chunks.text: River ice monitoring in Alaska is critical because ice dynamics affect ecosystems, transportation, and public safety, especially in remote areas. Many Alaskan communities rely on rivers and coastal waterways rather than roads, so freeze-up and breakup strongly influence accessibility. Ice decay and breakup processes can trigger spring flooding, and early freshet conditions can increase ice-jam risk and flood severity. These regional realities motivate improved, timely ice observation tools.
supporting_quote: The monitoring of river ice conditions, particularly in northern regions like Alaska, is of paramount importance due to the direct impact of ice dynamics on local ecosystems, transportation, and safety
86% of communities depending on rivers and coastal waterways as the primary means of transportation
the gradual weakening and eventual fragmentation of the ice cover... amplify the risk of ice jamming, thus intensifying the severity of flood events

chunks.text: Google Earth Engine (GEE) provides cloud-based access to large satellite archives and scalable computation, enabling rapid environmental monitoring without local downloads. Prior work has shown GEE’s usefulness across hazard applications (e.g., floods, droughts, wildfires) and its integration with supervised classification methods. This study positions river ice monitoring as a practical extension of these cloud-enabled workflows for under-observed northern regions.
supporting_quote: The Google Earth Engine (GEE), launched in 2010... provides a webbased platform that facilitates the manipulation and analysis of large-scale geographical datasets
The platform's ability to provide high-resolution satellite images without the need for local downloading streamlines the process
studies have effectively utilized the GEE's capabilities to address and manage natural disasters such as... floods, droughts, and wildfires

chunks.text: Citizen science can complement remote sensing by providing ground observations for validation and filling gaps when satellites are obstructed. The paper focuses on contributory citizen science where participants collect and submit observations, which can support operational forecasting and community engagement. Large-scale and regional initiatives (e.g., GLOBE, Fresh Eyes on Ice) provide structured pathways for these observations to be used in decision support.
supporting_quote: Citizen science is defined in this paper as a collaboration between public environmental observers and professional scientists
we focus here on contributory citizen science where public participants primarily collect, submit observations, and access data products
regional initiatives like the Fresh Eyes on Ice project in Alaska, offer valuable ground-truthing and observational data

chunks.text: The study aims to introduce an automated, FAIR-aligned framework that integrates multi-satellite remote sensing and citizen science data within Google Earth Engine for river ice monitoring. The goal is to support reliable, timely observations of river ice dynamics and enable analysis and visualization via a public-facing GEE application. The work also emphasizes community impact by supporting diverse stakeholders who need freeze-up and breakup information for transportation, safety, research, and hazard response.
supporting_quote: we introduce an automated framework that supports FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) science principles, facilitating remote sensing and citizen science data sharing
we introduce an automated framework... in the Google Earth Engine
The system's architecture was tailored to support information dissemination across this wide span of users

chunks.text: A central objective is to quantitatively assess the VIIRS-based river ice mapping product using Fresh Eyes on Ice citizen science observations. The paper targets evaluation during water year 2023 by matching photo observations to VIIRS pixels and computing standard accuracy metrics from a confusion matrix. This goal demonstrates how community observations can serve as ground truth when benchmark datasets are limited.
supporting_quote: citizen science data were leveraged for the assessment of the VIIRS River Ice product, focusing on images collected during the water year 2023
The evaluation of the accuracy... was conducted through the generation of a confusion matrix and the calculation of various assessment metrics

chunks.text: Alaska’s remote geography limits consistent in situ ice observations, creating gaps in monitoring needed for safety and operations. Access constraints and sparse measurements make it difficult to validate or interpret ice conditions across large areas. This motivates using remote sensing and community-contributed data to improve spatial and temporal coverage.
supporting_quote: In situ measurements of ice conditions are often spatially and temporarily limited by geographical inaccessibility and logistical constraints
The accurate detection of river ice conditions poses significant challenges, one of which is the scarcity of in situ observations in the remote and often inaccessible regions of Alaska

chunks.text: Optical satellite monitoring is often hindered by cloud cover and temporal revisit limitations, reducing the reliability of near-real-time ice detection during critical periods. These issues are especially problematic during breakup and freeze-up windows, when timely observations are needed. The paper addresses this by combining optical sensors with all-weather SAR and leveraging multiple platforms to improve continuity.
supporting_quote: common limitations in river ice monitoring caused mainly by cloud blockage and revisit cycle
the issue of cloud cover, which often obscures optical sensor data, can be bypassed by the all-weather, dayand-night imaging capability of SAR

chunks.text: Google Earth Engine is powerful for hosting and visualizing data, but it has limitations for running high-computation algorithms and offers a limited suite of machine learning methods. These constraints can hinder real-time or near-real-time posting of advanced products like segmentation outputs. The study therefore uses external cloud services to run the deep learning pipeline and then publishes results to GEE.
supporting_quote: limitations of the GEE in hosting high computational algorithms and a limited suite of machine learning algorithms
This poses a challenge in real-time or near-real-time data posting

chunks.text: Moderate-resolution sensors provide frequent coverage but may not detect ice processes in narrow rivers, limiting hazard monitoring in small channels. The paper illustrates that some ice jam events are missed by VIIRS segmentation because river width is too small. This necessitates complementary higher-resolution optical imagery (e.g., Sentinel-2) and other sources.
supporting_quote: The moderate resolution of sensors limits the effective monitoring of smaller rivers
the VIIRS River Ice product encountered limitations due to the narrow width of the river, failing to capture the ice jam event effectively

chunks.text: The monitoring approach integrates multiple satellite platforms to mitigate cloud blockage, revisit constraints, and resolution tradeoffs. It combines optical sensors (Landsat 8/9, Sentinel-2/3, VIIRS) and radar (Sentinel-1) within a single system hosted on Google Earth Engine. This multi-sensor strategy aims to provide more continuous and precise river ice monitoring across Alaska.
supporting_quote: we leverage multisatellite imagery that integrates various sources of remote sensing observations, detailed in Table 1
This integrated method combines the strengths of both optical sensors and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) sensors
ensuring a more continuous and precise monitoring system

chunks.text: The core remote sensing product is the Stevens River Ice Mapping System derived from VIIRS observations and implemented with automated deep learning. A U-Net model performs semantic segmentation to classify pixels into land surface and atmospheric categories relevant to ice monitoring. Output classes include water, snow, river ice, cloud, and cloud shadow, enabling monitoring during freeze-up and breakup.
supporting_quote: The cornerstone of our methodological framework is the Stevens River Ice Mapping System, derived from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) observations
A U-Net deep learning algorithm is employed for the semantic segmentation of images
The automated system generates detailed maps, delineating classes such as water... snow, river ice, cloud, and cloud shadow

chunks.text: Additional datasets are integrated directly from the GEE data catalog to provide higher-resolution and radar-based perspectives. Sentinel-1 uses the VV band to differentiate open water and ice under all-weather conditions. Sentinel-2 and Landsat 8/9 surface reflectance RGB bands support high-resolution visual interpretation of ice and water, while Sentinel-3 provides daily moderate-resolution RGB coverage with scale-factor conversion.
supporting_quote: additional remote sensing products are also integrated... including Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, Sentinel-3, and Landsat 8 and 9 datasets
Sentinel-1 data play a crucial role, leveraging the single co-polarization (VV) band
Sentinel-2... surface reflectance... Red (B4), Green (B3), and Blue (B2) bands, each pixel measuring 10 m

chunks.text: Citizen science integration is implemented through the Fresh Eyes on Ice program, which collects photo observations and ice/snow thickness data via a website or the GLOBE Observer app. Observations are transmitted to NASA/GLOBE and, for Alaska frozen seasons, incorporated into the Fresh Eyes on Ice database. Fixed river ice cameras complement participant submissions by providing continuous reach-based observations.
supporting_quote: Fresh Eyes on Ice... Interested individuals... collect photo observations and ice and snow thickness data
Data are submitted through the program's website or the GLOBE Observer app
the project is augmented by groundbased photographic data from fixed river ice cameras

chunks.text: The automated processing workflow generates segmented VIIRS river-ice products, then projects and crops to the region of interest and publishes outputs through a public GEE application. The pipeline reduces posting latency by running computation outside GEE and then uploading results for visualization. The authors report that their posted segmented VIIRS images are available with about a 1-day delay.
supporting_quote: The automated system operates through a series of methodical steps, presented in Figure 2
A pre-trained U-Net model then processes these data, producing segmented images
the images posted in our system are available with a significantly reduced delay, which we have quantified to be just 1 day

chunks.text: Data integration and posting to GEE uses a cloud workflow with Google Storage and Google Compute Engine. Segmented images and ice concentration images are uploaded to separate Google Storage buckets, and citizen science data are fetched through an API using an OGC Web Feature Service (WFS). An automated Compute Engine script transfers these assets into public GEE image collections and tables for use in the web app.
supporting_quote: uploading both ice concentration images and their segmented counterparts into separate, designated buckets in Google Storage
fetched via an Application Programming Interface (API), specifically using a Web Feature Service (WFS)
An automated code... deployed on... the Compute Engine... transferring the data from the Google Storage buckets directly to the GEE

chunks.text: The GEE user interface supports interactive exploration of river ice information by enabling layer control, date selection, side-by-side comparison, and time series analysis. Users can draw a rectangle, polygon, or point to define an area of interest and then observe changes in water, ice, and snow over time. The app also provides GeoTIFF download via a “Get Download URL” option, with a stated file-size limit.
supporting_quote: Users have the capability to select specific dates for visualizing available remote sensing observations
the drawing mode toolbox... allows users to conduct time series analysis within a defined area of interest
download a GeoTiff file using the "Get Download URL" button... limited to files up to 30 MB in size

chunks.text: The study integrates a set of satellite missions spanning optical and radar, each contributing different spatial resolutions for ice monitoring. Included sources are Landsat 8/9 (30 m), Sentinel-1 SAR (10 m), Sentinel-2 MSI (10 m), Sentinel-3 (300 m), and NOAA-20 VIIRS (375 m). This dataset selection supports both high-resolution mapping and frequent, broad-coverage monitoring.
supporting_quote: Overview of integrated satellite data sources
Landsat 8... 30 m... Sentinel-1... 10 m... Sentinel-3... 300 m... NOAA-20... 375 m

chunks.text: Ice-jam hazard context is informed using the CRREL Ice Jam Database for water years 2000–2023. The database documents hundreds of events and includes many occurrences at ungauged sites, expanding understanding beyond traditional gauging networks. The paper highlights the rivers with the highest ice-jam frequencies in this record.
supporting_quote: We utilize data from the Cold Regions Research and Engineering Laboratory (CRREL) Ice Jam Database, spanning the water years from 2000 to 2023
documents a total of 649 ice jam events, with a significant number of these occurrences reported at ungauged sites
The rivers experiencing the most ice jams... include the Yukon, Kuskokwim, Tanana, Buckland, and Kobuk

chunks.text: Citizen science inputs come from the Fresh Eyes on Ice project, including participant photo observations and ice/snow thickness measurements submitted through the website or GLOBE Observer app. The program also provides near-real-time imagery from fixed river ice cameras deployed across multiple Alaska rivers. These data streams support validation and situational awareness during cloud-obscured periods.
supporting_quote: Fresh Eyes on Ice... collect photo observations and ice and snow thickness data
Data are submitted through the program's website or the GLOBE Observer app

chunks.text: For quantitative evaluation, the authors used Fresh Eyes on Ice images from water year 2023 and applied a GIS-based filtering and spatiotemporal matchup to VIIRS pixels. From an initial pool of 1027 images, they restricted analysis to mid-size and large rivers likely captured by VIIRS and excluded cloud and snow pixels. The resulting matched dataset contained 165 observations corresponding to VIIRS water-or-ice pixels.
supporting_quote: A total of 1027 images... were initially available for analysis
exclusion of pixels classified as cloud or snow, limiting the assessment to those indicating water or ice
As a result... a total of 165 citizen science observations were identified

chunks.text: The VIIRS River Ice product showed strong agreement with Fresh Eyes on Ice observations during water year 2023 after filtering and matchup. Reported performance metrics include F1 score 0.90 and proportion correct 0.88, indicating accurate ice detection. The critical success index was 0.82, emphasizing skill in capturing true ice events.
supporting_quote: The F1 score, standing at 0.90
the proportion correct metric, at 0.88
The critical success index value of 0.82

chunks.text: The evaluation indicates a slight overestimation tendency for ice detection, with a bias ratio of 1.14. The paper attributes this to breakup-period complexity when mixed water and ice conditions create ambiguous pixels. False positive detections were primarily concentrated in April and May, consistent with breakup timing.
supporting_quote: the bias ratio of 1.14 reveals a slight tendency towards overestimation in ice pixel predictions
false positive detections... occurring predominantly in April and May, reflecting the breakup period
the presence of a mix of open water and ice cover on the rivers introduces complexity to the classification task

chunks.text: The system can depict seasonal evolution of snow, ice, and open water using the VIIRS segmentation classes, supporting spatiotemporal analysis of freeze-up and breakup. In an example over the Yukon River, snow cover began in October 2022 and ice cover persisted through winter. By May 2023, open water became predominant with reduced snow cover, illustrating transition timing.
supporting_quote: the onset of snow cover... was observed to begin in October 2022
Throughout the winter season, ice cover remains prevalent, as evident in the imagery from March 2023
A significant shift is observed in May, where open water conditions become predominant, accompanied by a notable reduction in snow cover

chunks.text: The GEE interface provides multiple operational features that broaden usability across stakeholders. It supports activating/deactivating layers, date selection for retrospective comparison, and a split-screen tool to compare two dates simultaneously. It also includes layers for recent citizen science observations (past 15 days), historical observations, and live camera feeds for local validation when satellite views are limited.
supporting_quote: Users have the capability to select specific dates for visualizing available remote sensing observations
The interface splitter... allowing users to simultaneously view ice conditions from different selected dates
recent citizen science data collected over the past 15 days
near real-time images from eight strategically deployed cameras across Alaska

chunks.text: Multi-source observations enabled analysis of an ice jam-induced flooding event at Fort Yukon on 14 May 2023. The VIIRS River Ice segmentation depicted broad-scale ice and water-over-land patterns suggestive of flooding, while Sentinel-2 provided finer detail in narrower channels. Fresh Eyes on Ice photos added ground-level evidence about severity and impacts not visible from satellites alone.
supporting_quote: ice jam-induced flooding event along the Yukon River in Fort Yukon on 14 May 2023
segmented images from the VIIRS River Ice product... demonstrate the extent of ice and the associated water over land, indicative of flooding
high-resolution imagery from Sentinel-2... offers a clearer and more detailed view of ice and water extents
Images from the Fresh Eyes on Ice portal offer ground-level insights into the severity and consequences

chunks.text: A Forty-Mile River ice jam near Chicken on 11 May 2023 demonstrated the importance of high-resolution imagery and citizen science for narrow rivers. The paper reports that VIIRS failed to capture the event due to river width limitations, while Sentinel-2 clearly showed accumulated ice and open water sections. Citizen science imagery helped identify the event as a breakup jam and provided additional details about ice characteristics.
supporting_quote: Forty-Mile River near Chicken on 11 May 2023
the VIIRS River Ice product encountered limitations due to the narrow width of the river, failing to capture the ice jam event effectively
The high-resolution imagery from Sentinel-2 successfully captured sections where ice was accumulated, as well as areas of open water
helped in identifying the nature of the jam as a breakup jam

chunks.text: For the near-record flooding at Circle on 16 May 2023, different sensors provided complementary information about floating ice and inundation impacts. The VIIRS River Ice product showed channels mostly as open water, while the VIIRS ice concentration product indicated concentrations exceeding 60%. Sentinel-3 RGB captured accumulated ice near banks, and Sentinel-1 SAR clearly depicted floating ice where available, while citizen science photos documented impacts on the ground.
supporting_quote: post-ice jam event... on 16 May 2023... near-record flooding at Circle
VIIRS ice concentration product... concentrations exceeding 60%
RGB images from Sentinel-3 observations... captured the accumulated ice near the river banks
high-resolution SAR... clearly depicted the floating ice
photographic images... accessible through the Fresh Eyes on Ice portal

chunks.text: The paper notes that GEE image collections are advantageous but limited for advanced image processing such as filtering, segmentation, and classification. These constraints motivate the framework’s approach of running computational steps externally and then publishing results back to GEE as public collections. The discussion frames this as a pathway for transitioning research outputs to operational tools despite platform limitations.
supporting_quote: limitations in terms of advanced image processing capabilities like image filtering, segmentation, and classification
The framework developed in this study addresses these limitations by guiding users on how to create and publicly share their own image collections within the GEE

chunks.text: A current limitation is that download functionality is restricted, and users do not have access to raw imagery within the app for custom preprocessing. The system uses pre-processed Sentinel and Landsat products from GEE, which restricts tasks like thermal noise removal or radiometric calibration. This limitation may affect users who need tailored calibration workflows for specialized analysis.
supporting_quote: the image download capability is currently confined to the river ice product
these images are provided in a pre-processed format
This limits the users' ability to further preprocess or calibrate the raw images... such as thermal noise removal or radiometric calibration

chunks.text: Citizen science observations are valuable for validation and context, but the paper emphasizes that they often lack detailed information about ice type and thickness during hazardous events. Even with accurate geolocation, photos alone may not characterize ice properties required to understand jam mechanics. The authors highlight the need for more in situ measurements and water-level change information to complement remote sensing and citizen observations.
supporting_quote: these observations have a major limitation: they do not provide detailed information regarding ice type and thickness
highlighting the necessity for more in situ measurements
importance of capturing changes in water levels during breakup and ice jam events

chunks.text: The study concludes that an automated, multi-source river ice monitoring system can provide near-real-time insights for Alaska by integrating cloud computing, deep learning, satellite remote sensing, and citizen science. The approach supports FAIR principles and provides an accessible tool for monitoring ice conditions and hazards. The paper positions this as a foundation for future enhancements and broader operational use.
supporting_quote: This study represents a significant advancement... particularly in... Alaska
integrating a range of technologies, including the Google Earth Engine, cloud computing, and deep learning... and citizen science data
offering a robust and accessible tool for river ice monitoring

chunks.text: The authors conclude that citizen science meaningfully complements satellite monitoring by providing ground-truth observations that enrich analysis and validation. They emphasize that this integration improves monitoring of dynamic river ice conditions and related hazards. The work underscores the value of combining technological innovation with community engagement.
supporting_quote: The inclusion of citizen science data is particularly noteworthy, as it provides groundtruth observations that greatly complement satellite imagery
This synergistic approach, combining technological innovation with community engagement

chunks.text: River ice dynamics are an important part of hydrologic processes in northern regions and serve as a key indicator of climate change. Ice formation and breakup affect fluvial processes, ecosystems, water resources, and infrastructure, and are driven by interacting thermodynamic, hydrodynamic, meteorological, and geomorphic processes. Recent assessments emphasize widespread declines in Northern Hemisphere river and lake ice, including later freezing and earlier thawing, motivating regional analyses of freshwater ice regimes.
supporting_quote: River ice dynamics, a crucial component of hydrologic processes, play a significant role in hydroclimatology in northern regions
IPCC Sixth Assessment Report underscores an accelerating decline in Northern Hemisphere lakes and river ice, with evidence of systems freezing later and thawing earlier each year

chunks.text: The Northeast United States is a densely populated region that is experiencing rising temperatures and changing precipitation patterns, and it is annually prone to ice jams and ice-induced flooding. The study area is framed by the NOAA National Weather Service Northeast River Forecast Center (NERFC) domain, where river ice hazards and human interventions (e.g., dams, hydropower, thermoelectric cooling) coexist with diverse river systems and variable climate conditions.
supporting_quote: The current study presents a comprehensive analysis of the Northeast United States, a region that is annually prone to ice jams and ice-induced flooding.
In the NERFC domain, human activities such as the operation of 5,443 dams ... and 313 hydropower plants ... Additionally, the region includes 384 thermoelectric plants

chunks.text: Operational hydrologic forecasting is hindered by the inability of the NOAA National Water Model (NWM) to represent streamflow under icy conditions and by the impact of ice on assimilated USGS streamflow observations. Improving regional understanding of ice phenology and climatology is positioned as a pathway to enhance monitoring, forecasting, and model reliability during cold seasons in ice-prone basins.
supporting_quote: a notable operational gap in the NWM is its inability to simulate streamflow in the presence of ice.
the model's reliance on assimilating the United States Geological Survey (USGS) streamflow observations, which can be impacted by ice presence

chunks.text: The study aims to characterize river ice phenology and climatology across the Northeast United States (NERFC domain) using both in situ and satellite observations. It targets spatial and temporal patterns in ice formation, ice breakup, ice concentration, and breakup ice jams. It also seeks to examine variability over 1985–2023 and evaluate linkages between ice phenology and major climate oscillations to inform hydrologic operations and hazard management.
supporting_quote: conduct a comprehensive assessment of river ice phenology and climatology in Northeast United States, utilizing a combination of in situ observations and satellite imagery.
Spatial and temporal patterns of ice formation, ice breakup, ice concentration, and breakup ice jams were analyzed.

chunks.text: A specific goal is to assess teleconnections between river ice variables and large-scale climate modes, including AMO, NAO/NAOJ, PNA, and ENSO (via SOI). The analysis is intended to identify seasons and lags where climate indices have the strongest associations with freeze-up, breakup, and breakup-related peak flows, as well as with ice jam frequency.
supporting_quote: river ice phenology variability in the NERFC region was analyzed in relation to dominant climate variability modes: the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO), North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO), Pacific North American pattern (PNA), and El Niño–Southern Oscillation.
These indices were averaged over threemonth moving windows, aiming to pinpoint the seasons and their associated lags that most significantly influence river ice characteristics.

chunks.text: Another objective is to demonstrate how integrating satellite-derived river ice products with in situ records improves the completeness of river ice climatology, especially for spatial mapping along river reaches. The study develops mapped climatologies of ice formation, breakup timing, and ice concentration integrated with NHDPlus reaches, laying groundwork for future applications in streamflow estimation using the National Water Model hydrofabric.
supporting_quote: the necessity of integrating satellite imagery with in situ observations to develop a comprehensive river ice climatology was emphasized.
The obtained river ice climatology results were then integrated into the NHDPlus river reaches.

chunks.text: The paper addresses a regional knowledge gap in freshwater ice climatology for Northeastern U.S. rivers, in contrast to the heavier focus on sea ice and ice sheets in broader assessments. Prior work often targeted continental or watershed scales, and the region lacks comprehensive, multi-source, recent regional analyses needed to infer region-specific variability and improve hazard management and forecasting.
supporting_quote: we address a notable gap identified in the Fifth National Climate Assessment, which focuses predominantly on sea ice and ice sheets, by providing insights into freshwater ice systems in the Northeastern U.S. rivers.
a comprehensive regional scale analysis using more recent data from multiple sources is needed to infer region-specific variability of ice cover occurrence.

chunks.text: Long-term climatological assessment of river ice is limited by the lack of detailed ice-related data and inconsistencies in historical in situ reporting. The paper notes that older USGS records often lack explicit ice flags, and estimating ice-affected periods can be subjective, complicating consistent detection of freeze-up and breakup timing across stations and years.
supporting_quote: Previous studies have highlighted a significant gap in longterm climatological assessments due to the lack of detailed ice-related data.
In recent years, the USGS has incorporated an explicit 'ice' flag in their records ... It is noteworthy that this explicit flagging is absent in older records.

chunks.text: A key operational problem is that current hydrologic forecasting tools do not simulate ice effects, creating errors in cold-season streamflow prediction. Because the NWM assimilates USGS streamflow that can be biased by ice, and because the NWM does not represent ice processes, forecasting performance can degrade in ice-prone regions during winter.
supporting_quote: a notable operational gap in the NWM is its inability to simulate streamflow in the presence of ice.
Abdelkader et al. (2023), highlighted a decrease in the NWM performance in regions prone to ice during cold seasons.

chunks.text: Ice phenology dates from USGS in situ records were derived using a rule-based approach applied by water year. Freeze-up was defined as the first ice-affected (flagged) streamflow measurement followed by at least ten consecutive flagged days, with cross-verification using water temperature where available. Breakup was defined as the end of a flagged sequence, with an added requirement of no flagged data in the subsequent month to confirm ice cessation.
supporting_quote: The initiation of ice formation was determined by spotting the first flagged streamflow measurement but conditional that the flagged measurement should be followed by at least ten consecutive days of flagged data
The breakup dates were obtained by identifying the end of a sequence of flagged measurements... after the identified breakup date, there should be an absence of flagged data for the subsequent month

chunks.text: To characterize breakup hydrology, peak discharge during breakup was computed with a station-specific window tied to the timing of flagged ice-affected flow. The study defined breakup peak discharge as the maximum discharge recorded during the last 15 days that had the 'A: e' (estimated, often ice-affected) flag, capturing regional fluctuations near breakup while allowing for upstream–downstream lag considerations.
supporting_quote: the peak discharge was identified as the maximum discharge value recorded during the last 15-days with a 'A: e' flag.
Recognizing this hydrological phenomenon, we first identified the breakup timing

chunks.text: Satellite-based river ice detection was produced from daily VIIRS imagery using a U-Net deep learning semantic segmentation approach. The segmentation classified pixels into multiple surface types including river ice, and was applied across the NERFC domain for October 1, 2012 to May 31, 2023. A predefined land/water mask derived from Landsat imagery was used to better constrain river pixels and improve detection on wider rivers.
supporting_quote: Remote sensing data on ice formation, breakup, and ice concentration were obtained from Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) observations.
analysis spanning the period from October 1st, 2012, to May 31st, 2023
a land/water mask was predefined using higher-resolution Landsat imagery

chunks.text: The VIIRS U-Net river ice model performance was summarized using detection metrics from prior work, supporting its use for operational monitoring and climatological analysis. The paper reports a Probability of Detection of 0.77 and a False Alarm Rate of 0.12, with noted robustness particularly when surrounding land is not snow covered.
supporting_quote: It has achieved a Probability of Detection of 0.77 and a False Alarm Rate of 0.12
particularly when the surrounding land is not snow-covered

chunks.text: Trend and change-point analyses of ice phenology and hydroclimatic variables used non-parametric methods suited for hydrologic time series. The Modified Mann-Kendall test assessed statistical significance, Sen’s slope quantified trend magnitude, and the Pettitt test identified single change points in series central tendency. Stations with fewer than 15 years of data were excluded from trend analysis to improve robustness.
supporting_quote: For trend analysis, the Mann-Kendall (MMK) ... test and Sen's slope estimator ... were employed.
the Pettitt test ... was applied specifically for change point detection
stations with less than 15 years of data were excluded from the trend analysis

chunks.text: Teleconnection analysis related river ice variables to climate indices by averaging indices over three-month moving windows and computing correlations. Significance was tested with a Student’s t-test at the 10% level, after confirming approximate normality via the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. Indices examined included AMO, NAO/NAOJ, PNA, and ENSO conditions represented by SOI.
supporting_quote: These indices were averaged over threemonth moving windows
The significance of these correlations is evaluated here with the student's t-test at a significance level of 10%.
ENSO conditions, indicated by the Southern Oscillation Index (SOI)

chunks.text: Remote-sensing climatology products mapped ice formation dates, breakup timing, and ice concentration along river reaches, with uncertainty primarily from cloud cover. Because neighboring pixels can show variable dates (often cloud-influenced), freeze-up and breakup dates from imagery were presented in 10-day intervals. Results were integrated with NHDPlus streams to support future use of ice information in streamflow estimation.
supporting_quote: the primary source of uncertainty in remote sensing-based analysis stems from cloud cover obscuration
these dates are presented in 10-day intervals.
The obtained river ice climatology results were then integrated into the NHDPlus river reaches.

chunks.text: In situ ice phenology data were derived from USGS stations within the NERFC domain selected through a multi-step screening process. Rivers with more than 10 ice jams after 1970 were identified using the CRREL Ice Jam Database, then USGS stations were filtered using NHDPlus and record-length criteria. The final dataset included 31 stations with records spanning 1985–2023, including 12 reference sites from Gages II.
supporting_quote: rivers that exhibited more than 10 ice jams post the year 1970 were shortlisted.
Only those stations maintaining records from the years 1985 to 2023 were considered... narrowed down the number of sites to a total of 31 stations, of which 12 were recognized as reference sites

chunks.text: Satellite observations used daily VIIRS imagery from the Suomi NPP platform to map river ice classes and ice concentration across the NERFC domain. The analysis period was October 1, 2012 through May 31, 2023, enabling a 12-year view of spatial ice patterns. The study focused on wider rivers because of the moderate spatial resolution of optical sensors.
supporting_quote: VIIRS observations onboard the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership (S-NPP) satellite platform
analysis spanning the period from October 1st, 2012, to May 31st, 2023
the study focused primarily on the wider rivers in the Northeast region

chunks.text: Breakup ice jam occurrence data came from the CRREL Ice Jam Database, used to build a spatio-temporal climatology of breakup jams across 1970–2023. The analysis emphasized breakup jams (rather than freeze-up jams) because of their higher destructive potential and examined seasonal categories including mid-winter and spring breakup events.
supporting_quote: using the CRREL database... spanning from 1970 to 2023, specifically focused on breakup jams due to their higher destructive potential
with a total of 1,102 recorded ice jam events

chunks.text: Hydroclimatic drivers were characterized using ERA5-Land reanalysis, aggregated daily from hourly data for 1985–2023. Variables included 2 m air temperature and snow cover fraction, and were aggregated to HUC-12 basins for each station. These data were used to contextualize changes in freeze-up and breakup timing.
supporting_quote: For the purposes of this study, data spanning from 1985 to 2023 were obtained, with a specific focus on 2 m air temperature and snow cover records.
Data was aggregated to the Hydrologic Unit Code level 12 (HUC-12) corresponding to each station's drainage basin

chunks.text: Climate oscillation indices were sourced as monthly series from NOAA PSL, including AMO, NAO, NAOJ, PNA, and SOI for ENSO. The NAOJ dataset extends NAO back to 1821 using early instrumental pressure observations, providing a longer historical perspective even though the study focuses on 1985–2023. Indices were used in correlation analysis with ice phenology and ice jam frequency series.
supporting_quote: Monthly data for these indices were retrieved from NOAA's Physical Sciences Laboratory
The NAOJ... extends the NAO index back to 1821 using early instrumental surface pressure observations

chunks.text: Spatial patterns show earlier ice formation in northern NERFC rivers and later formation in southern rivers, with latitude and coastal influence shaping timing. Northern rivers such as the Saint John and Allagash typically begin forming ice by mid to late November, while southern rivers like the Hudson and downstream Connecticut form ice later, often mid to late January. Discrepancies between in situ and VIIRS were noted in some locations (e.g., upstream Hudson), where remote sensing detected ice presence not reflected as ice-affected flow at gauges.
supporting_quote: rivers like the Saint John, Allagash... begin forming ice covers by mid to late November.
in rivers like the Hudson River, downstream Connecticut River, and Mohawk River, later ice formation dates were observed, occurring from mid to late January.
in-situ measurements indicated a median ice formation date in late January, contrasting with early January dates from remote sensing

chunks.text: Freeze-up trend analysis across 1985–2023 found no statistically significant trends at any site using the Modified Mann-Kendall test. Trend magnitudes nonetheless indicated a regional tendency toward later freeze-up, averaging about 0.47 days per year. About 85% of sites showed delayed ice cover formation according to Theil–Sen slopes, with the largest delays reported for the Housatonic River (1.42 days/year) and Schoharie Creek (0.8 days/year).
supporting_quote: The MMK test indicated no statistically significant trends in freeze-up dates at all study sites.
average trend magnitude suggested a shift toward later freeze-up at a rate of 0.47 days/year
delay in ice formation rates was quantified at 1.42 days/year for the Housatonic River and 0.8 days/year for Schoharie Creek

chunks.text: Change-point detection for ice formation identified significant shifts at two isolated sites, suggesting local drivers. Pettitt test results indicated significant change points for Cazenovia Creek in 2002 and Little Salmon River in 2005. The associated later-freeze-up rates were reported as 0.53 days/year and 0.27 days/year, and the study suggests these isolated signals may reflect human interventions or lake influences rather than broad regional climate forcing.
supporting_quote: revealed significant shifts in two isolated sites, Cazenovia Creek in 2002 and Little Salmon River in 2005
displaying rates of change (later freeze-up) at 0.53 days/year and 0.27 days/year, respectively
suggest alterations in ice formation dates could be due to human interventions or influenced by nearby lakes

chunks.text: Hydroclimatic context for freeze-up shows statistically significant warming in autumn and early winter, while snow cover tended to decrease without significant trends. The study reports significant increases in average temperature of about 0.05 °C/year in SON across most sites and similarly significant warming during OND averaging 0.05 °C/year. Snow cover declines were reported (e.g., -0.06%/year in SON and -0.10%/year in OND), but these changes were not statistically significant.
supporting_quote: significant increase in average temperatures... rise of 0.05 °C/year in SON
A similar statistically significant increase during OND was noted at all study sites, averaging 0.05 °C/year.
Snow cover showed declining rates of -0.06%/year in SON, -0.10%/year in OND... but these changes were not statistically significant.

chunks.text: Freeze-up teleconnections showed significant associations with the NAO/NAOJ primarily in late summer through early winter windows for early freeze-up dates. Significant correlations were found for NAO during September–November and October–December, and for NAOJ in August–October, September–November, and October–December. The interpretation given is that positive NAO/NAOJ phases are linked to delayed freeze-up and negative phases to earlier freeze-up, with stronger effects at higher-latitude sites.
supporting_quote: Significant correlations with freeze-up dates were observed for NAO during September-November and October-December
NAOJ showed significant positive correlations with early freeze-up dates particularly in August-October, September-November, and October-December.
positive phases of NAO/NAOJ are associated with delayed freezeup dates, while negative phases align with earlier freeze-up dates

chunks.text: Breakup climatology spans mid-February to mid-April, with earlier breakup in southern rivers and later breakup in northern rivers. Southern regions such as the Hudson, Housatonic, and lower Connecticut show breakup from late February to early March, while northern rivers including the Saint John, Allagash, and Big Black often break up in mid-April. Both in situ and VIIRS support this latitudinal pattern, though VIIRS may detect lingering floating ice later than flow-based in situ flags.
supporting_quote: Earlier breakup dates, typically from late February to early March, were noted in the southern regions such as the Hudson, Housatonic, and lower Connecticut Rivers
The latest breakup dates were typically recorded in mid-April in NERFC's northern rivers, including the Saint John, Allagash, and Big Black Rivers.
Overall, the median breakup dates in NERFC span the period between mid-February to mid-April.

chunks.text: Breakup trend analysis found a general tendency toward earlier breakup dates but no statistically significant trends across sites. About 70% of locations had earlier breakup trends by Theil–Sen estimates, averaging 0.24 days/year earlier with a standard deviation of 0.45 days/year. Breakup peak flow increased at about 60% of sites but was generally not significant, except for a significant increase at the Big Black River site.
supporting_quote: Approximately 70% of the sites showed trends toward earlier breakup dates
The average change in breakup dates during the study period was measured at 0.24 days/ year, with a standard deviation of 0.45 days/year
these increases were not statistically significant, except for a significant increase observed at the Big Black River.

chunks.text: Breakup teleconnections indicated ENSO influence as measured by SOI, with significant seasonal correlations for breakup timing and breakup peak flows. Significant positive correlations were reported between SOI (NDJ and DJF windows) and earliest/ latest breakup dates, and the maximum breakup peak flow series had its highest significant correlation with SOI NDJ. The authors interpret this as La Niña conditions tending to delay breakup dates and El Niño tending to produce earlier breakups.
supporting_quote: highlighted a notable influence of the Southern Oscillation Index
the highest significant correlation observed with the SOI NDJ series
La Niña associated with delayed breakup dates and El Niño potentially leading to earlier breakups

chunks.text: Breakup ice jam climatology from 1970–2023 documented 1,102 breakup jam events occurring mainly from December to April, with peaks in January and March and a substantial role for mid-winter breakups. Decadal counts rose to 304 events in 2010–2023, and mid-winter breakup accounted for around 50% of events in the 1990s and subsequent decades. The strongest mid-winter breakup jam concentrations occurred in the upper Connecticut (33 events), Lamoille (21), Missisquoi (12), and Cazenovia Creek (23).
supporting_quote: with a total of 1,102 recorded ice jam events
The peak periods for ice jams were identified in January and March, with an unexpectedly high occurrence in January and February
the frequency of ice jams during the past decades was recorded as follows... and 304 in 2010–2023.

chunks.text: Trend and change-point analysis of five-year running sums showed statistically significant increases in mid-winter breakup and total ice jam frequency, with a pronounced shift after 1992 for mid-winter events. Mid-winter breakup events had Z-MMK=3.029 with Sen slope 1.238 and a significant change point in 1992, with mean frequency increasing from 30.4 (m1) to 76.8 (m2). Total events increased (Z-MMK=2.794; Sen slope 1.037) with a change point in 1988.
supporting_quote: Mid-winter breakup events | 3.029 | increasing | 1.238 | 1992 | 30.4 | 76.8
Total events | 2.794 | increasing | 1.037 | 1988 | 73.3 | 124.6
average ice jam occurrences increasing from approximately 30 events per year prior to 1992 to about 77 events post-1992

chunks.text: The 12-year VIIRS record limits the ability to infer long-term trends from satellite observations alone. The paper notes that robust trend analysis typically requires several decades to separate natural variability and climatic cycles. This limitation motivates combining remote sensing with ground-based observations and historical records for a fuller climatological assessment.
supporting_quote: the temporal availability of VIIRS data, limited to 12 years, prevents definitive conclusions about long-term trends.
comprehensive trend analysis... often necessitates several decades of data to account for natural variability and climatic cycles

chunks.text: Accurately detecting breakup dates from in situ observations is challenging because ice flags can be subjective and there is no unified methodological framework for flagging measurements. The authors assume reliability of available flags but argue that more robust, systematic approaches are needed for broader-scale assessments. They suggest that improved databases and complementary monitoring (e.g., cameras) could enhance the reliability of ice presence indicators.
supporting_quote: Detecting breakup dates accurately from in-situ observations poses considerable challenges due to the subjectivity and lack of a clear unified methodological framework
utilizing camera footage in conjunction with flow data could yield more precise ice presence flags

chunks.text: Remote sensing uncertainty is dominated by cloud cover obscuration, which can also create spatial inconsistencies in apparent freeze-up dates across neighboring pixels. To manage this, the study presents formation and breakup dates from imagery in 10-day intervals. The paper notes that classification uncertainties between ice-covered and ice-free reaches are secondary relative to cloud limitations.
supporting_quote: the primary source of uncertainty in remote sensing-based analysis stems from cloud cover obscuration
Due to variances in ice formation dates across neighboring pixels, possibly influenced by cloud cover, these dates are presented in 10-day intervals.

chunks.text: The paper highlights a tradeoff between extending satellite time coverage and maintaining spatial resolution suitable for rivers. MODIS could extend the record to about 22 years, but its thermal band resolution (1 km) can miss smaller river ice features, whereas VIIRS has finer thermal resolution (370 m) but only 12 years of coverage. The authors argue that integrating multiple satellite platforms may best advance long-term river ice phenology studies.
supporting_quote: MODIS data could be utilized, offering up to 22 years of observations.
its thermal band's coarser spatial resolution of 1 km
VIIRS remains a more suitable alternative due to its finer spatial resolution of 370 m

chunks.text: Teleconnection assessment was limited to linear correlation methods, which may miss non-linear or time-varying relationships between climate oscillations and river ice. The authors propose that future work could apply wavelet analysis to examine variability in both time and frequency domains. This is framed as a way to uncover more complex connections between ice phenology series and climate indices.
supporting_quote: the correlation between ice phenology series and climate indices was limited to linear methods.
Future research may explore... through advanced methodologies like wavelet analysis, which allows for the examination of variability in both time and frequency domains

chunks.text: The study concludes that river ice phenology across the NERFC exhibits strong latitudinal structure: northern rivers form ice earlier (mid/late November) and break up later (to mid-April), while southern rivers form later (mid/late January) and break up earlier (late February/early March). Trend magnitudes suggest later freeze-up and earlier breakup at many sites, but these tendencies were not statistically significant for 1985–2023. The work emphasizes that combining satellite and in situ observations is important to capture both ice presence and ice-affected flow.
supporting_quote: ice formation initiates earlier in northern rivers... from mid to late November, and later in southern rivers, around mid to late January.
ice breakup patterns are earlier in southern rivers... late February to early March, and later in northern rivers, extending to mid-April.
a tendency towards later freeze-up dates across most sites and a general trend towards earlier breakup dates, though both trends remain statistically insignificant.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that climate oscillations are linked to regional ice phenology: positive NAO phases delay freeze-up while negative phases accelerate it, and ENSO conditions in autumn and winter influence breakup. The authors interpret La Niña as associated with delayed breakup and El Niño with earlier breakup, consistent with the reported SOI correlations. These relationships are presented as relevant for improving understanding of ice regime variability.
supporting_quote: positive phases of the North Atlantic Oscillation typically delay freeze-up dates, whereas their negative phases tend to accelerate these dates.

El Niño-Southern Oscillation patterns during autumn and winter significantly affect breakup dynamics, with La Niña conditions delaying breakup dates and El Niño conditions facilitating earlier breakups.

chunks.text: A major conclusion is that mid-winter breakup ice jams have increased significantly, with a marked shift after 1992, and this increase largely drives the upward trend in total ice jam frequency. The study reports significant change points in 1992 for mid-winter events and 1988 for total events, highlighting growing mid-winter hazard potential. The authors frame these findings as important for river management strategies and adaptation to ice-induced hazards.
supporting_quote: A considerable increasing trend was identified in the frequency of mid-winter breakup ice jams, with significant shifts... noted in 1992 for mid-winter events and 1988 for total events.
the observed increase in ice jam frequency across the NERFC is predominantly due to the rise in mid-winter breakup jams.

chunks.text: Streamflow estimation is central to water resources management because it supports reservoir operations, irrigation planning, hydropower scheduling, and flood warnings. Hydrologic prediction is challenging due to system nonlinearity, nonstationarity, complex drivers (precipitation, evaporation, groundwater, land use), and limited long-term observations for calibration in many basins. Large-scale hydrologic models help extend streamflow information across space and time, but require systematic evaluation against observations to build confidence and identify weaknesses.
supporting_quote: The estimation of streamflow plays a pivotal role in water resource management. It facilitates the forecasting of forthcoming flood events and contributes to the optimization of water demand processes
Simulating streamflow is complex due to the intricate nature of the hydrologic system

chunks.text: In the United States, national-scale forecasting has evolved from River Forecast Center-specific guidance to continental modeling frameworks. NOAA’s National Water Model (NWM), implemented in 2016, produces streamflow forecasts at millions of locations across CONUS using the WRF–Hydro framework. Retrospective simulations (reanalyses) are valuable for evaluating how well such models reproduce historical streamflow patterns and for diagnosing bias sources.
supporting_quote: In 2016, the National Water Model (NWM), a group of physics-based, hydrodynamic, and hydrologic models, was implemented by NOAA's Office of Water Prediction (OWP). The NWM is based on the Weather Research and Forecasting Model Hydrological modeling system (WRF–Hydro) framework
With an hourly modeling cycle, the NWM simulates streamflow for 2.7'million river reaches across the CONUS

chunks.text: Model evaluation for operational and decision-support applications typically compares modeled streamflow to gauge observations using multiple performance metrics and trend consistency. Retrospective runs provide an opportunity to assess spatial heterogeneity in performance and examine whether simulated time series preserve observed historical trends. This is particularly relevant for continental-scale applications where climate gradients and human regulation vary widely.
supporting_quote: A key component of model evaluation involves comparing model estimates to observed data and assessing the model's ability to reproduce historical streamflow patterns.
Retrospective simulations are a valuable tool in assessing the performance of continental-scale hydrological models.

chunks.text: The study evaluates NWM V2.1 multi-decadal retrospective streamflow performance across CONUS in both time and space. It aims to identify limitations revealed by retrospective runs that could indicate improvements needed for operational forecasts. A specific objective is to examine spatial and temporal variability of streamflow bias to determine where and when NWM overestimates or underestimates flow, enabling recommendations for improved hydrologic process modeling across the U.S.
supporting_quote: This study aims to evaluate the performance of the NWM V2.1 through the analysis of the results of multi-decadal retrospective simulations across the contiguous United States (CONUS).
The study investigates the spatial and temporal variability of streamflow bias, with the objective of identifying instances and locations where the model underestimates or overestimates streamflow.

chunks.text: A further goal is to assess whether the retrospective NWM dataset is useful for representing historical behavior beyond pointwise accuracy by comparing monotonic trends between simulated and observed flows. Trend evaluation is applied to natural flow series to test NWM’s ability to replicate historical streamflow patterns over 1979–2020. This complements metric-based evaluation and informs suitability of retrospective products for downstream uses such as frequency analysis.
supporting_quote: Further analysis of streamflow time series for monotonic trends (one direction, either increasing or decreasing) was performed using the non-parametric Modified Mann–Kendall trend test.
It is crucial to note that the trend analysis test was applied exclusively to natural flow series.

chunks.text: Accurate streamflow simulation at continental scale is difficult because hydrologic processes are complex and data limitations can restrict model calibration and evaluation. Nonlinear and nonstationary behavior means small forcing differences can cause large discharge changes. Additional uncertainty arises from simplified or incorrect process representation and from changes in land use and climate, which can alter runoff generation and seasonality.
supporting_quote: Simulating streamflow is complex due to the intricate nature of the hydrologic system
The estimation of streamflow is further complicated by the nonlinearity and nonstationary of the hydrological system.

chunks.text: Operational forecasting systems benefit from advanced models, but there has been a gap between state-of-the-art modeling and what is used in practice, motivating evaluation and improvement. Even with national systems like the NWM, stakeholders need clear understanding of model capabilities and limitations. Therefore, a structured evaluation against long observational records is necessary to identify where the model performs poorly and why.
supporting_quote: the National Research Council identified a discrepancy between the state-of-the-art modeling capabilities currently considered cutting edge and those utilized in the AHPS
Thus, it is imperative to evaluate hydrological models' performance.

chunks.text: Regulated rivers pose a specific challenge because dams and management practices alter timing and magnitude of flows, which a continental model may not represent. The study notes that the NWM retrospective does not incorporate reservoir management and that regulated basins can have human interventions not captured by static inputs. This can create systematic bias, especially in summer and early fall when reservoir operations may strongly affect downstream flow.
supporting_quote: regulated flow watersheds exhibit altered hydrological regimes due to the presence of water control structures, such as dams, weirs, and other hydraulic structures.
The larger PB values can be attributed to the fact that the NWM does not incorporate reservoir management practices.

chunks.text: The study uses NWM V2.1 retrospective simulations to compare modeled streamflow against USGS observations at collocated forecast points. NWM is described as a distributed framework based on WRF–Hydro, with Noah-MP land surface processes and multiple routing modules (diffusive wave, subsurface, and Muskingum–Cunge channel routing). Retrospective simulations span 42 years and exclude streamflow observations from assimilation, enabling an independent evaluation of model physics and forcing impacts.
supporting_quote: The National Water Model is a parallelized distributed hydrologic modeling framework based on the WRF–Hydro hydrologic model architecture
Version 2.1 includes an extended retrospective simulation spanning 42 years, from February 1979 to December 2020.

chunks.text: Stations are filtered to ensure robust long-term evaluation: at least 30 years of record, less than 10% missing data, and no consecutive missing gap exceeding 24 months. Forecast points showing constant or zero flows across the entire period are treated as simulation failures and excluded. This creates a quality-controlled evaluation dataset aligned in time and space between NWM outputs and USGS records.
supporting_quote: we uphold the need for a minimum of 30 years of records to ensure a reliable long-term analysis.
Our stringent data completeness criteria stipulate less than 10% missing data, with no consecutive gaps exceeding 24 months

chunks.text: Performance is evaluated using multiple statistics to capture complementary aspects: modified Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE) at hourly scale, percent bias (PB), Pearson correlation coefficient (CC), RMSE, and NRMSE. KGE is decomposed into correlation, bias ratio (β), and variability ratio (γ), and the formulas are explicitly defined. The authors emphasize that RMSE is sensitive to peak errors and therefore include additional metrics for a comprehensive assessment.
supporting_quote: Five statistics were used, including the modified Kling–Gupta efficiency metric (KGE), Percent Bias (PB), Pearson Correlation Coefficient (CC), the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), and the Normalized Root Mean Squared Error (NRMSE).

chunks.text: Climate-region stratification is performed using the Aridity Index (AI), computed as mean annual precipitation divided by mean annual potential evapotranspiration. NLDAS precipitation and PET are aggregated over HUC8 basins for 1979–2020, and basins are classified into arid, semi-arid, sub-humid, and humid using UNEP thresholds. Seasonal PB distributions are then analyzed by climate type for natural and regulated flows.
supporting_quote: AI = \frac{MAP}{MAE}
The classification was performed based on the AI values, and the resulting categories were Arid (0.03 < AI < 0.2), Semi-Arid (0.2 < AI < 0.5), Sub-Humid (0.5 < AI < 0.65), and Humid (AI > 0.65)

chunks.text: Trend analysis uses the Modified Mann–Kendall (MMK) test to compare monotonic trends between observed and simulated natural flow series. MMK is chosen because it is non-parametric, less sensitive to abrupt shifts, and accounts for autocorrelation in streamflow time series. Agreement is assessed spatially by comparing trend directions and Z-MMK outcomes for NWM vs USGS series.
supporting_quote: streamflow trend analysis utilizing the Modified Mann–Kendall (MMK) trend test
selected for this investigation due to its lack of requirements for data to adhere to a specific distribution... and its ability to account for autocorrelation in streamflow time series.

chunks.text: The primary model dataset is the NWM V2.1 retrospective reanalysis spanning February 1979 to December 2020. Outputs are available in NetCDF and Zarr; the study uses Zarr from the AWS-hosted archive to retrieve streamflow time series by forecast point reference number. Retrospective runs do not assimilate streamflow observations, allowing an evaluation of baseline model behavior.
supporting_quote: Version 2.1 includes an extended retrospective simulation spanning 42 years, from February 1979 to December 2020.
Our study utilized the Zarr format, a cloud-friendly format, to obtain streamflow data.

chunks.text: Observed streamflow comes from USGS gauging stations, with locations identified using GAGES-2 and natural-flow status referenced via HCDN and NHDPlus 2.1. Discharge records are obtained from USGS NWIS and assumed accurate without explicitly modeling rating-curve uncertainty. Stations are collocated with NWM forecast points to ensure spatial alignment of modeled and observed series.
supporting_quote: the Geospatial Attributes of Gages for Evaluating Streamflow, Version II (GAGES-2) database... was utilized to obtain stream gage locations.
streamflow data were obtained from the USGS National Water Information System (NWIS) portal

chunks.text: After applying record-length and completeness screening and removing simulation-failure points, the final evaluation dataset contains 3260 stations. Of these, 548 stations are in catchments with natural flow and 2712 are in regulated catchments. The stations are distributed across 12 River Forecast Centers (RFCs) to support regional comparisons.
supporting_quote: The final list of streamflow gauging stations used in this study consisted of 3260 stations, with 548 stations located in catchments with natural flow and 2712 located in regulated catchments
12 River Forecast Centers (RFCs)

chunks.text: Ancillary hydroclimate inputs for aridity classification are derived from NLDAS and processed over HUC8 basins for 1979–2020. Total precipitation and potential evapotranspiration are aggregated annually to compute AI and assign climate classes following UNEP thresholds. This supports analysis of seasonal and regional differences in NWM bias by climate type.
supporting_quote: Total precipitation and potential evapotranspiration data for the period spanning from January 1979 to December 2020 were obtained from the North American Land Data Assimilation System (NLDAS)
HUC-8 basins were classified into different climate types based on the calculated AI values

chunks.text: Spatial performance differs between natural and regulated conditions: a larger fraction of natural-flow sites meet commonly used performance thresholds. Specifically, 57% of natural flow forecast points have KGE > 0.5, versus 43% for regulated flow. Poorer performance clusters in MBRFC, ABRFC, and WGRFC, while better performance appears in NERFC, MARFC, and NWRFC.
supporting_quote: 57% of natural flow forecast points exhibit KGE values exceeding 0.5
43% of forecast points associated with regulated flow present KGE values surpassing 0.5

chunks.text: Bias patterns show underestimation in eastern/northwestern RFCs and overestimation in central/western RFCs for both flow regimes. For natural flow, 50% of points achieve low bias (PB between −10% and 10%), while regulated flow has only 36% within that range. The study links lower bias to humid, higher-precipitation regions and larger bias to drier areas.
supporting_quote: For natural flow, a satisfactory agreement... with PB values ranging between −10% and 10%.
The results revealed that 36% of regulated flow estimates demonstrated low bias error with PB values between −10% and 10%.

chunks.text: Error magnitude metrics indicate natural-flow simulations outperform regulated-flow simulations across CONUS. Regulated flow shows higher RMSE and NRMSE across many RFCs, reflecting difficulty representing human alterations. NRMSE < 5% is achieved by 86% of natural forecast points but only 63% of regulated forecast points, highlighting reduced reliability under regulation.
supporting_quote: Regulated flow data exhibited inferior performance compared to natural flow, as indicated by higher RMSE and NRMSE values
NRMSE values below 5% were obtained for 86% of natural forecast points and 63% of regulated forecast points

chunks.text: Correlation is generally high for both regimes, implying NWM often captures timing/variability even when biased. For natural flow, 89% of sites have CC > 0.5, and for regulated flow 88% exceed 0.5; around 30–31% exceed 0.8. The authors infer that KGE shortcomings often stem more from bias than from correlation.
supporting_quote: Overall, 89% of the natural flow forecast points had CC values exceeding 0.5.
88% of the regulated flow forecast points had CC values greater than 0.5

chunks.text: Drainage-area stratification shows no strong, systematic bias dependence on watershed size at national scale, though tendencies exist. Natural flow is slightly underestimated in milli- and sub-watersheds (median PB −3.90% and −3.60%) and slightly overestimated in the largest class (>50,000 ha) with median PB −1.51% and a tendency to overestimate. Regulated flow displays broader PB spread, consistent with heterogeneous regulation effects.
supporting_quote: Overall, the model exhibited a propensity for underestimating streamflow for Milli-watersheds (1000–10,000 ha) and sub-watersheds... with median PB values of -3.90% and -3.60%
for the watershed class (>50,000 ha), the results demonstrated a lower median PB value of -1.51%, with the model tending to overestimate streamflow.

chunks.text: Bias varies with stream order, especially for regulated rivers. Natural-flow PB is approximately symmetric with relatively small interquartile ranges across orders, whereas regulated-flow PB varies considerably. First- and second-order regulated streams show particularly high bias, suggesting limitations in representing small-catchment and low-order channel processes and assumptions that vary with stream order.
supporting_quote: PB values vary considerably as a function of stream order, exhibiting a substantial spread in IQR.
high bias streamflow estimates obtained from first- and second-order regulated streams

chunks.text: Monthly bias shows seasonal structure: natural flow tends to overestimate from August to January and underestimate from March to June, with the most negative biases in March and April. The spring underestimation is associated with seasonal transition and snowmelt timing and is consistent with potential SWE underestimation. This indicates that snow processes and wet-season forcing errors may drive seasonal bias swings.
supporting_quote: the model has a tendency to overestimate streamflow during the period between August and January
Natural flow estimates are predominantly underestimated during the period between March and June

chunks.text: Regulated-flow monthly PB is positive throughout the year, indicating systematic overestimation. Performance improves in February and March, but the poorest months are July–September with median PB of 23.90%, 27.37%, and 23.59%. The authors attribute these larger summer biases to missing reservoir management and retention effects in the model.
supporting_quote: PB for NWM estimates exhibited positive median values for all months, indicating a general propensity for the model to overestimate regulated flow
median PB values of 23.90%, 27.37%, and 23.59%, respectively

chunks.text: Seasonal bias depends strongly on climate type. For natural flow, humid regions show the best agreement with median PB near zero and the best performance in winter; arid regions generally overestimate in all seasons. Semi-arid and sub-humid regions show comparatively good spring performance, demonstrating that both aridity and seasonality shape NWM errors.
supporting_quote: The most favorable agreement between the NWM estimates and observed data was obtained for simulations conducted in humid regions.
In arid regions, the results revealed that the model generally overestimates streamflow values across all seasons

chunks.text: Trend consistency between observed and simulated natural-flow series is moderate-to-strong overall but with regional mismatches. The MMK comparison shows satisfactory agreement in temporal evolution for 74% of sites. Notable discrepancies occur in NERFC and parts of SERFC where simulated trend direction opposes observed trends, often coinciding with negative PB (underestimation) or positive PB (overestimation).
supporting_quote: Overall, the MMK test results disclosed a satisfactory agreement between the temporal evolution of the observed and simulated natural streamflow series for 74% of the studied dataset.
in the NERFC... 40% of the forecast point series revealing an opposing trend direction (decreasing trend) in comparison to the in-situ measurement trend direction (increasing trend).

chunks.text: A major uncertainty source is hydrometeorological forcing error, especially precipitation and temperature, which propagate into runoff, evapotranspiration, and snow processes. The retrospective uses AORC forcing, but the paper notes that continental-scale assessments of AORC hourly variables are lacking. Prior studies cited indicate AORC can overestimate daily precipitation and underestimate heavy rains, with larger bias in cold months, potentially affecting soil conditions and streamflow simulation.
supporting_quote: For the NWM V2.1 retrospective simulations, the Analysis of Period of Record for Calibration (AORC) dataset was employed as forcing data.
To our knowledge, there are no continental scale assessments of AORC forcing hourly data

chunks.text: Static input datasets can bias long retrospective simulations because land cover, soils, and channel geometry may not match historical conditions. The paper states it is unclear which land cover dataset was used for the retrospective, and using static layers over decades may misrepresent changing catchment response. River geometry assumptions (e.g., trapezoidal channels, constant roughness by stream order) also introduce routing uncertainties that can affect streamflow and flood mapping products.
supporting_quote: In the case of the NWM retrospective simulation, it is unclear which land cover dataset was used.
the adoption of trapezoidal channel geometry, uniform flow, and constant channel roughness that only varies depending on the stream order

chunks.text: Regulated-flow errors are linked to missing knowledge of reservoir operations and other human interventions. The paper identifies the lack of reservoir operation rules as a potential source of error and recommends more sophisticated approaches (e.g., physics-informed machine learning) to infer and incorporate operational behavior. Without such representation, the model tends to overestimate regulated flows, particularly when retention and managed releases dominate.
supporting_quote: the uncertainty associated with the lack of knowledge regarding reservoir operation rules has been identified as a potential source of error in the model's performance.
we advocate for the exploration and integration of advanced computational methods, such as physics-informed machine learning and data mining, into the operational procedures of the NWM.

chunks.text: Observation uncertainty can affect evaluation, since USGS discharge relies on rating curves that may change due to ice, debris, or backwater effects. Although the study assumes rating curve accuracy and does not consider associated uncertainty, it notes that ice-affected streamflow correction is important in cold regions. This limitation means some discrepancies between NWM and observations may reflect measurement issues rather than model errors.
supporting_quote: It is important to note that the accuracy of the USGS rating curves was assumed in the analysis, and their uncertainty was not considered.
the correction of ice-affected streamflow is critical for evaluating models' simulations in cold regions

chunks.text: The retrospective simulations evaluated do not assimilate streamflow observations, so operational performance may be better in areas where nudging is applied. The paper emphasizes that nudging in operations updates streamflow estimates but not other hydrologic components, implying remaining weaknesses in soil moisture, snow, and other states. This distinction limits direct transfer of retrospective skill to operational forecasts while still highlighting parameterization and forcing issues.
supporting_quote: it should be noted that streamflow observations are not incorporated into the retrospective simulations.

the operational version of the NWM actively nudging streamflow data from USGS stations. This nudging process is critical in updating the streamflow estimates within the model, but it does not affect the other hydrological components.

chunks.text: Across CONUS, NWM V2.1 retrospective performance varies regionally, with better skill in humid regions and poorer skill in the Great Plains and other drier areas. Natural-flow simulations generally agree better with observations than regulated-flow simulations. The paper attributes performance differences to aridity/precipitation dynamics, snowmelt contributions, runoff seasonality, and potential biases in static inputs and forcing data.
supporting_quote: The performance of the models was found to vary regionally, with the primary factors influencing this variation being aridity and precipitation alternation and chaotic dynamics, snowmelt contribution, and runoff seasonality.
The model performance was notably poor in the Great Plains region, while it demonstrated better performance in estimating streamflow in the Northeastern and Northwestern regions.

chunks.text: Quantitatively, a higher share of natural sites achieves acceptable skill than regulated sites, reinforcing that human regulation is a key modeling gap. The study reports 57% of natural flow forecast points with KGE > 0.5 versus 43% for regulated flow. It also emphasizes that bias correction is needed before using retrospective datasets for applications such as flood thresholds and inundation triggers.
supporting_quote: 57% of natural flow forecast points exhibited KGE values greater than 0.5, while 43% of regulated flow forecast points surpassed a KGE value of 0.5.
bias correction of the NWM retrospective data

chunks.text: Seasonal and climate controls matter: NWM performs best in humid regions during fall and winter, while semi-arid/sub-humid regions show better agreement in spring and arid regions in fall. The authors suggest that the model-agnostic NextGen framework could improve continental prediction by enabling regionally appropriate model choices and better representation of processes and regulation. Future work includes bias correction and frequency analysis to improve exceedance thresholds used for flood mapping.
supporting_quote: In humid regions, streamflow estimates were more accurate during fall and winter, while for arid regions, the model demonstrated better agreement with in-situ observations during the fall season.
the model-agnostic NextGen NWM framework, which accounts for regional performance of the utilized model, could be more suitable for continental-scale hydrologic prediction.

chunks.text: Land models (LMs) simulate terrestrial exchanges of heat, water, and carbon and are widely used in weather prediction, hydrology, ecosystem studies, and climate projections. Because these models underpin scientific inference and societally relevant predictions, their evaluation and benchmarking are critical. Flux-tower site simulations provide high-frequency in situ meteorological forcing and directly comparable turbulent flux observations, offering a promising evaluation environment.
supporting_quote: Land models (LMs) simulate terrestrial water, energy, and biogeochemical cycles.
meteorological variables that drive LMs are directly measured at tower sites at a time resolution appropriate for LM simulation (typically 30 min)

chunks.text: The work builds on the original PLUMBER benchmarking project but expands scope and addresses shortcomings. PLUMBER2 increases site diversity and record length and adds sensitivity tests for energy-balance correction and low-turbulence periods. It also broadens participating model types and strengthens empirical benchmark baselines to contextualize expected performance.
