supporting_quote: It follows the first Protocol for the Analysis of Land Surface Models (PALS) Land Surface Model Benchmarking Evaluation Project (PLUMBER; Best et al., 2015; Haughton et al., 2016) and addresses many of the shortcomings in its first iteration.
PLUMBER2 examines a much broader range of environments (170 sites instead of 20).

chunks.text: Turbulent flux observations from eddy covariance have known uncertainties, particularly around energy balance closure and low-turbulence conditions. Because LMs must conserve energy, mismatches can reflect observational issues rather than model flaws. PLUMBER2 therefore evaluates both raw and energy-balance-corrected fluxes and tests filtering of time steps to exclude low-turbulence periods.
supporting_quote: Site measurements regularly do not close the energy balance ... and measurements are likely to have much greater uncertainty in periods of low turbulence
evaluation involving both raw and energy-balance-corrected site data as well as filtering to remove periods of low turbulence

chunks.text: The paper aims to define how to fairly assess land model fidelity by creating an evaluation framework that supports attribution of model–observation mismatch to model shortcomings. It frames this as two questions: what simulation environment best constrains models observationally, and how to structure evaluation so attribution is fair. PLUMBER2 is presented as an experimental design to implement and demonstrate this framework.
supporting_quote: This paper focuses on a relatively simple question: how should we fairly assess the fidelity of land models?

First, what kind of simulation environment allows for the best observational constraint of LMs... Second, how do we best structure an evaluation framework to give us confidence in this kind of attribution?

chunks.text: A central goal is to quantify benchmark performance expectations for LMs using out-of-sample empirical models trained on the same forcing variables. By building a hierarchy of empirical models of increasing complexity, the study seeks to estimate what level of predictability is achievable from the available inputs. This provides a reference for identifying where mechanistic models can demonstrably improve.
supporting_quote: This idea can be approximated by using out-of-sample empirical models to predict site fluxes using the same meteorological driving variables as the LMs as predictors
By varying the complexity of empirical models and the number and types of predictors we provide them with, we create a hierarchy of benchmark levels of performance

chunks.text: Model evaluation is often conducted without explicit consideration of observational constraint and uncertainty and without benchmark expectations for what counts as good performance. This can lead to partial or misleading assessments depending on metric choice, data choice, and other factors. The study positions PLUMBER2 as addressing these shortcomings by explicitly incorporating observational uncertainty and benchmark-based performance thresholds.
supporting_quote: often without explicit consideration of the degree of observational constraint or uncertainty and typically without quantification of benchmark performance expectations
We aim to develop an evaluation framework that gives us confidence that LM evaluation is not partial

chunks.text: Large-scale grid-based evaluation is difficult because reanalysis forcing uncertainty is often unquantified and flux evaluation products can be coarse in time. This makes attribution of mismatches inconclusive and hinders process-level diagnosis. Site-based simulations alleviate some issues but introduce other challenges such as limited parameter measurement and flux observational uncertainty.
supporting_quote: LMs need to be driven by reanalysis-based meteorology with unquantified uncertainty ... making the attribution of model–observation mismatch inconclusive
Site-based LM simulations using observational data collected at flux towers offer a solution ... but they come with their own challenges.

chunks.text: Energy balance non-closure in flux-tower data complicates evaluation because LMs are structurally constrained to conserve energy. Observations may also be less reliable during low turbulence (often nighttime). PLUMBER2 treats this by considering energy-balance-corrected fluxes and by filtering to wind speeds above a threshold.
supporting_quote: Energy balance closure in flux tower data is particularly relevant ... LMs are fundamentally constrained to conserve energy.
run separately filtered by time steps with wind speeds above 2 m s−1

chunks.text: Using ranks (as in PLUMBER) can distort summarised model comparisons when models have very similar metric values at some sites but differ strongly at others. The paper illustrates how rank averaging can misleadingly label a model as worst even when differences are small at most sites. This motivates alternative summative indicators based on normalised metric values.
supporting_quote: In PLUMBER, each LM was ranked ... However, it has since become clear that this can create misleading results.
This summative indicator misleadingly suggests that the LM is comfortably the worst model of the four

chunks.text: PLUMBER2 runs mechanistic land models offline in single-site mode at flux-tower locations using observed half-hourly or hourly meteorological forcing. Models are requested to run “out-of-the-box” with default vegetation-type-based parameters as in global applications, using IGBP vegetation type mapping to model PFTs where possible. Calibration to site fluxes is prohibited to focus on predictive skill rather than fitting.
supporting_quote: Mechanistic LMs ran offline in single-site mode ... forced by observed meteorology from the 170 sites.
Simulations were requested as "out-of-the-box", using default (usually vegetation-type-based) parameters
Models were not allowed to calibrate to site fluxes

chunks.text: The experiment includes two physical benchmark models: a Manabe bucket and a Penman–Monteith model with reference stomatal resistance and unrestricted water availability. These provide simplified physically based baselines alongside empirical benchmarks. Analyses focus on latent heat flux (Qle), sensible heat flux (Qh), and net ecosystem exchange (NEE) to maximise inclusion across submissions.
supporting_quote: two "physical benchmarks" ... an implementation of a Manabe bucket model (Manabe, 1969) and a Penman– Monteith model
the analyses here focus on latent heat flux (Qle), sensible heat flux (Qh), and net ecosystem exchange (NEE)

chunks.text: Empirical benchmarks are required to be out-of-sample: each site prediction is made by training on other sites only. The benchmark hierarchy ranges from simple linear regression using SWdown (1lin) to multiple regression (2lin), clustered regression with 27 clusters (3km27) and 729 clusters (6km729), a lagged version (6km729lag), random forest (RF), and an LSTM that ingests dynamic meteorology plus static site attributes and predicts Qle, Qh, and NEE jointly.
supporting_quote: all empirical models need to provide out-of-sample predictions ... training on 169 sites and predicting on 1, repeated 170 times
A hierarchy of different empirical models was used ... 1lin ... 3km27 ... 6km729 ... RF ... LSTM

chunks.text: Flux-tower forcing data are processed with quality-control requirements on key variables and metadata. Sites must have whole years of data and avoid substantial missing periods in SWdown, Tair, Qair, or Rainf (gap-filling counted as missing). LWdown is gapfilled using a synthesis approach, pressure is derived from elevation and temperature, and ambient CO2 uses global values.
supporting_quote: after processing with the FluxnetLSM package ... had whole years of data; and were not missing significant periods of key forcing variables ... SWdown, Tair, specific humidity (Qair), or precipitation (Rainf).
Gapfilling ... of downwelling longwave radiation (LWdown) used the approach of Abramowitz et al. (2012).

chunks.text: To reduce inter-model differences due to missing site LAI observations, PLUMBER2 provides a remotely sensed LAI time series per site, derived from MODIS (MCD15A2H, 2002–2019) or Copernicus (1999–2017), with climatology outside product periods. Models that prognose LAI can ignore prescribed LAI. This is intended to standardise vegetation inputs where possible.
supporting_quote: we specified a remotely sensed LAI time series for each site to try to minimise differences between LMs.
derived from either MODIS (8-daily MCD15A2H product, 2002–2019) or the Copernicus Global Land Service (monthly, 1999–2017)

chunks.text: Analyses address observational issues by comparing against both uncorrected and energy-balance-corrected fluxes, restricting to non-gap-filled flux time steps. Additional sensitivity is tested by filtering to time steps with wind speed above 2 m s−1 to assess low-turbulence impacts. Forcing and evaluation files are distributed in updated ALMA NetCDF with CF and CMIP-equivalent names where possible.
supporting_quote: The analyses below consider both uncorrected and corrected latent and sensible heat fluxes, were only conducted on flux time steps that were not gap-filled
run separately filtered by time steps with wind speeds above 2 m s−1
Forcing and evaluation files were produced in an updated version of ALMA NetCDF

chunks.text: The paper proposes two summative indicators based on normalised metric values: dependent NMV (dNMV) normalises using the range that includes the LM and reference benchmarks, while independent NMV (iNMV) normalises using only the benchmark range so expectations are independent of the LM. iNMV allows values below 0 or above 1 when LMs outperform or underperform the benchmark range. Both are computed per metric, site, variable, and then aggregated.
supporting_quote: we define the *dependent* normalised metric value (dNMV)
The second approach, *independent* NMV (iNMV), defines the normalised metric range using only the reference benchmark models

chunks.text: PLUMBER2 initially ran at 170 flux-tower sites using in situ half-hourly or hourly forcing, drawing from FLUXNET2015, FLUXNET La Thuile, and OzFlux. After post-hoc identification of anomalous precipitation records, 16 sites were removed, and analyses are conducted on the remaining 154 sites. The dataset includes key site metadata such as canopy height, reference height, and IGBP vegetation type.
supporting_quote: LMs completed simulations at 170 flux tower sites for PLUMBER2
Sixteen sites were removed from the analysis as a result ... analyses below are conducted on the remaining 154 sites.
we ensured that the sites had a reference (measurement) height, canopy height, and IGBP ... vegetation type

chunks.text: Key forcing variables required include SWdown, Tair, Qair, and Rainf, with additional variables such as LWdown, wind, and pressure provided or derived. LWdown can be fully synthesised when needed, while PSurf is estimated from elevation and temperature and CO2air is assigned from global values. Data are stored in ALMA NetCDF with standardised naming attributes.
supporting_quote: key forcing variables ... incoming solar radiation (SWdown), air temperature (Tair), specific humidity (Qair), or precipitation (Rainf).
Surface air pressure (PSurf) was based on elevation and temperature, and ambient CO2 was based on global values
Forcing and evaluation files were produced in an updated version of ALMA NetCDF

chunks.text: Energy-balance correction is applied following the FLUXNET2015 approach (and replicated for other site collections), enabling evaluation against both raw and corrected latent and sensible heat fluxes. Analyses exclude gap-filled flux time steps to focus on measured periods. Sensitivity analyses also filter by wind speed above 2 m s−1 to examine low-turbulence measurement concerns.
supporting_quote: Energy balance closure correction was part of the FLUXNET2015 release ... and we replicated this approach for sites from the other sources.
were only conducted on flux time steps that were not gap-filled
run separately filtered by time steps with wind speeds above 2 m s−1

chunks.text: Remotely sensed LAI time series are provided for each site because most sites lack public and time-evolving in situ LAI. LAI is derived from MODIS (8-daily) or Copernicus (monthly) products, with a climatology used outside product coverage. This LAI forcing is meant to reduce differences between LMs, while models that predict LAI can opt not to use it.
supporting_quote: most sites had no publicly available leaf area index (LAI) data and none had time-evolving LAI data
The LAI time series were derived from either MODIS ... or the Copernicus Global Land Service
LMs that predict LAI would clearly not utilise this

chunks.text: Across sites, models vary more in partitioning energy between Qle and Qh than in total available energy, consistent with prior findings. Stand-alone ecosystem models show broader spread from observed Bowen ratio than models used in coupled systems. Empirical out-of-sample models cluster near observed mean flux partitioning, indicating meteorological forcing alone contains enough information to predict mean fluxes well out-of-sample.
supporting_quote: models differ most in their partitioning of surface energy ... rather than the amount of available energy
Those LMs that do not operate in a coupled modelling system ... appear to have a much broader spread of estimates
out-of-sample, demonstrating that forcing meteorology alone provides enough information to predict mean fluxes accurately out-of-sample

chunks.text: Energy-balance-corrected observations shift mean available energy substantially and do not improve alignment with mechanistic LMs. The corrected flux observations add about 16 W m−2 (about 23%) of energy across sites, placing observations further outside the LM spread of available energy. Similar conclusions hold when filtering to wind speeds above 2 m s−1, indicating low-turbulence filtering does not materially change the comparison.
supporting_quote: the corrected version of the flux observations contains an average of 16 W m−2 additional energy across these sites, an increase of about 23 %
the LMs' performance is not improved with energy-balance-corrected flux data
when we filter analyses ... wind speed above 2 m s−1 ... changes surprisingly little

chunks.text: Errors in mean energy evaporative fraction (Qle/(Qle+Qh)) show mechanistic benchmarks and ecosystem models deviate most, while empirical models remain near zero-centered with less spread as complexity increases. There is no clear observational bias implied in partitioning because some LMs have high EF bias and others low EF bias. This pattern is reported as largely insensitive to energy-balance correction and wind-speed filtering.
supporting_quote: the mechanistic benchmarks and ecosystem models show the largest deviation from the site observations, and empirical approaches are reliably zero-centred
The equivalent plots using energybalance-corrected data and data filtered for wind speed are almost indistinguishable from Fig. 2

chunks.text: For Qle versus NEE averaged across sites, most LMs predict less net carbon uptake than observed, with exceptions including Noah-MP and STEMMUS-SCOPE. Empirical models, despite lacking site history and often lacking LAI inputs, remain close to observed average NEE within about 0.35 μmol m−2 s−1. This suggests missing site history information does not strongly reduce out-of-sample predictability at the aggregate level.
supporting_quote: With the exception of Noah-MP, STEMMUS-SCOPE, and some empirical models, all LMs predict less net carbon uptake than is observed.
all the empirical models are within 0.35 μmol m−2 s−1 of the observations
The empirical models also do not have any site history and indeed in most cases do not even use any estimate of LAI.

chunks.text: Water use efficiency (−NEE/Qle) is generally underestimated by LMs, typically by about 50%, consistent with underprediction of carbon uptake. Noah-MP shows a very high WUE bias linked to overprediction of carbon uptake and high dynamically predicted LAI. Empirical models are more symmetrically spread around observed WUE despite predicting variables independently.
supporting_quote: almost all LMs underestimate WUE, typically by about 50 %
Noah-MP shows a very high WUE bias ... due to a high dynamically predicted LAI
The empirical models ... are better spread around the observed values.

chunks.text: Using dependent normalised metric values (dNMV) against reference benchmarks (1lin_raw, 3km27_raw, LSTM_raw) shows LMs perform relatively better for Qle and NEE than for Qh. Specifically, 15 of 18 LMs are worse than the simple out-of-sample 1lin_raw benchmark for Qh, while many fall within benchmark ranges for Qle and NEE. Sensitivity tests with energy-balance correction and wind filtering do not qualitatively change this overall pattern.
supporting_quote: 15 of 18 worse than the out-of-sample simple linear regression (1lin_raw) for Qh
LMs tend to perform better against the benchmarks for Qle and NEE than Qh
Filtering for higher wind speed time steps ... appears to make no qualitative difference

chunks.text: Independent normalised metric values (iNMV) reveal substantially poorer LM performance relative to empirical expectations because the benchmark range is defined without the LM. Averaged over all fluxes, no LM outperforms the out-of-sample linear regression against SWdown (1lin). Performance is especially poor for Qh: no mechanistic models lie within the benchmark range for Qh, versus about 40% within range for Qle and 29% for NEE.
supporting_quote: no LM outperforms the out-of-sample linear regression against SWdown
LM performance is particularly poor relative to the benchmarks for Qh, with no models within the range of the benchmarks
compared to 40 % of them for Qle and 29 % for NEE

chunks.text: Vegetation-type stratification of LM versus LSTM performance for Qle shows variability: average LM performance is worst for OSH, EBF, and MF, while grass-dominated types appear somewhat better. However, equivalent analyses for Qh and NEE suggest no consistent vegetation type is categorically anomalous. The study notes that some apparent shifts after energy-balance correction are partly driven by outlier models rather than broad changes.
supporting_quote: the mean LM performance is worst for open shrubland (OSH), evergreen broadleaf forest (EBF), and mixed forest (MF)
equivalent plots for Qh ... and NEE ... suggest that there is no clear differentiation of performance by vegetation type
this seems to be at least partially because of significant changes to outlier LMs

chunks.text: About 30% of sites show average evapotranspiration exceeding precipitation, indicating strong local water subsidies (e.g., groundwater access, hillslope flow, irrigation) or data issues. Despite many LMs being structurally unable to reproduce such water balances, sites with Qle exceeding precipitation do not show systematically worse LM performance in iNMV comparisons. Poorly simulated sites appear spread across dryness and energy regimes rather than concentrated in the anomalous water-balance subset.
supporting_quote: around 30 % of the sites showing an average evapotranspiration exceeding the average precipitation
despite there being a structural impediment to LMs simulating these sites, that impediment is clearly not the major cause of the LMs' poor performance
the sites worst simulated by LMs, shown in blue, seem evenly spread throughout the figures

chunks.text: Although energy-balance-corrected and raw fluxes differ substantially, conclusions about relative performance are qualitatively similar with or without correction, and wind-speed filtering does not materially improve LM comparisons. The authors suggest evidence that energy-balance correction may reduce predictability for Qle: an LSTM trained on corrected Qle does not outperform one trained on raw Qle when predicting corrected targets. This raises the possibility that the correction procedure for Qle is problematic, whereas Qh correction may be more defensible.
supporting_quote: our conclusions about model performance are relatively similar with or without the correction
restricting analyses to low-turbulence periods does not result in a qualitative change
it performs better than LSTM_eb for Qle ... This suggests that the correction to Qle makes these fluxes *less* predictable

chunks.text: A key limitation is incomplete site parameter and history information, which can affect mechanistic LM performance. While many sites lack measured soil properties and detailed land-use history, PLUMBER2 runs models as they would in global simulations (default parameters, no calibration). The study notes that NEE underprediction may relate to missing site history, but empirical models still predict NEE well out-of-sample, challenging assumptions about history/LAI necessity for flux prediction.
supporting_quote: not all LM parameters are measured at sites, and indeed at some sites little information is available beyond a broad indication of vegetation type
Simulations were requested as "out-of-the-box"
While it seems obvious that a lack of site history ... is the cause ... it is intriguing to see that empirical models (also not given this information) were able to predict NEE

chunks.text: The paper argues that rank-based or dependent normalisation summaries can give an artificially positive impression of LM performance because poor performance is not penalised proportionally when LMs fall outside benchmark expectations. Independent NMVs avoid including the assessed LM in defining the benchmark range, allowing much worse-than-expected performance to be reflected. This methodological choice strongly affects interpretation and is presented as necessary for fair attribution.
supporting_quote: The difference in apparent LM performance between dN-MVs and iNMVs as a summative indicator is stark.
By excluding the LM we are evaluating from the criteria that define good or bad performance ... we define benchmark levels of performance that are independent of the LM being evaluated.
Using metric ranks or dNMVs instead limits the cost of poor performance

chunks.text: Many sites violate the common LM assumption of negligible horizontal water transport, as shown by water evaporative fraction above 1. The authors interpret this as indicating roles for groundwater access, bedrock/landscape hydrology, or lateral moisture redistribution at flux-footprint scales and potentially larger. Few global coupled models represent these processes, which complicates site-level evaluation and may matter at sub-basin scales.
supporting_quote: A significant number of sites show a water evaporative fraction greater than 1
either (a) access to groundwater ... (b) below-surface bedrock structure ... and/or (c) horizontal advection of moisture in soil
Very few global coupled models include any of these effects.

chunks.text: The study concludes that flux-tower site simulations combined with out-of-sample empirical benchmarks provide enough observational constraint to diagnose land-model performance. The consistent outperformance of mechanistic LMs by out-of-sample empirical models indicates that LMs have information available in forcing data that they are not effectively using. This framework defines performance in terms of demonstrated achievable improvement rather than raw mismatch alone and supports targeted future model development.
supporting_quote: we can conclusively say that this simulation environment does offer enough observational constraint to diagnose model performance.
The fact that a broad range of empirical models ... can reliably outperform LMs tells us that enough information is available to LMs to do better.
defines model performance in terms of demonstrated capacity for improvement rather than model– observation mismatch alone

chunks.text: Independent NMV-based benchmarking is presented as a fairer summarisation than ranks or dependent normalisation because it sets performance expectations independently of the LM and can reflect extreme underperformance or outperformance. Applying iNMVs shows that no LM outperforms the simplest out-of-sample shortwave linear regression when averaged across fluxes, with particularly poor performance for sensible heat flux. The authors recommend incorporating empirical performance estimates into routine community evaluation tools to distinguish incremental from qualitative improvements.
supporting_quote: We suggest that the summative analysis we present here using iNMVs is a fairer, more comprehensive representation of LM performance
no LM outperforms the out-of-sample linear regression against SWdown
inclusion of empirical performance estimates, such as those shown here, will be key to distinguishing incremental improvements from qualitative improvements

chunks.text: Flood events are increasing in frequency and impacts, motivating regional-to-continental high/hyper-resolution flood forecasting. While streamflow forecasting has advanced (e.g., the National Water Model), converting streamflow into time-varying inundation maps with adequate speed and accuracy remains challenging. Operational settings require solutions that balance realism with computational efficiency and cyberinfrastructure constraints.
supporting_quote: With an increasing stress of climate and land use changes in recent times, flood events are becoming more frequent and perhaps more disastrous
translating streamflow forecasts into time-varying flood inundation maps with reasonable accuracy and speed remains an outstanding concern.
Choice of a hydraulic/hydrodynamic model as component of a large scale framework is determined less by the superior model physics and more by its suitability to be executed in cyber infrastructures

chunks.text: HEC-RAS has been widely used for flood hazard mapping in the United States, including FEMA and NOAA applications, and has recently added 2D capabilities. However, most hydraulic/hydrodynamic models require extensive spatial detail and manual setup, limiting their scalability and timeliness for high-resolution, large-area operations.
supporting_quote: HEC-RAS (Hydrologic Engineering Center-River Analysis System), with 1D flow simulation functionality, has been the principal model used in US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA)'s
The ability of performing coupled 1D/2D analysis has been recently added to HEC-RAS (hereafter, HEC-RAS 2D;
Executing most of the hydraulic/hydrodynamic models requires modelers' intervention to provide substantial spatial details

chunks.text: New low-complexity inundation mapping tools such as AutoRoute and HAND were developed to support rapid, large-scale flood mapping with simplified input needs. AutoRoute has been used to generate ~10 m flood maps over very large regions, and HAND has been used to couple NWM streamflow with a national HAND raster for near real-time mapping. Their relative skill versus each other and against advanced 2D hydrodynamics needs systematic evaluation.
supporting_quote: Follum (2012) introduced AutoRoute (Table 1) as a rapid tool to create flood inundation mapping over large scales.
generated high resolution  (∼10 m)  flood maps for the Midwest US (230,000 km2) and the Mississippi Delta (109,500 km2).
The new-generation low-complexity inundation mapping tools, such as AutoRoute and HAND, have not been compared with each other, or with advanced hydrodynamic models (e.g. HEC-RAS 2D).

chunks.text: The study’s main goal is to evaluate relative accuracy of AutoRoute, HAND, and HEC-RAS 2D across different flood magnitudes using two contrasting U.S. test cases. Evaluation targets both inundation extent and inundation depth, and includes sensitivity to terrain features such as bathymetry and a levee in the smaller, controlled domain. The work aims to inform whether low-complexity tools can serve operational hyper-resolution flood mapping needs.
supporting_quote: The main objective of this study is to evaluate the relative accuracy between AutoRoute, HAND, and HEC-RAS 2D for different magnitudes of flooding events, in terms of both inundation extents and depths.
The Cedar River (CR) in Iowa and Black Warrior River (BWR) in Alabama in the US were considered as test-cases
For one of the test-cases (BWR), models are compared after incorporating geophysical and man-made attributes (e.g. channel bathymetry and levee)

chunks.text: A secondary goal is to use FEMA estimates as a reference where available, enabling an external benchmark beyond inter-model comparisons. This benchmark is applied in the BWR domain for a 100-year event to compare extents and depths produced by the three modeling approaches. The intent is to judge practical reliability under operationally relevant conditions with a levee present.
supporting_quote: In one of the configurations of BWR, FEMA estimated flood extents and depths were also used as a reference to compare with model simulations.
Fig. 15 compares model simulated inundation extent and depth for a 100-year flood event with the corresponding FEMA estimates.
comparing the models with FEMA estimates seemed justified only for the ''NED + Levee" terrain setup.

chunks.text: Hydrodynamic and hydraulic models commonly require detailed cross-sections, bathymetry, and calibration inputs that are often unavailable, making them difficult to operationalize at continental scales. Their “black-box” setups and heavy computation become bottlenecks with high-resolution river networks. This motivates evaluation of simpler tools that reduce data and setup burdens while remaining accurate enough for emergency response.
supporting_quote: provide substantial spatial details (e.g. channel and flood-plain cross-sections, optimum parameter values), which are often not readily available.
the majority of these modeling packages come with a "black-box" configuration that can be executed only for research purposes
These models also require considerable setup and computation time, especially with high resolution river networks.

chunks.text: Key floodplain processes and man-made controls (bathymetry, levees, dams, bridges) are not consistently represented across models, and their influence on inundation is underexplored. Simplified physics in low-complexity methods may further reduce already-limited realism, especially under extreme events and complex hydraulic settings. The study frames this as a need for multi-model comparison to quantify relative performance under varied terrain setups.
supporting_quote: Ability to capture natural floodplain processes and the influence of man-made control structures is different in each model.
Effects of other geophysical and man-made attributes including channel bathymetry, levees, and bridges on model-simulated flood inundation has remained relatively unexplored
a multi-model comparison can help measure relative accuracy of each model.

chunks.text: Low-complexity tools (AutoRoute and HAND) had not been comprehensively compared to each other or to an advanced 2D hydrodynamic model, leaving uncertainty about their operational suitability. While AutoRoute had been compared against reference extents, HAND’s efficacy was described as not yet tested. This gap motivated systematic evaluation across two domains, multiple flood magnitudes, and multiple terrain configurations.
supporting_quote: The new-generation low-complexity inundation mapping tools, such as AutoRoute and HAND, have not been compared with each other, or with advanced hydrodynamic models
Although AutoRoute was compared with reference inundation extents (Follum et al., 2017), HAND's efficacy is yet to be tested.
attempts to fill this gap with a view to provide a "practical, yet reliable" flood inundation modeling alternative

chunks.text: The evaluation uses a multi-model comparison workflow across 39 configurations combining three models, multiple flood events, terrain setups, and two test beds. BWR uses 10-, 100-, and 500-year events and four terrain setups (NED; NED+Bathymetry; NED+Levee; NED+Bathymetry+Levee). CR uses a single 100-year event and a simplified NED-only terrain setup.
supporting_quote: The assessment presented in this study is based upon 39 model configurations involving three models, three flood events, four terrain setups, and two test beds.
BWR test-case separately for three flood events (10-, 100-, and 500-year return per-
CR... only a single flood event (100-year return period) and terrain setup (without channel bathymetry and levee)

chunks.text: To keep comparisons fair, the study holds key inputs consistent across models for a given configuration, including forcing streamflow, topographic resolution, land cover, and Manning’s roughness values. Differences in outputs are therefore attributed primarily to model structure and physical process representation. This setup supports relative accuracy assessment rather than calibration to observations.
supporting_quote: To enable an even assessment, the forcing data (i.e. input streamflow), topographic resolution, land cover classification, and the values of channel/surface roughness parameters were kept identical

Hence, plausible differences in simulated inundation depth and extent while using these different terrain setups evolve solely from the respective ability of the models to capture floodplain hydrodynamics.

chunks.text: Hypothetical flood-event streamflows are constructed via a fusion approach that scales National Water Model hydrographs using USGS and FEMA return-period peak-flow estimates, while preserving network connectivity. In BWR, an event-specific scaling factor at the outlet is applied to all reaches. In CR, scaling uses estimates at the outlet plus 14 upstream gauges, applying nearest downstream scaling where estimates are absent.
supporting_quote: input streamflow data for the three hypothetical flood events (10-, 100-, and 500-year return periods) were constructed by fusing NWM simulated outputs with USGS and FEMA estimates.
an event-specific scaling factor was calculated for the outlet of BWR, being defined as the ratio of corresponding USGS estimated magnitude and the NWM peak flow
calculation of scaling factor for this case involved using USGS estimated peak flow at 14 upstream gauge stations

chunks.text: Terrain setups for BWR are created by mosaicking 10 m NED with field-derived channel bed/water surface elevations (bathymetry) and a levee representation, producing four distinct terrain rasters. chunks.text: HAND is implemented as a raster terrain-analysis approach where cells with HAND values below a derived stage are inundated. The study creates 10 m HAND rasters for each terrain setup, builds stage–geometry relationships per reach, and generates synthetic rating curves with Manning’s equation using reach length/slope and channel roughness. Peak flow is converted to stage via rating curves and then used to delineate inundation from the HAND raster.

This frames a pathway for improving scalability while retaining physical relevance.

chunks.text: Frozen ground (permafrost and seasonally frozen soil) is widespread in the Northern Hemisphere and can strongly influence infiltration and runoff partitioning because soil ice reduces permeability and changes thermal properties. Snowmelt runoff over frozen ground has been linked to major floods, and in many regions snowmelt contributes a large share of annual streamflow. Yet, observed catchment-scale responses often show weak or inconsistent frozen-soil effects compared with strong laboratory evidence, suggesting scale- and site-dependent mechanisms.
supporting_quote: Permafrost and seasonally frozen ground account for about 58% (or 55 million km2 ) of the land surface in the Northern Hemisphere
The presence of ice in soil reduces soil permeability while increasing thermal conductivity, which affects partitioning of snowmelt water into infiltration and surface runoff.
At lab scales, the presence of ice in the soil matrix largely reduces soil permeability

chunks.text: Field evidence indicates that preferential flow through macropores can allow snowmelt infiltration even when soils are partly frozen, weakening the expected ice-blockage effect. Dye tracer studies show infiltration to deeper layers via preferential pathways, influenced by antecedent conditions and potential refreezing that can block pathways. This complexity contributes to contradictory findings across scales and motivates testing alternative frozen-soil parameterizations in large-scale models.
supporting_quote: More field studies using dye tracer techniques ... revealed that water can infiltrate into deeper soils through preferential pathways
Air-filled macropore networks allow preferential flow under partially saturated conditions due to substantial increases in infiltration capacity.
The effects of frozen soil on snowmelt infiltration/percolation, surface runoff, groundwater recharge/discharge, and hence streamflow remains "controversial and contradictory"

chunks.text: Land-surface and hydrological models have used contrasting frozen-soil hydraulic property schemes, ranging from very low permeability formulations to approaches that enhance infiltration by representing spatial heterogeneity or preferential pathways. Some schemes reduce conductivity using ice impedance factors, which can improve simulations in some basins but degrade others. This history underscores the need to evaluate how frozen-soil hydraulic parameterizations affect streamflow prediction skill.
supporting_quote: Early models treated the freezing-thawing processes as drying-wetting processes when parameterizing frozen soil hydraulic properties (SHPs), resulting in extremely low permeability
Niu and Yang (2006) developed a scheme of SHP ... to enhance infiltration.
the NCAR Community Land Model (CLM4.5; and later versions) reduced the permeability by applying an ice impedance factor in hydraulic conductivity.

chunks.text: The study aims to resolve conflicting evidence about frozen-ground effects by testing how alternative frozen-soil parameterizations influence streamflow predictions at basin to continental scales. The authors evaluate multiple Noah-MP frozen-soil options and route resulting runoff with RAPID to compare modeled daily discharge against observations across the Mississippi River Basin. They also assess the robustness of conclusions under two different precipitation forcing products.
supporting_quote: We aim to understand this conflicting phenomenon through modeling using the Noah land surface model with multi-physics (MP; Noah-MP) options and the Routing Application for Parallel computatIon of Discharge (RAPID) over the Mississippi River Basin.
we investigate the impacts of soil freeze-thaw parameterizations on streamflow simulations at a large spatial scale and at a high temporal resolution.

To address the impacts of uncertainties in climatic forcing on frozen soil effects, we drive Noah-MP with IMERG-Final precipitation and North American Land Data Assimilation System Phase-2 (NLDAS-2) precipitation.

chunks.text: A core challenge is the mismatch between strong small-scale evidence that soil ice blocks infiltration and larger-scale hydrologic observations showing weak or absent impacts on runoff timing and magnitude. This discrepancy complicates how frozen-soil processes should be represented in operational land-surface and hydrologic models. The paper frames this as a controversial, scale-dependent issue influenced by vegetation, snow conditions, and preferential pathways.
supporting_quote: Despite plentiful evidence of frozen ground effects on snowmelt infiltration from lab experiments at pedon scales, streamflow observations show a weaker or no effect in terms of timing and magnitude at larger scales.
Shanley and Chalmers (1999) found no clear effects of frozen soil on the runoff ratio in the Sleepers River watershed
The effects of frozen soil on snowmelt infiltration/percolation, surface runoff, groundwater recharge/discharge, and hence streamflow remains "controversial and contradictory"

chunks.text: The modeling framework couples Noah-MP land-surface simulations with RAPID river routing over the Mississippi River Basin. Noah-MP produces hourly surface runoff and groundwater discharge, which are aggregated to daily lateral inflows and routed through a high-resolution NHDPlus-based river network to predict daily discharge at gauges. This setup enables testing the impact of frozen-soil process options on routed streamflow.
supporting_quote: We then transferred surface runoff and groundwater discharge from Noah-MP to RAPID to simulate discharge at the 52 USGS gauge locations in the MRB.
We use daily mean gridded lateral inflow, that is, surface runoff and groundwater discharge outputs ... as the forcing to the RAPID model to predict daily discharge in the river network.
The NHDPlus V2 data set is used to develop the geospatial framework for the entire MRB

chunks.text: Sixteen experiments are created by combining two supercooled liquid water (SLW) schemes with four frozen soil hydraulic property (SHP) schemes, then driving each set with two precipitation products. The eight frozen-soil scenarios (S1–S8) are defined by SLW1/SLW2 crossed with SHP1–SHP4. This factorial design isolates sensitivity of streamflow skill to parameterization choices under different forcing uncertainty.
supporting_quote: We conduct 16 experiments with combinations of two supercooled liquid water (SLW) parameterization schemes and four soil hydraulic property schemes in Noah-MP driven by two gridded precipitation products
Combining the eight frozen soil schemes and the two precipitation products generates 16 model scenarios
Table 4  Model Scenarios ... S1 SLW1 and SHP1 ... S8 SLW2 and SHP4

chunks.text: The study tests two SLW formulations for maximum liquid water under subfreezing temperatures. SLW1 uses a freezing-point depression relationship based on Niu and Yang (2006), while SLW2 adds a (1+8θice) term following Koren et al. (1999) and requires iterative solution. These options affect the liquid-ice partitioning used by Noah-MP under frozen conditions.

Option 2 (SLW2) is a variant ... with an additional term of (1+8ice) following (Koren et al., 1999)
This equation needs to be iteratively solved.

chunks.text: Four SHP schemes represent different frozen-soil permeability assumptions for hydraulic conductivity and diffusivity. SHP1 uses a fractional impermeable area Ffrz that linearly reduces permeability, representing permeable/impermeable subdomains. SHP2 uses the Koren et al. (1999) approach, SHP3 uses liquid-water-only formulations, and SHP4 uses effective porosity with an ice-impedance factor (E=6.0).

Option 4 (SHP4) ... accounts for reduction in infiltration by the ice blocking effects through an impedance factor, E (E = 6.0 in this study).

chunks.text: Noah-MP was run at hourly time step and 0.125° resolution, initialized with uniform warm/wet conditions and spun up using three loops over 2014–2019, with the last loop used for routing. The model was updated with a wet-bulb temperature rain/snow partitioning and a two-stream radiation scheme, and snow liquid holding capacity was increased to 0.08 to better match observation-based SWE. Frozen-soil parameters were not calibrated to focus comparisons on scheme structure.

chunks.text: Model performance is evaluated using Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE), including a rescaled form following Knoben et al. (2019). KGE values are computed for daily streamflow over 2015–2019 at 52 gauges, with January–June analyzed separately to emphasize snowmelt and freeze-thaw impacts. Percent KGE gain of the best-performing scenario (S5) relative to others is used to summarize improvements.

chunks.text: Two precipitation forcing products are used: NLDAS-2 and GPM IMERG-Final (V06B), both prepared at hourly resolution and 0.125° grid to drive Noah-MP from 2014–2019. IMERG is originally half-hourly at 0.1° and is interpolated to 0.125°; NLDAS-2 provides hourly precipitation and other near-surface forcings over CONUS. Using both forcings helps assess sensitivity to climatic input uncertainty.

chunks.text: Streamflow observations for evaluation come from USGS daily discharge records at 52 gauges across the Mississippi River Basin for 2015–2019. Gauge drainage areas span from 178 km2 to about 2.9 million km2, covering diverse hydrologic regimes. Four representative gauges are selected for detailed hydrograph analysis corresponding to major sub-basins.
