chunks.text: Snow and freeze-thaw products are used to validate Noah-MP states relevant to frozen-soil processes. The study uses a 4-km University of Arizona gridded SWE and snow depth product for 2015–2019 basin-mean SWE evaluation. It also uses NASA SMAP Level-3 freeze-thaw retrievals (36 km) downscaled to the 0.125° grid to compare annual frozen days in the top 10 cm soil layer.
supporting_quote: We also used the 4-km gridded snow water equivalent (SWE) and snow depth developed at the University of Arizona (UA) ... to validate
we used the NASA Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) Level-3 data set ... to validate the frozen soil days simulated by Noah-MP.
SMAP L3 gridded daily estimates of freeze-thaw are available at 36 km spatial resolution ... downscaled to the 0.125° NLDAS-2 grid

chunks.text: Geospatial river network and catchment information are derived from NHDPlus version 2, enabling large-scale routing with RAPID. The merged MRB dataset includes millions of vector reaches and associated catchment polygons, along with attributes used to build connectivity and slopes. This dataset supports routing across the basin to compare discharge at gauges under different land-surface runoff scenarios.
supporting_quote: The NHDPlus data set includes approximately 2.7 million vector-based reaches, each of which is associated with a catchment polygon.
NHDPlus attributes that were used to create a river connectivity file and to calculate flowline slopes.
The NHDPlus V2 data set is used to develop the geospatial framework for the entire MRB

chunks.text: Across the 52 gauges, streamflow predictions are much more sensitive to frozen-soil hydraulic property (SHP) schemes than to supercooled liquid water (SLW) schemes. The study reports that SLW1 vs SLW2 produces negligible differences in KGE, while changing SHP leads to material changes in performance. The best-performing scenario is S5 (SLW2+SHP1), and the worst is often S7 (SLW2+SHP3).
supporting_quote: Different SLW schemes demonstrate negligible effects on streamflow predictions.
implementing SLW1 or SLW2 does not have an apparent effect on model performance, whereas sensitivity to different SHP schemes has a material effect on model performance.
Of all scenarios, regardless of precipitation product used, S7 performs the worst, and S5 and S1, with higher permeability, perform the best.

chunks.text: A higher-permeability frozen-soil scheme yields higher streamflow prediction skill irrespective of precipitation product. The model with the highest permeability improves mean daily KGE by 20%–57% over a water year and by 29%–113% for spring, averaged across gauges. These improvements support the claim that weaker ice-imposed permeability reduction better matches basin-scale streamflow observations.
supporting_quote: A model with the highest permeability performs better than other schemes on daily streamflow predictions by 20%–57% throughout a water year and 29%–113% for the spring
Schemes with higher permeability resulted in mean values of KGE improvement ... of 20%–57% throughout a water year and 29%–113% for the spring and early summer relative to lower permeability schemes.
irrespective of the precipitation product used to drive the Noah-MP-RAPID model, a model with higher frozen soil permeability ... produces more accurate streamflow simulations

chunks.text: IMERG-forced simulations generally outperform NLDAS-forced simulations at most gauges, indicating substantial forcing-data influence on routed streamflow skill. The paper notes that many gauges have higher KGE with IMERG S5 than NLDAS S5, and differences can be large. Nevertheless, the ranking that higher-permeability schemes perform better is consistent across both precipitation products.
supporting_quote: Models forced by IMERG show a better prediction skill compared with those forced by NLDAS at most of the gauges.
32 out of the 52 gauges show improved KGE values for IMERG S5 as compared to NLDAS S5, with a magnitude of improvement of up to 3.1 in KGE.
Both precipitation products confirm that a scheme of higher permeability yields more accurate streamflow predictions over frozen ground.

chunks.text: Model validation indicates acceptable snowpack simulation for studying frozen-soil effects on discharge. Basin-averaged SWE from Noah-MP reproduces observed UA SWE with NSE above 0.76 for five of six HUC-2 basins, with some overestimation in Missouri and Arkansas-White-Red and underprediction in Lower Mississippi. The authors conclude SWE realism is sufficient to proceed with frozen-soil scheme comparisons.
supporting_quote: The modeled SWE reproduces the observed SWE averaged over most river basins with slight overestimations in the Missouri and Arkansas-White-Red Rivers.
The model efficiency (NSE) is above 0.76 for all river basins except the Lower Mississippi River
The modeled SWE is generally acceptable ... for investigating the effects of different SLW and SHP schemes

chunks.text: Comparison of simulated frozen days with SMAP freeze-thaw shows moderate agreement, providing partial confidence in modeled freeze occurrence. Noah-MP predicts up to 191 maximum frozen days versus 210 detected by SMAP over the MRB, with Noah-MP averaging 68 frozen days (about 18 more than SMAP). Spatial agreement is weaker in densely vegetated northeastern areas, and the overall correlation is 0.58.
supporting_quote: Noah-MP predicted 191 maximum frozen days whereas SMAP L3 FT detected 210 days
Noah-MP simulates 68 average frozen days, about ~18 days greater than what is detected by SMAP L3.
The correlation between SMAP L3 FT frozen days and Noah-MP simulated frozen days is 0.58.

chunks.text: Scenario S5 achieves the highest overall KGE distributions across gauges for both forcings, with higher median performance under IMERG than NLDAS. For IMERG, mean KGE across the eight scenarios ranges from 0.32 to 0.46, and S5 attains 0.46. For NLDAS, mean KGE ranges from 0.18 to 0.29, with S5 highest at 0.29.
supporting_quote: The mean KGE for the eight model scenarios increases from 0.32 to 0.46 when they are driven by IMERG, and S5 performs the best with KGE_SS = 0.46
For the NLDAS scenarios, the mean KGE values range from 0.18 to 0.29, and S5 performs the best with KGE_SS = 0.29

chunks.text: Improvements from high-permeability schemes are geographically concentrated where frozen ground is more prevalent. The Missouri basin (H10) and the broader West region (H10 and H11) show much larger percent KGE gains for S5 relative to low-permeability alternatives than the East region. This pattern aligns with modeled soil ice content, indicating frozen-soil parameterizations matter most in frozen-soil dominated basins.
supporting_quote: KGE improvements using IMERG S5 in the Missouri River (H10), which has a greater proportion of soil ice content ... are greater than in all other HUC-2 regions
IMERG S5 shows improvements ... by up to 203% for the West region but less than 7% in the East region.
Streamflow prediction improvement with a scheme of higher frozen soil permeability is pronounced in basins dominated by frozen ground

chunks.text: Hydrograph comparisons at representative gauges show that higher frozen-soil permeability improves timing and magnitude particularly in frozen-dominated basins. At the Missouri River at Hermann, IMERG S5 increases KGE from 0.59 (IMERG S2) to 0.69 and avoids early/overestimated peaks seen in lower-permeability cases. In contrast, at the Red River at Spring Bank, Arkansas, performance is high (KGE > 0.84) and insensitive to precipitation product or frozen-soil scheme, consistent with minimal soil ice influence.
supporting_quote: IMERG S5 shows improved performance relative to IMERG S2 with KGE increasing from 0.59 to 0.69
The modeled streamflow at the Spring Bank station agrees well with the observed discharge (KGE >0.84) with both IMERG and NLDAS precipitation products and both scenarios (S5 and S2).
the scenario with higher soil permeability (S5) more accurately captures the phase of the hydrograph than the one with lower soil permeability (S2).

chunks.text: Higher-permeability frozen-soil schemes increase the modeled contribution of baseflow to total runoff, especially in frozen-soil dominated basins. The study reports that IMERG S5 and NLDAS S5 raise baseflow ratio by 10.95% and 13.66% compared to S7, respectively. This mechanism provides a process-based explanation for improved discharge simulations under higher infiltration/percolation during melt seasons.
supporting_quote: This is also reflected by increases in the modeled ratio of baseflow (or groundwater discharge) to total runoff (Figure 12).
IMERG S5 and NLDAS S5, with higher permeability, increase the baseflow ratio by 10.95% and 13.66% compared to IMERG S7 and NLDAS S7, respectively.
The increase in baseflow ratio is most pronounced over basins dominated by frozen soil

chunks.text: The analysis keeps the same frozen-soil matric potential (water retention) treatment across scenarios and focuses on permeability differences, which limits attribution to other frozen-soil physics. The authors explicitly note they do not investigate (a) alternative water retention characteristics under freezing or (b) preferential flow impacts on streamflow predictions. As a result, improved skill with high permeability is demonstrated, but the study cannot isolate the role of retention hysteresis or explicit macropore flow dynamics.
supporting_quote: we focus on the effects of frozen soil permeability on streamflow predictions ... with all the simulations sharing the same soil water retention scheme under freezing conditions
This study, however, does not investigate the effects of (a) soil water retention characteristics under freezing conditions or (b) preferential flow on streamflow predictions

chunks.text: Preferential flow is only implicitly represented in SHP1/SHP5 via fractional permeable areas and does not explicitly increase saturated conductivity to macropore-domain magnitudes found in other studies. The paper notes that Ksat values remain soil-texture-based (around 10−6 m/s), whereas macropore-aware models enhance Ksat by 10^1–10^3 or calibrate to ~10−3 m/s to match infiltration under frozen conditions. This highlights a structural limitation and suggests future improvements should represent macropore networks more physically.
supporting_quote: but not actually enhancing the Ksat values, which are based on soil texture and are around 10−6 m/s for most soil types.
Ksat is enhanced by 101 –103 times to account for the presence of macropores in topsoil
Ksat for the macropore domain is calibrated at ∼10−3 m/s to match observed infiltration data under frozen conditions

chunks.text: The SMAP freeze-thaw comparison is acknowledged as imperfect because SMAP does not sample the full diurnal cycle and its signal mixes soil, snow, vegetation, and surface water contributions. Retrievals are degraded by complex terrain, seasonal transitions, thick snow, surface water, and dense vegetation. Therefore, agreement between modeled frozen days and SMAP is only a rough continental-scale validation and may miss key freeze-thaw dynamics affecting hydrology.
supporting_quote: the SMAP FT retrieval is based on radiometer observations at 6:00 a.m. ... and does not sample the entire diurnal cycle.
the SMAP FT retrieval does not distinguish individual contributions from soil, snow, vegetation, and surface water components
The detection of FT is also degraded over complex terrain, during seasonal FT transitions ... presence of thick snow, surface water, and dense vegetation cover

chunks.text: The paper argues that calibrating parameters like Ksat in fully integrated 3D models can improve streamflow but may confound parameter uncertainty with uncertainty in model structure and underlying mechanisms. It suggests model selection approaches that evaluate competing hypotheses while considering parameter uncertainty. This limitation underscores that the current work prioritizes comparing scheme structures without calibrating frozen-soil parameters.
supporting_quote: The calibration, however, confused the uncertainties in model structure (or understanding) of key mechanisms controlling flow ... with model parameter uncertainties.
model selection techniques should be used to evaluate model structures (or competing hypotheses) while considering model parameter uncertainties
In this study, we did not calibrate the parameters associated with frozen soil schemes.

chunks.text: The study concludes that representing higher frozen-soil permeability in Noah-MP improves routed daily streamflow predictions across the Mississippi River Basin. Sensitivity is substantial for SHP schemes but negligible for SLW schemes, and benefits are strongest in frozen-soil dominated basins. Overall, higher-permeability parameterizations yield mean KGE improvements of 20%–57% annually and 29%–113% for January–June relative to lower-permeability schemes.
supporting_quote: parameterization schemes that represent higher permeability in frozen soil produce more accurate streamflow simulations at most gauges in the MRB
While the effects of SLW on streamflow simulations appear to be negligible, simulations appear to be substantially sensitive to SHP schemes.
Schemes with higher permeability resulted in mean values of KGE improvement ... of 20%–57% ... and 29%–113% for the spring and early summer

chunks.text: Improvements from high-permeability frozen-soil schemes are pronounced in western MRB regions with greater soil ice, while effects attenuate downstream and in regions with little soil ice. The paper notes that downstream reaches with large drainage areas show weaker sensitivity, likely due to attenuation of frozen-soil effects across upstream catchments. This supports targeting frozen-soil physics improvements where frozen ground dominates hydrologic response.
supporting_quote: The impacts of frozen soil effects are particularly evident for frozen soil dominated regions.
The effects on downstream reaches (with larger upstream drainage areas) appear to be weaker, which may be due to attenuation of the frozen soil effects.
IMERG S5 shows improvements ... by up to 203% for the West region but less than 7% in the East region.

chunks.text: The authors recommend that future models explicitly represent preferential flow through macropore networks to better capture frozen-soil infiltration and its translation to basin-scale discharge. They interpret the high-permeability scheme as consistent with preferential pathways but emphasize current parameterizations are still highly simplified. Physically based dual-permeability models are proposed as a promising next step for linking lab-scale infiltration to basin-scale streamflow.
supporting_quote: Future models should represent preferential flows through macropore networks to improve the understanding of frozen soil effects on infiltration and discharge across scales.
Further research ... should rely on physically based models, for example, the dual permeability flow model to represent preferential flow
The Niu and Yang (2006) model represents a dual domain model with enhanced permeability, but the effects of frozen soil on infiltration and runoff are highly parameterized.

chunks.text: Manning’s roughness coefficient (n) represents frictional resistance from channel beds, banks, and floodplains, and strongly controls velocity, shear stress, and thus flood timing and related risks. It is widely used for flood propagation, pollutant transport, infrastructure design, and aquatic habitat applications. Despite this importance, large-scale, holistic understanding of its spatiotemporal variability has been limited by data availability.
supporting_quote: Manning's roughness coefficient, n, is used to describe channel roughness, and is a widely soughtafter key parameter for estimating and predicting flood propagation.
Due to its control of flow velocity and shear stress, n is critical for modeling timing of floods and pollutants, aquatic ecosystem health, infrastructural safety, and so on.

chunks.text: Engineering practice commonly treats n as temporally constant, relying on lookup tables or calibration, which hinders large-scale estimation and can mask true dynamics. Some field studies suggest n depends on discharge and may be overestimated at high flows, motivating examination of temporal dependence. Alternative resistance formulations (e.g., Chezy, Keulegan) exist but have not been leveraged for large-scale prediction.
supporting_quote: open-channel n is typically regarded as temporally constant, determined from lookup tables or calibration
In current practices and guidelines, n is predominantly viewed as a temporally constant (but often spatially varying) parameter
some field studies... recognize that Manning's roughnessis a function of discharge and that flow resistance tends to be overestimated at high flows

chunks.text: The study leverages the USGS HYDRoSWOT dataset, built from ADCP surveys, to examine roughness at continental scale. Large, diverse observations enable machine learning to link roughness to integrative basin signals like discharge and drainage area, along with local environmental covariates. This creates an opportunity to quantify spatial versus temporal components of n variability across the conterminous United States.
supporting_quote: HYDRoSWOT contains, among other attributes, discharge, flow velocity, and flow depths for over 200,000 observations from thousands of sites across the United States.

Since all these channel properties covary, we hypothesize that catchment area or discharge as integrative signals, along with local environmental predictors, could present a pathway toward better determination of n at large scales.

chunks.text: The work aims to build a continental-scale dataset of Manning’s n (and alternative resistance parameters) from observations and evaluate whether n can be accurately predicted using machine learning and environmental inputs. It seeks to identify which predictors are most important and whether n exhibits geographic patterns. A further objective is to quantify how much of n variance is temporal (linked to discharge changes) versus spatial, and evaluate consequences for flood peak modeling when temporal variability is ignored.
supporting_quote: Here, we developed and analyzed a continental-scale n dataset (along with alternative formulations)
We investigated the following questions.
Q1: Given a comprehensive dataset of continental‐scale Manning's roughness coefficient n... can n be well predicted by machine learning methods...
Q2: At the continental scale, how much variance in n is due to temporal variation in discharge, in comparison to its spatial variability
Q3: How many errors in flood peak modeling will be encountered if the temporal variation of n is not considered?

chunks.text: Channel roughness is often estimated from lookup tables or calibrated locally, approaches that are difficult to scale and for which underlying raw data are frequently unavailable. This limits the ability to estimate n across large regions and to understand its drivers systematically. As a result, the magnitude and predictability of spatiotemporal variability of n have remained unclear at continental scale.
supporting_quote: roughness is overwhelmingly either determined from published tables... or calibrated through matching simulations
Due to the need for local investigation or calibration, either approach would preclude the estimation of n at large scales.
limitations in the scale of available datasets have created knowledge gaps in understanding how much and how fast n varies in space and time

chunks.text: Assuming n is constant over time can produce substantial errors in modeled velocities, especially during extreme flows, and thus distort flood timing and magnitude. If n decreases at high flows, using low-flow or mean-flow n can overestimate resistance and delay simulated flood peaks. These potential errors motivate explicitly modeling temporal dynamics of n rather than using static values.
supporting_quote: Since flow velocity is inversely proportional to n, if temporal variability is substantial then current models risk significantly miscalculating velocity for extremely high or low flows.
Ignoring temporal dynamics means flood peaks could arrive days before predicted, and peak magnitude estimation might also be erroneous

chunks.text: Manning’s n was computed from observed hydraulics using the uniform-flow Manning equation, combining hydraulic radius, slope, and velocity. Hydraulic radius (R) was approximated by observed maximum depth under a rectangular cross-section assumption, and slope (S) was derived from reach-averaged NHDPlus V2 and treated as time-constant. Sensitivity tests with triangular/trapezoidal geometry were conducted and found not to change main conclusions about variability impacts.
supporting_quote: Assuming the channel cross‐sectional geometry to be rectangular, R was approximated by the observed maximum depth.
Slope was determined using the National Hydrography Dataset version 2 (NHDPlus V2) and averaged for each reach. Therefore,slope wastreated as a temporally constant parameter.
we ran sensitivity tests where either triangular or trapezoidal geometry... was assumed... We found the geometric assumption to have little impact

chunks.text: Multiple machine-learning regressors were evaluated to predict calculated n from environmental covariates while excluding variables directly used in the n formula to avoid leakage. Models included Random Forest (RF), MLP, XGB, and KNN; RF was selected due to best performance. Hyperparameters were tuned via grid-search cross-validation and transferability was assessed using spatial k-fold cross-validation clustered into 18 hydrologic-region folds.
supporting_quote: To avoid information leakage, we excluded variables directly involved in calculating n in Equation 1 from the inputs to our models.
including Random Forest (RF), Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN).
As the RF model exhibited the top performance among all other regressors with a NSE of 0.7, it was selected
Spatial k-fold cross-validation was performed... clustered into 18 folds according to hydrologic regions

chunks.text: Feature preparation involved trimming extreme n values and transforming some predictors to improve learning. n values were trimmed to be less than 0.33 following guidance, and some variables such as land cover, soil contents, and sinuosity were log-transformed. Data were standardized and split into training (70%), validation (15%), and testing (15%) sets.
supporting_quote: Based on previous literature and guidelines... we trimmed the n values to be less than 0.33 (Arcement, 1989).
A few input variables(e.g., land cover, soil contents, sinuosity) were transformed using logarithmic functions
Seventy percent of the dataset was used for training and the rest was used for validation (15%) and testing (15%).

chunks.text: Temporal and spatial contributions to n variability were decomposed using sums of squared errors. Within-site temporal variability was quantified via residuals around site-mean n (SSE_s), total variance via residuals around global mean (SSE_A), and additional explainable variance captured by an RF model using time-varying discharge and static covariates (SSE_RF). This framework enabled partitioning of variance into spatial, predictable temporal, and remaining unexplained components.
supporting_quote: To decompose the spatiotemporal variability of n, we calculated Sum-of-Squares Error (SSE) to quantify the variability.
SSE_s is the sum of the squares of the residuals when using the mean n to predict n for a particular site
SSE_RF shows the RF performance with the original spatiotemporally varying n as an input
SSE_A denotes the total sum-of-squares of n for all the data

chunks.text: Physical significance of the calculated n and the importance of combining components consistently in Manning’s formula were tested through perturbation and hypothesis tests. They modified the n formula by substituting global or site-specific median/mean values for components (v, R, S) and retrained RF models; predictability declines supported that the original combined quantity is meaningful. F-tests and randomized shuffling of S, R, and v were used to reject null hypotheses that components were irrelevant.
supporting_quote: We modified the terms of n and retrained random forest RF(X) models to predict them.
Every time one of the variables in v, R, or S was replaced by either this variable's global mean value or its at‐a‐site mean... the predictability... declined significantly (Table 2).
An F-test was performed to analyze the variance in populations for all parts of the hypothesis.
The NSE values from the RF models with randomized S, R, and v values were, respectively, 0.29, − 18.20, and − 0.38

chunks.text: To quantify implications of n time-variability on velocity, the study compared velocities derived from a time-dependent RF model versus a temporally static model trained on site-mean discharge, at both high-flow and low-flow conditions. Metrics r_maxQ and r_minQ expressed the ratio of dynamic to static velocity estimates under max-Q and min-Q conditions, respectively. A separate non-ML metric r′ compared observed max-Q velocity to the velocity estimated by applying min-Q-derived n at max-Q.
supporting_quote: we compared the estimated flow velocities using the time-dependent RF model and a static RF model trained on the mean conditions
r_maxQ = \frac{v(n_{maxQ}^{RF(Q^i, x)}, R_{maxQ})}{v(n_Q^{RF(Q, x)}, R_{maxQ})}
r_minQ = \frac{v(n_{minQ}^{RF(Q^{\prime},x)}, R_{minQ})}{v(n_{\underline{Q}}^{RF(\underline{Q},x)}, R_{minQ})}
r' = \frac{v_{maxQ}}{v(n_{minQ}, R_{maxQ})}

chunks.text: Flood-routing implications were demonstrated using a Muskingum–Cunge (MC) routing model in the Juniata River basin (~5,000 km²). n values from ADCP sites were simplified into drainage-area-threshold assignments with different values for min-Q, mean-Q, and max-Q conditions. Simulations compared hydrographs and peak timing/magnitude across these n scenarios to illustrate modeling errors when static roughness is used.
supporting_quote: We further used a Muskingum-Cunge (MC) routing model (Bindas et al., 2024)
We chose the Juniata River basin in central Pennsylvania, USA, with a size of around 5,000 km2
These values were different for min‐Q, mean‐Q, and max‐Q conditions
This experiment quantified the error if measured n values under mean flow conditions were used to simulate flood propagation under a flooding scenario.

chunks.text: Core hydraulic observations came from the USGS HYDRoSWOT ADCP survey dataset, providing discharge, velocity, depths, and widths for thousands of sites across the conterminous United States. The paper reports 5,228 total sites with 67,433 observations used, while the broader compilation contains over 200,000 ADCP surveys. Median site characteristics include width 28.4 m, maximum depth 1.22 m, drainage area 4.55 km², and mean velocity 0.44 m/s.
supporting_quote: HYDRoSWOT contains... over 200,000 Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler (ADCP) surveys from thousands of sites across the United States.
There are 5,228 total sites, with 67,433 observations.
Median characteristics of the sites in the dataset include channel width (28.4 m), maximum depth (1.22 m), drainage area (4.55 km2 ), and mean velocity (0.44 m/s).

chunks.text: Static and ancillary geospatial predictors were assembled from multiple national and global products to support modeling. These included drainage area, stream order, slope, and mean elevation from NHDPlus V2; land cover, sinuosity, and stream density from NHDPlus-derived attributes; and median streambed particle size D50 from a CONUS-wide dataset. Climate/vegetation and soil predictors included MODIS NDVI (MOD13Q1 V6.1), aridity index, and sand/clay/silt contents at shallow depths.
supporting_quote: Drainage area, stream order, slope, mean elevation | National Hydrography Dataset... | Coverage CONUS
Land cover, sinuosity, stream density | Wieczorek et al., 2018... | Coverage CONUS
Channel bed particle size D50 | Abeshu et al., 2022 ... | Coverage CONUS
NDVI | MOD13Q1 V6.1 ... | Global/250 m
Aridity index... Global Aridity Index... V2
Sand, clay, silt ... at 250 m resolution... only depths of 0 and 10 cm were considered

chunks.text: Land cover information was represented as percentages of classes compiled using the 2011 National Land Cover Dataset and linked to NHDPlusv2 reach catchments and accumulated upstream catchments via COMID identifiers. Sinuosity attributes were also compiled along NHDPlusv2 flowlines. These engineered predictors were incorporated as covariates for ML models of roughness.
supporting_quote: This dataset leverages data from the 2011 National Land Cover Dataset (NLCD 2011) and compiles the percentage of land cover classes into two distinct spatial components of the NHDPlus version 2 (NHDPlusv2)
The inclusion of a unique identifier, COMID, facilitated the linking of this dataset to the NHDPlusv2 data suite.
Similarly, information on flowline reach sinuosity was compiled along the flowline NHDPlusv2 COMID data.

chunks.text: Random Forest models predicted Manning’s n with high accuracy when using time-varying discharge together with static covariates, reaching NSE around 0.71. Predictability dropped when models attempted to predict n at max discharge using only static covariates, indicating that temporal discharge information adds substantial explanatory power. This supports the claim that n is predictable in both space and time from integrative environmental signals.
supporting_quote: RF model performance with the observed discharge as an input, RF( Q^t , x), with Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) of 0.71 ( R^2 = 0.7 , RMSE = 0.037)
RF(x) model to predict n at maximum discharge at individual sites, with NSE of 0.63.

chunks.text: Variance decomposition indicated that spatial variability explains about 50% of total n variance, while predictable temporal variability explains about 35%, leaving about 15% as unexplained fluctuations and noise. This directly challenges the prevalent assumption that n is temporally constant. The analysis implies that time-varying discharge contributes meaningfully to roughness variability at continental scale.
supporting_quote: predictable time variability explains a large fraction ( ~ 35%) of n variance compared to spatial variability (50%).
The remaining 15% of the variance (SSE_RF/SSE_T = 15%) includes unpredictable fluctuations and measurement/calculation noise.

chunks.text: Hypothesis tests supported that the calculated n values are physically meaningful and linked to Manning’s equation components. F-tests on shuffled or randomized components showed significant variance differences with p-values approximately zero. Randomizing S, R, or v drastically reduced RF model NSE, indicating that the structure of the Manning formulation and its matched measurements are essential to obtain predictable n.
supporting_quote: The ratios of the variances were found to be 1.15 for S, 0.23 for R, and 0.02 for v, with all the p-values being approximately zero.
The NSE values from the RF models with randomized S, R, and v values were, respectively, 0.29, − 18.20, and − 0.38

chunks.text: Perturbation experiments replacing Manning components with mean or site-median values reduced model predictability sharply, reinforcing that n must be computed from co-located, contemporaneous measurements. The baseline formula achieved NSE 0.71, while substituting global or site medians in slope, radius, or velocity led to much lower NSE (e.g., 0.43, 0.26, down to near 0). A control altered formula using v instead of 1/v also had low NSE, supporting the physical relevance of the standard form.
supporting_quote: Control experiments with an altered formula | n'' = v R^{2/3} S^{1/2} | 0.16

chunks.text: Spatial maps showed no simple continental-scale gradient in n, but regional patterns exist: lower n is prominent in the Great Plains and Appalachian Plateau, while higher n is more common along the west coast and parts of the northeastern Appalachians. The dataset also shows unexpectedly high n concentrations on Coastal Plains (e.g., Florida and southern/coastal Texas), potentially linked to backwater flows, wetlands, and high sinuosity. Reported n values range from about 0.02–0.05 for larger rivers up to 0.33 at some sites.
supporting_quote: The spatial distribution of the calculated n shows no major large-scale gradients for either median- or max- discharge
low n values are quite prominent over the Great Plains... and in the Appalachian Plateau
High n values are more common along the west coast and parts of the northeastern Appalachian Mountains.
a substantial concentration of high n values for streams on the Coastal Plains, especially Florida and southern/coastal Texas.
The values of n in this dataset are around 0.02–0.05 for the larger rivers and can be as high as 0.33 for some sites.

chunks.text: Across discharge percentiles, both the mean and variability of n are higher under low-flow conditions and lower/more stable under high flows. This indicates roughness becomes more predictable near peak flows, while low flows show greater scatter. The authors note a model predicting n at maximum discharge with inputs including Qmax achieved NSE 0.63, higher than models targeting mean-flow conditions (NSE 0.36).
supporting_quote: both the mean value and the variability of n in a flow percentile band were larger for low flow conditions compared to high flows
a RF model, RF( Q_max^s , x), that was given at-a-site maximum discharge ( Q_max^s ) obtained an NSE of 0.63
higher than the models for n under mean flow conditions (NSE = 0.36).

chunks.text: Permutation feature importance indicated discharge is the most important predictor of n, followed by drainage area, land cover variables (forest and agriculture), sinuosity, and bed particle size. This differs from traditional handbook approaches that do not explicitly emphasize discharge and drainage area. Partial dependence plots showed an exponential decay relationship between n and discharge, and similarly decreasing n with drainage area, implying smaller streams tend to have larger n.
supporting_quote: discharge was found to have the highest relative importance in estimating Manning's n compared to the other input features, followed by drainage area, land cover factors... sinuosity, bed particle size
The n ∼ Q relationship is exhibited by an exponential‐decay curve.
Drainage area (DA) acts in a similar manner... Overall, they point to much larger n values for the smaller streams.

chunks.text: Ignoring temporal variability can lead to large velocity estimation errors: under max-Q conditions, the time-dynamic model produced velocities that were 45% higher (median across 333 sites) than a static RF model trained on mean conditions. Under low flows, the time-dynamic model produced velocities 45% lower than the static model. A direct observational comparison showed the observed max-Q velocity was about 125% larger than an estimate obtained by applying min-Q-derived n at max-Q conditions.
supporting_quote: For measured max‐Q conditions, the time‐dynamic model would produce velocities that are, for the median of 333 sites, 45% higher than the static RF model's results
for low flows, the time‐dynamic model leads to velocities that are, at the median, 45% lower than the static model's results.
the observed max‐Q velocity is, at the median, 125% larger than what would be estimated if we applied Manning's formula with n from min‐Q measurements

chunks.text: In the Muskingum–Cunge routing case study, using mean-Q n instead of max-Q n delayed simulated flood peaks substantially and affected peak magnitudes. Peak timing using mean-Q n lagged the max-Q n simulation by 23 hours for one event and 36 hours for another. The dynamic effect also altered peak superposition, producing about a 15% higher peak under max-Q n relative to mean-Q n in one scenario.
supporting_quote: The flood peak using mean‐Q n values lags the one with max‐Q n values by 23 hr
and 36 hr for another larger peak
a ∼15% higher peak than was simulated using the mean‐Q n.

chunks.text: The analysis treats channel slope as temporally constant, which is common in large-scale modeling but may be problematic where effective slope varies due to coastal or backwater influences. The paper notes that in regions with minimal elevation change, water surface slope critically influences velocity, and tidal or storm-surge driven changes can alter hydraulic conditions. This assumption could introduce inaccuracies, particularly in coastal rivers.
supporting_quote: slope wastreated as a temporally constant parameter.
in regions with minimal elevation change, such as coastal rivers, the water surface slope is a critical factor influencing flow velocity.
The assumption of a time‐constant slope in such settings could introduce inaccuracies in flood modeling

chunks.text: HYDRoSWOT width measurements were considered less reliable than depth because transects may not cover the full cross-section or be perpendicular to flow, potentially affecting hydraulic radius estimates when using geometry-based calculations. The study primarily uses maximum depth under a rectangular assumption, and only uses trapezoidal geometry as a robustness check. This measurement limitation motivates caution when interpreting geometry-dependent quantities.
supporting_quote: we found that the width value in HYDRoSWOT is deemed less reliable than depth as the surveys may not cover the entire cross section
we found max‐Q width to be sometimes smaller than that min‐Q width, an issue which never occurred with depth.
As mentioned earlier, we deemed the width measurements to be less reliable than those of depth, and thus mainly used the rectangular assumption.

chunks.text: The Muskingum–Cunge routing demonstration has limitations because its kinematic-wave approach does not represent slope dynamics or the feedback between roughness, velocity reduction, and increased water levels. The paper notes that diffusion or dynamic wave models can adjust water surface slope, whereas MC may overestimate the impacts of roughness errors. Thus, the case study is positioned as qualitative rather than definitive for all hydraulics contexts.
supporting_quote: the MC model's exclusion of slope dynamics overlooks the feedback loop between channel roughness and flow velocity

Unlike models that adjust for water surface slope, such as diffusion or dynamic wave models, the MC model's kinematic approach could potentially overestimate the impacts of roughness errors on flow simulations.

chunks.text: The paper notes that noise in mapped n values may be partly due to non-uniform flow conditions (e.g., coastal zones and reservoirs) where Manning’s uniform-flow assumption does not apply. This can contribute to apparent high n values and variability in some regions, complicating geographic interpretation. The authors suggest some observed anomalies may reflect these violated assumptions rather than true roughness differences.
supporting_quote: the noise in n values could partially be due to non‐uniform flow conditions (like in coastal zones and reservoirs) for which Manning's equation (with its assumption of uniform flow) does not apply.
we found a substantial concentration of high n values for streams on the Coastal Plains... could potentially be attributed to backwater flows

chunks.text: The study concludes that Manning’s n exhibits substantial and predictable temporal variability at continental scale, so treating it as temporally constant is conceptually flawed for many applications. Predictable time variability accounts for about 35% of total variance, large enough to materially affect modeled velocities and flood-wave timing. The authors call for the community to consider n as temporally variable and caution against using low-flow n values for flood modeling.
supporting_quote: predictable time variability explains a large fraction ( ~ 35%) of n variance compared to spatial variability (50%).
since neither theory nor data support the concept of a time‐constant n, we call for the larger community to start considering Manning's n as being temporally‐variable.
we should not use n measured under low flow conditions for flood modeling.

chunks.text: Machine learning using widely available geospatial datasets can provide accurate, practical predictions of roughness across space and time, with RF achieving NSE greater than 0.7. The findings emphasize that basin-scale integrators like discharge and drainage area are key predictors, suggesting a scalable path beyond traditional lookup tables. The resulting model is positioned as practically useful for improving flood and river-transport modeling.
supporting_quote: trained accurate random forest models to predict them
Random Forest (RF) model capable of predicting n... at high accuracy (Nash Sutcliffe model efficiency >0.7)
our study suggests that more attention needs to be paid to basin‐scale variables like discharge, catchment area, and sinuosity

chunks.text: The paper concludes that neglecting n’s discharge dependence can create large errors in flood timing and magnitude, with routing experiments showing peak lags of roughly a day or more under static roughness. Because peak roughness tends to be smaller at high flows, static calibration at one event may not generalize to other extremes. Incorporating dynamic n (or dynamic roughness parameters) is presented as a more viable near-term approach than simple equation tweaks.
supporting_quote: The flood peak using mean‐Q n values lags the one with max‐Q n values by 23 hr... and 36 hr
This dynamic effect also means that even if we calibrated n based on an observed streamflow peak, the calibrated value would not be guaranteed to perform well for other extreme scenarios.
it is unlikely that any simple modification to the equation could yield a robust universal model. Therefore, setting n as being dynamic may be a more viable approach

chunks.text: Agent-based models (ABMs) are widely used for studying complex, emergent dynamics in integrated socio-environmental systems where actors adapt and respond to context. Prior ABMs often encode behavior through theories such as bounded rationality or the theory of planned behavior, but have difficulty representing adaptive learning under uncertainty. The paper positions deep reinforcement learning as a way to model agents with memory and foresight who learn from feedbacks between human and environmental systems.
supporting_quote: Agent based models (ABMs) are particularly well-suited to model complex, emergent, scalable phenomena typically observed in integrated Socio-Environmental Systems (SESs)
One of the issues that many agent-based models (ABMs) deal with is a difficulty in simulating intelligent and adaptive agents with the ability to learn from their past failures or successes

chunks.text: Water quality is threatened by nutrient pollution from agriculture, particularly phosphorus and nitrogen, which can cause eutrophication and harmful algal blooms. Best management practices (BMPs) are commonly recommended to reduce nutrient mobility and downstream impacts, but adoption is often below needed levels. This creates a need to understand how policy, social factors such as memory, and environmental extremes interact to drive heterogeneous farmer adaptation.
supporting_quote: The health of waters across the country and around the world is compromised by excessive availability of nutrients, particularly phosphorus and nitrogen, leading to eutrophication, toxic algae blooms, and hypoxic dead zones.

Despite recommendations, BMPs are often not adopted at the needed scales to affect downstream change, leading to significant interest in understanding the policy (e.g. taxes, subsidies, regulations), social (e.g., memory and foresight of agents) and environmental (e.g., floods and droughts) drivers

chunks.text: The case study is motivated by the Missisquoi watershed in the Lake Champlain basin, where agriculture is a major contributor to phosphorus pollution and large reductions are required to meet future targets. EPA estimates suggest agriculture contributed 42% of phosphorus pollution in 2000–2010, and an 80% reduction from agriculture is recommended to meet targets by 2035. The authors note this would require BMP adoption by more than 80% of farmers, which frames their modeled adoption threshold.
supporting_quote: in the Missisquoi watershed of the Lake Champlain basin... agriculture was estimated to contribute 42 percent of the phosphorus (P) pollution between 2000–2010.

US EPA recommended an 80 percent reduction in P pollution from the agricultural sector to meet water quality targets by 2035, for which widespread adoption of BMPs by more than 80 percent of the farmers would be required.

chunks.text: The study aims to improve representation of intelligent, adaptive decision-making in ABMs by embedding deep reinforcement learning-derived behavioral rules in agents. It calibrates a deep reinforcement learning enabled ABM (DRL-ABM) to simulate 480 farmer agents and a policy agent in the Missisquoi watershed. The focus is to predict adoption of adaptation actions (BMPs) that reduce water-quality impacts under changing extreme-event conditions and policy incentives.
supporting_quote: this paper presents a novel ABM, in which intelligent agents are embedded with deep reinforcement learning derived behavioral rules.

A Deep Reinforcement Learning enabled ABM (DRL-ABM) is calibrated in this paper to simulate the behavior of 480 farmer agents engaged in joint production of food and water pollution in Missisquoi Watershed

chunks.text: The experimental goal is to test how policy incentives, environmental variability in extreme events, and agent memory affect BMP adoption, including conditions that can achieve more than 80% adoption. Simulations manipulate incentives (taxes/subsidies) set by a policy agent, frequencies of extreme events, and farmer memory of extreme events that cause damage without adaptation. The study also varies learning hyperparameters and compares homogeneous versus heterogeneous agent memory configurations.
supporting_quote: Experimental simulations manipulate incentives (taxes and subsidies)... frequencies of extreme events and the memory of farmer agents to these extreme events
We also test variations in learning related hyper-parameters for homogeneous and heterogeneous configurations of intelligent agents.

chunks.text: A central modeling problem is that ABMs often rely on fixed rules or probabilistic heuristics and struggle to represent agents that learn endogenously from experience under uncertainty. This limits the ability to capture adaptive behavior as environments and policies change over time. The paper targets this gap by integrating deep reinforcement learning to provide adaptive decision policies within an ABM setting.
supporting_quote: difficulty in simulating intelligent and adaptive agents with the ability to learn from their past failures or successes and environmental and social uncertainties

In traditional agent-based models, agents make decisions according to rule-based decision-policies or probabilistic methods. In integrating machine learning, agents instead make decisions according to an internal decision-policy function

chunks.text: The applied socio-environmental problem is insufficient adoption of agricultural BMPs needed to reduce phosphorus pollution to meet water quality targets. The Missisquoi watershed context highlights that large-scale adoption is required, yet adoption is often low. The model is used to explore combinations of policy, social memory, and environmental extremes that can induce high adoption rates.
supporting_quote: BMPs are often not adopted at the needed scales to affect downstream change
widespread adoption of BMPs by more than 80 percent of the farmers would be required. In this study, we simulate alternate policy, social and environmental drivers of farmer behaviors

chunks.text: The DRL component is based on deep double q-networks (DDQN) and incorporates improvements from the Rainbow algorithm, integrated into episodic training within ABM runtime. Each agent is equipped with active and target networks that periodically transfer weights to stabilize learning and reduce divergence. Unlike approaches that train one shared network for all agents, this model assigns each agent its own neural-network weights, increasing computational intensity but enabling finer-grained causal analysis of state-action relations.
supporting_quote: we apply deep double q-networks (DDQN) algorithm [1], a type of q-learning [13], to model the DRL component of DRL-ABM.
each agent has its own set of weights for a neural network architecture... significantly more computationally intensive modeling effort

chunks.text: Agent networks are organized as paired actor-critic architectures with an active pair for acting/learning and a target pair for more stable evaluation. The actor network selects actions from states, and the critic estimates the value of taking those actions; the actor is trained to maximize critic value while the critic minimizes prediction error. Target weights are updated periodically toward active weights to prevent overfitting and divergence.
supporting_quote: each agent has two paired actor-critic neural network architectures — one pair, which is used for 'active' learning, and a 'target' pair which is used for passive learning.
The target pair is updated periodically with the weights of the active pair... to prevent the networks from diverging during training.

chunks.text: Action selection uses an epsilon-greedy exploration strategy. With probability 1-ε the agent executes the action produced by the policy network μ(s), and with probability ε it takes a random action to encourage exploration and avoid local optima. States are vectorized inputs, and outputs encode the selected action.
supporting_quote: It performs this action with some probability 1 - \varepsilon. With probability \varepsilon, the agent will instead take a random action.
the decision-policy function is being approximated by an artificial neural network (ANN), \mu:S\to A

chunks.text: Learning updates follow q-learning with a DDQN target and experience replay. The critic network is updated using a gradient step on the TD error between Q(S_t,A_t) and Y_t^{DDQN}, while the actor updates via policy gradient using critic valuations from sampled experience batches. Target-network parameters are softly updated after episodes using a transfer rate τ.
supporting_quote: The policy evaluation network, Q, is updated using the q-learning update function (Eq. 1)... and the target Y_t^{DDQN} is calculated using the double q-learning target function (Eq. 2).
the target weights are updated towards the main weights using the transfer learning function (Eq. 3)... \tau \ll 1

chunks.text: Agents maintain a finite memory buffer of state transitions (s_t, a_t, r_t, s_{t+1}) for experience replay. A forgetfulness factor F (0 to 1) injects increasing noise into older memories to represent imperfect recall, where F=0 yields perfect recall and F=1 yields strong forgetting of distant experiences. The memory algorithm samples minibatches, optionally perturbs records by temporal distance and F, then performs Q and actor updates.
supporting_quote: These records are stored in a memory buffer B of fixed length N. When the memory buffer is full, new records overwrite the oldest records
An agent with F=0 will have perfect recall... whereas an agent with F=1 will have perfect recall of its most recent state transition with actions taken in the distant past being completely forgotten

chunks.text: Farmer agents make annual decisions about BMP adoption and adjusting productivity across four agricultural industries (beef, dairy, corn, hay). The action space includes adopt vs not adopt BMP and increase/maintain/decrease production in each sector, selecting one action from each group per time step. Farmer state inputs include land cover areas, sector productivities, 5-year histories (profit, storm losses, BMP usage, extreme events), and information from the 5-nearest neighbors.
supporting_quote: They make annual decisions... whether they should implement an agricultural BMP

Conditions that factor in as components of a farmer agent's state... 5-year history of the farm's profitability, storm losses, and BMP usage; and similar historical information from the agent's k-nearest neighboring farmer agents.

chunks.text: A single policy agent adjusts incentive structures every five time-steps by changing taxation rate, BMP subsidy, and the phosphorus runoff threshold that triggers penalties. These actions modify the phosphorus taxation function G1 and the BMP subsidization function G2, which influence farmer net profits. The policy agent’s objective is to minimize aggregate phosphorus output and storm loss across farmers using a weighted inverse reward signal.
supporting_quote: This agent acts more slowly than the farmer agents, once every five time-steps, and decides if/how it should modify its incentive structure — changing its taxation rate, the subsidization given to an agent for adopting a BMP, and the phosphorus runoff threshold
The goal of the policy agent is to minimize the aggregate phosphorous output and storm loss of all farmer agents

chunks.text: Farmer production is computed through calibrated production functions for corn, hay, dairy, and beef over years 2001–2040, with a BMP-dependent exponent b affecting effective land/productivity. If BMP is adopted, b=0.6; otherwise b=1.1, representing reduced workable land or productivity under BMPs. Extreme-event damages scale outcomes via S(B,EE), where exceeding expected events reduces productivity, with mitigation depending on BMP efficacy parameter B_e.
supporting_quote: calibrated for the years 2001-2040. These functions are shown below for the production of corn (Eq. 4)...
If the BMP has been adopted, the factor b is 0.6; otherwise, b is 1.1.
S(B, EE) = 0.1, E \ge N, \neg B ... S(B, EE) = (0.1 + 0.9B_e), E \ge N \ B

chunks.text: The modeled system represents the Missisquoi Bay area in the Lake Champlain Basin and instantiates 480 farmer agents corresponding to 480 agriculturally-zoned land parcels. The spatial layout is used to define neighborhood interactions (e.g., 5-nearest neighbors) included in agent state. The model structure thus ties agent decisions to parcel-level representation and local network context.
supporting_quote: There are two types of agents present in the DRL-ABM — 480 farmer agents, corresponding to the 480 agriculturally-zoned land parcels in the study area
historical information from their 5-nearest neighbors.

chunks.text: Farmer agent state inputs include land cover (cropland and pasture areas), sector productivity levels (corn, hay, dairy, beef), five-year histories of extreme events, finances, and BMP adoption, plus neighbor-derived financial loss and BMP usage summaries at 1-year and 5-year horizons. These elements are enumerated as grouped state components used as ANN inputs for decision-making.
supporting_quote: This subset of state factors is summarized in Table 1... information about their own land cover... the productivity... a 5-year history... and historical information from their 5-nearest neighbors.
Table 1... Land cover... Cropland... Pasture... Productivity... Corn... Hay... Dairy... Beef... History (5-year)... Network information

chunks.text: The action space for farmer agents consists of BMP adoption (adopt vs don’t adopt) and production adjustments in four sectors, each with increase/maintain/decrease options and bounded step sizes. One action from each group is selected each time step, creating a multi-dimensional decision per year that jointly influences profitability and pollution outcomes.
supporting_quote: The actions that the farmer agents can take are listed in Table 2... Adopt BMP... Don’t adopt BMP
One action from each group is selected during each time step

chunks.text: The policy agent state is defined using aggregate metrics over farmer agents (BMP adoption, net profits/losses, phosphorus runoff) plus historical records including extreme events over 5-year and 15-year windows. Its action space includes increasing/decreasing tax rate, providing/removing BMP subsidy, and scaling a phosphorus threshold. These are the primary policy levers manipulated during experiments.
supporting_quote: Table 3... Aggregate data... BMP adoption... Financials... Net profits/losses... P runoff
Table 4... Tax rate... Increase... Decrease... BMP subsidy... Provide/increase... Remove/decrease... Phosphorus threshold... Scale

chunks.text: Key learning hyperparameters are specified and largely held constant across experiments, including exploration rate ε=0.1, discount factor γ=0.99, transfer rate τ=0.001, replay memory size M=10000, and 1000 episodes with 40 steps per episode. Network architectures differ by agent class, with farmer μ outputting 17 nodes and policy μ outputting 5 nodes. These settings define the training regime used to obtain converged policies before testing runs.
supporting_quote: held constant were the exploration rate at \varepsilon = 0.1, the discount factor at \gamma = 0.99, the learning transfer rate at \tau = 0.001, the number of steps within a training episode at N = 40, the relay memory size at M = 10000.
Table 6... Number of episodes N 1000... Number of steps per episode T 40
Table 5... Output nodes... Agricultural \mu ... 17... Regulatory \mu ... 5

chunks.text: Experiments vary BMP efficacy B_e from 0 to 1 (step 0.1), change in extreme-event frequency ΔEE from -0.2 to 0.2 (step 0.05), regulation change limiter g in {0, 0.05, 0.2}, and memory/forgetfulness factors. Uniform memory runs vary F in {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1}, while mixed-memory runs vary population mixing P in {0.25, 0.5, 0.75}. These parameters define scenario grids for testing adoption outcomes.
supporting_quote: BMP efficacy (B_e) was varied from 0 to 1 in increments of 0.1.
Change in weather event frequency (\Delta EE) was varied from -0.2 to 0.2 in increments of 0.05.
Three values were tested: ... g = 0.2... g = 0.05... g = 0
Forgetfulness Factor F : 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1 ... Population mixing P : 0.25, 0.5, 0.75

chunks.text: Training generally produced stable policies across configurations: agents were trained for 1000 episodes and runs were screened for convergence, discarding and retraining when more than 10% of agents failed to converge. This failure criterion was triggered in fewer than 2% of model runs. Convergence was defined by small net change in target-network weights after an initial 50 episodes, using a threshold ε=1e-5.
supporting_quote: agents were trained for 1000 training episodes. If more than 10% of the agents (n=48) failed to converge... the model was discarded and retrained; however, this occurred in less than 2% of model runs.
considered to have converged if... the net change in the weights... was less than \varepsilon=1e-5

chunks.text: BMP adoption above the 80% benchmark is difficult without active policy adjustment. In the absence of policy action (g=0), adoption reaches close to 80% in only one scenario: extreme-event frequency increased by 20%, BMP efficacy at its highest, and agents having perfect memory. This highlights that environmental pressure plus highly effective BMPs and strong memory can drive adoption even without policy changes, but only in a narrow configuration.
supporting_quote: in the absence of a policy action (g=0), BMP adoption rate goes close to 80 percent in only one scenario configuration
When extreme precipitation event frequency increases by 20 percent, BMP efficacy is highest, and agents have perfect memory (F=0).

chunks.text: Policy adaptability increases the likelihood of achieving high BMP adoption. The likelihood of adoption above 80% increases when the policy agent’s action is moderate to aggressive, compared with static policy settings. However, the results emphasize that policy action alone is not sufficient if BMP efficacy is low.
supporting_quote: The likelihood of BMP adoption rate above 80 percent increases when policy agent action is moderate to aggressive
However, higher BMP efficacy always appears to be a critical condition for attaining 80 percent or higher BMP adoption rate.

chunks.text: BMP efficacy is consistently a key determinant of reaching very high adoption levels. Across scenarios, attaining 80% or higher adoption depends critically on high B_e values. This implies that even well-designed incentives or increased extreme events may not lead to widespread adoption if the modeled BMPs do not meaningfully reduce nutrient loading and/or damages.
supporting_quote: higher BMP efficacy always appears to be a critical condition for attaining 80 percent or higher BMP adoption rate.
BMP efficacy (B_e)... represents the effectiveness of a BMP in reducing nutrient loading from agricultural fields.

chunks.text: Memory loss reduces the chance of widespread adoption. As the forgetfulness factor increases (interpreted as more memory loss of distant extreme events), the likelihood of achieving 80% or higher BMP adoption declines substantially. This indicates that the persistence of past extreme-event experience in agent learning is important for sustained adaptation behavior.
supporting_quote: as we increase the Forgetfulness factor (i.e. more memory loss of distant extreme events), the likelihood of attaining 80 percent or higher BMP adoption rate reduces significantly
Forgetfulness factor, F... An agent with F=1 will have perfect recall of its most recent state transition with actions taken in the distant past being completely forgotten

chunks.text: Introducing heterogeneous memory across the population makes achieving the 80% adoption target harder under minimal policy action. When the model shifts from homogeneous memory to mixed populations of agents with perfect and imperfect memories, the likelihood of attaining 80% BMP adoption becomes 0% under minimal policy action. This suggests that population heterogeneity in recall can suppress collective adoption dynamics unless policy is strengthened.
supporting_quote: when we replace homogeneous memory populations of agents to heterogeneous memory populations... the likelihood of attaining 80 percent BMP adoption rate is 0 percent under minimal policy action.
In heterogeneous agent populations... a proportion of agents (P) had accuracy F = 1 and all other agents (1 - P) had accuracy F = 0.

chunks.text: The model simplifies real decision-making by restricting farmer and policy agent action spaces. Wider action spaces were considered, but the authors reduced scope because maintaining clear causal relationships between actions and outcomes became difficult. This limitation implies that results speak to a constrained set of decisions rather than the full complexity of real farming and policymaking.
supporting_quote: Farmers in this model have a fairly limited set of decisions that they are capable of making, and the policy agent is even more limited compared to real-world policymakers.
wider action spaces... were considered; however, the causal relationships between agents and their actions became increasingly difficult to maintain

chunks.text: Stochasticity and neural-network randomness make outcomes sensitive to pseudo-random seeds, initialization, and early experiences. The study addresses this by running the model many times per configuration and using long episodic training, but acknowledges these steps cannot fully remove bias. This affects reproducibility and necessitates interpreting results as distributions rather than single-run outcomes.
supporting_quote: the stochastic nature of many model components and artificial neural networks in particular make the model sensitive to the state of a machine's pseudo-random number generation.
each agent's artificial neural networks are biased by their random initialization and early experience... however, it cannot be entirely removed.

chunks.text: The authors caution that an optimized neural-network policy is not evidence of real-world realism or human rationale. The learned strategies are those that optimize rewards within the modeled problem space and input data, and may not correspond to what actual humans would do. Therefore, the DRL-ABM can suggest possible strategies and likelihoods but cannot predict specific human decisions with certainty.
supporting_quote: that a network is able to optimize a problem space... is not necessarily proof that the solution has a real-world analog
it cannot say with absolute certainty what specific human agents would do under similar circumstance.

chunks.text: The discussion interprets mixed-memory results as implying that real populations’ heterogeneous memory may require stronger policy action and better BMP technology to achieve both food and water security under increasing extremes. It also suggests that social action to reinforce memory of changing extreme-event frequencies could improve adaptation. These implications connect the modeled mechanisms (policy aggressiveness, BMP efficacy, memory) to potential interventions.
supporting_quote: Since human populations tend to have a mixture of perfect and imperfect memories, our findings imply that aggressive policy action... coupled with efforts... to identify most efficacious BMPs
Social action to reinforce the memory of changing frequencies of extreme events could also improve the likelihood of effective adaptation actions.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that integrating deep reinforcement learning with ABMs provides a new approach for modeling adaptive human decision-making in complex socio-environmental systems. Applied to the Missisquoi Bay farmer-policy setting, the DRL-ABM can explore how regulatory designs and environmental variability shape adaptation decisions. The authors emphasize that while the method may better capture decision processes, its computational intensity and technical complexity require careful design and parameterization.
supporting_quote: we discuss the implementation of the DRL-ABM, an agentbased model that incorporates classical agent-based modeling methodology with deep reinforcement machine learning
Results indicate that this technique could be used to model human decision-makers... however, its technical complexity and computational intensity demand that the design of such models is intentional

chunks.text: The work positions DRL-ABM as generalizable beyond the case study and argues it can support future applications to other integrated socio-environmental systems. The authors suggest these extensions could improve integration of AI/machine learning with intelligent systems to address sustainability challenges. This frames the contribution as methodological and transferable rather than purely case-specific.
supporting_quote: Extended applications of DRL-ABM in other integrated socioenvironmental systems can be tested in future research
improve the integration of AI/machine learning with Intelligent Systems and address pressing socio-environmental sustainability challenges.

chunks.text: The paper situates HELPING in the context of the Anthropocene, where climate change, consumption, and population growth are pushing Earth systems beyond safe boundaries. Water-cycle impacts are central to this crisis, expressed as shortages, floods, and pollution, with highly uneven consequences across regions and social groups. The authors argue hydrological sciences must adapt its procedures and scope to remain relevant to accelerating global change and emerging tipping risks.
supporting_quote: The Earth is facing severe problems caused by climate change, global consumption, and population growth that are pushing the Earth system out of safe and just boundaries
freshwater supply often varies between being too much, too little or too polluted for sustainable development

chunks.text: HELPING is presented as the third IAHS scientific decade, building on a trilogy of prior community-wide initiatives: PUB (2003–2012) and Panta Rhei (2013–2022). The authors frame the decades as a succession: first addressing prediction under data scarcity, then change and human–water coevolution, and now solution-oriented science. This continuity is used to justify a broad yet coordinated global agenda for hydrological research.
supporting_quote: Predictions in Ungauged Basins (PUB): 2003–2012
Change in hydrology and society – Everything Flows (Panta Rhei): 2013–2022
We capitalise on previous IAHS Scientific Decades shaping a trilogy; from Hydrological Predictions (PUB) to Change and Interdisciplinarity (Panta Rhei) to Solutions (HELPING).

chunks.text: IAHS is positioned as a global facilitator rather than a funder, providing long-term infrastructure for networking, synthesis, and publication across a large membership base. The association’s scale (10,000+ members in 150 countries) is argued to be suitable for linking local hydrological work to global patterns and policy processes. This platform role is central to HELPING’s ambition to coordinate bottom-up, locally grounded solution science.
supporting_quote: As a global organization with more than 10 000 individual members from 150 countries
IAHS supports hydrology and related sciences as a nonprofit, nongovernmental charity, in the form of networking; hence, it is not a conference, research council or a donor.

chunks.text: The decade’s overarching research goal is to integrate understanding of hydrological diversity across scales and regions, connecting local processes to global patterns. The paper emphasizes that solutions must be actionable and context-aware, requiring synthesis and transferability of knowledge. The authors frame the goal as advancing hydrology into decision support that can serve multiple societal sectors and support sustainable development beyond SDG 6.
supporting_quote: The overarching goal for the Science for Solutions decade HELPING was set as: "Understanding hydrological diversity and integrating knowledge across scales and regions."
provide science-based watercentric decision support

chunks.text: Theme 1 aims to accelerate understanding of interactions between local and global hydrological processes and their effects on water resources in context. The paper highlights example questions on morphology–hydrodynamics links, thresholds and feedbacks that may trigger transitions and tipping points, and surface–groundwater interactions across regions. Expected products include case studies for the Digital Water Globe, large-sample datasets, and methods linking global estimates to local conditions.
supporting_quote: This first theme of the HELPING decadal initiative aims to accelerate hydrological understanding of hydrological processes at local and global scales, how they interact
What is the influence of local morphology on hydrodynamics?
Which local thresholds and feedback mechanisms trigger global transitions and tipping points?
Case studies populating the Digital Water Globe platform

chunks.text: Theme 2 targets holistic solutions for water security, focusing on managing current crises and mitigating future ones. The paper prioritizes evaluating solution impacts (including nature-based solutions), developing criteria for selecting measures with high success rates, and ensuring inclusiveness via co-creation with stakeholders. The planned outputs include a catalogue of solutions and effects, assessment guidelines, and a dedicated catalogue of nature-based solutions with guidelines.
supporting_quote: Embarking on the second theme within the HELPING decadal initiative, our aim is to effectively manage existing water crises and proactively mitigate potential future challenges.
Catalogue of solutions and potential effects
Catalogue of NBS and their guidelines

chunks.text: Theme 3 establishes cross-cutting facilities to support co-creation, adoption, and equitable implementation of solutions in local societal contexts. It emphasizes selecting appropriate co-creation methods, understanding how scientific engagement can change attitudes and actions, and rigorously integrating Indigenous knowledge with evidence-based analysis. The intended products include open data repositories, a catalogue of local associations and co-creation training, and a database of examples merging practical/Indigenous knowledge with science.
supporting_quote: The third theme revolves around cross-cutting objectives, aiming to enhance capacity within local societies
Methods and training in co-creation activities
Database of good examples merging practical/Indigenous knowledge with evidence-based science

chunks.text: The paper identifies a global water crisis with manifestations of scarcity, excess, and pollution that undermine sustainable development. These impacts are accelerating due to global change and can push systems toward irreversible tipping points. The authors argue this creates an urgent need for hydrological engagement and coordinated action to address multidimensional water security issues.
supporting_quote: freshwater supply often varies between being too much, too little or too polluted for sustainable development
may soon put the planet into an emergency state caused by passing irreversible tipping points

chunks.text: Hydrological knowledge and infrastructure are described as fragmented and declining in key areas, limiting effective decision support. The authors point to problems with data and information that are not open or FAIR, inconsistencies in data chains, and declining in situ monitoring. They also emphasize a lack of synthesis and digestible messages across disciplines and between scientists, practitioners, decision makers, and communities.
supporting_quote: scientific knowledge on waterrelated robustness, resilience and security is fragmented; related data and information are often not Open, unFAIR, not chained and inconsistent
in situ monitoring is declining
there is a substantial lack of synthesis and of easily digestible scientific messages

chunks.text: The paper argues that water management and hydrological science must better connect local problems with global drivers and cross-sectoral needs. Heterogeneity in water issues across the planet and dispersed actors make coordination difficult. The authors call for holistic systems analysis linking scales, disciplines, and societal demands to improve water-centric decision support.

chunks.text: The authors contend hydrology is insufficiently considered in global policy frameworks, even where water is explicitly targeted. They argue that SDG 6 does not imply adequate attention to hydrological issues and that hydrology is "hardly considered" despite being essential. This mismatch motivates a decade aimed at making hydrology better recognized and integrated into SDG achievement.

chunks.text: HELPING’s scope and organization were developed through a participatory strategic planning process during the first year of the decade. The approach emphasized inclusiveness using online meetings across time zones, open forum discussions, and in-person workshops. The process is described as three steps moving from visions and topics, to goals and strategies, to launching working groups and implementation mechanisms.

chunks.text: Step 1 gathered candidate topics via a web forum (late 2022) and interactive meetings in three time zones, followed by an in-person Córdoba workshop. Participants brainstormed around tables, consolidated ideas, and used a SWOT approach to analyze candidate themes. The group agreed the decade focus should be "Science for Solutions," and a member-wide questionnaire then helped prioritize topics and support methods.

chunks.text: Step 2 reopened the forum for feedback on the concept note and held additional meetings (EGU splinters and a Vienna workshop) to define goals and strategies. chunks.text: The paper concludes that the global water crisis is central to security and human rights, and that the hydrological community is motivated to reverse current trends. HELPING is proposed as a decade focused on science for solutions via co-creation with disciplines and stakeholders to produce actionable knowledge across scales and contexts. The authors emphasize three focal directions: global–local interactions, holistic solutions including nature-based measures and nexus analysis, and methods for Indigenous knowledge, citizen science, and communication.
supporting_quote: Water-related issues are at the heart of the emergence and acceleration of the Anthropocene, and so strongly underlie security and human rights dimensions.
a new scientific decade was therefore suggested to focus on science for solutions to the water crisis, using co-creation processes
IAHS encourages the hydrological community to focus on: (1) global and local interactions
(2) holistic solutions to the water crisis
(3) development of methods that appreciate Indigenous and local people's knowledge, citizen science, engagement and communication

chunks.text: The authors assert that IAHS enables the decade by providing coordination mechanisms, communication, and platforms that support inclusive community-based efforts. They emphasize that the decade presumes open science and co-creation, aligns with UN and intergovernmental agendas, and seeks empowerment through capacity development and open access to data and information. The closing message is that collective action across the community can make the decade successful.
supporting_quote: IAHS enables these community-based efforts by providing support and facilitation.

As such, the new decade is well aligned with other global agendas, within the UN and with international policymakers

chunks.text: Flood inundation maps (FIMs) at national scale are needed to extend National Water Model (NWM) reach-scale discharges to high-resolution flood extents, but full 2D hydrodynamic modeling at continental scale is too expensive operationally. Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) provides a terrain-normalized relative elevation framework that can be coupled with synthetic rating curves (SRCs) to map inundation from stages. Prior work has demonstrated the viability of HAND+SRC for large-scale mapping, motivating its use in operational pipelines like OWP FIM.
supporting_quote: The need for high resolution FIM at 10 m or better requires additional post-processing from the principal output of the NWM which is forecast river discharges at the reach scale. The use of a 2-dimensional (2D) hydrodynamic model across a continental-scale and high spatial resolutions is very cost prohibitive

The Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) terrain model is one such technique that can be used, along with synthetic rating curves (SRC), to convert 1-dimensional (1D) riverine discharges to stages, and finally to inundation extents.

chunks.text: OWP Flood Inundation Mapping (OWP FIM) is an operational pipeline that builds a HAND-based FIM hydrofabric (HAND grid, catchments, SRCs, and crosswalks) and can generate inundation maps rapidly at HUC8 processing units. The system relies on extensive hydro-conditioning to enforce drainage, flowpaths, and monotonic thalweg elevations so that HAND assumptions hold. It packages open-source tools into a reproducible workflow and supports large domains including Hawaii and Puerto Rico.
