supporting_quote: OWP FIM is a fully operational pipeline of software tools to help acquire datasets, cache hydrofabrics, produce FIMs, and evaluate results.
The standard processing unit of OWP FIM is a HUC8
An enhancement of OWP FIM over previous HAND based FIM versions is the support for Hawaii and Puerto Rico

chunks.text: The NWM forecasts discharges at millions of points across several forecast horizons and uses NHDPlus-derived hydrofabric. A smaller Mainstems (MS) network is defined as reaches at or downstream of AHPS forecast points and is used for special assimilation operations. This MS subset is roughly 4.4% of reaches, motivating targeted approaches for key rivers while maintaining full-resolution coverage elsewhere.
supporting_quote: The NWM forecasts river discharges at more than 2.7 million forecast points
The river network upon which this special assimilation technique operates on is herein referred to as the Mainstem (MS) stream network.
The MS network contains roughly 120 thousand forecasting points or roughly 4.4% of the reaches of the FR stream network.

chunks.text: The study aims to mitigate HAND’s nearest-flowpath constraint in flood inundation mapping by enabling inundation sourced from multiple fluvial sources. The authors propose reducing HAND computation units to stream segments of effective unit Horton–Strahler order (level paths), computing HAND independently, and mosaicing the resulting inundation maps. They evaluate whether this stream-order reduction reduces false negatives at confluences and improves overall inundation skill against benchmarks.
supporting_quote: HAND is limited to producing inundation only when sourced from its nearest flowpath, thus lacks the ability to source inundation from multiple fluvial sources.
We seek to resolve this catchment boundary problem or nearest drainage limitation by discretizing the target stream network into stream networks of reduced, unit stream order
Here we demonstrate how reducing a HAND processing unit's stream network into discrete LPs of singular, effective stream order, can enhance FIM skill

chunks.text: A secondary goal is to implement the proposed multi-source extension within an open-source OWP FIM framework that incorporates updated hydro-conditioning and supports large-scale processing. The work frames MS and GMS as progressive degrees of stream-order reduction (4%–5% to 100% of the network). The evaluation seeks to quantify how much performance gain is achieved and whether improvements exhibit diminishing returns relative to computational expense.
supporting_quote: We present two successive methods, National Weather Service MS (Section 2.5.1) and Generalized Mainstems (GMS) (Section 2.5.2)

We observe that the improvement of this method applied at 4%–5% of the entire stream network to 100% of the network is about the same magnitude improvement as going from no drainage order reduction to 4%–5% of the network.

chunks.text: HAND-based flood inundation maps are constrained by the “nearest drainage” rule: inundation for a pixel is sourced only from its nearest flowpath and limited to its catchment. At confluences where a high-flow mainstem meets lower-flow tributaries, this causes underprediction and visible false negatives because mainstem water cannot spill into adjacent tributary catchments. This issue is known operationally as the “catchment boundary problem.”
supporting_quote: HAND assumes only fluvial inundation sourced from its nearest flowpath is accounted for

At the junction of high stream order and high flow rivers with lower flow tributaries, there can be a lack of inundation extents exhibited which is known colloquially in the forecasting community as the "catchment boundary problem."
the discharge along the main segment ... of 1,900 cubic meters per second (cumecs) does not translate to the lower flow rates along the tributaries

chunks.text: The nearest-drainage limitation interacts with routing that does not represent backwater dynamics, worsening errors near junctions. In such cases, a large discharge on the mainstem cannot extend beyond its catchment boundary and can instead “pool” along boundaries, distorting flood extents and the implicit behavior of rating curves. These limitations can lead to both missed inundation at junctions and unrealistic spatial patterns of flooding.
supporting_quote: model but fails to consider backwater dynamics
the flow of 1,900 cumecs from the main segment cannot extend to the neighboring catchments belonging to its tributaries
Water pools up vertically along the catchment boundaries of the higher order segment distorting rating curve behavior

chunks.text: The Generalized Mainstems (GMS) method discretizes the NWM full-resolution network into level paths (LPs), each representing a unit Horton–Strahler stream order. LPs are assigned by computing arbolate sums and propagating an LP identifier upstream from the HUC8 outlet, choosing the branch with maximum arbolate sum at each confluence. HAND, catchments, crosswalks, and SRCs are computed independently for each LP, and LP-level inundation maps are mosaiced into a single FIM.
supporting_quote: A version of HAND, known as Generalized Mainstems (GMS), is proposed that discretizes a target stream network into segments of unit Horton-Strahler stream order known as level paths (LPs).
we first compute arbolate sums which are defined as the cumulative drainage distance of all upstream flowpaths.
At every confluence, the direction of maximum arbolate sum is sought to propagate the current LP identifier.

chunks.text: The NWS Mainstems (MS) method applies stream-order reduction only to the subset of the network at or downstream of AHPS forecast points. HAND is derived on both the full-resolution (FR) and the MS network, and inundation is computed independently from each hydrofabric. The MS FIM is then formed by mosaicing the FR and MS inundation maps to better represent high-impact mainstem flooding while retaining FR coverage elsewhere.
supporting_quote: The Mainstems (MS) network is a subset of the NWM FR network at and downstream of AHPS forecast points
The MS network comprises about 200 thousand km of stream length which is less than 4% of the FR total stream length
we derive HAND using the FR stream network as well as the MS network

chunks.text: For mosaicing multiple inundation sources (MS or GMS), the study aggregates LP- or network-specific water depth rasters by taking the maximum depth at each pixel. This is intended to represent areas with multiple possible fluvial sources by retaining the dominant inundation depth. Binary extents are mosaiced similarly by taking the maximum of inundation indicators across contributing sources.
supporting_quote: For mosaicing the depths, we select the maximum inundation depth from the all the contributing areas
D_{ij} = \max_{k=[1,\dots,K]} D_{ijk}
Equation (5) illustrates the same process but for mosaicing the binary inundation maps, F_{ij} = \max_{k=[1,\dots,K]} F_{ijk}

chunks.text: Synthetic rating curves (SRCs) are generated using a reach-averaged Manning relationship, sampling volume and wetted bed area from DEM-derived geometry across discrete stages. The study computes discharge values for 84 stage depths from 0 to 25 m in one-third meter increments. Manning’s n is tested at 0.06 and 0.12 to assess sensitivity of HAND-based inundation to roughness assumptions.
supporting_quote: the reach averaged Manning's formula is derived as Q(y) = \frac{1}{n} \frac{V(y)^{5/3} S^{1/2}}{LB(y)^{2/3}}
We constrain the equation by selecting 84 stage values ... from 0 to 25 m in depth at a third of a meter increments
we examine the SRCs with Manning's n set to both 0.06 and 0.12

chunks.text: The workflow derives DEM-based flowpaths and reach segmentation to support HAND and SRC computation. Stream links are split into equidistant reaches not exceeding 1.5 km, with additional breaks at lakes and HUC8 boundaries. Catchments are delineated using D8 flow directions, with pixel-level catchments used for HAND computation and reach-level catchments used for mapping stages and inundation.
supporting_quote: Each stream link in this derived FIM stream network is split into equidistant reaches of 1.5 km in length
Catchments were derived using the D8 connectivity established by O'Callaghan and Mark (1984).
Two sets of catchments are derived, one set ... for each thalweg pixel ... The other catchments are derived for the drainage region for each stream reach

chunks.text: OWP FIM applies a sequence of hydro-conditioning steps to make DEMs suitable for HAND, including stream network enforcement, levee enforcement, depression filling, and thalweg elevation conditioning. Depression filling uses a Priority-Flood variant, and thalweg conditioning includes a zonal minimum approach and a breaching procedure to enforce monotonically decreasing thalweg elevations. HAND is computed using thalweg-conditioned elevations while retaining native elevations outside excavated channels, with negative relative elevations set to zero.
supporting_quote: The DEM is subject to a series of hydro-conditioning procedures
The depression filling algorithm used in our pipeline is a Priority-Flood variant developed by Zhou et al. (2016)
We found it more fitting to use the native elevations this final HAND computation thus avoid the use of manipulated values

chunks.text: Model performance is evaluated against FEMA Region 6 Base Level Engineering (BLE) HEC-RAS 1D inundation extents using CSI, POD, and FAR. To avoid hydro-climatic uncertainty from NWM forecasts, HEC-RAS recurrence discharges are spatially intersected with NWM reaches and assigned using the median value when multiple cross-sections intersect a reach. Metrics are computed per HUC8 and also recomputed after aggregating TP/FP/FN across the domain.
supporting_quote: evaluation ... was conducted by comparison to the HEC-RAS 1D models produced within FEMA region 6
we elected to spatially intersect the HEC-RAS cross sections with the NWM stream network assigning the 1% and 0.2% flow rates to each NWM reach.
The metrics employed in this study ... include CSI, Probability of Detection (POD), and False Alarm Ratio (FAR)

chunks.text: The study uses USGS NHDPlusHR hydrography and DEM (1/3 arc-sec, ~10 m) as core elevation and hydro-enforcement inputs, alongside NOAA OWP NWM v2.1 hydrofabric (streams, catchments, waterbodies). Additional geospatial constraints include USACE National Levee Database elevations and land/sea and land/Great Lakes borders for masking. These inputs are assembled within HUC8 processing units to build the FIM hydrofabric and support HAND computations.
supporting_quote: We utilized ... NHDPlusHR ... BurnLineEvents ... Water Boundaries (WBD) ... and the DEM elevation rasters
NWM Hydrofabric V2.1 ... used to define reservoirs for exclusion and catchments to cross-walk against
For enforcing levee data, the USACE NLD is used to burn feature elevations into DEMs

chunks.text: Validation data come from the Interagency Flood Risk Management (InFRM) Base Level Engineering (BLE) program in FEMA Region 6. BLE provides HEC-RAS 1D inundation extents and cross-sections with discharges for 1% (100-year) and 0.2% (500-year) recurrence interval events. The analysis uses 49 HUC8 watersheds spanning about 185,000 km² across nine states.
supporting_quote: Base Level Engineering (BLE) datasets within FEMA Region 6 ... at two recurrence intervals, 1% ... and 0.2%
We selected 49 available HUC8s ... which span about 185 thousand km2 across nine states.
Cross-Sections ... Includes discharges for 1% and 0.2% recurrence interval events.

chunks.text: The NWM full-resolution (FR) stream network represents the entire modeling domain, while the Mainstems (MS) network includes reaches at or downstream of AHPS forecast points. MS spans 121,724 reaches across 1,608 HUC8s and is less than 4% of FR stream length (~200,000 km vs ~5.5 million km). These network definitions drive the FR, MS, and GMS processing variants used for HAND computation.
supporting_quote: The FR network constitutes the entire NWM stream network while the MS resolution network is the FR network at or downstream of the AHPS forecast points
The MS network comprises about 200 thousand km of stream length which is less than 4% of the FR total stream length of 5.5 million km.
It also spans 121,724 reaches across 1,608 HUC8s.

chunks.text: Across 49 BLE HUC8s, inundation skill generally improves as HAND is computed on reduced stream-order units (FR → MS → GMS). Table-level aggregation shows CSI increases relative to FR: for Manning’s n=0.06, CSI improves by 2.53% (MS) and 3.95% (GMS) for 100-year flows, and 2.59% (MS) and 4.04% (GMS) for 500-year flows. Similar CSI gains occur for n=0.12, indicating consistent benefits of stream-order reduction and mosaicing.
supporting_quote: CSI generally increases from FR to MS and MS to GMS

chunks.text: Most of the performance improvement from stream-order reduction is driven by better detection of inundation (higher POD), implying reduced false negatives near confluences. Aggregated metrics show POD increases relative to FR by ~2.7% for MS and ~4.4%–4.9% for GMS across Manning’s n settings and event magnitudes. This aligns with the proposed mechanism that larger, overlapping catchments allow inundation from major rivers to extend into areas previously blocked by tributary catchment boundaries.
supporting_quote: This increase is primarily driven by an increase in POD thus generally increasing the probability of correctly detecting inundation.

chunks.text: False alarm behavior improves modestly with stream-order reduction. FAR decreases slightly from FR to MS and more for GMS in several settings, indicating a small reduction in overprediction. For example, with n=0.12 the aggregated FAR change is −2.31% (100-year) and −2.72% (500-year) for GMS, suggesting that SRC and catchment changes can also slightly reduce false positives.
supporting_quote: FAR is somewhat, albeit marginally, decreased from FR to MS and MS to GMS

chunks.text: Higher Manning’s n (0.12) produces better overall skill than n=0.06 across models and magnitudes, likely because it is closer to the BLE model’s roughness (~0.11). The improvement is mainly reflected in POD, but is accompanied by increased FAR, showing a tradeoff between detecting inundation and overpredicting. This sensitivity indicates that roughness parameterization remains an important control on HAND+SRC flood mapping performance.
supporting_quote: The higher Manning's n value enhances performance ... Most of this improvement is driven by significant increases in POD, but unfortunately, it also leads to a significant amount of over-prediction as observed by the increase in FAR.
seems to better agree with the value of 0.11 used in the BLE model
we examine the SRCs with Manning's n set to both 0.06 and 0.12

chunks.text: Larger recurrence events (500-year) tend to show better CSI, POD, and FAR than 100-year events across methods. This indicates that higher-magnitude floods may be less sensitive to bathymetry and near-channel elevation errors that dominate lower stages. The trend appears consistently in the reported distributions and aggregated domain metrics.
supporting_quote: We also observe additional trends associated with the magnitude ... with the higher flow rates exhibiting better overall CSI, POD, and FAR values than the lower, 100 years magnitude.
BLE maps are produced for two recurrence flows, 1% (100 years) and 0.2% (500 years)

chunks.text: The authors report substantial improvements in computational performance for producing HAND at full NWM resolution compared with earlier efforts. They estimate producing FR HAND at 0.13 CPU years, MS requiring an additional 0.05 CPU years (total ~0.18), and GMS increasing cost to ~1.17 CPU years. Thus, the more extensive stream-order reduction of GMS yields higher compute expense than FR/MS processing.
supporting_quote: For our work, we were able to produce HAND at the full NWM resolution in 0.13 CPU years
For the MS resolution, an additional 0.05 CPU years is required ... bringing the total to about 0.18 CPU years
GMS ... adds a significant amount of CPU time ... bringing the estimate total to about 1.17 CPU years.

chunks.text: Stream-order reduction enlarges catchments and reduces false negatives, but it also alters synthetic rating curves (SRCs). Average SRCs shift “down and to the right” from FR to MS to GMS, which the authors attribute to increased volume and bed area sampled within larger catchments that may include neighboring tributary geometry not aligned with the main flow direction. This can reduce false positives but may also introduce new false negatives due to biased stage–discharge relationships.
supporting_quote: we found some areas of slight reductions in FPs ... pointed to changes in the SRCs introduced by stream order reduction
Sub-Figure (11a) shows how the average SRCs ... tend to shift the curve down and to the right with ever increasing stream order reduction (FR to MS to GMS).
These tributaries ... contribute volume and bed area that is technically not perpendicular to the flux of streamflow ... thus leading to biases in the SRC.

chunks.text: Benefits from stream-order reduction show diminishing returns: applying it to the MS portion (~4%–5% of the network) yields an improvement comparable to applying it to the remaining network via GMS. This motivates future work to identify an optimal spatial coverage for unit-order processing that balances accuracy gains against increased computational costs. The paper suggests that excluding very low stream orders from reduction could be one possible strategy.
supporting_quote: reducing stream order does suffer from diminishing returns where the increase in mapping skill for applying stream order reduction to roughly 4%–5% of the stream network is about the same as the increase for applying stream order reduction to the remaining 95%–96% of the stream network.
One option could be removing lower stream orders (e.g., 1 and 2) from stream order reduction and simply using the inundation from FR from these areas.

chunks.text: Cross-walking between multiple stream networks introduces evaluation and mapping errors. The study conflates a DEM-derived FIM network to NWM identifiers and separately intersects BLE cross-sections with NWM reaches, which can create mass conservation issues and misassignment of discharges. Additionally, BLE flowpaths are denser than NWM, producing unavoidable false negatives where headwater inundation exists in BLE but no corresponding NWM reach exists.
supporting_quote: the methods that intersect HEC-RAS cross-sections with NWM reaches could introduce errors that violate mass conservation.
the BLE network is denser than that of the NWM which leads to FNs due to headwater streams that are present in the BLE but not within the NWM.
While these conflation methods are approximate, they can lead to some substantial errors

chunks.text: The approach inherits limitations from DEM resolution and bathymetry representation. The 10 m DEM lacks true channel bathymetry, affecting geometric parameters used in SRCs, and performance differences between 100-year and 500-year events may reflect this sensitivity. The authors note that AGREE conditioning introduces artificial geometry parameters that can affect SRC quality, and suggest higher-resolution lidar and improved bathymetric data assimilation as future improvements.
supporting_quote: The bathymetry of the 10 m DEM from 3DEP is known as lacking proper representation thus leading to inadequate representation of volume and bed area
We suspect that a significant amount of the difference in performance between 100 and 500 years magnitude events can be attributed to poor SRC performance due to poor bathymetric representation.
While the AGREE DEM procedure is meant to add some bathymetry ... it does introduce three parameters that have major implications in the quality of SRCs

chunks.text: HAND requires that the entire processing area drains to the stream network and that elevations decrease monotonically to a single outlet, so significant DEM manipulation is often needed. These enforced assumptions can introduce errors because real terrain and flood dynamics do not strictly follow drainage patterns. The authors suggest that more advanced 2D hydrodynamic models would better address this but are costly at large scales and high resolution.
supporting_quote: To derive HAND and create a FIM for a given area, that area must entirely drain to the stream network and the stream network must also drain itself.
Enforcing this assumption for HAND leads to significant amount of DEM manipulations that introduce basic errors.
Ultimately, the use of more advanced 2D hydrodynamic models should be considered ... but would come at significant expense

chunks.text: The paper concludes that HAND-based flood inundation mapping is fundamentally limited by its nearest-flowpath assumption, which prevents inundation from being sourced by multiple nearby rivers. Reducing effective stream order for HAND computation—via MS on the NWM mainstems subset and via GMS using level paths across the full network—reduces false negatives at major junctions and improves overall mapping skill. The improved FIMs are produced by mosaicing independently computed inundation maps from these unit-order processing units.
supporting_quote: The main contribution and conclusion of this work centers around a fundamental limitation in HAND based FIM which is a failure to account for multiple possible sources of fluvial inundation since HAND only considers inundation from the nearest flowpath.
We illustrate that reducing the Horton-Strahler stream order of a HAND processing unit down to one enhances skill by significantly reducing false negatives at junctions of major streams.
The Generalized Mainstem (GMS) technique discretizes the NWM FR network into level paths (LP) of unit stream order for HAND computation.

chunks.text: The study finds that extending stream-order reduction from MS coverage (~4%–5% of the network) to GMS coverage (100%) yields similar-magnitude additional improvements, implying diminishing returns. This supports the idea that targeting the most influential parts of the network may capture much of the benefit while controlling computational costs. GMS still increases computational expense substantially compared to FR/MS processing.
supporting_quote: we conclude that deriving HAND with independent stream networks of unit Horton-Strahler stream order enhances the skill of FIM but offers diminishing returns

the increase in mapping skill for applying stream order reduction to roughly 4%–5% of the stream network is about the same as the increase for applying stream order reduction to the remaining 95%–96% of the stream network.
GMS ... adds a significant amount of CPU time to the process bringing the estimate total to about 1.17 CPU years.

chunks.text: A noted side effect of stream-order reduction is a shift in stage–discharge behavior due to changes in reach-averaged geometry (volume and bed area) when catchments become larger and overlap. This shift can reduce false positives but highlights sensitivity to SRC assumptions, Manning’s n, and bathymetry limitations. The paper leaves improved roughness localization and bathymetry integration as key future research directions to further enhance HAND-based inundation mapping.
supporting_quote: This primary contribution also affects the parameters used to compute stage-discharge relationships shifting discharge higher at given stages which reduced the rate of false positives.
We leave questions related to Manning's n localization as well as bathymetry integration, estimation, and/or calibration open for future research to answer.
Manning's n ... could be tuned to account for these DEM limitations

chunks.text: Seasonal streamflow forecasts support major water decisions such as water supply management, hydropower operations, and irrigation scheduling, and they can aid early warning for floods and droughts. In cold headwater basins of North America, seasonal predictability depends strongly on initial hydrologic conditions, especially snowpack and soil moisture. Snowmelt acts as a natural reservoir (“water towers”) that releases water downstream during spring and early summer, making snow observations central to seasonal forecasting in many regions.
supporting_quote: Seasonal streamflow forecasts provide key information for decision-making in fields such as water supply management, hydropower generation, and irrigation scheduling.
The predictability of streamflow on seasonal timescales relies heavily on initial hydrological conditions, such as the presence of snow and the availability of soil moisture.

chunks.text: A range of seasonal forecasting methods exist (process-based, data-driven, and hybrid), and the paper emphasizes the value of relatively simple, regression-based approaches. Principal component regression (PCR) is highlighted as established in water supply forecasting and attractive due to speed, low compute cost, interpretability, and local applicability. The authors argue that more methodological complexity does not necessarily improve forecasts, motivating a simple benchmark workflow as a platform for reproducible development.
supporting_quote: a wide range of approaches now exists for streamflow forecasting on seasonal timescales, including process-based, data-driven, and hybrid models
Simple statistical regression methods such as PCR offer several key advantages, including their local applicability, intuitive nature ... speed, and low computational resource requirements.

chunks.text: Snow-driven water supply is threatened by climate change, which may alter snow accumulation, melt timing, and thus streamflow predictability. The paper frames understanding snowmelt-derived predictability as important for managing future water resources. It also notes observed and projected decreases in snow storage and shifts toward more rainfall influence in flood regimes, implying potential future degradation of SWE-based forecast skill.
supporting_quote: This important natural water supply is however threatened by climate change.
snow extent, snow cover duration, and accumulated snowpack are virtually certain to decline in subarctic regions of North America.

chunks.text: The study presents and evaluates a reproducible, data-driven workflow for probabilistic seasonal streamflow forecasting in snow-fed basins across North America. The workflow uses SWE measurements as predictors and streamflow volume observations as predictands, producing ensemble hindcasts across many basins. The work aims to provide user-oriented evaluation insights for monitoring experts, forecasters, decision-makers, and workflow developers, and to enable broader adoption through open notebooks.
supporting_quote: This study presents and evaluates a data-driven workflow for probabilistic seasonal streamflow forecasting in snow-fed river basins across North America (Canada and the USA).
The workflow employs snow water equivalent (SWE) measurements as predictors and streamflow observations as predictands.

chunks.text: A central research question is whether SWE alone can reliably predict future streamflow volumes in nival basins across the continent. The authors explicitly pose this question and then analyze hindcasts to assess predictability over different lead times, basins, and target periods. The goal is to characterize the spectrum of predictability and identify conditions where SWE-based forecasts are most and least effective.
supporting_quote: Through the analysis of the hindcasts produced with this workflow, we address this research question: can SWE be used as a reliable predictor of future streamflow in nival river basins across North America
The analysis presented here unveils a wide spectrum of predictability

chunks.text: Using station SWE time series for continental-scale forecasting is hindered by missing values, but PCA and regression modeling require complete predictor matrices. The workflow therefore needs robust gap-filling to maximize usable years and stations. Without infilling, many basins and predictor–predictand combinations would lack sufficient overlap to train and evaluate probabilistic hindcasts.
supporting_quote: we processed the SWE data to fill gaps because the subsequent principal component analysis (PCA) does not allow missing values.
The basin must have at least 20 years of overlapping SWE and streamflow data

chunks.text: Not all basins are appropriate for SWE-based volume forecasting because snow may not dominate runoff generation and human regulation can alter streamflow relationships. The study must identify basins with a nival regime and limited regulation to ensure SWE has a plausible causal relationship to spring–summer volumes. This basin selection step is critical to avoid evaluating SWE predictors in unsuitable regimes.
supporting_quote: we subset these basins to only keep those that experience nival regimes – i.e., basins for which we can reasonably expect SWE to have substantial predictability for streamflow forecasting.
This methodology was applied to 75 basins characterized by a nival (snowmelt-driven) regime and limited regulation

chunks.text: SWE-only forecasting is expected to lose skill when future precipitation during the target period becomes a dominant driver of streamflow. This is a key predictability challenge because precipitation during the forecast window is unknown at initialization, and its influence increases later in the season or in mixed regimes. The paper frames this as a limitation to SWE-based predictability and an indicator of possible future predictability loss under warming climates.
supporting_quote: high precipitation during the target period presents challenges to forecast skill and streamflow predictability.
we expect higher hindcast quality for hindcasts with high antecedent SWE content and low precipitation during the hindcast target period

chunks.text: FROSTBYTE is implemented as five modular Jupyter Notebooks covering regime classification, streamflow preprocessing, SWE preprocessing, forecasting, and verification. Each notebook is in Python with annotated steps and visuals, supporting traceability and adaptation. The workflow is shared openly (with sample basins) to facilitate reproducible application and further development.
supporting_quote: The workflow developed is structured into five Jupyter Notebooks: (1) regime classification, (2) streamflow preprocessing, (3) SWE preprocessing, (4) forecasting, and (5) hindcast verification.
The workflow, called FROSTBYTE (Forecasting River Outlooks from Snow Timeseries: Building Yearly Targeted Ensembles), is available on GitHub

chunks.text: Basins are classified as nival using circular statistics on observed streamflow timing and regularity of peak-flow events. Three peak metrics are computed—annual maxima, peaks-over-threshold, and center of mass—and nival basins are those with mean occurrence dates between 1 March and 1 August and regularity ≥ 0.65. Only basins identified as nival by all three metrics are retained.
supporting_quote: To classify the streamflow regimes, we used circular statistics (Burn et al., 2010).
we identified nival basins as those with an average date of occurrence of peak flow events between 1 March and 1 August and a regularity above or equal to 0.65

chunks.text: Streamflow predictands are seasonal volumes formed by summing daily flows over multiple target periods ending 30 September (e.g., 1 January–30 September, 1 February–30 September, etc.). Prior to aggregation, daily streamflow gaps are filled via linear interpolation with a maximum allowable gap length of 15 days to maximize data availability. The resulting volume dataset is saved in NetCDF for each basin.
supporting_quote: We first performed gap-filling through linear interpolation of the daily streamflow data ... The maximum allowable gap length for interpolation was set to 15 d
We then computed volumes ... 1 January to 30 September, 1 February to 30 September, 1 March to 30 September, etc.

chunks.text: SWE preprocessing uses a two-stage gap-filling strategy: short gaps are filled by linear interpolation (≤15 days), and remaining gaps are filled using quantile mapping from neighboring SWE and precipitation stations. Quantile mapping constructs day-of-year CDFs using a ±7 day window and selects donor stations with the highest Spearman correlation exceeding 0.6. Filled values are flagged to distinguish estimates from original observations.
supporting_quote: we applied linear interpolation to fill gaps in the daily SWE records. The maximum allowable gap length for interpolation was set to 15 d
we utilize quantile mapping to fill the remaining gaps using data from neighboring stations
exceed a minimum correlation threshold of 0.6

chunks.text: Forecasting uses principal component regression to reduce intercorrelation among multiple SWE stations within a basin. A PCA is computed for each predictor–predictand combination and only the first principal component (PC1) is used to avoid overfitting; PC1 explains about 90% of SWE variance on average. An OLS regression is trained under leave-one-out cross-validation for each initialization date and target period.
supporting_quote: We then transform the gap-filled SWE ... into principal components (PCs) to eliminate any intercorrelation
on average the first PC explains 90 % of the total variance
We only select the first PC in order to avoid any overfitting

chunks.text: Probabilistic hindcast ensembles are generated by perturbing deterministic regression predictions using Gaussian error sampling. For each left-out year, the deterministic hindcast is computed, then 100 ensemble members are drawn from a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation equal to the RMSE of deterministic hindcasts versus observations in training. Hindcasts are produced monthly (1 January–1 September) for multiple target periods ending 30 September when at least 10 training years exist.
supporting_quote: An ensemble of 100 members is then generated ... drawing random samples from a normal (Gaussian) distribution.
a standard deviation equal to the root mean squared error (RMSE) between the deterministic hindcasts and observations during the training period.
Hindcasts are initialized on the first day of each month between 1 January and 1 September

chunks.text: Hindcast verification combines deterministic and probabilistic metrics, computed with bootstrapping (100 resamples) to quantify sampling uncertainty. Metrics include KGE″ (computed on ensemble medians), Reliability Index (RI), fair CRPSS against observed climatology, and ROC AUC for low/high tercile events. Evaluation is focused on each basin’s “period of interest,” defined from the month of Qmax to the end of the water year.
supporting_quote: all metrics are computed using bootstrapping ... We draw 100 random samples
KGE'' ... computed on the ensemble hindcast medians.
For each nival basin, the period of interest begins in the month of the basin's Qmax and extends until the end of the water year.

chunks.text: Streamflow and basin boundary data come from reference networks designed to minimize human disturbance. US basins use USGS HCDN-2009, and Canadian basins use WSC HYDAT RHBN-N. Streamflow is downloaded for 1 January 1979 to 31 December 2021 to provide multi-decadal records suitable for hindcast evaluation.
supporting_quote: For the USA, we use shapefiles and streamflow observations for basins with limited regulation from the USGS Hydro-Climatic Data Network 2009 (HCDN-2009
For Canada, we use shapefiles and streamflow observations ... from the Water Survey of Canada (WSC) HYDAT Reference Hydrometric Basin Network (RHBN) subset, called RHBN-N
We downloaded streamflow data for the period 1 January 1979 to 31 December 2021

chunks.text: SWE measurements span 1 October 1979 to 31 July 2022 and integrate multiple national and regional sources. Canada uses CanSWE (with additional Quebec MELCCFP data not shareable publicly), and the USA uses NRCS snow courses, SNOTEL (BCQC), and northeastern state agency surveys compiled in Mortimer and Vionnet (2024). All SWE data are quality-controlled, with an additional systematic procedure applied except for the already BCQC SNOTEL dataset.
supporting_quote: SWE measurements were downloaded for the period 1 October 1979 to 31 July 2022.
For Canada, measurements are from the Canadian historical Snow Water Equivalent dataset (CanSWE, Version V5
For SNOTEL, we use data from the bias-corrected and quality-controlled (BCQC) dataset
All SWE data used for this study were quality-controlled.

chunks.text: Precipitation station data are taken from the Serially Complete Dataset for North America (SCDNA, v1.1) for 1979–2018. Precipitation is not used directly as a forecast predictor; instead, it is accumulated over water years and used as a proxy to increase donor availability during SWE gap-filling. The precipitation network provides additional neighboring-station information where SWE observations are sparse.
supporting_quote: Precipitation station data were downloaded from the Serially Complete Dataset for North America (SCDNA, Version 1.1) for the period 1 January 1979 to 31 December 2018
The precipitation data are used to maximize the number of data available as predictors. They were accumulated over water years for each precipitation station to serve as proxies for SWE.

chunks.text: The analysis domain includes 75 snowmelt-driven (nival) basins across Canada and the USA with limited regulation, each containing at least one SWE station and sufficient overlap of SWE and streamflow. However, only 62 basins are evaluated in detail because 13 lacked enough overlapping predictor–predictand years to produce hindcasts for required combinations. The period analyzed for hindcasts is 1979–2021.
supporting_quote: generate ensemble hindcasts ... for 75 nival basins with limited regulation from 1979 to 2021
we quantify the range of predictability for 62 of the 75 identified nival basins
A total of 13 basins were excluded from this analysis as no hindcasts could be generated for those basins due to a limited number of overlapping predictor–predictand training data

chunks.text: Across basins, deterministic hindcast performance (KGE″) is generally higher for earlier target periods and declines for later summer–fall target periods, indicating reduced snow-driven predictability later in the year. For target periods up to 1 June–30 September, performance improves as initialization approaches the target period start (shorter lead). Later target periods like 1 August–30 September and 1–30 September show overall declining KGE″, consistent with a shift from snow to rain influence.
supporting_quote: Overall, the KGE00 is higher for the early target periods and decreases with the later target periods.
For hindcasts generated for the target periods 1 January to 30 September until 1 June to 30 September, the KGE00 increases towards the perfect value as we approach the start of the target period

chunks.text: Decomposition of KGE″ indicates that correlation and variability ratio broadly mirror overall KGE″ patterns, while variability is commonly underestimated. Hindcast medians show a slight positive bias (overestimation of observed volumes), especially for late-season initializations (1 July to 1 September). These patterns suggest that the simple PC1-only predictor setup may not fully capture interannual variability.
supporting_quote: The correlation and the variability ratio show similar patterns to the KGE00.
The variability tends to be underestimated overall.
The bias ratio is overall slightly positive, indicating that the hindcast medians overall overestimate the observed volumes.

chunks.text: Ensemble reliability is generally high, consistent with the error-sampling ensemble construction, but not perfect. Reported RI values span roughly 0.55 to 0.9 across basins, initialization dates, and target periods. Reliability decreases with later initialization dates, and the lowest reliability is associated with the late-season 1–30 September target period, where snow is less relevant.
supporting_quote: overall, hindcasts display a high RI (ranging between 0.55 and 0.9) across all river basins, initialization dates, and target periods.

We expect this effect to be more noticeable when the sample size is smaller and hypothesize that it may partially account for the decrease in hindcast reliability with the increasing initialization dates

chunks.text: Skill relative to climatology (fair CRPSS) is near the baseline for 1 January initializations, improves for initializations between 1 February and 1 June, and then becomes unskillful overall for summer–fall target periods beyond 1 June. Earlier target periods are more skillful than later ones, again pointing to diminishing SWE relevance as the season progresses. Skill varies widely across basins, with interior western basins often showing higher and longer-lasting skill than many northern and eastern basins.
supporting_quote: hindcasts are as good as the baseline when they are initialized on 1 January.
They gradually get more skillful ... between 1 February and 1 June.
Beyond 1 June, hindcasts for the summer–fall target periods exhibit no overall skill

chunks.text: Spatial patterns of fair CRPSS show that skill generally decreases with increasing lead time and that after about 3 months lead, little skill is evident for many basins. Pockets of higher skill persist across multiple lead months in western North America around the Rocky Mountains and Sierra Nevada. Some basins exhibit low to negative skill throughout, emphasizing heterogeneity in SWE-based predictability even within nival-selected basins.
supporting_quote: Overall, the fair CRPSS decreases with increasing lead time, and at a lead time of 3 or more months there is little skill evident.
Pockets of higher skill are seen across several lead months for basins situated in western North America in and around the Rocky Mountains and Sierra Nevada ranges.

chunks.text: ROC AUC analyses for high- and low-flow tercile events are similar, and in most periods of interest the highest ROC AUC occurs for 0-month lead time. ROC AUC generally decreases with increasing lead time, indicating reduced discrimination of events as forecasts are made earlier. An exception is the 1 July–30 September target period, where ROC AUC peaks around 1 May initialization (about a 2-month lead), again reflecting seasonal shifts in drivers.
supporting_quote: For most of the target periods of interest, the peak ROC AUC is obtained for hindcasts with a 0-month lead time
This is however not the case for hindcasts for 1 July to 30 September, where the ROC AUC is highest when hindcasts are initialized on average on 1 May (with a 2-month lead time).

chunks.text: Late-season snowpack holds important predictability: although peak SWE typically occurs around 1 April across North America, skillful performance can still be achieved using SWE observations up to 1 June. This indicates that persistent snowpack after peak accumulation contributes meaningfully to predicting spring and summer streamflow volumes. Elevation influences peak SWE timing, with higher-elevation stations tending to peak later.
supporting_quote: peak SWE typically occurs around 1 April across North America
high performance in streamflow forecasts can still be achieved by using SWE observations up until 1 June.
stations situated at higher elevations have later peak SWE

chunks.text: Forecast skill is linked to the balance between antecedent snowpack and precipitation during the target period. For most target periods, fair CRPSS increases as the P/SWE ratio decreases, indicating higher skill with higher SWE at initialization and/or lower target-period precipitation influence. The relationship is statistically stronger for target periods 1 March–30 September through 1 May–30 September and breaks down for the latest target periods (1 August–30 September and 1–30 September).
supporting_quote: for most target periods, the hindcast skill increases as the P /SWE ratio decreases.
There is a stronger correlation (with statistical significance) for hindcasts generated for the target periods 1 March to 30 September, 1 April to 30 September, and 1 May to 30 September
this relationship does not hold for the target periods 1 August to 30 September and 1 to 30 September

chunks.text: Streamflow regime classification may be affected by the linear interpolation used to fill daily streamflow gaps, potentially missing flow peaks in small fast-responding basins. The authors argue this risk is reduced because reference datasets are nearly complete and the regime classification uses three complementary peak metrics plus a regularity threshold. Nonetheless, interpolation choices can influence inferred peak timing and basin inclusion decisions.
supporting_quote: The streamflow linear interpolation could have impacted the regime classification, leading to missed flow peaks, especially for smaller river basins with faster response times.
the use of three metrics for peak flow event identification ... potentially mitigates some of these issues.

chunks.text: SWE gap-filling can be substantial because the workflow does not impose a total maximum allowable gap length per station. This choice was made to avoid losing predictors, but it means some stations may be heavily infilled, and linear interpolation may affect donor/target CDF construction in quantile mapping. The paper flags these as potential sources of inaccuracy and motivates future sensitivity analyses on gap-filling design choices.
supporting_quote: no threshold was set to define a total maximum allowable gap length for each station. Consequently, certain stations may have undergone substantial gap-filling
linear interpolation might have impacted the construction of CDFs for donor and target stations, possibly introducing inaccuracies into the gap-filled data.

chunks.text: Using only the first principal component as a predictor may contribute to underestimation of variability, but the paper prioritizes overfitting avoidance given short records. The authors note that even including two PCs can overfit in related settings and that stopping criteria (e.g., BIC or regularization) could be explored. This is a key modeling limitation and development pathway for improving forecast dispersion and fidelity.
supporting_quote: The variability tends to be underestimated overall. This may be a direct consequence of using only PC1 as a predictor
We only select the first PC in order to avoid any overfitting
even using only the first two PCs could lead to overfitting for many river basins

chunks.text: Leave-one-out cross-validation supports maximum data use but can degrade reliability and introduce operational inconsistency because models and PC matrices change across years and months. The paper notes that this approach may create “artificial quality” in verification and that operational practice might instead use fixed PC matrices and models for consistency. However, fixed approaches can be problematic under nonstationarity, so cross-validation strategy is a key open issue.
supporting_quote: The reliability of hindcasts is not entirely perfect, which is primarily due to the leave-one-out cross-validation approach used.
this approach might introduce inconsistency from month to month and from year to year
might introduce ... some artificial quality in the hindcast verification process

chunks.text: Precipitation used for SWE gap-filling comes from SCDNA and is accumulated over entire water years without distinguishing between solid and liquid precipitation or accounting for snowmelt onset. The paper notes these choices could weaken correlations between cumulative precipitation and SWE, affecting donor-station selection and gap-filling quality. Future work could test alternative precipitation handling and other infilling strategies.
supporting_quote: We used the SCDNA precipitation data for infilling, which do not distinguish between solid and liquid precipitation.
the precipitation was accumulated during the entire water year and did not consider the onset of snowmelt.
Both of these decisions could have led to lower correlations between the SWE and the cumulative precipitation

chunks.text: The paper delivers a reproducible, open workflow (FROSTBYTE) for probabilistic seasonal streamflow forecasting in snow-fed North American basins using SWE-based PCR and ensemble generation. It is applied to 75 nival, minimally regulated basins (1979–2021), with hindcast quality assessed using deterministic and probabilistic metrics. The workflow is designed to be modular and extensible, supporting broader cold-regions applications and community improvement.
supporting_quote: We developed a systematic and reproducible data-driven workflow for probabilistic seasonal streamflow forecasting in snow-fed river basins across North America, including Canada and the USA.

This structured workflow consists of five essential steps: (1) regime classification and basin selection, (2) streamflow preprocessing, (3) SWE preprocessing, (4) forecasting, and (5) hindcast verification.

chunks.text: Key findings emphasize that late-season snowpack after peak SWE retains predictive value, making post-peak SWE measurements important for skillful spring–summer volume forecasts. Forecast skill is higher when antecedent SWE is high and precipitation influence during the target period is low, and the method can be useful for probabilistic prediction of low and high flows for many basins. The approach generally produces statistically reliable ensembles.
supporting_quote: the late-season snowpack (i.e., after 1 April) has significant predictability for spring and summer volumes.
higher hindcast skill is achievable ... when basins exhibit high antecedent SWE content and low precipitation during the forecast period.
this statistical forecasting approach ... can generate ensemble hindcasts that are statistically reliable.

chunks.text: From a decision-relevant perspective, the authors report that for periods of interest up to and including 1 June–30 September, lower-than-normal and higher-than-normal streamflows can be predicted with lead times up to 5 months in some basins. They also argue that an optimal future approach should incorporate additional predictors (e.g., climate) where SWE is insufficient, especially as snow-to-rain shifts reduce predictability. The paper positions FROSTBYTE as a benchmark for such extensions.
supporting_quote: for all periods of interest up to and including 1 June to 30 September, we can predict lower-than-normal and higher-than-normal streamflows with lead times of up to 5 months.
In many river basins and at many times of the year, the SWE is not a key predictor. Therefore, an optimal approach should leverage climate predictors

chunks.text: Canada’s hydrology spans highly diverse regimes across a vast landmass, with cold-regions processes strongly shaping the terrestrial water cycle. Historically, Canadian floods have commonly been triggered by snowmelt, ice jams, and heavy rainfall, with event types varying from flash floods to large basin-scale floods. Flooding is described as the country’s costliest natural disaster, and recent decades have seen unprecedented events with major economic impacts.
supporting_quote: Canada is one of the most diverse countries in the world with its large landmass, complex, and wide-ranging hydrological regimes
Floods in Canada have historically been caused by snowmelt, ice jams, and heavy rainfall

chunks.text: Operational large-domain fluvial flood forecasting has become feasible due to scientific and computational advances, typically relying on hydrological models driven by deterministic or ensemble NWP meteorological forecasts. The field has shifted toward probabilistic forecasting to better represent uncertainties and potentially provide earlier awareness of extreme-event risk. International communities such as HEPEX have supported this transition and learning across operational systems.
supporting_quote: Existing operational large-domain fluvial flood forecasting systems... aim to provide flood early warnings by running a hydrological model into the future, forced with a deterministic or an ensemble of meteorological forecasts
flood forecasting has shifted from deterministic to probabilistic forecasting... to characterize the irreducible uncertainties

chunks.text: Flood forecasting in Canada is largely a provincial/territorial responsibility delivered through multiple independent entities, including municipalities and conservation authorities. This fragmentation can provide locally tailored systems, but also creates inefficiencies and inconsistencies at national scale. The paper frames national coordination as increasingly important given flood impacts and evolving climate risks.
supporting_quote: Flood forecasting in Canada is largely considered a provincial responsibility and is carried out to varying technical levels by many of the 13 provincial and territorial governments

The main disadvantages of this incoherence are the dispersion of capacity, lack of integration with weather forecasting, inconsistent resource levels, and the duplication of forecasting services on transboundary river basins.

chunks.text: The paper aims to outline a route toward a nationally coherent flood forecasting framework for Canada that can enable advanced capabilities across responsible authorities. It situates Canada’s needs within global large-domain forecasting practice, with emphasis on cold-regions challenges. The authors also aim to provide recommendations spanning cooperation, governance, and knowledge mobilization to support framework creation and deployment across large geographical domains.
supporting_quote: Towards a coherent flood forecasting framework for Canada: Local to global implications
forecasting challenges are identified (with a focus on cold regions), and recommendations are made to promote the creation of this framework.

chunks.text: A specific objective is to describe current Canadian regional approaches, summarize ongoing national operational efforts and research advances, and use these to define future directions. The article frames Canada as a late adopter that can learn from international systems while contributing cold-regions expertise to global operational forecasting.
supporting_quote: Section 2 briefly describes the current regional approaches to flood forecasting within Canada.
Section 3 highlights ongoing national operational water modeling and forecasting efforts, and research advances

chunks.text: Canada is described as the only G7 country without a national flood forecasting or flow guidance system. The current distributed responsibility across provinces/territories leads to fragmented capacity and duplicated services, especially in transboundary basins. This limits consistent integration with weather forecasting and contributes to uneven resources and technical levels across jurisdictions.
supporting_quote: Canada is the only G7 country without a national flood forecasting or flow guidance system.

The main disadvantages of this incoherence are the dispersion of capacity, lack of integration with weather forecasting, inconsistent resource levels, and the duplication of forecasting services on transboundary river basins.

chunks.text: Flood-generation mechanisms are diverse and changing across Canada, complicating forecasting and model design. The paper highlights a declining role of snowmelt-driven floods in some regions and increasing importance of rain-on-snow and rainfall-driven floods, along with climate-driven changes to timing and antecedent moisture. Such shifts can produce unprecedented events in regions previously dominated by different regimes.
supporting_quote: highlight the large but declining magnitude of snowmelt-driven events, the increasing importance of rain-on-snow and rainfall-driven flood events
Cunderlik and Ouarda (2009) report the decreasing importance of spring snowmelt flood events across Canada

chunks.text: Ice-jam flooding is a major Canadian challenge because water levels for a given discharge can vary widely and can exceed open-water floods by meters. Forecasting requires coupling flow forecasting with complex river-ice processes (formation, breakup, jamming) and resulting stage impacts. Despite research progress, operational translation is limited and most provinces/territories lack operational ice-jam forecasting systems.
supporting_quote: Ice jams can result in high water levels that can be many meters above summer floods for equivalent or lower discharges
most provinces and territories in Canada do not have an operational ice-jam flood forecasting system

chunks.text: Observation scarcity and measurement uncertainty, especially in cold regions, constrain reliable forecasting and model evaluation. The paper notes that only a small fraction of Canada meets minimum hydrometric network density standards, and snow/precipitation measurement faces undercatch and scale challenges. These constraints increase uncertainty and hinder accurate depiction of key states like snow water equivalent.
supporting_quote: only about 12% of the Canadian terrestrial area is covered by hydrometric networks that meet the World Meteorological Organization (2008) minimum network density standards
surface precipitation... is difficult to measure accurately... and persistent undercatch in rain (and especially snow) observations

chunks.text: Many Canadian river forecast centers have adopted the Delft Flood Early Warning System (Delft-FEWS) as a model-agnostic platform to manage operational forecasting workflows. The paper lists multiple provincial users and key utilities, and notes prototype developments in the Yukon and Northwest Territories using MESH and Raven. A common platform has enabled shared development and improved integration of multiple hydrological models and remote-sensing river-ice monitoring.
supporting_quote: Delft-FEWS... is an open data handling model-agnostic platform developed for flood forecasting and early warning systems.
It is... used by Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Québec, and New Brunswick's river forecast centers

chunks.text: Environment and Climate Change Canada’s Canadian Meteorological Centre developed the National Surface and River Prediction System (NSRPS) as a modular national flow guidance capability. NSRPS combines analyses and deterministic (and developing ensemble) predictions on a national grid, producing hydrometeorological products such as runoff and river flow. The system is designed to inform provincial/territorial users and broader hydrological applications while not publicly disseminating river flow forecasts.
supporting_quote: constructed the National Surface and River Prediction System (NSRPS; Durnford, Carrera, et al., 2021), which was implemented... in 2019 with experimental status.
The NSRPS does not publicly disseminate river flow forecasts, as predicting floods is the jurisdiction of provinces and territories.

chunks.text: NSRPS hydrological analyses use the SVS land surface scheme driven by a deterministic meteorological analysis and an ensemble precipitation analysis (HREPA). HREPA assimilates ground-based and radar precipitation observations, and SVS is coupled with CaLDAS to assimilate satellite-derived variables including soil moisture and snow cover. These components support physically coherent land-surface states and runoff estimates used by downstream routing.
supporting_quote: A land surface analysis... is produced by driving the Surface Vegetation Snow land surface scheme (SVS)... with a meteorological analysis... and an ensemble precipitation analysis, called the High Resolution Ensemble Precipitation Analysis (HREPA)
HREPA assimilates ground-based and radar observations of precipitation.

chunks.text: River flow analysis and deterministic forecasting in NSRPS are produced by DHPS using the WATROUTE 1D routing model, including reservoir management via the Dynamically Zoned Target Release (DZTR) model. DHPS assimilates river flow observations from multiple sources (ECCC, USGS, and provincial networks) to constrain analyses. Deterministic river flow forecasts are generated twice daily to 6 days lead time, driven by land prediction outputs.
supporting_quote: DHPS provides a single river flow analysis at 1 km resolution using the 1D channel and reservoir routing model WATROUTE
river flow observations from ECCC, the United States Geological Survey (USGS) and the provincial networks of Alberta and Québec are assimilated into DHPS.

chunks.text: NSRPS deterministic land forecasting uses HRDLPS with HRDPS forcing for days 1–2 and GDPS forcing for days 3–6, providing land-surface forecasts (including runoff) to 6 days. NSRPS ensemble forecasts are being developed with 20 members, driven by REPS (days 1–3) and GEPS (days 4–16, extending to 32 days on Thursdays). The design supports scaling from short-range forecasts to subseasonal outlooks.
supporting_quote: HRDLPS... provides deterministic forecasts of the land surface (including runoff )... for up to 6 days lead time
Ensemble forecasts (20 ensemble members)... driven by... REPS for days 1–3 and... GEPS for days 4–16 (extended to 32 days on thursdays).

chunks.text: Global Water Futures (GWF) advances support national forecasting through development of meteorological ensembles, improved snow process simulation, modular model approaches, and operational prototypes. The paper highlights SnowCast, driven by 2.5 km HRDPS forecasts, providing mountain snow predictions down to 50 m. GWF also supports operationalization partnerships (e.g., Yukon) and model-agnostic development philosophies to enable reuse across modeling groups.
supporting_quote: Developing ensemble meteorological datasets for North America and the globe
SnowCast... provides predictions in the mountains of western Canada at scales down to 50 m.

chunks.text: The paper describes building a national ‘community of practice’ through Canadian flood forecasting workshops/forums co-hosted by GWF and ECCC (2019, 2021). This mechanism is presented as a structured approach to share experiences, identify common priorities (e.g., river ice, snowpack, basin characterization, communication), and recommend areas for further study. The goal is to strengthen collaboration between operational centers, academia, industry, and government.
supporting_quote: GWF and the NHS have co-hosted two Canadian flood forecasting workshops/forums (2019, 2021), with the aim to develop a community of practice
The community of practice aims to facilitate sharing of information on available products, tools, applications, common experiences, bestpractices

chunks.text: Canada’s near-real-time monitoring backbone includes hydrometric and meteorological station networks operated by ECCC with partners. The paper reports over 2500 active hydrometric stations and over 1800 active meteorological stations, with data disseminated publicly in standardized formats for operational ingestion. Despite the apparent density, the paper notes that spatial coverage meeting WMO minimum standards is limited nationally.
supporting_quote: The WSC operates over 2500 active hydrometric stations
The MSC operates over 1800 active meteorological stations

chunks.text: Hydrometric network adequacy is limited over large portions of Canada, especially in the north. The paper states that only about 12% of Canada’s terrestrial area is covered by hydrometric networks meeting WMO (2008) minimum density standards, with most stations south of 55N. This creates constraints for calibration, validation, and operational situational awareness in sparsely monitored basins.
supporting_quote: only about 12% of the Canadian terrestrial area is covered by hydrometric networks that meet the World Meteorological Organization (2008) minimum network density standards
most of which are situated south of 55N

chunks.text: NSRPS incorporates multi-source precipitation and satellite observations through HREPA and CaLDAS. HREPA assimilates ground-based and radar precipitation observations, while CaLDAS assimilates satellite-derived information including GOES temperatures, SMOS and SMAP soil moisture, and IMS snow cover. These integrated datasets provide gridded land-surface analyses used in national guidance workflows.
supporting_quote: HREPA assimilates ground-based and radar observations of precipitation.
CaLDAS... assimilates observations... including skin and brightness temperatures from GOES-16 and GOES-17, soil moisture from... SMOS... and... SMAP... and snow cover from... IMS

chunks.text: The paper highlights increasing operational use of remote sensing for river ice monitoring within Canadian forecasting workflows. In particular, Delft-FEWS enabled operational use of RADARSAT Constellation Mission and Sentinel-1/2 data for river ice monitoring in initiatives led by Alberta and Québec. Such datasets support enhanced monitoring to identify ice-jam flood risk and communicate early warnings.
supporting_quote: Delft-FEWS has also enabled the operational use of Canadian Space Agency RADARSAT Constellation Mission and European Space Agency Sentinel 1 and 2 data for river ice monitoring
Enhanced monitoring of river ice, for example using remote sensing data or flight observations, remains a key component

chunks.text: GWF provides ensemble meteorological forcing datasets that can support hydrological modeling and prediction across Canada and beyond. The paper notes development of ensemble datasets for North America (EMDNA) and the globe (EM-Earth), which can help address forcing uncertainty and data sparsity. These datasets are positioned as foundational inputs for large-domain hydrologic prediction systems.
supporting_quote: Developing ensemble meteorological datasets for North America and the globe (Tang et al., 2020; 2021; 2022);
EM‐Earth: The Ensemble Meteorological Dataset for Planet Earth.

chunks.text: The paper identifies a national structural gap: Canada lacks a unified national flood forecasting or flow guidance system compared to peer countries. It frames the current provincial responsibility model as producing locally tailored systems but also creating dispersion of capacity and duplication. This diagnosis motivates the push toward national flow guidance and a coherent framework that preserves local decision authority.
supporting_quote: Canada is the only G7 country without a national flood forecasting or flow guidance system.
The benefit of this fragmented approach is that the bespoke operational modeling and forecasting systems are specifically tailored to work at regional scales

chunks.text: Canadian flood regimes are categorized into rainfall-driven, snowmelt-driven, and mixed regimes, with evidence of ongoing regime shifts. The paper reports declining magnitude of snowmelt-driven events and increasing importance of rain-on-snow and rainfall-driven floods, alongside increased flooding occurrence. This regime evolution is presented as a key driver for modernizing forecasting systems and process representation.
supporting_quote: classify flood behavior in Canada into three major flood generation regimes: rainfall-driven, snowmeltdriven and mixed.
highlight... declining magnitude of snowmeltdriven events, the increasing importance of rain-on-snow and rainfall-driven flood events, and an overall increase in the occurrence of flooding in Canada.

chunks.text: The contrasting 2011 and 2014 Assiniboine River floods are used to illustrate changing Canadian flood drivers. The 2011 event was linked to high antecedent moisture, above-normal snowpack, and a very wet spring, producing peak flows lasting more than 120 days. The 2014 event is described as the first pluvial flood in 130 years of record for the area, driven by heavy rains on a saturated basin with summer peaks exceeding spring freshet.
supporting_quote: The 2011 flood was caused by high antecedent moisture conditions... followed by high snowpack accumulation... and by a very wet spring
This resulted in peak flows that lasted more than 120 days.

chunks.text: Ice-jam flood impacts can exceed open-water floods for similar discharges, and their predictability is low due to multiple possible backwater levels for a given discharge. The paper reports that ice-jam damages can surpass ice-free flood damages and cites the 2020 Fort McMurray ice-jam flood exceeding a billion Canadian dollars. These characteristics underscore the need for improved operational ice-jam forecasting and monitoring.
supporting_quote: a range of ice jam induced backwater levels are possible for a given discharge, which makes an ice-jam flood difficult to predict
the 2020 ice-jam flood in Fort McMurray in western Canada caused more than a billion Canadian dollars in damages

chunks.text: A key operational capacity development is the spread of Delft-FEWS across multiple Canadian jurisdictions and utilities, enabling shared tool development and integration of multiple hydrologic models. The paper describes this convergence as encouraging and contributing to a national (not federal) approach and a community of practice. It also notes that some jurisdictions are developing Delft-FEWS prototypes using different model backends, suggesting increasing interoperability.
supporting_quote: Delft-FEWS... is used by Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Québec, and New Brunswick's river forecast centers
This convergence of technology and methods is encouraging and is leading to a national (not federal) approach to flood forecasting

chunks.text: NSRPS has been implemented operationally at experimental status and provides national hydrometeorological analyses and forecasts on common grids and databases. The system includes land-surface analyses, deterministic land and river forecasts to 6 days, and developing ensemble capabilities. The paper presents NSRPS modularity and physical coherence as enabling component-by-component updates and a ‘numerical laboratory’ for operational Earth-system prediction development.
supporting_quote: National Surface and River Prediction System (NSRPS)... implemented... in 2019 with experimental status.
The NSRPS system is physically coherent across components (i.e., use of the same national grid, geophysical databases, and model versions).

chunks.text: The paper reports a demonstrated value of subseasonal ensemble runoff guidance in anticipating flood potential. It cites that before the 2019 spring floods in the Ottawa and St. Lawrence basins near Montréal, flood potential was predicted 2 weeks in advance and refined over time. This experience led to adding surface runoff from GEPS and REPS to the CCMEP Vigilance series for operational alerting.
supporting_quote: before the 2019 spring floods... the potential for flooding was predicted for the region 2 weeks in advance.
surface runoff from both... GEPS and REPS... were added to... CCMEP)'s Vigilance series.

chunks.text: Cold-region measurement challenges create persistent uncertainty in operational datasets used for flood forecasting. The paper notes that ice and sediment effects at gauge sites require frequent adjustments and increase uncertainty. It also highlights precipitation undercatch—especially for snow—and difficulties measuring snow water equivalent at scales needed for operations.
supporting_quote: Ice, sediment, and other effects at river gauge locations require frequent adjustment... such dynamic changes increase uncertainty
persistent undercatch in rain (and especially snow) observations

chunks.text: Operational implementation of ensemble forecasting and probabilistic communication remains challenging in Canada. Some provinces/territories use ensembles only for guidance, and obstacles include reliability and availability of ensembles, resource limitations, and dissemination of probabilistic information. The paper emphasizes that probabilistic products require careful communication to decision-makers who may fear blame for yes/no actions based on probabilities.
supporting_quote: a few provinces/territories use ensemble forecasts for guidance only (i.e., not operationally).
current challenges... are linked with the reliability and availability of ensembles, the dissemination of probabilistic information and resources limitations.

chunks.text: Although research progress on ice-jam flood forecasting is substantial, operational adoption is constrained by computational and software barriers and site-specific model designs. The paper states that computational resources limit operational uptake and calls for parallelization, model-agnostic couplers, and open-source codes to speed adoption. It concludes that end-user-friendly, large-domain operational approaches remain a major gap.
supporting_quote: the computational resources required to simulate ice-jam events is still limiting the application of these research advances into operational practice.
Advances in model-agnostic couplers are needed to embed river ice models into existing forecasting frameworks

chunks.text: Greater data availability does not automatically translate to operational value, due to processing burdens, expertise requirements, and product suitability issues. The paper notes impediments to remote sensing use in operations and warns that some widely available SWE products can be biased and unsuitable for forecasting. It argues that guidance and careful evaluation are needed before adopting novel products in forecasting systems.
supporting_quote: data provision alone does not guarantee added value to the forecasting community.
the quantity and processing time can be prohibitive for use in operational settings.

chunks.text: AI/ML approaches face constraints in Canada because many basins are sparsely gauged or ungauged, limiting training data and robustness. The paper adds that changing flood generation processes (e.g., snowmelt, glacier melt, ice breakup) complicate purely data-driven predictions. It suggests that hybrid approaches incorporating process-based constraints may improve applicability in Canada’s data-limited landscape.
supporting_quote: AI/ML methods are primarily data driven and so are challenged by sparsely gauged and ungauged basins in Canada
changes in flood generation processes... can make it more difficult to use data-driven models for predictions.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that Canada should develop a coherent national flood forecasting framework to coordinate local, regional, and international efforts and to operationalize state-of-the-art science. It recommends combining top-down and bottom-up approaches to build trust and remain mindful of local realities, while clearly articulating accountability and responsibility across the early-warning chain. It also emphasizes that a community of practice is essential for cooperation and for surfacing operational needs.
supporting_quote: A coherent national flood forecasting framework should be developed to coordinate local, regional, and international efforts
The national framework should follow both a topdown and bottom-up approach to be mindful of local realities and to build credibility and trust

chunks.text: The authors recommend that national coordination address the proliferation of available data and forecast products by enabling access while clearly communicating which forecast is authoritative. They also encourage the use of creative methods and education to improve communication and public engagement, supporting resilience. These recommendations are presented as relevant not only for Canada but also for other large-domain forecasting efforts globally.
supporting_quote: provision alone does not guarantee added value to the forecasting community... while clearly communicating the authoritative forecast.
Creative methods and educational campaigns could be explored to help build societal resilience to floods

chunks.text: The paper closes by arguing that recent investments in Canadian hydrological science and the national flow guidance initiative create an opportunity for Canada to contribute to next-generation flood forecasting internationally. It positions Canada’s cold-regions challenges as both difficult and uniquely valuable for advancing global operational guidance. The proposed Canada Water Agency is framed as a key institutional foundation to support coherent national flood prediction while meeting obligations to protect communities.
supporting_quote: recent investments in hydrological science in Canada are creating opportunities for Canada to make greater contributions in developing the next generation of flood forecasting systems.
A new Canada Water Agency is well-placed to successfully deal with Canada's... aspiration to contribute to global forecasting capabilities

chunks.text: USGS streamflow estimation relies on converting stream stage to discharge using rating curves that assume open-channel, free-surface flow. River ice can disrupt stage measurements and can force under-ice pressurized flow, violating rating-curve assumptions. To warn users, USGS applies ice-related quality flags in NWIS and later replaces ice-impacted observations with estimates.
supporting_quote: The stream stage is then converted to streamflow using an empirical site-specific relationship, known as a rating curve
the water beneath a fully covered river by ice can flow under pressure which is different from open channel flow conditions
the USGS adds quality flags in the USGS National Water Information System (NWIS) database ... to ice-affected observations

chunks.text: NIMS is a USGS operational network of ground-based cameras, publicly accessible via HIVIS, used for real-time remote monitoring at many streamgaging stations. As of January 2025, the network includes about 830 cameras, with roughly 630 in northern watersheds that are prone to ice. USGS currently uses these images qualitatively via visual inspection to assess river conditions during ice seasons.
supporting_quote: NIMS consists of a cloudbased database and software system supporting a network of cameras
The network comprises about 830 cameras, as of January 2025
Approximately 630 NIMS monitoring sites are located in the northern watersheds

chunks.text: Prior work has applied computer vision and deep learning to river ice detection using shore-based photos, UAV aerial imagery, and public cameras. These studies include region-based CNN approaches, U-Net variants, and other neural networks targeting segmentation and characterization of river ice. This paper positions RIce-Net as an operationally focused framework tailored to NIMS camera imagery and USGS needs.
supporting_quote: Ansari et al. (2021) used the region-based convolution neural network to detect and segment river ice
Pei et al. (2023) used a U-Net model to segment river ice images from public cameras
This study aims to introduce a novel computer vision-based framework, called River Ice Network (RIce-Net)

chunks.text: The study’s goal is to develop RIce-Net, a computer vision framework that automatically detects river ice from NIMS camera images and generates a near real-time ice flag. The intended use is to support USGS operations by reducing manual visual inspection while producing flags that match or improve agreement with USGS-reported ice flags. The authors emphasize robustness and minimal computational cost to enable scalable operational deployment.
