supporting_quote: This study aims to introduce a novel computer vision-based framework, called River Ice Network (RIce-Net), to support USGS monitoring of river ice conditions
The intention of this study is to test the reliability of the proposed framework over selected ice-prone USGS stations
A particular focus was put on developing a robust and reliable system that could run operationally at a minimal computational cost

chunks.text: A specific objective is to quantify the percentage of river ice coverage from segmented images and convert that into an automatic flagging rule that can reproduce USGS ice flags. The system is trained on one station’s imagery (Milwaukee River) and tested both temporally (2024 vs. 2023) and spatially via transfer to an unseen station (Missouri River at Bismarck). This evaluates both performance and transferability of the approach.
supporting_quote: This is done by calculating the percentage of river ice coverage using a segmentation model
RIce-Net was trained using images from selected NIMS stations collected in 2023 and tested using images collected in 2024
the framework's scalability and transferability were tested over another station that was not included in the training process

chunks.text: Ice conditions can make stage measurements unreliable, and the need to apply ice flags is currently determined using information sources that are labor-intensive and sometimes delayed. Frequent site visits are difficult during cold seasons and hazardous ice conditions, and other reports (e.g., from other agencies) share similar logistical constraints. Consequently, there is an operational gap for systematic, frequent, and consistent ice-condition assessment.
supporting_quote: it may not be feasible to visit all stations frequently, especially during the cold seasons and the hazardous conditions associated with ice processes

USGS relies on these images to qualitatively assess the conditions of the ice in the rivers. This is carried out through a visual inspection of the images, which makes the process subjective and time-consuming

chunks.text: Satellite and aerial methods for river ice monitoring have limitations for operational flagging at many sites. Issues include delays in dissemination, sparse measurements, and coarse spatial/temporal resolution; moderate-resolution polar-orbiting satellites are mainly suitable for large rivers. Aerial photos can be expensive and infrequent, and citizen science contributions may not be available when needed.
supporting_quote: these methods come with inherent limitations, such as data dissemination delays, sparse measurements, and coarse spatial and temporal resolution
satellite observations ... have a spatial resolution of a few hundred meters, which is only suitable for large rivers
aerial photographs may be expensive to collect and may not be available frequently

chunks.text: Running semantic segmentation on all NIMS images is computationally expensive given the scale of the network and image frequency. The paper notes 800+ stations capturing images every 15 minutes, and a segmentation inference time of about two seconds per image. This motivates a design that reduces the number of images requiring segmentation while maintaining reliable ice detection.
supporting_quote: The large number of NIMS stations (800+ stations), which capture images every 15 min
the inference time of the segmentation model, about two seconds per image, makes such models computationally expensive
a preliminary classification step was introduced so that only images that may contain ice are segmented

chunks.text: RIce-Net uses a two-stage pipeline to reduce computation: first classify images as ice-free or ice-affected, then segment only ice-affected images to compute ice coverage. The system shares the same encoder between classification and segmentation to avoid redundant computation. High-level features feed the classifier, and high- and low-level features feed the decoder for segmentation.
supporting_quote: RIce-Net implements a two-stage process: (1) introducing an image classification layer before the segmentation step
sharing the encoder network between the image classification and segmentation models to reduce computation redundancy
The high- and low-level features of the iceaffected images only are then passed to the decoder network of the segmentation model

chunks.text: Input preprocessing focuses the models on the river water surface by masking non-water regions. The authors manually define site-specific polygons to mask the water surface and crop black regions, reducing confusion between snow on banks and ice on water. Cropped images are resized/zero-padded to 1152×640, scaled by 255, and normalized using ImageNet mean and standard deviation.
supporting_quote: we use manually predefined polygons for each station to mask the water surface, and crop the black regions from the images
the cropped images are resized or zero-padded to 1152 × 640
normalized using mean [0.485, 0.456, 0.406] and standard deviation [0.229, 0.224, 0.225]

chunks.text: The segmentation component uses a ResNet50 encoder pretrained on ImageNet to improve training efficiency, with multiple decoder architectures tested. Models were implemented using Segmentation Models PyTorch, and evaluated by IoU and Dice-Sørensen coefficient (DSC). Training used Dice-Sørensen loss (1−DSC) and ADAM with a learning-rate schedule from 0.0001 to 0.00001 after 25 epochs.
supporting_quote: The pre-trained residual network (ResNet50) using the ImageNet dataset ... is used to enhance training efficiency
The performance of the segmentation model ... assessed using the Intersection over Union ... and the Dice-Sørensen coefficient (DSC)
The adaptive moment estimation (ADAM) optimizer was used, with an initial learning rate set to 0.0001 and then reduced to 0.00001 after 25 epochs

chunks.text: The classification model is binary (ice-free vs ice-affected) and uses transfer learning from the trained segmentation encoder. The encoder is frozen, and a fully connected output layer is trained with cross-entropy loss. A softmax activation with a 50% threshold is used for decision-making, optimized with ADAM at a learning rate of 1−4.
supporting_quote: leveraging the encoder network from the trained segmentation model
A softmax activation function with a 50% threshold was used for classification, while the encoder network was frozen during training
Crossentropy loss was used to train the classifier ... ADAM optimizer with a learning rate set to 1 − 4

chunks.text: Ice coverage (IC) is computed from segmented images as the fraction of pixels classified as ice over total river-surface pixels after cropping. An ice flag is triggered when IC exceeds a threshold for eight consecutive hours. Different thresholds are used for onset and breakup (15% and 20%, respectively) to reflect differences between shore-ice formation impacts and floating ice pans during breakup.
supporting_quote: dividing the total number of pixels classified as ice by the total number of pixels representing the river surface after cropping
An ice flag is triggered when the exceeds a specific threshold for a set amount of time, eight consecutive hours in this study
values of 15% and 20%, respectively

chunks.text: Segmentation annotations were created primarily from a single NIMS station: 1,829 images from the Milwaukee River near Cedarburg, Wisconsin. For segmentation training/validation, 1,359 images from January–December 2023 were used, and 470 images from January–March 2024 were used for testing. Images were manually annotated using the Pixel Annotation Tool.
supporting_quote: we manually annotated 1,829 NIMS images collected at the Milwaukee River near the Cedarburg station in Wisconsin only
a total of 1,359 images, which were taken between January and December 2023, were used
The remaining images, captured between January and March 2024, were used for testing
The Pixel Annotation Tool ... was used to manually annotate the images

chunks.text: To improve generalization, the segmentation dataset was augmented with two public datasets: NWPU_YRCC and Alberta River Ice Segmentation. NWPU_YRCC provides 1,517 UAV aerial images (1600×640) from the Yellow River (2015–2019) with classes including water and ice. The Alberta dataset has 50 images (1281×1081) with two ice types that were merged into a single ice class for this study.
supporting_quote: augmented with publicly available river ice segmentation datasets, such as the NWPU_YRCC ... and Alberta River Ice Segmentation
The first dataset contains 1,517 aerial images, of size 1600 × 640
The latter dataset contains 50 images, of size 1281 × 1081
the two ice classes are merged as ice while training the segmentation model

chunks.text: Overall, the combined annotated segmentation corpus totals 3,396 images, with 2,926 used for training and 470 for testing. The training set used a 20% validation split and extensive augmentation, including flips, rotations, noise, and brightness adjustments via Albumentations. All datasets used a land/water mask to exclude sky, structures, and vegetation and focus on the water surface.
supporting_quote: Combining all the aforementioned annotated images leads to a big dataset of 3,396 annotated images
A total of 2,926 images were used to train the segmentation models, of which 20% were randomly selected to validate
data augmentation techniques such as random flips, rotations, scales, crops, adding Gaussian noise, and brightness adjustments were applied during training using the Albumnetation python library
a land/water mask was used to delineate the water section in all images and to exclude all other objects such as the sky, structures

chunks.text: The classification dataset used only NIMS images and was balanced across ice-free and ice-affected classes. It includes 1,055 ice-free and 886 ice-affected images. For temporal separation, 2023 images were used for training/validation (20% validation), and 2024 images were used for testing.
supporting_quote: The dataset is balanced where the number of ice-free images is 1,055, while that of ice-affected images is 886
images captured in 2023 were only used to train and validate the classification model, where 20% of the images were used for validation
images captured in 2024 were used to test the model

chunks.text: Two ice-prone NIMS stations were used for evaluation: Milwaukee River near Cedarburg (site 04086600) and Missouri River at Bismarck (site 06342500). The Milwaukee site drainage area is 1,572.12 km2 and the camera covers ~65 m river width; the Bismarck site drains 482,774 km2 with a ~350 m wide viewed section. Only Milwaukee imagery was used for model training; Missouri was used to test generalization.
supporting_quote: the Milwaukee River site covers 1,572.12 km2 and the Missouri River at Bismarck site covers a larger area of 482,774 km2
The installed camera captures a river section approximately 65 meters wide
the camera at this location covers a wider river section, measuring about 350 meters in width
Only images from the Milwaukee River station were used to train the classification and segmentation models

chunks.text: Across tested segmentation decoders, PAN achieved the best overall performance for ice segmentation and ice-coverage estimation on the test dataset. PAN reached DSC=0.989 and IoU=0.981, with ice-coverage correlation R=0.982 and R2=0.962 and MSE=28.6%. It was also faster than DeepLabV3+ on CPU, motivating its selection for RIce-Net’s segmentation stage.
supporting_quote: the CPU inference time for the PAN was 14% faster than that of DeepLabV3+
Consequently, the PAN model was selected for the segmentation task

chunks.text: The PAN training process ran for 200 epochs and showed stable convergence without apparent overfitting. Training was stopped when performance changes were minimal over five consecutive epochs. Reported learning curves became asymptotic with loss around 0.04 and mean-IoU around 0.94, indicating consistent training and validation behavior.
supporting_quote: The training of the PAN model was carried out for 200 epochs
terminated as there were minimal changes in the performance metric over five consecutive epochs
loss and mean-IOU values become asymptotic around 0.04, and 0.94, respectively, indicating that the model is not overfitted

chunks.text: The binary classifier performed strongly on the 2024 test set, correctly separating ice-free from ice-affected images. Reported metrics were accuracy=0.977, precision=1, recall=0.954, and F1-score=0.976. Errors were mainly false negatives when ice coverage was very small (below about 5%).
supporting_quote: An accuracy of 0.977, with a precision of 1, recall of 0.954, and F1-score of 0.976
the model misclassified 12 images as false negatives
the ice coverage was minimal, with the percentage of ice coverage being less than 5%

chunks.text: RIce-Net’s automatically generated ice flags aligned closely with USGS flags for both the Milwaukee River and the Missouri River stations during January–March 2024. At Milwaukee, RIce-Net started flagging on January 12 (one day earlier than USGS) and removed the flag two days earlier than USGS; it also flagged Feb 17–20. At Missouri (Bismarck), RIce-Net started on January 9 like USGS but had a short gap March 2–5, whereas USGS was continuous to March 12.
supporting_quote: The results indicate a strong alignment between the RIce-Net ice flags and those reported by USGS
at the Milwaukee River station, the RIce-Net framework began flagging ice-affected readings on January 12th, one day earlier than USGS
At the Missouri River station, the RIce-Net ice flag started on January 9th as the USGS flag

chunks.text: The generated RIce-Net ice flag tracked observed stream-stage anomalies consistent with ice onset and breakup timing. At Milwaukee, the onset flag on January 12 matched a sudden stage drop and coincided with an image showing ice coverage exceeding 20%. During breakup around January 31, the flag ended when ice coverage fell below 15% and stage dropped. At Missouri, low ice coverage (<15%) on March 2 corresponded to no flag and a sudden stage drop, with flag resuming on March 5 as ice coverage increased.
supporting_quote: during the ice onset period on January 12th, the RIce-Net ice flag matches the sudden drop in the stream stage at that time
The NIMS image from January 12th shows ice presence that exceeds 20%
ice coverage was less than 15% and the reading was not flagged which matches the sudden drop in the stream stage

chunks.text: The classification stage reduces total computation by skipping segmentation on ice-free images, which is important for large-scale deployment. In the test set, about 50% of images had no ice, and bypassing their segmentation reduces computational time by about 32%. At network scale (830+ stations, 96 images/day), this can avoid segmenting large volumes of ice-free images, improving feasibility for operations and edge computing.
supporting_quote: approximately 50% showed no ice presence. Bypassing the ice-free image segmentation process would reduce the overall computational time by approximately 32%

chunks.text: The NWM’s groundwater exchange scheme is limited by design choices intended to support computational efficiency at continental scale. It assumes one-way aquifer-to-stream exchange and represents the aquifer as a two-meter soil column, while not explicitly representing stream losses to groundwater. The paper argues these limitations impact forecasts, particularly under low-flow conditions and in systems with losing and gaining reaches.

chunks.text: Computational constraints shape both groundwater and routing representations in the NWM, which can introduce systematic errors. chunks.text: NASA’s Earth Information System (EIS) emerged from the vision of systematic global Earth measurements and an advanced data-and-information infrastructure (EOSDIS). Over time, EOSDIS evolved into today’s EIS, which supports Earth system science by processing, distributing, and integrating observations with models. This evolution reflects decades of progress in remote sensing and Earth system modeling aimed at describing and predicting Earth system change.
supporting_quote: The report called for the development of an advanced information system—the Earth Observing System Data and Information System (EOSDIS).
Originally aiming to support models describing Earth system dynamics... the EOSDIS has evolved into today's Earth Information System (EIS).

chunks.text: The Earth system comprises interacting subsystems (atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, geosphere, biosphere) coupled across vast ranges of time and space. These couplings span roughly 14–16 orders of magnitude, and the underlying dynamics are nonlinear with incomplete physics understanding. This complexity motivates integrated observation-model approaches to monitor, diagnose, and predict Earth system behavior.
supporting_quote: The Earth system is composed of highly complex subsystems (e.g., the atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, geosphere, and biosphere).
The subsystems interact with each other via coupling mechanisms at time and spatial scales, spanning 14–16 orders of magnitude...

chunks.text: Modern EIS practice relies on data assimilation that merges models and observations to reconstruct recent and past states and to improve predictive skill. This approach has proven particularly successful in weather prediction, motivating recommendations to integrate models with all Earth observations for holistic Earth system descriptions. The EIS is framed as a foundation for actionable Earth science applications by enforcing physical laws and constraints in geospatial information products.
supporting_quote: Between the 1990s and 2000s, data-assimilation frameworks integrating ocean, weather, and hydrologic models with observations were developed and implemented with great success, improving weather prediction in particular.
The EIS integrates observations and models to produce geospatial information that follows physical laws and constraints.

chunks.text: The article aims to position Digital Twins of Earth (DTE) as the next-generation Earth Information System by explaining how recent advances in sensor technology and computing enable a step-change in observation resolution. It clarifies that DTEs often take the form of partial models that represent specific Earth processes or subcomponents, rather than a fully comprehensive Earth system replica. The editorial uses a terrestrial water-cycle digital twin as a concrete example of this framing.
supporting_quote: Digital Twins of Earth (DTE) are the "next-generation EIS", leveraging a step-change in spatial resolution in Earth observations...
The water cycle Digital Twin described in the lead article by Brocca et al. ... is a partial DTE designed to represent terrestrial hydrologic processes

chunks.text: A central objective is to emphasize that understanding and quantifying uncertainty in DTE models and analyses is a scientific imperative. The article also calls for coordinated action by major agencies and international programs to establish modern standards and rules for scientific data exchange. These standards are intended to support rigorous uncertainty characterization and robust research and applications as DTE capabilities expand.
supporting_quote: Understanding and quantifying uncertainty in DTE models and analyses is a scientific imperative

The leading governmental agencies [NASA, the European Space Agency (ESA), the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), and others]... need to collaboratively define modern standards and new rules for scientific data exchange
chunks.section_hint: Uncertainties in Digital Twins of Earth

chunks.text: A key challenge is that a DTE should not be interpreted as an engineering-style digital twin with the same ability to iteratively eliminate undesirable outcomes through design. The Earth system is a “complex system of systems” with incomplete scientific understanding and measurement/modeling limitations. This mismatch creates risk of overpromising what DTEs can do compared with industrial digital twin expectations.
supporting_quote: The DTE is not to the Earth system as the Digital Twin construct used in engineering design is to the industrial product.
despite major advances in the last 50 years, there remain important limitations to our scientific understanding and our ability to measure and model processes.

chunks.text: Remote-sensing observations that drive DTEs introduce uncertainty due to resolution averaging, sensor errors, retrieval algorithms, and interpretation limits. These uncertainties can be highly nonlinear and nonstationary, especially for water-cycle variables such as precipitation. Such behavior complicates both the integration of observations into models and the propagation of uncertainty through DTE analyses.
supporting_quote: The measurements are averaged to coarser resolutions... introducing errors from sensors, data estimation algorithms, and uncertainty in the interpretation of the observations.

Extensive studies over the last 30 years have documented the highly nonlinear and nonstationary nature of observational uncertainty in remote sensing of the water cycle, and precipitation in particular.
chunks.section_hint: Uncertainties in Digital Twins of Earth

chunks.text: On the modeling side, physical uncertainty arises from missing processes, unresolved scales, and parameters that cannot be directly measured or theoretically quantified. Parameter calibration further introduces ambiguity because it mixes forcing uncertainty with parameter uncertainty, tying fitted parameters to uncertain forcing regimes. This reduces interpretability for change monitoring and hampers prediction, particularly given heavy-tailed water-cycle statistics and extremes.
supporting_quote: physical uncertainty (PU) stems from missing processes, unresolved spatial and temporal scales, and the need to specify representative parameters that cannot be measured directly
Calibration of model parameters mixes the forcing and parameter uncertainties, thus introducing ambiguity.

chunks.text: Computational uncertainty is highlighted as an often-neglected component of model uncertainty, stemming from numerical formulation, implementation, and even hardware/architecture differences. In hydrologic models, structural uncertainty (computational plus physical) varies across space and time because landscapes and processes are heterogeneous. This variability complicates consistent uncertainty characterization across domains and model subsystems.
supporting_quote: Computational uncertainty (CU) is another, often-neglected, type of model uncertainty.
In hydrologic models, the total structural uncertainty (CU+PU) varies in space and time
chunks.section_hint: Uncertainties in Digital Twins of Earth

chunks.text: The EIS methodology is described as integrating models and remote-sensing data using data assimilation to generate physically consistent geospatial information products. Assimilation enables reconstruction of recent and past states, supports scientific exploration to find missing processes or improve parameterizations, and provides updated initial and boundary conditions for predictions and applications. This integration is presented as a defining operational mechanism of EIS and a foundation for DTE implementations.
supporting_quote: NASA)'s classical Earth Information System (EIS) integrates models and remote-sensing data using assimilation techniques to produce geospatial information
Dataassimilation techniques integrate observations and models to produce Earth information on recent and past states.

chunks.text: A proposed conceptual method for building DTE capability is a hierarchical ontology of multiple interconnected digital twins. These act as building blocks that represent networks of processes within subsystems (land, oceans, etc.) and progressively incorporate interactions and feedbacks across subsystems. The hierarchy provides a stepwise strategy to manage complexity and uncertainty while scaling from local to global representations.
supporting_quote: It is possible to envision a hierarchy of Digital Twins as interconnected building blocks to capture networks of processes
The Digital Twin hierarchy articulated earlier [Figure 1] provides a stepwise strategy to handle complexity and understand and characterize uncertainty.

chunks.text: To reduce calibration-related ambiguity, the article suggests leveraging Earth observations to derive consistent multidimensional parameter datasets directly from measured radiometric quantities. Parameters can be derived from reflectances, brightness temperature, and backscatter rather than being independently fixed or tuned against uncertain forcing. This approach aims to eliminate or dramatically reduce calibration, thereby making parameter uncertainty more independent of forcing uncertainty.
supporting_quote: an alternative approach is available to DTEs... leverage—to the largest extent possible—existing Earth observations to derive consistent multidimensional parameter datasets from direct measurements (reflectances, brightness, temperature, and backscatter)
thereby eliminate or dramatically reduce calibration.

chunks.text: The paper describes how uncertainty should be approached by distinguishing observational uncertainty, physical uncertainty, and computational uncertainty, and tracking how forcing errors propagate into internal process uncertainty. It provides an example pathway where precipitation uncertainty affects infiltration and runoff, which then impacts soil moisture, evapotranspiration, streamflow, and land–atmosphere interactions. This framing is intended to guide rigorous characterization and propagation of uncertainty within DTEs.
supporting_quote: For instance... uncertainty in precipitation is transformed into uncertainty in infiltration and runoff processes, which then impacts soil moisture, evapotranspiration, streamflow, and land-atmosphere interactions.
physical uncertainty (PU)... Computational uncertainty (CU) is another
chunks.section_hint: Uncertainties in Digital Twins of Earth

chunks.text: DTEs are enabled by high-resolution Earth observations made possible by newer measurement technologies and platforms. The editorial highlights synthetic aperture radar, hyperspectral sensors, and high-performance computing as drivers, alongside the proliferation of CubeSats and small satellites. These data sources underpin the ‘big data’ era that motivates the DTE concept as a step-change in the EIS.
supporting_quote: a step-change in spatial resolution of Earth observations enabled in the last decade by synthetic aperture radar, hyperspectral sensors, and high-performance computing.
the proliferation of CubeSats, small satellites, and constantly improving measurement technologies.

chunks.text: For water-cycle digital twins, key forcing inputs include precipitation and winds, while model parameters include surface energy budget controls such as albedo and surface roughness and soil-moisture dynamics such as soil hydraulic properties. Remote sensing is positioned as a means to observe and derive several of these quantities. These forcing and parameter datasets are central to both model performance and uncertainty characterization.
supporting_quote: uncertainties include those in forcing elements (precipitation, winds, etc.)
parameters that govern surface energy budget (e.g., albedo and surface roughness) and soil moisture dynamics (e.g., soil hydraulic properties).

chunks.text: The article notes that parameter datasets can be derived from direct measurement channels used in remote sensing, including reflectances, brightness temperature, and backscatter. Such measurement-derived parameters can replace or reduce reliance on literature values or independently produced datasets. The intended outcome is more internally consistent parameterization aligned with Earth observations.
supporting_quote: derive consistent multidimensional parameter datasets from direct measurements (reflectances, brightness, temperature, and backscatter)
Remote-sensing technologies provide a powerful tool for measuring various properties on the Earth's surface for use in hydrological models

chunks.text: The editorial contrasts satellite precipitation products with ground-based reference products, cautioning that references can still contain systematic errors. It lists sources such as observing geometries, sampling limitations, operational biases, and estimation algorithms, including issues in precipitation radar networks. This comparison is used to motivate careful treatment of uncertainties regardless of product provenance.
supporting_quote: ground-based reference products can also be riddled with systematic errors in observing geometries, sampling limitations, operational biases, and estimation algorithms
such as in the case of precipitation radar networks.

chunks.text: A cited quantitative finding is that deriving the diurnal cycle of albedo directly from reflectance measurements can significantly affect modeled surface energy budgets in complex terrain. The reported impact is on the order of tens to 100 W/m^2, comparable in magnitude to cloud radiation feedbacks in the climate system. This result supports the argument that observation-derived parameters can materially change model behavior without relying on calibration.
supporting_quote: Tao and Barros [4] showed that the impact of deriving the diurnal cycle of albedo directly from reflectance measurements on the surface energy budget in complex terrain could be of an order of tens to 100 W/m2
a value similar in magnitude to cloud radiation feedbacks in the climate system.

chunks.text: Even with high-performance computing and high-resolution observations, DTEs face limitations because measurements are often averaged to coarser resolutions to meet sensitivity requirements and quantify change. This introduces additional errors from sensors and retrieval algorithms, compounding interpretation uncertainty. The paper stresses that observational uncertainty for water-cycle variables is nonlinear and nonstationary, making it difficult to robustly characterize and propagate through models.
supporting_quote: The measurements are averaged to coarser resolutions to meet measurement sensitivity requirements and to quantify change, introducing errors from sensors, data estimation algorithms
highly nonlinear and nonstationary nature of observational uncertainty in remote sensing of the water cycle
chunks.section_hint: Uncertainties in Digital Twins of Earth

chunks.text: Calibration is discussed as a limitation because global error minimization makes calibrated parameters dependent on uncertain forcing regimes. As a result, parameters can become product-specific, undermining comparability across different precipitation datasets and complicating change detection and prediction. The heavy-tail nature of water-cycle processes and extremes further amplifies the consequences of this ambiguity.
supporting_quote: Because calibration involves some form of global error minimization, the calibrated parameters are tied to the uncertain forcing regime.
This handicaps the ability to monitor change, and to make predictions also because of the heavy-tail statistical nature of water cycle processes, including extreme events.

chunks.text: The paper notes that ground-based reference products, often assumed to be lower-uncertainty, can still exhibit systematic error sources. These include observing geometry issues, sampling limitations, operational biases, and estimation algorithm errors, such as those affecting precipitation radar networks. This undermines simple assumptions that ‘reference’ data are definitive, complicating validation and uncertainty benchmarking for DTEs.
supporting_quote: As reference products rely on ground-based observations, they are presumed to have lower uncertainty than satellite products.
Nevertheless, ground-based reference products can also be riddled with systematic errors... such as in the case of precipitation radar networks.

chunks.text: As Earth observation becomes more distributed across private sector and international actors, the volume of data outside NASA’s EIS is growing rapidly. The editorial warns that without rigorous documentation, metadata, and uncertainty characterization, the trustworthiness of DTE-derived information may be compromised. It argues that excitement about new observations should not override the need for rigorous data characterization and exchange standards.
supporting_quote: the volume of Earth data available outside of NASA's EIS framework is growing exponentially.
the exhilaration created by the potential of this new era of Earth observations must not trump the need for rigorous characterization of the data and their uncertainty.
chunks.section_hint: Not missing the trees for the forest trustworthy information

chunks.text: The editorial concludes that DTEs represent a next-generation EIS driven by high-resolution observations, but their value depends on rigorous uncertainty understanding, representation, and propagation. It calls for the Earth sciences to focus on reducing ambiguity and scrutinizing uncertainty as models and observations grow in complexity and volume. It also emphasizes the need for collaborative, modern standards for scientific data exchange to ensure robust research and applications.
supporting_quote: The DTE is the next-generation EIS.
The grand challenge of understanding, quantifying, representing, and propagating uncertainty is a sobering one
need to collaboratively define modern standards and new rules for scientific data exchange

chunks.text: Flood events are increasing globally, intensifying the need for rapid, large-scale flood inundation mapping (FIM). High-fidelity hydrodynamic models (e.g., 1D/2D shallow-water equation solvers) can be accurate but are computationally expensive for real-time, continental-scale mapping. Remote sensing and data-driven methods can provide alternatives, but they have limitations such as cloud cover, coarse resolution, and generalization challenges. Terrain-based approaches like HAND provide a practical trade-off, enabling fast mapping over large domains.
supporting_quote: The global rise in flood events driven by climate change, environmental challenges, and rapid urbanization has heightened the need for rapid Flood Inundation Mapping (FIM) at large scales
While these models offer high accuracy, they also entail significant computational costs ... running such models in real time at this resolution remains computationally impractical.
In recent years, the Height Above the Nearest Drainage (HAND) method, a terrain-based model has been commonly used in FIM.

chunks.text: In the U.S., NOAA’s Office of Water Prediction uses the National Water Model (NWM) and a HAND-based Flood Inundation Mapping (OWP HAND-FIM) framework to translate discharge into inundation extent. The framework uses a hydro-conditioned 10 m DEM converted to HAND rasters and reach-specific synthetic rating curves (SRCs) to convert discharge to stage. It produces hourly flood maps at the HUC-8 watershed scale and is being expanded toward national coverage.
supporting_quote: The OWP HAND-FIM utilizes detailed hydro-conditioning of a 10m DEM, converts it to HAND raster ... and uses discharge data from the National Water Model (NWM) to produce hourly flood maps at the watershed scale (Hydrologic Unit Code (HUC)-8).
These FIM services are currently supplied to 30 % of the population in the United States ... will be expanded to nearly 100 % of the U.S. population by 2026
Tarboton et al. (2018) proposed a novel approach that determines the stage-discharge relationship using Synthetic Rating Curves (SRCs).

chunks.text: The OWP HAND-FIM pipeline is open source and widely used, but executing it can be difficult for end users due to configuration and environment constraints. The published implementation relies on Docker, which improves portability but is not supported in some interactive notebook platforms. This restricts accessibility for education, prototyping, and collaboration in lightweight cloud notebook environments. A Docker-free pathway can broaden the user base and reduce barriers for non-technical users.
supporting_quote: end users often face challenges in configuring and running the model to generate FIMs.
The published version relies exclusively on Docker for FIM execution.
interactive notebook platforms such as Google Colab and JupyterHub via 2i2c ... currently do not natively support Docker.

chunks.text: The paper introduces FIMserv (“FIM as a Service”), an open-source Python toolset that streamlines OWP HAND-FIM flood map production using operational inputs. The goal is to enable straightforward FIM generation from both retrospective and forecast NWM discharge, including multi-watershed simulations. FIMserv also aims to support additional discharge sources (GeoGLOWS) and provide discharge evaluation against USGS observations. The tool is designed to run as a standalone notebook locally or in cloud environments, including CIROH cyberinfrastructure.
supporting_quote: we introduce "FIM as a Service (FIMserv)", an open-source toolset that streamlines OWP HAND-FIM predictions with enhanced functionalities
(1) FIM generation from retrospective and forecasted NWM discharge
(3) FIM from Group on Earth Observations Global Water Sustainability (GeoGLOWS) discharge
FIMserv operates as a standalone notebook on local/cloud systems and as a Community Resource within the CIROH cloud cyberinfrastructure.

chunks.text: A key objective is to replicate the environment-configuration role of Docker without containerization, improving usability in notebook-based platforms. FIMserv uses localized environment variable files to manage required OWP HAND-FIM paths and dependencies, allowing dynamic adaptation to the user’s system. The tool emphasizes a user-friendly notebook interface, embedded visualization, and flexibility across local and cloud execution contexts. This goal directly targets broader accessibility for non-technical users and collaborative environments.
supporting_quote: This approach leverages virtual. env files to define essential environment variables, such as input and output directories
By replicating Docker's role in environment configuration in a simplified manner, this method bypasses containerization
FIMserv includes the following additional functionalities: - 1. User-friendly and customizable notebook interface - 2. Embedded visualization - 3. Flexibility to run both locally and on the cloud

chunks.text: Operational HAND-based inundation mapping represents an accuracy–applicability trade-off and carries known conceptual limitations. HAND methods often act as an inundation proxy and can miss floodplain spillover behavior. The approach assumes inundated areas drain toward a nearby flow path and that the drainage network collectively drains to a single outlet. These assumptions can reduce realism in certain hydrologic and floodplain settings.
supporting_quote: HAND methods generate an inundation proxy and often fail to capture spillover effects across the floodplain.
The HAND method also assumes that all inundated areas must drain toward a nearby flow path
and that the thalweg network drains collectively to a single outlet point

chunks.text: Although OWP HAND-FIM is open source, running it remains challenging for many end users because the published workflow relies on Docker. Some widely used interactive notebook environments do not support Docker natively. This creates a practical barrier to rapid prototyping and education-oriented usage. The paper positions FIMserv as a response to these usability constraints.
supporting_quote: end users often face challenges in configuring and running the model to generate FIMs.
The published version relies exclusively on Docker for FIM execution.
Google Colab and JupyterHub via 2i2c ... currently do not natively support Docker.

chunks.text: OWP HAND-FIM generates inundation by hydro-conditioning a 10 m DEM to create HAND grids and a hydrofabric with reach attributes and synthetic rating curves. For each NWM river segment, Manning-based SRCs translate discharge (m3/s) into stage (m). The stage is applied to the HAND raster to inundate the floodplain and produce a binary flood map. Outputs are saved as GeoTIFF at 10 m resolution.
supporting_quote: The model involves a series of DEM hydro-conditioning processes
Synthetic Rating Curves (SRCs). SRCs are calculated for each NWM river segment using Manning's equation to translate the discharge (m3 /sec) into a stage (m).
produce a binary FIM output saved in GeoTiff format.

chunks.text: FIMserv is implemented as a modular Python package with notebook-oriented execution. It uses a DownloadHUC8 module to set up code/input/output directories and retrieve pre-processed HAND grids for a user-selected HUC-8 (optionally filtered by stream order). It then clones the OWP inundation-mapping repository and creates a localized .env file to manage required environment variables. This structure supports repeatable runs without Docker while keeping OWP code compatibility.
supporting_quote: Within the working directory, the DownloadHUC8 module generates three primary subdirectories: code, input, and output
The second step is to clone the OWP HAND-FIM source code from GitHub into the code directory
This process also creates a localized environment (.env) file within the code directory to manage essential variables.

chunks.text: FIMserv automates acquisition of NWMv3.0 retrospective discharge from NOAA’s public AWS S3 bucket using feature_id identifiers. Retrospective discharge is hourly and spans 1979–2023, provided in parquet format, and is downloaded for the reaches within a selected HUC-8 and event period. Forecast discharge is retrieved from Google Cloud Storage in NetCDF format for short-, medium-, and long-range horizons. Downloaded discharge is stored as CSV in the input directory for subsequent inundation mapping.
supporting_quote: The NWMv3.0 retrospective dataset consists of hourly simulated historical discharge data available from 1979 to 2023.
These datasets are stored in a public NOAA AWS S3 bucket ... and are provided in parquet format
This dataset is stored in Google Cloud ... and is provided in NetCDF (.nc) format.

chunks.text: To generate flood maps, the runOWPHANDFIM module combines discharge inputs from the input directory with downloaded HAND grids to produce binary inundation rasters at 10 m resolution. Users can generate time-series flood maps at the temporal resolution of the discharge data, with unique filenames based on event date. The framework also supports subsetting by user-defined boundaries via subsetFIM and includes interactive visualization using geemap and localtileserver. Visualization requires a Google Earth Engine project ID.
supporting_quote: the "runOWPHANDFIM" module uses discharge data from the input directory and the downloaded HAND grids (HUC-8 scale) to generate binary FIMs at a 10-m resolution.
Another sub-setting functionality, "subsetFIM", allows users to mask out specific portions of the flood inundation maps based on an Area of Interest (AOI) shapefile.
users need to have a valid Google Earth Engine account and create a projectID.

chunks.text: FIMserv integrates GeoGLOWS discharge by spatially joining GeoGLOWS streamlines with NWM flowlines and transferring identifiers. A conservative 100 m buffer around GeoGLOWS lines is used to join with NWM flowline midpoints, then connectivity tracing adds downstream-aligned segments. The GeoGLOWS LINKNO attribute is appended to NWM flowlines to enable discharge retrieval by LINKNO and assignment back to NWM feature_id. A dedicated module, getGEOGLOWSstreamflow, downloads GeoGLOWS discharge for an event date and prepares it for inundation mapping.
supporting_quote: For spatial joining, a conservative 100 m buffer was created around the GeoGLOWS streamlines.
After this, the LINKNO field from the GeoGLOWS streamline was appended to the corresponding NWM flowline
we have developed a module ... "getGEOGLOWSstreamflow". It is callable with "fimserve.getGEOGLOWSstreamflow (huc, event_time, hydrotable)".

chunks.text: FIMserv provides discharge comparison between NWM and USGS observations for NWM reaches associated with USGS gauges within the selected HUC-8. It retrieves USGS gauge IDs intersecting NWM reaches, downloads USGS time series, and computes summary metrics. The implemented statistics include Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE), Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), and percent bias (pBIAS). These diagnostics quantify flow uncertainties that can propagate to inundation maps.
supporting_quote: FIMserv includes functionality for statistical evaluation of NWM discharge predictions against USGS gauge data
Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE) ... Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) ... and percent bias (pBIAS) is considered to quantify the error
Table 4 Statistical metrics used in discharge comparison.

chunks.text: The paper describes FIM evaluation using benchmark inundation maps derived from remote sensing and synthetic hydraulic modeling. For Hurricane Matthew flooding in North Carolina, benchmarks come from high-resolution Planet imagery enhanced with a hydrologically guided region grow algorithm. For Oklahoma, benchmarks are HEC-RAS-derived synthetic inundation maps using 100- and 500-year return period flows (Base Level Engineering). A pixel-based framework (FIMPEF) computes F1 score, probability of detection (POD), and critical success index (CSI).
supporting_quote: validated against two sets of benchmarks FIM derived from 1) High-resolution Remote sensing flood maps for Hurricane Matthew flooding
and 2) HEC-RAS derived synthetic FIM (100 and 500-year return period flow) referred to as Base Level Engineering (BLE)
A pixel-based evaluation framework Flood Inundation Mapping Prediction Evaluation Framework (FIMPEF) ... is used to calculate the performance scores (Table-6).

chunks.text: FIMserv uses pre-processed OWP HAND raster hydrofabric data at 10 m resolution for CONUS, distributed via CIROH’s public S3 bucket. It uses NWMv3.0 retrospective hourly discharge (1979–2023) from NOAA’s public AWS S3 bucket and NWMv3.0 forecast discharge from Google Cloud in NetCDF format. It also supports GeoGLOWS discharge products (global retrospective and forecast) as a potential alternative input. Supporting lookup datasets include HUC-8 IDs, NWM river IDs, and USGS gauge sites hosted via ArcGIS Online.
supporting_quote: OWP-HAND raster 10m HAND raster across CONUS ... CIROH s3 bucket (s3://ciroh-owp-hand-fim)
NWMv3.0 retrospective discharge Hourly Discharge across CONUS (1979–2023)
NWMv3.0 forecast discharge Long-range ... Medium-range ... Short-range
GeoGLOWS Global 3 hourly/Daily Discharge data (1940–Current)
HUC-8 ID, NWM River ID and USGS gauge sites ... ArcGIS Online

chunks.text: The NWMv3.0 retrospective dataset provides hourly simulated historical discharge for 1979–2023 and is accessed using NWM stream network identifiers (feature_id). Forecast products are organized by horizon: short-range (18 h), medium-range (10 days), and long-range (30 days). Forecast data are stored in Google Cloud Storage and provided in NetCDF format for extraction by feature_id. FIMserv converts these into CSV discharge inputs for inundation mapping.
supporting_quote: The NWMv3.0 retrospective dataset consists of hourly simulated historical discharge data available from 1979 to 2023.
NWMv3.0 discharge forecasts are available for three forecast horizons: (a) short-range (18 h), (b) medium-range (10 days), and (c) longrange (30 days)
This dataset is stored in Google Cloud ... and is provided in NetCDF (.nc) format.

chunks.text: GeoGLOWS v2.0 is described as a global discharge dataset based on ECMWF forcing and Muskingum channel routing. It includes more than 7 million streams and 125 computational watersheds. Retrospective discharge spans 80 years (1940–2020) at daily resolution, while forecasts range from 3-hourly to 15-day horizons for 2021–current. In FIMserv, GeoGLOWS is accessed via unique LINKNO identifiers after joining with NWM flowlines.
supporting_quote: The latest version, Geo-GLOWS v2.0, includes more than 7 million streams and 125 computational watersheds.
retrospective discharge data ... available for 80 years (1940–2020) at a daily temporal resolution
forecasted discharge data ranging from 3-h to 15-day (2021-Current).

chunks.text: The authors demonstrate automated generation of flood inundation maps using NWM retrospective discharge and NWM forecasts (short-, medium-, and long-range). Short-range forecasts produce hourly maps up to 18 hours, medium-range produces 10 daily maximum maps, and long-range produces 30 daily maximum maps. FIMserv can default to the current date-time when not specified. It can also select maximum, minimum, or average discharge values from forecast ensembles to drive mapping.
supporting_quote: The short-range forecast provides deterministic discharge predictions at an hourly interval for up to 18 h.
The medium-range forecast ... every 3 h for up to 10 days
For the long-range forecast, daily maximum FIMs for 30 days are generated ... The medium-range forecast generates 10 daily maximum FIMs, while the short-range forecast produces 18 hourly FIMs.
By default, FIMserv selects the maximum discharge values from the forecast, but users can customize this ... based on maximum, minimum, or average discharge.

chunks.text: Computational testing across 66 randomly selected HUC-8 watersheds shows runtime increases with watershed area. A fourfold increase in catchment area (900–22000 km2) led to roughly a sixfold increase in computation time (30–180 seconds) for the tested setup. Platform tests on a single HUC-8 (17020006; 12,120.92 km2) indicate total workflow times of 3.3 minutes (Google Colab), 3.05 minutes (Windows-11), and 2.2 minutes (Mac). The paper also cites an in-prep comparison indicating much longer runtimes for LISFLOOD-FP and HEC-RAS versus FIMserv.
supporting_quote: tested on 66 randomly selected HUC-8s across the United States
a factor of four increase in catchment area (900–22000 km2 ) yielded a computational time increased by a factor of 6 (30 s–180 s
HUC-8 watershed (ID: 17020006), which has a catchment area of 12,120.92 km2
Google Colab ... Time (min) 3.3 ... Windows-11 ... 3.05 ... Mac ... 2.2
FIMserv takes approximately 1 min for data downloading and FIM generation, whereas LISFLOOD-FP and HEC-RAS required between 4 h and 17 days

chunks.text: The tool supports domain filtering by river stream order, enabling users to generate inundation maps for only higher-order streams. This is motivated by evaluation challenges where remote-sensing benchmark flood extents often exclude small tributaries. The paper demonstrates this for the Middle Neuse watershed (HUC 03020202), comparing full-domain results with results using stream_order > 3. Such filtering can make model outputs more comparable to benchmark maps and tailored to user needs.
supporting_quote: FIMserv can filter and subset the (HUC-8) study domain based on river stream order.
Benchmarks flood inundation maps derived from remote sensing imagery, often exclude small tributaries
This functionality is demonstrated in the Middle Neuse watershed, North Carolina (hucID − 03020202) ... for higher-order streams (stream_order>3).

chunks.text: In a discharge comparison example for the Middle Neuse watershed (feature_ids 11239465 and 11239241; USGS gauges 02089500 and 02091814) over 2015–2022, NWM discharge achieved satisfactory efficiency scores but showed high bias. The paper reports KGE and NSE values greater than 0.7 while pBIAS exceeded 30%. This highlights that good correlation/efficiency can coexist with substantial volume bias. The diagnostic supports interpreting downstream inundation uncertainty.
supporting_quote: Middle Neuse watershed ... for two NWM river segments (feature_ids = 11239465, 11239241) having USGS gauges (ID:02089500, 02091814) for the year 2015–2022.
we found that the NWM discharge exhibits satisfactory KGE and NSE score (>0.7) with respect to observed flow
however, there is a relatively higher value of pBIAS, (pBIAS>30 %).

chunks.text: The plotSRC module allows inspection of synthetic rating curves and stage values for specified reaches. In the Upper Clear Fork Brazos watershed (HUC 12060102), the paper reports example stage lookups for two feature IDs. For feature_id 5490493, a discharge of 3000 m3/s maps to a stage of 8.23 m; for feature_id 5490541, 3500 m3/s maps to 9.75 m. This helps users interpret how discharge translates to inundation-driving stage.
supporting_quote: This functionality is demonstrated for the Upper Clear Fork Brazos (hucID-12060102)
for feature-id 5490493, a discharge of 3000 m3 /s corresponds to a stage of 8.23 m
for feature-id 5490541, a discharge of 3500 m3 /s corresponds to a stage of 9.75 m

chunks.text: A GeoGLOWS vs NWM discharge comparison for Middle Brazos Lake Whitney (HUC 12060202) in 2016 shows mixed performance depending on metric and station. For USGS gauge 08091000, NWM had NSE 0.21 and pBIAS 158.11%, while GeoGLOWS had NSE 0.01 and pBIAS 91.44%; for another station (reported as USGS gauge ID 08091500), NWM had NSE 0.55 and pBIAS 70.15% while GeoGLOWS had NSE 0.06 and pBIAS 69.37%. The results illustrate that neither dataset is universally superior and that bias can be large in both.
supporting_quote: Table 5 Comparison of GeoGLOWS and NWM discharge for the year 2016.
NWM ... NSE 0.21 ... pBIAS 158.11 ... GeoGLOWS ... NSE 0.01 ... pBIAS 91.44
NWM ... NSE 0.55 ... pBIAS 70.15 ... GeoGLOWS ... NSE 0.06 ... pBIAS 69.37

chunks.text: For a low-flow event in Middle Brazos Lake Whitney on October 15, 2016, NWM and GeoGLOWS produced similar inundation extents. The reported maximum discharge was 29.88 m3/s (NWM) versus 24.85 m3/s (GeoGLOWS), and the paper suggests SRC-derived stage was not sensitive to that small difference. For a peak-flow event on June 2, 2016, NWM predicted 549 m3/s while GeoGLOWS predicted 234.22 m3/s, leading to underestimation of stage and inundation extent for GeoGLOWS-driven maps. This demonstrates how discharge bias propagates through SRCs to mapped flood extent.
supporting_quote: On October 15, the maximum predicted discharge from NWM for the catchment was 29.88 m3 /s, while GeoGLOWS predicted 24.85 m3 /s. The resulting FIM extents were found to be nearly identical
During the peak-flow event on June 2, the maximum predicted NWM flow ... was 549 m3 /s, while GeoGLOWS predicted 234.22 m3 /s.
This underprediction in streamflow from GeoGLOWS translated into an underestimation of stage from the SRC and to the FIM extent

chunks.text: Benchmark evaluation for Hurricane Matthew in North Carolina reports moderate-to-satisfactory pixel-based performance. For October 10, CSI was 0.63, POD 0.88, and F1 0.77; for October 14, CSI dropped to 0.55, POD to 0.68, and F1 to 0.61. These scores indicate the method detects much of the flooded area but performance varies across dates. The results support FIMserv as a rapid operational mapping option rather than a high-fidelity solver.
supporting_quote: On October 10, the CSI score was 0.63, the POD was 0.88, and the F1 score was 0.77.
On October 14, the CSI score dropped to 0.55, the POD to 0.68, and the F1 score to 0.61

chunks.text: For synthetic flooding benchmarks in Oklahoma using BLE/HEC-RAS extents, average scores are reported for both 100- and 500-year return period flows. For 100-year flow, mean CSI is 0.6, mean F1 is 0.74, and mean POD is 0.72. For 500-year flow, mean CSI is 0.63, mean F1 is 0.77, and mean POD is 0.75. The distributions suggest stable performance across multiple HUC-8 watersheds for scenario-based mapping.
supporting_quote: for 100-year return period flow, the mean values of CSI, F1, and POD were 0.6, 0.74, and 0.72, respectively.
for a 500-year return period flow, the mean values of CSI, F1, and POD were estimated as 0.63, 0.77, and 0.75, respectively

chunks.text: When comparing NWM-driven inundation (NWM-FIM) to USGS-driven inundation (USGS-FIM) in the Upper Neuse watershed on Oct 9, 2016, the paper reports overall satisfactory agreement except one station. The mean CSI across five stations was 0.62, mean POD 0.81, and mean F1 0.76; the median CSI was 0.55, median POD 0.69, and median F1 0.71. A notable underprediction occurred at station 020868449 due to NWM underestimating discharge (18.54 m3/s predicted vs 91.22 m3/s observed). This illustrates how flow errors can dominate inundation mismatch at specific locations.
supporting_quote: The mean CSI score across the five stations was 0.62, the mean POD was 0.81, and the mean F1 score was 0.76.
The median CSI score was 0.55, the median POD was 0.69, and the median F1 score was 0.71.
The predicted flow from NWM was 18.54 m3 /s, while the observed flow was 91.22 m3 /s.

chunks.text: HAND-based flood mapping has structural limitations that can affect realism, especially across complex floodplains. The paper notes that HAND often produces an inundation proxy and may not capture spillover effects. It also assumes inundated areas drain toward a nearby flow path and that the network drains collectively to a single outlet. These assumptions represent known caveats when interpreting FIMserv outputs based on OWP HAND-FIM.
supporting_quote: HAND methods generate an inundation proxy and often fail to capture spillover effects across the floodplain.
HAND method also assumes that all inundated areas must drain toward a nearby flow path
and that the thalweg network drains collectively to a single outlet point

chunks.text: FIMserv currently relies on existing OWP-produced HAND rasters and does not provide terrain conditioning as part of the tool. Users who want to test alternative DEM resolutions or conditioning choices must run the separate OWP HAND pipeline to generate new HAND inputs. This limits experimentation within FIMserv to discharge inputs and downstream mapping steps. The design emphasizes operational usability over end-to-end terrain processing.
supporting_quote: Currently, FIMserv uses the 10m HAND rasters generated by NOAA OWP ... and does not offer terrain conditioning capabilities to users.
if a user wants to evaluate the impact of different DEM resolutions on FIM, they must follow the HAND pipeline developed by OWP and use the processed HAND rasters as input

chunks.text: The GeoGLOWS integration in the current framework is limited to retrospective discharge. The paper states that GeoGLOWS forecast discharge is not yet supported but planned for future versions. This constrains GeoGLOWS-based FIM generation to daily retrospective workflows rather than real-time forecasting. As a result, forecast comparisons still rely on NWM forecast products.
supporting_quote: Currently, the framework only supports the use of retrospective GeoGLOWS discharge data.
However, in future versions, GeoGLOWS forecast discharge will also be integrated.

chunks.text: FIMserv’s discharge comparison tools do not apply bias correction or statistical adjustments to NWM or GeoGLOWS flows. Instead, the framework exposes bias and uncertainty through metrics such as KGE, NSE, and pBIAS to support user judgment. This means inundation maps may directly reflect biases in input hydrographs. Users must decide whether and how to correct flows before mapping.
supporting_quote: The framework does not apply any bias correction or statistical adjustments to the GeoGLOWS or NWM discharge data.
Instead, this functionality helps users understand the bias and uncertainty associated with the input flow data.

chunks.text: The paper frames FIMserv as a pragmatic trade-off between accuracy and usability, rather than a replacement for high-fidelity hydrodynamic solvers. Although performance scores are not described as outstanding, the tool is argued to be efficient given limited input requirements and rapid runtimes. It requires only 10 m HAND rasters and streamflow data, both accessible through the platform. This positioning clarifies appropriate use cases such as rapid mapping and scenario testing.
supporting_quote: although the performance scores may not be outstanding, FIMserv offers an efficient and practical platform for rapid flood inundation mapping.
It represents a reasonable trade-off between accuracy and usability
The model requires only two primary inputs for FIM generation 10m HAND rasters and streamflow data

chunks.text: The paper concludes that FIMserv is an efficient, user-friendly toolset that streamlines the OWP HAND-FIM inundation mapping module and runs on local workstations and cloud platforms. It extends the original workflow with features including stream-order/AOI subsetting, discharge evaluation versus USGS, use of NWM retrospective and forecasts, SRC visualization, and GeoGLOWS daily discharge support. The authors emphasize cross-platform usability (Windows, macOS, and cloud notebook environments). Overall, FIMserv is positioned as enabling rapid 10 m operational flood maps with minimal effort for a broad user community.
supporting_quote: we present an efficient and user-friendly Flood Inundation Mapping (FIM) toolset (FIMserv) based on the NOAA Office of Water Prediction (OWP) operational hydrological forecasting framework.
FIMserv introduces functionalities beyond the original OWP HAND-FIM framework including (1) domain filtering based on river stream order and AOI, (2) accuracy assessment ... against USGS discharge
enabling them to generate high-resolution (10m) operational flood maps with minimal effort.

chunks.text: Future development directions include integrating additional discharge datasets (e.g., SWOT), improving visualization via open-source web mapping, adding building footprints for risk/vulnerability analysis, and deploying a WebGIS portal as part of CIROH. These plans aim to broaden data inputs and move from notebook-based use toward web-service delivery. The roadmap also suggests extending operational relevance beyond inundation mapping to exposure and impact studies. This aligns with the paper’s emphasis on accessibility and community use.
supporting_quote: Further development of FIMserv will include (1) introduction of additional discharge dataset (e.g. SWOT)
(3) inclusion of building footprints for risk and vulnerability studies, and (4) development of a webGIS portal for deployment as a web service

chunks.text: Colorado extreme precipitation arises from multiple storm types interacting with complex terrain, producing strong spatial and seasonal variability. Areas west of the Continental Divide tend to receive most precipitation in the cool season, while the Front Range and eastern plains are more warm-season dominated. Orographic effects and varied moisture pathways make extremes difficult to anticipate and categorize using a single storm archetype.
supporting_quote: Extreme weather triggered by multiple storm types pose significant challenges to both forecasting and water resources management in Colorado (CO

Regions located west of the Continental Divide receive most of their precipitation during the cool season, whereas regions located on the Front Range and the Eastern plains receive most of their precipitation during the warm season.

chunks.text: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are corridors of enhanced integrated vapor transport (IVT) associated with a low-level jet within extratropical cyclones in midlatitude westerlies. When AR IVT intersects major mountain barriers, it can produce large orographic precipitation and strongly influence the western U.S. water cycle. Some West Coast landfalling ARs can penetrate inland through topographic gaps and contribute to interior precipitation extremes.
supporting_quote: Landfalling ARs along the West Coast of North America are regions of enhanced integrated vapor transport (IVT) along a low‐level jet stream (LLJ)

Previousstudies demonstrated the pathways by which cool‐season ARs landfalling on the West Coast can penetrate inland through gaps in these major mountain barriers and influence precipitation across the interior West

chunks.text: Gulf of America ARs can transport moisture poleward via cyclones and low-level jets, and can also reflect anticyclonic transport around the North Atlantic Subtropical High (NASH). The Great Plains low-level jet (GPLLJ), including both baroclinic and thermally driven components, can contribute to warm-season hazards like flash flooding and severe weather. These diverse mechanisms motivate separating Colorado extremes by synoptic regime and moisture-transport pathway.
supporting_quote: These Gulf of America ARs also have an upstream continental cyclone and LLJ that facilitates poleward water vapor transport
The development of an AR over the Central Plains is also likely a combination of poleward water vapor transport by both a baroclinic‐forced LLJ
The GPLLJ moisture transport is often implicated in contributing to warm‐season severe hail, tornadoes, and flash flooding

chunks.text: The study aims to classify synoptic regimes associated with Colorado top-decile precipitation days and quantify how much precipitation in each regime is associated with inland-penetrating ARs. It focuses on distinguishing contributions from West Coast ARs, Gulf of America ARs, and non-AR precipitation. The intent is to provide a storm-typing framework that supports future evaluations of predictability and forecast skill for high-impact precipitation extremes.
supporting_quote: The goal of this paper is to classify these synoptic regimes associated with top‐decile precipitation days across CO HUC8
quantify the contributions of West Coast ARs, Gulf of America ARs, and non‐ARs with these regimes.

chunks.text: A further objective is to leverage the AR framework to compute regime-specific AR probabilities and anomalies leading up to top-decile events. By examining AR probability two days prior through the event day, the authors seek to connect regime evolution with anomalous AR occurrence. Representative storm case studies are used to illustrate processes and impacts for each regime.
supporting_quote: Anomalous AR probability on and 2 days prior to the top‐decile precipitation events for each regime was computed
Representative storm examples were analyzed from each regime to illustrate processes related to top‐decile precipitation in CO.

chunks.text: Forecasting and managing extreme precipitation in Colorado is challenging because of complex terrain and the presence of multiple storm types and moisture pathways across seasons. This complexity yields spatially and seasonally anomalous extremes, complicating process-based understanding and prediction. The paper frames the need to categorize synoptic processes and quantify AR associations as a way to address this challenge.
supporting_quote: Forecasting precipitation in Colorado (CO) is challenging due to the complex terrain and multiple storm types that bring precipitation throughout the year.

The complex topography of CO and its influence on orographic precipitation during periods of moisture transport via multiple pathways result in spatially and seasonally anomalous extreme precipitation

chunks.text: The authors define top-decile precipitation days as those when any Colorado HUC8 basin daily precipitation exceeds the 90th percentile for 1981–2023. They then apply k-means clustering to 3,025 such days to identify distinct synoptic regimes. The clustering uses a set of least-correlated ERA5 variables averaged over Colorado, including 700-hPa specific humidity and winds and temperature at 700 and 500 hPa.
supporting_quote: The top‐ decile precipitation days are defined as days when daily precipitation in any HUC8 watershed exceeded the 90th percentile of the climatological period from 1981 to 2023.
We applied k‐means clustering to categorize regimes over the 3,025 top‐decile precipitation days in CO.
The clustering algorithm was initialized using a set of least correlated meteorological variables from the ERA5 reanalysis

chunks.text: Four regimes are selected from the k-means solution and analyzed via composite fields and representative case studies. The analysis uses ERA5 to create composites of sea-level pressure, geopotential height, IVT, and precipitation for each regime. Case-study storms are used as illustrative examples of mechanisms and impacts within each regime.
supporting_quote: Four regimes were identified from the clustering algorithm which were further analyzed using composite analyses and representative case‐studies
The synoptic analysis of the geopotential height, sea‐level pressure (SLP), IVT, and precipitation within the regimes, as well as for independent storms representative of each regime

chunks.text: AR occurrence is quantified using the Guan & Waliser ERA5 AR catalog and an IVT-feature-based detection approach. Detection uses seasonal IVT thresholds from the 85th–95th percentile with a minimum of 100 kg m−1 s−1, and geometric filters requiring IVT length > 2,000 km and length-to-width ratio > 2. The study notes ARs are identified solely from IVT structures, while the associated physical mechanisms are inferred through regime characterization.
supporting_quote: We used a catalog of ARs developed by Guan & Waliser (2024) using the ERA5 data set
The IVT threshold for AR detection was specified seasonally, ranging from the 85th to 95th percentile, with a lower limit of 100 kg m−1 s−1
Further filtering of ARs in the algorithm is based on length of IVT > 2,000 km and length‐to‐width ratio >2.
It should be noted here that ARs were identified based solely on IVT features.

chunks.text: Within each regime, AR probability is defined as the fraction of top-decile days that contain an AR. The authors compute anomalous AR probability for the event day and two days prior as the difference between regime AR probability and a regime-weighted climatological monthly AR probability. This links regime timing (monthly distribution) with AR anomalies preceding extremes.
supporting_quote: The "AR probability" in this study is defined as the fraction of days containing an AR among all days with top‐decile precipitation within each regime.

Anomalous AR probability on and 2 days prior to the top‐decile precipitation events for each regime was computed as the difference between the average regime AR probability and regime‐weighted climatological monthly AR probability.

chunks.text: AR contributions to top-decile precipitation are computed by summing precipitation on days when inland-penetrating ARs made landfall along the West Coast or the Gulf Coast. This approach separates precipitation totals associated with West Coast ARs, Gulf of America ARs, and non-AR days. The regime-based annual distributions are then compared across years.
supporting_quote: The contribution of ARs to top‐decile precipitation is calculated by summing precipitation on days when inland‐penetrating ARs made landfall along the West Coast or the Gulf Coast.
Annual distribution of top‐decile precipitation from inland penetrating West Coast ARs, Gulf of America ARs, and non‐ARs

chunks.text: The analysis uses precipitation aggregated over 92 HUC8 basins in Colorado (including basins intersecting seven other states), with basin boundaries from the USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset. Daily precipitation comes from PRISM, a 4 km × 4 km gridded product combining gauge, radar, and other datasets and interpolated using elevation and topographic information. Daily totals correspond to a 24-hr period ending at 1200 UTC.
