chunks.text: Because SAMs are monolayers, charge transport within the SAM-HTL and its exact functional mechanism remain debated. The review notes unresolved questions about whether SAMs primarily modify work functions or directly assist extraction and transport. This uncertainty is presented as a barrier to rational optimization and standardization of SAM contacts across different device stacks.
supporting_quote: understanding the charge transport within these HTLs remains challenging
ongoing debates about their function in modifying work functions or assisting with charge extraction and transport

chunks.text: Thermal and photostability of SAM-based HTLs remains a concern, especially because inverted PSCs place the SAM at the light incident side. The review highlights degradation of MeO-2PACz under light and electrochemical conditions and motivates molecular redesign. It discusses stabilizing modifications such as replacing alkyl linkers with conjugated phenylene to enhance charge delocalization and stability.
supporting_quote: concerns regarding their thermal and light stability... wherein the SAM layer is located at the light incident side
MeO-2PACz... undergoes significant degradation under light and electrochemical conditions.
substituting alkyl linkers with a conjugated phenylene group... enhancing the light and electrochemical stability

chunks.text: The paper notes that SAMs used as electron-transport materials in n-i-p devices generally underperform compared with traditional metal-oxide ETLs such as TiO2 and SnO2. This constrains SAM adoption as ETMs, even though they can reduce hysteresis and improve interfacial behavior in some cases. The review therefore treats ETM applications as less mature than SAM-HTLs.
supporting_quote: However, in n-i-p structures, SAMs used as ETMs tend to yield lower performance than traditional metal oxide substrates like TiO2 and SnO2.

chunks.text: Commercial integration requires that SAMs be compatible with scalable manufacturing while maintaining robustness. The review implies that interfacial defects, stability under outdoor stressors (oxygen, light, water), and incomplete mechanistic understanding remain key obstacles. It frames these as needing both new molecular designs and better characterization to support reliable scale-up.
supporting_quote: Degradation caused by oxygen, light, and water is a major factor contributing to their reduced stability.
several key challenges... Choosing an anchoring group that forms a strong covalent bond with the surface of the TCO is vital.

chunks.text: The review concludes that SAMs are promising HTLs for high-performance PSCs because they can improve efficiency through better energy-level tuning and reduced interfacial recombination while also simplifying processing. It highlights that SAMs can enable lower-cost, solution-processed, scalable selective contacts compatible with large-area and flexible devices. The paper emphasizes that continued progress depends on improved molecular design and deeper mechanistic understanding.
supporting_quote: SAMs have recently emerged as a promising type of molecule for wide use as the HTL of high-performance PSCs.
Simplified manufacturing process: Compared with traditional HTL materials, SAMs can be prepared through a straightforward solution-processing method
Scalability: SAMs' self-assembly properties allow their application on large areas and flexible substrates

chunks.text: The paper provides design recommendations for high-performance SAMs, prioritizing strong anchoring groups, appropriate functional groups for energy levels, and molecular planarity and intermolecular interactions for ordered packing. It also stresses the need for environmental stability, including thermal and photostability, for outdoor operation. These guidelines are presented as a roadmap for future SAM development in PSCs.
supporting_quote: Anchoring groups: Choosing an anchoring group that forms a strong covalent bond with the surface of the TCO is vital.
Molecular planarity and intermolecular interactions (such as π-π stacking) are crucial for forming ordered SAMs.
Environmental stability... SAMs molecules should have good thermal and photostability

chunks.text: River routing is essential for simulating how runoff converges through networks and controls flood peak timing and magnitude in stem rivers. Traditional routing methods (e.g., Muskingum-Cunge) are widely used but require parameter choices that represent channel geometry and flow resistance. These properties influence flood wave propagation and therefore the coincidence and size of downstream flood peaks.
supporting_quote: Routing describes how the stream network conveys runoff downstream while accounting for mass balances and the speed of flood wave propagation
The timing of flood convergence and peak flood rates are influenced by the channel's geometries and flow resistance properties

chunks.text: Large-scale routing parameterization is difficult because reach-scale heterogeneity is hard to represent and field-based roughness selection is impractical at scale. Many calibration efforts use one parameter set for an entire basin, which can neglect spatial variability. Some simplified relationships for roughness have been proposed, but their realism relative to data is uncertain.
supporting_quote: they have been difficult to parameterize at large scales, especially in a way to both sensibly represent basin-internal spatial heterogeneity and adapt to discharge data
Many calibration exercises ... have used only one set of parameters for an entire basin, neglecting fine-scale spatial heterogeneity in river-reach characteristics

chunks.text: Deep learning has improved rainfall-runoff modeling, but these advances have not been widely applied to routing modules that matter for large heterogeneous basins. Differentiable modeling, enabled by automatic differentiation, provides a way to couple neural networks with physical formulations and train parameters end-to-end while keeping physical priors. This approach may offer interpretability and better extrapolation than purely data-driven networks.
supporting_quote: these methods have not been applied to routing modules in order to benefit the simulation of stem river floods
"Differentiable" models can rapidly and accurately compute the gradients of the model outputs with respect to any input

chunks.text: The study aims to develop a differentiable routing framework that mimics Muskingum-Cunge routing across a river network while learning reach-scale parameterizations from attributes using a neural network. The learned parameters are intended to be inferred only from downstream hydrograph training signals, enabling end-to-end training without direct supervision for the parameters themselves. The work evaluates whether this improves routing for large basins with heterogeneous runoff sources.
supporting_quote: We present a novel differentiable routing method (δMC-JuniatahydroDL2) that mimics the classical Muskingum-Cunge routing model over a river network but embeds an NN to infer parameterizations for Manning's roughness (n) and channel geometries
the whole framework is trained together based on the overall loss function. The loss function ... was calculated at the furthest downstream node of the graph

chunks.text: A central goal is to test identifiability: whether downstream discharge observations contain sufficient information to recover reach-scale relationships, especially Manning’s roughness n and channel geometry parameter q. The authors use synthetic parameter-recovery experiments to quantify what can and cannot be learned. They then examine whether short real-data training windows can produce parameterizations that generalize across years.
supporting_quote: Synthetic experiments show that while the channel geometry parameter was unidentifiable, n can be identified with moderate precision.

Do short periods of downstream discharge contain sufficient information to train a reliable parameterization scheme or to identify the parameterizations for channel roughness and hydraulic geometries?

chunks.text: The work explicitly asks whether routing parameterizations can be learned despite substantial errors in runoff inputs produced by a separate rainfall-runoff model. It also evaluates whether learned parameterizations improve performance at untrained inner gages and how performance changes with basin drainage area. These questions are framed to assess utility in large river networks.
supporting_quote: Given substantial errors with estimated runoff as inputs to the routing module, can we learn effective routing parameterization schemes that can produce reliable results for long-term simulations in large river networks?
Do the learned parameterization perform well for both trained and untrained downstream/upstream gages and how does performance vary as a function of basin area?

chunks.text: Routing parameters are influential yet hard to estimate at scale because commonly used methods rely on lookup tables or calibration and often assume basin homogeneity. This can omit reach-to-reach heterogeneity in channel properties such as roughness. Practical acquisition of Manning’s n via field scouting is infeasible for large-scale applications.
supporting_quote: routing parameters often rank among the important ones for discharge simulation ... they have been difficult to parameterize at large scales
Using traditional roughness values tabulated for various land covers ... requires in situ scouting ... which is currently impractical for large-scale applications

chunks.text: Pure deep-learning approaches tend to work better for smaller, more homogeneous headwater basins and may underrepresent spatial heterogeneity in forcings and basin characteristics. Large basins can exhibit poorer performance for LSTM models, motivating explicit routing across heterogeneous subbasins. Routing is needed to account for flow convergence and timing in stem rivers.
supporting_quote: these approaches are mostly suitable for relatively homogeneous headwater basins; spatial heterogeneities in forcings and basin characteristics are generally not well represented
In our previous studies we observed that large basins often have poorer performance for LSTM models than smaller basins

chunks.text: Learning in a complex river network is challenging because the hierarchical graph can be deep in space and time, potentially causing vanishing gradients during training. Additionally, routing depends on runoff inputs that must often be modeled rather than observed, and such errors could obstruct learning routing parameters. It is unclear whether downstream discharge alone can identify reach-scale relationships given integrated signals.
supporting_quote: could potentially lead to a training issue known as the vanishing gradient
runoff data ... must be estimated by models, but models for runoff could incur substantial errors which could potentially prevent the routing parameters from being learned
it was further unclear if downstream discharge data alone contain enough information to enable learning of reach-scale relationships

chunks.text: Channel hydraulic geometry parameters used in routing may have weak influence on downstream hydrographs, raising identifiability concerns. The paper anticipates that some parameters (e.g., channel shape coefficients) might not be invertible from available data even if included for model completeness. This is a key risk for learning-based parameterization.
supporting_quote: we do not posit that q is invertible from available data because it may not be that significant for the downstream discharge
The non-identifiability of q was likely because q has only a small influence on the storage capacity of the stream

chunks.text: The authors implement a differentiable Muskingum-Cunge (MC) routing model over a river network in PyTorch, enabling automatic differentiation through the routing computations. This allows end-to-end training of a neural network that outputs reach-scale parameters used by MC. The overall loss is computed at the downstream-most node, and gradients are backpropagated through the network routing sequence.
supporting_quote: The model is programmatically differentiable as it is fully implemented in PyTorch, leveraging AD.
the whole framework is trained together based on the overall loss function. The loss function ... was calculated at the furthest downstream node of the graph

chunks.text: MC routing is formulated with a finite-difference update where outflow depends on current/next inflow, previous outflow, and lateral inflow. The method uses coefficients c1–c4 determined by timestep Δt, travel time K, and weighting X. K is set as reach length divided by wave celerity, updated each time step based on discharge-dependent velocity.
supporting_quote: We adopted the simple linear form of the Muskingum equation: X is constant and K = Δx/c

chunks.text: To update velocity and celerity, the study uses a power-law hydraulic geometry for top width as a function of depth, w = p d^q, and integrates to obtain cross-sectional area. Manning’s equation and discharge Q = v A are combined to solve for depth as a function of Q, n, slope, and q, then compute v and celerity (c = 5/3 v). The model assumes wide channels (d ≈ hydraulic radius) and uses simplifying assumptions to avoid numerical instability.
supporting_quote: w = pd^{q}
Manning's equation is: v = k/n R_h^{2/3} S_0^{1/2}
we can use d, n, p, S_0, and q, to estimate v, and then wave celerity, c = 5/3v

chunks.text: A multilayer perceptron (MLP) provides reach-scale parameterization by mapping normalized reach attributes to Manning’s n and channel shape q. The MLP has two hidden layers and a sigmoid output activation, and parameters are initialized with Xavier initialization and optimized with Adam. n and q are assumed time-invariant and computed per reach prior to routing.
supporting_quote: an MLP is incorporated, featuring two hidden layers and a sigmoid activation function in the output layer
The network then outputs the Manning's roughness coefficient (n) and channel bathymetry shape coefficient (q): n, q = NN(A_JRB)

chunks.text: Runoff inputs for routing are produced by a separate, pretrained LSTM rainfall-runoff model that outputs daily basin discharge for HUC10 watersheds. The LSTM is not updated during routing training to disentangle runoff errors from routing learning and test robustness. The daily runoff is disaggregated to hourly values via quadratic interpolation for use with the hourly MC timestep.
supporting_quote: we employed a pretrained LSTM ... and we chose not to further update the LSTM in order to disentangle the rainfall-runoff and routing parts
we quadratically interpolated ... daily data into hourly time steps

chunks.text: A mass transfer matrix maps HUC10 runoff to reach-scale lateral inflows by distributing subbasin runoff according to incremental reach catchment areas. The model accounts for time alignment issues by shifting runoff for time zone differences and applying an additional uniform inverse-routing shift τ. τ is treated as a hyperparameter and is tuned manually; the study uses τ = 9 hours across experiments.
supporting_quote: Lastly, we computed a mass transfer matrix, which tabulates the fraction of a subbasin draining into a river reach
we first shifted the LSTM-produced runoff outputs by 5 hr
we opted for a simple approach that shifted the runoff back in time by τ hours ... We found τ = 9 (hours)

chunks.text: Training uses 8-week windows, 50 epochs, and an hourly warm-up of 72 hours where loss is not computed to allow network states to stabilize. The loss includes mean squared error plus penalties to keep parameters within literature bounds and encourage monotonic behavior for low drainage area reaches. Hidden size and training setup were chosen through trial and error; the MLP hidden size is set to six.
supporting_quote: These trials led us to choose a hidden size of six for our MLP, and a training size of 8 weeks.
a period of 72 hr was employed to "warm up" the model states ... and the loss function and NSE were not calculated within this period
Our loss function is a combination of Mean Squared Error, a range-bound penalty, and a monotonic penalty

chunks.text: Three synthetic experiments assess parameter recovery: (1) recover spatially constant n and q values across the network; (2) recover constant values using the NN parameterization while adding small noise; and (3) recover power-law relationships between n, q and drainage area (DA) within literature bounds. These tests evaluate identifiability and the ability of the NN+routing system to learn functional relationships from downstream signals.
supporting_quote: Our first experiment tested if we could correctly recover a single, spatially constant set of assumed values for both n and q
In our second experiment, we assumed constant n throughout the reaches but set the trained model as n,q = NN(A)
Our third synthetic experiment examined if we could retrieve simple assumed relationships within realistic literature bounds (power-law)

chunks.text: The river network is built for the Juniata River Basin using NHDPlus v2 and discretized into approximately 2-km reaches. The resulting graph contains 544 nodes and 582 reaches, and a stream-density threshold is applied to reduce computation. Reach slope and sinuosity are derived by overlaying NHDPlus with the 10-m National Elevation Dataset.
supporting_quote: We discretized the river network into approximately 2-km reaches, resulting in 544 junction points (or nodes) and 582 river reaches (or edges).
We then calculated slope and sinuosity for the reaches by overlaying NHDplus v2 with the 10-m resolution National Elevation Data set

chunks.text: The primary training target is the hydrograph at the furthest downstream JRB gage, USGS 01563500, corresponding to node 4809. This gage drains 5,212 km2 and integrates contributions from the 582 simulated reaches. Seven upstream USGS gages are used for additional validation of inner-basin performance.
supporting_quote: USGS gage 01563500 (node 4809 in our graph) ... has a catchment area of 5,212 km2 contributed from the 582 simulated reaches upstream.
Seven USGS gages are located upstream of this node which enables further validation

chunks.text: Runoff forcings for routing come from a pretrained LSTM trained on 3,213 CONUS gages from the GAGES-II dataset using inputs from 1990–1999. In the JRB, the LSTM achieved a median daily NSE of 0.7849 across eight gages. The LSTM is then run for 2000–2009 to generate discharge for 17 HUC10 watersheds used as lateral inflows.
supporting_quote: we focused on training the LSTM on 3,213 gages selected from the USGS ... GAGES-II data set ... between 1990/01/01–1999/12/31
The LSTM streamflow model achieved a median daily Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) ... of 0.7849 for the eight gaging stations in the JRB
the model was run from 2000/01/01–2009/12/31 to predict discharge for the 17 HUC10 watersheds

chunks.text: The LSTM uses daily meteorological forcings from NASA NLDAS-2 and 29 basin attributes similar to prior continental LSTM studies. Forcings include precipitation, radiation, pressure, and temperature, while attributes include topography, land cover, soils, and dam-related variables. These inputs enable seamless prediction for basins across CONUS and are aggregated to HUC10 for this study.
supporting_quote: Meteorological forcings ... were obtained from the NASA NLDAS-2 forcing data set
We selected 29 basin attributes (Table A1 in the Appendix A) similar to those chosen in previous LSTM studies

chunks.text: The MLP for parameterization uses constant reach attributes describing geometry and landscape context. Inputs include reach width, elevation, slope, reach area, total drainage area, length, sinuosity, and bank elevation. These are normalized and supplied per reach to generate n and q used in routing.
supporting_quote: The MLP accepts a normalized array of attributes (A) for each reach (Table A2)
Table A2 ... Reach Width ... Slope ... Total drainage area ... Sinuosity ... Bank elevation

chunks.text: Real-data training uses selected 8-week high-flashiness periods in years where LSTM performance is reasonable (2001, 2005, 2007, 2008). Periods include 02/01–03/29 and 11/01–12/27 for each selected year, yielding eight training periods. Observed USGS discharge and model inputs are disaggregated to hourly time steps for MC routing evaluation.
supporting_quote: Periods of such "high flashiness" in the JRB occurred during both 02/01–03/29 and 11/01–12/27
the years 2001, 2005, 2007, and 2008 had decent LSTM accuracy, giving us eight time periods on which to train NN models
The observed discharge data were similarly disaggregated to hourly data.

chunks.text: In synthetic experiments with spatially constant parameters, the framework recovered Manning’s n with moderate accuracy across 15 runs, while failing to recover the channel geometry parameter q. n converged rapidly, typically within 20 epochs, whereas q stayed near initial guesses. Gradient analysis supports that loss is much more sensitive to n than to q.
supporting_quote: recovered the assumed n values with moderate accuracy, but not the channel geometry parameter q (Table 1)
The training led n to the assumed values rapidly, typically within 20 epochs
the time-averaged gradient of the loss function with respect to n is much larger than that with respect to q

chunks.text: When n and q were generated per reach by the NN, the model could approximately recover constant n levels and simple drainage-area power-law patterns for most reaches. Recovery was less accurate for headwater (small-DA) reaches where sharp changes occur and for large-DA reaches that are underconstrained. Despite these deviations, recovered n overlapped substantially with the synthetic target relationships.
supporting_quote: either constant values or simple functions could be roughly recovered for most of the reaches, while there may have been additional uncertainty for the furthest upstream and downstream reaches
The n values and the declining trends were somewhat underestimated for the headwater reaches (small-DA).
Toward the higher range of DA, the recovered values were lower than the assumed relationship

chunks.text: Training on 8 weeks of real data at the downstream gage produced a routed hydrograph that better aligned peak timing compared to direct summation of runoff inputs. For the illustrated 2001 training window, the model achieved a training NSE of 0.8381. The routed hydrograph was smoothed and delayed relative to Q′, matching observed peak timing closely even with biased runoff magnitudes.
supporting_quote: The hydrograph generated by the differentiable routing model was, as expected, smoothed and delayed compared to the summation of runoff generated during the training period.
leading to a high training NSE of 0.8381
the peaks of the routed hydrograph are placed almost exactly under the observed peaks

chunks.text: The year-long test in 2001 showed that a short 8-week calibration can generalize to long-term routing at the training gage. The differentiable routing model achieved NSE = 0.8587 over the year, outperforming both summation of Q′ (NSE = 0.7569) and a uniform whole-basin LSTM (about 0.802). Routing improved timing but could not correct rainfall-runoff bias due to MC mass balance.
supporting_quote: The differentiable model obtained a year-long NSE of 0.8587
In contrast, the summation of Q′(τ = 9) and the whole-basin LSTM were at 0.7569, and 0.801 (Table 2), respectively.
the mass balance dictated by the MC formulation, which prevents the model from adding or removing mass to remove the bias

chunks.text: The trained model learned a power-law-like relationship between Manning’s n and drainage area without being explicitly constrained to that functional form. n was highest in small drainage-area reaches and declined toward larger rivers, aligning with common expectations and regional understanding. The learned n–DA relationship had a logarithmic trendline with R² = 0.7032 for the shown training period.
supporting_quote: the scheme recovered a power-law-like relationship between n and DA (Figure 6)
The n values were highest (near n = 0.66) for smaller DA and declined gradually, approaching 0.04
on a logarithmic scale with a logarithmic trendline (R2 = 0.7032)

chunks.text: Performance at inner, untrained gages depended on basin size: routing became more competitive and often superior for larger drainage areas. For basins above roughly 2,000 km2, the differentiable routing model outperformed the uniform LSTM at multiple gages and generally outperformed the simple Q′ summation at most gages. For the smallest basin (94.8 km2), the uniform LSTM was noticeably better than the routing-based approach.
supporting_quote: for gages with larger than ∼2,000 km2 of catchment area, the differentiable routing model performed noticeably better than the uniform LSTM models
For the small subbasins, and especially gage 01557500 (94.8 km2 ), the uniform LSTM was noticeably better.
Our differentiable model was also better than the summation of Q′ for seven of the eight gages

chunks.text: Including multiple internal gages in the loss function produced only marginal changes in performance and slightly improved some smaller-DA locations while barely affecting large-DA results. The improvements were small enough that practical implications were limited in this basin. This suggests downstream-only calibration already constrained tributary behavior reasonably in the Juniata River Basin setting.
supporting_quote: When we used multiple internal gages within the NN loss function ... results improved very slightly at smaller DA gages, while barely degrading at larger DA reaches.
the differences introduced by calibrating at inner gages are too small to have real-world implications

chunks.text: Across eight 8-week training periods (two seasons across 2001, 2005, 2007, 2008), most trained models yielded acceptable NSEs when tested on different years, but some periods produced notably inferior results. Table 3 shows that models trained on 2007b or 2008a led to markedly lower NSEs for several test years. Better-performing training windows tended to include complete flood rising and recession phases and had higher Q′ NSE during training.
supporting_quote: choosing 2007b or 2008a led to notably inferior results in both NSE values (Table 3) and in timing
periods selected for training should (a) contain full flood rise and recession phases; and (b) have high Q′ NSE values

chunks.text: Channel geometry parameter q was consistently unidentifiable from downstream hydrographs in both constant and distributed synthetic experiments. The authors attribute this to q having limited influence on stream storage and to weak gradients with respect to q during training. As a result, the study focuses on n as the learnable routing parameter and treats learned q as not meaningful.
supporting_quote: recovered the assumed n values with moderate accuracy, but not the channel geometry parameter q
The non-identifiability of q was likely because q has only a small influence on the storage capacity of the stream
Similar to the two-constant-parameter retrieval experiment, the q parameter was not recoverable

chunks.text: The inverse problem is underdetermined: many reach parameters are constrained by only one downstream output, especially when training windows are short. This leads to uncertainty in estimated reach-scale n values and makes precise identification difficult, even when the learned pattern is plausible. The paper emphasizes that the method can yield performant parameterizations but does not guarantee recovery of true n.
supporting_quote: it is an underdetermined system
short training periods may not be sufficient to identify the true n values
we do not claim that the procedure retrieved the "true" n parameterization

chunks.text: Bias in runoff inputs from the pretrained LSTM can create low-biased simulated peaks that routing cannot fix because MC enforces mass balance. The routing model can improve timing and smoothing but cannot add water to correct magnitude biases. This limits achievable peak-flow accuracy when runoff forcings are biased.
supporting_quote: We noticed a substantial low bias in this training period, witnessed by much lower peaks with the simulated flow compared to the observed flow.
the mass balance dictated by the MC formulation, which prevents the model from adding or removing mass to remove the bias

chunks.text: Model skill at very small basins is limited by the runoff-producing unit size (HUC10), since some gage basins are smaller than the smallest HUC10 in the study area. Below this threshold, mapping runoff to reaches can be error-prone and uniform LSTM predictions may be preferable. The authors suggest using smaller runoff-generating units and improving mass transfer procedures in future work.
supporting_quote: The subbasin for 01557500 is smaller than our runoff-producing unit (HUC10s, with the smallest one ∼200 km2 ). This means predictions below this threshold can be error-prone.
The issues for the smallest basins could be attributed to the procedure that transfers mass from HUC10 subbasins to regular grids on the river network, which should be improved in future work.

chunks.text: Recovered n depends on modeling choices and simplifications, including the linear MC form, celerity approximations, and other hyperparameters such as τ and training period selection. The paper notes that using nonlinear MC formulations or different hydraulic-radius treatments could change inferred n values. Therefore, inversely obtained parameter values are not fully model-independent even if spatial patterns are informative.
supporting_quote: We adopted the simple linear form of the Muskingum equation
preliminary studies show that deriving c using the full equation leads to instability
using the nonlinear MC equations may generate somewhat different n values

chunks.text: Training-period choice can produce equifinality-like behavior where different n distributions yield similar routing performance, especially with short windows. The paper reports that some periods lacking full rising–recession cycles lead to poor test timing and extreme n values. Longer training periods with diverse storm patterns are suggested to better constrain inversion and reduce uncertainty.
supporting_quote: periods selected for training should (a) contain full flood rise and recession phases
not enough information exists in a short period to distinguish between possible solutions of n, similar to the problem of parameter equifinality
Future work needs to employ longer training periods to compromise across different periods and obtain broadly performant parameterizations.

chunks.text: The paper introduces a differentiable Muskingum-Cunge routing framework coupled to a neural network parameterization, functioning like a physics-informed graph neural network for river networks. Implemented in PyTorch, it can be trained end-to-end from downstream hydrographs to infer reach-scale parameters. This provides a modular approach that can be coupled to other runoff models and potentially ported to traditional modeling systems.
supporting_quote: we developed a novel differentiable modeling framework to perform routing and to learn a "parameterization scheme"
we used a combination of a pre-trained LSTM rainfall-runoff model and MC routing to create a learnable routing model, or, from the perspective of ML, a physics-informed GNN

chunks.text: Synthetic tests show the method can recover the overall spatial pattern of Manning’s n with moderate accuracy, but it cannot reliably recover channel geometry parameter q. Real-data experiments show that short 8-week training windows can yield parameterizations that improve long-term routing and peak timing even when runoff inputs contain significant errors. However, short training data may only constrain broad n patterns rather than precise values.
supporting_quote: Our synthetic experiments recovered the overall spatial pattern of n with moderate accuracy but could not recover the channel cross-sectional geometry parameter (q).
Eight weeks of real-world data produced decent long-term streamflow routing and improved upon approaches that did not use routing

chunks.text: Evaluation across inner gages indicates routing provides increasing advantage for larger basins, with best competitiveness in stem rivers above about 2,000 km2 where heterogeneity and flow convergence matter more. The learned n–drainage area patterns are consistent with literature expectations, suggesting potential for knowledge discovery. The trained n parameterization can be used to improve larger-scale hydrologic flood simulations by coupling with traditional routing models.
supporting_quote: For basins >2,000 km2 , our framework outperformed deep learning models that assume homogeneity
The learned n pattern was consistent with literature expectations, demonstrating the framework's potential for knowledge discovery
The trained n parameterization can be coupled with traditional models to improve national-scale hydrologic flood simulations.

chunks.text: Excess phosphorus loading to surface waters drives eutrophication and related impacts such as harmful algal blooms and oxygen depletion. Watershed-scale phosphorus mass balance and spatial targeting of critical source areas are widely used to inform water quality initiatives, especially in agricultural landscapes where nonpoint losses can dominate terrestrial P export. Despite advances in modeling capability, challenges remain in scaling and representing heterogeneity across landscapes.
supporting_quote: Excess phosphorus (P) loading to surface waters contributes to eutrophication, symptoms of which can include harmful algal blooms, oxygen depletion, and fish kills
nonpoint source losses from agricultural land account for a substantial portion of terrestrial P export in such watersheds

chunks.text: The Missisquoi Bay watershed is a major management focus within the Lake Champlain Basin because of historic and ongoing nutrient loads and frequent cyanobacteria blooms. The basin is subject to total maximum daily load limits for P, and agricultural activity is estimated to account for a large share of total P load to Missisquoi Bay. This study focuses on the Vermont portion of the watershed (MBB).
supporting_quote: Lake Champlain is subject to USEPA total maximum daily load limits for P
It has been estimated that 64% of the Missisquoi Bay watershed's total P load to Missisquoi Bay can be attributed to agricultural activity

chunks.text: Most watershed-scale nutrient status analyses rely on aggregated data sources and make broad assumptions across a landscape. While such data can represent averages, they often do not capture spatial variability in phosphorus flows and soil metrics, which can obscure high-risk areas. Preserving heterogeneity is important for identifying critical source areas that disproportionately contribute to P losses.
supporting_quote: Past studies have typically relied on aggregated county, state, regional, or federal data sources and used these data to make broad assumptions across the landscape.
This homogeneity of data across a watershed limits the ability of a model to represent conditions at smaller spatial scales within the watershed, which inherently obscures high-risk areas

chunks.text: The study aimed to develop a bottom-up approach that uses field-level nutrient management plan information to predict watershed-scale spatial patterns in agricultural phosphorus status. Specifically, it sought to predict and visualize partial P mass balance, soil phosphorus saturation ratio (PSR), and soil test P metrics for all agricultural parcels in the Vermont portion of the Missisquoi Bay Basin. The approach targets improved representation of heterogeneity and uncertainty at the watershed scale.
supporting_quote: we developed methods in this study that use field-level data from farm nutrient management plans (NMPs) to predict partial P mass balance and key soil test parameters for all agricultural land in the Vermont portion of the 184,297 ha Missisquoi Bay Basin (MBB).
predict and visualize partial P mass balance, soil P saturation ratio (PSR), and soil test P for agricultural parcels across a watershed

chunks.text: A secondary goal was to produce spatial visualizations that can help identify areas with higher P loss potential and support decision making and subsequent watershed modeling. The authors intended these methods to serve as a transferable framework for bottom-up nutrient status modeling in other regions where similar field-level data exist.
supporting_quote: Results were used to visualize areas with high P loss potential.
These techniques can also serve as a framework for bottom-up modeling of nutrient mass balance and soil metrics in other regions.

chunks.text: A key barrier in watershed-scale phosphorus assessment is reliance on aggregated datasets that cannot represent field-to-field variability in management and soil nutrient status. This limits the ability to identify spatially concentrated high-risk areas and to quantify uncertainty associated with heterogeneous conditions. The paper frames this as a gap between farm-scale nutrient accounting and watershed-scale predictions.
supporting_quote: Analysis of nutrient balance at the watershed scale, including for phosphorus (P), is typically accomplished using aggregate input datasets, resulting in an inability to capture the variability of P status across the study region.
Given the current gap between farm scale and regional or watershed-scale P data use, management, and decision making

chunks.text: Scaling nutrient and transport models across spatial extents can create additional issues, including overgeneralization of data, uncertainty, and computational burden. These challenges can reduce confidence in representing conditions at small spatial scales that matter for targeting management actions. The study positions its bottom-up approach as a way to preserve heterogeneity while acknowledging uncertainty.
supporting_quote: issues have arisen in scaling between models of various sizes, including data overgeneralization, overparameterization, uncertainty, and high computational demand
This homogeneity of data across a watershed limits the ability of a model to represent conditions at smaller spatial scales

chunks.text: The authors used K-means clustering to link field-level nutrient management plan (NMP) parcels to all agricultural parcels in the watershed based on physical characteristics. They clustered by slope and soil clay content and performed clustering separately for the two dominant crop types (corn and hay). After establishing centroids from the full watershed agricultural layer, they assigned NMP fields to those clusters and extrapolated management and soil-test distributions within clusters.
supporting_quote: we employed K-means clustering
Note that clustering was done separately for the two dominant crop types: corn and hay.
clustering parameters (slope and soil clay content)

chunks.text: Partial phosphorus mass balance was computed for each parcel as manure P plus fertilizer P minus crop P uptake. The approach used per-cluster mean manure, fertilizer, and uptake rates derived from NMP data and applied them to watershed parcels within corresponding clusters. The authors emphasized that this is a partial balance because it excludes P losses to water and system-boundary fluxes such as atmospheric deposition.
supporting_quote: we calculated a partial P mass balance (kg P ha−1 year−1) for each agricultural land parcel as P applied via manure plus P applied via fertilizer minus crop P uptake.
This partial mass balance does not account for P losses to water.
We also did not account for atmospheric deposition into nor leaching/export via surface waters out of the system boundary (hence, the "partial" mass balance).

chunks.text: To preserve soil-test variability, the model transferred entire distributions of PSR observations from NMP clusters to the corresponding watershed clusters rather than using only cluster means. When sampling a PSR value, the associated soil-test variables were also sampled together to maintain their pairing. This was designed to better represent heterogeneity in soil P status across the basin.
supporting_quote: To preserve variability of the NMP clusters in MBB predictions, we assigned the same distribution of PSR values from each cluster in the NMP dataset to its corresponding cluster in the MBB dataset.
For each PSR observation pulled, we pulled along the associated MMP, MMAl, M3P, and M3Al.

chunks.text: Uncertainty from random assignment of manure and fertilizer application across fields and the use of in-cluster means was addressed using Monte Carlo-style repetition. The NMP-to-watershed extrapolation was run 10,000 times, saving basin-wide mean outcomes for P balance and PSR (overall and by crop type) and the area fraction exceeding a PSR threshold. The authors then selected a 'centrally trending model iteration' whose outputs were close to the 10,000-run means within specified standard-deviation tolerances.
supporting_quote: we ran the NMP → MBB extrapolation 10,000 times.
we refer to this result as the "centrally trending model iteration"

chunks.text: To protect farmer privacy in map products, the field-scale predictions were aggregated for visualization. Spatially weighted means of P balance, PSR, and Modified Morgan P were computed within each HUC-12 subwatershed and land use type combination, producing smoother patterns and discouraging interpretation at the individual-field level.
supporting_quote: To protect farmer privacy when displaying the prediction in GIS, we performed some minor aggregation.
We computed spatially weighted mean values of P balance, PSR, and MMP for the centrally trending model iteration within each combination of land use type and NHDPlus HR HUC-12 subwatershed.

chunks.text: The spatial agricultural layer for the Vermont Missisquoi Bay Basin (MBB) was assembled from multiple GIS sources and field boundary polygons to better capture variability. Common land unit (CLU) polygons were used to define field boundaries. The final dataset included 5,557 fields totaling 35,688 ha, with agricultural land comprising about 21% of the watershed and dominated by hay/forages and corn.
supporting_quote: Agricultural land comprised approximately 21% of the MBB watershed.
Notably, the CLU polygons were used to define field boundaries
A total of 5557 fields were established, totaling 35,688 ha.

chunks.text: Ten nutrient management plans (NMPs) for the 2022 growing season from dairy farms in the MBB provided field-level cropping, nutrient management, and soil test information along with GIS polygons. All farms were large farm operations (>700 mature dairy cows). The NMP dataset covered 7,347 ha and 1,422 fields, representing approximately 21% of total agricultural land area in the basin.
supporting_quote: 10 NMPs prepared for the 2022 growing season from dairy farms operating within the MBB
All 10 farms were categorized as large farm operations (LFOs) by the VAAFM (>700 mature dairy cows).
The NMPs contained a total of 7347 ha of agricultural land, accounting for approximately 21% of the total agricultural land area in the MBB.
There were 1422 fields included in the dataset

chunks.text: Soil and topographic covariates used for clustering and interpretation were compiled for each polygon. Soil clay percentage, soil organic carbon percentage, and pH came from SSURGO, while mean slope was derived from NHDPlus HR. These variables supported the bottom-up extrapolation of NMP-derived parameters to all agricultural parcels.
supporting_quote: we compiled data on soil clay percentage, soil organic carbon percentage, and soil pH from the Soil Survey Geographic database (NRCS, 2022), and mean parcel slope from the USGS's NHD-Plus HR

chunks.text: Across 10,000 extrapolation runs, the basin-wide net partial phosphorus balance for MBB agricultural land was estimated at about 196,249 ± 7,861 kg P per year. The per-hectare partial P balance averaged 5.5 ± 0.2 kg P ha−1 year−1 across all agricultural land. Crop-specific surpluses were higher for corn than hay, indicating different management and/or uptake patterns between crop types.
supporting_quote: The mean agricultural land partial P balance for the MBB watershed was 196,249 ± 7861 kg P year−1
The MBB had an average P balance of 5.5 ± 0.2 kg P ha−1 year−1 for all agricultural land, 13.3 ± 0.8 kg P ha−1 year−1 for corn cropland, and 3.2 ± 0.2 kg P ha−1 year−1 for hay.

chunks.text: The model estimated mean phosphorus saturation ratio (PSR) for agricultural parcels in the MBB at 0.0399 ± 0.0002. Predicted PSR differed by crop type, with corn higher than hay on average. Model runs produced normal distributions for mean PSR, indicating stable central tendencies under the uncertainty procedure.
supporting_quote: We found that the average agricultural parcel in the MBB had a PSR of 0.0399 ± 0.0002
corn and hay cropland ... had PSR means of 0.0492 ± 0.0008 and 0.0373 ± 0.0002, respectively.

chunks.text: Using the PSR threshold of 0.1, the model estimated that a small fraction of agricultural land area had the highest risk for dissolved P loss. Across 10,000 runs, the mean area proportion with PSR > 0.1 was 1.7% ± 0.2%. All fields allocated PSR > 0.1 in the extrapolation were corn fields.
supporting_quote: the broadly applicable M3-PSR threshold value identified by Dari et al. (2018)
the mean percentage of the MBB agricultural land at highest risk for P loss was 1.7% ± 0.2%.
Note that all fields receiving a PSR > 0.1 in the NMP → MBB extrapolation were corn fields.

chunks.text: Predicted Modified Morgan P (MMP) categories suggested most agricultural land was at or above optimum, with substantial area in high and a smaller area in excessive classes. In the centrally trending iteration, 38% of land was 'optimum' and 29% 'high'. The combination of 'high' and 'excessive' summed to about 31% of agricultural land area, indicating widespread above-optimum soil test P levels.
supporting_quote: approximately 6% of the MBB's agricultural land had "low" MMP concentrations, 25% was "medium," 38% was "optimum," 29% was "high," and 2% was "excessive"
We predicted MMP above optimum for approximately 31% of the watershed's agricultural land

chunks.text: Cluster-level analysis showed strong differentiation among clusters in predicted P balance and PSR, and identified specific combinations of slope, clay content, and crop type associated with higher surplus. The highest mean P balance occurred in a corn cluster with medium slope and high clay (27.38 ± 1.22 kg P ha−1 year−1). Hay clusters generally had lower mean P balances, ranging from near 1 to about 8 kg P ha−1 year−1.
supporting_quote: The corn cluster with medium slope and high soil clay content had the highest P balance (27 ± 1 kg P ha−1 year−1)
all hay clusters had mean P balances between 1 and 8 kg P ha−1 year−1

chunks.text: Cluster-mean PSR and P balance were not significantly correlated, suggesting that P surplus and P saturation do not necessarily co-vary across landscape clusters. This indicates that management-driven surpluses and soil sorption capacity/chemistry can produce different spatial patterns. The authors report a moderate Spearman rho but non-significant p-value.
supporting_quote: Cluster-mean PSR and P balance values were not correlated (Spearman rho = 0.36; p = 0.34).

chunks.text: The authors note potential bias because the NMP dataset came from only 10 large dairy operations, which may not represent all farm types or nutrient strategies in the basin. They highlight that the dataset may overrepresent manure-applied fields and underrepresent fertilizer inputs. As a result, the inferred basin-wide balance could be sensitive to differences between NMP-covered fields and others.
supporting_quote: we recognize that the NMP polygon dataset from a limited number of LFOs may bias the dataset.
it seems that the NMP dataset may overrepresent manure and underrepresent fertilizer inputs.

chunks.text: The mass balance is explicitly partial and excludes key fluxes relevant to water quality outcomes. It does not include atmospheric deposition or exports via leaching and surface waters, and does not represent P losses to water directly. Therefore, results should be interpreted as surplus/deficit indicators rather than direct estimates of P delivery to streams or the bay.
supporting_quote: This partial mass balance does not account for P losses to water.
We also did not account for atmospheric deposition into nor leaching/export via surface waters out of the system boundary (hence, the "partial" mass balance).

chunks.text: The authors simplified minor land-use classes by assigning a zero mass balance to pasture, soybean, and other agriculture because these represent less than 2% of agricultural land. While consistent with prior assumptions for pasture grazing/dung dropping, this removes potential variability in those categories. The choice reduces complexity but could miss localized effects in small areas.
supporting_quote: we assumed a value of "0" for nutrient mass balance for agricultural land categorized as pasture, other ag, or soybean due to their combined contribution of <2% of agricultural land
to be in agreement with pasture grazing/dung dropping balance assumptions made by Meals et al. (2008b)

chunks.text: The model’s mapping outputs should not be used to infer field-level conditions, in part because of privacy protection aggregation and because predictions are spatial estimates. The authors intentionally computed HUC-12 and land-use weighted means to smooth patterns and reinforce appropriate interpretation. This limits applicability for parcel-specific decision making without additional field data.
supporting_quote: These results are spatial estimates and should not be interpreted as actual P balance values of real fields.
smoothing the data for public representation reinforces that the model is an informed estimate ... but should not be used to make field-level conclusions.

chunks.text: PSR and MMP are mainly source indicators for dissolved phosphorus loss and do not capture erosion-driven particulate P risk without transport factors. The authors caution that neither metric inherently represents particulate loss potential, which requires tools that incorporate transport processes. They point to the Vermont P Index and watershed models as approaches that include transport.
supporting_quote: PSR is best interpreted as a risk factor for dissolved P loss
Neither metric inherently captures risk for particulate P loss via erosion, which requires accounting for transport factors in addition to source factors.
This is achieved at the field level by tools such as the Vermont P Index

chunks.text: The study concludes that the highest predicted PSR and MMP areas tend to occur on flatter ground with lower-permeability soils and in locations more prone to flooding, implying heightened loss vulnerability where hydrologic connectivity is strong. The authors interpret these patterns as consistent with concerns about legacy P and continued surpluses affecting water quality over long timescales. The results are positioned as actionable for integrating nutrient management and watershed planning, including targeting restoration or BMPs.
supporting_quote: agricultural land in the MBB with highest PSR and MMP values is on flatter ground, with soils having lower permeability, in areas more susceptible to flooding.
the impacts of legacy soil phosphorus and repeated nutrient balance surplus will continue to impact river and lake water quality for years to come

chunks.text: The authors present their approach as a new bottom-up method for predicting watershed-scale P balance and soil nutrient status using field-level management data in a watershed larger than 100,000 ha. They state it can be replicated elsewhere when nutrient management plans cover a sizable portion of agricultural land, have similar spatial distribution, and are representative of practices. They emphasize that their case met coverage and spatial distribution criteria and largely met representativeness, though with some bias risks.
supporting_quote: we have pioneered a bottom-up method to predict P balance and soil nutrient status for agricultural land in a >100,000-ha watershed by leveraging field-level management data

key requirements being access to NMPs that (1) cover a sizable portion of the agricultural land within the watershed, (2) have similar spatial distribution to agricultural land in the watershed, and (3) are largely representative

chunks.text: Compound flooding in low-lying estuarine systems occurs when elevated sea level above normal tide coincides with high river flow, producing longer-duration and more widespread flooding than purely fluvial or coastal events. Because these drivers can co-occur, flood risk assessments should consider their joint behavior rather than treating them independently. Understanding how river discharge and storm surge depend on each other is therefore central to estuarine hazard characterization.
supporting_quote: Compound floods may happen in low-lying estuarine environments when sea level above normal tide co-occurs with high river flow.
Such events typically produce floodwaters that are longer in duration and more widespread, in comparison with purely fluvial or ocean-driven estuarine floods.

chunks.text: Traditional coastal flood risk assessments often model each driver separately, implicitly assuming no important interaction. The paper argues that comprehensive estuarine flood management requires multivariate modeling that captures the dependence structure between drivers. Multivariate hazard curves can then be used to estimate return periods for compound scenarios.
supporting_quote: The traditional approach to coastal flood risk assessment addresses flood hazard from each driver independently, i.e., employs univariate statistical modeling
comprehensive flood risk management for estuarine systems requires consideration of a probable co-occurrence (or sequence) of flood mechanisms

chunks.text: Non-stationarity in dependence can arise when the strength or form of dependence changes over time, potentially due to climatic variability and change. Prior large-scale studies have examined changing dependence among coastal flood drivers, but physically meaningful modeling that links dependence changes to mechanisms (rather than abstract time covariates) remains limited. This study positions large-scale climate teleconnections as interpretable covariates for dependence changes.
supporting_quote: Complications in multivariate hazard modeling arise when the dependence structure of the flood drivers does not remain unchanged, but rather exhibits non-stationarity.
There appears to be, in addition, a shortage of scientific literature concerning a realistic and physically meaningful modeling of the possibly varying dependence structure of compound flood drivers

chunks.text: The study searches for evidence of non-stationary dependence between estuarine river discharge and storm surge along the East and Gulf coasts of the United States. It specifically tests whether large-scale climate variability, particularly ENSO (via ONI) and NAO, explains changes in dependence strength. The goal includes building and comparing stationary versus physics-informed dynamic copula models in a Bayesian framework.
supporting_quote: we demonstrate our search for evidence of non-stationarity in the dependence between river discharge and storm surge along the East and Gulf coasts of the United States, driven by large-scale climate variability, particularly El-Niño Southern Oscillation and North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO).
Physics-informed copulas are developed by modeling the magnitude of dependence as a linear function of large-scale climate indices, i.e., Oceanic Niño Index or NAO index.

chunks.text: A second objective is methodological: to provide a parsimonious framework that both detects potential non-stationarity and models the bivariate distribution of discharge and surge. The framework emphasizes Bayesian estimation (to quantify uncertainty) and Bayesian model comparison (to decide between stationary and dynamic dependence). It also aims to reduce parameter uncertainty using informative priors based on observed dependence variability.
supporting_quote: here we develop a parsimonious framework to simultaneously search for non-stationary dependence between co-occurring flood variables as well as model their multivariate distribution.
Bayesian model intercomparison through appropriate metrics casts light on whether there is evidence for a non-stationary dependence.

chunks.text: Estimating joint estuarine flood hazard is difficult because it requires a statistically robust characterization of dependence between discharge and storm surge. The challenge is compounded when dependence may be non-stationary, since it is hard to prove changes in dependence magnitude and incorporate them into a multivariate model. Many existing approaches allow dependence to vary with abstract time rather than physically interpretable drivers.
supporting_quote: it is a rather difficult task to provide statistically robust evidence that the magnitude of dependence has been changing over the years and to subsequently incorporate this change into the construction of the multivariate probability distribution.
the majority of studies published on the matter have let multivariate distributions co-vary with , i.e., an abstract quantity not directly linked to the physical mechanisms

chunks.text: Observed records may not contain enough cases where both river discharge and storm surge are simultaneously extreme, limiting the ability to study true compound-flood extremes. As a result, dependence assessment often relies on conditionally sampled pairs where only one variable is extreme, which mixes event types. This can blur inference about drivers of actual compound floods.
supporting_quote: the overlapping time period is still considered rather short for us to extract many compound events where both variables, and , are considered extremes.
As a result, these data comprise a mixture of pairs

chunks.text: Storm surge is derived from still water level (SWL) by removing predicted tides via tidal harmonic analysis. The analysis is performed annually, includes 60 influential tidal constituents, and subtracts predicted tidal level (including mean sea level) from SWL to obtain the non-tidal residual (surge). This approach aims to isolate the meteorological, stochastic component of sea level variability.
supporting_quote: to obtain the storm surge... we conducted a tidal harmonic analysis.
we predicted the tidal level, including mean sea level (MSL), and subtracted it from SWL to extract the random nontidal residual, or else, surge.

chunks.text: The study constructs bivariate samples of discharge and surge using a two-way conditional sampling procedure. Annual maxima of a conditioning variable are paired with the maximum of the other variable within lags of +/- 1 to 10 days, producing Q_S and S_Q samples. The optimal lag and pairing direction are chosen to maximize statistically significant Kendall’s tau.
supporting_quote: We followed a two-way conditional sampling approach in order to extract co-occurring discharge () and surge () with at least one variable being extreme.

chunks.text: Dependence strength between discharge and surge is quantified using Kendall’s rank correlation coefficient, selected because it can capture non-linear dependency. Statistical significance of Kendall’s tau is computed, and the analysis proceeds using only the pairing direction and lag that yield the maximum statistically significant tau. This serves as a precursor to copula fitting and model comparison.

chunks.text: The dependence structure is modeled using copulas, leveraging Sklar’s theorem to connect a bivariate distribution to its marginal distributions. The paper uses an empirical copula to guide selection of a parametric copula family. It focuses on three Archimedean copulas—Frank, Gumbel, and Clayton—chosen for closed forms and their ability to represent symmetric dependence or tail dependence.

chunks.text: Copula family selection is based on goodness-of-fit testing with the Frank copula as the null hypothesis, using a parametric bootstrap with B = 500 replications. If Frank is rejected, Gumbel and Clayton are tested to identify whether upper- or lower-tail dependence better describes the data. The rationale links Frank to symmetry and lack of tail dependence, Gumbel to upper-tail dependence, and Clayton to lower-tail dependence.

the Gumbel copula is asymmetric and exhibits upper tail dependence

chunks.text: Non-stationarity is modeled via a physics-informed dynamic copula in which the copula parameter varies linearly with a large-scale climate index. The model specifies δ = b + w * Climate_Index, where Climate_Index is ONI or NAO depending on the estuary. Stationary and dynamic copula parameters are inferred in a Bayesian framework to represent uncertainty.
supporting_quote: we modeled a physics-informed copula by allowing the parameter to linearly co-vary with a large-scale climatic pattern (\_) as follows:

chunks.text: Bayesian inference is implemented with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) using Stan and rstan. The setup uses four parallel HMC chains and 16,000 total iterations, with half used as warm-up. Convergence is evaluated with split-Rhat and effective sample size, complemented by trace plot inspection.

We employed four parallel HMC chains
The total number of iterations was = 4 × 4,000 = 16,000, with half of them considered as warm-up phase.

chunks.text: Stationary and dynamic copulas are compared using Bayesian information criteria suited for MCMC output: DIC and WAIC. The paper states that lower DIC and WAIC indicate preferred models, and notes that WAIC averages over the posterior distribution and can approximate leave-one-out cross-validation. Model comparison is used to assess evidence for non-stationary dependence.

chunks.text: River discharge data are average daily values from the Global Runoff Data Center (GRDC), quality-controlled by retaining years with more than 80% non-missing entries. Still water level (SWL) is obtained as hourly measurements from tide stations in the GESLA database, and surge series are quality-controlled by removing years with at least 20% missing data. These constraints aim to ensure robust long-term overlap between the two datasets.

Consequently, the inferred (non-)stationarity pertains to potentially compounding conditions, not necessarily to observed compound flood events.

chunks.text: Continental-scale hydrologic and hydraulic models often use simplified river cross sections because detailed bathymetry/topography data are scarce, expensive to collect, and difficult to incorporate at large scale. This motivates assumptions like rectangular or trapezoidal channels when a model is primarily hydrology-driven. Such simplifications can impact computed routing and stage dynamics compared to real channels.
supporting_quote: For continental-scale modeling, the large amount of high-resolution data required, as well as the considerable computational effort needed to incorporate such data, has led to simplifying assumptions such as rectangular or trapezoidal channels for river reaches.
While topographic and bathymetric surveying can be used to acquire channel geometry, they are costly and thus relatively scarce.

chunks.text: The National Water Model (NWM) forecasts discharge for the continental U.S. using simplified channel geometry for millions of reaches. NWM v1.2 uses trapezoidal channels whose bankfull width and area come from regional curves relating drainage area to bankfull characteristics, with nationwide side slope assumptions. Errors in simulated stage can propagate into Muskingum-Cunge routing parameters that depend on stage-derived hydraulic properties.
supporting_quote: The National Water Model (NWM) uses a trapezoidal channel representation for 2.7 million river reaches to forecast water discharge for the entire continental United States (U.S.).
The channel side slopes in NWM v1.2 are currently assumed to be 1 horizontal unit to 20 vertical units (1H:20V) nationwide
Since the NWM-simulated stage is used internally for Muskingum-Cunge method flow routing, errors in simulated stage affect time-varying properties

chunks.text: New observation approaches could help improve channel geometry inputs, but each has limitations. SWOT is expected to help with river widths and potentially discharge estimation, yet it targets rivers wider than about 50 m and misses many headwater streams. The authors also point to citizen-science-style data collection as a possible way to gather geometry information for smaller streams with relatively simple measurements.
supporting_quote: the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT; expected launch in 2021; NASA 2016; Biancamaria et al. 2016) mission, hold potential for building datasets of channel geometry data, especially river flow width.
the SWOT mission was understandably designed with larger-scale features in mind, that is, river widths more than 50 m

chunks.text: The study aims to quantify how simplified NWM trapezoidal channel geometry affects hydrologic-model-relevant predictions and to propose a more realistic but still parsimonious geometry representation. The goal is to improve stage and routing-related behavior while keeping input requirements and runtime feasible for large-scale deployment. The evaluation is performed via controlled comparisons across multiple geometry scenarios.
supporting_quote: The aim of this study is to: (1) evaluate the impact of simplified (NWM trapezoidal) channel geometry representation on hydrological model predictions and (2) suggest an improved representation of channel geometry while maintaining parsimony in model input and runtime.
The overarching goal of this study was to assess the effects of incorporating more realistic channel geometry into continental-scale hydrological models and propose a generalized cross section

chunks.text: A key intended outcome is to determine whether better stage prediction from improved geometry will yield improved Muskingum-Cunge routing parameter estimates. Because NWM updates routing parameters K and X based largely on simulated stage, the study tests whether geometry-driven stage differences translate into materially different routing travel times. This provides evidence about the likely influence of geometry updates on discharge routing quality.
supporting_quote: Since the updates of routing parameters K and X throughout a simulation are based largely on the simulated stage, we test here whether better prediction of stage during simulations will lead to improved estimates of these routing parameters

chunks.text: Simplified trapezoidal channel representations in NWM v1.2 produce unreliable stage behavior and are poorly suited to overbank flow. The implementation includes steep assumed side slopes and an "infinite" depth assumption that limits representation of floodplain processes. Because stage is used internally for Muskingum-Cunge routing updates, stage errors can adversely affect discharge routing through K and X estimation.

chunks.text: Continental-scale models face a fundamental tradeoff: realistic channel and floodplain geometry requires high-resolution data that are hard to obtain and integrate at large scale. Even if such data existed, incorporating them in a large-scale hydrologic framework is challenging due to data volume and computation. This has driven continued reliance on simplified cross-sectional assumptions that can limit accuracy for hydraulics-relevant outputs like stage and inundation.

chunks.text: The study uses one-dimensional HEC-RAS unsteady simulations to compare stage and discharge responses under different channel geometry representations.
