chunks.text: The paper links shorter travel times under S2 to previously observed NWM issues of flow moving too quickly through reaches. The Hackensack comparison suggests that the S2 geometry’s high simulated stage yields lower computed K, meaning faster routing. Using S3/S4 would route discharge more slowly, which would be expected to add lag and attenuation and potentially better match observed hydrographs under Muskingum-Cunge routing.
supporting_quote: these higher S2 stages introduced low bias to the computed values of travel time K

The S2-predicted travel times are shorter by a factor of 2.16 on average for the full three-year simulation, which would correspond with unpublished assessments of the NWM v1.2 rushing flow through reaches about twice as fast as expected.
using the simplified geometries would cause discharge to be routed through the reach more slowly due to the longer expected travel times

chunks.text: Inundation mapping outcomes were highly sensitive to geometry choice in the Big Canoe Creek flood case. The NWM geometry (S2) produced much larger inundated area and depth than surveyed geometry (S1), while the proposed S3 geometry was intermediate. Specifically, S2 yielded 11.39 km^2 inundated with 26.51 m average depth, S1 yielded 3.52 km^2 and 1.84 m, and S3 yielded 7.16 km^2 and 13.21 m.
supporting_quote: The S2 geometry simulation resulted in an inundated area of  11.39 km^2  and an average depth of  26.51 m
The surveyed S1 geometry yielded only  3.52 km^2  and  1.84 m
the proposed S3 geometry resulted in an inundated area of  7.16 km^2  and an average depth of  13.21 m

chunks.text: For North Second Creek, travel-time differences among S2 and proposed geometries largely vanished during higher flows, suggesting geometry changes did not strongly alter K in that case. The paper attributes this to reliance on engineering-assumed trapezoidal bathymetry (2H:1V) in the underlying S1 dataset used to generate S3/S4, making scenarios similar at higher discharge. Differences were more evident at low flows and in long-term averages dominated by baseflow.
supporting_quote: While travel times are significantly different at the 95% confidence level for low discharge values, these differences quickly become nonsignificant as the peak event occurs in Figure 7c.
The lack of differences in S2 and other scenario travel times is likely indicative of the detrimental effect of the engineering assumptions that were made for North Second Creek.
a trapezoidal main channel with 2H:1V side slopes, 0.91 m (3 feet) deep

chunks.text: A major limitation is that HEC-RAS was forced with NWM retrospective hydrographs, and those hydrographs had substantial bias relative to USGS observations at many sites. The paper reports negative discharge NSE values, indicating poor forcing quality, which can influence simulated stage and any inferred routing improvements. As a result, the analysis emphasizes relative differences among geometry scenarios rather than absolute agreement with observations.
supporting_quote: The limitation of this approach is that biases in the NWM discharge predictions will affect the analysis of the HEC-RAS simulations.
the majority of the sites have a negative NSE for discharge, which indicates that the NWM discharge predictions for those river reaches have a high degree of bias.
The analysis is therefore based on evaluating the relative differences between the simulations and the observed hydrograph.

chunks.text: The computed Muskingum-Cunge K values are not a full replication of how K would evolve within an actual Muskingum-Cunge routing run, because flows were produced by the HEC-RAS solver rather than by Muskingum-Cunge routing. The authors caution that cascading timestep dependencies in Muskingum-Cunge prevent drawing conclusions from K time-series alignment in time under biased forcing. They recommend comparing travel times at given discharge and stage values rather than interpreting time-series trends directly.
supporting_quote: While this method does not completely replicate the potential changes in K due to the use of the RASsolver for the St. Venant equations instead of using actual Muskingum-Cunge routing
conclusions cannot be directly drawn based on the time-series of calculated travel time
it is most appropriate to compare the two sets of routing parameter values at a given stage for a given discharge rather than inferring time-series trends.

chunks.text: Because only the main channel geometry was updated in each study reach while tributary inflows were still driven by NWM retrospective outputs, the setup reflects a piecemeal update scenario. The authors note that differing geometry resolution between main channels and tributaries could affect travel time and model accuracy. This design helps explore whether improving only the main channel can still yield meaningful stage and routing-parameter improvements.
supporting_quote: This study's approach of only updating the main channel in each study site allows the exploration of whether substantial improvements in stage and discharge simulation in the main channel are possible by only improving the main channel representation.
In the likely case where channel geometry of larger rivers in the NWM are updated while tributary channels are not
Since flow travel time is strongly affected by geometry representation, this discrepancy could have a major effect on the model accuracy.

chunks.text: Engineering assumptions used to fill gaps in channel bathymetry can introduce systematic errors that propagate into generalized cross sections. At North Second Creek, faulty assumed depth led to thalweg placement that was too low, shifting simulated stages downward across scenarios. The paper emphasizes that ground-truthing and validation are important when deriving geometry from assumptions rather than direct measurements.
supporting_quote: the peak stage is underpredicted as compared to observed stage, but this is due to a faulty assumed depth of the cross section leading to vertical thalweg placement which is too low
The North Second Creek site channel geometry therefore represents potential shortcomings of adopting engineering assumptions directly; ground-truthing of channel geometry data is key

chunks.text: Citizen-science collection of channel geometry is presented as feasible but subject to uncertainty that depends on task complexity and training. The authors note that simpler tasks generally yield more reliable volunteer data and that moderate training and clear instructions can approach professional quality. This motivates the evenly spaced point design of S4 to reduce complexity, while acknowledging S3’s thalweg location may be harder for non-experts to determine.
supporting_quote: it is important to consider potential uncertainties which may arise, which will differ based on the type of data and the level of involvement in the data collection process
volunteer-collected data typically provides reliable information when tasks are relatively simple
the points at which depths are to be taken for the proposed S4 geometry were deliberately spaced evenly to be able to simplify data collection instructions
the proposed S3 geometry intentionally captures the position of the channel thalweg, which might be more difficult to ascertain in the field

chunks.text: The study concludes that improving channel geometry representation can substantially improve hydrologic-model-relevant outputs, particularly stage prediction and Muskingum-Cunge routing parameter estimation. Across the evaluated cases, substituting the proposed S3/S4 geometries for NWM v1.2 geometry reduced peak stage errors and decreased stage RMSE for both long runs and peak events. The authors argue that more accurate geometry is an important step toward better large-scale hydrologic prediction and flood forecasting.
supporting_quote: Improvement in model predictions was shown both in terms of stage prediction and Muskingum-Cunge routing parameter estimation.

When substituting S3 and S4 geometries for S2 NWM v1.2 geometry, peak stage errors were reduced by 80.4%–93.0%; stage RMSE decreased by 14.42%– 54.33% for the full three-year time-series and by 45.54%–78.56% for the selected peak events.
representing channel geometry more accurately has the potential to substantially improve hydrologic model predictions compared to the simple trapezoidal geometry assumptions

chunks.text: For sites with surveyed geometry, the proposed five-point generalizations produced statistically significantly longer travel times than the NWM v1.2 geometry at the 95% confidence level. The authors infer that these longer travel times would attenuate and lag Muskingum-Cunge routed hydrographs, improving realism relative to observed behavior. They identify direct integration of these geometries into large-scale models as a key next step for future work.
supporting_quote: For sites with surveyed S1 geometry (Hackensack River and Big Canoe Creek), the S3 and S4 five-point generalizations produced travel times that were statistically significantly longer than the S2 NWM v1.2 geometry travel times at the 95% confidence level.
These longer travel times will attenuate and lag hydrographs produced using Muskingum-Cunge routing
Additional future work can integrate the proposed channel geometry representations with large-scale hydrology models and evaluate the expected improvements of discharge simulations directly.

chunks.text: Flood hazard mapping and forecasting carry substantial societal value because flood damages are large and expected to rise with land use and climate change. In the U.S., FEMA Flood Insurance Rate Maps commonly depict single deterministic boundaries (e.g., the 100-year flood), which do not communicate uncertainty. Researchers have advocated probabilistic flood maps to better convey uncertainty to decision makers and the public.
supporting_quote: inflation adjusted economic damages from floods were in excess of 500 billion for the 1980-2005 period
a single line is used to represent the flood inundation boundaries for each flood recurrence level

chunks.text: Ensemble prediction systems are increasingly used to extend flood warning lead times by generating multiple plausible meteorological realizations. Translating coarse runoff/streamflow forecasts into local inundation requires hydraulic computations (Saint-Venant equations), but stable, efficient unsteady simulations over large networks remain challenging. These constraints motivate computationally cheaper approaches that still provide actionable inundation information.
supporting_quote: Increasingly, ensemble prediction systems are being used to extend flood warning lead times beyond the 48 h
Translating this coarse scale runoff and streamflow into local, actionable information such as inundation extents, depths, and velocities requires solving ... the Saint-Venant equations.

chunks.text: Rating curves relate discharge and stage at a cross section and are widely used because direct discharge measurement is difficult, especially during floods. Their validity depends on stable channel geometry and an effectively constant energy slope; violations can produce shifted or looped (hysteretic) relations. Backwater and rapidly changing flow can cause the same stage to correspond to different flows.
supporting_quote: A rating curve prescribes a one-to-one mathematical relation between stage and streamflow at a particular cross section
Changes in the value of the energy slope leads to a hysteresis effect known as a looped rating curve

chunks.text: The study aims to present a rating curve library method that converts ensemble streamflow forecasts into probabilistic local inundation maps at low computational cost. It also seeks to describe and demonstrate the Rating Curve based Automatic Flood Forecasting (RCAFF) software that automates the workflow. Feasibility is evaluated on Onion and Shoal Creeks in Austin, Texas, using downscaled ECMWF ensemble runoff forecasts.
supporting_quote: we present a new method for probabilistic flood inundation forecasting that involves using an ensemble of streamflow forecasts to compute inundation depths and extents from rating curve libraries
We also present the Rating Curve-based Automatic Flood Forecasting (RCAFF) software that we have developed to automate the workflow

chunks.text: A central evaluation goal is to check whether RCAFF-derived water-surface elevations and inundation extents match those from the underlying hydraulic models used to build the rating curve libraries. The authors also assess how well the two-day-ahead ECMWF-RAPID ensemble streamflows translate into water-surface elevation forecasts at USGS gages, recognizing that input streamflow uncertainty can dominate overall performance.
supporting_quote: we compared the flood inundation depths and extents produced by RCAFF to those produced by the HEC-RAS model
we compared the water surface elevations from RCAFF to observed water surface elevations at the most downstream USGS gages

chunks.text: Full ensemble flood inundation forecasting with hydraulic models is often impractical because many hydraulic simulations are computationally expensive and require careful boundary-condition specification. At regional and continental scales, additional issues include stability limits for unsteady flow solvers and complexities in representing bathymetry, reservoirs, and structures. These barriers hinder operational systems that can produce timely, accurate inundation forecasts with sufficient lead time.
supporting_quote: the high computational expense of many hydraulic models renders their use impractical for ensemble forecasting
challenges related to characterizing river bathymetry, incorporation of reservoir operations, inclusion of hydraulic structures, prescribing boundary conditions, as well as the computational expense

chunks.text: Static flood risk products such as Flood Insurance Rate Maps provide deterministic boundaries based on historical conditions and do not communicate uncertainty or provide forward-looking storm impacts. This limits their usefulness for decision-making during evolving events and for communicating uncertainty to policy makers and the public.
supporting_quote: This single line does not convey the inherent uncertainties in the hydrologic and hydraulic analysis
Flood Insurance Rate Maps provide static flood risk maps based on historical climate and hydrological conditions. They do not provide any insights on the potential impacts of future storms

chunks.text: Even with ensemble meteorological prediction, precipitation dynamics remain a dominant uncertainty for streamflow forecasting, and coarse model scales reduce the ability to represent local rapid hydrologic responses. This is especially problematic for flash-flood-prone basins where hydrographs can change quickly, limiting forecast reliability and local applicability without downscaling and improved routing.
supporting_quote: precipitation dynamics remain the largest source of uncertainty for streamflow predictions
These two watersheds are located in an area that is prone to flash flooding, leading to the National Weather Service nicknaming it "Flash Flood Alley"

chunks.text: The proposed rating curve library method pre-runs a hydraulic model across a range of steady inflows and extracts rating curves at multiple cross sections. During forecasting, predicted streamflow is used to interpolate stage from the library at each cross section, then stages are triangulated into a water surface. Subtracting bathymetry from the water surface yields inundation depths and extents at substantially lower computational cost than re-running hydraulics for each ensemble member.
supporting_quote: pre-running a hydraulic model using multiple inflows and extracting rating curves
For a given streamflow, flood stage at each cross section is interpolated from the pre-computed rating curve library to delineate flood inundation depths and extents at a lower computational cost.

chunks.text: Downscaling of ECMWF H-TESSEL runoff to local streamflow is accomplished by routing runoff through the RAPID model on the NHDPlus river network. The workflow transforms gridded runoff to NHDPlus catchment runoff using an overlap-area matrix, applies it as lateral inflow, and routes flows with RAPID’s parallelized Muskingum formulation. Outputs are produced at 6-hour resolution and stored as NetCDF files.
supporting_quote: routing runoff through the Routing Application for Parallel Computation of Discharge (RAPID) (David et al., 2011) on the National Hydrography Dataset Plus (NHDPlus)
Outputs were produced at a 6-h temporal resolution and saved in the NetCDF file format.

chunks.text: RCAFF Step 1 builds the rating curve library from a HEC-RAS model containing many steady-state flow profiles. RCAFF extracts cross-section rating curves and cutlines via the HEC-RAS COM HECRASController library and stores them in an XML library. The inflow boundary conditions for the steady profiles must span anticipated flows so the library captures water-surface and inundation evolution.
supporting_quote: provide RCAFF with a HEC-RAS model containing a series of steady-state simulations (i.e., flow profiles)
RCAFF creates a library saved in an Extensible Markup Language (XML) file format that stores the rating curves for each cross section

chunks.text: RCAFF Step 2 links NHDPlus reaches (COMIDs) to rating-curve cross sections using a CSV mapping file. The mapping can include a manually specified flow multiplier per cross section to adjust for downstream flow increases because RAPID provides flow at the downstream end of each reach. In this study, multipliers were estimated based on the fraction of total catchment area contributing at each cross section.
supporting_quote: RCAFF creates a comma separated values (CSV) mapping file with placeholders for the COMID
a multiplier can be specified manually in the mapping file for each cross section ... to account for the increase in streamflow as one moves downstream

chunks.text: In the forecasting step, RCAFF retrieves streamflows by COMID (from iRODS or local NetCDF/CSV), interpolates cross-section water-surface elevations from the rating curve library, and builds a constrained triangulated water surface using the Triangle library. DEM pixels are mapped to overlapping triangles to accelerate repeated interpolation, and inundation depth is computed as water surface minus DEM elevation. RCAFF outputs depth rasters and a raster of the fraction of ensemble members inundating each pixel as an inundation probability estimate.
supporting_quote: interpolating the water surface elevation at each cross section ... using the rating curve library and the streamflows retrieved
RCAFF also produces an output raster showing the fraction of the ensembles that predicted inundation for each pixel.

chunks.text: The feasibility study focuses on Onion and Shoal Creeks in Austin, Texas, chosen due to available high-quality HEC-RAS hydraulic models and LiDAR data provided by the City of Austin. These basins are prone to flash flooding and experienced significant flooding during the time window with available ECMWF forecasts. Model evaluation uses USGS gages located on these streams for observed stage and discharge comparisons.
supporting_quote: we applied the method to the Onion and Shoal Creeks located in Austin, Texas
selected these watersheds for our assessment because of the availability of existing high quality hydraulic models and LiDAR data from the City of Austin

chunks.text: ECMWF ensemble forecasts used here come from a 51-member medium-range ensemble (50 perturbed members plus 1 deterministic control). The ensemble is produced at ~32 km horizontal resolution for 10 days, then ~64 km for days 11–15, with 3-hour time steps for the first 144 hours and 6-hour thereafter. These atmospheric forecasts are coupled to the H-TESSEL land surface model that produces runoff inputs for routing.
supporting_quote: a 51-member ensemble medium range forecast with 50 perturbed members and 1 unperturbed deterministic control run
produced at a horizontal resolution of ~32 km for 10 days, increasing to ~64 km from day 11 to 15

chunks.text: Downscaled streamflow inputs are generated by routing ECMWF H-TESSEL runoff through RAPID on the NHDPlus network. NHDPlus provides reach-catchment connectivity and unique identifiers (COMIDs) used to connect reaches and extract corresponding forecast flows. Outputs are saved in NetCDF and stored on iRODS for retrieval.
supporting_quote: Each river reach and its contributing catchment is assigned the same unique identifier called the COMID
Outputs were produced at a 6-h temporal resolution and saved in the NetCDF file format.

chunks.text: To build the rating curve libraries, the authors ran each creek’s HEC-RAS model for 160 steady-state profiles spanning from 20 m³/s up to the 1% annual chance streamflow. The 1% flow targets were approximately ~703 m³/s for Shoal Creek and ~3,745 m³/s for Onion Creek, with profile selection aiming for ~0.5 m water-surface elevation increments between simulated flows.
supporting_quote: we ran their respective HEC-RAS model for 160 steady state profiles with streamflows ranging from 20 m³/s to their 1% annual chance streamflow (i.e., ~703 m³/s for Shoal Creek and ~3,745 m³/s for Onion Creek)
We chose the streamflows so that the change in water surface elevations between each simulated streamflow was close to 0.5 m.

chunks.text: Inundation delineation uses DEMs derived from LiDAR provided by the City of Austin, with reported vertical root-mean-square error of 10 cm. The DEM spatial resolutions were 0.3 m for Shoal Creek and 1.5 m for Onion Creek. The same DEM and projection/datum alignment were used for both HEC-RAS-based and rating-curve-based inundation delineations to ensure comparability.
supporting_quote: The spatial resolutions of the DEMs we used ... were 0.3 m and 1.5 m for the Shoal Creek and Onion Creek watersheds, respectively.
LiDAR dataset with a vertical root-mean-square error of 10 cm supplied by the City of Austin

chunks.text: When comparing ECMWF-RAPID ensemble streamflows with observed USGS hydrographs, the ensembles largely underpredicted peak flows at both creeks’ downstream gages. The underprediction was worse for the smaller Shoal Creek watershed, and the ensembles did not capture the rapid rising limb or smaller time-scale fluctuations. These deficiencies limited the usefulness of Shoal Creek forecasts for subsequent inundation prediction in this study.
supporting_quote: the ECMWF-RAPID ensembles largely under predicted the peak observed streamflows at the USGS gages
This under prediction of the peak streamflow was worse for the smaller Shoal Creek watershed

chunks.text: RCAFF inundation extents closely matched those produced by HEC-RAS when both used observed peak flows as inputs. Agreement quantified by the fitness index yielded F values of 95–96% for Shoal and Onion Creeks. Mean differences in predicted water-surface elevations between the two approaches were small (0.06 m for Shoal; 0.09 m for Onion), supporting that the library interpolation preserves the underlying hydraulic model behavior.
supporting_quote: good agreement ... with F values of 95-96% for the Shoal and Onion Creeks, respectively
mean difference ... only 0.06 and 0.09 m for Shoal and Onion Creeks, respectively

chunks.text: The authors report substantial computational savings from RCAFF relative to manual hydraulic-model execution and GIS-based delineation. For Onion Creek, RCAFF required about ~10 minutes per time-step for all 51 ensembles (~16 minutes including probability calculation), compared with ~130 minutes for manual HEC-RAS execution plus HEC-GeoRAS processing. This demonstrates the intended efficiency advantage for ensemble-based inundation products.
supporting_quote: RCAFF took ~10 min (16 min total if the inundation probabilities are calculated) for each time-step for the 51 ensemble members vs. ~130 min
providing savings on the computation time required to run each of the ensemble members

chunks.text: Because ECMWF-RAPID streamflow forecasts were poor for Shoal Creek, inundation forecasting was continued only for Onion Creek. For Onion Creek, the HEC-RAS-derived rating curve library compared well with measured USGS stage-discharge data for flows below ~2,000 m³/s, which exceeds the May 25, 2015 flood peak. This supports using the hydraulic-model-derived library for the evaluated event range.
supporting_quote: Since the ECMWF-RAPID streamflow forecasts were poor for Shoal Creek, we proceeded ... using only Onion Creek.
The rating curves compared well for streamflows below ~2,000 m3 /s

chunks.text: For Onion Creek, RCAFF generally underpredicted water-surface elevations because the ECMWF-RAPID ensembles underpredicted streamflow. However, at the downstream gage 08159000, RCAFF predicted higher water levels than observed on the rising limb despite underpredicted flows, consistent with hysteresis/looped rating behavior at that location. On the recession limb, when ensemble flows matched observations, water-surface elevations matched well (e.g., ensemble 47).
supporting_quote: RCAFF tool generally under predicted water surface elevations because the ECMWF-RAPID outputs under predicted streamflows
for ensemble 47 was 252.8 m3 /s vs. an observed value of 260.8 m3 /s ... 141.0 m vs. an observed value of 140.8 m

chunks.text: RCAFF produced ensemble-specific inundation depth rasters and an inundation probability map based on the fraction of ensemble members inundating each pixel. An example depth map is shown for Onion Creek at May 26, 2015, 06:00 using the ensemble member with the highest peak flow (252.8 m³/s). The probability map is computed for the same time to depict spatial variability in ensemble inundation agreement.
supporting_quote: inundation depth map ... for ... Onion Creek at May 26, 2015, 06:00
ensemble member with the highest peak flow of 252.8 m3 /s at May 26, 2015, 06:00

chunks.text: The study identifies multiple reasons for mismatch between ECMWF-RAPID flows and observed hydrographs, emphasizing scale and representation limits. Cited causes include sub-grid dynamics from coarse ECMWF/H-TESSEL grids and time steps, smoothing introduced by the downscaling workflow, and omission of hydraulic structures in RAPID routing. The authors note that bridges and dams exist in the basins and that incorporating such structures in RAPID is ongoing research.
supporting_quote: inability to capture some of the sub-grid dynamics due to coarseness of the computational grid and time-step
hydraulic structures including dams, reservoirs, etc., that can influence the predicted streamflows were not incorporated in the RAPID model

chunks.text: The rating curve library approach inherits classic rating-curve limitations: channel changes can shift stage-discharge relations over time. The authors highlight scouring/deposition, seasonal vegetation, and ice formation as processes that can make cross sections unstable and invalidate a previously derived library. Maintaining accuracy may require updating or shifting curves when conditions change.
supporting_quote: Unstable cross sections arising from scouring and deposition of sediment, seasonal vegetation growth within or along river reaches, and ice formation can shift the rating curves over time.

chunks.text: When the energy slope varies, rating curves can become looped (hysteretic), and the library may overpredict stages on the rising limb. The paper attributes looped conditions to rapidly changing flows and backwater effects, and notes that such overprediction can be conservative for risk assessment. The authors suggest hybridizing with unsteady simulations during rapidly changing flows to reduce this limitation.
supporting_quote: Streamflow conditions that cause the energy slope to change can lead to looped rating curve conditions
A hybrid approach that incorporates unsteady simulations with hydraulic models for periods with rapidly changing flow conditions may be employed

chunks.text: Backwater effects tied to downstream boundary conditions can reduce applicability of simple rating-curve-based forecasting. The authors suggest extending models downstream so backwater does not affect upstream locations of interest, and cite an alternative of extending the library to include possible backwater profiles via a hydraulic performance graph approach. These steps aim to address cases where downstream controls materially alter water levels.
supporting_quote: models can be extended downstream to ensure that backwater effects do not affect water surface elevations at the locations of interest upstream
Yen and Castro (2000) proposed the hydraulic performance graph approach, where the rating curve library is extended to include all possible backwater profiles.

chunks.text: The uncertainty treatment emphasized here primarily reflects meteorological and land-surface-model ensemble uncertainty, while other sources remain unaccounted. The authors list remaining uncertainties in RAPID parameters/initial conditions, downscaling, hydraulic-model parameters and boundary conditions used for the library, and interpolation methods. They propose extending libraries with Monte Carlo simulations over hydraulic parameter distributions to better represent hydraulic uncertainty.
supporting_quote: treatment of uncertainty ... only accounts for uncertainty related to the numerical weather predictions and the runoff from the ECMWF-HTESSEL simulations
uncertainty remains in the prescription of the initial conditions and parameters associated with the RAPID model

chunks.text: The paper concludes that the rating curve library method is a practical alternative to running full hydraulic models for ensemble inundation forecasting, offering a scalable path for operational use. RCAFF treats each river reach independently, making computations “embarrassingly parallel” and suitable for high-performance computing scaling. The approach can leverage the many existing calibrated hydraulic models developed for flood insurance studies to support local forecasting systems.
supporting_quote: a new rating curve library method for flood inundation delineation as an alternative to running full-blown hydraulic models
RCAFF treats each river reach as an independent element, placing its computations into the so-called "embarrassingly parallel" class of algorithms.

chunks.text: The authors conclude that interpolated water-surface elevations from RCAFF are comparable to the underlying hydraulic models used to build the rating curve libraries. This supports the idea that precomputed steady simulations can be reused to rapidly translate streamflow forecasts into inundation products without substantial loss of hydraulic fidelity for the tested conditions.
supporting_quote: The interpolated water surface elevations from the RCAFF tool were as good as results from the hydraulic models from which we generated the underlying rating curve library.
results from this rating curve library approach are comparable to the hydraulic models underlying the rating curve libraries

chunks.text: A key conclusion is that the largest impacts on inundation forecast accuracy come from numerical weather prediction, land-surface runoff generation, and the downscaling process used to produce local streamflows. Because streamflow ensembles underpredicted the event, RCAFF inundation predictions were correspondingly biased, indicating that improving upstream hydro-meteorological components will directly improve inundation forecasts derived from the library method.
supporting_quote: numerical weather predictions, runoff from land surface models, and the downscaling process ... have the largest impacts on the ability to accurately forecast flood inundation
ensemble streamflow forecasts used as inputs to RCAFF are the largest source of uncertainty in predicting observed floods

chunks.text: Accurate river width and depth are foundational inputs for large-scale hydrologic and hydraulic prediction because they influence flood magnitude, frequency, inundation extent, and ecosystem habitat conditions. Operational systems such as NOAA’s National Water Model (NWM) require channel geometry for millions of reaches, motivating scalable estimation approaches. Traditional workflows often simplify cross sections and rely on empirical curves to provide geometry at national scales.
supporting_quote: “widths and depths of rivers are fundamental characteristics of river geometry and have profound effects on flood magnitudes, frequency, and inundation”
“The National Water Model includes a network of 2.7 million river reaches”

chunks.text: Hydraulic geometry has historically been represented with power-law relationships linking discharge to channel width and depth, derived from log-log regressions on observations. In ungauged contexts, these equations are commonly simplified further by replacing discharge with drainage area. These relationships have been widely used for decades to parameterize river geometry in modeling and mapping applications.
supporting_quote: “The power‐law‐based hydraulic geometry curves... were first proposed by Leopold and Maddock... as follows: w = aQ^b (1) ... d = cQ^f (2)”
“In practice, these equations are usually simplified further, relying on catchment area instead of discharge”

chunks.text: Machine learning has emerged as a promising alternative for river geometry prediction, with prior studies showing improved predictive power over power-law approaches, particularly for width and depth separately. Tree-based methods and neural networks can incorporate multiple environmental covariates beyond drainage area or discharge alone. This work builds on those early results but expands scale and adopts a multi-model strategy.
supporting_quote: “Lin et al. (2020) developed an XGBoost approach... R^2 = 0.81 for a global‐scale test data set”
“For depth, Raney et al. (2021) developed a calibrated Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) model, increasing the R^2 from 0.32... to 0.58”

chunks.text: The study aims to evaluate whether machine-learning models can outperform traditional regionalized power-law hydraulic geometry methods for predicting median river width and depth across the contiguous United States. It explicitly compares ML and power-law approaches and examines variation in model skill by stream order and by geographic region. The work also targets producing a publicly usable national river geometry product derived from the trained models.
supporting_quote: “we are attempting to answer... (a) How do ML‐based models compare to traditional power‐law approaches... (b) How does model performance vary across stream orders and geographical regions?”
“develop a comprehensive... river geometry database... STREAM‐geo... for the nearly 2.7 million reaches across the contiguous US”

chunks.text: A central objective is to create STREAM-geo, a reach-scale prediction database for NHDPlus flowlines that includes width, depth, width-to-depth ratio, and river/stream surface area under median flow conditions. The dataset is intended to support hydrology, ecology, and water management applications that require consistent geometry estimates over very large spatial domains.
supporting_quote: “STREAM‐geo... provides river width, river depth, river width to depth ratio, and the river and stream surface area (RSSA) for the nearly 2.7 million reaches”
“The developed models have been used to create the newly publicly available STREAM-geo data set”

chunks.text: Power-law hydraulic geometry methods can be highly uncertain because they omit many controlling factors and depend on limited or uneven observation support. The paper describes uncertainties arising from poor observation quality/quantity, natural spatiotemporal variability, and theoretical shortcomings. These issues can propagate into large-scale hydrologic models that depend on empirical geometry parameterizations.
supporting_quote: “this regional regression approach suffers from substantial variabilities and uncertainties”
“mainly due to either the poor quality or quantity of hydraulic observations... the natural spatial and temporal variability of rivers... and theoretical shortcomings”

chunks.text: Large-scale models often simplify channel cross sections due to the difficulty and cost of bathymetric observations and computational constraints. The NWM uses trapezoidal channels and regional curves to estimate bankfull geometry, which can limit fidelity. This motivates improved data-driven estimation of width and depth for millions of reaches.
supporting_quote: “large‐scale hydrologic watershed models often have to simplify their channel cross‐section representations”
“the National Water Model assumes trapezoidal‐shaped channels with 11 parameters”

chunks.text: Remote sensing via SWOT will not fully solve national-scale geometry needs because it targets only wider rivers and has limited temporal sampling. Many U.S. reaches are narrower than SWOT’s effective threshold, leaving a large gap for headwaters and small streams. This creates the need for complementary approaches that can estimate geometry for small channels.
supporting_quote: “SWOT can only characterize rivers wider than 100 m, and that it provides only limited temporal sampling”
“the vast majority (>96.9%) of US stream reaches are narrower than that 50‐m threshold”

chunks.text: The study compares four modeling approaches for predicting median river width and depth: regional power-law equations, multiple linear regression, tree-based machine learning (Random Forest and XGBoost), and a neural network (multilayer perceptron). The ML methods use 17 predictors spanning climate, land use, geomorphology, and anthropogenic features. Power-law models are regionalized using Hydrologic Landscape Regions to mirror operational practice.
supporting_quote: “we used four different approaches... (a) multiple linear regression... (b) tree‐based approaches (Random Forest, XGBoost), and (c) a neural network (multilayer perceptron)”
“our data‐driven, machine‐learning approaches use 17 different predictors”

chunks.text: Regional power-law models were fit as functions of catchment area, with separate equations for width and depth. The authors developed 20 sets of coefficients corresponding to the 20 Hydrologic Landscape Regions across CONUS. This provides a benchmark aligned with regional hydraulic geometry usage in large-scale models.
supporting_quote: “w = aAw^b (3)”
“we developed 20 different equations for the 20 Hydrologic Landscape Regions”

chunks.text: Multiple linear regression was developed on log-transformed variables to address skewness, starting from the full predictor set and then reducing using forward stepwise selection. Predictors were removed if not significant (p > 0.05), and further removed if R-squared decreased by less than 0.05. Final equations are reported in supporting information.
supporting_quote: “all variables were log‐transformed, given the high degree of skewness”
“A forward stepwise regression technique was then used... p‐values > 0.05 being considered not significant”
“variables were removed... if their removal did not reduce the R‐squared value by more than 0.05”

chunks.text: Random Forest and XGBoost models were trained with hyperparameter tuning using GridSearchCV and five-fold cross-validation to limit overfitting. Random Forest tuning included maximum depth, number of trees, feature subsampling, and node-size constraints. The approach targets nonlinear relationships and interactions among the 17 predictors.
supporting_quote: “The GridSearchCV method... was applied to optimize... maximum tree depth, number of trees... minimum samples”
“Five‐fold cross‐validation... was also used with the training data set to prevent overfitting”

chunks.text: The multilayer perceptron (MLP) workflow included variable-specific transformations and scaling, random sampling of 100 hyperparameter sets, and early stopping with five-fold cross-validation. Discharge, watershed area, and slope received power-law transformations; other predictors were standardized then min-max normalized. Training used the Adam optimizer to minimize mean squared error.
supporting_quote: “we applied power‐law transformations to three predictor variables (discharge, watershed area, and slope)”
“Overall, 100 hyperparameter sets were generated”
“trained the model 100 times with an early stop function... with 5‐fold cross‐validation”
“Adam... was used to optimize a Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss function”

chunks.text: Model evaluation used a shuffled 75:25 train-test split and reported RMSE, PBIAS, R-squared, and Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency, computed on the held-out testing dataset. For models trained in log-space (power-law and MLR), predictions were back-transformed before metric calculation to ensure comparison in original units. Performance was additionally summarized by stream order and by Zone II North American Ecoregions.
supporting_quote: “randomly distributed to a 75:25 split of training and testing data sets”
“evaluation metrics... RMSE, Percent Bias (PBIAS), ... R^2, and Nash Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE)”
“back‐transformation... before calculating model performance”
“across stream orders... and... Zone II North American Ecoregions”

chunks.text: Predictor importance was analyzed using permutation-based out-of-bag mean squared error increases from the Random Forest model. For each predictor, the method compares out-of-bag MSE with and without permutation to quantify sensitivity. This supports interpretation of which covariates contribute most to width and depth predictions.
supporting_quote: “predictor importance was quantified using the method of permutation‐based mean‐squared error (MSE) reduction”
“we calculated the out‐of‐bag MSE (OOBMSE)... difference between the permuted and non‐permuted OOBMSE”

chunks.text: Observed width and depth targets were drawn from the USGS HYDRoSWOT dataset, consisting of ADCP-based cross-section hydraulics across the U.S. The dataset contains 220,000+ hydraulic records for more than 5,000 stations collected from the 1940s through 2014. The study uses water-surface width and weighted mean depth as targets.
supporting_quote: “HYDRoSWOT... includes 220,000 + records... for more than 5,000 stations”
“These data were collected... from the 1940s through 2014.”
“The water‐surface width and weighted mean river depth... were used as target variables”

chunks.text: The authors cleaned HYDRoSWOT by removing site-specific outliers (outside the 5th–95th percentile), NaNs, and sites with fewer than 6 measurements, then summarized each site by its median width and median depth. This converts time-varying series into time-stationary targets for model training. The final training dataset includes 5,269 reaches with width and 2,678 reaches with depth.
supporting_quote: “width and depth values above the 95th percentile or below the 5th percentile for each site were removed”
“Sites with fewer than 6 data points were removed”
“we calculated the median width and depth values”
“finalized training data set contained width measurements for 5,269... and depth measurements for 2,678”

chunks.text: A set of 17 stream and catchment predictors was assembled from multiple national datasets, covering climate, geomorphology, land use/vegetation, soils, and human impacts. Examples include aridity index, streamflow/discharge, elevation, slope, stream order, D50, catchment area, land use, vegetation indices, soil types, population density, and upstream dams. HYDRoSWOT points were matched to the nearest NHDPlus reach within 500 m to attach reach attributes.
supporting_quote: “A total of 17 stream and catchment attributes were collected”
“climatic variables such as the aridity index”
“reach metadata such as elevation, slope and stream order”
“anthropogenic features such as population density... and accumulated dam construction”
“matched with the closest NHDPlus reach within a 500‐m buffer”

chunks.text: STREAM-geo is the derived national product providing model-predicted geometry for NHDPlus reaches across CONUS. Out of 2,691,339 reaches, predictions are produced for 2,610,904 reaches; remaining reaches are NaN when key attributes (e.g., watershed area or mean annual flow) are invalid or missing. The dataset includes outputs from Random Forest, XGBoost, and MLP models.
supporting_quote: “STREAM‐geo provides river geometry data for nearly 2.7 million NHDPlus stream reaches”
“Among the 2,691,339 NHDPlus stream reaches... STREAM‐geo provides river geometry predictions for 2,610,904 reaches”
“we provide results from the three ML models (RFR, XGBoost, and MLP)”

chunks.text: Across all sites, machine-learning models substantially outperformed the regionalized power-law benchmark for predicting median river width and depth. For width, the best performance reached R^2 up to 0.75 (Random Forest) compared with R^2 = 0.45 for the power-law approach. For depth, ML achieved R^2 up to 0.67 versus R^2 = 0.18 for the power-law equations, showing especially large gains for depth estimation.
supporting_quote: “providing R-squared values of as high as 0.75 for width and as high as 0.67 for depth, compared with R-squared values of 0.45 for width and 0.18 for depth from the regional hydraulic geometry equations.”

chunks.text: Overall width prediction skill was high and similar across ML approaches, with Random Forest slightly best. Reported test metrics for width were approximately NSE=0.74 and R^2=0.75 for Random Forest, and NSE≈0.73 and R^2≈0.73 for both XGBoost and MLP. This indicates that tree ensembles and neural networks can both capture width variability when trained on the same predictor set.
supporting_quote: “For the median river width, the random forest model performed the best (NSE_RF = 0.74, R^2_RF = 0.75; NSE_XGB = 0.73, R^2_XGB = 0.73; NSE_MLP = 0.73, R^2_MLP = 0.73)”

chunks.text: Depth predictions were less accurate than width but still showed strong performance for Random Forest and XGBoost, with slightly lower results for MLP. Random Forest and XGBoost reported R^2=0.67 and NSE around 0.63–0.64, while MLP reported R^2=0.66 and NSE=0.57. The consistency across models suggests depth is inherently harder to predict from available predictors but remains improved relative to traditional methods.
supporting_quote: “For the median river depth... (NSE_RF = 0.63, R^2_RF = 0.67; NSE_XGB = 0.64, R^2_XGB = 0.67; NSE_MLP = 0.57, R^2_MLP = 0.66)”

chunks.text: Multiple linear regression (MLR) was not competitive for width, performing even worse than the power-law benchmark and yielding a negative NSE. For width, MLR explained only 33% of variance and had NSE = −0.26. For depth, MLR performed better (R^2=0.66; NSE=0.52) but still underperformed the best ML models.
supporting_quote: “multiple linear regression model performed even worse than the power-law predictions... (R^2_MLR = 0.33, NSE_MLR = -0.26)”
“The multiple linear regression model performed better for depth... (R^2_MLR = 0.66, NSE_MLR = 0.52)”

chunks.text: Discharge was the dominant predictor of both width and depth, based on both simple regressions and random-forest feature importance. Simple regressions showed discharge alone explained R^2=0.61 of median width and R^2=0.57 of median depth. Random forest relative feature importance similarly emphasized discharge (RFI_width=0.67; RFI_depth=0.78), indicating it contributes unique information beyond other catchment attributes.
supporting_quote: “discharge explains... variability in median width (R^2 = 0.61) and depth (R^2 = 0.57)”
“median river discharge... is by far the most important predictor (RFI_width = 0.67, RFI_depth = 0.78)”

chunks.text: Power-law predictions exhibited systematic bias and strong dependence on stream order, including large underprediction for high-order streams. Overall, the power-law approach underpredicted median width by about 24% and median depth by about 22%. By stream order, width underpredictions for higher-order streams were “50% or greater,” and depth underprediction reached −54.23% for 9th-order streams.
supporting_quote: “using the traditional power‐law models... results in an approximately 24% underprediction of median width values and a 22% underprediction of depth values”
“much poorer performance for the higher‐order streams, with underpredictions of width typically 50% or greater”
“median PBIAS = − 54.23% (9th‐order)”

chunks.text: Even though ML models improved average bias, their errors still varied by stream order, and different ML methods showed different patterns. Random Forest was comparatively consistent, while XGBoost and MLP showed a more pronounced U-shaped behavior across orders for width, with poorer performance for the smallest and largest streams. For 1st-order stream width, Random Forest had lower median PBIAS (22.6%) than XGBoost (30.0%) and MLP (28.9%).
supporting_quote: “there is a more pronounced U‐shaped behavior in the performance results... for XGBoost and the MLP models”
“for 1st‐order streams... median PBIASRF = 22.6%; median PBIASXGB = 30.0%; median PBIASMLP = 28.9%”

chunks.text: Model skill varied geographically across ecoregions, and the best-performing ML model could differ by region. For example, in the Southeastern U.S. plains (ER 8.3) all ML models achieved NSE > 0.84 for width. In the Appalachian region (ER 8.4), Random Forest (NSE=0.68) exceeded XGBoost (NSE=0.59), while in California’s mediterranean region (ER 11.1) XGBoost (NSE=0.81) and MLP (NSE=0.86) exceeded Random Forest (NSE=0.73).
supporting_quote: “Southeastern U.S. plains (ER 8.3) (NSE > 0.84)”
“Appalachian region... (ER 8.4)... random forest model (NSE = 0.68)... XGBoost model (NSE = 0.59)”
“mediterranean region of California (Ecoregion 11.1), XGBoost (NSE = 0.81) and MLP... (NSE = 0.86)... random forest... (NSE = 0.73)”

chunks.text: STREAM-geo derived metrics indicate width-to-depth ratios increase downstream and vary strongly by stream order. Under median flow, the median width-to-depth ratio rises from 13.0 for 1st-order streams to 48.4 for 10th-order streams, and then tends to plateau above 8th order. These ratios support broader characterization of depositional versus incisional channel tendencies across the network.
supporting_quote: “width‐to‐depth ratio varies greatly across stream orders, ranging from a median value of 13.0 for 1st‐order streams to 48.4 for 10th‐order streams”
“However, the ratios plateau above 8th order streams.”

chunks.text: The modeled river and stream surface area suggests substantial national coverage by surface waters under median flow. The paper reports nearly 75,000 km2 of streams and rivers across CONUS, representing 0.93% of the continental United States. The eastern half generally shows larger %RSSA than the west, except near the northwestern coast.
supporting_quote: “across the contiguous U.S., an area of nearly 75,000 km2 is covered by streams and rivers, constituting 0.93% of the continental United States.”
“The Eastern half of the CONUS generally has much larger %RSSA than the West (except near the northwestern coast).”

chunks.text: Performance differences across stream orders may be influenced by uneven training data availability, which over-represents mid-order streams and under-samples headwaters. The paper shows that sampling is concentrated in 4th–5th order streams while 1st-order streams are under-sampled relative to their prevalence in the national network. This uneven sampling may partially explain better width prediction performance for mid-order streams, though the authors note it does not fully explain depth behavior.
supporting_quote: “training data... disproportionately represents 4th‐ and 5th‐order streams”
“the sampling data represents an over‐sampling of middle‐order streams, while 1st‐order streams are under‐sampled.”
“This relationship between data availability and model performance does not hold, however, for the depth predictions”

chunks.text: HYDRoSWOT observations are spatially uneven, with denser sampling in the eastern U.S. than the west, leading to unequal geographic support for model training and validation. The paper highlights that there are more width measurements than depth measurements overall. Such imbalances can contribute to regional differences in model skill and to comparatively lower accuracy for depth.
supporting_quote: “the eastern U.S. has more intensive sampling than the west, leading to an uneven distribution of in situ river geometry knowledge.”
“overall, there are more river width data points than river depth data points”

chunks.text: Differences in which model performs best across ecoregions suggest no single ML algorithm is universally optimal, motivating selective or multi-model deployment. The authors propose that Random Forest may better capture complex nonlinear interactions, while MLP may perform better in more homogeneous feature spaces. This variability implies that operational systems could benefit from choosing models by region and/or stream order.
supporting_quote: “we can also see regional differences in performance with the individual models.”
“it may be beneficial to employ a multi‐model approach that allows for selective use of modeled results based on regional differences in model performance.”
“Random Forest models... might perform better... whereas MLPs... might perform better in areas with more homogeneous regions”

chunks.text: SWOT-derived products have limitations that constrain their ability to fully characterize U.S. rivers, especially headwaters. SWOT primarily observes rivers wider than 100 m and provides limited temporal sampling, and the paper notes most U.S. reaches are below even a 50 m threshold. As a result, the authors position their ML-based predictions as a complement to SWOT rather than a replacement.
supporting_quote: “SWOT can only characterize rivers wider than 100 m”
“uneven temporal sampling, leading to a limited ability to observe long‐term river geometry dynamics and flood events.”
“the vast majority (>96.9%) of US stream reaches are narrower than that 50‐m threshold.”

chunks.text: The paper concludes that Random Forest, XGBoost, and MLP models provide better continental-scale predictions of median river width and depth than regional physiographic power-law equations. These advances were achieved using publicly available land-surface predictors, without requiring detailed subsurface altimetry or satellite-derived channel measurements. The improvements support enhanced flood forecasting and hydrologic simulation parameterization for large networks.
supporting_quote: “All machine‐learning models provided exceptional evaluation metrics that outperformed... regional (physiographic) hydraulic geometry equations”
“achieved using only publicly available land surface information, without the need for detailed subsurface altimetry and satellite information.”

chunks.text: The authors emphasize that model performance varies by stream order and region, so a multi-model approach can be advantageous for operational use. They argue that large-scale systems like the National Water Model could improve by selecting or blending ML model outputs based on where each model performs best. This is presented as a step toward adaptive analytical frameworks for water system science.
supporting_quote: “performance outcomes across stream orders and geographical regions... demonstrating the value of using multi‐model approaches”
“large‐scale models like the National Water Model... stand to gain significantly from a multi‐ model strategy.”

chunks.text: A key deliverable is STREAM-geo, a publicly available dataset providing reach-scale predictions for most NHDPlus reaches across CONUS. It includes width, depth, width-to-depth ratio, and surface area metrics under median flow, supporting applications in hydrology, ecology, flood management, erosion, and sediment transport. The dataset is positioned as a comprehensive national resource for river geometry information.
supporting_quote: “STREAM‐geo... provides river width, depth, width‐to‐depth ratios, and stream surface area for nearly 2.7 million reaches”
“a groundbreaking new resource to promote new insights... to support hydrology, ecology, and river management.”

chunks.text: Coastal areas are vulnerable to extreme events, and accurate prediction of water levels is needed in the coastal transition zone (CTZ), the region between the coast and upland where tidal influence fades. Operational forecasting efforts such as enhancing NOAA’s National Water Model (NWM) aim to include CTZ water level predictions. Prior research shows tides, river discharge, storm surge, friction, and estuary geometry all affect propagation and amplification/attenuation of signals within estuaries and rivers.
supporting_quote: Vulnerability of coastal regions to extreme events motivates an operational coupled inland-coastal modeling strategy focusing on the coastal transition zone (CTZ)

infrastructure located in coastal areas require accurate estimations of water level ranges, magnitude, and frequencies in the areas between the coast and the upland where tides no longer influence water level variation, that is, the coastal transition zone (CTZ)
Understanding the processes that contribute to water levels in CTZs, such as mean sea level, tidal range, river discharge, and storm surge, is essential

chunks.text: Estuary hydrodynamics depend on frictional and topographical factors as well as channel convergence, which control tidal propagation, damping, and constituent behavior. Mathematical and semi-analytical studies have established that convergence affects tidal constituent amplitudes and velocity fields, and that nonlinear processes (e.g., overtides) and resonance can further modify water level amplification through estuaries and into rivers.
supporting_quote: Numerous studies mathematically defined the relationships between frictional and topographical factors, and their respective and combined influence on the tidal amplification in estuaries
Friedrichs and Aubrey (1994) and Jay (1991) show that convergence significantly influences amplitudes of tidal constituents and velocity fields.
Talke and Jay (2020) demonstrate the influence and importance of tidal resonance on the amplification of water levels

chunks.text: Existing sensitivity analyses and modeling studies are often site-specific, which limits generalization across broader regions. Recent calls argue for multidisciplinary regional-scale analyses of coastal interfaces to better understand seaward and landward extents and to assess compound hazards. This paper positions its approach as a response to that need by emphasizing scalable, region-informed analysis using idealized domains.
supporting_quote: Ward et al. (2020) and Harrison et al. (2021) argue that currently, many studies are site specific, and they fall short in advancing our understanding of the dynamic seaward and landward extent of coastal interfaces across the scale.
They suggest that researchers should instead steer their concerted effort toward multidisciplinary regionalscale analysis of coastal interfaces.

chunks.text: The paper aims to introduce a top-down framework for investigating how different physical processes and parameters affect hydrodynamics and total water level (TWL) predictions in coastal transition zones (CTZs). The framework incorporates geometry, physical properties, and forcing conditions, and is demonstrated across the U.S. East and Gulf coasts. A key intended use is to quantify the relative significance of parameter perturbations rather than estimating absolute parameter values.
supporting_quote: we propose a top-down framework for investigating the contributions of different processes and parameters to TWL prediction in CTZs.
This framework takes into account the effects of geometrical shapes, physical properties, and forcing conditions.
We note that our proposed framework focuses on the relative significance of the parameters rather than absolute values.

chunks.text: A second goal is to propose a new method—tidal vanishing point (TVP)—to delineate how far tidal signals reach inland, effectively estimating CTZ extent along the river. This delineation is meant to support decisions about the “handoff location” for exchanging information between inland and coastal models, helping balance accuracy and computational cost in coupled operational modeling.
supporting_quote: We further propose a novel method, called tidal vanishing point (TVP), for delineating the extent of CTZs through the upland.
This extent influences decisions on data exchange locations between an inland and a coastal model (i.e., handoff location)
We propose a novel method for delineating the reach of tidal signals through the upland called TVP

chunks.text: Operationally coupling inland hydrologic models with coastal hydrodynamic models is difficult because it can increase computational complexity and requires a priori parameter estimation. These difficulties motivate methods that can identify which processes and parameters most strongly influence CTZ water levels. The problem is not just simulation, but choosing efficient coupling strategies and calibration priorities under uncertainty.
supporting_quote: coupling the NWM to existing coastal hydrodynamic models in operational settings presents challenges such as increasing computational complexity and a priori parameter estimations
Understanding the processes that contribute to water levels in CTZs... is essential to tackling these challenges

chunks.text: The field lacks broadly transferable insights because many sensitivity studies focus on individual locations and do not readily generalize to regional-scale CTZ characterization. This creates a gap in understanding the dynamic extent of coastal interfaces across scales. The paper frames the need for a systematic regional approach that can compare geometry/forcing/process contributions in a unified way.
supporting_quote: many studies are site specific, and they fall short in advancing our understanding of the dynamic seaward and landward extent of coastal interfaces across the scale.
researchers should instead steer their concerted effort toward multidisciplinary regionalscale analysis of coastal interfaces.

chunks.text: Determining where tidal influence becomes negligible inland (the CTZ boundary) is challenging but important for coupled modeling and flood prediction. The paper highlights the need for a practical way to delineate CTZ extent through the upland. This motivates the creation of TVP as a procedural method based on tidal-constituent amplitude behavior along a river centerline.
supporting_quote: accurate estimations of water level ranges, magnitude, and frequencies in the areas between the coast and the upland where tides no longer influence water level variation
we define a new concept called TVP for characterizing the reach of tidal signals through the upland, that is, the extent of CTZs.

chunks.text: The proposed framework is organized into three groups of tasks: data analysis, modeling, and assessment. Data analysis compiles ground-truth and remote-sensing sources to summarize regional hydrodynamic characteristics and derive parameter ranges. Modeling uses idealized domains with a control (reference) model and systematic one-parameter perturbations. Assessment applies statistical comparison metrics and TVP to interpret parameter significance and CTZ reach.
supporting_quote: Figure 1 depicts a conceptual flowchart of the framework which we categorize into three groups: data analysis, modeling, and assessment.
we define a control model (a reference scenario) with some predetermined values for all the model parameters and then systematically perturb the parameters
We design the tasks in this category for gaining insights into the relative significance of contributing processes in coastal dynamics.

chunks.text: The assessment uses a significance-test style comparison that accounts for correlation between error scores when comparing scenarios. Errors (e.g., MAE) are computed relative to a reference scenario, then confidence intervals on differences are calculated using a correlation-adjusted formula. A signed distance (SD) metric summarizes whether Scenario 2 differs more significantly than Scenario 1 relative to the reference.
supporting_quote: we assess the changes between each prediction and the reference scenario for a variable of interest through an error estimation metric such as mean absolute error (MAE)
We compute this half-width confidence interval using  CIα = √(2(1−ρ)) × z* σ/√n
Finally, we compute  SD = sign(ΔE) × (abs(ΔE) − CIα)

chunks.text: TVP is defined via a procedure that tracks how dominant tidal-constituent amplitudes fluctuate along a centerline from ocean to river boundary. The method selects dominant constituents per category, filters amplitudes using a window based on centerline length, and defines thresholds using exceedance probabilities. TVPs are the inland locations where filtered amplitudes fall below thresholds, aggregated by taking the maximum TVP per constituent.
supporting_quote: This method relies on the amplitudes of the tidal constituents from the water level time series at grid points along the domain's centerline
Carry out three subsequent passes of low-pass filtering on the amplitudes.
Compute exceedance probability for the filtered amplitudes.
Compute locations across the centerline where the amplitudes onward fall below the thresholds for each constituent. We coin these locations' TVPs.

chunks.text: CTZ geometries are classified from satellite imagery into three main classes: direct river–coast connection (no estuary), triangular estuary, and trapezoidal estuary. Representative river–estuary systems are parameterized using ratios that relate estuary length and widths to river width. Additional within-class categories include straight rivers, sinuous rivers, and estuaries with barrier islands, though results focus on straight-river cases.
supporting_quote: manual labeling of RESs in the region suggests that either there is no estuary (direct river– coast connection), or the estuaries are mainly triangular or trapezoidal shaped.
we categorize the CTZs into three classes, namely, without estuary (direct river–coast connection) (C1), triangular-shaped estuary (C2), and trapezoidal-shaped estuary (C3).
we introduce three ratios to establish relationships among them, as follows: Rlb = Lb/Wb, Rbt = Wb/Wt, Rbr = Wb/Wr

chunks.text: Hydrodynamic simulations are performed in D-Flow Flexible Mesh (D-Flow FM) using unstructured grids in 2D. Idealized domains include ocean, estuary (if present), and river segments; the ocean segment is sized to minimize boundary effects. Bathymetry varies along the river direction and is set to allow upstream propagation and TVP estimation (e.g., upstream bottom elevation at −1 m).
supporting_quote: We conduct the simulations using the hydrodynamic model, D-Flow Flexible Mesh (D-Flow FM)
configured to perform 2D simulations.
we set the length of the ocean segment to 100 km... and its width to 50 km
in the river segment, we set the bottom elevation at the upstream boundary to −1 m, allowing the water to propagate upstream, and enabling the estimation of the TVP

chunks.text: Scenario design varies one parameter at a time relative to a reference to isolate contributions. Parameters include Manning’s roughness (R), upstream discharge (D), and ocean-boundary water level time series (tides alone vs. tides plus a storm surge pulse). The storm surge is represented as an isosceles triangular pulse superimposed on NOAA predicted tides, with fixed 2-day rise and fall durations.
supporting_quote: establish a procedure for setting up simulation by only changing one parameter per scenario
Manning's roughness at the bed level (R), the upstream river discharge (D), and the water level at the ocean boundary (T).
we superimpose an isosceles triangular surge pulse on the baseline water level time series
use a constant duration of two days for the rising and falling limbs of the pulse

chunks.text: For TVP computation in the case study, tidal constituents are obtained from simulated water level series using UTide. The study considers semidiurnal, diurnal, and short-period (overtide) categories because the simulation period is one month. The TVP filtering uses a rolling window width of 2% of the centerline length and a threshold based on 50% exceedance probability.
supporting_quote: we decompose the water level time series... into its tidal constituents using the Python implementation of the UTide package (Codiga 2011).
we take into account three of the four tidal constituents' categories, namely semidiurnal, diurnal, and short period (overtides).
determine the filtering window width of 2% of the centerline length and adopt 50% exceedance probability as the threshold to estimate TVPs

chunks.text: Multiple datasets are compiled to derive parameter ranges for tides, discharge, storm surge extremes, coastal slope, and geometry characterization. Water level observations and extreme water levels come from NOAA CO-OPS, while mean daily discharge is taken from USGS NWIS for stations influenced by tides. Coastal slope limits are sourced from Hammar-Klose and Thieler (2001), and satellite imagery from Stamen and Google Earth supports CTZ shape classification.
supporting_quote: TABLE 1. Datasets for obtaining sensible ranges for model parameters.
Water level observations   Oceanographic Products and Services (CO-OPS)  2000–2015
Mean daily river discharge  National Water Information System (NWIS)  2000–2015
Coastal slope  Hammar-Klose and Thieler (2001)
Satellite images  Stamen (2019... ) and Google Earth Pro

chunks.text: Tidal constituent dominance is assessed from 2000–2015 NOAA station data across the study region. The principal lunar semidiurnal constituent M2 is strongest over the U.S. East coast and much of Florida, while the lunar diurnal K1 is often strongest in the Gulf. Despite this spatial variability, the modeling study simplifies by considering only an M2-dominant tide.
supporting_quote: based on data from the period 2000–2015, the M2... tidal constituent is the strongest over the East and most of Florida coast, while the K1... is often the strongest tidal constituent in the Gulf.
Although there are two types of dominant tides in the region, we only consider an M2-dominant tide in this study.

chunks.text: River discharge bounds are estimated from USGS stations classified as tide stream (ST-TS) or estuary (ES). Out of 390 such stations, 26 provide mean daily discharge data used to summarize discharges for 2000–2015. The study defines the lower and upper discharge limits as the mean of means and mean of peaks, reported as 90 m³/s and 570 m³/s, respectively.
supporting_quote: Out of 390 ST-TS and ES stations, 26 have mean daily discharge data
Figure 3b... (mean of means = 90 m3/s and mean of peaks = 570 m3/s ).
We consider the mean of means... as the lower limit and the mean of peaks... as the upper limit for the river discharge values

chunks.text: Storm surge peak heights are bounded using extreme water levels defined as the 1% exceedance probability above mean higher high water (MHHW) for 2000–2015. The minimum and maximum extreme values, 0.769 m and 3.154 m, are used to parameterize two storm surge scenarios. These values are applied as surge peak amplitudes superimposed on predicted tides at the ocean boundary.
supporting_quote: The extreme water levels... are 1% exceedance probability of water levels above mean higher high water (MHHW).
We consider the minimum (0.769 m) and the maximum (3.154 m) values of the data as the lower and higher limits for the peak storm surge height
we produce two storm surge scenarios, S07 and S31, based on the minimum (0.769 m) and maximum (3.154 m)

chunks.text: Geometry parameterization is derived from manual labeling of over 400 river–estuary system (RES) satellite images, then narrowed to 46 representative cases. Summary statistics for these 46 RESs include a downstream estuary width Wb median of 8.9 km and mean of 11.9 km, along with ratio statistics such as Rbr median 8.1 and mean 10.1. These statistics inform scaling choices for idealized-domain dimensions (e.g., setting Wb to 10 km).
supporting_quote: we retrieve over 400 black and white satellite images of the RESs

Estuaries reduce the upstream extent of velocity-field changes relative to the no-estuary case, indicating attenuation.

chunks.text: Reproducibility is widely recognized as essential for scientific progress, yet many researchers report difficulties reproducing both others’ and their own results. Data-related work consumes a substantial share of data scientists’ time, limiting time for analysis. FAIR principles have become a central guideline for improving data management and access, and many repositories have adopted them. However, typical repository workflows emphasize publishing small files rather than enabling direct, machine-actionable reuse of subsets from larger datasets used in environmental modeling.

chunks.text: HydroShare is presented as a versatile online repository supporting diverse environmental data and models, including GeoTIFF, Shapefiles, and NetCDF, and it provides identifiers, metadata, and computational integration. It defines model programs and model instances, enabling sharing via URL or DOI. HydroShare’s hsclient and JupyterHub environments support programmable workflows. Despite these capabilities, HydroShare is mostly used for publishing collections of smaller files and is less commonly used to distribute multi-gigabyte gridded spatial datasets in a seamless, subsettable manner.

chunks.text: GeoServer and THREDDS Data Server (TDS) provide machine-to-machine protocols for subsetting and transmitting large geospatial and geo-temporal datasets. GeoServer supports OGC services such as WMS, WFS, and WCS, enabling retrieval and subsetting of raster and feature data through HTTP interfaces. TDS provides remote access to formats like NetCDF via DAP2/DAP4, and DAP2 enables dimensional constraints and efficient transport. DAP2 clients can lazily load metadata first, reducing network, time, and memory demands during analysis.

The work is positioned as a proof of concept using state-scale datasets, but intended to be adaptable to other spatial aggregations (e.g., watersheds or ecological regions). The goal is to enable reproducible, interoperable workflows where model inputs are subset programmatically from shared base datasets.

Finally, it evaluates whether results are consistent with conventional, manual file-based data preparation workflows.

chunks.text: Environmental models frequently rely on spatial inputs that are manually subset for each study area, which is time-consuming and can undermine reproducibility. Many online repositories support FAIR-aligned publication features but are oriented toward sharing small files, often subsets of larger spatial products. This limits the ability to programmatically find, access, and reuse consistent subsets of large-extent datasets across multiple applications. As a result, opportunities to foster reproducible science through seamless data access are missed.

When datasets are merged or transformed across coordinate systems, location shifts can occur and propagate into model inputs. These errors may be subtle and non-fatal, making them easy to overlook while still affecting model setup and output validity. The paper treats rigorous georeferencing as essential for consistent and reliable environmental modeling.

Land cover and soil differences became zero for Coweeta and Scotts Level, and also zero for Spout Run land cover and soils.
supporting_quote: we found that using a single control point was sufficient to align the merged DEM with the original raw DEM accurately.
we were able to eliminate the DEM differences except for the DEM of Spout Run (60 m resolution), where slight differences, within a range of ±6 cm
The difference between the conventionally accessed and LES datasets land cover, and soil at Spout Run (not shown in the figure) are zero.

chunks.text: Model outputs (daily streamflow) reflected the importance of georeferencing. Without georeferencing, agreement between conventional and LES-driven runs for Coweeta was imperfect, with NSE values 0.684 (conventional vs GeoServer) and 0.647 (conventional vs TDS). After georeferencing, the streamflow series matched perfectly across methods, with NSE 1.0 reported for conventional vs GeoServer and conventional vs TDS for Coweeta. The paper also reports perfect agreement after georeferencing for Scotts Level Branch and Spout Run.
supporting_quote: without applying the georeferencing tool (conventional vs. GeoServer: Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) 0.684, conventional vs. TDS: NSE 0.647)
Fig. 11 (a) and (b) showed perfect agreement ... (conventional vs GeoServer: NSE 1.0, conventional vs TDS: NSE 1.0)
other subplots in Fig. 11 showed perfect agreement after applying the georeferencing tool for the other two watersheds.

chunks.text: The approach still faces sustainability challenges common to API-based workflows: if APIs change, scripts may break and require maintenance. The paper notes this as a reason some researchers prefer manual data collection, despite the disadvantages for reproducibility. This limitation highlights that server-side interoperability does not eliminate the need for long-term workflow stewardship. It suggests that maintenance and adaptability remain important for data-driven modeling pipelines.
supporting_quote: The first challenge concerns API-based data access: when APIs are updated or changed, it can render hard-coded scripts obsolete over time.
it is a common issue that might contribute to why some researchers prefer manual data collection over APIs.

chunks.text: GeoServer and TDS have format and workload limitations that affect which datasets are easiest to serve and subset. The paper prioritizes GeoTIFF in GeoServer because subsetting SSURGO shapefiles with heterogeneous attributes can be computationally demanding. It suggests that more efficient ways to work with shapefiles and their attribute tables for modeling would be valuable. Thus, current best practice in their approach favors grid-based datasets for performance and manageability.
supporting_quote: our primary choice was the GeoTIFF format with Geo-Server.
subsetting SSURGO shapefiles can be resource-intensive due to the heterogeneous details of soil attributes
exploring alternative approaches or capabilities to work with shapefiles and their attributes (dbf table) ... would be a valuable pursuit.

chunks.text: The study’s choice of state-scale aggregation is pragmatic, but not necessarily optimal for all hydrologic applications. It notes that Hydrologic Unit Code (HUC) units could be more suitable for some use cases, while state-scale was selected because federal systems readily provide data in that form with minimal processing. The approach is described as agnostic to the aggregation unit, implying adaptation is feasible. Nonetheless, selecting an aggregation that aligns with study needs remains a design decision.
supporting_quote: We selected the state scale as the spatial unit for distributing LES datasets, though other spatial aggregations can also be considered.
For some hydrologic applications, the Hydrologic Unit Code (HUC) ... might be a more suitable scale than the state scale
We opted for the state scale because federal web-based distribution systems readily provide data at this aggregation level
