chunks.text: Creating LES datasets relied on proprietary GIS tooling (ArcPy/ArcGIS Pro), which creates barriers to full reproducibility and portability. ArcPy is Windows-only, and containerizing proprietary software requires license availability and compatible Windows container support. The paper suggests future work using open-source GIS such as GRASS GIS or QGIS to achieve end-to-end reproducible workflows. This highlights a tooling dependency that may limit adoption by researchers without access to ArcGIS.
supporting_quote: We used ArcPy to create the LES datasets.
ArcPy is currently compatible only with the Windows operating system.
the application of open-source GIS software such as GRASS GIS or QGIS will be a future work to achieve end-to-end environmental modeling.

chunks.text: The paper highlights broader concerns about data replication, ownership, and provenance when datasets are copied and modified across distributed systems. Even when data are free to copy, it can become difficult to verify which version was used, particularly after preprocessing to harmonize coordinate systems. It emphasizes the need to document changes and link processing procedures to derived products. As a future direction, it discusses using blockchain concepts and NFTs to track provenance and uniquely identify modeling data and scripts.
supporting_quote: data replication across distributed systems can present problems.
For reproducibility, it is important to document such changes and associate the procedure for making the changes with the new data product.
the concept of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs) ... could prove valuable for identifying digital objects ... and tracking the provenance

chunks.text: The paper concludes that integrating HydroShare with GeoServer and TDS enables programmatic, server-side access to large-extent spatial datasets that can support seamless, reproducible environmental modeling workflows. It provides methods to create, share, and subset large datasets as model inputs, advancing the concept of constructing inputs from common base datasets via reproducible scripts. Across three watershed applications, the study reports no significant error introduced relative to traditional manual data retrieval when georeferencing is handled properly. The approach is positioned as extensible to other spatial aggregations and repositories using existing distribution systems.
supporting_quote: The primary contribution of this research is the methods developed for integrating HydroShare with GeoServer and TDS for exposing Large Extent Spatial datasets to models
We demonstrate how to create, share, and subset large datasets as inputs to an environmental model
we show that no significant error is introduced when using the new data distribution system compared to traditional approaches

chunks.text: Georeferencing is identified as critical for maintaining spatial data accuracy and ensuring consistent model outputs when merging and transforming large-scale datasets. The study shows that small spatial shifts can create sizable differences in spatial inputs and streamflow simulations, but applying georeferencing corrections restores agreement. The conclusion emphasizes that georeferencing should be treated as a rigorous, necessary step, particularly for large-extent modeling applications spanning multiple coordinate systems. This improves reliability and reproducibility of derived modeling results.
supporting_quote: Georeferencing is critical in ensuring spatial data accuracy, especially when dealing with large-scale datasets spanning multiple coordinate systems.
without proper georeferencing, even small shifts in data can lead to considerable inaccuracies in model outputs.
By emphasizing the need for georeferencing ... we ensure that datasets from different sources are correctly aligned

chunks.text: The authors argue that the methods are useful not only for federal datasets but also for individual scientists who want to share processed datasets with robust metadata and API-based access without deploying their own data servers. They frame this as an extension beyond file-based publication toward direct programmatic reuse, aligning with FAIR principles. HydroShare plus GeoServer/TDS is presented as a practical way to share, update, and extend data for replication and reuse across case studies. The conclusion underscores interoperability and reusability as key outcomes of the demonstrated approach.
supporting_quote: Beyond sharing large, national-scale datasets maintained by federal agencies, individual scientists can also deploy the methods used in this work.
provide a means for scientists to create and share file-based scientific data in a way that provides programmatic access without the need to deploy their own web-based data distribution systems.
Creating and sharing datasets online using this approach offers a powerful means for scientists to achieve FAIR guiding principles

chunks.text: Multiple services now publish near-real-time flood inundation maps derived from satellite remote sensing, which are valuable for emergency response and for documenting historic events. These products efficiently map flood extent but typically do not provide floodwater depth, limiting their usefulness for operational decisions and damage assessment. Hydraulic models can produce water depths but often require substantial event and channel data, calibration, and time, making them less suitable for rapid, event-specific mapping.
supporting_quote: A number of organizations now provide flood inundation maps based on satellite remote sensing. These data products can efficiently and accurately provide the areal extent of a flood event, but do not provide floodwater depth

Although these tools can simulate water depths, they require information about the event hydrological characteristics and riverine morphology. Achieving accurate simulation of a flood event is often time consuming

chunks.text: Observed flood extent is used by first responders and relief agencies, and archived inundation maps support planning and model development. The paper positions flood extent mapping as widely available and operationally helpful, but highlights that depth information is a critical missing attribute. The intended use of the proposed approach is a rapid, first-order overview rather than a detailed representation of flood dynamics.
supporting_quote: Near-real-time observations of flood extent are useful for first responders, relief agencies, civil leaders, and recovery managers
The approach is intended for first-order overview, not detailed analysis of floodwater dynamics.

chunks.text: The study aims to introduce and test an automated methodology and GIS tool, Floodwater Depth Estimation Tool (FwDET), that estimates floodwater depth using only a flood inundation extent map and a DEM. A key goal is to determine whether this simplified approach can produce depth estimates comparable to those from a complex hydraulic model. The work emphasizes fast computation using readily available data for near-real-time use and large event archives.
supporting_quote: The objective of this paper is to introduce and test a new methodology for estimating water depths in flooded domains that relies on only flood extent and a digital elevation model (DEM).
We test whether our methodology can provide a comparable estimate of floodwater depth to a complex hydrologic model.

chunks.text: Flood inundation maps generally represent only the areal extent of flooding, and water depth cannot be readily derived from extent alone for most floods. Yet depth is crucial for rescue logistics, access and road closures, and post-event damage analysis. Existing model-based or simulation methods can provide depths but are often too data- and time-intensive for near-real-time, event-specific applications.
supporting_quote: Flood inundation maps provide information on the areal extent of a flood. With the exception of very small, i.e., easily surveyed, floods, water depth cannot be readily associated with or calculated from a flood extent map.
timely information about floodwater depth is important for directing rescue and relief resources, determination of road closures and accessibility, and post-event analysis of property damage

chunks.text: FwDET estimates floodwater depth by inferring a local floodwater surface elevation from the inundation boundary on a DEM. Boundary cells of the flooded polygon are identified and their elevations extracted from the DEM; each inundated cell is then assigned the elevation of its nearest boundary cell as a proxy for local water surface elevation. Depth is computed as the difference between this assigned boundary elevation and the DEM elevation at the cell, then clipped to the flooded domain and optionally smoothed.
supporting_quote: based on identifying the flooded domain boundary cells on a DEM, using a polygon layer delineating the flood extent

a cell within the flooded domain will be assigned the elevation of its nearest boundary cell, which is then used to calculate the local water depth by subtracting this value from a cell's surface elevation

chunks.text: Step 1 converts the flood extent polygon to a polyline and then to a raster so that only boundary grid cells are retained, with other cells set to No Data. This step can also capture boundaries of multiple polygons and holes within polygons, which become additional boundary cells. The raster resolution is chosen to be compatible with the DEM to align boundary cells with topography.
supporting_quote: A flood inundation extent polygon is converted into a polyline layer
The polyline layer is then converted into a raster layer ... with cells that are not corresponding to the polylines assigned with a "No Data" value
It is preferable to have the raster layer cell dimensions compatible to the available DEM

chunks.text: Step 2 extracts the DEM elevation at boundary cells using a conditional raster calculation, producing a raster that holds elevations only at the boundary. Step 3 then propagates boundary elevations inward by repeatedly applying focal statistics with an expanding neighborhood, ensuring each cell receives the nearest boundary elevation (smallest neighborhood iteration). A circular neighborhood was found to yield smoother surfaces, though other geometries are possible.
supporting_quote: cells corresponding to the boundary raster layer ... receive the value of the underlying DEM

To ensure that all cells are assigned with the elevation of their nearest boundary cell, a conditional loop is used in which the size of the "Focal Statistics" neighborhood is increased at every iteration
A circular "Focal Statistics" neighborhood was found to produce smoother results

chunks.text: The required number of focal-statistics iterations depends on flood extent width and DEM cell size; it can be approximated using maximum width divided by twice the cell size. The paper provides an example: a 1,000 m maximum width flood with a 10 m DEM needs about 50 iterations to reach the center from both sides. This operational detail links runtime and accuracy to domain geometry and resolution.
supporting_quote: The number of iterations needed is a function of the maximum flood extent width and the cell size used.
for a flood extent with a maximum width of 1,000 m and the DEM resolution is 10 m, at least (1,000/[2 9 10]) 50 iterations will be needed.

chunks.text: Step 4 computes floodwater depth via map algebra by subtracting the DEM elevation from the assigned nearest-boundary elevation raster, then clipping results to the flood polygon because focal statistics assigns values on both sides of the boundary. Step 5 optionally applies a low-pass 3×3 filter to smooth sharp depth transitions caused by mismatches or algorithmic artifacts. The authors caution that smoothing can also blur real sharp changes such as floodplain-to-channel transitions.
supporting_quote: A raster calculation (ArcGIS Map Algebra) expression is used to deduct the cell value of the output of Step 3 ... by the DEM value
In FwDET, the Clip tool is used with the flood extent polygon as the bounding feature
In FwDET, the "Filter" tool is used with the "low-pass" option. The tool calculates the average value for each cell based on its 3 9 3 neighborhood.

chunks.text: Two flood events were used to evaluate FwDET against hydraulic-model depth outputs: May 2016 on the Brazos River, Texas, and September 2013 on St. Vrain Creek near Lyons, Colorado. The Brazos event is large (about 4.5 km wide) and used a 10 m DEM; the St. Vrain event is small (about 0.3 km wide) and used a 1 m LiDAR-derived DEM. In both cases, iRIC-FaSTMECH simulations provided modeled depth for comparison.
supporting_quote: May 2016 at Brazos River, Texas, U.S., and September 2013 at St. Vrain Creek near Lyons, Colorado, U.S.
The Brazos River event was spatially extensive (width of about 4.5 km) and a 10 m resolution DEM is used as input.
a 1 m resolution, LiDAR-derived, DEM ... was used as input. In both cases, the iRIC-FaSTMECH model ... was used to simulate the floods.

chunks.text: For evaluation, the flood extent input to FwDET was taken from the hydraulic model’s predicted inundation area rather than from observations. This design choice aims to isolate differences attributable to FwDET’s simplifications by removing potential errors caused by mismatched or uncertain extent mapping. Thus, comparisons focus on methodological differences in depth estimation rather than discrepancies in extent inputs.
supporting_quote: Model-predicted flood inundation area is used as the flood extent input layer in FwDAT, serving as a substitute to an observed inundation map.
Using model-predicted flood extent input allows for a cleaner analysis ... and ensures that the differences ... are only due to the simplifications in FwDAT

chunks.text: Two remote-sensing flood maps were used for demonstrations: a MODIS-based DFO inundation map of the August 2016 Irrawaddy River flood in Myanmar (250 m), and a Sentinel-1 SAR-based USFIMR map of the May 30, 2016 San Jacinto River flood in Texas (10 m). The Myanmar case used a 3 arc-sec (~90 m) HydroSHEDS DEM. The San Jacinto case also supported testing DEM resolution effects with USGS NED 10 m and 30 m DEMs.
supporting_quote: a DFO map for the August 2016 flood event on the Irrawaddy River in Myanmar ... using 250 m spatial resolution MODIS imagery.
A 3 arc-sec (~90 m) resolution DEM (HydroSHEDS) ... is used as input topography.
a USFIMR map for the May 30, 2016 flood on the San Jacinto River, Texas using 10 m Sentinel-1
comparing floodwater depth predictions ... using 10 and 30 m resolution DEMs (from USGS National Elevation Dataset)

chunks.text: FwDET produced depth estimates that closely matched modeled depths for the May 2016 Brazos River case. Mean depth was 1.95 m (FwDET) versus 1.49 m (model), with RMSD 0.37 m, and maximum depths of 12.4 m (FwDET) versus 12.5 m (model). The authors interpret this as favorable performance because average deviation is under 40 cm for a flood exceeding 12 m maximum depth.
supporting_quote: The average depths estimated by our methodology and the model ... are 1.95 and 1.49 m, respectively.
The root-mean-square difference (RMSD ... ) is 0.37 m.
Maximum depths estimated by FwDET and the hydraulic model were 12.4 and 12.5 m, respectively.

chunks.text: For the September 2013 St. Vrain Creek case, FwDET again corresponded well with model results but showed larger relative bias given smaller depths. Mean depth was 0.72 m (FwDET) versus 1.28 m (model), maximum depths were 4.64 m (FwDET) and 4.26 m (model), and RMSD was 0.38 m. The similar RMSD to Brazos suggests consistent performance across scales, though errors are more consequential for shallow floods.
supporting_quote: The average floodwater depth estimated using FwDET and model-simulated depths ... are 0.72 and 1.28 m
maximum depths of 4.64 and 4.26 m, respectively, and an RMSD of 0.38 m.
The RMSD value is very similar to the Brazos River case study. However, it represents a more considerable bias as the average and maximum floodwater depths are smaller.

chunks.text: Runtime depended on grid size and iterations required to propagate boundary elevations. On a desktop with four 3.7 GHz processors and 7.5 GB RAM, St. Vrain (1 m, 640×615 cells, 100 iterations) ran in 3.6 minutes, while Brazos (10 m, 2087×1816 cells, 200 iterations) ran in 31.7 minutes. The paper links runtime to DEM resolution (per-operation cost) and flood-domain width relative to cell size (iterations).
supporting_quote: FwDET runtime ... varied from 3.6 min for the St. Vrain Creek case study, with a 1 m resolution, 640 9 615 (393,600) cells and 100 iterations, to 31.7 min for the Brazos River case study, with a 10 m resolution, 2087 9 1816 (3,789,992) cells and 200 iterations.
Runtime is a function of the input data resolution and the size of the flood inundation domain relative to the DEM resolution.

chunks.text: Error patterns in the Brazos case were mostly small, but notable discrepancies occurred near the main channel banks and at the upstream/downstream boundaries. Overestimation along banks was attributed to inability to capture fine-scale fluid dynamics, while strong underestimation at reach edges arose when boundary cells crossing the channel were used as references for nearby channel cells. The authors note this affects few cells and mostly within the active channel, reducing operational impact.
supporting_quote: The most extreme overestimations by FwDET ... are along the banks of the main river channel. These are due to FwDET's inability to calculate fine-scale fluid dynamic effects.
The greatest differences (>5 m) ... are the underestimation by FwDET at the up- and down-stream boundaries
Given the small number of cells affected by this problem and their location within the river channel, this bias does not greatly influence the utility

chunks.text: FwDET depth maps exhibited blocky, straight-line artifacts compared with smoother hydraulic-model surfaces, particularly visible as sharp transitions. The paper attributes these to the circular focal-statistics neighborhood used to propagate boundary elevations. A low-pass filter can smooth but not fully remove these patterns, and further filtering risks obscuring genuine abrupt depth changes.
supporting_quote: The floodwater depth estimation by FwDET ... shows sharp transitions ... These blocks and straight lines are artifacts of the Focal Statistics circular neighborhood.
The low-pass filter step smooths these artifacts but does not eliminate them.
Additional filtering passes and algorithms could be used but these may have adverse effects on capturing actual sharp transitions in water depth

chunks.text: In the Irrawaddy River demonstration, upstream depth estimates were unrealistic due to a narrow valley combined with coarse MODIS flood mapping and a relatively coarse DEM. Boundary cells were identified near valley ridges with high elevations, inflating inferred water surface elevation. This overestimation also affected visualization by saturating the color ramp and masking downstream depth variation.
supporting_quote: The Irrawaddy River (Myanmar) case study yielded unrealistic floodwater depth values at the upstream (northeastern) section of the river
The relatively coarse resolution of the MODIS-based water classification ... and the DEM resulted in boundary cells identification near the top of the valley ridges (with very high elevation).
One of the adverse effects of the overestimation ... is the masking of depth values along the downstream section of the flood (due to "color ramp" saturation).

chunks.text: In the San Jacinto River demonstration, much of Lake Houston was estimated at zero depth despite surrounding flooded classification because some boundary cells were erroneously placed on the reservoir surface. Where nonzero depths existed, banding artifacts appeared from the focal-statistics neighborhood and from misalignment between flood extent and DEM. The authors also observed that the DEM recorded water surface elevation rather than reservoir bed elevation, causing systematic underestimation over the reservoir.
supporting_quote: Much of the reservoir surface was estimated as having zero floodwater depth despite the fact the areas surrounding the reservoir were classified as flooded
This occurred in areas where one or more boundary cells were located, due to errors in the remote sensing-based map, on the reservoir itself.
it is clear that the DEM used recorded the water surface elevation, rather than the reservoir bed elevation, leading to considerable underestimation of water depth over the reservoir.

chunks.text: Comparing DEM resolutions for San Jacinto, the overall differences between 10 m and 30 m depth outputs were small, but local behavior differed by setting. A 10 m DEM reduced the spatial extent of deep overestimation hotspots in complex urban patterns by adding detail, whereas the 30 m DEM produced smoother outputs that could be preferable in flat wetlands. Reported summary depths were 0.75 m average and 11.7 m maximum (10 m DEM) versus 1.25 m average and 13.3 m maximum (30 m DEM).
supporting_quote: Using a higher resolution DEM (10 m; Figure 6a) improves the results for this section, primarily by providing additional detail that reduces the spatial extent of these deeper hotspots.
The 30 m DEM resulted in much smoother output which may be preferable for floodwater depth reporting in this case.
The average floodwater depths estimated are 0.75 and 1.25 m, with the maximum depths being 11.7 and 13.3 m for the 10 and 30 m DEMs, respectively.

chunks.text: FwDET is sensitive to misalignment between the flood inundation extent layer and the DEM, which can stem from coarse spatial resolution, projection differences, or grid-cell alignment. Such mismatches can place boundary cells outside the true floodplain or at high terrain, yielding biased depths and sometimes unrealistic alternating deep-shallow zones. The authors indicate that manual adjustment of boundary locations or using higher-resolution inputs may be required in problematic areas.
supporting_quote: FwDET can accurately calculate floodwater depth for diverse flooding scenarios but also leads to considerable bias in locations where the inundation extent does not align well with the DEM.
Such mismatch can result not only from relatively coarse spatial resolution but also from projection or grid-cell alignment issues.
manual adjustment or higher spatial resolution input is required.

chunks.text: Steep, confined terrain such as narrow valleys can drive major overestimation because boundary cells may be detected near ridge tops when flood mapping and DEM are too coarse. The Myanmar example illustrates this issue, where confined reaches produced unrealistic depths. The paper recommends excluding highly confined reaches unless high-resolution inputs and/or careful manual quality control ensure proper alignment.
supporting_quote: Steep terrain (e.g., narrow valley) may lead to considerable overestimations as they are highly sensitive to the resolution of the flood inundation map and DEM.
Highly confined river reaches should be excluded unless appropriate (high resolution) input data are available and/or careful manual quality control is implemented

chunks.text: Large water bodies and channels are prone to underestimation because DEMs often capture water surface elevation rather than bathymetry, and because classification errors can place boundary cells on open water. This can yield zero-depth estimates over reservoirs even when surroundings are flooded. Manual quality control can reduce boundary-placement errors, while bathymetry estimation is suggested to address DEM limitations over water surfaces.
supporting_quote: Large water bodies are prone to underestimation due to errors in the location of the flood boundary cells on the water body itself and the fact that DEMs typically record water surface elevation.
Much of the reservoir surface was estimated as having zero floodwater depth
Manual quality control should be used to prevent the former, whereas bathymetry estimations can address the latter.

chunks.text: Complex inundation patterns, especially in urban areas, can generate localized deep 'hotspots' in FwDET outputs. These may result from misclassified boundary locations and from low-elevation microfeatures (ponds or ditches) interacting with the nearest-boundary assignment. The authors found that higher-quality imagery and DEM inputs can limit the spatial footprint of such artifacts, and that choosing an appropriate DEM resolution is important for these settings.
supporting_quote: Complex inundation patterns and urban flooding are prone to localized hotspots of overestimation.
These were the result of (1) errors in the location of boundary cells ... and (2) areas of low elevation associated with small ponds or ditches.
Appropriate DEM resolution selection is needed to produce the best estimation under these settings.

chunks.text: Artifacts from the focal-statistics propagation can introduce straight transition zones and unrealistic banding, and smoothing is a tradeoff. While low-pass filtering can reduce blockiness, it may also smooth real sharp depth transitions such as between floodplain and active channel. The paper suggests discretion in applying smoothing and recognizes that the chosen algorithm geometry affects the appearance of outputs.
supporting_quote: There are a number of straight transition zones, mostly perpendicular to the flow direction. Similar to earlier examples, these are artifacts of the Focal Statistics neighborhood
This step can also smooth real, sharp changes in water depth, such as transition from floodplain to active channel, and so discretion should be used

chunks.text: The paper concludes that FwDET provides a useful approach for estimating floodwater depth from inundation extent and topography, performing well against hydraulic-model depths in both a large flood (Brazos River) and a small flood (St. Vrain) with RMSD on the order of 0.37–0.38 m. Demonstrations on satellite-derived flood maps show the tool can handle diverse scenarios but requires careful attention to input resolution and alignment. The authors position FwDET as a rapid, first-order depth estimation method rather than a replacement for detailed hydraulics.
supporting_quote: A new methodology, the FwDET, is presented ... estimating floodwater depth from remote sensing flood inundation maps.
FwDET performs well for both a large flood event (Brazos River, Texas; using a 10 m DEM) and a small event (St. Vrain River, Colorado), for which high-resolution 1 m DEM was used.
The approach is intended for first-order overview, not detailed analysis of floodwater dynamics.

chunks.text: Key takeaways emphasize where FwDET needs extra care: steep confined terrain can cause overestimation, large water bodies can be underestimated due to DEM water surface elevations and boundary errors, and complex/urban patterns can create localized overestimation hotspots. The paper recommends manual quality control, suitable DEM selection, and potentially adding bathymetry to reduce underestimation over large water bodies. These guidelines summarize when the method is most reliable and when additional steps are necessary.
supporting_quote: Steep terrain (e.g., narrow valley) may lead to considerable overestimations
Large water bodies are prone to underestimation ... and the fact that DEMs typically record water surface elevation.
Complex inundation patterns and urban flooding are prone to localized hotspots of overestimation.

chunks.text: The authors outline future work to improve usability and validation. They plan to test other geospatial toolchains (e.g., GDAL) to improve runtime and enable non-ArcGIS use, and to further validate FwDET using observed water depths such as USGS High Water Mark data. They also intend to deploy depth estimates within the USFIMR and DFO portals and provide the Python script via SDML and CSDMS repositories.
supporting_quote: Future research will focus on testing other tools and geospatial analysis packages to improve runtime and usability by non-ArcGIS users.
We plan to further test FwDET using observed water depth from sources such as the USGS High Water Mark (HWM) data (USGS, 2017).
Immediately, however, we will use FwDET to provide floodwater depth estimates for remote sensing products at the USFIMR and DFO portals.

chunks.text: Remote sensing flood inundation mapping is increasingly used for emergency response, damage assessment, planning, and forecasting. However, inundation extent products generally do not provide floodwater depth, which is critical for response and post-event assessment. Many depth approaches rely on hydraulic modeling or terrain-based methods that require additional hydrologic or oceanographic inputs, limiting near-real-time use in data-sparse regions. FwDET was created to estimate depth using only inundation extent and a DEM, enabling rapid, large-scale augmentation of remote-sensing flood maps.
supporting_quote: Remote sensing-based flood inundation mapping cannot be readily used to derive floodwater depth, which is an important attribute for near-real-time emergency response and post-event damage assessment
Both approaches require detailed hydrological, hydrometeorological, or oceanographic information ... hindering their utility in near-real-time and data-sparse regions.
FwDET ... calculates water depth based solely on an inundation polygon and Digital Elevation Model (DEM).

chunks.text: FwDET’s core concept is estimating local floodwater elevation from boundary cells and then deriving depth by differencing against the DEM inside the flooded domain. This method is computationally efficient and has low data requirements, which makes it appealing for large-scale and rapid analyses. Because it depends on local boundary elevations, performance is strongly influenced by DEM and inundation map quality, alignment, and resolution. The paper positions FwDET2.1 as a refinement to reduce artifacts and biases that occur when these inputs mismatch.
supporting_quote: The novelty of FwDET is its reliance on the identification of local floodwater elevation
The low data requirement and high computational efficiency of FwDET were shown to be advantageous
Local biases in FwDET predictions ... can be attributed to spatial or resolution mismatches between the inundation map and the DEM.

chunks.text: FwDET is implemented in desktop GIS and cloud platforms, including Google Earth Engine, to leverage broad DEM availability and scalable processing. The new version is designed to work with diverse DEM products and to support operational workflows. The paper emphasizes that visual quality and interpretability of depth products matter for adoption in emergency response contexts. Therefore, minimizing striping artifacts while maintaining accuracy is a key driver of the updates.
supporting_quote: Similar to FwDET2.0, the new version was adopted as ArcGIS Pro stand-alone script ... and a GEE script (referred to as FwDET-GEE)
One of the key limitations of FwDET is that its output floodwater depth maps often include sharp transitions in values, which leads to linear stripes along the flooded domain.
Visual representation of flood maps can be critical for the proliferation of their use, especially for emergency response and planning.

chunks.text: The study aims to describe the new FwDET2.1 algorithmic additions and evaluate their effects. It conducts an optimization study of the two new parameters—boundary smoothing iterations and slope threshold filtering—across multiple benchmark flood cases and DEMs. It also intercompares a large set of DEM products in Google Earth Engine and evaluates improvement over FwDET2.0 using a simulated flood. Finally, it demonstrates application to a large remote-sensing flood event in Myanmar and presents available deployment options for users.
supporting_quote: In this paper, we (1) describe FwDET2.1, (2) conduct an optimization study ... (3) analyze the tool's sensitivity to a range of DEMs in GEE, (4) compare the tool improvement over FwDET2.0, (5) discuss its application ... and (6) introduce new FwDET application options.

chunks.text: A central goal is to quantify how boundary smoothing and slope-based boundary filtering influence depth estimates and to identify parameter settings that work well across DEMs. The optimization is performed over 60 parameter combinations and evaluated using average absolute percent bias against hydraulic-simulation depths. The outcomes are intended to guide operational users in selecting parameters suited to DEM resolution and quality. The paper also examines whether a single configuration can be broadly effective across multiple DEMs.
supporting_quote: The sensitivity and optimal values of the two new FwDET2.1 parameters ... are analyzed by running the tool with 60 parameter combinations
Average absolute Percent Bias (absPBIAS) for all 16 case studies in each parameter space combination was used to infer the optimal combination for each DEM
A combination of ten smoothing iterations and a slope threshold of 0.5% was found to be optimal for most DEMs.

chunks.text: FwDET outputs can exhibit localized biases that appear as sharp transitions and linear stripes in the depth raster. These artifacts are linked to unrealistic differences between adjacent boundary-cell elevations, often caused by DEM errors or a spatial/resolution mismatch between the inundation map and DEM. Such artifacts degrade accuracy and reduce trust in products intended for operational use. The paper addresses this with boundary cell smoothing and additional filtering to remove anomalous boundary cells.
supporting_quote: Local biases in FwDET predictions, often manifested as sharp transitions or stripes in the water depth raster, can be attributed to spatial or resolution mismatches between the inundation map and the DEM.
These stripes are caused by unrealistic differences in elevation between adjacent boundary grid-cells
Improving FwDET's striping issues while maintaining or, preferably, improving its predictive ability is therefore meritorious.

chunks.text: In non-continuous flood domains, isolated non-flooded areas within the mapped flood extent may be real or may represent remote sensing classification errors (e.g., vegetation, clouds). FwDET may treat cells around these internal holes as boundary cells, which can either help (if real) or introduce substantial biases (if erroneous). Coastal boundaries also pose issues because DEM elevations at the ocean/coastline do not represent floodwater elevation. Prior versions handled coastal issues by filtering boundary cells at elevations equal to or below zero.
supporting_quote: Non-flooded isolated areas can be real or represent an error in the remote sensing analysis due to, for example, undetected flooding under dense vegetation or clouds.
FwDET identifies the cells around these areas as boundary grid-cells ... However, if these are not real, they can introduce considerable biases in the output.
Starting in version 2.0, FwDET addressed this issue by removing all boundary grid-cells that have, or are immediately adjacent to, grid-cells that have an elevation equal to or less than zero.

chunks.text: Remote sensing flood maps may contain gaps that are interpreted as flood boundaries, which can propagate incorrect water levels far into the domain. When such gaps occur over low-elevation features like the river channel, FwDET can assign low boundary elevations that lead to zero or underestimated depths spreading outward. These issues can arise from false negatives due to SAR/optical processing limitations or from true negatives linked to river migration relative to an outdated DEM. The study examines how FwDET2.1 filtering reduces the negative impact of these gaps.
supporting_quote: Gaps are identified as a flood inundation boundary and could thus propagate far into the water depth maps, causing low (or even zero) values if those (unrealistic) gaps are located within the river
In the case of false negatives, this can be caused by issues with the satellite processing chain
If the DEM no longer matches the actual location of a river, the combination of a flood map and DEM ... does not align well and can cause issues related to gaps

chunks.text: FwDET computes depth by estimating local floodwater elevation from boundary grid cells and subtracting it from DEM elevation within the inundated area. The procedure includes converting inundation extent to a boundary representation aligned to the DEM, extracting DEM elevations for boundary cells, assigning each flooded cell the nearest boundary-cell water elevation, and computing depth as the difference. The Google Earth Engine implementation follows the same concept but uses raster-native operations, such as rasterized border creation. This local-boundary approach differentiates FwDET from methods relying on cross-section maxima or global interpolation.
supporting_quote: FwDET calculates water depth by subtracting local floodwater elevation ... from topographic elevation at each grid-cell within the flooded domain.

(1) conversion of the inundation polygon to a polyline layer, (2) creation of a raster layer ... (3) extraction of the DEM value ... (4) allocation of the local floodwater elevation ... from its nearest boundary grid-cell, and (5) calculation of floodwater depth
The FwDET-GEE algorithm corresponds with the original but uses raster processes where available

chunks.text: FwDET2.1 adds a boundary grid-cell smoothing routine based on focal statistics. A 5 × 5 neighborhood Focal Statistics operation is applied to the boundary elevation raster, and multiple iterations can be run through a loop, including the option of zero iterations. By smoothing boundary elevations rather than smoothing final depths, the update targets striping artifacts at their source. Users can tune the number of iterations depending on DEM and inundation map characteristics.
supporting_quote: FwDET2.1 introduces a boundary grid-cell smoothing and filtering procedure.
A 5 × 5 grid-cell ... Focal Statistics tool is applied to the boundary elevation raster.
Multiple iterations of smoothing are supported ... The number of iterations is defined by the user (and can be zero).

chunks.text: FwDET2.1 introduces slope-based filtering to remove anomalous boundary cells, especially over permanent water bodies. The method computes a slope raster from the input DEM and removes boundary cells whose slope is below a user-defined threshold, under the assumption that true flood boundaries are less likely to have very low slope. This filtering is in addition to the elevation-based filtering from FwDET2.0 that removes boundary cells at or adjacent to elevations ≤ 0 for coastal contexts. Together, smoothing and filtering seek to reduce biases caused by erroneous boundary elevations.
supporting_quote: topographic slope-based filtering is introduced in FwDET2.1 to remove anomalous (and potentially erroneous) boundary grid-cells, primarily over permanent water bodies.
A topographic slope raster is calculated ... and a user-defined threshold is used to remove boundary grid-cells with a slope value below the threshold
FwDET ... removing all boundary grid-cells that have, or are immediately adjacent to, grid-cells that have an elevation equal to or less than zero.

chunks.text: Parameter sensitivity and optimization tested 60 combinations of smoothing iterations and slope thresholds across 16 benchmark flood case studies and five DEMs. Iterations ranged from 0–10 (increment 1) and slope thresholds from 0–2.5% (increment 0.5). Performance was evaluated using average absolute percent bias (absPBIAS) comparing FwDET-predicted depths to hydraulic-simulation depths at aligned resolutions via pixel-to-pixel analysis. The optimal parameter pair per DEM was inferred from the lowest average absPBIAS over all case studies.
supporting_quote: running the tool with 60 parameter combinations over sixteen (16) benchmark simulated flooding case studies, and for 5 different DEMs.
Iteration values ranged from 0–10 ... and slope values ranged from 0–2.5% at an increment of 0.5
Average absolute Percent Bias (absPBIAS) ... was used to infer the optimal combination

chunks.text: The absPBIAS metric was defined as 100 times the sum of absolute differences between observed and predicted depths divided by the sum of observed depths. Observed depths were taken from hydraulic simulations, and predicted depths from FwDET outputs. The study computed absPBIAS via pixel-to-pixel map algebra after aggregating benchmark rasters to match FwDET output resolution for each DEM. Averaging absPBIAS across case studies supported parameter selection across varied domains.
supporting_quote: absPBIAS = 100 [ \frac{\sum (|O_i - P_i|)}{\sum (O_i)} ]
where Oi is the observed water depth (hydraulic simulation) and Pi is the predicted water depth (FwDET)
The absPBIAS was calculated using a pixel-to-pixel (Map Algebra) analysis.

chunks.text: A DEM intercomparison in Google Earth Engine evaluated how different DEM products affect FwDET outputs for a single large USGS FIM case study (Amite and Comite Rivers, Louisiana). Sixteen DEM datasets spanning ~5–100 m resolution were used, and FwDET2.1-GEE was run without filtering to isolate DEM effects. Outputs were compared to a USGS FIM hydraulic depth layer using RMSE, absPBIAS, Pearson correlation (r), and area differences. This design emphasizes the dependence of depth estimates on DEM quality beyond nominal resolution.
supporting_quote: modeled using a comprehensive collection of DEMs ranging from 5 m to 100 m spatial resolution (Table 2).
used for this assessment without any filtering algorithms to test only the differences between the DEM products
RMSE, absPBIAS, and the Pearson correlation coefficient (r) comparison metrics were calculated

chunks.text: An evaluation case used the Brazos River (Texas) simulated May 2016 flood event to compare FwDET2.1 against FwDET2.0 under consistent terrain input. The benchmark was produced by the iRIC-FaSTMECH hydrodynamics model, and both simulation and FwDET used the 10 m NED DEM. Metrics included RMSE, PBIAS, and absPBIAS computed via pixel-to-pixel analysis. This case was selected because it better matches the intended remote sensing workflow than comparisons against 3–6 m simulation products.
supporting_quote: The Brazos River (Texas, USA) case study ... is a simulated May 2016 flood event using the iRIC-FaSTMECH hydrodynamics model
The simulation and the FwDET calculations use the 10 m NED DEM
RMSE, PBIAS, and absPBIAS statistics are calculated using pixel-to-pixel analysis.

chunks.text: The parameter optimization used 16 benchmark flood case studies from the USGS Flood Inundation Mapping (FIM) Program. Each includes a HEC-RAS simulated floodwater depth raster at 3–6 m resolution. Inundation extents were vectorized from the modeled depth rasters and used as FwDET inputs, then benchmark depths were aggregated to match each DEM resolution for comparisons. The set spans diverse rivers and flood extents, enabling evaluation across varied domains.
supporting_quote: The 16 benchmark case studies ... were retrieved from the USGS Flood Inundation Mapping (FIM) Program.
Each case study includes a floodwater depth raster calculated using HEC-RAS hydraulic model simulations at 3–6 m resolutions.
The inundation extent of each case study was vectorized from the modeled water depth raster and used as input to FwDET.

chunks.text: Five DEMs were used in the parameter sensitivity/optimization: NED (10 m), NASADEM (30 m), MERIT (90 m), ASTER (30 m), and SRTM90 (90 m). These were chosen for their wide use and availability in Google Earth Engine. Differences in resolution and vertical characteristics (e.g., ASTER integer elevations) were expected to influence FwDET behavior. The optimization derived best parameter settings for each DEM based on average absPBIAS across 16 case studies.
supporting_quote: The DEMs used were NED (10 m resolution; U.S. extent), NASADEM (30 m resolution; global extent), MERIT (90 m resolution; global extent), ASTER (30 m resolution; global extent), and SRTM90 (90 m resolution; global extent).
These DEMs were selected due to their wide use and availability in GEE.
The ASTER DEM ... yielded the highest absPBIAS. This can be explained by ASTER's low vertical resolution due to its integer data type.

chunks.text: The DEM intercomparison for the Amite and Comite Rivers used 16 DEM datasets in Google Earth Engine, including LSLP 5 m (uploaded asset), NED 10 m, 3DEP 10 m, Copernicus GLO 30 m, FABDEM 30 m, NASADEM 30 m, ALOS 30 m, ASTER 30 m, SRTM 30 m, SRTM 90 m, WWF HydroSHEDS 90 m, MERIT 90 m, and ASTER 100 m. The flood extent covered approximately 210 km² in central Louisiana. Outputs were compared against a USGS FIM reference layer with 5.5 m spatial resolution. The dataset selection enabled analysis across resolutions and DEM processing approaches.
supporting_quote: one of the USGS FIM case studies (Amite and Comite Rivers, Louisiana; case study #4 ... )
This analysis included 16 DEM datasets, listed in Table 2.
Error metrics relating FwDET-GEE output ... to the USGS FIM (5.5 m spatial resolution) reference flood depth dataset.

chunks.text: The Brazos River evaluation used a simulated May 2016 flood event produced with the iRIC-FaSTMECH hydrodynamics model. The simulation and FwDET calculations were both based on the 10 m NED DEM, enabling direct pixel-scale comparison. Two parameter settings were contrasted: [I0, S0] representing the FwDET2.0-equivalent configuration and [I10, S0.5] representing the overall optimal configuration. Accuracy was summarized with RMSE, PBIAS, and absPBIAS.
supporting_quote: The Brazos case study is a simulated May 2016 flood event using the iRIC-FaSTMECH hydrodynamics model
The simulation and the FwDET calculations use the 10 m NED DEM
FwDET2.1 using 0 iterations and 0 slope [I0, S0] (equivalent to FwDET2.0 ... ) and 10 iterations and 0.5 slope [I10, S0.5]

chunks.text: The remote sensing case study analyzed an upstream Irrawaddy River flood in Myanmar during July 2019 using a Sentinel-1 derived flood map (16 July 2019). The inundation extent was produced using an approach following Markert et al. (2020). FwDET2.1-GEE used this flood extent with four DEMs—ASTER, SRTM90, MERIT, and NASADEM—to examine sensitivity and the effect of boundary filtering. Because no reference depths were available, assessment relied on qualitative comparisons and water level statistics.
supporting_quote: Sentinel-1 satellite imagery was acquired on July 16.
The flood map derived from Sentinel-1 is used as FwDET2.1 inundation extent input, together with four DEMs: ASTER, SRTM90, MERIT, and NASADEM.
Since no validation or water depth reference data exists for these floods, we apply more qualitative means of assessing

chunks.text: Optimization over 16 USGS FIM cases showed that parameter sensitivity depends strongly on DEM resolution and quality. For NED 10 m, best performance occurred at [0 iterations, 0 slope] with limited sensitivity overall (absPBIAS range 5.6). For NASADEM 30 m, filtering improved accuracy, with the best run at ten iterations and slope 2.5 and a wider absPBIAS range (25.6). For MERIT 90 m, the best configuration was consistently slope 0.5 with ten iterations, and sensitivity was large (absPBIAS range 63.2). The average across all five DEMs favored [I10, S0.5].
supporting_quote: For the 10 m NED DEM ... the best performing run was for 0 slope and 0 iterations.
For the 30 m NASADEM ... optimal performance of ten iterations and slope of 2.5 (highest values tested)
For the 90 m MERIT, the optimal slope value was consistently 0.5 with ten iterations
[I10, S0.5] was also the optimal configuration when averaging the absPBIAS from all 5 DEMs.

chunks.text: The optimization summary table quantified best and worst absPBIAS for each DEM and showed increasing variability with coarser datasets. NED 10 m ranged from 40.5 to 46.1 absPBIAS, while NASADEM 30 m ranged 66.8 to 92.4. MERIT 90 m ranged 59.9 to 123.1, SRTM_90 ranged 78.2 to 137.3, and ASTER 30 m (integer) ranged 97.9 to 169.2. These results indicate that smoothing and slope filtering choices matter much more for coarse-resolution DEMs.
supporting_quote: NED ... Lowest absPBIAS 40.5 [0, 0] ... Highest absPBIAS 46.1 [1, 0]
The results show that the impact of the introduced boundary smoothing and slopefiltering procedures in FwDET2.1 increases for lower resolution DEMs.

chunks.text: ASTER 30 m produced the highest absPBIAS among the tested DEMs despite its moderate resolution, attributed to low vertical resolution from integer elevation values. MERIT 90 m outperformed the best NASADEM 30 m runs in the optimization, but also exhibited the highest variability across parameter combinations. The authors explain that coarse DEMs can yield extreme depth outliers from boundary mis-association because each cell represents a larger-area average elevation. Consequently, parameter choices can reduce some artifacts but also lead to unstable outcomes depending on the DEM.
supporting_quote: The ASTER DEM ... yielded the highest absPBIAS. This can be explained by ASTER's low vertical resolution due to its integer data type.
The 90 m MERIT DEM ... outperformed the best runs with the 30 m NASADEM.
MERIT, however, also yielded the highest variability in the results.

chunks.text: In the DEM intercomparison (Amite and Comite Rivers), the finest DEMs produced the best agreement with the USGS FIM reference depths. LSLP 5 m, NED 10 m, and 3DEP 10 m had RMSE of 0.63, 0.75, and 0.83 m and Pearson r of 0.95, 0.93, and 0.92. Among 30 m DEMs, FABDEM 30 m performed best (RMSE 2.26, r 0.55), while GLO 30 m performed worst (RMSE 4.37, r 0.33). These metrics align with visual differences in terrain clarity and water depth granularity.
supporting_quote: The lowest RMSE values were produced by the finest spatial resolution datasets— LSLP 5 m, NED 10 m, and 3DEP 10 m, with RMSE values of 0.63, 0.75, and 0.83 m
The highest RMSE value overall was observed in GLO 30 m at 4.37.
FABDEM 30 m had the lowest RMSE at 2.26

chunks.text: MERIT 90 m surpassed the 30 m global DEMs in the Amite/Comite intercomparison, indicating that DEM processing quality can outweigh nominal spatial resolution. MERIT achieved RMSE 1.58, absPBIAS 53.97%, and Pearson r 0.73, compared with NASADEM 30 m RMSE 2.73 and r 0.51 and SRTM 30 m RMSE 2.75 and r 0.50. MERIT also produced a larger modeled flood area (170.3 km²) closer to the USGS FIM area than most 30 m products, reducing area difference to 39.3 km². The paper attributes MERIT’s strong performance to artifact/noise removal and hydrological conditioning.
supporting_quote: MERIT 90 m surpassed the 30 m DEMs with an RMSE of 1.58.
MERIT 90 m surpassed the 30 m DEMs with a Pearson's r of 0.73.
MERIT 90 m ... absPBIAS (%) 53.97 ... Area Diff. (km2) 39.3

chunks.text: Depth distribution histograms showed that 3DEP 10 m most closely matched the USGS FIM reference, with remaining biases primarily in shallow depths. NASADEM 30 m tended to underestimate 0–2 m depths and overestimate 2–5 m depths and also produced depths up to 17 m compared to the USGS FIM maximum near 11 m. MERIT 90 m also underestimated 0–2 m depths and extended beyond 11 m, but its histogram shape tracked the USGS FIM reference more closely than NASADEM. These comparisons highlight that coarser DEMs can distort both shallow and extreme depth frequencies.
supporting_quote: There is a notable similarity between 3DEP 10 m and USGSFIM 5.5 m
NASADEM 30 m underestimates flood depths in the 0–2 m range and overestimates flood depths in the 2–5 m range.
NASADEM estimated floods reach depths of up to 17 m whereas USGS FIM extends to only 11 m depths.

chunks.text: In the Brazos River evaluation, FwDET2.1 with the overall optimal setting [I10, S0.5] improved accuracy relative to the FwDET2.0-equivalent setting [I0, S0]. RMSE decreased from 0.66 to 0.51 m, PBIAS improved from -13% to -7.2%, and absPBIAS decreased from 15.8% to 11.2%. The updated configuration also produced a smoother water depth map, reducing visible striping while maintaining a sharply peaked error distribution suggesting small biases over most pixels. Underpredictions were mainly along the flood boundary, while overpredictions appeared near channel peripheries and farther from boundaries.
supporting_quote: FwDET2.1 yielded strong results for the Brazos River case study, with an RMSE of 0.5 m and absPBIAS of 11%
FwDET2.1 yielded a smoother water depth map compared to FwDET2.0

chunks.text: For the Myanmar Irrawaddy remote sensing case study, water level variability depended on DEM choice and filtering settings. The spread of water levels was highest with ASTER, followed by SRTM90, and lower with both MERIT and NASADEM. Applying [I10, S0.5] slightly reduced the spread compared to [I0, S0] for all DEMs, with MERIT yielding the lowest spread in both cases. The authors note that full water level ranges remained large and likely unrealistic in places, consistent with substantial DEM errors possible in tropical mountainous areas.
supporting_quote: The spread of water levels is highest with ASTER, followed by SRTM90, and is lower with both MERIT and NASADEM.
[I10 S0.5] slightly reduces the spread compared to [I0 S0] for all DEMs.
the smallest range, found for MERIT at [I10 S0.5], was just below 15 m.

chunks.text: In the highlighted Irrawaddy sub-area, a single-pixel ‘gap’ in the Sentinel-1 flood map located over the low-elevation river channel caused FwDET to treat it as a boundary and propagate low water levels, producing an unrealistic zone of zero depth in the river and floodplain under [I0, S0]. The [I10, S0.5] configuration largely resolved this by filtering boundary cells, producing more continuous water level and depth fields. Longitudinal and cross-section profiles confirmed that [I10, S0.5] reduced variability and prevented water surfaces from being dragged down toward gaps. The gap pixel itself remained masked, but surrounding depths became more coherent.
supporting_quote: This gap is identified as an edge within FwDET and consequently, its elevation value is used as water level, propagating outwards ... resulting in an area of zero water depth
The issue is largely resolved in [I10 S0.5], where filtering of these boundary cells resulted in a more continuous water level and depth values.
[I10 S0.5] gives more continuous and less variable water levels than [I0 S0].

chunks.text: The USGS FIM benchmark datasets used for optimization are high resolution (3–6 m) and often include urban areas, which is not ideal for evaluating FwDET’s primary remote sensing-oriented use cases. The study acknowledges that FwDET can work well for urban floods with 1 m LiDAR DEMs, but this paper focuses on typical remote sensing applications that use 10 m and 30 m DEMs. To mitigate mismatch, the USGS FIM data were used primarily for optimization and DEM intercomparison, while a separate 10 m simulation (Brazos River) was used for more compatible evaluation. This highlights a broader challenge of limited open reference datasets spanning diverse domains.
supporting_quote: The high resolution of the USGS FIM maps and the fact that many of the 16 case studies are over areas with considerable urban land cover is not ideal for our comparison.
the main utility of the tool is to provide rapid calculations for remote sensing applications ... DEMs of 10 m resolution ... and 30 m resolution globally.
A different hydraulic model-driven flood simulation is used in Section 2.4 ... simulated flood depths at a 10 m resolution

chunks.text: The optimization analysis can yield relatively high absPBIAS values due to sensitivity to extreme depth outliers in a small number of pixels. FwDET often underpredicts average depth but can generate very high depths where nearest-boundary elevation is misplaced or misrepresented, which disproportionately impacts error statistics. This behavior is more prevalent with coarse DEMs because each cell represents an averaged elevation over a larger area. As a result, performance appears more variable and parameter-sensitive at coarser resolutions.
supporting_quote: The relatively high absPBIAS values ... can be explained by the sensitivity of this analysis to extreme values in individual grid-cells.
it can yield very high water depth values in a few grid-cells due to misplacement or misrepresentation of their nearest boundary-cell elevation.
This issue is more prevalent in coarse resolution DEMs

chunks.text: Remote sensing flood map gaps can strongly affect FwDET because gaps are treated as boundaries whose DEM elevations become water levels. False negatives may arise from SAR speckle filtering, cloud/shadow effects in optical imagery, algorithm limitations, or temporary objects that block the sensor signal. True negatives can also occur when rivers migrate but the DEM remains static and becomes misaligned with current channel location. While gap filling could mitigate some errors, it adds processing steps and may introduce commission errors, posing tradeoffs for emergency response decisions.
supporting_quote: Gaps are identified as a flood inundation boundary ... causing low (or even zero) values
In the case of false negatives, this can be caused by issues with the satellite processing chain
From a socioeconomic and environmental perspective ... whether accepting errors of commission would be preferable to accepting errors of omission.

chunks.text: The Myanmar case study lacked validation data, so usefulness and accuracy were assessed qualitatively through visual comparisons and water level statistics. The paper notes that DEM errors in tropical mountainous regions can be on the order of 10–20 m, which likely contributes to unrealistic water level ranges even after filtering. This limits the ability to determine whether FwDET2.1 outputs match actual depths at the pixel level. The authors suggest that while absolute values may be uncertain, relative spatial patterns can still be informative for prioritization.
supporting_quote: Since no validation or water depth reference data exists for these floods, we apply more qualitative means of assessing
errors in the DEMs themselves ... can be in the order of 10–20 m
the absolute depth values at the pixel level are likely not accurate enough to directly base decisions on

chunks.text: A key practical limitation in advancing flood depth estimation is scarcity of observational data for validation and development. While some datasets have improved (e.g., USGS High Water Mark and USGS FIM), the quantity, usability, and geographic coverage remain limited. This constrains robust evaluation of remote-sensing-derived depth products globally. The paper implies that better observational data would enable further refinement of coupling between flood mapping and terrain-based depth estimation.
supporting_quote: A limiting factor ... is the limitation of observational data.
While improvements in data availability have been made ... the quantity, usability, and geographic representation of these datasets remain limited.

chunks.text: FwDET2.1 adds boundary smoothing and filtering that improves visual quality and can also improve accuracy with minimal computational cost. The tool’s sensitivity to these parameters depends on DEM resolution and quality; higher-resolution DEMs generally yield better results. Across datasets, the authors identify ten smoothing iterations and a 0.5% slope threshold as a broadly effective configuration. The updated tool is distributed as open-source and is available across multiple platforms including ArcGIS and Google Earth Engine.
supporting_quote: The new version of the Floodwater Depth Estimation Tool (FwDET2.1) offers considerable visual improvement as well as accuracy improvement with nearly no computational costs.
A combination of ten smoothing iterations and a slope threshold of 0.5% was found to be optimal for most DEMs.
FwDET2.1 is provided as a free and open-source tool.

chunks.text: DEM selection strongly influences FwDET outcomes, and resolution alone does not guarantee better performance. While LiDAR and 10 m USGS DEMs are preferred where available, the global MERIT 90 m DEM outperformed several 30 m DEMs, attributed to artifact removal, smoothing, and hydrological conditioning. Parameter optimization further enhances MERIT performance, supporting its use for scaling FwDET beyond the U.S. These findings emphasize prioritizing DEM quality and conditioning for remote-sensing flood depth estimation.
supporting_quote: The 90 m MERIT dataset outperformed several 30 m DEMs, especially when FwDET2.1 boundary smoothing and filtering parameters are optimized.
This was attributed to MERIT's trees and building smoothing and hydrological conditioning.
if these are not available (e.g., outside the U.S.), MERIT outperforms the 30 m DEMs.

chunks.text: The National Water Center (NWC) is NOAA’s hub for the National Water Model (NWM), located at the University of Alabama. Through the NWC Innovators’ Program and partners, an annual Summer Institute was created to engage graduate students and researchers in rapidly prototyping applications of the NWM. Early efforts focused on demonstrating that real-time national-scale streamflow simulation and forecasting was feasible using NOAA weather products and WRF-Hydro.
supporting_quote: The National Water Center (NWC) ... is the hub for the new National Water Model (NWM) of the United States (U.S.).
launched the inaugural NWC Summer Institute to engage the academic community in developing applications of the NWM.
the overarching goal was to demonstrate a prototype NWM, exploring whether streamflow on 2.7 million stream reaches of the U.S. could be simulated and forecast in real time

chunks.text: The 2016 Summer Institute brought together 34 graduate students from 21 U.S. universities with theme leaders, coordinators, and NOAA staff. By mid-2016, the first version of the NWM was moving toward operations, shifting emphasis from basic feasibility to practical products and user-facing applications. The featured collection summarizes work aligned with this shift.
supporting_quote: The second Summer Institute (June 6–July 20, 2016) included 34 graduate students from 21 U.S. universities
By June 2016, a first version of the NWM was in the process of being made operational

chunks.text: A core enabling idea for national flood mapping is linking NWM discharge forecasts to terrain-based representations of inundation. The featured collection emphasizes tools like HAND and web-based dissemination platforms (e.g., Tethys) to translate model outputs into locally meaningful, actionable information across the continental U.S. The papers cover topics from inundation mapping to emergency response and precipitation evaluation.
supporting_quote: the focus of the 2016 Summer Institute was on translating the NWM forecasts of discharge into flood-inundation mapping and flood emergency response
broadly grouped into four research themes: Inundation Mapping, Flood Modeling, Forecast Errors, and Emergency Response.
The web apps were designed using the Tethys platform

chunks.text: The 2016 Summer Institute aimed to translate operationally oriented NWM discharge forecasts into products that support flood mapping and emergency response. Work was organized around four themes—Inundation Mapping, Flood Modeling, Forecast Errors, and Emergency Response—to move from raw hydrologic forecasts toward decisions and communication. The featured collection was assembled to represent these themes and demonstrate prototype capabilities.
supporting_quote: the focus of the 2016 Summer Institute was on translating the NWM forecasts of discharge into flood-inundation mapping and flood emergency response
broadly grouped into four research themes: Inundation Mapping, Flood Modeling, Forecast Errors, and Emergency Response.

chunks.text: A featured objective was to create a national-scale, high-resolution terrain derivative (HAND) that could support continuous flood-inundation mapping across the U.S. The intention was to enable locally informative, near-real-time inundation estimates when HAND is paired with NWM forecast information. This required continental-scale processing and cyberinfrastructure.
supporting_quote: a 10 m National Elevation Dataset of the U.S. was analyzed ... and transformed into a raster called Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND)
Coupled with flood forecasting from the NWM, the HAND approach establishes ... a foundation for locally informative, real-time flood-inundation mapping continuously across the continental U.S.

chunks.text: Another goal highlighted is converting NWM discharge predictions to stage (water depth) across the NWM network so that inundation mapping methods can be applied at scale. Because most reaches do not have surveyed channel geometry or long-term gage records, the aim was to develop alternatives that can derive channel geometry and rating curves from available national datasets.
supporting_quote: converting NWM water discharge predictions into water depth (flow stage) data in each of the NWM's 2.7 million stream reaches.
They proposed and tested a methodology for deriving channel geometry and synthetic rating curves from the 10-m HAND dataset for each stream reach.

chunks.text: The featured collection also seeks to demonstrate cyberinfrastructure and web applications that manage, visualize, and disseminate NWM outputs to intended users. By building tools such as explorer/viewer apps and gauge comparison utilities, the goal is to move NWM results into accessible interfaces and practical workflows for flood monitoring and mapping.
supporting_quote: presents the development of cyberinfrastructure and web apps designed to manage and disseminate NWM results.
develop two web apps for accessing NWM output: the NWM Explorer App ... and the NWM Viewer app

chunks.text: A central technical barrier to coupling NWM forecasts with inundation mapping is translating predicted discharge into water depth (stage) for each river reach. Traditional rating curves require surveyed channel geometry and long-term streamflow measurements at gaging sites, but these data are unavailable for most of the NWM’s reaches. This makes national-scale stage estimation difficult without synthetic or derived approaches.
supporting_quote: converting NWM water discharge predictions into water depth (flow stage) data in each of the NWM's 2.7 million stream reaches.
Traditionally, rating curves between discharge and stage are based on surveyed channel geometry and long-term measurement of streamflow at a gaging site.
Since such information is not available for the vast majority of the NWM stream reaches

chunks.text: A broader operational challenge is providing flood alerts that are precise and actionable for users. Existing flood alert systems are described as lacking sufficient spatial specificity, temporal precision, and actionable guidance. This motivates systems that integrate forecasts, warnings, and situational data at street-address resolution with response-oriented tools.
supporting_quote: FloodHippo prototype is designed to address several shortcomings of current flood alert systems, namely that they are spatially vague, temporally imprecise, and lack actionable information.
a web map displaying near-real-time flood information ... at the street-address level.

chunks.text: Flood-inundation mapping at national scale faces a feasibility tradeoff between accuracy and computational cost. Physically based hydraulic models can be more accurate but are less feasible for near-real-time coupling due to data and computational demands. Terrain-based methods like HAND are cheaper and data-light but may require modifications for complex hydrologic interactions.
supporting_quote: although the iRIC-FaS-TMECH model produced more accurate inundation extents, the HAND method still performed reasonably well

the minimal data requirements and computational cost of the HAND method mean it is much more feasible to couple to NWM forecasts for near-real-time flood-mapping than physically based hydraulic models.

chunks.text: Reliable precipitation inputs remain a limiting factor for hydrologic forecasting frameworks like the NWM. Spatial and temporal scaling of recent and forecast precipitation introduces complexities that are hard to evaluate. This motivates assessment of satellite precipitation products and the effects of downscaling relative to in situ observations.
supporting_quote: The accuracy of any hydrological model is dependent upon the robustness of its precipitation input.
In forecasting modeling frameworks (e.g., NWM), spatial and temporal scaling of recent and forecasted precipitation data add a layer of complexity which is challenging to evaluate.

chunks.text: A 10 m National Elevation Dataset was processed to create the HAND raster, where each cell stores its height above the nearest drainage cell on the corresponding NHDPlus stream reach. This was performed using the CyberGIS facility at the National Center for Supercomputer Applications. The method supports a national-scale HAND database used as a terrain basis for inundation estimation.
supporting_quote: a 10 m National Elevation Dataset of the U.S. was analyzed on the CyberGIS facility ... and transformed into a raster called Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND)
each cell contains the height difference between its elevation and the elevation of the cell in the National Hydrography Dataset Plus (NHDPlus) stream reach to which it drains.

chunks.text: Flood-inundation extent can be mapped from HAND by selecting raster cells whose HAND values are below a specified water depth for their nearest stream. When combined with NWM flood forecasts, this approach provides a mechanism for translating modeled flows into spatial inundation information across broad areas. The method is terrain-based and designed for continuous, near-real-time application.
supporting_quote: The HAND dataset can be used to map flood-inundation extent by identifying the cells whose HAND values are less than the water depth at their nearest stream.
Coupled with flood forecasting from the NWM, the HAND approach establishes ... real-time flood-inundation mapping continuously across the continental U.S.

chunks.text: To obtain stage estimates needed for HAND inundation mapping, a methodology was proposed to derive channel geometry and synthetic rating curves for each stream reach from the 10 m HAND dataset. This substitutes for traditional approaches that depend on surveyed cross-sections and long-term gage data. The method enables coupling of NWM discharge predictions with inundation estimates for data-sparse reaches.
supporting_quote: They proposed and tested a methodology for deriving channel geometry and synthetic rating curves from the 10-m HAND dataset for each stream reach.
Since such information is not available for the vast majority of the NWM stream reaches, the approach ... enables the coupling of NWM predictions and HAND inundation estimates.

chunks.text: Uncertainty in inundation predictions can be represented through a hydraulic multi-model ensemble built from two-dimensional iRIC-FaSTMECH and HEC-RAS simulations driven by NWM forecasts. The ensemble outputs are visualized through probability maps delivered via a web-based decision support tool implemented in the Tethys platform. This method emphasizes communication of uncertainty rather than a single deterministic flood extent.
supporting_quote: They used the two-dimensional ... iRIC-FaSTMECH) and ... HEC-RAS models to compile an ensemble of floodinundation predictions based on NWM forecasts
developed a web-based decision support tool (using the Tethys platform ... ) to disseminate the uncertainty ... through a series of probability maps.

chunks.text: A comparative evaluation approach for inundation mapping contrasted a simple terrain-based HAND method with the iRIC-FaSTMECH hydraulic model for the 2016 Brazos River flood. Model-derived inundation extents were validated against observed extents derived from satellite remote sensing. The HAND approach was also modified to explicitly represent intercatchment flows between the mainstem and tributaries.
supporting_quote: They compared the simple terrain-based HAND approach against the iRIC-FaS-TMECH model.
Flood-inundation extents estimated using both methods were compared to observed extents based on satellite remote sensing.
especially when modified to explicitly account for intercatchment flows between the mainstem and tributaries.

chunks.text: Observed inundation mapping was supported by intercomparing multiple Landsat 8 floodwater classification techniques against a reference map created from manual digitization and ancillary data. The evaluated techniques included supervised and unsupervised classification, delta cue change detection, and water indices (NDWI and MNDWI). This methodological comparison targets generating reliable observed flood maps for validation and impact assessment.
supporting_quote: compared several floodwater classification techniques, based on Landsat 8 satellite imagery, to a reference inundation map based on manual digitization and ancillary data
The compared techniques were supervised classification, unsupervised classification, delta cue change detection, normalized difference water index, and modified normalized difference water index.

chunks.text: Floodwater depth was estimated from remotely sensed inundation extent combined with DEM topography by identifying boundary cells, extracting their elevations, and using those to infer depth. Depth for inundated cells is computed by subtracting each cell’s elevation from the elevation of its nearest boundary cell. This leverages satellite-derived extents to obtain depth information needed for response and damage assessment.
supporting_quote: developed a novel floodwater depth detection algorithm based on remotely sensed flood-inundation extents and topography from digital elevation models (DEMs).
identifies boundary grid cells ... extracts their elevations from the DEM, and calculates the flood depth by subtracting the elevation of each inundated grid cell from its nearest boundary cell.

chunks.text: Cyberinfrastructure dissemination used the Tethys platform to build web apps for searching, viewing, and extracting NWM outputs, and for demonstrating applied uses like gauge comparison and county-scale flood mapping. The suite included an NWM Explorer App as a catalog, an NWM Viewer for visualization/extraction, a Gauge Viewer for comparing modeled vs observed flow, and additional flood-mapping apps. This method focuses on turning large forecast archives into user-accessible services.
supporting_quote: used Tethys to develop two web apps for accessing NWM output: the NWM Explorer App ... and the NWM Viewer app
a Gauge Viewer app that allows for comparisons between NWM and observed streamflow, and two flood-mapping apps

chunks.text: A key dataset underpinning the work is a 10 m National Elevation Dataset processed into a national HAND raster. HAND is defined relative to NHDPlus stream reaches by storing the elevation difference between a terrain cell and its nearest drainage cell on the stream network. This dataset is intended to support continental-scale inundation mapping.
supporting_quote: a 10 m National Elevation Dataset of the U.S. was analyzed ... and transformed into a raster called Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND)
each cell contains the height difference between its elevation and the elevation of the cell in the National Hydrography Dataset Plus (NHDPlus) stream reach to which it drains.

chunks.text: The NWM prediction domain referenced includes 2.7 million stream reaches, representing a national hydrographic network for simulating and forecasting streamflow. Forecast products from NOAA weather inputs and WRF-Hydro are described as drivers for real-time simulation and subsequent flood applications. This scale motivates automated methods for rating curves and mapping.
supporting_quote: streamflow on 2.7 million stream reaches of the U.S. could be simulated and forecast in real time
converting NWM water discharge predictions into water depth (flow stage) data in each of the NWM's 2.7 million stream reaches.

chunks.text: Observed flood inundation extents used for model comparison were derived from satellite remote sensing for the 2016 Brazos River flood. These observed products served as a benchmark to compare inundation mapping methods such as HAND and iRIC-FaSTMECH. The paper emphasizes the value of remote sensing observations in evaluating model performance.
supporting_quote: Flood-inundation extents estimated using both methods were compared to observed extents based on satellite remote sensing.
demonstrated the value of using observed (i.e., remote sensing-based) flood inundation for model comparison.

chunks.text: Landsat 8 satellite imagery is described as the basis for multiple floodwater classification techniques used to map inundation for the 2016 Brazos flood. A reference inundation map was created from manual digitization and ancillary data for accuracy assessment. These datasets support evaluation of mapping approaches and production of higher-quality observed flood layers.
supporting_quote: compared several floodwater classification techniques, based on Landsat 8 satellite imagery, to a reference inundation map based on manual digitization and ancillary data for the 2016 Brazos flood.

chunks.text: Precipitation evaluation used IMERG satellite products from the Global Precipitation Measurement mission and compared them to in situ observations at 214 rain gauges over the Lower Colorado River Basin in Texas. The analysis considered effects of spatial and temporal downscaling on correspondence with observed precipitation. These datasets are central for assessing precipitation input quality for hydrologic forecasting.
supporting_quote: evaluated the impact of spatial and temporal downscaling of the Integrated MultisatellitE Retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement mission (IMERG) products by comparing them to in situ observations at 214 rain gauges.

chunks.text: The HAND approach, when paired with NWM flood forecasting, is presented as enabling a first-of-its-kind foundation for continuous, locally informative, real-time flood-inundation mapping across the continental United States. The mechanism relies on comparing HAND cell heights to stream water depth to delineate inundation. This establishes a scalable pathway from national hydrologic forecasts to mapped impacts.
supporting_quote: The HAND dataset can be used to map flood-inundation extent by identifying the cells whose HAND values are less than the water depth at their nearest stream.

Coupled with flood forecasting from the NWM, the HAND approach establishes, for the first time, a foundation for locally informative, real-time flood-inundation mapping continuously across the continental U.S.

chunks.text: A key reported advance is a methodology to derive channel geometry and synthetic rating curves from 10 m HAND for each stream reach, enabling discharge-to-stage conversion at national scale. This provides an alternative where surveyed geometry and long-term gage observations are absent across most reaches. The result is described as enabling coupling between NWM discharge predictions and HAND inundation estimates.
