supporting_quote: They proposed and tested a methodology for deriving channel geometry and synthetic rating curves from the 10-m HAND dataset for each stream reach.
Since such information is not available for the vast majority of the NWM stream reaches, the approach ... enables the coupling of NWM predictions and HAND inundation estimates.

chunks.text: In an intercomparison for the 2016 Brazos River flood, the iRIC-FaSTMECH hydraulic model produced more accurate inundation extents than the terrain-based HAND approach when compared to satellite-observed extents. However, HAND still performed reasonably well, particularly after modification to represent intercatchment flows between mainstem and tributaries. The result highlights an accuracy-versus-feasibility balance for near-real-time national applications.
supporting_quote: although the iRIC-FaS-TMECH model produced more accurate inundation extents, the HAND method still performed reasonably well
especially when modified to explicitly account for intercatchment flows between the mainstem and tributaries.
Flood-inundation extents estimated using both methods were compared to observed extents based on satellite remote sensing.

chunks.text: A hydraulic multi-model ensemble approach was used to quantify and visualize uncertainty in flood-inundation simulations based on NWM forecasts, using iRIC-FaSTMECH and HEC-RAS. Uncertainty was disseminated through a Tethys-based web decision support tool using probability maps. The framework is positioned as improving communication capabilities of NWM predictions.
supporting_quote: compile an ensemble of floodinundation predictions based on NWM forecasts
disseminate the uncertainty in inundation forecasts through a series of probability maps.
This framework is envisioned to enhance the communication capabilities of NWM predictions.

chunks.text: Among Landsat 8 floodwater classification techniques tested for the 2016 Brazos flood, supervised classification achieved the highest accuracies relative to the reference inundation map. This finding supports using supervised approaches to generate higher-quality observed inundation layers. Such observed products are emphasized as important for validating models and assessing flood impacts.
supporting_quote: The authors found supervised classification resulted in the highest accuracies.
These results are important for producing highquality observed flood-inundation maps that can be used for validating models and assessing flood impacts.

chunks.text: A floodwater depth detection algorithm derived depths from satellite inundation extents and DEM topography, and test applications showed close correspondence with iRIC-FaSTMECH simulated depths. The method estimates depth by referencing boundary cell elevations and subtracting elevations of inundated cells. The result increases the potential use of remote sensing for emergency response and damage assessment where depth information is needed.
supporting_quote: Test applications ... indicated depths estimated by the new algorithm correspond well with depths simulated by iRIC-FaSTMECH.
calculates the flood depth by subtracting the elevation of each inundated grid cell from its nearest boundary cell.

chunks.text: Tethys-based web applications were developed to access, visualize, and extract NWM output and to demonstrate forecast usefulness. The described apps include the NWM Explorer (catalog/search), the NWM Viewer (visualization/extraction), a Gauge Viewer for comparing NWM to observed streamflow, and flood-mapping apps for Tuscaloosa County, Alabama, and Greenbrier County, West Virginia. These publicly available apps are presented as aiding dissemination and visualization of NWM results.
supporting_quote: develop two web apps for accessing NWM output: the NWM Explorer App ... and the NWM Viewer app
a Gauge Viewer app that allows for comparisons between NWM and observed streamflow, and two flood-mapping apps for Tuscaloosa County, Alabama, and Greenbrier County, West Virginia.
The development of these publicly available web apps contributes to the dissemination and visualization of NWM results

chunks.text: The FloodHippo prototype integrates operational model outputs, cloud-based GIS, and expanded communication channels to provide intelligent hazard alerts. It includes an Awareness Portal that aggregates near-real-time information (NWM forecasts, NOAA warnings, FEMA flood zones, and social media) at street-address level, and a Response Portal focused on navigation for avoiding flooded areas or evacuating. The system is positioned to improve public awareness and weather-readiness by making information more actionable.
supporting_quote: FloodHippo," a flood alert system that integrates operational model outputs, cloud-based geographic information systems, and expanded communication channels.
Awareness Portal ... displaying near-real-time flood information — NWM forecasts, NOAA warnings, Federal Emergency Management Agency flood zones, and social media data — at the street-address level.
Response Portal ... allowing users to plot routes to avoid flooded areas or to evacuate to the nearest accessible shelter.

chunks.text: IMERG satellite precipitation products were found to correspond better to observed precipitation after spatial and temporal downscaling, based on comparison to 214 rain gauges. Despite improvement, the evaluation notes that additional improvement is still needed. The result underscores the importance of precipitation scaling choices for forecasting frameworks like the NWM.
supporting_quote: comparing them to in situ observations at 214 rain gauges.
They found IMERG products better correspond to observed precipitation when downscaled, but more improvement is needed.

chunks.text: A major limitation for national-stage estimation is that traditional discharge–stage rating curves depend on surveyed channel geometry and long-term gaging records. Because these are unavailable for most of the NWM’s 2.7 million reaches, scaling conventional approaches is impractical. This limitation motivates synthetic rating-curve derivation using terrain products like HAND.
supporting_quote: Traditionally, rating curves between discharge and stage are based on surveyed channel geometry and long-term measurement of streamflow at a gaging site.
Since such information is not available for the vast majority of the NWM stream reaches

chunks.text: The comparison of inundation approaches illustrates a tradeoff: hydraulic models can be more accurate, but their data requirements and computational cost hinder near-real-time national coupling to NWM forecasts. The HAND approach is less costly and requires minimal data, making it more feasible operationally even if accuracy can be lower. This feasibility argument supports deploying HAND for broad coverage while reserving hydraulics for detailed studies.
supporting_quote: although the iRIC-FaS-TMECH model produced more accurate inundation extents

the minimal data requirements and computational cost of the HAND method mean it is much more feasible to couple to NWM forecasts for near-real-time flood-mapping than physically based hydraulic models.

chunks.text: The paper notes that hydrologic model performance is constrained by precipitation input quality, and that scaling precipitation in forecasting systems introduces difficult-to-evaluate complexities. Even when downscaling improved IMERG correspondence with observations, further improvement was still necessary. This limitation indicates that precipitation uncertainty remains an important factor for operational forecasting frameworks such as the NWM.
supporting_quote: The accuracy of any hydrological model is dependent upon the robustness of its precipitation input.
spatial and temporal scaling of recent and forecasted precipitation data add a layer of complexity which is challenging to evaluate.
better correspond to observed precipitation when downscaled, but more improvement is needed.

chunks.text: The featured collection demonstrates prototypes and demonstrations from the 2016 NWC Summer Institute spanning near-real-time inundation mapping, remote sensing integration for flood assessment, and cyberinfrastructure for disseminating NWM outputs. The editors conclude that such research advances the NWC mission by addressing contemporary water challenges. Overall, the collection emphasizes translating national forecasts into actionable flood intelligence.
supporting_quote: These projects include demonstrations and prototypes of innovative concepts such as nearreal-time flood-inundation mapping, integration of remote sensing into flood assessment, and development cyberinfrastructure and web apps for water resources.
Research like this is critical to advancing the mission of the NWC to address 21st-Century water challenges.

chunks.text: Forecast-Informed Reservoir Operations (FIRO) uses meteorological and hydrologic forecasts to guide reservoir releases and storage decisions, aiming to increase operational flexibility while balancing water supply, flood risk, and environmental objectives. Prior work at Lake Mendocino suggests FIRO can materially increase median storage while maintaining core objectives. The broader national viability of FIRO depends on having sufficiently skillful precipitation and streamflow forecasts at actionable lead times.
supporting_quote: Forecast-Informed Reservoir Operations (FIRO) seeks to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of reservoir operations by leveraging reliable and skillful meteorological and hydrological forecasts to inform water management decisions.

Model results (Delaney et al. 2020) and model-informed practices at Lake Mendocino... indicate that FIRO can increase median storage by >30% over conventional reservoir operations while maintaining water supply, mitigating flood risk, and providing healthy ecosystems.
the success of FIRO nationwide relies fundamentally on quantitative precipitation forecast (QPF) and streamflow forecast skill

chunks.text: National QPF skill has been evaluated previously using operational Weather Prediction Center (WPC) products and numerical weather prediction guidance, showing long-term improvements and strong regional dependence. Skill tends to be higher in regions dominated by cool-season synoptic storms and landfalling atmospheric rivers, and lower where warm-season convection dominates. These prior studies motivate a complementary watershed-based, nationwide skill assessment.
supporting_quote: Both of these studies highlighted steady improvements in year-over-year QPF skill at lead times of 1–3 days of 1-in. and 2-in. precipitation events since the 1960s
Both Sukovich et al. (2014) and Herman and Schumacher (2016) further demonstrate that QPF skill varies seasonally... higher QPF skill along the U.S. West Coast associated with landfalling ARs
lower QPF skill across the central and southeast United States dominated by warmseason convective processes

chunks.text: FIRO Phase III, the National Expansion Pathfinder effort (2023–27), is led by USACE and CW3E to support national expansion of FIRO. It includes objectives to assess and improve precipitation forecast skill, complete and conduct viability assessments, and apply a national screening process across the USACE portfolio. This manuscript provides a national view of watershed-scale QPF skill to support those Phase III objectives.
supporting_quote: The third phase of FIRO is the National Expansion Pathfinder effort and will span 2023–27.
The goals of the FIRO Phase III are to 1) perform a national precipitation forecast skill assessment and improvement campaign;
The purpose of this manuscript is to provide a national view of watershed-scale QPF skill as a key element of the National Expansion Pathfinder effort

chunks.text: The study’s goal is to produce a national, watershed-scale assessment of quantitative precipitation forecast (QPF) skill as an enabling input to FIRO Phase III’s national expansion. The assessment is intended to support development of a FIRO screening process across the USACE dam portfolio by characterizing where forecast skill is highest and how it degrades with lead time and season.
supporting_quote: The purpose of this study is to provide a national view of watershed-scale QPF skill as a key element of the "FIRO Phase III: National Expansion Pathfinder" effort.
support the first and sixth objectives of FIRO Phase III listed above.
The results of this study will be used to inform the development of a subsequent rigorous FIRO screening process for the USACE portfolio of dams.

chunks.text: A complementary objective is to summarize QPF skill not only by hydrologic regions (HUC-2) but also in the context of USACE organizational units (districts) and site locations. This supports identification of districts and site watersheds that may be promising for FIRO due to higher near-term forecast skill.
supporting_quote: The national variability in QPF skill is reflected within the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) portfolio of dams
Summation of the QPF skill for the top 1% and top 5% thresholds across the USACE portfolio is illustrated in Fig. 11
The locations of 749 sites with USACE regulatory involvement... are plotted and analyzed along with the spatial analysis in this study

chunks.text: FIRO viability is constrained by whether precipitation and streamflow forecasts are reliable and skillful at the lead times required for operational decisions. While many non-forecast factors affect feasibility at a reservoir, forecast skill is a fundamental national dependency for expanding FIRO beyond current pilots. Therefore, a quantitative, spatially explicit assessment of QPF skill is needed to inform screening and prioritization.
supporting_quote: the potential success of FIRO nationwide relies fundamentally on quantitative precipitation forecast (QPF) and streamflow forecast skill

While there are many physical, hydrological, environmental, and engineering considerations... the success of FIRO nationwide relies fundamentally on quantitative precipitation forecast (QPF) and streamflow forecast skill
apply a FIRO screening process nationally across the USACE portfolio of dams.

chunks.text: High-quality national QPF verification is challenged by data and model limitations: a long reforecast record with higher-than-C384 resolution is not available for CONUS as of early 2025. This constrains the ability to verify extremes at fine spatial scales and motivates watershed-mean (MAP) verification to reduce resolution mismatch impacts.
supporting_quote: A reforecast dataset with a period of record longer than 20 years and with a horizontal resolution greater than C384... would be ideal... however, such a dataset for CONUS does not exist (as of early 2025).

The methodology also indirectly measures the effectiveness of the relatively coarse resolution GEFS-R in resolving potentially localized extreme precipitation within the PRISM dataset. This resolution discrepancy is reduced by computing the MAP

chunks.text: QPF skill is evaluated using GEFSv12 reforecast precipitation aggregated to daily (24-h) totals for nine lead times from day 1 to day 9. The aggregation uses 24-h periods ending at 1200 UTC, matching the verification dataset’s daily accumulation window. Skill is computed for paired QPF–QPE days over 2000–19 (verification spanning 1200 UTC 10 January 2000–0000 UTC 31 December 2019).
supporting_quote: Six-hour forecasts of precipitation were subsequently aggregated into nine lead times corresponding to 24-h periods ending at 1200 UTC for forecast from hours 12–36 (day 1) to 204–228 (day 9).

The previously described choice to evaluate QPF in 24-h periods ending at forecast hour 36 (day 1) through hour 228 (day 9) is motivated by the 24-h aggregation period of the PRISM QPE analysis ending at 1200 UTC.
Paired QPF and QPE data are verified as a function of nine lead times during a period spanning 1200 UTC 10 January 2000–0000 UTC 31 December 2019.

chunks.text: The analysis converts both forecast (QPF) and observed estimates (QPE) into mean areal precipitation (MAP) for 2125 HUC-8 watersheds intersecting CONUS. MAP is computed by bilinear interpolation to a dense point array inside each watershed at ~0.05° spacing (≈4–6 km). This approach helps mitigate mismatches between the coarser GEFS-R grid and PRISM’s 4-km product.
supporting_quote: Both the QPF and QPE data are converted into mean areal precipitation (MAP) values for 2125 USGS Hydrologic Unit Code (HUC)-8-sized watersheds that intersect the CONUS boundary.

The MAP is constructed by downscaling the QPF and slightly upscaling the QPE using bilinear interpolation to an array of points within each watershed with a horizontal spacing of 0.058 latitude and longitude (;4–6 km depending on latitude).
This resolution discrepancy is reduced by computing the MAP

chunks.text: Skill is primarily measured using the critical success index (CSI) from a 2×2 contingency table, focusing on event-based thresholds. Thresholds include (1) MAP ≥ 1 inch (25.4 mm) in 24 h and (2) MAP ≥ the watershed-relative top 1% of wet days (QPE > 0.0 in.). The CSI is not computed when fewer than 10 forecast–observation pairs meet the event criteria to reduce instability from small samples.
supporting_quote: The QPF skill was assessed using the critical success index (CSI) derived from a 2 3 2 contingency matrix
These thresholds include 1) precipitation greater than or equal to 1 in. (25.4 mm) in 24 h and 2) precipitation greater than or equal to the QPEderived watershed-relative top 1% value
The CSI will not be calculated in this study where the number of forecast and observed pairs... is fewer than 10

chunks.text: To contextualize CSI patterns, the study also summarizes complementary contingency metrics: probability of detection (POD), false alarm ratio, and bias. In addition, less extreme percentile thresholds (top 20%, 10%, and 5% of wet days) are evaluated to show how skill varies with event rarity and intensity.
supporting_quote: The QPF skill will also be summarized... for the probability of detection (POD), false alarm ratio, and bias.
For comparison with less extreme events, the CSI will also be shown derived from the top 20%, top 10%, and top 5% thresholds.

chunks.text: For USACE portfolio visualization, a separate metric aggregates precipitation over 72 hours covering lead times days 1–3, then computes CSI for top 1% and top 5% events in that 72-h total. This is motivated by an operational use case where an operator may require roughly three days to release and route water downstream prior to an extreme inflow period. District averages are computed from the watersheds containing USACE sites.
supporting_quote: we construct an analysis of CSI for the top 1% and top 5% of 72-h aggregate QPE and QPF inclusive of lead times of 1–3 days.
motivated by a hypothetical use case where a reservoir operator may need 3 days to release water from their reservoir
The "days 1–3 aggregate CSI" for the watershed containing each site can be combined to create a USACE district average

chunks.text: Forecast precipitation comes from the NOAA Global Ensemble Forecast System v12 Reforecast (GEFS-R) for 2000–2019, using the control member initialized daily at 0000 UTC. Data are on a 0.25°×0.25° grid. Perturbed members were excluded because their degraded resolution produced noticeably lower QPF skill than the control.
supporting_quote: The QPF data in this study were derived from the NOAA Global Ensemble Forecast System v12 Reforecast (GEFS-R) dataset... for the period 2000–19
obtained with a horizontal grid spacing of 0.258 latitude 3 0.258 longitude.
The degraded resolution resulted in noticeably lower QPF skill of the GEFS-R ensemble members as compared to the control and is therefore not used in this study.

chunks.text: Observed precipitation estimates are from the PRISM daily gridded product at 4 km resolution, ending at 1200 UTC each day. PRISM was selected for robustness in data-sparse western U.S. regions where gauges and radar coverage can be limited. East of the Rockies, PRISM incorporates Stage-IV estimates where radar and observations are more available.
supporting_quote: The quantitative precipitation estimations (QPEs) used for evaluation... were derived from the Parameter-Elevation Regressions on Independent Slopes Model (PRISM)
generate a native 4 km 3 4 km gridded daily QPE ending at 1200 UTC each day
The PRISM QPE is chosen for this study... for its ability to provide robust estimates of precipitation over data sparse regions of the western United States

chunks.text: Verification is performed over 2125 USGS HUC-8 watersheds that intersect the CONUS boundary, using watershed boundaries from the USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset. The authors note PRISM does not extend beyond CONUS, so results for watersheds largely outside CONUS should be interpreted cautiously.
supporting_quote: mean areal precipitation (MAP) values for 2125 USGS Hydrologic Unit Code (HUC)-8-sized watersheds that intersect the CONUS boundary.
The geometries of the HUC-8 watershed boundaries were obtained from the USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset
the PRISM QPE does not extend beyond the CONUS boundary; therefore, interpretation of QPF skill for watersheds with a majority of their area outside of the CONUS should be approached with caution.

chunks.text: USACE infrastructure context includes 749 sites with regulatory involvement (e.g., dams, levees) from the National Inventory of Dams, plotted against watershed skill maps. The paper retains all sites even though not all are candidates for FIRO (for example, levees are not manageable outlets).
supporting_quote: The locations of 749 sites with USACE regulatory involvement (e.g., dams, levees, etc.) are plotted and analyzed
The locations of these sites were obtained from the National Inventory of Dams
All 749 sites are retained even though all infrastructures are not necessarily capable of supporting FIRO (e.g., a levee is not a manageable outlet).

chunks.text: For day-1 forecasts using a 1-inch/24h threshold, the highest watershed CSI is concentrated along the West Coast, with values exceeding 0.50 in parts of Washington, Oregon, and California; New England also shows relatively high skill with CSI above 0.30 in places. HUC-2 averages rank California highest (0.42), followed by New England (0.39) and the mid-Atlantic (0.35). The top individual CSI values (~0.65) occur in several Sierra Nevada watersheds (e.g., Upper King, Upper San Joaquin, Upper Yuba).
supporting_quote: The day-1 QPF skill using a threshold of 1 in. is highest for HUC-8 watersheds along the West Coast with CSI values . 0.50
When averaged across the regional USGS HUC-2 basins, the California region has the highest average day-1 CSI of 0.42, followed by the New England (0.39), mid-Atlantic (0.35)
The highest CSI using a threshold of 1 in. was in the Upper King (0.65) watershed in California

chunks.text: Using the watershed-relative top 1% extreme threshold, day-1 CSI remains highest along the West Coast with values above 0.50 in Washington, Oregon, and California, and additional local maxima appear in the Intermountain West and along the East Coast. HUC-2 average day-1 CSI is highest in California (0.34), followed by New England (0.29) and the Pacific Northwest (0.28). The Southeast shows lower CSI under the top 1% metric because its top-1% precipitation amounts exceed 1 inch, making events more extreme.
supporting_quote: The day-1 QPF skill using the top 1% threshold is similarly highest for watersheds along the West Coast with CSI values . 0.50
When averaged across the HUC-2 basins, the California region has the highest day-1 CSI of 0.34, followed by the New England (0.29) and the Pacific Northwest (0.28) regions.
The primary difference... is across the Southeast United States where the top 1% precipitation value is much larger than 1 in. and the CSI is lower

chunks.text: Seasonality matters: day-1 CSI for top 1% events is generally higher during the October–March cool season than during the April–September warm season, especially across the central and Northeast U.S. The highest top-1% day-1 CSI reported is 0.63 in the South Fork of the American River watershed, with multiple nearby Sierra foothill watersheds exceeding 0.55.
supporting_quote: Day-1 CSI values are generally higher for top 1% QPE days during the October–March cool season... as compared to the April–September warm season
The highest CSI of 0.63 was recorded on the South Fork of the American River in California with values . 0.55 on the Upper Cosumnes, North Fork of the American River, and Upper Mokelumne

chunks.text: Complementary contingency metrics align with CSI patterns: the West Coast and parts of the eastern U.S. show higher probability of detection, lower false alarm ratio, and lower bias for extreme precipitation compared with the central U.S. These diagnostics reinforce a coherent spatial contrast between higher-skill coastal/synoptic regimes and lower-skill regions.
supporting_quote: These complementary skill metrics similarly demonstrate a higher probability of detection, lower false alarm ratio, and lower bias for precipitation extremes along the U.S. West Coast and portions of the eastern United States as compared to the central United States.

chunks.text: Skill increases for less extreme events: CSI for top 20% and top 10% wet-day thresholds is higher than for top 5% and top 1% thresholds across the U.S. Despite higher absolute values, the spatial pattern remains similar, with the West Coast, Northeast, and mid-Atlantic showing particularly high CSI (often 0.50–0.70 for top 20%/10%).
supporting_quote: the QPF skill of less extreme QPE thresholds (e.g., top 20% and top 10%) is higher than more extreme QPE thresholds (e.g., top 5% and top 1%)
higher CSI values . 0.50–0.70 for watersheds along the West Coast and in the Northeast and mid-Atlantic for the top 20% and top 10% thresholds

chunks.text: Forecast skill decreases sharply with lead time, with top-1% CSI dropping to about 0.05–0.10 by 8–9 days. Regionally, California has the highest average CSI across all lead times, followed by the Pacific Northwest and lower Colorado. New England and mid-Atlantic start high on day 1 but lose skill faster during days 2–4, becoming comparable to other eastern regions by lead times beyond ~3–4 days.
supporting_quote: the QPF skill decreases as a function of lead time with CSI values that fall below ;0.05–0.10 at lead times of 8 and 9 days
The HUC-2 regionally averaged CSI values are highest in the California region... across all lead times followed by the Pacific Northwest
they feature a larger rate of decrease as a function of lead time during days 2–4.

chunks.text: Current FIRO-related West Coast watersheds (e.g., Russian, Santa Ana, North Fork Feather, Upper Yuba, North Fork American, Duwamish) generally lie in the upper decile of national QPF skill across lead times for both 1-inch and top-1% thresholds. Sierra Nevada basins show the highest CSI as lead time increases, while Russian, Duwamish, and Santa Ana are lower but still strong relative to national distribution. For some lead times and extreme thresholds, CSI is not computed due to fewer than 10 qualifying forecast events.
supporting_quote: watersheds in the Sierra Nevada... contain the highest CSI values as a function of lead time followed by relatively lower CSI values in the Russian, Duwamish, and Santa Ana watersheds
the 1-in. and top 1% CSI values at most lead times are in the upper 10% of nationwide watershed QPF skill (i.e., see the "P90" line
there were fewer than 10 GEFS-R forecasts at day 5 and day 9 above the top 1% threshold in the Russian River watershed, and the CSI was not calculated.

chunks.text: For a 72-hour (days 1–3) aggregated CSI view over USACE sites, the highest district-average skill for top 1% and top 5% events occurs in West Coast districts. Specifically, the Sacramento, Portland (Oregon), Seattle, and San Francisco Districts have the highest average CSI values based on watersheds containing USACE sites. District rankings beyond the top tier vary by threshold but include some Eastern Seaboard and interior river-valley districts.
supporting_quote: The highest average CSI values at lead times of 1–3 days for both the top 1% and top 5% are for watersheds containing 18 sites in the Sacramento District, 24 sites in the Portland (Oregon) District, 6 sites in the Seattle District, and 2 sites in the San Francisco District
Rankings of USACE districts by CSI vary for ranks 5–10 depending on threshold

chunks.text: The study identifies several methodological constraints that affect interpretation. It uses only the GEFS-R control member because perturbed members have degraded resolution and lower skill, and acknowledges that an ideal reforecast (longer than 20 years and higher than C384 resolution) is not available for CONUS. The reliance on MAP also means localized extremes can be smoothed, especially in regions with sparse 1-inch MAP events.
supporting_quote: The degraded resolution resulted in noticeably lower QPF skill of the GEFS-R ensemble members as compared to the control and is therefore not used in this study.
A reforecast dataset with a period of record longer than 20 years and with a horizontal resolution greater than C384... would be ideal... however, such a dataset for CONUS does not exist
the mean areal calculation masked these localized extrema.

chunks.text: Edge-of-domain limitations arise because PRISM QPE does not extend beyond CONUS. As a result, watersheds that lie mostly outside the CONUS boundary can have incomplete verification coverage, and their QPF skill estimates should be treated cautiously.
supporting_quote: the PRISM QPE does not extend beyond the CONUS boundary; therefore, interpretation of QPF skill for watersheds with a majority of their area outside of the CONUS should be approached with caution.

chunks.text: The authors note that in some regions (e.g., parts of the Intermountain West), the top-1% threshold may be relatively low due to MAP smoothing and/or climatological characteristics, which can affect frequency comparisons and relevance for extremes. They suggest that higher thresholds above the top 1% might be more appropriate in those areas, but such analyses were not pursued.
supporting_quote: This result is hypothesized to be related to the relatively low top 1% threshold in these locations due to a high frequency of "lighter" or "less extreme" precipitation events due to the MAP smoothing
In these locations, a higher threshold above the top 1% may be of relevance; however, it was not pursued for additional analysis in this study.

chunks.text: The paper emphasizes that FIRO screening must incorporate reservoir-specific operational constraints beyond the HUC-8 watershed framework. A reservoir’s effective catchment may not match HUC-8 geometry, and the lead time required for operational actions differs by site. Thus, skill metrics need to be aligned with each reservoir’s decision timelines and spatial hydrology.
supporting_quote: These screening processes will need to consider additional factors such as the appropriate lead time to evaluate skill that will differ from one reservoir to the next or the appropriate spatial area to evaluate skill (i.e., a reservoir's catchment may not match the HUC-8 geometry)

chunks.text: Future assessments should broaden the evaluation across models, forecast centers, verification datasets, and threshold definitions. The authors explicitly call for comparing NCEP and ECMWF, operational WPC forecasts, alternative QPE sources (e.g., Stage-IV or point-based), and model-climatology-based thresholds. This would provide a more complete and operationally relevant characterization of QPF skill for FIRO expansion.
supporting_quote: Future studies should also seek to assess the QPF skill using precipitation forecast data from different modeling centers [e.g., NCEP and the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF)]
QPF skill of operational forecasts (e.g., the Weather Prediction Center)
QPF skill computed from different ground-truth datasets for QPE (e.g., stage-IV or point-based verification with observations)

chunks.text: The national watershed-scale QPF skill patterns from GEFS-R and PRISM are consistent with prior studies: the highest skill occurs on the U.S. West Coast (especially the Sierra Nevada) and secondary maxima occur in the Northeast and mid-Atlantic, while a central U.S./Gulf Coast “skill desert” is evident. These spatial patterns are attributed to storm-regime differences, with synoptic-scale and atmospheric-river-related precipitation being more predictable than warm-season convection. The results provide a national baseline dataset to support FIRO Phase III screening and prioritization.
supporting_quote: Collectively, these results reaffirm that the QPF skill is generally highest within watersheds on the U.S. West Coast with maxima in the Sierra Nevada
Secondary maxima in the QPF skill... appear... within watersheds in the Northeast and mid-Atlantic regions.
The QPF skill is the lowest in a "skill desert" across the central United States and Gulf Coast where convective processes during the warm season are particularly challenging to predict

chunks.text: Watersheds hosting current FIRO or FIRO-related projects generally fall within the upper decile of national QPF skill and demonstrate actionable skill at lead times relevant to FIRO. The authors argue this skill baseline can be leveraged to identify additional USACE sites where enhanced QPF skill may support FIRO activities, forming a key input to a national screening process.
supporting_quote: The QPF skill at HUC-8 basins with current FIRO or FIRO-related projects is in the upper decile of all HUC-8 basins nationally and offers skill at lead times that make FIRO viable.
The national QPF skill assessment provides a dataset that can be leveraged to identify other sites within the USACE portfolio that may have enhanced QPF skill that can support FIRO activities

chunks.text: The paper concludes that national FIRO expansion should be paired with a precipitation forecast skill improvement campaign, potentially enabling more USACE dams to achieve FIRO viability. Proposed improvement pathways include model advances, targeted reconnaissance, data assimilation, and AI/ML postprocessing. This effort is framed as aligned with NOAA’s Precipitation Prediction Grand Challenge strategy.
supporting_quote: The FIRO Phase III effort will also be complemented by a QPF skill improvement campaign that should be incorporated into future assessments of the QPF skill.

This effort should quantify improvements in the QPF skill from recent successes in modeling advances... targeted ground and airborne reconnaissance... data assimilation techniques... and postprocessing using artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques
The national precipitation forecast skill assessment and improvement campaign is well aligned with the objectives of NOAA's Precipitation Prediction Grand Challenge

chunks.text: Stream water temperature (SWT) is a central variable in lotic systems because it influences water chemistry and aquatic ecosystem health. It regulates dissolved oxygen, biochemical oxygen demand, and chemical toxicity, and it shapes survival and distribution of fish, amphibians, and macroinvertebrates. As climate change progresses, SWT is increasingly used as a proxy for ecosystem health and function and for diagnosing cumulative anthropogenic impacts.
supporting_quote: Water temperature in a stream or river plays a vital role in nature and society, regulating dissolved oxygen concentrations
As climate change progresses, SWT will be an increasingly critical proxy for ecosystem health and function

chunks.text: SWT modeling has historically used statistical and physically based approaches. Statistical models rely on empirical relationships (often air–water temperature relations) and can be applied with relatively minimal input data. Physically based models attempt to represent energy transfer mechanisms and have been widely adopted and institutionalized through agency tools such as SNTemp and SHADE-HSPF, as well as commercial suites like MIKE.
supporting_quote: Statistical (also stochastic or empirical) models are governed by empirical relations between SWT and their predictors, which require fewer input data.
In the 1980s, the US Geological Survey (USGS) introduced a physically based model that simulated SWT called SNTemp

chunks.text: Machine learning (ML) has become increasingly popular in hydrologic sciences because it is data-driven, computationally efficient for prediction, and often open-source. The review distinguishes between traditional ML (e.g., K-NN, SVM, shallow neural networks) and newer ML (e.g., deep learning LSTM, extreme learning machine, hybrids). Recent neural network models have matched or exceeded performance of hybrid models like Air2stream in some SWT applications.
supporting_quote: One advantage that has made ML increasingly appealing includes its ability to learn directly from the data (i.e., datadriven)
Air2stream... initially outperformed earlier ML models... However, in the last few years, Air2stream has had its performance matched and even exceeded by recent neural network models

chunks.text: The paper’s first objective is to provide a concise review of how machine learning algorithms have been used for stream and river water temperature modeling, prediction, hindcasting, and forecasting. It aims to serve as an entry point for hydrologists interested in applying ML and as a reference for ML experts on existing SWT applications. The scope explicitly includes AI/ML methods beyond earlier ANN-only reviews.
supporting_quote: This review's first objective is to provide a concise review of ML algorithm use in SWT modeling.
we provide a comprehensive examination of peer-reviewed journals that use any type of artificial intelligence or ML algorithm to model or evaluate river or SWT.

chunks.text: A second objective is to synthesize the model evaluation metrics used in ML-SWT studies and propose guidelines that enable clearer comparison of ML performance across studies. The authors emphasize combining regression, dimensionless, and error metrics rather than relying on a single statistic. They also compile distributions and suggested rating ranges for key metrics to contextualize what “good” means in ML-SWT.
supporting_quote: Secondly, our goal is to examine the ML performance evaluation metrics used in SWT modeling and find the most-used metrics and suggest guidelines for clearer comparison of ML performance.
we recommend that a combination of standard regression... dimensionless... and error index statistics... be used for model evaluation and reported together

chunks.text: A third objective is to assess whether and how ML use has improved understanding of SWT’s spatial and temporal patterns, and to identify where progress is still needed. The paper aims to critique the state of SWT understanding amid rapidly increasing ML adoption, emphasizing needs around robustness and physical interpretability.
supporting_quote: The third objective is to discuss the community's use of ML to address physical system understanding in SWT modeling.
to examine how ML use in SWT modeling has enhanced our understanding... and examine where progress is still needed

chunks.text: In situ SWT monitoring remains limited due to accessibility, financial, and operational constraints. Streams may be remote, on private land, or dangerous to access, and instrumentation can fail or be lost, producing inconsistent time series. These barriers motivate alternatives such as statistical, process-based, and ML approaches to fill data gaps and support management.
supporting_quote: many stream reaches, stream segments, and entire catchments remain difficult to access
temporal limitations such as uncertainties and inconsistencies in the continuity of measurements or unforeseen equipment loss or failure

chunks.text: ML models are prone to overfitting when model complexity and feature counts are high relative to available observations, which can cause poor performance on unseen data. The paper stresses that underfitting is less common in ML for these applications, but overfitting can be widespread. To counter this, the authors highlight the need for stronger generalization testing beyond standard train/test splits.
supporting_quote: the model runs the risk of overfitting
Given the propensity of ML models to effectively learn the training data, underfitting is less of an issue in ML, whereas overfitting can be widespread.

chunks.text: Comparing ML-SWT studies is difficult because performance metrics and modeling phases are inconsistently reported. Some papers report only a single phase, others use “testing” and “validation” interchangeably, and split proportions are sometimes given only as years rather than percentages. This inconsistency undermines cross-study benchmarking and can inflate perceived performance.
supporting_quote: there was not a consistent way of reporting training, validation, and testing percentages
others used "testing" and "validation" interchangeably, which could affect interpretation of model performance

chunks.text: Data scarcity remains a major impediment for ML in SWT, and short high-frequency records can still be insufficient because of autocorrelation and limited exposure to diverse conditions. The paper argues that large numbers of points from sub-daily sampling do not necessarily translate into adequate training diversity. This limits extrapolation to extremes and to ungaged or shifting conditions.
supporting_quote: the scarcity of data remains a large impediment for the application of machine learning in SWT modeling
1 year of streamflow data... at 15 min intervals equal about ∼ 35 000 points... but is unlikely to be enough to properly train an ML model due to autocorrelation

chunks.text: The paper conducts an extensive literature review of peer-reviewed studies that apply ML to SWT modeling across hindcasting, prediction, and forecasting. It notes a publication surge: more ML-SWT studies appeared in 2020–2024 than in 2000–2019, totaling 57. The review includes studies covered by earlier ANN-focused reviews but broadens to all ML/AI approaches.
supporting_quote: in the recent 5 years (2020–2024), more studies using ML for SWT were published than in the previous 20 years (2000– 2019), totaling 57.
we provide a comprehensive examination of peer-reviewed journals that use any type of artificial intelligence or ML algorithm

chunks.text: To reduce overfitting and improve generalizability, the paper proposes a workflow emphasizing temporal, unseen, and ungaged region tests (TUURTs). Unseen tests remain within the development dataset, while ungaged tests evaluate predictions at new sites with no prior data exposure. The authors advocate broader adoption of TUURTs in ML-SWT to increase confidence in extrapolation.
supporting_quote: we suggest the need for "temporal, unseen, ungaged region tests" (TUURTs) in SWT ML modeling.
testing for "ungaged" cases means testing for new sites that have no data and have not been previously seen by the model at all

chunks.text: The review categorizes and describes traditional ML algorithms used for SWT, including K-nearest neighbors, clustering approaches (e.g., K-means, PCA), support vector methods (SVM/SVR), Gaussian process regression (GPR), generalized additive models (GAM), and decision trees/CART. It summarizes strengths and weaknesses such as scalability limits for K-NN and overfitting in CART. These methods are presented as common baselines and comparators in SWT studies.
supporting_quote: K-nearest neighbors (K-nn) is a versatile supervised ML algorithm
CART... is prone to overfitting and can be statistical unstable

chunks.text: The paper reviews ensemble tree methods frequently used in SWT prediction, particularly random forest (RF) and XGBoost, and notes their application across daily and regional studies. It highlights that these methods are often used for feature influence analysis, with drivers like air temperature, day of year, and discharge commonly identified. The review positions RF/XGBoost as strong nonparametric benchmarks against other ML and some nonparametric statistical models.
supporting_quote: RF and XGBoost have been used to predict daily SWT prediction
finding day of year, streamflow flux, and AT to be most influential in the prediction of SWT

chunks.text: Neural network approaches are summarized from traditional feed-forward ANNs to newer deep learning architectures. The paper describes RNNs for temporal data, the vanishing gradient problem, and LSTM as a solution using input/forget/output gates. It also notes emerging graph neural network approaches (e.g., RGCN, Graph WaveNet) for spatial-temporal stream networks.
supporting_quote: Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997) introduced the long short-term memory (LSTM) model... explicitly designed to overcome the vanishing gradient problem.
Graph WaveNet... has been used in spatial-temporal modeling of SWT

chunks.text: Hybrid and physics-informed approaches are described as a method direction, including coupling wavelet transforms with neural networks and differentiable modeling that inserts process-based structure into ML. The review cites examples where wavelet-ML couplings improved performance over standalone models and where adding components such as shallow subsurface flow and recency-weighted air temperature improved LSTM-based SWT predictions.
supporting_quote: the combination of WT and ML improved performance compared to the standalone models
adding a separate shallow subsurface flow component to the LSTM model and a recency-weighted averaging of past air temperature... resulted in improved predictions

chunks.text: For evaluation metrics, the paper organizes commonly used statistics into three categories: standard regression, dimensionless, and error indices. It provides definitions and equations for MAE, MSE, RMSE, PBIAS, NSE, KGE, Willmott’s d, and information criteria (AIC, BIC). The authors recommend reporting combined metric sets to better characterize fit, error magnitude, and bias.
supporting_quote: the quantitative statistics were split into three categories: standard regression, dimensionless, and error index
we recommend that a combination of standard regression... dimensionless... and error index statistics... be used for model evaluation and reported together

chunks.text: The review covers ML-SWT journal articles from 2000–2024 and compiles which performance metrics each study reported. The authors note that all examined papers used at least one metric, and that since 2019 the majority used multiple metrics. This compiled evidence supports their guidelines for standardized metric reporting.
supporting_quote: We considered journal articles from 2000– 2024 that used ML to evaluate, predict, or forecast SWT
two or more metrics used by >84 % of studies published in or after the year 2019

chunks.text: Across ML-SWT modeling studies, air temperature (AT) and SWT itself are the most commonly used predictors. Many studies also include discharge to constrain SWT, and recent work increasingly uses day of year (DOY), humidity, and remote sensing products such as solar radiation, sky cover, and potential evapotranspiration. The paper frames these inputs as a growing feature set with uncertain marginal benefits that require further study.
supporting_quote: the model inputs of AT and SWT continue to be the most used in ML modeling studies.
flow discharge has been used to attempt to constrain SWT

chunks.text: The paper reports that recent CONUS-scale ML-SWT studies have used very high-dimensional predictor sets. Examples include one study using over 20 variables and an LSTM study considering over 30 variables. Despite this broad data compilation, the authors report only satisfactory performance and limited generalizability, motivating feature selection and robustness testing.
supporting_quote: Wade et al. (2023) using a point-scale CONUS ML study using over 20 variables
Rahmani et al. (2023) created an LSTM model and considered over 30 variables to simulate SWT

chunks.text: For spatial-scale analysis of errors, the authors compiled RMSE values across publications and grouped them into local/watershed (<~100 km2) and regional/CONUS (>~100 km2) categories. They report the number of RMSE data points (900 local; 1369 regional) and summary statistics (average, median, max, min). This dataset underpins their claim that RMSE performance is broadly similar across spatial scales.
supporting_quote: Number of data points               | 900                                | 1369
Average                             | 1.52                               | 1.55

chunks.text: The paper makes its compiled data for figures and tables publicly available through HydroShare. The dataset includes the values used to create Figs. 1 to 4 and Tables 1 and 2. This enables reproducibility of the performance-metric synthesis presented in the review.
supporting_quote: Data used for Figs. 1 to 4 and Tables 1 and 2 are available online at CUAHSI HydroShare
http://www.hydroshare.org/resource/68edf1673096480bacc6bd104215e9dc

chunks.text: The review identifies a sharp increase in ML applications to SWT in recent years. Specifically, it reports that 2020–2024 produced more ML-SWT publications than the prior 20 years combined (2000–2019), and the 2020–2024 total is 57 studies. This trend supports the paper’s motivation to standardize evaluation and compare methods across a rapidly expanding literature.
supporting_quote: in the recent 5 years (2020–2024), more studies using ML for SWT were published than in the previous 20 years (2000– 2019), totaling 57.

chunks.text: Across the reviewed literature, the most-cited evaluation metrics were RMSE, NSE, MAE, and R2. The paper quantifies citations as RMSE (45), NSE (25), MAE (18), and R2 (17). Based on this, it recommends that future SWT-ML papers report a combined set of regression, dimensionless, and error-index metrics for better comparability.
supporting_quote: the most-cited performance metrics were RMSE (45 citations), NSE (25), MAE (18), and R 2 (17).
we recommend that a combination of standard regression... dimensionless... and error index statistics... be used for model evaluation

chunks.text: Reported R2 values in ML-SWT studies are generally high. Over 2001–2024, the reported R2 range is 0.65–1.00, and the median across 17 studies is about 0.93. The authors contrast these values with process-based guidelines where acceptable R2 can begin around 0.50, implying ML often achieves much tighter fits.
supporting_quote: with a median of R 2 ∼ 0.93 across 17 studies

chunks.text: NSE was not reported in ML-SWT papers from 2000–2010 but became common afterward. Across 2000–2024, NSE values range from 0.25–1.00, with a median NSE of about 0.93 across 25 studies. The paper argues that NSE and R2 should be reported together because they assess different aspects: predictive skill/error variance versus explained variability.
supporting_quote: NSE was not used as a metric in ML studies of SWT between 2000 and 2010
the NSE range reported... was between 0.25– 1.00... with a median NSE of 0.93 across 25 studies

chunks.text: Error indices show a wide spread in ML-SWT performance, with some extremely low errors and some much higher. The median RMSE across 45 studies is 1.35 °C, with medians ranging from 0.0002–3.50 °C in the review period. MAE is reported later in the literature, with a range of 0.14–2.19 °C and a median MAE of 1.09 °C across 18 studies.
supporting_quote: The median RMSE was 1.35 °C across 45 studies
the MAE range (Fig. 5) was 0.14– 2.19 °C. The median MAE overall was 1.09 °C across 18 studies

chunks.text: Spatial scale did not strongly differentiate RMSE performance in the compiled literature. Local/watershed studies (<100 km2) had average RMSE ~1.52 °C and median 1.38 °C, while regional/CONUS studies (>100 km2) had average RMSE ~1.55 °C and median 1.42 °C. The authors conclude neither category is significantly better or worse based on these summaries.
supporting_quote: the average RMSE was similar for the local (∼ 1.52 °C) and regional (∼ 1.55 °C) categories.
The median local RMSE was slightly better than the regional RMSE (∼ 0.04 °C)

chunks.text: The paper proposes updated, ML-specific performance ratings for cross-comparison (very good, good, satisfactory, unsatisfactory) for R2, NSE, RMSE, and MAE, separated by training, testing, and validation phases. For example, it classifies testing R2 as “very good” when >0.99 and “unsatisfactory” when <0.86, and testing NSE as “very good” when >0.98 and “unsatisfactory” when <0.70. The authors argue that values such as R2 ~0.91 should be considered only satisfactory in the ML-SWT context because typical reported values are higher.
supporting_quote: We posit that the definitions of satisfactory, good, and very good be updated
For example, R 2 values from ML-SWT studies that may appear to be very good, such as R 2 ∼ 0.91, should be considered satisfactory

chunks.text: The authors argue that ML-SWT research has largely prioritized model comparison and performance over explaining SWT dynamics and processes. They suggest this limits knowledge discovery and risks producing accurate but uninformative black-box models. As a remedy, they propose a baseline set of robustness tests (TUURTs) to make ML results more transferable and physically meaningful.
supporting_quote: Our review finds that ML studies examining SWT have been conducted from a computational perspective, one with a focus on comparing techniques and performance
we urge use of TUURTs (temporal, unseen, ungaged region tests) for future ML-SWT models

chunks.text: Although recent studies have expanded inputs and model complexity at CONUS scale, the review notes that performance remains only satisfactory and models are not generalizable. This suggests that simply adding more predictors does not guarantee transferable skill. The paper frames this as a major gap for decision-relevant applications requiring robust extrapolation.
supporting_quote: the models in these studies performed only satisfactorily and were deemed not generalizable
leaving much room for improvement in CONUS-scale modeling of SWT

chunks.text: Temporal-scale comparisons across studies were not performed because of inconsistent reporting and heterogeneity in sampling and output resolutions. Studies used inputs from minutes to months and produced outputs from hourly to monthly, with varying record lengths from weeks to decades. The authors recommend publishing metrics at the temporal scale of interest (not just aggregated metrics) in supplements to enable cross-study comparison.
supporting_quote: it was difficult to conduct statistical comparisons for temporal scales, so they are not further discussed in this review.
We strongly suggest to researchers that metrics be made available at the temporal scale of interest

chunks.text: Data scarcity and limited diversity in training sets constrain ML for SWT, even when point counts appear large due to high-frequency sampling. The authors emphasize that autocorrelation and short records reduce exposure to diverse hydrologic states, limiting model learning. They outline potential mitigations, including spatial/temporal data augmentation and transfer or semi-supervised learning strategies.
supporting_quote: the scarcity of data remains a large impediment for the application of machine learning in SWT modeling
1 year... at 15 min intervals equal about ∼ 35 000 points... but is unlikely to be enough to properly train an ML model due to autocorrelation

chunks.text: The review highlights challenges in integrating physics into ML: if adding physical structure degrades performance, the community should diagnose why. It also emphasizes the need to handle predictive uncertainty for decision support and risk assessment, noting that uncertainty analysis is often underdeveloped in ML-SWT. The paper points to methods such as Monte Carlo dropout and mixture density networks as steps toward uncertainty quantification in forecasts.
supporting_quote: In short, if our use of physics in machine learning makes our models worse, we should understand why.
researchers have attempted to address the role of uncertainty... using the Monte Carlo dropout

chunks.text: Trust and interpretability are framed as both technical and social barriers. Technically, ML can be a black box and is affected by data and parameter uncertainty; socially, hydrologists may be skeptical due to novelty and limited CS/coding experience. The authors argue that explainable AI, open repositories, and targeted education are necessary for ML to be accepted in decision-making contexts.
supporting_quote: a technical barrier (black-box issues, data limitations, model uncertainty) and a social barrier
If we are to incorporate ML into decision-making processes, it makes sense that ML must be transparent and understandable

chunks.text: The review concludes that ML use for SWT has expanded rapidly and spans local to continental scales and hourly to multi-decadal horizons. It emphasizes that ML metrics are consistently strong and often exceed traditional expectations, which complicates comparisons with statistical and process-based models. The authors call for redefining “model success” for ML-SWT and raising evaluation standards beyond headline accuracy.
supporting_quote: applications of ML in SWT modeling have ranged from the local to the continental scale
We find that ML performance metrics surpass all our preconceived notions of what makes a very good vs. satisfactory model.

chunks.text: The paper recommends standardizing metric reporting by jointly providing regression, dimensionless, and error-index metrics, and it offers ML-specific rating ranges derived from the literature. The intent is to make performance comparisons easier and to contextualize results within the ML-SWT field. It also urges making phase-specific and scale-specific metrics available in supplements to support benchmarking.
supporting_quote: we recommend that a combination of standard regression... dimensionless... and error index statistics... be used for model evaluation and reported together
we introduce updated designations (for ML studies only) of very good, good, and satisfactory performance metrics as derived from the literature

chunks.text: A central closing claim is that widespread ML adoption has not yet yielded commensurate gains in physical understanding of SWT drivers and mechanisms. The authors argue that model accuracy has overshadowed important trade-offs such as generalizability, knowledge discovery, and interpretability. They advocate for more purposeful ML development aimed at decision-relevant predictions, risk mitigation, and improved process understanding.
supporting_quote: the increased accessibility to ML and its use in SWT modeling has yet to lead to better physical understanding of SWT causes and effects.
we believe it is time to take a step back and purposefully consider more thoughtful creation and purposefulness of ML models

chunks.text: Hydrologic forecasting has long been part of NWS operations to support protection of life, property, and the economy. Floods are a major hazard in the U.S., producing large damages and high fatality counts among weather hazards, while drought can impose broader and longer-lasting impacts across many sectors. These water extremes motivate the need for accurate, timely hydrologic analyses and forecasts across the nation.
supporting_quote: Supporting the core NWS mission of the "protection of life and property and enhancement of the national economy"
Floods are devastating natural disasters, causing billions of dollars of damage each year and putting many lives in danger
drought has inflicted billions of dollars in damage to the U.S. economy since 1980

chunks.text: The National Water Model (NWM) is built on distributed hydrologic modeling concepts that can provide land-surface and streamflow information anywhere in a domain, complementing traditional basin-outlet forecasts. NWS already uses distributed approaches such as flash-flood-focused systems, demonstrating value for short lead time events. The NWM extends this paradigm to continental scale and multiple forecast horizons with consistent national coverage.
supporting_quote: An alternative to lumped modeling is spatially-distributed modeling, which can provide streamflow and land surface information at any grid point within the model domain

Other gridded models, like the Flooded Locations and Simulated Hydrographs (FLASH) system ... produce simulations of streamflow and surface runoff for direct characterization of flash flood conditions
NWM v2.1 is an hourly cycling analysis and forecast system that provides streamflow guidance for millions of river reaches

chunks.text: The NWM emerged in response to both a National Academy of Sciences (NAS) report and multiple enabling resources. The 2012 NAS guidance emphasized modernization, stronger research-to-operations pathways, forecaster roles shifting “over the loop,” and use of advanced models and data assimilation. Development was supported by IWRSS collaboration, the National Water Center, WRF-Hydro as a community foundation, summer institute efforts, and congressional mandates.
supporting_quote: the National Academy of Sciences (NAS) issued a report in 2012 with guidance on the improvements needed in the NWS hydrologic forecasting enterprise
Transition RFC forecasters away from the execution of labor-intensive models and towards an "over the loop" role
These outlines were translated into a physical system via a timely combination of five main resources

chunks.text: The paper aims to explain why the NWM was created, summarize the operational configuration and model components, and describe model performance. It also outlines ongoing and future development directions for improving NWM components and services. The focus is on the operationally implemented NWM v2.1 (April 2021) and how it advances continental-scale hydrologic modeling for NWS needs.
supporting_quote: This paper will discuss the driving factors underpinning the creation of the NWM, provide a brief overview of the model configuration and performance, and discuss future efforts to improve NWM components and services.
implemented version 2.1 of the National Water Model (NWM) into operations in April of 2021

chunks.text: Traditional lumped modeling provides information mainly at basin outlets and cannot resolve within-basin variability needed for distributed flooding characterization. This limits guidance for spatially heterogeneous flash flood and riverine flood conditions driven by fine-scale weather and land-surface variability. Distributed modeling is positioned as the alternative that can produce guidance at any grid point.
supporting_quote: they are limited by the fact that they only provide information at the outlet of the smallest basin modeling unit and cannot provide guidance inside of each basin
reflecting the highly variable land surface and meteorological conditions that impact spatially distributed flooding
spatially-distributed modeling, which can provide streamflow and land surface information at any grid point within the model domain

chunks.text: Forecast coverage based on existing RFC forecast points leaves large spatial gaps across the national river network. The paper notes that only a small fraction of river miles are covered by forecasts, leaving many critical locations without guidance. These gaps include infrastructure, ecological regions, cities, and recreation areas where flow guidance is needed.
supporting_quote: produce streamflow forecasts for approximately 3800 locations across the United States
only 100,000 out of 3,500,000 miles of river covered by a forecast
These spatial gaps include a wide variety of areas such as power generation sites, ecologically sensitive regions, cities and recreation areas

chunks.text: Regional RFC hydrologic models are described as manually labor-intensive and not fully representing coupled processes across inland, coastal, cryosphere, and groundwater components. Additionally, end users often need flood inundation extent maps, not only streamflow, to support decisions. Lack of comprehensive inundation information reduces actionable intelligence during flood events.
supporting_quote: manually labor-intensive and do not represent the full set of coupled inland-coastal-cryosphere-groundwater processes
the holy grail for emergency responders and many end users is flood inundation namely the extent of the ground which is covered by flood waters
Without direct knowledge of this quantity via maps of surface inundation for all portions of their area of interest, end users lack key, actionable intelligence

chunks.text: Operational NWM v2.1 runs multiple configurations on NOAA’s WCOSS to serve different needs: analysis/assimilation for initialization, deterministic short-range, and ensemble medium- and long-range forecasts, plus island domains. The CONUS includes hourly cycling AnA and 18-hour deterministic short-range, four-times-daily 10-day ensemble medium-range, and 30-day ensemble long-range. Open-loop (no data assimilation) versions are also executed to expose native model behavior and for certain initializations.
supporting_quote: Several configurations of the NWM are run operationally on the NOAA Weather and Climate Operational Supercomputing System (WCOSS)
CONUS Short-Range 18 h deterministic forecast
CONUS Medium-Range 10 day ensemble forecast
CONUS Long-Range 30 day ensemble forecast
Open-loop (no DA) configurations of the Analyses, CONUS medium-range, and island short-range forecasts are executed as well.

chunks.text: Short-range and medium-range CONUS forecasts are initialized from a continuously linked analysis cycle rather than event-based runs, avoiding spin-up. The short-range forecast cycles hourly and uses HRRR and RAP forcings for deterministic 18-hour guidance. The medium-range forecast runs four times daily, uses GFS forcing, and produces a seven-member time-lagged ensemble with members 2–7 using successively older GFS cycles to build an 8.5-day ensemble horizon.
supporting_quote: Each of these analysis cycles is started from the previous AnA iteration, making them continuously linked rather than event-based in nature, and eliminating the need for spin-up simulations.
The Short-Range Forecast configuration ... cycles hourly ... forced with meteorological data from the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) and Rapid Refresh (RAP) ... out to 18 h.
The Medium-Range Forecast configuration ... executed four times per day at 00Z, 06Z, 12Z, and 18Z
members 2–7 ingest time-lagged forcing data from successively older forecast cycles of the GFS
creating an overall seven member equal-weighted medium range ensemble forecast with an 8.5 day forecast horizon

chunks.text: The long-range forecast is a forcing-based four-member ensemble driven by different CFS members from a single cycle and runs to 30 days. Due to computational constraints, the long-range configuration does not use the 250 m overland/subsurface routing; instead it aggregates runoff and baseflow across NHDPlus catchments, which changes outputs and requires separate calibration. A specialized long-range analysis (AnA) with simplified routing is run four times daily with a 12-hour lookback to initialize these forecasts.
supporting_quote: At 30-days in length, the longest set of NWM forecasts is produced by the Long-Range Forecast
it consists of four members which are each forced with a different Climate Forecast System (CFS) forecast member from a single CFS model cycle.
the long-range, 30-day forecast configuration due to computational constraints

This more simplistic formulation ... also requires a separate calibration due to differing process representations.
Executed four times per day with a 12 h lookback period, this configuration differs further ... via its use of the simplified approach to routing surface water

chunks.text: Island (Hawaii and Puerto Rico/USVI) configurations produce only analyses and 48-hour short-range forecasts, reflecting available forcing data. Island forcings use NAM-Nest for shortwave/longwave radiation and WRF-ARW for remaining fields, and routing is performed at 100 m (vs 250 m CONUS) due to high topographic relief. USGS streamflow observations are assimilated in island analyses; Hawaii ingests MRMS precipitation, while Puerto Rico/USVI relies on HIRESW with NAM-Nest precipitation as fallback.
supporting_quote: only Analyses and Short-Range forecasts are produced—the latter extending out to a 48-h forecast horizon.
meteorological input from (1) Shortwave and Longwave Radiation: ... NAM-Nest ... and (2) Remaining Fields: WRF-ARW models

chunks.text: Structurally, the NWM is described as an integrated system composed of WRF-Hydro, a hydro-geospatial fabric, a Meteorological Forcing Engine (MFE), and automated calibration. WRF-Hydro supports multiple process modules including NoahMP land surface physics, overland and subsurface routing, conceptual baseflow, channel routing, and reservoir routing. The modular design enables extensibility for adding new process capabilities.
supporting_quote: It consists of the community WRF-Hydro modeling system, a detailed geospatial-hydrofabric set of data layers, a Meteorological Forcing Engine (MFE) and an automated model calibration system.

The core physics ... consists of multiple process modules including a column land surface model, modules for overland and saturated subsurface lateral flows, a bucket-type parameterization for baseflow, a channel flow module, and a reservoir routing module.
The column land surface model used in the NWM is an updated version of the community NoahMP land surface model

chunks.text: Overland flow is routed on 250 m (CONUS) or 100 m (islands) grids using an explicit diffusive-wave formulation and a steepest-descent gradient option to reduce latency. A 10 s routing time step is used at 250 m to satisfy Courant constraints. Overland flow exceeding retention depth and intersecting channel grid cells is converted to channel inflow aggregated to NHDPlus catchments and reaches.
supporting_quote: overland and saturated subsurface flow routines execute on a 250 m CONUS (100 m over the Hawaii and Puerto Rico/Virgin Island domains)
an explicit formulation of the diffusive wave simplification of the full St. Venant equation for overland flow
To satisfy Courant constraints ... an overland flow routing time step of 10 s is used.
Overland flow ... intersecting ... 'channel' grid cells, is sequestered as channel inflow.
channel inflow for each NHDPlus channel reach is aggregated from all channel grid cells within each NHDPlus catchment

chunks.text: Saturated subsurface flow uses a Boussinesq approximation for effective 2D lateral transport on the routing grid and is synchronized to the 60-minute NoahMP timestep. Water table position is inferred from the 2 m deep, 4-layer soil moisture discretization, and the implementation does not represent perched lateral transport. Lateral redistribution can lead to full-column saturation and exfiltration that then participates in overland flow.
supporting_quote: A Boussinesq approximation is employed as in Wigmosta et al. (1994) which results in an effective 2-dimensional calculation
determined from the 2 m deep, 4-discretization soil moisture representation in NoahMP
the subsurface flow routine in WRF-Hydro does not represent perched lateral transport.
The 60-min time-step of saturated lateral flow is synchronized with the execution of the NoahMP time step.
can result in full column saturation and exfiltration of soil water to the land surface

chunks.text: Channel routing uses an iterative Muskingum-Cunge formulation, with channel inflows from overland flow and conceptual baseflow inserted at the upstream node of each NHDPlus reach. Reservoirs are represented for more than 5000 locations with a basic fill-and-spill approach, but v2.0 introduced a two-pronged method at several hundred sites that combines observation persistence using USGS/USACE streamflow near reservoirs and assimilation of RFC observations and forecasts of reservoir outflow.
supporting_quote: Channel flow is then estimated using the iterative Muskingum-Cunge hydrologic routing formulation
Channel inflow components coming from overland and baseflow are ingested into the channel at the upstream node of the relevant NHDPlus channel reach.
More than 5000 of these reservoirs are already represented in the NWM, but in a fairly simplistic fill-and-spill manner.
a new module was developed in NWM v2.0 ... a twopronged automated approach
USGS and USACE-supplied streamflow measurements ... are used to correct NWM reservoir states and releases.
RFC-supplied observations and forecasts of reservoir outflow are assimilated into the NWM

chunks.text: The operational NWM uses a consistent spatial framework: a 1 km land surface grid and an NHDPlus-derived channel network providing output for over 2.7 million stream reaches. Overland and subsurface routing uses 250 m grids over CONUS and 100 m over island domains. The hydrofabric is based largely on NHDPlus v2 medium resolution flowlines and catchments, with modifications to ensure a seamless, continuous flow network across an extended domain into Canada and Mexico.
supporting_quote: All of the analyses and forecasts are executed with the same 1 km resolution land surface grid

The NWM channel routing network is largely derived from the National Hydrography Dataset Plus Version 2 (NHDPlus)
a continuous flow network was ensured by examining all interior network endpoints and reconnecting the network wherever possible

chunks.text: Meteorological forcing is ingested from multiple observed and NWP sources and processed by the NWM Meteorological Forcing Engine (MFE). The model requires seven forcing variables, including precipitation rate, near-surface temperature and humidity, wind speed, surface pressure, and incoming shortwave and longwave radiation. MFE performs standardization, interpolation to the 1 km grid, downscaling (e.g., lapse-rate adjustments; terrain adjustments for shortwave), bias correction for some configurations, and precipitation layering using preferential datasets.
supporting_quote: it ingests meteorological forcing from a variety of external sources including ... MRMS ... MPE ... HRRR ... RAP ... NAM-Nest ... GFS ... and CFS

The NWM requires seven meteorological variables; precipitation rate, 2-m air temperature, 2-m specific humidity, 10 m wind speed, surface pressure, incoming shortwave radiation, and incoming longwave radiation.
each variable is interpolated to the 1 km NWM land surface model grid

chunks.text: Long-range forcing from CFS is statistically post-processed using quantile mapping to NLDASv2 climatology to enable enhanced bias correction. The method uses parametric distributions by variable type (e.g., Weibull for non-zero precipitation, Gaussian for temperature/pressure/longwave, gamma for humidity and wind) and a Dirac delta for zero precipitation cases. Parameters vary by grid point and forecast hour and use a centered ±2-day moving window to increase sample sizes.
supporting_quote: This bias correction approach is based on the quantile mapping ... of CFSv2 outputs to match the North American Land Data Assimilation (NLDASv2) climatology
a Dirac delta function to model instances of zero precipitation, and a Weibull distribution to model non-zero precipitation.

chunks.text: Calibration for CONUS NWM v2.1 used AORC meteorological forcing and spanned October 2008 through September 2013, with 2007 as spin-up and validation from October 2013 through September 2016. Direct calibration was limited to 1365 lightly regulated basins selected from USGS, CADWR, and Canadian sites. Hawaii and Puerto Rico/USVI were calibrated separately using NAM-Nest-based forcing datasets and local RFC precipitation, with 29 and 47 basins calibrated respectively.
supporting_quote: The calibration period for the CONUS domain ... extends from October 2008 through September 2013, with a validation period spanning October 2013 through September 2016, and 2007 used for spin-up.

chunks.text: Automated calibration optimized 14 parameters across CONUS using Dynamically Dimensioned Search, minimizing an objective function combining NSE and log-space NSE using hourly streamflow observations. After calibration, parameters for uncalibrated areas are transferred via regionalization; for full-physics configurations, similarity is measured using Gower’s distance metric, while the long-range configuration uses an ecoregion-based approach. This creates complete parameter fields for the national domain despite limited direct calibration sites.

chunks.text: Retrospective CONUS validation (2013–2016), driven by AORC forcing and without streamflow DA, showed reduced hourly streamflow bias across NWM versions. Using the full USGS gauge set, the share of sites within ±20% bias increased from 31% (v1.0) to 52% (v2.1). The bias histogram also tightened, with fewer wet and dry extremes, though wet bias remained more prevalent in the middle of the CONUS.

These include differing regions, cadence, forcing sources, and forecaster modifications to inputs, states, and parameters. A direct comparison would require reforecasts with consistent forcing but still would not capture other important differences, so such analysis is deemed beyond the scope of the article.

chunks.text: Subsurface flow in the v1.0–v2.1 NWM does not represent perched lateral transport, because saturation is inferred from a 2 m, 4-layer NoahMP soil column and the water table is defined by the top-most saturated layer. This structural choice limits the realism of certain hillslope and shallow subsurface processes. The paper flags this as a representation boundary within the subsurface routing approach.
supporting_quote: In versions 1.0–2.1 of the NWM, subsurface soil saturation characterization is determined from the 2 m deep, 4-discretization soil moisture representation in NoahMP.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that the NWM provides a nationwide operational hydrologic modeling platform with multiple forecast horizons (18 hours to 30 days) and high-resolution gridded and reach-based outputs. It emphasizes that the system complements RFC forecasts while filling spatial gaps by providing output for over 2.7 million reaches and high-resolution grids. The authors highlight that continued versioned upgrades and partnerships across government, academia, and industry support further advances and broader applications such as flood inundation mapping.

The conclusion frames this as a critical advance given growth in exposure and vulnerability.

The authors anticipate that NWM v4.0 will begin using the NextGen framework in late 2025 or 2026, signaling a strategic shift to broaden community innovation pathways into operations.
