chunks.text: Large-scale river routing in land surface modeling has traditionally relied on gridded river networks aligned with atmospheric/LSM computational grids. New GIS hydrographic datasets provide vector “blue-line” river representations with explicit connectivity and enable more detailed routing. Streamflow observations are also widely available with precise locations on these vector networks, enabling basin-wide diagnosis beyond outlet gauges.
supporting_quote: river routing within LSMs has traditionally been done using gridded river networks that best fit the computational domain used in LSMs.
These datasets provide a vector-based representation of the river network using the "blue line" mapped rivers and streams.

chunks.text: NHDPlus provides nationwide hydrography for the contiguous U.S. with millions of reaches and their connectivity, enabling network-scale modeling. USGS NWIS supplies extensive streamflow gauge observations located on the NHDPlus network, supporting parameter estimation and evaluation at many interior points in basins.
supporting_quote: National Hydrography Dataset Plus (NHDPlus). This hydrographic dataset has about 3 million river and water body reaches along with information on how they are connected into networks.
The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) National Water Information System (NWIS) provides streamflow observations at about 20 thousand gauges located on the NHDPlus river network.

chunks.text: Parallel computing is common in large-scale atmospheric and ocean modeling but less frequent for large river networks. Typical upstream-to-downstream routing is sequential, and naive parallelization by basin decomposition can lead to load imbalance. Alternatives that relax strict upstream-to-downstream dependence can achieve better speedup, motivating investigation of parallel-friendly formulations while retaining traditional routing logic.
supporting_quote: the use of parallel computing is quite common in regional- to global-scale atmospheric and ocean modeling but comparatively infrequent in modeling of large river networks.
one way to speed up river flow modeling is to use a sequential river routing code to compute independent basins on different processing cores

chunks.text: The study aims to develop RAPID, a river network routing model that can compute discharge and water volume across thousands of vector river reaches described by NHDPlus. It seeks a formulation that uses NHDPlus connectivity and can estimate flows at ungauged locations. The work also targets automated calibration using many gauges across basins, not only at outlets.
supporting_quote: The present study links a land surface model with a new river network model called Routing Application for Parallel Computation of Discharge (RAPID) using NHDPlus

The research presented in this paper aims at answering the following questions: how can a river model be developed for calculation of flow and volume of water in a river network of thousands of blue-line river reaches?

chunks.text: A central goal is to create a matrix-based river routing method that avoids spatial iterations by expressing the whole network in one linear system. This is intended to enable efficient computation for large networks and to facilitate parallel implementation while preserving upstream-to-downstream routing behavior.
supporting_quote: A matrix-based version of the Muskingum method is developed herein
The vector-matrix notation provides one flow equation for the entire river network, therefore avoiding spatial iterations.

chunks.text: The study evaluates RAPID in a real basin setting (Guadalupe and San Antonio, Texas) by estimating flow wave celerities from 15-min gauge data and checking whether routed dynamics can be reproduced. It also uses these data to explore parameter estimation and diagnostic use of interior gauges.
supporting_quote: RAPID is applied to the Guadalupe and San Antonio River basins in Texas, where flow wave celerities are estimated at multiple locations using 15-min data
Gauges situated across river basins (not only at basin outlets) are used to automatically optimize the Muskingum parameters and to assess river flow computations

chunks.text: Another goal is to assess speedup from parallel computing using the matrix formulation, especially in a large interconnected basin. The work tests whether an iterative linear solver can decouple subbasins enough to reduce wall-clock time compared to traditional sequential Muskingum routing.
supporting_quote: This river model can be adapted for parallel computing
Finally, the speedup of RAPID in a parallel computing environment is assessed.

chunks.text: Routing in very large river networks requires systematic handling of connectivity and simultaneous computation across many reaches. Traditional reach-by-reach formulations can become unwieldy at the scale of thousands to millions of reaches. The paper frames a need for matrix structures for connectivity and computation to manage large NHDPlus-like networks.
supporting_quote: In a network of thousands of reaches, matrices are needed for network connectivity and flow computation.
For a river network with m river reaches, all vectors are of size m and all matrices are square of size m.

chunks.text: Existing studies often rely on limited gauges and focus on outlets, which reduces ability to diagnose runoff and routing errors across a basin. As model resolution increases, interior gauges become valuable for assessing land surface runoff quality. The paper positions this as a motivation for using many gauges distributed across basins for calibration and evaluation.
supporting_quote: Most studies mentioned above... use a limited number of gauges throughout large river basins, often focusing on gauges located at river mouths.
using gauges located across basins would help in diagnosing the quality of LSM computations.

chunks.text: Coupling land surface model runoff to a vector river network is challenging because LSM runoff is produced on a grid while NHDPlus routing uses catchments and reaches. Running an LSM at 30-m catchment-grid resolution is computationally prohibitive, motivating a practical approach for mapping grid runoff to catchment inflow without expensive horizontal routing.
supporting_quote: The map of catchments is available in NHDPlus in both gridded (at 30-m resolution) and vector formats
Running a land surface model at a 30-m resolution is very resource demanding. Therefore, a coarser resolution of 900-m cell size is chosen.

chunks.text: Fully interconnected basins limit simple parallelization by subbasin decomposition because upstream-to-downstream dependencies require sequential waiting. This makes it hard to achieve strong speedup if the method strictly enforces causality along the longest flow path. The paper highlights this challenge when exploring parallel computation for large river networks.
supporting_quote: In a river network that is fully interconnected... I 2 C - N cannot be made diagonal by blocks
computations would have to be made sequentially from upstream to downstream, each core having to wait for its upstream core to be done prior to starting its work.

chunks.text: RAPID is based on the traditional Muskingum routing method but expressed in a vector-matrix form for entire networks. The core routing equation is a single linear system relating outflows at t+Δt to previous outflows and lateral inflows through sparse matrices for parameters and connectivity. This provides one equation for all reaches, avoiding explicit spatial loops over network topology.
supporting_quote: The backbone of RAPID is a vector-matrix version of the Muskingum method shown in Eq. (1)
The vector-matrix notation provides one flow equation for the entire river network, therefore avoiding spatial iterations.

chunks.text: Network connectivity is encoded as a sparse matrix N where entry (i,j)=1 when reach j flows into reach i, enabling upstream inflow computation by N·Q. The approach relies on graph-theory concepts and supports multiple upstream reaches. Divergences are handled by assigning all upstream flow to a designated major path, while minor branches receive only lateral inflow unless fractions are supplied.
supporting_quote: A value of one is used at row i and column j if reach j flows into reach i, and zero is used everywhere else:
In case of a divergence... a unique reach (the major divergence) is used to carry all the upstream flow

chunks.text: Muskingum coefficients are implemented as diagonal parameter matrices C1, C2, and C3 whose diagonal elements depend on reach-specific k and x values and the routing timestep Δt. RAPID allows k and x to vary by reach. The coefficients follow standard Muskingum formulas and satisfy C1+C2+C3=1 for each reach.
supporting_quote: The matrices C1, C2, and C3 are diagonal matrices with their diagonal elements being the coefficients used in the Muskingum method
In RAPID, the parameters k and x of the Muskingum method are allowed to differ from one river reach to another

chunks.text: RAPID computes reach water volume using an explicit forward Euler discretization of the continuity equation. Volume at t+Δt equals previous volume plus inflow (from upstream and lateral inflow) minus reach outflow, all multiplied by Δt. This supports potential coupling to groundwater models needing reach storage estimates.
supporting_quote: the first-order, explicit, forward Euler method is applied to the continuity equation to calculate the volume of water in each river reach
V(t + Δt) = V(t) + [NQ(t) + Qe(t)]Δt - Q(t)Δt

chunks.text: Parameter estimation is posed as an inverse problem minimizing a daily summed square-error cost function over all available gauged reaches. A sparse diagonal gauge-selection matrix G ensures only gauged locations contribute. The objective uses daily average modeled discharge and daily observed discharge, scaled by a factor f to keep the cost magnitude near 10^1 for optimization stability.
supporting_quote: A square-error cost function φ is chosen
G is a sparse diagonal matrix that allows the dot product to survive only where gauges are available

chunks.text: To reduce calibration dimensionality, k and x are parameterized with two basin-wide multipliers (λk, λx). Storage time k is tied to reach length and wave celerity via k=L/c, then scaled by λk, while x is set as 0.1·λx. Three different initial guesses for (λk, λx) are used and the best solution is selected by minimum cost.
supporting_quote: k_j = L_j/c_j
the search for optimal parameters is limited to determining two multiplying factors λ_k and λ_x

chunks.text: Flow wave celerities are estimated from 15-min gauge data by maximizing lagged cross correlation between hydrographs at consecutive stations. The lag τtravel at maximum correlation is interpreted as wave travel time, and c=d/τtravel is computed using NHDPlus curvilinear distances along the river network. These celerities are used to inform parameter sets and to validate simulated dynamics.
supporting_quote: The maximum lagged cross correlation between hydrographs at two consecutive gauging stations is used to determine the flow wave celerity.
The wave celerity c is then computed using Eq. (16): c = d/τ_travel

chunks.text: A flux coupler maps gridded Noah-MP runoff to NHDPlus reaches by aggregating surface and subsurface runoff over each reach catchment. Catchment boundaries are rasterized to a 900-m grid and runoff is superimposed and summed per catchment COMID for each 3-hour output. The scheme intentionally omits horizontal routing from hillslopes to channels, simplifying coupling to any gridded LSM.
supporting_quote: a coarser resolution of 900-m cell size is chosen.
no horizontal routing is used between the land surface and the river network in the proposed scheme.

chunks.text: The study uses the NHDPlus dataset to represent river reaches, catchments, and connectivity for Texas basins and for the upper Mississippi performance test. For the Guadalupe and San Antonio basins, 5175 reaches with average length 3.00 km and average catchment area 5.11 km² are routed. NHDPlus COMID identifiers, nodes, and connectivity fields (FromNode/ToNode, Divergence, Hydroseq) support network matrix construction and ordering.
supporting_quote: There are a total of 5175 river reaches with known direction and connectivity within the NHDPlus description of the Guadalupe and San Antonio river basins
These 5175 reaches have an average length of 3.00 km and the average catchment defined around them is 5.11 km2 in area

chunks.text: Streamflow observations come from USGS datasets at two temporal scales: 15-min IDA data for wave-celerity estimation and daily NWIS data for parameter optimization. Fifteen gauging stations are used in the celerity analysis across two 6-month periods (early 2004 and early 2007). For calibration, 36 gauges with full daily records from 2004–2007 are used in the cost function.
supporting_quote: The USGS Instantaneous Data Archive (IDA) provides 15-min flow data
36 of them having full records of daily measurements for the four years studied (1 January 2004–31 December 2007). These 36 stations are used for parameter estimation.

chunks.text: Runoff forcing for routing is produced by the Noah-MP land surface model with TOPMODEL-based runoff and a simple groundwater component. Noah soil hydrology runs at an hourly time step and produces runoff every three hours. The routing time step in RAPID is set to 900 s (15 min), and 3-hour runoff is held constant within the included 15-min steps.
supporting_quote: the runoff scheme is TOPMODEL based, using a simple groundwater model (SIMGM; Niu et al. 2007).
The soil hydrology of Noah (soil moisture) is run at an hourly time step and runoff data are produced every three hours.

chunks.text: Meteorological forcing for Noah uses hourly NEXRAD precipitation downscaled from 4.763 km to 900 m, and other variables from 3-hourly NARR interpolated from 32.463 km to 900 m. The forcing dataset spans four years from 1 January 2004 to 31 December 2007. Required variables include precipitation, humidity, temperature, pressure, wind, and shortwave/longwave radiation.
supporting_quote: Hourly precipitation is obtained from the Next Generation Weather Radar (NEXRAD) and downscaled from its original resolution (4.763 km) to 900 m
All other meteorological parameters are downloaded from the 3-hourly North American Regional Reanalysis (NARR) and converted from its original resolution (32.463 km) to 900 m

chunks.text: Parallel-performance evaluation is conducted on the upper Mississippi River basin (NHDPlus region 7) with 182 240 reaches. A synthetic runoff forcing is used: 1 m3 every 3 h for all reaches and time steps, and uniform routing parameters based on reach length with c=2.5 m s−1 and x=0.3. The benchmark computes 100 days at a 900-s time step.
supporting_quote: upper Mississippi River basin... has 182 240 river and water body reaches
runoff data... are synthetically generated and set to 1 m3 every 3 h for all reaches

chunks.text: RAPID is implemented in FORTRAN 90 using PETSc for sparse matrices/vectors and linear solvers, and TAO for optimization. It uses NetCDF for input/output and can run sequentially or with MPI in parallel. The reported platform includes Lonestar at TACC, with 1460 nodes and 5840 computing cores.
supporting_quote: The river network routing model is coded in FORTRAN 90 using the Portable, Extensible Toolkit for Scientific Computation (PETSc)
Lonestar has a total of 5840 computing cores.

chunks.text: Flow wave travel times and celerities were estimated for 11 pairs of consecutive gauges in the Guadalupe and San Antonio basins using 15-min data. Travel times ranged from 0 s (too fast to resolve at 15-min sampling) to over 162 000 s, and corresponding average celerities varied substantially across subbasins. These estimates provided spatially varying celerity inputs for reach-parameter construction.
supporting_quote: Travel times are estimated for 11 sets of two stations and are shown on Table 1. Travel times of 0 s are reported at two stations
The wave celerity has been estimated for 11 subbasins within the Guadalupe and San Antonio River basins.

chunks.text: Calibration using uniform celerity c0=0.28 m s−1 yielded optimized multipliers λkα=0.131042 and λxα=2.58128 for parameter set (kα, xα). A separate optimization using observed subbasin celerities gave λkγ=0.617188 and λxγ=1.95898 for (kγ, xγ). These values define basin-wide scaling applied to reach lengths and celerities to construct reach-level k values.

The γ-optimization indicated the best-fit k values were 38% smaller than those derived directly from IDA celerities, implying faster effective routing improved discharge fit. The paper interprets this as a mismatch between runoff timing/location and routing, rather than purely channel-wave physics. It signals that correcting runoff generation and delivery may be necessary for consistent celerity and hydrograph skill.
supporting_quote: The optimization converges to a value of k that is 38% smaller than that estimated with the IDA lagged cross-correlation
This suggests that runoff is either produced too slowly or too far upstream of each gauge

chunks.text: A 15-min routing time step (Δt=900 s) was selected based on typical reach length and observed celerities, while also matching an integer subdivision of the 3-hour land-surface runoff interval. Using the median reach length 2.4 km and c≈2.5 m s−1, the derived Δt was near 960 s; 900 s was chosen for compatibility. This timestep underpins the RAPID simulations over 2004–2007.
supporting_quote: Using the median value of the reach length along with c=2.5 m s−1, Eq. (20) gives Δt=960 s.
To have an integer conversion between the river routing time step and the land surface model time step (3 h), a value of Δt=900 s=15 min is chosen.

chunks.text: Compared to a lumped scheme that accumulates Noah runoff at gauges without routing, RAPID routing reduced RMSE and increased Nash efficiency for parameter sets (kα,xα), (kβ,xβ), and (kγ,xγ). The paper notes mass conservation within RAPID because average flows match the lumped approach (routing changes timing/shape, not volume). These improvements demonstrate benefit of explicit routing over direct accumulation.
supporting_quote: RAPID simulations (kα, xα), (kβ, xβ), and (kγ, xγ) lead to a smaller RMSE and a higher Nash efficiency than the lumped runoff.
mass is conserved within RAPID since the flow rates in the lumped simulation and in all four simulations of RAPID are the same.

chunks.text: Model-data comparisons showed strong spatial bias patterns in runoff-derived flows: observed-to-lumped flow ratios were near 1 downstream but exceeded 7 upstream at several gauges. Two spring-fed rivers just downstream of the Edwards Aquifer outcrop (Comal and San Marcos) had much larger observed flows than simulated runoff. This indicates major missing groundwater contributions and spatially varying runoff errors.
supporting_quote: This ratio is around unity downstream of the Guadalupe and San Antonio Rivers but is greater than seven upstream
the Comal River at New Braunfels and the San Marcos River at San Marcos... measure large average streamflow... These flows are much larger than the lumped runoff

chunks.text: Celerities computed from RAPID outputs were generally faster than observed for the first three parameter sets, consistent with Muskingum celerity dependence on x and Δt/L. Even when using observed celerities to define kβ, simulated celerities differed, and the average ratio of simulated-to-observed celerity for (kβ,xβ) was 1.54. This motivated an adjusted parameter set δ to better match observed propagation speeds.
supporting_quote: in the first three sets of model parameters used, the wave celerities simulated in RAPID are greater than those observed.
The ratio of the average celerities from RAPID using (kβ, xβ) over the average observed celerities is 1.54.

chunks.text: The δ parameter set used λkδ=1.54 and λxδ=1 to compensate for overly fast simulated waves and achieved average celerity within 3% of IDA estimates. However, this closer celerity match reduced overall discharge skill, decreasing RMSE/Nash performance relative to other parameter sets. The trade-off suggests timing corrections in routing alone cannot resolve hydrograph errors tied to runoff generation.
supporting_quote: The average flow wave celerity over the 11 calculations in RAPID is within 3% of that estimated with IDA flows. Unfortunately, these closer wave celerities also lead to a decrease in the quality of RMSE and Nash efficiency.

chunks.text: Wilcoxon signed-rank matched-pair tests across 15 gauges indicated improvements from routing were statistically significant. For example, lumped runoff vs RAPID (kα,xα) had one-sided p≈0.0615 for efficiency and p≈0.0897 for RMSE when testing improvement direction. In contrast, RAPID (kγ,xγ) vs (kδ,xδ) showed significant deterioration with p≈0.0212 (efficiency) and p≈0.0261 (RMSE).
supporting_quote: The Wilcoxon signed-rank test... motivate the use of the Wilcoxon signed-rank test in the study herein.
RAPID (k^{γ}, x^{γ}) | RAPID (k^{δ}, x^{δ}) ... p value ... 0.021 24
RAPID (k^{γ}, x^{γ}) | RAPID (k^{δ}, x^{δ}) ... p value ... 0.026 12

chunks.text: In the upper Mississippi synthetic performance test, the matrix-based Muskingum approach had higher overhead on one core but achieved speedup with multiple cores using an iterative solver. The paper reports that on 16 cores, the matrix method’s total computing time was almost one-third of the traditional Muskingum method, while producing byte-for-byte identical outputs. The number of iterations increased slowly with core count, enabling net gains despite solver overhead.
supporting_quote: On one processing core... solving the matrix-based Muskingum method... is about twice as long as solving the traditional Muskingum method
Figure 12 shows that the total computing time with an iterative matrix solver on 16 processing cores is almost a third of the time needed by the traditional Muskingum method
The output files match on a byte-to-byte basis

chunks.text: The coupling scheme assumes lateral inflow Qe is constant over all 15-min routing steps within each 3-hour land-surface output interval. This simplifies input requirements and coupling but is only valid except near the end of an interval before new runoff is provided. Such temporal uniformity can affect hydrograph timing around runoff updates.
supporting_quote: Qe is assumed constant [i.e., Qe(t+Δt)=Qe(t)] over all 15-min river routing time steps included within a given land surface model 3-h time step.
This assumption is valid at all times except at the last routing time steps before a new Qe is made available

chunks.text: The flux coupler does not model horizontal routing from land surface cells to the river reach; it simply aggregates grid runoff over each catchment. The authors note this differs from schemes that use 2D wave routing or linear reservoirs to move water to channels. Missing hillslope-to-channel travel time and pathways may contribute to the need for artificially fast river celerities during calibration.
supporting_quote: Therefore, no horizontal routing is used between the land surface and the river network in the proposed scheme.
This differs from some other models... the two-dimensional wave equation is used... or the linear reservoir equation is used

chunks.text: RAPID’s current divergence handling routes all upstream flow into a single “major” branch, while minor divergences receive only lateral inflow. This can misrepresent real flow splits where multiple downstream branches carry fractions of upstream discharge. The formulation could be extended if split fractions are available, but they are not used here.
supporting_quote: a unique reach (the major divergence) is used to carry all the upstream flow, and the other reaches (minor divergences) carry only the flow that results from their lateral inflow.
This formulation could be modified to take into account given fractions of flows that separate into different parts of a divergence

chunks.text: Simulated celerities and discharge-skill metrics could not be simultaneously optimized: matching observed celerities more closely (parameter set δ) reduced RMSE and Nash efficiency. The authors suggest this inconsistency likely arises because runoff is produced too slowly or too far upstream in the land surface model/coupling configuration. Thus routing parameter tuning may compensate for runoff errors rather than represent true channel physics.
supporting_quote: wave celerities closer to those estimated from gauge data generally deteriorate the other statistics of calculations.
This suggests that runoff is either produced too slowly or too far upstream of each gauge

chunks.text: The study constrains calibration to only two basin-wide multipliers (λk, λx), and treats x as constant over the basin to reduce cost. While practical, this limits spatial variability of parameters and may miss local hydraulic differences. The authors note that NHDPlus attributes (slope, velocity, mean flow) and subbasin optimization could improve parameter realism at larger scales.
supporting_quote: the search for optimal parameters is limited to determining two multiplying factors λ_k and λ_x
as a first step— x is here constant over a given basin
Some data available in NHDPlus (such as mean flow, mean velocity, slope, etc.)... could be used to improve the proposed method.

chunks.text: In parallel runs with many cores, residual-norm calculations within the iterative solver become a substantial fraction of solve time due to communication overhead. The paper observes this can reach nearly half of solving time at higher core counts, limiting further speedup. It anticipates this bottleneck may diminish with faster interconnects and improved communication performance.
supporting_quote: as the number of cores increase, the relative importance of the computation of residual norms within the iterative solver increases up to taking almost half of the solving time
This limitation will most likely disappear as computer technology advances and communication time decreases.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that NHDPlus connectivity and NWIS gauges enable nationwide-style river routing and assessment across many interior locations. RAPID’s matrix-based Muskingum formulation can compute flow and volume across thousands of reaches, including ungauged sites, while conserving mass. Using distributed gauges for optimization improves routing outcomes relative to lumped runoff accumulation.
supporting_quote: NHDPlus... connectivity information for the river networks is available.
It has been shown that a GIS-based hydrographic dataset can be used as the river network for a river model to compute flow in large networks of thousands of reaches, including ungauged locations.
RAPID produces better RMSE and Nash efficiency than the lumped model, and the improvements are statistically significant.

chunks.text: The study finds that better matching observed wave celerities does not necessarily improve discharge error statistics, likely because runoff timing/location errors dominate. This highlights the diagnostic role of routing with interior gauges: inconsistencies between celerity reproduction and RMSE/Nash can point to deficiencies in runoff generation and missing groundwater contributions.
supporting_quote: wave celerities closer to those estimated from gauge data generally deteriorate the other statistics of calculations.
This deterioration might be due to runoff being produced too slowly or too far upstream of each gauge.

chunks.text: For large, interconnected basins, the matrix-based routing with an iterative solver can achieve meaningful parallel speedup while producing identical results to traditional Muskingum routing. The paper reports that overhead diminishes with more processing cores and that distant subbasins can be effectively decoupled within one timestep. This supports feasibility of scaling toward very large domains such as the contiguous United States with millions of reaches.
supporting_quote: the matrix-based Muskingum method decreases the total computing time when run on several processing cores.
Figure 12 shows that the total computing time with an iterative matrix solver on 16 processing cores is almost a third of the time needed by the traditional Muskingum method
the entire contiguous United States... would represent a square matrix of the size of 3 million.

chunks.text: Emergency risk communication affects downstream public health system burden. Organizations issuing warnings must recommend different actions to different audiences on tight timelines and with uncertainty, and messages can be hard to translate into plain language. When communication fails, the consequences include injuries, loss of life, and longer-term mental and physical health challenges after the emergency.
supporting_quote: The success or failure of those communication efforts can affect patient volume at emergency medicine departments and workload for community health workers
Ineffective emergency health risk communication can result in significant burdens on human health, including acute injuries, loss of life, and mental and physical health challenges post-emergency.

chunks.text: Flooding is an increasingly important context for emergency communication because climate change is intensifying extreme weather. Flood risk is rising faster than household preparedness, producing high costs and health harms. The paper frames floods as both a financial and public health threat that warrants improved communication approaches.
supporting_quote: Climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, including floods (1,2).
Flood risk is increasing faster than household preparedness for flooding, resulting in higher costs when floods occur, and demonstrating a need for better flood risk communication (3,4).

chunks.text: Flood impacts are widespread globally and include substantial mortality. The paper cites disaster statistics to emphasize scale and urgency, positioning floods as a leading natural disaster type affecting tens of millions. This context supports the need to strengthen community-level flood risk communication.
supporting_quote: Globally in 2019, floods accounted for nearly half of all natural disasters, affected around 31 million people, and were responsible for 5,055 deaths (7).
In addition to financial costs, threats to human health from floods are also notable (6).

chunks.text: The paper aims to translate evidence-driven health risk communication principles to the flood context. It reviews relevant health communication insights and discusses how those insights can improve flood risk communication practices. The intent is to provide actionable considerations for warning design and delivery in communities facing flood threats.
supporting_quote: Here we review evidence-driven health risk communication insights in existing literature and discuss how they may apply to flood risk communication.
Flood risk communication, like other emergency communication, can prevent injuries and the loss of life.

chunks.text: A secondary goal is to inform implementation of NOAA flood warning tools by understanding how information moves within communities. The paper describes an ongoing interdisciplinary project working with six U.S. communities to map formal and informal communication channels. Outputs are intended to support adoption and effectiveness of Flood Inundation Mapping (FIM).
supporting_quote: The team is working with six communities in the United States with relatively recent flood experience to understand how flood communication moves within communities
the findings from this research will support the implementation of National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)'s newest flood warning technology, Flood Inundation Mapping (FIM)

chunks.text: Emergency preparedness officials must communicate complex and sometimes competing recommendations to varied audiences under time pressure and uncertainty. Those constraints make it hard to produce understandable messages quickly, increasing the risk that people misunderstand what to do. The paper frames this as a core communication challenge with direct health consequences.
supporting_quote: must offer recommendations about a range of actions (e.g., evacuate your area vs. find shelter where you are) to various audiences
with sensitive timelines, fluctuating certainty, and messages that are difficult to communicate in plain language.

chunks.text: Flood risk communication research has gaps in explaining what actually motivates preparedness and whether households can carry out recommended actions. Context can change motivating factors, and capability constraints may prevent action even when intent exists. The paper uses this uncertainty to justify leveraging established health risk communication best practices.
supporting_quote: there is limited clarity on what motivates preparedness behaviors, how context changes motivating factors, and whether households can perform behaviors even if they want to do so (3).
demonstrating a need for better flood risk communication (3,4).

chunks.text: During threatening flood situations, negative emotions and uncertainty can distort information processing and increase vulnerability to misinformation. The paper notes that anxious people may seek information and become more likely to believe what they encounter regardless of source, even if incorrect. This creates a need to deliver accurate information directly and design warnings that anticipate emotional states.
supporting_quote: When a person is anxious, for example, they can question existing beliefs, look for information, and be more likely to believe information they encounter in the moment regardless of source, even if it is incorrect (10).
audience members are likely to experience emotions with a negative valence

chunks.text: Social vulnerability and structural inequities complicate flood communication because high-exposure groups may have fewer resources to respond and less access to information. The paper highlights that socioeconomic disparities and structural racism in housing can increase injury risk and extend recovery. As climate change worsens disproportionate impacts, messaging must account for intersectional constraints beyond individual choice.
supporting_quote: people experiencing socioeconomic disparities are more likely to live in flood prone areas (2).
these groups also face structural racism in housing and have fewer resources to respond to floods, which increases likelihood of injury and extends recovery timelines (2,22).

chunks.text: The paper uses a narrative review approach, drawing on health risk communication literature to extract practical insights and then discussing their application to flood risk communication. Rather than presenting a single experiment, it synthesizes evidence about emotions, credibility, mental models, and group differences. The goal is to adapt these established concepts to community flood warnings and preparedness messaging.
supporting_quote: Here we review evidence-driven health risk communication insights in existing literature and discuss how they may apply to flood risk communication.
By taking into account audience emotions, perceptions of source credibility, audience past experiences, and potential group differences, communicators can optimize future message design and delivery.

chunks.text: As an application example, the authors describe an interdisciplinary project studying within-community flow of flood warnings. The team is engaging six U.S. communities with recent flood experience to understand formal and informal networks that shape whether people receive and share warning information. Findings are intended to guide message design/placement and improve adoption of NOAA Flood Inundation Mapping (FIM).
supporting_quote: partnering on a new project that focuses on flood risk communication, bringing together an interdisciplinary team including contributors with expertise in communication research, design thinking, economics, hydrology
working with six communities in the United States with relatively recent flood experience to understand how flood communication moves within communities

chunks.text: The paper recommends that message testing for flood warnings should account for heightened emotional conditions similar to real events. It suggests either conducting testing in environments that mimic stress or prompting participants to reflect on how they respond when emotions are elevated. This methodological recommendation is tied to evidence that anxiety and other emotions alter how people evaluate and remember risk information.
supporting_quote: Message testing research to develop warnings should either occur in conditions which mimic the stress audiences will face when an actual flood is looming
or should at least ask participants to reflect on how they respond in situations of heightened emotion.

chunks.text: The paper provides global burden figures to contextualize flood risk as a major disaster and public health concern. It reports that in 2019 floods represented nearly half of natural disasters, affected around 31 million people, and caused 5,055 deaths. These statistics function as descriptive evidence supporting the need for better flood risk communication and preparedness.
supporting_quote: Globally in 2019, floods accounted for nearly half of all natural disasters, affected around 31 million people, and were responsible for 5,055 deaths (7).

chunks.text: Emotions shape how people process flood risk information, affecting attention, counterarguing, avoidance, and memory. The paper highlights that anxiety linked to uncertainty and lack of control can make people more receptive to information they encounter, even if incorrect. This implies flood communicators should anticipate emotion-driven processing and deliver clear, accurate guidance with actionable steps.
supporting_quote: Emotional response can affect the way in which information is processed.
When a person is anxious... be more likely to believe information they encounter in the moment regardless of source, even if it is incorrect (10).

chunks.text: Perceived source credibility and trust influence whether people accept messages and follow recommended behaviors. Evidence summarized in the paper indicates trust is strengthened when audiences perceive shared interests with the messenger, and that local sources are often most trusted. For flood communication, this supports involving local partners who can credibly signal alignment with community social and economic interests.
supporting_quote: Messenger credibility and perceived trust can affect whether audience members believe a health-related message and whether they complete the message's recommended action
their likelihood of adhering to requested public health behaviors was specifically linked to whether the participants perceived shared interests with the source of health information (12).

chunks.text: People may rely on convenient and familiar sources even when those sources are not the most trustworthy, which can shape disaster information exposure. The paper notes that family, friends, neighbors, and television are often used regardless of trust levels, while more trusted sources (e.g., local fire departments) may be harder to access. It also reports that interactive sources and maps are viewed as useful/trustworthy, suggesting design opportunities for flood warnings that enable questions and location-specific exploration.
supporting_quote: People reported frequently using convenient or familiar sources of information such as family/friends/neighbors or television, regardless of trustworthiness levels
Participants tended to report that interactive sources were the most useful or trustworthy to them
Maps were the second most used information source; participants also tended to view maps as both useful and trustworthy

chunks.text: Audience mental models based on past experiences can help or hinder understanding of new risks. The paper describes how people interpret new threats by comparing them to familiar ones, which can obscure novel features and lead to faulty assumptions. In flood contexts, communicators can use analogies for first-time flood areas while emphasizing what is new (e.g., higher projected water levels) in historically flood-prone communities.
supporting_quote: What individuals hold in mind about past experiences can shape their perceptions of new risks
Their existing mental models... were in some ways helpful... but in other ways harmful
risk communication should emphasize what is new (e.g., underscore how much higher water levels are projected to be than previous floods).

chunks.text: Group differences in cognitive ability and numeracy affect how risk information is processed and recalled, with implications for equitable warning design. The paper reports that numeric risk presentations can yield higher knowledge gain for general audiences and that combining numeric and non-numeric formats is likely best practice, while highly numerate groups are less sensitive to format. It also argues that reducing complexity and using plain language benefits everyone and is essential for equity, particularly for older adults and lower-literacy groups.
supporting_quote: studies showed that presenting risk information numerically was more effective (e.g., higher knowledge gain) than presenting non-numerically, and that presenting in both numeric and non-numeric form is likely best practice (18).
Reducing message complexity (e.g., using plain language) benefits all audiences by increasing comprehension and is essential to ensure equity across audiences

chunks.text: The paper emphasizes that existing flood risk communication research does not yet clearly explain motivations and feasibility of preparedness behaviors across contexts. This limits the ability to design universally effective messages and highlights the need to draw from health communication evidence while filling flood-specific gaps. The authors position this uncertainty as a rationale for more targeted, context-aware research and message development.

chunks.text: The workflow has three parts: flood susceptibility assessment, social vulnerability assessment, and flood risk assessment. Flood susceptibility is modeled using Random Forest classification with flood inventory points as the target and 12 conditioning factors as predictors. Social vulnerability is computed as a PCA-derived SoVI at the census-tract scale. Flood risk is then computed by multiplying normalized SoVI with the flood susceptibility index to form a flood risk index and map.

chunks.text: The flood inventory map is created using Hurricane Harvey (August 2017) inundation information derived from Sentinel-1 SAR processing, plus ground-truthing with a flood fatality dataset and confirmation using NOAA storm events. The SAR workflow includes spatial filtering to reduce noise, a division band-ratio using pre- and post-flood images, and masking permanent water using the Global Surface Water dataset. The final inventory includes 250 flood points and 250 non-flood points.

These include elevation, slope, aspect, curvature, TWI, SPI, precipitation, LULC, distance to rivers, NDVI, drainage density, and soil texture. The flood susceptibility index produced by the model is categorized into five equal-interval classes from very low (0–0.2) to very high (0.8–1.0).

chunks.text: Random Forest modeling is implemented in Python (Jupyter Notebook) using scikit-learn. The 500-point inventory dataset is split into 70% training and 30% testing using train_test_split. Hyperparameter tuning yields n_estimators=700, criterion=gini, and max_features=log2. Model outputs include feature importance ranking and pixel-wise flood susceptibility probabilities via predict_proba.

chunks.text: Social vulnerability is computed using PCA following Cutter et al. (2003) with ten census-tract variables. Variables are standardized using Z-scores and PCA is run with varimax rotation (100 iterations). Three components with eigenvalues greater than 1 are retained and then combined into a weighted SoVI using weights based on the ratio of variance explained. The resulting SoVI is classified into five categories using natural breaks.
supporting_quote: This study adopts a widely recognized formula developed by Cutter et al. (2003) to map social vulnerability... known as PCA.

chunks.text: Flood risk mapping aligns susceptibility and vulnerability by normalizing SoVI to 0–1 using Min–Max normalization, converting SoVI polygons to raster, and matching spatial resolution with the FSM. The flood risk index is defined as FRI = SoVI × FSI, producing values from 0 to 0.79. The flood risk map is classified into five categories with natural breaks: very low (0–0.07) through very high (0.28–0.79).

chunks.text: Floodplains can reduce flood peaks by storing water and extracting momentum, but their effects are often simplified or omitted in broad-scale routing models. Prior work shows floodplain geomorphology and slope can materially change storage and peak attenuation. Growing availability of high-resolution topography enables automated extraction of features that may better represent hydraulically meaningful floodplain effects at scale.

chunks.text: The study frames a strong linkage between floodplain form and hydraulic function, motivating classification approaches that generalize behavior across landscapes. Existing floodplain classifications commonly emphasize formative processes rather than explicit hydraulic impacts on routing. The paper positions mesoscale topographic features as a missing bridge between floodplain mapping and flood-routing functionality.
supporting_quote: Physical characteristics of the floodplain are important for describing variability in floodwater routing, suggesting a strong linkage between floodplain form and hydraulic functioning.

existing floodplain classifications are largely focused on formational processes ... leaving a need for approaches that better define floodplain impacts, notably their influence on surface water hydraulics and flood routing.

chunks.text: The Lake Champlain Basin provides a diverse physiographic setting with confined mountain valleys and expansive lowland floodplains. Floodplain presence varies from absent or discontinuous in steep headwaters to more continuous unconfined lowlands. This variability is leveraged to test whether topographic feature extraction can distinguish hydraulically distinct floodplain settings.

In the region's mountainous terrain, floodplains are either absent or present in pockets separated by intervening, more confined reaches
to lower‐grade alluvial channels unconfined by valley walls in the lowlands where floodplains are more continuous and laterally expansive.

chunks.text: The paper’s objective is to identify broad-scale patterns in floodplain characteristics that matter for flood routing. It seeks to use high-resolution topography to derive reach-scale features, group reaches into hydraulically distinct types, and test whether those types show different routing behavior. The work aims to support improved routing representation in continental-scale models and practical floodplain management.
supporting_quote: The objective of this paper is to identify broad‐scale patterns in floodplain characteristics important for understanding flood routing.
we leverage broadly available high‐resolution topographic data sets to identify hydraulically distinct floodplains from reach‐scale topographic features.

chunks.text: A central goal is to define and characterize an “Energy Dissipation Zone” (EDZ) hypothesized to disproportionately dissipate energy and attenuate floodwaters. The authors propose that EDZ size and shape, derived from reach-averaged hydraulic geometry signals, can act as a proxy for routing behavior. They evaluate this hypothesis by comparing celerity and synthetic-hydrograph attenuation across EDZ-based reach clusters.
supporting_quote: hypothesized to define and characterize a zone within the floodplain that disproportionately dissipates energy and attenuates floodwaters, called the Energy Dissipation Zone.
The size and shape of such zones, we assert, may be used as a proxy for the routing behavior of that reach.

chunks.text: Broad-scale flood prediction remains difficult because flood wave dynamics are not adequately captured in many models. Floodplains influence routing but are often represented in simplified ways that cannot express spatial variability in confinement, geometry, and connectivity. Coarse-resolution floodplain mapping methods can miss smaller-river floodplains and omit topographic details important for routing.
supporting_quote: accurate assessments from broad‐scale water resources and hazard models are extraordinarily challenging to develop, in part because flood wave dynamics are not adequately captured
floodplain representation in broad‐scale flood routing models is typically limited or highly simplified

chunks.text: Existing floodplain and river classifications do not explicitly focus on the hydraulic impacts of floodplains on flood routing, creating a gap for operational and management use. The authors argue for a classification that reflects landscape potential to influence flood hydraulics rather than only geomorphic formation. This motivates an automated, repeatable workflow that can be used across broad regions.
supporting_quote: existing floodplain classifications are largely focused on formational processes ... leaving a need for approaches that better define floodplain impacts, notably their influence on surface water hydraulics and flood routing.
The objective of this paper is to identify broad‐scale patterns in floodplain characteristics important for understanding flood routing.

chunks.text: The workflow extracts reach-averaged hydraulic-geometry metrics from 1-m HAND rasters to detect zones of inefficient conveyance. For each reach, inundated area, volume, wetted area, and hydraulic radius are computed across 1,000 stages from 0 to 6× bankfull depth. Reach-averaged cross sections are derived by dividing area and volume by reach length, and stage is normalized by regression bankfull depth to compare shapes across catchments.
supporting_quote: we developed a fully automated workflow to extract topographic features from high‐resolution
were calculated at 1,000 stages (s) equally spaced between 0 and 6 times the bankfull depth
Reach‐averaged cross‐sectional data were then generated by dividing As and Vs by reach length

chunks.text: To address missing below-water topography in LiDAR DEMs, the authors impute a simple trapezoidal channel into the reach-averaged cross-section. The imputed top width uses the reach-average width at HAND stage 0.015 m, and the bottom width is the minimum of a bankfull-width regression or the imputed top width. Channel depth is computed to convey an estimated discharge via Manning’s equation and capped at two-times bankfull depth.
supporting_quote: Because the LiDAR‐derived DEMs used in our workflow did not incorporate below‐water topography
we imputed a simple trapezoidal channel into the reach‐averaged cross‐section.
To limit unreasonable channel depths, the depth was capped at two‐times the bankfull depth estimate

chunks.text: The Energy Dissipation Zone (EDZ) is identified from departures in hydraulic-radius behavior with stage. The first derivative of hydraulic radius with respect to stage (Rh′) is used, and an EDZ is defined where the Rh′ curve “deflected and remained left of 0.5”. If multiple candidate stage ranges exist, the zone with the largest diagnostic size (Rh′area) is selected; if Rh′ never falls below 0.5, no EDZ is identified.
supporting_quote: We took the first derivative of Rh with respect to s (Rh′)
The EDZ was defined by the range of normalized stages where the Rh′ curve deflected and remained left of 0.5 (m/m)
If there were multiple stage ranges that met the definition of an EDZ, we selected the zone with the largest diagnostic size (Rh'area)

chunks.text: Seven EDZ features quantify the size and shape of hydraulically effective floodplain zones. These include access and exit stages (EDZaccess, EDZexit), stage range (EDZht), EDZ width at exit (EDZw), relative width (EDZw,rel), minimum Rh′ (Rh′min) as an indicator of lateral expansion rate, and diagnostic size (Rh′area) as area between the Rh′ curve and the 0.5 threshold.
supporting_quote: we defined seven features that described the size and shape of the EDZ (Table 2)
These features included the normalized stage of the energy dissipation access and exit points (EDZaccess and EDZexit
Finally, we used the area of the deflection as a diagnostic of the size of the EDZ ... (Rh'area)

chunks.text: Reaches were filtered to separate non-riverine or minimally attenuating settings prior to clustering. Waterbody reaches were tagged when >5% of reach length intersected a waterbody polygon >0.05 km2. Additional reaches were pre-sorted as “non-attenuating” when EDZw,rel < 1.5 or slope > 0.003 m/m, based on expected routing behavior and preliminary attenuation experiments.
supporting_quote: Reaches with more than 5% of their length intersecting an NHDPlus‐HR waterbody ... polygon of more than 0.05 km2 were tagged as a "waterbody" reach.
Reaches with EDZw,rel less than 1.5, or slope greater than 0.003 m/m were separated ... as assumed "non‐attenuating" segments.

chunks.text: Hydraulically similar floodplain reaches were grouped using K-medoids clustering on the seven EDZ features. Skewed features were log-transformed, and all features were standardized to zero mean and unit variance. Because silhouette and Calinski-Harabasz suggested only two clusters, the final choice used visual evaluation of Rh′ curve spread and medoid cross-sections, resulting in six clusters for floodplain settings.
supporting_quote: We used the KMedoids clustering algorithm
Feature sets with a sample skew greater than 1.5 were log transformed
We varied the cluster count from three to 12 ... Six clusters yielded groups with relatively even spread of member counts

chunks.text: Routing relevance was evaluated via celerity metrics and Muskingum–Cunge routing of synthetic hydrographs. Kinematic celerity was computed as a function of stage assuming Manning flow, and a “shape celerity” variant removed slope effects. Flood peak attenuation was estimated by routing synthetic hydrographs representing four AEP magnitudes (50%, 10%, 2%, 1%) and three durations, and attenuation was reported per kilometer in absolute and percent terms.

we performed a routing assessment ... using the Muskingum-Cunge (MC) model
represents the cartesian product of four peak discharges (50%, 10%, 2%, and 1% AEP) and three durations (short, medium, and long).

chunks.text: The analysis uses 1-m LiDAR-derived, hydro-enforced DEMs to create HAND maps for the Lake Champlain Basin. The DEMs have QL2 rating with vertical accuracy at least 9.25 cm, and HAND values provide a proxy for stage relative to the nearest drainage. These inputs enable reach-scale hydraulic geometry extraction from topography without field surveys.

chunks.text: River reaches are based on the NHDPlus High-Resolution network and were modified by merging short reaches (<1 km) downstream to reduce geometric errors from sparse raster cells. The final network includes 2,629 reaches spanning 4,131 km. Reach attributes include drainage area, stream order, and recalculated slope with a minimum enforced slope of 0.00001 m/m.
supporting_quote: We defined river reaches based on the NHDPlus High‐Resolution network (NHDPlus‐HR)
merge short reaches (length < 1 km) with the next downstream reach
In total, we analyzed 2,629 reaches over a 4,131 km river network

chunks.text: Floodplain and valley widths were estimated using a HAND–Synthetic Rating Curve approach across AEP floods, with the 1% AEP extent used as floodplain width and the 0.2% AEP extent used as valley width. Valley confinement was computed as valley width relative to an estimated bankfull channel width from regional regressions. These derived widths contextualize EDZ footprints against mapped inundation extents.
supporting_quote: We defined the floodplain width for this study as the extent of the 1% AEP floodplain and used the broadest mapped extent (0.2% AEP floodplain) to define the valley width.
Valley confinement ... was then estimated for each reach by dividing 0.2% AEP by an estimate of bankfull channel width

chunks.text: Synthetic routing experiments used design hydrographs built from regional regressions of peak discharge and duration, scaled by drainage area. Peak magnitudes correspond to 50%, 10%, 2%, and 1% AEP, and durations are short, medium, and long. Hydrograph ordinates were generated with the Soil Conservation Service dimensionless unit hydrograph approach.
supporting_quote: suite of design hydrographs ... represents the cartesian product of four peak discharges (50%, 10%, 2%, and 1% AEP) and three durations (short, medium, and long).
Peak discharge and time to peak were converted to hydrograph ordinates using the Soil Conservation Service dimensionless unit hydrograph approach

chunks.text: After removing reaches with geometric errors, most reaches were pre-sorted as waterbody or non-attenuating, and the remainder formed six floodplain clusters. Specifically, 84 reaches (3%) were removed due to geometric errors; 210 (8%) were classified as waterbody (W); and 1,596 (61%) were classified as non-attenuating (X) based on slope and EDZw,rel. The remaining 739 reaches (28%) were clustered into six floodplain settings (I–VI) showing distinct Rh′ deflection patterns.

Cluster I had small EDZs and higher Rh′min, indicating narrow, gradually expanding floodplains on smaller, steeper rivers (median drainage area 24 km²; median slope 0.001 m/m). Cluster V had the widest EDZ footprint (high EDZw and EDZw,rel) and often occurred on larger rivers (median drainage area 230 km²). Shape celerity ranged from 0.04 to 9.1 m2/3 (median 0.5 m2/3) and was better explained by Rh′area (R2 = 0.35) than celerity was (R2 = 0.03), supporting its use to isolate topographic effects.

chunks.text: Synthetic hydrograph routing showed attenuation is greatest for smaller, shorter floods and declines with magnitude and duration. Some reaches attenuated strongly (e.g., 84% during a medium duration 50% AEP flood), but many had little attenuation. For a medium-duration 50% AEP flood, 22% of all reaches and 50% of floodplain-cluster reaches attenuated peak flow by more than 1% per km. About 10% of reaches showed amplification, more pronounced during larger floods.

Percent attenuation per kilometer tended to be largest on small drainage areas, while absolute attenuation in m3/s was largest on large drainage areas, indicating scale effects in how attenuation is expressed.

chunks.text: Floodplain clusters differed in routing behavior, supporting that EDZ-derived classes capture hydraulically meaningful variability. Cluster X (steep/confined) had the greatest kinematic celerity and negligible attenuation. Clusters V and VI showed the greatest attenuation and lowest celerity; in cluster V, larger EDZ footprints offset higher slopes, while cluster VI benefited from very low gradients. Clusters II and III had the lowest attenuation among floodplain clusters, linked to high slopes and/or small EDZ stage-range and very low EDZw,rel.

chunks.text: The authors propose a Hydraulic Floodplain Classification that ties clusters to expected routing effect classes. The scheme includes Negligible Attenuation Effect (X), Limited Attenuation Effect (II, III), Moderate Attenuation Effect (I), Large Attenuation Effect (IV, V, VI), and a Waterbody class (W). Subclasses are differentiated by EDZ access stage and EDZ footprint measures, and each class is associated with typical watershed locations and valley settings.

Negligible Attenuation Effect ... Cluster X

chunks.text: The EDZ is interpreted as a hydraulically effective subset of the floodplain that may be narrower than mapped inundation extents. The EDZ footprint is often contained within the 1% AEP floodplain, but its bounds reflect how width changes relative to depth as stage rises, not simply inundation area. Thus, EDZ delineation emphasizes routing-relevant conveyance transitions rather than the full hydraulic floodplain extent.
supporting_quote: We interpret these EDZs to be part of the hydraulically defined floodplain.
the footprint of the EDZ is highly correlated with the floodplain defined by inundation extents
the EDZ highlights the hydraulically relevant subset of the floodplain that is important for flood routing.

chunks.text: Topography alone cannot fully determine attenuation because roughness, slope, hydrograph shape, and smaller-scale floodplain features also matter. The authors used constant roughness and synthetic hydrographs to isolate topographic effects, but acknowledge covariation among drainage area, slope, and topography that confounds interpretation. They note that natural and human features such as vegetation and floodplain channel networks can alter velocities, storage, and residence times beyond what reach-averaged geometry captures.
supporting_quote: Other factors also have a significant impact on flood wave attenuation, including the nature of the hydrograph, slope, roughness elements (e.g., vegetation)
we took steps to remove the influence of roughness and down-valley slope
topography, slope, and even hydrologic regime naturally covary across the landscape

chunks.text: The routing evaluation relies on the simplified Muskingum–Cunge framework, which may not capture all floodplain routing dynamics. The authors used MC because it is computationally simple and commonly used in large-scale models, enabling consistent comparison across reaches. They acknowledge that some dynamics sensitive to the topographic features of interest may not be fully realized with this approach.
supporting_quote: We selected the MC routing model because it can be parameterized by reach-average geometry, is able to model hydrograph attenuation
we acknowledge that some of the routing dynamics that may be sensitive to the topographic features of interest are likely not fully realized.

chunks.text: Reach-averaging and the choice of reach delineations can misrepresent floodplain setting transitions. The workflow assumes reach-averaged cross-sections reflect average hydraulic template conditions. However, NHDPlus-HR reaches are hydrologically defined and can span segments with different confinement or slopes; averaging across such transitions can distort classification and routing relevance.
supporting_quote: assumes that the features extracted from a cross‐section reflect the average condition of the setting
NHD reaches are hydrologically defined (e.g., extending between tributary confluences) and often span segments of notably different valley confinement and/or longitudinal slopes.
By averaging these natural transitions in the landscape, such hydrologically based reach delineations may mis‐represent the type of floodplain setting

chunks.text: EDZ access stage may indicate bankfull or incision, but uncertainty in regional regressions and geomorphic complexity complicate interpretation. The authors suggest EDZaccess often occurs near regression-based bankfull, while large deviations may reflect incision, terraces, or reach-averaging of variable bank elevations. They emphasize that EDZaccess variability could also reflect uncertainty in regional hydraulic-geometry regressions.
supporting_quote: The EDZ access point (EDZaccess) ... can be interpreted as an indicator of the geomorphic top of the streambank.
We found that the EDZ access point for many reaches in our study area occurs around the value of bankfull estimated from regression estimates.
some of the variability in EDZaccess may also be a function of the uncertainty associated with regional regressions

chunks.text: The study concludes that reach-scale flood attenuation potential can be resolved from features extracted from high-resolution topography. An EDZ, derived from the stage dependence of hydraulic-radius change, provides a practical signature of hydraulically effective floodplain zones. Clustering EDZ features yielded floodplain types with distinct celerity and attenuation behavior under synthetic routing, motivating a hydraulic floodplain classification for the basin and a pathway to improve broad-scale routing models.
supporting_quote: Riverscape potential for flood attenuation can be resolved at the reach scale by relying on simple features readily extractable from high‐resolution topography.
We derived a reach‐scale signature of the rate‐of‐change in hydraulic radius with progressive inundation depth to define the presence (or absence) of an energy dissipation zone (EDZ).
Unsupervised clustering of these EDZ features revealed a range of floodplain types with variable influence on reach‐average flood wave celerity and flood peak attenuation

chunks.text: The authors emphasize that the workflow is fully automated and requires modest, widely available inputs, enabling rapid regional application and updates after landscape change. They propose that outputs can help prioritize where floodplains are likely most effective for peak reduction and where improved topographic representation would benefit large-scale models. Future work is framed around generating a heterogeneous stream-network layer to guide routing-model improvements.
supporting_quote: The fully automated workflow developed here can be applied quickly across a broad region
The workflow requires modest, and widely available inputs (high‐resolution topography, stream network with reach delineations)
A focus of future research is to generate a heterogeneous stream network layer identifying which reaches (characterized by floodplains) would benefit from improved topography representation

chunks.text: Broad-scale satellite remote sensing is increasingly used for water quality assessment, but most development and testing have focused on large rivers. Smaller rivers comprise most of the river network and can be major sources of sediment and nutrients, making them important targets for monitoring. Optical remote sensing can estimate total suspended solids (TSS) via empirical links between surface reflectance and suspended particle scattering/absorption, but inland waters add complexity from adjacency to land, variability, and atmospheric correction challenges.

The goal was to identify settings and conditions where broad-scale remote sensing could be feasible throughout smaller river networks.

chunks.text: Remote sensing algorithms for TSS face several inland-water-specific error sources. Atmospheric correction over inland water is a major uncertainty, and fluvial systems exhibit rapid temporal changes in discharge, sediment, and organic matter. Moreover, near-bank land reflectance can contaminate water pixels and disturb water-leaving radiance, complicating retrievals in small channels.

chunks.text: The authors interpret better performance on high-background rivers as reflecting finer-grained, wash-load-dominated sediment that is more optically detectable and more vertically mixed, aligning depth-integrated sampling with surface reflectance. Fine particles also reduce bed influence by increasing water-column absorption and decreasing bed detectability.

chunks.text: A key interpretive limitation is that sediment characteristics and river width are confounded in this study area. chunks.text: Flooding causes major social and economic losses, and flood warnings can reduce deaths and property damage. Prior work has improved forecast accuracy and warning lead time, and even modest lead time gains can substantially reduce damages. However, benefits depend on whether people act on warnings, not only on forecast quality. Therefore, understanding warning response is central to realizing the value of improved forecasts.
supporting_quote: Flooding is a common weather disaster in the United States (U.S.) that has caused significant social and economic loss (Smith and Matthews, 2015).
Some studies suggest that as little as 1 h of lead time can reduce flood damages by 10-20%, with potential savings of $1.62 billion annually in the U.S.

chunks.text: Flood warning systems involve forecasting, monitoring and warning, dissemination, and public preparedness and response. Their effectiveness is rooted not only in forecast accuracy and lead time but also in how the public interprets risk and translates it into action. Technology has enabled more reliable and timely information and longer planning horizons. Yet reliable warnings provide little benefit if actions do not follow.
supporting_quote: Flood warning systems... are composed of (1) knowledge-based modeling and forecasting of flooding; (2) a monitoring and warning system; (3) an information dissemination system; and (4) public preparedness and response.
improvements in these areas do not in themselves reduce risk in disaster situations as reliable and timely warnings do little good if not followed by (early) actions.

chunks.text: Agent-based modeling is presented as suitable for representing complex, interconnected human communities where individuals have heterogeneous attributes and adaptive decision rules. Traditional top-down approaches struggle with such dynamic feedbacks. With improved computing, agent-based models have been widely applied to human-environment and disaster contexts. This motivates using ABM to simulate flood warning-response and evacuation behavior.
supporting_quote: Agent-based modeling has often been suggested as an appropriate solution to this kind of problem for capturing the dynamic feedback of subsystem components and their inherent complexities
agent-based modeling takes a bottom-up approach in which each system component is simulated as an autonomous, interdependent, and adaptive agent with heterogeneous attributes and decision rules

chunks.text: The study proposes an agent-based modeling framework to incorporate human behavioral heterogeneity into flood warning-response systems. Its objective is to test the hypothesis that the benefits of flood warnings vary with heterogeneous responses to warnings. The work also explores how residential density of flood zones relates to warning benefits. The intent is to inform evacuation planning priorities and improve warning system effectiveness for specific communities.
supporting_quote: This study proposes an agent-based modeling framework to incorporate human behavioral heterogeneity into flood warning-response systems.

The objective is to test the hypothesis that the benefits of flood warnings will vary depending on heterogeneous responses to flood warnings. Furthermore, this study also explores the relationships between the benefits of flood warnings and residential density (RD) of flood zones.

chunks.text: A central aim is to understand the marginal benefit of providing more accurate forecasts and/or longer lead times given heterogeneity in risk aversion aptitudes and socioeconomic environments. The framework is positioned to bridge empirical findings about responses with uncertainty in warning information. By simulating how interpretation and response translate into actions, it targets the value of improved warning information under realistic behavioral variation. This focus emphasizes that information quality and human response jointly determine outcomes.
supporting_quote: The central premise of this study is to explore how interpretation and response to flood warnings affect the benefits of the information provided by the flood warning systems.

the study aims to understand the marginal benefit of providing a more accurate forecast and/or longer lead times given the heterogeneity in risk aversion aptitudes and their socioeconomic environments.

chunks.text: Improved warning accuracy and longer lead times do not automatically reduce flood risk because people may not take early action. Human behavior during disasters can strongly affect evacuation effectiveness, but many studies have limited consideration of heterogeneous responses to flood warnings. Evacuation decision-making is complex and uncertain due to cognition under stress, risk aversion, and preparedness. This creates a need to model how diverse interpretations of warnings translate into evacuation actions.
supporting_quote: improvements in these areas do not in themselves reduce risk in disaster situations as reliable and timely warnings do little good if not followed by (early) actions.
These studies have had limited consideration of how human's heterogeneous response to flood warnings affect the evacuation processes

chunks.text: Determining what warning level and lead time to issue is difficult because early warnings can be highly uncertain and may erode trust, while low-risk warnings can be catastrophic for more risk-averse people. Different risk aversion levels make it challenging to set a single warning threshold. The paper frames this as a motivation for a framework that explicitly represents heterogeneity in response to probabilistic warnings. Such a framework is needed to assess system effectiveness under varying tolerance and uncertainty.
supporting_quote: Earlier lead times have not proven to necessarily reduce the level of flood damages or loss of life, as the uncertainty with the forecast at those times is often quite high

High-risk warnings with high uncertainty could result in loss of trust in the flood warning system, whereas a low-risk warning can result in catastrophic consequences if people's risk aversion levels are above it.

chunks.text: Prior work either evaluates evacuation with traffic dynamics and decision rules or estimates economic value of probabilistic forecasts and lead times, but does not integrate behavioral heterogeneity with warning effectiveness. Many studies rely on historical data and do not connect empirical response data to decision rules while also representing uncertainty in warning information. The paper identifies a gap in bridging human decision heterogeneity, evacuation dynamics, and probabilistic warning attributes in one modeling framework. Addressing this gap is positioned as necessary to evaluate benefits under diverse communities.
supporting_quote: none of the previous studies has integrated the heterogeneity in people's behaviors with the effectiveness of flood warning information.

There is still a need for a framework that bridges the gap between these elements, where the empirical data gathered in previous studies would inform human decision-making rules and their interactions, while at the same time consider uncertainties in the flood warning information.

chunks.text: The framework is an agent-based model coupled with a traffic model to simulate evacuation on a road network under probabilistic flood warning scenarios. The model represents (1) a geographic system with residents and a transportation network, (2) probabilistic warnings giving flood probability within a lead time, and (3) household decision-making and evacuation actions. The architecture separates an upper level environment (geography and warning information) from lower level agent attributes and behaviors. This coupling allows assessment of how warning quality, behavior, and congestion interact to determine evacuation outcomes.
supporting_quote: This study develops an agent-based modeling framework that evaluates the impacts of heterogeneity in human behaviors... The framework is coupled with a traffic model to simulate evacuation processes within a road network under various flood warning scenarios.
The model simulates (1) a geographical system... (2) probabilistic flood warnings... and (3) decision-making processes that describe how the agents make evacuation decisions

chunks.text: Transportation networks are modeled as directed graphs with nodes and edges; edge weights represent costs such as route length or capacity. The paper illustrates a matrix representation where non-connected node pairs have infinite cost. This abstraction is used to manage network complexity while preserving route connectivity for path finding. It supports computing shortest evacuation paths from locations to a designated safe node.
supporting_quote: many studies have suggested the use of simplified representations of transportation networks, such as a directed graph... which contains a set of nodes, edges, and weights associated with edges.
Edges associated with nodes that are not directly connected are assigned an infinite cost to represent that no direct evacuation route exists between them.

chunks.text: Evacuation traffic is simulated using the Nagel–Schreckenberg (N-S) cellular automaton model, which updates each vehicle by acceleration, deceleration, randomization, and movement at discrete time steps. Vehicles accelerate when headway exceeds a safe distance and decelerate when it is below the safe distance; random speed changes occur with a probability. The model also assumes an all-way stop rule at intersections where the first arrival has precedence. This individual-oriented traffic approach enables capturing congestion effects during evacuation.
supporting_quote: The N-S model divides a road into cells and categorizes a vehicle's actions on the road into four groups in a time unit: acceleration, deceleration, randomization, and movement.

We assume that individuals follow the all-way stop rule when multiple vehicles arrive at a road intersection at the same time: a vehicle that arrives first has precedence over vehicles that arrive later.

chunks.text: Households are modeled as agents, assuming family members influence a unified household evacuation decision. Agents share the same transportation network and receive the warning at the same time. Physical attributes include geographic location in the network, maximum evacuation speed, and final evacuation status. Psychological behavior is summarized by a single risk tolerance threshold (RT), representing the maximum flood probability a household tolerates before deciding to evacuate.
supporting_quote: Therefore, each household is simulated as an agent in this study.
we summarize all of these factors into a single parameter, RT threshold, to measure an agent's maximum tolerance level for flood risk

chunks.text: Agent behavior is simplified into three steps: decide whether to evacuate based on flood probability versus RT, choose an evacuation path, and then evacuate following traffic rules. The evacuation decision rule is threshold-based: evacuate if predicted flood probability exceeds the agent’s RT threshold. For route choice, agents are assumed to know the network and select the shortest path to the safe area. Real-time speeds are constrained by maximum speeds, route limits, and other agents, governed by the N-S model.
supporting_quote: an agent's response to flood warnings is simplified into three steps: (1) decide if evacuation action should be taken... (2) choose an evacuation path... and (3) evacuate
An agent will decide to evacuate if the probability of flooding exceeds its RT threshold.
it is assumed that all of the agents have good knowledge about the transportation network and they will choose the shortest path

chunks.text: Model implementation is in Java and proceeds in three steps: build agents and network inputs, execute the simulation with a probabilistic warning, and analyze outputs.
