To speed computation, shortest paths to the evacuation destination are precomputed and stored in a Java hashtable keyed by an agent’s location. During execution, agents make decisions after receiving the warning and those evacuating are simulated at discrete time steps within the warning lead time. Benefits are then assessed from evacuation statuses at the end of simulation.
supporting_quote: We implement the agent-based model using an object-oriented programming language, Java.
To improve computational speed, the shortest path from any given location to this evacuation destination is calculated before model execution and is stored in a Java hashtable
the benefits of flood warnings are measured by the percentage of agents who have evacuated to safe area.

chunks.text: Behavioral heterogeneity is represented by drawing agents’ RT thresholds from a normal distribution parameterized by a mean (μRT) and coefficient of variation (CVRT). The mean reflects overall community risk tolerance, while CVRT quantifies heterogeneity; setting CVRT to zero produces homogeneous agents. This approach is used because empirical distributions are not available and CV is a standard dispersion measure. The framework then explores output sensitivity across broad parameter settings.
supporting_quote: this study applies the normal distribution to generate agents' risk threshold. The mean value... measures the agents' overall risk threshold for floods (lRT), whereas the coefficient of variation (CVRT) measures agents' behavioral heterogeneity.
Coefficient of variation is set to be zero to simulate agents with homogeneous risk threshold.

chunks.text: The case study uses a hypothetical transportation network with 16 nodes, 16 routes, and one node designated as the evacuation destination (safe area). All roads are two-way with one lane per direction, with a uniform speed limit of 10 L/T and all-way stop signs at intersections. The total network length is 2,210 L, and household agents are uniformly distributed along routes. Units are generalized as L (length) and T (time) to avoid committing to a specific scale.
supporting_quote: The evacuation transportation network has 16 nodes, with one node selected as the evacuation destination, and 16 routes.

The total length of the transportation network is 2,210 L. We assume that all lanes in this network have the same speed limit (10 L/T in this study) and all route intersections have an all-way stop sign

chunks.text: Residential density (RD) is defined as the total number of agents divided by the number of nodes in the network. The study varies the number of agents from 320 to 640, corresponding to RD from 20 to 40 agents/node, to evaluate how density affects evacuation and warning benefits. This parameterization is used to represent differing neighborhood crowding and traffic load conditions. Agents are assumed uniformly distributed along transportation routes.
supporting_quote: The RD of the neighborhood is defined as the total number of agents in the transportation system divided by the number of nodes in the network.
the total number of agents in the transportation network ranges from 320 to 640 (i.e., RD ranges from 20 agents/node to 40 agents/node)

chunks.text: Scenario design varies mean risk threshold, risk threshold heterogeneity, predicted flood probability, lead time, and residential density across three scenarios. For example, Scenario 1 uses mean RT 0.75 and CVRT 0.1, predicted probability 0.6:0.05:0.9, and lead time 100:100:700 with RD 30. Scenario 2 explores mean RT 0.6:0.05:0.9 with CVRT 0:0.05:0.3 at predicted probability 0.75. Scenario 3 fixes lead time at 400 and varies RD 20:10:40 while sweeping predicted probability 0.6:0.05:0.9.
supporting_quote: TABLE 2. Parameters for the Three Simulated Scenarios in the Case Study Area
Mean value of agents' risk threshold [-]1 Scenario 1 0.75 Scenario 2 0.6:0.05:0.9 Scenario 3 0.75
Residential density [number of agents/node] Scenario 1 30 Scenario 2 30 Scenario 3 20:10:40

chunks.text: Flood forecast accuracy is operationalized as the predicted flood probability in the warning, paired with a lead time. The study focuses on flood events without false alarms, so warnings are treated as given probabilities rather than verified outcomes. Agents receive one warning at the beginning of simulation and no updates afterward. The benefit metric is evaluated at the end of the lead-time simulation window.
supporting_quote: we consider flood forecast accuracy only in terms of the predicted flood probability.
we assume that the agents will receive a flood warning at the beginning of model execution, and will not receive any other flood warning information during the following simulation periods.

chunks.text: Model validation reproduces expected qualitative relationships: benefits rise with increasing lead time and with higher predicted flood probability. The results also show joint constraints: benefits remain low if predicted probability or lead time is near a lower limit and saturate beyond upper limits. In the case study, low-benefit lower limits are around 0.7 predicted probability and 200 T lead time, while saturation occurs around 0.75 predicted probability and 500 T lead time. This supports that the model captures expert-accepted patterns of warning effectiveness.
supporting_quote: Figure 5a shows that the benefits of flood warnings increase as flood warning lead time increases.
Figure 5b shows that the benefits of flood warnings increase as predicted flood probability increases.
upper limits also exist beyond which the benefits of flood warnings will not increase significantly (0.75 for predicted flood probability and 500 T for flood warning lead time in the case study).

chunks.text: Behavioral heterogeneity (CVRT) has opposite effects depending on whether the population is on average risk-tolerant or risk-averse relative to the warning probability. When μRT > pf (risk-tolerant), benefits increase as CVRT increases; when μRT < pf (risk-averse), benefits decrease as CVRT increases. The paper connects this to the fraction that decides to evacuate under a normal RT distribution. This indicates heterogeneity can either help or hurt warning effectiveness depending on where the mean risk threshold lies.
supporting_quote: The results show that the benefits of flood warnings increase as agent heterogeneity increases for risk-tolerant agents (μRT > pf). The opposite phenomena hold true for risk-averse agents (μRT < pf).
RT ∼ N (μRT, μRT CVRT) | RT ∈ [0,1])

chunks.text: The model derives the fraction of residents deciding to evacuate as a function of warning probability, mean risk threshold, and heterogeneity: pe = Φ((pf − μRT)/(μRT·CVRT)). This relationship explains why increasing CVRT increases pe when μRT > pf (because the standardized term becomes less negative in magnitude), and decreases pe when μRT < pf. The analytic form ties behavioral distribution assumptions directly to evacuation participation. It provides a quantitative bridge between heterogeneity metrics and warning benefits.
supporting_quote: the percentage of residents (pe) who decide to evacuate after receiving flood warning can be represented by:
pe = Φ((pf - μRT)/(μRT CVRT))

chunks.text: Increasing lead time generally improves benefits, but the marginal gain depends strongly on the population’s average risk threshold. Longer lead times outperform shorter ones, yet if agents are sufficiently risk-tolerant, additional lead time yields little benefit because they do not choose to evacuate. The paper notes an apparent threshold where no additional benefits occur when average RT exceeds about 0.85 in the case study. This emphasizes that improving lead time alone may be ineffective without changes in response behavior.
supporting_quote: modeled flood warnings with longer lead times outperform those with relatively shorter lead times
even a longer warning lead time yields no additional benefits if the agents' risk threshold exceeds a limit (0.85 in this case).

chunks.text: In the illustrated comparison, changing behavior can yield larger gains than increasing lead time. The paper reports almost no added benefit from increasing lead time from 200 T to 400 T when average RT is 0.80, but a benefit increase of 0.22 when average RT decreases from 0.8 to 0.75. This suggests education or interventions that reduce effective risk thresholds can enhance warning value. The result frames behavior modification as complementary to forecast improvements.
supporting_quote: there are almost no additional benefits if the flood warning lead time is increased from 200 T to 400 T when the agents' average risk threshold is 0.80.
a benefit increase of 0.22 is achieved if the agents become more risk averse, with the risk threshold reduced from 0.8 to 0.75

chunks.text: Residential density constrains the benefits of more accurate warnings because higher participation can trigger congestion that prevents timely evacuation. Benefits from higher predicted flood probability are larger in low-density areas, while in high-density areas improvements in predicted probability do not significantly increase benefits. The model interprets this as a reduced marginal benefit of accuracy under congestion. For dense areas, increasing lead time or improving routes may be more effective than raising predicted probability.
supporting_quote: the benefits associated with more accurate flood warnings is constrained in high residential areas because a large fraction of the agents that take evacuation actions may not successfully evacuate... as a result of traffic congestion
the marginal benefit of providing higher predicted flood probability is higher in low residential areas than in high residential areas.

chunks.text: As residential density increases, evacuation success declines even among those who decide to evacuate. In the case study, 100% of evacuees reach the safe area at RD = 20 agents/node, but only 81% at RD = 30 and 68% at RD = 40. This quantifies congestion effects on outcome-based warning benefits. It demonstrates that the same warning can produce very different realized benefits depending on density-driven network load.
supporting_quote: 100% of the agents that decide to evacuate can successfully evacuate to the safe area when the RD is 20 agents/node.
this value decreases to 81 and 68% when the RD is 30 agents/node and 40 agents/node, respectively

chunks.text: Average evacuation time increases with residential density, reflecting added delays under congestion. Reported mean evacuation times are 150.2 T at RD = 20, 162.3 T at RD = 30, and 169.6 T at RD = 40. These increases help explain why higher density reduces the proportion reaching safety within the warning lead time. The result implies managers should estimate evacuation time requirements especially for high-density zones.
supporting_quote: the average evacuation time for all of the agents increases as RD increases, which is 150.2 T, 162.3 T, and 169.6 T when RD is 20 agents/node, 30 agents/node, and 40 agents/node, respectively

chunks.text: The evacuation time required to achieve a given percentage evacuated rises notably with density. The time for 50% (100%) evacuated is about 150 T (430 T) at RD = 20, 200 T (580 T) at RD = 30, and 250 T (785 T) at RD = 40. A 33% RD increase from 30 to 40 raises the 50% time by 25% (200 to 250 T) and the 100% time by 35% (580 to 785 T). Achieving high benefits is thus substantially harder in dense areas.
supporting_quote: The time needed for 50% (100%) of the agents to evacuate... is approximately 200 T (580 T) when RD is 30 agents/node.
This time is approximately 150 T (430 T) and 250 T (785 T) when the RD is 20 agents/node and 40 agents/node, respectively.
when RD increases by 33% (from 30 agents/node to 40 agents/node)... 100%... increases by 35% (from 580 T to 785 T).

chunks.text: The study validates the model qualitatively because empirical output data are unavailable. Validation is described as comparing simulation outputs to expert knowledge and empirical findings from prior studies rather than conducting quantitative outcome validation. This limits confidence in predictive accuracy for specific real communities. The approach is framed as appropriate for a theoretical framework demonstration.
supporting_quote: In this theoretical study, with no empirical data about the model outputs, the model validation is conducted from a qualitative perspective with empirical findings from previous studies
The output validation was done by comparing the model output with the expert's knowledge about flood warning-response systems.

chunks.text: The simulations represent a single flooding event and do not allow behavior to evolve through learning from past experiences. The authors note that, in reality, risk tolerance may change after repeated floods and incurred costs. This omission may affect long-term assessment of warning programs and trust dynamics. Future work is suggested to obtain socioeconomic and response data to better model decision processes.
supporting_quote: First, we simulate a single flooding event without considering the public's behavioral changes resulting from past experiences of flood events.
In reality, people might change their flood RT based on their past experiences.

chunks.text: Flood dynamics are simplified by assuming anyone remaining at the end of the simulation is flooded and anyone who reaches the safe area is not. The model does not specify inundation direction, speed, or timing. This limits realism because evacuation risk depends on evolving floodwater and route impassability. The authors propose future work to simulate gradual inundation processes.
supporting_quote: we assume that all of the agents remaining in the area at the end of model execution will be flooded, and the agents who have evacuated... will not be flooded.
Thus, we did not specify the direction, speed, or timing of the flood inundation processes. In future work, we will simulate the gradual inundation processes

chunks.text: Route choice and information assumptions are idealized: agents are assumed to know evacuation paths and always select the shortest path, rather than adapting to real-time traffic or evolving warning updates. This may understate rerouting behavior and its effects on congestion. The authors note the need to explore individual route choice impacts on evacuation traffic. Such refinements could change predicted benefits and bottlenecks.
supporting_quote: we assume that all of the households are knowledgeable about evacuation paths and will choose the shortest one.
in reality the agents might dynamically change evacuation paths based on real-time traffic conditions and warning information.

chunks.text: The model assumes agents make independent evacuation decisions and do not communicate, despite evidence that social ties affect evacuation behavior. This excludes neighbor/relative influence and social contagion effects that can alter timing and participation. The authors suggest future work to represent interactions and other socioeconomic household characteristics. Including these heterogeneities could better capture emergent community-level response patterns.
supporting_quote: Finally, this study assumes that agents make independent evacuation decisions without communicating with each other.
In the real world, relatives, neighbors, and friends greatly affect evacuation decisions (Parker et al., 2009).

chunks.text: The paper concludes that flood warning benefits depend jointly on warning quality and human response, not on forecast improvements alone. It finds the marginal benefit of better warnings is significantly constrained when people are more risk-tolerant. It also concludes that residential density strongly affects evacuation effectiveness and thus benefits, implying that warning strategies should differ across flood zones by density. Overall, collecting behavioral and residential information is argued to improve warning efficiency.
supporting_quote: There are three important findings from this study: (1) the benefits of flood warnings are affected not only by the quality of flood warning information but also by responses to such information;

(2) the marginal benefit associated with providing better flood warnings is significantly constrained if people behave in a more risk-tolerant manner; and (3) RD plays an important role in evacuation effectiveness and ultimately the benefits of flood warnings.

chunks.text: The framework integrates predicted flood probability and lead time, heterogeneous response (mean and coefficient of variation in risk threshold), and residential density, and couples this with a traffic model to evaluate evacuation processes. The authors argue that, beyond improving forecast information, using data on human behavior and residential characteristics can make warnings more beneficial by helping managers decide when and how to release warnings. They suggest modern information technologies and social media could support real-time data availability and improved decision-making. This points toward more adaptive, context-specific flood warning management.
supporting_quote: This study proposes an agent-based modeling framework for incorporating the quality of flood warnings (i.e., predicted flood probability and lead time), the heterogeneous nature of response... and RD
this study suggests that collecting and using information on human behaviors and residential characteristics of flood-threatened areas will make flood warnings more beneficial.

chunks.text: Overtopping is a common trigger of embankment breach failure, where flow over the crest erodes material and forms a breach channel that deepens and widens, increasing discharge and hazard downstream. The societal risk is large and expected to increase as extreme storms intensify. Better breach modeling supports preparedness and timely mitigation actions such as breach closure and improved flood control planning.
supporting_quote: The most prevalent scenario of breach failure occurs when the water level overtops the embankment crest
As this channel extends, deepens, and widens, discharge through the breach increases

chunks.text: Existing breach models often focus on 1D planar failure or rely on empirical submodels, while 2D modeling is less developed because breach evolution depends on coupled hydraulic and geotechnical controls. Lateral erosion and bank collapse can strongly influence breach outflow, but their effects on the time evolution of breach geometry are not well explored. Prior approaches sometimes simplify collapse by distributing failed material uniformly or by linking widening to deepening through assumed geometry.
supporting_quote: Two-dimensional modeling of breaching has been limited due to the complexity of breach development, which depends on both hydraulic and geotechnical factors

Lateral erosion of breach channel related to slope instability of the banks is reported to have a considerable effect on the outflow hydrograph, but the effects on the time evolution of breach geometry remain mostly unexplored

chunks.text: Laboratory and field experiments provide key information for modeling breaching processes, because real-event observations are often limited to final geometry or brief notes during failure. The paper uses two controlled experimental setups to analyze time variation of reservoir level, inflow and breach discharge, and evolving breach cross sections. These data are used to infer a failure-angle-based representation of periodic slumping that drives breach widening.
supporting_quote: Measurements of breach geometry in real embankments are common, but often limited to cursory observations during the event
Results of controlled experiments performed in the laboratory and the field provide information on the processes that should be incorporated in breach evolution models

chunks.text: The study aims to develop a new two-dimensional numerical model for overtopping breach evolution in noncohesive, optimally compacted earthen dams. A central goal is to explicitly represent breach widening caused by side-slope instability through a bank-failure source term in sediment mass conservation. The model is intended to reproduce time-varying breach width/depth, breach discharge, and reservoir drawdown across different scales and conditions, and then be applied to a real dam failure case.
supporting_quote: A two-dimensional, finite-difference numerical model is developed to simulate the breach evolution of noncohesive optimally compacted earthen dams
The main feature of the model is the inclusion of a source term in the sediment mass conservation equation that explicitly describes breach widening due to mass slumping of the breach sides

chunks.text: The paper seeks to estimate a threshold soil failure angle from experimental breach cross-section evolution and to use it as the trigger for slumping-driven widening in the numerical model. This connects observed periodic mass failures to a simplified parameterization suitable for 2D simulation. The estimated failure-angle concept is designed to capture the transition from early incision (prewidening) to later widening.
supporting_quote: a threshold failure angle,  φ_f , is proposed to model breach channel widening due to bank failure
This failure angle is estimated from the analysis of the time evolution of the breach cross section recorded in the laboratory experiments

chunks.text: The model is also intended to be tested beyond the laboratory by simulating the October 2015 Gibson Pond Dam failure associated with Hurricane Joaquin. A further goal is to quantify how key uncertain inputs—such as inlet discharge, soil failure angle, and tailwater depth—affect predicted widening/deepening rates and the breach hydrograph metrics.
supporting_quote: Then, the model is applied to simulate the overtopping failure of an earthen dam that occurred due to Hurricane Joaquin in October 2015 in Lexington, South Carolina
A sensitivity analysis is conducted to assess the effect of the main model parameters on the prediction of breach evolution

chunks.text: A major challenge in breach prediction is representing two-dimensional, laterally varying breach growth when overtopping initiates at the lowest crest point. Such cases require modeling both breach deepening and widening under rapidly changing geometry and flow. The complexity of coupled hydraulics and geotechnics has limited development and testing of robust 2D models under unsteady conditions.
supporting_quote: In wide valleys, and when water levels increase gradually, water spills over the lowest point of the crest. In this case, a two-dimensional modeling approach is necessary
Two-dimensional modeling of breaching has been limited due to the complexity of breach development

chunks.text: Bank collapse and slope instability are known to affect breach outflow, but modeling their contribution to breach geometry evolution is difficult, especially under changing moisture and pore-pressure conditions. Many models rely on empirical sediment flux relations or simplified collapse handling that may not reproduce the time evolution of widening events. This motivates a simplified but explicit representation of slumping as a lateral sediment source.
supporting_quote: These models are rarely tested for unsteady conditions with rapidly changing geometries and sediment properties, such as soil moisture content and pore-water pressures
Bank collapse has also been modeled as planar failure in which collapsed materials from the breach sides are uniformly distributed across the breach channel width

chunks.text: The numerical framework solves 2D depth-averaged shallow-water equations for mass and momentum coupled with a 2D sediment mass conservation equation for bed evolution. Friction slopes are computed using the Manning formulation, and sediment transport uses Meyer-Peter and Müller bedload relationships. A key addition is a source term representing lateral sediment input due to breach-side slumping.
supporting_quote: The numerical model is based on the two-dimensional shallowwater equations of water mass and momentum conservations
The sediment transport rates are calculated using the Meyer-Peter and Müller (1948) formulation (MPM)

chunks.text: Bank failure is triggered by comparing local computed side-slope angles to a threshold failure angle φ_f. When the local angle exceeds φ_f, an unstable wedge is assumed to slump and the lateral sediment supply rate q_sf is computed from the failed area over the time step, scaled by a relaxation coefficient. The unstable area depends on grid spacing and elevation differences between adjacent transverse nodes.
supporting_quote: At each time step, the angle  φ  is compared to  φ_f . If  φ  is greater than  φ_f , slumping failure occurs
q_{sf} = \frac{\Delta A \zeta}{\Delta t}

chunks.text: The failed material slumps with a characteristic timescale T_b through a relaxation coefficient ζ, which controls how rapidly the bank-collapse sediment is delivered. This provides a computationally simple way to represent periodic failures without resolving detailed geotechnical processes. The approach lumps embankment properties into the single parameter φ_f, estimated from measured breach cross-section changes.
supporting_quote: The relaxation coefficient is defined as  ζ = \left(1 - e^{\left(\frac{\Delta t}{T_b}\right)}\right)
a simplified approach in which embankment properties are lumped into a single parameter, a threshold failure angle,  φ_f

chunks.text: A finite-difference MacCormack predictor–corrector scheme is used to solve the governing equations, providing second-order accuracy in space and time. Sediment fluxes (q_bx, q_by) and the slumping source term (q_sf) are computed at the start of both predictor and corrector steps using known and predicted flow variables, respectively. Boundary conditions include specified upstream inflow hydrograph (q_x) with q_y=0 and a downstream free-fall condition.
supporting_quote: the MacCormack scheme (MacCormack 1969, 2003) is employed to solve the governing equations
at the downstream boundary, a free fall condition is specified

chunks.text: Time stepping is controlled using a Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy stability condition with a chosen Courant number. For the complex breach geometry, the study reports that using C_n equal to or greater than 0.9 yields good agreement with experiments, especially for peak discharge timing and reservoir drawdown onset. Artificial viscosity (Jameson et al. 1981) is applied to suppress spurious oscillations near steep gradients.
supporting_quote: The computational time step is selected to satisfy the Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy stability condition
choosing  C_n  equal to or greater than 0.9 for MacCormack scheme produced good agreement

chunks.text: A grid-independence study is performed for Setup 2 by varying transverse spacing Δy, streamwise spacing Δx, and reservoir-only streamwise spacing (Δx)_reservoir. Model performance is evaluated using RMSE for top breach width, maximum breach depth, breach discharge, and upstream reservoir water depth, along with CPU time. The selected base grid emphasizes adequate transverse resolution to capture widening behavior.
supporting_quote: three groups of grid spacings are tested for Setup 2 (Table 2)
Table 2 lists the grid sizes, number of computational points, CPU time for simulating 300 s, and root mean squared error (RMSE)

chunks.text: Setup 1 is a large-scale experiment with a 1.8 m tall optimally compacted earthen dam in a 5 m wide flume at HRI (Cairo). The dam uses nonuniform sand with geometric mean size 0.5 mm, has symmetric 2.5:1 (H:V) slopes, and a 1.5 m crest breadth. Overtopping is initiated by a 0.5 m wide and 0.03 m deep pilot channel; reservoir level is measured with ultrasonic sensors and breach cross-sections are tracked by a dropping-rod technique.
supporting_quote: A 1.8 m tall optimally compacted earthen dam is constructed across a 5 m wide flume
Dam sediment consisted of nonuniform sand with geometric mean size equal to 0.5 mm

chunks.text: Setup 2 is a small-scale experiment with a 0.2 m tall optimally compacted earthen dam in a 1 m wide flume at the University of South Carolina. It uses nonuniform sand with geometric mean grain size 0.35 mm, 3:1 (H:V) slopes, and a 0.3 m crest width. A constant pump discharge of 0.0045 m3/s feeds the reservoir; a side weir maintains constant early-stage water level, and breach evolution is measured with a green laser scanner.
supporting_quote: a 0.2 m tall optimally compacted earthen dam is built in a 1 m wide flume
A pump delivers a constant discharge of 0.0045 m3/s into the reservoir

chunks.text: Failure angles used to parameterize bank slumping are estimated from the time evolution of breach side slopes between consecutive measurements. For Setup 1, estimated φ_f values are 45°, 56.7°, 45°, and 65° for intervals 300–360 s, 360–420 s, 420–480 s, and 480–540 s. For Setup 2, φ_f is estimated as 43.26° (70–130 s) and 63.81° (130–220 s).
supporting_quote: Table 1 lists the estimated failure angle between each periodic mass failure for Setup 1 and Setup 2

chunks.text: For the Gibson Pond Dam case study, the reservoir geometry is simplified as a rectangular planform 80 m wide and 1,276 m long. Field data reported after the event include measured top breach width 21.16 m, breach depth 3.4 m, dam height 4.6 m, crest width 6.6 m, and D50=0.7 mm. Because the inflow hydrograph was unavailable, a constant inflow equal to the estimated peak storm discharge 98.62 m3/s was used.
supporting_quote: the reservoir area is simplified as a rectangular shape with a breadth of 80 m, representing the dam width, and a reservoir length of 1,276 m
the estimated peak storm discharge of 98.62 m³/s (Tabrizi et al. 2017) is used as a constant inflow rate

chunks.text: Experimental observations show breach evolution occurs in two stages: an initial prewidening phase dominated by vertical incision with little lateral growth, followed by a widening phase in which periodic mass failures abruptly widen the breach while deepening continues. In Setup 1, the first 300 s are dominated by deepening, then widening occurs via periodic slumping. Similar behavior is observed in Setup 2, with a shorter prewidening duration before widening and deepening occur together.
supporting_quote: breach evolution may be described in two stages: Stage 1 (prewidening) dominated by a deepening of the breach channel
Stage 2 (widening) characterized by the widening and deepening of the breach channel caused by periodic mass failure

chunks.text: For Setup 1, the flow record indicates reservoir level was held near constant early, then dropped as breach discharge increased sharply. The measured breach peak discharge is 3.0 m3/s, occurring 618 s after overtopping began. These observed hydrograph characteristics are used to inform model inflow boundary representation and to evaluate model timing of peak and drawdown.
supporting_quote: The reservoir water depth was kept constant at 1.78 m
Breach peak discharge over the sharp-crested weir is 3.0 m³/s and time to peak is 618 s

chunks.text: The numerical model reproduces Setup 1’s two-stage breach development, including a prewidening period of about 300 s followed by widening driven by bank failure when slopes exceed the failure angle. The model predicts the timing of mass failures over intervals consistent with the experiment and captures widening and deepening rates satisfactorily. Peak discharge is predicted around 610 s, close to the observed 618 s.
supporting_quote: the model can effectively capture the two stages of breaching
the predicted breach peak discharge occurs around  610 s ... compares well with the experimental observation of peak discharge occurring 618 s

chunks.text: For Setup 2, grid-resolution tests show transverse grid spacing strongly affects the ability to capture widening, deepening, hydrograph, and reservoir level. When Δy equals the initial pilot channel width (Grid 3), the model fails to reproduce key breach characteristics; smaller Δy improves performance and Grid 1 best captures widening peaks and patterns. Streamwise refinement beyond Δx=0.01 m yields similar results to Δx=0.02 m, and coarsening reservoir Δx to 0.02 m reduces CPU time with little accuracy loss.
supporting_quote: When grid size in the transverse direction  (Δy)  equals the initial pilot channel width (Grid 3), the numerical model fails to capture the breach widening
Grid 1 and Grid 6 produces almost similar numerical results ... reduction in CPU time by 16.7%

chunks.text: In Setup 2 comparisons using the selected grid, the model predicts a 70 s prewidening stage followed by two bank-failure intervals (70–130 s and 130–220 s). It captures onset of widening at 70 s, widening peaks near 160 s and 250 s, and reproduces the reservoir level decline starting around 140 s. The breach hydrograph shows a slight time-to-peak shift, attributed to differences in how discharge is estimated in measurements versus simulations.
supporting_quote: predicts the breaching that begins with a 70 s prewidening stage, followed by two instances of bank failure: the first spanning from 70 s to 130 s, and the second from 130 s to 220 s
there is a slight time to peak shift between the model prediction and the actual observation

chunks.text: Applied to the Gibson Pond Dam failure, the model predicts final breach geometry close to field measurements by the end of an 800 s simulation. The simulated breach top width is 22.0 m and the maximum breach depth is 3.38 m, compared with measured 21.16 m and 3.4 m. The study notes these are within a 5% margin of the measurements.
supporting_quote: At the end of the simulation (t = 800 s), the simulated breach top width is 22.0 m, and the maximum breach depth is 3.38 m
The measured top breach width and breach depth are 21.16 m and 3.4 m, respectively

chunks.text: Sensitivity analysis indicates that increasing inlet discharge raises average widening and deepening rates and increases peak discharge, while slightly reducing time to peak. Tailwater depth has a strong damping effect: increasing tailwater reduces widening and deepening rates and peak discharge, and increases time to peak. This is interpreted as breaching being driven by upstream–downstream head difference.
supporting_quote: As inlet discharge increases, average breach widening and deepening rates as well as the peak discharge increase, while time to peak discharge decreases slightly
increasing tailwater depth causes notable reductions in both average deepening and widening rates, as well as peak discharge, while simultaneously increasing the time to peak

chunks.text: Changing soil failure angle strongly affects widening and hydrograph timing but has limited impact on deepening rate in the Gibson Pond sensitivity tests. A 50% reduction in φ_f produces a 210% increase in average widening rate, a 30% increase in peak discharge, and a 20% decrease in time to peak. Increasing φ_f by 50% leaves deepening rate unaffected but reduces widening rate and peak discharge and increases time to peak by about 200%.
supporting_quote: A 50% reduction in the soil failure angle leads to a substantial 210% increase in the average widening rate, a 30% increase in peak discharge, a 20% decrease in time to peak discharge
when the failure angle is increased by 50% above its base value, the deepening rate remains unaffected ... 200% increase in the time to peak discharge

chunks.text: The study emphasizes that directly modeling periodic bank failure is complex and computationally intensive because many interacting processes (e.g., porewater pressure changes) can drive slope instability. The proposed approach therefore simplifies these processes by lumping embankment behavior into a single failure-angle threshold that triggers slumping. This simplification is intended to be practical while still capturing the observed transition from incision to widening.
supporting_quote: Due to the complexity of all processes involved, modeling periodic bank failure is complicated and computationally intensive
a simplified approach in which embankment properties are lumped into a single parameter, a threshold failure angle,  φ_f

chunks.text: For the Gibson Pond Dam application, a key limitation is the absence of an inflow hydrograph; the model uses a constant inflow set to the estimated peak storm discharge. This assumption introduces uncertainty in predicted timing and hydrograph shape, even if final breach geometry matches field observations. The paper explicitly notes the inflow hydrograph was not available.
supporting_quote: The inflow hydrograph to the Gibson Pond Dam reservoir is not available; therefore, the estimated peak storm discharge of 98.62 m³/s ... is used as a constant inflow rate

chunks.text: The authors highlight substantial uncertainty in determining model inputs before and during breaching, motivating the sensitivity analysis. Such uncertainties include hydraulic forcing, geotechnical parameters like the soil failure angle, and downstream tailwater conditions. The sensitivity tests are framed as a way to understand how these uncertain inputs propagate to breach widening/deepening and hydrograph metrics.
supporting_quote: Acknowledging the substantial uncertainty in determining the model inputs, both before and during the breaching process
a sensitivity analysis is conducted for the primary input variables ... inlet discharge, soil failure angle, and tailwater depth

chunks.text: The paper notes that the failure angle is not a universal constant and depends on multiple geotechnical characteristics of the embankment material. Examples given include soil gradation, soil matric suction, and cohesion. As a result, the authors call for further experimental and numerical work to confirm and generalize the failure-angle concept.
supporting_quote: The failure angle depends on various geotechnical characteristics of the embankment, e.g., soil gradation, soil matric suction, and cohesion
Further experimental and numerical investigations are needed to confirm this

chunks.text: The study concludes that overtopping breach evolution in noncohesive compacted dams exhibits a two-stage pattern: prewidening dominated by vertical incision followed by widening triggered by bank slopes exceeding a failure angle and causing periodic slumping. Incorporating a slumping-driven lateral sediment source term enables the 2D model to reproduce measured time histories of width, depth, discharge, and reservoir drawdown in laboratory tests. The model also predicts final breach geometry for the Gibson Pond Dam within about 5% of measured width and depth.
supporting_quote: Analysis of laboratory data indicates a two-stage pattern in breach development
The numerical model accurately replicates the time variations of the key breach parameters measured during the experiments

chunks.text: The sensitivity analysis supports the conclusion that tailwater depth strongly controls breach evolution because breaching is driven by the head difference between upstream and downstream water levels. Increasing tailwater reduces widening/deepening rates and peak discharge and delays the time to peak. Soil failure angle mainly influences widening rate and timing, with minimal effect on deepening rate, while higher inlet discharge accelerates breaching and increases peak discharge.
supporting_quote: increasing tailwater depth causes notable reductions in both average deepening and widening rates, as well as peak discharge, while simultaneously increasing the time to peak
Notably, the soil failure angle has minimal impact on the deepening rate

chunks.text: Hydrology research increasingly depends on large and rapidly growing datasets from satellites, radars, sensors, and model outputs. These data are used to support analyses such as flood extents, rainfall distributions, and other environmental metrics needed for decisions. The paper frames modern web technologies as an opportunity to improve how these data are managed and distributed for analysis workflows.
supporting_quote: The amount of information being generated in contemporary earth sciences exceeds the capacity for easy ingestion and digestion by researchers
This challenge is particularly evident in hydrology, encompassing remote sensing, reanalysis data, sensor data

chunks.text: Traditional hydrological information systems primarily distribute data through centralized server-based architectures that scale by adding more servers. These systems commonly expose data via internet services based on TCP/IP and rely on database layers to satisfy heterogeneous user queries. The scalability of such systems depends on user volume, information needs, and transaction load.
supporting_quote: The conventional methods of managing, storing, and distributing data often revolve around server-based architectures, mostly growing through horizontal scaling
Data hosted on servers is accessible through various mechanisms, typically employing TCP/IP services over the internet

chunks.text: Recent advances in browsers and web communication have expanded peer-to-peer and hybrid server/peer approaches across domains such as telemedicine and scientific computing. In hydrology and environmental science, emerging work uses browser-to-browser communication to support distributed modeling and collaborative analysis. This context motivates tooling that better supports decentralized sharing and processing in web environments.
supporting_quote: peer-server systems have facilitated the development of tele-home monitoring setups
recent advancements in browser-to-browser communication have triggered a prevalent shift in distributed systems

chunks.text: The work aims to leverage web browser standards to democratize and decentralize hydrological and environmental data access across server and peer settings. It introduces HydroRTC as a server/peer library that supports real-time sharing and multi-user collaboration. The intent is to make server-to-peer, peer-to-peer, and peer-to-server communication easier to build for domain applications.
supporting_quote: we have developed HydroRTC—an advanced server and peer library
to promote information democratization through real-time data sharing and multi-user collaboration

chunks.text: A central objective is to provide a collaborative platform for data sharing, user collaboration, and efficient data analysis while establishing resilient peer-to-peer communication. The library is positioned to reduce barriers to accessing and using large-scale data by providing modular functionality and community extensibility. Case studies are used to broaden the vision and demonstrate integration patterns.
supporting_quote: provide a collaborative platform that promotes data sharing, encourages user collaboration, facilitates efficient data analysis
establishes a resilient peer-to-peer communication infrastructure, removing different barriers to accessing and utilizing large-scale data

chunks.text: The library is designed as a high-level API focused on data streaming, workload distribution, and leveraging client-side hardware. The paper’s use cases emphasize enabling real-time decision-making without excessive reliance on server-side implementations. The goal is to let applications flexibly route transfers via server-to-peer or peer-to-peer channels depending on needs.
supporting_quote: serve as a comprehensive resource facilitating server-to-client communication across a wide spectrum of functions, with a particular focus on data streaming, workload distribution, and leveraging client-side hardware

chunks.text: Centralized server architectures struggle when user counts and data volumes grow, leading to overload and degraded performance. They also create a single point of failure that increases vulnerability to technical faults and cyberattacks, requiring costly redundancy. Geographic distance can increase latency and slow data retrieval for remote users.
supporting_quote: centralized systems face several challenges. They often encounter difficulties when dealing with a large number of users or accommodating a high volume of data
relying on centralized servers poses a single point of failure
Geographical distance from a centralized server can also cause increased latency for users

chunks.text: Hydrological workflows commonly require accessing only specific temporal or spatial subsets of server-held datasets, but conventional transfers tend to move whole files or require complex server-side logic. This creates friction for applications that need scheduled updates or region-of-interest extracts. The paper frames this as a motivation for smarter, user-driven transmission scheduling.
supporting_quote: A common challenge when accessing data from a server to a peer is the need to access information at specific time intervals or spatial coordinates through a region of interest

we've developed a smart data transmission feature that enables users to instruct the server regarding when, in terms of time and space, a particular set of files for a specific region should be transmitted

chunks.text: Large file transfers and streaming in browser-based environments can congest the user interface and are constrained by Node.js and browser runtime limits. The paper notes that preventing UI blocking and managing throughput requires chunking and careful transport mechanisms. These constraints limit accurate assessment of very high transfer rates and motivate adaptive strategies.
supporting_quote: The purpose of the latter is to submit large data files through the data channels and not congest or block the user interface
limitations in Node.js memory and the browser's JavaScript runtime environment prevented accurate assessment of high transfer rates

chunks.text: Using Node.js, WebSockets, and WebRTC introduces security risks that can affect availability and privacy in multi-user systems. The paper highlights risks such as Denial of Service, memory access violations, and IP address leaks. This motivates adding authentication and server health/error tracking mechanisms within HydroRTC.
supporting_quote: specific attacks that could crash the server, such as Denial Of Service (DoS) and Memory Access Violation, are noteworthy, along with IP address leaks
one of the main features that should be addressed in the application is the authentication of users and peers connected through the system

chunks.text: HydroRTC is implemented as a web-based library built on Node.js, Socket.IO, and Peer.js to support server-to-peer, peer-to-peer, and peer-to-server interactions. Node.js provides an event-driven, non-blocking server runtime suited for real-time applications. Socket.IO provides bidirectional transport over WebSockets between clients and the server, while Peer.js leverages WebRTC for direct peer connections with signaling support.
supporting_quote: HydroRTC is a library built on top of Node.js, Socket.IO, and Peer.js to create full server-to-peer, peer-to-peer, and peer-to-server interactions
Peer.js is a library built on top of WebRTC ... to create peer-to-peer data streaming

chunks.text: The system uses a server component to manage sessions, peer information, and file/task requests, and a client component that connects via event listeners and user-triggered handlers. The server listens for events through a defined message passing interface and initiates WebRTC setup in the client using Peer.js. The client creates a unique identifier for peer-to-peer connections and manages direct interactions once the server verifies the requested peer is available.
supporting_quote: a server-side implementation responsible for providing an environment that facilitates peer connections, stores peer information
When a user connects, the component creates a unique identifier that is used to create peer-to-peer connections
the server checks for the user identifier and looks to see if there is no other connection already established

chunks.text: Client-side storage is handled using IndexedDB to support storing and exchanging data received from the server or other peers, as well as local files and simulation outputs. This enables users to retain streamed data within the web app or persist it elsewhere, and to later share or upload it. The design explicitly considers flows from server to user, user to server, and user to user.
supporting_quote: IndexedDB was utilized in the client-side implementation to establish a strong and reliable method for storing and exchanging data with the server
an IndexedDB interface serves as client-side storage for data sourced from the server, other peers, the user's local machine, or outputs

chunks.text: HydroRTC streams large files by creating ArrayBuffer binary streams divided into chunks for transmission between server and clients, and can also stream from client local storage to the server. It compresses packages to improve streaming efficiency and security. On the receiving side, users can choose to keep data in the web environment or download it to local storage.
supporting_quote: it creates array buffer binary streams divided into chunks that can be sent to the client
the packages are compressed to ensure secure and efficient streaming
the user can decide whether to retain this information in the local web environment or save it to their storage

chunks.text: The server and client coordinate behavior using explicit event triggers that cover joining sessions, validating usernames, streaming, listing peers, initiating peer connections, smart data transfer, peer-to-server uploads, and distributed task/result exchange. The server implementation defines these triggers and exposes emitters accessible from the client. Specific handlers also exist for reading certain scientific file types on the server side.
supporting_quote: Event triggers for the server and client implementations
Validate-Username
Stream-Data
Get-task & task-result
Netcdf-reader, hdf5-reader, tiff-reader, gribb-reader

chunks.text: For server-to-peer exchange, HydroRTC supports conventional file transfer with WebSocket-based retrieval and a simple authentication layer. Clients can request specific server data, preview it, and trigger retrieval of subsets via server-side handlers. This supports application workflows that need to inspect data before committing to full transfer.
supporting_quote: We facilitate this interaction via Web sockets for information retrieval while incorporating a straightforward authentication layer
a client to request specific data from the server, preview this data before finalizing the request, and trigger a subset of information from the file via a handling method on the server

chunks.text: Smart data transmission allows a client to specify when (time) and where (space/region) files should be sent from the server, enabling scheduled delivery for evolving events such as sequences of raster/image files. The system tracks requested data and determines what must be transmitted. This is presented as useful for retrieving multiple files like TIFF or GeoTIFF for a region of interest.
supporting_quote: smart data transmission feature that enables users to instruct the server regarding when, in terms of time and space
useful when retrieving multiple files from the server, such as multiple TIFF, geoTIFF, or image files depicting the evolving state of a specific area

chunks.text: Distributed tasks are supported by connecting multiple users to a shared server session and distributing work via an ID-Task mechanism. An admin peer distributes tasks to connected peers, who compute locally and send results back to the server. Returned results are stored in a designated folder for distributed task outputs.
supporting_quote: Through an ID-Task system, users receive multiple tasks distributed by an admin peer from the server
once they are completed, the results are sent back to the server and stored in a specified folder dedicated to distributed task results

chunks.text: HydroRTC targets common hydrological and environmental data types and explicitly supports a broad range of scientific, geospatial, and general formats. Examples include HDF5, NetCDF v3/v4, GRIB/GRIBB, TIFF/GeoTIFF, shapefiles, JPEG/PNG, and text-based formats such as CSV, JSON/GeoJSON, XML, and tabular data. The paper positions these formats as central to storing and sharing multidimensional observations and model outputs.
supporting_quote: Scientific formats considered ... HDF.v5, netCDF.v3 and v4, GRIBB
GIS files (i.e., shapefiles, raster files, TIFF and GeoTIFF)
general formats (i.e., CSV, JSON, GeoJSON, tabular, XML)

chunks.text: The system is designed to handle large data sizes, including many files and individual files reaching tens of gigabytes, covering sensor observations, satellite imagery, GIS inputs/outputs, and model analysis or reanalysis outputs. Streaming uses chunked binary transfers to move such datasets. Client-side storage can retain streamed data for later use or sharing.
supporting_quote: manage large data sizes, including numerous files or file sizes reaching the scale of tens of gigabytes
This data covers sensor observations, satellite imagery, ... GIS input/output data, or model analysis/reanalysis outputs

chunks.text: For server and browser testing, the project used a Windows 10 machine with an Intel Core i7-6700HQ at 2.60 GHz and 32 GB RAM, with a 10 TB hard drive for storage. Performance tracking used Google Chrome diagnostics and Socket.IO event monitoring. Peer-to-peer experiments also computed throughput based on streamed size and duration.
supporting_quote: Intel Core i7-6700HQ @ 2.60 GHz with 32 GB of RAM, running a 64-bit Windows 10 operating system
Data storage ... was conducted on a 10 TB hard drive
we utilized Google Chrome's admin server diagnostics and Socket.IO
we implemented throughput calculation methods

chunks.text: Case study 1 used multiple hydrologic file types to test server-to-peer streaming and load behavior, including NetCDF, GRIBB, TIFF, and HDF5. File sizes in this test ranged from 1 MB to 2.6 GB. The server streamed using chunks up to 10 MB with Node.js file system utilities.
supporting_quote: including netCDF, GRIBB, TIFF, and HDF5 files
These files ranged in size from 1 MB to 2.6 GB
using chunks of up to 10 MB

chunks.text: Case study 2 evaluated peer-to-peer transfer via a chat interface by sharing precipitation gridded NetCDF files stored on a peer’s local machine. The transferred dataset sizes ranged from 1 to 9 GB. The evaluation varied chunk sizes and measured throughput as the time to stream full files.
supporting_quote: sharing precipitation gridded netCDF files of varying sizes, ranging from 1 to 9 GB
The data used for analysis resided in the local machine of the requested peer
Data throughput was calculated by measuring the duration taken to stream the entire data size

chunks.text: In the server-to-peer load test, the system handled concurrent client requests using both WebSockets and HTTP long polling. The test increased requests at 5-second intervals until a disconnection occurred, recording the time until the server became unhealthy. The paper reports an example where a 200-client test was managed through long-polling until the server disconnected while processing requests.
supporting_quote: The test initiated a specified number of client requests at 5-s intervals, waiting until any server disconnection occurred
during a 200-client request test, the server managed a large number of requests through long-polling until it eventually disconnected

chunks.text: Server-side handler complexity affected observed performance during smart data transmission and streaming. The paper notes that TIFF manipulation was faster than parsing and abstracting information from HDF5, independent of file size. It also highlights that HDF5 transmissions required longer processing time per request compared with other handlers, impacting operational stability.
supporting_quote: manipulating TIFF files exhibited faster performance compared to parsing and abstracting information from HDF5 files, irrespective of data size
transmissions of HDF5 files that took a longer amount of time to process

chunks.text: For server streaming, Node.js file system streaming was implemented with chunk sizes up to 10 MB, and after completing a stream the application displayed file-related features in a pop-up. This demonstrates the feasibility of chunked delivery for large scientific files while supporting lightweight preview/inspection in the browser. The approach is presented as part of the server-to-peer feature set.
supporting_quote: Node.js file system was used for file streaming, using chunks of up to 10 MB
Once the server finished streaming a file, a pop-up window displayed various file-associated features

chunks.text: In peer-to-peer testing, the paper observed a linear relationship between transfer speed and chunk sizes or larger datasets, but runtime constraints limited the evaluation of very high rates. Smaller transfers were more stable due to Node.js and browser memory limits. These results motivated adaptive peer-to-peer transmission rates that consider latency, data size, and storage availability.
supporting_quote: An observed linear relationship highlighted the correlation between the speed of data transfer and the sizes of chunks or larger data sets
limitations in Node.js memory and the browser's JavaScript runtime environment prevented accurate assessment of high transfer rates
This observation led to the development of smart data transmission rates between peers

chunks.text: Varying chunk sizes from 3 to 80 MB did not yield significant transfer-speed gains compared to much smaller chunk sizes between 0.1 and 3 MB in the peer-to-peer experiments. This suggests diminishing returns from increasing chunk size beyond a threshold in their environment. The finding is explicitly tied to results shown for 1–9 GB transfers.
supporting_quote: For chunk sizes ranging from 3 to 80 MB per chunk, no significant improvements in transfer speeds were observed
compared to data chunks between 0.1 and 3 MB each
ranging from 1 to 9 GB

chunks.text: The authors emphasize that performance results come from controlled testing and may vary based on server/client architectures, hardware, and network conditions. They note that client and server hardware configurations and latency can change observed behavior. This limits how broadly the reported case study results can be generalized without additional testing.
supporting_quote: results highlight the system's performance within controlled environments
acknowledging potential variations due to system architectures, available hardware configurations of client and server systems, network conditions

chunks.text: The library faces limitations tied to data sizing and chunking, as well as event blocking and memory constraints in Node.js and browser runtimes. Network reliability and latency further complicate large transfers and interactive workflows. The paper suggests moving data grabbing/manipulation/sharing to separate threads using Web Workers or Service Workers to reduce blocking.
supporting_quote: The library is restricted by data sizing limits, with the ability to provide large data through smaller chunks
Issues such as event blocking, memory limitations, and variables such as network reliability and latency
use of Web and Service Workers to move tasks like data grabbing, manipulation, and sharing towards a separate thread

chunks.text: Security is not fully assured due to vulnerabilities in underlying technologies such as Node.js, WebSockets, and WebRTC. The paper identifies threats including DoS, memory access violations, and IP leaks, and notes the need for authentication and server health tracking. It also proposes blockchain integration as a potential future direction for secure transfer and tracking in distributed work sharing.
supporting_quote: there is no complete security assurance
Denial Of Service (DoS) and Memory Access Violation ... along with IP address leaks
the integration of blockchain technology has the potential to ensure secure data transfer and robust tracking

chunks.text: The paper concludes that HydroRTC advances hydrologic data handling by integrating modern web standards across server and client components. It enables server-client data retrieval, smart data transmission, peer-to-peer sharing, and distributed workload support. The authors position it as a step toward decentralized, real-time collaborative workflows for hydrology and environmental science.
supporting_quote: we have enabled different use-case scenarios, enabling smart data transmission, direct server-client data retrieval, peer-to-peer data sharing, and distributed workload capabilities
step towards employing decentralized systems for real-time and collaborative data and workflow sharing

chunks.text: HydroRTC is presented as a prototype that demonstrates the feasibility of using standardized browser technologies to improve connectivity between servers and peers in hydrology. The authors identify future growth through integrating with cloud providers and institutional hosting solutions. They also state that additional exploration is needed for scalability and broader domain generalization.
supporting_quote: integration with existing solutions for web hosting and data sharing such as cloud providers and institutional data solutions would be the next step
The project has been developed as a prototype
various aspects requiring further exploration for comprehensive scalability

chunks.text: Hydrologic and hydraulic models rely on river routing methods to simulate discharge through channels, and routing accuracy depends strongly on how channel geometry is represented. Because detailed channel surveying is costly, operational systems often use simplified cross-sections and regional hydraulic-geometry relationships. Large-sample datasets have become important enablers for robust regional calibration and benchmarking across diverse watersheds.
supporting_quote: Hydrological models often require a routing method to estimate discharge hydrograph through a river channel
The accuracy of the representation of channel geometry can significantly impact routing simulations within hydrological models
Since obtaining accurate channel geometry using surveying methods is costly, simplifying assumptions are often used

chunks.text: Existing river geometry information comes from field measurements and remote sensing, but each has coverage limitations. SWOT-type satellite products can provide width and water surface elevation, yet they cannot observe below the water surface and may miss small rivers. Field datasets such as HYDRoSWOT provide cross-sectional observations but can shrink substantially after quality filtering, limiting robust analyses and regionalization.
supporting_quote: remote sensing products such as those offered by SWOT, are not without limitations as they cannot observe below the water surface and the small rivers are unobserved
HYDRoSWOT dataset is a compilation of geometry and hydraulic observations from over 220,000 cross-sectional measurements
Bjerklie et al. (2020) imposed restrictions on HYDRoSWOT... resulted in a subset including only 20,625 records

chunks.text: Large public datasets can accelerate hydrologic discovery, but they also require careful screening because inconsistencies can mislead calibration and inference. The paper positions IFMHA in this context: as a large, integrated compilation intended to support statistically meaningful, site-level and regional analyses of hydraulic attributes and derived channel geometry parameters.
supporting_quote: care must be taken when using large datasets as data inconsistencies, sometimes referred to as disinformative data, can lead to model calibration and inference issues
the benefits of developing larger and improved datasets
the IFMHA dataset enables stochastic approaches to estimate channel geometry parameters given flow discharge

chunks.text: The study introduces IFMHA (Inventory of Field Measurement of Hydraulic Attributes), a new dataset intended to enable research on channel geometry and streamflow characteristics using USGS field measurement records. IFMHA is designed to merge NWIS surface-water field measurements with stream attributes from NHDPlusV2.1, building upon HYDRoSWOT station metadata. The paper also demonstrates dataset utility by presenting conceptual models that estimate additional channel parameters from the available field attributes.
supporting_quote: This paper introduce a new dataset, IFMHA (Inventory of Field Measurement of Hydraulic Attributes), to enable research studies on channel geometry and streamflow characteristics.
IFMHA is derived from the National Water Information System (NWIS) site inventory for surface water field measurements and stream attributes from the National Hydrography Dataset (NHD).
The dataset utility is demonstrated here by presenting a series of conceptual models for estimating channel geometry parameters

chunks.text: A second goal is to estimate (and potentially gap-fill) four channel geometry parameters—mean depth, maximum depth, wetted perimeter, and roughness—using conceptual models and to evaluate those models against HYDRoSWOT observations. By providing these derived attributes at scale, the dataset aims to improve initial conditions and parameterization used in hydrologic/hydraulic routing, supporting operational flood forecasting frameworks.
supporting_quote: IFMHA provides estimates for four channel geometry parameters (i.e., channel mean depth, maximum depth, wetted perimeter, and roughness) using conceptual models.
The proposed models are evaluated using the mean and maximum depth values measured from observations of HYDRoSWOT.
Such a dataset and attributed channel geometry parameters can enhance the performance of operational flood forecasting frameworks

chunks.text: Simplified channel representations and rating-curve approaches are often used because surveyed channel geometry is scarce and expensive to obtain. These simplifications can constrain models to limited functional forms and omit potentially important catchment and river attributes. As a result, routing simulations and flood-related predictions can be sensitive to poorly characterized geometry and roughness.
supporting_quote: Since obtaining accurate channel geometry using surveying methods is costly, simplifying assumptions are often used
Often, channel geometry is estimated using simple rating curves... However, such methods are limited to power law relations
The accuracy of the representation of channel geometry can significantly impact routing simulations within hydrological models

chunks.text: Remote sensing datasets can help but have observation constraints: they generally do not measure below-water geometry and may omit small rivers. This limitation motivates the continued need for comprehensive field-measurement compilations that include cross-section-based attributes over a wide range of sites and flows.
supporting_quote: remote sensing products such as those offered by SWOT... cannot observe below the water surface and the small rivers are unobserved
the lack of surveyed data in most rivers has motivated research in the field of hydraulic geometry

chunks.text: Existing field compilations can lose much of their value after applying quality filters and hydraulic-condition restrictions, leaving too few records per site for robust inference. Prior HYDRoSWOT-based studies reduced the dataset to tens of thousands of records across a few thousand stations, which can be insufficient for site-level stochastic characterization and regional calibration.
supporting_quote: by filtering zero, missing, suspicious values, and outliers, the number of records significantly diminished
resulted in a subset including only 20,625 records, representing 3519 gaging stations
The low number of records in many locations... underline the benefits of developing larger and improved datasets.

chunks.text: IFMHA compilation integrates three sources: HYDRoSWOT, NWIS field measurements, and NHDPlus V2.1. Station-level identifiers (USGS site number) and NHD feature identifiers (COMID/FLComID) are used to link variables across sources. A workflow (flowchart) describes sequential adoption, selection of desired variables, and attribution into a unified dataset.
supporting_quote: IFMHA consists of three main sources of data including HYDRoSWOT, NWIS field measurements, and NHDPlus V2.1 datasets.
The desired variables from each data source were linked to IFMHA using the USGS site number and common identifiers (COMID).
the sequential steps involved in dataset adoption

chunks.text: NWIS field measurements were programmatically retrieved for each station as tab-separated text and parsed into a unified dataframe spanning all sites. The process created URL links from site numbers, queried the NWIS web interface, and standardized the returned fields (e.g., discharge, gage height, width, velocity, and area). The authors provide code on the IFMHA GitHub repository to reproduce retrieval and parsing.
supporting_quote: field measurements were queried in a tab-separated format for each NWIS station and then parsed and converted into a unified data frame comprised of records for all sites.
URL links for each USGS site station were first created using the list of site numbers
The Python script for retrieving... field measurements from the NWIS web service... can be found on the public IFMHA GitHub page.

chunks.text: NHDPlus V2.1 attributes were added by extracting fields from GageLoc and NHDFlowline and linking them to IFMHA using site number and COMID. Where a site lacked a direct GageLoc correspondence, reach attributes were assigned from the nearest site within a 300 m buffer using a nearest-neighbor procedure in QGIS. This provides stream-network features such as stream order and slope alongside gage metadata.
supporting_quote: desired field attributes were extracted from the gage location (GageLoc) and NHD flow line network (NHDFlowline)... attributed to IFMHA using the USGS site number and the common identifiers (COMID)
assigned to the nearest site within a 300 meters buffer
StreamOrder... Slope of flowline (meters/meters)

chunks.text: Mean depth was estimated using the Mean Value Theorem for Integrals, implemented as cross-section area divided by top width. The approach was evaluated by computing mean depth from each record’s width and cross-sectional area and comparing against HYDRoSWOT measured mean depth. After validation, the same computation was applied to IFMHA to populate mean depth values and help address missingness.
supporting_quote: the values of the channel cross-section area were divided by their corresponding channel width
In order to estimate the mean depth, the ''Mean Value Theorem for Integrals'' is applied.
the mean depth is computed by dividing the area of the cross-section by the top width

chunks.text: Maximum depth was estimated from mean depth using line of organic correlation (LOC) regression. LOC is expressed as y = αx + β, where α and β are defined by the ratio of standard deviations and the means of variables. The HYDRoSWOT subset was used to calibrate the LOC slope and intercept and to evaluate predictive performance for maximum depth (thalweg proxy).
supporting_quote: adopted the line of organic correlation (LOC) regression to fit the best line
y = \alpha x + \beta
The HYDRoSWOT subset was used to calibrate the slope... and yintercept

chunks.text: Two conceptual cross-section shapes (trapezoid and parabola) were used to estimate channel geometry parameters at each site. For trapezoids, a half-channel relation T/2 = m*dmax + Bw/2 was fit using a Non-Negative Linear Regression (NNLR) so that side slope m remains nonnegative; the intercept represents half bottom width. For parabolic sections, dmax = a*(T/2)^2 was fit with no intercept to estimate the parabolic coefficient a.
supporting_quote: two different conceptual cross-section shapes (trapezoid, and parabola) were used to estimate channel geometry
a Non-Negative Linear Regression (NNLR) method was used
T/2 = m \times d_{max} + B_w/2
d_{max} = a \times (T/2)^2

chunks.text: Roughness (Manning’s n) was back-calculated using field discharge, area, slope, and hydraulic radius derived from estimated wetted perimeter. Hydraulic radius was computed as R = A/P, and wetted perimeter used trapezoidal geometry P = Btv + 2*dmax*sqrt(m^2+1). To assign a representative n per site, outliers beyond a 99% interval were removed and the median n was selected.
supporting_quote: using Manning's equation the roughness was calculated as follows, n = \frac{A \times R^{2/3} \times S^{1/2}}{Q}
R = \frac{A}{P}
P = B_{tv} + 2 \times d_{max} \times \sqrt{m^2 + 1}
the median of the calculated roughness coefficients was selected as the representative coefficient for that location

chunks.text: Filtering was applied before model evaluation to remove problematic measurements and isolate natural stream/channel conditions. Records with missing or zero values in key attributes were excluded, negative discharge observations were omitted (likely tidal/control sections), and only sites categorized as channels/streams were retained. For IFMHA analyses, sites with fewer than 50 observations were also removed to ensure meaningful statistics.
supporting_quote: records with missing and zero values for the desired field attributes... were excluded
sites that include negative discharge observations are omitted
Finally, only sites categorized as channels or streams are selected
only sites with over 50 observations were selected

chunks.text: IFMHA is a large compilation of USGS gage field measurements, totaling 2,802,532 records from 10,050 sites across the United States. Measurements span a long historical period, from 05-05-1845 to 10-24-2022 (retrieval date). The dataset is publicly available, together with source code, on GitHub.
supporting_quote: IFMHA includes 2,802,532 records from 10,050 sites (NWIS streamgaging stations).
The time span of these measurements is from 05-05-1845 to 10-24-2022
IFMHA dataset and the source codes used in this study are publicly available in the GitHub repository https://github.com/smhassanerfani/ifmha.

chunks.text: IFMHA extends HYDRoSWOT by incorporating the entire NWIS field-measurement record and multiple measurement methods beyond ADCP-only observations. The dataset includes method codes and frequencies, with large shares marked unspecified (UNSPE) and midsection mechanical methods (QSCMM), alongside ADCP moving-boat measurements (QADCP). This broad inclusion is intended to increase coverage and robustness compared to earlier compilations.
supporting_quote: IFMHA expands upon the HYDRoSWOT dataset by incorporating the entire record of field measurements within NWIS including different types of field measurement methods

chunks.text: HYDRoSWOT contributes station metadata and fixed attributes that can be linked by USGS site number, including station name, coordinates, drainage area, and site type. These common identifiers enable consistent attribution of station characteristics across IFMHA and HYDRoSWOT. The paper lists key HYDRoSWOT fields used for this linkage.
supporting_quote: constant stream and catchment features such as station names, geographic coordinates, drainage area, and steam types were extracted from HYDRoSWOT
site_no | Site number
drain_area_va | Drainage area (square mile)
site_tp_cd | Site type code

chunks.text: NWIS field measurement records provide per-visit hydraulic and cross-section attributes used in IFMHA, such as discharge, gage height, width, velocity, and area. These fields come from the NWIS web interface and were parsed into a unified dataframe. The dataset therefore supports computations based on the velocity-area method variables.
supporting_quote: The USGS provides public access to these measurements through the NWIS web interface under the category of surface water field measurement
discharge_va | The computed discharge (cfs)
chan_width | The channel width (ft)
chan_velocity | The mean velocity (ft/s)
chan_area | The channel area (ft²)

chunks.text: NHDPlus V2.1 adds geospatial stream-network attributes to IFMHA via GageLoc and NHDFlowline tables, linked using site number and COMID. Included attributes cover state identifiers, drainage area, stream feature type, modified Strahler stream order, and flowline slope. These enrich IFMHA with contextual variables useful for regional analysis and modeling.
supporting_quote: The desired field attributes were extracted from the gage location (GageLoc) and NHD flow line network (NHDFlowline)
StreamOrder | Modified Strahler Stream Order
Slope | Slope of flowline (meters/meters) based on smoothed elevations
ComID | Common identifier of the NHD feature

chunks.text: For model evaluation, a filtered HYDRoSWOT subset was created with 47,522 records across 5,914 sites after removing missing/zero values and excluding non-stream conditions. Summary statistics for discharge, area, width, and measured depths define the evaluation range, spanning very small to extremely large flows and cross-sections. This subset provides the ground truth for assessing mean and maximum depth models.
supporting_quote: After these filtrations, the subset of HYDRoSWOT used in the following analyses includes 47,522 records within 5914 sites
Count 47,522
Max depth (m) ... Max 62.69

chunks.text: The mean-depth model (area divided by width) matched HYDRoSWOT observations extremely well after outlier handling. Performance metrics show NSE of 0.99, correlation r of +0.99, RMSE of 0.17 m, and PBIAS of −3.46. The authors interpret these results as sufficiently strong to make alternative mean-depth models unnecessary for this application.
supporting_quote: Mean depth ... NSE 0.99 ... r +0.99 ... RMSE (m) 0.17 ... PBIAS −3.46
The results indicate a strong agreement between the estimated mean depth and ground truth data, with an NSE and r score of 0.99.
These exceptional results indicate that further exploration of alternative models is unnecessary.

chunks.text: Maximum depth estimated via LOC regression performed well against HYDRoSWOT measured maximum depth. Metrics report NSE of 0.94, r of +0.97, RMSE of 0.78 m, and PBIAS of 0.00. The results suggest the LOC relationship can reproduce both central tendencies and higher-end values in the filtered evaluation dataset.
supporting_quote: Max depth ... NSE 0.94 ... r +0.97 ... RMSE (m) 0.78 ... PBIAS 0.00
This model well performed on estimating maximum depth, with 0.94, and 0.97 for NSE and r scores, respectively.
model was able to cover a wide range of the upper bound values and outliers of data

chunks.text: The LOC calibration yielded a slope of 1.48 and intercept of −0.01 for predicting maximum depth from mean depth. Neglecting the small intercept implies a maximum-to-mean depth ratio near 1.50, which is consistent with parabolic cross-section behavior. The paper links this ratio to the parabolic identity d_mean = (2/3) d_max.
supporting_quote: The fitted parameters of the LOC regression... are 1.48 and −0.01, respectively.
the ratio of maximum-to-mean depth is close to the value of 1.50
d_{mean} = \frac{A}{T} = \frac{2}{3} \times d_{max}

chunks.text: For trapezoidal cross-section fitting, a maximum side-slope threshold of 12 (m/m) was applied, and negative bottom widths were omitted. Under these criteria, estimated parameters were within thresholds for 6,169 sites, representing 94.9% of all sites used in the cross-section parameter estimation.
