This indicates the NNLR-based trapezoid fitting was feasible for most sites.
supporting_quote: a maximum threshold of 12 (m/m) was set
negative values were omitted
calculated parameters were within the chosen thresholds for 6169 sites (94.9% of all sites)

chunks.text: Filtering produced large retained samples for IFMHA analyses: after removing missing/zero values and excluding non-natural stream conditions, and requiring at least 50 observations per site, 2,064,782 observations across 6,498 sites remained. This indicates that IFMHA can support statistically meaningful, site-level characterization across much of the continental US. The authors also map the spatial distribution of sites and record counts.
supporting_quote: Eventually, 2,064,782 observations (represented by 6498 sites) remained for the analyses.
only sites with over 50 observations were selected.
The geographical distribution of sites and the corresponding number of records are shown in Fig. 2.

chunks.text: When comparing wetted perimeter estimates derived from trapezoidal versus parabolic cross-sections at selected sites, the two approaches sometimes diverged substantially. The paper notes cases where results form a vertical line in scatter plots, implying trapezoidal wetted perimeter is dominated by bottom width for wide channels. Other sites show closer agreement along the diagonal, indicating a stronger role for side slopes in the trapezoidal parameterization.
supporting_quote: Fig. 8 compares the wetted perimeter estimated by trapezoidal and parabolic cross-sections for 12 randomly selected sites.
This shape implies that the wetted perimeter is dominated by the bottom width of the trapezoidal crosssection
For cases 03415000 and 02298123, the wetted perimeter estimated by both cross-sections aligns more with the diagonal line.

chunks.text: Manning’s roughness coefficients computed using trapezoidal and parabolic geometry were highly consistent across sites. The scatter comparison aligned closely with the identity line with R^2 = 0.98, with parabolic sections producing slightly higher n due to smaller wetted perimeter. This suggests cross-section shape choice has limited influence on the resulting n values for these computations.
supporting_quote: values of Manning's roughness coefficient on the scatter plot align closely with the identity line (R^2 = 0.98)
the parabolic cross-section yields slightly higher values for Manning's roughness coefficient
channel geometry does not have a significant impact on the values of Manning's roughness coefficient

chunks.text: To enforce a physically plausible upper bound on roughness, the study used a maximum Manning’s n threshold derived from roughness-selection guidelines. Among 6,169 sites with computed n values, 64 exceeded the maximum threshold (<0.4745) and were excluded from roughness comparison plots. This indicates a small subset of sites produced implausibly large n via back-calculation under the chosen assumptions.
supporting_quote: 64 had roughness coefficients calculated using Manning's equation that exceeded the maximum Manning's threshold (<0.4745)
these 64 sites were excluded from the plots presented in Fig. 10.

chunks.text: Comparisons of bankfull identification approaches showed that the 99th percentile discharge often exceeds the discharge associated with the stage–discharge curve inflection point (Parker’s rollover concept). In several examples, the 50th percentile (median) discharge appeared closer to the inflection point, though not consistently. The results indicate substantial variability across sites and motivate stochastic rather than deterministic bankfull inference from discharge percentiles alone.
supporting_quote: except for certain cases... the 99th percentile discharge is significantly higher than the inflection point.
for some locations... the median (50th percentile discharge) might better represent the inflection point
identifying bankfull characteristics given river discharge is not a straightforward task

chunks.text: The paper highlights that large datasets can contain inconsistent or misleading values that harm calibration and inference if not handled carefully. This is framed as a general limitation of large-sample hydrology that necessitates filtering, outlier handling, and cautious interpretation. IFMHA attempts to mitigate these issues through systematic exclusion of missing/zero values, negative discharges, and non-stream site types before analysis.
supporting_quote: care must be taken when using large datasets as data inconsistencies, sometimes referred to as disinformative data, can lead to model calibration and inference issues
records with missing and zero values... were excluded
sites that include negative discharge observations are omitted

chunks.text: Remote sensing river products are limited for geometry inference because they do not observe below the water surface and often miss small rivers. This constraint reduces their utility for deriving full channel cross-sections and motivates reliance on field measurements. The limitation also implies that even with new satellites, field-based compilations remain necessary for many hydraulic attributes.
supporting_quote: remote sensing products such as those offered by SWOT... cannot observe below the water surface
the small rivers are unobserved

chunks.text: The analysis suggests bankfull discharge identification is inherently uncertain when inferred from discharge statistics, because the stage–discharge relation is nonlinear and varies by site. The authors argue that watershed heterogeneity, turbulence, and erosion processes contribute to non-deterministic behavior, making a single percentile-based rule unreliable. They propose that stochastic approaches are more appropriate when sufficient samples are available.
supporting_quote: identifying bankfull characteristics given river discharge is not a straightforward task, as it depends on the nonlinear relationship between river discharge and stage.
influenced by other factors such as the heterogeneity of watersheds, the stochastic nature of turbulent flow
the modeling approach should also be stochastic

chunks.text: Back-calculating Manning’s n from field measurements and estimated geometry can yield extreme values that must be screened. The study applied a maximum threshold derived from roughness-selection guidance and excluded sites exceeding it from comparison plots. This reflects a limitation of indirect roughness estimation: errors or mismatches in geometry, slope, or discharge can propagate into implausible n values.
supporting_quote: used to estimate a maximum threshold for the roughness coefficients
exceeded the maximum Manning's threshold (<0.4745)
these 64 sites were excluded

chunks.text: The paper introduces IFMHA as a large-scale, publicly available dataset of USGS field measurements augmented with NHDPlusV2.1 attributes, providing hydraulic geometry information across 10,050 US streamgaging stations. By integrating multiple data sources and retaining extensive historical measurements, IFMHA is positioned as a resource for studying channel geometry and streamflow characteristics at scale. The dataset is intended to support improved flow routing, flood forecasting, and broader water-resources analyses.
supporting_quote: introducing IFMHA, a large-scale dataset for channel geometry and stream flow characteristics.
includes 2,802,532 records from 10,050 sites (NWIS gage stations)
IFMHA dataset and the source codes used in this study are publicly available in the GitHub repository

chunks.text: Conceptual models derived from IFMHA inputs can estimate mean depth, maximum depth, wetted perimeter, and roughness, and validation against HYDRoSWOT shows strong performance for depth estimation. Mean depth and maximum depth models achieved NSE values of 0.99 and 0.94, respectively, indicating reliable derivation of key geometry attributes from width and area measurements. These derived attributes can help fill missing values in existing records and provide consistent parameters for modeling applications.
supporting_quote: Mean depth ... NSE 0.99
Max depth ... NSE 0.94
IFMHA provides estimates for four channel geometry parameters (i.e., channel mean depth, maximum depth, wetted perimeter, and roughness) using conceptual models.
fill gaps in the existing channel geometry attributes, stemming from missing values

chunks.text: Because IFMHA provides many observations per site after filtering, it enables statistically significant, stochastic approaches for estimating channel properties and bankfull-related behavior. The paper argues that such probabilistic modeling is needed given the non-deterministic and site-specific nature of discharge–stage relationships. Overall, IFMHA expands the basis for regional and site-scale hydraulic geometry inference across the contiguous United States.
supporting_quote: To employ a reliable probabilistic approach, it is essential to have a sufficient number of samples for statistical significance.
By providing statistically significant data for each site, the IFMHA dataset enables stochastic approaches
Eventually, 2,064,782 observations (represented by 6498 sites) remained for the analyses.

chunks.text: The paper positions itself beyond using AI purely for environmental prediction and instead focuses on AI that assists the full hydrological modelling workflow. It highlights how foundation models and LLMs have recently shown capabilities in scientific reasoning and domain understanding, enabling new forms of AI-assisted model development and analysis. This shift opens possibilities for improved workflow efficiency and new modes of knowledge integration across studies, provided scientific interpretation remains grounded in human expertise.
supporting_quote: we depart from traditional applications of AI to environmental prediction through machine learning models ... and explore the potential of AI to assist in the modelling process itself.
The emergence of foundation models capable of reasoning about complex scientific problems ... opens new possibilities for AI-assisted model workflows

chunks.text: The authors frame hydrological modelling as increasingly complex, with many configuration choices across processes, scales, and parameterizations, and with uncertainty about which decisions matter most across diverse hydroclimatic settings. They argue this complexity creates high-dimensional decision spaces that are difficult to navigate consistently. AI agents are proposed as a way to reduce cognitive load and help users make context-sensitive modelling choices.
supporting_quote: Modern hydrological models demand complex decisionmaking across numerous processes ... scales ... and parameterizations
alleviate the cognitive load associated with decision-making in high-dimensional spaces
chunks.section_hint: How AI Agents Can Transform How Researchers Interact With Complex Modelling Systems

chunks.text: The commentary emphasizes the need to balance the opportunities of automation with the risk of weakening scientific understanding and amplifying biases present in existing hydrologic knowledge. It explicitly argues that AI tools should not replace scientists but should support them, while core scientific discovery activities remain under human agency. The paper frames AI as potentially helpful for managing technical complexity and suggesting hypotheses, but only with human validation and oversight.
supporting_quote: requires finding the appropriate balance between the transformative opportunities of automation and the real risk in deteriorating scientific understanding
AI systems should be viewed not as replacements for human scientists but as tools

chunks.text: The paper’s goal is to explore how AI systems can assist hydrological modelling workflows end-to-end, from conceptualization to calibration and uncertainty analysis, rather than acting only as predictive models. It aims to articulate theoretical foundations and an architecture for AI-assisted environmental modelling with expert-system characteristics. The discussion is grounded in the authors’ practical experience using LLMs to support modelling decisions and documentation.
supporting_quote: we explore the potential of AI systems to improve environmental modelling workflows ... from initial conceptualization through to parameter estimation and uncertainty analysis
We focus our discussion on our recent experience in using Large Language Models (LLMs) to assist in hydrological modelling workflows.

chunks.text: A central objective is to evaluate whether LLMs can help address three modelling challenges: expanding decision complexity, lack of reproducible and well-documented workflows, and barriers to adopting advanced practices. The paper frames these as actionable targets for AI agents within a modelling workflow. The evaluation is pursued through the design and use of a prototype framework.
supporting_quote: evaluate the extent to which LLMs can address three critical challenges in modern hydrological modelling: (1) The growing complexity ... (2) the need for reproducible ... workflows, and (3) the technical barriers limiting broader adoption
chunks.section_hint: How AI Agents Can Transform How Researchers Interact With Complex Modelling Systems

chunks.text: The framework is intended to maintain detailed provenance of modelling decisions and their justifications, forming a knowledge base that supports learning across studies. The authors aim for a system that can record alternatives and rationales so that workflows can be revisited, understood, and transferred to similar settings. This is presented as a pathway to improve community best practices and scientific rigor.
supporting_quote: maintain detailed provenance of modelling decisions and their justifications, creating a dynamic knowledge base that facilitates learning from past experiences
systematically logging all modelling decisions, complete with justifications and alternative options considered

chunks.text: Hydrological modelling requires many interacting choices across processes, scales, and parameterizations, yet the importance of these decisions and their best configuration is often unclear across environmental regimes. This creates a large decision space where users can struggle to select appropriate structures and settings. The paper frames AI support as potentially helpful for providing context-sensitive recommendations based on watershed attributes and data availability.
supporting_quote: The relative importance of these decisions and their optimal configuration remains unclear
supported by using LLMs to provide context-sensitive recommendations ... by selecting model structures and process representations
chunks.section_hint: How AI Agents Can Transform How Researchers Interact With Complex Modelling Systems

chunks.text: Reproducibility is identified as a persistent issue because modelling decisions and their rationale are frequently underdocumented. This underdocumentation makes it hard for other scientists to understand, evaluate, or reuse workflows. The authors propose AI-assisted logging and provenance tracking as a response to this reproducibility gap.
supporting_quote: Reproducibility remains a core challenge in hydrology, as modelling decisions and their rationale are often underdocumented
systematically logging all modelling decisions, complete with justifications
chunks.section_hint: How AI Agents Can Transform How Researchers Interact With Complex Modelling Systems

chunks.text: Technical barriers hinder broader adoption of advanced hydrological modelling because workflows often require extensive data preprocessing, parameter estimation, and integrating diverse data sources. These tasks create a high burden for researchers, especially in settings with limited training or resources. The paper frames automation and expert guidance as a way to reduce these barriers while preserving data integrity.
supporting_quote: Hydrological modelling involves extensive data preprocessing, parameter estimation, and the integration of diverse data sources, each posing substantial technical challenges.
Through automation of routine tasks like data acquisition and preprocessing, AI assistance could help reduce technical barriers
chunks.section_hint: How AI Agents Can Transform How Researchers Interact With Complex Modelling Systems

chunks.text: A key risk highlighted is that many regions—particularly the Global South and remote areas—are underrepresented in LLM training data due to historical data scarcity. This can perpetuate or amplify existing knowledge gaps if AI guidance is biased toward well-represented environments. The paper treats representativeness as both an equity issue and a technical threat to modelling validity.
supporting_quote: historical data scarcity in many regions of the world, particularly in the Global South and remote areas
critically underrepresented in the training data of large language models, potentially perpetuating and amplifying existing knowledge gaps

chunks.text: The authors introduce INDRA (Intelligent Network for Dynamic River Analysis) as a prototype AI-assisted framework built as a network of specialized LLM expert agents. INDRA uses a chairperson agent to coordinate dialogue among domain experts (e.g., hydrology, hydrogeology, meteorology, data science, geospatial analysis). The method is designed to mirror collaborative scientific discussions while preserving clear documentation of decision rationales and supporting extensibility to new agents.
supporting_quote: we introduce INDRA (the Intelligent Network for Dynamic River Analysis), a novel prototype framework that leverages AI through a network of specialised Large Language Model (LLM) expert agents.
The system implements a chairperson agent that coordinates interactions between domain experts, including specialists in hydrology, hydrogeology, meteorology, data science, and geospatial analysis.
chunks.section_hint: A Prototype Platform for Exploring AI Management of Workflows

chunks.text: INDRA is implemented to interface with CONFLUENCE, a configuration-driven modelling framework that manages steps from domain definition and discretization to evaluation and reporting. CONFLUENCE uses a centralized configuration file to control the workflow, and INDRA’s agents propose settings and changes for that file based on modelling context and objectives. This enables both generating new configurations and reviewing existing ones, potentially iteratively.
supporting_quote: INDRA operates by interfacing with CONFLUENCE ... a comprehensive modelling framework that manages the hydrological modelling process through a centralised configuration system.
each step controlled through a single, central configuration file
chunks.section_hint: A Prototype Platform for Exploring AI Management of Workflows

chunks.text: A core mechanism is translating agent recommendations into explicit configuration parameters while logging all modifications with justifications. This is meant to preserve provenance by directly linking the reasoning of expert agents to concrete model implementation choices. The system supports proactive guidance (suggesting settings) and reactive assistance (reviewing and improving existing setups) via the same configuration interface.
supporting_quote: These recommendations are translated directly into configuration parameters, maintaining a clear link between expert reasoning and model implementation.
All modifications to the configuration are logged with their justifications, creating a comprehensive record of modelling decisions and their rationales.
chunks.section_hint: A Prototype Platform for Exploring AI Management of Workflows

chunks.text: The paper proposes adding robust verification mechanisms in future INDRA development, notably retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) connected to domain-specific databases. This is intended to support authoritative information retrieval and reduce hallucinations in scientific workflows. The authors also plan to explore multi-model instantiation of agents using different LLM APIs to mitigate biases tied to any single model.
supporting_quote: Future development of INDRA will prioritise robust verification mechanisms, including the implementation of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems integrated with domain-specific databases
we plan to explore multi-model frameworks where different LLM APIs are used for agent instantiation
chunks.section_hint: A Prototype Platform for Exploring AI Management of Workflows

chunks.text: To address reproducibility, the authors propose systematic documentation that adheres to FAIR principles and records uncertainty and confidence associated with decisions. This approach aims to make modelling assumptions and limitations transparent and revisitable. The logged record is positioned as a tool for knowledge transfer between similar studies and for community best practices.
supporting_quote: This creates a dynamic record that adheres to FAIR principles
documenting the uncertainty and confidence levels associated with different choices
chunks.section_hint: How AI Agents Can Transform How Researchers Interact With Complex Modelling Systems

chunks.text: The paper states that the INDRA and CONFLUENCE codebases are openly available as GitHub repositories under the GNU General Public Licence v3.0. It also notes that template configurations and usage instructions are provided in repository README files. This availability is presented as enabling reuse and transparency.
supporting_quote: The code for the frameworks presented in this paper is openly available in the following GitHub repositories:—INDRA: https://github.com/DarriEy/INDRA—CONFLUENCE: https://github.com/DarriEy/CONFLUENCE
All repositories are released under the GNU General Public Licence v3.0 Licence.

chunks.text: In implementation experiments across LLM APIs, the authors observed substantial differences in reliability. Earlier and smaller models, particularly Llama variants, were described as unreliable for documentation generation, including producing plausible but non-existent citations. More recent models, specifically Claude-3.5-Sonnet, showed improved reliability in similar tasks, with no detected errors reported by the authors.
supporting_quote: Earlier and smaller models, particularly the Llama variants, were unreliable ... most notably in the generation of plausible but non-existent citations and references.
Claude-3.5-Sonnet ... demonstrated markedly improved reliability with no detected errors in similar tasks.
chunks.section_hint: A Prototype Platform for Exploring AI Management of Workflows

chunks.text: The paper warns that AI-augmented modelling can introduce computational overhead that may become a barrier in regions with limited computing resources. It also notes that these limitations may interact with historical data scarcity, worsening representational gaps in AI guidance. These issues could reduce the accessibility and fairness of AI-assisted hydrology if not addressed in system design and deployment.
supporting_quote: the computational overhead of AI systems may create new technical barriers, particularly in regions with limited computing resources.
historical data scarcity ... meaning that many hydrological environments ... are critically underrepresented in the training data

chunks.text: A central limitation is the risk that automated recommendations may obscure technical nuances or propagate errors if implemented without validation. The paper argues that AI guidance can influence scientific decisions, so insufficient scrutiny could degrade modelling quality. It emphasizes the necessity of maintaining human oversight in critical evaluation and decision-making.
supporting_quote: automated workflows risk obscuring important technical nuances or propagating errors if AI recommendations are implemented without sufficient validation.
maintaining the essential role of human expertise in critical evaluation and decision-making.

chunks.text: The authors identify several systematic biases that can arise in AI-assisted modelling platforms: documentation bias, consensus bias, data availability bias, and temporal bias. These biases can lead to overuse of well-documented or widely used configurations, neglect sparse-data processes, or under-account for non-stationarity under climate change. The paper presents these as key dangers requiring active mitigation.
supporting_quote: documentation bias may favour well-documented approaches
consensus bias can lead to over-reliance on widelyused model configurations
data availability bias may skew recommendations
temporal bias could result in recommendations that inadequately account for non-stationarity

chunks.text: As mitigations, the paper proposes design choices such as explicit diversity requirements in recommendations, uncertainty quantification that accounts for bias, transparent documentation of reasoning, and interfaces that prompt users to apply local knowledge. It also recommends regular validation comparing AI recommendations with expert decisions across diverse contexts. These steps are presented as necessary to prevent AI systems from constraining modelling choices and to support responsible adoption.
supporting_quote: implements explicit diversity requirements in recommendation algorithms
incorporates uncertainty quantification specifically accounting for potential biases
interfaces that actively prompt users to critically evaluate recommendations against their local knowledge
regular validation protocols comparing AI recommendations against expert decisions across diverse hydrological contexts

chunks.text: The paper cautions that over-reliance on AI could erode deep process understanding and stifle creative scientific thinking. It argues that AI knowledge is bounded by training data and might fail to represent emerging conditions under climate change. This is presented as a scientific, not only technical, danger of AI-augmented research workflows.
supporting_quote: there is a real danger that over-reliance on automated guidance could erode deep process understanding.
The system's knowledge base ... is inherently bounded by its training data
the convenience of AI assistance could potentially stifle the creative scientific thinking

chunks.text: The paper concludes that AI-assisted modelling frameworks should be treated as tools that enhance, not replace, human experts by shifting effort away from routine tasks and toward higher-level scientific questions. It argues that realizing benefits requires preserving human judgement and process understanding while using AI to manage complexity. The authors frame this as a responsibility of the hydrological community to define appropriate AI roles and oversight.
supporting_quote: Rather than replacing human experts, these tools should be viewed as enhancing their capabilities
allowing human experts to focus on higherlevel scientific questions and complex decision-making

chunks.text: A forward-looking conclusion is that AI assistance could help democratize hydrological modelling in understudied regions by reducing technical barriers and offering reasoned guidance, but only if equitable global access is ensured. The paper suggests cloud-based deployments and institutional partnerships as potential ways to reduce computational and financial barriers. This democratization is tied to improving understanding and management in watersheds with limited modelling capacity.
supporting_quote: The democratisation of hydrological modelling through AI assistance presents unprecedented opportunities
Realising this democratisation potential will critically depend on ensuring equitable access ... potentially through cloud-based deployments and institutional partnerships

chunks.text: The authors argue that AI-augmented workflows may reshape scientific discovery by identifying patterns across studies, suggesting hypotheses, and helping design experiments, but success depends on maintaining human oversight of interpretation. They conclude that the field must balance AI’s capabilities with protections for scientific innovation and understanding. The path forward is framed as leveraging AI while preserving fundamental human elements of discovery.
supporting_quote: they could begin to influence the trajectory of the scientific discovery process itself, identifying patterns across studies, suggesting novel hypotheses and helping to design experiments
requires careful balance—leveraging AI's capabilities ... while maintaining and enabling human oversight

chunks.text: Rapid urbanization alters land surface properties and local climate through reduced vegetation and increased impervious cover, affecting energy balance, moisture, and runoff. A key outcome is the urban heat island (UHI), where urban areas are warmer than surrounding rural areas due to heat-absorbing materials and anthropogenic heat. UHI intensity is also influenced by urban geometry, land cover, and prevailing climate conditions, and can be amplified during heatwaves.
supporting_quote: Urbanization significantly impacts the environment in many ways, including a substantial decrease in evapotranspiration... caused by the expansion of impervious surfaces
One of the most notable effects of urbanization is the emergence of urban heat islands (UHI)... natural landscapes... are replaced with hard, dry, and impervious materials

chunks.text: Urban heat poses major health risks, ranging from dehydration and heat stroke to exacerbation of cardiovascular and respiratory illnesses. During heat waves, UHI intensification can increase emergency service demand, morbidity, and heat-related deaths. Heat can also worsen air pollution (e.g., ground-level ozone), compounding health impacts.
supporting_quote: Exposure to heat is associated with a range of adverse health outcomes including dehydration, heat stroke, heat exhaustion
The amplification of UHI during periods of heat wave events exacerbates adverse health impacts... increased morbidity, and heat-related deaths

chunks.text: Heat impacts are unevenly distributed because vulnerability depends on neighborhood demographics and socioeconomic conditions. Older adults, low-income residents, and socially isolated people often face higher risk due to higher exposure, poorer housing conditions, limited resources, and reduced capacity to respond. Many studies also note that inner-city areas tend to be hotter and poorer, producing disproportionate impacts.
supporting_quote: UHI adverse impacts affect urban populations differently, and the associated risk is unevenly distributed
Older people are among those most likely to be affected by UHI adverse effects
Higher UHI intensity generally occurs over inner cities, where poorer populations tend to be concentrated

chunks.text: The study aimed to assess urban heat vulnerability at the block group level in Alabama cities using a vulnerability index that combines exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity. It targeted Birmingham and Montgomery (large cities) and Auburn–Opelika (smaller conurbation) to compare how drivers of vulnerability differ across urban contexts. The outputs were intended to support location-specific policy design through mapping and index deconstruction.
supporting_quote: This research assessed urban heat vulnerability at block group level in three Alabama cities: Birmingham, Montgomery, and Auburn-Opelika.
We then developed a UHI vulnerability index at block group level by aggregating environmental and socioeconomic variables into three determinants: exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity.

chunks.text: A methodological goal was to derive land surface temperature (LST) using multiple Landsat 8 images across several years rather than a single-day snapshot. By generating composite, cloud-minimized products for LST and NDVI, the study sought a more robust characterization of summer heat exposure. This approach supports block-group scale comparisons within and across cities.
supporting_quote: Unlike many studies that relied on satellite images capturing surface temperature for a single day to calculate LST, our approach involved utilizing a collection of satellite images spanning several years for each city.
Our study employed for each city a collection of ten images from Landsat 8 satellite data... ranging from 2013 to 2021

chunks.text: Despite broad interest in UHIs, the authors identify a research gap for mid-sized and small cities and for comparative, multi-city analyses. Because each city’s microclimate, urban form, and population characteristics differ, findings from large-city studies may not generalize. This motivates detailed, local-scale assessments and policy designs tailored to the specific city context.
supporting_quote: there exists a notable research gap regarding various aspects of UHI in mid-sized and small-sized cities
the case of each city is unique, given the varying regional geographic settings, microclimates, heterogeneity and diversity of local urban populations

chunks.text: Vulnerability to urban heat arises from intertwined physical, demographic, and socioeconomic factors, complicating interpretation based solely on temperature patterns. Neighborhood-level differences in exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity can yield different risk profiles even under similar heat conditions. The study frames this as requiring granular analyses to identify localized hotspots and their drivers.
supporting_quote: UHI impacts affect urban populations differently, and the associated risk is unevenly distributed
vulnerability to urban heat depends on a complex interplay of physical, social, and economic factors

chunks.text: The study defines vulnerability using the IPCC framework as the combination of exposure and sensitivity minus adaptive capacity. Exposure and sensitivity represent potential impacts of the hazard, while adaptive capacity reflects the ability to cope and adapt. The approach produces a composite index intended to highlight high-vulnerability block groups.
supporting_quote: vulnerability is considered as a function of three determinants: exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity
Vulnerability = (Exposure + Sensitivity) - Adaptive Capacity

chunks.text: Land surface temperature (LST) was retrieved from Landsat 8 using a multi-step algorithm that converts thermal band radiance to brightness temperature and then to LST with emissivity estimated from NDVI and proportion of vegetation. The study used ArcMap tools (Raster Calculator, Zonal Statistics) to compute average LST by block group. Processing was performed on clipped city subsets.
supporting_quote: Landsat 8 bands 4 and 5 and thermal band 10 were used to retrieve LST
The main steps are (1) to retrieve... TOA... (2) convert... to Brightness Temperature (BT)... (3) compute... NDVI... (6) calculate LST using BT and ε

chunks.text: To reduce cloud and noise effects across the multi-year image set, the study created maximum-value composites (MVC) for thermal band 10 and for NDVI derived from bands 4 and 5. The resulting single composite image represented the 2013–2021 summer period and was used for subsequent spatial analyses. This was intended to improve robustness compared to single-scene LST estimates.
supporting_quote: ArcMap's Cell Statistics tool was used to create a maximum-value composite (MVC) for band 10
This combination of all bands resulted in a single cloud-free image over the 2013–2021 period

chunks.text: Sensitivity and adaptive capacity subindices were built from normalized indicators using factor analysis (FA) with varimax rotation to derive weights. Suitability for FA was tested with KMO and Bartlett’s test; the number of factors retained was determined via parallel analysis. Final indicator weights were derived from squared loadings and factor variances, scaled to sum to one.
supporting_quote: Factor analysis (FA) with varimax rotation was used to assign weights to variables for two subindices: sensitivity and adaptive capacity.
The Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) test and Bartlett's test of sphericity were used to verify whether FA was suitable for the data.

chunks.text: Soil moisture memory (SMM) describes how long soil moisture perturbations persist and is important for land–atmosphere feedbacks relevant to subseasonal-to-seasonal prediction. SMM provides a way to evaluate how quickly models lose water through evapotranspiration and drainage. Prior work using satellite products (notably SMAP) has enabled large-scale assessment of soil moisture dynamics, though root-zone observations remain limited.
supporting_quote: Soil moisture memory (SMM), which refers to how long a perturbation in soil moisture (SM) can last, is critical for understanding climatic, hydrological, and ecosystem interactions.
The influence of soil moisture on climate predictions at seasonal-tosubseasonal (S2S) scales is well-recognized due to its role in the exchange of surface energy and water fluxes with the atmosphere

Recent advancements in remote sensing observations have enabled analyses of interactions between near-surface soil and the atmosphere. Nonetheless, the paucity of root zone data complicates the investigation of deep soil dynamics.

chunks.text: A hybrid view of SMM separates short-term (energy-limited) and long-term (water-limited) regimes. Energy-limited memory typically lasts hours to a few days, while water-limited memory spans weeks to seasons. In this framing, drainage and evapotranspiration dominate different parts of the memory behavior, motivating regime-specific metrics.
supporting_quote: McColl et al. (2019) organized soil water loss into two main categories: water-limited (long-term) and energylimited (short-term).
The energy-limited regime is a process where water loss is constrained by available energy and lasts from hours to a few days.
In contrast, the waterlimited regime is a process where water loss depends on the available water and spans longer periods, such as weeks, months, and seasons.
McColl et al. (2019) specified that ET and drainage are the main controllers of long-term and short-term memories, respectively.

chunks.text: Soil moisture memory can be computed using various autocorrelation-based approaches, but modern high-resolution data encourage event-based, drydown-focused calculations. The study adopts the hybrid model approach that treats water-limited drydowns deterministically and energy-limited behavior stochastically to account for unresolved processes. This provides comparable SMM estimates for satellite and model time series.
supporting_quote: Determining SMM is not straightforward due to the variety of calculation methods proposed by researchers
Traditionally, soil moisture has been conceptualized as a red noise process, forming the basis for SMM calculations
Consequently, there has been a shift away from their use towards recent high-resolution observational and modeling data.
McColl et al. (2019) proposed a stochastic equation to capture the unresolved nature of energy-limited processes.

chunks.text: The study investigates whether land surface models miss or misrepresent soil hydrological processes that control soil moisture memory. It evaluates how soil hydraulic parameterizations and explicit representations of surface ponding and preferential flow affect both surface (5 cm) and root-zone (up to 1 m) SMM. Model configurations are compared against SMAP and in situ benchmarks over the CONUS for 2015–2019 to identify key processes that reduce typical LSM SMM biases.
supporting_quote: We attempt to answer a question: do LSMs miss or misrepresent key hydrological processes controlling SMM?
we use a version of Noah-MP with advanced hydrology that explicitly represents preferential flow and surface ponding and provides optional schemes of soil hydraulics.

We compare SMMs computed from various Noah-MP configurations against that derived from the Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) L3 soil moisture and in situ measurements from the International Soil Moisture Network (ISMN) from the years 2015 to 2019 over the contiguous United States (CONUS).

chunks.text: A specific objective is to test whether switching soil hydraulics from Brooks–Corey/Clapp–Hornberger to Van Genuchten improves SMM, and how adding ponding thresholds and a dual-permeability preferential-flow representation changes SMM across regimes. The intent is to provide guidance for LSM development for S2S prediction by identifying which process representations most affect SMM timescales.
supporting_quote: we designed and implemented five scenarios to focus on the impacts of key missing processes and different hydraulic parameterizations.
These scenarios include two soil hydraulic models (Clapp and Hornberger and Van Genuchten), a dual-permeability model representing preferential flow, and three surface-ponding thresholds.
We suggest that LSMs for use in seasonal-to-subseasonal climate prediction should, at least, adopt the Van Genuchten hydraulic scheme.

chunks.text: Many land surface models tend to overestimate surface soil moisture persistence, producing overly long soil moisture memory and sustained evaporation during drydown. Prior multi-model evaluations have found LSMs overestimate long-term memory in water-limited regimes and underestimate short-term memory in energy-limited regimes compared to SMAP-derived estimates. This study frames these biases as potentially rooted in missing or misrepresented hydrological processes and soil hydraulic parameter uncertainty.
supporting_quote: Most land surface models (LSMs) tend to overestimate surface soil moisture and its persistency (or SMM), sustaining spuriously large soil surface evaporation during dry-down periods.
LSMs generally overestimate memory in water-limited regimes and significantly underestimate it in energy-limited regimes.

Current LSMs may not be enough to address the uncertainties in SMM estimates for incomplete representations of key hydrological processes controlling SMM and uncertainties in soil hydraulic parameters

chunks.text: Model refinement and evaluation are hindered by limitations in observations, particularly for the root zone, and by uncertainties in how SMM should be computed. Satellite observations have limited ability to resolve drainage, a key energy-limited process in the hybrid framework. These issues motivate using a hybrid SMM method and combining satellite with in situ data for benchmarking.
supporting_quote: Refinement of soil moisture–precipitation feedback in LSMs is hindered by the lack of large-scale observational data
Nonetheless, the paucity of root zone data complicates the investigation of deep soil dynamics.
McColl et al. (2019) highlighted that drainage is not a process that is completely resolved by satellite observations.

chunks.text: The study computes SMM using the hybrid model of McColl et al. (2019), separating long-term water-limited memory (τL) from short-term energy-limited memory (τS). Water-limited memory is estimated by fitting an exponential drydown curve to selected precipitation-free intervals and extracting τL. Short-term memory is computed directly from the hybrid formulation and is interpreted as being dominated by drainage at SMAP-like sampling frequency.
supporting_quote: McColl et al. (2019) considered the SMM concept as it relates to two regimes: (a) the memory of a water-limited regime (τL)
In the analysis of water-limited memory, we fitted Eq. (2) to the soil moisture time series during specific dry-down intervals. Then, τL was extracted as a parameter from the fitting curve
In contrast, short-term memory was determined directly using Eq. (3)
McColl et al. (2019) declared that the short-term memory in their hybrid model is dominated by drainage when the sampling is relatively high (as in the case of SMAP's sampling frequency of 3 d).

chunks.text: Noah-MP is configured with advanced soil hydrology by solving a mixed-form (θ–h) Richards equation that can represent saturated conditions. This enables explicit representation of surface ponding, infiltration of ponded water, and infiltration-excess runoff when ponding exceeds a threshold. The solver uses adaptive time stepping to improve pressure head accuracy and mass conservation.
supporting_quote: The current Noah-MP adopts the methodology of Celia et al. (1990) to solve the mass-pressure (θ − h) mixed-form (MF) RE.
Surface ponding occurs when the pressure head of the surface layer is greater than the air entry pressure
Infiltration-excess runoff occurs when the surface-ponding depth, Htop, surpasses a predefined threshold, Htop,max
To achieve a more accurate solution of h and the mass balance, the solver uses an adaptive time-stepping scheme.

chunks.text: The model includes optional soil hydraulic schemes, allowing comparison between Van Genuchten–Mualem and Brooks–Corey/Clapp–Hornberger parameterizations. The Brooks–Corey/Clapp–Hornberger retention curve is smoothed near saturation to facilitate convergence. These options are central experimental factors for assessing their effects on SMM.
supporting_quote: The current Noah-MP provides optional hydraulics schemes of the Van Genuchten–Mualem (VGM) and Brooks–Corey with Clapp–Hornberger (BC/CH) parameters.
To facilitate quicker convergence, particularly near saturation, we smoothed the BC/CH water retention curve using a polynomial function

chunks.text: Preferential flow is represented using a dual-permeability model that partitions the soil into macropore and matrix domains. The approach uses a macropore area/volume fraction (Fa) to aggregate water content and fluxes across domains and includes transfer between domains (lateral infiltration/diffusion). This representation affects infiltration, evaporation, and groundwater recharge flux partitioning.
supporting_quote: To represent preferential flow, the current Noah-MP adopts a Dual-Permeability Model (DPM) approach, partitioning the model grid into two domains
This approach represents subgrid variability in infiltration capacity through a fractional area of soil macropores in the fields Fa
The aggregated water content (θ) and vertical water flux (q) for a grid cell are given by θ = Faθa+(1−Fa)θi and q = Faqa+(1−Fa)qi

chunks.text: Five Noah-MP experiments are run over 2014–2019 with repeated spinup; the last iteration is analyzed for 2015–2019 SMM. Experiments vary by soil hydraulics (BC/CH vs VGM), ponding depth threshold (Htop,max = 0, 50, 200 mm), and inclusion of dual-permeability preferential flow. All experiments use the same soil layering strategy extending to bedrock (minimum 4.0 m; maximum 49.0 m).
supporting_quote: We conducted five experiments using the current Noah-MP driven by the hourly NLDAS-2 forcing data at a spatial resolution of 0.125°, starting with the same uniform initial conditions
The five initial iterations were dedicated to the model's spinup phase, and the resulting surface and root zone soil moisture from the last iteration were used for SMM analysis.
The first condition, designated MF_VGM0, excluded the ponding effect by setting Htop,max to 0 mm.
the second condition, identified as MF_VGM200, incorporated a significant ponding depth of 200 mm.

with a minimum bedrock depth of 4.0 m.
fixed layer thicknesses ... down to 49.0 m

Noah-MP soil moisture is sampled at corresponding SMAP observation times to minimize temporal sampling biases in SMM estimation.

Noah-MP simulations are run from 2014–2019 with multiple spinup iterations, and SMM is computed for both the surface 5 cm and root zone up to 1 m. This common spatiotemporal frame supports comparisons among SMAP, ISMN, and model scenarios.

chunks.text: Soil hydraulics strongly control long-term surface SMM patterns and biases. The MF_CH (Brooks–Corey/Clapp–Hornberger) setup produces a spatial pattern opposite to SMAP, with longer τL in arid western regions and shorter τL in wet northeastern regions. Switching to Van Genuchten hydraulics yields patterns more consistent with SMAP, with higher τL in the eastern humid regions and lower τL in the arid west.
supporting_quote: The MF_CH experiment displays a spatial pattern that contrasts with the SMAP data, with a longer memory in the arid western regions but a shorter memory in the wet northeastern regions
Further examination reveals that models using the Van Genuchten scheme reflect SMAP's patterns. Specifically, the eastern regions display higher τL values, while the western regions show lower values

chunks.text: In drier, less-vegetated regions (NDVI < 0.45), the CH hydraulics overestimate long-term surface τL relative to SMAP, while Van Genuchten configurations closely match SMAP’s distribution. The MF_CH median is 10.53 d versus SMAP’s 8.47 d. Van Genuchten experiments show medians around 8.6 d and produce PDFs similar to SMAP, mitigating long-term memory overestimation noted in earlier studies.
supporting_quote: In the dry areas (see Fig. 4a), the probability distribution function (PDF) of the surface SMM from MF_CH differs from that of SMAP and exhibits a higher median of 10.53 d compared to SMAP's 8.47 d (overestimation).
Other model scenarios using van Genuchten (VG) hydraulics, with an SMM median of around 8.6 d, show a PDF like SMAP's.
Note that the VGM scenarios effectively tackle the problem of long-term memory overestimation

chunks.text: Explicit surface ponding generally increases long-term memory in wet regions for the surface layer. Removing ponding (MF_VGM0, Htop,max=0 mm) leads to shorter τL than configurations with ponding thresholds of 50–200 mm. In wet regions, MF_VGM0 has a median τL of 10.72 d, whereas MF_VGM200 and MF_VGM are about 12.05 d and 12.03 d, respectively, implying that ponded-water infiltration sustains longer persistence.
supporting_quote: MF_VGM0 (with a zero ponding depth threshold) shows a shorter long-term SMM, with a median of 10.72 d, compared to MF_VGM200 ... with a median of 12.05 d and MF_VGM ... with a median of 12.03 d.
This suggests that extra water inputs from the surface-ponded water (MF_VGM200) can help extend the surface SMM.

chunks.text: Changing the ponding threshold from 50 to 200 mm has only a marginal effect on surface long-term τL, suggesting a non-proportional response once ponding is allowed. MF_VGM and MF_VGM200 have nearly identical wet-region medians (12.03 d vs 12.05 d). This indicates that enabling ponding matters more than increasing the maximum ponding threshold in this range.
supporting_quote: Changing the ponding depth threshold from 50 mm (MF_VGM) to 200 mm (MF_vGM200) has a marginal effect on τL
MF_VGM200 ... with a median of 12.05 d and MF_VGM ... with a median of 12.03 d.

chunks.text: Preferential flow (DPM_VGM) alters surface SMM by promoting faster drainage and reducing long-term τL compared to MF_VGM under the same ponding threshold. In wet regions, DPM_VGM has a median surface τL of 11.73 d versus 12.03 d for MF_VGM. The paper interprets this as preferential pathways accelerating topsoil water loss, shortening persistence in the surface layer.
supporting_quote: With the same 50 mm ponding threshold, DPM_VGM produces a shorter SMM, with a median of 11.73 d, than MF_VGM
indicating that the effects of faster water drainage of the topsoil water caused by the preferential flow (as represented by DPM_VGM)

chunks.text: For short-term surface SMM (τS), all scenarios broadly reproduce the SMAP spatial pattern, with longer τS in the drier western CONUS and shorter τS in the wetter east. The CH hydraulics underestimates τS in dry regions (median 1.9 d) compared with SMAP (median 2.02 d). Van Genuchten scenarios produce higher dry-region medians (~2.09 d), helping rectify the short-term underestimation reported for many LSMs.

chunks.text: Across experiments, soil water retention (soil hydraulics) is identified as the most important control on SMM. Adopting Van Genuchten parameterization mitigates the common LSM issue of overestimating long-term surface SMM associated with Brooks–Corey/Clapp–Hornberger. The paper recommends that LSMs used for subseasonal-to-seasonal prediction adopt Van Genuchten hydraulics.

chunks.text: Explicit representation of surface ponding increases the time available for infiltration, which extends long-term memory in both surface and root-zone layers while tending to reduce short-term memory. This effect arises because ponded water sustains soil wetness and prolongs persistence through the profile. The study treats ponding as a key missing process in many LSMs with implications for SMM biases.

chunks.text: Including preferential flow via a dual-permeability approach improves overall soil moisture dynamics and affects both short- and long-term SMM by accelerating drainage along macropore pathways. The paper concludes that combining improved hydraulics with ponding and preferential flow can address long-term memory overestimation and short-term underestimation problems seen in LSMs. It also notes that macropore parameterization may need refinement for best performance.

chunks.text: Hydrologic models are widely used for flood forecasting, water management, and climate change impact assessment. Deep learning models (notably LSTM) have recently shown superior streamflow and other hydrologic-variable prediction skill, but they are often difficult to interpret and lack explicit physical constraints. Process-based models, while constrained by physical laws like mass balance and able to output many diagnostic variables, often struggle to match DL accuracy and can be costly to calibrate basin by basin. This motivates hybrid approaches that integrate data-driven learning with physically based model structure.
supporting_quote: Hydrologic models are vital tools to model and elucidate the terrestrial water cycle, and they have been widely used in flood forecasting
Recently, deep learning (DL) models have demonstrated superior performance compared to traditional process-based hydrologic models

traditional process-based hydrologic models following physical laws like mass balances can provide a full set of diagnostic outputs

chunks.text: Differentiable modeling combines a process-based backbone with neural networks so that gradients can be computed via automatic differentiation and neural components can be trained by backpropagation. Neural networks can be inserted to provide parameters or substitute uncertain processes, enabling systematic learning from large datasets while retaining physical structure. Prior work applied differentiable HBV hybrids to the contiguous United States, showing performance close to LSTM while producing interpretable internal variables and improved spatial generalization when trained regionally. This paper extends that idea to global-scale hydrologic simulation.
supporting_quote: By combining a physical model with a DL model, differentiable modeling... provides a systematic solution
They are collectively called "differentiable models" in the sense that they can rapidly compute gradients... using automatic differentiation
applying differentiable modeling to the conceptual hydrologic model named... HBV... for basins in the contiguous United States (CONUS)
the differentiable hybrid models can approach the performance level of the LSTM model whilst being constrained to physical laws

chunks.text: Global hydrologic models are frequently uncalibrated or only calibrated on limited targets, and many regions (e.g., parts of Africa and Asia) have sparse public streamflow data. The paper argues for regionalized frameworks that can leverage basin attributes to generate parameters, reduce overfitting to local noise, and generalize to ungauged locations. It is uncertain whether deep learning and differentiable physics-informed models maintain their advantages at global scale due to diverse climates and forcing datasets with different bias characteristics. Therefore, large-sample global testing is needed to assess both accuracy and extrapolation.
supporting_quote: current global hydrologic models are largely either uncalibrated... or only calibrated on mean annual water budgets or in limited regions
many large regions such as in Africa and Asia lack publicly available streamflow data
it is unclear if their observed strengths... can carry over to global scales, where the climate is much more diverse and datasets differ widely in their biases

chunks.text: The study aims to apply physics-informed differentiable hydrologic models at global scale for the first time in this context. It uses δHBV-globe1.0-hydroDL (δHBV) to simulate rainfall–runoff processes for thousands of basins worldwide and compares it to a purely data-driven LSTM benchmark. The goal is to quantify achievable accuracy at global scale, diagnose geographic and process-related patterns in model performance, and rigorously test spatial generalization to ungauged regions across continents. The work is positioned as establishing a benchmark for global hydrologic estimates and informing next-generation global modeling choices.
supporting_quote: we use – for the first time at this scale – differentiable hydrologic models (full name δHBV-globe1.0-hydroDL, shortened to δHBV here) to simulate the rainfall–runoff processes for 3753 basins around the world
we compare the δHBV models to a purely data-driven long short-term memory (LSTM) model to examine their strengths and limitations
We first investigate what prediction accuracy can be achieved by different models at global scale

we provide evidence indicating which type of model may be more appropriate for next-generation global modeling by rigorously examining each model's generalizability to ungauged regions across the world

chunks.text: Pure deep learning models can be accurate but lack explicit physical constraints and interpretability, limiting their ability to predict untrained or unobserved hydrologic variables. Process-based models offer physical consistency and multiple diagnostic outputs but often underperform DL in daily hydrograph metrics and do not necessarily improve with more training data. Traditional calibration is typically performed site by site, making global calibration time- and labor-intensive. The paper frames hybrid differentiable modeling as a way to reconcile these competing drawbacks.
supporting_quote: purely data-driven models are limited in that they cannot predict unobservable or untrained physical variables
traditional physical model to approach the performance level of the DL models in daily hydrograph metrics

chunks.text: It is uncertain whether the strengths of deep learning and differentiable hybrid models observed at continental scales transfer to global scales. The global setting introduces highly diverse climates and multiple forcing products with different biases and uncertainty structures. The study highlights the need to evaluate whether models can leverage information from data-rich continents to predict hydrology in data-sparse regions, a key requirement for global applications. This uncertainty motivates the paper’s focus on spatial generalization and cross-continent extrapolation.
supporting_quote: it is unclear if their observed strengths... can carry over to global scales, where the climate is much more diverse and datasets differ widely in their biases and uncertainty characteristics

chunks.text: The benchmark data-driven model is an LSTM rainfall–runoff framework that takes meteorological forcings and basin attributes as inputs and predicts daily streamflow. Training uses mini-batches consisting of 2-year sequences from 256 randomly selected basins; the first year is used to initialize states and loss is computed on the second year. Training sequences are randomly sampled from the training period, and one epoch corresponds to seeing all training data. The LSTM is trained for 300 epochs to reach convergence.
supporting_quote: The framework takes meteorological forcings and basin attributes as inputs and generates daily streamflow predictions
each mini-batch was composed of 2 year sequences from 256 randomly selected basins
The firstyear sequences are only used for initializing the cell states, so we calculate the batch loss function only on the secondyear sequences
We trained the LSTM model for 300 epochs to achieve convergence

chunks.text: The differentiable model (δHBV) uses the conceptual HBV hydrologic model as a physical backbone and employs differentiable parameter learning (dPL) for regionalization. A neural network gA (implemented as an LSTM) ingests basin attributes and meteorological forcings to output static or dynamic HBV parameters. HBV then simulates storages and fluxes and predicts daily discharge and other variables, with the full system implemented in PyTorch for automatic differentiation. Training minimizes a two-part RMSE loss on discharge, including a transformed-flow term to better represent low flows.
supporting_quote: The HBV model used here as the physical backbone is a conceptual hydrologic model with representations of snowpack, soil, and groundwater storages
The differentiable parameter learning (dPL) framework... is used to provide parameter regionalization for HBV
The gA network, which is an LSTM unit here, takes basin attributes and meteorological forcings as inputs, and it outputs static or dynamic physical HBV parameters
we employed the loss function based on root-mean-square error (RMSE) with two weighted parts

chunks.text: Two evolved HBV variants are evaluated within the differentiable framework. Both use 16 parallel subbasin-scale response units to implicitly represent within-basin heterogeneity; fluxes are averaged across units and parameters for all units are produced by the same gA network. One variant uses only static parameters, while the other allows limited daily-varying dynamic parameters to increase flexibility without excessive overfitting risk. Dynamism is restricted to two empirical parameters: the soil-runoff shape coefficient β and an added evapotranspiration shape parameter γ.

The second version... further allows some formerly static parameters... to vary daily with the meteorological forcings
we restricted the dynamism to only two empirical parameters: the shape coefficient β... and... (γ ) which is involved in the calculation of evapotranspiration

chunks.text: The study runs one temporal and two spatial generalization experiments. Temporal generalization trains on 2000–2016 and tests on 1980–1997 on the same basins (excluding basins with insufficient test records). Spatial generalization includes (1) a 10-fold cross-validation prediction in ungauged basins (PUB) random holdout, and (2) a cross-continent prediction in ungauged regions (PUR) where all basins in a continent are withheld for testing. The PUR setup is treated as a harder extrapolation test than PUB, which is closer to interpolation.
supporting_quote: For the temporal generalization experiment, the models were trained for the period of 2000 to 2016... and tested for the period of 1980 to 1997
we randomly divided the whole global basin set into 10 folds (groups) and performed cross-validation across these folds

With random hold out... can be interpreted as spatial interpolation... PUR... is the much harder test of spatial extrapolation

chunks.text: Model performance is assessed primarily with Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE) and Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) on test datasets. KGE decomposes performance into correlation, mean bias, and variability bias, while NSE reflects variance explained. Extreme-flow behavior is evaluated using percent bias metrics for the top 2% peak flow range (FHV) and bottom 30% low flow range (FLV). These metrics are computed only on testing data not seen during training.
supporting_quote: we used the Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE)... and the Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE)
KGE has three components that account for correlation, mean bias... and variability bias
We also examined the percent bias of the top 2 % peak flow range (FHV) and bottom 30 % low flow range (FLV)
All the reported performance metrics in this study are from model evaluation on the testing dataset

chunks.text: The study uses a global basin dataset from Beck et al. (2020a) originally containing 4229 headwater catchments with basin-mean forcings, attributes, and discharge observations. After removing basins with potentially erroneous discharge records and those with severe missing data (less than 5 years available during 2000–2016), 3753 basins remain for evaluation. Basins are categorized into five Köppen–Geiger classes: tropical (489), arid (109), temperate (1423), cold (1593), and polar (139). These data support both model training and climate-group performance analysis.
supporting_quote: a global database... contains a total of 4229 headwater catchments
Thus, 3753 basins were finally used to evaluate different models
including tropical (489 basins), arid (109 basins), temperate (1423 basins), cold (1593 basins), and polar (139 basins)
excluded those with severe amounts of missing data (less than 5 years' worth of data points available in the study period from 2000 to 2016)

chunks.text: Meteorological forcings consist of daily precipitation from MSWEP and daily maximum/minimum temperature from MSWX, with potential evapotranspiration estimated using the Hargreaves (1994) method. Discharge observations at basin outlets are used as prediction targets for model training and evaluation. These basin-mean forcings are used both by the purely data-driven LSTM model and by δHBV as inputs to generate daily streamflow simulations. The paper notes that forcing bias (e.g., peak precipitation underestimation) can influence results.
supporting_quote: daily precipitation from the Multi-Source Weighted-Ensemble Precipitation (MSWEP)
maximum and minimum temperature from the Multi-Source Weather (MSWX)
Potential evapotranspiration (ET) was estimated using the method from Hargreaves (1994)

chunks.text: To evaluate an untrained variable (evapotranspiration), the study uses MOD16A2GF, a gap-filled 8-day composite MODIS-based ET product, as independent comparison data. Differentiable models output ET as a diagnostic flux without being trained on ET observations. Evaluation is performed at the basin scale, including mean annual ET and time-series agreement. This provides a test of whether the physical-backbone model can produce plausible internal fluxes beyond discharge.
supporting_quote: To evaluate the simulations of untrained variables like ET, MOD16A2GF... was used as independent observations
a gap-filled 8 d composite ET product estimated from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) satellite data

chunks.text: In temporal generalization (train 2000–2016; test 1980–1997), all three models achieved strong daily streamflow skill globally with median KGE near or above 0.7. LSTM performed best overall with median NSE 0.70 and median KGE 0.74. The differentiable HBV with dynamic parameters achieved median NSE 0.67 and KGE 0.69, while the static-parameter version achieved median NSE 0.65 and KGE 0.68. The results indicate differentiable models approach LSTM performance at global scale.

LSTM... achieving a median NSE (KGE) value of 0.70 (0.74)

chunks.text: For a subset of 1675 basins with long-term discharge records, LSTM performance improved further in the temporal test. The paper reports a median KGE of 0.78 for this subset, which requires at least 15 years of training-period data and at least 5 years of testing-period data. This suggests that longer records provide additional benefit to the data-driven benchmark. It also provides a more stringent benchmark against which differentiable models are compared.

at least 15 years' worth of streamflow data available in the training period and 5 years' worth of data available in the testing period

chunks.text: Low-flow and peak-flow diagnostics show different strengths. LSTM has advantages for low-flow prediction, indicated by the FLV metric, relative to differentiable models. For peak flows, LSTM and differentiable models behave similarly and tend to underestimate observed peaks, as indicated by negative FHV. The paper connects peak underestimation to precipitation forcing bias and aggregation effects.

for the peak flow predictions, the LSTM and differentiable models were quite similar, and they all underestimated the observed peaks (FHV in Fig. 3)
MSWEP is based on the ERA5 reanalysis, which is known to underestimate precipitation peaks
the use of basin-averaged, daily averaged precipitation may further suppress the peaks

chunks.text: Performance varies systematically by climate group. LSTM performs best in polar, cold, and temperate basins and deteriorates in tropical and arid basins. Differentiable models show strong skill in temperate and cold groups but worse in tropical and especially arid basins; dynamic parameterization improves performance in all climate groups except the arid group. These patterns help attribute errors to missing processes and data/forcing issues that differ by climate regime.
supporting_quote: The LSTM model behaved the best in the polar, cold, and temperate groups, while the performance deteriorated in the tropical and arid basins
differentiable models showed strong performance in temperate and cold groups and worse performance in tropical ones, with the worst performance in arid basins
The differentiable model with dynamic parameters performed better than the model with static parameters in all climate groups except the most challenging arid group

chunks.text: In polar and cold climates, LSTM notably outperforms differentiable HBV, indicating limitations of the HBV backbone for cryospheric and cold-region processes. The paper reports that in the polar group LSTM has a median KGE of 0.81 while the differentiable model reaches 0.62, and in the cold group LSTM has 0.78 versus 0.71. The authors relate this to missing glacier and frozen-soil processes in HBV and to snow undercatch biases that DL can learn to compensate but mass-balance-constrained models cannot. This highlights how structural physics choices affect hybrid-model performance.

the original HBV itself does not have a glacial module
HBV does not have the ability to simulate frozen soil, sublimation, or snow cover fractions
LSTM can learn to address such systematic bias, while physical differentiable models cannot due to mass balance

chunks.text: Spatial generalization shows that differentiable models can outperform LSTM under more data-scarce, cross-continent testing. In the global PUB test, LSTM has a median KGE of 0.67 versus 0.64 for differentiable models, both exceeding the traditional linear-transfer regionalization baseline (median KGE 0.46). In PUR with Europe held out, differentiable models reach median KGE 0.58, significantly higher than LSTM at 0.52 (Wilcoxon p < 0.01). These results support the claim that regionalized differentiable modeling improves extrapolation to ungauged regions.

traditional regionalization method using linear transfer functions... (Beck20, median KGE of 0.46)

p-value less than 0.01 using the one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test

Reported median KGE values are 0.28 for LSTM and 0.31 for the static-parameter differentiable model. The dynamic-parameter differentiable model appears somewhat overfitted in this scenario and performs worse than the static version. The result indicates that added flexibility can hurt extrapolation in very challenging regions.

chunks.text: Differentiable models can predict untrained evapotranspiration (ET) in agreement with independent MODIS estimates. Mean annual ET across basins clusters near the 1:1 line with a reported correlation of 0.75. Temporal agreement is also high, with median ET time-series correlations of 0.82 and 0.89 for the two differentiable models across 3753 basins. This demonstrates that the physical-backbone hybrid produces plausible internal fluxes without direct ET supervision.

chunks.text: The paper attributes systematic underestimation of peak flows to forcing and representation limits. MSWEP precipitation is based on ERA5, which is described as underestimating precipitation peaks, and basin-averaged daily precipitation further suppresses extremes. The authors also note numerical and structural issues in differentiable HBV, including explicit sequential solution schemes and threshold functions that can make results sequence-dependent, and structural limitations such as deeper groundwater not feeding back to upper layers. They call for community efforts to address peak-flow bias.

MSWEP is based on the ERA5 reanalysis, which is known to underestimate precipitation peaks
the use of basin-averaged, daily averaged precipitation may further suppress the peaks
numerical errors introduced by the explicit and sequential solution scheme of HBV with excessive use of threshold functions
deeper groundwater storage cannot feed back to the upper layers

chunks.text: Differentiable model deficits in polar and cold regions are linked to missing cryospheric and frozen-ground processes and to snow gauge undercatch. The HBV backbone lacks a glacial module and does not simulate frozen soil, sublimation, or snow cover fractions, which can be important in these climates. In addition, because the hybrid is constrained by mass balance, it cannot easily compensate for systematic precipitation biases from snow undercatch the way LSTM can. This structural mismatch explains why LSTM often outperforms δHBV in polar regions.
supporting_quote: the original HBV itself does not have a glacial module
HBV does not have the ability to simulate frozen soil, sublimation, or snow cover fractions
snow gauges at high altitude are known to suffer systematic bias due to undercatch problems
LSTM can learn to address such systematic bias, while physical differentiable models cannot due to mass balance

chunks.text: Arid-region performance is challenging for both modeling approaches due to hydrologic regimes requiring long memory and flash flooding not represented at daily scale. The paper notes that even LSTM may not retain year-long memory for baseflow in arid settings, while HBV’s linear slow-flow reservoir cannot generate zero baseflows and cannot represent intense hourly rainfall impacts well. The authors also point to missing reservoir management modules as another contributor, since arid regions often have significant infrastructure effects on streamflow. These limitations motivate future process improvements.
supporting_quote: A more prominent challenge is the arid regions

This challenge can be attributed to the long duration of low flows which requires long-term memory and to flash floods which result from intense short-duration storms not well represented at the daily scale
Because HBV has a linear reservoir for its slow-flow (lowest) bucket, it can neither generate zero baseflows nor simulate the impact of intense hourly scale rainfall well
Another reason for the challenge in arid regions is the lack of reservoir management modules

chunks.text: The physical backbone in differentiable models is described as a double-edged sword. When the backbone structure is essentially correct, it stabilizes learning, mitigates overfitting, and improves generalization. But missing critical processes (e.g., reservoir management, ground ice, glaciers) and large unexplained forcing/observation biases can drag down performance and cause process compensation. The authors suggest adding forcing data correction layers and incorporating additional observations to better constrain learning and improve robustness.
supporting_quote: The challenges facing the differentiable models in this study include not only missing processes like reservoir management, ground ice, and glaciers

While LSTM can easily adapt to systematic bias, such forcing errors put the differentiable models under stress because they cannot reconcile streamflow observations with such forcings given the constraint of mass balances
The backbone of a differentiable process-based model thus serves as a double-edged sword
we can set up forcing data correction layers that can, to some extent, shield the core processes

chunks.text: ET evaluation is limited by uncertainties in the MODIS ET product and by potential issues in streamflow records used for training in some regions. The paper notes relatively low ET correlation in South America, but also small coefficient of variation in ET residuals there, and highlights that MODIS ET has large uncertainties in Amazonia due to observation difficulties. It also reports that some South American streamflow stations show unrealistic hydrographs that may indicate data processing errors. Future work is suggested to improve data screening/correction and to constrain models with other datasets such as eddy covariance flux data.
supporting_quote: the correlation is relatively low in South America
MODIS ET itself is not the ground truth and always has large uncertainties in Amazonia regions
some stations in South America show unrealistic hydrographs that may indicate data processing errors
more in-depth data screening and correction or constraining the model using datasets other than streamflow, e.g., eddy covariance flux data, should be considered

chunks.text: The study demonstrates that both LSTM and physics-informed differentiable δHBV models achieve state-of-the-art daily streamflow performance at global scale, with median KGE near or above 0.7. LSTM is best for temporal generalization, while differentiable models approach LSTM skill and provide physical interpretability and additional hydrologic outputs. Spatial generalization tests show differentiable models have stronger extrapolation to ungauged regions than traditional regionalization and, in some PUR settings, than LSTM. The work establishes a benchmark and supports differentiable models as candidates for next-generation global hydrologic modeling.
supporting_quote: Both types of models achieved highly competitive performance overall for global basins... yielding median KGE values close to or higher than 0.7
The LSTM still achieved the best performance for the temporal generalization test, but the differentiable HBV models... approach the LSTM's performance level
spatial generalization experiments highlighted the stronger regionalization and extrapolation ability of differentiable models than the traditional modeling approach and LSTM
this study proves that differentiable models are strong candidates as global water models

chunks.text: Climate- and region-dependent comparisons reveal where the δHBV backbone is insufficient. All models perform well in temperate and cold climates and poorly in arid basins, while differentiable models are notably worse than LSTM in polar basins where glacier and multiyear ice processes matter. The paper emphasizes that missing processes (e.g., glaciers, reservoir management, frozen-ground effects) cannot be fully compensated by neural parameterization alone. These diagnostic insights are presented as directions for targeted process improvements in future differentiable global models.
supporting_quote: All models achieve good performance in the temperate and cold climate groups, while they all behave unsatisfactorily in the arid group
For the polar group, the differentiable model performed significantly worse than the LSTM
differentiable models are limited by the structure of their physical backbone model, which in this case does not simulate multiyear ice buildup and melt
missing processes like reservoir management, ground ice, and glaciers
