chunks.text: A key added value of differentiable models is producing a comprehensive, interpretable set of hydrologic variables beyond discharge, including evapotranspiration and storages/fluxes, while still achieving competitive streamflow accuracy. The paper reports that ET simulations agree with independent MODIS estimates in mean annual patterns and temporal dynamics, despite no ET supervision. This capability positions differentiable models as tools for diagnosing and characterizing hydrologic processes in ungauged regions by leveraging learned relationships between basin attributes and physical parameters. The authors note that river routing is not included and is future work.
supporting_quote: Compared to the LSTM model which only outputs discharge simulations, differentiable models offer a suite of interpretable variables, including ET, soil water, recharge, and baseflow
We did not use any ET observations as training targets to supervise the differentiable models
mean annual ET comparison... a correlation of 0.75 for all the basins
River routing is not included in this work and will be investigated in the future

chunks.text: Large-scale hydrologic prediction is often hindered by limited streamflow observations, especially in many regions where gauges are sparse or unavailable. Deep learning models such as LSTMs can achieve high accuracy on streamflow prediction, but they are difficult to interpret and generally cannot output variables that lack direct training observations. Differentiable, physics-informed modeling offers a way to combine process constraints with neural-network learning on big datasets.
supporting_quote: Many regions across the world, e.g., parts of South America, Africa, and Asia, suffer from a paucity of publicly available streamflow data (Hannah et al., 2011), which precludes calibration.
DL models are still difficult to interpret and do not predict variables without first having extensive observations to enable model training.
Differentiable modeling is a genre of physics-informed machine learning (or scientific machine learning; Baker et al., 2019).

chunks.text: Spatial generalization in hydrology is commonly evaluated via PUB (randomly held-out basins) and PUR (regional holdouts). PUB is closer to spatial interpolation because training gauges typically surround test basins, whereas PUR is spatial extrapolation and is more representative of real global data gaps. Prior work showed LSTM performance drops more severely in PUR, while systematic PUR tests for process-based models have been limited.
supporting_quote: PUB can be considered spatial "interpolation", as there will always be training gauges surrounding the test basins (Fig. 1a).
PUR scenario better represents the case of spatial "extrapolation" encountered in real global hydrologic assessment (Feng et al., 2021).
For PUR, the LSTM's performance further declines significantly (Feng et al., 2021). No systematic PUR tests have been done for process-based models

chunks.text: Differentiable process-based hydrologic models (δ models) previously achieved near-LSTM accuracy in temporal tests while producing diagnostic physical variables and enforcing conservation. They use neural networks to learn parameterization for a process-based backbone and can be trained end-to-end on streamflow without supervising intermediate variables. This positions δ models as potentially better constrained alternatives for regional and global simulation.
supporting_quote: differentiable process-based hydrologic models (abbreviated as δ or delta models) ... provide daily streamflow prediction performance closely approaching that of state-of-the-art long short-term memory (LSTM)
δ models provide a full suite of diagnostic physical variables and guaranteed mass conservation.

Importantly, there are no intermediate target variables to supervise the neural networks – the whole framework is trained on streamflow as the only focus of the loss function in an end-to-end fashion.

chunks.text: The study tests whether differentiable process-based δ models can generalize spatially beyond training gauges and produce credible long-term change signals. Specifically, it evaluates (1) extrapolation to basins far from gauges and (2) prediction of decadal-scale change trends relevant for climate impact assessment. Performance is benchmarked against a regionalized LSTM and, when available, a traditional regionalized process-based model.
supporting_quote: we ran experiments to test (1) their ability to extrapolate to regions far from streamflow gauges and (2) their ability to make credible predictions of long-term (decadal-scale) change trends.
Our main research question in this paper is whether differentiable process-based models can generalize well in space and provide reliable large-scale hydrologic estimates in data-scarce regions.
we designed both PUB and PUR experiments. Furthermore ... we also evaluated the simulated trends of mean annual flow and different flow regimes

chunks.text: A key hypothesis is that stronger structural constraints in δ models (e.g., regulated information flow and mass balance) will yield advantages in spatial extrapolation compared to LSTM and existing process-based models. The paper also implicitly tests whether the learned parameterization mapping from attributes/forcing to parameters transfers to untrained regions. These hypotheses are examined via PUB (interpolation) and PUR (extrapolation) cross-validation.
supporting_quote: Our hypothesis is that, since the differentiable models have stronger structural constraints, they should exhibit some advantages in extrapolation compared to both LSTM and existing process-based models.
An implicit hypothesis is that the relationships learned by the parameterization component are general, so they can be transferred to untrained regions.
In this paper, we designed both PUB and PUR experiments.

chunks.text: Global-scale hydrologic modeling commonly lacks calibration because streamflow data are unavailable or not public in many regions, producing large predictive uncertainty. This data scarcity complicates assessing future water-cycle changes and hazards under population pressure and climate change. The paper frames the need for models that can operate credibly in such ungauged settings.
supporting_quote: For global-scale applications, however, models are often uncalibrated (Hattermann et al., 2017; Zaherpour et al., 2018), leading to large predictive uncertainty.
Many regions across the world ... suffer from a paucity of publicly available streamflow data ... which precludes calibration.
Therefore, it is important to better quantify the impacts of these pressures in these regions (Sivapalan, 2003) and estimate changes in the future water cycle.

chunks.text: Pure deep learning approaches have limitations for scientific and operational hydrology: limited interpretability and inability to predict unobserved physical variables without supervision. These limitations make it difficult to answer process questions (e.g., soil moisture–runoff relationships) and to obtain multi-physics diagnostics needed for understanding and decision-making.
supporting_quote: DL models are still difficult to interpret and do not predict variables without first having extensive observations to enable model training.
it is challenging to answer specific scientific questions using DL models, e.g., what is the relationship between variable soil moisture and runoff?

chunks.text: Evaluating models only under PUB-style random holdouts can mask weaknesses because PUB resembles interpolation with nearby gauges, while PUR is a harsher extrapolation scenario. LSTM performance is known to drop significantly in PUR, and comparable systematic PUR testing for process-based models has been lacking. The paper targets this gap with explicit PUR regional holdouts.
supporting_quote: PUB can be considered spatial "interpolation"
PUR ... better represents the case of spatial "extrapolation" encountered in real global hydrologic assessment
For PUR, the LSTM's performance further declines significantly ... No systematic PUR tests have been done for process-based models

chunks.text: δ models are implemented as differentiable, learnable hydrologic models using HBV as a process-based backbone while training neural networks end-to-end on streamflow. An LSTM-based parameterization network (gA) maps static basin attributes and historical forcings to HBV parameters. The differentiable setup enables backpropagation through model operations and learning without intermediate supervision targets.
supporting_quote: we employed the Hydrologiska Byråns Vattenbalansavdelning (HBV) model ... a relatively simple, bucket-type conceptual hydrologic model.
The parameters of HBV are learned from basin characteristics by a DL network (gA, an LSTM unit in Fig. 2)

Importantly, there are no intermediate target variables to supervise the neural networks – the whole framework is trained on streamflow as the only focus of the loss function in an end-to-end fashion.

chunks.text: The HBV backbone is structurally modified to improve flexibility while retaining physical constraints. The first change increases within-basin heterogeneity by using 16 parallel storage components, averaging states and fluxes across components, with all component parameters learned by gA. The second change optionally introduces dynamic parameterization, converting static HBV parameters to time-dependent daily values such as βt and γt learned from attributes and climate forcings.
supporting_quote: The first modification was to increase the number of parallel storage components of the HBV model (16 used here) to represent the heterogeneity within basins.
The second modification was that ... we turned some static parameters of HBV into time-dependent parameters with a different value for each day (we call this dynamic parameterization or DP).
we set the runoff curve shape coefficient parameter to be time-dependent (βt )
we modified the static β and γ into dynamic parameters βt and γt , which change with time

chunks.text: A regionalized LSTM streamflow model is used as the primary benchmark, trained with meteorological forcings and basin attributes. Training uses minibatches of 100 instances, each containing two consecutive years of forcings per basin with a 1-year warmup and loss computed on the second year. RMSE is used as the training loss, with δ models using a combined loss on unnormalized and transformed predictions to better represent low flow.
supporting_quote: We compared the performance of δ models with a purely data-driven LSTM streamflow model
In our case, a minibatch is composed of 100 training instances, each of which contains 2 consecutive years' worth of meteorological forcings
The first year was used as a warmup period, so the loss was only calculated on the second year of simulation.
For the δ models ... the RMSE was calculated on both the unnormalized predictions and transformed predictions to improve low-flow representation

chunks.text: PUB experiments are conducted via 10-fold random basin holdouts to represent spatial interpolation, while PUR experiments use seven contiguous regional holdouts to represent spatial extrapolation. Each fold trains on the complement basins/regions and tests on the held-out group. Both tests use the same time period for training and testing but different basins, targeting purely spatial out-of-sample generalization.
supporting_quote: For PUB experiments, we randomly divided all the CAMELS basins into 10 groups, trained the models on 9 groups, and tested it on the one group held out.
For the PUR experiment, we divided the whole CONUS into seven continuous regions ... trained the model on six regions, and tested it on the holdout region.
These spatial generalization tests were trained and tested in the same time period but for different basins.

chunks.text: Daily hydrograph performance is evaluated using NSE and KGE, plus flow-regime biases for high and low flows. FHV is defined as percent bias of the top 2% peak flow range, and FLV is percent bias of the bottom 30% low-flow range. These metrics assess overall fit, correlation/variability/mean bias, and regime-specific errors.
supporting_quote: we calculated the Nash– Sutcliffe (NSE; Nash and Sutcliffe, 1970) and Kling–Gupta (KGE; Gupta et al., 2009) model efficiency coefficients
We also reported the percent bias of the top 2 % peak flow range (FHV) and the percent bias of the bottom 30 % low flow range (FLV; Yilmaz et al., 2008)

chunks.text: Decadal trend skill is assessed for mean annual flow and flow percentiles representing different regimes: Q98 (high), Q50 (median), and Q10 (low). For each year, a flow percentile value is extracted and Sen's slope estimator is computed over the 10-year test period (hydrologic years 1989–1999), then compared to observed slopes. Years with excessive missing daily data are excluded using a threshold of <61 missing days per year.
supporting_quote: We also evaluated the multi-year trend for streamflow values at different percentiles (Q98, Q50, and Q10), in addition to the mean annual flow.
Then, Sen's slope estimator (Sen, 1968) for the trend ... was calculated for the 10 years in the test period
we only considered years with <61 (about 2 months) daily missing values

chunks.text: Experiments use the CAMELS dataset with 671 basins across the contiguous United States, reporting test performance on a commonly used 531-basin subset that excludes basins with unclear watershed boundaries. The study period is 1 October 1989 to 30 September 1999. This shared benchmark enables comparison across δ models, LSTM, and available traditional model results.
supporting_quote: We used the CAMELS dataset ... which includes 671 basins across the contiguous United States (CONUS)
reported the test performance on a widely used 531-basin subset
The study period was from 1 October 1989 to 30 September 1999.

chunks.text: Meteorological forcing sensitivity is evaluated using two CAMELS-compatible products: Maurer et al. (2002) forcings (chosen for comparability with existing regionalized results) and Daymet forcings. δ models use precipitation, temperature, and potential evapotranspiration (Ep), with Ep computed using the temperature-based Hargreaves method and daily min/max temperatures. The LSTM uses five forcings including precipitation, temperature, solar radiation, vapor pressure, and day length.
supporting_quote: The Maurer et al. (2002; hereafter denoted as Maurer) meteorological forcing data were selected ... We also ran experiments with Daymet (Thornton et al., 2020) forcings

The LSTM model takes five forcing variables including precipitation, temperature, solar radiation, vapor pressure, and day length, while the HBV model only takes precipitation (P), temperature (T ), and potential evapotranspiration (Ep).
We used the temperature-based Hargreaves (1994) method to calculate Ep

chunks.text: Regionalized learning uses 35 basin attributes spanning climate indices, topography, land cover/vegetation, soils, and geology. In the LSTM, attributes are concatenated with forcings as inputs. In δ models, gA receives attributes and historical forcing inputs and outputs HBV parameters, enabling parameter fields across CONUS without direct parameter observations.
supporting_quote: To train regionalized models for dPL and LSTM, we used 35 attributes, as shown in Table A1
For the LSTM streamflow model, the attribute data were directly concatenated with the forcings and provided as inputs.
With the δ models, the neural network gA receives attributes and historical forcing data as inputs and then outputs parameters

chunks.text: Evapotranspiration evaluation uses an independent satellite-based ET dataset, MODIS MOD16A2, providing an out-of-training validation for δ model ET outputs. δ models are trained only on streamflow, so ET is not calibrated directly. This enables testing whether the physics-informed structure yields realistic ET seasonality and magnitude under spatial interpolation/extrapolation.
supporting_quote: For the comparison of evapotranspiration, we used a product derived from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) satellite
This ET product served as a completely independent, uncalibrated validation for the evapotranspiration simulated by the differentiable HBV models.
All models were trained only with streamflow as the target.

chunks.text: In randomized PUB (spatial interpolation), δ models match LSTM daily hydrograph performance under Maurer and can surpass LSTM under Daymet forcing. Under Maurer, δ(βt,γt) reaches median PUB NSE 0.64 vs LSTM 0.65, and KGE medians for δ(βt) and δ(βt,γt) are about 0.66 and 0.65 with smaller spread than LSTM. Under Daymet, δ(βt) and δ(βt,γt) reach median NSE 0.68 and 0.69, exceeding LSTM at 0.66.
supporting_quote: Under the Maurer forcings, δ(βt, γt) had a median PUB NSE of 0.64, which is only slightly lower than LSTM (0.65)
For KGE, δ(βt) and δ(βt, γt) models ... had median values of 0.66 and 0.65, respectively ... and also had a smaller spread
Under the Daymet forcings, δ(βt) and δ(βt, γt) models reached NSE (KGE) median values of 0.68 (0.68) and 0.69 (0.67) ... higher than the LSTM at 0.66 (0.66)

chunks.text: PUB decadal-trend skill is broadly comparable between LSTM and δ models for annual mean and high-flow trends, but all models struggle on low-flow trends. In PUB, both model types achieve high accuracy for annual mean flow (R2 > 0.80) and high-flow bands (R2 > 0.70), yet perform poorly for Q10 low-flow trends (R2 < 0.40). δ(βt,γt) is similar to LSTM for mean, Q50, and Q98 trends, while LSTM is better for Q10.
supporting_quote: Both LSTM and δ models accurately captured the trends in annual mean flow (R2 > 0.80) and high-flow bands (R2 > 0.70), but both struggled with low flow Q10 ... (R2 < 0.40).
δ(βt, γt) had similar trend performance to LSTM in terms of annual mean flow, median flow Q50, and peak flow Q98, while LSTM had the advantage for low flow, Q10.

chunks.text: In PUR (regional extrapolation), δ models outperform LSTM on daily hydrograph metrics and exhibit smaller performance degradation from PUB to PUR. Under Maurer, median NSE increases from LSTM 0.55 to δ(βt,γt) 0.59, and median KGE rises from 0.52 to 0.61. Under Daymet, δ models improve more strongly than LSTM, reaching median NSE/KGE of 0.62/0.63 for δ(βt,γt) compared with LSTM at 0.55/0.51.
supporting_quote: For the regional holdout test (PUR), surprisingly, δ models noticeably outperformed LSTM in most of the daily hydrograph metrics (KGE, NSE, and FHV)
Under Maurer forcings, the median NSE values for LSTM, δ, and δ(βt, γt) models were 0.55, 0.56, and 0.59, respectively, and the corresponding KGE values were 0.52, 0.59, and 0.61
The median NSE (KGE) values for LSTM, δ, and δ(βt, γt) models were 0.55 (0.51), 0.60 (0.61) and 0.62 (0.63), respectively.

chunks.text: PUR decadal-trend prediction shows a strong contrast: LSTM trend skill declines markedly from PUB to PUR, while δ model trend accuracy remains stable, especially for mean annual flow and Q98 high flows. The paper reports LSTM R2 for annual mean discharge dropping from 0.87 (PUB) to 0.64 (PUR), and for Q98 dropping from 0.76 to 0.27. In contrast, δ(βt,γt) maintains about R2≈0.88 for annual mean discharge and around 0.77 for Q98 in PUR.
supporting_quote: while the LSTM's trend metrics declined noticeably from PUB to PUR, the δ models' trend accuracy barely budged (Fig. 7).
The LSTM R2 for annual mean discharge dropped from 0.87 for PUB to 0.64 for PUR, but R2 remained at 0.88 for δ(βt, γt).
The LSTM R2 for high flow (Q98) trends dropped significantly, from 0.76 for PUB to 0.27 for PUR, whereas this metric remained around 0.77 for the δ models.

chunks.text: δ model parameter fields are spatially stable across in-sample, PUB, and PUR training regimes, even when regions are held out. Parameter maps for β show similar overall CONUS-scale patterns between temporal, PUB, and PUR cases; PUR introduces more regional differences but preserves broad patterns. This stability is presented as evidence that the learned parameterization mapping is transferable and contributes to robustness under extrapolation.
supporting_quote: the insample, PUB, and PUR experiments all produced similar overall parameter patterns (see Fig. 8; for PUB ... and PUR ... these parameters were generated when the basins were used as the test basins and excluded from training).
Despite these strong perturbations to the training data, such parameter stability under PUB and PUR is impressive. This stability is part of the reason for the mild performance drop under PUR.

chunks.text: Evapotranspiration (ET), an untrained variable, is simulated with good agreement to MODIS across temporal, PUB, and PUR settings, indicating preserved seasonality under extrapolation. For δ(γt,βt), the median ET correlation with MODIS stays around 0.84 and RMSE around 6.4 mm per 8 days across scenarios. Dynamic-parameterization δ variants perform better than static-parameter versions for ET in temporal, PUB, and PUR.
supporting_quote: from temporal tests to PUB and then PUR, the median correlation and RMSE between simulated ET and 8 d integrated ET from the MODIS satellite product did not vary much, around 0.84 and 6.4 mm per 8 d, respectively.
the dynamic parameterization (DP) models, δ(γt, βt) and δ(βt), were better than static parameter models in all comparable cases (temporal test, PUB, or PUR).
LSTM is not shown, as it is unable to output physical variables on which it has not been explicitly trained.

chunks.text: Low-flow trend prediction (Q10) is difficult for both δ models and LSTM, likely due to limited subsurface information, small trend magnitudes, structural limitations, and human impacts. The paper notes the linear HBV groundwater reservoir may not capture real dynamics, and LSTM memory may be insufficient for gentle multi-year baseflow changes. Human activities such as reservoir operations also affect low flows, and loss functions are more sensitive to high flows due to magnitude differences.
supporting_quote: both struggled with low flow Q10 ... (R2 < 0.40 ).

the linear reservoir formulation in the present HBV groundwater modules may not capture the realworld dynamics, while even the LSTM may not have the memory that is long enough to represent a gentle multi-year baseflow trend change.
The greater impact of human activities such as reservoir operations on low flow also needs to be considered
the greater sensitivity of the training loss function to high flows compared to low flows due to the difference in their magnitudes

chunks.text: δ models can be more sensitive to precipitation bias because they enforce mass conservation and do not implicitly correct precipitation amounts. The study observes stronger improvements for δ models when switching from Maurer to Daymet forcing, suggesting Maurer precipitation bias may penalize δ models more. The paper notes that LSTM may learn to correct precipitation biases, though the impact of precipitation bias remains debated.
supporting_quote: This result suggests that precipitation in the Maurer forcing data may have a larger bias, and as δ models conserve mass and cannot by default apply corrections to the precipitation amounts, they are more heavily impacted by such bias.
As mentioned earlier, LSTM may potentially learn to correct biases in precipitation (Beck et al., 2020a), but the impact of precipitation bias is under debate

chunks.text: δ model advantages in PUR are concentrated in mean and high flow rather than low flow, and the authors attribute this to the groundwater module inherited from HBV. They hypothesize the simple linear reservoir cannot represent long-term groundwater storage changes and suggest structural changes such as added nonlinearity or feedbacks between groundwater layers. They also note mass balance constraints create tradeoffs during training, potentially prioritizing peaks over low flows.
supporting_quote: we attribute the advantage in high flow to learning a more generalizable mapping between raw attributes and runoff parameters.
we hypothesize that the δ models' groundwater module, which is inherited from HBV and based on a simple linear reservoir, cannot adequately represent long-term groundwater storage changes.
the δ models face more tension (or tradeoffs) between the low and high flow regimes during training. The peak flow part tends to receive more attention due to its larger values.

chunks.text: Comparability choices constrain absolute performance: the study uses consistent setups (forcings, periods, random seeds) rather than tuning each model for maximum accuracy. It also omits enhancement strategies for pure LSTM such as auxiliary constraints, multi-precipitation inputs, and ensembles, which prior studies found beneficial. As a result, reported results emphasize controlled comparison rather than best-case scores.
supporting_quote: To ensure comparability across different models, we have chosen the same setups ... rather than configurations that would maximize performance metrics.
some auxiliary information like soil moisture can be integrated by a kernel to constrain and enhance the extrapolation

Ensembleaverage prediction from different initializations ... can often lead to higher performance metrics. Here, however, we used a less computationally expensive but comparable setup without these strategies applied

chunks.text: Differentiable, learnable δ hydrologic models are highly competitive for spatial generalization: they approach LSTM in PUB and outperform LSTM in PUR on daily hydrograph metrics. For decadal trends, δ models outperform LSTM in PUR particularly for annual mean flow and high flows, supporting their use for climate change impact assessment in data-scarce regions. The study also highlights δ models’ interpretability and ability to output multi-physics variables as key advantages.
supporting_quote: For the daily hydrograph metrics, the δ models closely approached the LSTM model in the PUB test ... and outperformed the LSTM model in the PUR test.
For the decadal-scale trends, the δ models outperformed the LSTM model noticeably in the PUR tests, especially for the annual mean flow and high flows
δ models provide a full suite of diagnostic physical variables and guaranteed mass conservation.

chunks.text: Among tested variants, the dynamic-parameterization model δ(γt,βt) delivers the best overall generalization and improves ET seasonality, with minimal deterioration in PUB or PUR. The paper concludes that increased complexity did not cause overfitting because computation is regulated through parameter interfaces in HBV. This suggests dynamic parameterization may be capturing missing processes such as deep storage and vegetation dynamics.
supporting_quote: δ(γt, βt) stood out for having the best overall test performance
Even though its structure is more complex, it was not more overfitted than other models.
It also showed markedly better ET seasonality than δ or δ(βt), which barely deteriorated in PUB or PUR scenarios.
It seems DP may have enabled the learning of some true processes that are missing from HBV, possibly related to deep soil water storage and/or vegetation dynamics

chunks.text: Training δ models yields remarkably stable spatial parameter fields despite large changes in training data density (temporal vs PUB vs PUR), reinforcing robustness in extrapolation. The authors argue δ models can guide improvements in traditional process-based model mechanisms, particularly for vegetation and deep subsurface storage. They also emphasize δ models as candidates for regional to global simulations and multi-source data assimilation.
supporting_quote: The training of the δ models resulted in remarkably stable parameter fields despite large differences in training datasets (temporal test vs. PUB vs. PUR).
the δ models are not only reliable candidates for global climate change impact assessment but also can highlight potential deficiencies in current process-based model structures
Combined with their interpretability and ability to assimilate multi-source observations, the δ models are strong candidates for regional and global-scale hydrologic simulations

chunks.text: Hydrological models are widely used to understand and manage flooding, sedimentation, and nonpoint source pollution. The SWAT model is especially common due to its interfaces, documentation, and global databases. Because such models have many spatially distributed parameters, multisite and multi-objective calibration approaches have become important for representing heterogeneous watershed processes.
supporting_quote: Hydrological models are important tools for improving our understanding of hydrologically related processes (Clark et al., 2016), such as flooding, sedimentation, and nonpoint source pollution
The SWAT model is the most widely used one featured by user-friendly interface to setup the model, structured documents and wide coverage of database around the world.

chunks.text: Multiple software frameworks exist to support calibration and uncertainty analysis for SWAT, including AMALGAM, IPEAT/IPEAT+, OSTRICH, SWAT-CUP, and RSWAT. These tools commonly implement multisite calibration by treating the watershed in a lumped manner, producing a single optimal parameter set for all outlets. This common workflow provides automation but can limit the ability to represent spatial variation across subwatersheds.
supporting_quote: Many tools have been developed to facilitate multisite and multiobjective calibration. These include... AMALGAM... IPEAT... OSTRICH... SWAT-CUP... and RSWAT
Multisite calibration in these tools are commonly conducted in a lump mode... and determines one optimal solution of parameter sets for the whole watershed.

chunks.text: For watersheds with complex stream networks or strong geographic heterogeneity, it can be preferable to calibrate parameters for different subwatersheds independently. Prior work indicates that modifying parameters identically across the entire watershed may be unsuitable in heterogeneous basins. This motivates approaches that allow spatially varying parameter adjustment across sites.
supporting_quote: For watersheds with complex stream network or geographical heterogeneity, multisite calibration in the distributed mode is preferred for the SWAT model because parameters for sub-watersheds are calibrated independently.
Changing parameters in an identical way may be suitable... but not suitable for watersheds with large area or higher geographical heterogeneity

chunks.text: The study aims to develop an open-source toolbox (DMPOTSWAT) that enables multisite calibration of SWAT in both lump and distributed modes. The goal includes automating watershed division, supporting calibration across multiple outlets simultaneously, and providing auxiliary capabilities such as sensitivity analysis, uncertainty analysis, and visualization. The toolbox is intended to facilitate distributed-mode calibration for SWAT and potentially other hydrologic models.
supporting_quote: an open source toolbox named Distributed Model Parameter Optimization Toolbox for the SWAT model (DMPOTSWAT) is developed to perform multisite calibration in both the distributed and lump modes.

Other functions including model evaluation with default parameter values, sensitivity analysis, selecting best parameter sets, uncertainty analysis, and visualization of calibration output are also provided.

chunks.text: A key objective is to introduce a distributed calibration mode that updates parameters for different subwatersheds simultaneously but independently, rather than through sequential upstream-to-downstream workflows. The approach is described as originating from sequential and cascading calibration, but designed to remove extra model runs and avoid negative downstream impacts from fixing upstream parameters. The authors emphasize this distributed mode as not available in existing multisite calibration tools.
supporting_quote: a distributed mode for multisite calibration is proposed in this study. In this mode, parameters for different parts of sub-watersheds in a watershed are calibrated simultaneously but independently.

The development of this mode originates from the sequential and cascading calibration techniques but is advanced by removing the extra model runs and the potential negative impacts by fixing parameters for some sites.

chunks.text: Existing multisite calibration tools often operate in a lump mode, where parameters are changed identically across all subwatersheds and a single optimal parameter set is selected for the entire basin. This can fail to capture spatial variation in hydrologic processes across geographically heterogeneous watersheds. The resulting solution may be a compromised optimum because the algorithm tries to improve objective functions for all sites simultaneously with one shared parameter evolution.
supporting_quote: Multisite calibration in these tools are commonly conducted in a lump mode by changing parameters in identical ways for sub-watersheds of different sites participating calibration and determines one optimal solution of parameter sets for the whole watershed.
This indicates that the optimal solution is not able to fit the whole watershed and fails to capture spatial variation in hydrologic and related processes across sub-watersheds of different sites.

chunks.text: Sequential and cascading calibration approaches can generate site-specific parameter sets, but they can require many model runs when multiple sites are calibrated. They can also introduce issues when upstream parameters are fixed while calibrating downstream sites, particularly when sites lie along the main stream. These disadvantages make calibration difficult for watersheds with complex stream networks and strong heterogeneity.
supporting_quote: calibrating each site might require many numbers of model runs, resulting large numbers of model runs for calibrating all sites in the watershed.
fixing parameters for sites located upstream can sometimes affect the calibration for sites located downstream if the sites all locate on the main stream.

chunks.text: Dividing a watershed into upstream contributing subareas for multiple outlets can be time-consuming and prone to errors, especially in complex stream networks. The paper identifies the need for automation to determine upstream subareas and generate subwatershed groupings for distributed calibration. Without algorithmic support, preparing these spatial units becomes a barrier to applying multisite calibration in practice.
supporting_quote: to determine all upstream subareas and divide a watershed into sub-watersheds is a timeconsuming and error-prone job, especially for watersheds with complex stream network.
In the DMPOTSWAT, the Depth First Search (DFS) algorithm is adapted to retrieve the upstream subareas of any outlet of a watershed.

chunks.text: DMPOTSWAT is implemented in Python 3.10.8 and provides a GUI built with Tkinter. The package is compiled into an independent executable using pyinstaller to avoid requiring users to set up a programming environment. The GUI supports default evaluation, sensitivity analysis, calibration (lump or distributed), visualization, and uncertainty analysis after a SWAT model is prepared in ArcSWAT or QSWAT.
supporting_quote: The framework is programmed in python (3.10.8)... A user-friendly GUI is developed using the Tkinter library.
The whole DMPOTSWAT package is compiled into an independent executable file with the pyinstaller library, and removes the necessities of setting up the programming enviro nment.

chunks.text: The GUI is organized into a notebook-style interface with ten tabs, each supporting a specific workflow stage such as setting up projects, defining SWAT model settings, selecting parameters, running sensitivity analysis, performing calibration, plotting outputs, selecting best runs, and conducting uncertainty analysis. Users configure outlets and variables, choose statistics and weights, and then run background processes to modify SWAT inputs and execute simulations. Detailed instructions are provided in a user manual distributed with the software repositories.
supporting_quote: The GUI is designed with a notebook style containing 10 tabs with 9 tabs... performing specific functions and one "About" tab

users can use this toolbox to conduct operations including: 1) default model evaluation, 2) sensitivity analysis, 3) model calibration with either the distributed or lump mode, 4) visualize the calibration output, 5) uncertainty analysis.

chunks.text: Sensitivity analysis is supported through three global methods—Sobol, Morris, and FAST—implemented via the SALib library. The toolbox generates parameter samples using SALib samplers, runs SWAT for each sample, computes outlet statistics and objective functions, and then calculates sensitivity indices using SALib analyzers. Results are saved to CSV for further inspection.
supporting_quote: three methods are provided for performing global sensitivity analysis, including the Sobol, Morris, and FAST methods. These methods are conducted by functions in the SALib library
Then, the sensitivity index are calculated by corresponding functions (sobol.analyze, morris_analyze.analyze, fast. analyze) in the SALib and saved into a csv file.

chunks.text: Calibration uses the DDS (dynamic dimension search) optimization algorithm, which performs stochastic search within user-specified parameter bounds. The probability of perturbing parameters decreases with run number according to an exponential-like schedule, and new candidates are generated by perturbing the current best parameter set with Gaussian noise scaled to 20% of the parameter range. The best parameter set from one run becomes the candidate baseline for the next run.
supporting_quote: In this toolbox, the DDS optimization algorithm is implemented estimating sample sets for parameter values.
x_{new} = x_{best} + Z*0.2*(x_{upper} - x_{lower})

chunks.text: In lump-mode multisite calibration, a single parameter set is updated per run and applied across the whole watershed, with the best set selected based on objective functions aggregated across all outlets. Objective functions are computed using weighted sums over statistics and outlets, and statistics are standardized to avoid domination by metrics with larger numeric ranges. The framework caps NSE minimum at −99 and caps PBIAS/MSE/RMSE maximum at 100 for standardization purposes.
supporting_quote: By calibrating in the lump mode, only one set of the user selected parameters will be updated... and applied to the whole watershed.
values of the five statistics have different ranges and are standardized using equation (4)... the minimum value of NSE is set to be − 99... maximum value is set to be 100

chunks.text: In distributed-mode calibration, the watershed is divided into subwatersheds based on user-specified outlet numbers. Each subwatershed receives its own copy of subarea- and HRU-level parameter sets that are updated independently during DDS, while basin-level parameters are still chosen based on the weighted sum of objective functions from all outlets. Subarea/HRU parameters for each outlet are optimized using the weighted sum of selected statistics at that outlet, targeting spatially varying best-fit parameterizations.
supporting_quote: In the distributed mode, the watershed is divided into subwatersheds based on the outlet numbers specified by users.
each sub-watershed will get its own copy of parameters sets at the subarea and HRU level, who are updated individually

chunks.text: Watershed division is automated by using a Depth First Search (DFS) graph traversal to retrieve all upstream subareas for any specified outlet. The toolbox can generate individual subwatershed shapefiles via a GUI button, grouping subarea IDs per outlet and extracting polylines using geospatial Python libraries. This design targets complex stream networks where manual upstream delineation is difficult.
supporting_quote: In the DMPOTSWAT, the Depth First Search (DFS) algorithm is adapted to retrieve the upstream subareas of any outlet of a watershed.
the "Create Sub-watershed Shape" button enables users to generate individual shapefiles for subwatersheds of each user specified outlets

chunks.text: The toolbox is demonstrated on the St. Albans Bay (SAB) watershed, which contains three independent streamflow gauging stations suitable for multisite distributed calibration. Daily streamflow is calibrated at three outlets (11, 19, and 48) for 2011–2014 and validated for 2015–2018, with a 2009–2010 warm-up period referenced in the sensitivity analysis setup. This case study is used to illustrate default evaluation, sensitivity analysis, and calibration workflows.
supporting_quote: The DMPOTSWAT framework was tested at the St. Albans Bay (SAB) watershed
simulation of daily streamflow for 3 outlets (outlet 11, 19, and 48) at the watershed were calibrated from 2011 to 2014, and validated from 2015 to 2018

chunks.text: Sensitivity analysis for SAB streamflow used 30 parameters (Tables S1-1) evaluated with Sobol, Morris, and FAST methods over 2011–2014, using 2009–2010 as warm-up. Parameter ranges were drawn from literature sources and could be adjusted by users. In the sensitivity testing, NSE-based objective values were computed using 1−NSE.
supporting_quote: Sensitivity analysis of the simulated streamflow to the 30 parameters shown in Tables S1-1 were evaluated... for the period of 2011–2014, with 2009–2010 as the warm-up period.
In this testing, the NSE was selected for calculating the objective function, and the 1-NSE values were used.

chunks.text: The default-model evaluation reports multiple performance statistics at each outlet, including NSE, R2, PBIAS, MSE, RMSE, RSR, and an objective function. In the reported configuration, the objective function is computed from NSE as 1−NSE, and values are provided for outlets 11, 19, and 48. This baseline provides a reference point before calibration.
supporting_quote: Value of five statistics and objective function (OF) at each outlet by the default swat model of the SAB watershed.
In this testing, NSE was selected as objective function, which is calculated as 1-NSE.

chunks.text: Calibration experiments use 600 iterations in both distributed and lump modes and evaluate model fit using multiple statistics. During calibration, the study selects NSE and PBIAS as objective functions and applies outlet/statistic weighting, including a higher PBIAS weight for outlet 19. Performance is reported separately for calibration (2011–2014) and validation (2015–2018).
supporting_quote: For the demonstration purpose, 600 iterations were conducted with both modes
During the calibration with the two modes, the NSE and PBIAS were selected as objective functions. PBIAS has higher weight for outlet 19 than the other two outlets

chunks.text: Default SWAT performance in the SAB watershed was weak prior to calibration. Using recommended rating criteria, NSE and RSR were unsatisfactory across all three outlets, indicating poor baseline streamflow simulation. PBIAS was very good at outlets 11 and 48 but only satisfactory at outlet 19, suggesting bias differed by site even when other metrics were poor.
supporting_quote: Based on the recommended ratings of model performance (Moriasi et al., 2007), the NSE and RSR values were unsatisfactory for all outlets.
The PBIAS were very good for outlet 11 and 48, but satisfactory for outlet 19.

chunks.text: Sensitivity analysis indicated that the most influential parameters for streamflow differed by outlet in the SAB watershed. For the Sobol method, the top-8 parameter rankings varied among outlets 11, 19, and 48, demonstrating spatial heterogeneity in parameter sensitivity. Similar disagreements were observed when comparing Morris and FAST outcomes, motivating calibration of all 30 parameters for both modes.
supporting_quote: ranks for the sensitivity index for the top 8 parameters were quite different at the three outlets with the Sobol method.
The disagreements in ranks of sensitivity were also reflected by comparing results by the Morris and FAST method

chunks.text: After 600 iterations, distributed calibration achieved satisfactory NSE and R2 at all three outlets during the calibration period (2011–2014), whereas lump calibration remained unsatisfactory for outlet 11. For example, outlet 11 NSE improved to 0.57 (distributed) versus 0.41 (lump) during calibration. Outlet 48 also showed higher NSE under distributed mode (0.60) than lump mode (0.56).
supporting_quote: During the calibration period, the NSE and R2 values by the distributed mode were satisfactory for the three outlets. While by the lump mode... unsatisfactory for outlet 11.
Outlet 11 ... Cal ... D ... NSE 0.57 ... L ... NSE 0.41

chunks.text: During validation (2015–2018), distributed calibration produced satisfactory NSE and R2 at outlets 11 and 48 but remained unsatisfactory at outlet 19. Lump calibration was satisfactory only at outlet 48 and unsatisfactory at outlets 11 and 19. Numerically, outlet 48 validation NSE was 0.58 (distributed) versus 0.52 (lump), while outlet 11 validation NSE was 0.54 (distributed) versus 0.37 (lump).
supporting_quote: During the validation period, the NSE and R2 values by the distributed mode were satisfactory for outlet 11 and 48, but unsatisfactory for outlet 19.
Outlet 11 ... Val ... D ... NSE 0.54 ... L ... NSE 0.37

chunks.text: Bias performance after calibration was strong for both modes across outlets and periods. The paper reports PBIAS as very good during both calibration and validation for all three outlets under distributed and lump modes. This suggests that while overall fit metrics (e.g., NSE) differed by mode, systematic bias was effectively controlled by both calibration approaches in this case study.
supporting_quote: The PBIAS values were very good by the distributed and lump mode during both the calibration and validation period for the three outlets.
During the calibration with the two modes, the NSE and PBIAS were selected as objective functions.

chunks.text: Flow-duration and time-series comparisons showed that distributed calibration better captured high-flow behavior, particularly at outlet 11. The lump mode matched low-flow regimes but had poor agreement for high flow at outlet 11, whereas distributed mode matched both high and low flow regimes during calibration and validation. Similar trends were noted for outlet 48, indicating improved representation of extremes under distributed calibration.
supporting_quote: simulated streamflow by the distributed mode matched well for both high flow and flow regimes during both the calibration ... and validation ... period for outlet 11.
by the lump mode simulated streamflow matched well with low flow, but showed poor matching for high flow.

chunks.text: Uncertainty plots suggested improved overall performance for distributed calibration across flow regimes. The study infers that distributed-mode simulated flow performed better in both low and high flow regimes based on the uncertainty visualization. However, the authors note remaining mismatches between simulated and observed flow, indicating that calibration improvements did not fully eliminate discrepancies.
supporting_quote: From the uncertainty plot... it can be inferred that the simulated flow by the distributed mode performed better in both low and high flow regimes.
However, there are still mismatch between the simulated and observed flow, which needs further investigation.

chunks.text: The authors highlight that uncertainties during calibration can strongly affect results and may influence optimization scheme selection and parameter identifiability. They note that soil and land use properties may be geographically heterogeneous, while observed data may not adequately capture this heterogeneity. Addressing these uncertainty sources efficiently is identified as requiring substantial additional effort.
supporting_quote: The uncertainties during the calibration procedure might greatly affect the calibration results
soil properties and land use have large geographical heterogeneity, which might not be captured in observed data.

chunks.text: The paper notes the value of incorporating soft data (e.g., base flow ratios, groundwater depth, runoff coefficient) to add constraints during calibration and improve parameter identifiability. Such information may not be measurable in many study areas but can be important for predictive accuracy. The authors cite soft-data-constrained calibration as a future improvement direction.
supporting_quote: Information like general estimates of base flow ratios, depth of groundwater, runoff coefficient, might not be measurable in the study area but are essential to accuracy of model
These soft data are important for model calibration by providing extra constraints on objective functions among iterations and further increasing parameter identifiability

chunks.text: The toolbox currently demonstrates DDS but the authors suggest adding other optimization algorithms and comparing their applicability under different calibration modes. They argue that although algorithm efficiency has been widely tested, suitability with lump versus distributed calibration still needs evaluation. This is listed as a future feature to improve the framework’s capability for multisite calibration.
supporting_quote: Incorporation of other optimization algorithms.
their applicability with different calibration mode needs further comparison. These important features will be added to the framework

chunks.text: Subwatershed grouping is currently based on stream network upstream areas, but the authors note alternative grouping schemes based on soil, land use, or slope. They reference that such schemes are provided by SWAT-CUP and RSWAT, but emphasize that suitability across watersheds with varying conditions needs additional evaluation. This indicates potential limitations in generalizing the current division strategy without further testing.
supporting_quote: Besides dividing sub-watersheds based on stream network, they can also be grouped by factors including soil, land use, or slope properties
However, the applicability of these dividing schemes needs further evaluation on the applicability and suitability for watersheds with various conditions.

chunks.text: The study concludes that the new GUI-based DMPOTSWAT toolbox integrates key calibration-related functions for SWAT and supports both lump and distributed multisite calibration. The SAB case study illustrates how to use these functions and demonstrates advantages of distributed calibration over lump calibration. The software is distributed as an executable to lower barriers for users without programming environment setup.
supporting_quote: a new GUI-based toolbox called DMPOTSWAT is developed... can perform multiple functions relating to calibration of the SWAT model.
The testing results confirms the advantages of calibration by the distributed over the lump mode.

chunks.text: A central takeaway is that distributed-mode multisite calibration updates subwatershed parameters simultaneously within one calibration implementation, avoiding the need for multiple sequential calibrations. The authors present this as an advantage over sequential calibration because it reduces repeated calibration executions. This design is intended to improve feasibility for complex, heterogeneous watersheds.
supporting_quote: In the distributed mode, the parameters at different sub-watersheds are updated simultaneously in one implementation of model calibration.
One advantage of the distributed mode is that it avoids the necessity of multiple implementation of model calibration by sequential calibration.

chunks.text: Floods are among the most damaging natural disasters globally, with rising frequency and severe impacts on people, infrastructure, and economies. Decision-makers need timely and accurate flood information, but physically based hydraulic simulations are often too slow and costly at large scales. Machine learning approaches are increasingly used to support forecasting and mapping because they can learn relationships from data and provide faster predictions.
supporting_quote: Globally, the frequency of floods has increased by 40% in the last two decades (Khosravi et al., 2019).
Solving differential equations of conservation of mass and momentum for a large domain (national or continental scale) is tedious, time-consuming, and costly (Rahman et al., 2021).

chunks.text: Deep learning models, particularly convolutional neural networks, have emerged as promising tools for flood prediction and inundation mapping because they can perform automated feature extraction and spatial analysis. Prior research in Carlisle, UK showed that CNNs can outperform traditional regression baselines for predicting flood depth, motivating further investigation of CNN-based flood mapping frameworks.
supporting_quote: Since CNN accelerates feature extraction and spatial analysis, it has garnered considerable interest in flood prediction (Kabir et al., 2020; Moy de Vitry et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019; Kabir et al., 2020).
In a comparative analysis by Kabir et al. (2020), the CNN model outperformed the Support Vector Regression (SVR) method for predicting flood depth in the urban landscape of Carlisle, UK.

chunks.text: Digital elevation models are critical inputs for flood inundation mapping, but there is limited work on how DEM type (DTM vs DSM) and spatial resolution influence deep learning flood predictions. The paper positions this as a key knowledge gap, especially relevant where high-resolution DEMs are unavailable.
supporting_quote: In mapping the spatial extent of floods, the Digital Elevation Model (DEM), which provides information on the elevation and slope of the terrain, is proven to be a critical input
there is a significant research gap regarding the impact of DEM resolution on the performance of deep learning models for flood prediction.

chunks.text: The study aims to evaluate how DEM type (DTM versus DSM) and DEM spatial resolution affect rapid fluvial flood inundation prediction using a 1D CNN model. Carlisle, UK is used as a benchmark testbed to quantify impacts on flood depth and inundation extent. The paper also seeks to draw implications for data-scarce regions such as Pakistan where only coarser DEMs may be available.
supporting_quote: This paper aims to evaluate the influence of DEM type and resolution on the rapid prediction of fluvial flood inundation using a state-of-the-art 1-D CNN-based model.

Secondly, it aims to underscore the critical importance of providing higherresolution DEMs in regions with limited data availability, which are increasingly vital due to the escalating demand for machine learning techniques.

chunks.text: A secondary goal is to compare machine-learning-predicted inundation against a reference hydrodynamic model baseline and assess performance using depth errors and binary inundation classification metrics. This includes evaluating RMSE, Bias, Precision, Recall, and F1 across multiple flood stages to understand when and where DEM choices matter most.
supporting_quote: The models' performance is then evaluated and compared against an observed flood event using RMSE, Bias, and Fit indices.
Two metrics—RMSE and Bias—are used in this study to determine the CNN model's efficacy in predicting flood depth, and three additional metrics—Recall, Precision, and F1 score—are used

chunks.text: High-resolution DEM data are scarce in many flood-prone regions, which limits the accuracy and applicability of machine learning flood mapping. The paper highlights that rapid, operational flood prediction needs methods that remain useful when only coarser DEMs are available. This motivates studying whether coarser DTMs/DSMs can still provide viable performance and what accuracy trade-offs arise.
supporting_quote: Yet, data scarcity, especially high-resolution DEMs, challenges regions with limited access.
However, in this context, there has been a scarcity of research that has specifically examined the impact of DEM spatial resolution and type on flood prediction.

chunks.text: Large-scale or fine-resolution hydraulic simulations are computationally intensive and often impractical for real-time emergency response. Because running such models can be time-consuming and costly, surrogate approaches such as deep learning are needed to approximate hydrodynamic outputs quickly while retaining acceptable accuracy.
supporting_quote: Solving differential equations of conservation of mass and momentum for a large domain (national or continental scale) is tedious, time-consuming, and costly
running simulations in real-time, such as those needed for emergency response, using the hydraulic model is almost unfeasible

chunks.text: In data-scarce settings such as Pakistan, the commonly available DEM resolution is around 30 m, which can constrain flood inundation mapping quality. The paper frames this as a practical barrier to deploying advanced ML-based flood mapping and explores what performance to expect at 30 m and what added value higher resolution (e.g., 15 m) could bring.
supporting_quote: Ahmad et al. (2010) noted that the highest available DEM resolution in Pakistan is 30 m.
the use of digital elevation model (DEM) data in flood inundation mapping is limited by its low spatial resolution, which constrains the accuracy and applicability of ML methods.

chunks.text: The workflow generates training and testing datasets by coupling synthetic hydrographs with hydrodynamic simulations. LISFLOOD-FP is run using different DEM products to produce time series of raster water depths, which serve as targets for training a 1D CNN that predicts flood depth maps from upstream discharge inputs. The trained CNN for each DEM is then evaluated against pseudo-observed inundation derived from the higher-resolution baseline.
supporting_quote: multiple synthetic hydrographs with various peaks and durations are produced to represent flood scenarios of different magnitudes.

Considering DTMs and DSMs of different spatial resolutions, the LISFLOOD-FP is executed while employing sets of synthetic inflow hydrographs. The output of this process would be gridbased distribution of flood depths, which would serve as the target dataset for training the predictive model.

chunks.text: The study uses a 1D CNN architecture adapted for 1D signals, with convolutional layers for feature extraction and dense layers for mapping to spatial outputs. The model receives upstream flow discharge data and outputs a vector whose length equals the number of grid cells in the simulation domain. This implements a fast surrogate mapping from hydrograph conditions to spatial flood depths.
supporting_quote: The network comprises five hidden layers, two of which are convolutional and three of which are dense.
The output layer comprises nodes equal to the number of cells in the simulation domain, while the input layer receives the upstream flow discharge data.

chunks.text: Hydraulic simulations are performed with LISFLOOD-FP, a raster-based 2D inundation model. The study uses a reformulated LISFLOOD-FP configuration that solves shallow water equations while ignoring convective acceleration, and uses a sub-grid 1D channel representation when channel information is insufficient. These simulations provide the baseline water depth rasters for CNN training and evaluation.
supporting_quote: LISFLOOD-FP is a raster-based model for simulating fluvial or coastal flood inundation
a re-formulation of the LISFLOOD-FP model version 6.3.1 (Neal et al., 2012) is utilized, which solves the shallow water equations while simply ignoring the convective acceleration element

chunks.text: DTMs at coarser resolutions are created by resampling the highest-resolution terrain using bilinear interpolation. DSMs are generated by adding building footprints to the DTMs, representing buildings as raised elevations that obstruct flow. This design isolates the effects of DEM type (bare-earth vs surface with buildings) and resolution on inundation prediction.
supporting_quote: the DTM of various spatial resolutions is produced using the highest DEM resolution available using the bilinear interpolation approach.
Then to produce the DSMs, the building footprints are added to the constructed DTMs.

chunks.text: CNN training uses regularization to prevent overfitting, including early stopping, batch normalization, and dropout. The paper specifies key hyperparameters used during training, including patience and min delta for early stopping, batch size, dropout rate, optimizer, and learning rate. This setup aims to improve generalization across multiple synthetic flood scenarios and DEM configurations.
supporting_quote: regularization techniques are used during the training phase, such as "early stopping", "batch normalization" and "dropout"
the settings for patience ... and the improvement criteria (min delta) were configured as 5 and 0.001, respectively. Additionally, a batch size of 10 and a dropout rate of 0.2 were chosen.

chunks.text: Model performance is assessed for both continuous water depth accuracy and binary inundation extent accuracy. Depth performance uses RMSE and Bias across pixels, while extent performance uses Precision, Recall, and F1 derived from TP/TN/FP/FN classifications of wet vs dry pixels. LISFLOOD-FP outputs are treated as the baseline reference rather than field observations.
supporting_quote: Two metrics—RMSE and Bias—are used in this study to determine the CNN model's efficacy in predicting flood depth
three additional metrics—Recall, Precision, and F1 score—are used to demonstrate how well the model performs in identifying the correct binary inundation status

chunks.text: The case study is Carlisle, UK, a flood-prone urban area at the confluence of three rivers (Eden, Petteril, and Caldew). The modeled domain covers about 14.5 km^2 and benchmarks the well-documented 2005 flood event. Flood phases are evaluated at multiple timestamps to compare inundation depth and extent patterns.
supporting_quote: The research domain encompasses about 14.5 km2 of Carlisle's urbanized region (Figure 2)
The flooding that occurred in Carlisle in 2005 was selected for benchmarking and simulated using the LISFLOOD-FP.

chunks.text: High-resolution topography is sourced from a 1 m LiDAR DTM (Environment Agency, 2020) with stated vertical accuracy, and is processed into multiple coarser resolutions. DSMs are created by integrating building footprints from OpenStreetMap with the resampled DTMs. The 5 m DSM is treated as the baseline representation for inundation mapping.
supporting_quote: the LiDAR 1 m DTM released by the Environment Agency in 2020 with a vertical accuracy of +/-15cm RMSE

The associated DSMs were generated by combining the DTMs with the building footprint Polygons made available by OpenStreetMap (www.openstreetmap.org/). The DSM with a resolution of 5 m is considered to represent the baseline.

chunks.text: Hydrologic forcing includes three upstream boundary locations and 15-minute discharge hydrographs for the 2005 event, along with multiple synthetic hydrographs to provide training variability. The training set uses 24 synthetic hydrographs (eight per upstream location), while the observed/routed 2005 event is held out for testing. Synthetic hydrographs are adjusted to increase peak variability by scaling with a ratio to exceed observed peaks.
supporting_quote: This study uses 15 minute discharge hydrographs for the 2005 event that were generated using 1D flood routing (Kabir et al., 2020).
To train the ML model, 24 "synthetic" hydrographs—eight for each of the three upstream boundary locations—are created with variable peaks and durations

chunks.text: Hydrodynamic simulations output 15-minute water depth grids, using a uniform Manning coefficient and a depth threshold to remove small depths from targets. These rasters are converted to arrays and stacked to form the CNN target matrices, whose number of columns equals the number of domain cells at each DEM resolution. The input feature matrix has 2104 samples and 28 variables derived from timestamps and discharge antecedents across three upstream locations.
supporting_quote: The output files include 15-minute interval water depth grids in raster format. Each simulation has a uniform Manning coefficient of 0.055 sm−1/3
Therefore, timestamps, three upstream discharge values, and eight preceding discharges add up to a total of 28 input variables. The total number of samples amounts to 2104

chunks.text: The number of computational cells (and thus CNN output size) varies strongly with DEM resolution, affecting the target matrix dimensionality. For example, the 15 m resolution target has 64,668 columns (cells), while coarser grids have fewer cells. This links DEM resolution to both modeling detail and computational workload.
supporting_quote: the target matrix ... depends on the resolution of each DEM and the total number of cells within the domain, as indicated in Table 2.
At a spatial resolution of 15 m, the domain contains 64,668 cells, while at a 30 m resolution, there are 23,180 cells.

chunks.text: Using a 30 m DTM provided better flood depth prediction accuracy than a 30 m DSM, particularly during peak flooding. The paper reports that at the flood peak, a 30 m DSM increases RMSE relative to a 30 m DTM by about 21%. This indicates that at low resolution, bare-earth terrain representation can outperform surface models that include buildings.
supporting_quote: Results indicated that utilizing a 30 m DTM outperformed a 30 m DSM in terms of flood depth prediction accuracy by about 21% during the flood peak stage
In the case of Carlisle, employing a 30 m DSM resulted in a 21% increase in RMSE during the peak stage compared to the 30 m DTM.

chunks.text: At many validation stations, predicted water depth tends to increase as DEM resolution becomes coarser, especially for DTMs. Station-specific comparisons (e.g., Bus depot, Caldew level, Watermark 3, Eden level) show that coarsening can elevate peak depths and alter hydrograph shapes. Effects can differ by location, with river-proximal stations sometimes showing similar DSM/DTM depths due to limited building influence.
supporting_quote: In the Bus depot, the water depth is increased as the resolution of the DTM becomes coarser
The findings demonstrated a consistent trend of increasing water depth in most stations as the resolution of the DEMs became coarser.

chunks.text: Spatial error maps show that DTM-based CNN predictions have lower errors than DSM-based predictions in areas without buildings, while DSM can reduce errors near some built-up areas. For 15 m resolution, DSM errors are high near the main river early on, but small areas around building-related stations show low errors, suggesting localized benefit from representing structures.
supporting_quote: it is evident that the DTM exhibits lower error rates compared to the DSM in regions devoid of buildings

there are two small green areas surrounding Building 1 and Building 2 stations in the DSM maps ... that exhibit the lowest error rates. This indicates that the implementation of DSM positively influences flood inundation mapping for these built-up areas.

chunks.text: Depth error indices aggregated over control sites indicate DTM performance is slightly better than DSM performance, especially at flood initiation. During initiation, reported DTM15 depth errors are about RMSE 0.65 m and Bias 0.45 m, with positive bias indicating overestimation. DTM30 shows lower RMSE and Bias than DSM30, reinforcing the advantage of DTM at coarser resolution.
supporting_quote: During this stage, the RMSE and Bias values for the DTM15 indicated an inundation depth error of approximately 0.65 and 0.45 m, respectively.
Additionally, DTM30 shows lower RMSE and Bias values in comparison to the DSM30

chunks.text: Depth prediction error increases as the flood progresses, with RMSE rising substantially from early to peak stages. The paper notes an approximately 2-fold increase from the 48th to 96th time steps and a 4-fold increase from the 48th to 144th time steps, indicating deteriorating accuracy over longer durations and larger inundation. Bias also increases toward peak inundation, reflecting consistent overestimation tendencies.
supporting_quote: there is an approximately 2-fold increase from the 48th to 96th time steps, a 4-fold increase from the 48th to 144th time steps
the Bias values demonstrate a substantial increase starting from the early stages of the flood, reaching their peak at the time of maximum inundation.

chunks.text: Inundation extent metrics indicate DTM performs better in early stages at finer resolutions, while DSM becomes more competitive as flooding expands into built-up areas. At time step 48, F1 is higher for DTM at 15 m (0.644) and 20 m (0.538) than DSM at 15 m (0.573) and 20 m (0.522). At peak (time step 144), DSM shows higher precision and F1 across selected resolutions, consistent with buildings becoming more relevant.
supporting_quote: at resolutions of 15 and 20 m, the F1 scores are 0.644 and 0.538 for DTM, respectively, compared to 0.573 and 0.522 for DSM.
This trend is more evident at the peak flood (144th time step), where DSM exhibits greater precision and F1 scores for all selected spatial resolutions.

chunks.text: Recall values are consistently very high across resolutions and stages, approaching 1, indicating the models identify most truly inundated pixels. However, high recall with lower precision implies overprediction of wet areas, especially with coarser DEMs. As a result, F1 tends to track precision more closely than recall.
supporting_quote: the recall values approach a high value of 1, indicating accurate identification of true inundated pixels.
the recall values remain consistently high across various resolutions and stages, albeit with lower precision values. As a result, the F1 performance aligns more closely with precision.

chunks.text: Runtime comparisons show that coarser DEMs reduce training/testing time because they reduce the number of domain cells. The reported training/testing time is about 6 minutes at 15 m (64,668 cells) versus about 3 minutes at 30 m (23,180 cells) on an NVIDIA GeForce 940MX. This highlights the computational trade-off between resolution and speed in CNN-based inundation mapping.
supporting_quote: The CNN models developed for all DTMs and DSMs were trained on an NVIDIA GeForce 940MX.
At a spatial resolution of 15 m, the domain contains 64,668 cells, while at a 30 m resolution, there are 23,180 cells. The corresponding runtimes are approximately 6 and 3 minutes, respectively.

chunks.text: For a data-scarce context like Pakistan where 30 m DEMs are common, the Carlisle-based analysis anticipates DSMs would reduce depth accuracy relative to DTMs. The paper estimates that using a 30 m DSM increases RMSE by about 30% at initiation, 21% at peak, and 12% at recession compared to 30 m DTM, while F1 overlap may slightly improve. Overall, DTMs are recommended given current availability.
supporting_quote: Ahmad et al. (2010) noted that the highest available DEM resolution in Pakistan is 30 m.
This increase in RMSE is estimated to be around 30% during the flood initiation stage, 21% during the peak stage, and 12% during the recession stage.

chunks.text: DSM construction is simplified by adding building footprints with a constant height, which may not represent real variability in building and infrastructure heights. The paper notes that footprint accuracy and height assumptions can influence corrected DEM quality, especially in complex terrain. This simplification may limit how well DSM-based modeling captures true urban flow obstruction effects.
supporting_quote: the accuracy of the building footprints used in the correction process can impact the quality of the corrected DEM.
the constant height assumption may not always hold true, as buildings and infrastructures can have varying heights and the terrain can be complex

chunks.text: DSM benefits depend on whether buildings adequately occupy a grid cell; at low resolutions, many cells are only partially covered by buildings. The study notes that its selected resolutions (15–30 m) produce large cell areas (225–900 m^2), making it difficult to model building effects accurately when gaps and building sizes are smaller than the grid. This can lead to poorer inundation simulations for coarse grids relative to building scale.
supporting_quote: the size of each cell ranges from 225 m2 (15m×15m) to 900 m2 (30m×30m). Additionally, the cells might not be fully occupied by existing buildings in reality
modeling scenarios that are coarser than the size of the buildings and gaps lead to poor performance in inundation simulations.

chunks.text: Model evaluation uses LISFLOOD-FP outputs as the baseline instead of field observations, meaning accuracy is measured against a reference simulation rather than ground truth. While this enables controlled comparison across DEM configurations, it may not fully reflect real-world observational uncertainties or biases present in hydraulic models.
supporting_quote: In this study, instead of using actual field data, the outputs from the LISFLOOD-FP model are utilized as a baseline to evaluate the predictive abilities of the ML models

chunks.text: The paper notes memory limitations for 1D CNNs, which can restrict applicability to small domains at higher spatial resolution. For future work with higher resolutions, the study suggests reducing domain size or using alternative architectures such as 2D convolutions to handle increased memory demands.
supporting_quote: 1D CNNs are known for their memory inefficiency, limiting their applicability to smaller domains.
in future research endeavors involving higher spatial resolutions, it becomes necessary to either reduce the domain size or explore alternative network architectures (e.g., 2D convolutions)

chunks.text: Across the tested range, DTMs generally yield slightly lower RMSE and reduced bias than DSMs, and at 30 m the DSM produces notably worse depth accuracy at peak. Higher-resolution DEMs improve inundation extent accuracy; the paper reports that 15 m resolution provides better extent prediction than 30 m DTM, with average improvements across flood phases. The study emphasizes prioritizing higher-resolution DEM availability, particularly for data-scarce regions, while balancing computational constraints.
supporting_quote: we found that, within the range of resolutions examined, using a DTM yields slightly lower RMSE and reduced bias compared to a DSM.
employing a 30 m DSM resulted in a 21% increase in RMSE during the peak stage compared to the 30 m DTM.

chunks.text: The study concludes that even when only coarser DEMs are available, they can still support rapid CNN-based flood prediction, but modest resolution improvements can add substantial value. It argues that improving DEM accessibility and resolution can strengthen flood risk management by enabling more accurate ML-based inundation depth and extent estimates in vulnerable regions.
supporting_quote: The findings emphasize that while a coarser resolution DEM may impact the accuracy of machine learning models, it remains a viable option for rapid flood prediction.
even a slight improvement in data resolution in data-scarce regions would provide significant added value, ultimately enhancing flood risk management.

chunks.text: Hydrologic models are commonly used to represent complex environments, but their evaluation is complicated by multiple interpretations of outputs, differing process formulations, and uncertainty in inputs and parameters. Many parameter values used in computations are not directly measurable and therefore must be calibrated with objective functions such as NSE or RMSE. Understanding how each parameter influences model output is important for focusing calibration on influential parameters and reducing uncertainty.
supporting_quote: Difficulties frequently arise in model performance evaluation due to multiple interpretations of output or data products, differing mathematical descriptions of underlying processes, and uncertainties present in the input and parameter datasets

Model parameter values for numerical calculations are often not a direct physical interpretation and can rarely be measured in the field. Consequently, models are calibrated using objective functions (e.g., Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency [NSE], root mean squared error [RMSE]

chunks.text: Reproducibility and transparency are increasingly emphasized in hydrology, yet published studies often cannot be reproduced. The paper highlights community calls to make data, software, methods, and provenance accessible and well-documented. Technical barriers, insufficient documentation, and complex software packaging can hinder replication of computational hydrology studies.
supporting_quote: Previous studies have called for the adoption of reproducibility and transparency within hydrology to add credibility to scientific claims.
Stagge et al. (2019) found low reproducibility (5.6% of total sampled articles) in research published in 2017 from six hydrology and water resources journals.

Challenges to reproducibility include technical barriers, limited documentation of the research to be replicated and potentially complex requirements for how the software is packaged, installed, and executed

chunks.text: Although many tools exist for computing objective functions and conducting sensitivity analyses, they are often not integrated into unified workflows. The authors note that packages for goodness-of-fit and global sensitivity analysis rarely communicate, motivating a universal approach that integrates existing libraries. This integration is especially needed for large parameter sets and multi-metric evaluation.
supporting_quote: Many packages are available for calculating objective functions (e.g., the R package hydroGOF... ) and implementing sensitivity analyses (e.g., the python library SALib... ), but rarely do these packages communicate with one other.
The hydrologic community needs a common procedure to evaluate model output based on parameter sensitivities and uncertainties compared to performance metrics

chunks.text: The study aimed to develop a well-documented, adaptable, and reproducible workflow to evaluate hydrologic model parameter sensitivities and uncertainties. The workflow is intended to objectively evaluate model output as a function of parameter choice using both numerical indices and visualization products. Although motivated by National Water Model evaluation needs, it was designed to be universal and modular for integration across hydrologic frameworks.
supporting_quote: Our study objective was to develop a welldocumented, adaptable, and reproducible workflow for evaluating hydrologic model parameter sensitivities and uncertainties.
The workflow needed to objectively evaluate model output as a function of parameter choice using both numerical and visualization techniques.
our workflow was intended to be universal and modular for applications across a variety of hydrologic modeling frameworks.

chunks.text: A further goal was to integrate existing open-source tools into a single modular pipeline and demonstrate it across multiple hydrologic models with differing parameterizations and metrics.
