The authors deconstructed and integrated the R package hydroGOF and the Python SALib sensitivity library, adding new scripts within modules. They tested the workflow on SWMM, HBV, and TOPMODEL and provided reproducible notebooks and outputs via a community GitHub repository.
supporting_quote: We deconstructed and integrated an existing R package (hydroGOF) and a python sensitivity analysis library (SALib) with new R and python scripts executed within different modules of the resulting workflow.
We tested the workflow using three common hydrologic models: Storm Water Management Model (SWMM... ), ... HBV ... and TOPMODEL
For each case study, an executable Jupyter Notebook with all Python and R scripts was included in the github repository.

chunks.text: Hydrologic model evaluation is challenging because parameter uncertainty and alternative process representations can yield multiple plausible outputs. Since parameters are often not directly measurable, calibration depends on objective functions, which can obscure how individual parameters drive performance. The paper frames the need to understand parameter influence to better target calibration and uncertainty reduction.
supporting_quote: Difficulties frequently arise in model performance evaluation due to multiple interpretations of output or data products, differing mathematical descriptions of underlying processes, and uncertainties present in the input and parameter datasets

To effectively model hydrology, it is necessary to understand how the model output is impacted by each parameter and focus model calibration on decreasing the uncertainties of more influential parameters.

chunks.text: The hydrologic community lacks a common, reproducible framework that combines objective-function evaluation with parameter sensitivity and uncertainty analyses, particularly for large parameter sets and multiple metrics. Existing packages for metrics and sensitivity analysis typically do not interoperate, making comprehensive analyses harder to implement and reproduce. The paper positions the proposed workflow as addressing this procedural gap.
supporting_quote: The hydrologic modeling community needs common frameworks organizing the development of open source, multicriteria approaches that are reproducible, adaptable, and transferable for evaluating model parameter sensitivities and uncertainties
Many packages are available for calculating objective functions... and implementing sensitivity analyses... but rarely do these packages communicate with one other.

chunks.text: The workflow is a modular pipeline that ingests parameter sets, model simulations, observed data, and objective functions, then produces numerical sensitivity/uncertainty outputs and standardized visualizations. It expects four input matrices: parameters [n×K], simulations [n×t], observations [1×t], and objective functions [n×S]. The workflow can use hydroGOF or other evaluation tools (e.g., WRES) to compute objective functions, and outputs figures and files with generic labels and sizing to support diverse applications.
supporting_quote: The necessary input formats were a: (1) [n × K] matrix... (2) [n × t] matrix... (3) [1 × t] matrix... and (4) [n × S] matrix
Many coding packages are available for calculating common objective functions and we used the R package hydroGOF
The workflow was modular to allow users to run only scripts applicable to their parameter sets, model outputs, and objective functions.

chunks.text: Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) is used to quantify uncertainty in parameter spaces by estimating posterior distributions of parameters without explicitly computing a likelihood. The method draws parameters from priors, runs simulations, computes objective functions, and then filters parameter sets based on a distance criterion and a user-specified tolerance to approximate the posterior. The workflow saves parameter sets within tolerance and generates histograms, CDFs, and PDFs of prior vs posterior parameter distributions.
supporting_quote: One method integrated into the workflow was Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC)... to estimate posterior distributions of model parameters.
ABC is advantageous because it bypasses calculating the likelihood function by using the model simulations compared to the observed data
Remove parameter points beyond a user-specified tolerance interval to approximate samples from the posterior distribution.

chunks.text: The workflow includes three sensitivity analyses to cover different computational and inferential needs: Sobol variance-based indices, Delta moment-independent indices, and OLS regression. Sobol yields first-order, second-order, and total-order indices and can capture nonlinear responses and interactions; the workflow uses the Saltelli scheme to reduce the number of required runs. Delta quantifies effects on the output distribution (pdf) and is computationally efficient, while OLS provides an R² measure of linear parameter effects on objective function variance.
supporting_quote: Three sensitivity analyses were incorporated into the workflow: a variance-based sensitivity analysis, a moment-independent sensitivity analysis, and an ordinary least squares (OLS) regression.
The Sobol method... yields first-order, second-order, and total-order sensitivity indices.
Our workflow employed the Saltelli scheme... which allowed for the calculation of the first-order, second-order, and total-order sensitivity indices with fewer model runs
The Delta index... is a moment-independent global sensitivity analysis.
Lastly, the OLS regression yields an R2 coefficient, which quantifies the linear effects of model input parameters on model output variance.

chunks.text: Visualization is treated as a core part of the workflow: it produces observation time series and magnitude percentile plots to compare modeled vs observed frequency distributions, plus parameter-objective scatterplots. It generates spider plots to summarize parameter sensitivity magnitudes across indices and objective functions, portrait plots for multi-objective comparison, and radial convergence plots (RCPs) that display Sobol first-order, total-order, and second-order interactions as circles and connecting line thickness.
supporting_quote: To evaluate model performance, the workflow plotted observation datasets... and magnitude percentile plots comparing the frequency distributions
portrait and spider plots summarized the OLS and Delta sensitivity analysis of each parameter

Saltelli parameter sampling schemes provided the workflow with data necessary to generate radial convergence plots (RCPs)... plot the first order, total order, and second-order Sobol sensitivity indices for each parameter.

In the RCP figures, the size of the filled light blue circle represents the first-order... the size of the dark blue circle border represents the total-order... and the thickness of dark blue lines between points represents the second-order

chunks.text: In the SWMM case study, the Fall Creek watershed in New York (325 km² near Ithaca) was used because forcing data and parameter ranges were available. SWMM was chosen due to low computational cost (about four seconds per run). A Saltelli sampling scheme generated 24,000 unique parameter sets spanning 11 parameters, and each set was simulated from January 1, 2013 to June 30, 2013 with streamflow extracted for evaluation.
supporting_quote: The Fall Creek watershed, a 325 km2 basin, located near Ithaca, New York, was selected
SWMM was selected as the hydrological model because it is computationally inexpensive and was able to complete one model run in approximately four seconds.
we employed the Saltelli sampling scheme to generate 24,000 unique parameter sets. Eleven parameters (Table 1) were sampled
Each parameter set was run through the SWMM from January 1, 2013 to June 30, 2013, and the time series of simulated streamflow was extracted.

chunks.text: Observed streamflow for the SWMM evaluation came from a USGS stream gauge, enabling time-series comparison of simulated discharge to observations. Model performance was summarized with six objective functions computed using the hydroGOF R package: mean error, mean absolute error, mean squared error, NSE, percent bias, and RMSE. The paper focuses its detailed visualization examples on NSE while noting other objective-function outputs are available in the repository.
supporting_quote: Simulated streamflow was compared to USGS stream gauge data (https://waterdata.usgs.gov/nwis/uv? 04234000, Accessed July 1, 2019).
Six objective functions were calculated using the R hydroGOF package... mean error, mean absolute error, mean squared error, NSE, percent bias, and RMSE.
This section describes the complete workflow with NSE as the objective function

chunks.text: The SWMM sensitivity analysis varied 11 parameters spanning surface roughness, storage, routing, infiltration, snowmelt, and groundwater terms, each sampled over specified ranges. Examples include basin width (500–1,500 m), hydraulic conductivity (0.01–10.0 mm/hours), and groundwater parameters A1 (groundwater flow coefficient) and B1 (groundwater flow exponent). These parameter ranges defined the explored parameter space for the 24,000 model runs.
supporting_quote: TABLE 1. The 11 parameters... and parameter ranges sampled
w ... Range 500 to 1,500
k_sat ... Range 0.01 to 10.0
A1 Groundwater flow coefficient ... Range 0.0001 to 0.00
B1 Groundwater flow exponent ... Range 1.0 to 3.0

chunks.text: For the SWMM case study using NSE, the groundwater parameters were dominant in multiple sensitivity measures. Parameter A1 had the largest Sobol indices (S1=0.4894; ST=0.5790) and the largest OLS linear influence (R²=0.664), while B1 was the next most influential (S1=0.2219; ST=0.2609). Delta indices also ranked A1 and B1 highly (0.2939 and 0.1609, respectively), indicating strong influence on the objective function distribution.
supporting_quote: For the NSE objective function... the Sobol, Delta, and R2 sensitivity indices... were shown in Table 2.

chunks.text: Magnitude percentile curves revealed a systematic bias in the SWMM simulations relative to observations. The percentile plots showed that most simulated streamflow values fell below the historical data, especially in high-flow events (80th–100th percentile). This indicates the model configuration tended to underestimate discharge during larger flows for the study period.
supporting_quote: Figure 2 showed a time series of the historical data along with frequency magnitude percentile curves.
As shown in Figure 2 for the SWMM model simulations, the majority of simulated streamflow values fall below the historical data.
This implies SWMM tends to underestimate streamflow, especially for higher flow (80th–100th percentile) events.

chunks.text: The ABC uncertainty analysis, using a tolerance of NSE ≥ 0.0, filtered out most SWMM simulations and produced constrained parameter distributions. Approximately 20% of the 24,000 model runs achieved NSE greater than zero, meaning about 80% were removed by the tolerance. Posterior histograms and PDFs suggested that the best-performing configurations concentrated A1 values near zero, implying a potentially narrower effective range for that parameter under the chosen metric and tolerance.
supporting_quote: ABC was implemented with a tolerance specified at NSE ≥ 0.0
Of the 24,000 model runs, approximately 20% had an NSE greater than zero.
Approximate Bayesian Computation ("ABC Results") was applied with a NSE ≥ 0.0, removing ~80% of the modeled discharges.
The SWMM model configurations with the most positive NSE values have the A1 parameter equaling values near zero

chunks.text: OLS scatterplots and R² values indicated that A1 had the strongest linear relationship with NSE among the tested parameters, while Tb had minimal linear influence. The paper reports A1 with R²=0.66 and Tb with R²=0.01 for the SWMM runs, aligning with visible patterns in the parameter-objective scatterplots. This contrast helps distinguish parameters that affect performance linearly versus those with weak linear effects.
supporting_quote: For the SWMM model runs, it could be inferred that the A1 (R2 = 0.66) groundwater coefficient has the strongest linear impacts on the NSE objective function
The parameter with the weakest linear impacts on the NSE objective function was Tb (R2 = 0.01, Table 2).
A correlation between an objective function and a model parameter directly corresponds to the linear relationship indicated by the R2 value from the OLS sensitivity analysis.

chunks.text: Sobol radial convergence plots highlighted key second-order interactions affecting NSE in addition to main effects. The paper identifies notable second-order interactions between n_perv and k_sat, cmelt and Tb, cmelt and A1, and A1 and B1. These interactions indicate that parameter effects on performance are not purely additive and that some parameter pairs jointly influence objective function outcomes.
supporting_quote: Second-order indices indicated how much the interactions between two parameters influenced model output
Parameters with large second-order indices are n_perv and k_sat, cmelt and Tb, cmelt and A1, and A1 and B1.

chunks.text: The workflow was demonstrated as adaptable across multiple hydrologic models and configurations beyond the SWMM example. For HBV-light, the authors report 30,000 parameter sets with 14 parameters and four objective functions, applying ABC with tolerances and computing OLS, Delta, and Sobol indices with multiple visualization types. For TOPMODEL, they used 5,000 parameter sets with 10 parameters and NSE, applying ABC (NSE ≥ 0) and OLS with scatterplot visualizations.
supporting_quote: The workflow (Figure 1) was adapted and easily implemented across the various case study domains and models: SWMM, HBV-light, and TOPMODEL.
HBVlight case study, we calculated four objective functions from 30,000 model parameter sets (each consisting of 14 parameters)
TOPMODEL was configured with 5,000 unique parameter sets (each consisting of 10 parameters) and output was evaluated using one objective function, NSE.
ABC was applied with a tolerance of NSE ≥ 0 and OLS was calculated

chunks.text: Computational cost can limit the use of Sobol second-order indices because the number of required model evaluations grows quickly with the number of parameters. The paper notes that computing second-order Sobol indices needs N × (2K + 2) model runs, which may be infeasible for expensive models or large parameter spaces. To address this, the workflow also includes Delta and OLS methods that have no minimum run requirement.
supporting_quote: since the calculation of Sobol second-order indices requires N × (2K + 2) model runs (where N is preset model runs and K is number of parameters)
some models may be too computationally expensive to run with multiple input parameters.
Consequently, we included two additional sensitivity analyses which have no minimum number of model runs.

chunks.text: The authors caution that ABC-based parameter constraints and interpretations depend on understanding relationships and dependencies among parameters. While ABC suggested A1 values near zero under NSE ≥ 0.0, they state it is not possible to conclude how constraining one parameter will affect others without knowledge of parameter dependencies. This motivates using additional sensitivity analyses to characterize interactions before making strong inferences about parameter range refinement.
supporting_quote: One might conclude the A1 parameter should be sampled from a constrained range of values, skewed toward zero.
However, it is impossible to conclude this without understanding the relationships and dependencies between the various parameters of the model.
Additional sensitivity analyses were required to adequately describe the parameter interactions within the hydrologic model configuration.

chunks.text: Large ensembles can make traditional time-series plots difficult to interpret due to heavy overlap among simulations. The paper notes that comprehensive sensitivity analyses often produce thousands of time series, and overlapping plots provide little insight into output frequency. The workflow therefore includes magnitude percentile curves to summarize distributions, but the underlying limitation remains that dense ensembles require specialized visualization to be interpretable.
supporting_quote: Comprehensive sensitivity analyses require a large number of model runs, resulting in plots with sometimes thousands of overlapping time series displayed on them.
The overlapping time series of historical and simulation data provides little insight into the frequency of various model output values.
Magnitude percentile curves allow for the interpretation of less and more frequent observation values by grouping the individual time series into percentile ranges.

chunks.text: The paper presents a documented, transferable workflow that integrates numerical sensitivity/uncertainty analyses with visualization to support hydrologic model evaluation. The authors conclude that the workflow can aid model selection, simplification, and parameter definition, and is designed for integration with the NWC WRES performance metric tool. They also emphasize its modularity, enabling future expansion with additional analyses and iterative parameter sampling based on sensitivity results.
supporting_quote: We developed a well-documented, easily adaptable, and transferrable workflow to visualize parameter sensitivities and uncertainties for hydrologic models.
Numeric and visual output from the workflow can aid hydrologic modelers in model selection, simplification, and parameter definition.
The workflow was designed for easy integration with the current NWC performance metric tool, WRES.
There is potential to expand on the sensitivity analyses and visualization techniques based on user needs due to the modular setup of the workflow.

chunks.text: Sequential Bayesian estimation (data assimilation, DA) is central to hydrologic and Earth-system modeling for inferring time-evolving system states from imperfect observations. DA merges observations with a dynamic model via a conditional probability formulation to improve accuracy and quantify uncertainty. This framing motivates methods that explicitly target posterior state trajectories rather than only point predictions.
supporting_quote: Sequential Bayesian estimation often referred to as data assimilation (DA) lies at the core of hydrologic modeling
DA aims to infer the temporal evolution of the states of dynamic systems using imperfect observation data

chunks.text: The Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) is widely used in hydrologic DA, but its performance can be suboptimal due to assumptions that are often violated in nonlinear hydrologic systems. In particular, EnKF relies on Gaussian error distributions and a linear update rule, which can limit posterior representation when dynamics and errors are non-Gaussian or strongly nonlinear.
supporting_quote: The most widely used DA method in hydrologic modeling is the Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF)
Key constraints of the EnKF include the Gaussian assumption of error distributions, and the linear updating rule inherent to the EnKF

chunks.text: Particle filters (PF) relax Gaussian assumptions and can assimilate observations with non-Gaussian errors, but practical limitations remain. Earlier PF variants suffer from weight degeneracy and challenges representing filtering densities with finite particles in high dimensions. These constraints motivate alternative approaches that can better approximate posteriors in complex hydrologic settings.
supporting_quote: Unlike the EnKF, the PF can relax the Gaussian assumption of error distributions
the earlier versions of the PF are limited by the weight degeneracy
the inherent limitation of representing the filtering density with a finite number of particles remains unchanged

chunks.text: The study aims to develop a new hydrologic data assimilation method that integrates deep generative modeling with ensemble DA in a unified latent space. The approach is designed to condition model state trajectories on observations using a generative model, then refine results with resampling in physical space. The goal includes outperforming a leading hydrologic DA baseline (HEAVEN) in both synthetic and real watershed experiments.
supporting_quote: we propose the Hydrologic Generative Ensemble Data Assimilation (HydroGEnDA) method
to condition the state trajectories of a dynamic model to the observed data using a generative model within a unified latent space
The performance of the developed DA method is compared to ... (HEAVEN)

chunks.text: A key objective is to enable training of the deep learning components without requiring batches of observations, improving practicality for real-world hydrologic DA. The method separates an offline training stage that uses hydrologic model outputs from an inference stage that assimilates observations to update states. This design targets applicability when observed data availability is limited or inconsistent.
supporting_quote: The HydroGEnDA involves an offline training stage without relying on observations, utilizing hydrologic model outputs instead
The generative and deep learning models in the proposed method are trained during the offline stage without requiring observed data

chunks.text: Conventional DA methods often rely on simplifying assumptions to obtain tractable analysis updates, which can be mismatched to hydrologic reality. Hydrologic systems are nonlinear and high-dimensional, making posterior characterization difficult under Gaussian/linear update frameworks. These issues can lead to suboptimal analyses and inadequate uncertainty representation.
supporting_quote: Conventional DA methods typically depend on simplifying assumptions to derive closed-form expressions for analysis.
the hydrologic systems' underlying dynamics are nonlinear and difficult to capture within a manageable state-space model

chunks.text: Many prior ML+DA attempts do not fully integrate DA and deep learning; instead they often use model reduction or surrogate models for propagation. Studies coupling deep learning with DA frequently focus on synthetic scenarios where observations are noisy versions of states, limiting relevance to hydrologic problems. This leaves a gap for methods that can handle realistic observation–state relationships.
supporting_quote: In most previous attempts, DA and machine learning were not indeed integrated; rather, model reduction or surrogate models were typically employed
typically have focused on synthetic scenarios, where observation data are the noisy versions of the states

chunks.text: A practical challenge in hydrology is that observed variables may not directly correspond to model states (e.g., assimilating streamflow to improve soil moisture dynamics). Some prior DA frameworks cannot assimilate observations that are not directly related to the dynamic model states, restricting real-world usability. The proposed approach targets relaxing assumptions about observation operators via latent-space conditioning.
supporting_quote: the proposed DA methods are not capable of assimilating observed data that are not directly related to the states of the dynamic model
in real world hydrologic modeling, the observed variables may not directly correspond to the model states

chunks.text: Latent-space DA using autoencoders can propagate autoencoder errors into the assimilation, due to encoding/decoding biases affecting reconstructions. Additionally, some approaches train deep learning components using observed data batches, which may be unavailable in operational hydrologic contexts. HydroGEnDA introduces physical-space resampling and observation-free offline training to mitigate these barriers.
supporting_quote: errors in the AE model, such as biases in the encoding or decoding processes, could propagate through the DA process
training the deep learning components ... using a batch of observed data, which is not always accessible in real-world DA applications

chunks.text: HydroGEnDA is a two-stage framework: an offline stage that trains an autoencoder and a score-based generative model using open-loop hydrologic model simulations, and an inference stage that assimilates observations. The offline stage perturbs forcings and initial conditions to generate an ensemble of trajectories capturing uncertainty, then learns a latent prior distribution. The inference stage conditions latent sampling on observations, decodes samples back to physical states, inflates them, and finally resamples in physical space to produce the analysis.
supporting_quote: HydroGEnDA comprises two primary stages: an offline training phase ... and an inference phase for state estimation
The HydroGEnDA method begins with ... the "offline stage," during which runoff is simulated using a dynamic model
Finally, resampling in physical space further improves the performance of the DA method.

chunks.text: The method performs dimensionality reduction with an autoencoder to create a unified latent space that can include both model states and observations (or model outputs). The encoder maps from a combined feature space to latent dimension L, and the decoder reconstructs physical states. The autoencoder is trained end-to-end using an L2 reconstruction loss to preserve information through the bottleneck.
supporting_quote: The Encoder transfers the data from the physical space (x) into a reduced-order latent space (z) to reduce dimensionality.
The reconstruction loss used in the AE model is defined as:  L_AE = E_x [ || x - g_phi ( f_theta(x) ) ||_2^2 ]

chunks.text: HydroGEnDA models the latent prior distribution with score-based diffusion (SDE) generative modeling. A forward SDE progressively perturbs latent samples with drift f(t) and diffusion g(t), producing a Gaussian perturbation kernel p(x(t)|x). A reverse SDE then removes noise guided by the score ∇_{x(t)} log p(x(t)), generating samples from the learned distribution.
supporting_quote: samples (x) drawn from a distribution (p_x) are progressively perturbed ... described by ... SDE
the perturbation kernel is considered Gaussian ... p(x(t)|x) = N(x(t)|mu(t)x, Sigma(t))
the reverse denoising process can be described by a reverse SDE

chunks.text: The paper uses a sub-Variance Preserving SDE (sub-VPSDE) parameterization with explicit μ(t) and Σ(t) to satisfy boundary conditions from data-like samples at t=0 to near-Gaussian noise at t=1. A small numerical stability term η=10^-3 is included. This choice supports stable diffusion training and sampling in the latent space.
supporting_quote: we use the sub-Variance Preserving SDEs (VPSDE)
where  η  is a small numerical stability term (10^-3).
mu(t) = cos^2(cos^-1(sqrt(eta)).t)

chunks.text: The score function in the reverse SDE is approximated by a neural score network trained with a denoising objective. The paper adopts an ε-parameterization to reduce instability near t=0 and trains by minimizing an L2 loss between predicted and true noise. After training, the score network is inserted into the reverse SDE to simulate denoising and generate samples.
supporting_quote: the score function ... can be approximated using machine learning methods called score networks
The objective function to train the score network can be expressed as ... || ε_φ(...) - ε ||_2^2

chunks.text: To assimilate observations without retraining a new conditional score model at each time, the posterior score is decomposed using Bayes’ rule into prior score and likelihood score. The likelihood is approximated assuming a differentiable observation operator A and Gaussian observation process, using Tweedie’s formula to estimate E[x|x(t)]. This enables conditioning sampling on observations while keeping a single learned prior score network.
supporting_quote: decomposing the posterior score using the Bayes' rule ... ∇ log p(x(t)|y) = ∇ log p(x(t)) + ∇ log p(y|x(t))
assuming a differentiable observation operator (A) and a Gaussian observation process
Using Tweedie's formula ... E_{p(x|x(t))}[x] ≈ (x(t) + σ(t)^2 s_φ(x(t), t)) / μ(t)

chunks.text: To reduce data demands and improve stability, the method leverages local score approximations based on (pseudo) Markov blankets over time windows. A local score network is trained on a window x_{i-k:i+k}(t), approximating the local gradient of log density. Sampling is implemented with an exponential integrator discretization for the reverse SDE and augmented with Langevin Monte Carlo correction steps to improve sample quality.
supporting_quote: a pseudo Markov blanket is used instead ... a window ... {i - k, ..., i + k}\{i}
The exponential integrator discretization scheme ... can be used to simulate the reverse SDE
add a few steps of Langevin Monte Carlo Correction (LMC)

chunks.text: After latent-space conditional sampling and decoding, HydroGEnDA performs inflation and then physical-space likelihood-based resampling to mitigate errors propagated from the autoencoder and generative model. Likelihoods are computed from model simulations versus observations using a Gaussian likelihood, converted to normalized weights, and Sampling Importance Resampling (SIR) selects higher-probability ensemble members. The post-resampling set is treated as the final analysis.
supporting_quote: The likelihood is calculated as ... exp[-1/2 (y_t - h(x_t^i))^T R_t^-1 (y_t - h(x_t^i))]
w_i = l_i / sum l_j
The Sampling Importance Resampling (SIR) algorithm is used for resampling

chunks.text: Synthetic experiments are conducted with the Lorenz-63 chaotic system, integrated using a fourth-order Runge–Kutta method with time step Δ=0.025. The study generates 1,024 trajectories and splits them into 70% training, 15% validation, and 15% testing for the deep learning components and assimilation evaluation. Observations are created by adding heteroscedastic noise with relative error levels 0.15, 0.30, 0.45, and 0.60.
supporting_quote: we use fourth order Runge-Kutta (RK4) integrating method with 0.025 time units (∆ = 0.025)
we generate a set of 1,024 trajectories ... 70% ... training ... validation (15%) and testing (15%)
relative error levels of 0.15, 0.30, 0.45, and 0.60

chunks.text: Real hydrologic experiments use the coupled SNOW-17 snow model and SAC-SMA soil moisture accounting model to simulate streamflow, with PET computed via Priestley–Taylor. chunks.text: Hydrologic model predictions can be biased due to uncertainty in forcing data, parameters, structural representation, and initial/boundary conditions. Operational forecasting therefore requires continual adjustment of forecasts as new observations become available. Data assimilation integrates observations with dynamic models to improve forecast accuracy and quantify uncertainty, but most DA research has emphasized theory rather than operational modular deployment.

These issues motivate enhanced PF variants that improve particle diversity.

chunks.text: The EnKF is implemented as an ensemble-based Kalman filtering approach that propagates ensembles through the nonlinear model and updates states using a Kalman gain and perturbed observations. Forecast ensembles are generated via model propagation, then updated using the innovation between perturbed observations and predicted observations. Observation replicates are generated as Gaussian noise around the actual observation with covariance Σy.

Method selection should therefore consider operational requirements such as reliability and integration ease.

chunks.text: The study delivers a standards-based, BMI-compliant, model-agnostic data assimilation module for the NextGen framework, including procedures to tune hyperparameters and dynamically adjust ensemble spread using VVM. The module supports dual state-parameter updating and is structured to allow additional DA methods to be integrated following the same development approach. Testing with the CFE model demonstrates operational feasibility for real-time assimilation within NextGen.
supporting_quote: This study outlines the process of incorporating DA into a standardsbased operational model interoperability framework as a modelagnostic module
The VVM method is presented in both filters to dynamically adjust the distribution of the ensemble using the prediction errors in real-time.
The module is structured to facilitate integration of additional DA methods into the NextGen framework

chunks.text: Assimilating streamflow observations improves model performance for both EnKF and EPFM, with EPFM showing superior performance in most cases across probabilistic and deterministic metrics. The paper concludes EPFM’s advantages are linked to enhancements that address PF issues via genetic algorithms and MCMC. These findings support EPFM as a strong candidate for operational streamflow DA in NextGen when adequate ensemble sizes are available.
supporting_quote: The EPFM demonstrates superior performance over the EnKF in most cases considering both probabilistic and deterministic metrics after assimilating streamflow observations into the model.
Across all basins, the EPFM consistently outperforms the EnKF across all performance metrics after the ensemble size reaches 500.
enhanced versions of the PF, such as the EPFM, have addressed these issues through the integration of more robust algorithms, such as genetic algorithms and MCMC method.

chunks.text: The operational U.S. National Water Model (NWM) has historically been based on WRF-Hydro and has been running since 2016. In parallel, machine learning methods for hydrologic forecasting have advanced rapidly and are increasingly considered for operational deployment. NOAA’s Nextgen framework was initiated to support standards-based, model-agnostic coupling of heterogeneous models and to enable community contributions at continental scale.
supporting_quote: The operational U.S. National Water Model (NWM) is based on WRFHydro ... originally deployed in 2016.
NOAA's Office of Water Prediction initiated the development of the standards based, model agnostic, next-generation water resources modeling framework (Nextgen; Ogden et al. 2021)

chunks.text: Nextgen relies on a component-based approach that allows spatially varied model formulations to be integrated under a shared interface. This approach is motivated by calls for heterogeneous model formulations and diagnostic model selection in large-domain hydrologic modeling. Standards-based frameworks are intended to facilitate research-to-operations contributions, including student-led efforts.
supporting_quote: Johnson et al. (2023) called for heterogeneous model formulations and diagnostic model selection for large-domain hydrological modeling.
Nextgen uses BMI as a common model code architecture and component-based abstraction enabling the integration of plugand-play models in a heterogeneous modeling framework

chunks.text: Two ML-related model classes are highlighted for Nextgen: LSTM rainfall–runoff models and differentiable parameter learning conceptual models (δ conceptual models). LSTMs are described as strong performers for streamflow prediction and already compatible with Nextgen. δ conceptual models use neural networks to learn parameters through differentiable process equations and have been proposed to unify ML and conceptual modeling, especially for ungauged regionalization.
supporting_quote: Among the various ML models, long short-term memory (LSTM) network models for hydrological forecasting excel in terms of streamflow prediction skill and accuracy
Differentiable parameter learning conceptual hydrological models (δ conceptual models) utilize neural networks to generate static, or time-varying, parameters for process-based equations

chunks.text: The technical note aims to integrate ML and physics-informed ML models into the Nextgen framework to support future versions of the NWM. It targets three methodological gaps: evaluating performance across many ungauged catchments, enabling diagnostic-based model selection, and developing regionalization strategies using catchment attributes. The work synthesizes student-led contributions primarily developed through the NOAA Summer Institute.
supporting_quote: integrate machine learning (ML) models ... into the nextgeneration water resources modeling framework (Nextgen) to enhance future versions of the U.S. National Water Model (NWM).

We address three specific methodology gaps ... (1) assess model performance across many ungauged catchments, (2) diagnostic-based model selection, and (3) regionalization based on catchment attributes.

chunks.text: A central objective is to demonstrate that an LSTM trained on gauged CAMELS basins can be deployed at the finer catchment scale of the Nextgen hydrofabric, supporting distributed simulations. The New England (HUC 01) region is used as a regional case to compare predicted flow duration curves from hydrofabric catchments against gauge-based flow duration curves.
supporting_quote: We demonstrate that an LSTM trained on CAMELS catchments can make large-scale predictions with Nextgen across the New England region
We compared the FDC from each hydrofabric catchment with the FDC from stream gauges corresponding to CAMELS basins.

chunks.text: Another objective is to test a machine-learning-driven model selection approach that predicts which model or weighted ensemble of models is likely to perform best in a basin. The paper proposes using catchment attributes to predict comparative model performance and then form an ensemble streamflow prediction with weights derived from those predictions, targeting applicability to ungauged basins.
supporting_quote: Our approach uses a random forest regressor (RFR) to predict the most performant multi-model ensemble of streamflow predictions.
an estimate of model performance for any basin can be obtained using only catchment attributes.

chunks.text: The note also seeks to evaluate δ conceptual modeling by implementing a differentiable version of the CFE model (δCFE) that can learn time-varying parameters via gradient descent. The aim is to improve streamflow prediction performance while maintaining Nextgen interoperability through BMI compliance.
supporting_quote: We implemented the CFE model using a differentiable (δ) platform (PyTorch) to enable gradient tracking through the model.
Our model fully complies with BMI standards, keeping its direct applicability to Nextgen.

chunks.text: A key operational challenge is determining the most appropriate model formulation across hundreds of thousands of catchments in a continental hydrofabric. Because catchments differ widely, a single model may not be best everywhere, making region-specific model selection essential. The paper frames ML as a natural tool for this high-dimensional model selection and classification problem, especially in ungauged basins.
supporting_quote: Given the hundreds of thousands (~800,000) of catchments within the CONUS scale Nextgen hydrofabric, one of the most pressing challenges is identifying the region-specific most performant modeling approach
ML provides an ideal toolkit for dealing with the model selection problem, specifically high dimensional classification

chunks.text: Nextgen models are deployed on catchments smaller than typical gauged basins, creating a scale mismatch between available training/evaluation data and operational model units. The paper highlights that the USGS gauge network has a median catchment area much larger than Nextgen catchments, so runoff prediction must be assessed in distributed ungauged sub-catchments contributing to downstream gauges.
supporting_quote: The USGS stream gauge network across the United States has a median catchment area of 167 km2.
the models in Nextgen will be deployed on catchments smaller than the gauged watersheds of which they are part.

chunks.text: Regionalization and catchment attribute representation are emphasized as critical for ungauged prediction and for deciding which models to apply. The paper notes the lack of comprehensive sensitivity testing of static attributes for LSTM, δ models, and model selection. It also points out that differences in attribute calculations can degrade ML performance, motivating the use of consistent attribute products such as HydroAtlas.
supporting_quote: The need for static attributes as model inputs to represent true basin characteristics, for regionalization and ungauged predictions, cannot be understated.
no comprehensive sensitivity test of static attributes has been presented in the literature.

chunks.text: Model evaluation is conducted against stream gauges using multiple performance metrics. The paper uses NSE, NNSE, and KGE to summarize predictive skill, and also uses the flow duration curve (FDC) to compare distributions of flows. These metrics are used consistently across experiments to compare models and ensembles.
supporting_quote: We evaluate streamflow predictions against stream gauges using four metrics of performance. Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE)
Kling–Gupta Efficiency (KGE) combines correlation, variability, and bias into one statistic
The flow duration curve (FDC) describes the frequency and magnitude of flows

chunks.text: For the distributed catchments experiment, an LSTM trained on CAMELS basins is applied to the Nextgen hydrofabric in New England (HUC 01). The hydrofabric contains about 10,000 catchments, and the analysis compares predicted FDCs from many sub-catchments to observed FDCs from CAMELS stream gauges. This tests whether runoff prediction transfers from larger training basins to smaller operational catchments.
supporting_quote: We applied the LSTM to the HUC 01 (New England) region.
The hydrofabric for this region includes about 10,000 catchments
We compared the FDC from each hydrofabric catchment with the FDC from stream gauges corresponding to CAMELS basins.

chunks.text: For model selection, the study trains a random forest regressor (RFR) to predict model performance from catchment attributes and then form a weighted ensemble. Four candidate models are included: CFE, LSTM, NWM v2.1, and a linear regression using precipitation. Predicted NNSE values determine the weights and a threshold rule drops models whose predicted NNSE is more than 0.2 below the best predicted NNSE.
supporting_quote: Our approach uses a random forest regressor (RFR) to predict the most performant multi-model ensemble of streamflow predictions.
The diverse set of candidate models included: ... CFE ... LSTM ... the NWM v2.1 ... and a simple linear (regression) model
We included a threshold ... predicted NNSE must be within 0.2 of the highest predicted NNSE, otherwise it is dropped from the ensemble.

chunks.text: The multi-model ensemble discharge is constructed as a weighted sum of member streamflows, where weights are proportional to predicted NNSE for each model in the basin. This yields a single ensemble hydrograph per basin based on attribute-driven performance predictions. The framework is intended to estimate performance and guide selection in ungauged basins using only static attributes.
supporting_quote: The resulting multi-model ensemble streamflow prediction for each basin (Q*) is the weighted sum:
Q* = \sum ... ( NNSE_i / \sum ... ( NNSE_j ) ) * Q_i
an estimate of model performance for any basin can be obtained using only catchment attributes.

chunks.text: A differentiable conceptual model (δCFE) is built by implementing CFE in PyTorch to enable gradient tracking and parameter learning through the conceptual equations. A neural network learns time-varying parameters at an hourly time step, specifically saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ks) and a groundwater flux coefficient (Cgw). The authors validate that δCFE matches standard CFE predictions and can recover synthetic parameters from a digital twin experiment.
supporting_quote: We implemented the CFE model using a differentiable (δ) platform (PyTorch) to enable gradient tracking through the model.
The predicted, dynamic, parameters are: saturated vertical hydraulic conductivity (Ks) ... and the primary groundwater flux coefficient (Cgw)
We also tested to ensure that δCFE recovers synthetic parameters

chunks.text: To test sensitivity to static attributes, the study uses HydroAtlas attributes processed to the hydrofabric and then aggregated to represent CAMELS basins for training. Attribute sets are expanded by sampling HydroAtlas variables over hydrofabric feature extents. Performance is assessed as static attributes are added, including an approach that selects attributes via PCA and a comparison to using random attribute subsets.
supporting_quote: There are 280 HydroAtlas attributes, which include physical, biological, and climatological basin characteristics.
we incrementally added static attributes from a principal component analysis (PCA) of the HydroAtlas attributes.
We found that selecting any 10 random HydroAtlas attributes results in median, 75th, and 25th percentile NSE values of 0.61, 0.71, and 0.43

chunks.text: The study uses CAMELS for training, calibration, and validation, including daily USGS streamflow and meteorological forcings, and also relies on hourly streamflow records compiled by Gauch et al. (2021). CAMELS provides both observed hydrologic responses and basin attributes used for ML training and for relating performance to catchment characteristics.
supporting_quote: The experiments presented in this note utilize the Catchment Attributes and Meteorological dataset for Large Sample Studies (CAMELS)
CAMELS data include corresponding daily streamflow records from US Geological Survey (USGS) gauges, and meteorological forcing data.
We use hourly streamflow records compiled by Gauch et al. (2021).

chunks.text: The paper incorporates NWM retrospective simulation output for benchmarking and comparison. Specifically, it uses the 25-year (1993–2019) retrospective simulation from NWM version 2.1. The description notes that NWM includes Noah-MP land surface modeling and multiple routing components for national-scale prediction.
supporting_quote: We include streamflow output from the 25-year (1993–2019) retrospective simulation by the NWM version 2.1
NWM versions 3.1 and below apply Noah-MP (Niu et al. 2011) on a 1km grid

chunks.text: The Nextgen hydrofabric is used to represent catchment discretization and routing topology for distributed simulations. It is generated with tools such as hyRefactor and includes catchments, flow paths, water bodies, and network topology. The Nextgen NWM hydrofabric realizes catchments at approximately 3–15 km2 with minimum channel reach lengths of 500 m.
supporting_quote: NOAA and the USGS have jointly developed a set of tools called "hyRefactor"
The Nextgen NWM hydrofabric realizes catchments at a scale of 3–15km2, and imposes minimum channel reach lengths of 500m.

chunks.text: HydroAtlas is used as a spatially complete source of static basin attributes to support regionalization tests and sensitivity analysis. The dataset provides about 280 hydro-environmental attributes spanning physical, biological, and climatological characteristics. Attributes are processed to hydrofabric basins and then averaged to represent CAMELS basins for ML training.
supporting_quote: We use HydroAtlas static attributes (Linke et al. 2019)
There are 280 HydroAtlas attributes, which include physical, biological, and climatological basin characteristics.
Then, for model training, we averaged hydrofabric basin attribute values to represent the CAMELS basins.

chunks.text: In the New England distributed-catchment experiment, average predicted flow duration curves from hydrofabric catchments agree well with observed high flows but diverge at low flows. Specifically, the average predicted streamflows match higher flows (low exceedance probability) while slightly overestimating the lowest flows (high exceedance probability). The range between minimum and maximum predicted FDCs across many hydrofabric catchments is much wider than the observed CAMELS FDC, consistent with the increased variability at finer spatial scales.
supporting_quote: The average of predicted streamflows match up well with the higher flows (lower percent exceedance), but tend to slightly overestimate the lowest flows (highest percent exceedance).
The minimum and maximum FDC of the HUC 01 LSTM Nextgen have a much greater variation than the observed CAMELS FDC.

chunks.text: The distributed simulation suggests that an LSTM trained on larger gauged basins can be applied to much smaller hydrofabric catchments and still produce effective runoff predictions. The paper notes that hydrofabric catchments are 3–15 km2, while CAMELS training basins can be much larger, yet the LSTM still provides plausible catchment responses across the network.
supporting_quote: we are predicting runoff on catchments much smaller (3–15km2 ) than the training set of CAMELS basins with areas up to 20,000km2.
This demonstrates that the LSTM can make effective runoff predictions at each catchment within the hydrofabric

chunks.text: Model-selection results show that the random-forest-weighted ensemble (WE) performs comparably to the best actual model when basins have higher skill and is robust in lower-skill basins. For NNSE above about 0.6, WE closely matches the best actual model, while for NNSE below 0.6 the ensemble remains the most effective approach. The study also notes that the weighted ensemble generally outperforms the LSTM, which is the best individual model among those tested.
supporting_quote: For catchments with NNSE values above approximately 0.6, the performance of the WE predictions closely matches that of the best actual model.
the multi-model ensemble streamflow prediction remains the most effective approach for catchments with NNSE values below 0.6
Notably, the multi-model ensemble generally outperforms the LSTM model

chunks.text: The δCFE experiment shows improved representation of peak runoff events relative to a calibrated conceptual baseline, with a sharper recession behavior. The hydrograph analysis attributes peak matching to dynamic parameter adjustments that release more water during stormflow-generating events. Time-varying parameters show systematic shifts: Ks becomes smaller than the original value while Cgw becomes larger.
supporting_quote: The hydrograph demonstrates that δCFE closely matches the observed peak runoff events and shows a sharper recession curve compared to its calibrated counterpart
The δCFE matching of observed peaks is the result of the dynamic parameters adjusting to release more water than usual
The predicted time-varying Ks is smaller than the original value, and the time-varying Cgw is larger.

chunks.text: Static-attribute sensitivity experiments show that LSTM performance improves as HydroAtlas-derived attributes increase up to a point, but degrades when too many attributes are added. Using PCA-ordered attributes, the best median NSE reported is 0.62 with 10 PCA attributes. Beyond 10 attributes, performance declines for the tested LSTM configuration.
supporting_quote: The best median NSE score of 0.62 is made with 10 PCA attributes.
Model accuracy improves as the number of HydroAtlas attributes increases to 10; beyond this point, adding more attributes lowers performance

chunks.text: The study finds that PCA preprocessing does not meaningfully improve attribute usefulness compared to selecting a random subset of the same size. Any 10 random HydroAtlas attributes yield a median NSE of 0.61, while the “optimal” 10 PCA attributes yield a median NSE of 0.62, with identical 25th percentile values (0.43) and near-identical 75th percentiles (0.71 vs 0.72).
supporting_quote: selecting any 10 random HydroAtlas attributes results in median, 75th, and 25th percentile NSE values of 0.61, 0.71, and 0.43, respectively.
The optional number of HydroAtlas PCA attributes (10) results in median, 75th, and 25th percentile NSE values of 0.62, 0.72, and 0.43, respectively.
This indicates that the PCA preprocessing of static attributes contributes nothing of value for model predictability.

chunks.text: Calibrated NOAH-MP parameters were tested as static attributes for LSTM prediction but were not beneficial. The paper reports that these parameters fail to provide useful information for improving LSTM streamflow predictions in the conducted sensitivity analysis.
supporting_quote: Static attributes from other sources were also tested. The analysis shows that calibrated parameters from the NOAH-MP model fail to provide useful information for LSTM predictions.

chunks.text: The low-flow bias in the distributed LSTM experiment is discussed as a known weakness and may be exacerbated by spatial-scale mismatch between training and deployment. The paper notes that ML and δ models are known to struggle with low flows, and here the LSTM is applied to 3–15 km2 catchments despite being trained on much larger CAMELS watersheds. This suggests a need for training approaches that better reflect distributed-catchment deployment.
supporting_quote: tend to slightly overestimate the lowest flows (highest percent exceedance).
It is known that both ML and δ models struggle to predict low flows
we are predicting runoff on catchments much smaller (3–15km2 ) than the training set of CAMELS basins with areas up to 20,000km2.

chunks.text: The paper raises an architectural and methodological question about whether LSTMs should be trained with an explicit routing scheme when used in a distributed hydrofabric. Nextgen needs routing to combine runoff across catchments, but current training may not incorporate this structure. The authors suggest distribution-based training/evaluation such as training on the flow duration curve rather than squared error to better match operational needs.
supporting_quote: In the Nextgen framework, a routing scheme is required to combine the runoff through a network of smaller catchments
There is a lingering question of whether or not the LSTM model should be trained in a manner that includes this routing scheme.
Training the LSTM on the flow duration curve itself, rather than a squared error metric, could be more suitable

chunks.text: While the ML-weighted ensemble can improve robustness, the approach may reduce computational efficiency because candidate models must still be run wherever predicted weights are non-zero. The paper notes this could offset gains from using streamlined conceptual models like CFE directly. This trade-off matters for large-scale operational deployments.
supporting_quote: this approach necessitates running all candidate models with predicted ensemble weights significantly greater than zero across each appropriate catchment
which might offset the computational efficiencies gained, especially in scenarios where computationally streamlined models like CFE could be directly applied.

chunks.text: δ conceptual modeling may improve peak flows but can distort internal hydrologic states and process interpretations. The authors describe sharper recessions driven by depleted state values and caution that time-varying parameters may increase equifinality. They warn that δ models could be misinterpreted as physically representative even when states and processes are misrepresented.
supporting_quote: The sharper recession curve following peak events suggests an accelerated drainage effect caused by the model's depleted state values.
The effect of greater equifinality is potentially much larger with time-varying parameters.
there is a risk that such δ conceptual models may misrepresent physical states and processes of hydrologic systems

chunks.text: A practical limitation for ML development in Nextgen is that the framework currently supports inference but not training. ML models must be trained externally and then imported via saved weights, adding friction to iterative development and operationalization workflows. This limitation is presented as a barrier to rapid improvement within the Nextgen architecture itself.
supporting_quote: A potential limitation within the current Nextgen software architecture, in terms of ML, is its inability to train ML models (it can only make inferences with previously trained models).
ML models destined for Nextgen must be trained using external tools, with their weights saved and then imported into Nextgen.

chunks.text: The authors conclude that Nextgen’s standards-based, model-agnostic design can incorporate ML models such as LSTMs and δ conceptual models, enabling heterogeneous modeling to improve operational forecasting. They recommend continuing LSTM development as a benchmark model within Nextgen, emphasizing its adaptability and accuracy, especially in ungauged basins. They also recommend continued δ model development for regionalization benefits, coupled with careful assessment of impacts on hydrologic states.
supporting_quote: We recommend the continued development of LSTM as the benchmark model for hydrologic predictions within Nextgen
the continued development of δ models should be pursued for their unique strength in regionalization and enhancing model performance
it is crucial to examine potential degradation of hydrologic states

chunks.text: The paper concludes that heterogeneous ensembles guided by ML can address the basin-specific model selection problem, including in ungauged basins. Their results support using ML not necessarily to identify a single universally optimal model, but to combine multiple models effectively. They also propose that further attribute analysis can refine model selection criteria and reliability.
supporting_quote: we showed that machine learning can offer effective strategies to combine multiple models, even in ungauged basins.
A continued attribute analysis would inform and refine the criteria for model selection

chunks.text: The authors recommend near-term work to expand δCFE to additional time-varying parameters and to evaluate δ approaches in ungauged basins against standard regionalization methods. They propose coupling δ modeling with the model-selection framework to compare deep learning, process-based models, and hybrid δ conceptual models. This is positioned as a path to improved operational workflows and better understanding of attribute effects on skill.
supporting_quote: Immediate future progress should expand δCFE to include more time-varying parameters and performance assessment in ungauged basins
Such advances could be coupled with the model selection framework

chunks.text: Deep learning has become a leading benchmark for rainfall–runoff prediction because it often outperforms conceptual models and can generalize to new locations and extremes. This has motivated hybrid and physics-informed approaches that incorporate physical theory into machine learning. The paper positions mass conservation as a central physical principle often assumed foundational in hydrologic modeling and examines whether enforcing it actually benefits prediction at catchment scales.
supporting_quote: Deep learning (DL) models are becoming the standard benchmark for predictive hydrologic modelling in the current literature because of their high accuracy relative to conceptual models
we use physicsinformed machine learning to explore the longstanding assumption that mass conservation should be the foundation of hydrological models

chunks.text: A key physical constraint for hydrologic systems is the mass balance relation that storage change equals inputs minus outputs. While conservation laws are physically true, the paper argues their usefulness as a modeling foundation is not guaranteed at watershed scales given observational uncertainty and mismatches between modeled control volumes and real system boundaries.
supporting_quote: dS/dt = I(t) - O(t)

While conservation laws are considered to be a fundamental truth about (classical scale) systems in our physical world, it is not necessarily the case that this makes them a proper or useful foundation for either understanding or modelling watershed systems.

chunks.text: Beven’s closure-violation hypothesis suggests that enforcing conservation constraints may harm model accuracy because observed inputs and outputs may not close due to epistemic uncertainty and missing fluxes. Deep learning may appear superior because it is not constrained to conserve mass and can implicitly learn systematic error structures in data. This paper frames its analysis as bounding the size of that closure-related skill gap.
supporting_quote: Beven (2020), who proposed that the closure problem might explain the poor performance of conceptual and physicallybased (PB) hydrology models relative to DL
the observational data do not themselves provide consistent mass and energy balance closure.

chunks.text: The study tests whether strictly enforced mass conservation is responsible for the performance gap between conceptual/process-based rainfall–runoff models and deep learning models. It uses a mass-conserving neural architecture to isolate the effect of closure constraints when precipitation forcing data are biased. The goal is to quantify how much predictive skill is lost by forcing closure on error-prone inputs and targets.
supporting_quote: We designed an experiment to test the hypothesis proposed by Beven (2020) that the lack of mass conservation in DL rainfall-runoff models explains the difference in skill relative to PB models that are constrained by closure.
Our goal is to understand how much of the difference in skill between the PB and DL models can be accounted for by forcing closure on biased data.

chunks.text: The paper aims to place an upper bound on the ‘closure effect’—the information loss or error attributable to enforcing mass conservation when data contain biases or unobserved sources/sinks. It compares an unconstrained LSTM to an MC-LSTM that strictly enforces mass conservation at every timestep, and to a calibrated conceptual benchmark, to isolate constraint-driven differences.
supporting_quote: we place a bound on this 'closure' effect (i.e., an upper bound on the information loss due to enforcing closure over error-prone data)
The internal calculations of the MC-LSTM ensure mass-conservation, at every timestep

chunks.text: A further goal is to evaluate whether deep learning models can accommodate spatiotemporally heterogeneous biases in forcing products, in contrast to conceptual models, and whether this explains differences in skill. This is tested using two precipitation products that disagree substantially in long-term totals and by examining long-term runoff bias patterns regionally across CONUS.
supporting_quote: We used Daymet and NLDAS for this project because the disagree in their total precipitation amounts
the DL-based LSTM network was able to learn the non-uniform patterns of biases in input–output data

chunks.text: Hydrologic models often assume mass balance closure, but observed precipitation and streamflow data can be inconsistent due to measurement errors and missing fluxes (e.g., springs, anthropogenic inputs). This creates apparent closure violations that can degrade calibration and performance, especially for models that demand strict conservation. The paper treats this as a possible explanation for why deep learning can outperform conceptual and physically inspired models.
supporting_quote: conceptual and PB models typically demand a degree of closure that may not necessarily be achievable given sparse and error-prone observation data
mass contributions to the system through natural springs and anthropogenic water resources can come from outside of the watershed 'boundary' and are not often directly observable

chunks.text: Forcing datasets can exhibit large, nonlinear, location-specific differences in long-term precipitation totals, implying systematic bias in at least one product. When such biased inputs are used, models that enforce water balance may propagate the bias into runoff predictions. This makes it difficult to disentangle whether poor performance comes from model structure or from closure constraints applied to biased data.
supporting_quote: two meteorological data sets with a large, nonlinear, and locationspecific disagreement in long-term precipitation totals, assuming that at least one of these datasets is biased
This systematic difference must be either a positive Daymet bias or a negative NLDAS bias in long-term precipitation totals

chunks.text: The study highlights a broader conceptual issue: the typical fixed catchment control-volume representation may not align with mesoscale storms or groundwater aquifer scales. If watershed boundaries and internal state assumptions are scale-mismatched, enforcing strict conservation within that conceptualization may be inappropriate or unhelpful for prediction. This motivates testing whether mass conservation is a useful scale-relevant modeling foundation.
supporting_quote: it is possible that no successful scale-relevant theory of watersheds has been developed to-date because the fundamental conceptual basis for a 'watershed' is itself incorrect
the typical 'fixed catchment control-volume' represented by our watershed delineations with closed internal states cannot represent mesoscale storm-system scales and groundwater aquifer scales.

chunks.text: The experimental design benchmarks three model classes under two forcing datasets that disagree in long-term precipitation: a per-basin calibrated conceptual model (SAC-SMA with SNOW-17 and unit hydrograph routing), a regionally trained LSTM, and a regionally trained mass-conserving MC-LSTM. By holding training procedures consistent and varying whether strict closure is enforced, the study attributes performance differences to conservation constraints versus model flexibility.
supporting_quote: to benchmark three models: (i) a standard PB model calibrated per-basin; (ii) a standard DL model trained regionally (over all basins, not per-basin), and (iii) a physicsinformed DL model that is constrained to enforce mass conservation trained regionally
The conceptual model that we used as a benchmark was the Sacramento Soil Moisture Accounting model (SAC-SMA) with SNOW-17 and a unit hydrograph routing function.

chunks.text: The MC-LSTM architecture enforces mass conservation at every timestep between designated mass inputs and outputs. Precipitation is treated as a conserved mass input, while other meteorological variables are auxiliary. Unobserved sinks (e.g., evapotranspiration, recharge) are represented by cell states that accumulate mass not released as streamflow.
supporting_quote: The internal calculations of the MC-LSTM ensure mass-conservation, at every timestep, between any number of inputs (here precipitation) and outputs (here streamflow).
accounts for unobserved sinks (e.g., evapotranspiration, aquifer recharge and anthropogenic water resources) using a subset of cell states to accumulate mass that does not translate to streamflow.

chunks.text: Both LSTM and MC-LSTM are trained using daily forcings and static catchment attributes with a normalized squared-error loss (NSE*) that standardizes by basin discharge variability to avoid overweighting large basins. Training uses sequence-to-one minibatches, Adam optimization with a learning-rate schedule, gradient clipping, and added heteroscedastic noise to targets. The models are trained across basins simultaneously, not calibrated per basin.
supporting_quote: we used daily streamflow records as training targets with a normalized squared-error (NSE*) loss function that does not depend on basin-specific mean discharge
Both models were trained for 30 epochs using sequence-to-one prediction to allow for randomized, small minibatches.

chunks.text: The main training/test split follows prior CAMELS benchmarks: training includes water years from 1 October 1999 through 30 September 2008, and testing includes water years 1990–1999. This split is used to ensure comparability with earlier studies, and an alternate period is evaluated in the Appendix for robustness and NWM overlap.
supporting_quote: the training period included nine water years from 1 October 1999 through 30 September 2008, and the test period included 10 water years 1990–1999
Appendix includes an analysis of a different time period (the train period included water years 1981–1995, and the test period included water years 1996–2014)

chunks.text: Model evaluation uses two metric sets: standard hydrologic benchmarking metrics over the full test period per basin, and long-term mass balance metrics based on cumulative discharge bias. The mass balance evaluation uses absolute mass bias and separated positive/negative bias so opposing errors do not cancel. Regions are also analyzed using USGS Water Resources Regions for spatial aggregation.
supporting_quote: We report two sets of performance metrics.
total absolute mass bias = |∑ obs.Q - ∑ sim.Q| / ∑ obs.Q

chunks.text: To quantify information loss from constraints, the study applies an information-theoretic framing that expects information to decrease as constraints are added. It computes mutual information (MI) between observed and simulated flows using histograms with 100 bins, and also computes KGE skill scores comparing constrained models (MC-LSTM, SAC-SMA) to the unconstrained LSTM baseline.
supporting_quote: We quantified this (hypothesized) chain of inequalities using two difference metrics. The first metric is the standard mutual information (MI) metric calculated by histograms with 100 bins
KGEskillscore = (KGEmodel - KGEbaseline) / (1 - KGEbaseline)

chunks.text: Training/calibration uncertainty is handled using an ensemble of eight models differing only by random weight initialization, with the ensemble mean used as the final estimate. This approach is used for DL models and aligns with prior benchmarking practices. Confidence intervals are reported over the large sample of basins to indicate stability of summary statistics.
supporting_quote: we treat training/calibration uncertainty by using an ensemble of eight models, where the only difference between the ensemble members are different random weight initializations, and we take the ensemble mean of streamflow as our final model estimate.
We include 95% confidence interval of the summary statistics, and these are relatively low given our large sample size.

chunks.text: The study uses the CAMELS dataset for CONUS, which provides daily meteorological forcings, discharge observations, and static basin attributes for benchmarking rainfall–runoff models. The widely used CAMELS benchmarking subset includes 531 basins with largely natural flow regimes and long records (1980–2008). One basin is omitted here because continuous observation records are required for mass-balance metrics during the test period.
supporting_quote: we used the Catchment Attributes and Meteorological Large Sample (CAMELS) data set
This results in the large-sample ... data set with 531 basins ... In the current study, we had to omit one of these 531 basins

chunks.text: Daily discharge observations come from the USGS Water Information System and serve as training targets and evaluation data. Static catchment attributes (soils, climate, vegetation, topography, geology) are used as input features for the DL models along with meteorological forcings. The study follows the same feature set used in prior LSTM CAMELS work.
supporting_quote: CAMELS includes daily discharge data from the USGS Water Information System, which are used as training and evaluation targets.
CAMELS also includes several static catchment attributes related to soils, climate, vegetation, topography, and geology ... that are used as input features to the DL models.

chunks.text: Two forcing products from CAMELS are central to the experiment: Daymet and NLDAS. They differ systematically in long-term precipitation totals in a way that is nonlinear and location-specific, enabling tests of how models behave under biased inputs. The disagreement is used to assume at least one product is biased and to observe how closure constraints propagate that bias.
supporting_quote: We used Daymet and NLDAS for this project because the disagree in their total precipitation amounts
This systematic difference must be either a positive Daymet bias or a negative NLDAS bias in long-term precipitation totals

chunks.text: The MC-LSTM distinguishes mass-conserving versus auxiliary forcing variables. Precipitation is the conserved mass input (mm), while minimum/maximum temperature, solar radiation, and vapour pressure are treated as auxiliary inputs not subject to conservation. This separation determines which inputs are constrained by the conservation mechanism in the network.
supporting_quote: Both the LSTM and MC-LSTM use the same forcing variables, but the MC-LSTM distinguishes between mass inputs ... and auxiliary
Average daily precipitation   Mass conserving (mm)

chunks.text: Regional analyses group basins into USGS Water Resources Regions (from Water-Supply Paper 2294), enabling spatial summaries of mass-bias behavior. Eighteen regions exist, but only 17 are used due to insufficient CAMELS basins in the Souris-Red-Rainy region (HUC 09). These regions support the study’s evaluation of geographic bias patterns.
supporting_quote: The regions were delineated according the United States Geological Survey (USGS) Water Resources Regions outlined in Water-Supply Paper 2294
only 17 of which have enough CAMELS basins for meaningful statistics (leaving out Souris-Red-Rainy, hydrologic unit code 09).

chunks.text: Across standard performance metrics on the 1990–1999 test period, LSTM and MC-LSTM show broadly similar median skill, with only small basin-wise differences, while both outperform SAC-SMA on average. With Daymet, LSTM has higher KGE in 323 basins (average difference 0.06) versus 208 for MC-LSTM. With NLDAS, MC-LSTM has higher KGE in 282 basins (average difference 0.05) versus 249 for LSTM, indicating that strict mass conservation does not systematically improve performance.
supporting_quote: With Daymet forcings, the LSTM had a higher KGE score in 323 basins, with an average difference of 0.06, and the MC-LSTM had a higher KGE score in 208 basins.
With NLDAS forcings, the LSTM had a higher KGE in 249 basins, while the MC-LSTM had a higher KGE score in 282 basins, and the average difference between KGE score was 0.05.

chunks.text: Median benchmark metrics confirm that both LSTM and MC-LSTM outperform SAC-SMA across multiple criteria for both forcings. For example, with Daymet forcing median NSE is 0.77 (LSTM) and 0.76 (MC-LSTM) versus 0.65 (SAC-SMA), and with NLDAS median KGE is 0.74 for both LSTM and MC-LSTM versus 0.68 for SAC-SMA. These results indicate that differences between DL and conceptual models are not primarily explained by whether mass conservation is explicitly enforced.

Long-term cumulative discharge analysis shows that with NLDAS forcing, LSTM, MC-LSTM, and SAC-SMA have similar total mass bias, but with different balances of positive versus negative errors; MC-LSTM is generally between LSTM and SAC-SMA. With Daymet forcing, SAC-SMA exhibits streamflow predictions biased toward very high positive mass error, while MC-LSTM slightly outperforms LSTM. Overall, LSTM and MC-LSTM yield more accurate long-term cumulative discharge than calibrated SAC-SMA.
supporting_quote: The LSTM, MC-LSTM and SAC-SMA all have a similar total mass bias with the NLDAS forcing.
With Daymet forcing SAC-SMA's streamflow predictions are biased toward a very high positive mass error.

chunks.text: Spatial patterns of mass bias show that SAC-SMA with Daymet forcings has a clear positive mass bias in the eastern half of CONUS, while SAC-SMA with NLDAS shows mixed biases. LSTM and MC-LSTM patterns are relatively similar to each other across forcings, including a notable negative mass bias corridor through central CONUS (from about Montana through East Texas). This suggests DL models are less sensitive to the Daymet/NLDAS bias discrepancy than the conceptual benchmark.
supporting_quote: The result of the SAC-SMA simulation with Daymet forcings shows a clear positive mass bias error in the eastern half of CONUS.
There is a clear negative mass bias error down the middle of CONUS from about Montana through East Texas.

chunks.text: Regional box-and-whisker analyses indicate SAC-SMA has very high mass balance error in eleven eastern USGS regions under Daymet forcings, while western regions are better. Under NLDAS, SAC-SMA does not show a consistent mass bias pattern like Daymet. All three models show relatively high mass bias errors in the central CONUS regions, consistent with the negative bias corridor identified spatially.
supporting_quote: SAC-SMA shows a very high mass balance error in the eleven eastern regions, but does much better in the western regions.
All three models show relatively high mass bias errors in the CenCon region

chunks.text: Mutual information analysis shows a consistent ordering where the unconstrained LSTM retains the most information about observed runoff, followed by MC-LSTM, then SAC-SMA. For concatenated flows across all 530 basins, MI with NLDAS is 0.39 (LSTM), 0.37 (MC-LSTM), 0.34 (SAC-SMA); with Daymet it is 0.40, 0.37, 0.33. Basin-wise CDFs also show the same ranking across both forcings.
supporting_quote: with NLDAS forcings are: 0.39 (LSTM), 0.37 (MC-LSTM) and 0.34 (SAC-SMA)
with Daymet forcings for models LSTM, MC-LSTM and SAC-SMA are 0.40, 0.37 and 0.33, respectively.

chunks.text: KGE skill score results generally support the hypothesized ordering that adding constraints degrades performance, consistent with an information-loss perspective. The analysis also indicates Daymet is more informative for DL models than NLDAS despite Daymet showing biases, while SAC-SMA performs significantly worse with the biased data. Adding mass balance constraints appears to provide more benefit when using NLDAS inputs than when using Daymet inputs.
supporting_quote: The left subplot ... shows a clear ordering of model performance that agrees with what we hypothesized in Equation (6)—generally, model performance degrades as more constraints are added.
This subplot shows that adding mass balance constraints to the LSTM has more benefit when using NLDAS inputs than when using Daymet inputs

chunks.text: The long-term mass balance results imply that Daymet is likely positively biased rather than NLDAS being negatively biased, because SAC-SMA forced with Daymet shows strong positive mass bias in the Eastern U.S. This bias propagation reduces efficiency metrics but not correlation or peak timing error. The inference is based on how forcing differences translate into systematic runoff bias patterns in the conceptual model.
supporting_quote: SAC-SMA includes a strong positive mass bias in the Eastern U.S. with Daymet forcings.
This indicates that ... Daymet is likely positively biased, rather than NLDAS being negatively biased

chunks.text: The paper constructs an estimated upper bound on error introduced by adding a mass balance constraint by comparing MC-LSTM to LSTM per basin. This difference is treated as conservative because other architectural differences (e.g., handling unobserved sources/sinks) may also contribute. The distribution includes cases where MC-LSTM performs better (negative difference), indicating constraints do not uniformly harm performance.
supporting_quote: In each basin, this difference represents an upper bound on the error introduced by mass balance constraints, relative to the LSTM.
