however this difference (which is sometimes negative) is a conservative estimate of the error due to mass conservation in DL rainfall runoff models.

chunks.text: A more rigorous long-term water balance assessment is constrained by limited availability of accurate evapotranspiration, percolation, and related flux observations at watershed scales. Consequently, the study focuses on cumulative discharge bias as a practical proxy for closure behavior. This limitation affects how directly the models’ internal sink/source representations can be validated.
supporting_quote: Our ability to properly conduct a more rigorous and detailed analysis of long-term water balances is limited by the fact that accurate evapotranspiration and percolation data (etc.) are not readily available at watershed scales.
what our analysis based on examining cumulative discharge shows

chunks.text: Interpretation of MC-LSTM versus LSTM differences is nuanced because MC-LSTM includes a flux term for unobserved sinks and explicitly accounts for all water across boundaries. Performance differences may therefore reflect not only conservation constraints but also how unobserved sinks and sources are represented. This complicates attributing all skill changes solely to enforced mass balance.
supporting_quote: There is some subtlety to this conclusion due to the fact that the MC-LSTM includes a flux term that accounts for unobserved sinks
There are other possible reasons why the MC-LSTM might not perform as well as the LSTM (e.g., the way that it handles unobserved sources and sinks)

chunks.text: The National Water Model comparison is limited because it is only available with NLDAS forcing and cannot be re-calibrated or run with Daymet due to data and operational constraints. Its calibration period (water years 2009–2013) differs from the study’s train/test periods, making results not directly comparable. Therefore, NWM results are relegated to the Appendix with caveats.
supporting_quote: we present the results of the NWM benchmarks in Appendix ... because (i) the NWM is only available for NLDAS forcing; and (ii) we are not able to calibrate the NWM to match our other models, so the NWM results are not directly comparable.
The NWM calibration time period is on water years 2009–2013. Because of the inconsistencies ... we cannot directly compare the NWM to the other models.

chunks.text: The paper argues that catchment-scale predictive success may require imposing as few physical constraints as possible unless the constraints add predictively useful information not already extractable from data. This implies that some classical hydrologic theory may not aggregate well to watershed scales. The discussion highlights a tension between interpretability and predictive accuracy under available data limitations.
supporting_quote: A likely reason for this is that that the current body of hydrological theory does not aggregate well to the scale of unorganized complex watershed systems
the most accurate way to generate a predictive model is to impose as few 'physical constraints' as possible on its ability to extract information from the available data

chunks.text: The study notes that strict mass conservation becomes essential in Earth-system-scale modeling because unaccounted residuals can accumulate and invalidate long-term simulations. This contextualizes why a mass-conserving architecture like MC-LSTM may be more valuable for global modeling than for catchment-scale discharge prediction. The discussion suggests extending MC-LSTM with additional targets for atmospheric and subsurface transfers.
supporting_quote: a particular application of rainfall-runoff modelling that necessarily requires the imposition of strict mass-balance constraints is 'Earth-system-scale' modelling.
could be implemented by training additional model targets of mass-loss representations of 'losses' (transfers) to the sub-surface and 'losses' (transfers) to the atmosphere.

chunks.text: The study finds that imposing conservation laws is generally harmful for hydrologic prediction, but this accounts for only a small fraction of the skill gap between deep learning and traditional conceptual models. Deep learning can learn systematic, spatially and temporally heterogeneous biases in input–output data, including under biased precipitation products. Therefore, closure violations due to data errors are not the primary explanation for the superior performance of DL rainfall–runoff models.
supporting_quote: While Beven (2020) was correct that the imposition of conservation laws is generally harmful for hydrologic prediction, this fact does not help to explain most of the significantly better skill provided by DL over traditional (theory-based) rainfall-runoff models.
the DL-based LSTM network was able to learn the non-uniform patterns of biases in input–output data

chunks.text: Cumulative discharge analyses indicate that Daymet likely overestimates precipitation in the eastern U.S., as evidenced by SAC-SMA’s strong positive mass bias when forced with Daymet. DL models, including the mass-conserving MC-LSTM, largely avoid this systematic propagation by learning heterogeneous bias structures. This shows that biased data may still contain useful predictive information when used with flexible models.
supporting_quote: Daymet is likely positively biased, rather than NLDAS being negatively biased (i.e., Daymet overestimates precipitation magnitudes, rather than NLDAS underestimates).
Daymet seems to actually contain more information about streamflow than the less biased NLDAS precipitation product.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that conservation laws may not be a good foundation for scale-relevant hydrological theory at catchment scales, and that what appears as ‘disinformation’ in data may instead reflect limitations of prevailing model architectures. In this view, theory-based constraints can remove information needed for accurate prediction, whereas DL can better extract effective water balance behavior from available data. The work reframes the main bottleneck as model conception rather than data quality alone.
supporting_quote: that conservation laws may not be a good foundation for scalerelevant hydrological theory,
for catchment-scale rainfall-runoff prediction it is arguably the current hydrological theory that is (more) disinformative, not the hydrological data.

chunks.text: Deep learning has recently become the most accurate approach for rainfall–runoff prediction in hydrology, but its adoption is tempered by long-standing skepticism about whether data-driven models generalize reliably beyond their training data. Earlier debates contrasted process-oriented confidence in physically based models with empirical claims that data-driven models can forecast better. Modern deep learning models have shown strong spatial and temporal generalization, motivating a direct test of reliability for extremes.
supporting_quote: Deep learning (DL) provides the most accurate rainfall– runoff simulations available from the hydrological sciences community
"physical process-oriented modellers have no confidence in the capabilities of data-driven models' outputs with their heavy dependence on training sets"

chunks.text: The belief that physically based hydrologic models are more reliable out of sample was influenced by early experiments with shallow neural networks, but it has not been evaluated with modern deep learning architectures. Recent work suggests deep learning can generalize to challenging conditions such as ungauged basins and shifting climates by learning transferable hydrologic behavior. Because deep learning is now state of the art, identifying its limits is important for scientific and operational use.
supporting_quote: it has not been tested in the context of modern DL models, which are able to generalize complex hydrological relationships across space and time
DL can generalize to ungauged basins with better overall skill than calibrated conceptual models

chunks.text: The study emphasizes the value of standardized, comparable benchmarking practices in large-sample hydrology experiments. Using common datasets and consistent training/testing protocols enables direct comparison across studies and models. The authors build on prior CAMELS benchmarking and extend evaluation toward extreme-event performance and peak flows.
supporting_quote: we used open community data sets and consistent training/test procedures that allow for results to be directly comparable between studies
we continue that practice here to the extent possible

chunks.text: The primary goal is to test whether data-driven rainfall–runoff models lose predictive accuracy during extreme (high-return-period) streamflow events more than models based on process understanding. The evaluation focuses on rare annual peak flows and examines performance when extreme events are excluded from the training data. Four model classes are compared: standard deep learning, physics-informed deep learning, a conceptual model, and a process-based model.
supporting_quote: The primary objective of this study is to test the hypothesis that data-driven models lose predictive accuracy in extreme events more than models based on process understanding.
compare four models: a standard deep learning model, a physics-informed deep learning model, a conceptual rainfall—runoff model, and a process-based hydrological model.

chunks.text: A secondary goal is to explicitly assess extrapolation by training on only common (≤ 5-year return period) years and testing on rarer (> 5-year return period) years. This design aims to mimic practical out-of-sample conditions, including situations that can represent nonstationarity relative to the training period. Performance is assessed both over full hydrographs and specifically for annual peak-flow errors.
supporting_quote: The third training/test period split used all water years in the CAMELS data set with a 5-year or lower return period peak flow for training, whereas the test period included water years with greater than a 5-year return period peak flow
stationary return period calculations directly test predictability on large events that are out of sample relative to the training period

chunks.text: A central concern in hydrology is that deep-learning streamflow predictions may be unreliable during extrapolation, especially for extreme events that are rare or absent from training. This concern is widely voiced by physical scientists and users of model-based information products. The paper frames this as a testable hypothesis about comparative degradation in extremes for data-driven versus physically based models.
supporting_quote: There is a concern among hydrologists that the predictive accuracy of data-driven models based on deep learning may not be reliable in extrapolation or for predicting extreme events.
The hypothesis tested in this work was that predictions made by data-driven streamflow models are likely to become unreliable in extreme or out-of-sample events.

chunks.text: Extreme-event evaluation is complicated by basin-to-basin differences in what counts as “extreme,” since the same discharge magnitude can be rare in one basin and normal in another. The study addresses this by using return periods of annual peak flows so that extremes are defined relative to each basin’s flood frequency. This allows training/test splits and performance summaries that are hydrologically meaningful across many basins.
supporting_quote: a similar flow volume may be "extreme" in one basin but not in another.
The return periods of peak annual flows provide a basis for categorizing target data in a hydrologically meaningful way.

chunks.text: Benchmarking is hindered by the lack of standardized community procedures, making it difficult to compare new models and to deploy them reliably. The authors emphasize consistent datasets and shared splits to improve comparability. This limitation motivates using CAMELS and aligning certain experiments with the National Water Model retrospective dataset.
supporting_quote: The hydrological sciences community lacks communitywide standardized procedures for model benchmarking, which severely limits the effectiveness of new model development and deployment efforts
we used open community data sets and consistent training/test procedures

chunks.text: The study compares four modeling approaches for rainfall–runoff prediction: an unconstrained LSTM, a mass-conserving (physics-informed) LSTM variant, a conceptual SAC-SMA model, and the process-based NOAA National Water Model retrospective product (NWM-Rv2). The MC-LSTM is architecturally constrained to conserve mass, while the LSTM is purely data-driven. All comparisons are conducted at the daily time scale, with metrics computed across basins and by return-period bins for extreme-event analyses.
supporting_quote: We focus specifically on high-return-period (low-probability) streamflow events and compare four models
a physics-informed LSTM that is architecturally constrained to conserve mass – we call this a mass-conserving LSTM (MC-LSTM; Hoedt et al., 2021).
All experiments in the present study were done at the daily timescale.

chunks.text: Return periods are computed per basin by fitting annual peak flows (log-transformed) to a Pearson type III distribution following Bulletin 17b guidance. Annual peak flow observations come directly from USGS NWIS to satisfy guidelines requiring annual peaks rather than daily averages. Each basin-year in CAMELS is then classified by the return period of its observed peak annual discharge for use in performance stratification and training/test splits.
supporting_quote: fit all available annual peak flows (log transformed) for each basin to a Pearson type III distribution
we used annual peak flow observations taken directly from the USGS NWIS, instead of from the CAMELS data
we classified each water year of the CAMELS data from each basin (each basin-year of data) according to the return period

chunks.text: The LSTM and MC-LSTM are trained jointly across basins using daily meteorological forcings and static catchment attributes, with daily streamflow as the target. Training uses a basin-normalized squared-error loss (NSE*) that scales errors by each basin’s discharge standard deviation to avoid overweighting wet or large basins. Sequence-to-one training with a 365-day sequence length enables randomized minibatches containing samples from multiple basins.
supporting_quote: Daily meteorological forcing data and static catchment attributes data were used as inputs features
a normalized squared-error loss function that does not depend on basin-specific mean discharge
The standard LSTM had 128 cell states and a 365 d sequence length.

chunks.text: Training details include 30 epochs, minibatch size 256, gradient clipping to a global norm of 1, and adding heteroscedastic noise to targets (standard deviation 0.005 times the target). Optimization uses Adam with a fixed learning-rate schedule and forget-gate bias initialization to 3 to help gradients persist through long sequences. The MC-LSTM uses similar hyperparameters but 64 cell states, reflecting its different interpretation of states as physical quantities.
supporting_quote: Both models were trained for 30 epochs
We used a minibatch size of 256
Gradients were clipped to a global norm (per minibatch) of 1.
Heteroscedastic noise was added to training targets ... with a standard deviation of 0.005 times the value of each target datum.
Biases of the LSTM forget gate were initialized to 3

chunks.text: Three training/test regimes are used: (1) training on water years 1999–2008 and testing on 1990–1999 to match prior studies, (2) training on 1981–1995 and testing on 1996–2014 to align with NWM-Rv2 availability, and (3) training on all years with ≤5-year return period peaks and testing on years with >5-year return period peaks (within 1996–2014). For regime (3), training and test years are separated by at least one year to accommodate the 365-day sequence length and prevent leakage.
supporting_quote: training period included 9 water years, from October 1 1999 through September 30 2008, and the test period included 10 water years, from 1990 to 1999
The training period included water years 1981–1995, and the test period included water years 1996–2014
training ... with a 5-year or lower return period peak flow ... test period included water years with greater than a 5-year return period peak flow
we separated all training and test years in each basin by at least 1 year

chunks.text: Benchmark models include SAC-SMA (with SNOW-17 and unit hydrograph routing) and NWM-Rv2 (WRF-Hydro with Noah-MP and routing components). SAC-SMA is recalibrated to match each training/test split, with separate calibration per basin using a Python implementation and SPOTPY. NWM-Rv2 outputs are extracted at CAMELS gauges, aggregated from hourly to daily for 1980–2014, but its calibration period differs from the other models.
supporting_quote: The conceptual model ... was the Sacramento Soil Moisture Accounting (SAC-SMA) model with SNOW-17 and a unit hydrograph routing function.
we recalibrated SAC-SMA to be consistent with our training/test splits
NWM-Rv2 ... hourly ... we pulled hourly flow estimates ... and averaged these hourly data to daily
NWM-Rv2 was calibrated by NOAA personnel ... on water years 2009– 2013.

chunks.text: Model performance is assessed using established CAMELS metrics (e.g., NSE, KGE, Pearson-r, α-NSE, β-NSE, FHV/FLV/FMS, Peak-Timing) and a peak-flow error metric. For contiguous splits, metrics are computed over the whole test period per basin. For return-period-based splits, metrics are computed per water year and basin to enable stratification by return-period bins, and absolute percent error is computed for the largest event in each water year.
supporting_quote: A full list of these metrics is given in Table 1.
it is necessary to calculate separate metrics for each water year and each basin in the test period.
absolute percent bias of peak flow only for the largest streamflow event in each water year

chunks.text: The primary dataset is CAMELS, providing daily meteorology and discharge for 671 CONUS catchments (1980–2008) plus static catchment attributes. The study uses 498 basins after filtering consistent with prior benchmarking work (excluding area discrepancies and basins >2000 km²). USGS discharge is used as the training/evaluation target, and inputs include meteorological forcings and static attributes following a prior feature set.
supporting_quote: The CAMELS data set consists of daily meteorological and discharge data from 671 catchments ... (1980–2008).
We used 498 of the 671 CAMELS catchments
removed basins ... with areas larger than 2000 km².
We used the same input features ... that were listed in Table 1 by Kratzert et al. (2019b).

chunks.text: Meteorological forcing is taken from NLDAS within CAMELS, chosen to match the forcing used by NWM-Rv2 for fairer benchmarking. Static catchment attributes span soils, climate, vegetation, topography, and geology. This combination supports large-sample learning across basins while enabling comparison to the National Water Model retrospective simulations.
supporting_quote: We used NLDAS for this project because we benchmarked against ... the NOAA National Water Model (NWM) ... which also uses NLDAS.
CAMELS also includes several static catchment attributes related to soils, climate, vegetation, topography, and geology

chunks.text: Return-period estimation uses annual peak flow observations from USGS NWIS rather than CAMELS daily flows, and leverages all available peak-flow records per basin (26 to 116 years). These return periods are then mapped to CAMELS basin-years by matching each water year’s observed annual peak. The resulting labels support both binning of evaluation metrics and the extreme-exclusion training regime.
supporting_quote: we used annual peak flow observations taken directly from the USGS NWIS
The Bulletin 17b (IACWD, 1982) guidelines require the use of all available data, which range from 26 to 116 years for peak flows.
we classified each water year of the CAMELS data ... according to the return period of its observed peak annual discharge.

chunks.text: NWM-Rv2 benchmark data are obtained from the public archive as hourly, CONUS-wide estimates, then extracted at CAMELS gauge locations and averaged to daily values for 1 October 1980 through 30 September 2014. This enables comparisons at the daily scale used in the study, and accommodates the longer test period needed for extreme-event analysis. However, NWM-Rv2 calibration years differ from the other models’ training years.
supporting_quote: Public data from NWM-Rv2 are hourly and CONUS-wide
averaged these hourly data to daily over the time period from 1 October 1980 through 30 September 2014.
All experiments in the present study were done at the daily timescale.

chunks.text: Across 498 basins, the deep learning models show stronger median performance than SAC-SMA and NWM-Rv2 for whole-hydrograph metrics. In the 1996–2014 test period, LSTM achieves median NSE 0.71 and KGE 0.77, compared to SAC-SMA NSE 0.63 and KGE 0.68, and NWM-Rv2 NSE 0.63 and KGE 0.67. Pearson-r is also higher for LSTM (0.86) than SAC-SMA (0.81) and NWM-Rv2 (0.82).
supporting_quote: Table 2. Median performance metrics across 498 basins
Test period: 1996 – 2014 ... NSE ... LSTM 0.71 ... SAC-SMA 0.63 ... NWM-Rv2 0.63
Test period: 1996 – 2014 ... KGE ... LSTM 0.77 ... SAC-SMA 0.68 ... NWM-Rv2 0.67

chunks.text: When testing only on low-probability years (years whose annual peak is > 5-year return period) after training only on ≤ 5-year years, the data-driven models remain superior on key correlation metrics. In this “low-probability years” test, median NSE is 0.81 for LSTM and 0.77 for MC-LSTM versus 0.66 for SAC-SMA and 0.67 for NWM-Rv2. Pearson-r is 0.91 (LSTM) and 0.90 (MC-LSTM) compared to 0.84 (SAC-SMA) and 0.85 (NWM-Rv2).
supporting_quote: Test period: low-probability years ... NSE ... 0.81 ... 0.77 ... 0.66 ... 0.67
Test period: low-probability years ... Pearson-r ... 0.91 ... 0.90 ... 0.84 ... 0.85
testing across years with a peak annual event above a 5-year return period

chunks.text: Performance behavior differs by metric in the extreme-year test: correlation-based metrics improve while variance-based α-NSE degrades. The authors attribute this to wet conditions increasing variability, which can raise correlation even when variance matching worsens. Despite this metric tension, data-driven models remain better than both benchmarks for NSE, KGE, Pearson-r, and α-NSE in the return-period test period.
supporting_quote: Model performance generally improves overall in this period according to the three correlation-based metrics (NSE, KGE, Pearson-r), but it degrades according to the variance-based metric (α-NSE).
the data-driven models remained better than both benchmark models against all four of these metrics

chunks.text: Adding mass balance constraints via MC-LSTM does not improve extreme-event skill relative to the unconstrained LSTM and can reduce it. The paper reports that differences between LSTM and MC-LSTM are small in nominal test periods, but “clear differences” emerge for high-return-period metrics. In out-of-sample return-period years, MC-LSTM shows reduced performance compared to LSTM, even though both remain better than SAC-SMA and NWM-Rv2 in most cases.
supporting_quote: There were clear differences between the physicsconstrained (MC-LSTM) and unconstrained (LSTM) datadriven models in the high-return-period metrics.
adding mass balance constraints resulted in reduced performance in the out-ofsample years.

chunks.text: Peak-flow evaluation shows errors increase with event extremity for all models, but LSTM has the lowest average absolute percent bias across return-period bins in the contiguous-split experiment. The conceptual SAC-SMA is the worst for peak-flow bias and deteriorates more strongly with increasing return period than LSTM. This indicates that the deep learning model maintains comparatively robust peak-flow prediction across rare-event categories.
supporting_quote: All models had increasingly large average errors with increasingly large extreme events.
The LSTM average error was lowest in all of the return period bins.
SAC-SMA was the worst performing model in terms of average error.

chunks.text: In the return-period-based training setup (training on ≤ 5-year years), peak-flow performance degrades as return period increases, but LSTM and MC-LSTM deteriorate less rapidly than SAC-SMA. The LSTM is best on average among the trained/calibrated models for extreme events, while NWM-Rv2 is slightly better only in the 25–50 and 50–100 return-period bins. The authors caution that NWM-Rv2’s calibration did not exclude extremes, complicating direct comparisons.
supporting_quote: SAC-SMA performance deteriorated faster than LSTM and MC-LSTM performance with increasingly extreme events.
except for the 25–50 and 50–100 cases, where NWM-Rv2 performed slightly better on average.
remember that the NWM-Rv2 calibration data were not segregated by return period.

chunks.text: The return-period analysis assumes stationarity and does not incorporate climate or land-use driven nonstationarity, because there is no agreed method for doing so in flood frequency estimation. The authors argue this does not undermine the paper’s purpose because stationary return periods still test predictability for events that are out of sample relative to the training period. Thus, the method is positioned as a practical stress test for extrapolation even if real-world nonstationarity exists.
supporting_quote: This return period analysis does not account for nonstationarity
There is currently no agreed upon method to account for nonstationarity
stationary return period calculations directly test predictability on large events that are out of sample relative to the training period

chunks.text: NWM-Rv2 cannot be recalibrated to match the irregular return-period-based training years used for LSTM/MC-LSTM and SAC-SMA, limiting strict comparability. NWM-Rv2’s calibration was performed on different years (2009–2013) and across about 1400 basins, which may provide an advantage over models trained/calibrated on the study’s chosen periods. The authors still treat NWM-Rv2 as a useful benchmark, but interpret results with this caveat.
supporting_quote: Without the ability to recalibrate NWM-Rv2 on the same time period as the LSTM, MC-LSTM, and SAC-SMA, we cannot directly compare the performance of NWM-Rv2 with the other models.
NWM-Rv2 was calibrated by NOAA personnel on about 1400 basins ... on water years 2009– 2013.

chunks.text: Some metrics are unstable and may not support strong general conclusions, especially those based on flow duration curve tails. The paper notes FHV, FLV, and FMS are less stable and depend heavily on test-period characteristics. It specifically highlights FLV fragility when flows approach zero and attributes large discrepancies to a few regionally clustered outlier basins, due in part to log terms in the FLV equation.
supporting_quote: with the exception of the FHV (high flow bias), FLV (low flow bias), and FMS (flow duration curve bias). These metrics depend heavily on the observed flow characteristics
we caution that the FLV metric is fragile, particularly when flows approach zero
The FLV equation includes a log value of the simulated and observed flows. This causes a very large instability

chunks.text: The MC-LSTM imposes strong conservation constraints but represents unobserved sources and sinks with an aggregated residual mechanism, including a designated “trash cell.” Because evapotranspiration and other fluxes are not observed and provided, the model uses one state to absorb unobserved sinks, and its output is ignored in computing discharge as the sum of outgoing mass. This design is a pragmatic workaround but simplifies the true catchment water balance structure.
supporting_quote: accounts for unobserved sinks in the modeled systems by allowing the model to use one cell state as a "trash cell".
The output of this cell is ignored when we derive the final model prediction as the sum of the outgoing mass  ∑h .
Because we did not provide the model with (for example) observations of evapotranspiration, aquifer recharge, or baseflow

chunks.text: The paper argues that adding physical constraints to neural networks can only help if it improves optimization, because constraints restrict (rather than expand) the set of functions a network can emulate. Since neural networks can emulate large classes of functions, constraints act as regularization and are beneficial only if they guide training toward better minima. This perspective is used to interpret why the physics-constrained MC-LSTM may underperform the unconstrained LSTM for extremes.
supporting_quote: by adding constraints to this type of model, we can only restrict (not expand) the space of possible functions that the network can emulate.
This form of regularization is valuable only if it helps locate a better ... local minimum on the optimization response surface

chunks.text: The results reject the hypothesis that deep-learning rainfall–runoff models become comparatively unreliable in extreme or out-of-sample events. Both data-driven models outperform the conceptual and process-based benchmarks for peak flows under almost all conditions, including when extreme events are excluded from training. Therefore, modern deep learning appears robust for high-return-period event prediction in this large-sample setting.
supporting_quote: Our results indicate that this hypothesis is incorrect

the data-driven models ... were better than benchmark models at predicting peak flows under almost all conditions, including extreme events or when extreme events were not included in the training data set.

chunks.text: Contrary to expectations, the physics-constrained MC-LSTM does not improve extreme-event peak-flow prediction and can reduce performance relative to the unconstrained LSTM, especially for out-of-sample return-period events. The study suggests that conservation constraints may not automatically enhance extrapolation and highlights the need to understand when physical constraints actually aid optimization and generalization.
supporting_quote: It was somewhat surprising to us that the physicsconstrained LSTM did not perform as well as the pure LSTM at simulating peak flows and out-of-sample events.
we saw the greatest differences between the LSTM and MC-LSTM when predicting out-of-sample return period events.

chunks.text: The U.S. National Water Model (NWM), built on WRF-Hydro, is a large-scale hydrology simulator used operationally for national forecasting. It covers the contiguous U.S. with very high stream-network detail and is intended to represent hydrologic dynamics, including response timing. Prior evaluations show that NWM performance varies substantially by region and conditions, with hypothesized error sources including engineered features and land-surface parameter issues.
supporting_quote: The United States (U.S.) National Water Model (NWM), based on WRF-Hydro (Cosgrove et al. 2015), is an emerging large-scale hydrology simulator.
including increased resolution and number of stream reaches (2.7 million) for a model covering the contiguous United States (CONUS).

chunks.text: Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are recurrent deep learning models that have become effective tools for hydrologic time-series prediction. They are well suited to rainfall–runoff modeling because they can carry information over long time windows and mimic aspects of dynamical systems. Prior work has demonstrated strong daily and even hourly streamflow performance, including in ungauged basins, motivating comparisons with process-based models like the NWM.
supporting_quote: One example of an ML approach that has been effective for hydrologic prediction is the "long short-term memory" network (LSTM)
LSTMs have been effective at simulating predictions of surface runoff at the daily time scale ... including in ungauged catchments

chunks.text: A practical way to merge process-based and data-driven modeling is hydrologic post-processing, where model outputs are corrected using a learned mapping. This approach can reduce systematic errors and has been used to improve forecast accuracy under certain conditions. In this paper, the authors frame LSTM post-processing of NWM outputs as a straightforward form of theory-guided or physics-informed machine learning.
supporting_quote: Hydrologic post-processing can remove systematic errors in the model prediction, and has been shown to improve real-time forecast accuracy
This is a straightforward method of theoryguided (or physics-informed) ML, but is commonly referred to as post-processing

chunks.text: The study aims to build and compare three daily LSTM streamflow models across 531 CONUS basins: a post-processor using only NWM outputs (LSTM_PP), a post-processor using NWM outputs plus atmospheric forcings (LSTM_PPA), and a model using only atmospheric forcings (LSTM_A). The central question is whether including NWM outputs provides added value beyond what an LSTM can learn directly from forcings. The authors also target model diagnostics to identify which NWM components contribute to mass bias and timing errors.
supporting_quote: We build three long short-term memory (LSTM) daily streamflow prediction models ... (1) ... (LSTM_PP), (2) ... (LSTM_PPA), and (3) ... (LSTM_A).
Finally, we performed a sensitivity analysis to diagnose the land surface component of the NWM as the source of mass bias error and the channel router as a source of simulation timing error.

chunks.text: The authors seek to evaluate whether LSTM post-processing can improve NWM predictive performance while preserving operational constraints that require the NWM to continue producing other hydrologic states. They emphasize that an ML streamflow model must run in parallel and therefore ask if the NWM formulation benefits already-accurate LSTM streamflow predictions. The study uses mostly headwater, minimally engineered basins to focus on close-to-natural rainfall–runoff response.
supporting_quote: an ML prediction for streamflow that does not also include predictions of the other hydrologic states and variables must be run in parallel with the existing process-based hydrologic model.
The basins chosen for this largescale analysis are mostly headwater catchments without engineered control structures

chunks.text: Calibrating the NWM everywhere is computationally expensive, and despite targeted calibration, many basins remain ungauged or uncalibrated. Regionalization can reduce costs but often reduces accuracy compared to direct calibration, motivating alternative approaches for large-scale prediction. This motivates exploring data-driven methods that might offer high accuracy without per-basin calibration.
supporting_quote: NOAA personnel calibrated the NWM (version 2.0) at 1,457 gauged basins within the CONUS domain.
Calibrating the model at each stream gauge ... is a large computational expense, and while regionalization strategies can be used ... accuracy typically suffers compared to direct calibration.

chunks.text: The NWM shows uneven predictive skill across regions, and prior work suggests specific weaknesses such as poor performance in the Southwest and Northern Plains. Hypothesized sources of error include lakes/reservoirs, floodplain dynamics, and soil parameter calibration. Such heterogeneous errors create a need for methods that can correct systematic biases and diagnose process components responsible for mass and timing errors.
supporting_quote: WRF-Hydro has generally poor performance in the Southwest and Northern Plains (Salas et al. 2018).
Salas et al. (2018) hypothesized that error in WRF-hydro might come from lakes, reservoirs, floodplain dynamics, and soil parameter calibration.

chunks.text: A core uncertainty is whether using NWM outputs as inputs to an LSTM helps or harms streamflow prediction relative to an LSTM trained only on atmospheric forcings. Since LSTMs can already learn rainfall–runoff relationships, NWM outputs could add useful physical context or instead inject error. This uncertainty is especially important for ungauged or atypical basins where generalization is critical.
supporting_quote: A natural question arises: does the existing NWM formulation benefit the already highly accurate LSTM predictions of streamflow?
LSTM_A outperforms LSTM_PP and LSTM_PPA in ungauged basins.

chunks.text: The experimental design compares four model variants over the same evaluation period: NWM daily mean streamflow, LSTM_PP (NWM outputs only), LSTM_PPA (NWM outputs plus atmospheric forcings), and LSTM_A (atmospheric forcings only). Models are evaluated on identical daily data for 1994–2002, while LSTMs are trained on 2004–2014 with a one-year gap to avoid information bleed due to a 365-day lookback. Performance is assessed with NSE/KGE and focused metrics for peak timing error and total bias.
supporting_quote: We trained the LSTMs on water years 2004 through 2014 and tested on water years 1994 through 2002.
The LSTMs used a 365-day LSTM look-back period, so a full year gap was left between training and testing
We tested/evaluated all models (NWM and all LSTMs) on the same daily data and the same time period (years 1994–2002).

chunks.text: The LSTM implementation follows prior hydrology LSTM work and is built using the NeuralHydrology codebase in Python/PyTorch. Inputs include dynamic meteorological forcings and static catchment attributes; for post-processing experiments, NWM outputs are added as dynamic inputs. All inputs are normalized using the training-period mean and standard deviation, and models are trained across all basins simultaneously to learn basin-specific behavior via static attributes.
supporting_quote: using a codebase that is now referred to as NeuralHydrology
We normalized all inputs to the LSTM, including static and dynamic inputs by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation of the training data.
Catchment attributes are static for each basin ... allowing us to train a single model that can be applied on any basin

chunks.text: To reduce stochastic dependence on initialization, the authors train ensembles of LSTMs with multiple random seeds and report statistics based on the ensemble mean hydrograph. They report small variability across seeds, supporting stability of conclusions. Dropout is used during training to mitigate overfitting and is disabled during testing.
supporting_quote: We trained separate LSTMs with 10 unique random seeds for initializing weights and biases, and calculated benchmarking statistics using the ensemble mean hydrograph.
the dropout rate ... in our case with a probability of 0.4. ... Model runs during testing did not include dropout.

chunks.text: NWM outputs are converted to daily values for compatibility with the one-day LSTM timestep by averaging hourly NWM outputs across UTC calendar days for LSTM inputs. For direct NWM streamflow diagnostics, the authors instead use local calendar day to match USGS gauge records. Basin-level land-surface variables are spatially aggregated by averaging 1 km Noah-MP cells within basin boundaries, and routing variables are summarized using mean and maximum within basins.
supporting_quote: we took the mean values of these model outputs across UTC calendar days ... to produce daily records from the hourly NWM when used as input to the LSTM
but for NWM streamflow diagnostics we used the local calendar day ... to be compatible with the USGS gauge records.
calculated the averaged to produce a single representative (lumped) value for each catchment.

chunks.text: Model performance is quantified with NSE and KGE plus decomposed components (variance, bias, correlation). Metrics are computed both per-basin (then summarized) and by pooling flows across all basins. Additional analyses stratify results by flow regimes (rising/falling limbs, high/low flows) and by USGS water resource regions.
supporting_quote: We calculated several metrics ... including the NSE and Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE)
We calculated the metrics in two ways: (1) at each basin and then averaged together, and (2) using all of the flows from all basins combined.
High flows were characterized as all flow above the 80th percentile ... and low flows as below the 20th percentile

chunks.text: The paper uses interpretability analyses to connect post-processing gains to NWM variables. Integrated gradients are computed for each input and timestep to attribute contributions to predicted streamflow, producing very large attribution sets per basin. A complementary analysis correlates basin-mean NWM feature values with basin-level performance changes to identify which NWM states/fluxes relate to improvements.
supporting_quote: We calculated integrated gradients ... to attribute the LSTM inputs ... to the total prediction of streamflow.
for nine years of test data with a 365-day lookback there were about 1.2 million integrated gradients per input, per basin.
We calculated Pearson R values between the basin average value of each NWM input feature and the total performance change

chunks.text: A sensitivity and diagnostic experiment trains additional LSTMs using subsets of NWM outputs to isolate information content from different NWM components. These include models using only NWM streamflow, excluding streamflow and velocity, using only channel routing variables, or using only land-surface outputs. Comparative performance is then interpreted as qualitative evidence of information loss in the NWM modeling chain.
supporting_quote: We trained a set of LSTM post-processors using different combinations of NWM outputs as input to the LSTM, as described in Table 5.
LSTM_Q_only ... only streamflow from the NWM output.
We tested the sensitivity to the channel routing (LSTM_chrt) and land surface (LSTM_ldas) components

chunks.text: The study uses 531 CAMELS basins selected for benchmarking and generally representing smaller, less engineered headwater catchments. CAMELS provides daily USGS streamflow and catchment attributes, while meteorological forcings come from NLDAS (precipitation, temperature, vapor pressure, solar radiation). Newman et al. (2015) selection criteria exclude basins larger than 2,000 km² and those with area discrepancies.
supporting_quote: we used the 531 (out of 671) basins that Newman et al. (2015) chose for model benchmarking.
Newman et al. (2015) excluded basins ... also basins larger than 2,000 km2.
meteorological forcing data ... come from North American Land Data Assimilation System (NLDAS

chunks.text: NWM version 2.0 reanalysis outputs are used as both a baseline streamflow model and as potential LSTM inputs. The reanalysis is a 25-year retrospective simulation from January 1993 through December 2019, with both channel routing point outputs and land-surface gridded states/fluxes. A defined set of NWM variables (e.g., streamflow, velocity, soil moisture, snow, underground runoff) is used in the post-processing models.
supporting_quote: We used the NWM version 2.0 reanalysis, which contains output from a 25 year (January 1993 through December 2019) retrospective simulation
NWM reanalysis output includes channel outputs (point fluxes: CHRT) and land surface (gridded states and fluxes: LDAS and RT) outputs.
The specific features that we used from the NWM reanalysis are shown in Table 1.

chunks.text: Dynamic inputs for LSTM_A consist of five NLDAS forcing variables: precipitation, max/min air temperature, vapor pressure, and solar radiation. Static inputs include catchment attributes spanning climate, vegetation, topography, geology, and soils, enabling a single regional LSTM trained jointly across basins. For post-processing, additional dynamic inputs are drawn from NWM outputs, increasing input dimensionality as summarized in the model table.
supporting_quote: meteorological forcing data (precipitation, max/min temperature, vapor pressure, and total solar radiation) come from ... NLDAS
We used 18 catchment attributes from the CAMELS dataset related to climate, vegetation, topography, geology, and soils.
LSTM_PP     | 28 ... LSTM_PPA    | 33 ... LSTM_A      | 5

chunks.text: The study aligns target and prediction units by converting LSTM-predicted runoff in millimeters to volumetric streamflow using catchment area. USGS gauge records and NWM predictions are in [L^3/T], while LSTM outputs are in [mm], reflecting area-normalized discharge. The conversion uses the CAMELS geospatial fabric estimate of basin area for diagnostic comparisons.
supporting_quote: The LSTMs make predictions representing runoff in units [mm]
USGS gauge records (and the NWM predictions) are in streamflow units [L3/T].
We used the geospatial fabric estimate of the catchment area provided in the CAMELS dataset to convert all streamflow

chunks.text: A calibrated-vs-uncalibrated split is constructed based on NWM calibration coverage overlapping CAMELS. Of the NWM calibrated basins, 480 overlap with the 531 CAMELS catchments, leaving 51 uncalibrated in the CAMELS set. Separate experiments train LSTMs on only the 480 calibrated basins and evaluate performance on both calibrated and uncalibrated basins to emulate ungauged-type settings.
supporting_quote: Of the NWM calibrated basins, 480 overlap with the 531 CAMELS catchments used in this study.
We then used the full set of 531 catchments to test the performance out-of-sample.
We analyzed the 480 in-sample basins and 51 out-ofsample basins separately

chunks.text: Hydrologic signature evaluation uses a set of 13 signatures (e.g., runoff ratio, baseflow index, flow quantiles, zero-flow frequency). Observed signatures are computed from USGS data, and modeled signatures from predicted daily streamflow, then compared across basins using r². Statistical comparison across models uses the Steiger method for dependent correlations.
supporting_quote: We analyzed the hydrologic signatures described by Addor et al. (2018), and these are listed below in Table 4.
We compared true values and predicted values with a correlation coefficient (r2) across basins
We used the Steiger method to test for statistically significant changes

chunks.text: Across 531 basins, all three LSTM models outperform the NWM in median NSE during the 1994–2002 evaluation period. Median NSE values are 0.73 for LSTM_PP, 0.75 for LSTM_PPA, and 0.74 for LSTM_A, compared to 0.62 for the NWM. This indicates that LSTM-based approaches provide substantial accuracy gains relative to the NWM reanalysis baseline.
supporting_quote: Overall performance of the three LSTMs is similar, with median NSE scores of 0.73 (LSTM_PP), 0.75 (LSTM_PPA), and 0.74 (LSTM_A), and all three LSTMs outperform the NWM validation scores of 0.62.

chunks.text: Post-processing improves the NWM in most basins, but does not clearly beat the LSTM that ignores NWM outputs. LSTM_PP improves NWM NSE in 465 basins (88%) and LSTM_PPA improves NWM NSE in 488 basins (92%). However, the paper also notes that LSTM_A is the overall better performing model, implying that NWM outputs add limited incremental value beyond atmospheric forcings.
supporting_quote: The LSTM_PP improved the NSE score of the NWM mean daily streamflow at a total of 465 (88%)
The LSTM_PPA postprocessor improved the NSE score ... at a total of 488 (92%)
The LSTM_A, however, is the overall better performing model.

chunks.text: By flow regime, LSTM post-processors generally improve NSE/KGE and components versus NWM, especially on rising limbs and high flows. Table results show significant improvements for post-processing over NWM in multiple regimes, including rising limbs and flows above the 80th percentile. Low-flow performance remains problematic for all models, with extremely negative NSE values per-basin when focusing on below-20th-percentile flows.
supporting_quote: In general Table 6 shows that the LSTM postprocessors improved over the NWM in nearly all flow regimes
The prediction of rising limb and high flow regimes was improved upon by the LSTM postprocessors according to every metric.
Below 20th percent ... NWM ... -18,384.37 ... LSTM PP ... -6,941.62

chunks.text: Regionally, post-processing significantly improves NWM NSE and timing in most USGS water resource regions but rarely improves bias. The post-processors significantly improve NSE in 15 of 18 regions and peak timing error in 16 regions with sufficient basins. Bias is significantly improved in only one region, and in five regions the NWM represents bias better than the post-processor, including the East Coast and Pacific Northwest.
supporting_quote: The LSTM postprocessors significantly improved the NSE over the NWM in 15 of the 18 regions
the peak timing error in 16 regions (all regions with enough basins for a statistical evaluation)
and significantly improved bias in only one region.

chunks.text: Improvements from the two post-processing approaches occur in largely the same basins. The basin-wise improvement patterns of LSTM_PP and LSTM_PPA are almost identical, with an r² of 0.995 between their improvements across basins. This indicates that adding atmospheric forcings to the post-processor changes average performance little and does not fundamentally alter where post-processing helps.
supporting_quote: The improvements of the two post-processing methods are correlated across all basins (r2 = 0.995).

chunks.text: Integrated gradients show that in the combined-input model (LSTM_PPA), precipitation is the top driver and NWM routed streamflow is second. This means the model tends to learn directly from forcings rather than relying primarily on NWM streamflow output, even when NWM variables are available. In the NWM-only post-processor (LSTM_PP), NWM streamflow overwhelmingly dominates the attributions, indicating reliance on the NWM hydrograph when forcings are absent.
supporting_quote: The most important dynamic features for the LSTM_PPA were: (1) precipitation from NLDAS, and (2) routed streamflow from the NWM point data.
Precipitation inputs were weighted higher than the NWM streamflow output itself
Without the atmospheric forcings included ... the NWM streamflow output was by far the highest contributing dynamic input feature to the LSTM_PP.

chunks.text: Post-processing benefits are linked to specific NWM variables, with strongest relationships for timing and bias differences rather than NSE differences. Performance changes are most strongly (anti)correlated with stream velocity and accumulated underground runoff: basins with lower velocity and less UGDRNOFF see greater improvements from daily post-processing. By contrast, higher TRAD and higher LH are associated with larger improvements, suggesting certain hydroclimatic settings benefit more from post-processing.
supporting_quote: Performance differences ... were most strongly (anti)correlated with stream velocity from the channel router and accumulated underground runoff
basins with lower stream velocity (velocity) and less underground runoff (UGDRNOFF) saw greater performance improvement
basins with higher total radiation (TRAD) and higher latent heat flux (LH) saw greater improvement due to post-processing.

chunks.text: Hydrologic signature analysis shows that post-processing can improve some signatures relative to NWM but worsens representation of zero-flow frequency. Among 101 basins with any zero-flow periods, the NWM predicts zero flow in 56 basins, while LSTM_A, LSTM_PPA, and LSTM_PP do so in only 35, 29, and 25 basins, respectively. This indicates a systematic weakness of these LSTM approaches in capturing intermittency compared to the NWM.
supporting_quote: There were 101 basins with any periods of zero flow.
The NWM is better at handling this situation, predicting zero flow periods in 56 of the 101 basins.
The LSTM_A, LSTM_PPA, and LSTM_PP only predicted periods of zero flows at 35, 29, and 25 basins, respectively.

chunks.text: A sensitivity/diagnostic experiment using different subsets of NWM outputs shows that each post-processor variant still outperforms the NWM, implying information loss in the NWM chain. LSTMs trained only on LDAS land-surface outputs or only on CHRT channel-routing outputs both beat the NWM, suggesting those components contain information not translated into NWM streamflow. This supports using ML post-processing as a diagnostic tool for identifying where process-model information is lost.
supporting_quote: Each of the LSTM post-processors made better average daily streamflow predictions than the NWM itself
the LSTM that took as inputs only the LDAS model output from the NWM made better predictions than the NWM itself
The same was true for the states and fluxes of the CHRT component of the NWM

chunks.text: The authors caution that LSTM post-processing is unreliable for improving NWM predictions in all settings, especially when generalizing to ungauged-type basins. In the calibrated-only training experiment, post-processors were severely detrimental for two outlier basins that were much smaller than any training basin, while LSTM_A generalized better. This suggests that including NWM outputs can constrain learning and reduce extrapolation robustness when basin characteristics fall outside the training distribution.
supporting_quote: The LSTM postprocessors are unreliable for improving predictions of the NWM.
The post-processors both failed to make reasonable predictions at two basins that were much smaller than any basins included in the training set. The LSTM_A was able to make good predictions

chunks.text: All models struggle in low-flow and zero-flow conditions, which affects low-flow regime metrics and signature representation. The paper attributes poor below-20th-percentile performance partly to difficulty predicting zero streamflow, with 101 basins exhibiting zero-flow periods. Although LSTMs improve many metrics, the NWM better captures zero-flow events, limiting the suitability of LSTM post-processing in intermittent-flow regions without further methodological changes.
supporting_quote: All models poorly predicted flows below the 20th percentile.
This is likely due to the fact that all models tend to have difficulty predicting zero streamflow, and the 101 basins with periods of zero streamflow affected the average performance metrics.
The LSTM post-processors hurt the representation of the frequency of days with zero flow.

chunks.text: Because regression-based prediction of where post-processing will help depends on knowing NWM performance, it is not directly applicable to ungauged basins. The authors achieve high r² in predicting LSTM improvement over NWM, but note this requires streamflow observations to compute NWM performance. This limits operational pre-screening of post-processing benefits in locations without gauges.
supporting_quote: Figure 7 shows the results predicting the LSTM improvement over the NWM at each basin with an r2 value of 0.97, 0.88, and 0.89
a problem is that this requires knowing ahead of time the NWM performance.
This prevents us from predicting post-processing improvement in ungauged basins, since calculating the NWM performance requires streamflow observations.

chunks.text: The experiments focus on relatively undisturbed headwater basins and do not represent many human-managed processes relevant to national operations. The authors explicitly selected basins with few engineered control structures to capture close-to-natural rainfall–runoff response. As a result, further work is needed to extend conclusions to reservoirs, urban areas, and other managed hydrologic conditions.
supporting_quote: The basins chosen for this largescale analysis are mostly headwater catchments without engineered control structures
We trained the LSTMs on headwater basins, so further work would be needed to include reservoirs, urban areas, and other management practices.

chunks.text: The NWM’s calibration details are not thoroughly documented in the literature, which constrains interpretation of calibration impacts on comparative performance. The authors note NWM was calibrated over 2007–2013 but that no journal publications fully describe the calibration. This uncertainty motivates evaluating the NWM reanalysis on a fixed historical test window shared with the LSTMs.
supporting_quote: The NWM was calibrated by NOAA on the time period 2007–2013
though no journal publications thoroughly describe the details of this calibration.
For this study, we tested the performance of the NWM reanalysis only on the time period 1994–2002

chunks.text: The study concludes that LSTM post-processors significantly outperform the NWM but do not consistently or significantly outperform an LSTM trained only on atmospheric forcings. Because the LSTM can learn rainfall–runoff dynamics directly from forcings, NWM outputs provide limited added information and can sometimes hinder generalization. The authors recommend professional judgment in choosing post-processing and suggest using LSTM_A in uncalibrated or poorly understood locations.
supporting_quote: The LSTM post-processors (LSTM_PPA and LSTM_PP) significantly outperformed the NWM, but did not consistently, nor significantly, outperformed the LSTM_A
LSTMs, in general, are capable of learning the dynamics of rainfall– runoff processes, gaining little additional information from the conceptualizations coded within the NWM.
In locations where the NWM is not calibrated ... it would be best to use the LSTM without the influence from the NWM.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that the NWM loses information from atmospheric forcings to streamflow outputs, and that different NWM components relate to different error types. The land surface component (LDAS) is identified as a source of mass/bias error, while the channel routing component (CHRT) is identified as a source of timing error. Based on these diagnostics, improving the NWM routing scheme is highlighted as a priority.
supporting_quote: The NWM land surface component (LDAS) loses information about mass conservation (shown from the bias error), and the channel router (CHRT) loses information about streamflow timing.
This indicates that the NWM channel routing scheme should be considered a priority for NWM improvement.

chunks.text: For practical forecasting, the authors suggest deploying an atmospheric-forcing LSTM for streamflow in undisturbed catchments and upstream of managed systems, while retaining NWM for other states and engineered processes. This positioning leverages the low training/inference cost of LSTMs and the broader state simulation provided by the NWM. The approach can thus improve streamflow predictions without replacing the NWM’s full hydrologic forecasting suite.
supporting_quote: The immediate potential for improving realtime forecasting could be deploying an LSTM_A for streamflow prediction in undisturbed catchments
This would allow for retaining conceptual representations of lakes and reservoirs that already exist in the NWM.
these LSTM models can be trained on a laptop computer in a few hours ... and the computational cost of forward prediction is negligible.

chunks.text: Snowmelt is a dominant contributor to runoff in the western United States, so accurately simulating snowpack evolution is essential for water resources management. This need is especially acute in the Upper Colorado River Basin (UCRB), where snowmelt runoff supports tens of millions of people and major economic activity. Prior model intercomparisons show that both model physics/parameterization choices and errors in meteorological forcing can strongly influence simulated snowpack and melt timing.
supporting_quote: Snowmelt plays a crucial role in driving streamflow throughout the western United States (US; ...), accounting for 50%–80% of the region's annual runoff
runoff generated by snowmelt supplies to ∼40 million people across five US states and Mexico and supports ∼$1.4 trillion in annual economic activity

chunks.text: Differences in snow model structure and parameterization have been repeatedly shown to cause large spreads in simulated SWE and snowmelt, and snow simulations are also highly sensitive to forcing errors. Mountain regions amplify these issues because terrain modulates meteorology and observation networks are sparse. As a result, both forcing uncertainty and parameterization uncertainty must be considered when diagnosing SWE biases.
supporting_quote: intercomparison projects ... have shown that (a) differences in model physics and parameterization schemes often result in large differences in simulated snowpack and snowmelt, and (b) simulated snowpack evolution is highly sensitive to the errors in the prescribed forcings.
their roles can be particularly prominent in mountain regions where meteorological variables are strongly modulated by terrain and where observation networks are sparse

chunks.text: The National Water Model (NWM) uses Noah-MP with a default parameterization set, but prior work reported pronounced negative SWE bias in the UCRB when driven by common forcings. This motivates a targeted investigation that separates forcing-driven errors from model-physics and parameterization limitations. Understanding these contributions can guide improvements to both forcing preparation and model configuration.

chunks.text: The study aims to distinguish how much SWE simulation uncertainty in the UCRB arises from meteorological forcing errors versus Noah-MP physical parameterization choices within NWM. It specifically evaluates the AORC forcing product for SWE simulation and tests the impact of bias-correcting AORC precipitation and temperature using SNOTEL observations. It further seeks to identify which parameterization processes/schemes most influence SWE and whether an optimized scheme combination plus corrected forcings can substantially improve SWE predictability.

chunks.text: The paper frames four guiding questions: how precipitation and air temperature forcing errors affect snowpack precision, how parameterization schemes influence snowpack accuracy, whether combining optimal parameterization with bias-corrected forcing improves snowpack evolution in the UCRB, and what broader lessons apply to mountainous regions. Quantifying the isolated effects of precipitation and temperature bias correction is therefore a central problem addressed by the experiments.

chunks.text: The experimental design has three steps: evaluate SWE driven by default AORC forcings (control), quantify the role of forcing by bias-correcting AORC precipitation and/or temperature using SNOTEL observations, and quantify the role of parameterization using an ensemble of scheme combinations for five snow-related processes. Comparisons are made at grid cells containing SNOTEL sites and aggregated across sites. The approach is intended to isolate forcing impacts and then assess parameterization sensitivity under corrected forcings.

chunks.text: Bias correction of forcings is performed using SNOTEL daily observations at available grid cells. Observed daily precipitation is disaggregated to hourly using either the forcing’s diurnal distribution when daily forcing precipitation is nonzero or a uniform distribution when it is zero, then substituted for hourly AORC precipitation. Hourly forcing temperature is scaled to match the observed daily mean temperature. These adjusted forcings are then used in NWM runs to quantify SWE improvements.

SWE performance differences among these runs indicate relative sensitivity to precipitation versus temperature forcing errors.

chunks.text: Suspended sediment concentration (SSC) is a key control on river ecosystems and morphology. Unlike sediment flux, SSC directly influences light penetration, primary production, habitat suitability, and transport of carbon, nutrients, and contaminants. Rivers with similar sediment flux can still have very different ecological conditions if SSC differs. Understanding how human actions alter downstream SSC patterns is therefore important for both geomorphology and ecology.

chunks.text: Human activities have disrupted sediment delivery in many river systems, often through sediment trapping by dams and increased erosion from land-use change.
