On the hold-out test set (n = 2407), the model produced RMSE of 29 mg l−1, MAE of 12 mg l−1, bias of 4.2 mg l−1, and relative bias of 0.59. The authors also report no evidence of spatial or temporal bias in error metrics when stratified by latitude, longitude, and time period.
supporting_quote: Hold out test results (n=2407) ... RMSE of 29 mg l−1, mean absolute error (MAE) of 12 mg l−1, bias of 4.2 mg l−1, and relative bias of 0.59.
we examined error metrics stratified by latitude, longitude, and time period and found no evidence of spatial or temporal biases

chunks.text: Across 1984–2018, SSC declined in a substantial fraction of US rivers. By river length, mean annual SSC decreased in 32% of rivers, increased in 2%, and showed no significant trend in 66%. Declining rivers experienced a mean SSC reduction of 40% over the 34-year period, with reductions ranging from 9% to 98%.
supporting_quote: Mean annual SSC decreased in 32% of US rivers by length, increased in 2%, and had no significant trend ... in the remaining 66%
showed a mean SSC reduction of 40% across all declining rivers with a range of 9%-98%

chunks.text: Where declines occurred, rates varied widely. The study reports Theil–Sen decline rates from 0.02 to 15.6 mg l yr−1, with a mean decline rate of 0.52 mg l yr−1. These values quantify the pace of multi-decadal SSC change across the reaches that met the representativeness criteria.
supporting_quote: Rates of decline ranged from 0.02 to 15.6 mg l yr−1 with a mean decline of 0.52 mg l yr−1

chunks.text: Longitudinal SSC patterns among well-sampled rivers were diverse, but downstream increases were most common. SSC increased downstream in 117 rivers (48%), decreased downstream in 68 rivers (28%), and showed no significant pattern in 59 rivers (24%). Rivers with decreases or no pattern exhibited greater spatial variability in SSC compared with rivers showing downstream increases.
supporting_quote: SSC increased downstream in 117 rivers (48%), decreased downstream in 68 rivers (28%), and had no significant pattern ... in 59 rivers (24%).
Rivers with longitudinal decreases or no longitudinal pattern had greater spatial variability in SSC on average than rivers with longitudinal SSC increases

chunks.text: Dam characteristics differed across rivers with different longitudinal SSC patterns. Rivers with longitudinal decreases or no pattern had larger dams on average than rivers with longitudinal increases, including median dam height 16.6 m versus 11 m (difference 5.6 m; p = 0.009) and median reservoir water storage 0.96 mm versus 0.46 mm (p = 0.008). In contrast, cumulative reservoir storage was not different (p = 0.56), and dam density was higher where SSC increased downstream (0.012 vs 0.009 dams km−1; p = 0.02).
supporting_quote: a 5.6 m taller median dam height of 16.6 m compared to 11 m (p = 0.009, Kruskal–Wallis test)
double the median reservoir water storage of 0.96 mm compared to 0.46 mm (p = 0.008).
there were no differences in cumulative metrics ... total reservoir water storage (p = 0.56)
dam density was surprisingly higher in rivers with longitudinal SSC increases, 0.012 compared to 0.009 dams km−1 (p = 0.02

chunks.text: Comparisons to a modeled no-dam scenario suggest that damming has altered downstream SSC structure in many rivers. For the 66 rivers with modeled SSC profiles, 53% changed their longitudinal trend category when comparing the modeled no-dam profiles to contemporary observed profiles. Examples include the Colorado, Snake, and Rio Grande shifting from modeled increases to observed decreases.
supporting_quote: Modeled SSC profiles were available for 66 rivers. Of the 66 rivers, 53% changed longitudinal patterns comparing modeled no-dam profiles to contemporary observed profiles
the Colorado, Snake, and Rio Grande Rivers showed longitudinal SSC increases before damming, but now show rapid longitudinal decreases.

chunks.text: Annual SSC profile shapes within a river were generally consistent across years since 1984. The distribution of stability values was skewed toward high stability, indicating that persistent spatial zones of relatively high and low SSC recur over time. Stability tended to be slightly lower during the most extreme high or low flows, while most other flow conditions showed no differences.
supporting_quote: the shape of observed SSC profiles are remarkably similar from year to year within a river since 1984
SSC profile stability values are skewed toward high, more stable values
Less stable SSC profiles are slightly more likely to occur during the most extreme high or low flows

chunks.text: A multiple linear regression related mean SSC profile stability to basin and management factors. Drainage area, median dam height, and percent cropland explained 41% of the variation in mean stability. Larger basins with taller storage dams and minimal cropland tended to have the most stable SSC profiles.
supporting_quote: we found 41% of the variation in the mean stability was explained by drainage area ... median dam height along the river ... and percent cropland in the drainage area
Larger basins with minimal agriculture and tall storage dams have the most stable SSC profiles on average

chunks.text: The SSC model is constrained by the range of conditions represented in the training data. The authors note that machine-learning models cannot reliably extrapolate beyond the training SSC range of 0.1–2228 mg l−1. This limitation implies that extremely low or high SSC outside that range may be poorly estimated and motivates future model improvements.
supporting_quote: ML models are limited to the range of the training data, here 0.1–2228 mg l−1.
Further limitations and future improvements of our SSC model are discussed in supplemental information.

chunks.text: Trend comparisons with prior in-situ synthesis show agreement in magnitude but differences in the fraction of sites/river length showing declines. The paper reports a mean SSC reduction of 40% for declining rivers and cites a similar 37% reduction across 140 US sites, yet finds fewer declining trends than the in-situ analysis. The authors attribute disparities to limited representativeness of small in-situ samples and different record lengths (1992–2012 vs 1984–2018).
supporting_quote: mean SSC reduction of 40% across all declining rivers
found a mean SSC reduction of 37% across 140 sites in the US (Murphy 2020).
we found fewer declining SSC trends with 33% (n = 28 397) ... compared to 58% (n = 140 sites)
different record lengths, from 1992 to 2012 in Murphy (2020) compared to 1984-2018 reported here.

chunks.text: The analysis relies on Landsat Collection 1 Tier 1 Surface Reflectance because it was the best option at the time, rather than the newer Collection 2 product. The authors indicate they plan to release a Collection 2 update in future work. This implies that some estimates may change with updated atmospheric correction and calibration in Collection 2.
supporting_quote: We used the USGS Collection 1 Tier 1 Landsat Surface Reflectance product (T1-SR) because it was the best available product at the time of analysis
we will release a Collection 2 update in future work.

chunks.text: The study concludes that one-third of large US rivers show declining SSC since 1984, with a mean reduction of 40%, while increases are rare (2%). It argues that dams and land use influence not only temporal trends but also the longitudinal shape and stability of SSC profiles. Modern rivers with a few large dams often exhibit altered yet stable SSC profile shapes compared to modeled historical conditions without dams.
supporting_quote: One-third of large US rivers have declining SSC trends, with a mean reduction of 40% since 1984, while only 2% of rivers show increases.
our results also link dams and land use to the shape and stability of SSC profiles.
Modern rivers with at least a few large dams now have different, yet stable, SSC profile shapes compared to historical patterns before dams.

chunks.text: RivSed is presented as the most comprehensive spatial accounting of SSC trends in large US rivers to date, enabling identification of where rivers are changing and supporting geomorphic and ecological applications. The authors emphasize that this spatially continuous perspective provides broad utility and forms a basis for future expansion to global SSC monitoring. They highlight potential integration with future global flow observations (e.g., SWOT) to track sediment movement through rivers.
supporting_quote: Our spatially continuous view provides the most comprehensive accounting of SSC trends to date.
RivSed has broad applications in river geomorphology, hydrology, and ecology and we are expanding the database to a global scale.
With global SSC observations combined with river flow from the NASA Surface Water Oceanography and Topography mission ... we will gain an unprecedented view of suspended sediment movement

chunks.text: Accurate quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) is a core requirement for hydrologic and climate applications such as land surface modeling, flood forecasting, and drought monitoring. Existing precipitation datasets from gauges, satellites, and reanalysis differ in uncertainty, spatial/temporal coverage, and bias. Because each source has strengths and weaknesses, fusing multiple sources has become a key strategy to improve overall QPE quality.
supporting_quote: Accurate quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) is essential for various applications, including land surface modeling, flood forecasting, drought monitoring and prediction.
In situ precipitation datasets, remote sensingbased estimations, and reanalysis products have heterogeneous uncertainty.

chunks.text: Rain gauges directly measure rainfall and are often considered the most reliable QPE reference, but they are spatially sparse and contain missing values, and interpolation introduces additional uncertainty. Satellite remote sensing offers global spatiotemporal coverage and captures precipitation patterns, but many satellite products have systematic biases relative to gauges. Reanalysis products integrate models and observations via assimilation, yet can still exhibit significant systematic error and bias depending on inputs and algorithms.
supporting_quote: Although suffering from temporal and spatial sparsity, rain gauge measurements are still considered the most reliable source for QPE
However, many of these products suffer from large systematic biases and uncertainties compared to rain gauge estimates
many of the reanalysis datasets still have high systematic error and bias

chunks.text: Many existing merging approaches rely on traditional interpolation, weighting, cokriging, or Bayesian methods, but they often depend on assumptions that can be violated and treat spatial and temporal relationships separately. Machine learning and deep learning have stronger capacity to learn complex patterns in large datasets. The paper motivates using deeper spatiotemporal architectures to exploit precipitation autocorrelation and spatial context at scale.
supporting_quote: However, many of these methods are traditional regression models that are highly reliant on assumptions that in many cases do not hold.
the discrete spatial and temporal associations between satellite-derived precipitation and gauge observations are evaluated independently, rather than in conjunction
machine learning (ML) models have stronger learning abilities and generalization capabilities in capturing the complex inherent patterns in data

chunks.text: The study aims to develop a general framework that can simultaneously fuse and downscale multiple user-selected precipitation products using rain gauge observations as targets. The intended contribution is a deep learning architecture that captures spatiotemporal dependencies by combining 3D convolutions and ConvLSTM layers. The framework is designed to be flexible so users can choose products and tune parameters such as window size, temporal depth, and network structure.
supporting_quote: we developed a general framework that can simultaneously merge and downscale multiple user-defined precipitation products by using rain gauge observations as target values.
A novel deep learning-based convolutional neural network architecture, namely, the precipitation data fusion network (PDFN), that combines multiple layers of 3D-CNN and ConvLSTM

chunks.text: A specific goal is to evaluate how spatial neighborhood size and temporal depth affect fusion accuracy, quantifying the benefit of spatiotemporal dependencies. The study also seeks to identify the best-performing combination of input products among seven candidates. Finally, it compares the proposed approach against simpler merging baselines such as arithmetic mean and one-outlier-removed (OOR) mean.
supporting_quote: We also investigate the effect of window size and temporal depth to determine how much the spatiotemporal correlations of adjacent cells can affect the accuracy of the final product.
Here, we used 7 precipitation products and employed our framework to fuse various combinations of these datasets and to identify the best possible combination
Finally, we compare our framework with different competing approaches, such as the arithmetic mean and one-outlier-removed (OOR) mean

chunks.text: A key gap is that many precipitation fusion methods focus on either spatial or temporal correlations separately and do not jointly model spatiotemporal dependencies. This limitation can prevent models from capturing the inherent dynamics of precipitation fields that may improve estimates. The paper positions a combined spatiotemporal deep learning approach as necessary to overcome this shortcoming.
supporting_quote: many of these attempts are mainly focused on spatial or temporal correlations between various remote sensing sources and/or gauge data separately
thus, the developed model cannot fully capture the inherent spatiotemporal dependencies that could potentially improve the precipitation estimations.

chunks.text: Precipitation datasets exhibit strong class imbalance because no-precipitation days substantially outnumber precipitation days. This imbalance increases the risk of overfitting and biased learning in deep models, requiring explicit mitigation strategies. The authors highlight data augmentation and regularization as responses to this challenge.
supporting_quote: address skewed class proportions due to the highly imbalanced nature of the precipitation datasets.
the number of precipitation days significantly lower than the number of no-precipitation days.

chunks.text: Gauge observations, while reliable, contain missing values and can be spatially sparse, which complicates building consistent training targets and can introduce uncertainty through interpolation. Satellite and reanalysis inputs also include missing values and outliers, requiring preprocessing to avoid NaNs in model inputs. The paper frames these data quality issues as practical barriers for large-scale fusion modeling.
supporting_quote: the poor and uneven spatial resolution and the plethora of missing values in rain gauge estimates significantly affect the accuracy
The missing values and outliers in the gauge stations and satellite products are processed to ensure that input images to the networks do not contain NaN values.

chunks.text: The precipitation data fusion network (PDFN) combines multiple 3D-CNN and ConvLSTM blocks to extract spatial and temporal features from multi-product precipitation inputs. 3D-CNN blocks first convolve over the 4D inputs to produce feature maps, which are then processed by ConvLSTM blocks for more rigorous spatiotemporal feature extraction. The final feature maps are flattened and passed through dense layers with dropout to reduce overfitting.
supporting_quote: PDFN architecture, which is comprised of multiple 3D-CNN and ConvLSTM blocks
the 3D-CNN blocks will perform several convolutions on the 4D input images and prepare the final feature maps to be fed to the ConvLSTM blocks.
Finally, the feature maps will be flattened and then fed to multiple dense layers followed by dropout layers to avoid overfitting.

chunks.text: Input construction uses station-centered spatiotemporal windows. All products are resampled with nearest-neighbor interpolation to a common 0.1° grid, then clipped in a user-defined spatial window around each gauge station and over a user-defined temporal depth. The clipped 3D arrays (time × width × height) for each product are concatenated across products to form 4D tensors (time × width × height × products) used as network inputs.
supporting_quote: resampling is performed on all datasets using the nearestneighbor interpolation method to achieve a spatial resolution of 0.1◦.
A window with a user-defined size is created that is centered around each gauge station.
concatenated over the 7 products to create 4D input images with the shape of time × width × height × products.

chunks.text: The preprocessing pipeline removes problematic stations and cleans NaNs by handling missing values and outliers. Stations with more than 5% missing values are excluded, and remaining datasets are aligned in space and time and then clipped to the CONUS domain. The pipeline is computationally heavy, so clipping operations were parallelized on a high-performance computing cluster.
supporting_quote: First, the stations with *>5% missing values are disregarded.
The satellite products are first evaluated for their spatial and temporal characteristics, and subsequently matched to ensure consistency.
120,907,710 clipping operations are needed... this process was parallelized over the Center for Complex Hydrosystems Research High-Performance Computing (CCHR-HPC) cluster

chunks.text: To address imbalance in precipitation days, the training data is augmented using simple image transformations that preserve spatial structure. The authors apply rotation and horizontal/vertical flipping to increase the number of precipitation-day samples. Inputs are normalized per variable using the training-set mean and standard deviation for consistency across products.
supporting_quote: This study addresses the challenge of imbalanced and sparse precipitation data by utilizing image augmentation techniques
two simple data augmentation techniques, rotation and horizontal/vertical flipping, were employed to augment the training dataset
we normalized the input images by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation of each variable

chunks.text: Model training uses mean square error (MSE) loss and the Adam optimizer. The learning rate is set to 0.0001, mini-batch size to 4096, and training runs for 30 epochs based on loss convergence. Batch normalization is included to stabilize training by mitigating internal covariate shift, and dropout with rate 0.5 is used in the last layer as regularization.
supporting_quote: The current study uses the mean square error (MSE) as the loss function
we use the Adam optimizer
the learning rate value of 0.0001 resulted in the best outputs
The mini-batch size is selected to be 4096... the epoch number is set to 30
a dropout rate of 0.5 was used in the last layer.

chunks.text: The study uses a spatiotemporally separated split to test generalization across both station locations and time. From 2629 GHCNd stations, 50% are used for training, 25% for validation, and 25% for testing, with 3-fold cross-validation for tuning. Training uses 2003–2008, validation 2009–2014, and testing 2015–2020, ensuring the test period differs from training.
supporting_quote: 2629 stations were chosen for this study that had *<*5% missing values for the period of 2003 to 2020.
50% were chosen for the train (1314 stations), 25% for the test (658 stations), and another 25% for the validation (657 stations)
The period of 2003–2008 was chosen for training, while 2009–2014 was selected for validation, and... 2015–2020, were used for the test set.

chunks.text: Evaluation relies on continuous and event-based metrics to assess accuracy and detection skill. The paper defines and uses MSE, Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC), and Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE), along with POD, FAR, and CSI for rain/no-rain detection. These metrics are computed between predicted precipitation and gauge observations over the evaluation sets.
supporting_quote: The accuracy evaluations... are performed using the mean square error (MSE), pearson correlation coefficient (PCC), and Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE)
Probability of Detection (POD), False Alarm Ratio (FAR) and Critical Success Index (CSI) are defined in Eqs. (6)–(8).

chunks.text: Seven gridded precipitation products plus gauge stations are used, representing satellite-based, gauge-based, and reanalysis sources. The gridded products include PERSIANN-CDR, IMERG, CPC Unified, NLDAS, CMORPH, GSMaP, and CHIRPS, while GHCNd provides station observations. The study focuses on CONUS and harmonizes products for fusion experiments.
supporting_quote: Here, we used 7 precipitation products
Table 1  A summary of the precipitation products used in this study.
GHCNd... This dataset is used as the target dataset in this study.

chunks.text: IMERG Final V06 is used as a satellite-gauge adjusted precipitation input. IMERG provides global coverage from 60°N to 60°S and offers 0.1° spatial resolution with 30-minute temporal resolution, with Early/Late/Final runs differing by latency and gauge adjustment. The study specifically states it uses IMERG “Final” version 6.
supporting_quote: provide precipitation estimates with a 0.1◦ spatial resolution and 30-min temporal resolution.
In this study, IMERG "Final" version 6 was used.

chunks.text: CPC Unified provides gauge-based daily precipitation and is used as an input product. It has global coverage and uses over 30,000 stations, with 0.5° spatial resolution since 1979; for CONUS it uses more than 8000 stations at 0.25°. The study uses the CPC Unified version and notes its quality control based on independent sources.
supporting_quote: utilizes over 30,000 stations worldwide.
offers daily precipitation data with a spatial resolution of 0.5◦ since 1979.
For the Continental United States (CONUS)... employs *>8000 stations with a spatial resolution of 0.25◦.
Here, we used the CPC Unified version.

chunks.text: NLDAS-2 is used as a reanalysis forcing dataset over North America. It spans 25°–53°N and 125°–67°W and provides hourly forcing and land-surface model outputs at 1/8° resolution, incorporating a gauge-based daily precipitation dataset that is disaggregated to hourly. The record runs from 1979 to present.
supporting_quote: spans across the CONUS... with the geographical coordinates of 25◦-53◦N and 125◦-67◦W
at a spatial resolution of 1/8◦.
variables are estimated at a spatial resolution of 12.5 km from 1979 to the present day

chunks.text: CHIRPS is a land-only satellite-station blended precipitation product used as an input. It provides 0.05° spatial resolution and daily (also pentadal/monthly) estimates from 1981 to present, covering 50°S to 50°N. The study uses CHIRPS version 2.0.
supporting_quote: offered at 0.05◦ spatial resolution and daily, pentadal, and monthly temporal resolution from 1981 to present.
the spatial coverage of the product is 50◦ S to 50◦ N latitude band
In this study CHIRPS version 2.0 was used.

chunks.text: GHCNd station observations serve as the target/reference dataset for supervised learning. From nearly 12,000 CONUS stations, 2629 stations with less than 5% missing values (2003–2020) are selected, with a minimum 50 km spacing to reduce window overlap. The target variable is daily precipitation at these stations.
supporting_quote: This dataset is used as the target dataset in this study.
From nearly 12,000 stations over the CONUS in the GHCNd dataset, 2629 stations were chosen for this study that had *<*5% missing values for the period of 2003 to 2020.
the distance between any two stations must be *>50 km

chunks.text: Fusion accuracy improves as spatial window size increases, indicating the value of spatial context. In the window-only experiments (temporal depth 0), test MSE decreases from 27.23 at 0×0 to 22.61 at 15×15, while test PCC increases from 0.7670 to 0.7915. The authors select 15×15 as the final input window size based on test-set performance.
supporting_quote: the MSE gradually decreases by increasing the window size
the lowest MSE and the highest PCC are achieved by the window size of 15 × 15 according to the test set

chunks.text: Increasing temporal depth alone yields modest improvements until an optimal point, after which performance degrades. With window size 0×0, test MSE decreases from 27.23 (depth 0) to 25.95 (depth 11), but then increases at depth 13 (26.11) and depth 15 (26.21). This suggests temporal context helps but must be tuned to avoid adding noise or irrelevant history.
supporting_quote: after the depth of 11, the MSE starts to increase.
0 × 0 ... Temporal depth 0 ... Test ... MSE ... 27.23
0 × 0 ... Temporal depth 11 ... Test ... MSE ... 25.95
0 × 0 ... Temporal depth 13 ... Test ... MSE ... 26.11

chunks.text: The best spatiotemporal configuration is achieved by increasing window size and temporal depth simultaneously. The strongest test performance in Table 2 occurs at window size 15×15 and temporal depth 15, with test PCC 0.7888 and test MSE 21.69. This supports the claim that jointly modeling spatial neighborhoods and temporal sequences improves QPE.
supporting_quote: the MSE decreases at a higher rate by increasing the window size and temporal depth simultaneously
the best performance is achieved for a window size of 15 × 15 and a temporal depth of 15.

chunks.text: Using all seven products as inputs yields the best overall fusion accuracy compared with reduced input sets. In Table 3, the all-input scenario (IM_NL_CM_CP_GS_PE_CH) achieves test PCC 0.7888 and test MSE 21.69. Removing CPC and NLDAS together substantially degrades performance (IM_CM_GS_PE_CH: test PCC 0.6571, MSE 35.82), showing key contributions from high-performing inputs.
supporting_quote: IM_NL_CM_CP_GS_PE_CH ... Test ... PCC 0.7888 ... MSE ... 21.69
IM_CM_GS_PE_CH ... Test ... PCC 0.6571 ... MSE ... 35.82
removing these inputs would show a significant reduction in model performance.

chunks.text: Even the poorest individual product (GSMaP) can improve fusion when included, contradicting the intuition that weak products should be discarded. Table 3 shows that removing GSMaP from the full input set (IM_NL_CM_CP_PE_CH) increases test MSE from 21.69 to 23.20. The authors note this corresponds to a 7% MSE increase, implying the network can extract useful complementary signals from less accurate products.
supporting_quote: Even removing the GSMaP with the lowest performance increased the MSE by 7%.
IM_NL_CM_CP_GS_PE_CH ... Test ... MSE 21.69
IM_NL_CM_CP_PE_CH ... Test ... MSE 23.20

chunks.text: PDFN outperforms standard products across CONUS test stations (2015–2020). Relative to CPC (best baseline), PDFN reduces MSE from 33.56 to 21.69 (35% improvement) and increases PCC from 0.674 to 0.789 (16% improvement). PDFN also improves KGE to 0.718, exceeding NLDAS (0.608) and CPC (0.595).
supporting_quote: NLDAS ... KGE ... 0.608
PDFN outperforms other datasets in terms of MSE and PCC, with 35% and 16% improvement compared to CPC

chunks.text: When restricted to non-gauge-based/corrected products, PDFN still improves accuracy and event detection. For 2017–2020, PDFN achieves MSE 33.99 and PCC 0.654, improving MSE by 33% relative to the best individual product (SM2RAIN MSE 50.43). It also shows strong rain/no-rain skill with POD 0.98 and CSI 0.65 while reducing FAR to 0.34.
supporting_quote: SM2RAIN ... MSE ... 50.43
IM% represents the improvements with respect to the best performing product.

chunks.text: PDFN can act as a recalibration method even when using a gauge-based product alone. Using CPC as the only input (Table 3: CP), PDFN achieves test MSE 24.67, which is lower than CPC’s standalone test MSE 33.56 reported in Table 5. The authors interpret this as evidence that CPC’s calibration may be suboptimal for CONUS and that PDFN can learn improvements from station targets.
supporting_quote: when the PDFN is applied using CPC as the sole input product, the MSE is reduced to 24.67, as demonstrated in Table 3

chunks.text: Compared with simple merging baselines, PDFN performs better across multiple measures on the test dataset. The paper evaluates arithmetic mean and one-outlier-removed (OOR) mean and reports that PDFN “significantly outperforms” both. The stated reason is that PDFN learns spatiotemporal dependencies, while the baselines do not account for such relations.
supporting_quote: The results of the PDFN were compared with two other optimal merging methods, namely, the arithmetic mean and one-outlierremoved (OOR) arithmetic mean.
According to this figure, the PDFN significantly outperforms the arithmetic mean and the OOR mean in all measures.
the PDFN merging method is better equipped to learn the spatiotemporal patterns and dependencies

chunks.text: The study produces a fused daily precipitation dataset over 2015–2020 at 0.1° resolution. The authors state this dataset follows the proposed PDFN framework and integrates the spatiotemporal patterns across all seven products. Visual comparisons on selected days suggest the fused product’s spatial patterns are consistent with major storms while differing in intensity from any single parent product.
supporting_quote: Following the proposed PDFN framework, a fused daily precipitation dataset from 2015 to 2020 with a spatial resolution of 0.1◦ is produced.
Considering both the spatial and temporal patterns of all 7 precipitation products, the PDFN can better exploit the spatiotemporal patterns and produce a fused product

chunks.text: Daily temporal resolution limits applicability for real-time hazards such as flood forecasting that require hourly or sub-hourly precipitation. The authors note users could fuse higher-frequency products, but the fused output will then depend on each product’s availability and latency. They also emphasize that changing the input products requires updating the fusion model.
supporting_quote: in some applications, such as real-time flood forecasting, the temporal resolution of daily precipitation data is insufficient
users can access and fuse products that provide precipitation data at hourly or sub-hourly intervals.
any modifications to the input products necessitate corresponding updates to the fusion model.

chunks.text: The framework downscales products only to the finest resolution among the inputs and does not use ancillary high-resolution predictors. The authors state that without DEM, cloud data, infrared, or radar observations, the model cannot fully capture fine-scale precipitation variability. They suggest incorporating ancillary datasets in future work to improve high-resolution representation.
supporting_quote: it was designed to fuse and at the same time downscale the precipitation products to match the resolution to the finest product used as input.
it cannot fully capture the variability in precipitation at fine resolutions since no ancillary data, such as DEM, cloud data, and/or IR and radar observations, are used.
For future works, other ancillary datasets at finer resolutions can be used

chunks.text: Temporal information contributed less than spatial context in the reported experiments. The authors observe from Table 2 that performance improves more rapidly with increased window size than with increased temporal depth. They call for further research to understand why and how to better exploit temporal correlations in the fusion model.
supporting_quote: the temporal contributions are not as much as spatial ones as evidenced in Table 2.
More research is needed to explore the reasons and how we can take advantage of temporal correlations as much as spatial relations.

chunks.text: Including gauge-based or gauge-corrected products as inputs may reduce independence from the gauge reference because some of the same stations could have been used in calibration. The authors note this could be a concern in some applications, and users can remove such products thanks to the framework’s input flexibility. They caution that integrating gauge-based and satellite products requires careful consideration to avoid overfitting.
supporting_quote: It is possible that the gauges employed in this study have already been employed in the calibration or correction process of generating these products, making them non-independent from the reference dataset.
users can simply remove these products from the fusion process by taking advantage of the input flexibility of the PDFN framework.
users can integrate gauge-based and satellite products in the presented framework with careful consideration to avoid overfitting.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that PDFN, a deep architecture combining 3D-CNN and ConvLSTM, improves QPE by jointly learning spatial and temporal precipitation patterns from multiple products with gauge targets. Regularization and augmentation (batch normalization, dropout, and image transformations) are emphasized as important to handle vanishing gradients, overfitting, and data imbalance. The authors highlight that larger window sizes and temporal depths improve performance when tuned appropriately, and that using all seven products provides the best fusion accuracy.
supporting_quote: A novel deep learning-based convolutional neural network architecture that combines multiple layers of the 3D-CNN and ConvLSTM, namely, the PDFN, was developed to extract the spatial and temporal patterns of precipitation simultaneously.
This architecture benefits from techniques such as batch normalization... and data augmentation schemes and dropout layers
by increasing the window size and temporal depth simultaneously, superior results with lower MSE and higher PCC can be achieved.
We found that using all 7 products will result in the best performance

chunks.text: Overall, the fused PDFN product outperforms the parent precipitation products on the CONUS test set, with substantial improvements in accuracy metrics. The study reports improvements of 35% in MSE and 16% in PCC relative to CPC, the best-performing baseline product, alongside improved KGE. The authors argue these gains demonstrate the value of exploiting spatiotemporal dependencies for precipitation fusion.
supporting_quote: The results showed that the fused daily product remarkably improved the mean square error (MSE) and Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) by 35% and 16%, respectively, compared to the best-performing product.

chunks.text: The authors suggest the PDFN framework is general and can be extended beyond precipitation to other Earth system variables. They propose that the success of learning spatiotemporal dependencies for precipitation fusion indicates similar potential for datasets like soil moisture, evapotranspiration, and temperature. The framework’s user-defined inputs and parameters are positioned as enabling broader applications.
supporting_quote: the framework is general in the sense that users can choose their desired sets of products and modify the parameters of the algorithm
The success of the PDFN for precipitation data fusion demonstrates the great potential of this approach... for other datasets, such as soil moisture, evapotranspiration, temperature, etc.

chunks.text: Environmental modeling is increasingly converging toward Earth System modeling, where land-surface, hydrology, and ecology models incorporate more processes and require interdisciplinary expertise. This shift increases the complexity of model configurations and the variety of spatial representations used. As a result, workflows depend heavily on geospatial and meteorological datasets prepared for the model’s specific discretization.
supporting_quote: Process-based models developed across different areas of the environmental sciences are now converging to the interdisciplinary ''Earth Systems'' modeling paradigm.
Such terrestrial systems models require expertise from scientists across multiple disciplines

chunks.text: Earth System modeling uses multiple landscape discretizations (e.g., grids, triangles, irregular polygons), and scientific datasets are often provided in different spatial configurations. Moving variables like precipitation and temperature between these configurations is a common prerequisite for model forcing and evaluation. The paper positions remapping as a central step in efficient, reproducible environmental modeling workflows.
supporting_quote: The Earth System modeling community uses different methods to discretize a landscape in model elements, such as square grids, triangles, or irregular shapes.
Mapping data from one spatial configuration to another is an essential part of environmental modeling

chunks.text: Preparing forcing and geospatial inputs commonly requires multiple remapping-related tasks beyond grid-to-grid interpolation. These include mapping to subbasins/HRUs, extracting point time series for stations, summarizing regional averages, and visual checks. The authors summarize these repeated needs as community-wide tasks that motivate a generalized tool.
supporting_quote: A key task in complex environmental models is preparing the necessary geospatial and meteorological data used to force models.
These tasks can be summarized as follows: Remapping variables... Extraction of data for a given point... Generating summary metrics... Visualization of variables

chunks.text: The work introduces EASYMORE, a Python package intended to make remapping between spatial representations fast, efficient, reproducible, and transparent. The package is designed to remap variables from a source (often netCDF) to a target polygon representation (shapefile) and output ready-to-use datasets. The manuscript aims to explain the package, show example applications, and describe its impact for Earth System modelers.
supporting_quote: we present a Python package called EASYMORE.
The package is aimed to increase the efficiency of data preparation for Earth System modeling in a reproducible and transparent manner.
In the following, the EASYMORE package is explained, a few examples are provided and its impact on the Earth System modeling community and ongoing research is presented.

chunks.text: A practical objective is to reduce the time costs of preparing inputs for Earth System Models by streamlining remapping steps into a single, easy-to-use workflow. The authors emphasize accessibility compared with comprehensive but complex alternatives. EASYMORE is positioned as a focused remapping tool that helps users efficiently handle common Earth System modeling and hydrology use cases.
supporting_quote: Our goal with EASYMORE is to reduce the time costs needed to prepare inputs for Earth System Models.
EASYMORE is a focused tool that provides easy-to-use remapping capabilities commonly needed in Earth System Modeling and catchment hydrology.

chunks.text: Remapping data between spatial configurations is frequently time-consuming and cumbersome in environmental modeling workflows. Different models and datasets use incompatible discretizations, so users must repeatedly transform forcing and outputs between grids, stations, and irregular polygons. The paper highlights this as a pervasive barrier to efficient and reproducible Earth System modeling.
supporting_quote: Mapping data from one spatial configuration to another is an essential part of environmental modeling, and can be time-consuming and cumbersome.
station and gridded data... often needed to be remapped from their native spatial resolution to the modeling elements used in terrestrial systems models, such as grids, subbasins

chunks.text: The community needs to support multiple remapping scenarios, including regular grids, rotated grids, and non-regular shapes such as Thiessen/Voronoi polygons. In addition to areal remapping, common tasks include point extraction, regional summaries, and visualization checks. The authors frame these needs as not fully met by existing ad hoc scripts or tools that require extensive training.
supporting_quote: Remapping variables from one spatial representation (e.g., regular grids, rotated grids, or non-regular shapes such as Thiessen polygons or Voronoi diagrams) to another spatial representation
Usually, research groups and model developers use in-house scripts that are tuned for their modeling approach purposes.
A part of the community uses packages that might need extensive training

chunks.text: A recurring operational challenge is handling partial spatial overlap between a source dataset domain and a target shapefile. Without tooling, users often must manually pre-select or clip shapes to avoid invalid outputs. The paper presents this as a frequent issue when administrative boundaries or limited domains do not cover all desired target subbasins.
supporting_quote: There might be cases in which the target shapefile and the domain of the source netCDF file(s) do not overlap.
EASYMORE allows the user to keep the nonoverlapping shapefile values as nan or fully remove them from the remapped file

chunks.text: Missing values in source netCDF files can cause remapped values to be biased if weights are not adjusted. The paper notes that per-time-step missing data should not break conservation or produce artifacts due to weights that no longer sum to unity. Addressing this is presented as important for Earth System modeling because it preserves mass or energy during remapping.
supporting_quote: The second layer of normalization of weights is based on the existing missing values in the source netCDF files and it is performed per time step.
This is important for Earth System modeling as it preserves the mass or energy during the remapping from source to target shapes.

chunks.text: EASYMORE’s architecture centers on an "easymore" class implemented in easymore.py, with nc_remapper as the core function. nc_remapper orchestrates other helper functions depending on user choices, while utilities like make_shape_point and dataframe_to_netcdf_xr can also be called directly. This structure supports both integrated end-to-end remapping and modular use of components.
supporting_quote: EASYMORE functions are prepared in an easymore class of functions in a file called easymore.py. The core functionality of EASY-MORE is the function nc_remapper.
All other functions in the easymore class... can also be called individually and directly.

chunks.text: The nc_remapper workflow takes source netCDF files with latitude/longitude coordinates, a target polygon shapefile, and optionally a source shapefile or an existing remap file. It computes areal overlaps between source and target polygons to derive weights, then applies those weights to map source values to target polygons. Outputs are written as a new netCDF file and optionally CSV files.
supporting_quote: EASYMORE's core function nc_remapper takes the following inputs: A (collection of) source netCDF file(s)... A target shapefile...
EASYMORE nc_remapper then calculates the areal overlap between each source polygon... and each polygon in the target shapefile and saves this information in a so-called remap file.
Finally, EASYMORE uses the areal overlaps to remap values in the source netCDF onto the polygons in the target shapefile and saves the results as a new netCDF file (and optionally CSV files).

chunks.text: If a source netCDF is not on a regular or rotated grid, EASYMORE assumes each point represents an area and automatically builds Thiessen (Voronoi) polygons from the latitude/longitude coordinates. Users can override this by providing a custom source shapefile that defines representative areas, which can be useful in complex terrain. This enables remapping from stations or irregular point datasets to target polygons.
supporting_quote: If this is not the case, EASYMORE assumes that each data-point... is representative of an area around these coordinates and EASYMORE will automatically create Thiessen polygons (also known as Voronoi diagrams)
This behavior can be overridden if the user provides a ''source shapefile'', that contains the polygons for which each data value is considered to be representative.

chunks.text: To accelerate repeated remapping for the same spatial configuration, nc_remapper can reuse a precomputed remap file that stores source–target overlaps and weights. When an existing remap file is provided, EASYMORE skips GIS-based processing steps. This is intended for workflows remapping multiple netCDF files that share identical spatial organization.
supporting_quote: The user can short-circuit this procedure by specifying an existing remap file as an input to the nc_remapper function.
If such a remap file is provided EASYMORE nc_remapper will skip all GIS-based processing steps.

chunks.text: EASYMORE uses first-order conservative remapping weights based on the fraction of source areas overlapping target areas. The paper notes that more advanced schemes (e.g., second-order conservative remapping or Kriging) can be emulated by creating remap files outside nc_remapper. The examples in the manuscript follow the first-order conservative approach.
supporting_quote: the internal remapping weights are first-order conservative
This means the weights used for remapping are based on the fraction of areas from the source shape in the target shape.
examples that are presented in this study follow first-order conservative assumptions

chunks.text: nc_remapper can rescale and normalize weights in two stages to handle partial overlap and missing data. First, it normalizes when source and target shapes do not fully overlap. Second, it adjusts weights per time step to account for missing values in the source netCDF so the remaining weights sum to unity, helping preserve conservation properties during remapping.
supporting_quote: nc_rempper has the capability to rescale the remapping weights and normalize them in two steps (by default).
The first normalization of weights is when the source and target shapes do not fully overlap.
The second layer of normalization of weights is based on the existing missing values in the source netCDF files and it is performed per time step.

chunks.text: EASYMORE’s main file formats are netCDF for array-oriented scientific variables and ESRI shapefiles for vector geometries used as source/target representations. netCDF is used for scalable spatial-temporal Earth System data storage, while shapefiles store polygon/point/line geometries and associated attributes across multiple companion files. The remapping workflow combines these formats to compute overlaps and produce remapped outputs.
supporting_quote: EASYMORE uses two file formats as its main input and output files. These two formats are netCDF and ESRI shapefile.
NetCDF... support the creation, access, and sharing of array-oriented scientific data.
A shapefile... is a widely used format to represent spatial data or features as a vector

chunks.text: One example dataset is ERA5, used to demonstrate remapping a regularly spaced gridded temperature field to irregular subbasin polygons of the South Saskatchewan River up to Medicine Hat, Alberta. The example emphasizes grid-to-polygon remapping for model forcing preparation. The manuscript visualizes both the original grid field and the remapped subbasin representation.
supporting_quote: ERA5... provides an example of remapping the variables from a netCDF file with regularly spaced grids into the subbasins of the South Saskatchewan River up to the city of Medicine Hat
This example is based on the remapping of the temperature field from grids to subbasins

chunks.text: A second example uses WRF-CONUS-I, a dynamically downscaled atmospheric product with rotated coordinates where each grid cell has distinct latitude/longitude. The dataset is used to show that EASYMORE can handle non-uniformly spaced grids and remap temperature variables to the same South Saskatchewan subbasins. This illustrates remapping from rotated grids to irregular polygons.
supporting_quote: The second example provides the remapping of rotated coordination for netCDF file(s) in which each grid has a different latitude and longitude (not uniformly spaced).
WRF-CONUS-I... is selected for this example.

chunks.text: A third example uses SCDNA, a serially complete station dataset (about 26000 stations across North America) for precipitation and temperature. EASYMORE creates Voronoi/Thiessen polygons from station latitude/longitude in the netCDF and remaps variables from station-representative areas to target subbasin polygons. This shows support for station-based datasets via polygon construction.
supporting_quote: SCDNA... provides a serially complete station dataset for approximately 26000 stations across the North American domain.
EASY-MORE package can create the Voronoi diagram or Thiessen polygons for stations based on the latitude and longitude provided in the netCDF file.

chunks.text: Another example uses Canadian census 2016 dissemination areas (polygons representing 400 to 700 inhabitants on average) to remap population density to South Saskatchewan subbasins. The workflow converts census tabular data to netCDF using dataframe_to_netcdf_xr, then uses the dissemination-area shapefile as the source geometry for areal remapping. This demonstrates remapping for socio-environmental covariates beyond meteorology.
supporting_quote: The Canadian census of 2016 and its dissemination area... account for 400 to 700 inhabitants on average
census data... are converted into a netCDF file from CSV files using EASYMORE dataframe_to_netcdf_xr.
nc_remapper is called using the created netCDF file as the source file and its associated shapefile

chunks.text: The final example reads GRACE terrestrial water anomaly at 1-degree resolution and extracts values for a point shapefile of world capital cities. It highlights handling of differing longitude conventions between data (0 to 360) and shapefiles (−180 to 180). The paper illustrates the extracted time series for Tehran as a representative output.
supporting_quote: GRACE... provides an understanding of freshwater changes over the world at a resolution of 1 degree
GRACE dataset is provided with a longitude of 0 to 360 while the target shapefile... is given with a longitude between −180 to 180 degrees.
The GRACE anomaly is extracted for the point shapefile of all the capital cities around the world.

chunks.text: EASYMORE can remap from regularly spaced latitude/longitude grids to irregular subbasin polygons, producing subbasin-level fields suitable for modeling. The ERA5 example demonstrates remapping a temperature field from grid cells to the South Saskatchewan subbasins. The paper presents visual comparisons of original gridded temperature and remapped subbasin values.
supporting_quote: Remapping of ERA5 data on a regularly spaced grid to sub-basins of the South Saskatchewan River
Visualization of temperature field for ERA5 dataset from (left) the original grids to (right) remapped variables at subbasins.

chunks.text: The software supports rotated-grid netCDF inputs where latitude and longitude vary per grid cell, enabling remapping from such grids to irregular basin polygons. The WRF-CONUS-I example shows temperature remapped from original rotated grids to South Saskatchewan subbasins. This indicates EASYMORE is not limited to uniformly spaced regular grids.
supporting_quote: remapping of rotated coordination for netCDF file(s) in which each grid has a different latitude and longitude (not uniformly spaced).
EASYMORE can remap the temperature variables to the subbasins of the South Saskatchewan River

chunks.text: For station datasets, EASYMORE can automatically create Voronoi/Thiessen polygons from station coordinates and use them as source areas for areal remapping. The SCDNA example demonstrates precipitation mapped from Thiessen polygons to subbasins, bridging point-based measurements and polygon-based model units. The paper visualizes stations, their Thiessen polygons, and the resulting subbasin precipitation field.
supporting_quote: EASY-MORE package can create the Voronoi diagram or Thiessen polygons for stations based on the latitude and longitude provided in the netCDF file.
Remapping of precipitation field for SCDNA dataset from (left) Voronoi diagram or Thiessen polygons to (right) subbasin

chunks.text: EASYMORE provides mechanisms to handle non-overlapping areas and missing values by rescaling weights and optionally retaining or removing non-overlapping targets. In the ERA5 example with nan values and partial domain overlap, the tool can produce conserved remapped variables by adjusting weights for missing grids and non-overlapping shapes. This reduces the need for manual preprocessing of shapefiles and source domains.
supporting_quote: EASYMORE allows the user to keep the nonoverlapping shapefile values as nan or fully remove them from the remapped file
EASYMORE can rescale weights for the non-overlapping shape or grids without values and provide conserved remapped variables

chunks.text: EASYMORE can reconcile longitude conventions between source netCDF and target shapefiles for point extraction use cases. In the GRACE example, the dataset uses 0–360 longitude while capital-city shapefiles use −180–180, and EASYMORE corrects the shapefile to extract the intended grid values. The extracted anomaly time series is illustrated for Tehran.
supporting_quote: GRACE dataset is provided with a longitude of 0 to 360 while the target shapefile... is given with a longitude between −180 to 180 degrees.
EASYMORE can recognize this difference and correct the shapefile so they can read the right values from the source netCDF file.

chunks.text: The authors note that remapping accuracy depends on the nc_remapper workflow assumptions, how the remap file is created, and the behavior of underlying geospatial and scientific Python libraries. They recommend careful assessment and comparison of generated grids/Thiessen polygons, remap files, and remapped values against other packages. This is framed as future work for validating and benchmarking EASYMORE outputs across cases.
supporting_quote: We would like to emphasize that the accuracy of remapping is based on nc_remapper workflow in creating the remapping file, its assumptions, and underlying packages and libraries.
A careful assessment and comparison of generated grids, Thiessen polygons, the remapping file, and remapped values with other similar packages is necessary in the future.

chunks.text: While EASYMORE aims to simplify remapping, the paper acknowledges that other tools (e.g., ESMF) are more comprehensive scientifically and computationally, but can have steep learning curves. EASYMORE is positioned as a focused alternative that covers common remapping cases, complemented by example notebooks on GitHub. This discussion implicitly limits EASYMORE’s scope to frequently needed workflows rather than full generality of broader frameworks.
supporting_quote: other tools can be used for remapping purposes such as ESMF. These tools are often very comprehensive on the scientific and computational fronts. However, users may experience a steep learning curve.
EASYMORE is a focused tool that provides easy-to-use remapping capabilities commonly needed in Earth System Modeling and catchment hydrology.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that EASYMORE is an open-source Python package for remapping variables from netCDF files to arbitrary shapes defined in a shapefile, distributed via PyPI and GitHub. It is intended to facilitate data preparation workflows for Earth System modeling and support broader adoption and future improvements. The authors emphasize continued development toward greater efficiency and handling of more complex cases.
supporting_quote: EASYMORE provides a Python package for remapping variables from netCDF file(s) to any desired shape provided within a shapefile.
The package is part of the Python indexing package and is open-source and available to the public on GitHub.
We look forward to more use of this package and improvement in the future both in the sense of efficiency and complexity

chunks.text: EASYMORE is intended to streamline remapping in Earth System modeling workflows and has been adopted in projects emphasizing reproducible science. The paper highlights its role in the CWARHM initiative, where remapping many ensemble members and databases is streamlined within the single package. It also notes uptake beyond the original developers and visibility through PyPI downloads.
supporting_quote: A notable use of EASY-MORE in Earth System modeling is given in the CWARHM initiative, which is focused on reproducible science and transparent modeling workflows
These studies are easier to carry out because the remapping of many ensemble members and databases is streamlined within the single EASYMORE package.

chunks.text: Lakes and reservoirs are major components of the terrestrial water cycle, influencing hydrology, climate, and ecosystems. Reservoir construction has greatly expanded storage capacity and altered natural river systems to support irrigation, municipal supply, and hydropower. Because these water bodies affect mass, energy, and momentum conservation in Earth system modeling, their representation is important for credible simulations, especially for water balance and regulated outflows.
supporting_quote: Lakes store a large fraction of terrestrial water and have considerable impacts on the terrestrial water cycle, global and local climate, and ecosystems
From the year 1950–2000, the total volume of water stored by large dams increased from 1,000 to 11,000 km3

chunks.text: Routing schemes for rivers, lakes, and reservoirs are often embedded within hydrological, land surface, or water management models, but typically reflect a single lake/reservoir formulation. The land modeling community needs frameworks that can flexibly represent different lake and reservoir behaviors within a consistent river-lake network, allowing complexity to vary by data availability and study purpose.
supporting_quote: River, lake, and reservoir routing schemes are often embedded within existing hydrological, land surface, or water management models
there is a pressing need for frameworks that can simulate different types of lake and reservoir models within a defined system of rivers, lakes, and reservoirs network

chunks.text: mizuRoute is a vector-based routing model intended for large-scale water cycle studies and CESM coupling, supporting multiple in-channel routing schemes and parallel computation. Its vector nature enables use of existing river network fabrics (e.g., NHDPlus) and avoids rasterization of water bodies. This provides a foundation for scalable integration of lakes and reservoirs into routing computations.
supporting_quote: mizuRoute is a vector‐based routing model

The current version of mizuRoute includes four options for in‐channel routing schemes: (a) impulse response function, IRF, (b) kinematic wave tracking, KWT, (c) Muskingum‐Cunge, and (d) Diffusive Wave.
mizuRoute can internally decompose the routing domain into regions and pass calculations to multiple processors for faster simulation

chunks.text: The study introduces mizuRoute-Lake, which integrates lake and reservoir water balance into the mizuRoute vector routing framework. A central goal is to provide a seamless way to switch among multiple lake/reservoir formulations within the same routing configuration. The framework is intended to support both parametric models and data-driven specification of lake/reservoir behavior using observations or external water management information.
supporting_quote: we introduce mizuRoute‐Lake to simulate lakes and reservoirs within the routing model mizu-Route
The advantage of mizuRoute‐Lake can be summarized as the flexibility in seamless alternative lake and reservoir models.
Users can also use existing data such as historical observations or water management models to specify the behavior

chunks.text: Another goal is to demonstrate mizuRoute-Lake versatility across scales through global, regional, and local applications. The paper aims to show how lake/reservoir modeling choices and network topology (resolvable vs unresolved water bodies) affect streamflow and storage/outflow behavior. The applications are designed to highlight both scientific evaluation and practical scenario analysis for management-relevant events.
supporting_quote: We demonstrate the flexibility of mizuRoute‐Lake by presenting global, regional, and local scale applications.
In this section, four mizuRoute‐Lake case studies are presented.

chunks.text: Accurately representing lakes and reservoirs in Earth system models is challenging because they influence multiple conservation laws, but water balance is especially critical due to direct links to human activity. Many modeling systems include only one lake/reservoir representation, limiting the ability to evaluate alternative formulations and uncertainties. This motivates a flexible framework that can host multiple lake/reservoir models within a consistent network topology.
supporting_quote: the representation of lakes and reservoirs in Earth system models is a challenging task
water balance has understandably attracted substantial attention because the inflow and outflow fluxes to and from lakes and reservoirs are directly linked to human activity

chunks.text: Switching among lake/reservoir formulations is often not seamless in existing frameworks because changes can require reconfiguring routing or other model components. This limits isolating the effect of lake water balance representations from changes in river topology or other parameters. mizuRoute-Lake is presented as addressing this need for interchangeable formulations within one routing setup.
supporting_quote: switching between the different options for lake and reservoir models is seamless, and therefore the impact of different lake water balance models can be evaluated in isolation from changes in river network topology

chunks.text: Lake Victoria water-balance reconstruction is difficult due to major data and process uncertainties, including precipitation over the lake, tributary inflows, evaporation validation, and human regulation of outflow. The controversy and lack of public outflow observations after 2000 make it hard to infer the lake level–outflow relationship. This motivates exploring interactions between hydraulic parameters and climatic forcing using an adaptable modeling platform.
supporting_quote: Modeling the Lake Victoria water balance is challenging due to (a) a lack of comprehensive rainfall data on the lake
(b) a lack of upstream discharge measurements
(c) a lack of data to validate and estimate evaporation from the lake surface
There are no lake outflow observations publicly available

chunks.text: At regional scales, river network density controls how many lakes and reservoirs are resolvable, which can affect routing and streamflow simulations. In the South Saskatchewan example, different topologies (HDMA vs MERIT-Basins) resolve different numbers of water bodies. This creates uncertainty about how much results depend on topology versus the chosen lake/reservoir water balance model and parameters.
supporting_quote: MERIT‐Basins is 10 times denser than the HDMA data set and resolves 70 water bodies while the HDMA resolves only 7 water bodies in this basin.

chunks.text: mizuRoute-Lake represents lake and reservoir storage dynamics with a water balance equation that accounts for inflow, outflow, precipitation, evaporation, groundwater exchange, and abstraction/injection. The formulation allows time series of abstraction/injection to be provided externally and applied to river segments, lakes, or reservoirs. When lake/reservoir modules are active, precipitation and evaporation must be supplied and can be remapped to lake area by the model.
supporting_quote: The water balance of lakes and reservoirs in mizuRoute-Lake can be written as:
dS/dt = I - O + (P - E + G)A - F_{a,i}
mizuRoute provides the capability to use externally calculated or prepared abstraction and/or injection of water to and from river segments, lakes, or reservoirs.

chunks.text: mizuRoute provides two-stage runoff routing: hillslope (in-basin) routing via a gamma-distribution unit hydrograph and in-channel routing using selectable schemes. Four in-channel routing options are available, and the model can parallelize computations through domain decomposition. These capabilities support efficient simulations including global river-lake networks with millions of segments and lakes.
supporting_quote: mizuRoute then performs two stages of runoff routing. First, in‐basin or hillslope routing
Currently, this is performed using a gamma‐distribution‐based unit‐hydrograph
four options for in‐channel routing schemes: (a) impulse response function, IRF, (b) kinematic wave tracking, KWT, (c) Muskingum‐Cunge, and (d) Diffusive Wave.
This parallelization is also used in river‐lake combined networks which makes global simulations with millions of river segments and lakes feasible.

chunks.text: The framework includes multiple parametric outflow models for lakes and reservoirs. Time-invariant options implemented include the Döll formulation and a HYPE hydropower reservoir formulation based on elevation zones (spillway crest, limiting level, turbine intake, and minimum level). These parametric models relate outflow to storage and parameters, supporting use when operational details are limited or when representing hydropower behavior.
supporting_quote: Currently, there are two time‐invariant parametric models implemented in mizuRoute.
Döll: The simplest lake model implemented in mizuRoute‐Lake is the formulation of Döll et al. (2003)
HYPE: The second time‐invariant parametric model in mizuRoute is the HYPE formulation of lakes and reservoirs
The operation rules for the HYPE reservoir model depend on four elevation zones

chunks.text: A time-varying parametric model is implemented as “Hanasaki with memory,” which adapts monthly inflow and demand parameters over time using a window of past years. This adds flexibility to reflect long-term changes (e.g., climate change effects on inflow or evolving irrigation demand). The method updates inflow and demand parameter estimates from stored histories and then computes target releases and actual outflow based on reservoir type and storage state.
supporting_quote: we have implemented the "Hanasaki with memory" parameterization
allowing the inflow and demand parameters to be adjusted over a past window of simulation, for example, every 5 years.
This enables adjustment of time‐varying parameters by considering how long‐term changes in environmental conditions, such as climate change, affect inflow

chunks.text: mizuRoute-Lake supports data-driven lake/reservoir modeling by allowing users to prescribe abstraction/injection time series and/or target reservoir volumes. When a target volume is provided, the model adjusts outflow to store water if current volume is below target, or release water when above target. This enables coupling with water management models, observations, or scenario-based operations without relying solely on parametric release rules.
supporting_quote: mizuRoute‐Lake allows the user to provide a time series of abstraction and injection fluxes
a user can identify target volumes (at the time step of the model simulation, e.g., hours or days). mizuRoute‐Lake then adjusts the outflow.

chunks.text: Endorheic and exorheic lakes are handled differently: exorheic water bodies are assumed to have one outlet, while endorheic lakes have no outlet and therefore set outflow to zero. This provides a consistent treatment of closed-basin systems within the same routing framework. The simplifying one-outlet assumption constrains exorheic representation but supports scalable network integration.
supporting_quote: mizuRoute-Lake assumes one outlet for the exorheic lakes and reservoirs.
Endorheic lakes are treated as water bodies in which outflows from the outlet, O from Equation-1, are assumed to be zero.

chunks.text: Lake Victoria case-study experiments perturb hydraulic parameters of the outflow curve and optionally scale precipitation and evaporation over the lake to explore joint effects on lake levels. The study runs 1000 post-2000 simulations per scenario with uniformly sampled parameters and evaluates fit to satellite altimetry lake-level data using Nash Sutcliffe Efficiency. Sensitivity is assessed with the VISCOUS global sensitivity analysis method, and behavioral simulations are defined by ENSE > 0.5.
supporting_quote: 1000 simulations are performed for the post‐2000 period for each scenario
The goodness of fit is evaluated, using ENSE, comparing simulated lake level time series to the remotely sensed DAHITI data set
a global sensitivity analysis is performed ... using the VISCOUS method
Simulations and their associated parameters with ENSE values higher than 0.5 are considered behavioral

chunks.text: For the Lake Diefenbaker local study, the model is run in data-driven mode: observed upstream discharges are injected at gauged locations, a downstream demand term represents Qu'Appelle canal abstraction, and historical reservoir volume is used as a target volume to emulate operations. River routing parameters for the impulse response function (velocity and diffusivity) are calibrated using the pygmo package with Particle Swarm Optimizer. Scenario analysis is then performed by constructing alternative drawdown trajectories and evaluating resulting peak flows at Saskatoon.
supporting_quote: forced with discharge estimation at hydrometric stations upstream of Lake Diefenbaker
the parametric lake models are replaced with the target lake volume, which mizuRoute‐Lake replicates by adjusting the reservoir outflows
Calibration of velocity and diffusivity parameters is performed using the pygmo Python package
The algorithm used for this optimization is Particle Swarm Optimizer (PSO)

chunks.text: The global case study uses the HDMA river network with approximately 300,000 river segments and adds resolvable lakes and reservoirs from HydroLAKES. About 4,200 lakes/reservoirs are resolvable at this topology, compared to 1.43 million water bodies in HydroLAKES overall. Parameters for Döll are set using HydroLAKES volumes and assumed active storage depth, enabling global assessment of lake impacts on discharge extremes.
supporting_quote: Hydrologic Derivatives for Modeling and Applications with approximately 300,000 river segments worldwide (HDMA)
adds approximately 4,200 resolvable lakes and reservoirs globally from the 1.43 million lakes in the HydroLAKES data set
the inactive storage of each lake is set to the total volume provided by the HydroLAKES data set, and the maximum active storage is considered to be 5 m of water volume over the area of lake

chunks.text: Runoff forcing for the global evaluation is taken from a 0.25° VIC simulation forced with MSWEP precipitation and includes lake precipitation and open-water evaporation for the water balance. The study emphasizes that the runoff product is bias-corrected to better match observed streamflow when routed. Open-water evaporation is computed with a Penman formulation within VIC and passed to mizuRoute-Lake.
supporting_quote: The simulated runoff is from the Variable Infiltration Capacity, VIC, with a resolution of 0.25° forced with MSWEP precipitation data set
The advantage of this product is its bias‐ corrected runoff fields
Simulated open water evaporation, based on Penman formulation, is used from the VIC model.

chunks.text: Performance evaluation in the global case study uses streamflow observations from GRDC at stations downstream of resolvable lakes and reservoirs. The analysis compares Nash Sutcliffe Efficiency between simulations with and without lakes/reservoirs. The paper reports results for 1600 GRDC gauges identified as downstream of resolvable water bodies in the HDMA+HydroLAKES configuration.
supporting_quote: We also investigate the simulation performance with and without lakes compared to observation stations from the Global Runoff Data Center, GRDC
75% of stations from the total of 1600 GRDC stations that are downstream of lakes and reservoirs within the network of HDMA and Hydro-LAKES

chunks.text: For Lake Victoria, the basin contains 207 HydroLAKES water bodies but only 6 are resolvable on the HDMA river network. Lake level observations for evaluation are taken from the remotely sensed DAHITI dataset, and the outflow-release relationship is represented by the Agreed Curve. The Agreed Curve is expressed with parameters 66.3, 7.96, and 2.01 for outflow-rate, reference elevation, and exponent, respectively.
supporting_quote: According to the HydroLAKES data set, 207 lakes and reservoirs exist in the Lake Victoria basin. From this number, only six lakes and reservoirs, including Lake Victoria itself, are resolvable given the HDMA river network
comparing simulated lake level time series to the remotely sensed DAHITI data set
Therefore, the default parameters of the Agreed Curve are 66.3, 7.96, and 2.01

chunks.text: The South Saskatchewan regional study uses two alternative river network topologies: HDMA and MERIT-Basins. MERIT-Basins is reported as 10 times denser than HDMA, resolving 70 water bodies compared to 7 in HDMA for the basin. Simulations are compared against observed streamflow at locations including Banff, Calgary, Medicine Hat, and Saskatoon.

The simulations ... are visualized ... namely Banff, Calgary, Medicine Hat, and Saskatoon.

chunks.text: The Lake Diefenbaker study uses Canadian hydrometric observations to drive and evaluate data-driven operations, including upstream inflows and downstream flow at Saskatoon, plus reservoir level at Gardiner Dam. The paper lists station IDs for key inflows (South Saskatchewan at Medicine Hat 05AJ001; Red Deer at Bindloss 05CK004; Swift Current River 05HD039) and the downstream gauge at Saskatoon (05HG001). Reservoir elevation at Gardiner Dam (05HF003) is used with elevation-storage relationships to approximate storage and define target volumes.
supporting_quote: South Saskatchewan at Medicine Hat and Red Deer at Bindloss (station IDs of 05AJ001 and 05CK004 respectively)
Swift Current River is the biggest contributor (station ID of 05HD039).
The streamflow from Gardiner Dam is measured at Saskatoon (station ID 05HG001).

chunks.text: At the global scale, including lakes and reservoirs in the HDMA routing network changes downstream discharge extremes, with larger effects near large lakes and diminishing influence farther downstream. The study maps the absolute difference in maximum discharge (ΔQ) between simulations with and without lakes for 1985–2010. The reported spatial pattern supports assumptions about downstream distance of lake/reservoir influence and demonstrates the hydraulic damping effect of storage.
supporting_quote: Figure 2 indicates changes in maximum discharge values per river segment with and without lakes for the period of 1985–2010.
the impact of lakes on streamflow is diminishing further downstream of lakes and reservoirs.

chunks.text: Including resolvable lakes and reservoirs improves agreement with observed streamflow at many global stations. For the 1985–2010 period, the paper reports that about 75% of 1600 GRDC gauges downstream of resolvable water bodies show improved Nash Sutcliffe Efficiency compared to the no-lake simulation. This indicates that even with bias-corrected runoff forcing, representing lake/reservoir storage and release can add measurable skill in routed streamflow.
supporting_quote: 75% of stations from the total of 1600 GRDC stations ... exhibit improved performance in Nash Sutcliffe Efficiency, ENSE, in comparison to the case without lakes and reservoirs.
This demonstrates the added value of the inclusion of lakes and reservoirs in streamflow simulations

chunks.text: For Lake Victoria after 2000, simulations using the default Agreed Curve produce lake levels higher than DAHITI observations, indicating that the pre-2000 level–outflow relationship is no longer representative. Behavioral ensembles show that allowing both hydraulic parameter perturbations and climate scaling can substantially improve fit, with best ENSE increasing from 0.61 (hydraulic-only) to 0.86 (hydraulic + climate). This demonstrates that reproducing observed lake levels requires considering both operational and forcing uncertainties.
supporting_quote: The simulation based on the Agreed Curve results in a higher lake level than the DAHITI observed data.
The best‐performing simulation for scenario‐A and ‐B are 0.61 and 0.86 respectively, in scale of ENSE.

chunks.text: Uncertainty in Lake Victoria outflow increases when both hydraulic parameters and climate forcings are perturbed. The paper reports that scenario-B (hydraulic + climate scaling) produces “much larger outflow simulation ranges” compared with hydraulic-only perturbations. Because outflow observations are unavailable, the outflow ensembles are not constrained directly, emphasizing that lake-level fitting alone may not uniquely identify outflow behavior.
supporting_quote: scenario‐B, due to its degree of freedom, results in much larger outflow simulation ranges.
This is expected as the outflow is not used to constrain behavioral parameters in this case study.

chunks.text: Sensitivity analysis for Lake Victoria identifies the emergency spillway exponent parameter Pemg as dominant for both scenarios. Table 1 reports first-order and total-order sensitivity of Pemg as 0.68 and 0.88 for scenario-A, and 0.37 and 0.77 for scenario-B. The increased total-order sensitivity relative to first-order for Qemg,rate in scenario-B suggests stronger interactions with climate-scaling parameters.
supporting_quote: Table 1 indicates, for scenario‐A and ‐B, the parameter Pemg is the most sensitive in its first and total effects.
Pemg ... Scenario‐A ... First 0.68 ... Total 0.88 ... Scenario‐B ... First 0.37 ... Total 0.77

chunks.text: In the South Saskatchewan River case study, differences among lake/reservoir model categories become more pronounced downstream, especially at Saskatoon. Upstream at Banff, simulated streamflow is similar across categories, implying limited lake/reservoir influence there. Downstream, category choices (No lake, Döll, Döll+HYPE, Döll+HYPE+Hanasaki) lead to substantial hydrograph differences, highlighting the importance of lake/reservoir representations.
supporting_quote: For the most upstream locations, such as the town of Banff, streamflow remains similar across categories
