These buildings were classified using Google Earth's Street view maps. A GIS tool was used to create a shape file for each building

chunks.text: Simulations indicate that dynamic adaptation by government and residents can generate abrupt changes in system behavior, consistent with a regime shift between two states of ice-jam flood risk. One state exhibits higher flood risk and higher variability, implying a stronger role of adaptation dynamics, while the other state reflects lower risk and lower variability. The results emphasize that perturbations in model factors can switch the system between these two states.
supporting_quote: the dynamic adaptation of governments and residents can play an important role in abrupt changes and sudden shifts between two different system states... known as regime shifts
Fig. 9.b shows two different patterns and trends in the dynamics of ice-jam flood risk.
The variability of the icejam flood risk of state 1 is higher than that of state 2

chunks.text: Results identify a tipping-point behavior tied to the economic feasibility of artificial breakage. A regime shift in ice-jam flood risk occurs when tax levels surpass a critical threshold related to the cost of artificial breakage, stated as about $1.65 million. Beyond this point, flood risk drops abruptly, illustrating that policy-controlled funding can trigger large reductions in risk.
supporting_quote: sudden shift in flood risk beyond a critical cost threshold for artificial breakage, estimated at $1.65 million.
Fig. 12... shows the regime shift and an abrupt reduction in ice-jam flood risk when the parameter of tax surpasses the tipping point (i.e., 1.65 million $ in the y-axis).
According to (CBC, 2019), the annual cost of artificial breakage is 1.65

chunks.text: The model shows a trade-off between government-led artificial breakage and resident flood-proofing adoption. While artificial breakage can substantially reduce flood risk, it also reduces residents’ incentive to adopt flood-proofing, lowering the number of newly adapted residents and diminishing the community’s role in risk reduction. This highlights that effective top-down measures can unintentionally suppress bottom-up adaptation.
supporting_quote: artificial breakage by the government can lead to a regime shift and a decrease in the ice-jam flood risk.
However, it can also decrease the number of newly adapted residents to flood-proofing and the role of residents in ice-jam flood risk.
While artificial breakage significantly reduces flood risk, it also decreases the incentive for residents to invest in floodproofing measures

chunks.text: Adaptation trajectories for newly adapted residents vary over time, with a pronounced peak at the start of the simulation period and additional changes aligned with risk fluctuations. The paper reports a peak in adaptations in 2001 and another increase in 2016, while adaptation is low in 2006 and 2011 when ice-jam flood risk decreases. These patterns suggest residents’ flood-proofing responses track perceived or modeled risk levels over time.
supporting_quote: the model simulation highlights a peak in adaptations during 2001
The model simulation also shows another increase in newly adapted residents in 2016 with an increase in the ice-jam flood risk.
the adaptations show low numbers in 2006 and 2011 due to a decrease in ice-jam flood risk.

chunks.text: Variance-based global sensitivity analysis finds that income tax is the dominant driver of variability in averaged ice-jam flood risk. The first-order Sobol index for income tax is reported as more than 90%, while the cost of flood-proofing contributes less than 10%. Minimal difference between first- and total-order effects indicates parameter interaction has little influence on flood-risk variability.
supporting_quote: Fig. 13.a shows that the individual contribution... of the income tax to the variability of the ice-jam flood risk is more than 90 % while that of the cost of flood-proofing is less than 10 %.
As there is almost no difference between the first-order effect and the total-order effect, the parameter interaction does not affect the variability of the ice-jam flood risk.

chunks.text: Sensitivity analysis for the number of newly adapted residents shows both main effects and interactions matter. The cost of flood-proofing contributes around 50% to variability, income tax contributes less than 20%, and about 30% is attributed to interaction effects. The paper further interprets income tax as having a negative effect on newly adapted residents, meaning higher tax can reduce flood-proofing adoption.
supporting_quote: Fig. 13.b shows that the individual contribution of the cost of flood-proofing... is around 50 % while that of the income tax is less than 20 %, and the rest (around 30 %) is the effect of parameter interaction

it can be interpreted that the income tax has a negative effect on the newly adapted residents. In other words, an increase in the income tax can decrease the newly adapted residents to flood-proofing.

chunks.text: Averaged risk surfaces suggest that increasing income tax (enabling artificial breakage) or decreasing flood-proofing costs (via subsidy) can reduce ice-jam flood risk over 2001–2021. The plot of averaged risk under dynamic adaptation shows an abrupt reduction when tax surpasses the tipping point. This reinforces the combined importance of public financing capacity and private adaptation affordability for lowering long-run risk.
supporting_quote: This plot shows how the ice-jam flood risk can reduce... by an increase in income tax or a decrease in the cost of flood-proofing via government subsidy.
Fig. 12... also shows the regime shift and an abrupt reduction in ice-jam flood risk when the parameter of tax surpasses the tipping point

chunks.text: The authors note that their agent-based model is not calibrated or validated, emphasizing that its purpose is exploratory rather than reproducing historical events. The model is used to present a range of outputs to inform policymakers about how individual decision-making could shape ice-jam flood risk management. This limitation indicates that quantitative predictions should be interpreted cautiously.
supporting_quote: While our agent-based model lacks calibration and validation, its primary aim is not to replicate past events but rather to explore the potential outcomes
By presenting a range of model outputs, we offer policymakers valuable insights into the influence of individual decision-making

chunks.text: The paper acknowledges simplifications in representing decision-making using rational behavior, despite criticisms that rational choice overlooks real-world complexities. It suggests that future research should test alternative social theories, such as protection motivation theory, to strengthen the framework and examine sensitivity to behavioral assumptions. This highlights behavioral realism as a key avenue for refinement.
supporting_quote: Both types of agents are assumed to make their decisions based on rational behavior
Despite the recent criticism of the use of rational behavior for overlooking the complexities of decision-making processes
future research should explore alternative social theories, such as protection motivation theory

chunks.text: Transferability is framed as feasible but conditional: applying DIFRA elsewhere requires tailoring to local hydraulic and socioeconomic conditions. The authors stress adapting the model to case-specific contexts to ensure effectiveness in informing local strategies. This indicates that DIFRA is not a plug-and-play tool and depends on local data and parameterization.
supporting_quote: the underlying modeling approach holds broader applicability to other riverine communities facing similar ice-jam flood risks in cold regions.
It is important to tailor the model to the unique hydraulic and socio-economic conditions of a case study to ensure its transferability

chunks.text: The study concludes that incorporating dynamic human adaptation is essential for understanding ice-jam flood risk over time, and that DIFRA provides a holistic framework integrating hydraulic hazard modeling with agent-based adaptation. In Fort McMurray, government-led artificial breakup can trigger a regime shift and reduce risk, but it can also reduce resident flood-proofing uptake. The paper positions DIFRA as potentially useful for other cold-region riverine communities when tailored to local conditions.
supporting_quote: our study introduced the conceptual framework of Dynamic Ice-jam Flood Risk Assessment (DIFRA), which integrates agent-based modeling with hydraulic modeling
government-led artificial breakup initiatives can lead to a regime shift in ice-jam flood risk
the underlying modeling approach holds broader applicability to other riverine communities facing similar ice-jam flood risks in cold regions.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that explicitly modeling interactions between micro-level individual adaptation and macro-level government decisions improves understanding of ice-jam flood risk management. It emphasizes that combining top-down and bottom-up measures reveals cross-scale feedbacks and trade-offs. These insights are intended to support more informed policy design around artificial breakage, subsidies, and community participation.
supporting_quote: explicitly modeling the interactions between micro-level (i.e., individual adaptation) and macro-level (i.e., government adaptation) dynamics

By including the interaction between top-down and bottom-up risk reduction measures, such as artificial breakup and floodproofing, our study showed the role of human adaptation across different scales

chunks.text: Ice-jam flooding is a distinct hazard in northern rivers because jams can form rapidly during breakup, producing high backwater levels and overbank flooding. Small changes in jam morphology and location can strongly amplify flood stages, and design flood levels for some exceedance probabilities can exceed open-water flood levels. Because forecasting lead time is limited, both structural thresholds and preparedness measures must explicitly consider ice-jam processes.
supporting_quote: During ice-cover breakup, the damming effect of ice jams... can cause very high backwater levels and overbank flooding.
Important characteristics of ice-jam flooding... is the rapidity of the formation of ice jams... very difficult to forecast with very little response time

chunks.text: Ice-jam risk mitigation spans top-down actions by governments (e.g., artificial breakup) and bottom-up actions by asset owners (e.g., flood-proofing). These choices are shaped by social preferences, values, budgets, regulations, and land constraints. Effective assessment therefore requires models that combine physical flood processes with social and cultural decision contexts.
supporting_quote: These measures can be in the form of large-scale, top-down projects... (e.g., the artificial breakup of the ice cover) or... bottom-up measures... (e.g., flood-proofing of buildings).
Both topdown and bottom-up measures do involve decisions... within the constraints of financial budgets, policy regulations, and land availability.

chunks.text: Agent-based modeling is presented as a bottom-up approach well suited to water-human systems because it can represent heterogeneous individual decision-making and feedbacks across scales. In flood-risk contexts, ABMs have been used to explore interactions among households and institutions and how micro-level behaviors generate system-scale outcomes. This paper positions ABMs as a way to link resident adaptation with government actions in ice-jam flood management.
supporting_quote: Agent-based modeling is a valuable bottom-up approach... capturing individual decisionmaking, heterogeneity of human decision-making, and feedback mechanisms
enabling the study of how individual behaviors and interactions propagate and shape emergent phenomena.

chunks.text: The study aims to enhance an existing ice-jam flood risk agent-based model by integrating Protection Motivation Theory (PMT) as a bounded-rationality decision framework for residents. It evaluates whether and to what extent PMT improves representation of ice-jam flood risk dynamics compared with Rational Choice Theory (RCT). The case study is the Athabasca River at Fort McMurray.
supporting_quote: The objective of this study is to explore the potential enhancements... through the integration of the PMT as a decision-making framework under uncertainty.
assess whether and to what extent such integration can improve the modeling of ice-jam flood risk with the case study of the Athabasca River at Fort McMurray.

chunks.text: A further goal is to compare model outputs under PMT and RCT to understand how alternative social theories shape outcomes of flood risk management, including adaptation patterns and risk trajectories. The study also aims to quantify which socio-economic parameters most influence total flood risk and adaptation adoption by conducting sensitivity analyses.
supporting_quote: By comparing the model outputs under both the RCT and PMT, this research seeks to assess the impact of different social theories on the model response
Furthermore, a sensitivity analysis is conducted to explore the significance of socio-economic factors in the model and evaluate their influence on the overall results.

chunks.text: Ice-jam floods are difficult to manage because their formation is rapid and sensitive to small morphological changes, leaving little time for warning and response. This creates high uncertainty in anticipating impacts and complicates preparedness. The problem motivates the need for risk models that can better account for fast-onset dynamics and limited response windows.
supporting_quote: very difficult to forecast with very little response time to prepare and counter the impacts
small changes in the morphology of ice jams... can exacerbate the flooding situation.

chunks.text: Despite growing flood-risk modeling literature, the paper identifies a gap in incorporating bounded rationality into flood risk models, especially for ice-jam flood contexts. The authors argue that representing how people perceive threats and coping capacity under uncertainty remains insufficiently addressed. This gap is linked to improving realism in modeled adaptation behaviors.
supporting_quote: there remains a gap in understanding the importance of incorporating bounded rationality (e.g., PMT) into flood risk modeling, particularly in the context of ice-jam floods.
a critical research gap remains in the specific domain of ice-jam flood risk.

chunks.text: Another identified gap is understanding cross-scale interactions between resident adaptation and government interventions in flood risk management. The study highlights the need to investigate interplay between local-scale household measures and larger-scale governmental actions. Addressing this is necessary for comprehensive ice-jam risk management strategies.
supporting_quote: more studies are needed to investigate the interaction across scales... interplay between local-scale residents' adaptation and basin-scale government adaptation.
The interactions between residents and the government influenced the overall flood risk.

chunks.text: The work builds on a prior Fort McMurray agent-based model that coupled physical ice-jam flood processes with resident and government adaptation. In the earlier implementation, both residents and the government used Rational Choice Theory, comparing benefit-cost ratios for flood-proofing and artificial breakup decisions. This study retains the ABM structure while changing the resident decision rule to PMT to represent bounded rationality.
supporting_quote: Residents considered the benefit-cost ratio to decide whether to implement flood-proofing measures, while the government used the same ratio to determine whether to carry out artificial breakage.
This study builds upon the methodology developed by Ghoreishi and Lindenschmidt (2024)

chunks.text: Physical ice-jam processes were simulated using RIVICE, a one-dimensional hydrodynamic and river-ice hydraulic model. It solves the dynamic wave form of the St. Venant equations to simulate backwater flow and includes river-ice processes such as border ice, frazil ice, and consolidated cover. Flood risk was then estimated from water levels via flood depth/extent and depth-damage relationships for economic damages.
supporting_quote: they used RIVICE, which is a one-dimensional, hydrodynamic, and river-ice hydraulic model.
The study also estimated ice-jam flood risk by assessing the potential economic damages... applying a depth-damage relationship to estimate damages

chunks.text: In the PMT-based model, residents’ flood-proofing decisions depend on threat appraisal and coping appraisal. Threat appraisal is represented by flood risk, while coping appraisal includes response efficacy, self-efficacy, and adaptation costs. Two additional determinants—social network and past flood experience—were added to reflect peer influence and learning from prior floods.
supporting_quote: According to the PMT, residents make decisions based on threat appraisal and coping appraisal.
This study incorporated two supplementary factors, namely social network and appraisal of past flood experience

chunks.text: A logistic (logit) choice model was used to convert socio-economic predictors into a probability that a resident adopts flood-proofing at each time step. The model includes flood risk (FR), cost of flood-proofing (CP), response efficacy (RE), self-efficacy (SE), flood experience (FE), and social network (SN) with coefficients β0–β6. Adoption occurs stochastically by comparing the computed probability to a random number in [0,1].
supporting_quote: a logit model was used... Eq. 1 represents the probability of residents adopting risk reduction measures
If this number is lower than the calculated probability... the agent decides to adopt flood-proofing.

chunks.text: The PMT decision probability is explicitly defined as a logistic function of a linear index containing FRi,t, CP, REi, SEi, FEi,t, and SNi,t. Response efficacy and self-efficacy are bounded between 0 and 1, and parameter values and weights are sampled from normal distributions to represent heterogeneity. This setup follows prior ABM practice for representing diverse agent characteristics and uncertainty in behavioral parameters.
supporting_quote: RE and SE vary between 0 and 1.
the values of response efficacy, self-efficacy, and weights are sampled from a normal distribution for agents in the model setup

chunks.text: Flood experience for each resident is updated using the difference between the resident’s observed water level and averaged historical water levels from 40 years ago over the model timespan. This mechanism represents learning from prior exposure to ice-jam flooding and allows experience to evolve through time. It provides a pathway for past events to influence present adaptation decisions.
supporting_quote: The flood experience variable is updated... by the difference between their observed level of water and the averaged historical water level data from 40 years ago
capturing the residents' past exposure to ice-jam flooding and facilitates modeling of their adaptation decisions

chunks.text: Social network influence is operationalized as the fraction of connected agents within a specified radius that have already adopted risk-reduction measures. Specifically, SNi,t equals Ai,t divided by Ni, where Ai,t is the number of adopters and Ni is the number of agents in that radius. This implements peer effects by making adoption more likely when nearby agents have adopted.
supporting_quote: The social network... is calculated as the ratio of the number of agents... who have adopted... (Ai,t) ... to the total number of agents... (Ni)
SN_{i,t} = A_{i,t} / N_i

chunks.text: Sensitivity analysis used a two-part strategy: multiple stochastic repetitions and a global sensitivity analysis (GSA). The model was run 1 to 1000 repetitions to assess stochastic variability, and VARS (Variogram Analysis of Response Surfaces) was used for GSA with 50 stars and resolution 0.1, totaling 5000 runs. Responses analyzed were ice-jam flood risk and newly adapted residents averaged over time.
supporting_quote: running the model multiple times... ranging from 1 to 1000 repetitions.
VARS... 50 stars and a sampling resolution of 0.1, resulting in a total of 5000 model runs

chunks.text: The case study focuses on the Athabasca River at Fort McMurray, where geomorphic transitions promote ice-jam lodgement. The river shifts from a steep, narrow reach upstream of the town bridge to a flatter, wider downstream reach with islands and constrictions that encourage jamming. Tributary conditions on the Clearwater River increase severity by enabling backwater flow into the tributary and inundation of downtown floodplains.
supporting_quote: The study site is the Athabasca River at Fort McMurray.
water flows from a relatively steep and narrow stretch... to a flatter, wider downstream stretch... providing areas where the ice rubble... can easily lodge and jam.

chunks.text: Parameter ranges for global sensitivity analysis were set using localized information and external sources. Economic parameters include Income Tax between $1500000 and $1800000 and Cost of flood-proofing between $200 and $2000. Multiple PMT-related parameters (means of normal distributions for coefficients and efficacy variables) range from 0 to 1, and heterogeneity (standard deviations) ranges from 0 to 0.3.
supporting_quote: Income Tax... Lower Bound 1500000 Upper Bound 1800000
Heterogeneity (standard deviations of normal distributions)... Lower Bound 0 Upper Bound 0.3

chunks.text: Scenario analysis defined contrasting economic conditions for RCT and then extended them with social-factor configurations under PMT. Scenario A used high income tax ($1700,000) and low flood-proofing cost ($200), while Scenario B used low income tax ($1600,000) and high cost ($1800). PMT sub-scenarios varied social factors, heterogeneity, and economic-factor coefficients using values such as 0.8, 0.3, 0.2 and 0.2, 0, 0.8.
supporting_quote: Scenario A... high-income tax and low cost... at $1700,000 and $200
Scenario B... lowincome tax and high cost... as $1600,000 and $1800

chunks.text: The model timeframe for comparing trajectories spans 2001 to 2021, and flood experience is computed relative to averaged historical water level data from 40 years earlier. The results also reference historical ice-jam floods (e.g., 1875, 1977–1979, 1997) as context for early-period adaptation assumptions. These temporal elements define how adaptation and risk evolve in the simulations.
supporting_quote: from 2001 to 2021 under the dynamic adaptation through the RCT and the PMT
averaged historical water level data from 40 years ago

chunks.text: Across sampled factor boundaries from 2001–2021, PMT and RCT simulations show similar overall trends in total ice-jam flood risk, including evidence of regime shifts driven by adaptation dynamics. However, PMT produces a smoother response surface with more gradual changes across variables, while RCT appears more discrete. The PMT outputs also show higher variability across sampled factors, interpreted as increased behavioral uncertainty consistent with bounded rationality.
supporting_quote: The simulation based on the PMT captures gradual changes... compared to... the RCT, which covers the response surface in a more discrete way.
the results of the PMT model exhibit higher variability in ice-jam flood risk across the sampled factors.

chunks.text: Both theoretical frameworks exhibit regime shifts in ice-jam flood risk associated with dynamic adaptation by governments and residents. The paper interprets this as the system switching between two distinct states with different patterns and trends in flood risk when model factors are perturbed. This aligns with the notion that adaptation feedbacks can induce abrupt transitions in socio-hydrological systems.
supporting_quote: PMT also shows a regime shift attributed to the significant role of dynamic adaptation by governments and residents.
shift... resulting in two states characterized by different patterns and trends in the dynamics of ice-jam flood risk.

chunks.text: Despite PMT introducing more uncertainty, the lower bound of PMT uncertainty indicates the possibility of larger reductions in ice-jam flood risk compared to RCT under some factor settings. The paper attributes this gap to the strong influence of socio-economic factors on decision-making within PMT. In other words, bounded-rational behavioral representation can yield more optimistic risk-reduction outcomes in certain configurations.
supporting_quote: Although the PMT model introduces more uncertainty...
the lower bound of uncertainty in the PMT model highlights the potential for a greater reduction in ice-jam flood risk when compared to the RCT model.

chunks.text: For newly adapted residents, PMT and RCT show similar trends from 2001 to 2021 but PMT exhibits greater uncertainty in 2001 due to socio-economic factor effects on decisions. After 2001, both models show similar variability, yet in 2011 PMT shows more newly adapted residents than RCT even though total flood risk decreases. The paper links this increase to social factors captured in PMT.
supporting_quote: the model simulation by the PMT indicates a higher degree of uncertainty... in 2001.
Although the total flood risk decreases in 2011, the PMT model shows an increase in newly adapted residents compared to the RCT model.

chunks.text: Multi-run experiments suggest stochasticity in the ABM has relatively small impact on outputs. An envelope of 1000 trajectories for one socio-economic setting showed low variability attributable to stochastic decision-making. Based on this, the study used 100 repetitions for global sensitivity analysis to reduce computational cost while maintaining robustness.
supporting_quote: revealed a low variability attributed to the stochastic features of the model.
Thus, in this study, we chose 100 for model repetitions.

chunks.text: Global sensitivity analysis rankings indicate economic factors are most influential in both RCT and PMT. Income tax is ranked most critical for total flood risk in both models, and is also top-ranked for adapted residents under RCT. Under PMT, the mean coefficient for cost of flood-proofing becomes the most important driver of adapted residents, surpassing income tax.
supporting_quote: economic factors exhibit the highest level of sensitivity in both models.
the coefficient of cost of flood-proofing surpasses income tax in terms of importance when considering the number of newly adapted residents.

chunks.text: Heterogeneity is identified as a key factor affecting both total flood risk and adoption of flood-proofing in the PMT model. This emphasizes that diverse resident characteristics and decision rules materially change system outcomes. The ABM structure is highlighted as enabling explicit representation of heterogeneous behaviors compared to more aggregated approaches.
supporting_quote: the sensitivity analysis highlights the significance of heterogeneity as one of the key socio-economic factors affecting both total flood risk and the adoption of flood-proofing measures
emphasizing the influence of heterogeneity in decision-making processes.

chunks.text: Response efficacy and self-efficacy coefficients are important contributors to both total flood risk and newly adapted residents in the PMT analysis. This indicates that beliefs about the effectiveness of protective actions and confidence in implementing them can meaningfully shift adaptation uptake and risk outcomes. These factors provide policy levers beyond purely economic incentives.
supporting_quote: the coefficients of response efficacy and self-efficacy emerge as important factors contributing to both total flood risk and the number of newly adapted residents.
demonstrate the significance of response efficacy and self-efficacy in flood risk management strategies.

chunks.text: Scenario analysis under PMT shows that high income tax and low flood-proofing costs (A–A4) yield lower total flood risk than low tax and high costs (B–B4). Within both A and B sets, scenarios with high social factors (A1/A2 and B1/B2) produce lower flood risk and higher adoption compared to low-social-factor cases (A3/A4 and B3/B4). The mechanism is a surge in newly adapted residents around 2011 that reduces subsequent risk.
supporting_quote: In scenarios A-A4... income tax is high and the cost of flood-proofing is low, the total flood risk is lower compared to... scenarios B-B4
scenarios with high social factors... showcases lower total flood risk values and higher numbers of newly adapted residents compared to scenarios with low social factors

chunks.text: The discussion frames a trade-off between model complexity and uncertainty, noting that adding processes can reduce structural error but also increases parameters and potential over-parameterization. The PMT model is more complex than RCT because it includes more socio-economic factors and thus can introduce added uncertainty. The paper argues an equilibrium is needed to avoid over-parameterization and preserve predictive power.
supporting_quote: A more complex model encompasses a broader range of processes... However, an increase in complexity also introduces a higher number of parameters and variables
a complex model can introduce the issue of over-parameterization... increase model uncertainty, and limit the model's predictive power.

chunks.text: The authors emphasize that the relationship between complexity and uncertainty is not universal: in some ABMs, added complexity (e.g., learning) can reduce uncertainty over time depending on structural assumptions. Therefore, evaluating complexity-uncertainty trade-offs requires attention to domain-specific mechanisms and model structure rather than assuming monotonic effects.
supporting_quote: such a conclusion is not universally applicable.
instances exist where heightened model complexity results in a reduction of uncertainty... agent-based models incorporating learning capabilities among agents

chunks.text: The paper notes that focusing only on PMT and RCT may miss the influence of other behavioral theories on flood adaptation. It explicitly suggests considering theories such as the theory of planned behavior in future work. This limitation affects how broadly the behavioral conclusions can be interpreted across decision-making paradigms.
supporting_quote: the study focuses on the PMT and RCT as the guiding social theories, potentially overlooking the impact of additional theories
future studies need to explore the influence of other social theories such the theory of the planned behavior

chunks.text: The study acknowledges general modeling limitations: results depend on assumptions and data availability, and uncertainties are inherent in agent-based simulations. The authors caution that accuracy and reliability hinge on these assumptions and therefore findings should be interpreted carefully. This frames uncertainty as both structural and data-driven.
supporting_quote: there are inherent uncertainties and assumptions associated with the agent-based model used in the analysis.
The model's accuracy and reliability depend on the underlying assumptions and data availability.

chunks.text: Generalizability is limited because results may be specific to Fort McMurray conditions, socio-economic context, and ice-jam characteristics. The paper recommends expanding to diverse case studies to support broader inference about patterns and trends. This limitation constrains direct transfer of parameter sensitivities and scenario outcomes to other regions.
supporting_quote: The study's findings and conclusions may be specific to the context and conditions considered in the analysis.
Future research endeavors should systematically broaden their scope by focus on diverse case studies with distinct conditions.

chunks.text: Human decision-making is recognized as difficult to represent fully because it involves cognitive biases, social norms, and external influences beyond modeled variables. While the study uses social theories to approximate decisions, it cannot capture all variability. The authors propose collecting more extensive observational datasets to refine model development.
supporting_quote: Human decision-making processes are inherently complex... including cognitive biases, social norms, and external influences.
future research should focus on accumulating a more extensive dataset through systematic observation.

chunks.text: The study concludes that integrating PMT into the ice-jam flood ABM can provide a more comprehensive socio-economic representation than RCT, but at the cost of increased uncertainty and possible over-parameterization. Even so, both frameworks reproduce similar overall trends and show regime shifts driven by dynamic adaptation by governments and residents. The comparison clarifies strengths and limitations of each framework for ice-jam risk assessment.
supporting_quote: the study acknowledges the potential benefits of a more complex model (PMT model)... However, it also acknowledges the challenges... higher uncertainty and the issue of over-parameterization.
Both the RCT and PMT models exhibit similar trends... The results show a regime shift in ice-jam flood risk due to significant dynamic adaptation

chunks.text: Economic factors are concluded to be the dominant drivers of modeled flood risk and adaptation, especially income tax and the cost of flood-proofing. The paper highlights that cost of flood-proofing can become more influential when government artificial breakup is not implemented. It also concludes that social factors can increase adoption even when overall risk is low.
supporting_quote: The sensitivity analysis underscores the significance of economic factors... particularly the income tax and the cost of flood-proofing
despite a low overall flood risk, focusing on social factors can result in a higher rate of residents adopting adaptive measures.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that heterogeneity, response efficacy, and self-efficacy are important social-behavioral determinants affecting both flood risk and the adoption of flood-proofing. Enhancing residents’ beliefs in action effectiveness and their confidence to self-protect is framed as a pathway to more effective flood risk management. These findings support designing strategies that account for diverse decision-making processes.
supporting_quote: The analysis underscored the importance of heterogeneity in decision-making processes
The response efficacy and self-efficacy coefficients played a significant role in influencing flood risk and the adoption of flood-proofing measures.

chunks.text: Real-time flood inundation mapping supports emergency response by translating rainfall and discharge forecasts into spatially explicit flood extent and depth information that is easy for responders to interpret. Traditional inundation maps are often prepared locally and mainly for populated areas, leaving many rural areas unmapped. Automated approaches using topographic data can enable broader-coverage mapping needed before, during, and after disasters.
supporting_quote: Real-time flood inundation mapping is vital for emergency response to help protect life and property.

Flood inundation maps have traditionally been prepared by local agencies... generally only been produced for densely populated areas and are usually not produced at all for less populated and rural areas.

chunks.text: The National Water Model forecasts discharge for millions of river reaches in the continental U.S., and these discharges can be converted into inundation maps using the Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) method combined with synthetic rating curves (SRCs). SRCs use Manning’s equation to translate discharge to stage height, while HAND converts stage height to flood extent based on relative elevation above drainage. This workflow is computationally inexpensive and suited for continental-scale mapping.
supporting_quote: The National Water Model (NWM)... produces daily and subdaily discharge forecasts for over 2.7 million reaches spanning the continental U.S.

The NWM forecasted discharge is converted to inundation extent by combining the Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) method... and synthetic rating curves (SRCs)... SRCs converting discharge to stage height using Manning's equation, and HAND converting stage height to flood extent using relative elevation.

chunks.text: Topographic data availability and resolution improvements have made large-scale flood hazard modeling increasingly feasible, but fully detailed hydrodynamic modeling everywhere remains expensive and difficult. Manning’s equation can be inaccurate under complex hydraulic controls (e.g., bridges, culverts, dams), yet it is still used here for scalable approximate inundation mapping. Therefore, performance assessment of these simplified methods is essential before broad operational use.
supporting_quote: Improvements in the resolution of topography data have made it possible to analyze and advance inundation modeling

A dense network of gauging stations or the application of hydrodynamic models... for every river in the country would provide very accurate flood maps but would be prohibitively difficult and expensive
Manning's equation is known to not accurately relate discharge to stage height under many hydraulic conditions such as where bridges, culverts, and dams influence flow

chunks.text: The study’s main objective is to evaluate the accuracy of synthetic rating curves derived from 10 m National Elevation Dataset topography for use with HAND inundation mapping. The authors compare SRCs to rating curves obtained from calibrated hydrodynamic (HEC-RAS) models tied to observed stage heights and compute statistics to quantify agreement. This evaluation is intended to determine whether SRCs are sufficiently accurate for large-scale approximate inundation mapping.
supporting_quote: In this study we assess the accuracy of the SRCs derived from 10 m National Elevation Dataset (NED) topography data
We address the accuracy of SRCs by comparing them to HEC-RAS rating curves that were calibrated against observed stage heights, and we quantify their performance using appropriate metrics.
We find SRCs are accurate enough for large-scale approximate inundation mapping while not as accurate when assessing individual reaches or cross sections.

chunks.text: A second goal is to identify terrain and channel characteristics associated with SRC errors and to test a practical enhancement to SRC construction. The authors examine whether reach length, slope, and other attributes predict divergence from HEC-RAS rating curves. They propose recalculating slope in Manning’s equation as a weighted average over a minimum distance (moving window) and evaluate performance across a range of window lengths.
supporting_quote: Additionally, we investigate the effect of channel features and terrain characteristics on SRC performance and propose an approach to adjust the slope in Manning's equation used for calculating the SRCs.
We propose an approach to recalculate the slope in Manning's equation as the weighted average over a minimum distance and assess accuracy for a range of moving window lengths.

chunks.text: Flood inundation information is often unavailable or unsuitable for forecasting across much of the U.S. because existing products are incomplete and/or not designed for real-time river forecasts. FEMA maps cover less than half of the continental U.S. and focus on a theoretical 1% chance flood, limiting operational usefulness. This motivates automated inundation mapping approaches that can run nationwide from topographic data.
supporting_quote: The Federal Emergency Management Agency flood maps cover less than half of the continental United States (U.S.), are based on the theoretical 1% chance flood and have limited use for river forecasts.
Thus, an automatic process that uses topography data as the only input for inundation mapping would allow flood maps to be produced for the entire country

chunks.text: Synthetic rating curves are used operationally to convert discharge to stage height, but their validity must be demonstrated against trusted standards before they can be relied on. There is no standardized method for statistics in rating-curve comparisons, and different metrics can introduce different biases. Without systematic evaluation, SRC-driven inundation mapping may misrepresent stage heights and flood extents.
supporting_quote: To be used with any degree of confidence, SRCs must be evaluated for accuracy against standardized or observed data.
Currently there is no standardized method for statistics in rating curve comparisons.

chunks.text: Applying Manning’s equation uniformly can yield inaccurate stage estimates when local hydraulic controls or complex flow regimes exist. Features such as bridges, culverts, and dams can alter depth-velocity relationships and violate assumptions underlying a simple uniform-flow formulation. This creates a challenge for a national-scale automated approach that does not explicitly model these local hydraulics.
supporting_quote: Manning's equation is known to not accurately relate discharge to stage height under many hydraulic conditions such as where bridges, culverts, and dams influence flow
The presence of a control structure upstream and a dam downstream can result in a mixed flow regime of supercritical and subcritical flow conditions along a given stream reach

chunks.text: SRCs are constructed by using HAND-derived reach-averaged hydraulic properties at specified water levels and then applying Manning’s equation with an assumed roughness coefficient to obtain discharge. Repeating this for a series of water levels yields a stage–discharge relationship for each reach. This study follows the SRC development approach described in Zheng et al. (2018) using 10 m NED topography.
supporting_quote: SRCs are first constructed using HAND to estimate the channel hydraulic properties, such as cross-sectional area, wetted perimeter, slope, etc., of a stream reach at a uniform water level
Provided with an in-channel roughness coefficient (n), Manning's equation is applied to obtain a uniform discharge (Q) corresponding to a given water level.
for a series of different water levels and corresponding discharges, an SRC for a stream reach is obtained

chunks.text: HEC-RAS rating curves are produced from provided 1-D steady-flow models run with the standard step method for gradually varied flow, incorporating backwater effects. Each HEC-RAS cross section includes stage values for a set of discharge conditions spanning annual low flow through multiple return periods (10-, 25-, 50-, 100-, and 500-year events). These cross-sectional rating curves serve as the calibrated reference for evaluating SRC stage estimates.
supporting_quote: The provided HEC-RAS models are run under a 1-D steady flow analysis with the standard step method assuming gradually varied flow.
The method uses the energy, momentum, and continuity equations, with backwater effects being modeled.
Each cross section has a set of discharge values that relate to the 10-, 25- 50-, 100-, and 500-year frequency events as well as typical annual low flow conditions.

chunks.text: Because SRCs are reach-based while HEC-RAS curves are cross-section-based, the study aggregates HEC-RAS cross-section rating curves to reach scale when multiple cross sections fall within a reach. For each discharge value, the median HEC-RAS stage height across cross sections is taken as the reach representative to reduce the impact of outliers. SRC error is computed as the vertical stage difference relative to this median reach-averaged HEC-RAS curve.
supporting_quote: The discharge and stage height relationships for SRCs are valid for a reach, whereas for HEC-RAS the rating curves are valid for a cross section.
We took the median of the HEC-RAS cross-sectional stage height values for each discharge value as the representative value for the reach rating curve.
we take the vertical stage height difference between the SRC and the median HEC-RAS rating curve as the error.

chunks.text: SRC performance is quantified primarily using normalized RMSE (NRMSE), computed from stage-height differences between SRC and HEC-RAS at the set of discharge points, and normalized by the HEC-RAS stage range between the 500-year event and annual low flow. Secondary metrics include mean absolute depth (stage) difference and percent bias to capture absolute magnitude and systematic over/underprediction. The normalization enables comparisons across rivers of different sizes.
supporting_quote: The primary metric used to assess performance in this study is the RMSE normalized by difference in stage height between the 500-year event and annual low flow conditions.
We have chosen to normalize by stage height range... allowing comparison across all scales.
We therefore use absolute depth difference... and percent bias
Percent Bias = ... \left(\frac{\sum_{n \in R} (\hat{y} - y)}{\sum_{y} y}\right) \times 100

chunks.text: To explore drivers of accuracy, the authors analyze relationships between SRC error and reach attributes: reach length, reach slope, bankfull width, bankfull depth, and location/proximity to structures. Errors are grouped into five equal bins for each variable, and box plots of absolute depth difference summarize distributions within bins. Bankfull width and depth are derived from HEC-RAS geometry files using bank points and cross-section minima.
supporting_quote: The terrain characteristics and channel features we chose to assess are reach length, reach slope, bankfull width, bankfull depth, and location of the reach.
We calculate and group SRC accuracy by range... breaking up the reaches into five equal bins
We calculated bankfull width and depth from HEC-RAS geometry files... width was taken as the difference in station between the two bank points and depth was taken as the vertical difference

chunks.text: To address poor performance associated with short reaches and extreme slopes, the study recalculates slope for reaches shorter than a chosen minimum moving-window length. A new river segment centered on the reach is extended upstream and downstream to meet the minimum length, then slope is computed as a weighted average across included reaches. SRCs are recomputed using this adjusted slope and evaluated over a range of window lengths to identify an optimal length per river.
supporting_quote: very short reaches and reaches with very low slope values were observed as more likely to exhibit poor SRC performance.
We therefore calculated the slope of short reaches by introducing a variable minimum length moving window.
The new slope value is calculated as a weighted average of the slope across this new stretch of river, as: S_{new} = \frac{1}{L_{total}} \sum_{i=1}^{N} S_i L_i
For each minimum length value, we recalculate SRC accuracy... computing the change in performance as we increase the minimum distance

chunks.text: The evaluation uses four Coastal Texas rivers with available calibrated HEC-RAS models: the San Antonio, Guadalupe, Lower Colorado (main stems), and the smaller Blanco River. These rivers span different basin sizes and elevation gradients, with Blanco notably steeper (0.19%) than the others (0.03%–0.08%). Tributaries are not examined because USACE-provided HEC-RAS models only covered main stems.
supporting_quote: The study areas consist of four rivers in Coastal Texas: The San Antonio, Guadalupe, and Lower Colorado Rivers... and the Blanco River.
The San Antonio, Guadalupe, and Lower Colorado Rivers have lengths of approximately 386, 370, and 665 km... The Blanco River is much smaller, with length of 90 km
mean elevation gradients of 0.04%, 0.08%, and 0.03%, whereas Blanco has a much greater gradient of 0.19%.
The HEC-RAS models provided by USACE had only the main stem of each river available, so no tributaries were examined in this study.

chunks.text: Synthetic rating curves are derived from 10 m National Elevation Dataset topography, following the HAND-based approach used in prior work. Reach slope inputs are computed from channel bed elevation values derived from the 10 m NED, and compared against NHDPlus attribute slopes for sanity checking. The analysis focuses on reach-averaged properties and rating curves compatible with HAND inundation mapping.
supporting_quote: we assess the accuracy of the SRCs derived from 10 m National Elevation Dataset (NED) topography data
An initial slope value for each reach was obtained from channel bed elevation values derived from topography of the 10 m NED.
the values were compared to averaged slopes from the current version of the National Hydrography Dataset (NHDPlus) attributes table... and were found to be generally similar.

chunks.text: The hydrodynamic reference consists of calibrated HEC-RAS models produced by USACE and the San Antonio River Authority, with stage–discharge information at multiple discharges including return-period flows. Blanco, Guadalupe, and Lower Colorado HEC-RAS models are not publicly available, while the San Antonio River model is available via SARA’s repository. These model outputs provide cross-sectional rating curves later aggregated to reach scale.
supporting_quote: HEC-RAS models calibrated against observed stage heights that were produced and provided by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) and San Antonio River Authority (SARA).
Each cross section has a set of discharge values that relate to the 10-, 25- 50-, 100-, and 500-year frequency events as well as typical annual low flow conditions.

The HEC-RAS models for Blanco, Guadalupe, and Lower Colorado Rivers were provided by USACE and are not publicly available. The HEC-RAS model for the San Antonio River are provided by SARA in a public repository

chunks.text: Channel geometry attributes used in exploratory analyses are taken from HEC-RAS geometry files. Bankfull width is computed as the station difference between left and right bank points, and bankfull depth as the vertical difference between the median bank elevation and the minimum cross-section elevation. These derived variables are used to test whether cross-section size relates to SRC error.
supporting_quote: We calculated bankfull width and depth from HEC-RAS geometry files, where width was taken as the difference in station between the two bank points
depth was taken as the vertical difference between the median of the two bank points and the minimum elevation value across the cross section.

chunks.text: Across the four Texas rivers, SRCs show moderate agreement with calibrated HEC-RAS reach-averaged rating curves but with substantial remaining deviations. Mean normalized RMSE ranges from 20.6% to 31.2%, suggesting approximate but imperfect stage estimation. Blanco shows the best NRMSE performance (20.6%), while Lower Colorado shows the worst (31.2%).
supporting_quote: We find that the mean normalized RMSE ranges from 20.6% to 31.2%
The SRCs of the Blanco River have the best performance, whereas the SRCs of the Lower Colorado River have the most deviation
Lower Colorado | 31.2
Blanco | 20.6

chunks.text: Absolute stage-height errors vary widely by river, with mean absolute depth differences from 0.65 m to 2.42 m. The San Antonio River SRCs have the smallest mean absolute depth difference (0.65 m), while the Guadalupe River has the largest (2.42 m). These magnitudes indicate that while SRCs may be useful for broad inundation approximation, vertical errors can be large for some rivers.
supporting_quote: The mean absolute depth differences for the four rivers range from 0.65 to 2.42 m.
San Antonio | 0.65
Guadalupe | 2.42

chunks.text: Bias results show SRCs tend to over-predict stage height for a given discharge in most rivers, though the Guadalupe River under-predicts on average. Mean percent bias ranges from -9.5% to 35.5%. The Lower Colorado River exhibits particularly large over-prediction with 35.5% mean percent bias, while Guadalupe’s mean percent bias is -9.5%.
supporting_quote: The mean percent bias values of the four rivers range from -9.5% to 35.5%
only the Guadalupe River has SRCs that overall under-predicted the stage height with a mean percent bias value of -9.5%.
The over-prediction is particularly large for the Lower Colorado River with a mean percent bias of 35.5%

chunks.text: Reach length is associated with SRC performance in several rivers: short reaches are more likely to show poor accuracy, while medium-length reaches tend to perform better. For Blanco, Guadalupe, and San Antonio, the shortest reach-length bins (shorter than about 1.2–1.3 km) exhibit worse performance than other bins in max, upper quartile, and median errors. This trend is not observed for the Lower Colorado River.
supporting_quote: There seems to be a trend where short reach lengths are more likely to exhibit poor SRC performance and medium length reaches are likely to exhibit better SRC performance.
reaches shorter than 1.2, 1.2, and 1.3 km, respectively, exhibit worse performance than all other groups
This trend, however, is not present for the Lower Colorado River.

chunks.text: Reach slope also relates to accuracy: low-slope reaches are more likely to exhibit poor SRC performance. The lowest-slope groups in Blanco and Guadalupe (reach slopes <0.13%) perform worse than other groups, and in San Antonio and Lower Colorado the minimum slope group (0.001%) is also the poorest performer. However, performance does not monotonically improve with slope; the steepest groups can degrade again.
supporting_quote: There is a visible trend where reaches with low slope are more likely to exhibit poor SRC performance.
Blanco River and Guadalupe River with reach slopes <0.13% performance worse than all other groups
San Antonio River and Lower Colorado River where all reaches have the minimum slope value of 0.001% perform worse than all other groups
there is not a visible trend where performance improves as reach slope increases.

chunks.text: Bankfull width and bankfull depth generally do not show strong relationships with SRC accuracy across the four rivers. Only the Guadalupe River shows minor trends of decreasing performance in wider and deeper sections. For the other three rivers, no meaningful relationship is observed between error and these size-related channel attributes.
supporting_quote: There does not seem to be any significant trend between SRC accuracy and bankfull width... or bankfull depth... when the four rivers are examined together.
Only for the Guadalupe River does there seem to be a minor trend where SRC performance decreases for wider sections of the river
The three other rivers do not exhibit any meaningful relationship between SRC accuracy and bankfull width or depth.

chunks.text: Spatial inspection suggests proximity to roads and bridges may coincide with worse SRC performance, although broad geographic location (upstream vs. near the Gulf Coast) does not show a clear bias. The map-based comparison highlights that reaches affected by roads and bridges appear more error-prone. This supports the idea that hydraulic structures can contribute to divergence between simplified SRCs and calibrated hydrodynamic rating curves.
supporting_quote: There does not seem to be any bias toward better or worse performance in upstream locations or areas near the Texas Gulf Coast.
However, there is a possible trend where reaches affected by roads and bridges appear to exhibit worse SRC performance.

chunks.text: Recalculating slope with a moving-window weighted average can improve SRC performance, but gains vary by river. For Blanco, mean normalized RMSE decreases substantially from about 20.7% to 7.8% at a 1.25 km moving window. For Guadalupe, San Antonio, and Lower Colorado, improvements are smaller, with optimal NRMSE reductions to 26.4% (2.25 km), 21.6% (1.25 km), and 29.2% (0.75 km), respectively.
supporting_quote: the improvement in normalized RMSE is quite large, decreasing from 20.7% to 7.8% with a moving window length of 1.25 km.
For the Guadalupe River... 29.0%, whereas the optimal value is found to be 26.4% for a moving window length of 2.25 km.
For the San Antonio River... 23.1%, whereas the optimal value is found to be 21.6% for a moving window length of 1.25 km.
For the Colorado River... 31.2%, whereas the optimal value is found to be 29.2% for a moving window length of 0.75 km.

chunks.text: The authors emphasize that SRCs are not suitable for assessing flood risk at individual locations, but may be acceptable for large-scale approximate inundation mapping. They note that coarse elevation data can misrepresent channel shape, length, and thalweg, and that improved terrain models could enhance SRC alignment with calibrated rating curves. In emergency response, they argue that over-predicting stage is preferable to underprediction.
supporting_quote: While SRCs are not appropriate to assess flood risk for individual locations, these results show promise for automated national-scale inundation mapping.
higher resolution terrain models which may better represent the shape and length of channels... can strengthen the information displayed by SRCs
There is an overall trend of the SRCs over-predicting stage height for a given discharge... which is preferable to underprediction in the context of emergency response.

chunks.text: Flat coastal terrains may be particularly challenging for HAND/SRC mapping because small elevation errors can cause very low or erroneous slope estimates. The study notes that inundation mapping is harder where terrain convergence is weak, and that derived slopes can be extremely low, leading to incorrect stage estimates. This may help explain differences between Blanco (steeper) and the other coastal main stems.
supporting_quote: Flood inundation mapping is more difficult in flat, coastal terrains which lack terrain convergence.
This problem may be exaggerated in particularly flat terrains where the terrain model derived slope can be very low, leading to erroneous estimation of stages.
The Blanco River is generally the steepest compared to the other rivers

chunks.text: The paper argues that reach length and extreme slope values affect the validity of using Manning’s equation with local bed slope estimates. Short reaches may be more prone to extreme slopes due to local variability, while very long reaches violate the assumption of uniform water surface elevation. These issues suggest that network segmentation (combining very short reaches and splitting long ones) could improve continental inundation mapping performance.
supporting_quote: We suggest that short reaches are more likely to have extreme slope values due to local terrain variability
Manning's equation is only accurate for overall slope values rather than purely local bed slope values.
The NHDPlus network... contains reaches shorter than ten meters as well as reaches over 10 km. Both short and long reaches pose significant barriers

chunks.text: Roughness is recognized as a major source of uncertainty in Manning-based SRCs, but the study assumes uniform roughness due to lack of field data. The authors note that roughness varies spatially and seasonally, and that composite in-channel and overbank roughness values could improve accuracy. However, estimating roughness from only topography remains difficult.
supporting_quote: Roughness has a significant effect on Manning's equation, but in this study we simply assume a uniform roughness for all reaches since we do not have data
An improvement... is to use composite values of in-channel roughness and overbank roughness rather than a bulk value
in-channel roughness is challenging to estimate from only topography data.

chunks.text: Local hydraulic structures likely degrade SRC performance because the automated approach does not explicitly model these controls. The analysis suggests poorer accuracy near roads and bridges, and the authors expect culverts and dams to have similar impacts. They note that fully mitigating this would require more detailed hydrodynamic modeling, though systematic study might support correction factors where consistent bias is observed.
supporting_quote: reaches affected by roads and bridges appear to exhibit worse SRC performance.
Proximity to other hydraulic structures such as culverts and dams are similarly expected to negatively impact SRC performance.
the automated SRC process is designed as an alternative to the detailed hydrodynamic modeling that is most appropriate to approximate local hydraulics.

chunks.text: The study presents a framework for evaluating HAND/SRC inundation components by comparing SRCs to calibrated HEC-RAS rating curves aggregated to reach scale. The results show significant differences between detailed hydrodynamic rating curves and SRCs derived from coarse elevation data. The authors conclude SRC performance is acceptable for large-scale approximate inundation mapping, but not reliable for inundation assessment at an individual location.
supporting_quote: We developed a framework to compare SRC performance to HEC-RAS rating curves.
our results showed that there are significant differences between rating curves derived from detailed hydrodynamic modeling and SRCs developed from coarse resolution elevation data.
We found that SRC performance is acceptable for large-scale approximate inundation mapping although not reliable for assessing inundation at an individual location.

chunks.text: Reach length, reach slope, and possibly hydraulic structures are identified as predictors of poor SRC performance. In particular, short reaches, low-gradient reaches, and reaches near structures like roads/bridges tend to have larger errors. These findings point to where future improvements should focus when scaling inundation mapping nationally.
supporting_quote: we find that reach length (Figure 2), reach slope (Figure 3) are likely to predict SRC accuracy.
Short reaches, reaches with low gradient, and reaches in close proximity to hydraulic structures were found to predict poor SRC performance.

chunks.text: A moving-window slope recalculation approach can improve SRC accuracy by replacing purely local slope with a weighted-average slope over a minimum river length. The method produced very large improvement for one river (Blanco) but only minor gains for the others, indicating that effectiveness depends on river and terrain context. The authors recommend further testing across diverse terrains and additional refinements (e.g., roughness and structures) to produce more accurate real-time inundation maps.
supporting_quote: We proposed a moving window approach to recalculate reach slope and assessed the impact of this change on SRC performance
The improvement was found to be very significant for one river but relatively minor for the three others.
Further exploration of the proposed moving window approach across different terrains and rivers will be necessary

chunks.text: Groundwater depletion is a growing threat to water security, driven by increasing demand and declining surface water availability. In the Southeastern US, depletion in the Mississippi embayment section of the Gulf Coastal Plain has been substantial over the last century. Because recharge is a key flux controlling aquifer sustainability, improving understanding of its spatial and temporal variability is important for effective management.
supporting_quote: Groundwater depletion (larger withdrawals than natural recharge) is a growing threat to groundwater management and water security.
in the Southeastern US... groundwater depletion has occurred at a rate of 1.2 km3=year between 1900 and 2008

chunks.text: Local-scale recharge information is needed for tasks such as contamination assessment, evaluating pumping impacts, and understanding climate and land cover effects on storage. Because drivers like precipitation, pumping, and land cover can vary over 1–10 km², recharge estimates at comparable resolution are valuable for basin stakeholders and planning.
supporting_quote: Groundwater recharge information at local scales is essential for various tasks
Because precipitation, pumping rates, land cover changes... can vary significantly at a local scale (on the order of 1 to 10 km2), having recharge estimates at a similarly fine scale will be useful

chunks.text: A prominent data-driven CONUS recharge product provides annual recharge at 800 m resolution for 2000–2013, derived from empirical regression equations. Its validation relied on limited point observations, leaving uncertainty about accuracy, especially in regions with sparse measurements. This motivates alternative evaluation approaches, including comparison with process-based models.
supporting_quote: Reitz et al. (2017) employed a data-driven approach to estimate annual values of recharge... at an 800 m resolution for the period 2000–2013
validating a large-scale dataset with a small number of point estimates is not adequate

chunks.text: The study aims to compare a process-based, semi-distributed hydrologic model’s recharge estimates against the USGS data-driven recharge product for a major Alabama river basin. By implementing SWAT at a scale comparable to the 800 m product, the authors seek to infer strengths and limitations of empirical recharge mapping when direct validation data are scarce.
supporting_quote: the objective of this study is to implement a process-based, semi-distributed hydrological model... using the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT)... and compare the model results with the recharge product developed by the Reitz et al. USGS study.
we hypothesize that a comparison with a processbased model that explicitly resolves hydrological processes at a scale similar to the USGS product would still provide insights

chunks.text: A further goal is to use SWAT’s finer temporal resolution to examine seasonal recharge dynamics and how precipitation, evapotranspiration, runoff, and soil moisture influence recharge generation. This analysis is intended to clarify when recharge occurs and which fluxes are most associated with recharge variability within the basin.
supporting_quote: The finer temporal resolution of the SWAT model allows us to assess the seasonal dynamics of recharge and the impact of precipitation, ET, and soil moisture on it.
Fig. 13 shows the monthly dynamics of... soil water content (SWC), and groundwater recharge.

chunks.text: Quantifying aquifer recharge remains difficult and is one of the most uncertain parts of the hydrologic cycle. Reliable recharge estimates are needed for sustainable groundwater policies, but uncertainty persists due to limited direct observations and complexities of processes controlling recharge across space and time.
supporting_quote: quantifying this flux continues to be a challenge and remains one of the most uncertain components of the hydrological cycle.
Reliable estimates of aquifer recharge have the potential to help develop sustainable groundwater management policies.

chunks.text: The USGS empirical recharge product has weak validation due to sparse and unevenly distributed point-based recharge estimates. Some states have very limited measurements, and even where data exist, the measurement period may not align with the modeled period. This raises concerns about the accuracy of annual recharge maps.
supporting_quote: validating a large-scale dataset with a small number of point estimates is not adequate, because a sample of 45 sites in an area as big as the United States is not representative.
there was just one recharge estimate for the entire state of Alabama... data collected in 1993, whereas the USGS product was developed... 2000 to 2013.

chunks.text: Even if basin-scale averages match, empirical relationships fitted at basin scale may not hold at finer spatial resolutions such as 800 m pixels. This potential scale mismatch can lead to spatial discrepancies that matter for local management decisions.
supporting_quote: good agreement at the basin scale, but significant discrepancies at finer spatial resolutions.
the empirical relationships modeled at the basin scale by the USGS empirical equations might not hold at smaller spatial scales.

chunks.text: A semi-distributed SWAT model was developed for the Black Warrior–Tombigbee Basin, discretized into subbasins and HRUs to represent spatial variability in land use, soils, and slope. The model used SCS curve number for runoff and Penman–Monteith for potential evapotranspiration. It was run daily from 1997–2013 with a 3-year warm-up, analyzing outputs for 2000–2013 to match the USGS product period.
supporting_quote: The final model consists of 40 subbasins and 3,774 HRUs.
For this study, we used the SCS curve number method.
Penman-Monteith (selected for this study)
The model was set to run from January 1, 1997, to December 31, 2013... generating results from January 1, 2000, to December 31, 2013.

chunks.text: SWAT recharge computation in this study relied on the model’s total recharge formulation at HRU scale, which is routed into aquifer stores with a drainage time parameter and partitioned between shallow and deep aquifers. The study used SWAT total recharge (Eq. 5) at HRU scale for comparison to the USGS total recharge product.

chunks.text: Calibration targeted both streamflow and baseflow using NSE as the objective function, with different aggregation choices suited to each variable. Streamflow calibration used monthly data, while baseflow was estimated via PART and calibrated using annual aggregates due to method guidance that daily values are only valid when aggregated. Calibration was performed at the basin outlet and validated at two upstream gauges.

For total streamflow... a monthly time scale was selected for calibration.
baseflow estimates from this software... are valid only if the values are aggregated at least at a quarterly time scale. Therefore, baseflow values were calibrated using annual estimates

chunks.text: A global sensitivity analysis was conducted using the Fourier Amplitude Sensitivity Test (FAST) to identify influential SWAT parameters for streamflow and baseflow performance. The most sensitive parameters were then perturbed using Latin hypercube sampling to search parameter combinations yielding improved model performance. Final parameter selection combined independent calibrations with trial-and-error to achieve acceptable joint streamflow and baseflow fits.

the most sensitive parameters were perturbed in the model with a Latin hypercube sampler (LHS)
