chunks.text: For spatial comparison with the USGS 800 m product, SWAT HRU-level annual recharge outputs were rasterized to 800 m resolution. The analysis focused on the driest year (2007) and wettest year (2009) to illustrate spatial differences and evaluate pixel-scale agreement between the approaches.
supporting_quote: The annual recharge estimates for the driest (2007) and the wettest (2009) years were selected for the spatial analysis.
The SWAT model estimates at the HRU level were rasterized at an 800 m resolution to allow comparison with the USGS data products at every pixel.

chunks.text: Seasonal recharge dynamics were evaluated using monthly time series from SWAT, including net surface flux (PCP–ET), subsurface flux proxy (PCP–ET–QF), soil water content, and recharge. Pearson correlations were used to compare how the relationship between net fluxes and recharge changes across wet and dry seasons.
supporting_quote: Fig. 13 shows the monthly dynamics of... (PCP – ET)... (PCP–ET – QF), soil water content (SWC), and groundwater recharge.
recharge occurred mainly from December to May... correlates better with monthly recharge according to Pearson's correlation coefficient (ρ) (ρ = 0.45).

chunks.text: The study basin drains to the USGS Coffeeville gauge and spans about 48,300 km² across Mississippi and Alabama, covering the period 2000–2013 for comparison with the USGS recharge product. Land cover is dominated by forests and pastures (~65%), with woody wetlands (~13%), urban (~7%), and agricultural land (~3%).
supporting_quote: The Basin drains an area of approximately 48,300 km2 , overlying portions of Mississippi and Alabama.
The streamflow record available at the Basin outlet is for January 2000 to December 2013 period, and the USGS recharge product includes this period.
the Basin is covered by various types of forests and pastures over approximately 65% of the area; about 13% is woody wetland, 7% is urban, 3% is agricultural land

chunks.text: Model setup used a USGS 1-arc-second DEM, STATSGO soils, and NLCD 2016 land cover. Meteorological forcing for SWAT came from NCEP CFSR daily data (precipitation, wind, humidity, solar) for 1997–2013. The study notes prior findings that CFSR forcing can produce streamflow simulations comparable to or better than traditional station inputs.
supporting_quote: The DEM was obtained from the USGS The National Map... The 1-arc-second DEM version was selected.
ArcSWAT was used to retrieve the STATSGO soil dataset
land cover-land use data was retrieved from National Land Cover Database version 2016.
This dataset provides daily precipitation, wind, relative humidity, and solar data... For this study, we downloaded data between January 1, 1997, and December 31, 2013.

chunks.text: Streamflow calibration and validation relied on three USGS gauges with minimal missing data and substantial contributing area: Northport (02465000), Geiger (02448500), and Coffeeville (02469761). Baseflow was not directly observed and was estimated from daily streamflow using USGS PART for annual aggregation in calibration.
supporting_quote: Streamgauges with less than 5% of gaps between 2000 and 2013, and a drainage area greater than 10% of the Basin, were selected; a total of three stations meet these criteria
02465000 Black Warrior River, Northport AL
02448500 Noxubee River Nr, Geiger, AL
02469761 Tombigbee R At, Coffeeville, AL
Baseflow was estimated using PART

chunks.text: The comparison dataset consisted of USGS annual estimates of recharge and ET for CONUS at 800 m resolution for 2000–2013, produced by Reitz et al. using empirical regression equations. Recharge was computed as a residual water budget term assuming negligible long-term storage change, and the published 'Total Recharge' adds 5% of ET uniformly to account for riparian interception. This study compares SWAT recharge with that Total Recharge product.
supporting_quote: Reitz et al. (2017) provided estimates of annual quick-flow runoff, ET, and groundwater recharge for CONUS
applied directly to annual and pixel scale (800 m resolution) data
R = P - Q - ET - ΔS
The authors assumed that the change in sub-surface storage is negligible
the authors added 5% of ET uniformly to the effective recharge (this dataset is called Total Recharge). In the current study, the total recharge product is compared with SWAT recharge estimates.
chunks.section_hint: USGS Annual Estimates of ET and Groundwater Recharge

chunks.text: Sensitivity analysis indicated different dominant parameters for streamflow versus baseflow performance at the basin outlet. For streamflow, ESCO was most influential, followed by ALPHA_BF, SOL_AWC, and CN2. For baseflow, CN2 was most sensitive, followed by ESCO and SOL_AWC, highlighting how runoff generation and soil evaporation controls affect groundwater contributions differently.
supporting_quote: For streamflow, the model is most sensitive to the soil evaporation compensation factor (ESCO)... followed by the baseflow recession constant (ALPHA_BF), soil available water content (SOL_AWC), and curve number (CN2)
For baseflow, the model is most sensitive to curve number, followed by the soil compensation factor, and soil available water content.

chunks.text: The calibrated SWAT model reproduced monthly streamflow well across calibration/validation stations, with NSE values at or above 0.61 and R² above 0.65. Baseflow performance was weaker in NSE, including negative NSE at Northport, though R² exceeded 0.53. The authors attribute low baseflow NSE partly to an outlier year (2009) in a short annual series.
supporting_quote: Streamflow prediction performance is good for the three locations; coefficient of determination (R2) values are above 0.65 for all stations, while NSE values are greater than 0.61.
For baseflow prediction, R2 values are above 0.53.
the reason for these low NSE values is that baseflow predictions for the year 2009... deviated significantly... and because the time series contains only 11 points

chunks.text: At the basin scale, SWAT and USGS annual recharge estimates agreed strongly for 2000–2013 when spatially averaged over the basin. Agreement metrics were high (NSE 0.84, R² 0.83) with minimal bias and RMSE 46 mm. This indicates that, when aggregated, the empirical USGS product aligns closely with the process-based SWAT estimates in this basin.
supporting_quote: We can observe that the two recharge estimates are in good agreement. The NSE is equal to 0.84, R2 is equal to 0.83, percent bias (PBIAS) is equal to 0.4, and the root mean squared error (RMSE) is equal to 46 mm.

chunks.text: Mean recharge over 2000–2013 was nearly identical between the two approaches: 256 mm/year from SWAT and 257 mm/year from USGS. These correspond to about 18% and 17% of precipitation, respectively, expressed also as 12.36 and 12.41 km³. Despite similar recharge, the precipitation forcing differed, with SWAT using CFSR and USGS using PRISM.
supporting_quote: Between 2000 and 2013, the mean recharge value was 256 mm= year (12.36 km3) (18% of precipitation) according to the SWAT model, while the USGS model estimate is 257 mm (12.41 km3), which is equivalent to 17% of precipitation.
The SWAT model uses precipitation from the CFSR dataset... 1,415 mm
The USGS model uses the PRISM dataset... equals 1,481 mm=year

chunks.text: Precipitation estimates used by SWAT (CFSR) and USGS (PRISM) were strongly correlated but PRISM was slightly higher on average. The reported precipitation comparison shows R² of 0.85 and PBIAS of 4.7, indicating PRISM tends to overestimate relative to CFSR in this basin during 2000–2013.
supporting_quote: we can observe a strong correlation between precipitation estimates (R2=0.85 ); however, PRISM tends to slightly overestimate with respect to CFSR (PBIAS = 4.7)

chunks.text: At 800 m resolution during the dry year 2007, the two recharge products diverged substantially. SWAT estimated 92 mm (4.44 km³) while USGS estimated 48 mm (2.32 km³), a 44 mm difference corresponding to a 48% relative error (taking SWAT as reference). Pixel-scale agreement was weak with R² 0.16 and RMSE 65 mm, and USGS generally underpredicted recharge across the basin.
supporting_quote: In 2007... 92 mm (4.44 km³) of recharge according to the SWAT model, while the USGS model estimates 48 mm (2.32 km³)
an average difference of 44 mm, or a relative error of 48%
The coefficient of determination between recharge estimates at the 800 m scale across the Basin is R2=0.16, and the RMSE is 65 mm.
The USGS model generally underpredicts for this dry year across the Basin

chunks.text: SWAT produced more spatially heterogeneous recharge patterns than the USGS product across 2000–2013. The coefficient of variation of annual recharge averaged over years was higher for SWAT (mean CV 0.67) than for USGS (mean CV 0.51). This indicates the process-based model expresses greater fine-scale variability in recharge across the basin.
supporting_quote: The SWAT model predictions are more heterogeneous in space than the USGS model, as indicated by the coefficient of variation (CV).
The mean CV of SWAT recharge estimates between 2000 and 2013 is 0.67, while USGS recharge estimates present a lower mean value equal to 0.51.

chunks.text: In 2007, basin-mean ET differed little between models (SWAT 733 mm vs USGS 745 mm), yet pixel-scale agreement was very poor. The ET spatial comparison showed absolute differences up to 300 mm at 800 m, with R² 0.04 and RMSE 135 mm. The mismatch in ET patterns coincided with areas where USGS underpredicted recharge, consistent with recharge being a residual in the USGS water budget.
supporting_quote: For the year 2007, the SWAT model predicts 733 mm of ET, while the USGS model predicts 745
the models show absolute differences of 300 mm at the 800 m resolution. The correlation coefficient for this year is R2=0.04, and the RMSE is equal to 135 mm.
Because the annual recharge estimates from the USGS model are the residual of the water budget after estimating ET

chunks.text: For the wet year 2009, basin-average recharge was more similar: SWAT 524 mm (25.31 km³) versus USGS 493 mm (23.81), a 31 mm difference (6% relative error). Spatial consistency improved but remained limited (R² 0.29; RMSE 227 mm). Both models showed a shared region of lower recharge, though SWAT captured an additional low-recharge zone in the northeast that USGS did not.
supporting_quote: recharge is estimated as 524 mm (25.31 km3) according to the SWAT model, and 493 mm (23.81) according to USGS estimates, a difference of 31 mm or a relative error of 6%.
The spatial distribution of recharge for this year is marginally more consistent... R2 = 0.29, and RMSE = 227 mm.
while the SWAT model predicts a low-recharge zone in the northeastern portion of the Basin, the USGS model fails to capture this lower recharge zone.

chunks.text: In 2009, ET differed substantially in magnitude between models, with SWAT at 826 mm and USGS at 940 mm (114 mm difference; 14% relative error). Spatial agreement for ET remained low (R² 0.06; RMSE 160 mm), with USGS predicting very high ET over most of the basin. This reinforces that model agreement at basin scale can mask large fine-scale differences in flux partitioning.
supporting_quote: ET in 2009 is estimated to be 826 mm by the SWAT model, while the USGS model estimates 940 mm, a difference of 114 mm or a relative error of 14%.
There is not much consistency in the spatial pattern... R2 = 0.06, and RMSE = 160 mm.

chunks.text: Direct validation of recharge products is limited by scarce measurements, making it difficult to definitively judge which model is more accurate at fine scales. The paper emphasizes that comparing two models can provide insights, but cannot replace ground-truthing, especially at subbasin or pixel scales where discrepancies are largest.
supporting_quote: Because a full validation is not possible due to the lack of direct measurements
we cannot conclude that the SWAT model results at the HRU or 800 m scale are more accurate
more ground-truthing recharge datasets are necessary to properly evaluate subbasin-scale models

chunks.text: The USGS recharge product is based on empirical regressions fitted at basin scale, which likely explains why agreement is better when data are aggregated. Applying these basin-scale relationships to 800 m pixels can break the scale-dependent relationships, contributing to poor pixel-scale agreement in recharge and ET patterns.
supporting_quote: The USGS recharge and ET products are based on regression equations fitted with data at a basin scale, which might explain why the agreement between model estimates occurs at larger scales.
When these equations were used to obtain recharge and ET values at the fine 800 m scale, the relationships found at the basin scale by the regression equations were not necessarily preserved.

chunks.text: Baseflow was used as a calibration proxy for groundwater processes, but the paper notes limitations of baseflow for resolving fine-scale recharge behavior. While baseflow may be adequate at coarser regional scales, it may not reliably constrain subbasin-scale process representation without additional recharge measurements.
supporting_quote: While using baseflow as a proxy for groundwater recharge might be adequate for coarser scales (regional or larger), there are limitations in using baseflow data to resolve processes at finer scales.
Baseflow was estimated using PART

chunks.text: Baseflow calibration performance (NSE) was sensitive to outliers due to the short annual record used for evaluation. The authors note that the year 2009, the wettest year, strongly influenced NSE because the annual baseflow series contains only 11 points, illustrating statistical fragility in performance metrics for short time series.
supporting_quote: The reason for these low NSE values is that baseflow predictions for the year 2009 (the wettest in the period of analysis) deviated significantly
because the time series contains only 11 points, the NSE value is highly penalized by this outlier.

chunks.text: SWAT and the USGS empirical recharge product agree well at the basin scale for 2000–2013, but show notable disagreement at 800 m resolution. The weak pixel-scale correlations in both dry and wet years and large RMSE values indicate that fine-scale recharge mapping remains uncertain. The findings suggest basin-fitted empirical equations may not transfer reliably to smaller spatial scales.
supporting_quote: The two datasets exhibited good agreement (NSE = 0.84, R2 = 0.83) at the basin scale.
There is a weak correlation (R2 = 0.16 for the driest year, and R2 = 0.29 for the wettest year)
These results suggest that the application of the empirical equations derived by Reitz et al. (2017) at the basin scale might not be valid at lower scales.

chunks.text: Seasonal analysis indicates recharge is concentrated in winter and spring when soils are wetter, and that soil moisture conditions modulate how precipitation and evapotranspiration translate into recharge. In summer and fall, low soil water content coincides with recharge near zero even when net water flux increases. This points to soil moisture as a key control for seasonal recharge dynamics in the basin.
supporting_quote: recharge occurred mainly from December to May
The period from December to May also coincides with high values of soil water content.
during this period (June–November)... recharge remains constant at values near zero.
The result highlights that soil moisture helps to determine the extent to which PCP-ET influences groundwater recharge.

chunks.text: The study emphasizes the need for more direct recharge measurements at finer spatial and temporal scales to calibrate and validate models intended for subbasin-level applications. It suggests that ground-truthing is essential to evaluate competing recharge estimates and to reduce uncertainty in fine-scale predictions, potentially aided by targeted benchmarking field sites and probabilistic approaches.
supporting_quote: we do point out the need for groundwater recharge data at finer spatial and temporal scales to better calibrate and verify recharge models.
In general, more direct recharge measurements are needed to validate hydrologic models that aim to resolve processes at subbasin scales.
probabilistic models could be developed to provide a range of values for recharge estimates.

chunks.text: Precipitation phase partitioning (e.g., rain, snow, sleet, hail) is a key variable for hydrology, climate science, and water management because it controls water storage and release dynamics. Climate change is increasing the importance of monitoring phase transitions to better assess flood/drought risks and impacts on terrestrial water storage. Existing monitoring approaches include threshold meteorology methods and sophisticated remote sensing instruments, but coverage and resolution gaps remain, especially in complex terrain.
supporting_quote: “PRECIPITATION phase partitioning is the classification of various types of precipitation, such as rain, snow, sleet, and hail”
“With climate change and its impacts on precipitation patterns… accurately monitoring precipitation phase transitions is increasingly important to assess flood and drought risks”

chunks.text: Acoustic sensing has emerged as a non-invasive, cost-effective option for environmental monitoring, including rainfall detection and snow sensing. A common approach is to extract Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), which compactly represent the short-term spectral envelope on a perceptual Mel scale. MFCCs have been broadly used for acoustic classification tasks and are noted to often outperform other acoustic features in such settings.
supporting_quote: “Recently, acoustic detection in environmental monitoring has gained significant attention”
“MFCCs are features widely used in audio signal processing that represent the short-term power spectrum of a sound, based on a perceptual scale that mimics the human ear”

chunks.text: IoT growth has increased demand for running machine learning directly on edge devices to reduce latency and bandwidth costs compared with cloud offloading. Edge analytics can enable real-time classification using lightweight models on constrained hardware. This motivates embedding precipitation-phase inference directly on sensor nodes for remote deployments.
supporting_quote: “The significant growth of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has enabled and intensified demand for ML and computing at the edge”
“Instead of offloading sensor data to the cloud (which adds latency and bandwidth costs), emerging approaches run ML inference locally on devices”

chunks.text: The paper aims to build an integrated, low-power edge device that performs real-time precipitation phase prediction from precipitation acoustics. The system combines on-device MFCC feature extraction with lightweight ML (SVM/RF) and supports near-real-time reporting. It is also designed to integrate additional meteorological sensors needed for snow hydrology studies.
supporting_quote: “we propose a novel multimodal wireless acoustic system that leverages a support vector machine (SVM) classifier and MFCC feature extraction on the edge device to provide real-time multitype precipitation phase prediction”

“we present the design, fabrication, and validation of the Advanced Unified Rainfall and Atmospheric Monitoring (AURA) system, integrating sensors for temperature, humidity, ultrasonic snow depth, solar radiation, and wind velocity”

chunks.text: A central goal is to make MFCC computation feasible on microcontrollers by reducing memory and computation requirements of the Mel filter bank. The authors target storing compact Mel filter representations in program memory and computing filter outputs efficiently at runtime. This enables the full DSP+ML pipeline to run on the ATmega 2560.
supporting_quote: “To address the intense memory and computational needs for MFCC extraction, we introduce two lightweight methods for applying Mel filters”
“both of which are stored in the program memory of microcontrollers, such as the AVR family”

chunks.text: The work also targets a remote-ready communications design using LPWAN and satellite uplink. A LoRa star topology with TDMA is used to avoid collisions and reduce power, and an Iridium-enabled gateway provides reliable transfer from remote sites. The objective is scalable deployment in mountainous regions with near-real-time transmissions.
supporting_quote: “The low-power AURA network uses a long range (LoRa) star topology with time-division multiple access (TDMA) and an Iridium gateway for reliable data transfer from remote sites.”
“The AURA system is designed for deployment in mountainous regions.”

chunks.text: Conventional precipitation phase detection methods struggle near freezing conditions, where phase transitions are ambiguous, and are not well suited for widespread deployment in remote terrain due to practical constraints. The paper highlights cost, size, and power limitations as major barriers. This motivates a low-cost, low-power distributed sensing approach.
supporting_quote: “conventional methods struggle to distinguish precipitation phase near freezing”
“unsuitable for distributed deployment in remote, complex terrain due to cost, size, and power constraints”

chunks.text: Implementing MFCC extraction on microcontrollers is constrained by limited RAM, because applying many Mel filters to an N-point DFT implies a large filter-bank matrix. The required storage for a full P×(N/2+1) filter bank can exceed available memory. This necessitates alternative representations that avoid storing the full matrix in RAM.
supporting_quote: “MFCC extraction is constrained by RAM limitations. Applying P Mel filters to an N-point DFT requires a matrix of size R^{P × ((N/2)+1)}, often exceeding available memory.”
“the lookup table approach requires R^{30 × 257} and the linear approach fits in R^{30 × 7}”

chunks.text: Remote mountainous deployments face energy limitations, especially in winter when solar irradiance can be low for extended periods. Limited solar charging can hinder continuous operation. The system therefore needs strategies to reduce duty cycle and wake only when precipitation is likely.
supporting_quote: “Under harsh mountainous conditions and snow, limited solar irradiance during extended winter periods can hinder battery charging.”
“The system applies a dew point threshold to opportunistically wake and record audio only when conditions suggest a high likelihood of precipitation.”

chunks.text: AURA is an embedded sensing platform built around an ATmega2560 microcontroller (16 MHz) that runs audio sampling, STFT/MFCC feature extraction, ML inference, LoRa communication, and scheduling. The board includes RTC timestamps and micro-SD storage, along with power distribution switches to manage peripheral power. The design supports both leaf nodes and a gateway configuration.
supporting_quote: “The 5-V ATmega2560 MCU clocked at 16 MHz runs the trained ML algorithm, signal processing… LoRa communication, and scheduling tasks.”
“The AURA board adopts a DS3231 RTC chip and an SD card socket.”

chunks.text: Audio is sampled on the microcontroller at 24 kHz in 8-bit ADC mode and recorded for 10 seconds per event, saved as uncompressed PCM in WAV format to the SD card. The 24 kHz rate captures frequencies up to 12 kHz per Nyquist. This audio becomes the input for on-device STFT and MFCC computation.
supporting_quote: “sampling rate of 24 kHz (8-bit ADC mode), accurately capturing frequencies… (12 kHz)”
“The audio is recorded… for a time length of 10 s… written to the SD card in the Waveform Audio (WAV) File Format”

chunks.text: The DSP pipeline computes an STFT over overlapping 512-sample frames (powers of two for radix-2 DFT) using a Hamming window to reduce spectral leakage. MFCCs are derived from the power spectrum |X(m,k)|^2 filtered by a Mel filter bank, followed by log energies and DCT. The system retains the first 13 MFCC coefficients and averages them over time for ML input.
supporting_quote: “Hamming window function… To reduce the spectral leakage”
“In this work, we compute the first 13 MFCCs on the edge device (ATmega 2560 MCU)”

chunks.text: The paper implements two memory-efficient Mel filter bank methods for microcontrollers: (1) storing a precomputed filter weight lookup table in program memory, and (2) storing a compact linear (slope-intercept) representation for each triangular Mel filter. The linear method computes filter weights on the fly using stored parameters, reducing storage from a 30×257 table to 30×7 parameters. Both approaches avoid large RAM allocations for the filter bank.
supporting_quote: “we implement two novel memory-efficient methods: 1) a lookup table storing precomputed filter weights… and 2) a multiplication-based… linear model”
“we apply 30 Mel filters and a 512-point DFT… the lookup table approach requires R^{30 × 257} and the linear approach fits in R^{30 × 7}”

chunks.text: Noise robustness of the MFCC-DFT pipeline is evaluated by generating a synthetic five-tone, 10-second signal (2, 4, 6, 8, 10 kHz) sampled at 24 kHz and injecting white Gaussian noise at controlled SNRs. The baseline is set at 45 dB to respect 8-bit WAV quantization limits, and SNR is verified via signal and noise power calculations. MFCC degradation is quantified using mean absolute coefficient differences and Euclidean distances relative to the baseline.
supporting_quote: “We synthesize a five-tone sequence with frequencies f_i ∈ {2, 4, 6, 8, 10} kHz, sampled at f_s = 24 kHz for a total duration of T = 10 s.”
“we select A_p ≈ 0.57 to result in a 45-dB SNR as the baseline reference… We then inject different noise levels”

chunks.text: Two lightweight classifiers are trained on MFCC features for precipitation categorization: random forest and linear-kernel SVM, evaluated with leave-one-out cross-validation. Models are trained on a computer and ported to the Arduino environment as header files for on-board inference. The selection for the prototype emphasizes memory footprint, favoring the SVM implementation.
supporting_quote: “Leave-oneout cross-validation (LOO-CV) is used for verification”
“The SVM shows the lowest memory footprint among ML models and higher accuracy than RF”

chunks.text: The IoT network uses a LoRa star topology with a TDMA protocol to prevent packet collisions and reduce power use. A gateway node (ID 0) transmits sync packets and collects data from leaf nodes during assigned time slots with guard periods. The gateway forwards aggregated data through a RockBlock Iridium 9603 modem using Iridium Short-Burst Data.
supporting_quote: “The LoRa network is based on a star topology with AURA nodes transmitting to a central Iridium-enabled gateway”
“The TDMA protocol… controls the wireless node communication by dividing time into fixed intervals, ensuring accurate data transmission while preventing LoRa packet collisions”

chunks.text: The study uses both simulated precipitation acoustics and real environmental recordings collected during Winter 2025 to train and validate models. Environmental recordings are labeled by precipitation category and include mixed precipitation, rain, snow, and a no-precipitation/noise class. These datasets support assessing performance differences between synthetic and real-world acoustics.
supporting_quote: “we have developed both simulated precipitation acoustics datasets and collected real (naturally occurring) precipitation acoustic data during Winter 2025.”
“Environmental audio files with 83 samples for Mixed Precip., 62 samples for rain, 101 samples for snow, and 70 samples for WGN”

chunks.text: Field validation data were collected in a campus deployment in Burlington, Vermont, in May 2025, with a measurement interval of every 10 minutes over 66.5 hours. The deployment recorded acoustic predictions and meteorological variables including sonar distance, solar radiation proxy, temperature, relative humidity, and wind velocity. This dataset served as a proof-of-concept for integrated sensing and on-device inference.
supporting_quote: “The sensor leaf node was deployed on the UVM campus in Burlington, Vermont, in May 2025, with a measurement interval set to every 10 min.”
“The AURA system was deployed for 66.5 h (2.77 days) in a controlled environment to validate its performance.”

chunks.text: Acoustic data collection for training uses an Enviro DIY Mayfly board to record 8-bit audio from a MAX9814 microphone placed in an aluminum conical chamber. A Raspberry Pi 3B+ triggers recording and logs weather data via a local API, while a nearby Google Nest camera provides visual context for labeling. This setup supports synchronized audio capture and ground-truth assignment.
supporting_quote: “An Enviro DIY Mayfly board is utilized to record 8-bit audio from a MAX9814 microphone (40 dB AGC) in a conical chamber made from aluminum.”
“A Raspberry Pi 3B+ is connected… to trigger recording and logging weather data from a local API… Google Nest camera… for data labeling (ground truth).”

chunks.text: Calibration datasets were collected for the ultrasonic snow-depth sensor by moving MB7060 sensors through known distances from 30 cm to 2.55 m in 15 cm steps and recording voltages. Linear regressions map voltage to time-of-flight, and temperature-dependent speed of sound is used for distance computations. Illuminance sensor calibration uses seven lighting conditions against a reference light meter.
supporting_quote: “MB7060 sensors are placed and moved at known distances (d) in 15-cm increments ranging from 30 cm to 2.55 m”
“The light sensor and its voltage are calibrated against an MT-912 light meter under seven different light conditions”

chunks.text: On simulated precipitation acoustics, both models achieve very high testing accuracy. Random forest reaches 97.35% testing accuracy, while the SVM reaches 98.07%. These results demonstrate that MFCC features with lightweight classifiers can separate precipitation classes effectively in controlled synthetic conditions.
supporting_quote: “RF model achieves testing accuracy of 97.35% on simulated precipitation acoustics”
“The SVM classifier achieves 98.07% accuracy on simulated acoustics”

chunks.text: On consolidated-class (CC) environmental recordings, the system attains mid-80% accuracy, indicating a performance drop from simulations to real-world audio. Random forest achieves 85.67% and SVM achieves 85.99% accuracy under these conditions. This suggests real environmental variability and noise make the task harder but still feasible on-device.
supporting_quote: “85.67% in consolidated class (CC) environmental recordings”
“85.99% on CC environmental recordings”

chunks.text: Memory profiling shows the linear-model Mel filter approach and SVM provide the smallest combined DSP+ML footprint on the ATmega2560. SVM+LM uses 65.10 kB flash (26.25%) and about 3.93 kB RAM (~49%), whereas RF-based options consume substantially more flash. These results justify selecting SVM for the prototype while keeping RF feasible if more flash is available.
supporting_quote: “SVM+LM uses 65.10 kB (26.25%), the smallest overall”
“RF+LM and RF+LUT require 156.12 kB (62.95%) and 184.61 kB (74.44%), respectively”

chunks.text: Power profiling indicates the board’s peak active consumption varies by operating state, with LoRa TX/RX and satellite TX drawing the most. Deep sleep draws 260 µA, and low-voltage-disconnect mode drops to 140 µA. A battery-life estimate suggests about 15.2 days operation without solar under an average 20.2 mA draw (ideal conditions).
supporting_quote: “In deep sleep operation mode, only the MCU draws 260- μA current. In the LVD mode, the current drops to 140 μA”
“with an average current draw of 20.2 mA, the device should run for approximately 15.2 days without solar panels”

chunks.text: Quantization analysis sets an upper bound on SNR for 8-bit WAV audio and guides the baseline for noise-robustness tests. The theoretical maximum SNR is about 49.92 dB for 8-bit PCM at normalized peak amplitude 1. The authors choose a baseline around 45 dB by setting peak amplitude near 0.57.
supporting_quote: “With b = 8… this yields a maximum SNR of 49.92 dB.”
“we select A_p ≈ 0.57 to result in a 45-dB SNR as the baseline reference”

chunks.text: Noise robustness analysis finds MFCC 1 deviates the most under additive white Gaussian noise, while higher-order coefficients remain more stable. Euclidean distance to the baseline decreases as SNR increases, showing expected feature stabilization at lower noise levels. This provides guidance for potentially excluding noise-sensitive coefficients in future models.
supporting_quote: “MFCC 1 shows the greatest deviation across noise levels.”
“presents a descending mean Euclidean distance from baseline as SNR value increases”

chunks.text: A campus field deployment validates integrated sensing and on-device inference over 66.5 hours. Sonar measurements averaged about 1.75 m, which is 2.78% lower than a 1.8 m reference, indicating generally stable operation. During this deployment, no frozen precipitation was observed, so snow/hail performance could not be validated in situ.
supporting_quote: “deployed for 66.5 h (2.77 days)… Sonar… averaging approximately 1.75 m, 2.78% lower than the reference value of 1.8 m.”
“No frozen form of precipitation (i.e., hail or snow) was observed during the deployment course.”

chunks.text: In the May 2025 field deployment, SVM-based classification identified three states: no precipitation (WGN), rain, and mixed precipitation. The predictions were reported as aligning with visually observed events and historic weather timing, supporting the viability of on-device ML. A separate station-based comparison for precipitation vs. non-precipitation yielded 72.73% correct detections after timestamp adjustments.
supporting_quote: “SVM-based precipitation classification… identified three weather states: no precipitation (WGN), rain, and mixed precipitation”
“In total, 72.73% of events are correctly detected.”

chunks.text: The paper attributes prediction mismatches partly to non-collocation between the deployed sensor and the ground-truth weather station, so precipitation may differ spatially. This limits the interpretability of station-based validation for a specific sensor location. The authors frame this comparison mainly as proof-of-concept.
supporting_quote: “the ground truth weather station is not collocated with the deployed system”
“Due to spatial variability and distance from the weather station, the comparison mainly serves as proof-of-concept.”

chunks.text: Hardware acoustics can limit sensitivity for certain precipitation regimes. The authors note that the aluminum cone produced weak acoustic responses to light rain because rigid walls dampened small droplet impacts. They propose redesigning the resonance structure to improve sensitivity.
supporting_quote: “the aluminum cone produced weak acoustic responses to light rain, as its rigid walls dampened small droplet impacts.”
“A redesigned pyramid structure with transparent, flexible sheets is proposed to improve sensitivity.”

chunks.text: Model generalization is limited by the size and diversity of the training dataset. The authors state that the model was trained on a limited dataset, which can reduce robustness across conditions. They plan to collect additional verified events with a Parsivel2 disdrometer to improve ground-truth quality and expand training data.
supporting_quote: “the model was trained on a limited dataset, reducing generalization.”

chunks.text: Low-gradient coastal regions are vulnerable to both heavy precipitation flooding and storm-surge flooding, and their combination can produce compound flooding impacts. Sea level rise and projected increases in tropical cyclone rainfall are expected to increase the likelihood and severity of extreme coastal flooding. chunks.text: Compound coastal flooding is defined as flooding where inland processes (fluvial/pluvial) and coastal processes (storm surge, tides, etc.) jointly contribute to impacts. Prior work indicates that coupling inland hydrologic models and coastal circulation models can improve flood depth and extent estimates in compound-flood-prone areas. chunks.text: The NextGen Water Resources Modeling framework was designed for model interoperability via the Basic Model Interface (BMI), enabling different hydrologic and related models to interact within one system. chunks.text: The study develops a new BMI wrapper for the GeoClaw coastal model and uses it to couple GeoClaw with the National Water Model Conceptual Functional Equivalent (CFE) hydrologic model through the NextGen framework. chunks.text: A practical goal is to show that NextGen can support coupled hydrologic and hydrodynamic analyses in coastal regions by running GeoClaw within the NextGen ecosystem and connecting it to inland discharge outputs. chunks.text: Accurately representing compound flooding in low-gradient coastal regions requires accounting for mutual interactions between river discharge and storm surge. Without coupled modeling, water levels can be misrepresented in coastal watersheds that experience both drivers during extreme storms.

chunks.text: Within NextGen, the absence of a coastal/ocean-hydrodynamics BMI prevented direct coupling of coastal surge models with hydrologic models. chunks.text: Coastal regions face increasing flood hazard when multiple drivers such as rainfall, river discharge, storm surge, wind, and low pressure co-occur. chunks.text: Hydrodynamic flood model accuracy is sensitive to terrain representation through DEMs. Even with modern InSAR and LiDAR, DEMs retain uncertainties, particularly in representing underwater bathymetry and in urban areas where vegetation, defenses, and built structures create artifacts. Many DEM improvement techniques exist (e.g., hydro-flattening, burning, subgrid correction), but they can miss opportunities to incorporate local ground-truth surveys.

chunks.text: Grid discretization also controls accuracy and computational cost in 2D hydrodynamic modeling. Curvilinear grids can align with channel flow and reduce nodes but struggle with complex geometries; unstructured triangular meshes are flexible but may not align with flow direction and can impose small time steps when elongated. Hybrid meshes combine structured and unstructured elements and have been reported to improve accuracy and efficiency, yet are rarely applied to compound coastal flood assessments due to generation complexity.
supporting_quote: two-dimensional horizontal hydrodynamic models employ two common methods... structured, boundary-fitted curvilinear and unstructured triangular mesh.

chunks.text: The study’s main goal is to quantify how DEM correction and mesh generation choices affect compound coastal flood simulation accuracy and efficiency. The authors propose a mesh tailored to topobathymetry and flood dynamics, and evaluate how using corrected terrain data changes results. chunks.text: The research demonstrates the use of locally accurate cross-sectional survey data to produce realistic DEM improvements for urban river channels. This is intended to reduce uncertainty in simulated inundation depth and extent maps for decision-making.

chunks.text: In metropolitan coastal regions, model setups often emphasize bays and deep channels while overlooking smaller upstream tributaries that strongly affect urban flooding. chunks.text: The application performs SAR-based flood extraction using change detection between pre- and post-flood Sentinel-1 imagery, computing two indices: Normalized Difference Flood Index (NDFI) and Difference Image Index (DII). A threshold is applied to each SAR index image using a mean ± kf times standard deviation rule. Flood pixels are identified using a minus sign for NDFI (below threshold) and a plus sign for DII (above threshold), and the final flood map is produced by merging NDFI and DII results.
supporting_quote: calculates the Normalized Difference Flood Index (NDFI) and the Difference Image Index (DII)
Thr = mean(SAR \ Index \ Image) \pm k_f \times stdev(SAR \ Index \ Image)
The ultimate flood map is then derived by merging the final NDFI and DII flood maps

chunks.text: To improve SAR threshold selection, the tool can run an automated sensitivity analysis that iteratively tests different kf values and compares SAR-derived flood maps to an optical flood map derived from Sentinel-2. Optical flooding is extracted using the Modified Normalized Difference Water Index (MNDWI) with a default threshold (0.4). The sensitivity analysis chooses kf values that maximize Total Agreement (intersection over union) between SAR and optical flood extents.
supporting_quote: includes an automated sensitivity analysis algorithm that identifies optimal threshold values using flood maps derived from available optical data
MNDWI = (Green Band - SWIR Band) / (Green Band + SWIR Band)

This creates a need for drought- and low-flow-specific validation in the Colorado River Basin.
supporting_quote: Because of complexity of the interactions between deeper groundwater and surface water and the simplified treatment in WRF-Hydro (Broda et al. 2013)
the evaluation was limited to a single season (May–August 2015) and limited in its exploration of watershed and stream characteristics.

chunks.text: The study compares NWM retrospective streamflow to USGS observations using relative streamflow (percentiles) and goodness-of-fit metrics. GOF includes R^2, percent bias (PBIAS), and Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE), computed with hydroGOF. Metrics are summarized by water year (Oct 1–Sep 30) from 1994–2015 to characterize annual and seasonal performance.
supporting_quote: Relative streamflow values were compared between modeled and observed records
These measures include: coefficient of determination or  R^2 , Percent Bias (PBIAS), and Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE).
Both measures of GOF and low flow events were summarized by water year (October 1–September 30) from 1994 to 2015.

chunks.text: Low-flow events are defined using a monthly 7Q10 threshold calculated separately for modeled and observed datasets. Hourly modeled streamflow is aggregated to daily mean, and monthly low-flow thresholds are computed to reflect seasonality. Separate thresholds are used to avoid masking differences due to systematic modeled-vs-observed bias and to identify abnormally low flow relative to the same season.
supporting_quote: modeled streamflow data were aggregated from an hourly to a daily mean streamflow
The 7Q10 statistic represents the minimum seven-day average discharge with a nonexceedance probability of 10% (or recurrence interval of 10 years).
Separate thresholds were calculated for gaged streamflow and modeled streamflow to reduce the effects of potential systematic differences between the gaged and modeled streamflow records.

chunks.text: Drought severity is classified using the U.S. Drought Monitor Index, aggregated into two categories: low-moderate (No drought, D0, D1) and severe-exceptional (D2–D4). Years are assigned based on dominant drought coverage in Upper and Lower basin aggregates. Model performance is then contrasted between these drought classes.
supporting_quote: For simplicity, these classes are aggregated into two classes as follows: low-moderate = No drought, D0 and D1, and severe-exceptional = D2, D3 and D4.
Years were classified as either low-moderate drought or severe to exceptional drought, depending on the dominant coverage of drought severity.

chunks.text: To link performance to watershed characteristics, Pearson correlations are computed between GOF and continuous basin attributes from GAGES II, and ANOVA is used for categorical variables. Categorical tests include dominant geology (sedimentary vs nonsedimentary), Upper vs Lower basin, and drought severity. This approach screens which attributes may indicate better suitability of NWM streamflow for low-flow and drought analysis.
supporting_quote: Pearson's correlation, or r, was calculated between measures of GOF and the continuous variables
The influence of categorical variables (Dominant Geology Type, Upper vs. Lower subbasin, and drought severity), were evaluated using a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA).

chunks.text: Modeled streamflow comes from a nearly 24-year NWM v1.0 retrospective simulation spanning Jan 1, 1993 to Oct 31, 2016, without streamflow data assimilation. Analysis is restricted to Colorado River Basin stream segments with Strahler order at least 3. The period used for annual summaries is water years 1994–2015.
supporting_quote: Historical modeled streamflow data were obtained from a nearly 24-year retrospective simulation (from January 1, 1993 to October 31, 2016) of the NWM (version 1.0).
the retrospective simulation does not include any data assimilation for streamflow
Stream segments were limited to those within the CRB with a Strahler stream order ≥3.

chunks.text: Observed streamflow is taken from USGS gages over the same period, matched to NHD stream segments, with basin characteristics from GAGES II. After filtering for missing observations and GAGES II availability, 179 matched gages are retained for evaluation. The set includes 112 gages in the Upper basin and 67 in the Lower basin, with many having major dams upstream.
supporting_quote: Historical streamflow data were obtained from USGS gage locations during the same time period
After eliminating locations with missing observations or those not included in the GAGES II dataset, a total of 179 matches remained for evaluation.
112 gages are located in the Upper CRB (78 of which have at least one major dam upstream of the gage) and 67 gages are located in the Lower CRB (39 of which have at least one major dam upstream).

chunks.text: Watershed and riparian attributes used to interpret performance include climate, hydrology, geomorphology, development, and infrastructure measures from GAGES II. Anthropogenic disturbance is summarized using the Hydrologic Disturbance Index (HDI), ranging from 2 to 42, with higher values indicating greater human impact. In this dataset, mean HDI differs between subbasins (13.6 Upper vs 8 Lower).
supporting_quote: The Hydrologic Disturbance Index (HDI) is used to quantify the cumulative impact of anthropogenic disturbance surrounding each stream gage
HDI ranges from 2 to 42, with higher values indicating a greater anthropogenic impact.
HDI is higher in the Upper CRB than the Lower CRB (an average HDI of 13.6 compared to 8).

chunks.text: Across 3,938 stream-years (179 sites over 22 years), NWM relative streamflow shows a wide range of performance but is generally well correlated with observations. KGE indicates relatively good structural agreement in percentiles, while PBIAS is centered near zero, implying roughly balanced over- and under-estimation across stream-years. Seasonal patterns differ by subbasin when summarized monthly.
supporting_quote: 3,938 stream-years were compared (179 locations multiplied by 22 years) over the period of 1994–2015.
Generally, relative streamflow values are well correlated, and the KGE indicates relatively good matches in structure
The PBIAS is centered nearly around zero

chunks.text: Seasonal goodness-of-fit differs between Upper and Lower basins. In the Upper basin, performance improves in summer months with better correlation, lower bias, and higher KGE, while the Lower basin shows the opposite pattern with lower summer correlations and efficiencies and greater biases. The paper attributes these contrasts to differing dominant hydrologic drivers, especially snowmelt influence in the Upper basin.
supporting_quote: For the Upper CRB, the model is generally better correlated, less biased, and has greater KGE during the summer months than the rest of the year.
In contrast, the Lower CRB exhibits lower correlations, greater biases, and lower efficiencies in the summer months.
the Upper CRB is largely influenced by snowmelt processes, whereas the Lower CRB streamflows may be more influenced by other hydrologic processes

chunks.text: Low-flow comparisons indicate NWM tends to underestimate low streamflows in multiple ways across the basin. The model often yields fewer low-flow events than USGS, fewer years with at least one low-flow event, and fewer sites flagged with low flows. Several of these differences are statistically significant (p values around 0.02 and below 0.01).
supporting_quote: there are many sites and years when the NWM underestimated the number of low flow events compared to the USGS record
The difference between low frequency by site (averaged from 1994 to 2015) is significant (p = 0.02).
The difference in number of years with a low flow is significant (p < 0.01) and the difference in number of locations with low flows is significant (p = 0.02).

chunks.text: The onset of low-flow conditions (measured as first day-of-year with a low-flow event) is often later in NWM than in observations. This is reflected by many negative USGS–NWM differences for first occurrence. The difference in first occurrence timing is significant when aggregated by site (p < 0.01), though not significant by year (p = 0.11).
supporting_quote: The first occurrence of a low flow event ... is often later in the NWM, resulting in many negative differences
The difference in first occurrence of a low flow is significant by site (p < 0.01) but not by year (p = 0.11)

chunks.text: Watershed characteristics most associated with better GOF are higher precipitation, higher snow fraction, higher baseflow index, and higher elevation, which show the strongest positive correlations with R^2 and KGE (r about 0.41 to 0.59). Basin temperature shows a strong negative relationship with these measures (reported as 0.57). PBIAS relationships with basin attributes are generally weaker.
supporting_quote: Basin precipitation, snow percent, baseflow index, and basin elevation have the strongest positive correlations with R^2 and KGE values (r values between 0.41 and 0.59), whereas basin temperatures are negatively correlated with these measures (0.57).
Relationships between these (and other) characteristics and PBIAS are much weaker

chunks.text: Categorical comparisons show no significant performance difference between sedimentary and nonsedimentary geology types, likely due to limited representation of other geology categories. In contrast, Upper vs Lower basin membership is significant for R^2 and KGE, and nearly significant for PBIAS (p = 0.068), with the Upper basin showing better average GOF.
supporting_quote: Because of the low representation of other geology types, we simply compared sedimentary to nonsedimentary and found no significant difference
the levels of the Upper and Lower CRB are significant for R^2 and KGE (and nearly significant (p = 0.068) for PBIAS), with the Upper CRB having better mean values of GOF than the Lower CRB.

chunks.text: Model performance differs by drought severity, with worse GOF during severe-exceptional drought years. In the Upper basin, PBIAS is four times greater (20% vs 5%) and KGE is lower during severe-exceptional drought years; similar degradation (higher PBIAS, lower KGE) occurs in the Lower basin. R^2 does not significantly differ between drought categories.
supporting_quote: In the Upper CRB, model performance is worse during severe-exceptional drought conditions: PBIAS is four times greater (20% compared to 5%) and KGE is lower
For the Lower CRB, PBIAS is also greater and KGE is lower years dominated by severe-exceptional during drought indices than during low-moderate years.
There are no significant differences in  R^2  values between periods of severe or low drought indices.

chunks.text: Low-flow underestimation also varies with drought severity and subbasin. In the Upper basin, severe-exceptional drought years show much larger underestimation of low-flow events (over 40 fewer events per year on average) than low-moderate years (about 5 fewer). In the Lower basin, underestimation is larger during low-moderate years (about 25 fewer) than severe-exceptional years (about 9 fewer).
supporting_quote: The number of low flows that occurred during years with severe-exceptional drought were more heavily underestimated in the Upper CRB (on average, over 40 fewer events per year) than during years with low-moderate drought (on average, 5 fewer events per year).

low flow events during low-moderate droughts are more heavily underestimated (on average, 25 fewer events per year) than during years with severe-exceptional droughts (on average, 9 fewer events per year).

chunks.text: The authors note that performance variability across space and seasons can affect how and where modeled streamflow products should be used. Despite the Upper basin having higher disturbance and more dams on average, model fit is generally better there, suggesting the model captures snowpack-driven hydrology more reliably. The Lower basin appears to need improvements where flows are less tied to snowmelt processes.
supporting_quote: Performance of the modeled streamflow produced by the NWM retrospective analysis showed major variation within the CRB and on a seasonal basis.
it is interesting to note that the degree of development ... is greater ... for the Upper CRB ... yet the GOF is generally better.
In the Lower CRB, however, there is an apparent need for improvement where flows are more removed from snowpack/snowmelt-related processes.

chunks.text: The paper warns that overestimating streamflow during droughts and underestimating low-flow frequency/extent could yield overly optimistic information for forecasting and planning. Such bias could lead to inadequate management strategies and underestimation of historical drought impacts. Accurate estimation is emphasized as particularly important in a water-stressed basin like the Colorado River Basin.
supporting_quote: Overestimating streamflow during droughts and underestimating the frequency and extent of low flows may lead to overly optimistic forecasts.
there is a risk of underestimating the impacts of past droughts.
In areas that are as water-stressed as the CRB, it is especially important to accurately estimate streamflow

chunks.text: Low-flow event records depend on the threshold definition, and the authors caution that threshold choice should match stream type and application. They also note opportunities to extend analyses using ecological perspectives, such as habitat-specific thresholds. This frames low-flow detection as a methodological sensitivity that can influence conclusions.
supporting_quote: the record of low flow events may vary depending on the definition of low flow threshold.
Definitions of low flow need to be considered carefully and a particular threshold may be more appropriate for some streams or applications than others.
including linking information about the unique habitat and ecological needs of a stream network to determine thresholds.

chunks.text: Because many basin attributes are intercorrelated (e.g., temperature and elevation), the paper cautions that broader analyses beyond the Colorado River Basin are needed to isolate drivers of poor performance. This limits causal interpretation of attribute–performance relationships from the current study alone. The authors suggest further evaluation across more varied conditions to identify key physical and climate contributors.
supporting_quote: some of these characteristics are strongly related to others (e.g., temperature and elevation)
further analysis across more widely varying conditions than those in the CRB will help identify which physical and climate characteristics may be contributing most to poor model performance.

chunks.text: The retrospective NWM evaluation provides a baseline for judging improvements in future model versions, especially for drought and low-flow applications. The authors recommend running similar analyses on future retrospective simulations to verify improvements, particularly in areas less influenced by snowmelt and during severe droughts. They also emphasize that retrospective simulations can enhance understanding of historical streamflow where observations are incomplete.
supporting_quote: Evaluation of retrospective NWM data provides a useful baseline for comparisons of updated iterations of the model.

we recommend exploring future retrospective simulations in a similar manner to ensure improvements, particularly in areas that are less directly influenced by snowmelt processes and during periods of severe droughts.
Retrospective simulations have the potential to also enhance understanding of historical streamflow, especially in areas where historical observations are incomplete or unavailable.

chunks.text: Overall, comparisons indicate NWM underestimates low-flow frequency, timing, and spatial/temporal extent in the Colorado River Basin, with performance depending on drought severity and watershed characteristics. Better performance is associated with the Upper basin and basins with higher precipitation, snow percent, baseflow index, and elevation. These findings highlight where model development and application should focus to avoid misleading drought and low-flow assessments.
supporting_quote: these comparisons suggest that the NWM is underestimating low streamflows in the CRB on a variety of measures.
We found model performance to be more accurate for the Upper CRB and at sites with higher precipitation, snow percent, baseflow index, and elevations.
This highlights characteristics on which to focus future model development efforts.

chunks.text: Remote sensing is increasingly used to observe and monitor geohazards after extreme events, including wildfires, because it can measure surficial changes over large spatial and temporal extents. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) is particularly useful as an active sensor with near all-weather capability and frequent repeat acquisitions, enabling deformation monitoring with interferometric methods. Differential InSAR (DInSAR) methods have been widely applied to slow deformation phenomena and can extend monitoring to locations without in situ instruments.
supporting_quote: One of the most significant applications of remote sensing is the observation and monitoring of geohazards following extreme events.
SAR is an active sensor, providing its own energy source that allows for measurement at any time of day
DInSAR has been applied primarily to geophysical phenomena where associated ground changes are slow

chunks.text: Wildfires can disrupt hillslope hydrology and mechanics, increasing short-term hazards like debris flows and flooding and longer-term hazards such as shallow landslides. Short-term effects include reduced interception and evapotranspiration and potential hydrophobic soil layers, increasing runoff. Over several years, root degradation can reduce slope reinforcement and create preferential flow pathways that contribute to instability.
supporting_quote: Wildfires pose a significant threat to the natural and built environment and may alter the hydrologic cycle
burning of vegetation (trees and groundcover) reduces water interception and evapotranspiration, and the burned material may create a hydrophobic layer
the degradation of the root systems, which act to anchor the slope, can lead to instability

chunks.text: The 2017 Eagle Creek Fire in Oregon burned about 200 km2 in a steep, landslide-prone basalt terrain with thick Douglas Fir forests and many debris-flow-active drainages. The central region including the Tanner Creek basin was among the most severely burned, with estimated vegetation recovery times of 5–10 years. These site characteristics create both elevated post-fire hazard potential and an opportunity for radar-based monitoring where canopy loss exposes the ground surface.
supporting_quote: burning an estimated 200 km2
Bedrock geology at the site is predominantly basalt belonging to the Grande Ronde and Northwest Cascade Volcanoes formations
the central region, comprising the Eagle Creek and Tanner Creek drainage basins, was the most severely burned area with an estimated ground vegetation recovery time ... of 5–10 years

chunks.text: The study evaluates whether SBAS-DInSAR can be used to interpret post-wildfire ground-surface elevation change in the Tanner Creek drainage basin after the 2017 Eagle Creek Fire. It aims to assess temporal changes in the distribution of estimated displacement and examine spatial interferometric coherence patterns. It also explores links between displacement, precipitation, soil moisture, and burn severity to understand drivers of post-fire surface change.
supporting_quote: investigate the feasibility of using small-baseline subset differential interferometric synthetic aperture radar (SBAS-DInSAR) to interpret changes in ground surface elevation following large wildfires
We assess the temporal changes in the distribution or the estimated displacement, the spatial interferometric coherence, and explore connections to precipitation, soil moisture, and burn severity.

chunks.text: Post-wildfire landscapes can be hazardous and difficult to access, making widespread deployment of in situ monitoring instrumentation impractical. Traditional burn-hazard estimates can be one-time assessments and may not reflect evolving site-specific hydrologic and ecological conditions such as vegetation regrowth. A monitoring approach that can repeatedly measure ground-surface change over large areas would improve ongoing hazard mitigation and prioritization.
supporting_quote: the potentially remote and vast areas impacted, and the hazards encountered in accessing burned sites
remote sensing tools have particular utility for monitoring and assessing the impact of wildfires when widespread in situ instrumentation is not feasible.
this model is a one-time estimation ... and does not necessarily consider ... regrowth of vegetation, or the potential impacts of evolving hydrologic conditions in the years following a fire.

chunks.text: C-band DInSAR commonly performs poorly in dense forests because canopy interactions cause volume scattering and phase decorrelation. This limitation reduces measurement reliability in vegetated terrain, motivating careful coherence masking to isolate locations where phase changes are more likely due to ground deformation. In this study context, wildfire-induced canopy loss partly alleviates the limitation but regrowth can reduce coherence over time.
supporting_quote: C-band radiation only partially penetrates forest canopies, resulting in volume scattering and decorrelation of the phase signal in heavily forested areas.
heavy vegetation and tree cover is one of the main limitations of C-band SAR.
Vegetation regrowth will limit the measurable area over time due to decreases in interferometric coherence.

chunks.text: The analysis used the SBAS technique to generate an InSAR displacement time series from multiple small-baseline interferograms, reducing noise associated with large spatial and temporal baselines. Processing was performed in MintPy, starting from phase-unwrapped interferograms, selecting a high-coherence reference pixel, correcting unwrapping errors, and inverting the interferogram network. Additional corrections included tropospheric delay (ERA-5) and topographic error correction using an SRTM DEM.
supporting_quote: The small baseline subset technique (SBAS), developed by Berardino et al. [10], was used for this study.
processed following the SBAS technique using Miami InSAR Time-series Software in Python (MintPy, v1.60)
The phase timeseries then undergoes correction for tropospheric delay using ERA-5 dataset and topographic errors using a digital elevation model (3-arc second SRTM DEM).

chunks.text: SAR acquisitions were sourced from Sentinel-1A and interferogram pairs were formed primarily with short temporal baselines. Interferograms were generated with 12–36 day separations, with one manually created 90-day pair due to missing products. The time series epoch is driven by Sentinel-1A’s 12-day repeat cycle, and single-track constraints in MintPy required using a consistent track.
supporting_quote: Interferogram pairs were generated using a temporal baseline (time between acquisitions) of 12 to 36 days
pairs were manually created ... 19 December 2021–19 March 2022 (temporal baseline of 90 days).
The time step of the timeseries ... is 12 days for the Sentinel-1 A satellite used in this study. MintPy only supports single-track processing

chunks.text: Line-of-sight displacement was projected to vertical displacement using a cosine relationship with the incidence angle, assuming LOS change is dominated by vertical motion. The authors argue this is appropriate because they interpret deformation as spatially distributed erosional change triggered by precipitation events that are intermittent and short-lived relative to satellite repeat passes. Horizontal components were therefore not modeled in the projection.
supporting_quote: Line-of-sight (LOS) displacement was projected to vertical displacement using the following formula: dLOS = dv cos(θinc)
This projection assumes that all displacement observed by the satellite in the LOS direction is derived from vertical displacement
the predominant driver of changes in the ground surface elevation is erosion following intense precipitation events

chunks.text: A relatively high coherence threshold was selected to mask pixels likely affected by vegetation-induced decorrelation and to retain exposed slopes burned at high severity. The study notes typical vegetation-area thresholds of about 0.2–0.3, but uses 0.5 to exclude adjacent forested terrain. This masking step is positioned as critical for ensuring phase changes reflect ground-surface displacement rather than scattering noise.
supporting_quote: Generally, coherence threshold of 0.2 to 0.3 is used in vegetated areas
a coherence threshold of 0.5 was selected for this study which effectively masked adjacent vegetated areas and retained pixels within the exposed slopes burned to a high severity.
Determining an appropriate interferometric coherence threshold was critical to maintaining the integrity of the results

chunks.text: The study used Sentinel-1A C-band SAR data (wavelength ~5.55 cm) because canopy removal after the fire increased ground visibility and coherence on burned slopes. Imagery was ordered via ASF Vertex and processed as on-demand Level-2 products for ascending path 137. Multi-looking (10×2) yielded an approximate pixel size of 38 m × 55 m.
supporting_quote: Sentinel-1 A is equipped with a C-band microwave sensor that has a wavelength of approximately 5.55 cm.
order on-demand Level-2 SAR imagery from the Sentinel-1 A satellite, ascending path 137, and processing with multi-look factor of 10 × 2
for a pixel size of approximately 38 m × 55 m in the range and azimuth directions

chunks.text: Processing and computation were carried out using ASF’s OpenSARLab cloud environment and MintPy time-series software. The workflow relied on a DEM for terrain and topographic error corrections and tropospheric corrections derived from ERA-5. These inputs enabled generation of displacement time series across the area of interest.
supporting_quote: The data were brought into the OpenSARLab computing environment
processed ... using Miami InSAR Time-series Software in Python (MintPy, v1.60)
includes digital elevation model terrain corrections and tropospheric delay corrections

chunks.text: Hydrometeorological covariates included precipitation from a nearby SNOTEL station and soil moisture from SMAP root-zone products. Precipitation came from the North Fork SNOTEL station 666, about 7 km southwest of the basin at 932 m elevation, summarized as cumulative precipitation across water years. Root zone soil moisture was queried from the SMAP L4 Global 3-hourly 9 km dataset, representing moisture volume fraction in the upper 1 m of soil.
supporting_quote: Precipitation data were obtained from the North Fork SNOTEL station 666, located approximately 7 km southwest ... at an elevation of 932 m
Soil moisture data ... query the SMAP L4 Global 3-hourly 9 km Root Zone Soil Moisture dataset
estimated as the volume fraction of moisture in the upper 1 m of soil

chunks.text: Burn severity classification used MTBS/BAER products derived from Landsat and Sentinel-2 comparisons before and after the fire, with limited field survey. The study also references dNBR as an indicator used to categorize burn severity, and uses OSIP aerial imagery (2016, 2018, 2022) to visually contextualize vegetation changes and define subbasins for analysis.
supporting_quote: leverages satellite imagery from Landsat satellites and imagery from Sentinel-2 from before and after the fire, to determine the extent and severity of the fire
Figure 2 ... MTBS burn severity map developed after the fire
Ortho imagery (0.3 m resolution) ... from 2016 (pre-fire), 2018, and 2022 (both post-fire)

chunks.text: Interferometric coherence was substantially higher in high burn severity areas where vegetation was removed, and lower in moderate/low and unburned forested areas. The coherence distributions by MTBS class suggest coherence can differentiate burn severity categories and could complement dNBR-based burn assessments. Coherence also declined from 2021 to 2022, consistent with vegetation regrowth reducing signal stability.
supporting_quote: interferometric coherence in areas burned with high severity is much higher than in low burn severity and unburned forested areas
coherence appears positively correlated with the burn severity class
There is an overall reduction in interferometric coherence from 2021 to 2022, possibly indicative of the effect of vegetation regrowth

chunks.text: After applying a coherence mask, the analysis showed that most severe ground-surface changes occurred in the first two years following the fire. However, subbasin comparisons revealed heterogeneous behavior: some subbasins showed significant erosion early while others had little change over the same period. The authors interpret negative vertical displacement as erosion and positive displacement as accretion on slopes, noting possible mass transfer into masked (incoherent) areas.
supporting_quote: most of the severe ground surface changes occurred in the two years following the fire.
Subbasins 1 and 3 experienced generally significant erosion during the wet season of 2018–2019, while Subbasin 2 ... experience little to no erosion or accretion.
negative values are likely due to erosion and those indicated by positive values are likely due to accretion.

chunks.text: The number of coherent pixels decreased over time, which the study attributes to vegetation regrowth reducing coherence. This contraction of usable measurement area is visible across wet-season displacement maps spanning 2018–2022. Despite reduced coverage, high burn severity areas still maintained comparatively higher coherence than surrounding forested zones.
supporting_quote: The number of coherent pixels (masked at average coherence of 0.51) decreases with time, likely due to regrowth of surface vegetation.
Vegetation regrowth will limit the measurable area over time due to decreases in interferometric coherence.

chunks.text: Elevation patterns in displacement suggested greater erosion at higher elevations and near-zero to slightly positive deformation at lower elevations, implying downslope migration and deposition. In Subbasin 1, higher elevation points showed more negative vertical displacement during the 2018–2019 wet season. This spatial pattern is consistent with material being mobilized from upper slopes and accumulating lower in the landscape.
supporting_quote: slopes at higher elevation have greater negative deformation (erosion), with near zero or slightly positive deformations (accretion) occurring at lower elevations
Figure 12. Relationship between projected vertical displacement, elevation, and dNBR in Subbasin 1.

chunks.text: For areas burned at high severity, burn intensity (dNBR) increased with elevation in the study area. The paper notes that lower elevations are typically wetter while higher elevations are drier and can burn more intensely, and that fire spread can accelerate upslope. This helps contextualize why exposed, high-severity slopes at higher elevations may show strong post-fire geomorphic response.
supporting_quote: For areas burned to a high severity (dNBR values greater than 660), there is a clear positive relationship between the dNBR and elevation
Lower elevations tend to contain more moisture, with higher elevations being dryer and thus more susceptible to more intense burning.

chunks.text: Long-term time series indicated distinct mean vertical displacement rates by subbasin over 2018–2022. Subbasin 1 showed a steady mean displacement of about −3.34 cm/yr and Subbasin 3 about −2.64 cm/yr, while Subbasin 2 had little trend until around January 2020 and then shifted to about −2.21 cm/yr. These trends suggest spatially variable post-fire evolution and delayed response in some locations.
supporting_quote: Subbasin 1 appears to experience a steady displacement of −3.34 cm/yr on average.
Following January 2020, Subbasin 2 begins to experience vertical displacement rate of about −2.21 cm/yr
Subbasin 3 ... displacing at a rate of about −2.64 cm/yr on average.

chunks.text: Displacement time series showed seasonal correspondence with hydrologic conditions: increased precipitation and higher root-zone soil moisture aligned with faster erosion, while summer low soil moisture aligned with slower or negligible erosion. The paper describes an approximately one-month lag at the start of the water year between precipitation onset and notable deformation. Erosion accelerated near peak soil moisture and slowed as precipitation accumulation rates and soil moisture declined.
supporting_quote: periods of precipitation corresponding to periods of increased erosion.
periods of lower soil moisture (i.e., June through October) align with slower or generally no erosion
there appears to be a lag of about one month until the initiation of significant ground surface displacements (erosion).

chunks.text: Across water years 2019–2022 in Subbasin 1, accumulated precipitation showed a linear relationship with projected vertical displacement, summarized as a mean erosion rate per unit precipitation. The reported mean rate was −0.014 m of vertical displacement per 1 m of accumulated precipitation. This provides a simple quantitative link between hydrologic forcing and observed surface lowering in the burned terrain.
supporting_quote: Combining all four study years (2019–2022), there is a clear relationship between the accumulated precipitation and erosion in Subbasin 1
which suggests a mean rate of erosion of −0.014 m per 1 m of accumulated precipitation

chunks.text: A key limitation is that many burned areas lack colocated instrumentation (e.g., GPS) to validate DInSAR estimates, which can reduce confidence in absolute displacement magnitudes. The authors argue DInSAR is still valuable for unmonitored locations but suggest it can help prioritize where limited sensors should be installed. This positions InSAR as complementary to targeted field monitoring rather than a complete replacement.
supporting_quote: the area being monitored may be devoid of existing instrumentation (i.e., GPS stations) that could be used to verify the DInSAR measurements.
If limited in situ monitoring is an option, DInSAR could first be used to assess potential locations for deployment of sensors

chunks.text: DInSAR’s spatial and temporal resolution can be insufficient for some monitoring needs. The paper notes that spatial resolution may not capture fine details at smaller sites, and the 12-day repeat interval may miss short-lived, critical events such as debris flows or sudden landslide motion, capturing only before-and-after differences. Thus, DInSAR is best suited to longer-term processes like erosion/accretion and vegetation change at the scale resolvable by Sentinel-1.
supporting_quote: the spatial resolution may not be fine enough to capture refined details in some smaller sites.
in some cases the 12-day repeat pass interval may not be a fine enough temporal resolution to capture short-term critical events.
the progression of short-term phenomena such as a sudden movement of material (i.e., debris flows, landslides) may not be captured, except before and after.

chunks.text: Vegetation regrowth progressively reduces interferometric coherence, shrinking the area where reliable displacement can be estimated. The paper observes decreasing coherent pixels over time and frames this as a practical limit on the monitoring window after wildfire. Nonetheless, it suggests high burn severity zones may retain useful coherence for several years to a decade, and coherence itself may help track regrowth as a complementary indicator to dNBR.
supporting_quote: Vegetation regrowth will limit the measurable area over time due to decreases in interferometric coherence.
the area covered by coherent pixels decreases with time from the wildfire or disturbance.
areas that experience high burn severity, may maintain relatively high coherence ... for several years to a decade

chunks.text: The study concludes that SBAS-DInSAR can measure post-wildfire ground surface displacements in areas not obscured by vegetation and that coherence is related to burn severity. Using a coherence mask, the authors mapped projected vertical displacement and found the largest erosion occurred within about two years after the fire, while some areas showed minimal change for up to four years. Displacement patterns were generally consistent with precipitation and soil moisture variability, including a lag after precipitation onset.
supporting_quote: DInSAR is capable of measuring ground surface displacements in burned areas not obscured by vegetation cover and that interferometric coherence can differentiate between areas that experienced different burn severities.
the most significant measured erosion occurred two years after the fire.
some areas showing little to no ground surface displacement for up to four years after the fire.

chunks.text: The findings support the idea that precipitation and soil moisture dynamics are linked to periods of accelerated erosion inferred from vertical displacement time series. The authors highlight an approximately one-month lag at the start of water years during which root-zone soil moisture steadily rises before notable deformation begins. This suggests hydrologic state, not just rainfall occurrence, influences when measurable surface change occurs.
supporting_quote: Comparison of ground surface displacement to precipitation and soil moisture suggested that trends in increased precipitation and increased soil moisture are generally consistent with the computed accelerated erosion.
This lag period of approximately one month is associated with a steady increase in the rootzone soil moisture.

chunks.text: The paper situates flood response within a context of high national impact and persistent risk to both the public and responders. It cites substantial U.S. damages and fatalities from flooding and notes that even trained responders can be harmed when situational hazards are not well understood. The authors frame these outcomes as motivation for improving how actionable flood information is communicated and used during emergencies.
