supporting_quote: According to NOAA statistics, in 2015, water related events alone affected 7 million citizens in 15 states...cost exceeding $4.8 billion with 176 lives lost due to flooding alone (NOAA, 2015).
Police officers have been swept away in their vehicles and drowned, after driving into swift water currents that overtop roadways.

chunks.text: Prior work and incident learning consistently highlight that flood decision-making is not adequately supported by model outputs in practice. The authors point to a growing opportunity created by increased geospatial “big data,” sensors, and models such as the National Water Model, but emphasize that these advances are not automatically usable by emergency organizations without better packaging and delivery mechanisms.
supporting_quote: Decisions during active flood disasters have had little support from flood model information (Leskins et al., 2014).

Addressing the communication gap...will leverage the increased availability of scientific geographic "big data" from the advancement of processing power, internet-of-things, sensor proliferation and new and emerging models like the National Water Model.

chunks.text: The study draws on literature trends advocating simulation, serious games, visualization, and web-based decision support for emergency management. It notes existing systems and approaches (e.g., RimSim, SDSS, TETHYS) and stresses that cognitive and visual analytics considerations matter for how stressed users interpret information during emergencies.
supporting_quote: There is a growing trend toward adopting serious game software approaches to significantly enhance the "reality" factor in training simulations
The best of computerized implementations, however, cannot ignore human cognitive predispositions and perceptions.

chunks.text: The primary objective is to propose a conceptual model that first supports training and can later expand to operational use. Specifically, it aims to integrate pre-event training, live event command-and-control coordination, and post-event analysis and recovery management within a unified platform.
supporting_quote: The objective and scope of this study is to propose a conceptual model that has the initial capability to integrate (1) training... (2) live event command & control coordination and (3) post-event analysis and recovery process management.

chunks.text: The study’s guiding research question is how to facilitate effective use of water science among emergency flood responders. The authors pursue this by exploring translation and delivery mechanisms that convert scientific outputs into operationally relevant information for emergency roles.
supporting_quote: we were able to present the major visual components of our conceptual approach and address the research question of "How can utilization of water science research among emergency flood responders be effectively facilitated?"

chunks.text: A key design goal is to deliver role-tailored information to the right person at the right time, using only need-to-know content. The platform is envisioned as scalable across hazards, hierarchical levels, and time phases (pre-event, event, post-event).
supporting_quote: The operationalized intelligent and integrated expert decision support system communicates with just the right person, at just the right time, with only the parsed information that individual requires.
This threedimensional platform would scale (1) horizontally to all hazards; (2) vertically...with a (3) a third axis of time (pre-event, event and post-event).

chunks.text: The paper identifies a persistent communication gap between water science researchers and emergency responders, which inhibits effective use of scientific data in operations. It argues this gap is primarily a translation and interpretation issue rather than an engineering or hydrologic science limitation. The mismatch includes differing vocabularies and preferred representational forms.
supporting_quote: We posit that this communication gap...does not represent an engineering or hydrologic science problem but rather a translation and interpretation problem.
the lack of transparency...between the invariant vocabulary of the hydrologic science community and the visual language preferences of flood emergency first responder communities

chunks.text: After-Action Reviews frequently cite ineffective communication as a major obstacle in incident response, reinforcing the need for improved information synthesis and dissemination. The authors frame the challenge as turning complex scientific products into simplified, timely, and actionable guidance that can be applied under stress.
supporting_quote: After-Action Reviews (AARs) from past incidents consistently mention "lack of effective communication" as a primary and frustrating issue in responding to incidents (Donahue, 2006).
The potential to significantly reduce the loss of life...rests with simplifying complex science domain data and information...so that it can be translated into "socially" applicable domain knowledge

chunks.text: The authors claim that conventional decision-making during flood disasters is poorly supported by flood model outputs, contributing to underutilization of valuable geospatial and temporal data. They describe the science and social domains as so misaligned that they effectively use different “alphabets or symbols,” which obstructs operational uptake.
supporting_quote: Decisions during active flood disasters have had little support from flood model information (Leskins et al., 2014).
not only do the "science cloud" and the "social cloud" not speak the same language... they do not use the same alphabet or symbols.

chunks.text: The proposed approach centers on an ontological “knowledge warehouse” that stores reusable scenarios, SOPs, and best practices, and delivers them through a serious game-like environment. The platform is intended to translate scientific outputs and then parse them into role-specific “packets” of information, akin to customized tweets. This is framed as a mechanism to make products like the National Water Model more usable in training and operations.
supporting_quote: The core of our approach evolves around an ontological knowledge warehouse (Yacci, 1999) of re-useable scenarios, standard operating procedures (SOPs), and best practices ultimately to be delivered in a serious gamelike software environment.
the parsing or filtering...into basic need-to-know "packets" of information... An analogy might be drawn with the social media "tweet" packet

chunks.text: The authors structure requirements and capabilities using a three-dimensional framework spanning time, hazard type, and organizational hierarchy. Time is broken into pre-event, event, and post-event phases; hazards include multiple flooding types; and hierarchy captures different information needs by role. The framework is used to guide how information is categorized and delivered.
supporting_quote: we categorized each capability along 3D spatial thinking dimensions as (1) Temporality (2) Hazard and (3) Hierarchy.
[A] Temporal...**Pre-Event**...**Event:**...**Post-Event:**
[C] Hierarchy...**parsed information packets (e.g. "tweets")** required for each hierarchical level role with **"need-to-know-only"** information

chunks.text: A Rosetta Stone metaphor is used as a conceptual device for bridging the science and social domains, motivating translation and synthesis mechanisms at high spatial and temporal resolution. The metaphor guides how the authors think about mapping scientific sources to responder applications and building anticipatory computing translators.
supporting_quote: Thus by redefining the communication gap to be one of a translation problem...we have been able to use a Rosetta Stone metaphor
We utilized the Rosetta Stone metaphor to guide our thinking visually (see Figure 1)

chunks.text: The empirical component uses a qualitative design combining interviews, observations, and documentary analysis to validate the communication-gap hypothesis and elicit user needs. The study was executed under tight constraints within a rapid prototyping environment, aiming to identify improvements for training, migration to live command and control, and post-event recovery processes.
supporting_quote: We selected a qualitative research design with a mix of research methods such as Interviews, Observations, and Documentary Analysis
This research design also allowed us to expedite the study within the tight time and resource constraints associated with a 7-week, rapid prototyping environment.

chunks.text: Primary data collection relied on open-ended, face-to-face interviews with a convenience sample of emergency managers, responders, and National Water Center scientists, complemented by informal interviews and observations during demonstrations and a tabletop exercise. The authors emphasize careful selection of a cross-section of roles but acknowledge the non-random sampling frame.
supporting_quote: We began our investigation with primary research in the form of open-ended personal interviews, using a small convenience sample

We formally interviewed Tuscaloosa County Fire and Rescue Deputy...Northport Fire and Rescue Chief...Tuscaloosa County EMA Director as well as water resource and flood scientists at the National Water Center.

chunks.text: Because a full prototype was infeasible, the team pivoted to a web-based mock-up to demonstrate the concept and its information flow. The proof of concept was implemented using WIX and simulated geo-visualizations-as-a-service and flood information-as-a-service components to communicate how the platform could work.
supporting_quote: the project was too large to obtain a working prototype... Therefore, we pivoted and opted to visualize through a mocked-up, proof of concept knowledge warehouse "platform" (via a free web page design site called WIX.com).
The web-based visualizations simulate geo-visualizations-as-a-service, flood information-as-a-service

chunks.text: The platform logic is described as IF-THEN driven and oriented toward decision support, incorporating lessons learned and best practices from After Action Reports. It also proposes redundancy strategies for degraded communications, including offline client-side GEO-PDFs on battery-powered mobile devices.
supporting_quote: It provides a "simulated" knowledge warehouse that categorizes information using an IF-THEN algorithmic logic engine.
In terms of fault tolerance and redundancy...use battery powered mobile client side devices to operate standalone GEO-PDF's (a form of lite geographical information system-GIS)

chunks.text: The paper draws on primary qualitative evidence from interviews with local fire/rescue leadership, an EMA director, and National Water Center scientists, as well as informal interviews and observations during equipment demonstrations and a tabletop exercise in the National Water Center operations room. These inputs were used to validate perceived communication and empathy gaps and inform platform requirements.
supporting_quote: We formally interviewed Tuscaloosa County Fire and Rescue Deputy...the Northport Fire and Rescue Chief...and the Tuscaloosa County EMA Director as well as water resource and flood scientists at the National Water Center.

it was clear from the information obtained, all interviewees felt there was a serious communication gap and lack of communication (several used the word "empathy") between scientists and first responders.

chunks.text: Secondary inputs included documentary and literature sources spanning serious games, simulation and visualization for emergency response, anticipatory computing, and web-based decision support. The authors describe conducting keyword “topic search swarms” to structure the review and support the conceptual model.
supporting_quote: Our secondary research focused on the following keyword topic search swarms: (1) serious game... (3) utilization of semiotics and anticipatory computing... (4) web-based modeling and simulation for decision support systems

chunks.text: The concept relies on hydrologic and geospatial data sources, emphasizing the National Water Model as a basis for both archived historical scenarios and real-time streams. The model’s national coverage is presented as enabling local training anywhere in the contiguous United States using familiar conditions.
supporting_quote: First responders could then use hydrologic models such as the National Water Model (NWM)
since the National Water Model covers all of the contiguous United States, any first responder within that area...would be able to train with their own local and familiar real-time data.

chunks.text: The envisioned repository would ingest multiple operational artifacts over time, including dispatcher activity logs, media files, and training manuals/documents from agencies, along with lessons learned. The authors describe automated import mechanisms (e.g., FTP) contingent on standard file structures, and emphasize ongoing curation and governance.
supporting_quote: the conceptual model...would be populated with data from various sources including... (1) activity logs from dispatchers...automatically imported using FTP
(2) media files (photos and video gathered from previous disasters, training videos, etc.), (3) training manuals and documents from different agencies.

chunks.text: The investigation reports two primary results: a need for more frequent pre-planning practice opportunities and a need to tailor those services to different roles. Regular tabletop exercises are emphasized as a mechanism for integrating responders with recent engineering and modeling advances, especially the National Water Model.
supporting_quote: The investigation to date has identified two main results (1) what is needed and (2) by whom.

A higher frequency of regular pre-planning opportunities (i.e., table top exercises) for practicing and integrating with the latest engineering science advances exemplified by the National Water Model.

chunks.text: Role and hierarchy are identified as central determinants of information needs. The authors conclude that the organizational structure—from on-the-ground responders to leadership—requires different types of pre-planning information and services for distinct job functions, motivating role-based parsing and delivery.
supporting_quote: The hierarchical structure of emergency management organizations (from on-the-ground first responders to chiefs and directors) dictates the need for various types of pre-planning information and services for different roles

chunks.text: Interview and observational evidence indicates widespread agreement among participants that a serious communication gap exists between scientists and first responders. Respondents also emphasized a lack of “empathy” across groups, reinforcing the paper’s translation-and-synthesis framing of the problem.
supporting_quote: it was clear from the information obtained, all interviewees felt there was a serious communication gap and lack of communication (several used the word "empathy") between scientists and first responders.

chunks.text: The web-based proof of concept demonstrates a potential solution pattern: a user-friendly visual interface with need-to-know access controls by organization, online tabletop exercise templates, and an IF-THEN categorization logic. It illustrates how best practices and lessons learned from AARs could be used to trigger role-specific actions (e.g., dam breach response steps).
supporting_quote: It provides first responders and emergency managers access to a user friendly visual interface that is deliverable on a need-to-know basis by organization
It provides online tabletop exercise templates (powered by the ESRI Story Map Interface)
IF a dam breaches, THEN certain actions must be taken... These actions are taken from best practices and lessons learned...After Action Reports (AARs).

chunks.text: The authors identify specific follow-on development opportunities suggested by the findings: testing visual stories (e.g., ESRI Story Maps), improving the realism and delivery of tabletop exercises, implementing reverse lookup inundation mapping from windshield surveys, and developing spatial-temporal 3D visualizations for situational awareness across hierarchical levels.
supporting_quote: further research opportunities exist for (1) developing and testing visual stories like "ESRI Story Maps"
(3) Reverse lookup, inundation-mapping on-the-fly through first responder windshield survey methods and (4) spatial-temporal visualizations

chunks.text: The study explicitly states its primary research is not statistically significant due to non-random, convenience sampling and constrained scope. The authors warn against generalizing findings to the national emergency management population and call for additional qualitative and quantitative research to validate relationships and significance.
supporting_quote: Our research approach was not statistically significant and does not constitute a random sample, nor should any of our results be inferred to the general emergency management population across the country.
More qualitative and quantitative research must be done to further validate and study the statistical significance among relationships and variables.

chunks.text: The authors note that building a full knowledge warehouse platform would require extensive software engineering beyond what was possible in their rapid prototyping timeframe. As a result, they presented a mocked-up proof of concept rather than an operational prototype, which limits validation of real-world performance and integration complexity.
supporting_quote: We quickly determined the conceptual knowledge warehouse (Yacci, 1999) platform would require extensive software programming resources and planning.
because of the scale and scope of the knowledge warehouse and the limited rapidprototyping timeframe, the project was too large to obtain a working prototype

chunks.text: The paper concludes that emergency flood responders’ scientific information needs can be met through an “intelligent” knowledge warehouse that functions as a Rosetta Stone between science and social domains. By instantly interpreting, parsing, and connecting sources to applications based on responder roles, the approach is argued to close communication gaps and improve preparedness and response effectiveness, initially via training and potentially later in operations.
supporting_quote: The scientific information needs of emergency flood responders...can be met through a comprehensive "intelligent" mechanism; to use a metaphor, a Rosetta stone concept that we propose as the Knowledge Warehouse (KW).

The KW instantly interprets, parses and connects appropriate pre-defined "sources" of information with pre-defined "applications" of information based on the specific emergency responder role being supported.

chunks.text: The authors assert that translating up-to-date hydrologic models into the operational language of responders, structured through SOPs and role-based delivery, can prepare responders across hierarchical levels for more efficient response. They frame the platform as a way to interface interdisciplinary information sources toward the core goal of saving lives and property.
supporting_quote: By translating the most up-to-date hydrologic models and scientific information into the language of emergency flood responders through standard operating procedures (SOPs); this platform has the ability to prepare emergency responders at every hierarchical level

Given emergency management's interdisciplinary nature, it is well positioned also to interface with other disciplinary sources of information to facilitate the common goal of saving lives and property.

chunks.text: Environmental sensor networks are expanding and producing continuous, high-volume time series that require robust infrastructure for collection, storage, metadata management, and sharing. Organizations face challenges from sensor and telemetry costs, heterogeneity of data and sensors, and the need to modernize long-lived software stacks. IoT platforms offer connectivity but are often generalized, requiring domain-specific metadata and context to make environmental observations interpretable. Standards for metadata, interfaces, and encodings are emphasized as key to interoperability for publishing and exchanging sensor observations.
supporting_quote: Operating sensor networks and managing the observations produced by continuous data collection require robust infrastructure enabling collection, communication, storage, management, and eventual sharing of data.

Challenges in provisioning this infrastructure include the cost associated with environmental sensors... variety of data produced... and the velocity and volume of data produced that must be stored, managed, and shared.

chunks.text: The OGC SensorThings API (STA) provides a RESTful, JSON-based standard API and data model aimed at interoperability for IoT and sensor applications. STA has a Sensing part for CRUD operations on data and metadata and a Tasking part for parameterizing taskable devices, and it follows OData URL conventions. STA was designed to be lighter weight and more suitable for resource-constrained devices than older XML-based OGC services such as SOS/SPS. Because STA is a general standard, domain applications may require extensions and operational software implementations.
supporting_quote: STA offers a RESTful interface with JSON data encoding
The API specification consists of two parts: 1) a Sensing part... CRUD operations...; and 2) a Tasking part
STA... follows modern representational state transfer (REST) principles, and uses efficient JavaScript object notation (JSON) message encoding

chunks.text: The Observations Data Model (ODM/ODM2) is a relational model developed to store hydrologic and broader environmental observations with sufficient metadata for unambiguous interpretation, particularly for in situ sensor time series. Historically, ODM was paired with WaterOneFlow and WaterML (XML) for web-based sharing, but these technologies are now dated. The paper positions STA as a replacement for WaterOneFlow/SOS and JSON as a modern alternative to WaterML/XML while retaining rich metadata patterns from ODM. HydroServer is a legacy platform built around ODM and WaterOneFlow that the authors aim to modernize using STA.
supporting_quote: ODM... was focused primarily on storing the necessary metadata to describe time series of hydrologic observations from in situ environmental sensors and to enable their unambiguous interpretation.
the technologies on which the WaterOneFlow service interface is based are now quite dated and in need of replacement.
describe how the WaterOneFlow web service interface... can be replaced by STA and how the ODM/WaterML information model and XML data encoding... can be replaced by STA's data model and JSON encoding

chunks.text: The work aims to specialize the OGC SensorThings API and data model for managing and sharing in situ environmental sensor time series within HydroServer. Key objectives include extending STA entities with required and optional ODM metadata, implementing the enhanced model in a relational database, and delivering a Python-based STA service for ingest and query. The system is intended to support both IoT devices and traditional sensing stations and to operate as a modern, deployable web-based platform. A complementary data management API is introduced to manage extended metadata and multi-user workflows.
supporting_quote: we describe a specialization of the STA data model and application programming interface (API) designed to adapt them for supporting the data collection and sharing workflow associated with data generated by in situ environmental sensors.

specific contributions... include: 1) adaptation of the STA data model... 2) a physical implementation of the enhanced data model...; and 3) a Python-based implementation of the STA... along with a complementary data management API

chunks.text: HydroServer modernization targets three STA-aligned components: an enhanced observational database/data model, a standardized API for ingest and query, and interoperable JSON encoding for data exchange. The design is driven by functional requirements including efficient storage, robust metadata (location, variable/units, procedures, responsible parties, annotations, and processing level), standardized ingest endpoints, flexible query (spatial/temporal filtering), scalability, and multi-user security. These requirements guide how STA is extended and how additional APIs are structured around STA.
supporting_quote: development of three components... including: 1) an enhanced data model... 2) a standardized web service interface... and 3) an interoperable data encoding... implementations of OGC's SensorThings specification.
Multi-user support: Security and access control must be implemented to ensure secure access to authorized users and to restrict access to data based on user roles and permissions.

chunks.text: Environmental sensor data management is hindered by heterogeneity across sensors, variables, platforms, protocols, and by the scale and velocity of streaming observations. Many monitoring programs have long-lived systems that require modernization across multiple software generations to remain viable. General IoT platforms do not automatically capture the context and metadata needed for environmental observations, making customization necessary and often beyond the expertise of many organizations. Lack of standards reduces interoperability in publishing and sharing time series observations.
supporting_quote: Challenges... include... variety of data produced... and the velocity and volume of data produced that must be stored, managed, and shared.
many sensor networks... have been faced with updating and/or modernizing software technologies given that they have lasted through multiple generations of software development.
software platforms that support IoT data collection have been generalized... requires customization to ensure that necessary context and metadata are created, stored, and maintained

chunks.text: STA’s generic, domain-agnostic model does not, by itself, ensure that environmental sensor data are described with sufficient metadata for interpretation, and the standard does not dictate physical storage. The paper highlights that applying STA in a particular sensing domain requires extending the base information model to add necessary metadata. In addition, STA is a specification that must be implemented as operational software, and usable implementations are limited. These gaps motivate an adapted model and a new implementation tailored to environmental time series.
supporting_quote: applying it for any particular sensing domain... requires extension of the base information model to add metadata necessary to maintain the context and interpretability of observational data;
while OGC provides the standard specification, physical implementation of the standard as useable software is left to the community

chunks.text: STA Part 1 does not include parties (people/organizations) and does not specify security or ownership mechanisms, yet HydroServer requires multi-user operation with authorization, entity ownership, and privacy controls. The authors note STA assumes a single provider is responsible for observations, which is insufficient for shared platforms. Managing ODM-derived metadata entities also lacks standard STA endpoints. These issues necessitate additional data model entities and a separate data management API.
supporting_quote: the SensorThings API Part 1: Sensing... data model specifically excludes information about people and organizations
The STA specification does not prescribe how security and access control should be handled.
the STA specification does not include endpoints to manage creation of instances of those entities (e.g., ... Person or an Organization)

chunks.text: The authors extended STA by mapping STA entities and attributes to corresponding ODM entities, then adding additional required and optional ODM metadata. They used STA’s per-entity "properties" extensibility field to incorporate extra ODM attributes while retaining STA compliance. The approach proceeded in two passes: first mapping equivalents (e.g., Thing to SamplingFeatures), then enriching entities with additional ODM elements not represented in core STA attributes. This design targets environmental sensor time series while keeping STA’s standard interface behavior.
supporting_quote: We adapted the basic STA data model... by extending the attributes of each entity... to include required and optional metadata elements from ODM.
we made a first pass... map them to corresponding entities from ODM... the STA "Thing" entity was mapped to the ODM "SamplingFeatures" entity.
We used the "properties" extensibility mechanism to add additional required and optional attributes from ODM.

chunks.text: To support storage and query performance, the paper implements the enhanced STA model in a relational database, noting that STA specifies JSON responses but not disk storage. Additional normalized tables were introduced where STA expects structured JSON objects, such as a separate Unit entity to populate Datastream.unitOfMeasurement (name, symbol, definition). The relational design is presented as an ER diagram, distinguishing core STA entities from added ODM-compliance entities. This enables efficient querying and JSON encoding for the API.
supporting_quote: the STA specification does not designate how data should be stored on disk to support the API.
we developed an implementation of the STA data model for storing sensor data in a relational database management system (RDBMS).
we added a "Unit" entity... the JSON object should contain... "name"... "symbol"... and "definition"

chunks.text: HydroServer implements STA Part 1 (Sensing) GET endpoints for all STA entities to be fully compliant for querying. Because extended ODM entities and ownership constructs are not covered by STA, a separate HydroServer data management API provides POST/PATCH/DELETE for all entities except Observations. Observations are created using standard STA POST endpoints, including individual observations and the Data Array extension for bulk insertion. This separation preserves STA compliance while enabling complete operational metadata management.
supporting_quote: We implemented the GET endpoints for all of the STA entities such that the query interface... is fully compliant with the OGC specification.
we developed a separate data management API... endpoints for creating (POST), updating (PATCH), and deleting (DELETE) instances for all of the data model entities except for Observations.
For Observations, we implemented the standard POST endpoints... and one for posting multiple observations using the STA Data Array extension

chunks.text: The data model adds explicit multi-user ownership by introducing Organization, Person, and ThingAssociation and extending ownership to Sensors, ObservedProperties, ProcessingLevels, Units, and ResultQualifiers. Ownership is designed to support primary and secondary owners for a Thing, with downstream propagation of control to related Locations, Datastreams, and Observations. The authors chose not to adopt STAplus 1.0 because it targets citizen-science use cases, excludes personal data, and does not support ownership of Sensor or ObservedProperty, which HydroServer requires. The result is a custom ownership model integrated with HydroServer’s metadata workflows.
supporting_quote: we designed an ownership model that enables users to own instances of the STA Sensor, Thing, and ObservedProperty entities
the STAplus extension... specifically excludes storage of any personal data.
the STAplus extension does not allow ownership of instances of the Sensor or ObservedProperty entities

chunks.text: For access control, HydroServer uses OAuth 2.0 for authorization and supports account creation via Google or ORCID identity providers, then secures API calls with JSON Web Tokens (JWT). Privacy and visibility flags at the Thing and Datastream levels determine public accessibility of metadata and observations. Owners can modify and post observations, and only primary owners can delete Things and transfer ownership. This approach provides a practical security model absent from the base STA specification.
supporting_quote: we designed and implemented an access control system... based on the OAuth 2.0 protocol
After a user account has been created, JSON Web Tokens (JWT) are used to secure communication
The Thing entity stores an "isPrivate" attribute... two attributes are stored for each Datastream – "isVisible"... and "isDataVisible"

chunks.text: Physical storage targets PostgreSQL with optional TimescaleDB to support time series performance via partitioning, indexing, and compression while preserving SQL and Django ORM compatibility. The design supports deployment on-premise, on virtual machines, or as managed SaaS such as Timescale Cloud. The Timescale extension is optional; the system can run on plain PostgreSQL, enabling flexible adoption based on scale and performance needs. The authors used Timescale Cloud for the example deployment.
supporting_quote: We have targeted implementation... using the PostgreSQL RDBMS... along with the optional TimescaleDB extension.
TimescaleDB can be used to extend PostgreSQL to provide specific functionality for time series data, including automatic time partitioning, optimized indexing, and data compression.
For the LRO instance, we set up the database using Timescale Cloud

chunks.text: ODM-to-STA mapping decisions include using Thing/Location/HistoricalLocation to represent monitoring stations and potential station moves over time, rather than ODM’s SamplingFeatures alone. People and organizations are added as first-class entities to support multi-user contexts absent in STA. Actions are omitted for simplicity because sensor time series usually do not require complex action chains; instead, people are linked directly to owned metadata entities. The Sensor entity is enhanced with ODM Methods metadata to represent procedures that may not be physical sensors (e.g., derived discharge).
supporting_quote: monitoring station metadata was mapped to the generic Thing entity, and the monitoring station's location information was mapped to the Location entity.
Thus, we kept the HistoricalLocation entity from STA as specified to take advantage of this STA functionality.
we did not include Actions... Instead, people are associated directly with the metadata describing Things, Sensors, ObservedProperties
we added specific metadata from the ODM Methods entity to the STA Sensor entity

chunks.text: A demonstration deployment was conducted using the Logan River Observatory (LRO), a research watershed with dozens of monitoring locations and hundreds of sensors, many collecting at 15-minute intervals for over a decade. The HydroServer instance and its STA endpoint are publicly accessible, and the LRO data are openly available. This deployment serves as a representative operational setting for long-term, high-volume environmental time series management.
supporting_quote: typical of many research watersheds having dozens of monitoring locations with hundreds of deployed sensors, many of which have been collecting data at 15-min spacing for more than a decade.
The Hydro-Server instance for the LRO is available at https://lro.hydroserver.org, and the HydroServer STA... at https://lro.hydroserver.org/api/sensorthings/v1.1/
LRO data is openly and freely available.

chunks.text: Benchmark datasets were simulated to evaluate database performance, including PostgreSQL databases with 1e6, 100e6, and 1e9 Observations and Datastream sizes of 50,000, 500,000, and 5e6 observations. Datastreams were simulated over a common 10-year period, with larger Datastreams implying denser time spacing. The Observations table was tested both as a standard PostgreSQL table and as a TimescaleDB hypertable with ten time partitions. Queries representative of UI needs included last 72 hours, last year, and full Datastream retrieval.
supporting_quote: We performed some simple benchmark testing by setting up a PostgreSQL database containing 1e6, 100e6, and 1e9 observations with three Datastream sizes (50,000, 500,000, and for the latter two database sizes 5e6 Observations).
All of the Datastreams were simulated over the same 10-year period
We then tested three queries... fetching the last 72 h of data... the last one year of data, and the whole Datastream.

chunks.text: The LRO HydroServer database scale is described as approximately 250 million observations, providing a real-world reference point between the simulated 100 million and 1 billion benchmark cases. This contextualizes expected operational workloads for long-running observatories and informs whether TimescaleDB features are necessary. The paper uses this scale to motivate performance expectations for interactive visualization and API responsiveness.
supporting_quote: For comparison, the LRO HydroServer database contains approximately 250e6 observations.
retrieving Datastream Observations for visualization... must be performant enough to meet user expectations

chunks.text: The HydroServer STA data model integrates ODM metadata into STA core entities and adds new entities where STA lacks structure needed for environmental time series context. Key additions include Person and Organization for parties, ProcessingLevel for QC/processing state, Unit to support Datastream.unitOfMeasurement requirements, and ResultQualifier to represent data qualifying comments as arrays on Observations. Datastreams map closely to ODM Results and Observations to ODM ResultValues, preserving the time series pattern while enabling richer interpretation metadata. HistoricalLocation is retained to represent station moves over time.
supporting_quote: we added two entities... Person... and Organization
We created an equivalent entity... called ProcessingLevel.
we added a Unit entity to the Hydro-Server STA data model implementation.
we added an entity called ResultQualifier... The ResultQualifier attribute in the Observation entity is defined as an array

chunks.text: HydroServer’s STA query interface is implemented to be OGC-compliant for GET endpoints across all STA entities, while JSON responses are expanded via the standard "properties" field to include ODM-derived metadata. Standard STA POST endpoints are used for inserting Observations, including the Data Array extension for multi-observation payloads. Non-STA metadata entities are managed through a separate data management API rather than altering STA endpoints, keeping sensor/device ingest standardized. The approach enables both compact and expanded response styles supported by STA.
supporting_quote: We implemented the GET endpoints for all of the STA entities... fully compliant with the OGC specification.
JSON responses from STA have been expanded to include the specific metadata fields... within the "properties" attribute
For Observations, we implemented the standard POST endpoints... including... the STA Data Array extension

chunks.text: A multi-user ownership model is implemented using Organization, Person, and ThingAssociation, allowing primary and secondary ownership of Things. Ownership extends downstream to associated Locations, HistoricalLocations, Datastreams, and Observations, giving owners control over related resources. Only primary owners can delete a Thing, and primary ownership can be transferred to prevent “stranding” of data when responsibilities change. Sensors, ObservedProperties, ProcessingLevels, and ResultQualifiers can also be owned, with constraints to maintain coherence between owned metadata and Datastreams.
supporting_quote: users (Person)... can be given ownership over Things, categorized as primary or secondary owners
only primary owners possess the capability to delete a Thing
primary owners can transfer primary ownership to another designated user
Instances of the Sensor, ObservedProperty, ProcessingLevel, and ResultQualifier entities can also be owned

chunks.text: The physical database implementation targets PostgreSQL with optional TimescaleDB hypertables for time series optimization and cloud deployment. The authors report that, for tested sizes up to 1e9 observations and representative UI queries, TimescaleDB showed no appreciable performance improvement over standard PostgreSQL. As a result, most HydroServer instances with fewer than 1e9 observations may not require TimescaleDB. TimescaleDB remains an option for larger scales, high insert rates, compression needs, or more advanced aggregations.
supporting_quote: We implemented the Observations table as both a standard PostgreSQL table and as a TimescaleDB hypertable
we found no appreciable improvement in performance with TimescaleDB
for most practical applications of HydroServer having less than 1e9 Observations, the TimescaleDB extension is not needed.

chunks.text: HydroServer’s API services are implemented as a Django project with separate apps for STA, the data management API, and account services, using Django ORM mappings to the database. The STA app builds on an STA Django extension and adds HydroServer-specific JSON schemas to support the extended metadata. This modularity is intended to decouple STA interface complexity from database specifics, potentially enabling support for additional database backends in the future. The implementation is designed for deployment as part of HydroServer or as an independently reusable Django extension.
supporting_quote: The HydroServer API Services Django project... consists of three apps... STA, HydroServer's data management API, and HydroServer's account services API.
The project uses Django's Object-Relational Mapper (ORM)
This approach helps decouple the complexities of STA implementation from the specific database implementation

chunks.text: HydroServer implements OAuth-based account linking (Google/ORCID) and JWT-secured API communication, with optional basic authentication for flexibility. Authorization is enforced primarily through ownership and privacy/visibility flags: Thing.isPrivate controls public access, and Datastream.isVisible and Datastream.isDataVisible separate metadata visibility from observation visibility. Even though Sensor and ObservedProperty instances have owners, they are treated as publicly retrievable to support query filtering across related entities. Non-owners requesting private Things or Datastreams receive appropriate HTTP error codes.
supporting_quote: use OAuth to allow users to securely create their HydroServer account using either Google or ORCID
After a user creates their account, client applications request JSON Web Tokens (JWT)
The Thing entity stores an "isPrivate" attribute... "isVisible"... and "isDataVisible"
If a non-owner requests a private Thing or Datastream through the API, they receive an appropriate HTTP error code.

chunks.text: Adding ODM metadata substantially enlarges the STA data model, which may be unnecessary for lightweight retrieval use cases. Although STA supports compact versus expanded responses, the richer model introduced a practical need for create/update/delete endpoints for extended metadata not covered by STA. HydroServer addresses this with a separate data management API, but the authors identify an opportunity to harmonize these endpoints with STA via future core changes or an extension. They are evaluating moving metadata management endpoints into an STA extension to consolidate STA-related functionality.
supporting_quote: The HydroServer STA data model implementation adds a significant number of entities and attributes to the base STA data model.
adding the additional metadata to the data model required that we add additional API endpoints that go beyond the OGC STA specification
we are currently evaluating moving the POST, PATCH, and DELETE endpoints for metadata... to an STA extension

chunks.text: HydroServer’s ownership model differs from the STAplus 1.0 extension, and the authors did not adopt STAplus because it lacks ownership of Sensors and ObservedProperties and includes additional entities not needed for their use cases. They argue there is room to rethink and broaden ownership concepts, potentially blending HydroServer’s approach with STAplus to serve more domains. This divergence can limit interoperability with communities adopting STAplus conventions. It also implies that standardization of ownership across STA implementations remains unsettled.
supporting_quote: The structures for expressing ownership... are different from those in the STAplus 1.0 extension to STA.
we would have needed to extend it to include ownership of Sensors and ObservedProperties.
We suggest that there is an opportunity for rethinking and broadening the ownership concept

chunks.text: Including personal and organizational party metadata in HydroServer can complicate international adoption due to privacy laws. STAplus explicitly avoids storing personal data, whereas HydroServer treats responsible-party contact and affiliation as essential observation metadata. The authors note that relying on an external identity management system was beyond scope, but acknowledge that legal compliance may require modifications for international deployment. This highlights a tension between complete metadata and privacy-by-design approaches.
supporting_quote: the STAplus extension... specifically excludes storage of any personal data.

international use of the HydroServer STA data model and API implementation may require modifications to ensure compliance with laws related to collection, storage, and dissemination of personal information

chunks.text: TimescaleDB performance depends on partitioning and chunking parameters, and default settings may degrade query performance when mixing high-frequency short-duration data with low-frequency long-duration data. The authors observed significant delays with the default seven-day chunk size in such mixed datasets. Adjusting chunk size to one year drastically improved performance in their case. This indicates that operational deployments must tune time-series storage parameters based on data characteristics.
supporting_quote: We found that query performance degraded significantly when we loaded high frequency data... into the same database with lower frequency data
TimescaleDB's default data chunking scheme of seven days caused significant delays
Changing the default chunk size to one year drastically improved performance

chunks.text: Several STA extensions remain unimplemented in HydroServer, limiting functionality for some IoT workflows. The authors implemented the Data Array extension but not MultiDatastream (complex result arrays) and have not yet implemented MQTT, though they are investigating it. MQTT could improve operation in low-bandwidth or unreliable IoT networks. The current scope reflects prioritization of in situ sensor time series of individual observations.
supporting_quote: We implemented the Data Array extension
We have not yet implemented the MultiDatastream extension
While we have not yet implemented the MQTT extension, we are investigating how it could be integrated

chunks.text: STA standardizes endpoints and encodings but does not provide controlled vocabularies, leaving semantic heterogeneity as a barrier to integration. With ODM metadata added, HydroServer could use ODM controlled vocabularies to populate metadata fields where available. Without vocabularies, different providers may encode observed properties and other metadata inconsistently, complicating interpretation and harmonization. The paper frames vocabulary adoption as an opportunity rather than a solved aspect of STA-based interoperability.
supporting_quote: The STA specification does not specify controlled vocabularies for use in populating metadata elements.
the opportunity exists to use values from the ODM controlled vocabularies... to populate metadata elements
semantic heterogeneity may still exist... making data integration and interpretation more difficult.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that lack of standardized, accessible software remains a barrier to effective environmental sensor data management and sharing, and that STA provides a modern REST/JSON standard that helps address variability across devices and systems. By extending STA with ODM metadata and implementing it in Python/Django with a PostgreSQL-based model, HydroServer offers an additional open-source implementation option for researchers and practitioners. The authors emphasize that STA responses can remain lightweight or be expanded to include richer metadata. Deployment instructions and code availability are provided to support stand-alone or integrated HydroServer use.
supporting_quote: Access to standardized software tools remains a barrier to effective collection, storage, management, and sharing of time series data from in situ environmental sensors.
The Python and Django-based HydroServer implementation of STA adds an additional deployment choice
STA responses can be expanded to include full metadata or kept compact to keep responses lightweight.

chunks.text: The authors find that STA generally satisfies HydroServer’s core use cases for environmental sensor time series when extended via the built-in extensibility mechanism to include ODM-required metadata. The main exception is management of additional metadata and ownership, which required non-standard endpoints (handled in the data management API). They anticipate usefulness for both IoT and traditional monitoring stations, supporting modernized interoperability and sharing. The work positions HydroServer as a componentized platform that can be deployed in cloud or stand-alone contexts.
supporting_quote: After using the extensibility mechanism built into the STA data model to add additional required and optional metadata attributes from ODM, we found that STA generally satisfied the major use cases
The exception was in managing metadata entities we added from ODM and to support ownership.
Instructions... detail how the HydroServer STA implementation can be deployed... or as a stand-alone database and web service API

chunks.text: HydroServer originated in the CUAHSI Hydrologic Information System as a platform for hosting observational databases and publishing them via web services. Early versions used the Observations Data Model (ODM) for storage and WaterOneFlow services with WaterML (XML) for standardized querying and retrieval. Over time, CUAHSI moved toward a centralized cloud-hosted model for ODM and WaterOneFlow, changing how HydroServer-like functionality was delivered to users.
supporting_quote: HydroServer was developed as part of the CUAHSI HIS ... populate any number of databases conforming to the Observations Data Model (ODM) ... and then connect those ODM databases to WaterOneFlow web services
WaterOneFlow was an early attempt at a standardized web service interface ... used ... XML schema called WaterML for encoding data

chunks.text: Standards for sensor web services evolved substantially after HydroServer’s original design. OGC advanced WaterML 2.0 and multiple Sensor Web Enablement standards (e.g., O&M, SOS, SensorML). More recently, OGC released the SensorThings API and data model using REST principles and JSON encodings, motivated in part by IoT and modern web practices.
supporting_quote: OGC also developed and advanced a suite of web service interface standards ... including the OGC Observations & Measurements Schema (O&M)
OGC released a twopart SensorThings API and data model ... introduce modern ... REST principles and efficient ... JSON data encodings

chunks.text: HydroServer’s modernization is motivated by growth in operational streaming sensor networks and long-term time series volumes. The authors’ Logan River Observatory (LRO) provides an example of sustained, multi-site monitoring generating frequent observations and accumulating very large databases. This operational context drives requirements for scalable ingestion, storage, and management.
supporting_quote: the Logan River Observatory (LRO) ... consists of nearly 30 continuous monitoring sites generating new data every 15 min
the LRO observations database now contains more than 253 million individual observations, with approximately 43,000 new raw observations added daily

chunks.text: The paper aims to describe a modernized HydroServer software stack that supports collection, storage, management, and sharing of in situ environmental sensor data. The modernization centers on adopting OGC SensorThings API (STA) for standardized ingest and retrieval, while keeping the system deployable and open source. The work extends a prior paper on STA adaptation by documenting the full stack and user-facing tooling.
supporting_quote: In this paper we describe a modernized version of the HydroServer software, which is a generalized HIS ... support collection, communication, storage, management, and sharing of data from in situ environmental sensors.
HydroServer has been redesigned and modernized using the OGC's STA

chunks.text: A central goal is to provide an open-source, deployable hydrologic information system that integrates standards-based web service interfaces and encodings for both ingestion and access. The paper positions its contributions as a full software stack plus client and web tools that support multi-user metadata management, sensor data handling, and interoperability.
supporting_quote: specific contributions of this paper include: 1) an open-source, deployable HIS software stack
2) integration and implementation of standards-based web service interfaces and data encodings that promote interoperability

chunks.text: Environmental monitoring organizations face heterogeneity in sensing hardware and manufacturer-specific protocols, making reliable multi-vendor networks and workflows difficult. Inconsistent data collection, storage, and communication approaches force users to operate across multiple systems. This creates barriers to generalized, scalable data management for continuous sensing.
supporting_quote: Heterogeneity in sensing hardware and software ... makes it difficult to assemble a reliable network of in situ sensors from different manufacturers
Inconsistencies between communication protocols and software from different sensor/datalogger manufacturers may require researchers to work across multiple systems

chunks.text: There are few complete off-the-shelf solutions that cover the end-to-end needs of collecting, communicating, storing, managing, and sharing environmental sensor time series. Commercial systems can be expensive or proprietary, while other tools are tied to specific manufacturers. This leaves gaps for users who need generalized and affordable solutions.
supporting_quote: there remain few complete, generalized, offthe-shelf software solutions that enable collecting, communicating, storing, managing, and sharing time series
Commercial options range from excellent (but expensive and proprietary) ... to more specialized software solutions that remain specific to a particular sensor or datalogger manufacturer

chunks.text: Centralization of the CUAHSI HIS reduced operational functionality needed for day-to-day data management. In particular, upload of streaming sensor data was not supported via the public query services, and near real-time ingestion tooling was not maintained. This made the system stronger for sharing than for operational management.
supporting_quote: WaterOneFlow provides a public data query API, but does not allow data upload.
CUAHSI did not advance or maintain HydroServer's Streaming Data Loader software ... As a result, dynamic uploading of streaming sensor data was disabled

chunks.text: Existing platforms often lack support for IoT devices, IoT protocols, and open standards for interfaces and encodings. IoT platforms can be application-agnostic and require customization, and may assume data are short-lived with limited long-term management capabilities. These issues constrain interoperability and operational monitoring needs.
supporting_quote: Additional limitations of existing software include lack of support for IoT devices, IoT protocols, and open standards for interfaces and data encodings.
IoT software systems also often assume that data are short lived with little support for the type of long term data management required for environmental monitoring.

chunks.text: HydroServer’s architecture follows a generalized hydrologic information system pattern with four primary components: acquisition, operational storage, data management/processing, and publication/exchange. The design explicitly places ingestion and query web services as a central connector between components. Requirements and assumptions were derived from use cases, earlier HydroServer versions, and a literature-based generalized HIS architecture.
supporting_quote: This generalized architecture consists of four primary components: 1) data collection and acquisition ... 2) operational storage ... 3) data management, curation, and processing ... and 4) publication, sharing, and exchange
HydroServer's overall software architecture (Fig. 1) follows this general HIS architecture pattern, but explicitly groups the web service interfaces for data ingestion and query

chunks.text: The data acquisition design supports three ingestion pathways: direct posting by internet-connected dataloggers to HydroServer’s ingestion API, loading by scripts or software via the API (optionally through the Python client), and loading CSV outputs using a Streaming Data Loader. This approach intentionally complements, rather than replaces, proprietary field interfacing tools. Automation can be implemented with local scheduling or cloud orchestration tools.
supporting_quote: three main pathways for loading data into HydroServer: 1) Internet connected dataloggers can post data directly through Hydro-Server's web service API
3) CSV files ... can be loaded using a "Streaming Data Loader" software app

chunks.text: Operational storage is based on an extended OGC SensorThings API (STA) data model, augmented with ODM metadata for unambiguous environmental monitoring description. HydroServer also adds entities for multi-user security and access control. The model is used both for the database schema and as the basis for API input/output encodings.
supporting_quote: Hydro-Server was designed to use an extended version of the OGC STA data model ... to which we added metadata ... from the Observations Data Model (ODM)
We also added additional entities and attributes to the data model to enable HydroServer to handle data from multiple users and to provide security and access control.

chunks.text: HydroServer implements OGC STA Part 1: Sensing v1.1 for standardized ingestion and query, following OData URL conventions and JSON formats. Because HydroServer extends STA with additional entities, it provides a complementary data management API to support user management, access control, and orchestration metadata. Together, these APIs support full CRUD of metadata and observational data.
supporting_quote: include an implementation of the OGC STA Part 1: Sensing Version 1.1 API
we developed a data management web service API that is complementary to STA

chunks.text: A web-based data management application provides GUI-driven workflows for accounts, workspaces, metadata creation, data browsing/visualization/export, access control, and data loading setup. QC functionality is designed for scriptability via Python functions and a separate QC GUI application that is under development. The GUI complements the APIs by enabling common tasks without writing code.
supporting_quote: we designed a data management web application ... creating user accounts; creating workspaces; creating and managing metadata ... browsing, inspecting, and visualizing available data
We designed QC functionality for scriptability via data QC functions coded within HydroServer's Python client package ... the QC software application is currently under development

chunks.text: The hydroserverpy Python client abstracts HTTP requests, authentication, and JSON-to-object conversion to simplify automation and analysis workflows. It is organized into api (CRUD + retrieval to Pandas), etl (extract/transform/load with extensible extractors/transformers/loaders), and quality (QC filters and edits) sub-packages. The ETL components enable loading from multiple transfer protocols and nonstandard formats by extension.
supporting_quote: We developed a Python client package called hydroserverpy ... abstracts low-level details of making HTTP requests ... handles user authentication
The hydroserverpy package currently consists of three sub-packages ... api ... etl ... quality

chunks.text: The Streaming Data Loader (SDL) is a cross-platform desktop application that automates loading observations from CSV files into HydroServer. It runs as a background service with scheduled jobs, retrieving its configuration from HydroServer’s data management API, and loading new records via STA. Job setup maps CSV columns (payloads) to specific datastream IDs within defined workspaces.
supporting_quote: The Streaming Data Loader (SDL) is a desktop app that can be used to automatically load data into HydroServer from CSV files containing sensor data
The SDL retrieves all information about which data to load from HydroServer's data management API

chunks.text: The authors provide operational scale characteristics from the Logan River Observatory deployment to motivate requirements and demonstrate applicability. The observatory contains nearly 30 sites producing data every 15 minutes, with a long-term record exceeding 10 years at some sites. The database size is reported as more than 253 million observations and about 43,000 new observations per day.
supporting_quote: Logan River Observatory (LRO) ... consists of nearly 30 continuous monitoring sites generating new data every 15 min
the LRO observations database now contains more than 253 million individual observations, with approximately 43,000 new raw observations added daily

chunks.text: HydroServer’s operational data store is implemented in PostgreSQL, with optional Timescale extension for very large deployments. Entities are uniquely identified using GUIDs to ensure uniqueness across systems that contribute or consume data. The database can be hosted locally or via cloud-based managed PostgreSQL services.
supporting_quote: HydroServer uses ... PostgreSQL ... For very large HydroServer instances, the Timescale extension for PostgreSQL may provide some performance benefits
HydroServer uses globally unique identifiers (GUIDs) to uniquely identify entities in its database

chunks.text: HydroServer’s data model is an adaptation of OGC STA with additional entities for environmental monitoring and multi-user operations. Core STA entities include Thing, Location, Sensor, ObservedProperty, Datastream, and Observation, while HydroServer adds metadata such as ProcessingLevel, Unit, ResultQualifier, Photo, and Tag. It also adds user/workspace/access-control entities and orchestration entities such as DataSource, DataArchive, and OrchestrationSystem.
supporting_quote: HydroServer adopted important entities from the STA data model ... "Thing" ... "Location" ... "Sensor" ... "ObservedProperty" ... "Datastream" ... and "Observation"
we added the "DataSource", "DataArchive", and "OrchestrationSystem" entities to the data model

chunks.text: HydroServer delivers a full software stack implementing a standards-based HIS centered on OGC SensorThings API with added data management capabilities. It supports comprehensive CRUD for sensor metadata and observations via STA plus a complementary data management API. The platform is open source and designed for cloud or local deployments, aiming to make operational sensor data management more accessible to researchers and practitioners.
supporting_quote: HydroServer provides an open-source, standards-based software platform for environmental sensor data management.
Together, HydroServer's STA and data management web service API provide the ability to comprehensively create, read, update, and delete (CRUD) metadata and observational data

chunks.text: HydroServer provides role-based access control via workspaces to support multi-user data management. Users can create workspaces and add collaborators with roles of owner, editor, and viewer; public workspaces can be browsed by general users. This approach replaced station-level access control to reduce management burden as the number of stations grows.
supporting_quote: we implemented role-based access control over "workspaces" ... roles of owner, editor, and viewer

We originally implemented access control at the individual monitoring station (Thing) level but found that this required a lot of work ... As an alternative, we implemented role-based access control over "workspaces".

chunks.text: The hydroserverpy client package simplifies both management and analytics workflows by providing high-level objects and methods for entity CRUD and data retrieval to Pandas. It includes convenience functions similar to USGS dataretrieval for obtaining datastream subsets and loading them into DataFrames. This makes scripting ingestion, querying, and QC more practical for users working in Python.
supporting_quote: The api sub-package provides functionality ... for creation, editing, retrieval, or deletion
provides functionality that is similar to the United States Geological Survey's (USGS) dataretrieval package ... retrieving datastreams ... and loading them into a Pandas DataFrame object

chunks.text: HydroServer’s etl tooling supports generalized data loading beyond CSV-by-SDL, including extensible extractors and transformers for multiple protocols and formats. It defines a generic loader interface where a datastream loads observations from a Pandas DataFrame through a load_observations method. The ETL classes are explicitly designed to be extensible so users can integrate nonstandard or legacy formats.
supporting_quote: We implemented a set of extractors capable of authenticating with and retrieving data from various endpoints using HTTP, SFTP
defined a loader that uses a generic load_observations method ... takes as input a pandas DataFrame object

chunks.text: The data management web app provides core HIS user functionality, including maps of sites, station landing pages, datastream configuration, sparkline views of recent data, interactive plotting, and downloadable CSV exports. Users can filter datastreams by site, observed property, and processing level and share plot state via URL. The web app is implemented with Vue.js/TypeScript and integrates Google Maps for site browsing.
supporting_quote: HydroServer's data management web app provides a graphical user interface that allows users to create and manage monitoring sites and their associated datastreams and metadata.
The data management app was developed using the Vue.js 3.4 framework ... Google Maps Java-Script API

chunks.text: The Streaming Data Loader enables scheduled ingestion of new records from CSV sources by mapping file columns to HydroServer datastream identifiers. Configuration is managed through the Job orchestration page and stored as OrchestrationSystem and DataSource metadata. The SDL detects new data not previously loaded and pushes status updates back to HydroServer for monitoring.
supporting_quote: On the user-defined schedule, the SDL will parse the data source file, detect any new data that has not already been loaded into Hydro-Server, and then load new data
Configuration information for orchestration systems, data sources, and mappings ... are stored in the OrchestrationSystem, DataSource, and Datastream tables

chunks.text: HydroServer supports archiving operational time series to HydroShare, enabling long-term sharing and a project end-of-life off-ramp. Users authorize via OAuth 2.0, configure archival per monitoring site, and export one CSV per selected datastream including descriptive headers. Archived files can be written to new or existing HydroShare resources and organized by folders per site.
supporting_quote: OAuth 2.0 is then used to authorize the data management web app to access HydroShare on the user's behalf.
One data file containing the entire period of record is exported per selected datastream ... written in a CSV format with a descriptive header

chunks.text: The authors deployed HydroServer for the Logan River Observatory at a public URL and provide a public playground instance for testing. The LRO instance hosts watershed monitoring data intended to support water management decision-making and hydrologic research, while the playground allows users to create accounts and try functionality. These deployments demonstrate operational readiness and accessibility for evaluation.
supporting_quote: we have deployed an instance of HydroServer for the LRO at https://lro.hydroserver.org
We also provide a public testing instance of HydroServer at https://playground.hydroserver.org that allows users to create a user account and test HydroServer's functionality

chunks.text: HydroServer has been adopted for operational modernization of Utah’s Division of Water Rights infrastructure, which manages data from more than 1500 continuous stations. The system is used for water distribution accounting in Utah’s legal water rights system, serving as a data management platform and data source for decisions. This illustrates applicability beyond the authors’ research observatory.
supporting_quote: UDWRi operates or retrieves data from more than 1500 continuous data collection stations throughout Utah
with HydroServer serving as a data management platform and the source of data for operational decision making

chunks.text: HydroServer’s adoption of OGC STA positions it for interoperability with international initiatives such as WMO WHOS and potential GEOGloWS use cases. The paper argues that standards-based interfaces and encodings allow integration with broker and discovery systems. HydroServer’s access control allows providers to choose what becomes public while still supporting interoperability.
supporting_quote: HydroServer fits with the architecture of WHOS by enabling data providers to share hydrologic data via standards-based web service interfaces and data encodings (using OGC's STA)
HydroServer is also under consideration by the GEOGloWS Initiative ... as a platform for enabling hydrologic measurement services

chunks.text: HydroServer’s specific technology choices may not align with all organizations’ existing expertise or systems, limiting customization for some advanced groups. Some potential users may also lack the expertise to deploy and operate HydroServer themselves. This creates an opportunity for hosted HydroServer-as-a-service models.
supporting_quote: our specific technology choices may or may not be compatible with their expertise or other systems they maintain
Other groups may lack the expertise to deploy an instance of HydroServer for their own use, leaving an opportunity for potential hosting of Hydro-Server instances as a service

chunks.text: Because HydroServer is relatively new, the authors report continued discovery and fixing of bugs during operational use. This implies maturation work is ongoing as deployments expand. Users should expect iterative stabilization as the system is exercised under varied real-world conditions.
supporting_quote: since HydroServer is relatively new, we are still uncovering bugs and fixing them as we use HydroServer in operational contexts.

chunks.text: Performance and scalability can depend on appropriate cloud configuration and resource sizing, which requires specialized expertise. Although issues can be addressed through deployment choices, managing costs while meeting performance objectives is nontrivial. This can be a barrier for organizations without cloud operations capacity.
supporting_quote: Issues with performance and scalability, particularly for instances with large data volumes, can be solved with appropriate configurations within cloud deployment environments
expertise is required to "right-size" cloud resources to minimize costs while meeting performance objectives

chunks.text: The paper concludes that HydroServer provides an open-source platform enabling effective collection, communication, storage, management, and sharing of in situ environmental sensor data. It emphasizes that using the open OGC SensorThings standard makes the system interoperable and adaptable to different organizations. Deployments for the LRO and Utah’s Division of Water Rights are cited as evidence of capacity to manage large sensor data volumes.
supporting_quote: HydroServer provides a software platform designed to meet these needs for organizations that operate sensors for environmental monitoring.
Successful deployment of HydroServer for the LRO and UDWRi's water use data infrastructure demonstrates its capacity to manage large volumes of sensor data.

chunks.text: HydroServer’s flexibility in deployment (cloud or local infrastructure) is presented as enabling tailoring and scaling for diverse organizational requirements. The authors also highlight automation via the SDL and Python client and the availability of HydroShare archival as a practical off-ramp when projects end. These features aim to reduce long-term maintenance burdens while preserving access to curated datasets.
supporting_quote: HydroServer's flexibility in deployment, whether through commercial cloud platforms or local infrastructure, ensures that it can be tailored and scaled
Archival to HydroShare provides an off-ramp at the end of a project or data collection initiative so that an organization need not maintain an active HydroServer instance in perpetuity.

chunks.text: Backwater (BW) conditions occur where a river meets standing water (ocean, lake, reservoir) or upstream of dams, forcing water surface elevation to “back up” and altering depth, velocity, and sediment transport over long distances. In BW zones, water surface slope decreases independent of bed slope, changing longitudinal depth and velocity profiles. These hydraulic shifts can substantially influence erosion and deposition patterns and thus flood dynamics and land topography in coastal and dam-influenced rivers.
supporting_quote: This condition can occur as a river joins a body of standing water (e.g., ocean, lake, and dam reservoir)
The shift in BW hydraulics causes the water surface slope to decrease independent of the bed slope

chunks.text: Observed and modeled studies suggest BW hydraulics can either reduce or enhance shear stress and sediment transport depending on flow conditions. In low to moderate flows, expanding cross-sectional area downstream can reduce shear stress and transport, promoting deposition. During high flows, drawdown to match downstream water levels can decrease cross-sectional area downstream and increase shear stress and transport, intensifying geomorphic activity.
supporting_quote: during low-moderate flows, resulting in a decrease in shear stress and sediment transport
during high flows, the cross sectional area decreases downstream and results in a substantial increase in shear stress and sediment transport

chunks.text: Darby Creek in metro-Philadelphia is an urban, flood-prone creek whose lower reach is influenced by the Delaware River, creating a substantial BW segment. The study reach spans about 15 river kilometers from Mt. Moriah Cemetery to the Delaware River confluence. Approximately 7 river kilometers of the lower creek are estimated to be in BW conditions, and the downstream wetland area (Heinz National Wildlife Refuge) increases the importance of understanding channel and floodplain evolution.
supporting_quote: reaching to a length of approximately 15 river kilometers (rkm)
Approximately 7 rkm of the lower part of the creek is estimated to be in BW conditions

chunks.text: The study aims to present an integrated iterative two-dimensional fluvial morphological model that can quantify spatio-temporal morphological alterations from quasi-normal flow through transitional and backwater conditions. The approach integrates a 2D normal-flow model with a 1D gradually varied flow backwater profile to generate a consistent water surface elevation field. Using that integrated water surface, the study develops an analytical 2D approach to estimate shear stress and predict erosion/deposition patterns over time for Darby Creek.
supporting_quote: This study presents an integrated iterative two-dimensional fluvial morphological model to quantify spatio-temporal fluvial morphological alterations in normal flow to backwater conditions.
an analytical 2D model is established to estimate shear stresses and morphological alterations in the normal, transitional, and backwater zones

chunks.text: A further goal is to test whether the model’s predicted locations of geomorphic change are consistent with observations, given limited direct before/after topography. The paper verifies the integrated water surface profile against LiDAR-derived water surface elevation for a moderate discharge. It then compares predicted erosion/deposition patterns with Landsat-based change detection over a window that includes the largest recorded flood (164 cms on 8 September 2011).
supporting_quote: The LiDAR data collected on 25 April, 2015 was used to determine the measured water surface elevation along the creek.
the highest registered flood happened on 8 September, 2011 with a maximum discharge of 164 cms

chunks.text: Predicting morphodynamics in BW zones is challenging because BW hydraulics complicate hydrometric measurements and produce spatially varying depths and velocities that differ from uniform flow assumptions. The presence of BW complicates measuring water surface slope, velocity, and discharge, and transitional areas are particularly data-poor. These issues limit conventional sediment-transport-based approaches that rely on measured or estimated hydraulic parameters.
supporting_quote: The presence of the BW complicates different types of hydrometric measurements including the water surface slope, velocity, and discharge
A lack in measured data is even more severe for transitional areas where the flow state changes from normal to a gradually varied flow

chunks.text: The paper identifies a methodological gap: two-dimensional morphological models for BW and transitional zones are not well known or available for predicting morphological alterations. While hydraulic models exist for gradually varied flow water surface profiles, integrating them with 2D morphodynamics remains underdeveloped. This motivates building a coupled 1D–2D framework to address BW-driven changes.
supporting_quote: there is no two-dimensional river model available for predicting morphological alterations in backwater zones
the 2D morphological models currently available for BW and transitional zones are not well known

chunks.text: A practical challenge for Darby Creek is the lack of frequently updated elevation datasets needed for direct geomorphic model verification. LiDAR collection is difficult in this area because it would require shutdown of the Philadelphia airport, making recent floodplain DEMs scarce.
