As a result, the study must rely on older LiDAR/bathymetry merging and indirect validation via satellite reflectance changes.
supporting_quote: Collecting LiDAR data for the study area is extremely difficult since it requires shutdown of the Philadelphia airport.
In the absence of more recent data, the LiDAR based DEM and bathymetry data were merged

chunks.text: The integrated modeling workflow iteratively links hydraulic simulation, backwater profiling, and morphodynamic updating. First, iRIC is used to generate a 2D normal-zone water surface elevation for a discharge. Second, a 1D backwater profile is generated for the BW zone using a modified Parker approach, and then the two surfaces are integrated with a linearly adjusted transitional zone. Finally, an analytical 2D method estimates shear stress and erosion/deposition, generating a new DEM that becomes the input for the next discharge iteration.
supporting_quote: (1) iRIC model is used to generate a 2D normal water surface; (2) a 1D water surface is developed for the backwater; (3) the normal and backwater surfaces are integrated
The integrated model generates a new digital elevation model based on the estimated erosion and deposition.

chunks.text: The BW water surface profile is computed regressively from the known downstream boundary condition at the river mouth. The BW length scale is characterized as Lb = H/S using mouth depth and average bed slope to differentiate normal and BW regions. The gradually varied flow equation dH/dx = (S0 − Sf)/(1 − Fr2) is used, with frictional slope related to bed friction (Sf = Cf Fr2) and Manning-Strickler roughness to link depth and friction.
supporting_quote: the water surface profile was generated regressively from the known water surface elevation at the mouth
Lb = H/S
dH/dx = (S0 - Sf)/(1 - Fr^2)

chunks.text: To estimate depths across BW cross sections, the study assumes water surface elevation is approximately constant laterally. Node depth is computed from the integrated WSE and the node ground elevation using hi = WSE − Zi. This provides 2D depth values in BW and transitional zones even though the WSE is computed along the thalweg using the 1D model.
supporting_quote: By assuming that the water surface elevation was constant across the cross section, the depth at each node in the cross section was calculated as: hi = WSE - Zi
By assuming that WSE does not change substantially across the cross sections in the BW zone

chunks.text: A cross-section segmentation method is used to compute shear stress in the BW zone. Each cross section is divided into segments between adjacent nodes; segment area is computed as Ai = L (h1 + h2)/2 and wetted perimeter approximated by node spacing. Hydraulic radius Ri = Ai/Pi and segment conveyance Ki = (1/n) Ai Ri^(2/3) are computed, with segment discharge apportioned by area Qi = Q Ai/ATotal. Segment friction slope follows Sfi = (Qi/Ki)^2, enabling shear stress estimation via τb = γ RH Sf.
supporting_quote: Qi = Q , Ai/ATotal.
Sfi = (Qi/Ki)^2

chunks.text: Sediment transport is computed using the Meyer-Peter and Müller (MPM) relation based on excess non-dimensional shear stress. The non-dimensional bedload rate is q* = α(τ* − τ*c)^β with τ*c = 0.047, and q* is converted to volumetric bedload discharge per unit width. To better represent sand, α is adjusted from 8 to 12 while β remains 1.5. Bed elevation change is then computed using the 2D Exner equation with sediment porosity.
supporting_quote: τ*c is the non-dimensional shear stress associated with incipient motion equal to 0.047
the α value was adjusted from 8 to 12 to make the equation applicable for sand

chunks.text: To avoid numerical artifacts near the normal-to-BW transition, the study applies smoothing and under-relaxation to bed elevation updates. A diffuser function averages neighboring node elevation changes using ηsmooth = (1 − ε)η + (1/n)Ση, with ε = 0.1 and n = 2. An under-relaxation update ηnew = (1 − ω)ηold + ω ηsmooth is applied with ω = 0.1, and ηnew updates the DEM each timestep.
supporting_quote: ε = 0.1 and n = 2 were used in the calculations
the under-relaxation coefficient, ω, was set to 0.1
ηnew = (1 - ω) ηold + ω ηsmooth

chunks.text: Model verification uses two complementary remote sensing checks: LiDAR-based water surface elevation and Landsat-based surface change detection. For LiDAR, the integrated model is run at 0.42 cms (the discharge on 25 April 2015) and compared to water surface points extracted near banks. For geomorphic validation, two cloud-free Landsat images (14 July and 16 September 2011) are differenced after masking water using NDWI, and the mapped reflectance changes are compared to simulated erosion/deposition patterns.
supporting_quote: the discharge associated with that date was 0.42 cms
Two cloud-free Landsat images from 2011 (14 July and 16 September) were obtained
The normalized difference water index (NDWI) was used to differentiate between the water, vegetation and soil

chunks.text: The study integrates multiple geospatial and hydrologic datasets into a single geodatabase to support hydraulic and morphodynamic simulations. Inputs include LiDAR-based basin DEM (2006–2008), LiDAR point cloud (2015), and NOAA bathymetry (2008) merged to represent floodplain and channel bathymetry. Time series discharge and water surface elevation come from a USGS gage, while downstream stage boundary conditions come from NOAA tidal gages on the Delaware River.
supporting_quote: The data used for this study was collected from a range of open disparate sources and integrated in a single geodatabase (Table 1).
Basin DEM based on LiDAR (2006–2008)
Discharge (2006–2016) and measured water surface elevation (2015)

chunks.text: Hydrologic forcing is derived from USGS and NOAA stations. Upstream discharge and water surface elevation are obtained from the USGS Cobbs Creek at Mt. Moriah Cemetery gage (01475548) using fifteen-minute discharge records. Downstream stage is taken from Delaware River NOAA gages 8540433 and 8545240 referenced to NAVD88, providing boundary conditions needed for the backwater profile.
supporting_quote: Water surface elevation and the discharge data were obtained from the USGS gage ... (USGS gage 01475548). The hydrograph was constructed from fifteen-minute discharge data.
Stage ... obtained from NOAA gages of the Delaware River (8540433, and 8545240, recorded at NAVD88 vertical datum).

chunks.text: Bed sediment characteristics are informed by field sampling and sieving analysis at two locations along the creek. Samples were collected on 9 November 2017 at rkm 2 (bed, point bar, substrate) and rkm 4 (bed, bank), when discharge was 0.1 cms (5th percentile). For morphological analysis, the downstream substrate grain sizes D50 = 0.0016 m and D90 = 0.0027 m are used.
supporting_quote: At 2 rkm, three sediment samples were collected
At the time of sampling (9 November 2017), the discharge was 0.1 cubic meters per second (cms), which was the 5th percentile discharge
grain sizes ... downstream with D50 = 0.0016 m and D90 = 0.0027 m were considered

chunks.text: Event-based calibration and validation data include a major flood used to calibrate the 2D iRIC hydraulics and a separate extreme flood window used for geomorphic comparison. iRIC calibration targets an event on 30 August 2009 with peak WSE of 12 m and maximum discharge of 184 cms using a 72-hour observed hydrograph and friction coefficients. For geomorphic verification, the highest registered flood on 8 September 2011 (164 cms) anchors a July–September 2011 period assessed with Landsat imagery.
supporting_quote: selected event for the model calibration occurred on 30 August, 2009 and registered a peak water surface elevation of 12 m with the maximum discharge of 184 cms.
the highest registered flood happened on 8 September, 2011 with a maximum discharge of 164 cms

chunks.text: A critical (incipient) discharge threshold for selecting peak events is computed using the Schoklitsch equation and local slope/sediment parameters. Using S = 7.04 × 10−4, d40 = 0.0013 m, and an average width of 70 m, the study estimates and rounds the critical discharge up to 10 cms. This threshold filters out low discharges when selecting peak flows between the two Landsat image dates.
supporting_quote: the Schoklitsch Equation [71] was used to find the critical discharge as
By considering S = 7.04 × 10−4, d40 = 0.0013 m and an average width of 70 m ... rounded up to 10 cms.

chunks.text: The integrated water surface profile captures differences between quasi-normal hydraulics and gradually varied BW hydraulics and is qualitatively supported by LiDAR-derived water surface elevations. For a moderate discharge of 0.42 cms, the model-generated water surface profile is compared to water surface points extracted from the 25 April 2015 LiDAR dataset. The paper notes uncertainty is concentrated around the transitional zone where the 1D and 2D profiles differ abruptly and are interpolated to create a smooth transition.
supporting_quote: The integrated model was then run for a discharge of 0.42 cms to obtain the estimated water surface elevation.
The red vertical lines show the transitional zone, which indicates uncertainty in the estimated water surface elevation.

chunks.text: Hydraulic classification indicates mild-slope M-type profiles and an M1 backwater condition under the chosen downstream boundary. The critical depth for the maximum simulated discharge (164 cms) with average width 70 m is estimated as 0.82 m and is smaller than the normal depth from iRIC in the BW zone. With an average downstream WSE boundary of 1 m on the Delaware River, the BW depth is above normal (y > yn; y > yc), consistent with an M1 profile for all discharges.
supporting_quote: The critical depth associated with the maximum discharge in the simulations (164 cms) and the average river width of 70 m was estimated as 0.82 m
An average WSE of 1 m was used in the hydraulic models for the downstream boundary condition ... suggesting an M1 water surface profile. This was true for all discharges.

chunks.text: Spatial patterns of modeled geomorphic change generally align with Landsat-detected surface reflectance changes from July to September 2011. Both approaches show reduced geomorphic activity in the transitional zone between quasi-normal and BW flow and limited change at the initiation of the BW zone. They also broadly agree on active morphological alterations in the lower marsh area of the BW zone, indicating bank activity and sediment exchange between channel and banks.
supporting_quote: The results of the integrated model showing areas of change generally agreed with the surface changes captured by the Landsat images.
Both methods captured the reduction in the geomorphic changes in the transitional zone between the quasi-normal and the BW zones.

chunks.text: The model produces mapped erosion and deposition locations and integrated DEM change over the study window. For example, for a discharge of 99 cms with a 1 h duration, the model identifies predicted erosion and deposition points. By integrating node-based erosion and deposition across the domain, the study generates a raster of elevation change where positive values indicate deposition and negative values indicate erosion, including localized changes at the entrance of the BW zone.
supporting_quote: Erosion and deposition locations were identified by the integrated model for a discharge of 99 cms ... with the duration of 1 h.
Positive and negative values in DEM change indicate deposition and erosion respectively.

chunks.text: Discharge sensitivity differs between BW and quasi-normal zones, with BW requiring higher flows before morphological activity initiates. The study finds that for discharges lower than 42 cms, no morphological alterations occur in the BW zone, whereas quasi-normal zone alterations below 22 cms are negligible. The authors interpret this as a higher critical discharge threshold for morphologic activity in BW conditions compared with quasi-normal flow.
supporting_quote: For discharges lower than 42 cms, no morphological alterations took place in the BW zone
in the quasi-normal zone, the morphological alterations below 22 cms were negligible

chunks.text: Grain size sensitivity analysis shows decreasing geomorphic activity with increasing sediment size, with stronger sensitivity in the BW zone. The model predicts almost no geomorphic changes in the BW zone for grain sizes larger than 6 mm. In the normal zone, it predicts no geomorphic changes for grain sizes larger than 35 mm, highlighting differing mobility thresholds across hydraulic regimes.
supporting_quote: The sensitivity analysis ... showed that the geomorphic activities in both the quasi-normal and BW zones decreased with an increase in sediment size
The model predicted almost no geomorphic changes in the BW zone for any grain size larger than 6
in the normal zone, no geomorphic changes for grain sizes larger than 35 mm.

chunks.text: The paper emphasizes that the validation against Landsat is qualitative and intended to confirm spatial patterns rather than quantify sediment volumes. It states the model predicts where erosion or deposition occurs on a relative scale, not the quantity of moved material. The authors note that improved verification requires recently measured elevation datasets, which are currently lacking for the site.
supporting_quote: The purpose of validating the integrated model by using Landsat images was not to compare it with the model output in quantifiable terms
The model predicts where erosion or deposition occurs on a relative scale, rather than predicting the quantity of the moved or deposited sediment.

chunks.text: Several factors may explain discrepancies between satellite-detected changes and simulated geomorphic activity, especially in the lower BW marsh where Landsat indicates more activity than the model. Proposed causes include water covering land in imagery, vegetation effects, and the limitation of simulating a single discharge instead of a full hydrograph. The paper also points to model sensitivity to chosen sediment size and to the selection of the sediment transport equation.
supporting_quote: The satellite images captured more morphologic activity in the marsh relative to the model prediction.
A single discharge simulation rather than a full hydrograph did not capture the differences.
The discrepancy ... might stem from sensitivity of the model toward the selected sediment size

chunks.text: Water surface elevation extraction from LiDAR is described as potentially arbitrary due to point-cloud noise and lateral WSE variability. The authors note adjacent-point elevation differences over the water surface can vary by about 10 percent, potentially reflecting lateral WSE variations, remote sensing errors, suspended materials, and waves. This limits the certainty of WSE verification, particularly near the transition zone.
supporting_quote: Choosing points from LiDAR data to obtain water surface profiles can be arbitrary
The elevation differences in adjacent points over the water surface—which may vary approximately up to 10 percent

chunks.text: The morphodynamic model simplifies sediment properties by using a single representative grain size, creating uncertainty in predicted geomorphic alterations. The authors explicitly flag sensitivity to D50 and suggest that incorporating multiple transport models could better represent mobility across different sizes. This limitation is highlighted in relation to differences between modeled and satellite-observed activity in parts of the BW zone.
supporting_quote: The developed geomorphic model was based on a single grain size, which may result in an uncertainty in the predicted geomorphic alterations.
The integrated model can be enhanced by including other transport models that can address the mobility of different sediment sizes.

chunks.text: Remote sensing change detection can be biased in heavily vegetated upstream areas, which may affect the comparison with model outputs in the quasi-normal zone. The paper notes that trees and bushes along the creek might bias Landsat change results, while the lower BW zone is less affected due to less dense vegetation. This underscores the unequal reliability of satellite-based verification across the study reach.
supporting_quote: In the upstream area (normal zone ...), the presence of the trees and bushes along the creek might bias the Landsat change results
for the lower part in the BW zone that issue is less significant, as the vegetation is less dense

chunks.text: The study concludes that an integrated 1D–2D framework can simulate spatial patterns of erosion and deposition across normal, transitional, and BW zones and iteratively update topography through time. The approach integrates and adjusts water surface profiles across zones, then derives shear stress and sediment transport to estimate bed elevation change. The model is positioned as an intermediate time-scale tool (decades) to inform land/resource management, infrastructure planning, and climate-change impact mitigation in BW-affected rivers.
supporting_quote: The integrated model generated a new DEM of the study area, which served as the starting point for the next iteration of flow, ultimately modeling geomorphic changes through time.
can simulate continuous morphological changes in BW conditions for an intermediate time scale (over decades)

chunks.text: Application to Darby Creek suggests distinct morphodynamic behavior in BW zones relative to quasi-normal flow. The simulations indicate a higher discharge threshold for morphological activity in the BW zone than in the quasi-normal zone. The model also indicates actively eroding and depositing banks in the BW zone and reduced morphological alterations in the transition from normal to gradually varied flow.
supporting_quote: the critical discharge ... for the BW zone is higher than the one for the quasi-normal flow.
The model results show that the banks in the BW zone in Darby Creek are actively experiencing erosion and deposition of the sediment.
the model showed a reduction in morphological alterations at transitioning zone from normal to a gradually varied flow.

chunks.text: The authors emphasize that the model is intended to identify representative areas or gradients of change rather than precisely quantify magnitudes of sediment movement. It is framed as an initial, simplified integrated model that advances 2D geomorphic assessment in BW and transitional zones, where such tools are limited. Verification using LiDAR WSE and Landsat change detection supports that the model captures major spatial patterns of geomorphic change.
supporting_quote: The intention of this paper is to initially develop the integrated model in a simple form to show a representative change or gradient of change.
This model does not attempt to truly quantify the degree of change, just the areas of change.
Landsat images spanning three months suggested a strong spatial correlation between the model results and the presence of geomorphic change.

chunks.text: Recent advances in internet technology, WebGL, and computing hardware have made it feasible to deliver flow simulation results as interactive visualizations in a web browser. Flow visualization converts hydrodynamic model outputs into images/animations so that complex flow behavior can be understood intuitively. When combined with geospatial and monitoring data, web visualization platforms can support integrated watershed management and decision-making such as scheduling and disaster relief.
supporting_quote: Thanks to the rapid development of internet technology and computer hardware, it is now possible to use web services to provide visual simulations of flow field calculation results.
Flow visualization technology uses computer graphics and image processing technology to convert the data computed by hydrodynamic models into images or animations

chunks.text: Water flow visualization methods can be categorized by purpose (visual effect vs scientific visualization), by data type (scalar vs vector), and by temporal behavior (static vs dynamic). Vector and dynamic flow fields carry more information and are therefore harder to visualize effectively than scalar and static fields. Practical visualization relies on visual mapping methods such as direct, geometric, texture-based, and feature-based approaches.
supporting_quote: Water flow visualization techniques are generally classified into two categories: visual effect visualization and scientific visualization
the visualization of vector and dynamic flow fields is more difficult than that of scalar and static fields due to their higher amount of information.
There are four main types of visual mapping methods for water flow data ... direct ... geometric ... texture-based ... feature-based

chunks.text: Earlier watershed flow visualization applications were often built with Client/Server architectures, which are harder to maintain and use across platforms. As web technology matured, Browser/Server architectures became attractive due to cross-platform access and easier maintenance and expansion. However, web-side water flow visualization remains relatively rare due to limited graphics libraries, performance constraints, and insufficient integration with virtual earth/geospatial environments.
supporting_quote: The above-mentioned water flow visualization applications are all based on C/S architecture, which means that it is difficult to work across different platforms and maintain systems
As web technology has developed, B/S architecture, with effective cross-platform features, convenient maintenance, and expansion capability, has gradually replaced C/S architecture.
there are few applications of water flow visualization technology on the web because of a lack of graphics libraries and poor performance

chunks.text: The study aimed to develop a watershed water-flow visualization platform using B/S architecture on top of the Cesium web rendering framework. The platform targets visualization of scalar, vector, and dynamic flow field outputs directly in the browser. The authors also aimed to test the platform in the Beijiang River Basin to demonstrate usability across devices and realistic management scenarios.
supporting_quote: we developed a platform for visualizing flow in a watershed based on a Cesium rendering framework with Browser/Server (B/S) architecture
tested it in the Beijiang River Basin using scalar field, vector field, and dynamic flow field visualization techniques

chunks.text: Another central goal was to improve web rendering efficiency for large-scale flow fields without sacrificing precision. The work focused on combining frame interpolation for time-varying flows with a viewpoint-driven dynamic rendering strategy to reduce data transfer and rendering load. Performance testing was used to verify that rendering speed could meet practical requirements for large datasets.
supporting_quote: our performance test results indicate that the rendering performance meets the practical application requirements for visualizing large-scale flow fields by employing frame interpolation and viewpoint-based dynamic rendering techniques.
An attempt has also been made to optimize the display method to improve the efficiency of the visual rendering of largescale data plotted in a flow field.

chunks.text: Web-based water flow visualization faces challenges including lack of mature graphics libraries, lower performance than desktop, and limited ability to simulate diverse flow data types. Many existing web or desktop tools do not integrate geospatial data well or cannot be placed within a virtual earth context, reducing usefulness for basin-wide information integration. This motivates a platform that can overlay flow results with 3D geospatial context in a browser.
supporting_quote: there are few applications of water flow visualization technology on the web because of a lack of graphics libraries and poor performance, meaning that there are few ways to simulate different types of water flow data.
the vast majority of applications do not integrate geospatial data or cannot be combined with the virtual earth environment

chunks.text: Large-scale, refined flow simulations generate massive datasets, which create slow loading, low frame rates, and unsmooth interaction in web visualization. Transmission limits between server and browser can cause blocking when frequent file requests occur, leading to black or stuck screens. Rendering also stresses GPU memory, especially for time-varying fields requiring frequent updates.
supporting_quote: thus slow data loading, the low frame rate of the visualization display, and non-smooth interactions that occur when massive data are used in the visualization process on the web side
frequent requests for files will cause blockages on the browser side, resulting in, e.g., black screens and stuck screens.
the real-time updates of the large-scale data drawing will also place demands on the GPU Video RAM (VRAM).

chunks.text: Optimizing large-scale river flow visualization is harder than terrain or ocean currents because river models often use unstructured grids with complex topology and boundaries, making spatial hierarchies difficult. Simplifying the flow data may omit key river features and degrade accuracy. Few studies have achieved smooth display for enormous river flow datasets while maintaining high simulation precision.
supporting_quote: it is more difficult to visualize large-scale river flow data and provide precise simulations of the river, because the boundaries are mostly fitted by unstructured grids and the topology is complex, meaning that it is difficult to build a spatial hierarchy
if the flow field data are simplified, river features may be omitted, thereby affecting the visualization.
few researchers have managed to optimize the display when visualizing the enormous volume of large-scale river flow data

chunks.text: The system is designed with a three-layer B/S architecture: data, application, and display layers. The data layer stores monitoring, simulation, and geospatial datasets in databases and file servers. The application layer implements flow calculation, flow visualization, and 3D visualization modules to process data and prepare renderable content. The display layer renders results in the browser and sends user interactions to the server for responses.
supporting_quote: the platform is divided into three levels, namely the data layer, application layer, and display layer.
The application layer includes three modules, namely the flow calculation module, the flow visualization module, and the 3D visualization module.
The display effect of the client is rendered in the browser.

chunks.text: Implementation uses front–back end separation with open-source tools. The front end uses Bootstrap for UI and CesiumJS for rendering, with shader work based on OpenGL ES 2.0. The back end uses Flask to respond to requests and provides module interfaces, while MySQL stores structured data. Large unstructured resources like high-precision images and videos are served through file servers.
supporting_quote: The platform was developed in front- and back-end separation mode
CesiumJS as the rendering engine
In the back end, Flask was used as the web server framework
The data were stored in the MySQL database.
Access to large unstructured data, such as high-precision images and videos, was provided in the form of file servers.

chunks.text: Scalar fields such as water depth and water level are visualized as an isosurface rendered through the GPU pipeline. Scalar values are converted to textures and fitted to terrain, and fragment shaders compute color based on interpolated per-fragment scalar values. A piecewise color-mapping function assigns RGB colors by scalar ranges, enabling contour-style rendering while leveraging Cesium primitives and shader-based raster interpolation.
supporting_quote: The scalar field data, including water depth and water level
the web-side isosurface was drawn through the GPU rendering pipeline using the raster interpolation feature of the shader.
The scalar data were converted to textures and then fitted to the terrain
a color mapping relationship for this study was defined by Equation (1)

chunks.text: Slope confluence (hillslope-to-channel flow) is visualized using particles driven by DEM-derived flow directions. The study uses the D8 algorithm to compute flow direction based on the maximum descent gradient between a cell and its neighbors. Particles have lifecycle, motion (velocity/direction), and appearance properties; motion is updated in real time via Cesium's CallbackProperty, and particles regenerate when they expire or exit the field.
supporting_quote: The commonly used D8 algorithm ... was selected to calculate the flow direction in this study.
FlowDir = Max{(H(x) - H(x_i))/D(x_i)}
By updating the particle properties with the CallbackProperty function, the particle motion can be plotted in real time.

chunks.text: River vector fields are visualized with the Image-based Flow Visualization (IBFV) algorithm via texture advection. Each new frame blends the previous frame texture with a new noise texture controlled by a blending parameter. Implementation includes texture mesh warping based on integrated velocity, generating cyclic random white noise textures in shaders, and saving frames using Render-to-Texture with ping-pong frame buffer objects to access the previous frame.
supporting_quote: The IBFV algorithm is based on the principle of texture advection
This problem can be solved by combining the RTT (Render to Texture) technology and ping-pong technology
two frame buffer objects (FBOs) are created

chunks.text: Dynamic (time-varying) flow visualization is achieved by updating vertex attributes and grid positions over time while keeping grid topology constant. To avoid choppy transitions between discrete time-step files, the method performs frame interpolation within each time interval by computing a gradient between two time steps and updating the field for any intermediate time. Cesium DrawCommand mechanisms push updated data to refresh buffers and execute rendering.
supporting_quote: There are a large number of time-step files in the dynamic field rendering. While the topology of the grid does not change with time, the vertex attribute value and the grid position both change over time.
the flow field data over a short period of time are interpolated to fill the animation frames
f = F0 + δ0 × t
The gradient matrix of the flow field file is updated by the push mechanism of DrawCommand to refresh the vertex buffer data

chunks.text: To reduce web-side I/O delays and rendering pressure for large-scale time-varying data, the platform applies a viewpoint-based dynamic rendering strategy. Grid and flow files are preprocessed into blocks with file–block indexing so only relevant areas are loaded. At runtime, the viewport range is obtained from camera changes, corresponding blocks are requested on demand, and only the visible region is drawn by updating the RTT camera texture. Adjacent regions are preloaded asynchronously into cache.
supporting_quote: we adopted the viewpoint-based dynamic rendering strategy to reduce the amount of data calls and rendering data and improve the rendering efficiency.
divide the blocks and to establish the indexing relationships between the files and blocks
the area to be drawn is determined according to the location of the camera viewpoint
only draws the area within the viewport range
the adjacent region file is asynchronously requested and read into the cache

chunks.text: The platform’s data layer includes real-time hydrological station monitoring data (water level and flow), hydrodynamic simulation results, and geospatial datasets. Monitoring data are transmitted to the server in real time and used as initialization conditions for a 2D hydrodynamic model. Geospatial data include imagery, terrain (DEM), vector layers, and scalar layers, which are processed and loaded to build a 3D basin environment.
supporting_quote: the monitoring data, water flow simulation results, and geospatial data were stored in the data layer.
The monitoring data, including water level and flow data, were mainly sourced from hydrological stations and were transmitted to the data server in real time
Geospatial data, including image, terrain, vector layer, and scalar layer data, were processed and loaded to establish a 3D environment in the basin.

chunks.text: Performance tests were conducted for IBFV rendering using multiple scenarios with different mesh sizes, and reported counts of vertices, triangles, file sizes, and fps. The largest case listed includes 12,378,489 vertices and 24,742,804 triangles with 1,044 MB vertex file size and 484 MB flow field file size, yielding 18 fps. Mid-scale cases (e.g., 3,371,295 triangles) retained about 59–60 fps.
supporting_quote: Table 1   Rendering frame rate of the IBFV flow field for different amounts of meshes
Vertex file size (MB) ... 1,044
Flow field file size (MB) ... 484
Average frame rate (fps) ... 18

chunks.text: Cross-device compatibility was tested using a server deployment and clients accessing via Google Chrome over a local network. The hardware set included a server with Intel Xeon E5-2609 v4 *2 and NVIDIA Quadro P2000, and user devices including a Windows laptop (Ryzen 7 5800H, RTX 3060 Laptop), an Android phone (Snapdragon 888, Adreno 660), and an iPad (Apple A12X). These devices were used to benchmark visualization projects such as isosurface, particles, IBFV, and dynamic flood evolution.
supporting_quote: Different devices, namely a host, mobile phone, and tablet, were selected as client devices for testing
the user side used Google Chrome for access through the local area network.
Server ... Intel Xeon E5-2609 v4 *2 ... NVIDIA Quadro P2000
Android 12 ... Qualcomm Snapdragon 888 ... Qualcomm Adreno 660
iPad OS 15 ... Apple A12X

chunks.text: The case study area is the Beijiang River Basin reach between Feilaixia and Qingyuan hubs, covering 46 km of channel. The numerical simulation uses an unstructured triangular grid with 266,007 triangular cells and 134,060 grid nodes, with local grid refinement near spur dikes and bridges. A scenario library contains 63 working conditions derived from upstream/downstream flows and downstream water level, computed by a 2D hydrodynamic model and stored in a database.
supporting_quote: the river reach between the Feilaixia Water Conservancy Hub and the Qingyuan Water Conservancy Hub ... the length of the river channel in the study area is 46 km.
an unstructured triangular grid ... with a total of 266,007 triangular cells and 134,060 grid nodes.
divided into 63 working conditions.
calculated by a two-dimensional hydrodynamic model, and the results were stored in the database.

chunks.text: The platform constructs a 3D Earth scene using online imagery and terrain from the Map World web map server and loads hydraulic-structure vectors (e.g., spur dikes and bridges) as GeoJSON. For other 3D model formats (osgb, obj, fbx), conversion to Cesium-supported 3dTiles is required for distribution. These geospatial data provide context for overlaying and interpreting flow field visualizations.
supporting_quote: constructed a 3D Earth map from image and terrain data obtained online through the Map World web map server.
Vector graphics of, for example, the spur dikes and bridges were loaded into the scene in Geographic JavaScript Object Notation (GeoJSON) format files
they need to be converted to the 3dTiles format supported by Cesium

chunks.text: The IBFV performance test indicates the platform can render large vector-field meshes at interactive rates for several million triangles. Rendering stayed around 60 fps through case sizes up to about 3,371,295 triangles (59 fps) and remained 52 fps at 8,757,647 triangles. As mesh sizes grow beyond this, fps degrades (e.g., 28 fps at 17,484,490 triangles and 18 fps at 24,742,804 triangles), consistent with GPU memory pressure.
supporting_quote: generally stable at 60 fps under the rendering of 3 million meshes
Case 4 ... Number of triangles 3,371,295 ... Average frame rate (fps) 59

chunks.text: Richards' equation (RE) is the standard governing equation for variably saturated flow in soils and is widely used in vadose zone, ecohydrology, and land-surface modeling. Despite its importance, reliable numerical solution is difficult because soil hydraulic properties depend nonlinearly on pressure head and saturation. RE is particularly valuable for matrix drainage and capillary flows and for coupling with heat and solute transport.
supporting_quote: Richards' equation (RE) describes the movement of water in variably saturated porous media.
Almost any practical application of RE requires a numerical solution; yet RE remains challenging to solve reliably and accurately for a given set of boundary conditions and soil hydraulic properties

chunks.text: A common view is that pressure-head form solutions can suffer from mass conservation issues, while mixed-form approaches can enforce mass balance. Adaptive time-stepping (ATS) has been shown to effectively control mass balance errors. This paper positions generic ODE/DAE solvers as practical “black-box” ATS tools for RE when implemented carefully.
supporting_quote: Some numerical solutions to the  ψ  form of RE are reportedly subject to poor mass conservation
it has been shown that mass balance errors can be effectively controlled using ATS

chunks.text: For near-saturated conditions, the storage term dθ/dψ approaches zero, so an elastic storage term is needed to solve RE robustly. The paper incorporates specific storage SS into the capacity term so that saturated and unsaturated conditions can be handled with a unified ψ-based formulation. Setting SS=0 recovers the usual unsaturated form.
supporting_quote: Because  dθ/dψ=0  in saturated, or close to saturated, soils, an elastic storage term is needed to solve RE in these conditions.
for convenience, hereafter we define  C(ψ) = SS θ(ψ)/θS + ∂θ/∂ψ , such that elastic storage can be ignored by setting  SS = 0

chunks.text: The paper aims to implement a simple, practical, efficient, and mass-conservative RE solver using open-source Python tooling and off-the-shelf ODE solvers. A second goal is to improve mass balance calculations for ATS solvers by addressing boundary-flux evaluation under adaptive stepping. The work also provides guidance on maximizing efficiency/accuracy and avoiding subtle implementation pitfalls.
supporting_quote: Our objective in this paper is to (i) implement a simple and practical approach to solve RE that is efficient, is mass conservative, and uses open-source software (written in Python)
and (ii) present an improved mass balance calculation procedure for use with ordinary differential equation (ODE) solvers that apply adaptive time-stepping (ATS) schemes.

chunks.text: The authors define five success criteria for evaluating an RE solver: reproduce benchmark states, conserve mass, minimize truncation errors in boundary fluxes for chosen time steps, be computationally efficient, and prefer simpler code when performance is comparable. These criteria motivate comparing ATS+ODE methods to classic fixed-step iterative schemes and Hydrus 1D.
supporting_quote: we define the following five criteria for success for an RE solver: (i) ... reproduce benchmark solutions
(ii) ... mass conservative
(iii) truncation errors in the simulated boundary fluxes should be negligible
(iv) ... computationally efficient; and (v) ... the simplest code should be preferred.

chunks.text: Even when a method enforces water balance closure, boundary fluxes can still have substantial truncation error that depends on the user-selected time step. This creates a situation where inflow and storage-change terms both shift with Δt while the balance still “closes,” potentially misleading evaluations that focus only on mass balance. The paper highlights this as an underappreciated issue for mixed-form fixed-step solutions using backward-difference flux integration.
supporting_quote: This solution has excellent mass balance closure, but because it uses a fixed-step iterative solution procedure with a backward difference approximation for  Q_{j → j+1} , the simulated boundary fluxes can be shown to be sensitive to the time step
even though for larger  Δt  the water balance is still perfectly closed, the actual terms within the water balance have changed

chunks.text: ATS ODE solvers produce many internal calculation steps between reporting outputs, but naive flux calculations based only on reporting-step states can miss nonlinear evolution of q(t). Using dense output or forcing reporting steps to equal calculation steps can address this but increases memory and runtime demands. The paper frames this as the key practical obstacle to accurate boundary fluxes and water balance under ATS.
supporting_quote: To accurately calculate the boundary fluxes, it is necessary to use the  ψ  information from the calculation time steps
enable dense output ... or ... force the ODE solver to make the reporting steps equal to the calculation steps. However, both of these approaches are more computationally demanding

chunks.text: Mass balance metrics computed only over the full simulation can hide large internal errors that cancel over time. The paper therefore introduces a daily (or chosen increment) RMSE metric in addition to overall bias to detect error accumulation or cancellation. This reframes model evaluation beyond a single end-to-end balance check.
supporting_quote: The bias error can be treated as a mass balance performance metric for the model, but this metric may underestimate the true errors in the water balance that occur within the time period simulated, which may cancel out over the entire run.
A more rigorous mass balance performance metric is the root mean squared error of the daily (or some other time increment) cumulative net flux minus the change in storage,  εR

chunks.text: Generic ODE-solver implementations of RE can fail on challenging boundary conditions such as ponded infiltration into profiles with a water table, where perched saturation and strong nonlinearity occur. In the Miller benchmark, the ATS approach required many more internal steps and tighter tolerances to propagate the wetting front correctly. This shows that robustness depends on solver configuration, not only on the discretized equations.
supporting_quote: For the ATS solutions using the default ODE solver settings, the models failed to propagate the wetting front into the soil correctly.
It was necessary to increase the maximum number of calculation steps allowed per reporting time step ... from the default 500 to 10 000

chunks.text: The core numerical approach is the method of lines: a finite-difference spatial discretization of the ψ-form RE reduces the PDE to a system of ODEs dψ/dt = f(ψ,t,z), which is then integrated with an off-the-shelf ODE solver. The scheme uses a cell-centered (staggered) grid with states at cell centers and fluxes at boundaries, and computes dq/dz from adjacent boundary fluxes. Boundary conditions include specified flux (type II), specified ψ (type I), and free drainage.
supporting_quote: apply the method of lines to reduce the partial differential equation (PDE) in Eq. (7) to a system of ODEs of the form  dψ/dt = f(ψ, t, z)
We will use a cell-centered grid ... state variables are stored at nodes ... while fluxes are defined at the cell boundaries
There are three commonly used boundary conditions for this problem, namely i. a specified flux ... ii. a free-drainage boundary ... iii. a fixed  ψ  (type-I)

chunks.text: Fluxes at internal cell boundaries are computed using Darcy’s law with the arithmetic mean of nodal conductivities at adjacent nodes. The discrete flux-gradient is then used in the continuity equation to compute dψ/dt at each node. The paper presents concise pseudocode (Box 1) implementing K(ψ), C(ψ), internal fluxes, and boundary fluxes.

To quantify mass balance, the paper uses a bias error over the full simulation interval and an RMSE over shorter reporting increments. Bias compares cumulative net boundary flux to the depth-integrated change in θ. RMSE computes the squared mismatch per reporting interval and averages across intervals to detect transient errors that might otherwise cancel.
supporting_quote: εB = ∫ (q(t,0) - q(t,zN)) dt - ∫ (θ(tM,z) - θ(t0,z)) dz
εR = sqrt( (1/M) Σ ( ∫_{tj}^{tj+1} (q(t,0) - q(t,zN)) dt - ∫ (θ(tj+1,z) - θ(tj,z)) dz )^2 )

chunks.text: The solver flux output method (SFOM) augments the ODE system with cumulative boundary flux states QT and QB so the ODE solver directly integrates dQ/dt = q alongside dψ/dt. The dependent variable vector F includes QT, all ψ nodes, and QB, enabling accurate integrated fluxes at reporting times without dense output or saving all internal steps. Fluxes are optionally scaled (e.g., ×1000) inside the solver for numerical conditioning, with rescaling on output.
supporting_quote: At an instance in time, the cumulative boundary flux, Q, is related to the instantaneous flux, q, by  dQ/dt = q.
We therefore use the ODE solver to integrate this expression and solve for Q.
We shall refer to this method for calculating the boundary fluxes as the solver flux output method (SFOM).

chunks.text: Efficiency improvements include supplying the Jacobian sparsity (pattern) rather than a full Jacobian, exploiting the tridiagonal structure induced by the 1D finite-difference stencil. SciPy solvers can accept banded Jacobian structure (uband=lband=1) or a general sparsity pattern, reducing computation in stiff integrators. The paper recommends the banded pattern as a good complexity–benefit trade-off.
supporting_quote: all the terms of the Jacobian are zero, except for where j = i - 1, j = i, and j = i + 1
The Jacobian pattern is a simple tridiagonal matrix, with ones on the three main diagonals and zeros everywhere else.
setting uband and lband arguments to 1 tells the ODE solver that the Jacobian is a tridiagonal matrix

chunks.text: A second efficiency technique is just-in-time compilation with Numba for the right-hand-side evaluation routines in Python. Numba compiles selected functions once and accelerates repeated calls during ODE integration. The paper reports up to ~10× speedups in general discussion and a much larger improvement in the appendix benchmark for the 10-year test case.
supporting_quote: Numba compiles selected Python functions once at the start of the runtime, and then all subsequent calls to the code run much faster.

These models use the Thomas algorithm for the tridiagonal linear system. Code simplicity is quantified by lines of code for solver and configuration.

This can mislead diagnostics if one only checks closure without assessing flux truncation error.

Across multiple benchmarks, the approach reproduces published solutions, yields negligibly low mass balance errors, and produces boundary fluxes independent of reporting time step. chunks.text: Estimating nutrient and pollutant loads from discrete water-quality samples paired with discharge is central to freshwater management and regulation. Many approaches rely on concentration–discharge (C–Q) relationships, with regression-based tools like LOADEST and WRTDS widely used. These models are foundational inputs for government targets and scientific studies assessing receiving-water responses to external loads.
supporting_quote: Estimating constituent loads from discrete water quality samples coupled with stream discharge measurements is critical for management of freshwater resources.
A number of regression models are available for load estimation... such as LOADEST ... or Weighted Regressions on Time, Discharge and Season (WRTDS)

chunks.text: C–Q relationships are not stationary because catchment processes and human activities vary seasonally and over time. While some models include seasonality through day-of-year or sinusoidal terms, these may not fully capture complex seasonal dynamics. Antecedent conditions and hysteresis at storm-event and longer time scales can substantially modify C–Q behavior.
supporting_quote: C-Q relationships are known to vary over time as a result of a variety of factors.

it may be important to account for antecedent conditions when modeling C-Q relationships, because hysteresis (both at the scale of individual storm events and at longer timescales) can modify C-Q relationships

chunks.text: Machine-learning methods, especially random forests, are increasingly used in aquatic science because they can perform well, are straightforward to implement, and provide interpretability via variable importance and related visualizations. Despite their use for predicting nutrients in unmonitored streams and other aquatic applications, established approaches for using random forests specifically for C–Q load estimation are limited.
supporting_quote: Random forests are a family of machine learning models which has been widely used in aquatic sciences because they are easy to implement
I am not aware of established methods to use random forests to model C-Q relationships.

chunks.text: The study developed a random-forest regression model to estimate concentrations and loads of TP, DP, TN, and chloride using daily discharge time series and periodic grab samples. The model was applied to 17 Lake Champlain tributaries monitored over multiple decades. Performance was benchmarked against WRTDS and a WRTDS extension using Kalman filtering.
supporting_quote: In this study, I developed a random forest regression model for nutrient load estimation
applied to estimate concentrations and loads of total phosphorus, dissolved phosphorus, total nitrogen, and chloride, using data from 17 tributaries to Lake Champlain monitored from 1992 to 2021.

chunks.text: A design objective was to build a load-estimation approach that uses only discharge- and time-related predictors, similar to common management models, while retaining flexibility to incorporate additional covariates when available. The intent was a broadly applicable method that can be applied to existing datasets and customized for different applications.
supporting_quote: My goal was to create a model which relied only on discharge data coupled with concentration measurements (similar to currently used load estimation models)
I designed this model to be widely applicable, utilizing only discharge- and time-related variables as predictors.

chunks.text: Seasonal variability and changing catchment processes can cause standard seasonal representations to miss important concentration dynamics. Approaches that use day-of-year functions or seasonal smoothing may not capture interannual variability in event timing or abrupt transitions. This can impair the accuracy of estimated concentrations and loads derived from discrete sampling.
supporting_quote: these formulations may fail to capture variability of seasonal processes.
does not account for year-to-year variability in the timing of cardinal events such as the spring snowmelt pulse, which can vary by months from year-to-year.

chunks.text: Hysteresis and antecedent hydrologic conditions can alter concentration–discharge relationships in ways not captured by models that ignore hydrograph position. Differences between rising and falling limbs of storm events, and longer-term antecedent wetness, can change concentrations at similar discharge levels. Ignoring these effects can bias event and annual load estimates, especially for particulate-associated constituents.
supporting_quote: hysteresis (both at the scale of individual storm events and at longer timescales) can modify C-Q relationships
which does not consider position on the hydrograph

chunks.text: For the Lake Champlain tributary dataset, true annual loads are unknown, making it hard to determine which model best estimates annual fluxes based solely on comparison to sparse samples. This motivates additional evaluation using a river with daily concentration records, where modeled annual fluxes can be compared against observed annual fluxes after downsampling.
supporting_quote: Because it is difficult to determine which model produces the best estimate of annual fluxes using the Lake Champlain dataset (because the true annual flux is not known)
daily concentration data for TP, soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP) and total suspended solids (TSS) allowed direct comparisons of observed and modeled annual fluxes

chunks.text: WRTDS was used as the primary benchmark model. It estimates concentrations using regressions trained with observations weighted by similarity in time, discharge, and day of year, emphasizing recent years and comparable seasonal and flow conditions. The implementation used EGRET (version 3.0.7) with default smoothing parameters.
supporting_quote: WRTDS calculates C-Q relationships which are trained using data weighted by time, discharge, and day of year
WRTDS is implemented in the EGRET R package (version 3.0.7). Default settings were used for all smoothing parameters.

chunks.text: A WRTDS extension with Kalman filtering (WRTDS-K) was also evaluated to better align modeled concentrations with observed samples. The filter uses an autocorrelation-based correction, adjusting predicted concentrations depending on distance in time from observed values. The autocorrelation parameter rho was set to 0.9 for all analytes.
supporting_quote: implemented the Kalman filtering method available in the EGRET package
Rho (which describes the degree of autocorrelation assumed in the filter) was set to 0.9 for all analytes.

chunks.text: The random forest regression model used predictors derived solely from discharge and time information to match typical data availability for load estimation. Predictors included log10 discharge at time t, antecedent discharge means over 7 and 30 days, 1-day discharge change (ΔQ1 day), day of year, and water year. These features were designed to capture hysteresis, antecedent wetness, seasonality, and long-term trends.
supporting_quote: The complete list of predictors used in the random forest model is:
Mean Q over days t-7 through t-1... Mean Q over days t-30 through t-1.
ΔQ1 day (calculated as Q at time t minus Q at time t-1).
Day of year.
Water year.

chunks.text: Random forest fitting used the randomForest R package with 500 trees and two variables tried at each split. Each tree was trained using a bootstrap subset equivalent to 63% of samples. Permutation importance (%IncMSE) ranked predictors by the increase in model error when a variable was shuffled.
supporting_quote: All random forest analyses used the randomForest R package
The random forests were run with forests of 500 trees, with two variables tried at each split. 63 % of samples were used in each tree
we used the increase in model error upon random permutation of each variable (%IncMSE) as our variable importance metric

chunks.text: Model performance was assessed using repeated holdout testing. For each run, 20% of sample data were withheld as an independent test set, using the same splits for WRTDS and random forest to ensure comparability. The process was repeated 20 times with separate test sets, and metrics were summarized with means and 95% confidence intervals computed as 1.96 times standard error.
supporting_quote: independent test datasets were withheld using a randomly assigned 20 % of the sample data
all models were run 20 times with 20 separate test sets.
95 % confidence intervals around the mean estimates were calculated as 1.96*standard error.

chunks.text: Evaluation metrics included R2 and RMSE on held-out sampling dates and flux bias on the test-set days. Flux bias was defined as the percent difference between predicted and observed flux summed across all test-set days, rather than averaging per-day percent bias. For full-dataset comparisons, out-of-bag R2 from the random forest was compared against WRTDS R2 trained on the full dataset.
supporting_quote: R2 and root-mean-squared error were assessed
Flux bias was also calculated... calculated as the percentage difference in predicted flux summed across all days in the test set, minus observed flux summed across all days in the test set.
R2 for the base WRTDS model was compared to out-of-bag R2 for the random forest model when both were trained on the complete dataset.

chunks.text: To compare annual-load bias against a known reference, the study used a Maumee River dataset with daily concentrations. The daily record was downsampled to 7-day and 30-day intervals, models were fit on the downsampled data, and percent bias of annual loads was computed relative to annual flux calculated from the original daily dataset.
supporting_quote: daily concentration data for TP, soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP) and total suspended solids (TSS) allowed direct comparisons of observed and modeled annual fluxes
I calculated percent bias of annual loads... when the data was downsampled to 7 day and 30 day intervals.
compared to observed annual flux calculated from the daily dataset.

chunks.text: To illustrate event-scale and seasonal hysteresis differences, selected time windows from DP in the Missisquoi River were analyzed with reduced risk of overfitting. Samples within the target windows were removed from training, then WRTDS and RF models were trained on the remaining data and used to predict concentrations during the removed windows. This focused the comparison on generalization performance during representative hydrologic events.
supporting_quote: To illustrate model differences when representing event-scale or seasonal hysteresis
samples from within these time windows were removed from the training datasets
the resulting models were used to predict concentrations during the selected windows.

chunks.text: The main dataset came from the Lake Champlain Long-Term Chemical and Biological Monitoring Project and included 17 tributaries with sufficient data for analysis. Discharge data were obtained from corresponding USGS gage stations. The monitoring design targeted discharge peaks, with additional base-flow samples from May–November and few samples in December–February.
supporting_quote: All chemistry data were collected as part of the Lake Champlain Long-Term Chemical and Biological Monitoring Project
Data were used from 17 monitored tributaries
All discharge (Q) data were collected by USGS gage stations.
The sampling plan targets discharge peaks... Very few samples were taken in December, January, and February.

chunks.text: Analytes modeled for Lake Champlain tributaries were total phosphorus (TP), dissolved phosphorus (DP), total nitrogen (TN), and chloride (Cl). The study period for these tributaries spanned 1992 to 2021. Daily discharge series were paired with periodic grab-sample concentrations for model training and testing.
supporting_quote: four analytes (total phosphorus (TP), dissolved phosphorus (DP), total nitrogen (TN), and total chloride (Cl))
using data from 17 tributaries to Lake Champlain monitored from 1992 to 2021.
daily discharge time series and measured nutrient concentrations

chunks.text: An external validation dataset was obtained for the Maumee River, Ohio, from Heidelberg University’s National Center for Water Quality Research. It included daily concentration data enabling direct comparisons of observed and modeled annual fluxes. Variables used there included TP, soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP), and total suspended solids (TSS).
supporting_quote: Additional data were acquired... at Heidelberg University... for the Maumee River, OH, where daily concentration data for TP, soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP) and total suspended solids (TSS) allowed direct comparisons of observed and modeled annual fluxes

chunks.text: The random forest predictor set was built from daily discharge and calendar information. It comprised log10 Q at time t, antecedent mean Q over t-7 to t-1 and t-30 to t-1, 1-day discharge change (ΔQ1 day), day of year, and water year. These predictors were computed for each day to support daily concentration estimation.
supporting_quote: Log10 Q at time t
Mean Q over days t-7 through t-1.
Mean Q over days t-30 through t-1.
ΔQ1 day (calculated as Q at time t minus Q at time t-1).
Day of year.
Water year.

chunks.text: Across Lake Champlain tributaries, the random forest generally improved predictive performance relative to base WRTDS on independent test sets. For test-set R2, RF exceeded WRTDS in 15/17 tributaries for DP, 17/17 for TP, 16/17 for TN, and 13/17 for chloride. Improvements were also reflected in RMSE comparisons and were often strongest for TP.
supporting_quote: The RF model tended to outperform the base WRTDS model for all analytes, with the greatest improvement demonstrated for TP
the RF had higher R2 for 15 of 17 tributaries for DP, 17 of 17 tributaries for TP, 16 of 17 tributaries for TN, and 13 of 17 tributaries for Cl

chunks.text: The random forest also outperformed WRTDS-K in most test-set comparisons, while WRTDS-K only slightly improved over base WRTDS. RF achieved higher R2 than WRTDS-K for 13/17 tributaries for DP, 17/17 for TP, 13/17 for chloride, and 14/17 for TN. This indicates that the additional RF predictors and nonlinear structure often provided more benefit than the autocorrelation correction.
supporting_quote: The RF model also outperformed WRTDS-K in most cases on the test set
the RF had higher R2 relative to WRTDS-K for 13 of 17 tributaries than WRTDS-K for DP, 17 of 17 tributaries for TP, 13 of 17 tributaries for Cl, and 14 of 17 tributaries for TN.
WRTDS-K slightly outperformed WRTDS in the test-set comparisons

chunks.text: When RF was best, it often substantially exceeded WRTDS performance, especially for total phosphorus. In TP models, RF R2 was frequently 0.2–0.4 higher than the WRTDS models, implying 20–40% more variance explained and often a doubling of explained variance. Cases where RF was not best were typically only slightly worse than the best-performing model.
supporting_quote: when the RF was the best model, it often substantially outperformed the WRTDS models.
particularly true in the case of TP, where the RF R2 was frequently 0.2–0.4 higher than the WRTDS models

chunks.text: In Lake Champlain test sets, none of the models consistently dominated for flux bias. WRTDS and WRTDS-K tended to overestimate TP and DP and slightly underestimate chloride, while RF tended to slightly overestimate chloride and was roughly balanced between over- and under-estimation for TP and DP. All models were relatively unbiased for TN on average.
supporting_quote: None of the models consistently outperformed the others with respect to flux bias over the test sets in the Lake Champlain dataset.
Both WRTDS and WRTDS-K tended to overestimate TP and DP, and to slightly underestimate Cl
The Random forest tended to slightly overestimate Cl, and had a roughly equal probability of overestimating or underestimating TP and DP.
All of the models were relatively unbiased with respect to TN

chunks.text: On the Maumee River with known daily-derived annual fluxes, RF had lower annual-load bias than base WRTDS for SRP, TP, and TSS at both 7-day and 30-day sampling intervals. WRTDS-K matched RF median bias only for TP at 7-day sampling, but was worse for SRP and TSS at 7 days and for all analytes at 30 days. RF median bias was very close to 0, within ±5%, though variance increased at 30-day sampling.
supporting_quote: Using the Maumee River dataset... compare bias in annual flux estimates for SRP, TP, and TSS
the RF model had lower bias (closer to 0) relative to the base WRTDS model for all three analytes, at both 7-day and 30-day sampling intervals.
The RF model had median bias very close to 0 (within 5 %) for all analytes for both 7-day and 30-day sampling intervals

chunks.text: Variable-importance results highlighted different dominant predictors by constituent class. For total nutrients (TN and TP), ΔQ 1 day was the most important predictor for TP and second most important for TN. For dissolved constituents, 7-day antecedent discharge was most important for DP and second most for chloride, and logQ was most important for only 2 of 4 analytes (TN and chloride).
supporting_quote: For the "total" nutrient variables (TN and TP... ), ΔQ 1 day was the most (TP), or the second most (TN) important predictor variable
for the two dissolved constituents 7-day antecedent Q was the most (DP) or the second most (Cl) important predictor
LogQ was the most important predictor for just 2 of 4 analytes (TN and Cl).

chunks.text: RF produced hydrograph-limb asymmetry consistent with event hysteresis that WRTDS cannot represent. For Missisquoi River DP events, both models predicted rapid increases at event onset, but RF predicted quicker declines on the falling limb while discharge remained high. RF also showed seasonal dilution effects via antecedent discharge, with early snowmelt peaks often higher than later peaks, a pattern not seen in WRTDS.
supporting_quote: RF modeled concentrations decline quickly on the falling limb of the hydrograph while discharge remains high, whereas the WRTDS concentrations remain high throughout the discharge event.
In wet periods of the year, high antecedent discharge is associated with lower nutrient concentrations, consistent with a dilution effect.

the RF model frequently shows hydrograph peaks towards the start of the snowmelt period having higher concentrations than peaks later in the snowmelt period, which is a pattern not seen in the WRTDS model

chunks.text: Partial dependence plots for Missisquoi DP indicated nonlinear and seasonal effects captured by the RF. The logQ effect resembled a logistic response where concentrations rose at low discharge and plateaued at high discharge. Day-of-year showed spring-flood dilution and high concentrations in fall, while ΔQ1 day showed strong increases with rapidly rising discharge; longer antecedent discharge windows emphasized dilution after prolonged wet periods.
supporting_quote: The partial effect of logQ shows a logistic relationship with DP
The partial effect of the "day of year" variable shows a clear dilution effect during the spring flood
The ΔQ1 day variable reveals a strong impact of rapidly rising discharge on nutrient concentrations
The 30 day leading average shows a strong dilution effect following prolonged periods of high discharge

chunks.text: The RF partial effect of water year tracked long-term trends similarly to WRTDS flow-normalized concentrations. The study reports that flow-normalized annual concentration from WRTDS and the RF partial effect of water year were highly correlated. This suggests RF can provide a management-relevant trend diagnostic analogous to WRTDS flow normalization.
supporting_quote: The partial effect of the water year variable is useful as an indicator of long-term trends
across the models tested here the flow-normalized annual concentration and the partial effect of water year were highly correlated

chunks.text: Despite differences in concentration dynamics, annual load estimates across models were often broadly similar and ranked years similarly, but discrepancies increased in wet years. For Missisquoi DP, Spearman correlation between WRTDS and RF was 0.97 for annual loads, yet only 0.77 for flow-weighted mean concentrations. WRTDS models substantially overestimated flow-weighted mean concentrations relative to RF during wet years.
supporting_quote: the load estimates were largely similar, with low-load years in one corresponding to low-load years in another model
Spearman's rank-based correlation between the WRTDS and RF models was 0.97 for annual loads, but only 0.77 for flowweighted mean concentrations.
both WRTDS models substantially overestimating mean nutrient concentrations relative to the RF model during wet years.

chunks.text: A key interpretation is that RF’s improved performance stems from both explicit process representation and model flexibility. Including ΔQ1 day and antecedent discharge terms likely helped represent hysteresis and antecedent effects, and random forests can fit complex interactions and threshold behaviors without specifying functional forms in advance. This may be especially beneficial for particulate-dominated constituents like TP.
supporting_quote: The strong performance of the RF model likely resulted from a combination of more explicit process representation... and the inherent flexibility of random forests to fit observed data distributions.
I attempted to capture the effects of hysteresis through the inclusion of ΔQ1 day and leading-averaged discharge variables as predictors.
This is particularly true in the case of TP

chunks.text: Using day-of-year as a seasonal predictor in RF can create an artificial discontinuity at the year boundary. The paper notes this is most problematic when the transition occurs during data-scarce periods such as winter, potentially producing nonsensical or biased estimates at the start or end of the year. A sin/cos seasonal representation avoids discontinuity but reduced RF performance and interpretability in tests.
supporting_quote: the use day-of-year to represent season is potentially problematic, because it leaves open the possibility for abrupt shifts in modeled concentration at the annual transition
This is particularly true when the annual transition happens during a time of year with relatively few samples (e.g. winter in the Lake Champlain Basin).
A sin and cos representation of date was tested... but generally resulted in slight declines in model performance.

chunks.text: The study’s main comparison in Lake Champlain cannot definitively validate annual-load accuracy because the true annual flux is unknown. This limitation prompted use of the Maumee River daily dataset for explicit annual-bias evaluation. Even with that supplement, broader validation across other systems and sampling designs is needed.
supporting_quote: it is difficult to determine which model produces the best estimate of annual fluxes using the Lake Champlain dataset (because the true annual flux is not known)
Using the Maumee River dataset, it was possible to explicitly compare bias in annual flux estimates

chunks.text: Generalizability may be constrained by watershed context and monitoring protocols. The Lake Champlain tributaries have limited urbanization, so performance in more urbanized catchments is uncertain. Aside from the Maumee River, tributaries were sampled under a similar protocol, leaving open how RF would perform under different sampling intervals and program designs.
supporting_quote: There is limited urbanization within the Lake Champlain basin... so it is not clear how the RF model would perform in more urbanized catchments.

With the exception of the Maumee River, all of the tributaries presented in this study are sampled using a similar protocol, so it is not yet clear how the model would perform in other monitoring programs.

chunks.text: RF adoption in management contexts is limited by missing features that are well developed in WRTDS. The paper highlights that WRTDS provides established uncertainty quantification and quality-control and visualization tools, which were not replicated for RF here. RF may also be more sensitive to outliers, especially during data-scarce seasons such as winter.
supporting_quote: WRTDS also has well-developed methods for the quantification of uncertainty... which I have not attempted to replicate here.
WRTDS also has well-developed visualization tools and quality control steps
RF models may be more sensitive to outliers than WRTDS, particularly in data-scarce times of year such as winter

chunks.text: The paper concludes that random forests can improve estimates of nutrient concentrations and loads relative to WRTDS approaches in many cases, as monitoring datasets grow. The method is robust and easy to apply using common inputs (discharge and grab samples) and also supports process insight through variable importance and partial dependence plots. This makes RF useful for both research and management applications.
supporting_quote: Random forests offer a robust and easy-to-apply modeling framework, which in this case worked well to improve estimates of nutrient concentrations and loads in the majority of tests.
Random forests also have the ability to provide process insights by looking at variable rankings and partial dependency plots

chunks.text: The RF approach was intentionally designed for broad applicability with only discharge- and time-related predictors, but it is readily extendable. The paper notes it can be supplemented with additional predictors such as sensors (turbidity, fluorescence, temperature) and can be adapted to higher-resolution gage data (e.g., 15-minute) for flashy streams. This flexibility positions RF as a practical framework for future improvements in load estimation.
supporting_quote: I designed this model to be widely applicable, utilizing only discharge- and time-related variables as predictors.
the approach developed here would be easy to supplement with additional data sources as predictor variables
The model developed here could also be easily adapted to use higher resolution (e.g. 15-minute) gage data

chunks.text: Surface water and groundwater are connected through stream–aquifer exchanges that can occur in both directions. Many large-scale hydrologic models simplify this coupling due to data and computational constraints. The National Water Model (NWM) represents groundwater contributions to streams but omits stream losses back to aquifers, which can be important where the water table is below the stream stage and streambeds are permeable.
supporting_quote: Surface water and groundwater are intimately connected by a two-way flux between the stream and underlying aquifers.
The National Water Model (NWM) currently only considers a one-way flux, where groundwater can enter a stream but cannot return to the aquifer.

chunks.text: The Northern High Plains Aquifer (NHPA) is a large, heavily used groundwater system spanning five U.S. states, where drought and pumping have caused substantial groundwater-level declines. These declines can increase the likelihood of losing streams and disconnection between streams and aquifers. Historical studies reported notable transmission losses, making the NHPA a relevant testbed for evaluating impacts of missing losing-stream mechanisms in large models.
supporting_quote: The NHPA is an extensive groundwater resource that spans nearly 250,000 km2 and underlies five states: South Dakota, Wyoming, Nebraska, Colorado, and Kansas
drought and groundwater pumping within regions of the basin result in groundwater level declines of up to 30 m

As early as the 1970s, losing stream conditions were identified in NHPA with transmission losses of streamflow to groundwater throughout the region of an average of 1.2% per km traveled (Jordan 1977).

chunks.text: Stream exchange depends on streambed properties and hydraulic gradients, and it can vary in space and time. Losing conditions occur when groundwater levels fall below stream levels, enabling infiltration from stream to aquifer if streambeds are sufficiently permeable. Such conditions may be exacerbated by drought and pumping, so assuming all streams are gaining can bias streamflow forecasts.
supporting_quote: Stream exchange is controlled by the hydraulic conductivity of the streambed... and the hydraulic gradient between the stream level and the underlying groundwater
flow from the stream to the groundwater when the water table of the surrounding aquifer is below the water surface of the stream, provided the streambed is sufficiently permeable

ignoring the effects of losing streams... may especially impair streamflow forecasts in areas where prolonged drought or aquifer depletion from agricultural pumping has lowered the groundwater table below the streambed

chunks.text: The study aims to quantify how excluding two-way groundwater–surface water exchange (specifically stream losses to groundwater) affects NWM streamflow predictions in the NHPA. The authors test whether model errors during floods and droughts correlate with whether reaches are likely losing or gaining. They also develop a scalable reach-classification approach using existing datasets rather than new field campaigns.
supporting_quote: The objective of this study was to understand how the omission of a two-way exchange mechanism for streams in the Northern High Plains Aquifer (NHPA) impacts the NWM's capacity to forecast the hydrologic extremes it was designed to predict.
we aim to directly evaluate the NWM's streamflow prediction ability... correlated with the effects of losing stream regimes

chunks.text: A key goal is to classify stream reaches within the NHPA as potentially losing, gaining, or neutral using an integrated approach. The classification is used as a prerequisite for evaluating NWM performance by stream regime during extreme events. The approach combines USGS gage comparisons, flux outputs from a USGS groundwater model, and remote sensing vegetation/water indices.
supporting_quote: First, hydrologic regimes for stream reaches within the NHPA are classified as potentially losing, gaining, or neutral.

hydrologic regime identification is achieved by a composite method to include historical United States (U.S.) Geological Survey (USGS) streamflow data, an existing USGS Groundwater Availability Model (GWAM), and remote sensing of the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI).

chunks.text: The authors state hypotheses about NWM behavior under floods and droughts when losing-stream processes are absent. For floods, they expect amplified and earlier modeled peaks relative to observations, particularly in losing reaches. For droughts, they expect NWM to simulate flow where observations show no-flow because the model cannot drain streamflow into groundwater.
supporting_quote: For flood events, we hypothesize that the lack of a losing mechanism in the NWM will result in a higher intensity flood response forecast compared to the observed streamflow
we hypothesize that the omission of a losing stream mechanism will result in stream reaches with modeled flow in the NWM when the reach is observed to have no flow.

chunks.text: The NWM’s one-way groundwater-to-stream coupling prevents simulation of losing streams, meaning modeled discharge cannot decline downstream due to infiltration to aquifers. This structural limitation can be unrealistic in regions with depressed groundwater tables from drought or pumping. Consequently, NWM streamflow forecasts may be biased, especially during hydrologic extremes.
supporting_quote: The NWM currently only considers a one-way flux, where groundwater can enter a stream but cannot return to the aquifer.
there is no mechanism for streamflow to decline in the downstream direction (known as a losing stream).
the assumption underlying the NWM that streamflow losses do not exist is not realistic for the NHPA

chunks.text: Prior evaluations found NWM often overpredicts streamflow, but the sources of bias remain uncertain. Many studies focus on flood inundation mapping rather than directly assessing streamflow prediction skill. This paper targets direct comparison of NWM discharge to observed gage hydrographs with attention to groundwater–surface water exchange mechanisms as a potential driver of error.
