supporting_quote: Previous studies have evaluated the NWM prediction performance and found that the NWM overpredicts streamflow in many cases, but the causes of this overprediction are not fully understood

these studies do not directly evaluate the streamflow prediction ability of the model (Afshari et al. 2018; Zheng et al. 2018; Johnson et al. 2019; Shastry et al. 2019) In this study we aim to directly evaluate the NWM's streamflow prediction ability.

chunks.text: Identifying losing versus gaining reaches at regional scales is challenging because traditional methods require intensive field measurements that are costly and represent only local conditions at specific times. The NHPA has strong spatial and temporal heterogeneity in pumping, geology, and groundwater levels, complicating direct characterization of stream–aquifer fluxes across the domain.
supporting_quote: Traditionally, stream classification requires field measurements including seepage meters... sediment temperature, and groundwater modeling
For regions as large and as spatially and temporally heterogeneous as the NHPA, determining groundwater-surface water flux at a stream reach level would be expensive.

chunks.text: The study classifies reaches using three independent indicators of losing conditions and then synthesizes them into a final label. For each reach and season, a segment is deemed likely losing if at least two methods indicate losing. A segment is deemed gaining only if both the USGS gage method and the USGS GWAM method indicate gaining; otherwise, uncertain segments are discarded.
supporting_quote: Losing stream reaches were identified using three independent data sources: USGS stream gages, the USGS GWAM, and remote sensing products.
If at least two methods identified stream segments as losing, then they were considered to be likely losing for this analysis.
Both the USGS Groundwater Availability Model and the USGS Gage method had to indicate the stream segment as potentially gaining for it to be listed as gaining.

chunks.text: The USGS gage method infers losing or gaining by comparing upstream and downstream mean discharges for pumping (May–September) and nonpumping (October–April) periods. If upstream discharge exceeds downstream discharge over a period, the segment is flagged as potentially losing; the reverse indicates potentially gaining. A small threshold difference (>0.01) is used to treat changes as meaningful given uncertainty.
supporting_quote: If the upstream gages had a higher mean discharge for the five-month pumping period May–September or the seven-month nonpumping time period of October through April, then the segments were considered to be potentially losing.
If the downstream gages had a higher discharge than the upstream gage for the time period, then the segment was potentially gaining.
a difference in streamflow between gages >0.01 cm (cubic meters per second) was considered viable

chunks.text: The USGS GWAM method uses simulated groundwater–surface water flux along streams to label reaches as losing, gaining, or neutral. The GWAM is a MODFLOW-NWT regional model providing flux outputs for 1 km grid cells along streams from 1940–2009, separated into pumping and nonpumping time periods each year. For this paper, the flux sign is used qualitatively: negative for losing and positive for gaining.
supporting_quote: Model outputs include groundwater-surface water flux for 1 km grid cells along simulated streams from 1940 to 2009 for two timeperiods each year, designated as pumping and nonpumping.
For this study, stream reach classification was derived directly from the calculated groundwater-surface water flux term in the USGS GWAM.
the quantitative flux from GWAM was qualitatively expressed for this study as losing (negative flux from surface water), gaining (positive flux to the surface water), or neutral.

chunks.text: Remote sensing provides a third indicator of potential losing reaches using vegetation and water indices. Landsat imagery (water years 1994–2009) is used to compute NDVI and NDWI on 1 km grids along streams. Cells with low NDVI (0–0.2) and NDWI < 0.3 are flagged as possible losing reaches, based on the idea that sparse riparian vegetation and dry indicators reflect deeper groundwater tables.
supporting_quote: Landsat 5 and 7 images with <10% cloud cover from water years 1994–2009 were used to calculate NDVI and Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI) for 1 km grids along the streams.
Grids with low NDVI values (0–0.2)... were cross-referenced with NDWI values <0.3
If the grids had both low NDVI and NDWI values, they were identified as possible locations of losing reaches

chunks.text: Hydrologic extremes are identified before evaluating model performance. Flood events are defined where USGS discharge exceeds bankfull discharge (from the Groundwater Toolbox), or otherwise using a 5-year return period threshold. Drought events are chosen from U.S. Drought Monitor periods of severity D1–D4, and results are also summarized by pumping (May–October) and nonpumping (November–April) seasons.
supporting_quote: Flood events were chosen by identifying where the USGS discharge at the gage was above the bankfull discharge value calculated using the Groundwater Toolbox
For gages that did not have a bankfull discharge available, a return period of five years was used to estimate flooding events
Drought events are selected using the US Drought Monitor records for events from D1 to D4 severity
extreme events were subset into annual periods of groundwater pumping (May– October) and nonpumping (November–April)

chunks.text: NWM performance is evaluated by comparing NWM simulated discharge to USGS gage observations and using the difference as an error metric. Differences in mean event error between losing and gaining classes are tested with a t-test to assess whether stream regime is associated with systematic NWM bias. The analysis focuses on water years 1994–2009 to match availability across classification datasets.
supporting_quote: Hydrographs from the predicted discharge from the NWM are compared with observed discharges at USGS stream gages
the difference in the USGS streamflow and the NWM predicted streamflow is used as a metric to describe NWM error
The differences in mean streamflow prediction error in each event between gaining and losing reaches were analyzed using a t-test
Data were analyzed from the water years 1994–2009

chunks.text: The study area is the Northern High Plains Aquifer, which spans roughly 250,000 km2 across South Dakota, Wyoming, Nebraska, Colorado, and Kansas. The analysis focuses on stream reaches within this region and leverages its documented groundwater declines and pumping impacts. Spatial patterns (e.g., Sand Hills vs. central/southern basins) provide contrasting hydrogeologic settings for losing and gaining behavior.
supporting_quote: The NHPA is an extensive groundwater resource that spans nearly 250,000 km2 and underlies five states: South Dakota, Wyoming, Nebraska, Colorado, and Kansas
The portion of the northern subbasins in the NHPA... Sand Hills region... minimal surface or groundwater irrigation
regions in the central and southern Platte and Republican River Basins... characterized by larger depths to groundwater where streams are more likely disconnected from the underlying aquifer

chunks.text: USGS National Water Information System stream gage records are used both to infer reach regime (via upstream–downstream discharge comparisons) and as the observational benchmark for evaluating NWM hydrographs. The study compares NWM retrospective streamflow to these observed gage time series. Because NWM uses data assimilation from roughly 8,000 gage observations, the retrospective product is expected to match gage behavior at many locations.
supporting_quote: The USGS National Water Information System provided streamflow data
Hydrographs from the predicted discharge from the NWM are compared with observed discharges at USGS stream gages
Forecasted streamflow in the NWM is calibrated using nudging-based data assimilation of roughly 8,000 streamflow observations from USGS gages.

chunks.text: The USGS Groundwater Availability Model (GWAM) provides simulated groundwater–surface water fluxes along streams at 1 km grid resolution. Outputs span 1940–2009 with two seasonal periods (pumping and nonpumping) each year, enabling classification over the 1994–2009 overlap window. Flux values are converted into qualitative reach labels (losing, gaining, neutral) for integration with other indicators.
supporting_quote: Model outputs include groundwater-surface water flux for 1 km grid cells along simulated streams from 1940 to 2009 for two timeperiods each year, designated as pumping and nonpumping.
For this study, stream reach classification was derived directly from the calculated groundwater-surface water flux term in the USGS GWAM.

chunks.text: Landsat 5 and 7 remote sensing imagery is used to compute NDVI and NDWI along stream corridors to help locate potential losing reaches. The dataset includes images with less than 10% cloud cover for water years 1994–2009. Indices are computed on 1 km grids along streams and combined with threshold criteria to flag possible losing segments.
supporting_quote: Landsat 5 and 7 images with <10% cloud cover from water years 1994–2009 were used to calculate NDVI and Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI) for 1 km grids along the streams.
Grids with low NDVI values (0–0.2)... NDWI values <0.3

chunks.text: Flood events are detected using USGS discharge relative to bankfull thresholds computed with the Groundwater Toolbox; where bankfull is unavailable, a 5-year return period is applied. Drought events are derived from the U.S. Drought Monitor and include severities D1–D4. The paper reports analyzing 42 flood events and 116 drought events over the study period.
supporting_quote: Flood events were chosen... above the bankfull discharge value calculated using the Groundwater Toolbox
a return period of five years was used to estimate flooding events from stream gage data.
Drought events are selected using the US Drought Monitor records for events from D1 to D4 severity
A total of 42 flood events and 116 drought events were analyzed between water years 1994 and 2009.

chunks.text: The USGS GWAM indicates that gaining conditions are more prevalent than losing across modeled stream cells in the NHPA. Specifically, 55% of stream cells are gaining, 25% are losing, and 20% have negligible flux. This distribution supports the need to distinguish regimes when evaluating NWM performance because a substantial fraction of the network may experience streamflow losses to groundwater.
supporting_quote: According to the USGS GWAM, 55% of the stream cells were gaining, 25% were losing, and 20% of stream cells had negligible groundwater-surface water flux.

chunks.text: Estimated streamflow loss rates differ depending on how they are aggregated. For losing reaches, the average loss is about 1% per km, similar to a historical estimate of 1.2% per km. When normalized at basin scale (total loss relative to total basin streamflow), the implied average is smaller: about 0.1% per river km across the NHPA.
supporting_quote: For the losing reaches, the average percent of streamflow loss was 1% per km, similar to the 1.2% per stream km from Jordan (Jordan 1977).
As a result, the average loss factor when viewed at a basin-scale is 0.1% per river km

chunks.text: During floods (42 events), the NWM shows statistically significant differences in error between losing and gaining reaches across the rising, peak, and falling limbs when pumping and nonpumping periods are combined. Table 1 reports significant p-values for all three hydrograph regions, indicating regime-dependent performance. The authors describe losing streams as showing earlier and overestimated flood volumes relative to gaining streams.
supporting_quote: A total of 42 events were included in the analysis.
Statistically significant differences in the mean flows between NWM predictions and USGS gages were found in all portions of the flood hydrograph (Table 1).

For flood events, the modeled flood response for losing streams is characterized by statistically significant earlier peak discharges and an overestimate of the observed flood volume when compared to gaining streams.

chunks.text: For an example flood on a losing reach of the Republican River (May 26, 2008), the NWM peak is much larger and earlier than observed. The paper reports the NWM predicted the peak discharge to be 481 cm higher and to occur 8 hours earlier than the USGS peak. This illustrates how missing losing-stream processes can contribute to exaggerated flood response in certain reaches.
supporting_quote: For the losing reach, the NWM predicted a peak discharge of 481 cm higher and eight hours earlier than the observed flow.
FIGURE 7. (a) Hydrograph for May 26, 2008 flood event on the Republican River on a losing reach.

chunks.text: For the same May 26, 2008 flood event on an upstream gaining reach, the NWM still predicts an earlier and higher peak but with smaller magnitude than in the losing example. The paper states the NWM overpredicted peak discharge by 60 cm and that it occurred 8 hours earlier than observed. This demonstrates that timing biases can occur in both regimes, though magnitude biases differ.
supporting_quote: For the gaining reach in Figure 7b, the NWM overpredicted peak discharge by 60 cm and occurred eight hours earlier than the observed event.
FIGURE 7. (b) hydrograph for the same flood event on an upstream gaining reach.

chunks.text: In pumping-season floods, the study reports significant differences between losing and gaining reaches for peak and falling limb errors, and also lists a significant result for the rising limb in Table 2. The NWM tends to underpredict rising and falling limbs for both reach types during pumping season. However, it overestimates peak flow for losing reaches and underpredicts peak flow for gaining reaches during pumping season.
supporting_quote: During the annual groundwater pumping season, there were significant statistical differences in the peak and falling limb of the hydrograph, but not the rising limb (Table 2).
The NWM tended to underpredict the rising and falling limbs of the hydrograph for both gaining and losing reaches.
However, the NWM overestimated the peak flow for losing reaches and underpredicted peak flow for gaining reaches.

chunks.text: Flood peak timing differences between losing and gaining reaches are not statistically significant. Table 3 reports p-values of 0.16 (All) and 0.28 (Pumping), indicating no regime-based timing difference. Nevertheless, the paper notes that peaks in USGS data are on average later than those in the NWM for both reach types, and losing reaches tend to be earlier in NWM than gaining reaches.
supporting_quote: Overall, there was no statistical difference in flood peak timing between losing and gaining reaches
TABLE 3... p-Values | All ... 0.16 ... Pumping ... 0.28
the timing of maximum flow during flood events was on average later in the gage data than simulated NWM results in both losing and gaining reaches.

chunks.text: For droughts (116 events), the NWM overestimates streamflow for both losing and gaining reaches, and the difference in mean error between regimes is not statistically significant. Table 4 shows p-values of 0.23 (pumping), 0.16 (nonpumping), and 0.07 (all). The paper emphasizes that the NWM fails to represent no-flow conditions observed at gages.
supporting_quote: A total of 116 droughts were identified
there were no statistically significant differences... during drought events between identified losing and gaining reaches (Table 4).
However, NWM predictions overestimated streamflow regardless of gaining or losing classification (Figure 8).
In both cases, the NWM fails to model a dry stream when the USGS gage indicates that the stream is not flowing.

chunks.text: In the example 2006 drought event on the Republican River, the NWM overestimation is larger for the losing reach than for the gaining reach. The reported mean overestimate is 5.3 cm on the losing reach versus 2.1 cm on the gaining reach (Figure 8). The NWM also shows a spike in August 2006 that is not present in the USGS observations.
supporting_quote: For the losing reach, the NWM's mean overprediction is 5.3 cm compared to 2.1 cm for the gaining reach.
FIGURE 8. (a) Hydrograph for a 2006 drought event on a losing reach... The mean overestimate of discharge by the NWM is 5.3 cm; (b)... The mean overestimate of discharge by the NWM is 2.1 cm.
there is a spike in the NWM streamflow occurring in August of 2006 that is not represented in the USGS streamflow data.

chunks.text: The USGS gage-based losing/gaining inference is subject to measurement uncertainty and confounding factors. The paper notes that streamflow values include uncertainties from stage, velocity-area discharge calculation, and rating curves. Diversions or other sinks can also cause downstream decreases unrelated to losing conditions, and gage spacing can mask sub-reach variability.
supporting_quote: An inherent source of error associated with using the USGS gages is the uncertainty in the published streamflow values.

One limitation to this approach is the influence of diversions or other discharge sinks that may result in a decrease in discharge in the downstream direction that does not otherwise satisfy the losing stream condition
because gages may be several miles apart, smaller segments between the reaches may be losing, whereas the reach average is gaining

chunks.text: The integrated reach-classification methods are not validated against direct field measurements in this study, limiting certainty in the losing/gaining labels. The authors explicitly state that none of the three methods directly measures groundwater–surface water flux and recommend field validation before broader adoption. They also note that previous losing/gaining studies in the NHPA fall outside their study window, preventing agreement checks.
supporting_quote: These methods have not been validated by field measurements; thus, before adopting the method and applying it broadly, stream classification through field techniques should be employed to validate the accuracy
none of the three methods presented here directly measures the groundwater-surface water flux
Two studies identifying stream reaches as losing or gaining in the NHPA were published in 1977 and 2013 which were outside of this study's time frame

chunks.text: The NDVI/NDWI approach uses vegetation and surface wetness as proxies for losing conditions, which may not generalize to all regions. The paper acknowledges that vegetation patterns can be influenced by factors other than groundwater access and that the cutoff thresholds were not sensitivity tested. The authors also note it cannot identify gaining reaches because lush vegetation is not uniquely indicative of gaining conditions.
supporting_quote: this remote sensing technique uses vegetation as a proxy for streamflow and does not consider other factors that might affect the vegetation–streamflow relationship.
While the sensitivity of these cutoff values was not tested
this method was not used to identify potentially gaining reaches because lush vegetation does not particularly indicate a gaining stream.

chunks.text: A reach-averaged loss percentage can be misleading when aggregated across a basin because small intermittent streams can dominate normalized loss metrics. The authors caution that a 1.2% per km loss rate would imply near-total loss over a few hundred kilometers, which may not reflect basin-scale volumetric importance. They propose a basin-normalized loss factor (0.1% per km) to reduce bias from ephemeral reaches.
supporting_quote: a value of 1.2% loss per river km should be viewed with some skepticism as it would indicate that in 375 km of losing conditions, a stream would lose 99% of the streamflow.
small intermittent or ephemeral streams have a disproportionate weight as 100% of their streamflow is lost when the streamflow goes dry
As a result, the average loss factor when viewed at a basin-scale is 0.1% per river km

chunks.text: The authors note that missing a losing-stream mechanism may not fully explain NWM errors; other model components could contribute. They suggest improving baseflow and interflow estimation, routing schemes, and channel geometry representation. This positions the losing-stream exchange as a partial explanation within a broader set of potential NWM structural issues.
supporting_quote: The results suggest that there may be other sources within the NWM that contribute toward errors in streamflow predictions.
Other areas of the NWM that could be simulated to improve streamflow forecasts include improved baseflow and interflow estimation
optimized channel routing schemes... and incorporation of varying channel geometries for different stream types

chunks.text: Across flood and drought extremes, the NWM systematically overestimates streamflow compared with USGS gages in the NHPA, consistent with effects of excluding losing-stream processes. Flood errors differ by reach type, with significant regime dependence in hydrograph magnitudes, while drought errors are similar across regimes but still show persistent overprediction and failure to simulate no-flow. The paper concludes that incorporating a losing-stream mechanism could improve NWM performance in regions like the NHPA.
supporting_quote: For both flood and drought events, the NWM systematically overestimates streamflow when compared to the USGS gage observed streamflow
For floods... statistically significant differences... earlier peak discharges and an overestimate
For drought events... the NWM overpredicted streamflow and did not simulate no-flow conditions.

chunks.text: The authors propose implementing a stream-loss term as a pragmatic step toward two-way exchange in the NWM. Using the GWAM, they estimate losses of about 1% per km for losing reaches, or a uniform 0.1% per river km when expressed as a basin-wide fraction of total streamflow. They argue this type of loss term must be region-specific and computed before being applied at CONUS scale.
supporting_quote: This study proposes using an average stream loss term for a region to represent a losing stream reach.
The total water lost from the stream that went into the aquifer is 1% per km in losing stream reaches, or alternatively 0.1% of the total streamflow per km in the entire region of the NHPA
this method of applying a blanket percent loss term will vary across regions and thus would need to be calculated before being applied to the NWM on a CONUS-wide scale.

chunks.text: Applying the basin-normalized loss factor can materially reduce NWM overestimation in a demonstrated case, though it does not fully close the gap. For the Republican River summer 2006 example, the paper states that applying 0.1% loss per km along upstream river lengths to two gages would reduce NWM mean streamflow by about half. This supports the claim that missing losing-stream losses explain part, but not all, of the NWM bias.
supporting_quote: The loss factor... is equivalent to applying the 0.1% loss to the 725 and 627 km upstream river length to gages 06844500 and 06837000, respectively.
This alone would decrease the mean streamflow estimate of the NWM by 51% and 47%, respectively, and decrease the streamflow gap... by a factor of two.
While the loss factor does not close the gap between the NWM's streamflow prediction and the USGS observed streamflow, it does represent one explanation for part of the discrepancy

chunks.text: Flooding is a dominant global hazard with major human and economic consequences, and its risk is increasing due to climate change and expanding exposure in flood-prone areas. Reported evidence links recent decades to increased frequency and severity of key hazard drivers such as precipitation extremes and sea level rise. The paper frames riverine and coastal flooding as requiring understanding across meteorological, hydrologic, and hydrodynamic processes to support risk management and forecasting.
supporting_quote: flooding accounted for 43.4% of all 7,255 disaster events recorded globally between 1998 and 2017
climate change associated with global warming has increased the frequency and severity of flood hazard drivers (e.g., precipitation and sea level rise, SLR)

chunks.text: The review distinguishes flood forecasting (future estimation) from flood prediction (hindcasting/nowcasting), highlighting that forecast precipitation drives forecasting models while observed precipitation supports prediction studies. It positions ensemble prediction systems as a major development for probabilistic flood forecasting because they provide ensembles of meteorological forcings that can be propagated through hydrologic models to produce ensemble streamflows.
supporting_quote: "Flood forecasting" pertains to the estimation of future floods, while "flood prediction" is typically used to describe the characterization of past flood events (hindcasting) or provid near-real-time information (nowcasting).
the EPS outputs (e.g., an ensemble of precipitation and temperature) can be used as inputs to a hydrologic model to propagate the uncertainty and forecast an ensemble of streamflows

chunks.text: Coastal flooding is driven by interacting processes that contribute to extreme coastal water levels, including mean sea level, tides, storm surge, and wave setup/runup. The review notes the magnitude of coastal exposure and projects that frequent exceedance of present-day 100-year extreme sea levels is expected by the end of the century even under low warming scenarios. This motivates detailed modeling of coastal water level components and their coupling.
supporting_quote: One billion of the world's population currently dwells on land less than 10 m above the high tide line
a majority of coastal communities around the globe will experience the present-day 100-yr extreme sea level at least once a year by the end of this century, even under 1.5 °C of warming

chunks.text: The paper aims to summarize recent advances, identify key challenges, and propose pathways for improving riverine and coastal flood characterization and modeling. It emphasizes better understanding of causative mechanisms, uncertainties, and risks in coupled hydrologic-hydrodynamic modeling for forecasting and inundation mapping. It also points to opportunities for state-of-the-art data assimilation and machine learning to support operational transition.
supporting_quote: The overarching goal of this review paper is to summarize the past advances, describe our current capacity and limitations, and recommend potential pathways to further advance our flood characterization and modeling skills.

identify challenges in understanding flood processes, associated uncertainties and risks in coupled hydrologic and hydrodynamic modeling for forecasting and inundation mapping, and the potential use of state-of-the-art data assimilation and machine learning

chunks.text: A stated objective is to provide a more comprehensive review than prior work by covering both riverine and coastal flooding mechanisms, and by treating riverine flooding end-to-end from meteorological drivers through hydrology to hydrodynamics. The review also highlights a perceived gap in prior literature for coastal flooding reviews and sets out to appraise process-based, data-driven, and hybrid methods. It additionally organizes inundation models by flood type and includes a dedicated discussion of hydrodynamic data assimilation.
supporting_quote: Considering the lack of a review paper for coastal flooding in the literature, a thorough appraisal of the state-of-the-art methods that include process-based hydrodynamic modeling, data-driven, and hybrid methods is noticeably warranted.
we cover both of these topics and review both hydrologic and hydrodynamic processes involved in riverine flooding while providing the latest end-to-end approaches

chunks.text: Despite decades of development of physically based flood models, accuracy and reliability remain insufficient for many applications, and computational demands hinder full operational use. The paper attributes these shortcomings to limited understanding of flood-generating mechanisms, simplifying assumptions in model development, and inadequate treatment of uncertainty. This creates a persistent gap between scientific advances and robust operational flood forecasting and mapping.
supporting_quote: these models still fall short in accuracy and reliability and are often considered computationally intensive to be fully operational.
This could be attributed to insufficient comprehension of the causative mechanisms of flood processes, assumptions in model development and inadequate consideration of uncertainties.

chunks.text: Hydroclimatic classifications that link floods to atmospheric circulation patterns or climate indices can omit key watershed preconditions. In particular, the review notes that soil saturation and snow processes are often not captured well, which limits explaining flood-generating processes in many basins, especially mountainous snow-dominated catchments. This motivates combining hydroclimatic and hydrological perspectives.
supporting_quote: the key role of soil saturation in flood-generating processes ... is commonly disregarded by linking the circulation patterns with flood characteristics.
they cannot properly explain snow processes, which results in a poor description of flood-generating processes in mountainous snow-dominated catchments

chunks.text: Operational flood forecasting chains often end at streamflow hydrographs and do not routinely produce spatially explicit inundation forecasts. The review argues that inundation maps are more actionable for emergency response, but coupling hydrodynamic models into operations is difficult due to setup, calibration, and computational costs. This motivates simplified and surrogate approaches and better integration strategies for real-time inundation forecasting.
supporting_quote: The outcome of most operational flood forecast systems is often limited to these streamflow forecast hydrographs without the simulation of a physical model to convert streamflow forecasts to flood inundation areas.
The setup, calibration, and computational time required to simulate flooding via these models are also significantly high.

chunks.text: Hydrodynamic data assimilation for inundation mapping is constrained by the lack of observations with suitable spatial and temporal resolution. The paper states that ideal gridded water level observations at meter-scale resolution and daily/sub-daily frequency are unlikely soon. Existing satellite products often have long revisit times or coarse resolution, limiting the ability to track flood dynamics and update models in real time.
supporting_quote: an ideal observation for DA-hydrodynamic modeling is fine-grided water level data (grid size ∼ DEM resolution) at high temporal resolution (daily/sub-daily scale).
access to such a product seems almost impossible in the near future.

chunks.text: Compound and coastal flood analysis faces challenges for both process-based and data-driven approaches, particularly due to sparse overlapping records and limited validation archives. The review highlights that dependence assessment between sea level and river discharge is often impeded by insufficient co-located records. This data limitation restricts purely statistical dependence modeling and motivates hybrid and coupled approaches.
supporting_quote: a sufficient length (usually decades) of overlapping (both in time and space) records of contributing variables is crucial
only found four sites in the entire African continent and three sites in South America with sufficient overlapping records to enable dependence assessment and compound flood analysis

chunks.text: The review outlines a hydrological ensemble prediction system (HEPS) framework that couples ensemble weather forecasts with hydrologic modeling to produce probabilistic flood forecasts. It describes core components including meteorological preprocessing, hydrologic simulation, hydrologic data assimilation, postprocessing/product generation, and verification. The intent is to propagate meteorological uncertainty into streamflow ensembles and provide decision-relevant products.
supporting_quote: The whole process of generating ensemble meteorological forecasts within an EPS and coupling them with a hydrologic model to produce probabilistic flood forecasts is implemented within an integrated system referred to as the hydrological ensemble prediction system (HEPS).

A HEPS contains several key components, including meteorological preprocessing ... a hydrological modeling component ... a hydrologic data assimilator ... a hydrological postprocessor ... and a verification system

chunks.text: For streamflow forecasting, the paper reviews data-driven approaches that learn input-output relationships from historical data without explicit process representation. Common predictors include lagged streamflow alone or streamflow plus precipitation; recent work also uses satellite-based gridded precipitation and soil moisture. Deep learning, particularly LSTM, is highlighted for capturing long temporal dependencies in hydrologic sequences.
supporting_quote: data-driven methods ... only rely on historical data and do not consider the underlying physical processes in the catchment
LSTM has the ability to memorize long sequences of data (more than years), which is significantly important for hydrological predictions

chunks.text: Hydrological data assimilation is presented as a Bayesian updating framework to incorporate observations into hydrologic models and improve initial conditions and forecasts. The review emphasizes EnKF and particle filter families, noting EnKF’s practical popularity and PF’s ability to handle non-Gaussian and multimodal posteriors. It also discusses multivariate assimilation (e.g., soil moisture and streamflow) and smoothing approaches (REnKF, EnKS) to address routing-related time lags.
supporting_quote: The main DA techniques used in the hydrological forecasting context include the ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) and particle filter (PF).
PF DA has garnered increasing attention ... as a viable alternative to the EnKF ... characterizing multimodal or skewed distributions

chunks.text: Riverine flood inundation mapping is described as numerical hydrodynamic modeling that solves reduced forms of the Navier–Stokes equations (e.g., shallow water equations) in 1D, 2D, or coupled 1D/2D configurations. The review highlights computational-efficiency strategies such as reduced physics (diffusion/local inertial), hybrid 1D/2D schemes, code optimization/parallelization, and GPU/HPC acceleration. Model setup typically requires terrain data, roughness, boundary conditions, and initial conditions.
supporting_quote: The central premise of hydrodynamic models ... is to numerically solve derivations of the Navier-Stokes (NS) equations
most important recent numerical developments have focused on improving the computational efficiency of numerical 2D simulations
hydrodynamic models are set up with (a) terrain data ... (b) channel/ floodplain roughness coefficients ... (c) upstream/ downstream river boundary conditions ... and (d) the initial condition

chunks.text: Topography-based simplified inundation methods use DEM-derived geomorphic descriptors to rapidly classify flood-prone areas or estimate flood extent. The review emphasizes HAND as a widely used feature for binary floodplain classification and for real-time mapping by combining forecast discharge with Manning’s equation and synthetic rating-curve libraries. These approaches trade physical completeness for speed and scalability.
supporting_quote: the height above nearest drainage (HAND) ... has received a great deal of attention for flood inundation and extent mapping
HAND-based real-time flood inundation mapping can be carried out by inserting forecasted discharges ... into Manning's equation, which results in generating a library of synthetic rating curves

chunks.text: Surrogate (response surface) methods emulate high-fidelity hydrodynamic models by training machine learning models on many physics-based simulations, mapping boundary conditions to inundation depth outputs. Approaches include SVMs, random forests, and ANNs; the review notes efforts to manage spatial correlation via clustering into homogeneous regions and hybrid ANN structures that link data-rich channels and data-sparse floodplains. CNN-based domain-wide surrogates are also mentioned but can be parameter-heavy.
supporting_quote: ML models are trained on the results of a high-fidelity hydrodynamic model to emulate its response more efficiently.
divide the study area into homogenous regions using clustering methods
develop a single complex ANN model for the whole domain using a CNN model ... it has a large number of parameters (order of millions)

chunks.text: Flood inundation forecasting approaches include coupling hydrologic streamflow forecasts to hydrodynamic models, using low-fidelity hydrodynamics (e.g., coarse grids with subgrid channels), or selecting from libraries of precomputed inundation scenarios. HAND-based operational mapping is framed as an offline rating-curve library approach used to convert forecast streamflows into inundation extents. Surrogate models can also be run in forecast mode by using forecast hydrographs as inputs.
supporting_quote: A common approach for forecasting flood inundation areas is to feed a hydrodynamic model with ... streamflow data
coupled the VIC hydrologic model and ... ensemble ... and then fed an ensemble of streamflow forecasts into a low fidelity ... hydrodynamic model
Another approach ... develop a library of prerecorded flood inundation maps

chunks.text: Hydrodynamic data assimilation methods are summarized as assimilating gridded water levels, flood extent maps, and point observations (water levels/discharge) into 2D models using EnKF/LETKF/ETKF, PF, and limited 4DVAR implementations. The review highlights SAR as a key remote-sensing source for flood extent, with approaches assimilating either derived water levels or flood extent directly. It also notes emerging directions such as assimilating SAR backscatter directly via a new observation operator and using mutual information in PF likelihood weighting.
supporting_quote: a wide range of observations has been assimilated into 2D hydrodynamic models ... water level ... binary flood extent maps ... channel water level and discharge hydrographs
active microwave technology using synthetic aperture radar (SAR) has been shown to be the best source of remotely sensed flood extent and water level data
proposed a novel observation operator that directly uses backscatter values from SAR instruments as observations
proposed the use of mutual information (MI) for the estimation of particle weights

chunks.text: The paper identifies key data used in flood modeling and evaluation, including gauge observations (streamflow and water level), high water marks from field surveys, and remote sensing flood extent products. It highlights that observed streamflow used for forcing and for hydrologic model calibration can be substantially uncertain, especially during floods. These observational uncertainties propagate into inundation modeling and can dominate error budgets even when high-quality topography is available.
supporting_quote: streamflow/water level data at gauge stations ... provide extremely beneficial pieces of information for calibrating, assimilating and validating flood inundation models.
Errors are 20% for average flow conditions, and perhaps as much as 40% or more for flood flows are not atypical

chunks.text: Topography and terrain datasets are treated as foundational inputs for hydrodynamic inundation modeling, including DEMs and LiDAR. The review states LiDAR offers high vertical accuracy and fine horizontal resolution that improves inundation mapping, but global coverage is extremely limited and computational costs can be high. The paper also notes global terrain products from radar/optical interferometry as alternatives.
supporting_quote: LiDAR provides the most accurate flood inundation maps ... due to its great vertical accuracy of 0.05–0.1 m and fine horizontal resolution of 0.5–3 m
it covers just 0.005% of the Earth's land area
global terrain data collection efforts using a variety of radar and optical interferometric techniques

chunks.text: Remote sensing data are highlighted as both forcing-related predictors for data-driven hydrologic forecasting and as observations for inundation mapping and assimilation. The review points to satellite-based gridded precipitation, gridded soil moisture, SAR-derived flood extent, and satellite altimetry water levels for large rivers. It also notes the forthcoming SWOT mission as providing water levels at approximately 100 m resolution, enabling new assimilation opportunities.
supporting_quote: satellite-based gridded precipitation data as predictors
adding gridded soil moisture data as a new predictor
SAR data can be converted to flood extent maps
SWOT ... will be the first satellite altimeter that records water levels at a fine spatial scale (∼100 m)

chunks.text: The paper discusses practical constraints of satellite flood extent archives for validation and assimilation, emphasizing tradeoffs between spatial and temporal resolution. It notes SAR can provide 10–30 m resolution but revisit times of 10–14 days, while MODIS provides daily coverage but coarse resolution exceeding 500 m. These constraints limit detailed hourly/daily validation of fine-resolution inundation simulations.
supporting_quote: SAR satellites are available every 10–14 days, but their spatial resolution ranges are 10–30 m
give coarse resolution maps (>500 m) at the daily scale (e.g., MODIS)

chunks.text: Crowdsourced Volunteered Geographic Information (VGI) is presented as an emerging observational dataset for hydrodynamic model updating, collected via citizen devices to report flood locations, extents, or water levels. The review notes its promise for assimilation frameworks and also flags challenges around uncertainty and the need for standardized real-time platforms. VGI is thus positioned as complementary to gauges and satellites.
supporting_quote: The crowdsource data referred to as Volunteered Geographic Information (VGI)
georeferenced data that provide information about the location of a flood, flood extent, or water level

chunks.text: The paper reports evidence that atmospheric rivers are globally important contributors to runoff and flooding, linking them to both coastal and inland riverine floods. It cites a global estimate that ARs contribute about 22% of total runoff and explain more than 80% of floods in several regions. This supports prioritizing AR characterization in flood hazard studies.
supporting_quote: Paltan et al. (2017) demonstrated that ARs contribute to approximately 22% of the total global runoff and explain more than 80% of floods in several regions.

chunks.text: Hydrologic-process-based classification studies show that pre-event watershed conditions, especially soil moisture, play a major role in flood behavior beyond meteorological forcing alone. The review summarizes findings that weather patterns tend to control flood magnitude while soil moisture affects flood extent. It also notes that for the United States, precipitation variability alone poorly explains flood variability, with evaporation and soil-moisture-controlled precipitation excess dominating many extremes.
supporting_quote: they found that weather patterns mostly control the flood magnitude, soil moisture affects the flood extent
flood variability in the United States is poorly explained by precipitation variability, whereas evaporation and soil moisture-controlled precipitation excess are dominant factors

chunks.text: Comparative modeling literature summarized in the review indicates that 2D hydrodynamic models generally outperform 1D approaches for inundation mapping, albeit at higher computational cost. The paper cites empirical studies that demonstrate clear superiority of 2D over 1D in most circumstances. It also discusses that hybrid 1D/2D schemes can retain efficiency by representing channels in 1D and floodplains in 2D.
supporting_quote: large-scale empirical studies ... have demonstrated the clear superiority of 2D over 1D methods in most circumstances, but 2D models can be computationally expensive.
Hybrid approaches ... using a 1D model for the channel and a structured 2D model for the floodplain

chunks.text: For reduced-physics flood models, the local inertial approximation is highlighted as producing near-identical results to the full shallow water equations for subcritical flows. The review states agreement at Froude numbers less than 0.5, with increasing divergence toward Fr = 1.0 but typically still smaller than typical input-data errors. It cautions against use for supercritical flows where omitted convection becomes dominant.
supporting_quote: The local inertial form ... has been shown to give near-identical results to the full equations at Froude (Fr) numbers less than 0.5
For Fr > 1.0, the flow becomes supercritical ... the simpler models are contra-indicated

chunks.text: The review identifies boundary forcing uncertainty—especially discharge—as a major limitation for hydrodynamic inundation simulations, even when high-quality LiDAR topography is used. It reports typical gauged flow errors of around 20% for average conditions and 40% or more for flood flows. Consequently, forcing data can be the greatest source of uncertainty in LiDAR-based hydrodynamic modeling.
supporting_quote: Errors are 20% for average flow conditions, and perhaps as much as 40% or more for flood flows are not atypical
for a hydrodynamic model built using LiDAR, it is likely that the forcing data used to drive the simulation currently constitutes the greatest source of uncertainty.

chunks.text: The paper summarizes evidence that current HAND-based real-time inundation mapping can underperform physically based hydrodynamic models. It notes that HAND simplifications (steady Manning’s equation and reach-averaged depth/discharge assumptions) contribute to poorer performance compared to hydrodynamic approaches, and that HAND tends to work mainly in confined floodplains. This supports using HAND primarily for rapid preliminary estimates.
supporting_quote: has led to its poor performance compared to hydrodynamic models
HAND methods do not conserve mass or momentum and tend only to work in confined floodplains.

chunks.text: A cited nonselective comparison study found that HAND can fail to capture flood extent in many cases, while hydrodynamic models generally perform better and 2D models provide higher accuracy than 1D models. The review treats this type of evaluation as rare but important for selecting modeling approaches. The result underpins the paper’s call for broader, rigorous inter-model comparisons using high-quality validation datasets.
supporting_quote: They demonstrated that the HAND method fails to properly capture the flood extent in many cases and that hydrodynamic models outperform in the majority of rivers.
They also showed that 2D hydrodynamic models have higher accuracy than 1D models.

chunks.text: For coastal flooding, the review notes that wave setup can be a meaningful fraction of peak storm-tide water levels in tropical cyclones. It reports a finding that wave setup contributed up to 17% to peak water levels for historical tropical cyclones along U.S. East and Gulf Coasts. This supports coupled wave–hydrodynamic modeling for coastal flood hazard assessment.
supporting_quote: Marsooli and Lin (2018) found that wave setup contributed up to 17% to the peak water levels induced by historical tropical cyclones at the U.S. East and Gulf Coasts.

chunks.text: The review argues that hydroclimatic approaches alone may be questionable for explaining physical flood-generating mechanisms because flood events are relatively rare compared to total days, and because key antecedent conditions are ignored. Specifically, it notes soil saturation is often disregarded and snow processes are not adequately explained by circulation patterns. These limitations motivate combined hydroclimatic–hydrological analyses.
supporting_quote: Since the sample of flood events is much smaller than the total number of days, the validity of using circulation factors/climate indices for explaining underlying physical flood-generating processes is still a matter of question
the key role of soil saturation ... is commonly disregarded
they cannot properly explain snow processes

chunks.text: Pre- and postprocessing can improve forecast quality, but the paper highlights mixed evidence for preprocessing benefits after propagation through nonlinear hydrologic models. It stresses that gains depend on region, catchment, and season, and that methods trained on recent data can struggle with nonstationarity and longer-range changes. This limits generalizability of processing-method performance across systems.
supporting_quote: some publications also clearly state that preprocessing can even lose any impact on discharge when fed through the nonlinear system.
Hegdahl et al. (2021) find that ... the answer depends on "region, catchment and season"

chunks.text: Hydrodynamic data assimilation is limited by observation availability that meets meter-scale spatial needs and sub-daily temporal needs. The paper states that gridded water-level products with these properties are essentially unavailable, while satellite flood maps often provide only snapshots and gauge data are point-based. This mismatch restricts robust, operational DA for inundation forecasting.
supporting_quote: the spatial resolution of observational data should be on the order of meters
The rapid changes in the dynamics of flooding at sub-daily scales also require access to observations at daily/sub-daily temporal resolution.
the gridded observations ... are usually available for a given instance ... and cannot track the flood wave dynamics over time.

chunks.text: LiDAR-based terrain improves inundation accuracy but is not widely available and can impose major computational burdens. The review reports that LiDAR covers only a tiny fraction of Earth’s land area and that fine-resolution simulations can be costly. This limits global deployment of high-accuracy topography for flood inundation modeling.
supporting_quote: LiDAR provides the most accurate flood inundation maps
it covers just 0.005% of the Earth's land area
the huge computational cost of running hydrodynamic models with this data set

chunks.text: The paper highlights a persistent validation gap for flood inundation models, noting that many studies are weak, selective, and not comprehensive due to limited high-quality observed flood extent data. It also explains that satellite-derived extent maps carry substantial uncertainty from image-to-flood extraction and have inadequate spatiotemporal coverage for validating hourly/daily flood-wave simulations at <30 m resolution. It recommends data fusion and downscaling to create better validation archives.
supporting_quote: Flood inundation models are often not properly validated; specifically, many model testing studies are weak, selective, and not comprehensive.
available satellites ... provide fine-scale spatial resolution with a long revisit time ... or give coarse resolution maps (>500 m) at the daily scale
we are interested in simulating flood waves propagating hourly/daily at fine spatial resolutions (e.g., <30 m).

chunks.text: The review identifies structural data gaps—channel bathymetry and flood defense information—as major limitations for large-domain inundation modeling. It states that missing bathymetry reduces routing accuracy, and that global datasets for structures such as levees and dams (including fragility and reservoir performance curves) are needed. It proposes extrapolating from surveyed samples using statistical and remote sensing methods or estimating bathymetry through calibration/assimilation.
supporting_quote: The lack of access to detailed information on channel bathymetry and flood defenses globally (location, fragility curves) decreases the accuracy
Channel bathymetry information is critical to properly route flood waves along rivers.
we need to allocate additional resources and investments to develop a comprehensive global data set that accurately displays the geographical locations of river structures

chunks.text: The paper concludes that improved flood understanding requires a holistic perspective integrating hydroclimatic, hydrological, hydrodynamic, and human influences. It recommends shifting operational forecasting toward innovative earth system modeling frameworks where components interact and feedbacks are represented. This integration is positioned as key for more consistent predictions and improved flood risk management.
supporting_quote: we suggest a more holistic approach that considers human influence, hydroclimatic, hydrologic, and hydrodynamic drivers.
We recommend transitioning to an innovative earth system modeling approach that connects meteorological, hydrologic, hydrodynamic, and decision-making components and allows for feedback exchange.

chunks.text: For inundation modeling, the review emphasizes that physical hydrodynamic models can now achieve accurate simulations given high-resolution topography and computational advances, and that HPC enables more efficient parallel modeling. It still supports simplified methods as useful when time is extremely limited (e.g., flash floods) or where access to HPC is constrained. The paper calls for rigorous, nonselective comparisons and better validation archives to strengthen model selection and trust.
supporting_quote: physical models have the capability to accurately simulate flooding rivers and estimate spatiotemporal water depth distributions these days.
Given the recent advances in HPC, parallel simulation of hydrodynamic models opens a future pathway for efficient simulation of flooding conditions.
they are still useful in remote regions where access to HPC is limited or during flash floods when the required time for simulation is too short.

chunks.text: For coastal and compound flooding, the paper concludes that hybrid approaches linking multivariate statistics with process-based coupled models can improve efficiency and realism. It stresses that nonstationarity from sea level rise and climate change must be addressed in hazard projections, using semi-stationary or fully nonstationary statistical methods and climate-forced simulations. Coupled modeling (including biological and wave processes) is highlighted as necessary for comprehensive coastal flood risk assessment.
supporting_quote: Hybrid methods, via systematic links between advanced data-driven methods and process-based coupled models help address these issues.
Nonstationarity of coastal flooding dynamics due to sea level rise
semi-stationary methods ... or fully nonstationary methods that let the probability distribution parameters vary over time or co-vary with SLR are useful

chunks.text: Hydrologic forecasts can be degraded by model structural inadequacies, parameter uncertainty, and errors in meteorological forcings, which can accumulate in internal hydrologic states over time. Data assimilation (DA) is widely used to incorporate near-real-time observations and improve operational forecasts. Variational DA updates adjustable variables by minimizing mismatch with observations using gradients, and can be “training-free” compared with data-driven approaches.
supporting_quote: because of model structural inadequacies, parametric uncertainty, and unpreventable meteorological forcing data errors, significant errors can linger and accumulate in the model's hydrological states
variational DA relies on the calculation of gradients ... with respect to the adjustable states, parameters, or inputs
Variational DA is "training-free" --- it solves an optimization problem

chunks.text: Deep learning methods, especially LSTM networks, have shown strong performance for streamflow prediction, and can incorporate recent observations via data integration (DI) by using lagged streamflow as an input. DI can be very effective but relies on systematic training data to learn relationships and may degrade when applied to untrained sites. Variational DA for LSTM can update hidden and cell states using automatic differentiation, but has not clearly surpassed DI.
supporting_quote: data integration (DI) ... directly include recent streamflow observations along with other forcings and geographic attributes as inputs
Using LSTM with DI, Feng et al. (2020) improved streamflow performance from a median NSE of 0.73 to 0.86 on the CAMELS dataset
this type of data integration depends on the availability of sufficient systematic training data ... otherwise the resulting models may degrade in effectiveness when applied to untrained sites
Nearing et al. (2022) implemented variational DA with LSTM ... achieving a median NSE of 0.86

chunks.text: Differentiable hydrologic models embed physical equations while using neural networks to supply parameters, enabling end-to-end training with automatic differentiation. The δHBV model reimplements HBV equations in PyTorch and uses an LSTM to generate static and dynamic parameters, maintaining interpretable physical states such as soil moisture, snowpack, and subsurface storages. While differentiable models have shown strong accuracy and generalization, DA had not been implemented for them before this study.
supporting_quote: differentiable models directly embed the physics inside the model system, training connected neural networks along with the equations
developed a differentiable ... (δHBV) model for streamflow prediction, which incorporated an LSTM network to calculate and provide static or dynamic parameters
Although DA has not yet been implemented for differentiable models

chunks.text: The study aims to develop and test variational DA schemes for a differentiable hydrologic model (δHBV) by optimizing adjusters for precipitation, internal hydrologic states, or both. It seeks to determine whether differentiable models with a small set of physical states can benefit from variational DA as much as LSTM-based DA approaches. It also aims to identify which combination of adjusters yields the most effective streamflow forecast improvements.
supporting_quote: Here we developed variational DA methods for differentiable models, including optimizing adjusters for just precipitation data, just model internal hydrological states, or both
We sought answers to the following questions:
can differentiable models with limited physical states benefit as much from variational DA as LSTM?
What is the most effective combination of model hydrological state and/or precipitation adjusters

chunks.text: It is unclear which DA approaches are optimal for physics-informed machine learning (“differentiable”) models, which have relatively few, physically meaningful states compared with the large hidden state dimension of LSTMs. The study highlights uncertainty about whether the differentiable model structure limits DA effectiveness, and whether adjusting hydrological states versus meteorological forcings yields different benefits. The work frames state errors as long-term mass distribution issues and forcing errors as short-term input errors, motivating an explicit comparison.
supporting_quote: it is unclear which methods are performant or optimal for physics-informed machine learning ("differentiable") models
it remains unclear if variational DA can benefit differentiable models as much as it benefited LSTM
There are multiple ways in which DA can be applied ... the hydrological state variables and the input forcings can each be adjusted

chunks.text: Variational DA can become underconstrained because there may be many adjustable variables but limited observational constraints, producing uncertainty in optimal adjustments. Historically, implementing variational DA for complex models has been difficult due to the need for gradient calculations, although automatic differentiation platforms reduce this barrier. These issues motivate developing practical DA schemes in differentiable modeling frameworks.
supporting_quote: there are often a large number of adjustable variables and not enough constraints, leading to substantial uncertainty in the optimal adjustments
for complex models, the significant effort of building the software infrastructure needed to calculate the gradients can be daunting
AD ... significantly alleviated the challenges of calculating gradients

chunks.text: The differentiable δHBV model uses an LSTM to generate static and dynamic HBV parameters and then runs differentiable HBV equations to simulate streamflow and states. The model represents physical states including soil moisture, snow water equivalent, meltwater, and upper/lower zone storages (SUZ, SLZ). Training and DA both use a normalized squared-error loss that scales residuals by basin streamflow standard deviation to reduce dominance of highly active basins.
supporting_quote: θ_{b,s}, θ_{b,d}^t = LSTM(x_b^t, A_b)
Q_b^t, S_b^t = HBV(θ_{b,s}, θ_{b,d}^t, x_b^t, S_b^{t-1})
include soil moisture (SM) ... upper zone storage (SUZ) ... lower zone storage (SLZ)
normalized square-error loss function

chunks.text: Precipitation-adjustment DA (δHBV-DA-P) optimizes a basin-specific multiplier k to adjust precipitation on a specific lag day within a 5-day assimilation window. For forecasting at day t+1, precipitation at day t−a is adjusted as p' = k^4 p, with a=2 selected as best and w=5 chosen from tested windows (1,3,5,10,20). Gradients of window loss with respect to k are computed by automatic differentiation and optimized with AdaDelta; adjustments are accepted only if loss decreases and are not applied on dry days.
supporting_quote: called δHBV-DA-P, we utilized a multiplier adjuster for short-term precipitation inputs in the assimilation window
We tested assimilation window lengths of 1, 3, 5, 10, and 20 days ... with w = 5 showing the highest performance
we found that a = 2 provided the highest performance improvement
The AdaDelta optimizer based on gradient descent is used
If the loss function within the window is decreased after DA, we accept the adjustment ... The adjustment is not applicable on dry days

chunks.text: State-adjustment DA (δHBV-DA-S) optimizes the initial hydrologic states at the start of the 5-day DA window to minimize streamflow loss over that window. The model runs HBV forward within the DA window using candidate states S' and uses gradient descent to find states that reduce the loss. As with precipitation adjustment, updates are accepted only when the window loss decreases; then the model is run forward to produce the day t+1 forecast with adjusted states.
supporting_quote: called δHBV-DA-S ... enhance streamflow forecasts by correcting the model's internal hydrological states
adjusting the initial states at the beginning of DA window (day t-w+1
S_{b}^{\prime(t-w+1)} = argmin_{S_{b}^{(t-w+1)}} ( Loss(...) )
If the loss function is decreased after DA, the state updates are accepted

chunks.text: Combined DA (δHBV-DA-PS) applies both precipitation and state adjustments within the same assimilation window to jointly reduce DA-window streamflow loss. The combined procedure follows the same steps as the individual adjusters, but optimizes both the precipitation multiplier and the initial states. This design targets both short-term forcing errors and accumulated state errors.
supporting_quote: For combined precipitation and state adjustment ... (δHBV-DA-PS), we aimed to adjust both the short-term precipitation inputs and the internal hydrological states simultaneously
The procedures are exactly as described above, only that both of them are employed

chunks.text: Benchmark models include: (1) a standalone LSTM for streamflow driven by Daymet forcings and basin attributes; (2) LSTM with data integration (LSTM-DI) that uses 1-day-lagged streamflow observations as an input; and (3) LSTM with variational DA (LSTM-DA) that updates cell and hidden states by minimizing loss over 5-day windows, repeating 20 windows to assimilate 100 days before predicting t+1.
supporting_quote: a standalone LSTM for streamflow ... given on atmospheric forcings (f^t) and static site attributes (A_b) to predict streamflow (Q_b^t)
integrates most recent (1-day-lagged) streamflow observations
the third LSTM model used data assimilation (LSTM-DA) ... In each five-day window (w = 5
They repeatedly update states with 20 windows to assimilate 100-day observations

chunks.text: Models are trained on CAMELS basins for 1999/10/01–2008/09/30 over 100 epochs with batch size 100. Both δHBV parameterization LSTM and the streamflow LSTM use hidden size 256 and sequence length 365. DA is conducted in 1989/10/01–1999/09/30 after saving and freezing δHBV parameters and states unless adjusted by DA.
supporting_quote: trained on 531 CAMELS basins, with streamflow observational data from 1999/10/01 to 2008/09/30 over 100 epochs, with a batch size of 100
used a hidden size of 256 and a sequence length of 365 days
tested the model from 1989/10/01 to 1999/09/30 to save HBV parameters and states and conducted data assimilation in the same time span
parameters and states over the forecasting timespan are saved and frozen

chunks.text: Evaluation uses NSE and KGE for overall accuracy, plus RMSE for low flows (bottom 30%) and high flows (top 2%). The study also calculates annual relative peak errors (%) to assess peak-flow prediction quality. These metrics are reported as medians over basins for core comparisons.
supporting_quote: Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE ...)
Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE ...)
RMSE of the bottom 30% flow and of the top 2% flow
annual relative peak errors (%)

chunks.text: Experiments use the CAMELS dataset, including streamflow observations, basin attributes, and basin-averaged meteorological forcings from Daymet. Inputs for δHBV include precipitation, mean temperature, and potential evapotranspiration (computed via Hargreaves) along with CAMELS geographic attributes. The study uses 531 basins selected from 671 by excluding basins with area discrepancies and basins larger than 2000 km².
supporting_quote: We employed the Catchment Attributes and Meteorology for Large-Sample Studies (CAMELS) dataset
basinaveraged meteorological forcing data from Daymet
We utilized 531 basins from a total of 671 CAMELS watersheds ... removed ... basins ... larger than 2000 km^2
x_b^t represents ... forcings (precipitation, mean temperature, and potential evapotranspiration calculated using the method from Hargreaves et al. (1994))

chunks.text: For δHBV, forcing variables include PRCP, temperature (T), and potential evapotranspiration (Ep), and attributes span climate, aridity, precipitation frequency/duration, topography, vegetation, soils, and geology from CAMELS. The paper summarizes these inputs in Table A1 and uses them consistently across δHBV variants. These attributes are used alongside time-varying forcings for basin-specific simulations.
supporting_quote: Table A1. Summary of the forcing and attribute variables used in all δHBV models
Forcings PRCP ... T ... Ep
Attributes ... p_mean ... aridity PET/P ... elev_mean ... soil_porosity ... geol_permeability

chunks.text: Across 531 basins, combined DA on δHBV (δHBV-DA-PS) improves median NSE from 0.75 to 0.82 and median KGE from 0.754 to 0.852, making it the best δHBV DA scheme in aggregate. This improvement comes with reduced low-flow RMSE to 0.01 mm/day and high-flow RMSE to 2.66 mm/day relative to the baseline δHBV (0.06 and 3.36 mm/day). These medians are reported in Table 1.
supporting_quote: The resulting forecast ... one-day lead time median Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) elevated from 0.75 to 0.82

chunks.text: State adjustment alone (δHBV-DA-S) provides the dominant gains, substantially reducing both high- and low-flow RMSE and increasing median NSE to 0.82. Specifically, high-flow RMSE drops from 3.36 to 2.69 mm/day and low-flow RMSE drops from 0.06 to 0.01 mm/day compared with baseline δHBV. The precipitation adjuster alone yields smaller benefits, mainly for high flows.
supporting_quote: The state adjuster (δHBV-DA-S) was the main effective DA mechanism which reduced both the high- and low-flow RMSE
δHBV-DA-S ... highflow RMSE ... from 3.36 ... to 2.69 mm/day
lowflow RMSE ... from 0.06 mm/day to 0.01 mm/day
resulting in a median NSE (KGE) of 0.82 (0.84)

chunks.text: Precipitation adjustment alone (δHBV-DA-P) is only moderately effective and can even reduce median NSE relative to baseline δHBV (0.74 vs 0.75) while increasing KGE (0.800 vs 0.754). It reduces high-flow RMSE by 0.21 mm/day (3.36 to 3.15) and low-flow RMSE by 0.01 mm/day (0.06 to 0.05). The paper attributes its limited effectiveness to its short-term nature and inability to correct long-term storage/snow errors.
supporting_quote: the precipitation adjuster alone was only moderately effective, reducing high-flow RMSE by 0.21 mm/day (to 3.15 mm/day) and low-flow RMSE by 0.01 mm/day (to 0.05 mm/day)
cannot correct errors that happened a long time ago, e.g., with long-term water storage and snow accumulation processes

chunks.text: Adding precipitation adjustment to state adjustment (δHBV-DA-PS vs δHBV-DA-S) yields small additional gains, largely confined to high flows. Median low-flow RMSE remains 0.01 mm/day for both, while high-flow RMSE improves slightly from 2.69 to 2.66 mm/day and KGE increases from 0.841 to 0.852. This indicates precipitation errors matter more for quick-flow peaks than for low-flow recession behavior.
supporting_quote: When we added the precipitation adjuster to δHBV-DA-S, it did not further improve low flow, but did have a moderate benefit for the high flow
δHBV-DA-S ... KGE 0.841 ... High Flow RMSE 2.69
δHBV-DA-PS ... KGE 0.852 ... High Flow RMSE 2.66
suggests precipitation error matters more for quick flow processes

chunks.text: δHBV-DA-PS and LSTM-DA achieve the same median NSE (0.82) using a single forcing source (Daymet). δHBV-DA-PS improves δHBV by 0.07 NSE (0.75→0.82), while LSTM-DA improves LSTM by 0.08 (0.74→0.82). This shows differentiable models with limited physical states can benefit from variational DA similarly to LSTM-based DA.
supporting_quote: achieving the same performance with a single source of forcing data (Daymet): an NSE value of 0.82
δHBV-DA-PS improved δHBV's median NSE by 0.07 (from 0.75 to 0.82)
LSTM-DA improved LSTM's NSE by 0.08 (from 0.74 to 0.82)

chunks.text: LSTM with data integration (LSTM-DI(1)) attains a higher median NSE (0.84) than δHBV-DA-PS or LSTM-DA (0.82), but has worse RMSE for low and high flows than the DA methods. Table 1 reports LSTM-DI low-flow RMSE 0.04 and high-flow RMSE 2.83, while δHBV-DA-PS has 0.01 and 2.66 and LSTM-DA has 0.01 and 2.63. This supports the paper’s claim that DI can be moderately more effective on NSE but not necessarily on flow-magnitude errors.
supporting_quote: LSTM-DI(1) ... presented a slightly higher NSE (0.84) ... but had higher RMSE values for both low and high flow prediction
LSTM-DI (1) ... Low Flow RMSE 0.04 ... High Flow RMSE 2.83
δHBV-DA-PS ... Low Flow RMSE 0.01 ... High Flow RMSE 2.66
LSTM-DA ... Low Flow RMSE 0.01 ... High Flow RMSE 2.63

chunks.text: Across basins, δHBV-DA-PS improves over δHBV in 80% of basins, whereas LSTM-DA improves over LSTM in 74% of basins. The comparison also indicates δHBV-DA-PS performs better for lower-performing basins (NSE < 0.8), while LSTM-DA has a slight advantage when NSE exceeds 0.8. These patterns are shown in the scatter and CDF comparisons.
supporting_quote: δHBV-DA-PS improved the simulation against δHBV in 80% of basins, while LSTM-DA improved 74% of basins against LSTM
δHBV-DA-PS outperformed LSTM-DA for low-performing basins (NSE < 0.8)
LSTM-DA exhibited a slight advantages for basins with NSE values above 0.8

chunks.text: Regional analysis (Eastern/Central/Western CONUS) shows δHBV-DA-PS outperforms LSTM-DA in the Eastern and Central regions, while LSTM-DA leads in the Western region. Table 2 reports Eastern NSE 0.782 (δHBV-DA-PS) vs 0.770 (LSTM-DA) and Central NSE 0.660 vs 0.614, but Western NSE 0.907 vs 0.924. Western high-flow RMSE is also higher for δHBV-DA-PS (3.10) than LSTM-DA (2.42).
supporting_quote: δHBV-DA-PS performed better than LSTM-DA mostly in the Eastern US
In the Western region (Region C), LSTM-DA performed better than δHBV-DA-PS
Eastern US (A) ... LSTM-DA NSE 0.770 ... δHBV-DA-PS NSE 0.782
Central US (B) ... LSTM-DA NSE 0.614 ... δHBV-DA-PS NSE 0.660
Western US (C) ... LSTM-DA NSE 0.924 ... δHBV-DA-PS NSE 0.907

chunks.text: The precipitation adjuster is constrained to short-term effects on runoff and can be ineffective for short, flashy events due to its time lag; it may also worsen performance in some regions. The paper notes cases where the adjuster is applied on a zero-precipitation day during a brief peak, making it ineffective. Spatially, precipitation adjustment shows benefits in the western US but negative impacts in central and southeastern coastal areas.
supporting_quote: precipitation adjuster's lackluster effectiveness could result from its restriction to short-term impacts on direct runoff
With such a shortterm peak, the adjuster ends up being applied on a zero-precipitation day, making it ineffective
The precipitation adjuster shows benefits in the western US while negatively impacting simulations in the central US and the southeastern coastal region

chunks.text: State adjustment is broadly effective but may not correct very short-term errors because it modifies the initial states at the first day of the assimilation window rather than the most recent day. It also struggles with storm regimes featuring frequent peaks, limiting performance in flashy basins. These limitations are linked to the window-based variational formulation and reliance on state changes propagating through the HBV dynamics.
supporting_quote: the state adjuster ... is more evenly distributed across CONUS
cannot respond quickly for correction of short-term errors ... relies on modifying the states for the first day in the DA window rather than those of the last
It also struggles with storm-induced streamflow that involves frequent peaks

chunks.text: The paper argues LSTM-DA can be prone to over-tuning because it adjusts a larger number of states, whereas δHBV-DA-PS has fewer states and stronger physical constraints, which may help in some basins. Conversely, where rainfall-runoff processes are complex and less accurately represented by HBV, LSTM-DA can have advantages due to its flexibility to adjust many states. This highlights a tradeoff between physical constraint and adaptive capacity.
supporting_quote: LSTM-DA, with adjustments to a larger number of states, is prone to over-tuning (overfitting)
δHBV-DA-PS, having fewer states as well as stronger physical constraints between these states, can be more effective
in regions where rainfall-runoff processes are more complex and less accurately represented by HBV ... LSTM-DA offered greater advantages

chunks.text: The variational DA formulation for δHBV can be overly flexible and underdetermined, allowing multiple adjustment combinations to fit the same observations. The paper notes discrepancies between states adjusted by state-only DA versus combined precipitation+state DA, suggesting non-uniqueness. It proposes adding additional physical or data constraints to preserve spatial patterns and reduce underdetermination.
supporting_quote: it remains overly flexible, leading to an underdetermined problem
discrepancies arise between states adjusted solely by the state adjuster and those adjusted when both components are applied
can be further improved to preserve the spatial pattern of simulation with more physical or data constraints

chunks.text: Differentiable physics-informed models can benefit from variational DA as much as LSTM-based DA, with δHBV-DA-PS matching LSTM-DA performance at median NSE 0.82 using Daymet forcing. The approach leverages physically interpretable state and precipitation adjusters to improve forecasts and provides mechanistic insight into corrections. The authors suggest exploring other DA methods (e.g., particle filtering and Kalman filters) to further assess accuracy and uncertainty handling.
supporting_quote: differentiable physics-informed machine learning models ... can effectively compete with ... LSTM-DA
achieving the same performance ... an NSE value of 0.82
incorporates physically based hydrological state and precipitation adjusters, offering a structured approach
Exploring other data assimilation approaches such as Particle Filtering and Kalman Filters

chunks.text: The best-performing DA configuration for δHBV uses both state and precipitation adjusters, where state adjustment provides most of the improvement and precipitation adjustment adds moderate benefit for high flows. Across basins, δHBV-DA-PS improves δHBV’s median NSE from 0.75 to 0.82 and reduces high-flow RMSE from 3.36 to 2.66 mm/day. This indicates that correcting internal hydrologic states is central, while precipitation correction complements peak-flow simulation.
supporting_quote: Both precipitation and state adjusters were needed to achieve these results, with the latter being substantially more effective on its own, and the former adding moderate benefits for high flows
δHBV ... NSE 0.75 ... High Flow RMSE 3.36
δHBV-DA-PS ... NSE 0.82 ... High Flow RMSE 2.66

chunks.text: Unsteady flow in open-channel networks is commonly modeled with the nonlinear Saint-Venant equations, and many operational flood-routing tools rely on implicit finite-difference schemes. For subcritical conditions, the four-point implicit Preissmann scheme is widely adopted and considered robust. However, network coupling through junction backwater effects often forces a simultaneous system solution across all channels, increasing computational cost for large sparse matrices.
supporting_quote: Flow in an open channel is modeled by numerically solving the non-linear, hyperbolic Saint-Venant equations of conservation of mass and momentum.
The fourpoint implicit Preissmann scheme is the widely adopted method for the solution of Saint-Venant equations
This requires the solution of a system of equations, with a large sparse coefficient matrix, which is computationally intensive.

chunks.text: To reduce the burden of solving a global matrix for channel networks, an iterative alternative was proposed that solves each channel independently and then couples channels by predicting and correcting junction water stages. The junction point water stage prediction and correction (JPWSPC) method targets subcritical flows and has been further improved using recursive coefficients and under-relaxation for faster convergence. The same line of work noted that regions with high transient activity can dictate a globally small time step, causing over-discretization elsewhere.
supporting_quote: an iterative method which solves each channel independently and subsequently integrates the channels by the prediction and correction of junction point water stages (JPWSPC) was introduced for sub-critical flows in channel networks
