supporting_quote: An evaluation of the roughness coefficient used in the production of synthetic rating curves suggests it is the most important parameter for correcting these errors.
SRCs are insensitive to changes in hydraulic radius... but are very sensitive to changes in Manning's N.
As a general rule we believe the default Manning's coefficient used by HAND is too small in low-order reaches and arguably too large in higher-order reaches.
observed streamflow (NWIS)–stage (USFIMR) relationships could be achieved by varying N except in catchments with zero relief

chunks.text: Bias from NWM streamflow forecasts meaningfully degrades inundation mapping primarily when normalized mean absolute error exceeds 60%, above which large, directional over- or underprediction occurs. Low-relief terrain remains a major challenge, sometimes causing inundation exaggeration regardless of accurate flow inputs due to DEM limits. Despite these issues, the authors argue no fundamental flaws prevent NWM–HAND from being useful for guidance and express optimism that targeted improvements can raise operational value.
supporting_quote: found the method to be relatively insensitive until the normalized absolute error between NWM and observed flow exceeded 60 %. Above this threshold, predictable patterns of large under- or overprediction occur
Another reoccurring error in our simulations was overprediction in catchments with low relief.
our analysis revealed no fundamental errors that would render NWM–HAND unusable... we end with great optimism

chunks.text: Western US municipal water systems rely on winter snowpack and spring snowmelt for most surface-water supply, while municipal demand peaks in mid-to-late summer due to outdoor irrigation. This seasonal mismatch, plus interannual variability and persistent drought, requires utilities to forecast key system states (e.g., reservoir levels) to support operations and planning under changing climate conditions.
supporting_quote: The accumulation of winter precipitation (e.g., snow-water-equivalent (SWE)) functions as a high-elevation storage reservoir... providing the greatest surface water yield during spring snowmelt (April through early July).
Municipal water demand exhibits an opposing seasonal pattern... high peak during the mid-to late-summer as outdoor water use for irrigation increases

chunks.text: A standardized way to evaluate water-system performance is the reliability–resilience–vulnerability (RRV) framework, which compares component behavior to thresholds defining satisfactory versus unsatisfactory states. Reliability measures non-exceedance probability, resilience indicates recovery speed after failure, and vulnerability measures failure magnitude. This framework supports comparing operational strategies and future scenarios.
supporting_quote: Hashimoto et al. (1982) applied the concepts of reliability, resilience, and vulnerability (RRV), based on predetermined thresholds
The framework defines reliability as the probability of the non-exceedance of the threshold... and vulnerability as the severity of an exceedance event (i.e., the magnitude of a failure).

chunks.text: Systems models can represent municipal water system interactions via mass balance and operating rules, but are complex and require extensive parameterization and calibration. Urban water systems can include multiple sources, pressure zones, infrastructure constraints, and prioritization rules, making development time-consuming and difficult to transfer between utilities. These burdens motivate alternative approaches.
supporting_quote: Systems models use the continuity equation to define the intrasystem interactions, accounting for system-wide mass balance changes
Fu et al. (2022) identifies multiple obstacles... (2) ... calibrating a large number of model parameters... (4) the models are system-specific preventing the transferability

chunks.text: The study introduces the Machine Learning Water Systems Model (ML-WSM), a modular, model-agnostic workflow that uses data-driven models to predict key municipal water system components and support vulnerability assessment. The intent is to reduce barriers associated with traditional systems modeling while still capturing operational feedbacks and climate-driven supply/demand effects.
supporting_quote: We develop the Machine Learning Water Systems Model (ML-WSM) as a novel application of ML
we design the ML-WSM as a modular and model-agnostic workflow to extend its application to any MWS with ample data

chunks.text: The ML-WSM is applied to Salt Lake City’s utility to predict daily reservoir levels, groundwater withdrawal, and imported water requests under dry, average, and wet climate scenarios. Performance is benchmarked against an existing systems model to test whether machine learning can replicate system dynamics and produce useful vulnerability classifications for decision-making.
supporting_quote: We apply the ML-WSM framework to the Salt Lake City Department of Public Utilities (SLCDPU) water system... predicts the response of reservoir levels, groundwater withdrawal, and imported water use at a daily temporal resolution
benchmarking model performance to an existing systems model.

chunks.text: Although systems models can represent municipal system interactions, their high complexity and long development cycles impede widespread adoption by utilities. The paper highlights that accurately integrating system connectivity, assumptions, and calibration across many parameters demands significant expertise and time, limiting transferability and slowing research-to-operations.
supporting_quote: extensive parameterization, high complexity, and long development cycles present barriers to widespread adoption.
there are nearly 4,300 elements that required manual calibration over a 10-year period.

chunks.text: Prior machine-learning work has shown value in hydrology and water resources, but ML specifically as a tool to inform municipal water system decision-making under climate anomalies has not been studied. This gap leaves uncertainty about whether ML can capture operational feedbacks among storage, groundwater, and imported supplies for vulnerability assessment.
supporting_quote: While previous research explores the expansion of ML approaches throughout many aspects of water resources, the application of ML to inform MWS decision-making to climate anomalies has not been studied to date.

chunks.text: Data-driven models can produce physically impossible outputs when unconstrained, which is problematic for operational water components like reservoir storage, pumping rates, and imported conveyance. The study encountered predictions exceeding maximum pumping or below minimum aqueduct flow, indicating the need for incorporating constraints or physics-aware learning.
supporting_quote: we discovered physically impossible prediction values. Predictions of groundwater withdrawal exceeded the maximum allowable rate (11 × 10^4 m^3/day)
predictions of Deer Creek requests were below 7.3 m³/s, which is the minimum combined flow rate

chunks.text: The ML-WSM workflow is a four-step process: choose the key municipal components to model, identify features that influence those components, evaluate candidate ML algorithms, and assess model performance. The framework is intended to be iterative, encouraging feature engineering and algorithm testing to improve skill while keeping the approach system-agnostic.
supporting_quote: The conceptual workflow of the ML-WSM initiates by (1) the user determining conceptual components... (2) identifying components (features)... (3) investigating ML algorithms, and (4) evaluating model performance
The workflow encourages the iterative evaluation of different formulations to optimize ML-WSM performance.

chunks.text: Feature engineering emphasizes representing supply availability, demand drivers, hydroclimate, and system connectivity. The paper recommends including previous-timestep component states as features to capture memory and interactions (e.g., reservoir levels or imported water requests from day t−1). This reduces the need to explicitly encode all physical connections as in a systems model.
supporting_quote: Features describing the connectivity of the MWS can improve model performance and we recommend exploring MWS components from the previous timestep as features
For example, reservoir A levels from the preceding timestep... could be a feature of reservoir B levels

chunks.text: To manage feature collinearity, the study recommends a variance inflation factor (VIF) screening, using VIF > 10 as a practical indicator of problematic collinearity. Features with high collinearity are candidates for removal, balancing statistical concerns against the value of connectivity features in municipal systems.
supporting_quote: We recommend a variable inflation factor (VIF) test to address collinearity among features
VIF values exceeding 10 indicate high levels of collinearity among features and we recommend removing the features displaying the lower correlation to the target

chunks.text: Dimensionality reduction and feature selection are described as core steps to improve learning accuracy and reduce model complexity. The paper discusses PCA, LASSO, recursive feature elimination (RFE), and autoencoders, and in the application uses RFE to identify strong predictors via cross-validation and recursive pruning.
supporting_quote: Common methods include PCA, LASSO regularization, recursive feature elimination (RFE), and auto-encoders.
We use RFE within the Scikit-Learn package (v1.0.2) to identify the optimal features for each MWS component

chunks.text: The application adopts a multimodel (submodule) design where each key component (reservoirs, groundwater, imported water) is modeled separately. Two supervised algorithms are explored: a multilayer perceptron (MLP) and XGBoost. XGBoost hyperparameters are tuned using GridSearchCV across learning rate, depth, subsampling, regularization, and number of estimators.
supporting_quote: a multimodel approach, through the use of submodules for the modeling of each key MWS component, best replicates the interactions
We use the Scikit-Learn GridSearchCV package to perform an exhaustive grid search across hyperparameter combinations

chunks.text: Model evaluation uses standard hydrologic metrics: RMSE, Kling–Gupta Efficiency (KGE), and Percent Bias (PBias). KGE integrates correlation, variability, and bias, with values approaching 1 indicating strong agreement. A 10–30% test split is recommended; the study uses 17 years training and 3 years testing.
supporting_quote: We use standard metrics within water resources... including the root-mean-square error (RMSE), Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE), and Percent Bias (PBias)
The 85%/15% training–testing split (17 years for training, 3 years for testing) fits within the recommended testing partitioning of 10–30%

chunks.text: A coupled vulnerability assessment converts predicted component time series into satisfactory/unsatisfactory states using thresholds and computes reliability and vulnerability metrics. The study uses SPI (0/1 status) and RRV-style calculations, and then applies Jenks natural breaks to classify vulnerability and peak severity into Low/Medium/High categories to improve interpretability.
supporting_quote: we calculate the system performance index (SPI)... either one or zero depending on whether the prediction exceeds a threshold
we apply the Jenks classification algorithm to categorize the level of vulnerability and severity... three categories ranging from Category 1 (Low) to Category 3 (High)

chunks.text: The case study is the Salt Lake City Department of Public Utilities system serving about 350,000 people across four cities. It relies on Wasatch mountain creeks for over 60% of annual supply, with groundwater and imported Deer Creek Reservoir water providing the remaining portion when surface water is insufficient. The Dell reservoirs are the only long-term storage owned by the utility.
supporting_quote: The municipality serves approximately 350,000 people across residential, institutional, and commercial sectors in four cities
City Creek, Parleys Creek, Big Cottonwood Creek, and Little Cottonwood Creek contribute over 60% of the annual supply

chunks.text: Reservoir capacities and supply limits define key constraints in the study system. Mountain Dell and Little Dell have storage capacities of 3.2×10^6 m^3 and 25×10^6 m^3, respectively. The utility can use up to 22×10^6 m^3/year of sustainable groundwater and up to 61×10^6 m^3/year of imported water from Deer Creek Reservoir.
supporting_quote: Mountain Dell Reservoir and Little Dell Reservoir with a storage capacity of 3.2 × 10^6 m^3 and 25 × 10^6 m^3, respectively
access to up to 22 × 10^6 m^3 per year of sustainable groundwater... imported water from Deer Creek Reservoir supports up to 61 × 10^6 m^3 per year

chunks.text: Model inputs combine long historical records and administrative datasets. The utility provided near-continuous daily streamflow observations from 1910–present at canyon mouths, which are aggregated into a total surface-water supply feature. Municipal demand data comes from the Utah Division of Water Rights, and population from the Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute.
supporting_quote: The utility provided a near-continuous long-term record of daily streamflow observations (1910–present)
The Utah Department of Water Rights provides the total volume of water entering the distribution system

chunks.text: Targets for machine-learning training and benchmarking are simulated system states from an existing GoldSim-based systems model (SLC-WSM). The ML-WSM is trained to replicate the SLC-WSM programming, using simulated reservoir levels, groundwater withdrawal, and imported water requests, because the systems model is treated as the performance baseline.
supporting_quote: We use the simulated reservoir levels, groundwater withdrawal, and imported water requests from the SLC-WSM.
the motivation is to train the ML-WSM to replicate the SLC-WSM programming and use the SLC-WSM simulations to benchmark the prediction performance

chunks.text: Evaluation uses three climate scenarios selected from the Alta Guard MesoWest station snowfall record: dry (2015, 680 cm), average (2017, 1,270 cm), and wet (2008, 1,660 cm). A Log-Pearson Type III analysis assigns approximately 150-year and 15-year return intervals to the dry and wet years, respectively. Simulations run daily from April 1 after initializing on March 31.
supporting_quote: we identify the most recent dry (2015, 680 cm), average (2017, 1,270 cm), and wet (2008, 1,660 cm) conditions
A Log-Pearson Type III analysis... indicates the dry year and wet year having a 150 year and 15-year return interval

chunks.text: Across dry and average conditions, the ML-WSM reproduces seasonal dynamics of reservoir levels, groundwater withdrawal, and imported water requests with high skill. Reported KGE values are around 0.88–0.98 for reservoirs and about 0.89–0.91 for groundwater and Deer Creek requests, and PBias values are small (roughly within a few percent). Performance is strongest during supply-limited conditions that are operationally important.
supporting_quote: The ML-WSM accurately predicts the seasonal dynamics of all components; especially during supply-limiting conditions (KGE . 0.88, PBias , +3%).
Table 3 | ... Dry... Little Dell Reservoir level... KGE 0.97... PBias 2.85... Deer Creek request... KGE 0.91... PBias 3.45

chunks.text: During wet conditions, reservoir predictions remain reasonably skillful but imported water (Deer Creek) requests are challenging because requests are near zero and harder to model. The Deer Creek request model shows poor KGE (−0.33) and large PBias (87.16) in the wet scenario, while groundwater and reservoirs maintain higher KGE values (e.g., groundwater KGE 0.94).
supporting_quote: Extreme wet conditions challenged model skill
Deer Creek request | Wet | ... KGE | -0.33 | PBias | 87.16

chunks.text: In the dry scenario, the ML-WSM captures key operational patterns such as snowmelt-driven reservoir filling, subsequent drawdown, early-season elevated groundwater pumping, and late-season bimodal imported-water request peaks. Timing and magnitude are close enough to produce similar management signals, such as crossing the 45% Mountain Dell threshold within about two days of the benchmark simulation.
supporting_quote: The ML-WSM accurately predicts the seasonal time series of each MWS component during dry climate conditions.
Figure 5 illustrates the Mountain Dell Reservoir predictions surpassing the 45% of capacity threshold within 2 days of the observed

chunks.text: Iterative feature adjustment beyond initial RFE improved performance for imported water requests. For Deer Creek requests, adding features reflecting physical influences reduced RMSE from 8.4×10^4 m^3 to 2.5×10^4 m^3 for MLP, and the final XGBoost further reduced RMSE to 1.4×10^4 m^3. This indicates that embedding connectivity-relevant inputs can be more effective than purely automated feature selection.
supporting_quote: Integrating features related to the physical influences on Deer Creek requests improved the prediction performance, displayed by a reduction in RMSE from 8.4 × 10^4 m^3 to 2.5 × 10^4 m^3.
the final XGBoost and MLP models... a reduction in RMSE... to 1.4 × 10^4 m^3 for the Deer Creek requests model

chunks.text: The coupled vulnerability assessment largely matches the systems-model benchmark. The ML-WSM correctly estimates vulnerability classification in 10 of 12 component-by-scenario cases and matches all peak severity classes. Misclassifications occur for groundwater in the dry scenario (predicted High vs observed Medium) and Deer Creek in the wet scenario (predicted Medium vs observed Low).
supporting_quote: The ML-WSM correctly estimates the vulnerability classification in ten out of twelve scenarios/components.
resulting in the correct classification of 10 out of 12 vulnerability classes and all peak severity classes

chunks.text: Reliability, vulnerability, and peak severity values computed from ML-WSM outputs are close to benchmark values, with some larger deviations for reservoir reliability in specific cases. For example, Mountain Dell reliability is 0.85 versus 0.94 in the wet scenario, and Little Dell reliability is 0.79 versus 0.88 in the dry scenario. Even when reliability differs, peak severity levels remain correctly classified.
supporting_quote: The reliability estimates for the Dell reservoir system exhibit the greatest difference from the observed with an underprediction of 0.09 during wet (Mountain Dell, 0.85 vs. 0.94) and dry (Little Dell, 0.78 vs. 0.88) conditions.
Peak severity level | ... matches the observed for each climate scenario.

chunks.text: Compared to the benchmark systems model, the ML-WSM is much faster to run and far less parameterized. The paper reports ML-WSM simulations around 2 seconds versus 120 seconds for the systems model, and notes about 36 ML hyperparameters (nine per component) versus about 4,300 calibrated elements in the SLC-WSM. This supports rapid scenario screening as a practical benefit.
supporting_quote: the ML-WSM consistently predicted 60 faster than the systems model (2 s vs. 120 s, respectively)
collectively has 36 parameters... compared to the 4,300 parameters in the SLC-WSM

chunks.text: A key limitation is that ML models can produce physically impossible outputs, requiring post-processing constraints. The study observed groundwater withdrawal exceeding 11×10^4 m^3/day and Deer Creek requests below 7.3 m^3/s, then constrained predictions to acceptable bounds. This motivates future work on physics-informed ML that enforces mass balance and operational limits directly in the model.
supporting_quote: Predictions of groundwater withdrawal exceeded the maximum allowable rate (11 × 10^4 m^3/day)
Future applications of the ML-WSM could explore physics-informed ML models which can address the physical limitations of the system

chunks.text: The wet scenario exposes reduced skill for imported water requests, indicating challenges when the system operates in regimes with low or near-zero values. The paper notes that extreme wet conditions challenged model skill, and the Deer Creek request KGE becomes negative with very high PBias. This suggests additional feature/algorithm work is needed for rare-event or low-flow regimes.
supporting_quote: Extreme wet conditions challenged model skill
Deer Creek request | Wet... KGE | -0.33 | PBias | 87.16

chunks.text: Another limitation is potential degradation under non-stationarity, when feature–target relationships change due to climate change or service-area evolution. The authors caution that changes in statistical behavior can challenge ML model skill, while systems models may better handle new regimes through explicit physical connections. They propose reservoir computing RNNs and physics-informed ML as possible ways to improve extrapolation beyond training bounds.
supporting_quote: Alterations of the statistical behavior between feature-target responses, such as from a changing climate or a change in service area composition, can challenge ML model prediction skill
Evolving ML methods utilizing reservoir computing RNN models show promise in the prediction of long-term dynamical systems behavior influenced by non-stationarity

chunks.text: The study trains ML-WSM to replicate an existing systems model rather than observed system measurements, which frames performance as emulation of SLC-WSM logic. The paper notes observed data could enable direct comparison between ML-WSM and systems models, but the current motivation is to replicate the systems model programming. This limits conclusions about absolute real-world accuracy unless validated with observations.
supporting_quote: We use the simulated reservoir levels, groundwater withdrawal, and imported water requests from the SLC-WSM.
the motivation is to train the ML-WSM to replicate the SLC-WSM programming

chunks.text: The ML-WSM demonstrates that machine learning—particularly XGBoost—can reproduce daily municipal water system component dynamics (reservoir levels, groundwater, imported water) with minimal error relative to a benchmark systems model. Coupling predictions to a threshold-based vulnerability assessment yields interpretable measures of reliability, vulnerability, and peak severity. The approach substantially reduces development burdens compared to a highly parameterized systems model.
supporting_quote: Using the Xtreme Gradient Boosted (XGBoost) algorithm, the ML-WSM captures the defined feedbacks and interactions... with minimal error and without the high parameterization
We couple the predictions to a vulnerability assessment that categorizes peak severity and vulnerability for each key component

chunks.text: The authors argue ML-WSM can complement rather than replace systems models by providing a fast first approximation for screening scenarios and guiding management actions, especially for utilities lacking an existing model but having ample data. They emphasize future improvements via physics-informed constraints and methods for non-stationary dynamics, while maintaining the open-source and transferable nature of the workflow.
supporting_quote: we see a synergistic approach... the ML-WSM does not need to replace the systems model to be beneficial.
We recommend future work exploring physics-informed ML... and reservoir pool algorithms to examine the feasibility of ML for modeling non-stationarity

chunks.text: Snowpack-dominated municipal water systems in the western United States face strong seasonal coupling between climate, supply, and demand. Snowpack functions as a high-elevation reservoir, while summer heat and drought drive peak outdoor water use. Climate change is expected to alter runoff timing and reduce late-season flows, increasing stress during peak demand months. These dynamics motivate evaluating both supply and demand under changing climate conditions for water system planning.
supporting_quote: Seasonal climatic drivers of water supply and demand determine the ability of a snowpack-dominated municipal water system (MWS) to deliver clean and reliable water.
projections from general circulation models (GCMs) suggest a 1.5–3°C increase in mean temperature by 2060 throughout the western U.S.

chunks.text: Water resource assessments are often supply-centric, emphasizing spring runoff and low flows when computing reliability, resilience, and vulnerability (RRV). However, municipal demand also responds to climate variability and can exhibit nonstationarity. Assuming static per-capita demand can misrepresent system performance when climate variability and trends shift outdoor use. Integrating climate influences into demand modeling is therefore important for vulnerability assessments.
supporting_quote: Water resource management efforts are routinely supply-centric, with water system performance evaluations biased to the examination of spring runoff and late-season low-flow impacts on reliability, resilience, and vulnerability (RRV).
the assessments neglect the influences of climate distributed elsewhere, such as the assumption of water demand as a static, per-capita estimate that is independent of dynamic climate conditions

chunks.text: Salt Lake City’s system illustrates the seasonal mismatch between supply and demand: snowmelt peaks in May–June, while irrigation-driven demands peak in July–August. When surface water becomes limited later in summer, the utility relies more on groundwater and imported water from Deer Creek Reservoir. Imported water is the least prioritized source and above-average imports are used as a vulnerability indicator. This context makes imported water requests a relevant performance indicator for climate vulnerability analysis.
supporting_quote: Peak surface water supply occurs in May and June from snowmelt whereas peak demands occur in July and August to maintain landscaping health.
SLCDPU identifies imported water from Deer Creek Reservoir as the least prioritized source and uses above-average use as an indicator of system vulnerability

chunks.text: The study aims to quantify how integrating climate-sensitive demand estimates changes modeled municipal water system performance under wet, average, and dry climate states. Using Salt Lake City’s calibrated systems model, it compares climate-independent per-capita demand assumptions with a climate-sensitive demand model. The intent is to see how demand modeling choice affects vulnerability indicators tied to imported water requests. The work is positioned as planning guidance for climate-related vulnerability assessment.
supporting_quote: we use the documented performance of a real-world MWS with a calibrated systems model to investigate how demands modeled with and without the influences of climate impact system vulnerability indicators
The study uses the Salt Lake City, Utah MWS and the documented performance of an existing systems model to explore the research questions.

chunks.text: Two explicit research questions guide the analysis: expected modeling accuracy gains from climate-sensitive demand estimates, and whether performance metrics are more sensitive to supply variability or demand variability. The study evaluates these questions by linking climate scenarios to both surface-water supply inputs and demand forcings. It then computes RRV metrics based on imported water requests. This supports assessing where improved modeling fidelity matters most for vulnerability assessment.
supporting_quote: What degree of water system modeling accuracy can be expected from integrating climate-sensitive demand estimates for assessing MWS performance to climatic extremes?
To which source of variability do the RRV metrics defining MWS performance exhibit greater sensitivity: supply or demand?

chunks.text: Common econometric demand models often assume stationarity and exclude climate drivers such as temperature and precipitation. This can bias demand forecasts, especially during droughts when outdoor use dynamics shift. Such disconnects can cascade into incorrect system vulnerability classifications and misguided management actions. The paper frames this as a key weakness in climate vulnerability assessments that treat demand as climate-independent.
supporting_quote: Econometric-based methods embedded with assumptions of stationarity and independent from influencing factors traditionally define methods for estimating MWS demand
ignoring the influences of temperature and precipitation, among other externally influencing factors, challenges a comprehensive assessment of water system vulnerabilities

chunks.text: Nonstationarity in both supply and demand complicates estimating reliability, resilience, and vulnerability metrics that depend on the mismatch between supply and demand. Climate change can produce trends or a “new normal” beyond historical bounds, while urban densification can reduce outdoor use. These changing conditions can confound a priori RRV estimation if models rely on historical central tendencies. The paper highlights the need to address the intersection of nonstationarity and variability across both processes.
supporting_quote: nonstationarity surrounding climate, supply, and demand (e.g., prolonged irrigation season, increased evapotranspiration demands) due to evolving climate conditions challenges system management
Nonstationarity within the processes influencing supply and demand confounds the a priori estimation of water system RRV metrics

chunks.text: Imported water from Deer Creek Reservoir is a critical but constrained resource, making accurate timing and magnitude of imports important for operations and planning. Constraints include reservoir multi-user allocation and potential water quality issues such as harmful algal blooms. Because imported water is least prioritized and more costly, overestimating its need can distort vulnerability indicators and conservation staging decisions. This elevates the importance of accurate demand modeling when supplies become limiting.
supporting_quote: Imported water can present several challenges: (1) HABs are increasing in frequency in western U.S. reservoirs which can compromise imported water supplies
Due to the limitations surrounding the imported water, SLCDPU identifies imported water from Deer Creek Reservoir as the least prioritized source

chunks.text: The study constructs three climate scenarios—dry, average, and wet—using October–April snow accumulation at the Alta Guard station as a proxy for regional climate anomalies. It selects recent representative years and aligns observed daily streamflow at canyon mouths to drive surface water supply inputs to the systems model. Snow depth is used as a generalized indicator even though snow water equivalent is the usual metric. These scenarios are intended to test the system under extremes and average conditions.
supporting_quote: we identify the most recent dry (2015, 680 cm), average (2017, 1270 cm), and wet (2008, 1660 cm) years to serve as a proxy for the regional climate
The daily streamflow observations at the canyon mouths, before diversions, align with the scenarios to form the surface water supply inputs to drive the SLC-WSM.

chunks.text: Two demand estimation approaches are compared: a climate-independent model and a climate-sensitive demand model (CSD-WDM). The climate-independent approach uses long-term historical monthly per-capita averages to generate monthly lpcd values. The climate-sensitive approach integrates climate forcings and service area characteristics to predict demand. Observed scenario-aligned per-capita demands provide a baseline for evaluating demand-model accuracy.
supporting_quote: The analysis uses two methods to estimate water demands; (1) a climate-independent model based on historical monthly percapita water use and (2) the climate-sensitive demand model demonstrated in Johnson et al. (2021).
we use Equation (1) to calculate per-capita water use for each month

chunks.text: Monthly per-capita demand series are downscaled to the daily timestep required by the water systems model. The paper uses cubic-spline interpolation to create continuous daily values while iteratively adjusting residuals so monthly totals match the original monthly demand. This supports focusing on average seasonal performance rather than short-lived daily spikes. The assessment targets April–October outdoor-demand seasonality in the modeling.
supporting_quote: The monthly per-capita demands require downscaling to match the daily time step of the SLC-WSM and we use cubic-spline interpolation to produce a continuous daily time series.
the assessment intends to evaluate the average MWS performance from April to October.

chunks.text: The climate-sensitive water demand model (CSD-WDM) is implemented as a Python-based platform that uses an ordinary least squares algorithm. Inputs include air temperature, precipitation, conservation goals, surface water supplies, snow accumulation, and land use metrics. Training uses data from 1980–2017 with fivefold cross-validation to reduce overfitting, and predictions are generated at a 95% confidence level. The study reports standard accuracy metrics for the evaluation scenarios.
supporting_quote: The CSD-WDM is a Python-based modeling platform integrating service area characteristics
we select an ordinary least squares algorithm in the Statsmodels v0.13.0 package
Model training uses climate, service area, and supply data from 1980 to 2017... and fivefold cross-validation to prevent overfitting.

chunks.text: Municipal water system performance is simulated with the Salt Lake City Water Systems Model (SLC-WSM) built in GoldSim. The model is mass-balance based, includes over 4300 components, and runs at a daily timestep. It replicates real-world source prioritization: surface water first, then groundwater, then imported Deer Creek water if needed. A 20-year warm-up is applied so scenarios begin from comparable reservoir, groundwater, and import initial conditions.
supporting_quote: GoldSim uses the conservation of mass to track water throughout the water system, consisting of over 4300 system components
The SLC-WSM replicates the source prioritization strategy; beginning with surface water sources... groundwater, and then imported Deer Creek Reservoir water
Each scenario undergoes a 20-year warm-up to ensure reservoir levels, groundwater levels, and imported water begin with the same initial conditions.

chunks.text: RRV performance metrics are computed using imported water requests from Deer Creek Reservoir as the system performance indicator (SPI). Satisfactory states are requests below the daily mean imported request, while unsatisfactory states exceed it. Reliability is computed from the frequency of unsatisfactory states, resilience from transitions back to satisfactory states (reported as 1/RS), and vulnerability as a weighted function of exposure and severity. Vulnerability categories are defined using Jenks natural breaks derived from historical simulations.
supporting_quote: We determine MWS RRV using imported water from Deer Creek Reservoir as the system performance indicator (SPI)
Reliability describes the relative frequency of the system operating in a satisfactory state
Vulnerability = f(exposure, severity) = WRI_S β_WR + S β_S
We categorize vulnerability into five categories using the historical simulations (2000-2020) and the Jenks natural breaks technique

chunks.text: A sensitivity analysis assesses how imported water use responds to variation in supply and demand. The study performs 99 simulations, bounding supply by ±50% and demand by ±40% of average values and varying each in 10% steps. Imported water request volumes are recorded to quantify relative sensitivity. This isolates which side of the water balance more strongly drives vulnerability-relevant performance changes.
supporting_quote: We investigate MWS performance sensitivity to 99 simulations of varying supply and demand
we bound the supply by ±50% of the average and demand by ±40% of the average, varying in 10% intervals.

chunks.text: Climate scenario selection is based on the long-term snowfall record at the Alta Guard station in the headwaters of Little Cottonwood Creek. The record spans 1945–present and provides dry, average, and wet reference magnitudes. The chosen scenario snow depths are 680 cm (dry), 1270 cm (average), and 1660 cm (wet). The paper uses snow depth as a proxy for climate anomaly and links scenarios to observed daily streamflow inputs.
supporting_quote: From the long-term (1945–present) snowfall record at the Alta Guard station
dry (680 cm) and wet (1660 cm) years demonstrate an approximate 400 cm deviation from the long-term average snowfall (1270 cm/year)

chunks.text: Municipal demand data come from utility-reported monthly treatment facility releases into the distribution system, covering multiple sectors and system losses. The study area population is about 350,000 people, and demand shows strong seasonality and large interannual variability. Examples include a minimum of 428 lpcd in April 2017 and a maximum of 2635 lpcd in July 1991. The analysis uses historical monthly per-capita demand observations across decades to build the climate-independent baseline and train the climate-sensitive model.
supporting_quote: The utility reports monthly treatment facility releases into the distribution system
with the service area population (i.e., ~350,000 people)
a minimum of 428 liters per-capita day (lpcd) in April 2017; a maximum in July 1991 (2635 lpcd)

chunks.text: The climate-independent demand model uses 30 years of monthly per-capita observations spanning 1980–2017, excluding testing years and missing data. The climate-sensitive model training also uses climate, service-area, and supply data from 1980 to 2017 with cross-validation. Demand modeling focuses on the April–October period because outdoor use dominates seasonal variability. Monthly per-capita values are interpolated to daily series for the systems model.
supporting_quote: We used 30 years of SLCDPU demand observations (n) spanning 1980–2017 (omitting testing years and missing observations) to develop the climate-independent model
Model training uses climate, service area, and supply data from 1980 to 2017
Demand modeling focuses on April-October outdoor water use

chunks.text: The systems model represents Salt Lake City’s portfolio of surface water, groundwater, and imported water, and operational prioritization among them. The paper reports approximate annual access magnitudes and key operational constraints, including reduced imported water availability under supply-limited conditions. Imported water is sourced from Deer Creek Reservoir and can be restricted based on broader basin conditions. These system attributes shape how supply deficits translate into modeled imported water requests.
supporting_quote: Salt Lake City has access to surface water (50,000 × 10^4  m^3 /year), groundwater (22,000 × 10^4  m^3 /year), and imported water contracts (48,000 × 10^4  m^3 /year)
Imported water comes from Deer Creek Reservoir... but reduces to 48,000 × 10^4  m^3 /year during supply-limited conditions

chunks.text: Historical simulations from 2000–2020 provide the baseline for computing exposure in the vulnerability metric and for classifying vulnerability levels. The paper defines historical water requests (WR_H) from this period and computes scenario-specific requests (WR_S). Jenks natural breaks are then used to define vulnerability categories from low to extreme. These historical baselines operationalize “bounds of stationarity” for classification.
supporting_quote: We use the 2000–2020 simulation period to determine the WR_H and calculate the WR_S for each climate/demand scenario.
We categorize vulnerability into five categories using the historical simulations (2000-2020) and the Jenks natural breaks technique

chunks.text: Under wet climate conditions, simulated system performance showed minimal vulnerability across demand-modeling approaches. RRV metrics indicated near-complete reliability and resilience, and low vulnerability when using observed demands. The climate-independent simulation produced a small number of days with above-average imports, leading to a higher (medium) vulnerability classification than observed. Climate-sensitive demand slightly improved alignment with observed RRV classification.
supporting_quote: No simulations produced any severe system vulnerabilities during the wet climate scenario
There were 4 days during the climate-independent demand simulation... resulting in a medium versus low (observed) vulnerability

chunks.text: For average climate conditions, climate-independent demand estimates materially degraded modeled RRV performance relative to observed. The climate-independent model showed 25% lower reliability and 53% higher vulnerability than observed, and it misclassified vulnerability one level too high. In contrast, the climate-sensitive demand simulation closely matched observed RRV metrics and classifications. This indicates that incorporating climate drivers into demand estimates improves vulnerability assessment even without extreme drought.
supporting_quote: The climate-independent model exhibits 25% less reliability, 53% greater vulnerability
Integrating climate-sensitive demand estimates results in a strong agreement with all the observed RRV metrics and classifications.

chunks.text: During the dry climate scenario, demand-model choice produced the largest divergence in modeled system vulnerability. The climate-independent demand run yielded vulnerability 39% higher and peak severity 133% higher than observed, leading to an extreme classification rather than very high. Climate-sensitive demand produced RRV metrics that matched observed vulnerability closely, with remaining error mainly in monthly peak severity (+20%). Overall, climate-sensitive demand better represented timing and magnitude of imported water needs under supply-limited conditions.
supporting_quote: The climate-independent demand model resulted in vulnerability and peak severity being 39% and 133% greater than the observed, respectively, and classified as extreme versus very high.
The climate-sensitive demand estimates produced accurate RRV metrics, except for monthly peak severity (+20%)

chunks.text: Operationally relevant performance indicators show that omitting climate effects in demand overstates imported water volumes and distorts timing during dry conditions. For the dry case, seasonal Deer Creek requests were 3040×10^4 m^3 under climate-independent demand versus 2080×10^4 m^3 observed, while climate-sensitive demand produced 2030×10^4 m^3. Peak request month was incorrectly shifted to July under climate-independent demand but remained September under observed and climate-sensitive cases. These differences affect the inferred duration and seasonality of unsatisfactory states.
supporting_quote: Seasonal deer creek requesta 2080 ... 3040 ... 2030 (1200–2900)
Peak deer creek request month Sep ... Jul ... Sep (Aug–Sep)

chunks.text: The study reports improved demand-model accuracy for the climate-sensitive approach used in evaluation scenarios. Performance metrics include Kling–Gupta efficiency of 0.96, RMSE of 74.0 lpcd, and percent bias of 3.4%. This level of accuracy supports using the climate-sensitive model as an input to system simulations that depend on daily demand patterns. The paper emphasizes that uncertainty bounds can also be carried into performance assessment.
supporting_quote: Model accuracy for the evaluation scenarios is as follows; Kling–Gupta efficiency = 0.96, root mean squared error = 74.0 lpcd, and percent bias = 3.4%.

chunks.text: Sensitivity analysis shows imported water use is more responsive to changes in demand than to changes in supply. Across the tested ranges, a 1% increase in demand produced a 3% increase in imported water use, while a 1% reduction in supply produced a 1% increase in imported water use. Under average supply, imported use varied by about 6000×10^4 m^3 across demand changes, compared to about 2000×10^4 m^3 across supply changes under average demand. This indicates demand forecasting accuracy strongly influences vulnerability-relevant outcomes.
supporting_quote: a 1% increase in demand produces a 3% increase in imported water use whereas a 1% reduction in supply produces a 1% increase in imported water use.
Under average supply conditions, there is a 6000 × 10^4 m^3 range of imported water use over the range in demands
Under average demands, there is a 2000 × 10^4 m^3 range in imported water use across their range in supply

chunks.text: The analysis focuses on April–October outdoor demand because indoor demand is treated as relatively constant. This narrows the study’s applicability to seasonal irrigation-driven variability rather than year-round total demand dynamics. The approach also emphasizes average daily performance over the season rather than capturing short-term demand spikes. As a result, operational impacts from unusual daily events (e.g., infrastructure failures) are not a target of the evaluation.
supporting_quote: Demand modeling focuses on April-October outdoor water use, with the climate-independent model representing the current status quo
we focus on outdoor demands as indoor demands remain consistent throughout the year
While spikes in daily use (e.g., unexpected pipe breaks) can impact short-term MWS performance, the assessment intends to evaluate the average MWS performance from April to October.

chunks.text: Snow depth is used as a proxy for the climate anomaly even though snow water equivalent is typically preferred for supply estimation. The paper explicitly notes this generalization when linking climate states to system performance. While the selected snow years align with observed streamflow inputs, this proxy may not fully capture changes in density, melt dynamics, or rain-snow partitioning that affect runoff. The choice reflects a simplifying assumption for scenario development.
supporting_quote: While snow water equivalent is the standard for determining water supply availability, we generalize snow depth as a climate anomaly indicator.

chunks.text: The full Salt Lake City Water Systems Model (SLC-WSM) is not shared due to security restrictions, limiting external reproducibility of the end-to-end systems simulation. Although code and data for the Python-based demand modeling are publicly available, access to the GoldSim implementation requires permission. The authors instead provide simulation results and analysis tools in an open repository. This creates a partial transparency limitation for independent verification of the systems model behavior.
supporting_quote: The SLC-WSM is not provided for review due to security reasons specified by SLCDPU. Permission for this model requires direct consent from SLCDPU.
We do provide access to simulation results and analysis tools in an open-source data repository

chunks.text: The authors argue that future studies should expand beyond direct climate drivers to include additional demand drivers such as urbanization. They note that water-use efficiency and densification can reduce per-capita use but may also lead to demand hardening that reduces flexibility during drought. Because system performance is highly sensitive to demand, excluding these drivers could understate or mischaracterize future vulnerabilities. This is presented as an important direction for improving long-term vulnerability assessment frameworks.
supporting_quote: Future studies should consider additional drivers of demand, such as urbanization, that extend beyond the direct impacts of climate.
In addition to the climate-demand influence on water system performance, urbanization will likely alter per-capita water use

chunks.text: The study concludes that integrating climate-sensitive demand estimates yields a more representative understanding of water system vulnerabilities, with benefits increasing as supplies become limited. Climate-sensitive demand better captures the duration, timing, and magnitude of vulnerability indicators derived from imported water requests. The authors emphasize that realistic demand estimates are necessary to support proactive decision-making under climate extremes. This directly addresses shortcomings from treating demand as stationary and climate-independent.
supporting_quote: Integrating climate-sensitive demands results in a more representative understanding of water system vulnerabilities, becoming more significant as supplies become limited.
Demand estimates representing climate influences can accurately identify the duration, timing, and magnitude of system vulnerabilities to support proactive decision-making.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that water system performance can be more sensitive to percent changes in demand than to percent changes in supply. This was demonstrated by the quantified relationship between demand changes and imported water usage in the sensitivity analysis. The implication is that vulnerability assessments should complement supply-focused modeling with high-quality demand forecasts that reflect climate and other drivers. This helps avoid misclassification of vulnerability states and misinformed conservation staging.
supporting_quote: Water systems can exhibit a greater sensitivity to percentage changes in demand compared to supply
a 1% increase in demand produces a 3% increase in imported water use whereas a 1% reduction in supply produces a 1% increase in imported water use.

chunks.text: The authors identify future research needs to better characterize combined effects of supply and demand accuracy and to extend analyses to larger regional infrastructure serving multiple stakeholders. They suggest exploring coupled influences of modeled supply and demand accuracy on system performance and developing protocols for assessing nonstationarities driven by climate change. They also note the value of scaling refined demand estimates to reservoir operations and other sectors impacted by seasonal demand and supply timing. These directions aim to standardize and strengthen climate vulnerability assessment practice.
supporting_quote: Future studies should consider additional drivers of demand, such as urbanization

there is a research need to examine the impacts of refined demand estimates on regional management and operations to climate change-driven vulnerabilities, such as scaling the analysis to larger water resources infrastructure that supports many stakeholders.

chunks.text: Municipal water systems in the arid western U.S. face a difficult supply–demand nexus because water use peaks in hot summers while supplies depend heavily on snowmelt and stored water. Climate change is altering precipitation and temperature patterns, which affects both surface water availability and the timing/intensity of irrigation-driven demand. As a result, demand management and improved demand estimates are increasingly important for operational and planning decisions.
supporting_quote: Altered precipitation and temperature patterns from a changing climate will affect supply, demand, and overall municipal water system operations throughout the arid western U.S.
the persistent summer drought and high evapotranspiration drive increases in outdoor water use from April to October to maintain landscaping health

chunks.text: Traditional demand forecasting in utilities often relies on climate-independent, econometric or time-series approaches that assume historical patterns and serial correlations will persist. However, in highly seasonal arid regions, irrigation season length and intensity can deviate from historical behavior under climate variability and change. This challenges models that neglect climate influences and motivates incorporating climate and service-area drivers.
supporting_quote: demand forecasts typically estimate water use independent of climate and other externalities
because of a changing climate, irrigation season length and intensity deviate from historical use patterns

chunks.text: Machine learning has improved water-demand prediction accuracy in prior work, but utilities can be reluctant to adopt it due to overfitting risk, limited extrapolation under changing climate, and lack of interpretability. The paper frames model complexity as the number of parameters, linking complexity to interpretability and operational usability. This motivates comparing simpler interpretable models to more complex black-box methods under climate extremes.
supporting_quote: ML algorithms are susceptible to overfitting, can produce unreasonable estimates from inputs exceeding the bounds of training data
We define model complexity as the number of parameters within the model and translate the complexity to the interpretability given by the number of parameters

chunks.text: The study aims to evaluate accuracy-versus-complexity tradeoffs between simple climate-independent demand estimation and more complex climate-sensitive, data-driven models for an arid municipal system. It uses Salt Lake City, Utah as a test bed and assesses performance across wet, average, and extreme dry climate conditions that are framed as representative of a new climate normal. The work also seeks to characterize climate–demand interactions to support management decisions.
supporting_quote: assess model accuracy versus complexity tradeoffs between simple climate-independent econometric-based models and complex climate-sensitive data-driven models to average to extreme wet and dry climate conditions
We investigate the research questions using Salt Lake City Department of Public Utilities (SLCDPU) as a case application

chunks.text: Two explicit research questions guide the work: whether climate-sensitive models measurably improve seasonal forecasting skill compared with climate-independent models under extreme climate conditions, and whether increasing model complexity yields measurable changes in predictive skill across different climate regimes. The paper operationalizes this by training OLS, random forest regression, and multilayer perceptron models and comparing them to a climate-independent baseline.
supporting_quote: Is there a measurable change in seasonal water demand forecasting accuracy from more complex climate-sensitive models compared to climate-independent econometric-based models
Are there measurable changes in prediction skill from models of differing levels of complexity for estimating demands to various climate regimes?

chunks.text: Climate-independent demand estimation can perform poorly during climatic extremes because it relies on historical averages and serial correlation rather than explicitly modeling climate drivers. The paper reports that this baseline approach substantially overpredicts demand under dry conditions, leading to large monthly and seasonal errors. Such error propagation can undermine operational decisions such as supply acquisition and budgeting.
supporting_quote: The climate-independent model displayed low performance during extreme dry conditions with predictions exceeding 90% and 40% of the observed monthly and seasonal volumetric demands, respectively
The climate-independent model produces demand estimates greater than the observed for all scenarios

chunks.text: A key challenge for adopting machine learning in municipal demand forecasting is balancing improved accuracy with risks such as overfitting, poor extrapolation when future climate exceeds training bounds, and black-box interpretability barriers. These limitations contribute to reluctance in utility adoption even when ML can be accurate. The study positions interpretable modeling as important for management trust and use.
supporting_quote: ML algorithms are susceptible to overfitting, can produce unreasonable estimates from inputs exceeding the bounds of training data
the black box from high model complexity obscuring the relationships between input variables, model algorithm, and predictions

chunks.text: There is a stated research gap regarding how seasonal municipal demand forecast accuracy changes under current and projected climate-influenced conditions when model complexity varies. The paper argues that integrating complexity as an evaluation measure enables a more operationally relevant comparison that accounts for interpretability and efficiency. This gap motivates the cross-model comparison under multiple climate regimes.
supporting_quote: highlight a research gap surrounding the prediction accuracy of seasonal municipal demand, specifically, to current and projected conditions influenced by a changing climate while considering model complexity versus accuracy trade-offs
Integrating model complexity as an evaluation measure allows for a methodological investigation of accuracy changes to different model formulations

chunks.text: The climate-independent baseline model estimates monthly per-capita demand as the historical mean for each month over the training period, representing a low-complexity serial-correlation approach. It uses a 1980–2017 training period and assumes indoor use is consistent in November–March. This provides a simple benchmark against which climate-sensitive methods are evaluated.
supporting_quote: we calculate the monthly liters per-capita day water (lpcd) use from the training period spanning from 1980 to 2017
estimating monthly demands as a function of the historically observed monthly climate-demand interactions and the assumption that previous observations will reflect future demands based on Equation 1
We assume consistent per-capita water use during this period (i.e., 590 lpcd).

chunks.text: For climate-sensitive modeling, the authors isolate outdoor demand by subtracting an estimated indoor baseline from total demand. Indoor per-capita use is computed as the mean of November–March demands for each year, assuming minimal outdoor use during those months. Outdoor demand from April–October becomes the dependent variable for the climate-sensitive models.
supporting_quote: We calculate monthly outdoor water use (DOm ) using Equation 3,
DOm = DTm − DIy
we assume indoor water use activities ... remain relatively constant throughout the year ... and that there is minimal water applied for outdoor purposes from November to March

chunks.text: The workflow constructs climate and service-area predictors including temperature, precipitation, snowfall, and streamflow, as well as population/housing density, land-cover fractions, and a conservation-goal feature. Climate features are derived as spatial averages over the service area from March through October, and streamflow is assembled from four canyon-mouth gauges. The feature set includes antecedent climate variables to represent system memory affecting irrigation needs.
supporting_quote: We create temperature, precipitation, snowfall, and streamflow features to represent the dynamic climate conditions
We calculate monthly air temperature (°C) and precipitation (mm) features as a function of the spatial average of the service area from March through October
We calculate monthly streamflow (Qcms) from the daily discharge measurements at the canyon mouths of the four supply streams
We incorporate antecedent climate features to reflect the hydrological system memory

chunks.text: A conservation feature represents a planned 25% per-capita reduction goal by 2025, using 1980–2000 monthly averages as the baseline and linearly interpolating reductions from 2001–2025. This creates a continuous time series of expected conservation-driven demand reductions. The feature is intended to reflect policy-driven trends alongside climate influences.
supporting_quote: a statewide goal to reduce per-capita water use by 25% by 2025
The conservation features uses the long-term average demand of each month from the 1980–2000 period as the baseline
We use linear interpolation between 2001 to 2025 to create a continuous time series of conservation goals using Equation 4

chunks.text: To reduce dimensionality and collinearity, the study uses a Correlation Bias Reduction (CBR) procedure followed by Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE). CBR filters to features strongly correlated with demand while limiting feature-to-feature correlation, then RFE prunes predictors using cross-validation and grid searches over correlation thresholds. The resulting optimized monthly predictor sets are used consistently across OLS, MLP, and random forest models.
supporting_quote: Feature selection reduces model dimensionality, improves learning accuracy, and facilitates a better model understanding
Implementing a correlation bias reduction (CBR) strategy into the feature selection workflow can further improve model performance
We use Scikit-learn 0.24.1 RFE to identify the optimal monthly per-capita outdoor demand predictors

chunks.text: Three climate-sensitive models are trained: an interpretable ordinary least squares regression (fit without an intercept), a random forest regressor with hyperparameters tuned by GridSearchCV, and a deep multilayer perceptron built in TensorFlow/Keras. All models use five-fold cross-validation. Model complexity is quantified as number of non-zero OLS coefficients, number of trees for random forest, and number of network parameters for MLP.
supporting_quote: We train a lower complexity ordinary least squares (OLS) model and develop complex random forest regression (RFR) and multilayered perceptron (MLP) models
We train the OLS model using five-fold crossvalidation and fit without a y-intercept
use a five-fold cross-validation and a GridSearchCV function to optimize the hyperparameters
MLP network ... eight hidden layers ... and 500 epochs

chunks.text: Model evaluation uses wet, average, and dry scenarios defined by seasonal accumulated snowfall at the Alta Guard station, plus a 2018–2022 holdout period to test year-to-year variability and out-of-training-bounds inputs. Performance metrics include percent bias (PBias), RMSE, and Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE), along with volumetric seasonal and annual percent errors. This setup links demand forecasting skill to climate regimes relevant for operations.
supporting_quote: we use seasonal accumulated snowfall (Scm) as the metric to characterize the climate and establish wet, dry, and average testing
identify the most recent wettest (2008), driest (2015), and average (2017) seasonal snowfall
We use percent bias (PBias), root-mean-squared-error (RMSE), and Kling-Gupta Efficiency metrics (KGE)

chunks.text: The case study is the Salt Lake City Department of Public Utilities service area, serving about 350,000 people with strong seasonal demand driven by outdoor irrigation. Supply is snowpack dominated, with four mountain streams providing about 60% of annual water. The system’s long-term records enable analysis of seasonality and interannual variability relevant to climate-sensitive demand forecasting.
supporting_quote: use SLCDPU as a representative arid western U.S. water system ... (serving 350,000 people)
streamflow from City (CC), Parleys (PC), Big Cottonwood (BCC), and Little Cottonwood (LCC) creeks providing approximately 60% of the annual supply

chunks.text: Monthly treated water releases into the distribution system are available from 1980 onward and are used to compute per-capita demand; these data include residential, institutional, and commercial uses plus losses. The paper highlights long-term declines in per-capita demand over the past two decades. The April–October period exhibits high variability due to outdoor water use.
supporting_quote: SLCDPU has reported the total volume of monthly treated water releases into the distribution system ... from 1980 to the present
including leakage and unaccounted for system losses
Municipal demand has decreased from 1100 lpcd to 800 lpcd over the past two decades

chunks.text: Climate forcings for temperature and precipitation are obtained from NLDAS and aggregated as service-area spatial averages for March through October. Streamflow predictors are computed from daily discharge at the canyon mouths of the four supply streams, with limited missing values interpolated using nearby gauges. Snowfall features use November–April observations at the Alta Guard station to describe winter conditions relevant to summer demand and supply signals.
supporting_quote: use the North American Land Data Assimilation System (NLDAS) climate-forcing data products to retrieve temperature and precipitation estimates
We calculate monthly streamflow (Qcms) from the daily discharge measurements at the canyon mouths of the four supply streams
we used November to April monthly and seasonal snowfall from the Alta Guard station

chunks.text: Urbanization and land-cover predictors are constructed using U.S. Census population and housing counts (interpolated between decadal observations) and Landsat imagery classifications. Land-cover fractions (urban, residential, irrigated, vegetated) are derived at a 5-year frequency from 1985 through 2017 using a random-forest classifier on Landsat 5 and 8 imagery. These features are intended to capture service-area changes that may influence demand.
supporting_quote: We use the population and housing estimates from the U.S. Census ... to calculate population and housing densities
we use linear interpolation between decadal census observations
At a 5-year frequency, beginning in 1985 and including 2017, we retrieve USGS Landsat 5 and 8
create features as the percentage of the urban area, residential area, irrigated area, and vegetated area

chunks.text: Testing scenarios are defined using annual snowfall totals at Alta Guard with specified return intervals, including wet 2008 (1660 cm), dry 2015 (680 cm), and average 2017 (1347 cm), plus 2018–2022 additional years. A Log Pearson type III analysis on 78 years of snowfall data is used to characterize rarity, with the dry scenario described as a 150-year event. This enables evaluation across a broad range of climate conditions.
supporting_quote: wettest (2008), driest (2015), and average (2017) seasonal snowfall
dry scenario (680 cm) and wet scenario (1660 cm) have a 150-year and 15-year return period, respectively
include the climate conditions from 2018 to 2022 to extend the model evaluation period

chunks.text: Across wet, dry, and average climate scenarios, the climate-independent model systematically overpredicts demand and shows large negative PBias and high RMSE. Overall performance across the three climate states is PBias −27.3% and RMSE 294 lpcd, with particularly poor results during dry and average conditions. The paper reports monthly errors approaching 90% or about 700 lpcd during challenging conditions.
supporting_quote: The climate-independent model produces demand estimates greater than the observed for all scenarios
PBias metric characterizing the prediction trend at -27.3%
errors approaching 90% or 700 lpcd

chunks.text: Climate-sensitive models substantially reduce bias and error relative to the climate-independent baseline when evaluated across wet, dry, and average scenarios. The OLS model achieves PBias 3.4% and RMSE 74 lpcd overall, while RFR achieves PBias −1.7% and RMSE 109 lpcd, and MLP achieves PBias −2.5% and RMSE 153 lpcd. KGE values also improve, indicating better agreement in correlation, variability, and bias.
supporting_quote: PBias values of 3.4%, −2.5%, and 1.7% for the OLS, MLP, and RFR models
an ordinary least squares model demonstrating a measurable reduction in prediction bias (3.4% vs. −27.3%) and RMSE (74.0 lpcd vs. 294 lpcd)
The climate-sensitive models translated the climate influences on water demand with high prediction accuracy

chunks.text: Under the extreme dry scenario, OLS performs best among the climate-sensitive models, nearly eliminating bias and producing very low RMSE and high KGE. In Table 4, dry-scenario OLS PBias is 0.2%, RMSE is 48 lpcd, and KGE is 0.98. RFR and MLP degrade under dry conditions compared to OLS, with negative PBias and lower KGE.
supporting_quote: The OLS model displayed the highest model accuracy during the dry climate conditions, with a low PBias (0.20%), RMSE (48.4 lpcd), and high KGE (0.98).
The dry scenario presented challenging conditions for the MLP and RFR models, displayed by a PBias of −13.8% and −7.5%

chunks.text: Errors in the climate-independent model compound when converted to volumetric seasonal and annual demand, creating large operationally meaningful overestimates. Seasonal demand is overpredicted by 24.2 Mm³ (34%) in the dry scenario and 20.8 Mm³ (31%) in the average scenario. The annual volumetric error during dry conditions reaches 32.8 Mm³, which exceeds the Dell reservoir system capacity of 27.1 Mm³.
supporting_quote: overprediction of seasonal demand by ... 24.2 Mm3 (34%), and 20.8 Mm3 (31%) for the wet, dry, and average conditions
The annual volumetric error during the dry conditions (i.e., 32.8 Mm3 ) exceeds the storage capacity of the Dell reservoir system (i.e., 27.1 Mm3 )

chunks.text: In the 2018–2022 evaluation period, performance declines for climate-sensitive models relative to the three-scenario testing, suggesting sensitivity to conditions outside the training bounds and changing behavior. MLP shows the largest degradation (PBias −6.0%, RMSE 237 lpcd, KGE 0.62), while OLS and RFR retain PBias below 1% with RMSE around 170 lpcd and KGE near 0.80. Overprediction in 2021–2022 is attributed to drought-driven conservation behavior.
supporting_quote: The 2018–2022 period examines the impacts of inputs outside of the training bounds on model skill and we observed a decrease in prediction accuracy.
The MLP model ... PBias (−6.0% vs. −2.5%), an increase in RMSE (237 lpcd vs. 153 lpcd), and a reduction in KGE (0.62 vs. 0.86)
The OLS and RFR models displayed similar performance for the 2018–2022 period with a PBias less than 1%, RMSE around 170 lpcd, and a KGE close to 0.80.

chunks.text: The model accuracy versus complexity comparison shows that increasing complexity from the climate-independent baseline yields major accuracy gains, but very high complexity does not guarantee better performance than simpler climate-sensitive approaches. Complexity degrees reported are 1 (climate-independent), 18 (OLS), 33,721 (MLP parameters), and 60 (RFR trees). Accuracy ranking across scenarios is OLS, RFR, MLP, then climate-independent, with minimal differences between OLS and RFR.
supporting_quote: The climate-independent model has a complexity degree of 1
the OLS algorithm has a complexity degree of 18
the MLP model has a complexity degree of 33,721
the RFR model has complexity degree of 60
Model accuracy was consistent across all scenarios, with the greatest to least accuracy as follows: OLS, RFR, MLP, and climate-independent models.

chunks.text: OLS coefficients derived from selected predictors indicate temperature and precipitation dominate monthly demand sensitivity, helping interpret climate–demand relationships. The paper notes that 12 of 18 OLS predictors are monthly air temperature and precipitation variables. An example relationship is that a 1°C increase in April mean temperature corresponds to a 21.3 lpcd increase in April demand, consistent with outdoor irrigation behavior.
supporting_quote: We observe 12 of the 18 predictors connecting service area monthly air temperature and precipitation to demand
For example, for every degree increase in April mean temperature (°C), SLCDPU can expect a 21.3 lpcd increase in April demand.
April mean temperature ... 21.3

chunks.text: A key limitation is the assumption that indoor demand is constant and independent of dynamic conditions; observed errors in November–March suggest indoor use may change with drought awareness and conservation. Because outdoor demand is computed by subtracting indoor use from total demand, mischaracterizing indoor trends can propagate into outdoor-demand modeling error. The authors suggest integrating additional service-area characteristics for indoor modeling to improve performance.
supporting_quote: We can no longer assume indoor demands are independent of dynamic service area conditions, as errors in November through March demands indicate

Future research ... integrating service area characteristics for indoor demand modeling may improve overall modeling performance, leading to improvements in overall demand prediction accuracy (Equation 3)

chunks.text: The conservation feature is modeled as a linear trend toward a 2025 goal, but the authors note potential non-linear conservation behavior that could better fit observed patterns. They mention a negative exponential trend may partially describe error as scenarios approach 2025. This indicates that policy/behavioral dynamics may not be well represented by a simple linear reduction assumption.
supporting_quote: There is the potential for a non-linear conservation trend, as a negative exponential trend partially describes the observed error
We use linear interpolation between 2001 to 2025 to create a continuous time series of conservation goals

chunks.text: The study’s feature importance patterns may not transfer directly to other municipalities, where non-linear predictor–demand relationships could be stronger and challenge linear regression. The authors recommend trying multiple ML algorithms and even ensemble approaches when applying the framework elsewhere. They also suggest that sectoral decomposition and demographic/socioeconomic variables could improve skill if data are available.
supporting_quote: applying the climate-sensitive workflow to other systems may indicate a non-linear predictor-demand relationship that challenges linear regression-based algorithms
We encourage developers to explore many ML algorithms that increase prediction accuracy under non-linear relationships
Decomposing sector water use and including demographic and socioeconomic components could improve model skill

chunks.text: The paper concludes that climate-independent, low-complexity demand estimates can severely overestimate municipal demand under dry and average conditions, with monthly errors up to about 90% and seasonal errors up to about 40%. By incorporating climate and service-area features, climate-sensitive models substantially reduce bias and RMSE across wet, average, and dry regimes. These improvements are framed as important for water system management as conditions trend drier.
supporting_quote: we find the climate-independent model to overestimate monthly demands up to 90% and seasonally up to 40%
The climate-sensitive models produced measurable reductions in the overall prediction bias compared to the climate-independent model across wet, dry, and average testing scenarios

chunks.text: Among evaluated methods, OLS is identified as the best balance of interpretability and accuracy, matching or exceeding more complex models while providing transparent climate–demand relationships. The study emphasizes that the largest accuracy gains come from integrating key temporally dynamic service-area characteristics rather than maximizing algorithmic complexity. The authors encourage applying the workflow to other systems and exploring probabilistic, ensemble, and additional feature enhancements.
supporting_quote: The model accuracy versus complexity comparison identified the OLS algorithm as the ideal balance between interpretability and prediction accuracy.
The OLS model demonstrated that sufficient complexity could match or exceed the performance of greater complexity models (i.e., MLP, RFR)
Additional research opportunities include applying probabilistic algorithms, exploring ensemble modeling strategies

chunks.text: Hydrologic Information Systems (HIS) are integrated hardware and software used to collect, store, manage, and disseminate hydrologic observations and metadata for monitoring, modeling, and water-resource management. As costs and barriers have decreased, hydrologic observations are increasingly high-volume and high-frequency, requiring cyberinfrastructure to support the full data life cycle. HIS help reduce the time between data collection and analysis and commonly provide visualization to support interpretation and communication to diverse data consumers.
supporting_quote: Hydrologic Information Systems (HIS) consist of the integrated hardware and software systems used to collect, store, manage, and disseminate water observations data and metadata
Successful HIS enable scientific investigations and analysis as well as water resource management by providing reliable and accessible water data and information

chunks.text: The modern push for HIS accelerated around 2004 alongside information technology advances and community efforts such as CUAHSI’s national-scale HIS. Earlier uses of the term were often tied to GIS and spatial data, with ArcHydro supporting hydrologic time series within GIS. Operational systems like the USGS National Water Information System (NWIS), released publicly in the mid-1990s, demonstrated large-scale public internet access to hydrologic data and became foundational to later HIS developments.
supporting_quote: Scopus identified 65 documents ... dating back to 2004, which marked a major push to apply advances in information technology to the hydrology domain
Initially released to the public in the mid-1990s, USGS NWIS was an early HIS ... made it uniformly accessible to the public over the Internet

chunks.text: Recent HIS evolution reflects the growth of low-cost sensing platforms and Internet of Things (IoT) approaches. Monitoring networks increasingly use off-the-shelf microcontrollers, new data transfer protocols, and standards designed for Internet-connected sensing devices. These shifts influence mechanisms for sensing, logging, communicating, and managing observations, including adoption of standards like the OGC SensorThings API.
supporting_quote: several HIS ... were designed to support increasingly popular low cost sensing platforms using off-the-shelf microcontrollers
including technologies associated with the Internet of Things (IoT) ... supporting communication technology

chunks.text: The paper aims to provide an introductory overview of HIS focused on cyberinfrastructure supporting observational time series at fixed monitoring stations (e.g., discharge, water quality, precipitation, groundwater levels). It synthesizes universal and generic HIS functions and components from prior literature, then connects these concepts to implementations in current and emerging systems. It also identifies remaining gaps and deficiencies as opportunities to improve operational HIS.
supporting_quote: we present a synthesis and overview of HIS specifically focused on cyberinfrastructure to support time series of observational data at fixed monitoring stations
The objectives of this paper are to: 1) establish an introductory overview of HIS ... 2) describe implementations of HIS in current and emerging systems, and 3) identify gaps and deficiencies

chunks.text: A central goal is to distill common patterns across diverse HIS implementations into a generalized architecture. The authors characterize HIS as data pools and data fluxes, with key pools being collection/acquisition, operational storage, and publication/sharing/exchange. This synthesis is intended to provide foundational understanding for data collectors, developers, and practitioners and to frame modern challenges and modernization opportunities.
