supporting_quote: patterns emerged for universal and generic HIS functionality and components
We consider components to be either "data pools" in which data reside or "data fluxes" in which data are transferred.

chunks.text: Operational HIS details are often under-described in published hydrologic studies, limiting shared understanding of data management practices. The paper notes that methods for collection, management, quality control, processing, and dissemination are frequently presented only briefly because research emphasis is placed on process understanding rather than system implementation. This scarcity of detailed operational documentation constrains comparison across HIS and complicates learning and reuse.
supporting_quote: the details and challenges of data management are not often described in existing literature
the methods associated with collection, management, quality control, processing, and dissemination are often presented only cursorily

chunks.text: A persistent operational challenge is non-interoperability between sensing/datalogging systems and downstream HIS components. Although sensor-to-datalogger interfaces may use standards, the pathway from dataloggers to data management software is often proprietary and not standardized, forcing reliance on vendor software or custom middleware. This inhibits generalizable, hardware-agnostic acquisition workflows.
supporting_quote: Challenge 1: Non-interoperability of sensing and datalogging systems.
retrieving data from a fielddeployed datalogger still often requires proprietary software or custom middleware.

chunks.text: Heterogeneity in data models, metadata elements, and vocabularies remains a barrier to interoperability even when systems share similar concepts. Different HIS may represent concepts inconsistently or omit key metadata, and even when fields align, semantic heterogeneity persists if vocabulary values are not standardized. Prior controlled-vocabulary approaches exist but have seen inconsistent implementation and adoption.
supporting_quote: Challenge 2: Heterogeneity in data models, metadata, and vocabularies.
even when data collection organizations use the same metadata elements, if they do not use standardized vocabularies ... semantic heterogeneity persists

chunks.text: Modernization is difficult because many HIS components were built with now-dated technologies and accrue technical debt, while no single de facto standard has emerged across the community. Legacy standards and interfaces (e.g., older web service styles and encodings) complicate upgrades and integration. Terminology shifts (e.g., toward IoT) may also reduce visibility of relevant work labeled outside “HIS.”
supporting_quote: Many of the systems described in this review were developed using technologies and/or standards that are becoming outdated
none of them has emerged as a de facto standard that is widely used and maintained by broad communities

chunks.text: Multiple competing web service interfaces and exchange standards create uncertainty and duplication for data publication and interoperability. The paper highlights that standards and implementations exist (e.g., SOS, WOF, SensorThings; WaterML variants), yet guidance on applicability is inconsistent. This complexity can push data producers toward one-off or commercial solutions and risks lock-in as standards evolve.
supporting_quote: Challenge 4: Multiple different web service interfaces and exchange standards.
multiple web service interfaces (SOS, WOF, SensorThings) and encodings for data exchange ... yet there is no consistent guidance on applicability

chunks.text: The authors conducted a literature review to identify HIS components and universal functionality, starting from known papers and expanding via reference lists and citation tracking. They also searched Google Scholar and Scopus with keywords including “hydrologic information systems,” “water data management,” and “hydroinformatics.” Inclusion prioritized systems where observational time series are a key supported data type, including conference proceedings but excluding presentation abstracts.
supporting_quote: we performed a review of relevant literature ... identified by reviewing reference lists and by tracking the citations
selected via Google Scholar and Scopus using relevant keywords: "hydrologic information systems", "water data management", and "hydroinformatics"

chunks.text: To supplement the literature, the authors gathered information from operational HIS implementations not formally described in research publications. They contacted representatives of water monitoring networks and included systems the authors have worked on, such as USGS NWIS. They constrained the scope to systems supporting fixed-location time series, acknowledging the paper is not comprehensive and is mostly U.S.-focused due to available literature and experience.
supporting_quote: We also sought to gather information from currently operational implementations of HIS not formally described in the research literature.
we limited the search to systems that support fixed location time series ... thus the discussion in this paper is mostly U.S. focused.

chunks.text: The paper synthesizes a generalized HIS architecture by extracting common functional components from reviewed literature. It organizes HIS into “data pools” (where data reside) and “data fluxes” (how data move between pools), and then describes each component’s functionality, implementation considerations, and challenges. This approach supports comparison across diverse systems even when individual publications focus on specific workflows or components.
supporting_quote: commonalities emerged in the functional components of HIS ... which we synthesize here as a generalized HIS and data workflow
We consider components to be either "data pools" in which data reside or "data fluxes" in which data are transferred.

chunks.text: For collection and acquisition, the paper distinguishes pull-based versus push-based data acquisition architectures. In pull-based architectures, a central system requests data from remote loggers and may cache files before loading to operational storage. In push-based architectures, remote nodes initiate transmission through a service interface (e.g., HTTP, MQTT), often supporting lower power use and event-based or real-time reporting.
supporting_quote: an important distinction is between pull- and push-based architectures
in push-based architectures ... remote data collection nodes initiate data transfer ... using standardized and open communication protocols like HTTP ... or ... MQTT

chunks.text: For operational storage, the paper treats information models as the basis for consistent representation of fixed-point time series and associated metadata. It highlights prominent models and standards used to implement storage and exchange, including ArcHydro Time Series, OGC Observations and Measurements (O&M), ODM/ODM2, and OGC SensorThings. The paper uses a conceptual model comparison (Figure 4) to show how core entities are represented across multiple models.
supporting_quote: software applications are generally based on a common information model that describes the data in the domain
Fig. 4. Conceptual information model for hydrologic time series data with entity names from the ArcHydro data model ... Observations Data Model (ODM) ... OGC O&M ... and OGC SensorThings

chunks.text: For publication and sharing, the paper describes standards-based web service interfaces and encodings used to transfer time series over the Internet. Examples include WaterOneFlow (WOF) and WaterML from the CUAHSI HIS effort, OGC Sensor Observation Service (SOS) with encodings using WaterML 2.0 or O&M, and RESTful APIs returning formats such as JSON. The paper emphasizes how consistent interfaces enable federated discovery and retrieval across distributed data providers.
supporting_quote: developed the WaterOneFlow (WOF) web service interface ... and Water Markup Language (WaterML)
SOS is a web service interface that allows querying observations that are then encoded for response using WaterML 2.0 or O&M

chunks.text: The paper’s scope is observational time series at fixed monitoring stations, including discharge, water quality, precipitation, and groundwater levels. It explicitly excludes several other data categories such as gridded data, remotely sensed data, grab sample results, and numerical model results. This scoping decision is used to keep the HIS component synthesis focused on a core and widely needed data type.
supporting_quote: focused on cyberinfrastructure to support time series of observational data at fixed monitoring stations (this includes discharge, water quality, precipitation, and groundwater levels
but does not include gridded data, remotely sensed data, grab sample results, or numerical model results

chunks.text: The literature search identified a publication trend: Scopus returned 65 documents containing the keyword “hydrologic information systems” dating back to 2004, and Figure 1 summarizes counts from 1980 to 2023. The paper interprets the increase around 2004–2014 and later decline as potentially reflecting a shift from research to operationalization and/or terminological changes that reduce “HIS” keyword usage.
supporting_quote: Scopus identified 65 documents (articles, conference abstracts, etc.) with the keyword "hydrologic information systems"
Fig. 1. Count of publications identified by Scopus with the keyword "hydrologic information systems" from 1980 to 2023.

chunks.text: Hydrologic time series are captured by sensors and stored on dataloggers, then transmitted to centralized systems using telemetry or manual transfer. The paper cites telemetry options such as satellite, radios, and cellular modems and notes that transfer intervals are user-defined. It also discusses acquisition from external sources via web-scraping and ingestion templates that include associated metadata.
supporting_quote: Data are stored on dataloggers ... transmitted to centralized systems at user-defined time intervals using automated telemetry (e.g., satellite, spread spectrum radios, cellular modems, etc.) or manually
Other HIS acquire time series data from external sources ... using web-scraping mechanisms such as source-specific templates

chunks.text: A generalized HIS can be represented as three major data pools with data fluxes between them: (1) collection and acquisition, (2) operational storage, and (3) publication/sharing/exchange. Data move from sensors/dataloggers to storage via “sensor-to-storage transfer,” and from storage to users via web interfaces or web services, often supported by catalogs. Management, curation, and processing run in parallel to these pools and may read and/or write data within the operational store.
supporting_quote: We identify the following major data pools in HIS ... Collection and Acquisition ... Operational Storage ... Publication, Sharing, and Exchange
Storage-tosharing transfer is enabled by web user interfaces or web services for automated retrieval and may be facilitated by data registries and catalogs.

chunks.text: The paper identifies core metadata concepts needed to interpret hydrologic time series and shows how information models encode them. In ODM, key characteristics include sites, variables, methods, sources, and quality control levels, tied to date and time for each observation. These concepts align with OGC O&M (feature of interest, observed property, observing procedure, observer), supporting interoperability across storage and exchange implementations.
supporting_quote: In ODM, the concepts of sites ... variables ... methods ... sources ... and quality control levels ... are the key metadata characteristics that define each observation, along with the associated date and time.
ODM's concepts parallel those of OGC's O&M, (feature of interest, observed property, observing procedure, and observer).

chunks.text: The paper consolidates examples showing that HIS acquisition is implemented via both pull-based and push-based architectures. Pull-based systems request and cache files and then load them (e.g., scheduled jobs), while push-based systems have remote nodes send observations via service interfaces (e.g., HTTP or MQTT). Push-based approaches are highlighted as useful for lower power operation and event-based or real-time monitoring needs.
supporting_quote: In pull-based architectures ... a central system initiates a request to the remote logger or device
Push-based systems can have lower power requirements ... especially important for systems requiring event-based or real time data

chunks.text: CUAHSI’s HIS is described as a federated system built around a community observations data model (ODM), standardized terminology, and web services for data transfer. Distributed sources registered with HIS Central, a metadata catalog enabling discovery and access across providers. Client applications (HydroDesktop and HydroClient) leveraged consistent metadata and the WOF interface to download and visualize time series regardless of where providers hosted services.
supporting_quote: CUAHSI designed and implemented a federated HIS
Distributed data sources registered their data with CUAHSI's HIS Central, which was a metadata catalog and source for data discovery and access

chunks.text: USGS NWIS is characterized as a foundational and exceptionally large operational HIS enabled by internet distribution of standardized access to hydrologic data. The paper notes NWIS as the world’s largest enterprise HIS by number of sites and data values and emphasizes its role as a milestone for public data accessibility. NWIS also demonstrates that operational HIS may combine vendor systems with agency authoritative databases and reference lists.
supporting_quote: NWIS remains the world's largest enterprise HIS (in terms of number of sites and data values
USGS NWIS ... uses a combination of in-house designed software applications and a commercial vendor data management system.

chunks.text: The paper describes standards and tools that support publication and exchange of hydrologic time series, including WOF/WaterML, OGC SWE components such as SOS and SensorML, and RESTful APIs. It shows that adopting common interfaces enables uniform retrieval across distributed sources and supports catalogs for discovery. However, it also notes that not all organizations can sustain local publishing services, motivating hosted or cloud options.
supporting_quote: developed the WaterOneFlow (WOF) web service interface ... and Water Markup Language (WaterML)
many organizations did not have the resources or personnel to run, manage, or sustain a publishing service on their local computer infrastructure

chunks.text: Data consumer functionality frequently centers on map-based site discovery and time series plot visualization, with download options and programmatic access. Examples include USGS’s National Water Dashboard and WHOS’s Water Data Explorer, both offering maps, metadata views, plots, and downloads. The paper also highlights language-specific client packages (R, Python, Julia) that retrieve data via web services for analysis workflows.
supporting_quote: deployed project-based web applications/ portals that included, at minimum, a map for displaying the locations of monitoring sites and a time series plot viewer
packages in common programming languages ... for accessing USGS NWIS data

chunks.text: Beyond operational portals, long-term archival is presented as an additional sharing pathway because operational stores and websites can be deprecated. The paper describes publishing time series as CSV snapshots to repositories such as HydroShare and ESS-DIVE and notes that repositories support versioning, persistent identifiers, and citation. These archival practices address needs that operational HIS (e.g., NWIS) may not fully support.
supporting_quote: Web portals and operational data stores may be deprecated after a project ends or technology ages
archived hydrologic time series by publishing snapshots with persistent identifiers in the ESS-DIVE repository

chunks.text: The review is explicitly not comprehensive and is constrained by available literature and the operational nature of many HIS that are not formally published. The authors emphasize that presentations often reflect development work but were excluded due to lack of detail, and that their discussion is mostly U.S.-focused. These factors limit the ability to fully characterize global HIS diversity and detailed operational practices across organizations.
supporting_quote: We acknowledge that the coverage of HIS by this paper is not comprehensive
we found more literature describing systems within the United States ... thus the discussion in this paper is mostly U.S. focused.

chunks.text: The paper argues that despite many standards and system efforts, no broadly maintained de facto HIS standard has emerged, and many existing technologies are aging. It suggests the decline in “HIS” publications may reflect research moving into operations and shifting terminology (e.g., IoT), which complicates discovery of relevant work. This fragmentation motivates renewed community R&D to modernize HIS.
supporting_quote: none of them has emerged as a de facto standard that is widely used and maintained by broad communities
Another possible confounding factor is that with newer technologies and approaches (e.g., IoT), the terminology used to describe systems may have changed

chunks.text: A limitation in advancing interoperability is that mapping existing storage models to newer exchange standards can be difficult and may lose information when standards are not expressive enough. The paper notes that SensorThings is generic and uses a small set of entities with extensible attributes, requiring careful mapping of hydrology-specific metadata. It also raises the issue that discovery metadata needs may differ from interpretive metadata needs, potentially introducing additional translations such as Schema.org.
supporting_quote: This mapping process can be challenging, and may, in some cases be lossy
the SensorThings information model is not hydrology specific and relies on a relatively small number of entities with a few attributes – some of which are extendable

chunks.text: Automation of QA/QC remains limited because data review can be subjective and dependent on local knowledge. While anomaly detection research exists, operational adoption at scale is constrained by false positives, technician burden, computational costs, and the lack of consistently labeled “gold standard” datasets. The paper suggests that even with improved algorithms, technician review may remain necessary in many cases.
supporting_quote: data processing and review can be subjective and often require local knowledge
concerns remain with high levels of false positives resulting in an extra burden on technicians reviewing data

chunks.text: The paper concludes that HIS comprise hardware and software supporting hydrologic data from field observation to dissemination, including storage, transfer, curation, processing, and publication. It reiterates that the key HIS components for fixed-point time series are collection/acquisition, operational storage, and publication/sharing/exchange, with parallel management and processing tasks. The authors emphasize that HIS design and ease of management can facilitate or inhibit downstream scientific analyses.
supporting_quote: HIS are comprised of hardware and software that support the life cycle of hydrologic data from observation in the field to end user dissemination
For fixed point time series data, the key components of HIS support data collection and acquisition; operational storage; publication, sharing, and exchange

chunks.text: The authors argue that advancing HIS requires coordinated community action to improve interoperability, reduce heterogeneity, and converge on modern standards and mappings. They propose that generic, manufacturer-agnostic communication (e.g., HTTP with a shared ingest/egress encoding) and community-endorsed vocabularies and mappings could enable more “plug and play” integration. They also call for guidance on standards, participation in standards bodies, and improved operationalization of QA/QC automation.
supporting_quote: Interoperability between sensing and datalogging systems and downstream HIS components could be advanced through generic communication solutions that are agnostic to the hardware manufacturer.
Community-endorsed mappings are also vital in overcoming the challenge of aligning information models for hydrologic time series data with those of broader, more generic exchange standards

chunks.text: The paper closes by emphasizing that many groups lack resources to deploy and sustain HIS and would benefit from robust suites of commercial and open tools built on community-endorsed standards. It suggests that releasing agency-developed HIS software and building consensus around vocabularies and exchange protocols could help address these needs. While challenges are substantial, the authors consider them solvable through concerted community efforts to advance next-generation HIS.
supporting_quote: Research groups, citizen science efforts, and small municipalities may not have the resources, expertise, or bandwidth to effectively deploy HIS and sustain them
we conclude that these hurdles, while substantial, are not insurmountable. With concerted community efforts, we are poised to advance the next generation of HIS

chunks.text: Hydrology and meteorology increasingly rely on multidimensional, georeferenced datasets from Earth observations and models. Data volumes are growing rapidly, making storage, indexing, access, and analysis difficult, especially when datasets are too large to transfer and process efficiently. Web services can reduce data-transfer overhead by enabling remote access and subsetting, but they typically require datasets to follow specific standards and conventions.
supporting_quote: Earth observations are in the form of spatiotemporal gridded data, spanning multiple dimensions in space and time.
Several obstacles arise with the management of these large quantities of data, including storing, indexing, accessing, distributing, downloading, visualizing, and analyzing.
Web services provide methods of interacting with remote data that eliminate data transfer overhead. However, to use many services, data must be formatted properly

chunks.text: NetCDF is a common format for storing gridded multidimensional data because it is self-describing, portable, and supports flexible data types and structures. However, netCDF itself does not impose naming or organizational rules, so datasets can vary widely. To improve interoperability, communities use conventions such as the CF conventions and ACDD to standardize metadata and describe dataset structure for software and discovery.
supporting_quote: One widely used data format is the network common data form (netCDF) file.
This file format is widely used and popular because it is selfdescribing... portable between different computers and operating systems
The netCDF model does not impose any restrictions on naming variables and dimensions... Consequently... nearly limitless flexibility
Two notable examples are the Attribute Conventions for Data Discovery (ACDD) and the Climate and Forecast Conventions (CF conventions).

chunks.text: THREDDS Data Server (TDS) supports serving gridded datasets like netCDF through multiple remote-access protocols including OPeNDAP and OGC services. For smaller organizations, TDS can simplify publishing data services, but success depends on properly formatted datasets. Compliance with CF/ACDD metadata enables TDS to interpret datasets and expose them reliably to tools and applications.
supporting_quote: A THREDDS data server (TDS) can provide remote data access protocols... including OPeNDAP, OGC Web Coverage Service (WCS), OGC Web Mapping Service (WMS)
For organizations, using a TDS greatly simplifies the process of creating a web server and setting up data web services.
the metadata is defined and formatted in such a way so that tools such as... THREDDS can extract the metadata from the dataset

chunks.text: The paper proposes an open-source Python package to help users create or update netCDF datasets with metadata that meets ACDD and CF conventions. The intent is to reduce the expertise required to implement complex conventions while producing datasets that can be served through TDS and accessed via OPeNDAP. The authors emphasize automating metadata generation where possible, and guiding users to fill in remaining required information.
supporting_quote: we propose to develop an open-source Python package that generates the metadata necessary to make a netCDF file compatible with the ACDD and the CF conventions.
The cfbuild python package is intended to be used to streamline the process of adding metadata.
The package must produce a dataset that is sufficiently compliant with the CF conventions to be compatible with a TDS and OPeNDAP.

chunks.text: A key goal is to generate an NcML representation that both documents dataset organization and injects needed metadata for compliance. The workflow is designed so users can manually modify metadata or configuration elements that cannot be inferred programmatically. The approach supports running on arbitrary netCDF files to inspect contents and help standardize outputs.
supporting_quote: The ability to generate a netCDF markup language (NcML) file that displays the organization of the data and that generates the metadata necessary to make the dataset compliant
The ability for the dataset creator to manually enter or modify any metadata or file configuration properties that cannot be auto-configured;
The package must run on any netCDF file and generate information about the contents of the file;

chunks.text: The initial package targets explicit convention versions to ensure predictable validation and interoperability. The authors specify support for CF conventions version 1.9 and ACDD version 1.3. They also aim for usability by people unfamiliar with these standards, making compliance achievable without deep knowledge of file formats and conventions.
supporting_quote: The initial version of the package must have support for the CF conventions version 1.9 and ACDD version 1.3;
The package must be usable by people unfamiliar with the ACDD and CF conventions;

chunks.text: CF and ACDD conventions are comprehensive but complex to implement correctly, leading to many netCDF datasets that are not usable across tools and services. The paper argues that the complexity makes it hard for non-experts to configure metadata and structure properly. When files do not meet requirements, the surrounding technology stack for big-data access and web services becomes unusable.
supporting_quote: the most common conventions are complex and difficult to implement correctly, resulting in datasets that are unusable for many applications due to a lack of compliance
With over 250 pages of suggestions, rules, and specifications in the CF documentation, fully understanding the CF conventions can be daunting.
If netCDF files do not meet certain requirements, all the technology built to solve the problems associated with big data are unusable.

chunks.text: Large data volumes create practical barriers to transferring and processing gridded datasets over the web. These challenges are especially acute in developing countries with limited computational and storage resources. The paper highlights that limited in situ data can increase reliance on remote/model data, so inability to manage and serve these datasets has disproportionate impacts.
supporting_quote: Dataset repositories, and sometimes individual datasets, often become so large that transferring over the web and processing the datasets becomes impractical
These big data problems are especially prominent in developing countries, which have less computational and storage capacity.
they often do not have the same availability of in situ data as more developed countries and rely more heavily on remotely collected or model-generated data

chunks.text: Interoperable web-service access (e.g., OPeNDAP, WMS/WCS via TDS) depends on strict dataset formatting and metadata requirements. Even when web services exist to avoid data transfer overhead, noncompliant datasets prevent those services from working effectively. This links metadata compliance directly to whether distributed access technologies can be used.
supporting_quote: Web services provide methods of interacting with remote data that eliminate data transfer overhead.
However, to use many services, data must be formatted properly to comply with requirements specific to the service used
If these three constructs are properly configured in the dataset, there is a high probability that the dataset will be compatible with services such as OPeNDAP and TDS.

chunks.text: For ACDD compliance, the authors emphasize meeting required global attributes and required attributes on each data variable. ACDD defines levels of recommended global metadata, and specifies highly recommended variable attributes, some of which overlap with CF requirements. The method therefore includes ensuring that datasets contain the convention-specified global attributes and that each data variable has the needed variable attributes.
supporting_quote: The ACDD lists three levels of global metadata: highly recommended, recommended, and suggested.
To be compliant with the ACDD, datasets must contain all the global attributes specified by the convention, and each data variable within the dataset must have the required variable attributes.

chunks.text: For CF compliance in georeferenced multidimensional datasets, the paper focuses on configuring three essential CF constructs: dimension coordinate, field, and coordinate reference constructs. Correctly configuring these constructs is presented as a practical proxy for achieving compatibility with TDS and OPeNDAP. The method centers on ensuring coordinate variables and CRS information are present and interpretable by software.
supporting_quote: Three of the constructs in the CF data model are essential to defining a georeferenced multidimensional dataset.
These constructs are the dimension coordinate construct, the field construct, and the coordinate reference construct.
If these three constructs are properly configured in the dataset, there is a high probability that the dataset will be compatible with services such as OPeNDAP and TDS.

chunks.text: The dimension coordinate construct requires coordinate variables that match dimension names, are one-dimensional, and vary monotonically. CF gives special handling to latitude, longitude, height, and time axes, requiring an axis attribute with values Y, X, Z, and T. The method therefore checks coordinate variable naming, dimensionality, monotonic behavior, and required axis metadata for spatiotemporal coordinates.
supporting_quote: A coordinate variable is required to have the same name as the dimension for which it contains the value.
The coordinate variable array holding the values is required to be one-dimensional and to increase or decrease monotonically.
Each variable representing one of these axes must have the axis attribute with the corresponding values Y, X, Z, or T.

chunks.text: Field constructs require data variables to be organized so software can infer dimension order for indexing. The CF guidance highlighted in the paper orders dimensions by time (T), height (Z), latitude (Y), and longitude (X), with other dimensions placed to the left. The method also expects standard_name, units consistent with canonical units, and range attributes such as valid_range and actual_range.
supporting_quote: the dimensions defining the shape of the data array should be ordered by time (T), height (Z), latitude (Y), and longitude (X)
every data variable should contain, including a standard_name attribute
a units attribute with a value equivalent to the conical units listed with the standard name
a valid_range attribute... and the actual_range attribute

chunks.text: Coordinate reference information can be implicit for WGS84-like lat/lon datasets, but CF also supports explicit grid-mapping variables for other coordinate reference systems. The paper recommends latitude spanning -90 to 90 and longitude -180 to 180 to avoid software issues with coordinate warping. When not using WGS84, the method uses a grid-mapping variable containing grid_mapping_name and additional CRS attributes required by CF.
supporting_quote: It is recommended that the values for latitude should span from -90 to 90, and longitude should span from -180 to 180
If the coordinate reference system used is not WGS84, grid-mapping variables can be used
Each grid-mapping variable must contain the grid_mapping_name attribute

chunks.text: To improve OPeNDAP and tool compatibility, the paper notes constraints on data types and names. OPeNDAP does not support 64-bit integers, so the method recommends avoiding int64. It also avoids reserved keywords for variable names, and notes that some tools require the time dimension and coordinate variable to be named exactly "time".
supporting_quote: OPeNDAP does not currently support 64-bit integers, and therefore it is recommended that this data type be avoided
there are several reserved keywords which should not be used as variable names
the time dimension and associated coordinate variable must be named time.

chunks.text: The cfbuild package workflow programmatically inspects a dataset, assigns metadata, exports an NcML representation, then regenerates a new netCDF file. The described process includes opening the file, sorting content into global attributes, dimensions, and variables, determining variable types, assigning metadata, writing NcML, reading modified NcML, and writing an updated dataset to a new netCDF file.
supporting_quote: The process followed by the cfbuild package in reading and creating a dataset is as follows:
Determine the variable types.
Write the data structure with the assigned metadata to an NcML file.
Create a new netCDF file.
Write the updated dataset to the new netCDF file.

chunks.text: cfbuild identifies CF variable roles using a combination of attribute-based rules and fallback heuristics. The package first checks CF-recognized identifiers (e.g., axis, coordinates, bounds, grid_mapping_name) summarized in a table. If those checks fail, it attempts identification using standard_name or units, dataset structure, or variable name; if still unknown, it records the issue for manual assignment later.
supporting_quote: The accepted methods of identifying variables according to the CF conventions are summarized in Table 1.
If the variable cannot be identified using the methods shown in Table 1, then the cfbuild package attempts to identify the variable type using the standard_name or units attributes
If the variable type cannot be determined, the fact is noted, and the type can be manually assigned later in the process.

chunks.text: Package testing used datasets collected while building the Met Data Explorer, including data from national meteorological and hydrological services such as ONAMET (Dominican Republic), SENAMHI (Peru), and INAMHI (Ecuador). The authors evaluated these datasets against ACDD v1.3 and CF conventions using online compliance checkers. Compliance was assessed based on errors, missing elements, and the importance of missing elements for human/machine readability.
supporting_quote: we evaluated datasets from a number of organizations including the Oficina Nacional de Meteorologia (ONAMET)... SENAMHI... the Instituto Nacional de Meteorología e Hidrología (INAMHI)
These datasets were tested against the ACDD, version 1.3, using the... PODAAC online convention checker
and against the CF conventions, version 1.8, using the... online CF conventions checker

chunks.text: A web-application test case used TDS-hosted datasets accessed through WMS and OPeNDAP. The application targets organizations producing custom WRF model outputs and provides visualization, animation, dataset inspection, and complex subsetting. Updated files produced with cfbuild were used to validate that the datasets could be hosted and served via these services.
supporting_quote: The Met Data Explorer interfaces with a TDS using WMS and OPeNDAP to display and animate multidimensional data as a web map
We created this application specifically for organizations such as INAMHI, SENAMHI, and ONAMET that produce custom Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) models
Using the Met Data Explorer, we were able to verify that files updated using the cfbuild package were able to be hosted on a TDS and served via OPeNDAP.

chunks.text: INAMHI’s case study data included WRF model outputs for two domains at 3 km resolution over 3 days, with roughly 18 meteorological variables. Example variables listed include temperature, precipitation, cloud cover, and precipitable water. Additional datasets visualized include CHIRPS, CHIRTS, and GFS (0.25° for 15 days), enabling comparisons and short-term forecasting workflows in a single portal.
supporting_quote: The first domain includes continental Equator and the Galapagos Islands with a spatial resolution of 3 km over 3 days.
The two domains include an average of 18 meteorological variables, some of which include temperature, precipitation, cloud cover, precipitable water
the Met Data Explorer is used to visualize and analyze... CHIRPS... CHIRTS... and... GFS... of 0.25◦ for 15 days.

chunks.text: After updating datasets with cfbuild and re-running the same online checkers, the authors observed a substantial increase in ACDD and CF compliance for the tested datasets. They report that, at least for simple datasets, required metadata can be generated and many attribute values can be derived from the dataset itself. The improvement is illustrated in a figure showing approximate compliance before and after.
supporting_quote: We updated the datasets shown in Figure 6 using the cfbuild Python package and checked compliance with ACDD and CF conventions using the same online compliance checkers
We observed a significant increase in compliance, as shown in Figure 6.
the results of our testing showed that, at least for simple datasets, the needed metadata can be generated

chunks.text: The Met Data Explorer served as an end-to-end validation that cfbuild-updated netCDF files work in operational web-service contexts. The authors confirmed that updated files could be hosted on THREDDS and accessed through OPeNDAP. This demonstrates that the package can help produce datasets that are practically usable for web visualization and subsetting workflows.
supporting_quote: Using the Met Data Explorer, we were able to verify that files updated using the cfbuild package were able to be hosted on a TDS and served via OPeNDAP.
The Met Data Explorer interfaces with a TDS using WMS and OPeNDAP

chunks.text: The paper reports deployments of the Met Data Explorer for multiple national hydrometeorological services, enabling them to access both self-produced and external multidimensional datasets through a unified interface. Instances are noted for INAMHI (Ecuador), INDRHI (Dominican Republic), and SENAMHI (Peru). This suggests that convention-compliant datasets (supported by cfbuild) can be operationalized across organizations and reused in a generalized client.
supporting_quote: we have installed instances of the web app on servers for different national hydrometeorological services, including INAMHI in Ecuador, INDRHI in the Dominican Republic, and SENAMHI in Peru
These organizations have effectively used the Met Data Explorer as a one-stop web interface for accessing multidimensional, georeferenced data

chunks.text: INAMHI’s example demonstrates practical use of compliant WRF outputs for visualization and extraction. The paper describes temperature fields behaving as expected (warmer coastal region, cooler highlands) and the ability to extract and download time series by selecting meteorological station points. It also highlights comparing variables across provinces (Imbabura vs. Guayas) to support climate-relevant analysis.
supporting_quote: In Figure 8a, the temperature is accurately visualized, being greater for the coastal region and lower for the highlands.
the data timeseries can be extracted and downloaded for further analysis by selecting one of the points representing a meteorological station
In Figure 8d, the temperatures from two separate provinces, Imbabura and Guayas, are compared

chunks.text: The authors scope the work to hydrological, multidimensional, georeferenced netCDF datasets and note that they tested on comparatively simple datasets. They state it is impossible to account for every configuration given the varied nature of hydrometeorological data, and expect the range of supported datasets to expand with further testing. They also limit testing to software most relevant to their use case, notably THREDDS and OPeNDAP.
supporting_quote: Due to the varied nature of meteorological and hydrological data, it is impossible to account for every configuration of a dataset.
The datasets which were used in testing the cfbuild Python package were comparatively simple datasets.
we have focused our testing on software that is most useful for our application, namely THREDDS and OPeNDAP.

chunks.text: cfbuild can parse basic structures and add many attributes, but it does not infer complex inter-variable relationships or sophisticated dataset structures. The paper emphasizes that certain attributes cannot be programmatically specified and require manual review and completion in the generated NcML. As a result, final dataset quality and full compliance remain partly dependent on the dataset creator’s competency and choices.
supporting_quote: There are many attributes that cannot be programmatically specified, with the result that the generated NcML file needs to be reviewed and completed manually.
It cannot determine inter-variable relations or complex dataset structures.
The quality of the dataset will always be somewhat reliant on human competency.

chunks.text: The authors acknowledge that variable-type identification is inherently difficult and sometimes impossible without sufficient information already present in the dataset. The package attempts multiple identification methods and records uncertainty when it cannot determine a type. In those cases, users must manually assign types, indicating a limitation of purely automatic compliance enforcement.
supporting_quote: Assigning the variable type is one of the most difficult parts of process, as it is impossible to determine the variable type if certain information is not present.
If the variable type cannot be determined, the fact is noted, and the type can be manually assigned later in the process.

chunks.text: The reported compliance improvements are described as partly subjective because compliance depends on which missing elements matter most for usability. Even after using checkers, the authors manually judged compliance based on error counts, missing elements, and their importance for readability. They also emphasize that the dataset creator determines the final structure and metadata, so results vary with human decisions.
supporting_quote: we manually evaluated the results and determined how compliant each dataset was based on the number or errors shown in the results, the number of mis-sing elements, and the importance of the missing elements
The results of this test are somewhat subjective
it is ultimately the dataset creator that determines the final structure of the dataset and the metadata included in the dataset.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that while ACDD and CF conventions are comprehensive and valuable, their complexity creates a barrier for many data producers. As multidimensional data generation grows, programmatic approaches to enforce compliance will become essential. The authors also argue that conventions should be written more simply and unambiguously to be accessible to people unfamiliar with the standards.
supporting_quote: ACDD and the CF conventions are examples of excellent standards for multidimensional data. They are well-defined and comprehensive.
Programmatic methods to enforce compliance with standards will become essential.
conventions need to be written simply and concisely, in an unambiguous method that is understandable by people unfamiliar with the conventions.

chunks.text: The work highlights that tools like THREDDS, OPeNDAP, and generalized clients (Met Data Explorer) become powerful when datasets are properly configured. INAMHI is presented as a case where validated and updated datasets can be hosted on TDS and accessed globally through a web interface. The authors position cfbuild as supporting organizations to keep datasets compliant so they remain usable across web services and applications.
supporting_quote: INAMHI can host its self-produced datasets on a TDS, which can then be accessed anywhere in the world using its customized instance of the Met Data Explorer.
The cfbuild Python package helps INAMHI validate and update its data, keeping its datasets compliant with the ACDD and CF conventions
This case study shows exactly why the cfbuild package was developed, to help organizations such as INAMHI format its data so that it can be used

chunks.text: AI methods are increasingly used in hydrology for tasks such as rainfall–runoff modeling, water quality forecasting, data augmentation, and climate/hydrologic forecasting. Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4 and BERT provide human-like language understanding and generation. Recent efforts fuse visual representations with language models to process complex visual information, enabling joint vision-language reasoning relevant to hydrological analyses and communication.
supporting_quote: Such methods are increasingly being applied in hydrology to solve various problems such as rainfall-runoff modeling [2,3], water quality forecasting using deep learning [4], data augmentation [5], and climate and hydrologic forecasting using AI [6].
Models like Mini-GPT-4 [9] and LLaVA [10] have emerged... explored the fusion of visual representations with the language model's input space

chunks.text: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) combine language processing with computer vision to support flood and hydrology workflows. They can analyze sensor reports and government sources while also interpreting satellite imagery to detect land-cover or water-level changes. These capabilities support real-time monitoring, contextual understanding, predictive analytics, and decision-support reporting for hydrological events.
supporting_quote: The application of LLMs and vision models in flood detection and hydrology involves leveraging advanced language processing and computer vision technologies
Combining LLMs with vision models allows for the real-time monitoring of hydrological conditions.

chunks.text: Vision-language systems are positioned as general-purpose assistants that span generation and vision-language understanding (VLU) tasks. VLU includes classification (image-to-text retrieval) and text-based image retrieval (TBIR) in a joint embedding space. This background motivates benchmarking MLLMs on hydrology-relevant recognition, description, and reasoning tasks that require aligning text prompts with images.
supporting_quote: Vision-language multimodal tasks are typically categorized into two groups: generation and vision-language understanding (VLU).
Text-based image retrieval is another critical aspect of VLU models. In this task, the model undergoes training in a joint embedding space that encompasses both images and text.

chunks.text: The study aims to explore synergies between hydrology and MLLMs by empirically assessing four models—Multimodal-GPT, LLaVA, GPT-4 Vision, and Gemini—on hydrology-specific multimodal tasks. The focus is on how well models interpret images paired with prompts in real-world scenarios (e.g., flood management). Performance is assessed by comparing responses for accuracy, relevance, and comprehension in hydrological contexts.
supporting_quote: This study aims to explore the synergies between hydrology and Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), examining the contributions of models like GPT-4, Gemini, LLaVA, and Multimodal-GPT
This study is designed to evaluate the application of MLLMs in hydrology, particularly for real-world scenario analysis such as flood management.

chunks.text: The work targets practical hydrological applications including flood management, water level monitoring, agricultural water discharge, and water pollution management. By designing prompts to improve visual inference and contextual comprehension, the study seeks to determine real-time suitability of these MLLMs for complex field conditions. The overarching objective is to inform responsible integration of multimodal AI into water resource decision-making.
supporting_quote: The study aims to enhance multimodal technologies to address various challenges related to flood management, water level monitoring, agricultural water discharge, and water pollution management.
Prompts were designed to enhance the models' visual inference capabilities and contextual comprehension from images.

chunks.text: Although MLLMs can generate strong multimodal responses, their outputs can be deceptive or incorrect, which is risky for hydrological decision-making. The paper highlights that responsible adoption requires balancing excitement about breakthroughs with realistic awareness of model limitations. This motivates systematic evaluation of hydrology-specific performance rather than assuming general multimodal ability transfers reliably.
supporting_quote: While promising, the responses generated by these models may occasionally be deceptive, incorrect, or false.
Balancing the enthusiasm for the potential breakthroughs with a realistic understanding of the model's limitations is essential

chunks.text: MLLMs face practical barriers that hinder dependable deployment in hydrology, including high computational demands, dependence on large/balanced multimodal datasets, challenges in generalization and interpretability, and high inference time that can limit real-time use. Ethical issues such as bias propagation and environmental costs (carbon footprint) are also noted. These constraints define the evaluation and deployment concerns addressed in the study.
supporting_quote: Firstly, their complexity and resource demands are substantial, requiring extensive computational power for training and fine-tuning.
the high inference time for processing both language and vision concurrently can limit real-time applicability. The environmental impact of their computational demands also deserves attention

chunks.text: The study uses an empirical benchmarking design to evaluate four MLLMs—Multimodal-GPT, LLaVA, GPT-4 Vision, and Gemini—on hydrological tasks. Models are compared on their ability to interpret hydrology-specific multimodal inputs consisting of an image plus a textual prompt. The workflow is described as benchmarking in hydrological tasks with standardized presentation of cases across models.
supporting_quote: The study involves an empirical assessment of four advanced MLLMs: Multimodal-GPT, LLaVA, GPT-4 Vision, and Gemini.
These models are evaluated based on their ability to interpret and generate responses from hydrology-specific multimodal data, involving both textual prompts and visual inputs

chunks.text: Model outputs are evaluated using three criteria: accuracy, relevance, and comprehension. Accuracy is assessed by comparing model responses to predefined correct answers or known truths about the scenario in the image. Relevance checks alignment with the prompt and hydrological context, and comprehension measures integration of both visual and textual elements into consistent responses.
supporting_quote: The model's response is then evaluated based on three key criteria: accuracy, relevance, and understanding.
Accuracy refers to the model's ability to provide accurate and precise information... comparing the responses generated by the model with previously defined correct answers or known truths

chunks.text: Input preparation combines an image depicting a hydrological scenario and a textual question framing a task (e.g., counting buildings or reading a gauge). Image preprocessing includes resizing, normalization, and conversion to model-compatible formats (often tensors). Text is tokenized into numerical IDs with special tokens, and inputs are combined per model requirements, either as separate image/text inputs or a single packed structure.
supporting_quote: The input for each MLLM consists of a visual element—an image depicting a hydrological scenario...—and a textual prompt that frames a question or a task
the image data undergo preprocessing steps such as resizing... normalization... conversion into a format compatible with the model's input requirements

chunks.text: The paper characterizes each evaluated model to contextualize expected strengths. Multimodal-GPT is described as built on OpenFlamingo with a vision encoder and gated cross-attention, fine-tuned with LoRA, and trained with a unified instruction template to support multimodal dialogue. These architectural notes are used to interpret performance differences during benchmarking.
supporting_quote: Multimodal-GPT utilizes a vision encoder to efficiently extract visual information and integrates a gated cross-attention layer for seamless interactions between images and text.
Fine-tuned from OpenFlamingo... incorporates a Low-Rank Adapter (LoRA)

chunks.text: LLaVA is described as integrating a CLIP-based vision encoder with a Vicuna-based language model, trained via “Visual Instruction Tuning” that includes alignment pretraining and end-to-end fine-tuning using instruction-following data. The paper notes that multimodal language-image instruction-following data are generated in two stages and that the model is refined for domain tasks like science QA, illustrating generalization ambitions relevant to hydrology prompts.
supporting_quote: LLaVA architecture combines CLIP-based vision encoders with Vicuna-based language model decoders
The core of LLaVA training lies in "Visual Instruction Tuning", comprising pretraining for feature alignment and end-to-end fine-tuning

chunks.text: Gemini is presented as a multimodal transformer designed to integrate text, audio, and visual inputs, optimized for specialized hardware like Google TPUs. The paper highlights very long context capability (up to 32,000 tokens) and modality-specific handling (e.g., videos as sequences of frames; audio at 16 kHz). These properties motivate considering Gemini for long-form hydrological data analysis and multimodal inputs beyond single images.
supporting_quote: Designed to efficiently run on specialized hardware like Google TPUs, Gemini models excel in processing various media content, including text, audio, and visual data.
With the capability to handle very long context lengths of up to 32,000 tokens

chunks.text: Evaluation inputs are hydrology-specific multimodal cases pairing images with prompts about the depicted scenario. Example tasks include assessing a flooded area, determining the number/condition of buildings, and interpreting water level or flow contexts. The intent is to approximate real-world hydrological analysis by grounding questions in visual evidence plus short task instructions.
supporting_quote: The input for each MLLM consists of a visual element—an image depicting a hydrological scenario, such as a flood event—and a textual prompt that frames a question or a task
the model may be presented with an image of a flooded area and asked to determine the number of buildings visible and assess their condition.

chunks.text: The paper specifies image sourcing and copyright compliance: most images are licensed from Adobe Stock, with an exception for one image taken by the authors. This sourcing note clarifies that evaluation uses curated, publication-safe visuals rather than proprietary operational feeds. It also indicates the image set is embedded in the manuscript rather than in an external dataset repository.
supporting_quote: Unless otherwise is noted, the images used in this study were sourced from Adobe Stock, a licensed platform providing high-quality visual content, except for the image input in Table 6, which was taken by the authors.
This study used readily available models and tested them on the images provided in the manuscript.

chunks.text: The empirical comparison is organized as a set of image-question pairs with model responses reported in Tables 2–9. These tables cover recognition (e.g., identifying a cornfield), situational description (flood severity), counting (people/buildings), and pollution indicators (dead fish, algal bloom). The structure supports side-by-side qualitative assessment across models for the same visual prompt.
supporting_quote: Tables 2–9 present the questions asked based on input images and the corresponding responses generated by multimodal LLMs, including LLaVA, GPT-4 Vision, Multimodal-GPT, and Gemini.
In evaluating hydrology-related image samples, recent MLLMs such as Multimodal-GPT, LLaVA, GPT-4Vision, and Gemini are utilized.

chunks.text: Across the hydrology image tasks, GPT-4 Vision is reported as the most consistent performer, leading on visual accuracy, relevance, and contextual understanding. The paper clarifies that “accuracy” is visual accuracy, such as correctly identifying and quantifying objects/people. Overall, GPT-4 Vision produced more detailed and contextually rich hydrology responses than LLaVA, Multimodal-GPT, and Gemini.
supporting_quote: The evaluation demonstrated that GPT-4 Vision consistently outperformed the other models in terms of accuracy, relevance, and contextual understanding.
'accuracy' refers specifically to 'visual accuracy'—the ability of the model to correctly identify and quantify visual elements within an image

chunks.text: In crop-condition recognition, GPT-4 Vision correctly identifies the scene as a drought-impacted corn (maize) field and explains visual evidence such as cracked soil and withered plants. Other models also identify corn but vary in specificity and add unsupported location details. This example is used to illustrate GPT-4 Vision’s stronger hydrology-relevant visual interpretation.
supporting_quote: GPT-4 Vision: This is a corn (maize) field. However, it appears to be suffering from severe drought, as the soil is cracked and the corn plants are withered and brown
Table 2. Example of image-based recognition and response generation of MLLMs. GPT-4 Vision accurately identifies the crop as cornfield and assesses its condition.

chunks.text: For building damage assessment in a flood-related image, GPT-4 Vision provides a nuanced count separating severely damaged foreground buildings from intact background buildings. Competing models give conflicting counts and damage descriptions (e.g., “two buildings,” “three buildings,” “eight buildings” all severely damaged). The contrast demonstrates variability in visual quantification and condition assessment across MLLMs.
supporting_quote: GPT-4 Vision: In the foreground, there are two notably damaged buildings... In the background, there are at least five other buildings visible. These buildings appear to be intact
Gemini: There are eight buildings visible in the picture. All of them are severely damaged.

chunks.text: In flood-scene description and severity characterization, GPT-4 Vision produces the most detailed narrative, noting widespread inundation, depth, infrastructure damage, and the need for emergency response while acknowledging that precise severity needs on-the-ground assessment. Other models produce shorter descriptions with fewer contextual qualifiers. This supports the paper’s claim that GPT-4 Vision yields richer, more actionable situational understanding from images.
supporting_quote: GPT-4 Vision: The image depicts a severe flooding event affecting a residential area... it is clear that there is substantial inundation which would require emergency response efforts
LLaVA: The image shows a flooded neighborhood with houses and streets submerged in water.

chunks.text: For a safety-critical prompt (“This is happening in front of me. What should I do?”) with a tornado image, GPT-4 Vision and LLaVA both generate actionable sheltering guidance, while Multimodal-GPT outputs a generic definition of tornadoes. This qualitative difference highlights that some models may fail to follow instruction intent even when recognizing the hazard type. Such behavior affects usefulness for real-time emergency assistance.
supporting_quote: GPT-4 Vision: The image appears to show a tornado... Seek Shelter Immediately... Go to a pre-designated shelter area
Multimodal-GPT: A tornado is a violently rotating column of air that is in contact with both the surface of the Earth and a cumulonimbus cloud

chunks.text: In estimating water discharge from an image, GPT-4 Vision explicitly refuses to infer a cfs value from imagery alone and points to the need for on-site measurements or monitoring data. LLaVA similarly states it cannot determine the exact discharge without more information. In contrast, Multimodal-GPT and Gemini provide specific numeric values (“1000”, “900 cfs”) that the paper describes as arbitrary, illustrating hallucination risk in quantitative hydrology.
supporting_quote: GPT-4 Vision: I’m unable to determine specific quantitative data such as the water discharge rate in cubic feet per second (cfs) from an image alone.
Multimodal-GPT: The value of the water discharge in the image in cfs is 1000
Gemini: 900 cfs.

chunks.text: For counting people in an image, Gemini returns “6 people,” while GPT-4 Vision and LLaVA return “five people,” and Multimodal-GPT does not provide a numeric count. The table note states Gemini is more accurate than other models on this example. The result indicates that model leadership can vary by task type, particularly for counting.
supporting_quote: Gemini: There are 6 people in the image.
Table 7. Example of image-based recognition and analytics using MLLMs. Gemini demonstrates more accurate recognition of the number compared to other Multimodal LLMs.

chunks.text: In a water-quality image showing dead fish, GPT-4 Vision identifies a fish-kill event and suggests likely causes such as pollution or low oxygen, citing murky water, algae/debris, and litter on the shore. LLaVA provides a cautious description with multiple possible explanations but less direct inference. Multimodal-GPT misinterprets the scene as fish swimming, showing a failure mode in environmental hazard recognition.
supporting_quote: GPT-4 Vision: multiple dead fish floating... possibly related to pollution or a lack of oxygen in the water... There's also some litter visible on the shore
Multimodal-GPT: Aquatic life in the pond. The fish are swimming in the pond.

chunks.text: For algal bloom recognition, GPT-4 Vision provides an extended explanation of nutrient-driven blooms, visible surface scum, and contributing sunny conditions, while Gemini asserts a specific algae type (“Enteromorpha”) and Multimodal-GPT makes an unsupported claim about Lake Okeechobee being “the largest in recorded history.” The example is used to show GPT-4 Vision’s more grounded, descriptive output and other models’ tendency to over-specify without evidence.
supporting_quote: GPT-4 Vision: The image shows a coastal landscape where an algal bloom is apparent... excess nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen
Multimodal-GPT: The algae bloom in Lake Okeechobee, Florida, is the largest in recorded history.
Gemini: The specific type of algae appears to be Enteromorpha, also known as sea lettuce.

chunks.text: The paper outlines broad limitations of MLLMs that affect hydrology deployment: heavy compute and resource needs, reliance on large and unbiased multimodal datasets, limited generalization, and difficulties interpreting internal representations, reducing transparency. It also notes contextual understanding issues, adversarial vulnerability, and high inference time that can hinder real-time use. Ethical concerns include bias propagation and environmental impacts from compute demands.
supporting_quote: their complexity and resource demands are substantial, requiring extensive computational power
Interpreting the representations generated by MLLMs is another challenge... hindering transparency in decision-making processes.
Robustness against adversarial attacks is an ongoing challenge, and the high inference time... can limit real-time applicability.

chunks.text: A task-specific limitation observed in results is that some models generate arbitrary quantitative outputs from images when the value cannot be visually determined, which is dangerous for hydrological inference. In the discharge example, GPT-4 Vision and LLaVA refuse to guess, but Multimodal-GPT and Gemini provide specific cfs values without measurement context. The paper uses this pattern to argue that further refinement is needed for reliable response generation in operational settings.
supporting_quote: Multimodal-GPT and Gemini provide arbitrary water discharge values in their responses, whereas LLaVA and GPT-4 Vision offer more realistic and contextually appropriate responses.
Multimodal-GPT: The value of the water discharge in the image in cfs is 1000
Gemini: 900 cfs.

chunks.text: The study concludes that MLLMs can meaningfully contribute to hydrological decision-making, especially for flood detection and management, by interpreting hydrology-specific multimodal inputs in near real time. It frames the evaluation of Multimodal-GPT, GPT-4 Vision, Gemini, and LLaVA as a foundation for building intelligent flood monitoring and response systems. The conclusion emphasizes integrating these capabilities into operational water resource management to address complex hydrological challenges.
supporting_quote: The potential impact of this study on flood detection and management is significant.
The findings from our evaluation of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in hydrological tasks

chunks.text: The paper proposes actionable strategies for policy and management based on the evaluated capabilities: integrating models like GPT-4 Vision into early warning systems for flood risk management, continuous monitoring for water quality enforcement, and guiding sustainable water usage by predicting availability and demand. It also recommends collaborations between AI researchers and hydrological agencies to build tailored decision-support systems. These recommendations are positioned as near-term steps toward data-driven governance in water systems.
supporting_quote: Flood Risk Management: The advanced predictive capabilities of models like GPT-4 Vision can be integrated into national and regional early warning systems.
Water Quality Monitoring: MLLMs can be employed to monitor water bodies continuously, detecting pollution levels with high accuracy.
Governments should consider establishing collaborations between AI researchers and hydrological agencies to develop tailored MLLM applications

chunks.text: Future work directions include developing MLLM-based systems that generate realistic flood scenarios from text descriptions and deeper integration into decision-support systems combining textual and visual inputs. The paper also calls for research on mitigating biases, improving interpretability, strengthening robustness against adversarial attacks, and reducing carbon footprints by optimizing computational resources. These priorities aim to enable responsible and sustainable deployment of MLLMs in hydrology.
supporting_quote: future research... could focus... development of MLLM-based systems for generating realistic flood scenarios based on textual descriptions.
Research on mitigating biases, improving interpretability, and enhancing robustness against adversarial attacks would be valuable
investigating methods to optimize computational resources and reduce carbon footprints associated with MLLMs would be crucial

chunks.text: Urban watersheds with high imperviousness and intensifying extreme rainfall are highly susceptible to flooding, creating major economic and societal impacts. For densely populated regions, decision support systems that forecast flooding impacts are critical for preparedness and response. The Hackensack River watershed in the NYC metropolitan area has repeatedly experienced severe events, including Hurricanes Irene (2011) and Sandy (2012).
supporting_quote: Urban watersheds especially those with a high impervious percentage... are highly susceptible to urban fooding.

The Hackensack River watershed... is densely populated and food-prone... impacted by several extreme weather events, including hurricanes like Hurricanes Irene and Sandy, in 2011 and 2012, respectively.

chunks.text: The operational Stevens Flood Advisory System (SFAS) provides flood forecasts for the NYC metropolitan area by integrating coastal and inland hydrology components. Its inland hydrology relies on a lumped HEC-HMS model calibrated over a larger region and used to force hydraulic/coastal models. The study positions WRF-Hydro as a candidate replacement to improve spatially distributed simulation capabilities.
supporting_quote: Stevens Institute of Technology developed the Stevens Flood Advisory System (SFAS) specifcally for operational food inundation mapping in the New York City metropolitan area.
The inland hydrology component of the SFAS system relies on a lumped hydrological model, namely, the Hydrologic Engineering Center's Hydrologic Modeling System (HEC-HMS) ... to simulate streamfow.

chunks.text: Gridded hydrologic-hydraulic models like WRF-Hydro enable simulation of the spatial distribution of processes needed for small-scale flood impact assessment. Prior studies have applied WRF-Hydro for flash floods and urban flooding sensitivity to resolution. This study leverages that capability for block-scale inundation in a regulated urban watershed.
supporting_quote: The advent of gridded models like... WRF-Hydro... has certainly helped in the development of models that can simulate the spatial distribution of the hydrologic and hydraulic processes within the watershed.
The novelty of this study consists of simulating hyper-resolution food inundation in an urban environment with a controlled reservoir using WRF-Hydro.

chunks.text: The study aims to assess a high-resolution, gridded WRF-Hydro configuration for simulating streamflow and street/block-scale flood inundation in the Hackensack River watershed. A key objective is evaluating whether it can be integrated into the operational SFAS system, which currently uses HEC-HMS. Hurricane Irene (August 2011) is used as the main validation event, with comparisons to observations, HEC-HMS outputs, and crowdsourced inundation evidence.
supporting_quote: The goal of this study is to assess a new gridded WRF-Hydro-based model that simulates streamfow and food inundation in the Hackensack River Watershed in New Jersey.
The model is a candidate for deployment in the operational Stevens Flood Advisory System.
The case study is selected as Hurricane Irene which was recorded in August 2011.

chunks.text: The work specifically targets block-scale routing detail by configuring WRF-Hydro with 50 m channel routing and 200 m land-surface modeling, expecting improvements over the lumped hydrologic component used by SFAS. The evaluation is designed to measure both hydrologic performance (streamflow) and hydraulic outcomes (inundation depth/extent).
supporting_quote: The proposed WRF-Hydro model features a block-scale resolution of 50 m for the channel routing scheme and 200 m for the surface overland routing scheme.
The model is expected to ofer an improvement over the existing hydrologic component in the SFAS system which is a novel contribution

chunks.text: Lumped and data-driven models are limited for distributed flood inundation prediction because they do not represent spatial heterogeneity of hydrologic processes. They are typically calibrated or trained for streamflow at specific points, making it difficult to identify which blocks or intersections are most impacted. This limits their usefulness for targeted interventions and evacuation planning during extreme events in complex urban watersheds.
supporting_quote: The limitation of lumped and data-driven models consists of their non-suitability for the simulation of distributed food inundation within the watershed.
Both model categories are unable to simulate the spatial distribution of the hydrologic response in the watershed.

chunks.text: In WRF-Hydro’s channel routing, backwater effects for overbank flow from channels onto terrain are not represented, requiring a postprocessing approach for riverine inundation. This motivates the use of the HAND method and stage derivation from synthetic rating curves, but adds uncertainty in converting streamflow to flood depth and extent.
supporting_quote: However, the backwater efect accounting for the overbank fow from the channel to the terrain cannot be computed in the existing channel routing scheme.

A postprocessing step is needed to convert the volume of the overbank food into inundation maps... However, this step might introduce additional errors due to the synthetic rating curves (SRCs) utilized to convert streamfow to stage value

chunks.text: The study uses WRF-Hydro v5.1.1 in one-way coupled mode with Noah-MP as the land surface model at 200 m resolution and routing at higher resolution. The 200 m grids are disaggregated to 50 m for overland and channel routing, then aggregated back after routing. Routing uses a diffusive-wave formulation for both overland and channel flow.
supporting_quote: WRF-Hydro version 5.1.1
The proposed WRF-Hydro model features... 50 m for the channel routing scheme and 200 m for the surface overland routing scheme.
Diffusive wave formulation is adopted for the overland and channel flow routing schemes

chunks.text: Riverine inundation depth and extent are computed using the HAND method because channel routing does not compute overbank hydraulics. HAND layers were produced from a USGS 10 m DEM interpolated to 50 m. Streamflow outputs are converted to stage using CONUS-wide Synthetic Rating Curves (SRCs) for NWM reaches, and peak stages are used with HAND to create inundation maps.
supporting_quote: Therefore, to account for the riverine fooding over terrain, the Height Above the Nearest Drainage (HAND) method is adopted for the inundation depth and extent calculations.
HAND layers are calculated based on the USGS 10-m DEM which is interpolated to the 50-m resolution
River stage values... are generated by using Synthetic Rating Curves (SRC) defned CONUS-wide for each National Water Model (NWM) reach.

chunks.text: Reservoirs are explicitly represented in WRF-Hydro for three major water bodies (Lake Oradell, Lake Tappan, Lake DeForest). For each reservoir, weir and orifice structures are defined and routed using a simple level-pool scheme. This supports modeling of regulated flows that influence downstream flood response in the Hackensack watershed.
supporting_quote: Three major reservoirs (Lake Oradell, Lake Tappan, and Lake DeForest) in the study area are defned in the model.
For each reservoir, both weir and orifce structures are defned, and the outfow calculations are performed based on the simple level pool routing scheme

chunks.text: Model performance for hydrographs is quantified using RMSE, NSE, KGE, correlation, and PBias at an hourly time step. Water level comparisons against surveyed high-water marks use PBias, RMSE, and MAE. Inundation extent is compared via peak water depth and resulting inundated surface area.
supporting_quote: Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Nash–Sutclife Efciency (NSE), and Kling-Gupta Efciency (KGE)
These metrics are calculated based on the hourly time step same as the model time step.
Mean Absolute Error (MAE) is calculated to see the average residual for the evaluation of the simulated water level compared to the USGS HWMs

chunks.text: Calibration uses a two-stage Dynamically Dimensioned Search (DDS) procedure with 200 iterations per stage, first optimizing KGE then RMSE. Parameters target both hydrograph volume and timing/shape, including REFKDT, RETDEPRTFAC, SLOPE, OVROUGHRTFAC, MANN, and LKSATFAC. Calibration is performed at the downstream New Milford station due to the algorithm’s single-station configuration.
supporting_quote: It was determined that the combination of KGE-RMSE is the one that leads to the best agreement between observed and simulated streamfow.
running a frst two-hundred-iteration calibration with the KGE objective function... a second calibration stage with the same number of iterations utilizing the RMSE
The calibration was performed using streamfow observations at New Milford station... The confguration of the used DDS algorithm allows for the consideration of one single station.

chunks.text: The modeling domain is the Hackensack River watershed portion upstream of the tidally influenced reach, excluding the area downstream of New Millbrook station. The studied drainage area is about 294 km² and includes steep terrain in the northwest and developed/deciduous forest land cover. The watershed contains critical reservoirs supplying drinking water to over 1 million residents.
supporting_quote: the part of the watershed downstream of New Millbrook station was excluded from the studied domain
The drainage area of the studied part of the basin is around 294 km2
Over 1 million residents... receive~120 million gallons of drinking water every day from the reservoirs within the watershed

chunks.text: Hurricane Irene (August 2011) is the main validation event; rainfall totals in the basins ranged from 6.5 to 8.6 inches and antecedent wet conditions increased flood severity. Cumulative precipitation over the Hackensack basin from NLDAS-2 during a 25 h window varied between 188 and 214 mm, with higher amounts on the western side affecting tributaries like Pascack Brook.
supporting_quote: The total precipitation records range from 6.5 to 8.6 inches in the Passaic and Hackensack River Basins.
The cumulative precipitation varies between 188 and 214 mm (7.4–8.4 inches) over 25 h.
tributaries like the Pascack Brook (USGS station 01377500) that drains the western part of the watershed

chunks.text: Meteorological forcing comes from NLDAS-2, with precipitation and other atmospheric variables downloaded and bilinearly downscaled from 0.125° to 200 m to match the Noah-MP land surface grid. Terrain/routing parameters at 50 m are derived using the WRF-Hydro preprocessing toolbox from a USGS 1/3 arc-second (10 m) DEM. Land cover uses MODIS IGBP (500 m) and soils use STATSGO (1 km).
supporting_quote: The NLDAS-2 dataset is utilized as the forcing dataset
downscaled from 0.125°×0.125° to a 200-m resolution using the bilinear interpolation technique
generated based on the USGS 1/3 arc-second (10-m) Digital Elevation Model (DEM)
MODIS... landcover product with 500-m spatial resolution... soil classifcations are produced from the 1-km STATSGO database.

chunks.text: Streamflow evaluation uses multiple USGS gauges: West Nyack (01376800), Rivervale (01377000), Pascack Brook at Westwood (01375000), and New Milford (01378500).
