Water depth evaluation uses surveyed USGS high water marks, and qualitative inundation assessment uses manually geotagged photos from local media and residents compared to WRF-Hydro surface head outputs on Google Earth.
supporting_quote: USGS stations... West Nyack NY (01376800)... Rivervale NJ (01377000)... Pascack Brook at Westwood NJ (01375000)... New Milford NJ (01378500)
evaluated using surveyed USGS high water mark (HWM) data
pictures released in local media... were geotagged manually... overlaid on the Google Earth 3D map layer

chunks.text: Calibration materially changed key hydrologic and routing parameters relative to defaults to improve hydrograph fit. REFKDT increased from 3.0 to 4.68 and RETDEPRTFAC increased from 1.0 to 7.14, while OVROUGHRTFAC decreased to 0.42 and channel MannN decreased to 0.90 to reduce lag and accelerate routing. LKSATFAC dropped from 1000 to 220.42, slowing lateral subsurface movement.
supporting_quote: After the calibration the REFKDT value was increased from 3 to 4.68
RETDEPRTFAC increased from 1.0 to 7.1 mm
Both OVROUGHRTFAC and MannN are decreased to 0.4 and 0.9, respectively
reduced... LKSATFAC from 1000 to ~220 (Table 2).

chunks.text: For Hurricane Irene validation at New Milford, calibrated WRF-Hydro improved hydrograph agreement versus default settings. RMSE decreased from 37.95 to 31.53, NSE rose from 0.76 to 0.84, and KGE rose from 0.71 to 0.82; correlation remained 0.93. PBias decreased from 22.01% to 16.81%, indicating reduced volume overestimation.
supporting_quote: WRF-Hydro-default... Corr 0.93... PBias 22.01... RMSE 37.95... KGE 0.71... NSE 0.76
WRF-Hydro-validation... Corr 0.93... PBias 16.81... RMSE 31.53... KGE 0.82... NSE 0.84

chunks.text: Compared to the operational HEC-HMS run forced with the same NLDAS-2 data, WRF-Hydro performed substantially better at New Milford during Hurricane Irene. HEC-HMS showed lower correlation (0.72) and much worse overall fit (RMSE 61.86, NSE 0.38, KGE 0.36). HEC-HMS also had strong negative bias (PBias −32.47%), indicating systematic underestimation after the rising limb.
supporting_quote: HEC-HMS... Corr 0.72 | PBias -32.47 | RMSE 61.86 | KGE 0.36 | NSE 0.38
Figure 4 shows an underestimation of streamfow at New Milford with HEC-HMS.

chunks.text: Peak flow magnitude at New Milford was reduced by calibration, moving closer to observations while preserving peak timing. The reported peak flow decreased from 382 to 349 m3/s after calibration. Both default and calibrated versions showed underestimation of baseflow before the event, but the discrepancy was considered small relative to event peaks (~300 m3/s).
supporting_quote: The value of the peak fow was reduced from 382 to 349 m3 /s.
both configurations led to an underestimation of the baseflow prior to Hurricane Irene... discrepancy is in the order of 10 m³/s... event streamfow... in the order of 300 m³/s.

chunks.text: Eight USGS high-water marks (HWMs) in the southern watershed were compared against WRF-Hydro-derived water levels inferred via SRCs and HAND. Agreement was good overall: PBias about 4%, RMSE 0.8 m, and MAE 0.78 m. The study notes that proximity of HWM points to the river and floodplain may contribute to the apparent agreement.
supporting_quote: USGS reported eight HWMs
The PBias was limited to 4%, the RMSE was equal to 0.8 m, and the MAE was 0.78 m.

chunks.text: Inundation extent comparisons showed both over- and under-estimation depending on sub-catchment and station. For station 01377000, WRF-Hydro peak depth (6.56 m) exceeded USGS-based peak depth (3.74 m) and produced about double inundated area (1410 vs 747.5 ×10^3 m2). For station 01377500, WRF-Hydro peak depth (1.58 m) was below USGS (2.65 m) and inundated area was smaller (377.5 vs 502.5 ×10^3 m2).
supporting_quote: 01377000... Peak water depth (m) 3.74... Surface area (103 m2) 747.5... WRF-Hydro... 6.56... 1410
01377500... Peak water depth (m) 2.65... Surface area (103 m2) 502.5... WRF-Hydro... 1.58... 377.5

chunks.text: Crowdsourced photo evidence for Storm Ida showed WRF-Hydro can identify flooded locations but may misestimate depth locally. At Harding Avenue in Westwood, an inferred depth of ~365 mm from fence height contrasted with ~60 mm modeled surface head. At Ruckner Rd, a reported 6.4 inches (~163 mm) compared reasonably with modeled 193 mm (~7.6 inches).
supporting_quote: backyard... was fooded up to 1/5 of the height of the fences... This water depth corresponds to~365 mm.
WRF-Hydro... show that the same location is inundated with a water depth of around 60 mm.
Ruckner Rd... water level reached up to 6.4 inches (~163 mm)... WRF-Hydro... water depth of 193 mm (~7.6 inches)

chunks.text: Qualitative comparison using a Hurricane Irene image from Nanuet, NY indicated WRF-Hydro approximated shallow inundation depths visible in media photos. The photo-based estimate suggested 1–2 inches of water near a vehicle tire, while the corresponding WRF-Hydro map indicated about one inch or lower. The authors note that many images are not time-stamped, which may affect alignment with modeled peak conditions.
supporting_quote: image taken at a marketplace in Nanuet, NY, after Hurricane Irene
water depth... is between 1 and 2 inches... At the same location... WRF-Hydro map reports a water depth in the order of one inch or lower.
most of them are not time-stamped, which may introduce a discrepancy

chunks.text: Higher-resolution WRF-Hydro configurations (targeting ~10 m) were tested but were unstable despite timestep adjustments. The authors attribute instability to steep topographic gradients within the watershed and to cascading lakes/reservoirs. They also note that real reservoir bypass behaviors during overtopping are not represented because the model only includes orifice and weir structures.
supporting_quote: it is desirable to generate urban food inundation maps at higher resolution in the order of 10 m.
The simulations at higher resolution led to a signifcant instability of the model
This could be attributed to the topographic gradient in the Hackensack watershed
bypasses that divert the water... still not possible to capture... limited to the modeling of the orifce and weir

chunks.text: Reservoir operation representation in WRF-Hydro is comparatively basic and can increase uncertainty in regulated systems like Hackensack, where multiple reservoirs cascade discharge toward New Milford. The paper contrasts this with richer HEC-HMS options (e.g., storage-discharge, elevation-area relationships). The simplicity can propagate errors downstream and complicate calibration.
supporting_quote: The modeling of lakes and reservoirs in WRF-Hydro is somehow basic, unlike the modeling options that are available in HEC-HMS
the Hackensack watershed comprises a set of reservoirs that cascade the discharge towards the basin outlet at the New Milford station and so does the error in the simulation of reservoir releases.

chunks.text: WRF-Hydro does not include key urban infrastructure (levees, pumping stations, minor drainage networks, conduits) that can shape inundation in cities. The model also lacks two-way coupling between overland routing and overbank flooding, so overbank volumes are handled for mass conservation but do not hydraulically influence overland routing. Consequently, inundation mapping relies on postprocessing (e.g., HAND) that can introduce additional errors.
supporting_quote: While WRF-Hydro considers the urban land cover characteristics... it does not account for the impact of urban infrastructures like levees, pumping stations, minor drainage networks, or conduits.
there is no two-way coupling between overland fow and overbank fooding... A postprocessing step is needed... such as the Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) method

chunks.text: Aggregation of high-resolution topography to the 50 m routing grid can remove crucial urban details (street gutters, building obstructions) needed for realistic surface flow paths. The authors suggest refining DEMs by exaggerating building footprints to better represent drainage networks and obstructions. This is presented as important for assessing infrastructure-level impacts in urban environments.
supporting_quote: a signifcant part of the topographic details is lost when aggregating the information to match the overland fow grid scale (50-m in this study).
Future work should consider refning the DEM by exaggerating the building footprint to achieve a better-defned surface fow drainage network

chunks.text: Calibration was limited by the DDS implementation that only supports a single station, so parameters optimized for New Milford apply uniformly across the watershed. The authors note that multi-station, sub-watershed parameter calibration could reduce uncertainty caused by enforcing parameter homogeneity. They also highlight that inferring reservoir management rules from only downstream streamflow is not straightforward and may require multi-year upstream/downstream data.
supporting_quote: The confguration of the used DDS algorithm allows for the consideration of one single station. The adjusted parameters resulting from the calibration will apply to the entire watershed.
the inference of reservoir management rules through the calibration process... is not straightforward.
Future versions of the algorithm with the capability of including several stations and generating diferent parameter sets for diferent subwatersheds

chunks.text: A gridded WRF-Hydro configuration (200 m LSM, 50 m routing) was deployed for the Hackensack River watershed and validated for Hurricane Irene. The calibrated model improved agreement with observed streamflow and outperformed the HEC-HMS configuration used in SFAS for this event comparison. However, both default and calibrated runs showed limitations in representing baseflow and flood extents could be larger or smaller than USGS-inferred extents, partly due to synthetic rating curves and model structure.
supporting_quote: The model was confgured... land surface model has a 200-m resolution and the routing model for surface and channel has a 50-m resolution.
the calibrated version of the WRF-Hydro model led to a stronger agreement with the observed streamfow.
The food extents simulated with WRF-Hydro were either larger or smaller... attributed to the use of synthetic rating curves

chunks.text: USGS high water marks indicated that WRF-Hydro could reproduce maximum water depths reasonably well for the evaluated points, supporting its utility for inundation analysis in this watershed. The paper emphasizes the need for improved online inundation simulation and more reliable rating curves to reduce dependence on offline postprocessing. This is framed as a key direction for enabling operational integration.
supporting_quote: High Water Marks... showed that the model accurately simulated the water depth.

Future work should focus on enhancing WRF-Hydro capabilities to simulate food inundation online with more reliable rating curves without the need to infer food inundation ofine as a postprocessing step.

chunks.text: Overall findings support WRF-Hydro as a suitable candidate for eventual integration into SFAS to replace lumped HEC-HMS, primarily due to improved streamflow performance and the ability to produce 50 m overland flow detail for spatial inundation mapping. The study underscores that additional advances—especially better calibration across multiple gauges and improved representation of regulated systems—would further strengthen operational readiness.
supporting_quote: makes WRF-Hydro a suitable candidate for an eventual integration in the SFAS system to replace the lumped HEC-HMS model.
WRF-Hydro with its gridded confguration... can simulate at the 50-m pixel level overland fow which allows it to capture the spatial distribution of food inundation.
a more advanced calibration procedure that accounts for all existing USGS stations within the watershed remains necessary

chunks.text: The National Water Model (NWM) is an operational continental-scale system for hourly streamflow prediction across the United States, built on WRF-Hydro and the Noah-MP land surface model (LSM) with routing modules. Its design emphasizes physics-rich simulation and modular options, but the operational configuration is a single, complex setup spanning multiple spatial and temporal scales. This motivates exploring alternative architectures that can be more flexible and easier to modify for local applications while still leveraging LSM strengths.
supporting_quote: The National Water Model (NWM) is an operational system that provides hourly streamflow predictions for over 12.8 million km of streams and rivers in the Continental United States

The current version of NWM is based on the Weather Research and Forecasting Hydrologic model (WRF-Hydro) v5.1.2 ... which couples land surface model (LSM; Noah-Multi Parameterization [MP]) and routing modules

chunks.text: TOPMODEL is a watershed-scale conceptual model that uses terrain-derived Topographic Wetness Index (TWI) to represent hydrological similarity and variable contributing areas, providing computational and parametric efficiency with physical grounding. TOPMODEL concepts have been incorporated into or coupled with LSMs in prior work, often improving discharge prediction. However, previous coupling strategies are commonly two-way, and there remains scope to understand how coupling interface choices affect model behavior and process representation.
supporting_quote: TOPMODEL ... is based on a theory of hydrological similarity of points in a catchment, determined by deriving a Topographic Wetness Index (TWI) from a Digital Elevation Model (DEM)
the studies have shown similar conclusions that the coupling of TOPMODEL with LSM improved discharge prediction
there remains significant scope to improve our understanding of the effect of coupling interfaces on the coupled model's behavior

chunks.text: The paper frames model coupling in both hydrology and software design terms, emphasizing that coupling interfaces influence understandability, modifiability, and uncertainty. One-way coupling is treated as loose coupling, while two-way coupling is tighter and can be harder to analyze due to feedback loops and computational cost. The authors highlight that coupling design can be a source of structural uncertainty that should be explicitly considered alongside performance.
supporting_quote: One-way coupling transfers the data (flux) from one model to another model in sequential order and can be also called "external coupling"
"Coupling" and "cohesion" are two key elements of structured modular design that determine the ease of software maintenance or modification
The coupling interface represents a source of structural uncertainty

chunks.text: The study has two primary objectives. First, it aims to substitute the NWM runoff calculation with TOPMODEL to simplify NWM structure and address drawbacks in headwater catchments. Second, it investigates how changing the coupling interface—such as coupling location, transferred flux types, and sub-model modifications—affects the behavior and performance of a one-way coupled Noah-MP + TOPMODEL system across six scenarios.
supporting_quote: The study had two objectives; (1) Substitute National Water Model's (NWM) runoff calculation with a conceptual hydrologic model (TOPography-based hydrological MODEL [TOPMODEL])
(2) Investigate how varying the coupling interface (location of coupling, type of fluxes used, modification of sub-models) affects model behavior ... using six different scenarios

chunks.text: A key experimental intent is to use a low-coupling one-way design to enable controlled comparisons of predictive performance, uncertainty, and parameter sensitivity across coupling interfaces. By transferring Noah-MP hydrologic fluxes and internal states into a stand-alone TOPMODEL implementation, the authors aim to isolate how interface complexity changes model behavior without requiring full integration into WRF-Hydro.
supporting_quote: we aimed to establish a low level of coupling to perform a controlled model experiment
a stand-alone model was one-way coupled by transferring hydrologic flux data
we analyzed the coupled model's streamflow prediction performance, uncertainty, and parameter sensitivity

chunks.text: The NWM forecast skill can be limited by applying a uniform model structure and scale over diverse hydrologic settings, especially headwater catchments where topography strongly controls processes. NWM’s 250 m routing grid can miss important terrain details, and key interfaces among shallow soil water, conceptual groundwater, and discharge rely on simplified representations and calibrated parameters rather than detailed landform considerations. These issues motivate testing alternatives that more directly encode terrain controls.
supporting_quote: forecast skill is limited by model architecture that applies a uniform model structure and spatial scale over the whole domain

Topographical influence on hydrological processes can be significant in smaller catchments ... but the spatial resolution of NWM's terrain routing grid (250 m) is coarse enough to miss some topographic details
the interface between shallow soil water, conceptual nonlinear groundwater reservoir, and underground discharge is controlled by simplified representations and calibrated parameters

chunks.text: NWM’s computational demand hinders applying finer grids or watershed-by-watershed calibration, limiting practical tailoring to local basins. Increasing resolution expands cell counts and can require smaller routing timesteps to maintain stability, while calibrating many watersheds can require supercomputing even at HUC10 scales. This creates a need for approaches that support efficient calibration and experimentation at headwater scales.
supporting_quote: NWM has high computational demand due to LSM-based model structure, and it hinders solutions such as applying a finer resolution grid or applying watershed-by-watershed calibration
Finer resolution increases the number of cells to calculate by the square and requires a smaller flow routing time-step
Calibration of individual watersheds requires super computer support even at ... HUC10 watershed scale (160–1,010 km2)

chunks.text: Applying LSM-based streamflow prediction has known shortcomings in representing subsurface processes, such as macropore or preferential flow, because many LSMs rely on 1-D soil column physics. This can manifest as unrealistic hydrographs with flashy runoff and slow recessions, and improving such processes inside LSMs is still an ongoing research area. The paper frames coupling with a conceptual watershed model as a pragmatic alternative while larger redesign efforts mature.
supporting_quote: LSMs do not typically consider macropore water movement or preferential flow scheme in subsurface representation and rely solely on Richardson equation within 1-D soil column
This can result in poor streamflow prediction with flashy runoff superimposed on slow recessions
a solution to provide stable streamflow prediction with the current soil column grid-based LSM structure is still lacking

chunks.text: The paper argues that coupling design itself can introduce structural uncertainty because fluxes that are theoretically similar may be incompatible between sub-models due to differing assumptions and process delineations. In complex coupled systems, small changes in one component can cause ripple effects on subsequent steps. This motivates systematically testing coupling interface choices rather than focusing solely on prediction scores.
supporting_quote: a small change in one component's usage or option can affect the whole following process steps with a "ripple effect"
each sub-model might calculate a different internal value for certain hydrological variables used as coupling fluxes even when they are theoretically identical
The coupling interface represents a source of structural uncertainty

chunks.text: The study implements a one-way coupling where Noah-MP is run to generate hydrologic fluxes, which are then transferred to a stand-alone TOPMODEL run. The design focuses on low coupling to enable controlled experiments, rapid execution, and straightforward calibration and sensitivity analysis. Six coupling scenarios are tested, where the degree of TOPMODEL process modification and reliance on Noah-MP fluxes define the coupling interface complexity.
supporting_quote: we did not do two-way couple or integrate models into NWM, and instead, a stand-alone model was one-way coupled by transferring hydrologic flux data
We established six versions of Noah-MP + TOP-MODEL coupling options

The type of hydrological state or flux values transferred from Noah-MP to TOPMODEL varied from fluxes equivalent to meteorological input to fluxes that are comparable to the internal state variables of TOPMODEL

chunks.text: To generate coupling data, routing feedbacks were disabled and Noah-MP outputs and internal RESTART states were written every timestep, then reformatted for TOPMODEL ingestion. Soil and groundwater-related parameters were adjusted, including setting Noah-MP’s slope index parameter to 1 to allow free gravitational drainage to the groundwater reservoir. Flux variables were collated from LDASOUT, LSMOUT, and RESTART, and converted to m/h, with accumulated RESTART variables differenced to hourly changes.
supporting_quote: Surface and subsurface flow routing were turned off to prevent Noah-MP's soil moisture contents being disturbed by feedback
The RESTART output file ... was set to write every timestep
The slope index parameter of Noah-MP was modified (set to 1) to allow free gravitational drainage
Target output variables were collated from multiple output files, such as LDASOUT ... LSMOUT ... and RESTART

chunks.text: Coupling fluxes are organized using a Noah-MP water balance where precipitation minus canopy and snow storage changes, minus actual evapotranspiration, equals surface runoff, underground runoff, and soil moisture change. The study distinguishes input-equivalent fluxes (water flux toward soil and Noah-MP actual evapotranspiration) from counterpart fluxes (Noah-MP surface runoff Qsfc and underground runoff Qugd) that can override or constrain TOPMODEL processes. The dependency between models is defined by whether and how these counterpart fluxes are used.
supporting_quote: (P - Δ Can - Δ Snw) - ETa = Qsfc + Qugd + ΔS

Variables on the left-hand side ... are not identical but comparable to TOPMODEL's meteorological input (rainfall and PET rate). These coupling fluxes will be called "(meteorological) input-equivalent fluxes"
we refer to them as "counterpart" coupling fluxes

chunks.text: TOPMODEL is implemented in R (r.TOPMODEL) and uses a precomputed topographic index derived from a 10-m DEM processed with TauDEM. Parameter bounds are chosen from prior studies and sampled using a Sobol quasi-Monte Carlo sequence (26,000 sets) to support calibration and global sensitivity analysis. An exception is made for surface hydraulic conductivity k0, with an upper bound of 10 m/h and logarithmic sampling to allow near-zero infiltration-excess behavior.
supporting_quote: We used an R-implemented version of TOPMODEL (Buytaert 2011)
processed from a 10-m resolution DEM using the TauDEM package
26,000 parameter sets sampled by Sobol sequence were used for all six coupling options
exception for surface hydraulic conductivity (k0), setting the upper bound to a very high value (10 m/h) ... and sampled on a logarithmic scale

chunks.text: Model calibration uses Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) as the optimization objective, but performance assessment compares multiple metrics including NSE, RMSE, RSR, PBIAS, and KGE against benchmarks. Uncertainty in streamflow prediction is estimated using GLUE with NSE-based behavioral thresholds (0.7 for better models, 0.55 for worse models) and 90% confidence bounds. Bound quality is summarized with percent observations contained and Average Relative Interval Length (ARIL).
supporting_quote: Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (Nash and Sutcliffe 1970) was used as an objective function for model calibration
We investigated metric scores including NSE, root mean square error (RMSE) ... percent bias (PBIAS), and Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE)
GLUE ... threshold of NSE was set to 0.7 for better performing coupled models and 0.55 for worse performing models
Average Relative Interval Length (ARIL)

chunks.text: Global parameter sensitivity is computed using the Jansen (1999) estimator to obtain first-order and total Sobol-like indices. Because NSE can take extreme negative values that impair variance-based sensitivity methods, the study uses a bounded NSE transformation C2M = NSE/(2 − NSE) for sensitivity analysis. Flow duration curves (FDCs) are used as hydrologic signatures for qualitative assessment of water availability.
supporting_quote: We used the "Jansen (1999)" method to retrieve first order and total sensitivity indices for parameters
To resolve this issue, we implement a bounded formulation of the NSE called C2M
C2M = NSE/(2 - NSE)
the flow duration curve (FDC), was applied to review the model's capability to predict water availability

chunks.text: Six coupling options progressively modify TOPMODEL to reflect different coupling interfaces. Options 1–3 limit reliance on Noah-MP runoff fluxes by using input-equivalent precipitation and ETa, removing ET scaling and/or the root zone, and in Option 3 dynamically scaling vertical drainage using Qugd. Options 4–6 are more aggressive, overriding TOPMODEL vertical drainage and/or infiltration with Noah-MP counterpart fluxes, culminating in full override where TOPMODEL relies on Qsfc and Qugd rather than meteorological inputs.
supporting_quote: We established six versions of Noah-MP + TOP-MODEL coupling options
Option 3 (Dynamic Unsaturated-zone Delay) ... references underground runoff (Qugd) of Noah-MP
Coupling Option 4 ... vertical drainage calculation in TOPMO-DEL is overridden by counterpart flux Qugd
Coupling Option 6 (Full Override) ... fully relies on runoff-related counterpart fluxes from Noah-MP

chunks.text: The study site is the ~17 km2 Elder Creek catchment upstream of USGS gage 11475560 within the Angelo Coast Range Reserve in Northern California. The area has steep hillslopes (average 32°) and a coastal Mediterranean climate with most precipitation between October and May and little snow. The modeling domain corresponds to HUC12 180101060103, selected as a data-rich headwater catchment for testing coupling validity and interface effects.
supporting_quote: modeling was done for the sub-catchment upstream of the USGS "Elder Creek" stream gage site (11475560)
about 17-km2 Elder Creek catchment
The study site has a steep hillslope (average 32°)
The climate in the area is coastal Mediterranean ... most of the precipitation falling between October and May

chunks.text: The base modeling system uses NWM v1.2.2 with NLDAS-2 forcing data, and outputs from Noah-MP are harvested for coupling. Domain data are subsetted using the CUAHSI Domain subsetter, and Noah-MP outputs are processed from NetCDF using the rwrfhydro package. Coupling variables are assembled from LDASOUT, LSMOUT, and RESTART files, with RESTART providing internal state variables needed for water-balance calculations.
supporting_quote: NWM v1.2.2 was used as a base model
used North American Land Data Assimilation System-2 (NLDAS) as a forcing data
domain data ... subsetted using CUAHSI Domain subsetter
"rwrfhydro" package was used to disaggregate and reformat NetCDF files
collated from multiple output files, such as LDASOUT ... LSMOUT ... and RESTART

chunks.text: The simulation spans four water years from October 1, 2015 to September 30, 2019. Spin-up follows WRF-Hydro guidance using an idealized uniform precipitation initialization, then multiple repetitive runs using the first three months of WY2015 and a full WY2015 simulation to stabilize states. Performance figures often focus on the wet season of WY2017 (Oct 2016–Mar 2017) for legibility and event richness.
supporting_quote: We used a model simulation period from October 1, 2015 to September 30, 2019, covering four water years
The model spin-up used four repetitive model runs using the first three months of the first water year 2015
hydrograph figures are limited to the wet season of the water year 2017 (October 2016–March 2017) for legibility

chunks.text: TOPMODEL terrain inputs are derived from a 10-m DEM, with the topographic index computed using TauDEM. This enables TOPMODEL to represent hydrologic similarity and contributing area dynamics based on high-resolution topography, which is central to the rationale for coupling it to NWM’s LSM for headwater catchments.
supporting_quote: TOPMODEL requires precomputation of the topographic index, which was processed from a 10-m resolution DEM using the TauDEM package
TOPMODEL ... uses high-resolution topographical data not only to calculate surface routing but to represent hydrologic characteristics of the area

chunks.text: For the coupling experiments and calibration/sensitivity runs, 26,000 parameter sets are sampled using a Sobol sequence across defined parameter bounds. Evaluation uses USGS observed streamflow at the Elder Creek gage and multiple statistical scores computed over the full simulation period. GLUE ensembles are formed using NSE thresholds that differ for better versus worse performing coupled options.
supporting_quote: 26,000 parameter sets sampled by Sobol sequence were used for all six coupling options
compared the model performance based on simulated streamflow of the original NWM, original TOPMODEL, and Noah-MP & TOP-MODEL coupled versions
The threshold of NSE was set to 0.7 for better performing coupled models and 0.55 for worse performing models

chunks.text: The baseline NWM configuration performed poorly for this headwater catchment and did not meet common minimum standards, particularly during wet seasons. It produced overly flashy hydrographs, often overestimated peaks, and underestimated water availability in the flow duration curve. Quantitatively, NWM had NSE 0.488, RSR 0.715, and PBIAS −32.5 over the full period.
supporting_quote: The NWM did not meet the minimum standard suggested by Moriasi et al. (2007) (PBIAS lower than 25%, NSE over 0.5, and RSR lower than 0.7)
NWM showed a very flashy hydrograph ... and often overestimated the peak flowrate
The FDC showed the strong tendency of NWM to underestimate the water availability

chunks.text: The original stand-alone TOPMODEL control (forced by NLDAS precipitation and PET) outperformed NWM in metrics but had a much smaller behavioral parameter ensemble under GLUE. Over the full period, TOPMODEL-control achieved NSE 0.749 and PBIAS −23.9, but only 97 out of 26,000 parameter sets exceeded the GLUE threshold of NSE 0.7, indicating strong constraint/equifinality issues under the chosen forcing and structure.
supporting_quote: The original standalone TOPMODEL ... returned higher metric scores compared to NWM
TOPMODEL (control) | 0.749 ... PBIAS | −23.9
only 97 of 26,000 parameter-sets satisfied GLUE thresholds of NSE 0.7

chunks.text: All one-way coupled Noah-MP + TOPMODEL scenarios outperformed NWM and generally improved streamflow prediction relative to standalone TOPMODEL, but success depended on coupling interface. Moderate coupling options (1–3) performed reliably across seasons/years, while aggressive overrides (4–6) were only acceptable in limited periods and inherited undesirable NWM-like behavior. This demonstrates that relying on LSM fluxes to override TOPMODEL internal processes can degrade performance.
supporting_quote: The one-way coupled model outperformed NWM and noncoupled TOPMODEL
moderate options (1, 2, and 3) showed reliable performance through varying years and seasons
More aggressive coupling cases (from Option 4 to Option 6) that relied more heavily on Noah-MP output fluxes produced relatively lacking performance
Performance declined when coupling configurations relied more on LSM calculated fluxes to override TOPMODEL internal processes

chunks.text: Option 1 (removing TOPMODEL ET scaling while using Noah-MP ETa and effective precipitation) improved statistical scores over both controls and reduced bias relative to the TOPMODEL-control underestimation of high flows. Over the full period, Option 1 achieved NSE 0.789 and PBIAS −14.5, and it consistently outperformed NWM except near dry-season baseflow depletion. However, it still underestimated streamflow over parts of the flow duration curve (around the 40th percentile and above).
supporting_quote: Coupling Noah-MP and TOPMODEL with a minor change in ET scheme (Option 1, ET replacement) improved all the statistical scores and hydrographs
Option 1           | 0.789 ... PBIAS | −14.5
Option 1 consistently outperformed NWM except for the period when baseflow recesses near depletion
it tended to underestimate the streamflow over the 40th percentile

chunks.text: Option 2 (removing the root zone to constrain ET with local storage deficit) improved bias and KGE compared to Option 1, with PBIAS shifting to +5.4 and KGE to 0.829 while NSE remained similar (0.792). It better reproduced event peaks and recession shape in wet periods but increased uncertainty over the full period, with ARIL 2.69 and only 29.9% of observations within GLUE bounds. Performance tradeoffs were season-dependent: uncertainty metrics improved relative to Option 1 during the wet season of WY2017.
supporting_quote: In coupling Option 2 (Rootzone Removal), PBIAS and KGE noticeably improved compared to Option 1
Option 2           | 0.792 ... PBIAS | 5.4   | KGE   | 0.829 | ARIL | 2.69 | % within bound | 29.9
Coupling Option 2 had a recession curve that is closer to the observed recession shape and reproduced small peaks
when those metrics were calculated only for the wet season of the WY 2017 ... % of observation within bound was higher in Option 2 than Option 1 (49% vs. 42%)

chunks.text: Option 3 (dynamic unsaturated-zone delay that indirectly references Noah-MP Qugd) produced the best overall performance among the coupling schemes. It reached NSE 0.806, PBIAS 3.3, and KGE 0.821, and improved recession/baseflow representation compared to Option 2. The improvement was somewhat unexpected given TOPMODEL’s known low sensitivity to td, but dynamically scaling vertical drainage using LSM flux trends improved performance (e.g., WY2018 wet season NSE increased from 0.48 in Option 2 to 0.63 in Option 3).
supporting_quote: Coupling Option 3 (Dynamic Unsaturated-zone Delay) produced the highest scores of all the options
Option 3           | 0.806 ... PBIAS | 3.3   | KGE   | 0.821
baseflow increased and the recession curve fitted more closely to the observed streamflow
improved streamflow prediction during a wet season in the dry year (WY 2018) from NSE 0.48 (Option 2) to 0.63 (Option 3)

chunks.text: Aggressive coupling options that override TOPMODEL internal states with Noah-MP runoff/drainage fluxes (Options 4–6) reduced predictive skill and required lowering the GLUE behavioral threshold to NSE 0.55. These options often showed NWM-like behavior with flashy runoff and poor wet-season baseflow, indicating incompatibility between Noah-MP flux definitions and TOPMODEL’s groundwater dynamics. Option 4 was among the worst performers (NSE 0.599; PBIAS 25.3), while Option 6 had large uncertainty bounds (ARIL 5.11).
supporting_quote: The more aggressive coupling options ... required us to reduce the GLUE threshold value to an NSE of 0.55
they inherited the characteristics of NWM with lower predictive skill during the wet season showing "flashy runoff superimposed on slow recessions"
Option 4           | 0.599 ... PBIAS | 25.3
Option 6           | 0.605 ... ARIL | 5.11

chunks.text: Overriding infiltration with Noah-MP surface runoff (Option 5) yielded intermediate metric performance but introduced delayed peaks and high uncertainty. The hydrograph showed time-to-peak delays that could exceed 24 hours, and ARIL increased to 4.13 despite NSE 0.616. This suggests that forcing counterpart fluxes into TOPMODEL can disrupt compatibility with TOPMODEL’s routing and internal dynamics even when only one process is overridden.
supporting_quote: Coupling Option 5 (Infiltration Override) ... showed better scores compared to Options 4
Hydrographs of Option 5 suffered from delayed time-to-peak estimation, which extended in some extreme cases to over 24 h
Option 5           | 0.616 ... ARIL | 4.13

chunks.text: Coupling changed TOPMODEL’s behavioral parameter space: unlike TOPMODEL-control, the better coupled options (1–3) had thousands of parameter sets exceeding NSE 0.7. The TOPMODEL-control behavioral sets had a narrow range of the m parameter (0.02–0.056) relative to the sampled range (0.0001–0.25), whereas coupled runs did not show such narrowing. This indicates that LSM-derived surficial fluxes as inputs can reduce reliance on certain sensitive TOPMODEL parameters and improve robustness under input/structural uncertainty.
supporting_quote: only 97 of 26,000 parameter sets satisfied GLUE thresholds of NSE 0.7. However, better performing coupled Options (1, 2, and 3) had 2,000–4,000 surpassing the same threshold
these 97 parameter sets ... had a relatively narrow distribution of "m" parameter (transmissivity decline, 0.02–0.056) compared to the range of sampled space (0.0001– 0.25)
TOPMODEL's reliance on the "m" parameter ... was resolved when LSM surficial fluxes were used as model input

chunks.text: Parameter sensitivity indices shifted markedly across coupling interfaces, and sensitivities could diverge even when hydrographs or performance metrics appeared similar. As coupling became more override-driven, sensitivities of key TOPMODEL parameters declined; in Option 6, lnTe sensitivity dropped to 0.13 and m to 0.005, while surface routing velocity became most significant. The paper also reports that structural modifications (e.g., removing the root zone) changed sensitivity of parameters not directly involved, indicating nonlocal ripple effects within the model.
supporting_quote: As coupling options more aggressively modify TOPMODEL structure and rely on LSM fluxes, sensitivity indices of multiple parameters declined
In Option 6 ... sensitivity indices for lnTe and m became very small at 0.13 and 0.005 each
modification of model structure can significantly affect sensitivity indices of parameters that are not directly involved in the calculation

chunks.text: The authors interpret improved performance as arising from combining distributed LSM simulations with a simpler, calibratable watershed-scale runoff structure that better represents headwater processes. They note a substantial water-balance inconsistency among NLDAS rainfall, observed runoff, and Noah-MP AET (reported ratio 1:0.94:0.27), implying substantial forcing/observation uncertainty. Coupling can improve fit to given data but does not resolve input uncertainty; instead, it can bias performance differences between high-flow and low-flow regimes.
supporting_quote: a one-way coupling scheme with NWM's Noah-MP coupled to a calibrated TOPMODEL outperformed the NWM v1.2 and original TOPMODEL
the water budget between NLDAS rainfall, USGS observed runoff, and AET rate from Noah-MP was calculated at 1:0.94:0.27
Coupling models do not resolve input uncertainty, but were able to improve predictive performance

chunks.text: The paper argues coupling interface uncertainty should be treated as structural uncertainty, because superficially similar coupling choices can yield different parameter sensitivities and water budgets. Sensitivity analysis revealed that coupling can affect parameters far from the coupling location and that performance metrics alone may not indicate sound model behavior. The authors recommend avoiding forced overrides of internal states when models are incompatible, and instead using indirect constraints that translate flux trends into compatible internal states (as in Option 3).
supporting_quote: We, therefore, propose that coupling method uncertainty should be considered as a major source of model structural uncertainty
The parameter sensitivity can and did diverge rapidly even when model performance metrics or hydrographs were similar

it would be better to consider indirect use of coupling fluxes first. We suppose that extracting one sub-model's key component and embedding it into the other sub-model can also reduce incompatibilities

chunks.text: The study is limited by using one-way coupling and by not assessing or correcting uncertainty in inputs or observations. The authors state they did not analyze uncertainty from input data nor use calibration techniques designed to resolve forcing/observation errors. They also acknowledge that while one-way coupling simplifies experimentation, scaling the approach to many watersheds would require watershed boundary delineation and an NWM-compatible channel routing scheme embedded in the hydrologic model.
supporting_quote: Neither of analysis to assess the uncertainty from input data nor model calibration technique to resolve errors in input/observation data was considered due to the limited scope of the study
it is only targeted for an experiment in a single headwater catchment and was not designed for applying on a large scale
Applying this to multiple watersheds over large areas will require dedicated watershed boundary delineation and embedding an NWM-compatible channel routing scheme

chunks.text: Operationalization would require more efficient internal data management than the experiment used. The coupling relied on writing Noah-MP RESTART outputs every timestep and external post-processing to pass fluxes into TOPMODEL, which is sufficient for research but not for operations. The paper notes that an operational model would need an efficient flux transfer/exchange module while keeping software coupling levels low.
supporting_quote: The RESTART output file ... was set to write every timestep
any operational one-way coupling implementation would require a more efficient data management between Noah-MP and TOPMODEL
any operational model must include a data management module that can efficiently transfer/exchange model fluxes while keeping software coupling levels low

chunks.text: The one-way coupling of TOPMODEL with Noah-MP increased predictive skill compared to both NWM and standalone TOPMODEL in the headwater catchment, supporting the idea that replacing 1-D soil column-based runoff representation with a conceptual watershed structure can better upscale runoff processes. The one-way scheme enabled conventional calibration, performance evaluation, and uncertainty/sensitivity analysis to diagnose coupling interface effects. The authors emphasize that coupling interface strongly affects performance and can cause unexpected changes in parameter sensitivity and water balance even when metrics are similar.
supporting_quote: One-way coupling resulted in increased predictive skill compared to controls (NWM and original TOPMODEL)
One-way coupling scheme facilitated conventional model calibration, performance evaluation, and uncertainty-sensitivity analysis
Coupling interface strongly affected prediction performance ... led to unexpected shifts in TOPMODEL parameter sensitivity or water balance even when performance metrics were similar

chunks.text: Coupling interface should be treated as a source of structural uncertainty because fluxes can be incompatible across sub-models even when theoretically similar, due to different assumptions and process delineations. The paper recommends maintaining independence of key sub-model structures/processes and arranging coupling fluxes to establish consistency between internal model states, favoring indirect use of coupling fluxes over direct override when incompatibilities exist. These principles are presented as relevant to future modular, mix-and-match hydrologic modeling frameworks such as next-generation NWM concepts.
supporting_quote: Coupling interface should be considered as the source of structural uncertainty in coupled models
Incompatibility can exist between submodels' internal fluxes even when they are theoretically identical because of varying process delineation and assumptions
It is recommendable to maintain independency of sub-models' key structures/processes and to arrange coupling fluxes to establish consistency between sub-models' internal status

chunks.text: The paper is situated in the context of rising environmental hazards, especially extreme flooding, which heightens the need for effective crisis and risk communication. It focuses on Indigenous communities such as the Wyandotte Nation, where communication is shaped by Indigenous epistemologies and ontologies. The regional setting includes multiple sovereign tribal governments and overlapping jurisdictions, creating a complex governance environment for emergency communication. The work is motivated by the need for communication approaches that better fit local cultural contexts and decision-making realities.
supporting_quote: Given the increasing frequency of environmental hazards such as extreme flooding, effective crisis and risk communication is critical.
The Wyandotte Nation often face additional challenges due to cultural communication differences.
The Wyandotte Nation is situated in Ottawa County, Oklahoma, which is home to 9 federally recognized Native American tribes

chunks.text: The study emphasizes Indigenous storytelling as a central tradition that can convey technical information in culturally resonant ways. Prior research suggests one-way information provision often fails, while tailored communication can influence risk perceptions and behavior. The authors position storytelling as an ontological and practical framework to support understanding and action in the face of hazards. This background motivates using narrative-based tools to connect flood risk information to community values and lived experience.
supporting_quote: Communication is a two-way street, and simply providing information on hazards, risk, and adaptation strategies has not proven successful at encouraging evacuation.
Central to many Indigenous communication practices is the tradition and art of storytelling
These storytelling elements offer an opportunity for Indigenous populations to understand technical information

chunks.text: The paper adopts a co-production orientation, emphasizing shared authority with Tribal partners to counter extractive research dynamics. It connects this approach to trust building and the need for tangible community benefit, given histories of research fatigue and strained relationships. The background frames the project as relational and place-based, rather than purely technical. This sets up collaborative development of communication products that can be used by both community and external agencies.
supporting_quote: Following recent literature, this work will take a collaborative approach to the co-production of knowledge with our Tribal partners
To combat the effects of research fatigue, this study hopes to work with its partners to identify tangible benefits to the community
developed with equal participation and shared authority with Indigenous and community partners

chunks.text: A primary goal is to co-produce communication strategies with Tribal communities to strengthen decision-making capacity and understanding around Indigenous perspectives of water. The work is nested within a broader study on modeling community trust while scoping water forecast needs in northeast Oklahoma. The communication component focuses on building capacity through strategies that reflect Indigenous ontologies. This goal explicitly positions communication as part of governance and preparedness, not just information dissemination.
supporting_quote: One of the overarching goals of the study is to establish co-produced communication strategies with Tribal communities to build decision-making capacity and understanding around indigenous perspectives of water.
This research was part of a larger study focused on modeling community trust when scoping water forecast needs with tribal communities in Northeast Oklahoma.

chunks.text: The study aims to explore culturally adaptive communication practices with the Wyandotte Nation and translate them into usable crisis and risk communication strategies. It seeks to develop approaches that resonate with Indigenous communities by centering Tribal needs, prioritizing trust building, and grounding products in place-based knowledge. The project also intends to create a communication artifact that can help convey flood risks and related hazards in accessible ways. The resulting approach is intended as a model for cross-cultural hazard communication.
supporting_quote: This study sets out to explore communication practices with the Wyandotte Nation and develop more culturally adaptive communication strategies.
Taking a collaborative approach of coproduction, the centering of Tribal needs, and prioritizing trust building, the project was grounded in place-based knowledge.

chunks.text: A specific objective is to identify approaches to Indigenous community research that can be exported into NOAA operations. The authors argue these communities require different ontological positioning and cross-cultural governance requirements than typical research practices address. The focus spans multiple Tribal partners—Wyandotte, Miami, and Quapaw Nations—to examine how cultural pathways intersect with jurisdictional complexity. The work thus targets institutional learning and operational transferability for NOAA.
supporting_quote: Exploring new ways to work within the Indigenous community research space that can be exported into NOAA operations
these communities require different ontological positioning and cross-cultural governance requirements not currently addressed by researchers.
Our key focus is the co-production of communication strategies with the Wyandotte, Miami, and Quapaw Nations

chunks.text: Emergency response and risk communication in Ottawa County are complicated by overlapping jurisdictions and multiple governmental structures. Flood risk crosses political boundaries, including two state borders and several federal agencies, which undermines formal warning systems. The paper notes that official channels often fail to provide adequate warning, creating a gap between hazard monitoring and community action. This governance complexity makes it difficult to coordinate disaster response across Tribal and municipal entities.
supporting_quote: Emergency response in the area faces challenges stemming from the need to coordinate between different governmental structures and jurisdictional boundaries.
formal warning systems have proven to fall short due to jurisdictional challenges, including two state borders and numerous federal agency jurisdictions

chunks.text: The region faces significant flood hazards compounded by long-standing environmental contamination from the Tar Creek Superfund site. Mining waste from decades of lead and zinc extraction has left toxic piles across the landscape, intensifying community risk and complicating hazard communication. This environmental context creates layered threats where flooding can interact with contamination concerns. Communicating risk therefore requires integrating multiple hazards and histories in ways that make sense to local communities.
supporting_quote: The potential for crises and hazards in the area is further exacerbated by the Tar Creek Superfund site
has left enormous piles of toxic mining waste across the landscape.

chunks.text: The paper describes a "data desert" problem in which tribes often lack their own data and must rely on information from federal or state entities. This dependence limits the community’s ability to convey accurate risk communication and coordinate disaster response effectively. The gap is not about lack of expertise but lack of accessible, locally controlled data resources. This problem motivates creating tools that integrate datasets into more usable formats for Tribal decision-making.
supporting_quote: tribes often lack their own data and are limited to using information provided by others, such as federal or state entities.
These "data deserts" impact the community's ability to effectively convey accurate risk communication and properly coordinate disaster response

chunks.text: Trust barriers hinder effective communication, including mistrust of federal government actors tied to the Superfund site and the broader history of extraction and harm. The paper also highlights research fatigue, where communities experience repeated research engagement without tangible benefits. These dynamics reduce willingness to engage with outside information and can undermine uptake of risk communication products. Addressing trust is therefore positioned as a prerequisite for communication efficacy.
supporting_quote: mistrust of the federal government as a result of fractured trust due to the Superfund Site
the history of research fatigue from researchers who offer little tangible change or utility to the tribal community

chunks.text: The authors argue that many flood risk maps and one-way communication approaches fail to balance simplicity and complexity or reach communities in culturally relevant forms. Simply providing hazard information has not consistently driven protective behavior such as evacuation. The problem is framed as a "final mile" gap: research and technical products do not translate into accessible, trusted media for local audiences. This motivates experimenting with interactive, narrative-driven communication formats.
supporting_quote: many current flood risk maps still lack a balance between simplicity and complexity.
simply providing information on hazards, risk, and adaptation strategies has not proven successful at encouraging evacuation.
one-way communication often falls short, as it fails to reach the "final mile"

chunks.text: The study uses ArcGIS StoryMaps as an interactive, mixed-media platform to communicate flood risks through narrative. StoryMaps combine maps, videos, images, and graphs into an online interface, and the authors adopt it not only for information delivery but also as a storytelling medium. The platform choice is tied to the need for accessible and culturally relevant communication tools. The StoryMap is designed to disseminate flood and environmental hazard information in a digestible format.
supporting_quote: the use of online interactive communication tools such as StoryMaps to disseminate valuable information is becoming increasingly popular in risk communication (e.g., ArcGIS StoryMaps)
ArcGIS StoryMaps are a novel mixed-media approach that combines a wide variety of functionalities, including maps, videos, images, and graphs

chunks.text: A co-production process anchored the first year of work, focusing on discussions with the Wyandotte Nation to scope tangible benefits, define goals, and center Tribal priorities. Trust building is treated as a core methodological requirement for effective risk communication. The team also planned continued support and used the Wyandotte Nation’s judgment when engaging additional community partners. This approach aligns decision-making authority with Tribal leadership rather than researcher-only control.
supporting_quote: the majority of the first year of our project was dedicated to discussions with the Wyandotte Nation, scoping tangible benefits, defining project goals, and centering Tribal needs and priorities
Plans were made for a commitment to continued support and additional projects, and when bringing in additional community partners, we relied on the Wyandotte Nation's judgment

chunks.text: The StoryMap’s purpose was explicitly defined through partner discussions as serving both external visibility and local utility. This dual-purpose framing guided design choices about content, tone, and included features. The tool is meant to help external audiences understand Tribal challenges while also serving as a practical local communication asset. Structuring around these goals is part of aligning outputs with community-identified needs.
supporting_quote: Following discussions with Tribal leadership, we identified a dual purpose of the storymap based on these needs and priorities: increasing visibility for external audiences and providing utility for the local community.

chunks.text: The team conducted a guided tour of Ottawa County led by community members to identify key locations, risks, and challenges. They collected thorough notes and photographic documentation to ground the StoryMap in local, place-based knowledge. This field-based elicitation shaped the StoryMap’s structure, priorities, and the selection of sites and narratives. The approach emphasizes that local knowledge is foundational, not supplementary, to technical communication design.
supporting_quote: a guided tour of the county was conducted and led by community members.
During this tour, key locations, risks, and challenges were identified.
This centering of place-based knowledge of the local area was the foundation of the Storymap

chunks.text: The StoryMap integrates diverse media and interactive elements, including pictures, videos, interactive maps, sliders, and datasets. The authors used plain language to increase accessibility across stakeholders. Combining multiple media types is intended to make complex flood and contamination information understandable and engaging. This design choice operationalizes the broader aim of culturally adaptive, user-centered risk communication.
supporting_quote: there was integration of diverse media, including pictures, videos, interactive maps, and sliders in addition to datasets
Plain language was used to ensure accessibility to all stakeholders.

chunks.text: Narrative framing was central: the StoryMap was structured as a "journey down the river" using a visual of a person in a canoe moving through rivers and creeks. Each segment begins with a new depiction and vivid titles (e.g., "the canary in the coal mine" and "the toxic source") to emphasize distinct local challenges. This storytelling approach was deliberately designed to be more accessible and culturally relevant. The narrative device connects geographic progression with hazard understanding.
supporting_quote: framing the entire experience as a "journey down the river".
incorporated a visual storytelling element of a person in a canoe
reinforced with vivid title descriptions such as "the canary in the coal mine" or "the toxic source"

chunks.text: The StoryMap incorporates multiple external datasets to represent hazards and environmental conditions in the region. Specifically, it includes information from the Oklahoma Department of Environmental Quality, FEMA flood zones, and mining waste associated with the Tar Creek Superfund site. These datasets are integrated with interactive map elements to support exploration and understanding. The combination aims to connect official data sources with locally grounded storytelling.
supporting_quote: datasets from the Oklahoma Department of Environmental Quality, FEMA Flood Zones, and mining waste from the Tar Creek Superfund Site.

chunks.text: Field-based qualitative inputs were gathered during a community-led guided tour, including notes and photographic documentation. These materials captured key locations, risks, and challenges as identified by community members. The collected observations served as foundational inputs that shaped the StoryMap’s structure and priorities. This emphasizes place-based knowledge as a primary data stream for communication design.
supporting_quote: a guided tour of the county was conducted and led by community members.
Thorough notes and photo documentation were also taken.
key locations, risks, and challenges were identified.

chunks.text: In preliminary feedback, the Wyandotte Nation responded positively to the first iteration of the StoryMap. They emphasized its digestibility, its potential as a practical tool for future communication, and its capacity to increase visibility of local challenges. This reception suggests that the narrative-driven, co-produced format aligns with community expectations for accessible communication. The results are explicitly described as early-stage and tied to the initial version of the tool.
supporting_quote: results presented here are preliminary and reflect outcomes from the first iteration of the StoryMap.
the Wyandotte Nation, who expressed strong approval regarding its digestibility, its potential as a practical tool for future communication, and its ability to generate visibility

chunks.text: NOAA leadership at the National Water Center reacted favorably to the StoryMap’s cross-cultural communication utility. They viewed the approach as broadly applicable beyond the immediate case, implying potential for organizational adoption. This indicates institutional interest in the co-produced, storytelling-forward design as a method for communicating hazards across diverse communities. The result is framed as enthusiasm rather than a formal evaluation outcome.
supporting_quote: The StoryMap was similarly presented to NOAA leadership at the National Water Center, who were excited by its utility in addressing cross-cultural communication, which would be widely applicable for many other areas.

chunks.text: The project reports increased visibility as a measurable early outcome, using view counts for the StoryMap and a follow-up documentary. The StoryMap reached over 590 views in under a year, and the 12-minute documentary received 200 views on YouTube in a short timeframe. These numbers are used as evidence that the communication product is reaching audiences. Visibility is treated as one of the two partner-identified purposes of the StoryMap.
supporting_quote: garnering over 590 views in under a year.
A follow-up 12-minute short documentary was also produced several months later, which has already attracted 200 views on YouTube

chunks.text: The paper identifies the StoryMap as a concrete output of the collaboration, providing its public title and location. Naming and linking the product signals that the work resulted in a deployable communication tool rather than only conceptual recommendations. This artifact is positioned as the first iteration, with plans to expand it. The availability of the tool supports its stated intent to increase external visibility and community utility.
supporting_quote: The StoryMap itself is titled The Journey Through the River and the Tribes Caught Between and can be found at https://arcg.is/1qS8iq0
results presented here are preliminary and reflect outcomes from the first iteration of the StoryMap.

chunks.text: The authors argue that the work demonstrates co-produced, culturally adaptive communication as an effective alternative to one-way science communication. They frame science communication as relational, emphasizing collaboration and shared authority with Tribal partners. This discussion positions the approach as contributing to NOAA’s broader mission of delivering actionable water intelligence. The core implication is that culturally grounded storytelling combined with interactive tools can improve how NOAA products are used and delivered.
supporting_quote: demonstrating the efficacy of co-produced, culturally adaptive communication strategies.
science communication is a relational process of collaboration and shared authority rather than a one-way transmission of information.
we aim to better deliver our commitment to providing actionable water intelligence and improve the use and delivery of NOAA Products.

chunks.text: A key limitation and boundary condition is that Indigenous communities differ in ontological positioning, needs, and priorities, so approaches cannot be applied identically everywhere. While the authors emphasize scalability into NOAA operations, they caution against assuming a universal template. This implies that co-production must be re-done locally, with community-led priority setting each time. The discussion balances scalability claims with a requirement for contextual adaptation.
supporting_quote: methodologies and foundational strategies of the work are inherently scalable and should be exported into NOAA operations.
it is important to recognize that every Indigenous community will have a different ontological positioning and, therefore, a different set of needs and priorities.

chunks.text: The results are explicitly characterized as preliminary because the project is ongoing and reflects only the first iteration of the StoryMap. The authors describe the development as iterative and note that further versions are planned to enhance utility for Tribal communities. This limits the strength of claims about effectiveness at this stage, since systematic evaluation is still underway. The paper therefore treats current outcomes as promising but not final.
supporting_quote: As the project is ongoing, the results presented here are preliminary and reflect outcomes from the first iteration of the StoryMap.
the development of this tool and communication strategy is an iterative process, so there are still plans for further versions of the StoryMap

chunks.text: Planned evaluation work acknowledges that the StoryMap’s efficacy has not yet been measured against other flood risk communication tools. The authors propose measuring performance relative to products like the National Water Model or Flood Inundation Maps. They plan to use focus groups, semi-structured interviews, and a tabletop exercise to map decision-making and communication pathways during crises. This future work indicates that current evidence is based on reception and reach rather than comparative behavioral or decision outcomes.
supporting_quote: Future work and projects will firstly include finishing this project, with measurement of the efficacy of the StoryMap compared to other risk communication tools such as the National Water Model or Flood Inundation Maps.
there are ongoing focus groups and semi-structured interviews taking place
This information will then be used to inform a tabletop exercise to identify communication challenges and map decision-making

chunks.text: The paper concludes that combining Indigenous storytelling traditions with interactive tools like ArcGIS StoryMaps can make risk communication more culturally resonant and technologically innovative. It argues that the approach can enhance crisis communication within the Wyandotte Nation and potentially across NOAA operations and other communities. The conclusion emphasizes continued evolution of the project and the promise of a scalable framework. The intended impact is improved preparedness, response, and long-term resilience.
supporting_quote: By integrating Indigenous storytelling traditions with modern and novel interactive tools like ArcGIS StoryMaps, this study demonstrates how risk communication can be adapted to be a more culturally resonant
the scalable framework has the potential to enhance crisis communication not only within the Wyandotte Nation, but also across NOAA operations

chunks.text: The authors conclude that co-production centered on Tribal needs and trust building offers tangible benefits and broader applicability. They underscore that the framework can be used as a model for NOAA and risk communication more generally, while being grounded in place-based knowledge and community authority. The project’s communication product is presented as evidence that collaborative methods can produce usable tools. The conclusion ties these elements to broader goals of improving how actionable information reaches communities.
supporting_quote: Taking a collaborative approach of coproduction, the centering of Tribal needs, and prioritizing trust building, the project was grounded in place-based knowledge.

This scalable framework of co-production and incorporating Indigenous storytelling with modern interactive tools not only offers a tangible benefit to the Wyandotte Nation, but also holds the potential for broader applications across NOAA and risk communication more generally.

chunks.text: The actor model is a concurrency paradigm where computation is organized as independent actors that communicate via asynchronous message passing rather than shared state. Its primitive operations—create, send, and become—support scalable parallel execution while avoiding common issues like low-level data races and deadlock. Actor hierarchies formed through actor creation also naturally enable supervision-based fault handling, where parent actors can manage failures in children.
supporting_quote: The actor model is a mathematical model of concurrent computing where the fundamental unit of computation is called an actor.
Agha is also credited with formalizing the three primitive operations of the actor model, create, send, and become

chunks.text: Shared HPC systems rely on schedulers (e.g., Slurm) and tools (e.g., GNU Parallel) to manage fairness and performance, but users often still face inefficiencies such as idle CPU time and waste from imbalance. Failures in large simulations are common, and manual resubmission workflows can be time-consuming and resource-wasteful. The paper positions actor-based approaches as a way to reduce user burden while improving utilization and robustness in such environments.
supporting_quote: Examples of wasteful use of HPC resources include requesting more CPU cores than necessary, having a high idle CPU time, and having a low level of fault tolerance that necessitates re-running large portions of a computation.
The typical process followed by users when a job fails is as follows: Diagnose the problem... Re-submit jobs to the queue.

chunks.text: SUMMA is a process-based hydrological modeling framework that solves conservation PDEs for water and energy across land domains. It structures spatial domains into GRUs and HRUs and typically treats GRUs independently, but its standard execution model is serial per instance and does not use MPI. Large domains therefore require batching GRUs into scheduler jobs, which can trigger imbalance and failure amplification when a single GRU causes a whole batch to fail.
supporting_quote: SUMMA is a process-based hydrological modeling framework (a so-called land model) that simulates the hydrology and associated thermodynamics of a terrestrial landscape [8].
SUMMA is not designed to use MPI or any other multi-threading paradigms, meaning it does not use more than one CPU core per instance of the program.

chunks.text: The paper aims to show that applying the actor model at the application level can improve both resource utilization and fault tolerance for large-scale scientific simulations composed of many independent sub-simulations. The authors demonstrate this by building SUMMA-Actors, an actor-based version of SUMMA, and comparing it against standard Slurm array-job execution and GNU Parallel-based execution. The goal includes reducing wall-clock time, improving CPU efficiency, and eliminating manual intervention for recoverable failures.
supporting_quote: we propose the use of the actor model of concurrent computation as a way to improve resource utilization and fault tolerance in large-scale scientific computing simulations.
We compare the wall-clock time, CPU efficiency, CPU utilization, and fault tolerance of SUMMA-Actors against SUMMA run with a standard array job and against SUMMA run with GNU Parallel

chunks.text: A specific objective is to demonstrate that actors can be incorporated into a legacy scientific application without rewriting it from scratch, even when the legacy codebase lacks native actor support. The work targets Fortran-based codes and leverages C++ interoperability through ISO_C_BINDING to integrate actors while preserving existing data structures and computational routines. This goal is evaluated by implementing actor-managed execution around SUMMA’s existing Fortran components.
supporting_quote: Lastly, we demonstrate that the actor model can be incorporated into a legacy scientific computing application even when there is no pre-existing support for it.
SUMMA-Actors relies on the ISO_C_BINDING Fortran module to interface Fortran and C++.

chunks.text: Large simulations with many independent sub-simulations can suffer from severe load imbalance because completion times vary widely, producing unpredictable runtimes and poor utilization. In HPC jobs that allocate whole nodes, the straggler effect means the job lasts as long as the slowest sub-task, leaving many cores idle while resources are still reserved. This inefficiency is particularly problematic in shared environments where users are expected to optimize resource usage.
supporting_quote: sub-simulations may have wildly varying completion times or not complete at all, leading to unpredictable runtimes as well as unbalanced and inefficient use of human and computational resources.
the straggler effect [3], which is the consequence that a job takes as long as its longest running sub-task.

chunks.text: Standard scheduler-based batching can amplify failures: even if GRUs are theoretically independent in SUMMA, the program time-steps a batch together such that a single GRU failure causes the whole batch job to fail. The default manual workflow requires diagnosing the failure, modifying parameters, extracting and resubmitting the failed subset, and waiting again. This manual intervention adds latency and increases wasted compute due to rerunning successful work.
supporting_quote: despite the theoretical independence of each GRU simulation, in practice a failure from one GRU causes the simulation for the whole batch to fail.
The key drawback of this process is that it is typically carried out manually.

chunks.text: Existing tools such as GNU Parallel can dynamically distribute sub-tasks across cores to reduce the straggler effect, but they do not address application-level fault tolerance. Slurm’s fault handling is oriented toward isolating bad jobs rather than enabling recovery from software-level simulation failures. As a result, users still need to build and maintain fragile scripting logic or manually resubmit computations after errors.
supporting_quote: Recently, there have been efforts to address the straggler effect with software tools such as GNU Parallel [23] that attempt to dynamically distribute the sub-tasks across CPU cores. However, these tools do not address fault tolerance.

Slurm's fault tolerance ensures that when jobs go bad... they do not adversely affect other jobs. However, it is still up to the user/developer to write software that is robust enough to prevent the need for re-submitting jobs

chunks.text: The authors propose a design strategy for integrating actors into legacy batch-based scientific applications that interface with C/C++. The strategy targets workloads with many independent iterative sub-simulations that follow a read–compute–write pattern and have heterogeneous runtimes. It introduces three actor roles: a job_actor to supervise execution and error handling, a file_access_actor to mediate I/O and shared data structures, and subsimulation_actors to run each sub-simulation concurrently.
supporting_quote: Our design strategy specifically targets applications that meet the following criteria: The application is written in a language that can easily interface with C/C++.
Applications that meet these criteria can integrate the actor model by implementing three types of actors: a job_actor, a file_access_actor, and a subsimulation_actor.

chunks.text: SUMMA-Actors implements the actor-based design in SUMMA using the C++ Actor Framework (CAF). It provides a job_actor to initialize Fortran state, spawn worker actors, and supervise errors, plus a file_access_actor that performs NetCDF I/O and coordinates shared input/output structures. Each GRU is simulated by an hru_actor, enabling many GRUs to run independently and concurrently, with scheduling handled by CAF’s work-stealing scheduler.
supporting_quote: we took the proposed design strategy from Sect. 2.3 using CAF [7] and applied it to SUMMA to create a version called SUMMA-Actors.
the scheduling of the hru_actors is handled by CAF's scheduler, which is based on a work-stealing algorithm

chunks.text: An additional actor, summa_actor, is introduced to control batching inside an application instance to limit memory usage. It can split an initial request (e.g., 1000 GRUs) into smaller batches based on a configurable maximum size specified in a JSON configuration file. This provides flexibility in managing RAM constraints while preserving parallelism across hru_actor computations.
supporting_quote: One additional actor type, the summa_actor, was implemented to provide some extra flexibility
the summa_actor can be configured to split them into smaller batches of 125, 250, or 500 GRUs.

chunks.text: Fault tolerance in SUMMA-Actors is implemented via actor supervision, where failures from individual hru_actors are handled without aborting the whole job. The job_actor can re-spawn failed hru_actors with adjusted parameters and can limit retries via a maximum-attempts setting. For the benchmark, a known resolution strategy halves the timestep and retries the failing GRU until it succeeds or reaches the retry limit.
supporting_quote: Errors that arise from hru_actors are handled individually by re-spawning any failed hru_actors with adjusted parameters.
we implement an error resolution scheme that halves the timestep size and re-runs the GRU.

chunks.text: The evaluation compares three execution approaches for the same continental-scale SUMMA workload: SUMMA-Actors, standard SUMMA with manual sub-tasking inside Slurm array jobs, and SUMMA with GNU Parallel for dynamic load balancing of sub-tasks. All experiments are run on two Alliance Canada supercomputers (Graham and Niagara), with performance measured using wall-clock time, CPU efficiency (via Slurm seff), CPU utilization, and fault tolerance outcomes.
supporting_quote: We ran a large-scale simulation to compare SUMMA-Actors against two different job submission strategies for SUMMA.
performance was measured in terms of wall-clock time, CPU efficiency, CPU utilization, and fault tolerance.

chunks.text: Strong scaling of SUMMA-Actors is tested by running five jobs of 1000 GRUs each using 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32 CPU cores, and comparing wall-clock time as cores increase. SUMMA is also run with a single core on the same batches to check whether actorization introduces appreciable overhead at baseline. The expectation is near-ideal scaling because GRU computations are independent and actors are lightweight.
supporting_quote: five jobs of 1000 GRUs were assembled... and submitted using 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32 CPU cores.
We also ran the same five jobs with SUMMA using a single CPU core to determine whether SUMMA-Actors incurs any extra cost

chunks.text: To quantify actor overhead, the authors profile a SUMMA-Actors job on Graham using Intel VTune hotspots analysis. The analysis reports CPU time by module to see how much time is spent in original SUMMA code versus actor infrastructure (the application’s actor definitions and CAF core library). This profiling focuses on a job computing 4,000 GRUs on a full node.
supporting_quote: we profiled the first job from the SUMMA-Actors Graham submission using the VTune profiler from Intel.
This job used an entire node to compute the first 4,000 GRUs of North America
