chunks.text: The main benchmark is a hydrological simulation over North America consisting of 517,315 GRUs, each with a single HRU, using forcing data from 1979 to 2019 at an hourly timestep. The workload is embarrassingly parallel because lateral flux coupling between HRUs is absent in this configuration. The study also states that the dataset contains three GRUs that fail under default settings and can be fixed by reducing the timestep.
supporting_quote: The simulation consists of 517,315 GRUs using forcing data from 1979 to 2019 with an hourly timestep.
We know that the dataset includes three GRUs that fail under the default SUMMA settings.

chunks.text: Experiments are conducted on two Digital Research Alliance of Canada clusters: Graham and Niagara. Graham is heterogeneous with Broadwell CPUs, and Niagara is homogeneous with Skylake CPUs and hyperthreading enabled. To ensure consistency, only Broadwell CPUs are used on Graham and only Skylake CPUs are used on Niagara for the comparisons.
supporting_quote: Graham is a heterogeneous compute cluster... It consists of 1,185 nodes with a total of 41,548 CPU cores
Niagara is a homogeneous cluster... It consists of 2,024 nodes with a total of 80,640 CPU cores.

chunks.text: On Graham, the benchmark uses a Slurm array of 130 jobs with 4,000 GRUs per job (plus a smaller last job), allocating entire 32-core Broadwell nodes for a total of 4,160 CPUs. Standard SUMMA divides each job into 32 sub-tasks of 125 GRUs, while SUMMA with GNU Parallel divides each job into 160 sub-tasks of 25 GRUs. SUMMA-Actors does not require manual sub-division for load balancing.
supporting_quote: job arrays consisting of 130 jobs with 4,000 GRUs per job
For the SUMMA GNU Parallel simulation, each job was divided into 160 sub-tasks of 25 GRUs each

chunks.text: On Niagara, the benchmark uses a Slurm array of 104 jobs with 5,000 GRUs per job (plus a smaller last job), allocating entire 40-core Skylake nodes and submitting with cpus_per_task=80 due to hyperthreading. Standard SUMMA divides each job into 80 sub-tasks of 63 GRUs, while GNU Parallel uses 250 sub-tasks of 20 GRUs. This setup aims to exploit extra threads and reduce stragglers through smaller tasks.
supporting_quote: job arrays consisting of 104 jobs with 5,000 GRUs per job
Because the Niagara system has hyperthreading enabled, jobs were submitted using the Slurm setting cpus_per_task=80.

chunks.text: On Graham, SUMMA-Actors achieves the best overall runtime, with total wall-clock time summed across jobs of 667.01 h versus 875.05 h for standard SUMMA and 743.58 h for SUMMA with GNU Parallel. This corresponds to a 26.98% reduction compared to SUMMA and 10.86% compared to GNU Parallel. The paper reports that SUMMA-Actors finishes with the shortest wall-clock time for every job in the array.
supporting_quote: the total wall-clock times for SUMMA-Actors, SUMMA, and SUMMA GNU Parallel were 667.01 h, 875.05 h, and 743.58 h, respectively.
SUMMA-Actors reduces the overall wall-clock time by 26.98% when compared to SUMMA and 10.86% when compared to SUMMA GNU Parallel.

chunks.text: On Graham, CPU efficiency averages are highest for SUMMA-Actors at 98.30%, compared to 85.25% for SUMMA and 90.92% for SUMMA with GNU Parallel. The paper attributes this to better load balancing and reduced idle time, whereas standard SUMMA suffers from the straggler effect. Across jobs, SUMMA-Actors has the highest CPU efficiency in 122 of 130 jobs.
supporting_quote: The average CPU efficiency for SUMMA-Actors, SUMMA, and SUMMA GNU Parallel was 98.30%, 85.25%, and 90.92%, respectively.
SUMMA-Actors has the highest CPU efficiency for 122 jobs, while SUMMA GNU Parallel has the highest CPU efficiency for 8 jobs.

chunks.text: On Graham, SUMMA-Actors also reduces total CPU utilization compared to both baselines, indicating limited overhead for the actorization in this setting. Total CPU utilization is 20,941.47 h for SUMMA-Actors, 22,157.45 h for SUMMA, and 21,622.33 h for GNU Parallel. This is a 5.49% reduction versus SUMMA and 3.19% versus GNU Parallel.
supporting_quote: The total CPU utilization for SUMMA-Actors, SUMMA, and SUMMA GNU Parallel was 20,941.47 h, 22,157.45 h, and 21,622.33 h, respectively.
SUMMA-Actors reduces the overall CPU utilization by 5.49% when compared to SUMMA and 3.19% when compared to SUMMA GNU Parallel.

chunks.text: Fault tolerance differs sharply on Graham: SUMMA-Actors completes all jobs without manual intervention, while both SUMMA and SUMMA with GNU Parallel require three manual re-submissions each. The resubmissions for SUMMA involve larger re-run batches (125 GRUs) and take 8.25 h, 7.14 h, and 7.47 h, while GNU Parallel resubmissions are smaller (25 GRUs) and take 1.61 h, 1.69 h, and 1.65 h. SUMMA-Actors avoids these re-run cycles by retrying failed GRUs internally after halving the timestep.
supporting_quote: SUMMA-Actors completed all jobs without any manual intervention, whereas both SUMMA and SUMMA GNU Parallel required 3 re-submissions each
The re-submissions required for SUMMA had wall-clock times of, 8.25 h, 7.14 h, and 7.47 h. For SUMMA GNU Parallel, the resubmissions took 1.61 h, 1.69 h, and 1.65 h.

chunks.text: On Niagara, SUMMA-Actors again has the lowest total wall-clock time: 375.77 h versus 414.83 h for SUMMA and 420.38 h for GNU Parallel. The improvement is smaller than on Graham but remains substantial, with SUMMA-Actors faster by 9.88% compared to SUMMA and 11.20% compared to GNU Parallel. The authors also report that SUMMA-Actors has the shortest wall-clock time for every job in the Niagara array.
supporting_quote: The total wall-clock times for SUMMA-Actors, SUMMA, and SUMMA GNU Parallel were 375.77 h, 414.83 h, and 420.38 h, respectively.
SUMMA-Actors outperforms SUMMA by 9.88% and SUMMA GNU Parallel by 11.20%.

chunks.text: On Niagara, CPU efficiency remains highest for SUMMA-Actors with an average of 92.48%, compared to 81.60% for SUMMA and 84.65% for GNU Parallel. When comparing job-by-job, SUMMA-Actors has the best CPU efficiency in 91 jobs, versus 6 for SUMMA and 7 for GNU Parallel. The paper notes overall CPU efficiency is reduced versus Graham due to shorter runtimes and greater end-of-job idle effects.
supporting_quote: SUMMA-Actors, SUMMA, and SUMMA GNU Parallel have averages of 92.48%, 81.60%, and 84.65%, respectively.
SUMMA-Actors has the best performance 91 times, SUMMA has the best performance 6 times, and SUMMA GNU Parallel has the best performance 7 times.

chunks.text: On Niagara, CPU utilization totals show more overhead for SUMMA-Actors and GNU Parallel relative to SUMMA: 28,396.87 h (SUMMA-Actors), 27,472.14 h (SUMMA), and 28,688.37 h (GNU Parallel). Job-by-job comparisons show SUMMA has the lowest CPU utilization for 68 jobs, while SUMMA-Actors is lowest for 28 jobs. The authors attribute this to hyperthreading, smaller cache on Skylake relative to Broadwell, and scheduling/NUMA effects.
supporting_quote: The total CPU utilization for SUMMA-Actors, SUMMA, and SUMMA GNU Parallel were 28396.87 h, 27472.14 h, and 28688.37 h, respectively.
With the addition of hyper-threading and a smaller cache size on the Skylake CPUs compared to the Broadwell CPUs

chunks.text: Strong scaling experiments indicate that SUMMA-Actors scales well as CPU cores increase from 1 to 32 for five 1000-GRU batches. The figure and accompanying text state that scaling appears near-ideal relative to single-core performance. The paper also reports that comparing SUMMA-Actors on one core to SUMMA on one core shows no appreciable overhead for these batches.
supporting_quote: submitted using 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32 CPU cores.
there is no appreciable overhead in using SUMMA-Actors for these batches. Relative to the single CPU core performance, higher core counts appear to show ideal scaling for SUMMA-Actors

chunks.text: Profiling with VTune suggests actor overhead is negligible for the Graham job analyzed. The largest CPU time shares are in the original SUMMA library (libsumma.so, 35.4%) and standard math/runtime libraries, while the actor-definition module (summa_be) and CAF core library (libcaf_core.so) each account for less than 0.1% of CPU time. The paper links this to avoiding large message passing and keeping computation in SUMMA routines.
supporting_quote: Libsumma.so 35.4
Summa_be <0.1  Libcaf_core.so <0.1

chunks.text: SUMMA-Actors currently targets embarrassingly parallel configurations where HRU/GRU simulations are decoupled and does not support lateral flux coupling. The authors state that configurations involving lateral fluxes would make HRU sub-simulations no longer completely independent, and integrating such coupling into the actor-based design is left for future work. This limits the immediate applicability to operational modes of SUMMA without lateral coupling.
supporting_quote: At present, SUMMA-Actors does not support configurations that involve lateral fluxes because the HRU sub-simulations would no longer be completely decoupled.
The integration and subsequent parallelization of such configurations within SUMMA-Actors is a topic of future work.

chunks.text: The actor model is not portrayed as universally beneficial; the paper highlights trade-offs including higher memory usage from duplicated state and overhead from copying messages. Some frameworks allow shared state to reduce copying, but this violates actor principles and increases race-condition risk. Additionally, global mailbox designs can become bottlenecks for high-message actors, requiring architectural workarounds.
supporting_quote: First, the actor model isolates actors from each other, leading to higher memory usage through the duplication of state.
Lastly, many actor model implementations use a global mailbox, which can become a bottleneck for actors that receive frequent messages.

chunks.text: To preserve legacy Fortran data layouts and reuse existing code, SUMMA-Actors uses shared input/output structures coordinated by a single file_access_actor, which violates strict actor-model isolation. This design choice is motivated by constraints of libraries like NetCDF and HDF5 that may not allow thread-parallel file access. The paper notes that file_access_actor could be a bottleneck, though they expect it to be dominated by filesystem performance due to infrequent large I/O.
supporting_quote: Having shared states between the file_access_actor and the sub-simulation_actors does violate the principles of the actor model; however, it is necessary to maintain the original application data structure layout and re-use its source code.
some software libraries such as NetCDF and HDF5 do not allow thread parallel access to the file system.

chunks.text: The Niagara results indicate non-negligible overhead for SUMMA-Actors under certain architectural conditions. The authors suggest hyperthreading, smaller cache on Skylake compared to Broadwell, and NUMA/scheduling effects can increase cache misses or poor scheduling when tasks move across cores or NUMA zones. This can cause higher total CPU utilization even if wall-clock time improves due to better load balance.
supporting_quote: These results suggest that there is overhead associated with SUMMA-Actors and SUMMA GNU Parallel.
With the addition of hyper-threading and a smaller cache size on the Skylake CPUs compared to the Broadwell CPUs

chunks.text: The paper notes practical drawbacks of non-actor approaches in usability and portability: manual sub-tasking for SUMMA is error-prone, and GNU Parallel batch generation is described as tedious and not portable across HPC environments. Managing output logs for GNU Parallel within Slurm arrays also requires careful handling to distinguish sub-task logs. SUMMA-Actors is framed as reducing these operational complexities by internalizing load balancing and coordination.
supporting_quote: the submission process itself is prone to errors when manually sub-tasking for SUMMA.
With SUMMA GNU Parallel, we found the batch configuration generation tedious and not portable across different HPC environments.

chunks.text: The study concludes that actor-based management (SUMMA-Actors) improves resource utilization and reduces time-to-results for large ensembles of independent simulations on shared HPC systems. Across two clusters, it consistently achieves lower wall-clock time than standard SUMMA arrays and SUMMA with GNU Parallel, while also improving fault tolerance through supervised, per-GRU recovery. The authors emphasize that this can reduce both computational waste and user effort.
supporting_quote: SUMMA-Actors in fact requires less wall-clock time to perform a large hydrologic simulation over the North American continent
SUMMA-Actors shows how hierarchical failure handling can eliminate the need for users to manually re-submit jobs

chunks.text: The paper concludes that SUMMA-Actors demonstrates nearly ideal strong scaling on independent GRU workloads, indicating that the actor model can exploit increasing core counts effectively for embarrassingly parallel tasks. The scaling evidence is presented alongside a single-core comparison showing minimal baseline overhead versus SUMMA for the tested batches. This supports the claim that actorization can deliver parallel performance without heavy runtime cost.
supporting_quote: we demonstrate how the strong-scaling performance of SUMMA-Actors is nearly ideal.
higher core counts appear to show ideal scaling for SUMMA-Actors

chunks.text: A broader conclusion is that legacy Fortran applications can be converted into actor-based applications through C/C++ interoperability, extending their lifespan and enabling modern fault-tolerant execution patterns beyond MPI-centric designs. The authors argue that increasing Fortran interoperability standards make such conversions more feasible over time. SUMMA-Actors is presented as evidence that substantial reuse of existing Fortran routines is possible while gaining actor benefits.
supporting_quote: Finally, we demonstrate that Fortran applications can be converted into actors applications.
Interoperability between Fortran and C/C++ has increased in each new standard of Fortran, and this trend is expected to continue.

chunks.text: Hydrologic model studies commonly summarize agreement between observed and simulated streamflow using aggregated efficiency metrics such as MSE, NSE, and KGE. These metrics are convenient but their interpretation is often reduced to a qualitative “closer to ideal is better” view. The paper frames benchmarking as the practice of setting a-priori expectations for model performance by comparing a model to simpler alternatives rather than relying on absolute metric values.
supporting_quote: A common approach ... is to use some sort of aggregated efficiency metric ... Common metrics include the Mean Squared Error, Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency ... and Kling-Gupta Efficiency
This is often referred to as benchmarking: setting a-priori expectations for model performance

chunks.text: The paper positions simple benchmark models as tools that represent what should be expected, providing understandable context about explanatory power for a case study. Examples include regime statistics like seasonal cycles and simple precipitation-to-runoff transformations based on runoff ratios. Such benchmarks can indicate the level of predictability implied by the data and inputs before deploying complex hydrologic models.
supporting_quote: simple models that, in the words of Seibert et al. (2018): 'represent what could and should be expected'

Simple streamflow benchmarks could, for example, be statistical descriptors of the flow regime (such as the average seasonal cycle), or simple transformations of precipitation into streamflow based on average runoff-ratios

chunks.text: The study focuses on lower benchmarks as a way to define minimum expectations, following the definition that lower benchmarks set a priori expectations while upper benchmarks relate to maximum predictability. It argues that fixed thresholds like those associated with the mean-flow reference in NSE/KGE do not generalize to the proposed benchmark ensemble, because each benchmark must be calculated on calibration data and validated on an independent period.
supporting_quote: Clark et al. (2021) ... defines lower benchmarks as setting certain a priori expectations for models, whereas upper benchmark define the maximum predictability of the system.
the benchmarks should be seen as very simple models that need to be calculated/calibrated from/on the data, and validated on an independent part of the time series.

chunks.text: The paper aims to use an ensemble of very simple benchmark models to set expectations for hydrologic model performance during calibration and validation across a large sample of catchments. It intends to empirically demonstrate regional differences in expected performance, show that expectations are often far above the long-term mean-flow benchmark, and argue that benchmark ensembles provide objective, interpretable context for efficiency scores.
supporting_quote: In this commentary I use an ensemble of very simple models to set expectations for model performance during calibration ... and validation ... on a large (6250) sample of catchments.

I will show empirically (1) that expectations for model performance are subject to certain regional differences; (2) that in almost all cases one might reasonably expect model performance to be (far) above the long-term mean flow benchmark; and (3) that using an ensemble of simple benchmarks is a computationally efficient

chunks.text: A secondary goal is to provide a practical pathway for implementing benchmark ensembles by offering a Python package (HydroBM) that reproduces the listed benchmarks and computes common performance metrics. The package is intended to make it easy to apply benchmarks consistently to multiple basins and data formats, including an option to use a rain-plus-melt flux for snow-affected basins.
supporting_quote: I developed a simple Python package called HydroBM that implements the benchmarks listed in Table 1
The package also includes the basic snow accumulation and melt model that can be used to estimate a 'rain plus melt' flux.

chunks.text: Aggregating model errors into a single efficiency score can hide important information and create interpretation challenges. The paper notes that such metrics can suffer from information loss, sampling uncertainty, lack of universal applicability across hydrologic problems, and unintuitive behavior across different data partitions. This makes it difficult to infer model fidelity from a single number and encourages overreliance on vague notions of “high” performance.
supporting_quote: there is a distinct loss of information when aggregating a time series of model errors into a single number
the metrics may be subject to considerable sampling uncertainty
not every metric is equally applicable to every type of hydrological problem
the fidelity of the model system is often difficult to discern from single metrics

chunks.text: Using the long-term mean flow as a universal benchmark is too crude at sub-annual time steps and does not constrain model performance meaningfully. This leaves a large range of possible scores between the benchmark and the ideal metric value, shifting the burden to the modeler to decide whether a score is “high enough.” Such decisions are hard to reproduce and communicate and may become codified into inappropriate performance-class tables.
supporting_quote: the long-term mean flow benchmark is very crude predictor of streamflow at sub-annual time steps
This means the benchmark does not impose many constraints on the model of interest and leaves a wide range of scores between the benchmark and the metric's ideal value.
the judgement calls involved in deciding when a score is 'high' are not particularly objective and take place in the opaque areas of expert knowledge and experience.

chunks.text: Metric thresholds and value judgments do not transfer reliably across basins, regimes, or time periods. The mean-flow reference in NSE is an inappropriate baseline in basins with strong seasonality, making it easy to “outperform” the benchmark, while it may be harder elsewhere. Benchmark suitability can also vary within a year (e.g., dry season vs melt season), leading to unintuitive behavior when computing efficiencies over different periods.
supporting_quote: what constitutes a good score in one scenario does not necessarily imply a good score in a different experiment.
the reference model in the NSE (i.e., the long-term mean flow) is an inappropriate baseline model for any basin with a distinct seasonal flow regime
The mean flow may be more appropriate for certain parts of the regime than for others ... in snow-dominated basins the mean may be close ... during the dry season, but far ... during the melt phase.

chunks.text: The approach defines lower benchmarks using an ensemble of simple models computed from a calibration period and evaluated on an independent validation period. Because these benchmarks are derived from data, they do not correspond to fixed thresholds like NSE=0 or KGE=1-√2; instead, each benchmark yields its own calibration and validation scores. A seasonal-cycle benchmark is illustrated as repeating mean daily flows computed from the calibration period.
supporting_quote: expectations for model performance are defined through an ensemble of very simple benchmark models.
the benchmarks should be seen as very simple models that need to be calculated/calibrated from/on the data, and validated on an independent part of the time series.
the seasonal cycle may be calculated as a repeating sequence of mean daily flow values

chunks.text: Benchmarks are selected based on simple hypotheses and grouped into three categories: streamflow-only regime descriptors, rainfall-runoff-ratio transformations of precipitation, and very parsimonious empirical catchment-function models. Streamflow-only benchmarks assume regime stability; rainfall-runoff-ratio benchmarks assume a representative ratio from observations can be applied to new periods; parsimonious models include lagging and smoothing scaled precipitation to mimic travel time and diffusion.
supporting_quote: The benchmarks used in this work ... are derived from very simple hypotheses and can be divided into three categories
Benchmarks that rely on streamflow data only.
Benchmarks that rely on rainfall-runoff ratios.

Benchmarks that rely on (very) parsimonious models ... Adjusted Precipitation Benchmark (APB) ... shifted in time by some optimal lag ... Adjusted Smoothed Precipitation Benchmark (ASPB) ... smoothed by a moving average

chunks.text: The benchmark ensemble includes 17 specific benchmarks spanning mean/median annual flow, monthly and daily mean/median seasonal-cycle predictors, multiple runoff-ratio scalings from annual to per-timestep, and two calibrated precipitation benchmarks with lag and smoothing. Table 1 enumerates these benchmarks and their descriptions, including APB (optimized lag) and ASPB (optimized lag plus window length).
supporting_quote: TABLE 1 Overview of simple benchmarks.
17 | Adjusted Smoothed Precipitation Benchmark | As (11), smoothed by a moving average of optimized window length.
16 | Adjusted Precipitation Benchmark | As (11), with the whole time series shifted by an optimized lag value.

chunks.text: Benchmarks are treated like model experiments: computed or calibrated on a calibration period and then used to simulate the validation period. The study enforces a minimum of 2 years per period to prevent trivial perfect fits for daily mean/median benchmarks in very short records. Performance is computed with MSE, RMSE, NSE, and KGE, with the discussion focusing mainly on KGE.
supporting_quote: Each benchmark is calculated/calibrated and validated akin to a standard model configuration exercise.
I arbitrarily selected a minimum data length of at least 2 years for each period
I calculated MSE, Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) and Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE) scores for all benchmarks

chunks.text: To account for snow effects, a simple degree-day snow accumulation and melt routine is applied to derive a 'rain plus melt' flux, using a 0°C threshold and fixed melt rate. For APB and ASPB, integer parameters (lag; lag plus smoothing window) are optimized by brute-force search to minimize MSE, similar to the approach in Schaefli & Gupta (2007).
supporting_quote: I used a very simple degree-day snow accumulation and melt model ... The threshold for snowfall and melt was set at 0 C, and the melt rate was kept fixed at 3 mm C1 day1

Parameters for the Adjusted Precipitation Benchmark (APB; 1 integer parameter representing time lag) and Adjusted Smoothed Precipitation Benchmark (ASPB; 2 integer parameters representing time lag and smoothing window size) were optimized through a brute-force approach
found the value(s) that resulted in the lowest Mean Square Error (MSE)

chunks.text: Implementation is provided as the HydroBM Python package, which runs the benchmark ensemble and computes efficiency scores. It supports netCDF and CSV inputs via xarray and pandas, includes the snow routine, and exposes adjustable snow parameters. The package is distributed on PyPI with community contributions via GitHub.
supporting_quote: I developed a simple Python package called HydroBM that implements the benchmarks listed in Table 1
It can deal with hydro-meteorological data from both netCDF and CSV files through xarray and pandas respectively.
The package is available through the pypi repository
https://github.com/wknoben/hydrobm

chunks.text: The analysis uses precipitation, temperature, and streamflow from the global Caravan dataset, which aggregates multiple CAMELS-style regional datasets in a standardized format. This standardization enables consistent benchmark application across many basins. The study applies benchmarks across thousands of basins drawn from these sources.
supporting_quote: The precipitation, temperature and streamflow data used in this work are obtained from the Caravan dataset
Caravan aggregates data from the CAMELS ... CAMELS-AUS ... CAMELS-BR ... CAMELS-CL ... CAMELS-GB ... HYSETS, and LamaH-CE ... in a standardized format

chunks.text: Basins are filtered to require at least 2 years of data in both calibration and validation periods, to avoid degenerate perfect calibration for daily climatology benchmarks on very short records. This filtering removed 571 basins and left 6259 basins spanning 4 to 40 years of data. The stated target sample is about 6250 catchments.
supporting_quote: I arbitrarily selected a minimum data length of at least 2 years for each period
This resulted in 571 basins being removed from the analysis, leaving 6259 basins with at least 4 and up to 40 years of data
on a large (6250) sample of catchments

chunks.text: For climate context, the paper compares benchmark performance against aridity and snowiness indicators. Aridity is computed as PET/P using mean annual PET and precipitation from HydroATLAS attributes provided with Caravan. Snow influence is discussed via “fraction precipitation as snow.”
supporting_quote: Figure 5 shows a simple attempt to investigate the second by comparing benchmark performance against two common climate indicators (aridity, and fraction precipitation as snow).
Aridity was calculated as PET/P, using mean annual PET and P obtained from the HydroATLAS attributes in Caravan.

chunks.text: Across basins, the best-performing benchmark in the ensemble often achieves validation KGE scores higher than the traditional mean-flow reference (KGE = 1-√2). Many of these benchmark scores could be interpreted as “acceptable” or “good,” implying that unseen streamflow can be relatively predictable even under very limited hydrologic assumptions. Calibration-period benchmark scores are even higher, emphasizing that mean-flow baselines impose little constraint on model fitting.
supporting_quote: In all cases, performance on unseen data is better than what the traditional mean flow benchmark would indicate (i.e., KGE = 1-2)
in many cases these performance scores would be considered 'acceptable' or even 'good'.
the capability of the benchmarks to replicate calibration data is even better, highlighting that the mean flow benchmark ... does not impose many constraints on model calibration

chunks.text: No single benchmark dominates everywhere: rankings show different benchmarks perform best in different basins and regions. The mean annual flow benchmark is typically among the worst predictors during both calculation and evaluation, and it is never ranked as the best benchmark. Median annual flow tends to perform even worse, though it occasionally performs well for unseen data in some datasets.
supporting_quote: No single benchmark obtains the highest scores in every case
The traditional mean annual flow benchmark ... is typically one of the worst predictors of streamflow, both during benchmark calculation and for unseen data.
it is telling that ... the mean annual flow (benchmark 1) is never ranked as the most accurate or best predictive benchmark out of all the possibilities tested.
Only the median annual flow (benchmark 2) performs worse across most cases

chunks.text: The daily mean flow benchmark fits calibration data consistently well but has limited predictive power relative to other benchmarks, potentially due to short observational records that poorly define the true seasonal signal. Among rainfall-runoff-ratio approaches, the “monthly rainfall-runoff ratio to monthly precipitation totals” benchmark (benchmark 12) shows unexpectedly strong fitting and predictive capability, often comparable to or better than daily mean flow despite only monthly variability in its estimates.
supporting_quote: The daily mean flow (benchmark 5; mean flow for each calendar day) provides consistently good performance during benchmark calculation ... but has somewhat limited predictive power
A potential cause may be the presence of basins with a low number of observed streamflow years.
the 'monthly runoff-ratio to monthly precipitation totals' (benchmark 12) stands out as having surprising data fitting and predictive power.
this benchmark is on par with or better than the mean daily flow benchmark (benchmark 5)

chunks.text: The simplest calibrated empirical benchmarks (APB/ASPB) are consistently among the best performers. In most regions the 2-parameter ASPB (benchmark 17) outperforms the 1-parameter APB (benchmark 16), suggesting smoothing improves predictability by representing diffusion/storage effects. Australia is an exception where the 1-parameter model performs better, implying that adding diffusive smoothing can reduce predictability there.
supporting_quote: the simple calibrated models (orange) are consistently among the best benchmarks available.
in most regions the most complex 2-parameter model (benchmark 17) shows better performance than the simpler 1-parameter model (benchmark 16).
In the Australian basins this pattern is reversed ... suggesting that ... including diffusive processes in these catchments is detrimental for predictability.

chunks.text: Benchmark performance exhibits regional variability in both calibration and validation degradation. North America, South America, and Australia show noticeable degradation from calibration to validation in many basins, while Great Britain and Central Europe show more overlap between calculation and evaluation histograms. This supports the claim that expected performance levels depend on regional hydrologic and data characteristics.
supporting_quote: Some regional differences may be observed too.
basins in North America, South America and Australia experience a distinct degradation in validation performance
the performance histograms in Great Britain and Central Europe mostly overlap.

chunks.text: A worked example shows that conceptual rainfall-runoff models with typical complexity can achieve seemingly acceptable validation KGE, but still underperform simple benchmarks in specific aspects. Benchmarks reveal stable, easily predictable low winter flows (daily mean benchmark) that all models simulate poorly, and differences in snowmelt peak shape where models produce sharper peaks than benchmarks. This illustrates how benchmark context changes interpretation of model performance and points to specific process deficits.
supporting_quote: without the context provided by the benchmarks their validation KGE scores could be considered acceptable.

one deficiency in all models is their poor prediction of low winter flows, whereas the benchmark ensemble shows that these low flows are in fact very stable across years and easily predictable (benchmark 5).
the benchmarks have lower but wider snowmelt-driven flow peaks than the models do.

chunks.text: Climate indicators relate to benchmark predictability patterns: non-arid basins often allow higher efficiency scores and show less degradation on unseen data, while arid basins show more varied performance. The paper notes this is particularly evident in CAMELS-AUS and suggests the inverse framing may be more accurate: non-arid basins are easier to achieve high scores in. Snowiness also broadly aligns with increased predictability but with substantial scatter.
supporting_quote: It is commonly said that arid places are harder to model ... perhaps the inverse is more precise: it is much easier to obtain higher efficiency scores in non-arid basins
In arid basins performance seems more varied both in terms of data-fitting ... and predictive capability
an increase in snow also roughly aligns with an increase in predictability but with considerable variation

chunks.text: The paper cautions that benchmark ensembles provide context for efficiency scores but do not establish model realism. As argued by Kirchner, efficiency scores alone are not proof of correct process representation, and a model with lower scores than benchmarks may still be useful for internal states or unassessed fluxes. Conversely, high-scoring benchmarks can be purely empirical and provide no information about internal catchment states.
supporting_quote: The concerns expressed by Kirchner (2006) still apply: the scores themselves are not indicative of model realism.
It may be that a model with lower efficiency scores than the benchmarks still provides useful information about internal catchment states or fluxes not directly assessed.
despite their high scores, the benchmark models used here provide no information about internal catchment states at all.

chunks.text: Upper benchmarks aimed at maximum predictability are acknowledged but not addressed in this work. Quantifying information content in inputs relative to outputs requires a different approach than the lower benchmark ensemble presented. The paper explicitly scopes the contribution to generalized lower benchmarks based on simple models.
supporting_quote: Upper benchmarks can be seen as an attempt to quantify the information content in model inputs in relation to the variable of interest
This requires a different approach then I apply for the lower benchmarks and is out of scope for this discussion.

chunks.text: Performance thresholds based on specific metric values are argued to be non-transferable across regions and experiments. Instead of exporting standards like fixed “acceptable” KGE/NSE ranges, the paper advocates comparing the model of interest to the performance of benchmark models tailored to the same basin and period. This is presented as a shift in thinking away from absolute thresholds and toward relative, interpretable comparisons.
supporting_quote: specific metric values do not have the same meaning in different locations
standards for acceptable performance developed in one region (or experiment), should not be uncritically exported to other regions
instead of using specific values as performance thresholds, one can compare the performance of the model of interest to that of specific (benchmark) models or ensembles of benchmark models.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that benchmarking provides essential context for interpreting hydrologic model performance, and that the traditional mean annual flow baseline is an extremely low bar. Outperforming mean flow should be treated as a requirement rather than evidence of skill. An ensemble of simple benchmarks offers a practical, objective way to estimate expected calibration fit and validation predictability for a catchment.
supporting_quote: I show here that in almost all cases this is the lowest possible bar to ask a model to pass, and that outperforming this benchmark should be seen as a requirement and not an indication of skilful models.
an ensemble of very simple benchmark models ... can be used to provide an indication of how easily the calibration data can be replicated and how predictable unseen data in a catchment may be.

chunks.text: The work argues for presenting efficiency metrics in the context of benchmark ensembles rather than in isolation or against generic performance threshold tables. It emphasizes that benchmark ensembles enable more deliberate interpretation, including requirements like predicting deviations from the seasonal cycle. The author hopes this motivates a community shift toward benchmarking-informed reporting.
supporting_quote: I hope this work provides the hydrologic modelling community with both the means and the motivation to step away from presenting model performance scores in isolation or compared to 'performance threshold tables', and shift towards presenting these metrics in the context of a benchmark ensemble.

Relying on more than just the mean annual flow also lets us define more taxing requirements for acceptable model performance, such as requiring that a model can predict deviations from the seasonal cycle.

chunks.text: Computational cost is presented as minimal: applying the benchmark ensemble (including rain-plus-melt derivation) takes minutes per basin, supporting feasibility at scale. The paper highlights that expected achievable scores vary by region (e.g., Australia vs HYSETS), reinforcing that benchmarking should be catchment- and dataset-specific rather than based on universal thresholds.
supporting_quote: calculating a benchmark ensemble (including the derivation of a 'rain plus melt' flux) takes on average 3 min per basin, and 5 min at most.
in the Australian case, KGE scores above 0.8 seem beyond the ability of this benchmark ensemble
whereas in a large number of the HYSETS basins such scores could be considered a minimum requirement for models

chunks.text: Large-domain hydrologic prediction needs models that perform robustly across diverse basins. Two competing paradigms are emphasized: a single universal model structure versus a multi-model mosaic where different model structures are used in different places. The paper argues that single-model approaches face limits due to incomplete process equations, insufficient representation of diverse landscapes, and difficulties in configuration under heterogeneous data. Multi-model mosaics are appealing but hinge on credible model selection for each basin.
supporting_quote: The need for robust predictions of water availability and threats across large spatial scales ... requires models that work well across a variety of landscapes
An alternative paradigm is the "multi-model mosaic" approach ... where different models are selected for different regions

chunks.text: Hydrologic model selection is often based on aggregated efficiency metrics like NSE and KGE, but these single-number scores can hide important information and lead to equifinality. Many different model structures can yield very similar efficiency values, making it hard to identify a uniquely best model. The paper situates this challenge within broad evidence that multiple models can be close-to-best for most basins when judged by KGE-based comparisons.
supporting_quote: Differences in the performance of different models are typically expressed through differences in metrics such as the Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) or Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE)
equifinality ... different simulations ... may obtain very similar or identical efficiency scores, as a consequence of reducing an entire time series of errors into a single number

chunks.text: Recent work highlights that efficiency scores have substantial sampling uncertainty because a small subset of time steps can dominate total error. As a result, the exact validation period or days included can materially change NSE/KGE and thus change model rankings. The paper builds on bootstrap-jackknife/bootstrapping approaches (gumboot) to estimate uncertainty intervals for KGE and argues this is not yet standard practice in model selection studies.
supporting_quote: Recent work refers to this concept as "sampling uncertainty" in objective function values
for the majority of these basins tolerance intervals around NSE and KGE scores are larger than 0.10 NSE or KGE "points"

chunks.text: The study revisits a prior 36-model, 559-basin comparison and explicitly accounts for sampling uncertainty in validation KGE. The overarching aim is to determine how many distinct model structures are actually needed to achieve performance that is indistinguishable from the best model in each basin when uncertainty is considered. This directly informs large-domain multi-model mosaic design by quantifying the minimum model set required for domain coverage.
supporting_quote: we explicitly account for this sampling uncertainty to determine the number of models that are needed to simulate hydrologic processes across large spatial domains
we revisit the model comparison study of Knoben et al. (2020), who calibrate 36 different lumped conceptual models for 559 basins

chunks.text: Three research questions are defined using performance equivalence based on the 5th–95th sampling uncertainty interval of the best model’s KGE in each basin. The questions quantify (1) how many basins each model is performance-equivalent to the best model, (2) how many models are performance-equivalent within each basin, and (3) the minimum number of models required to cover all basins with performance-equivalent simulations.
supporting_quote: Uncertainty bounds ... refer to the 5th to 95th objective function sampling uncertainty interval calculated for the best model
3. What is the minimum number of models needed to obtain simulations with performance that is within the sampling uncertainty interval of the best model in each basin?

chunks.text: Model selection across large domains is commonly based on validation KGE/NSE values aggregated over long time series, yet these metrics can be ambiguous because different models can have similar scores. The paper frames this as equifinality in model identification: numerous model structures may be effectively indistinguishable in performance even if their internal dynamics differ. This ambiguity complicates implementing a multi-model mosaic because it becomes unclear which model should be chosen for a location.
supporting_quote: it is difficult to unambiguously select one model over another based on the aggregate NSE and KGE metrics alone
model structure equifinality tends to be high ... it is typically possible to find multiple models that produce simulations with close-to-best performance for a given basin

chunks.text: A key exacerbating issue is sampling uncertainty: a small number of days can contribute a large fraction of total model error, so the calculated KGE depends strongly on the sampled period. This means that model rankings based on single KGE values may be unstable and differences between models may be smaller than uncertainty intervals. The paper notes that explicitly accounting for such sampling uncertainty is uncommon and its effect on model selection across large domains is not well known.
supporting_quote: only 10 out of approximately 4000 time steps contribute some 70 % of the total model error

explicitly accounting for the sampling uncertainty inherent in aggregated model performance scores is not (yet) common practice, and it is unknown to what extent sampling uncertainty affects attempts at model selection

chunks.text: The workflow combines CAMELS observations with precomputed simulations from Knoben et al. (2020), then estimates KGE sampling uncertainty using gumboot. KGE uncertainty is computed via nonoverlapping-block bootstrapping of water years, generating percentile estimates (5th, 50th, 95th). The analysis then filters models per basin to retain those whose validation KGE lies within the uncertainty bounds of the basin’s best model.
supporting_quote: we can calculate the KGE scores and quantify their associated uncertainty with the gumboot package
gumboot returns ... the 5th, 50th, and 95th percentile estimates of the KGE score through a "nonoverlapping block" bootstrapping method

chunks.text: Gumboot is run with default settings to build 1000 bootstrapped realizations using October as the first month of the water year, and requiring at least 100 valid (larger than 0) flow values in a water year. For computational simplicity, uncertainty bounds are computed only for the best model (highest validation KGE) in each basin. Models with efficiency below the best model’s 5th percentile KGE are excluded from further analysis in that basin.
supporting_quote: This creates 1000 bootstrapped realizations, with October as the first month of the water year, and a water year must contain at least 100 valid (larger than 0) flow values
we only calculate the KGE uncertainty bounds for the best model ... we exclude all models with efficiency scores below the 5th percentile estimate

chunks.text: To answer the minimum-models question, the paper formulates coverage as a set-cover style optimization solved via linear programming. Each model defines a subset of basins where it is performance-equivalent to the best model. The optimizer searches for the smallest number of model subsets whose union covers the full basin set, avoiding infeasible brute-force enumeration of all model combinations.
supporting_quote: A faster way is to rewrite the problem as a linear programming problem
find the smallest number of subsets (i.e., models) needed to cover the full set (i.e., all basins)

chunks.text: The analysis is repeated for a low-flow-focused objective function by using KGE computed on reciprocal flows, KGE(1/Q). To handle zeros, a constant epsilon is added to observed and simulated flows at every time step, defined as 1% of mean observed flow. Steps of uncertainty estimation and model selection are then rerun on these low-flow calibration results to test sensitivity to the objective function.
supporting_quote: repeat steps (2) and (3) using the low-flow calibration results ... use the reciprocal of flows to calculate model performance as KGE(1/Q)
a constant epsilon equal to 1% of mean observed flows is added on every time step

chunks.text: Streamflow observations, gauge locations, and basin areas come from the CAMELS dataset, while simulations come from the Knoben et al. (2020) model outputs. Observed streamflow is converted from ft3 s−1 to mm d−1 using GAGES II areas provided with CAMELS to match simulation units. Basins were originally selected from CAMELS based on water balance closure and basin area error considerations.
supporting_quote: We obtained streamflow observations, gauge locations and basin areas from the CAMELS data set
We converted these observations from ft3 s−1 into mmd−1 using the GAGES II areas provided as part of the CAMELS data to match the simulations

chunks.text: The model ensemble contains 36 lumped conceptual models from MARRMoT, spanning a wide complexity range from 1 store/1 parameter to 6 stores/15 parameters, and includes variants mimicking published models. Only 8 models include a snow module; 28 have no explicit snow accumulation/melt capability. Models are calibrated on streamflow using KGE, with 10-year calibration and 10-year validation periods for each basin in the underlying dataset.
supporting_quote: Using a selection of 36 conceptual models and 559 basins
varying from a simple 1 store ... 1 parameter bucket model to ... up to 6 stores and 15 parameters. Of these models, 8 include a snow module

chunks.text: Sampling-uncertainty analysis is conducted on 555 basins because four basins cannot be processed by gumboot due to years with no observed flow. The issue affects bootstrapped computation of standard deviations and correlations. These four basins are excluded from all subsequent analyses, including performance-equivalence filtering and model-set optimization.
supporting_quote: We can use gumboot in 555 out of 559 basins. The remaining four basins contain years with no observed flow
These four basins are excluded from further analysis

chunks.text: Accounting for sampling uncertainty reveals that every model can be performance-equivalent to the best model in a nontrivial number of basins. Even the worst model is performance-equivalent in at least 50 basins. The most widely performance-equivalent model (m28; 4 state variables, 12 parameters) falls within the best-model uncertainty bounds in 362 basins, almost two-thirds of cases, despite lacking a snow routine.
supporting_quote: even the worst of these is performanceequivalent to the best model in at least 50 basins
The model that is performance-equivalent to the best model in the most basins is ... m28 ... within the uncertainty bounds ... in 362 basins

chunks.text: Performance-equivalent model counts vary widely by basin. In most basins, numerous models fall within the best model’s uncertainty bounds, indicating strong equifinality once sampling uncertainty is considered. In 7 basins (about 1.5% of cases), all 36 models are performance-equivalent to the best model under the defined uncertainty bounds.
supporting_quote: the number of performanceequivalent models varies strongly between basins
in 7 basins (approximately 1.5 % of all cases) every single model in the ensemble obtains validation KGE scores that are within the uncertainty bounds of the best model

chunks.text: Spatially, lower counts of performance-equivalent models occur in snow-influenced regions because only 8 tested models include snow routines. Mountain ranges and northeastern/Great Lakes regions show reduced equivalence counts, which the authors attribute to the experimental design rather than a universal geographic rule. Outside snow-dominated areas, the spatial pattern in the number of performance-equivalent models is weak.
supporting_quote: Only eight of the tested model structures include a snow routine ... regions that experience more snowfall ... thus have lower numbers of performance-equivalent models
Across the remainder of the domain where snow plays a smaller role, no clear patterns in the number of performanceequivalent models exist

chunks.text: A small set of models can cover most basins with performance-equivalent simulations when sampling uncertainty is used as the equivalence criterion. One model (m28) covers almost two-thirds of basins. Four models (m28, m34, m37, m36) cover more than 95% of basins, and 10 models are sufficient to cover all basins in the 555-basin analysis.
supporting_quote: a single model (m28 ... ) is performance-equivalent ... in almost two-thirds of the basins
only four models (m28, m34, m37, m36) are needed to get performance equivalence in more than 95 % of basins ... Another six models are needed to fill the remaining 21 basins

chunks.text: The models selected for the minimal covering set show interpretable process capabilities: m34 and m37 perform well in snow-dominated basins due to snow accumulation/melt routines, including degree-day snow and refreezing capability. The fourth key model (m36) is distinguished by representing losing streams, though its role is uncertain. The remaining basins require a few additional models in small counts, which the authors interpret as likely noise from data and parameter uncertainty.
supporting_quote: The next two models (m34 ... and m37 ... ) perform well in snow-dominated basins, due to their snow accumulation and melt routines
The distinguishing feature of the fourth model (m36 ... ) is its ability to represent losing streams

chunks.text: When using the low-flow objective KGE(1/Q), performance equivalence is reduced and more models are needed for coverage. The worst model is performance-equivalent in only 1 basin (versus 53 under KGE(Q)), and the best model is performance-equivalent in 263 basins (versus 362). Under KGE(1/Q), 8 models are needed for 95% coverage and nearly double the number of models is needed for full-domain coverage compared to the KGE(Q) case.
supporting_quote: the worst model is only performance-equivalent to the best model in a single basin (compared to 53 before)
almost double the number of models is needed ... with eight models being needed to obtain 95 % coverage

chunks.text: The paper argues that sampling uncertainty makes it hard to distinguish among competing models using aggregated objective scores: scores can eliminate extremely poor models, but cannot reliably identify uniquely appropriate structures beyond obvious needs (e.g., snow module in snowy basins). This challenges the idea that many different models are necessary for higher accuracy in large-sample KGE-based selection frameworks. The authors caution that high efficiency does not guarantee internally realistic process representations.
supporting_quote: accounting for sampling uncertainty makes it very difficult to distinguish among competing models
high efficiency scores do not guarantee internally realistic models

chunks.text: A methodological limitation is that sampling uncertainty is computed only for the best model in each basin, while other models are judged using their full-period KGE values. This can create edge cases where a model barely falls within the best model’s uncertainty bounds while its own uncertainty distribution would largely lie outside. The authors suggest future work should compute uncertainty for all models and compare distributions via fractional overlap.
supporting_quote: we only account for the sampling uncertainty of a single model in each basin
Future work could account for the objective function sampling uncertainty in all models and use the fractional overlap of objective function distributions

chunks.text: Another limitation is that the initial selection of the “best model” is based on full validation-period KGE without incorporating sampling uncertainty at that selection step. The authors note that full-period scores correlate with gumboot’s median (50th percentile) estimates but show scatter. They propose alternative definitions of best model that trade off estimated median performance and uncertainty-interval size.
supporting_quote: we select the single model in each basin using the KGE scores obtained for the full validation period, without accounting for sampling uncertainty
these full-period scores correlate with the estimated 50th percentile scores obtained with gumboot, but some scatter is present

chunks.text: The model ensemble is a limited subset of available hydrologic models and is imbalanced for snow processes: only eight conceptual models include a dedicated snow component. The authors highlight that the strong performance-equivalence of a “no-snow” model across many basins motivates future experiments that connect conceptual cores to snow routines. They also note value in extending comparisons to physics-based and machine learning models.
supporting_quote: The models used in this work were a convenient choice but represent a subset of the wider range of hydrologic models available
only eight of these models have a dedicated snow component

chunks.text: Findings are conditional on modelling purpose, illustrated by different results between KGE(Q) and KGE(1/Q). The authors suggest follow-up work that evaluates stability of conclusions for specific flow regimes (e.g., low-flow and high-flow percentiles). This underscores that geographic generalization may be easier than generalizing across different objective functions and decision contexts.
supporting_quote: The findings presented in this paper are thus conditional on the chosen objective function
followup work could investigate the stability of our conclusions for simulation of different flow percentiles

chunks.text: The study concludes that explicitly accounting for KGE sampling uncertainty greatly increases apparent equifinality and reduces the number of distinct models needed for large-domain streamflow simulation. Under KGE(Q), only four models are needed to achieve performance-equivalent simulations in 95% of basins, and 10 models cover 100% of basins in the analyzed set. The authors emphasize that KGE-based model selection would otherwise suggest nearly every model is “best somewhere,” but uncertainty-aware selection favors a small, carefully chosen model set.
supporting_quote: Only four models are needed to get simulations with acceptable accuracy in 95 % of basins. With 10 models, 100 % coverage is obtained
If we were to select models based on their validation KGE scores only, almost all of the investigated 36 models would be selected for at least a handful of basins

chunks.text: For a low-flow-focused objective function (KGE(1/Q)), the same qualitative message holds—sampling-uncertainty-aware selection reduces the number of models needed versus picking the best model per basin—but more models are required than for KGE(Q). Specifically, 8 models cover 95% of basins and 19 models are needed for full coverage. This reinforces that required model diversity depends on the objective function, even when uncertainty is accounted for.
supporting_quote: only 8 models are needed to cover 95 % of basins and 19 models for 100 % coverage
These findings hold for a different objective function aimed at low-flow simulation: the KGE of the reciprocal of flows

chunks.text: The authors interpret the results to mean that, within common large-domain workflows relying on aggregated objective scores, “uniqueness of models” does not necessarily translate into appreciable performance gains. They argue that progress toward realistic model selection likely requires perceptual models, hypothesis-testing links between processes and equations, and diagnostic evaluation beyond aggregate error metrics. Until then, KGE-based selection with sampling uncertainty suggests that a small handful of models can be adequate for streamflow simulation across large domains.
supporting_quote: the results of this analysis suggest that uniqueness of models does not necessarily lead to appreciable increases in model performance
diagnostic model evaluation approaches that go beyond aggregated error metrics are needed to quantify each models strengths and weaknesses

chunks.text: Rice is Nepal’s primary staple crop and a major contributor to agricultural livelihoods and GDP. Production is vulnerable to climate change and increasing extreme events, making timely, reliable, large-scale yield estimates important for food security planning. Remote sensing indicators combined with machine learning have become attractive alternatives to traditional statistical and process-based crop models due to scalability and reduced input requirements.
supporting_quote: In Nepal, it is the primary staple crop, cultivated by 76% of all agricultural households and contributing 21% to the agricultural gross domestic product (GDP)
To mitigate climate risks and ensure food security... it is imperative... to have timely and reliable rice yield prediction.
To address these challenges, remote sensing-based indicators of vegetation growth status combined with novel machine learning (ML) approaches offer improved yield prediction accuracy

chunks.text: Traditional yield modeling approaches have tradeoffs: statistical regressions can be computationally simple but often lack spatial generalization, while process-based crop models can be accurate but are data-intensive, costly, and difficult to scale. These constraints are especially problematic in developing-country contexts where detailed soils, management, and weather inputs may be limited. This motivates data-driven methods that learn relationships from multi-source satellite and environmental datasets.
supporting_quote: Traditional statistical methods predict yields... While these methods offer simpler computation... they face significant limitations due to their localized nature and restricted spatial generalization
process-oriented crop models... can accurately simulate crop development... but require extensive and detailed input data on local soils, crop management practices, and prevailing weather conditions
these models are time-consuming, costly, and challenging to implement on a larger scale, particularly in developing countries

chunks.text: Vegetation indices such as NDVI and EVI are widely used for yield estimation, but solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) is a more direct indicator of photosynthetic activity and can be more sensitive to plant function. The paper positions SIF as a promising but underused predictor for yield, especially when integrated with traditional remote sensing variables and environmental drivers. This integration is expected to improve regional yield prediction performance.
supporting_quote: Key indices such as the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI), enhanced vegetation index (EVI)... have been widely employed for estimating crop yields
Satellite-based solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF), which is more sensitive to photosynthetic capacity than traditional VIs, has recently been used to predict crop yield
integrating SIF with other remote sensing and environmental data for regional crop yield modeling still needs to be explored

chunks.text: The study aims to enhance district-level rice yield prediction in Nepal by incorporating SIF alongside traditional vegetation indices, biophysical variables, climatic variables, and soil properties within machine learning models. It evaluates which predictors and algorithms best support accurate yield estimation and quantifies the improvement from adding SIF. It also investigates the most reliable within-season time window to enable early yield forecasting in the Terai region.
supporting_quote: This study aims to address these gaps by incorporating SIF to enhance rice yield prediction in Nepal
we harnessed satellite-derived data, including the recently prominent SIF, along with VIs, biophysical, climatic, and soil variables, to develop and evaluate four ML models
we examined how these variations influence rice yield prediction... four specific time windows were established

chunks.text: The paper explicitly frames four research questions focused on: identifying the most effective input variables; determining the most suitable machine learning models; measuring accuracy gains from combining SIF with other variables; and selecting the most reliable time period within the growing season for prediction. These questions structure the experimental comparisons across feature sets and temporal windows.
supporting_quote: From this study, we aimed to answer the following questions: (i) Which input variables are most effective for rice yield predictions?
(ii) Which ML models are the most suitable for optimal rice yield predictions?
(iii) How much improvement can be achieved by combining SIF with traditional remotely sensed and environmental variables?

chunks.text: Rice yield prediction research in Nepal is limited, with only a small number of prior studies and limited predictor scope. Earlier work relied on restricted satellite datasets or combinations such as NDVI and meteorology, without using SIF and without incorporating soil properties. This narrow feature coverage likely constrained model predictive power at district scales.
supporting_quote: Despite rice being the most-grown crop in Nepal, research on rice yield prediction in the country remains sparse. Only two studies have been conducted on this topic.
these approaches were limited in scope, as they did not incorporate key predictors such as SIF
The exclusion of SIF and soil properties limited the predictive power of these models.

chunks.text: Existing Nepal-focused studies also did not evaluate how prediction performance depends on crop growth stages and feature time windows. Because environmental conditions and crop signals vary across the growing season, an optimal temporal window is needed for reliable early prediction. The paper addresses this by testing multiple within-season windows.
supporting_quote: Furthermore, existing studies need to explore the influence of different growth stages on model performance.
Identifying the most appropriate time window for capturing rice features is essential for accurate yield prediction.
four specific time windows were established... July–September, August–September, July–October, and August–October.

chunks.text: The study builds supervised machine learning yield models for Terai districts using multiple feature combinations and four algorithms: random forest, support vector regression, gradient boosting regressor, and LASSO. Models are trained on earlier years and tested on later years to evaluate generalization. The workflow includes data preprocessing, feature aggregation at district scale, model training/testing, and evaluation with RMSE, RRMSE, and R².
supporting_quote: Random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVR), gradient boosting regressor (GBR), and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) algorithms were employed to predict crop yield
data from 2003 to 2013 were used for training, while the remaining data from 2014 to 2017 was used for testing
The performance of models was done based on three statistical indicators: root mean squared error (RMSE), ratio of RMSE (RRMSE), and coefficient of determination (R2).

chunks.text: To capture growth-stage effects, the paper defines four time windows within the monsoon rice season and trains separate models for each: Jul–Sep, Aug–Sep, Jul–Oct, and Aug–Oct. The windows are intended to represent early growth and pre-harvest phases and to identify the earliest window that still yields strong prediction accuracy. This design supports evaluating lead time for forecasting before harvest.
supporting_quote: we developed ML models for four growing periods to pinpoint the optimal time window for rice yield prediction
four specific time windows were established... July–September, August–September, July–October, and August–October.
rice is typically planted in July and harvested in November

chunks.text: The study compares single-source and progressively richer multi-source feature sets. Scenarios include: VIs only; VIs + biophysical (LAI, FPAR); adding climatic variables; adding soil properties; and finally adding SIF. This structured feature ablation isolates the marginal value of each data source, especially SIF, for yield prediction.
supporting_quote: The feature combinations include VIs, VIs + Biophysical, VIs + Biophysical + Climatic, VIs + Biophysical + Climatic + Soil, and VIs + Biophysical + Climatic + Soil + SIF.
When using only the VIs (NDVI and EVI)... when biophysical variables (LAI and FPAR) were included... Substantial improvement was observed when adding climatic features
Finally, we achieved the best performance by incorporating SIF with all the previous data

chunks.text: Model interpretability and feature sensitivity are assessed using SHAP values to quantify each feature’s contribution to predicted yield. The paper interprets larger absolute SHAP values as higher impact and uses SHAP plots to infer whether high or low feature values increase or decrease yield predictions. This analysis is used to identify leading soil, climate, vegetation index, and SIF drivers.
supporting_quote: SHAP value analysis... to explain how each input feature influences the model's predictions.
A larger absolute SHAP value indicates a higher impact of a feature on the model's output.
In this study, SHAP value analysis was employed to quantify the contribution of each input feature to the predicted rice yield.

chunks.text: The study uses district-level rice yield records for 15 years (2003–2017) across the Terai region, compiling 330 observations from 22 districts. Yield data come from ICIMOD’s RDS for 2003/06–2013/14 and from Nepal’s Ministry of Agriculture publications for 2015/16–2016/17. These yields serve as the target variable for model training and testing.
supporting_quote: 330 yield data points were collected over 15 years from 2003 to 2017 from 22 districts in the Terai region.
District-level rice yield production data from 2003/06 to 2013/14 were obtained from the Regional Database System (RDS), managed by ICIMOD
for the years 2015/16 to 2016/17, the district-level data were sourced from the 'Statistical Information on Nepalese Agriculture'

chunks.text: Solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence is taken from a fused SCIAMACHY and GOME-2 high-resolution product (V2) with monthly values from 2003 to 2017 at 0.05° resolution. The study extracts district-average monthly SIF using district boundary masks in Python. SIF is integrated as a physiological predictor alongside conventional indices and environmental variables.
supporting_quote: We used the solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) from "Global High-Resolution Estimates of SIF from Fused SCIAMACHY and GOME-2, V2"
monthly SIF estimates from 2003 to 2017... at a spatial resolution of 0.05◦
we extracted district-level averaged monthly SIF values by masking the data with the shapefile of the district boundaries of Nepal

chunks.text: Vegetation indices NDVI and EVI (MODIS/Aqua MYD13A1) and biophysical variables LAI and FPAR (MODIS/Aqua MYD15A2H) are used as predictors. Data are collected for dominant rice-growing months (July–October) from 2003–2017 and aggregated to monthly district averages using a rice-field mask and a maximum value composite approach. These features represent canopy greenness and vegetation biophysical status.
supporting_quote: We used NDVI, EVI, LAI, and FPAR remote sensing products as predictive features
The datasets cover the dominant rice-growing months from July to October from 2003 to 2017.
all the VIs were averaged on a monthly scale using the maximum value composite method

chunks.text: Soil predictors come from Nepal’s Digital Soil Map (NARC, 2021) at 250 m resolution and include texture fractions (clay, silt, sand), pH, organic matter, and nutrients such as total nitrogen, P2O5, K2O, boron, and zinc. Values are masked to rice cultivation zones and aggregated to district means. Soil variables are treated as static over time for modeling.
supporting_quote: Soil data were obtained from the Nepal Agricultural Research Council (NARC) through its Digital Soil Map (DSM)

provides detailed essential soil properties such as texture (percentage compositions of clay, silt, and sand), pH, organic matter, and nutrient content, including total nitrogen, phosphorus pentoxide (P2O5), potassium oxide
We assumed soil variables were static and used the same values for all months and years.

chunks.text: Climatic predictors are sourced from TerraClimate at 4.6 km monthly resolution for 2003–2017. Variables include AET, PET, water deficit (def), PDSI, precipitation (Pr), soil moisture, solar radiation (srad), Tmin, Tmax, vapor pressure (vap), VPD, and wind speed (vs). These layers are masked to rice areas and aggregated to district level in Google Earth Engine.
supporting_quote: we incorporated climatic variables from TerraClimate (Abatzoglou et al., 2018)
The climatic data were obtained at a spatial resolution of 4.6 km and a temporal resolution of one month.
These variables encompass Actual Evapotranspiration (AET)... Precipitation accumulation (Pr)... Minimum temperature (Tmin), Maximum temperature (Tmax)... Wind speed (vs).

chunks.text: Among tested algorithms, the gradient boosting regressor achieved the strongest overall accuracy, especially when using the July–September window with combined multi-source features. In that setting, the model reached RMSE about 250 kg/ha, RRMSE 8.6%, and R² 0.73 on the test period. This identifies GBR as the best-performing model for early-season district-level rice yield prediction in the study region.
supporting_quote: GBR out-performed other machine learning algorithms when using input features from July to September, achieving root mean square error (RMSE)... of 250 kg/ha and 8.6%
The best performance was observed with GBR, which achieved an RRMSE of 8.6% and an R2 value of 0.73
Jul–Sep ... GBR ... R2 0.73 ... RMSE 249.8 ... RRMSE 8.6

chunks.text: Across scenarios, GBR and random forest consistently performed better than SVR and LASSO. Reported RRMSE ranges were 8.6%–16.9% for GBR and 11.0%–15.5% for RF, while SVR and LASSO showed larger errors (11.5%–20.8% and 12.6%–20.6%). This indicates tree-based ensemble methods were more robust for the multi-source, district-level yield task.
supporting_quote: The GBR and RF demonstrated superior performance across all scenarios, consistently delivering better results than SVR and LASSO.
the RRMSE for GBR ranged from 8.6% to 16.9%
the RRMSE for SVR, RF, and LASSO ranged from 11.5% to 20.8%, 11.0%–15.5%, and 12.6%–20.6%

chunks.text: Adding more data sources systematically improved prediction accuracy relative to using vegetation indices alone. RRMSE was 14.8%–20.8% with only NDVI and EVI, improved to 13.5%–20.1% when LAI and FPAR were added, and improved further with climate variables (as low as 11.7%). Including soil reduced RRMSE to 10.9%–13.5%, and the best performance occurred when SIF was also included (8.6%–14.1%).
supporting_quote: When using only the VIs (NDVI and EVI), the RRMSE ranged from 14.8 % to 20.8 %
when biophysical variables (LAI and FPAR) were included... the RRMSE improved... 13.5 %–20.1 %
Including soil variables... RRMSE dropping to between 10.9 % and 13.5 %... incorporating SIF... RRMSE values ranging from 8.6 % to 14.1 %.

chunks.text: Incorporating SIF alongside traditional remote sensing and environmental variables reduced prediction error substantially. The paper reports that adding SIF decreased RRMSE by 21% compared with models that excluded SIF. This supports the claim that SIF provides complementary information linked to photosynthetic activity beyond standard vegetation indices.
supporting_quote: After adding SIF to traditional remote sensing and environmental variables, we observed that RRMSE is reduced by 21 %.
incorporating SIF alongside traditional remote sensing and environmental variables significantly enhances the model's prediction accuracy.
Our findings revealed that incorporating SIF into the model reduced the prediction error by 21%.

chunks.text: The July–September feature window enabled reliable prediction with about two months lead time relative to harvest. Because rice harvest occurs in November in the Terai, using July–September inputs allows forecasting before the end of the season. The study highlights this as operationally useful for planning and decision-making.
supporting_quote: the GBR model demonstrates its capability to predict rice yield with the highest precision using data from July to September.
Consequently, this model can forecast rice yields two months before the actual harvest date.
Given that the rice harvest in Nepal occurs in November, yield predictions can be made as early as two months before harvest

chunks.text: Correlation analysis shows that among vegetation and physiological variables, EVI had the strongest positive association with yield (0.34), while NDVI (0.31), FPAR (0.28), SIF (0.25), and LAI (0.25) were also positively correlated. For climate variables averaged over the growing season, precipitation had the highest positive correlation (0.22), whereas solar radiation, wind speed, and Tmin were most negatively correlated (−0.17, −0.16, −0.13). These correlations provide context for feature relevance but are generally modest in magnitude.
supporting_quote: EVI demonstrates the strongest correlation with yield, with a coefficient of 0.34.
NDVI, FPAR, SIF, and LAI exhibit comparable correlations with yield, with coefficients of 0.31, 0.28, 0.25, and 0.25, respectively.
Precipitation shows the highest positive correlation with yield, having a coefficient of 0.22... srad, vs, and Tmin... − 0.17, − 0.16, and − 0.13

chunks.text: Soil-yield correlations indicated positive associations for silt (0.27), P2O5 (0.21), and Zn250 (0.18), while sand was most negatively correlated with yield (−0.23). These relationships align with subsequent model interpretability results that emphasize soil texture and nutrients. Overall, several soil variables had weak correlations, suggesting non-linear interactions captured better by machine learning models.
supporting_quote: silt, P2O5, and Zn250 demonstrate the strongest positive correlations with yield, with coefficients of 0.27, 0.21, and 0.18, respectively.
sand displays the highest negative correlations with yield, with coefficients of − 0.23.
The remaining variables exhibit correlations with yield below 0.1 in absolute value.

chunks.text: SHAP-based sensitivity analysis identified the most influential predictors in the best-performing setup, led by soil properties and selected monthly climate/remote sensing features. The top features included sand, P2O5, precipitation in August (pr_08), September water deficit (def_09), September NDVI (NDVI_09), and August SIF (SIF_08). The directionality indicated higher sand reduces predicted yield, while higher pr_08, NDVI_09, and SIF_08 increase predicted yield.
supporting_quote: The most crucial features identified include sand, followed by P2O5 (phosphate), pr_08 (precipitation in August), def_09 (water deficit in September), NDVI_09... and SIF_08
high values of sand are predominantly associated with negative SHAP values
Higher pr_08, NDVI, and SIF_08 values positively affect the model output, resulting in increased predicted rice yield.

chunks.text: Spatial validation for 2014 showed close agreement between predicted and observed district yields when using the GBR model with combined features (including SIF, VIs, biophysical, climatic, and soil variables). The paper notes that predictions remained consistently aligned with observations in later years as well (shown in supplementary material). This supports the model’s ability to generalize across districts during the test period.
supporting_quote: The spatial pattern of both observed and predicted rice yields for 2014, using the GBR model, is illustrated in Fig. 7.
This figure highlights the close alignment between the predicted rice yield across all districts and the observed rice yield in 2014
the model's predictions were consistently aligned with the observed rice yields in subsequent years

chunks.text: A key limitation is the use of static rice-field masks from only a few years due to lack of annual rice layers. Because rice area can change year to year, static masks may introduce errors in extracting remote sensing and environmental variables. The authors recommend developing annual rice maps using updated satellite data to reduce extraction errors and improve yield prediction reliability.
supporting_quote: due to the unavailability of dynamic annual rice layer data, we had to rely on static rice layers from 2010, 2012, and 2014
