replace the storage values with linearly interpolated values between the normal storage values in two adjacent days

chunks.text: Across the 452 reservoirs, operations can be approximated with a small number of modules, ranging from 1 to 8. Most reservoirs use fewer than six modules, and the distribution is strongly skewed toward low counts: 25% use one module; 54% use two or three; 19% use four or five; and only 2% use six or more. Module counts vary by purpose, with many hydropower and navigation reservoirs using one or two modules, while irrigation and flood control commonly require multiple modules.
supporting_quote: the operation of any of these reservoirs can be effectively approximated using 1–8 modules
25% of the 452 reservoirs use just one module; 54% use two or three; 19% use four or five; only 2% require six or more.
Nearly 80% of those reservoirs are operated with only a single or two modules

chunks.text: From 1,155 extracted modules, the paper identifies five basic module types based on the primary driver and functional form: constant release; inflow-driven piecewise constant release; inflow-driven linear release; storage-driven piecewise constant release; and storage-driven nonlinear (or piecewise linear) release. In addition, a joint-driven module type is recognized when both inflow and storage jointly define decision-tree splits. These types serve as reusable “Lego bricks” for describing operations across many reservoirs.
supporting_quote: Among the 1,155 modules derived from the 452 reservoirs ... five typical module types are identified ... constant release, inflow‐driven piecewise constant release, inflow‐driven linear release, storage‐driven piecewise constant release, and storage‐driven nonlinear (or piecewise linear) release
Besides the five basic module types, the joint‐driven modules do not determine the release solely depending on inflow or storage but on the combined information of both.

chunks.text: Constant release modules reflect near-constant discharge regardless of inflow and storage and often appear during low-release periods such as refill or dry conservation. They are also common in very large reservoirs where releases are stable and demand-driven. The paper provides examples such as Clark Canyon Dam using low constant releases in November–April for storage building and Garrison Dam applying constant release modules in most months, with non-constant modules mainly during floods.
supporting_quote: The constant release modules represent the operation scheme characterized by constant or near constant releases, regardless of the inflow and storage levels
The constant release modules are mainly found in operations with low releases during a low‐flow period ... or the restricted releases during dry periods for water conservation.
The constant release modules are commonly observed with extremely large reservoirs, where the releases are relatively stable and demand‐driven

chunks.text: Inflow-driven piecewise constant modules hold release constant within inflow ranges and are often used for low releases, whereas inflow-driven linear modules increase release linearly with inflow and are more associated with high releases. Storage-driven piecewise constant modules set different constant releases for storage levels, typically for low/normal releases and storage maintenance. Storage-driven nonlinear modules increase release sharply beyond a storage threshold, reflecting hedging-like behavior and also appearing during transition months between refill and high-release periods.
supporting_quote: Under the inflow‐driven piecewise constant release module, the release is constant within a certain inflow range.
For the inflow‐driven linear release modules, the release changes linearly with the inflow.

under the storage‐driven nonlinear release modules, the release remains relatively low when the reservoir storage is less than a threshold; beyond the threshold, the release significantly increases. This reflects the hedging policy

chunks.text: Module-type application differs by primary purpose. Constant release modules are used on over 20% of days for all listed purposes and are especially frequent for irrigation reservoirs (48%). Hydropower reservoirs show high use of inflow-driven linear modules (36%), consistent with many run-of-river plants. Flood-control reservoirs show notable complexity with joint-driven modules applied 21% of days, while storage-driven nonlinear modules occur relatively infrequently (5%–8%) across purposes.
supporting_quote: the constant release module type is applied in over 20% of days in a year for all primary operational purposes
This is particularly evident for irrigation reservoirs (48%)
hydropower reservoirs exhibit a high application of the inflow‐driven linear release module type
Flood control reservoirs have a high application of constant release (39%) and joint‐driven release modules (21%)
storage‐driven nonlinear module type has relatively low application frequencies 5%–8%

chunks.text: Seasonal module selection is linked to reservoir size ratio (storage capacity divided by average annual inflow). Small size-ratio reservoirs are more inflow-driven, with inflow-driven linear modules dominating year-round; reservoirs with size ratio 0.0–0.2 use inflow-driven linear modules for 58% of reservoirs on a monthly basis. Large size-ratio reservoirs are more stable, with constant release modules dominating; for size ratio >1, constant release is adopted for 71% of reservoirs on a monthly basis. Larger size ratios also show more frequent transitions between low-release constant modules and high-release inflow-driven modules, reflecting refill-to-release switching.
supporting_quote: size ratios (defined as the ratio of storage capacity to average annual inflow
for reservoirs with size ratio between 0.0 and 0.2 ... the inflow‐driven linear release modules are adopted for 58% of the reservoirs.
for those reservoirs with size ratio larger than 1, the constant release modules are adopted for 71% of the reservoirs.
The transition between constant ... and inflow‐ driven ... modules indicates the switch between storage refill and water release with large reservoirs.

chunks.text: Irrigation reservoirs exhibit a distinctive seasonal refill–release cycle. From September to March, constant release modules dominate for 74% of irrigation reservoirs on a monthly basis, consistent with storage refill and low releases. During May to July, constant release prevalence drops to 38%, while higher-release modules (e.g., inflow-driven linear and joint-driven) increase during the irrigation season. This reflects seasonal switching between low-release refill rules and high-release supply rules.
supporting_quote: For September to March, constant release modules prevail for 74% of the irrigation reservoirs on a monthly basis.
the percentage of constant release modules decreases to 38% during May to July.
This seasonal module transition reveals a distinctive seasonal operation cycle of refill and release essential to irrigation reservoirs.

chunks.text: Regional patterns modify seasonal operations for irrigation reservoirs in the western U.S. In the Pacific Northwest, inflow-driven linear modules are applied more from November to February due to high rainfall months. In California, storage-driven modules are applied more because summer rainfall is low and irrigation supply relies on stored water accumulated in wet months. Great Basin shows higher inflow-driven linear use in spring tied to snowmelt inflow and irrigation needs, while Upper Colorado shows more joint-driven modules in high-flow months, indicating combined inflow and storage considerations.
supporting_quote: In Pacific Northwest Region ... the inflow‐driven linear release module is more applied from November to February ... corresponding to the high rainfall months
In California Region ... the application of storage‐driven modules ... is significantly higher in this region than others.
Great Basin Region ... shows a higher application of inflow‐driven linear release modules during spring ... high inflow caused by snow melting.
Upper Colorado Region ... more applications of the joint‐driven modules ... implying that storage is jointly considered with inflow in high‐release decisions.

chunks.text: Flood-control reservoirs show strong regional contrasts tied to climate and flood types. In the Pacific Northwest, higher-release modules (inflow-driven linear and joint-driven) are emphasized during the rainy season, with low-release modules during summer dry months. In the Ohio region, floods are more episodic and storm-driven year-round, producing abrupt switches: low-release modules on non-flood days and joint-driven modules on flood days, with higher high-release module application in winter when storms are more frequent. Missouri region shows weaker seasonal switching because drought-prone conditions and agricultural demand reduce flood-control seasonality in normal and dry years.
supporting_quote: in Pacific Northwest Region ... corresponding to the rainy season when flood management is critical
Ohio Region ... flood events are mainly episodic and storm‐driven, which could occur all year long.
operation follows the low‐release modules ... applied for non‐flooding days and the high‐release ... modules applied for flood days.
For the Missouri Region ... most areas in this region are drought‐prone and have high agricultural water consumption ... the seasonality of flood control is hidden

chunks.text: Variable-importance analysis shows different hydroclimatic priorities by operation purpose. Inflow is nearly exclusively dominant for navigation reservoirs and is also most important for many hydropower and flood-control reservoirs, though storage remains non-negligible for flood control. Day-of-year (DOY) is most important for irrigation reservoirs, reflecting seasonally structured refill and release. Water supply and recreation reservoirs emphasize both inflow and storage, with slightly higher importance on storage, while PDSI rarely dominates because it overlaps with inflow and storage signals.
supporting_quote: the relative importance of inflow is near 1.0 (i.e., the highest importance) for almost all navigation reservoirs
it is found that DOY is the most important information for irrigation reservoirs
reservoirs primarily operated for water supply and recreation are found to have both inflow and storage critically accounted for release decisions, but with slightly higher importance on storage.
there are only a small number of reservoirs of which the operation is primarily operated by PDSI

chunks.text: The authors caution that the five basic module types derived from CONUS reservoirs may not universally apply to all reservoirs elsewhere, and should be validated as additional data become available. They also note that GDROMs may be limited for flood control because some reservoirs operate at sub-daily intervals during flood events, which daily models can miss. In addition, GDROM performance is weaker for extreme inflows and releases in some regions, motivating methodological improvements for robustness.
supporting_quote: the derived five basic types of operation modules from 452 CONUS reservoirs may not be applicable to some other reservoirs. The patterns can be validated and applied to new reservoirs when more data are available.
the data‐driven models (GDROMs) used in this work can be limited in representing flood control rules given that some reservoirs are operated in sub‐daily time intervals during a flood event.
the GDROM performs relatively weak ... with abnormally high inflows and releases in some regions such as the North and Mid‐Atlantic.

chunks.text: To address biases from extreme values, the paper suggests improving GDROM training with robust loss functions rather than mean squared error. As an alternative, it proposes modifying the model structure to fit extreme and regular releases separately, with a flood-event-specific tuning. These steps are framed as future work to improve simulation of extremely high releases.
supporting_quote: In the future, the GDROMs can be improved by using robust loss functions to overcome the bias caused by extreme values (outliers) to replace the currently employed mean square error
Alternatively, the model structure may be modified to fit the extreme and regular releases separately ... tuned for flood events for improved simulation of extremely high releases.

chunks.text: The study argues that typical module types and their transition patterns can inform reservoir operation model formulation, including representing seasonality and regional differences more explicitly. It emphasizes that regional features persist even among reservoirs with similar size and purpose, indicating that model transitions should consider climate and regulation context rather than only storage and seasonal inflow. The module “Lego bricks” are positioned as a way to build or improve operation models, especially when data are limited.
supporting_quote: the five types of modules and the joint module ... can be used as elementary components to build a new model or improve an existing model
the analysis presented in this study highlights the necessity to represent distinct regional features in an operation model
persistent differences in module application transitions even among reservoirs of similar size and same operation purpose

chunks.text: The paper concludes that reservoir operations across 452 CONUS reservoirs can be represented with a small set of modules (up to eight), and that these modules can be grouped into five basic types plus a joint-driven type. Seasonal and regional transition patterns differ systematically by size ratio, purpose, and location, such as refill–release cycles for irrigation and more climate- and flood-type-dependent dynamics for flood control. The inferred priorities of inflow, storage, DOY, and PDSI further clarify what information drives different reservoir operations.
supporting_quote: a small number of modules (up to eight in our findings) can effectively represent the operation of any of those reservoirs
the operation modules are categorized into five basic types and joint modules
the operation of flood control reservoirs is modeled with a more complex structure, with consideration of regional climate characteristics and flood types (storm‐driven or seasonal).
The roles of each hydroclimatic variable (inflow, storage, PDSI, and DOY) are prioritized for release decisions

chunks.text: A central takeaway is that inflow-determined modules tend to characterize small reservoirs, while constant/stable release or storage-related modules are more common for large reservoirs with high regulation capacity. The authors highlight practical implications: the discovered module types and transition conditions can help build models for data-scarce reservoirs and can be incorporated into large-scale hydrologic models due to GDROM’s interpretable structure and common inputs.
supporting_quote: In general, inflow‐determined modules are formulated for small reservoirs while modules with constant and stable release or storage are adopted for large reservoirs.
the findings with the 452 reservoirs across the CONUS can be used to build a data‐driven operation model for reservoirs with limited data availability

GDROMs have an interpretable and transparent decision tree‐based model structure and four input variables, they can be easily incorporated into the rainfall‐runoff processes of a large‐scale hydrologic model

chunks.text: Reservoirs strongly modify river flow regimes, so large-scale hydrologic models need realistic reservoir representations to simulate streamflow. Errors in simulated reservoir releases can accumulate and propagate downstream because upstream releases become inflows to downstream reservoirs. Many simplified routing schemes ignore human operational objectives, which limits their ability to reproduce regulated flows at continental scales such as in the U.S. National Water Model (NWM).
supporting_quote: Reservoirs exert a significant influence on streamflow regimes, necessitating their accurate representation in hydrological models
releases from upstream reservoirs influence inflows into downstream reservoirs; consequently, errors in reservoir release simulation propagate downstream.
the U.S. National Water Model (NWM), which is designed to produce streamflow simulations and forecasts at over 2.7 million river reaches across the U.S.

chunks.text: Operational purpose and human decision-making complicate reservoir simulation. Even when rule curves exist, operators may deviate based on hydrologic variability and forecast uncertainty, and multiple reservoirs may be coordinated. These realities motivate reservoir operation models that can capture operator behavior without requiring hard-to-obtain physical/demand data.
supporting_quote: it is difficult for reservoir operation models to explicitly capture reservoir operators' behaviors under different water availability and demand conditions
operators normally follow regulations (usually embedded in the predesigned reservoir operation rule curve), they have flexibility to use their own judgment
multiple reservoirs in intensively managed watersheds may be operated in coordination, which is particularly difficult for reservoir operation algorithms to simulate

chunks.text: Recent data-driven approaches infer reservoir operating rules from long-term records with low computational burden, making them suitable for large-scale hydrologic models. GDROM is one such algorithm, and derived rules for hundreds of CONUS reservoirs have been published for immediate use. This creates an opportunity to test whether a modern data-driven routing scheme improves NWM reservoir outflow simulations.
supporting_quote: Some recently proposed reservoir operation models have taken advantage of growing operation data availability for many reservoirs and advanced data-based techniques to derive reservoir operation rules from long-term operation records
the generic data-driven reservoir operation model (GDROM; Chen et al., 2022)
Derived operation rules for a large number of reservoirs of CONUS based on the GDROM ... are already published for immediate use by Li et al. (2023)

chunks.text: The study evaluates whether replacing the NWM reservoir representation with a data-driven routing algorithm (GDROM) improves reservoir outflow and streamflow simulation. It compares NWM versus NWM+GDROM using long retrospective simulations and multiple goodness-of-fit metrics. The evaluation targets both CONUS-wide performance and regional differences in regulated basins.
supporting_quote: This study investigates whether improvements could be achieved for the United States National Water Model (NWM) by using a data-driven reservoir operation simulation algorithm, that is, the generic data-driven reservoir operation model (GDROM), to replace the existing reservoir representation in NWM
The evaluations of NWM versus NWM + GDROM are conducted using 41 year NWM retrospective simulation products during 1979 to 2020.
The performance comparisons are carried out at both CONUS scale and regional scales.

chunks.text: A key objective is to diagnose how inflow accuracy and reservoir storage error accumulation affect the potential gains from GDROM in a large-scale model. The study explicitly tests two routing configurations (observed storage vs modeled storage) and also analyzes a subset of reservoirs with adequately simulated inflow (NSE > 0). This isolates temporal error accumulation and spatial upstream-downstream error propagation effects.
supporting_quote: we further examine the effect of error propagation over time due to water balance errors accumulating in reservoir storage
we also examine a subset of the reservoirs, the simulated inflow of which has relatively high accuracy (with an NSE value exceeding 0.)
evaluate the performance of reservoir outflow simulations when observed reservoir storage is used for the routing.

chunks.text: The NWM retrospective simulations route reservoirs using the level pool scheme (or limited specified rules), which largely ignores operational purposes and decision-making. Level pool makes releases mainly a function of storage elevation and structural parameters (weir/orifice), potentially missing regulated release patterns. This limitation can reduce outflow realism and thereby affect downstream streamflow.
supporting_quote: Retrospective simulations from the NWM use the level pool routing scheme (or specified operation rules existing with some reservoirs) to simulate reservoirs
The level pool method represents reservoir outflow as a function of the elevation of reservoir storage, discounting the effects of reservoir operation purposes
errors in reservoir release simulation propagate downstream.

chunks.text: Over long simulations, inflow and release errors can accumulate in reservoir storage, and storage errors can further degrade simulated releases. This creates a feedback where water-balance errors magnify over time, undermining routing accuracy. The study treats this as a central obstacle when applying reservoir algorithms for multi-decade retrospective runs.
supporting_quote: Over long time periods, errors in inflow and/or release can lead to the accumulation of errors in reservoir storage.
errors in reservoir storage can lead to further errors in reservoir releases and consequently magnify the effects of errors accumulation.

chunks.text: In large river networks, upstream reservoir routing affects downstream inflows, so inflow biases at one reservoir can propagate spatially to others. Using NWM inflows directly may be problematic for comparing routing methods because those inflows reflect upstream reservoir modeling choices. The study addresses this by examining a subset of reservoirs with NWM inflow skill above a threshold.
supporting_quote: upstream reservoir releases impact downstream flow and downstream reservoir inflows

the reservoir inflows directly obtained from the NWM may not be ideal for the comparative analysis via GDROM, that is, the error with the inflow will propagate the error of reservoir release and downstream flow.
the subset only includes reservoirs for which the NWM-modeled inflows obtain model performance evaluation metrics exceeding a threshold value

chunks.text: The workflow routes NWM retrospective inflows through GDROM to simulate daily reservoir releases and update storage by mass balance. GDROM uses inflow, current storage, day of year (DOY), and Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI) as predictors. The resulting GDROM releases are compared to NWM retrospective outflows produced by NWM’s built-in reservoir routing.
supporting_quote: using derived reservoir operation rules (GDROM) to route reservoir inflows, obtained from the NWM retrospective dataset version 2.1, through reservoirs
simulated inflows from the NWM retrospective dataset, along with daily reservoir storage, day of year (DOY), and Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI) values, are provided as inputs to GDROM.
Simulated releases of that day obtained from the GDROM algorithm may then be used to update the reservoir storage using the mass balance relationship.

chunks.text: GDROM is implemented as transparent if-then decision rules based on decision trees learned from long-term operation records. A classification tree selects among operation modules, and regression trees simulate releases from inflow and storage under the selected conditions. DOY and PDSI represent seasonality and drought intensity, enabling operational context without explicit reservoir attributes as inputs.
supporting_quote: GDROM is a data-derived reservoir simulation algorithm that uses long-term operation records to present reservoir operation rules as a set of transparent if-then rules based on inflow, current storage, PDSI and DOY
For each reservoir, GDROM determines a classification tree and a set of regression trees.
DOY and PDSI predictors capture seasonality and impacts of drought intensity on reservoir operation, respectively.

chunks.text: The baseline reservoir routing in the NWM retrospective dataset is the level pool method (or specified rules for some reservoirs). In level pool, outflow depends on reservoir storage elevation and spillway/orifice formulations, with no outflow until a threshold elevation is reached. For this study, the authors directly use NWM retrospective outflows rather than re-deriving structural details.
supporting_quote: Retrospective simulations from the NWM use the level pool routing scheme (or specified operation rules existing with some reservoirs) to simulate reservoirs
no outflow occurs until the reservoir storage reaches a certain elevation, beyond which the spill is modeled as a function of the weir coefficient
In our analysis, we simply take the simulated NWM outflows from the NWM retrospective dataset version 2.1

chunks.text: To test temporal error accumulation, two GDROM configurations are evaluated: routing with observed storage versus routing with modeled storage. In both cases, NWM inflow is used; the difference is whether storage is supplied from observations or updated internally via mass balance. This isolates how storage biases affect release simulation quality over long periods.
supporting_quote: evaluate the performance of reservoir outflow simulations when observed reservoir storage is supplied as an input to GDROM, which is referred as simulation with observed storage.
use GDROM simulated reservoir storage based on the mass balance relation, which is referred to simulation with modeled storage.
For both cases, NWM-based simulated inflow is provided as an input to GDROM

chunks.text: To test spatial error propagation from upstream regulation, the study analyzes a reservoir subset whose NWM-modeled inflows are sufficiently accurate. The selection criterion is inflow NSE greater than 0, separating cases where inflows are reasonable from those dominated by upstream modeling errors. This supports a fairer comparison of routing algorithms when inflow quality is a limiting factor.
supporting_quote: we also compare the model results with a subset of the original 452 reservoirs; the subset only includes reservoirs for which the NWM-modeled inflows obtain model performance evaluation metrics exceeding a threshold value
use zero NSE value as the cutoff to split all reservoirs into two groups
reservoirs with inflow simulation NSE greater than 0

chunks.text: Model performance is compared using three goodness-of-fit estimators that target different flow regimes: NSE and KGE for high flows, and tRMSE for low flows via a Box-Cox transformation. The paper notes that NSE and KGE emphasize high flows due to squared error terms and heteroscedasticity. The transformation for tRMSE uses λ = 0.3 to emphasize lower flows before computing RMSE.
supporting_quote: Three GoF estimators are used: the Nash Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE...)), the Kling Gupta Efficiency (KGE...)) and the transformed root mean square error (tRMSE...)
NSE and KGE are chosen to quantify high flow simulation performance because both estimators have squared error terms
We use the tRMSE estimator to evaluate simulation performance in terms of low flows (Equation 4)... Box-Cox transformation (Equation 5)..., λ = 0.3

chunks.text: The study uses NOAA’s NWM retrospective dataset version 2.1, forced by AORC meteorology, providing 41 years of simulations from February 1979 to December 2020. The dataset includes inflows and outflows for over 5000 reservoirs across CONUS. Retrospective runs do not apply data assimilation, so reservoir outflows reflect the level pool method outputs.
supporting_quote: NOAA NWM retrospective dataset version 2.1 ... spanning 41 years (from February 1979 to December 2020)
The streamflow simulations provide inflows and outflows from over 5000 reservoirs across the CONUS.
The retrospective dataset of historical streamflow simulations used in this analysis does not apply data assimilation

chunks.text: Observed reservoir release data for evaluation are taken from a published dataset that also contains GDROM-derived rules for the analyzed reservoirs. The study focuses on 452 reservoirs where GDROM has been validated and for which observed releases are available. Because record lengths vary, only overlapping periods between NWM retrospective outputs and the GDROM dataset are used.
supporting_quote: observed reservoir outflow values... are taken from Li et al. (2023) providing observed reservoir releases for all 452 reservoirs in the GDROM dataset.
GDROM has been validated to 452 reservoirs across the CONUS
we use periods that overlap between the NWM retrospective dataset and the GDROM dataset to conduct comparative analysis.

chunks.text: To ensure a fair evaluation on unseen data, the comparative analysis uses the testing period defined in the original GDROM development study. Simulation windows differ by reservoir but typically cover multiple years. The paper notes that for most reservoirs, the evaluation period spans at least five years.
supporting_quote: the testing period used to evaluate GDROM in Chen et al. (2022) is employed as the simulation period to conduct the comparative analysis
it is fair to apply both NWM and NWM + GDROM to "unseen" data.
One can observe that the simulation for most reservoirs covers at least 5 years.

chunks.text: Across CONUS, NWM+GDROM driven by observed storage shows widespread improvements over NWM for reservoir outflow simulation, with positive KGE and NSE differences for almost all reservoirs. With modeled storage, performance is mixed and a small number of reservoirs show worse performance in KGE. The paper attributes this to storage drift caused by accumulated inflow/outflow errors over long periods.
supporting_quote: most significant improvement is achieved by NWM + GDROM driven by observed storage with positive KGE and NSE differences for almost all reservoirs across the CONUS
a small number of reservoirs (51 out of 452 ... ) even show relatively negative performance with NWM + GDROM (in terms of KGE only).
storage simulation could largely deviate from the actual value due to the inflow and outflow simulation error accumulation over a long simulation period

chunks.text: When reservoir inflows are adequately simulated (inflow NSE > 0), NWM+GDROM substantially outperforms NWM for high-flow-focused metrics. The paper reports that with observed storage, median KGE approaches 0.8 and the lower quartile exceeds 0.6, while NWM’s median KGE is below 0.6 and lower quartile below 0.3. Similar improvements are reported for NSE, showing strong gains when inflow quality is not limiting.
supporting_quote: when using adequately simulated inflows (i.e., NSE > 0), NWM + GDROM substantially outperforms NWM in terms of KGE and NSE.
the median KGE from NWM falls below 0.6, with a lower quartile below 0.3.
NWM + GDROM with observed storage inputs achieves a median KGE nearing 0.8 and a lower quartile above 0.6

chunks.text: Improvements for low-flow simulation are limited. The distributions of tRMSE for NWM and NWM+GDROM are similar, indicating only slight or marginal low-flow gains. The paper links this to GDROM being trained to maximize NSE (favoring high flows) and to NWM’s poorer low-flow inflow performance relative to high flows.
supporting_quote: NWM and NWM + GDROM have comparable performance in terms of tRMSE, which suggests similar capabilities for the two models in capturing low flow patterns
GDROM is trained primarily to maximize NSE, which biases the model towards better performance in high-flow scenarios.
the NWM generally provides better simulations for high flows than low flows, as the distribution of NSE is skewed closer to 1 ... than that of logNSE.

chunks.text: Storage specification strongly influences NWM+GDROM high-flow performance across CONUS. Observed storage produces much better KGE/NSE distributions than modeled storage, especially for lower quartiles, while tRMSE is similar between storage settings. This indicates that long-term storage error accumulation mainly degrades high/mean flow skill rather than low-flow metrics in this setup.
supporting_quote: NWM + GDROM's performance with observed storage significantly exceeds its performance with modeled storage ... in terms of KGE and NSE.
The lower quartile for KGE increases from below 0.4 ... to around 0.6 with observed storage
the similar tRMSE values between the two storage settings

chunks.text: There are clear spatial patterns in performance gains: reservoirs in Western and Central U.S. see larger improvements from NWM+GDROM than those in the Eastern U.S., where the two models are more comparable. The authors suggest Eastern reservoirs are more inflow-driven and less storage-dependent, allowing simpler NWM routing to capture outflow dynamics reasonably. This leads to marginal incremental gains from GDROM in some Eastern areas.
supporting_quote: Reservoirs in Western and Central U.S. have larger outflow simulation improvement by using NWM + GDROM than those in Eastern U.S., where the NWM and NWM + GDROM have comparable performance.
reservoir operations in Eastern U.S. are more inflow-driven and less dependent on storage
thus NWM's relatively simple built-in reservoir module could reasonably capture outflow dynamics

chunks.text: Regional comparisons show consistent high-flow improvements from NWM+GDROM in the Ohio and Arkansas-White-Red regions when inflow skill is adequate, while tRMSE differences remain modest. In Ohio, the gap between observed vs modeled storage configurations is small, indicating storage plays a lesser operational role. In Arkansas-White-Red, improvements in NSE are strong, with NWM+GDROM lower-quartile NSE around 0.25 compared to NWM median near 0.20.
supporting_quote: Ohio Region... NWM + GDROM significantly outperforms the NWM in terms of both KGE and NSE
in the NWM + GDROM model, the difference between the two storage settings is not as significant in the Ohio region
Arkansas-White-Red Region... the NWM + GDROM models have the lower quartile of NSE around 0.25, which is even higher than the median NSE value achieved (≈0.20) by NWM

chunks.text: In the Upper Colorado region, NWM+GDROM’s success depends heavily on storage accuracy. With observed storage, median KGE and NSE reach about 0.7 and 0.4, but with modeled storage they drop to about 0.25 (KGE) and −0.5 (NSE). The paper connects this to the operational importance of large storage for supply and irrigation, making storage drift particularly damaging.
supporting_quote: Upper Colorado Region... With observed storage, NWM + GDROM achieves median KGE and NSE values of 0.7 and 0.4, respectively.
these values decrease to 0.25 for KGE and −0.5 for NSE when using the configuration with modeled storage.
given the extensive use of large reservoirs in the Colorado River Basin for water supply and irrigation

chunks.text: In the Pacific Northwest, NWM+GDROM with observed storage significantly outperforms NWM across metrics when inflows are accurately simulated, while modeled storage still improves but less strongly. The analysis also emphasizes that better inflow simulation substantially boosts performance for both NWM and NWM+GDROM. Storage accuracy mainly benefits high-flow metrics (KGE/NSE) and contributes little to tRMSE improvements.
supporting_quote: Pacific Northwest Region... NWM + GDROM employing observed storage data significantly outperforms NWM in all metrics.
the use of modeled storage with NWM + GDROM also enhances the performance largely compared to NWM
accurate storage data primarily enhances the accuracy of high flow patterns (as measured by NSE and KGE)... contributes less to improvements in tRMSE

chunks.text: A central limitation is that GDROM is not tightly coupled with NWM’s rainfall–runoff processes, so feedbacks between hydrology and reservoir operations are not fully represented. This means the analysis may not capture dynamic interactions that could affect inflow, storage, and release simultaneously. The authors suggest fully coupled modeling would enable a more complete comparison.
supporting_quote: our analyses in this study may not be able to completely capture the dynamic interactions between rainfall–runoff processes and reservoir operations.
This is because the NWM and GDROM are not tightly coupled, which misses feedback and interactions between the two components.
A fully coupled rainfall–runoff processes and reservoir operations in large-scale hydrological modeling is expected to provide a more complete comparison

chunks.text: The study notes limitations in performance evaluation: although NSE and KGE are widely used and emphasize high flows, their relationship can be unclear and they have known drawbacks. Because of the large number of sites, the authors cannot perform detailed hydrograph-by-hydrograph diagnostics, relying instead on aggregated goodness-of-fit metrics. They also propose exploring alternative metrics that better capture low-flow accuracy.
supporting_quote: We acknowledge, however, that a better approach for simulation performance evaluation, rather than using GoF estimators, is to conduct a detailed comparison of the observed and simulated hydrographs; unfortunately, the large number of study sites included in our analysis prevents us from doing so.
future work may need to explore the model performance difference based two KGE and NSE, which seem to be both high flow-prioritized metrics but their relationship remains unclear
a metrics with better measurement of low-flow simulation accuracy can be tested.

chunks.text: Low-flow improvements are limited partly due to GDROM’s training objective and NWM inflow weaknesses. GDROM is trained primarily on NSE, which de-emphasizes low flows and can lead to near-constant predictions during low-flow periods. Additionally, the paper notes that NWM itself performs relatively poorly for low-flow conditions, limiting what improved routing can achieve.
supporting_quote: GDROM is trained primarily to maximize NSE, which biases the model towards better performance in high-flow scenarios.
For lower flows, GDROM predictions tend to be a constant value close to the mean of the low flows
the NWM exhibits relatively poor performance in simulating low flow conditions, thus limiting the potential improvements that GDROM could introduce.

chunks.text: Incorporating GDROM for reservoir routing can significantly improve NWM reservoir outflow simulation across CONUS, especially when inflow and storage errors are controlled. For reservoirs with inflow NSE > 0 and when driven by observed storage, NWM+GDROM attains lower-quartile KGE and NSE around 0.60 and 0.15, exceeding NWM’s median performance. The study concludes that accurate inflow and storage are critical conditions for realizing GDROM’s benefits at scale.
supporting_quote: The results show that NWM + GDROM has significant improvement compared to NWM in simulating CONUS-wide reservoir outflow, especially when the errors with reservoir inflow and storage are controlled (i.e. reservoir with inflow NSE > 0 and using observed storage for outflow simulation).
NWM + GDROM yields lower quartile of KGE and NSE values around 0.60 and 0.15, respectively, which are even larger than the median value achieved by NWM.
the accuracy of inflow and reservoir storage simulation is also critical in reservoir outflow modeling in hydrological simulations.

chunks.text: Regional conclusions emphasize that observed storage-driven GDROM improves outflow simulations in all four examined regions, while modeled storage can fail in the Southwestern U.S. where storage regulation is crucial. In Upper Colorado, median KGE is about 0.7 with observed storage but about 0.2 with modeled storage, illustrating sensitivity to storage error accumulation. Overall, the study finds larger improvements for high flows than low flows.
supporting_quote: Results show when driven by observed storage, NWM + GDROM produces significant improvements in reservoir outflow simulations in all these regions.
in this region, the median KGE values are approximately 0.1 for NWM, and 0.2 for NWM + GDROM with modeled storage (much lower than 0.7 for NWM + GDROM with observed storage).
the improvement is less considerable in capturing low-flow patterns of reservoir outflow than the high and mean flow.

chunks.text: Hydrological modeling for streamflow is commonly split into data-driven approaches (e.g., LSTM, transformer networks) and process-based models derived from physical laws or conceptual system views. Data-driven models often achieve high predictive accuracy but can be less interpretable and may struggle with extremes. Process-based models offer process insight but can underperform due to structural inadequacies. This motivates approaches that combine strengths across model families.
supporting_quote: Hydrological models serve as indispensable tools for achieving this objective and can be traditionally categorized into two types: data-driven models ... and process-based (or physically-based) models
Data-driven models ... generally achieve high performance. However, they often lack interpretability and may not resolve extreme values very well

chunks.text: Differentiable process-based models aim to merge physical structure with learning by embedding neural networks inside process-based equations and training end-to-end. The differentiable HBV (δHBV) is an HBV formulation implemented in a differentiable framework with neural components for regionalized parameterization and missing processes. Prior work suggests such models can improve computational efficiency, spatial generalization, and representation of extremes, but their structural biases may persist due to prescribed equations.
supporting_quote: These differentiable models (Shen et al., 2023) connect (flexible amounts of) prior physical knowledge to neural networks
δHBV ... incorporates deep neural networks for both regionalized parameterization and missing process representations within a differentiable programming framework that supports "end-to-end" training

chunks.text: Meteorological forcing uncertainty strongly affects hydrologic model performance, and independent forcing products have distinct error characteristics. This paper leverages three CAMELS forcing datasets to expose differences in model behaviors. It contrasts two strategies: fusing forcings as simultaneous inputs to a single model versus training separate models per forcing and then ensembling their outputs.
supporting_quote: the performance of any type of hydrologic model heavily depends on the quality of input data, particularly meteorological forcing data

one could choose to use data fusion to combine them into a single coherent model input ... or to pass each forcing dataset through a model and then afterwards combine the multiple outputs in an ensemble

chunks.text: The study aims to systematically evaluate and leverage simulations from two structurally different high-performing models—an LSTM and a differentiable HBV (δHBV)—across multiple meteorological forcings. It focuses on whether ensembling across model types produces more robust deterministic streamflow predictions than ensembling within a single model class. It further examines benefits across temporal extrapolation and two spatial generalization settings (PUB and PUR).
supporting_quote: we systematically evaluated and utilized the simulations from two highly different models with great performances: a purely data-driven long short-term memory (LSTM) network and a physics-informed machine learning ("differentiable") HBV ... model (δHBV)
evaluating them under both temporal and spatial tests

chunks.text: A central goal is to compare alternative ways of using multiple meteorological forcing datasets. The paper tests whether separate training under single forcing sources followed by output ensembling is more effective than feeding all forcings into one data-driven model (LSTMmulti). This comparison is embedded within the same benchmarking framework and evaluation scenarios.
supporting_quote: It is not clear which approach is more beneficial.
we additionally trained a single LSTM model using all three forcing datasets as simultaneous inputs ... referred to as LSTMmulti

chunks.text: The work explicitly targets the value of process-based structural constraints within an ensemble, especially for spatial transfer. It investigates whether δHBV contributes unique spatial constraints that improve interpolation (PUB) and extrapolation (PUR), where data-driven models may fail to generalize. The evaluation is designed to quantify these effects with standardized metrics over many basins.
supporting_quote: Do process-based equations bring unique value to an ensemble, especially in terms of spatial generalizability?
δHBV significantly enhanced spatial interpolation when incorporated into LSTM, and provided even more prominent benefits for spatial extrapolation

chunks.text: Despite extensive work on ensembles, most hydrology ensemble studies either vary factors within a single model (e.g., initialization, training data, objective functions) or ensemble only process-based models. Large-sample tests across fundamentally different model types (data-driven vs process-based vs hybrid) remain limited. As a result, it is unclear whether crossing model-type boundaries in deterministic ensembles provides systematic benefits.
supporting_quote: These studies generally use one model to generate the differences among the ensemble members.
little work has tested an ensemble across the boundary of model types, particularly between data-driven, process-based, and hybrid models, especially on a large number of samples

chunks.text: Differentiable process-based models such as δHBV raise a specific uncertainty: while they improve over traditional process-based models, their prescribed equations may impose bias patterns that cannot be reduced. This creates ambiguity about their role in ensembles, because they might add structural bias even as they reduce variance. The paper frames this as an open question prior to experimentation.
supporting_quote: it is also unclear whether current differentiable models, e.g., δHBV, ... have unique bias characteristics that are associated with the process-based parts of their structures that cannot be reduced once the equations are prescribed

chunks.text: Prior ensemble evaluations have focused mainly on temporal prediction, but spatial extrapolation is harder and may lead to different conclusions. The paper distinguishes spatial interpolation (PUB) from spatial extrapolation (PUR) and notes that results from temporal tests may not carry over. This motivates evaluating ensembles under both spatial settings.
supporting_quote: previous studies have primarily focused on evaluating ensemble simulations for temporal predictions
streamflow simulation under spatial extrapolation scenarios presents greater challenges, and findings from temporal tests may not be directly applicable

chunks.text: How to best utilize multiple meteorological forcing datasets for streamflow simulation is unresolved. One option is forcing fusion into a single model input; another is to train separate models per forcing and then ensemble outputs. The paper highlights that the relative benefit of these approaches is not established, particularly when model types differ.
supporting_quote: Given the utilization of multiple forcing datasets, one could choose to use data fusion to combine them into a single coherent model input
It is not clear which approach is more beneficial.

chunks.text: The study trains two distinct model types: a benchmark LSTM rainfall–runoff model and a differentiable HBV (δHBV) that embeds HBV equations into a PyTorch differentiable framework. For comparability, the LSTM architecture and hyperparameters follow Kratzert et al. (2021). δHBV uses neural networks for regionalized parameterization and missing process representations and supports end-to-end training via backpropagation.
supporting_quote: we used the LSTM model and its hyperparameters as reported in Kratzert et al. (2021).
HBV is implemented on PyTorch so it is programmatically differentiable ... allowing this model to be trained together with neural networks in an endto-end fashion

chunks.text: The δHBV version used is δHBV1.1p, which adds a capillary rise module to improve low-flow characterization and introduces changes aimed at high-flow performance. These include three dynamic parameters (γ, β, k0), removal of precipitation log-transform normalization, and using a normalized squared-error loss. Dynamic parameters are also maintained during warm-up to reduce initial condition uncertainty.
supporting_quote: we used δHBV1.1p ... The main improvement is the addition of a capillary rise module, which enhances the characterization of low flows.

Three additional modifications ... the use of three dynamic parameters (γ , β, k0); the removal of log-transform normalization for precipitation; and the adoption of the normalized squared-error loss function

chunks.text: A factorial training design is used: each of the two model types (LSTM, δHBV) is trained separately with each of three forcings (Daymet, NLDAS, Maurer), yielding six single-model/single-forcing simulations per scenario. Models are evaluated under temporal extrapolation, PUB, and PUR tests, each repeated over three random seeds. Ensemble results are reported on a 531-basin subset for consistent comparison.
supporting_quote: we trained the two models ... each with one of three meteorological forcing datasets (Daymet, NLDAS, and Maurer), resulting in six corresponding streamflow simulations
We repeated all the simulations with three different random seeds.

chunks.text: Ensembles are created from the six base simulations using several tested weighting strategies; simple averaging is selected because it yields the best performance. The paper defines shorthand ensemble notation: superscripts 1/2/3 for Daymet/NLDAS/Maurer, and superscript clustering (e.g., 123) for forcing-ensembled results. Ensembles are grouped into LSTM, δHBV, cross-model (LSTM+δHBV), and their forcing-ensemble counterparts.
supporting_quote: we tested various weighting strategies and ultimately employed averaging to combine the six single-forcing, single-model-type simulations, as it yielded the best performance
Daymet, NLDAS, and Maurer are abbreviated as superscripts 1, 2, and 3, respectively.

chunks.text: To benchmark an alternative multi-forcing strategy, the study also trains LSTMmulti, a single LSTM that ingests all three forcing datasets simultaneously. This mirrors the approach in Kratzert et al. (2021) and allows direct comparison between (i) output ensembling across single-forcing models and (ii) fusing forcings at the input stage for a single model. This comparison is central to evaluating forcing-utilization paradigms.
supporting_quote: we additionally trained a single LSTM model using all three forcing datasets as simultaneous inputs as done by Kratzert et al. (2021), referred to as LSTMmulti
Ensembling models trained on a single forcing outperformed a single model using fused forcings

chunks.text: Three evaluation scenarios define generalization difficulty: temporal test (same basins, different periods), PUB (holdout basins for spatial interpolation), and PUR (holdout regions for spatial extrapolation). PUB uses 10 spatially stratified groups and PUR uses 7 disjoint regional groups, with round-robin holdouts. Performance is computed after concatenating test results across basins and rounds.
supporting_quote: Temporal Test: Models were trained using data from all basins and tested across different periods.
we conducted 10 rounds for the PUB test and 7 rounds for the PUR test, with a different group held out for testing in each round

chunks.text: Performance evaluation uses basin-wise metrics including NSE, KGE, PBIAS, and RMSE, plus flow-regime RMSE variants for high, low, and mid-range flows. The study also computes ensemble spread to analyze variability and complementarity among ensemble members. The main text emphasizes NSE, while additional metrics are reported in appendices.
supporting_quote: We calculated several well-established performance metrics: Nash-Sutcliffe model efficiency coefficient (NSE) ... Kling-Gupta ... percent bias (PBIAS), and root-mean-square error (RMSE).
We also considered RMSE values for high (top 2 % "peak" flow, highRMSE), low (bottom 30 % "low" flow, lowRMSE)

chunks.text: The experiments use the CAMELS dataset, which includes 671 basins across the conterminous US and provides streamflow, static basin attributes, and multiple meteorological forcing products. For evaluation reporting, the study focuses on a 531-basin subset that excludes basins with areas larger than 2000 km2 or with large area discrepancies. This selection follows prior benchmarking practice to ensure consistent comparisons.
supporting_quote: The CAMELS dataset encompasses 671 basins distributed across the conterminous United States
Test results and performance metrics for all models are reported for the 531-basin subset that excludes those with areas larger than 2000 km2

chunks.text: Three independent daily meteorological forcing datasets from CAMELS are used: Daymet, NLDAS, and Maurer. They include precipitation, temperature, vapor pressure, and surface radiation variables, with NLDAS and Maurer daily temperature extrema supplemented from Kratzert et al. (2021). The methodological differences among these forcings provide distinct error characteristics that can reveal different model behaviors.
supporting_quote: forcing datasets from three independent sources: Daymet ... NLDAS ... and Maurer
Each of the three meteorological forcing datasets operates at a daily temporal resolution, encompassing precipitation, temperature, vapor pressure, and surface radiation variables

chunks.text: Model inputs combine dynamic forcings and static basin attributes. For δHBV, potential evapotranspiration is computed using the Hargreaves method based on maximum/minimum temperatures and basin latitude, while precipitation and mean temperature come from CAMELS. Static attributes cover climate, topography, soils, land cover, and geology, and are normalized for learning-based components.
supporting_quote: potential evapotranspiration is calculated using the Hargreaves (1994) method based on maximum and minimum temperatures along with basin latitudes
Aattr consists of normalized observable basin-averaged attributes, encompassing basin area, topography, climate, soil texture, land cover, and geology

chunks.text: The evaluation periods differ by scenario. Temporal testing trains on 1980–1995 and tests on 1995–2010, using all basins. PUB and PUR train on 1980–1999 and test on 1995–1999, using basin or region holdouts respectively, with multiple rounds to cover all groups.
supporting_quote: Temporal      Alla ... 1980–1995b ... All      1995–2010

chunks.text: In the temporal test, cross-model-type ensembling (LSTM+δHBV) consistently outperforms within-class ensembles when using the same forcing conditions. With a single forcing dataset, median NSE rises from about 0.735 for LSTM to about 0.79 when δHBV is added. Even when LSTM already performs strongly via forcing ensembling (LSTM^123 ≈ 0.808), adding δHBV still improves results to about 0.818.
supporting_quote: With a single forcing dataset, the median NSE was elevated from ∼ 0.735 for LSTM to ∼ 0.79 with δHBV added
LSTM ... were ensembled (ef = 123, ∼ 0.808), adding δHBV still improved the results to ∼ 0.818

chunks.text: The study finds that using multiple forcings via output ensembling of single-forcing LSTMs is better than feeding all forcings into one LSTM (LSTMmulti). Specifically, LSTM^123 achieves NSE 0.8082 versus 0.7974 for LSTMmulti in the temporal test. This suggests the single-model fusion approach may overfit redundant forcing information, while separate training allows diverse errors that are reduced through ensembling.
supporting_quote: Ensembling LSTM simulations each using a single forcing dataset (LSTM123) resulted in an NSE value of 0.8082, higher than that of 0.7974 from feeding multiple forcing datasets into a single LSTM (LSTMmulti).
the trained LSTM in LSTMmulti may be overfit to the significant redundant information in these three forcing datasets

chunks.text: The most diverse ensemble reported combines cross-model forcing ensembles with seed ensembling and optionally adds LSTMmulti, setting new CAMELS benchmarks. The paper reports a median NSE of about 0.83 in the temporal test for (LSTM+δHBV)seed^123 + LSTMseed^multi, surpassing the previous benchmark near 0.82 from LSTMseed^multi. Improvements are also reflected in RMSE and high-flow RMSE when LSTMseed is incorporated.
supporting_quote: Our most diverse ensemble, (LSTM + δHBV)seed123 + LSTMseedmulti , achieved a median NSE value of ∼ 0.83, surpassing the ∼ 0.82 benchmark set by LSTMseedmulti
After incorporating the LSTMseed variant into (LSTM + δHBV)seed123 + LSTMseedmulti , overall RMSE and highRMSE both improved.

chunks.text: Cross-model-type ensembling yields increasing benefits as spatial generalization becomes harder. In PUB, adding δHBV to LSTM ensembles improves median NSE by about 0.02–0.03. In the harder PUR test, δHBV-only simulations and ensembles outperform LSTM-only counterparts under the same forcings, and the LSTM+δHBV gap rises to about 0.04–0.07 (e.g., LSTM^123 ≈ 0.656 vs (LSTM+δHBV)^123 ≈ 0.701).
supporting_quote: adding δHBV to the same-model-type LSTM ensembles improved median NSE by 0.02-0.03 for PUB
e.g., LSTM123 (median NSE ∼ 0.656) and (LSTM + δHBV)123 (median NSE ∼ 0.701 )

chunks.text: The previous temporal record-holder, LSTMseed^multi, shows large performance drops in PUB and PUR, demonstrating weaker robustness for spatial transfer. In contrast, δHBV provides systematic stabilization for ungauged regions, with δHBV-only models generally outperforming LSTM-only models in PUR. This supports the claim that process-based constraints reduce the risk of failed LSTM generalization.
supporting_quote: the previous record-holder for temporal test performance, LSTMseedmulti , incurred large drops in the PUB and PUR tests
δHBVonly individual simulations or ensembles consistently outperformed LSTM-only counterparts in the PUR test

chunks.text: Forcing quality interacts differently with the two model types. δHBV appears more reliant on forcing quality: δHBV with Maurer and NLDAS generally performs worse than with Daymet, which has lower biases. Nevertheless, adding δHBV still improves over LSTM alone even when δHBV’s single-member performance is reduced under certain forcings.
supporting_quote: δHBV models seem more reliant on the quality of the forcing data
δHBV with the Maurer and NLDAS forcing datasets generally performs worse than it does with Daymet, which has lower biases

chunks.text: A diagnostic comparison suggests that basins where LSTM outperforms δHBV under a single forcing are often the same basins that benefit from forcing ensembling within δHBV. This is illustrated by relating (LSTM^1 − δHBV^1) to (δHBV^123 − δHBV^1) for those basins, indicating forcing errors likely drive δHBV underperformance in those cases. The paper argues that ensembling forcings can suppress timing or bias errors that HBV structure cannot easily adapt to.
supporting_quote: the NSE differences between LSTM1 and δHBV1 (LSTM1 – δHBV1)
the NSE differences between δHBV123 and δHBV1 (δHBV123 – δHBV1)

chunks.text: Ensemble diversity increases when combining model types. The paper reports lower spread for δHBV (median spread 0.61) than for LSTM (mean spread 0.72), consistent with δHBV having lower variance. Combining δHBV and LSTM increases ensemble spread, which is associated with stronger ensemble benefits across temporal, PUB, and PUR tests.
supporting_quote: Although δHBV (median spread 0.61) exhibits lower spreads than LSTM (mean spread 0.72), their combination increases the ensemble spreads
This pattern holds across the temporal, PUB, and PUR tests.

chunks.text: Random-seed ensembling yields diminishing returns beyond a small number of seeds. When increasing seeds from 3 to 10, performance improves slightly for all approaches, but the relative gaps remain similar. The paper concludes that 3 seeds are sufficient for robust comparisons, and that LSTM shows higher seed-to-seed variation than (LSTM+δHBV)^123.
supporting_quote: When we changed the number of random seeds from 3 to 10, we found that although all model and ensemble performances slightly improved, the gaps between them did not change much
For LSTMs alone, different random seeds displayed higher variation

chunks.text: The authors note remaining deficiencies in challenging regions such as the Great Plains and areas with strong anthropogenic influence or heterogeneous conditions. Even the ensemble yields low NSE (around 0.3–0.4) for many Great Plains basins, indicating unresolved drivers like sparse stations, aridity, dams, and water use. They suggest multiscale formulations and inclusion of additional data or modules to address these issues.
supporting_quote: the Great Plains ... even the ensemble model had NSE values of only 0.3–0.4 for many of the basins there
regions with significant anthropogenic impacts, such as dam presence, as well as arid climatic and highly heterogeneous geological conditions

chunks.text: While averaging was the best among tested weighting strategies, the paper argues that adaptive or optimized weighting could further improve performance. Basin-specific optimized weights can be highly imbalanced, implying that static averaging is not always ideal. A genetic-algorithm example shows that optimized weighting can substantially raise NSE beyond averaged ensembles in all three test scenarios.
supporting_quote: we have explored various weighting strategies and found that averaging yields the best performance yet
Optimized weighted ... Temporal NSE ... 0.844303212 ... PUB NSE ... 0.842396015 ... PUR NSE ... 0.790796063

chunks.text: The study does not build a δHBVmulti model analogous to LSTMmulti, citing prior related experiments and expected limited gains from seed perturbations in δHBV. The authors argue δHBV has lower variance and potentially higher bias, so random seeds likely will not create sufficiently large perturbations to improve ensembles substantially. They propose that achieving comparable perturbation may require using multiple distinct hydrological model structures (e.g., SAC-SMA, PRMS, GR4J).
supporting_quote: we did not create a δHBVmulti model (in the same vein as LSTMmulti )
random seeds would likely not create large enough perturbations for δHBV and wouldn't bring the benefits seen with LSTMseed

chunks.text: Computational cost is a practical challenge for large ensembles, especially for differentiable process-based models. The paper reports that training LSTM (30 epochs) and δHBV (50 epochs) for temporal testing under a single forcing takes about 5 and 21 hours, respectively, on an NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU. The authors argue most cost is training and could be mitigated by model reuse, simplification, and scalable cloud computing.
supporting_quote: training LSTM (30 epochs) and δHBV (50 epochs) for temporal testing under a single meteorological forcing dataset takes approximately 5 and 21 h, respectively, using a single NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU
the majority of computational costs are incurred during model training

chunks.text: Across 531 CAMELS basins and three evaluation scenarios, cross-model-type ensembles combining LSTM and δHBV consistently outperform single-model and within-class ensembles. The improvements hold for temporal extrapolation as well as spatial interpolation and extrapolation tests, indicating complementary error characteristics. The work positions these results as new benchmarks on CAMELS and highlights the practical value of combining data-driven and physics-informed models.
supporting_quote: Cross-model-type ensembles (LSTM + δHBV) consistently outperformed single-model approaches across all test scenarios, setting new performance benchmarks on the CAMELS dataset.
reaching median NSE values of ∼ 0.83 for the temporal test ... ∼ 0.79 for the ungauged basin test (PUB) ... ∼ 0.70 for the ungauged region test (PUR)

chunks.text: The study concludes that ensembling models trained separately on different forcing datasets is more effective than merging forcings as simultaneous inputs to a single LSTM. Separate training allows each member to capture forcing-specific features and biases that can be mitigated by averaging. This finding challenges the default practice of feeding all available forcing data into one data-driven model.
supporting_quote: Ensembling models trained on different forcing datasets proved more effective than using multiple forcing datasets as simultaneous inputs to a single model.

The superior performance of ensembling models with different forcing datasets over using merged forcings as a single input highlights the risk of indiscriminately feeding all available data into one data-driven model.

chunks.text: A key conclusion is that δHBV contributes most strongly under spatial generalization, especially for the hardest PUR setting, where LSTM-only ensembles can degrade. The authors attribute this to the value of physics-informed constraints in improving transferability to ungauged basins and regions. Nonetheless, they note persistent weaknesses in certain regions, motivating future development that accounts for anthropogenic impacts and basin heterogeneity.
supporting_quote: δHBV provided significant benefits to ensemble simulations on spatial generalization.
Ensembling LSTM with δHBV showed increasing benefits as generalization challenges increased, from temporal to spatial interpolation (PUB) to spatial extrapolation (PUR) tests.

chunks.text: Snow water equivalent (SWE) is a key measure of mountain water storage and is central to predicting snowmelt runoff and water supply forecasting. Seasonal SWE dynamics also influence ecological processes and downstream hydrology, making timely characterization of peak SWE and melt timing valuable. Broad-scale SWE estimation remains difficult due to complex terrain and heterogeneous snow processes across scales.
supporting_quote: Snowpack, measured in the form of snow-water equivalent (SWE), is a fundamental component of the water supply in mountainous regions and the hydro-connected downstream environments
SWE represents the quantity of liquid water within a snowpack and is one of the key parameters in predicting snowmelt runoff and corresponding water supply forecasting

chunks.text: The western U.S. has an extensive in situ snow monitoring network (SNOTEL), and airborne LiDAR products (e.g., ASO) can provide high-resolution catchment-scale snow information. However, point networks are sparse and under-represent high-elevation complex terrain, while LiDAR campaigns are costly and not temporally continuous. These constraints motivate methods that can provide spatially continuous SWE at high resolution and frequent timesteps.
supporting_quote: the USDA Natural Resource Conservation Service (NRCS) has installed over 900 automated snow telemetry (SNOTEL) in situ monitoring stations

the sparsity of in situ sites throughout each basin, the under-representation of SWE measurements at high elevation and topographically complex terrain, and the cost and processing time of snow-on LiDAR observations confound accurate large-scale and temporally continuous snow estimates

chunks.text: Physics-based and remote-sensing-supported snow models can be accurate but face limitations when applied at national scales due to spatial heterogeneity, changing climate, and data constraints (e.g., cloud/vegetation). Machine learning offers flexibility by learning relationships between topography, observations, and snow properties without explicit process parameterization. Recent ML SWE work shows promise, encouraging development of adaptable frameworks for large, heterogeneous regions.
supporting_quote: limitations associated with spatial heterogeneity (e.g., highly variable topography and microclimates), calibration to changing trends in climate, and data limitations ... reduce the likelihood of developing a single national-scale SWE model

The basis for larger-scale model flexibility derives from ML frameworks effectively identifying key topographic and physical feature relationships to snow properties without the need for prior assumption or mechanistic parameterization

chunks.text: The study aims to demonstrate a hybrid ML workflow that estimates spatially continuous SWE across the western U.S. using a limited, publicly available feature set and relatively simple model architecture. The authors seek to quantify how performance varies across snow climate domains and over time, and how error behaves with elevation. A further objective is to outline steps to move the framework toward operational, near-real-time SWE estimation.
supporting_quote: we present an effective use case for hybrid-ML modeling of SWE with the following objectives: (i) quantify the regional variation in ML model performance across snow climate domains, (ii) quantify the temporal variability of model performance, (iii) quantify regional error as a function of elevation, and (iv) introduce future steps

chunks.text: A key goal is to build region-specific SWE sub-models that capture heterogeneity in western U.S. snow hydrology and can produce 1 km gridded SWE estimates at a daily timestep. The workflow uses feature optimization to identify regionally unique drivers and then trains regionally independent neural networks. The operational evaluation is framed as a hindcast of WY2019 excluded from training to reduce leakage.
supporting_quote: We segregated the model domain into 23 region-specific sub-models to account for the differences in western U.S. snow hydrology.
We developed a data-driven modeling framework to examine the operational capabilities of the ML model for extrapolating spatially continuous SWE estimates
We removed WY2019 from the training dataset to investigate the operational capacity of the model

chunks.text: Accurate, broad-scale SWE estimation is challenging because complex terrain drives highly variable snow accumulation and ablation processes. Scaling from point observations to catchment-to-region estimates is difficult when microclimates and topographic complexity dominate. These issues contribute to SWE remaining a longstanding challenge in snow hydrology.
supporting_quote: Complex terrain controls snow accumulation and ablation process, impacting the accurate scaling of SWE estimates from in situ point measurements to the catchment and greater scales
accurate estimation of SWE on a broad scale remains a longstanding challenge

chunks.text: Observation limitations hinder continuous SWE mapping: in situ stations are sparse and biased away from high elevations, and LiDAR-based products are expensive and infrequent. Remote sensing can also be limited by clouds or vegetation, complicating consistent SWE characterization. These data constraints make it hard to maintain high-resolution, temporally continuous SWE estimates.
supporting_quote: the sparsity of in situ sites throughout each basin, the under-representation of SWE measurements at high elevation and topographically complex terrain
data limitations (e.g., remote sensing snowpack properties below cloud cover or heavy vegetation)

chunks.text: Developing a single national-scale SWE model is difficult because heterogeneity, calibration challenges under climate change, and incomplete observations limit generalizability. Even with physics-based models and remote sensing assimilation, consistent performance across diverse regimes is hard to achieve. This motivates flexible modeling approaches that can adapt to regional conditions.
supporting_quote: limitations associated with spatial heterogeneity ... calibration to changing trends in climate, and data limitations ... reduce the likelihood of developing a single national-scale SWE model

chunks.text: The modeling pipeline is a hybrid approach: gradient-boosting decision trees (GBDT) are used for feature-space optimization, and an artificial neural network (ANN) then estimates SWE magnitudes on a 1 km grid. The GBDT stage uses LightGBM and recursive feature elimination (RFE) to select region-specific predictor subsets and representative monitoring sites. The resulting optimized feature set is used to train an MLP regression model for each of 23 regions.
supporting_quote: we utilize a hybrid-ML framework of gradient-boosting decision trees (GBDT) with feature optimization to inform regionally optimized ANNs
We selected the LightGBM framework ... to function as the GBDT algorithm in the ML pipeline.
we implemented Recursive Feature Engineering (RFE) ... within the gradient-boosting model

chunks.text: Study domain is partitioned into 23 sub-model regions aligned with mountain ranges and snow regimes (maritime, prairie, alpine). Regions are designed to avoid distant stations informing unrelated areas and ensure observations are relevant to regional snow hydrology. Sites belong to only one sub-model to keep regional training independent.
supporting_quote: We segregated the model domain into 23 region-specific sub-models to account for the differences in western U.S. snow hydrology.
we delineated the data domain into maritime, prairie, and alpine snowpack regimes to define the regions and to ensure in situ snow observations are relevant to the region of interest.
Observation sites located within a submodel are not considered in another sub-model.

chunks.text: Pre-processing derives terrain predictors from a DEM, including elevation and a combined slope/aspect metric called northness. Terrain values are mapped to 1 km grid cells using nearest-neighbor interpolation. Northness is computed as sin(slope) * cos(aspect) to reduce dimensionality while retaining slope/aspect information.
supporting_quote: Data pre-processing included the use of elevation, slope, and aspect, derived from DEM data, through nearest-neighbor interpolation
northness = sin(slope) * cos(aspect).

chunks.text: Temporal and observational features are engineered to capture accumulation and melt dynamics. The model uses a water-year week index (1–52), current and previous-week in situ SWE from neighboring stations, and a delta SWE feature defined as SWE_t minus SWE_{t-1}. A Previous SWE feature encodes serial correlation by using prior-week SWE (observed in training/testing; predicted during operational hindcast).
supporting_quote: Temporal features include a weekid ... representing the week of the water year (WY)
we calculated the difference to capture the trend ... in SWE dynamics ...  \n$$\Delta SWE_{xt} = SWE_{xt} - SWE_{xt-1}.
the model uses the SWE estimate of the previous week as a feature (Previous SWE).

chunks.text: Missing and inconsistent in situ observations are handled by dropping all records for dates associated with missing SWE values in key features. A specific quality-control case in the Southern Sierra Nevada removed implausible 0.0 cm SWE values above 2500 m during accumulation season and split the region into high/low elevation sub-domains using 2500 m. Features are min–max scaled to 0–1 per region prior to RFE.

chunks.text: LightGBM models are optimized per region using a 5-fold cross-validation grid search over key hyperparameters, including maximum depth, number of leaves, learning rate, subsample fraction, and number of estimators. RFE iteratively removes the lowest-importance feature (based on split counts) and selects the feature set that minimizes L2 loss. Feature importance is then summarized as gain to interpret influential predictors.

chunks.text: The ANN stage uses a multilayer perceptron (MLP) implemented in Keras/TensorFlow. Each regional model includes an input layer for optimized features, seven dense hidden layers (5 to 128 nodes), and an output layer for normalized SWE. Hidden layers use ReLU activation and training minimizes L2 loss with the Adam optimizer.

chunks.text: The model domain is constrained using VIIRS NDSI-derived fraction snow-covered area (fSCA). VIIRS 375 m fSCA is aggregated to 1 km grid cells, and a 10% threshold is used to define snow/no-snow. Locations with fSCA ≤ 10% are assigned 0 cm SWE, while fSCA and a derived HasSnow binary feature are also included as model inputs.

In situ SWE comes from nearly 600 SNOTEL and over 100 CDEC sites, and additional SWE observations come from ASO and NRCS Snow Course surveys. chunks.text: In the WY2019 hindcast (operational-style) evaluation across 23 regions, the model achieves strong overall agreement with observations. chunks.text: The hindcast evaluation indicates the workflow can capture peak SWE magnitudes for most regions. In a rigorous WY2019 hindcast, it achieves respectable performance metrics and captures regional accumulation, peak, and melt dynamics.

chunks.text: Recent improvements in numerical weather prediction have shifted hydrologic forecasting from observation-based statistical methods toward deterministic and probabilistic approaches driven by NWP. In the U.S., a continental-scale system has been developed using WRF-Hydro with a georeferenced vector river network (NHDPlus), enabling forecasts at millions of river reaches. This shift expands spatial coverage far beyond traditional gauge-based forecast points and motivates evaluation of model robustness at intended spatiotemporal scales.
supporting_quote: The ability and accuracy of weather prediction have greatly improved over the past decade, resulting in transformation of hydrologic forecasting approaches from statistical and stochastic methods

chunks.text: WRF-Hydro is a coupling architecture that links land-surface hydrology and routing, supporting both grid-based and reach-based routing. RAPID performs reach-based routing on the NHDPlus network with computational and GIS advantages. Noah-MP, a land surface model with multiple parameterization options, is used in the WRF-Hydro-RAPID framework and underpins the NFIE and the operational National Water Model.

RAPID directly resolves streamflow computations on the NHDPlus river network in a vector-based environment

chunks.text: Prior large-scale evaluations of Noah-MP were often performed at coarse resolution and focused on major rivers and basin outlets, while RAPID evaluations emphasized routing parameter optimization without connecting streamflow errors to land-surface water-flux biases. This creates a need for finer-scale assessment and explicit linkage between streamflow errors and runoff component biases across climatic gradients.

chunks.text: The study aims to evaluate an offline WRF-Hydro-RAPID configuration over Texas for its high-resolution simulation of evapotranspiration and streamflow. It targets understanding model behavior across a strong west–east climate gradient, emphasizing how ET biases relate to biases in individual runoff components. The work is intended as a baseline assessment using default Noah-MP parameters rather than an operationally optimized forecast system.

This responds to growing interest in using satellite-based ET for hydrologic model calibration, while keeping the current study focused on evaluation rather than parameter estimation.
