supporting_quote: our knowledge of HTF heavily relies on data collected from tide gauges, which are scarce and unevenly distributed in coastal systems
coastal systems with the nearest tide gauge located more than a hundred kilometers away ... hinder their use in the estimation of HTF

chunks.text: Prior work has projected water levels or HTF using tide-gauge locations, simplified assumptions (e.g., holding surge/tides constant), or without future projections. Some studies also do not represent how tides may vary with SLR, while others are limited to gauged locations only. The paper argues that these limitations reduce the usefulness of existing studies for decision-making in ungauged stretches of coastline. It situates this study as extending spatial coverage and producing more actionable coastal projections.
supporting_quote: all of these studies are subject to either of the following limitations: (a) being limited to areas with enough gauge readings ... (b) failing to consider how tidal characteristics(i.e., amplitude) vary with SLR in the future, or (c) only investigate the current changes in HTF frequency without making future projections.

chunks.text: The study aims to quantify how projected SLR will exacerbate HTF along the U.S. Atlantic and Gulf coasts assuming no additional flood protection. It produces continuous, spatially distributed estimates by combining high-resolution SLR projections with modeled tidal levels and comparing them against local HTF thresholds. The work targets ungauged coastlines by using a 10 km spacing of analysis points to fill gaps between NOAA gauges. Outputs are intended to support region-specific adaptation planning.
supporting_quote: we investigate the impacts of SLR on HTF along the Gulf and Atlantic Coasts of the United States.
We quantify the extent to which SLR is expected to exacerbate the HTF regime in the coming decades if no more flood protection is implemented.

chunks.text: A central objective is to provide relatively higher-resolution insights into future HTF regime changes under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5. The study combines past tidal estimates and future tide predictions with projected SLR for 2030, 2050, and 2100, then evaluates exceedances of high-resolution HTF thresholds. By doing so, it accounts for both spatial and temporal variability in flooding potential. This supports identifying HTF hotspots and informing local strategies.
supporting_quote: the primary objective of this study is to offer relatively higher resolution insights into the changes in HTF regimes over the coming decades under the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) scenarios
obtaining ... values of SLR projections under different SSPs 2–4.5 and 5– 8.5 and by comparing them to the recently developed HTF thresholds

chunks.text: Tide gauges alone cannot provide adequate spatial coverage for estimating HTF because they are sparse and unevenly distributed, leaving long ungauged coastline segments. Variability in topobathy, land cover, and flood defenses can also limit transferring gauge-derived thresholds to distant locations. This causes gaps in HTF characterization and undermines large-scale planning. The paper frames its analysis as overcoming these gaps via modeling and high-resolution thresholding.
supporting_quote: tide gauges, which are scarce and unevenly distributed in coastal systems
the limited availability of tide gauges restricts their effectiveness for large‐scale planning.

chunks.text: Existing SLR projections are often available only at coarse spatial scales (e.g., ~111 km grids or gauged basins), which are not recommended for simple interpolation in coastal applications. Nonlinear interactions among projection components can make neighboring points differ in ways that are not captured by coarse products. This limits the ability to deliver local, actionable guidance for HTF risk. The paper motivates generating higher-resolution SLR projections to match 10 km HTF analyses.
supporting_quote: SLR projections are available at gauged basins and gridded resolutions of approximately 111 km (IPCC, 2023; Sweet et al., 2022) for local analyses.
such coarse‐resolution SLR projections are not recommended for interpolation due to nonlinear interactions among their underlying influential components.

chunks.text: Long-duration physics-based simulations of tides across full tidal epochs are computationally expensive, complicating future scenario assessments at large spatial scales. Running multi-decade tidal simulations (e.g., the 18.6-year lunar nodal cycle) is described as inefficient for projecting future conditions. This creates a practical need for approaches that retain tidal physics while reducing computational burden. The paper addresses this with harmonic reconstruction driven by constituents from a baseline period.
supporting_quote: due to the computational cost associated with simulating long-term tidal epochs (e.g., the full 18.6-year lunar nodal cycle ...), such simulations become inefficient for future scenario assessments.
To overcome this limitation, harmonic tidal analysis is employed.

chunks.text: Future tidal levels are estimated by linearly combining projected SLR with reconstructed tidal levels. The authors acknowledge nonlinear tide–mean sea level interactions but argue that simply shifting water levels upward by SLR is conservative for design and adequate for their objectives. They cite evidence that storm-tide levels along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts may have insignificant or negative sensitivity to SLR, supporting the linear-combination approach. This framework follows prior projection approaches used in related work.
supporting_quote: In this study, we linearly combine SLR projections with reconstructed tidal levels to estimate tidal level projections.
Consequently, the conventional approach of shifting storm tides upward at the rate of SLR would be positioned on the conservative side of the design spectrum.

chunks.text: To obtain high-resolution future SLR values at 10 km spacing, the study uses a multiple linear regression approach. SLR projections are generated for central years 2030, 2050, and 2100 under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios. The SSP choices are described as representing moderate and high-end emission pathways with global mean SLR ranges by 2100. Regression model performance metrics are reported in supporting information to justify usability.
supporting_quote: To obtain a spatially distributed estimate of the projected values of SLR (for the years 2030, 2050, and 2100), we used a statistical approach based on multiple linear regression
we selected SSP2‐4.5 and SSP5‐8.5 as they represent moderate and high‐end greenhouse gas emission pathways

chunks.text: A physics-based hydrodynamic model (DFlow-FM) is used to simulate present-condition tidal dynamics across the Atlantic and Gulf coasts, with an unstructured triangular mesh and spatially variable bed roughness. Calibration adjusts roughness values by land cover class and compares simulated tides against NOAA CO-OPS tide gauge observations, targeting improved KGE performance. The study also evaluates fit using NSE, RMSE, KDE comparisons, and harmonic constituent comparisons computed via UTide. Remaining systematic mean bias is corrected and spatially interpolated to ungauged locations.
supporting_quote: a physics-based modeling approach is used to simulate tidal dynamics under present conditions.
calibration ... comparing the simulated tidal levels ... against NOAA's tide values ... at 89 ... CO‐OPS tidal gauges, with the goal of maximizing KGE score.

chunks.text: The model domain uses tidal forcing at open boundaries derived from TPXO 8.0 harmonic constituents via Delft Dashboard. Boundary points are taken in both the Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic Ocean, and multiple constituents are included (primary, long-period, and nonlinear). This provides astronomic tidal forcing needed to evaluate HTF evolution along ungauged coastlines. The approach bypasses the lack of offshore gauges by relying on global inverse tidal modeling products.
supporting_quote: boundary conditions in the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean were obtained from 99 to 34 computation points of the Global Inverse Tide Model (TPXO 8.0
Amplitudes ... are included in the TPXO models for eight primaries ... two long periods ... and three non‐linear ... harmonic constituents

chunks.text: To make future tidal projections efficiently, the study performs harmonic tidal analysis using UTide to extract tidal constituents from the baseline hydrodynamic simulation (2000–2021) and reconstruct future tidal time series. Reconstructed tides are produced for 2020–2040, 2040–2060, and 2090–2110, then combined with SLR projections for central years 2030, 2050, and 2100. Constituent selection can be based on statistical significance (SNR > 2), and nodal corrections and detrending options are noted. This hybrid approach reduces computation versus long forward simulations.
supporting_quote: UTide was used to (a) achieve the tidal constituents information ... at each calculation point ... and (b) to reconstruct tidal levels over three tidal epochs of interest (2020–2040, 2040–2060, and 2090–2110)
ensuring that only statistically significant components (SNR > 2) are included in the model.

chunks.text: HTF frequency changes are quantified by comparing current and projected tidal levels with previously developed local HTF thresholds available every 10 km. The analysis counts the number of hours within a 20-year span that projected tides exceed minor flooding thresholds, then compares current versus future exceedance hours to estimate regime change. This assumes HTF thresholds remain constant in the future, which the authors argue is reasonable at regional to continental scales for near- to mid-future assessments. Outputs are mapped as exceedance probability and exceedance hours.
supporting_quote: current states and projections of tidal levels were compared to the previously developed HTF thresholds ... to achieve the number of hours in a 20‐ year time span in which tides surpass the minor flooding thresholds locally.
This approach assumes that HTF thresholds are constant and unchanged in the future, which is a reasonable assumption

chunks.text: The coastline is classified into tidal regime clusters using tidal range and the form factor (FF) computed from diurnal and semidiurnal constituent amplitudes. The study defines FF = (K1+O1)/(M2+S2) and uses FF thresholds to distinguish semidiurnal (<1.5) versus diurnal (>1.5) systems, combined with microtidal (<2 m) and mesotidal (2–4 m) ranges. It then evaluates sensitivity using a normalized relative change (NRC) based on changes in hours exceeding thresholds between present and 2050. This helps identify which tidal regimes are more sensitive to projected SLR.
supporting_quote: we categorized the Atlantic and Gulf Coastlines into three different classes: microtidal semi‐diurnal, mesotidal semi‐ diurnal, and microtidal diurnal.

chunks.text: The study uses corrected DEMs for coastal wetland elevations from Holmquist and Windham-Myers (2022), originally referenced to MHW but transformed to NAVD88 using NOAA’s VDatum to match other modeling layers. It also uses CUDEM 2014 LiDAR-derived topobathy (10 m, NAVD88) and replaces areas with vegetation-corrected DEM where available. These elevation inputs are central for hydrodynamic modeling in low-slope coastal environments. The workflow explicitly addresses vegetation-related vertical bias in LiDAR.
supporting_quote: we utilized the generated elevation data by Holmquist and Windham‐Myers (2022)
To make the necessary adjustments, the vertical datum transformation tool (Vdatum) developed by NOAA was used.

chunks.text: The hydrodynamic model grid is an unstructured triangular mesh extending from Maine to Texas, refined to include urban and wetland areas. The mesh is based on an ADCIRC community grid, modified using Delft3D’s RGFGRID tool and trimmed to nearshore/offshore extents relevant to the Atlantic and Gulf coasts. It includes 34,387 nodes, with 100 m finest resolution in coastal parts and 30 km coarsest resolution offshore. This mesh supports spatially continuous tidal simulation along the study domain.
supporting_quote: The computational mesh ... covers the entire Atlantic and Gulf Coasts, extending from Maine to Texas.
It consists of 34,387 nodes, with the finest resolution of 100 m in the coastal parts and the coarsest resolution of 30 km offshore.

chunks.text: Astronomical tidal forcing for model boundaries is taken from the TPXO 8.0 Global Inverse Tide Model using Delft Dashboard. The forcing includes eight primary constituents (M2, S2, N2, K2, K1, O1, P1, Q1), two long-period constituents (Mf, Mm), and three nonlinear constituents (M4, MS4, MN4). Boundary points are specified separately for the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean. This dataset supplies amplitudes of elevations, transports, and currents needed for tidal simulations.
supporting_quote: Global Inverse Tide Model (TPXO 8.0; Egbert & Erofeeva, 2002) ... using Delft Dashboard
eight primaries (M2, S2, N2, K2, K1, O1, P1, Q1), two long periods (Mf, Mm), and three non‐linear (M4, MS4, MN4)

chunks.text: Model calibration and evaluation rely on NOAA CO-OPS tidal gauges, using 89 stations as calibration points. Observed NOAA tide values are compared to simulated tidal levels to tune roughness and compute skill metrics including KGE, NSE, RMSE, and KDE comparisons. The study also uses UTide on observed and simulated series for constituent amplitude/phase comparisons. These gauge datasets anchor the model’s realism before spatial interpolation to ungauged points.
supporting_quote: comparison of the simulated tidal levels ... against NOAA's tide values ... at 89 ... CO‐OPS tidal gauges
The accuracy of tidal levels ... were compared ... The median NSE of 0.74 ... and a median RMSE of 0.14 m

chunks.text: Spatially varying bed roughness is assigned using National Land Cover Database 2019 classes and ranges informed by Nyaupane et al. (2018). A Latin Hypercube Sampling scheme generates roughness parameter sets for calibration. Land cover classes include forests, grasslands, crops, wetlands, urban areas, and open water. This parameterization aims to improve tide simulations near wetlands and urban areas where friction effects are important.
supporting_quote: land cover classes were obtained from the National Land Cover Database 2019
A Latin Hypercube Sampling (LHS) scheme was used to generate uniformly distributed random samples of roughness values

chunks.text: To estimate societal exposure, the study uses Climate Central’s Risk Finder tool to translate projected tidal levels (relative to MHHW) into county-level exposure estimates. For counties of interest, the median projected tidal level across corresponding coastal points is used as input. The analysis considers property exposure, road closure, and protected lands, and evaluates included versus excluded levee scenarios. The method uses linear interpolation for exposures below 0.6 m and nonlinear regression between 0.6 and 3 m.
supporting_quote: we estimated the exposure associated with the projected tidal levels based on the Risk Finder interactive tool from Climate Central
we calculated the median of the projected tidal levels across these points. This median value represents the water level used as input for the Risk Finder website

chunks.text: Hydrodynamic model calibration produced generally strong agreement between simulated and observed tides across 89 NOAA stations after calibration and mean bias correction. The study reports a median NSE of 0.74 and a median RMSE of 0.14 m, supporting model applicability for tidal characterization. Median KGE is 0.75 with a reported 95% confidence interval of 0.26–0.86. Some Gulf Coast stations show difficulty reproducing diurnal constituent amplitudes (K1, O1), but overall performance remains acceptable.
supporting_quote: The median NSE of 0.74 ... and a median RMSE of 0.14 m ... supports the applicability of this hydrodynamic model
overall performance ... acceptable based on the median KGE of 0.75 (and 95% confidence interval of 0.26–0.86).

chunks.text: Under SSP2-4.5, 2050 projected tidal level (95th percentile over 2040–2060) values range from −0.88 to 2.02 m above MHHW, while projected SLR ranges from 274 to 625 mm. By 2030, projected SLR ranges 133–325 mm and tidal levels range −1.06 to 1.83 m above MHHW. By 2100, projected SLR ranges 647–1,394 mm and tidal levels range −0.42 to 2.49 m above MHHW. These results demonstrate large spatial variability in both tide levels and SLR along the coasts.
supporting_quote: The values of tidal level projections span from − 0.88 to 2.02 m above the MHHW datum, and the amount of SLR extends from 274 to 625 mm.
SLR shows a range of 647–1,394 mm, and tidal levels vary between − 0.42 and 2.49 m above the MHHW datum for 2100.

chunks.text: The study finds median absolute increases in tidal levels relative to MHHW over time, indicating accelerating future water level exceedances. By 2030, the median increase is 0.18 m (95% CI: 0.13–0.21 m). By mid-century, the median increase is 0.35 m (95% CI: 0.25–0.45 m), with Chesapeake Bay at 0.39 m (95% CI: 0.34–0.54 m). By end-century, the median increase reaches 0.84 m (95% CI: 0.69–1.93 m).
supporting_quote: by the year 2030, there will be a median increase of 0.18 m, accompanied by a 95% confidence interval ... 0.13 to 0.21 m
by the mid‐21st century, tidal levels are expected to undergo a median increase of 0.35 m ... 0.25 to 0.45 m ... In the Chesapeake Bay, a median increase of 0.39 m ... 0.34 to 0.54 m.

chunks.text: Comparing projected tidal levels with local HTF thresholds shows that most locations remain below 30 days/year of HTF in the 2030s under SSP2-4.5, with exceptions such as Wilmington (Delaware) and Boston (Massachusetts). By mid-century, multiple regions exceed 30 days/year, including parts of Texas, eastern Florida and South Carolina, Pamlico Sound, Chesapeake Bay areas, New Jersey, and parts of Massachusetts and Maine. Pamlico Sound, Chesapeake Bay, and Rockport (Maine) are identified as highly sensitive, with projections of more than 90 days/year by mid-century. The results emphasize strong regional differences in HTF escalation.
supporting_quote: all regions ... are projected to experience less than 30 days of HTF ... with the exception of Wilmington in Delaware and Boston in Massachusetts.
Pamlico Sound in North Carolina, Chesapeake Bay, and Rockport in Maine ... may endure more than 90 days/year of inundation.

chunks.text: The tidal histogram shapes indicate different tidal regimes between coasts: Atlantic stations show two peaks consistent with semidiurnal tides, while many Gulf stations show patterns consistent with diurnal tides. This supports classification of the Atlantic coast as predominantly semidiurnal and much of the Gulf as diurnal, with exceptions such as the eastern Gulf. The result provides process context for why HTF sensitivity may differ regionally. It also motivates the use of form factor and tidal range clustering in later analyses.
supporting_quote: stations located on the Atlantic Coastline have two peaks in their histograms ... classifying them as semidiurnal systems.
the Gulf coastlines typically experience one high tide and one low tide daily, categorizing them as diurnal systems.

chunks.text: By the end of the century under SSP2-4.5, the study projects widespread increases in HTF, with many locations from Texas to Alabama and from North Carolina to New Jersey experiencing more than half a year of HTF. South Carolina, New York, and Florida are projected to face over 90 days/year, while Maine and New Hampshire are expected to encounter less frequent HTF. This indicates strong north–south and Gulf–Atlantic contrasts in long-term HTF burden. The findings are framed as highlighting the urgency of tailored adaptation measures.
supporting_quote: By the end of this century, states spanning from Texas to Alabama, from North Carolina to New Jersey, and some parts of Massachusetts are anticipated to experience HTF for more than half of the year.
the states of Maine and New Hampshire are expected to encounter less frequent HTF during the same period.

chunks.text: Classification by tidal range and form factor divides the coast into microtidal semidiurnal, mesotidal semidiurnal, and microtidal diurnal regions, consistent with known tidal patterns. The eastern Gulf of Mexico is identified as semidiurnal despite the broader Gulf tendency, attributed to Atlantic influence near Florida. Using normalized relative change (NRC), the study reports that microtidal semidiurnal regions have more variation in sensitivity, while mesotidal semidiurnal regions have the highest median sensitivity. This supports the claim that mesotidal semidiurnal systems are, on average, more sensitive to SLR-driven HTF changes.
supporting_quote: we categorized the Atlantic and Gulf Coastlines into three different classes: microtidal semi‐diurnal, mesotidal semi‐ diurnal, and microtidal diurnal.
micro‐tidal semidiurnal will experience more variations in SRC, whereas the median of SRC is higher than the others in the meso‐tidal semidiurnal region.

chunks.text: Comparing HTF exceedance hours derived using Sweet et al. (2018) versus Mahmoudi et al. (2024) thresholds shows spatially structured, statistically significant differences. A paired t-test confirms significance, and the study attributes discrepancies to feature sets: Sweet et al. relies mainly on tidal range, while Mahmoudi et al. includes latitude/longitude and SLR. In Louisiana and east Texas, Mahmoudi et al. yields higher thresholds driven by higher SLR and latitude, whereas Sweet et al. can be lower due to low tidal range. On parts of the Atlantic coast, Mahmoudi et al. thresholds increase in northern states due to high latitude and tidal range and decrease southward as latitude and SLR decline.
supporting_quote: Sweet et al. (2018) ... relying predominantly on the tidal range as the sole feature. Alternatively, Mahmoudi et al. (2024) ... incorporates additional features, including longitude, latitude, SLR, and tidal range
A paired t‐test confirmed the statistical significance of these differences.

chunks.text: Exposure estimates using the Risk Finder tool suggest that, with levees included, New Orleans and Boston have the most severe end-of-century property exposure to projected HTF, followed by Washington, D.C. The study reports that New York, Houston, and Miami are projected to experience less than $1 billion exposure by end-century in this specific analysis. For road exposure by end-century, New Orleans is most affected, followed by Houston, with other cities below 100 miles of exposed roads. Over the next three decades, New Orleans is projected to face about $23 billion exposure and Boston about $3 billion, with several metros around $800 million.
supporting_quote: by the end of this century, New Orleans and Boston are expected to bear the most severe exposure ... whereas New York, Houston, and Miami are expected to experience less than 1 billion dollars exposure.
Over the next three decades ... New Orleans is projected to face the most significant exposure of $23 billion dollars, followed by Boston with an exposure of $3 billion dollars.

chunks.text: The exposure analysis uses Climate Central’s Risk Finder “bathtub method,” which the authors note can introduce significant inaccuracies because it assumes uniform horizontal spreading of water and neglects flow dynamics, topography, infrastructure interactions, and defenses. As a result, exposure estimates should be interpreted as illustrative rather than high-fidelity flood modeling. The study uses this approach to provide tangible, accessible outcomes but explicitly acknowledges its bias risks. This limitation affects the precision of county-scale exposure numbers.
supporting_quote: This tool estimates the different flood exposures ... using a bathtub method.
bathtub models can introduce significant inaccuracies and biases in flood risk estimates (Sanders et al., 2024).

chunks.text: The study assumes HTF thresholds remain constant in the future when comparing projected tides to minor flood thresholds. The authors argue this is reasonable at regional to continental scales for near- to mid-future projections, but it remains an assumption that could be affected by evolving coastal morphology, defenses, or local datum changes. This simplification helps isolate climate-driven changes in HTF frequency. However, it may under- or over-estimate future HTF if thresholds shift.
supporting_quote: This approach assumes that HTF thresholds are constant and unchanged in the future
which is a reasonable assumption at the regional to continental scale under near to mid‐future projections

chunks.text: Non-tidal residuals (NTR) are not projected forward in this study, and the authors justify this by showing that tides are the dominant driver for most HTF events near minor-to-moderate thresholds. They report that for 75% of stations, the tidal-to-still-water ratio exceeds 50% within the relevant threshold range. They also note uncertainty and contradictory findings on how storm surges may change with warming. This omission is presented as reasonable for HTF-focused projections but limits representation of surge-driven changes in HTF.
supporting_quote: we excluded the evolution of non‐tidal residuals (NTR) over time
the percentage ration in 75% of the stations is above 50%, which means that water levels in the range of minor to moderate thresholds is mostly driven by tides.

chunks.text: The paper emphasizes that the scenario analyzed assumes no significant additional flood protections, infrastructure improvements, or land-use changes through the end of the century. This is described as less likely in practice but useful for isolating climate effects on exposure and HTF escalation. The analysis does not include future levees/seawalls, urban planning changes, or relocation that could alter exposure levels and potentially the HTF regime. Therefore, results represent a baseline “no additional intervention” outlook rather than a policy-informed adaptation pathway.
supporting_quote: The results presented here are based on the assumption that, till the end of this century, no significant additional protection strategies, infrastructure improvements, or changes to land use and development will be implemented.
this analysis does not account for potential mitigation measures, such as the construction of new levees, seawalls, or other flood defenses

chunks.text: Some tidal environments such as narrow inlets, creeks, or channels would ideally require mesh resolutions finer than used here (1–30 m desired vs 100 m used), but computational constraints prevented further refinement. The authors note that ever-changing morphology also introduces bias and that systematic shifts between observed and simulated tides required mean bias correction. These model-structure and input limitations can affect local accuracy, especially in complex geomorphological settings. The study mitigates this via calibration and bias correction, but residual uncertainties remain.
supporting_quote: For tide gauges located in narrow tidal inlets, creeks, or channels, a mesh resolution of 1-30 m is desirable ... which is lower than the resolution we considered here (100 m).
there were systematic differences and shifts between simulated and observed tides. Hence, a bias correction toward observed values was required.

chunks.text: The authors caution that end-of-century predictions carry substantial uncertainty because of the long time horizon and potential changes in climate, technology, and protective infrastructure. They also note that terrestrial fluxes influencing estuarine water levels are not included, which could affect trends in estuarine systems like Chesapeake Bay. The discussion highlights the need to incorporate uncertainty quantification, distinguishing aleatory from epistemic uncertainty. This frames future work as expanding from deterministic projections to probabilistic risk ranges.
supporting_quote: making precise predictions about conditions by the end of the 21st century comes with uncertainties
A critical future direction for this work is the incorporation of methods to quantify and account for uncertainties

chunks.text: The study concludes that accelerating SLR will substantially increase HTF frequency along the U.S. Atlantic and Gulf coasts, with strong spatial variability. It identifies Chesapeake Bay and Pamlico Sound as early hotspots for major HTF increases, with other high-risk areas spanning states from North Carolina to New York and parts of the Gulf Coast including Texas and Louisiana. The results are positioned as a high-resolution baseline for regional planning, emphasizing that region-specific strategies are needed. The authors stress that local SLR information and localized HTF thresholds are essential for effective adaptation decisions.
supporting_quote: Chesapeake Bay and Pamlico Sound will be the first regions to experience the most significant increase in HTF.
Our findings highlight the need for region-specific flood strategies based on high-resolution SLR and HTF information

chunks.text: By end-century under SSP2-4.5, the paper projects very large increases in tidal levels above MHHW and widespread HTF, including the possibility of at least 180 days/year of inundation in Chesapeake Bay. The authors note that some regions (eastern Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, and Maine) may experience comparatively fewer inundation hours by mid-century relative to hotspots. The conclusion emphasizes differentiated regional impacts and calls for tailored flood mitigation strategies, prioritizing the most vulnerable regions first. This message is framed as supporting policymakers and planners in allocating resources efficiently.
supporting_quote: Chesapeake Bay will experience more severe consequences of tidal flooding as it will at least undergo 180 days/year of inundation
Chesapeake Bay, west and central parts of the Gulf Coast emerge as the initial frontline regions in urgent need of flood mitigation strategies

chunks.text: High tide flooding (HTF) is a minor coastal flooding category that can repeatedly disrupt communities through traffic and business interruptions and gradual infrastructure degradation. While individual events may be small, their chronic accumulation over time creates significant socioeconomic and policy challenges. Prior analyses of NOAA tide gauge records show HTF occurrence and duration have increased across U.S. coasts, and sea level rise (SLR) is identified as the primary driver of this trend.
supporting_quote: High tide flooding (HTF, a.k.a. sunny day flooding or nuisance flooding) is a category of minor floods driven by elevated coastal sea levels with a potential for business and traffic interruptions and infrastructure degradation
Previous studies examining still water levels recorded by tide gauges ... have revealed a discernible increase in the occurrence and duration of HTF events
Sea level rise (SLR) ... is known as the primary factor behind the increased frequency of HTF

chunks.text: Local relative SLR can deviate from global mean rates because of regional and local processes, which complicates planning and adaptation. The paper cites an accelerating global rate around 3.1 ± 0.3 mm/yr but emphasizes that local estimates differ due to local/regional factors. This motivates the need for local projections and metrics that can monitor and communicate SLR impacts across space and time.
supporting_quote: The local estimates of relative SLR would deviate from the estimated accelerating global rates  (3.1\pm0.3 \, \text{mm/yr}^{16,19-21})  due to local/regional processes
To facilitate effective long-term planning, it is imperative to prioritize the development of local projections for sea level analysis and prediction

chunks.text: Common HTF threshold setting combines tidal records with local flood impact monitoring to identify water levels where nuisance flooding begins. Tide gauges and satellite altimetry provide water level information, but impact-based monitoring is needed to tie water levels to actual nuisance impacts (e.g., closures). The resulting thresholds represent coastal water levels at which nuisance flooding begins for communities.
supporting_quote: to establish HTF thresholds ... a systematic approach is currently adopted. This involves ... local tidal records and a local flood monitoring system.
To accurately identify when nuisance flooding impacts begin to occur (e.g., road and business closures), it is imperative to implement a local flood monitoring system.
HTF thresholds, which represent the coastal water level at which nuisance flooding impacts begin to occur for coastal communities

chunks.text: The study proposes a machine-learning-based HTF thresholding system to estimate both relative SLR rates and HTF thresholds at fine spatial resolution along U.S. coastlines. The approach targets 10 km intervals and is designed to complement conventional linear and point-based estimates. A key goal is to provide estimates for ungauged stretches of coast by learning relationships from existing gauge data and physically relevant features.
supporting_quote: we propose a high tide flood (HTF) thresholding system that leverages machine learning (ML) techniques to estimate SLR and HTF thresholds at a relatively fine spatial resolution (10 km) along the United States' coastlines.
can estimate these values at ungauged stretches of the coast.
intended to facilitate the communication of SLR risk to vulnerable coastal communities, particularly in locations that lack gauge measurements.

chunks.text: A primary aim is to generate spatially distributed products for SLR rates and HTF thresholds along the CONUS coast every 10 km to support impact communication and adaptation planning. The paper frames these outputs as tangible metrics to raise awareness of chronic HTF signals and to inform risk-informed decision-making. The intended audience includes emergency managers, policymakers, and communities lacking nearby gauges.
supporting_quote: provide spatially distributed information on SLR rates and HTF thresholds every 10 km along the Continental United States (CONUS) coastline.
The results can raise community awareness about SLR impacts by documenting the chronic signal of HTF and providing useful information for adaptation planning.
This information plays a pivotal role in effective riskinformed decision-making and communication

chunks.text: HTF thresholds and SLR rates are often derived from point-based tide gauges, but gauge networks are sparse and uneven. The paper estimates that if U.S. coastlines are segmented into 10 km intervals, 75% of coastal communities lack a tide gauge within 10 km. This forces stakeholders to borrow thresholds from distant gauges, which may not share the same controlling coastal characteristics and introduces uncertainty.
supporting_quote: Our current understanding of SLR rates and HTF thresholds is heavily reliant on measurements from point-based gauges.
If the US coastlines were segmented into 10 km intervals ... 75% of the coastal communities in the United States lack access to tide gauges within a 10 km radius
They make assumptions and use the information available at the nearest tide gauge that might be located more than a hundred kilometers away

chunks.text: Impact-based threshold setting is limited where comprehensive local flood monitoring records are missing, preventing consistent separation of flooding and non-flooding conditions. This lack of monitoring impedes systematic HTF threshold determination at many sites. As a result, consistent and spatially complete HTF threshold datasets are difficult to produce using traditional approaches.
supporting_quote: the lack of a comprehensive flood monitoring system over the past few decades in many tide gauges does not allow for a systematic delineation between flooding and non-flooding conditions
it is imperative to implement a local flood monitoring system. This system is designed to continuously track and record favorable conditions at which flood impacts occur.

chunks.text: A univariate linear regression based on greater tidal range (GTR) is insufficient to capture spatial variability in HTF thresholds above the local high tide datum (MHHW). The paper shows poor skill for the MHHW-based formulation, including negative NSE in some cases, especially where GTR is large. This indicates HTF thresholds are controlled by multiple factors and require a multivariate, nonlinear approach.
supporting_quote: an insufficient skill of Eq. (2) to estimate HTF_MHHW is evident (i.e. with a negative NSE), especially for points with larger GTR.
a linear regression solely based on one independent variable (here GTR) generally fails to capture the stochastic nature of spatial variability in HTF threshold
The variability in HTF thresholds necessitates the incorporation of multiple features, and a simple linear regression method proves insufficient

chunks.text: There is an identified gap in consistent, generalizable metrics to monitor and communicate SLR impacts across spatiotemporal scales. Even with progress in SLR projection methods, the paper argues that severity of predicted impacts is not communicated effectively. A thresholding system that can be monitored across locations is positioned as one solution to make impacts more tangible and comparable.
supporting_quote: There is a general absence of reliable and generalizable metrics that allow for ongoing monitoring of SLR impacts across spatiotemporal scales.
there is a need to communicate the severity of predicted impacts more effectively.

chunks.text: The workflow clusters the coastline into regions with similar input-feature characteristics, then trains separate Random Forest (RF) models per cluster for SLR and HTF threshold estimation. K-means clustering is used, and the elbow approach selects the number of clusters. The process is applied first to SLR, then extended to HTF thresholds using the estimated/available SLR among other features.
supporting_quote: we used the K-means algorithm ... to cluster the HTF threshold's input data into different categories.
Based on the results of the elbow approach ... three different clusters were required

distinct Random Forest (RF) algorithms are developed for each cluster, specifically addressing SLR rates. Following this, the application of RF algorithms for each cluster is extended to the HTF threshold model.

chunks.text: The study uses K-means clustering with an elbow-method tradeoff to partition sites into three coastal regions. The resulting clusters are West Coast, Gulf and Southeast Coasts, and Northeast Coast. This regionalization is presented as physically consistent with differing still-water-level dynamics that govern HTF behavior.
supporting_quote: The elbow approach ... determine the optimal number of clusters
three different clusters were required for the dataset to be divided on
clustered ... into the following three regions ... i) West Coast, ii) Gulf and Southeast Coasts, and iii) Northeast Coast.

chunks.text: Relative SLR rates are estimated using an RF regression model at 10 km intervals after feature transformation and hyperparameter tuning via randomized search. The trained model is evaluated by comparing predicted SLR rates against target values from Kopp et al. Region-specific models are emphasized to capture spatially varying drivers.
supporting_quote: Feature transformation and randomized search are essential steps
RF regression algorithm was used to estimate the SLR rate at 10 km intervals along the U.S. coasts.
the predicted SLR rates were compared to the target values from Kopp et al.

chunks.text: HTF thresholds above MHHW are estimated with an analogous RF training/validation procedure and compared against a linear regression (Sweet et al.) approach. The paper frames the ML model as less constrained because it "puts more trust" in reported NWS thresholds, aiming to mimic observed thresholds more closely across a wider range. Model refinement includes removing low-impact features to improve performance and reduce computation.
supporting_quote: We went through an identical training and validation procedure
comparison between the observed and predicted values using ... the ML algorithm ... and the linear regression (LR) introduced by Sweet et al. (Eq. (2))
a necessary refinement was performed by removing two components, including coastal elevation and continental shelf slope, which were found to have relatively minimal impacts

chunks.text: Model validation uses a random 85%/15% training/validation split, repeated 100 times, and reports averaged evaluation metrics to assess generalization to unseen samples. This procedure is applied to both the SLR and HTF models. Performance is summarized with metrics including NSE, KGE, MAE, and R-squared.
supporting_quote: resulting in an 85% allocation to the training dataset and a 15% allocation to the validation dataset.
This process was repeated 100 times, and the average evaluation metrics were used
The performance metrics used ... show ... Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) ... Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE) ... mean absolute error (MAE) ... and R-squared

chunks.text: Because some predictors were only available at coarse resolution, the study interpolates them to desired coastal points using Empirical Bayesian Kriging (EBK). Values are then extracted to target points in ArcGIS Pro to form the feature matrix for RF training and for generating final 10 km products. This step is positioned as necessary for enabling predictions at every coastal interval.
supporting_quote: Empirical Bayesian Kriging was utilized to interpolate between the input feature data points in cases where input data had coarse resolution.
Next, Extract Multi Values to Point in ArcGIS Pro was used to provide the features' values at the available target points
generate spatially distributed SLR rates and HTF thresholds every 10 km.

chunks.text: To address limited target (output) sample size, the study uses a buffer-zone data augmentation approach around existing target points. A 2.5 km radius buffer is created and 2–3 additional points are generated within it, assigned the same target value as the original point. The justification is that coastal characteristics vary minimally within 2.5 km.
supporting_quote: we adopted a data augmentation technique referred to as the buffer zone method
a circular buffer with a radius of 2.5 km was created around each existing target point. Within this buffer zone, two to three additional points were generated
coastal characteristics exhibit minimal variation within a radius of 2.5 km

chunks.text: For SLR model training, the target variable is based on site-specific SLR rates from Kopp et al., covering 145 gauge locations along CONUS and multiple climate scenarios/percentiles. The study uses the 50th percentile estimate for year 2020 under RCP 4.5 as the present-day baseline. Other scenarios are analyzed in supplementary materials.
supporting_quote: we utilized the SLR rates from Kopp et al. which provided 145 SLR rates for gauges along the CONUS coastlines.
we have considered the 50th percentile of the estimated SLR for the year 2020 under RCP 4.5 ... as the baseline for present-day.
we analyzed other scenarios and presented the results in the supplementary information.

chunks.text: For HTF threshold modeling and validation, the study uses available threshold records including those provided by Sweet et al. and additional recently estimated thresholds. It reports obtaining thresholds at "one hundred additional gauges" along CONUS that will be made publicly accessible. NOAA/NWS official thresholds are used as reference for comparisons in mapping and evaluation.
supporting_quote: besides using the original records of HTF threshold provided by Sweet et al. 5, we have obtained recently estimated thresholds in one hundred additional gauges along the CONUS coastline
The proposed ML algorithm here ... puts more trust in the correctness of the reported NWS thresholds
the NOAA official thresholds are presented ... to facilitate the comparison

chunks.text: Input features for estimating relative SLR include multiple reanalysis-derived ocean/atmospheric variables and vertical land motion, assembled at 10 km resolution after interpolation when needed. Specifically mentioned predictors include ocean heat, ocean circulation, salinity, sea level pressure, surface pressure, and sea surface temperature, plus vertical land motion. Latitude and longitude are also included as geographic indicators.
supporting_quote: reanalysis records of global ocean heat, ocean circulation, salinity, sea level pressure, surface pressure, and sea surface temperature were obtained ... and considered as input features
The vertical land motion (VLM) was another input feature expected to contribute to the relative SLR.
latitude and longitude were considered among the input variables for both processes

chunks.text: For the HTF threshold model, the candidate predictors include relative SLR, greater tidal range (GTR), continental shelf slope, and coastal elevation, along with latitude and longitude. These variables are described as physically relevant to HTF exceedance changes, wave propagation modulation, and inundation vulnerability. Flood defenses are acknowledged as relevant but excluded due to lack of accessible public data.
supporting_quote: relative SLR, GTR, the continental shelf slope, and the coastal elevation were considered as effective variables on the HTF thresholding system
The continental shelf slope is specifically essential, given its contribution to the modulation of coastal wave propagation
Another aspect that merited consideration is the flood defenses ... However, the unavailability of easily accessible public data led to the decision not to incorporate this component

chunks.text: The study generates final products at 10 km intervals along the CONUS coastline and states that all data sources are publicly accessible, with links listed in Supplementary Table S1. It also provides a project link for final products and a GitHub repository for code and data. This supports reproducibility and access to outputs for practitioners.
supporting_quote: provide spatially distributed information on SLR rates and HTF thresholds every 10 km along the Continental United States (CONUS) coastline.
All data used in this study is publicly accessible. Please refer to Supplementary Table S1
The codes, input data, and output data of the ML algorithms are deposited on our GitHub page

chunks.text: K-means clustering identified three coastal regions as the optimal partition for modeling based on the elbow method. The clusters correspond geographically to West Coast, Gulf and Southeast Coasts, and Northeast Coast. The paper states this partition aligns with physical differences affecting still water level dynamics and HTF behavior.
supporting_quote: Based on the results of the elbow approach ... three different clusters were required
clustered ... into the following three regions ... i) West Coast, ii) Gulf and Southeast Coasts, and iii) Northeast Coast.
This is consistent with physical features in these systems that govern the still water level dynamics

chunks.text: The RF SLR model shows good agreement between observed and predicted SLR rates in validation comparisons. Under current climate, the Northeast cluster has the largest regional median SLR rate reported as 5.25 mm/yr, with smaller spread than other clusters. The West Coast shows a smaller median (~2 mm/yr) and includes locations below the global average SLR rate.
supporting_quote: Figure 3a illustrates a comparison between the observed rates of SLR and the rates predicted by the trained algorithm.
the Northeast cluster shows the largest regional median rate of SLR, which is 5.25 mm/yr
Similarly, the West Coast cluster shows a smaller median value of 2 mm/yr ... includes locations with rates of relative SLR that are below the global average rate of SLR.

chunks.text: Feature-importance analysis suggests different dominant drivers by region for SLR prediction. The West Coast model is most affected by latitude; the Gulf and Southeast region is most affected by ocean circulation; and the Northeast is driven mainly by latitude and vertical land motion. Removing low-importance variables degraded metrics, indicating even low-ranked predictors can matter locally.
supporting_quote: the West Coast is most affected by the latitude; the Gulf and Southeast Coasts are impacted by the ocean circulation the most; and the most important feature in the Northeast Coast is latitude and vertical land motion
we eliminated the variables with the least importance ... However, we found that the evaluation metrics worsened, indicating that all variables were essential as input data.

chunks.text: For HTF thresholds above MHHW, the ML approach better matches observed median and range across regions than the linear regression method based on Sweet et al. The LR method shows poor performance in capturing percentile range across all regions, while ML performs relatively well for both median and range. This supports using nonlinear multivariate models for HTF threshold estimation.
supporting_quote: Figures 4a and b show the comparison ... the ML algorithm ... and the linear regression (LR)
the LR approach fails to produce a percentile range that aligns with the reported values across all regions.
In contrast ... the ML algorithm performs relatively well in predicting both the median and the range of HTF thresholds.

chunks.text: Model refinement for HTF thresholds removed coastal elevation and continental shelf slope after they were found to have minimal impact, improving performance and reducing training time. The paper reports that percentile rankings of large disparities improved after omitting these features, and supplementary tables show evaluation metric improvements with this change. This indicates careful feature selection can strengthen the RF threshold model.
supporting_quote: removing two components, including coastal elevation and continental shelf slope, which were found to have relatively minimal impacts ... led to improvements in the model performance and a decrease of computational time
Supplementary Tables S6a and S6b show the evaluation metrics with and without considering the coastal elevation and continental shelf slope, demonstrating the improvement

chunks.text: Validation metrics are reported for both SLR and HTF models under current conditions, showing higher skill for SLR than HTF thresholds. For SLR estimation across clusters, NSE values are 0.74, 0.95, and 0.8 and KGE values are 0.82, 0.94, and 0.85. For HTF thresholds, average NSE values are 0.42, 0.4, and 0.3 with KGE 0.6, 0.54, and 0.48, indicating moderate predictive skill for thresholds.
supporting_quote: SLR estimation ... show a Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) of 0.74, 0.95, 0.8, Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE) of 0.82, 0.94, 0.85
Regarding the HTF thresholds ... NSE of 0.42, 0.4, 0.3, KGE of 0.6, 0.54, 0.48

chunks.text: The trained models are applied to produce spatially distributed maps of SLR rates and HTF thresholds every 10 km along CONUS. The spatial outputs indicate higher SLR rates along Louisiana and east Texas compared with other Gulf/Southeast areas closer to global averages. The Pacific Northwest shows the lowest SLR rates, attributed in part to isostatic adjustments.
supporting_quote: provide spatially distributed information on SLR rates and HTF thresholds every 10 km along the Continental United States (CONUS) coastline.
the coasts of Louisiana and east of Texas have experienced higher rates of SLR
The Pacific Northwest region displayed the lowest SLR rates ... partially due to isostatic adjustments

chunks.text: The study notes that vertical land motion appears least important for SLR prediction in the Gulf and Southeast cluster, which conflicts with prior local studies. The authors attribute this discrepancy to limited observational water level data in parts of the Gulf Coast, citing only three long-record tide gauges along Louisiana. This highlights how sparse observations can limit what data-driven models learn about key drivers in specific regions.
supporting_quote: vertical land motion (VLM) had the least importance in affecting SLR rates in the Gulf and Southeast cluster. This finding is in contrast to previous studies
Only three tide gauges with long enough records exist along the coast of Louisiana that enable the calculation of relative SLR rates.
our ML algorithm may not have sufficient information to learn the importance of VLM in this region

chunks.text: Providing spatially distributed SLR and HTF estimates is constrained by the coarse resolution of many input datasets, making interpolation unavoidable. The paper suggests that dynamically downscaled inputs could improve accuracy. It also flags an open question about the tradeoff between number of input features and reliable outputs, calling for further investigation with comprehensive dynamical modeling.
supporting_quote: the input data for the ML algorithm proposed here to predict SLR rates is available at coarse resolution, so interpolation between the available points is inevitable.
Dynamically downscaled input information can greatly improve the accuracy of these predictions.
the tradeoff between the number of input features to obtain reliable outputs is subject to further investigation.

chunks.text: Flood defenses are identified as a critical variable for flood thresholds, but they are excluded due to lack of accessible public data. The discussion also notes that NOAA impact-based thresholds can be inconsistent in impact-depth across locations, limiting their usefulness for spatial pattern/trend analysis. These issues motivate feature-based and ML approaches but also indicate missing variables and institutional inconsistencies remain challenges.
supporting_quote: Another aspect that merited consideration is the flood defenses, a critical parameter ... However, the unavailability of easily accessible public data led to the decision not to incorporate this component
impact-depth inconsistencies in NOAA thresholds pose a serious challenge in providing useful spatially distributed information on HTF patterns/trends

chunks.text: The paper concludes that an ML-based, regionally trained RF framework can provide spatially distributed estimates of relative SLR rates and HTF thresholds at 10 km resolution, including ungauged coastal stretches. It argues these products can improve flood risk communication by documenting chronic HTF signals and aiding adaptation planning. The findings encourage broader application of ML for distributed threshold development beyond traditional linear or point-based methods.
supporting_quote: we propose a high tide flood (HTF) thresholding system ... at a relatively fine spatial resolution (10 km) along the United States' coastlines.
can estimate these values at ungauged stretches of the coast.
The results can raise community awareness about SLR impacts by documenting the chronic signal of HTF and providing useful information for adaptation planning.
The findings encourage further application of ML in achieving spatially distributed thresholds.

chunks.text: The study positions the developed approach as a substantial advancement from impact-based local thresholding and univariate linear regression toward a multivariate, nonlinear, feature-based strategy. It emphasizes that ML better captures the natural regional differences in HTF thresholds and can generate reasonably accurate results across a wider range of observed threshold values than the LR method. This supports using ML to create more generalizable coastal threshold information for management and planning.
supporting_quote: The proposed methodology in this study represents a substantial advancement towards a global strategy that leverages ML algorithms to provide spatially distributed information efficiently.
our ML algorithm exhibits a capacity to generate reasonably accurate results across a more extensive spectrum of observed HTF threshold ranges.
The natural differences in HTF thresholds across regions highlight limitations in current methods that mainly use univariate linear regression and suggest a need to shift to nonlinear approaches.

chunks.text: Flooding is the most frequently experienced natural disaster in the United States and is a leading driver of federal disaster declarations and relief spending. Beyond property losses, floods cause loss of life, including risks to first responders during rescues. The paper frames improved real-time flood information as essential for saving lives and reducing damage during events.
supporting_quote: “Flooding is the natural disaster most frequently impacting people in the United States (U.S.).”
“the cost to the federal government for disaster relief for flooding exceeds that from any other form of natural disaster”

chunks.text: NOAA’s National Weather Service established the National Water Center to provide a focus for “total water prediction” in the U.S., and the NFIE emerged as an early collaborative activity around that center. The experiment connected academic, federal, and commercial partners to explore how national-scale hydrologic modeling and information exchange could be advanced and transitioned toward operations.
supporting_quote: “The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Weather Service (NWS) has established a National Water Center… intended to provide a focus for total water prediction for the U.S.”

“The National Flood Interoperability Experiment is a research collaboration among academia, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration National Weather Service, and government and commercial partners”

chunks.text: Multiple national geospatial datasets were integrated into NHDPlus, which subdivides the continental U.S. into 2.7 million reach catchments and associated flowlines with shared identifiers (COMID). This structure provides a high-resolution, connected representation of land and water suitable for localized computations while maintaining national consistency. FEMA’s flood mapping programs created DFIRMs and the National Flood Hazard Layer, offering floodplain extents over much of the country.
supporting_quote: “combined into a composite dataset called NHDPlus in which the land surface of the continental U.S. is subdivided into 2.7 million elementary ‘reach catchments’”
“The DFIRMs from individual cities and counties have been synthesized into a National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL) that covers 60% of the land area and 88% of the population of the U.S.”

chunks.text: A central goal was to demonstrate a near real-time, high spatial resolution flood data, modeling, forecasting, and inundation mapping system for the continental United States. The effort aimed to show that national computations at reach-catchment scale are feasible quickly enough to support operational decision-making. The paper also positions the work as preparation for the National Water Center Summer Institute in 2015.
supporting_quote: “create a demonstration version of a near real-time, high spatial resolution flood data, modeling, forecasting, and inundation mapping system for the continental U.S.”
“a demonstration version of a near real-time, high spatial resolution flood forecasting model was developed for the continental United States.”

chunks.text: The paper proposes a conceptual framework that links high-resolution flood forecasting with real-time observations, flood inundation mapping, and planning for local emergency response. It aims to clarify how national modeling outputs can be translated into actionable local intelligence. The framework is organized into five interacting components meant to partition and coordinate a complex end-to-end system.
supporting_quote: “This study presents a conceptual framework to connect information from high-resolution flood forecasting with real-time observations and flood inundation mapping and planning for local flood emergency response.”
“the overall task could be broken down into a series of five components”

chunks.text: NFIE explicitly asked how to build national, high-resolution real-time hydrologic simulations using a next-generation HydroFabric of open water data services in space and time. It further asked how such capability can improve emergency response and resilience, and how interoperability can sustain innovation from research to operations. These questions guide the design of components and services described in the paper.
supporting_quote: “How can real-time hydrologic simulations at high spatial resolutions, covering the nation, be developed using a next-generation ‘HydroFabric’ — a framework of open water data services in space and time?”
“How can an improved interoperability framework support the first two goals and lead to sustained innovation in the research to operations process?”

chunks.text: At the start, the paper characterizes the task as unprecedented: the U.S. had not previously operated a single, continental-scale, high-resolution flood forecasting system. Roles among partner agencies were uncertain, and the linkage from national forecasts to local emergency response was undefined. A key problem became how to decompose the overall effort into solvable subproblems that could later be integrated.
supporting_quote: “The U.S. has never had a single, continental-scale, high spatial resolution flood forecasting system.”
“How a national flood forecasting system could be connected to local flood emergency response was undefined.”

chunks.text: A major technical challenge is that flood hazard mapping coverage is incomplete nationally, which complicates connecting forecasts to floodplain impacts everywhere. The NFHL exists for only part of the U.S., with large gaps particularly in rural areas. This limits the ability to create reach-scale flood warning zones uniformly across the country.
supporting_quote: “A challenge for the NFIE is to allow for the fact that the NFHL does not exist for 40% of the land area of the U.S., including much of its rural lands.”
“The DFIRMs… synthesized into a National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL) that covers 60% of the land area”

chunks.text: Real-time flood inundation mapping is sparse relative to the national stream network because it relies heavily on gaged locations and precomputed inundation libraries. The national set of real-time inundation sites maps only a small fraction of total river miles. The paper highlights the need for methods that can extend inundation mapping beyond stream gages.
supporting_quote: “There are 134 of these real-time flood inundation mapping sites distributed across the nation”
“so the length of stream miles thus mapped in real time is small compared to the total of about 4 million miles of rivers and streams that exist nationally. Another solution is needed”

chunks.text: For NFIE-Hydro to function effectively, runoff produced on gridded atmospheric-land models must be converted quickly to the reach-catchment units used for routing on NHDPlus. This grid-to-catchment conversion is necessary to align model outputs with the national hydrographic framework. Without efficient conversion, national high-resolution modeling and routing would not be practical in near real time.
supporting_quote: “a rapid connection is needed to convert runoff between grid cells and reach catchments.”
“This ‘grid to catchment’ conversion can be done by intersecting the grid cells and the catchments and compiling a set of area weights”

chunks.text: The NFIE is structured into five integrated components: NFIE-Geo, NFIE-Hydro, NFIE-River, NFIE-Response, and NFIE-Services. Geo provides the national geospatial framework; Hydro produces reach-scale flow forecasts; River links flows to inundation and hydraulics; Response connects outputs to local emergency plans; and Services standardizes observation/forecast exchange. The arrows among components describe information flow from geospatial framework through modeling to mapping and response, all supported by web services.
supporting_quote: “broken down into a series of five components… NFIE-Geo… NFIE-Hydro… NFIE-Response… NFIE-River… foundation… NFIE-Services.”
“The direction of the arrows in Figure 1 conveys the flow of information through the NFIE components”

chunks.text: NFIE-Geo builds on NHDPlus reach catchments and the national flow network, using COMID identifiers shared between catchments and flowlines. The paper proposes intersecting NHDPlus with FEMA’s NFHL to define reach-based flood warning zones where floodplain mapping exists, enabling local warning and response at reach scale. HUC12 subwatersheds provide a larger planning unit that groups multiple reach catchments and aligns boundaries where they overlap.
supporting_quote: “Both the reach catchment and its flow line have a common identifier, or COMID”
“The NHDPlus and NFHL can be intersected so that an elementary flood warning zone is created for each reach catchment where flood mapping has been done”

chunks.text: NFIE-Hydro uses the WRF-Hydro framework to couple weather forecasts, land-atmosphere modeling, and channel routing. It connects gridded runoff fields to reach catchments via area-weight intersections between grid cells and catchment polygons. The paper emphasizes that similar weights can be computed for other hydrologic models with different grids, making the approach extensible.
supporting_quote: “WRF-Hydro is ‘both a stand-alone hydrological modeling architecture as well as a coupling architecture for coupling of hydrological models with atmospheric models’”
“intersecting the grid cells and the catchments and compiling a set of area weights”

chunks.text: For routing on the national river network, the experiment uses RAPID, which operates on NHDPlus reaches and solves Muskingum routing with parallel computation. Reach attributes like length and average velocity support travel-time estimation, and storage parameters support discharge computation at downstream ends. RAPID was coupled to WRF-Hydro to compute time-varying flows across the full 2.7 million-reach network.
supporting_quote: “RAPID… developed to operate on top of the NHDPlus stream reach network and uses parallel computation to solve the Muskingum flow equations on very large river networks”
“RAPID was coupled to WRF-Hydro and used to compute flows as a function of time on all 2.7 million NHDPlus reaches”

chunks.text: The paper describes a ‘static’ inundation mapping approach based on libraries of maps computed at discrete water-surface elevations near gaged forecast points. Discharge forecasts are converted to stage using rating curves, and the corresponding inundation map is selected from the library. It also outlines a ‘dynamic’ approach requiring unsteady 1D St. Venant equations and detailed channel geometry and roughness, as used in HEC-RAS-style modeling.
supporting_quote: “a flood inundation map library is computed in uniform increments of water surface elevation such as one foot.”
“A more complete ‘dynamic’ flood inundation mapping system requires a solution of the St Venant equations of unsteady, one-dimensional river flow”

chunks.text: To make forecasts actionable for responders and the public, the paper proposes mapping flood warning zones using the NWS color scheme and time-indexing the colors to forecasts. A more advanced method would build inundation libraries across all warning zones in a subwatershed and intersect them with roads, critical infrastructure, housing footprints, and address points to estimate exposure and impacts. Ensemble forecasts could then be converted into probabilistic impact and damage estimates.
supporting_quote: “adopt the NWS color scheme for the flood warning”
“By intersecting these maps with layouts of the road network, critical infrastructure and key resources, housing footprints, and address points, assessment can be made”

chunks.text: NFIE-Services emphasizes interoperable web services for observations and forecasts using shared standards. USGS serves time-series via WaterML2 as sequences of time-value pairs, and NWS committed to publishing prototype hydrologic forecast information similarly for 3,600 forecast points. This establishes a common internet-published representation of past, present, and future hydrologic conditions at points.
supporting_quote: “Instantaneous Values Service and a Daily Values Service, which both use the WaterML2 language for publishing hydrologic time series.”
“the NWS committed itself to similarly publishing as a prototype web service in WaterML2 its forecast information from its 3,600 hydrologic forecast points”

chunks.text: NHDPlus is the core national geospatial dataset used for NFIE-Geo, integrating hydrography, elevation, land cover, and watershed boundaries into a connected framework. It subdivides the continental U.S. into 2.7 million reach catchments and corresponding flowlines with shared COMID identifiers. Attributes include drainage area and land cover at catchment scale, and upstream-accumulated properties, mean annual flow estimates, and average velocity at flowline scale.
supporting_quote: “NHDPlus… land surface of the continental U.S. is subdivided into 2.7 million… ‘reach catchments’”
“Flow line attributes also include an estimate of the mean annual flow and the average velocity on the flow line.”

chunks.text: FEMA flood mapping products provide national-scale floodplain extents and related risk layers. DFIRMs were synthesized into the National Flood Hazard Layer, and later efforts include depth and velocity grids that allow homeowner-level risk assessment. These layers can be intersected with NHDPlus reach catchments to define reach flood warning zones where coverage exists.
supporting_quote: “A Digital Flood Insurance Rate Map (DFIRM)… define the spatial extent of flood inundation area for the 100 year flood”
“The DFIRMs… synthesized into a National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL) that covers 60% of the land area”

chunks.text: Watershed planning in NFIE uses the Watershed Boundary Dataset, especially HUC12 subwatersheds, which provide a hierarchical drainage-area unit larger than reach catchments. The paper notes the national subdivision into about 86,000 subwatersheds and shows how reach catchments nest within them. Subwatershed and reach-catchment boundaries are spatially coincident where they overlap, enabling aggregation and reporting.
supporting_quote: “most refined level… called the HUC12 Subwatersheds.”
“Subwatershed — … The continental U.S. is subdivided into approximately 86,000 Subwatersheds.”

chunks.text: NFIE uses operational observation and forecast point datasets tied to the national stream network. NWS River Forecast Centers issue official flood forecasts at about 3,600 forecast points, many collocated with USGS stream gages for verification. These points and related layers (water bodies, dams, gage locations) are intended to be topologically connected to the NHD stream network.
supporting_quote: “one location of about 3,600 in the country where the NWS issues official flood forecasts.”
“About three-quarters of the NWS forecast points are collocated with USGS stream gage sites”

chunks.text: For hydrometeorological forcing, the paper highlights NOAA’s HRRR model as a real-time, 3-km resolution atmospheric model updated hourly and used to forecast precipitation up to 15 hours ahead. NFIE also references ECMWF products used in GloFAS, producing ensemble forecasts at six-hour intervals. These provide alternative sources of precipitation and runoff guidance for hydrologic prediction over NHDPlus-based routing.
supporting_quote: “High-Resolution Rapid Refresh… ‘a NOAA real-time 3-km resolution, hourly updated’… forecast precipitation up to 15 h in advance”
“The ECMWF forecasts are for six-hour time intervals”

chunks.text: Local emergency response examples use address point datasets to connect flood hazard areas to potentially affected people and structures. The paper cites roughly 500,000 address points in Travis and Williamson Counties, Texas, and illustrates intersecting these with the floodplain to count addresses at risk. Such data could also support more targeted alerting based on geographic location within floodplains.
supporting_quote: “There are about 500,000 such address points in Travis and Williamson Counties, Texas”
“intersect the flood hazard zone map with the address points and the count of how many address points could be flooded”

chunks.text: A demonstration near real-time national modeling capability was achieved by dividing the river network into 2.7 million reaches and computing runoff and discharge rapidly at national scale. The paper reports that flows over the full NHDPlus network could be computed in about 10 minutes using the Texas Advanced Computing Center. This served as a key milestone validating national-scale high-resolution flood simulation feasibility.
supporting_quote: “The river and stream network was divided into 2.7 million reaches”
“it was demonstrated that the runoff into these stream reaches and the discharge within them could be computed in 10 min at the Texas Advanced Computing Center.”

chunks.text: During the mobilization phase, WRF-Hydro was coupled with RAPID routing to compute time-varying flows on all 2.7 million NHDPlus reaches. The paper reports the national computation could be completed in 10 minutes and was updated every 3 hours during the Summer Institute period. The author notes the speed and scale were surprising relative to initial expectations.
supporting_quote: “RAPID was coupled to WRF-Hydro and used to compute flows… on all 2.7 million NHDPlus reaches”
“this computation could be achieved in 10 min… and this computation was updated each 3 h during the NFIE Summer Institute period.”

chunks.text: The NFIE produced, for the first time in the U.S., a shared web-service ‘common language’ for publishing hydrologic conditions at a point across time horizons. USGS provided real-time observations via WaterML2, and NWS published prototype forecasts for 3,600 forecast points in WaterML2 as well. The paper characterizes this as a milestone enabling internet exchange of the past, present, and future of hydrologic conditions.
supporting_quote: “the USGS… both use the WaterML2 language for publishing hydrologic time series.”
“Together, these web services… established for the first time in the U.S. a common language for publishing through the internet the past, present, and future of hydrologic conditions at a point.”

chunks.text: The paper demonstrates how national reach-catchment forecasts can be related to existing NWS River Forecast Center products. An RFC forecast subbasin (ATIT2) contains 76 NHDPlus catchments, enabling comparisons between reach-based NFIE forecasts and RFC forecasts at the outlet point. This alignment supports potential reconciliation or adjustment so different forecast scales remain consistent.
supporting_quote: “this forecast subbasin ATIT2 contains 76 NHDPlus catchments”
“NFIE flood forecasts defined on NHDPlus stream reaches can thus be compared with forecasts coming from the NWS RFCs”

chunks.text: The paper presents an example of ensemble flood forecasting at reach-catchment scale using ECMWF/GloFAS coupled with RAPID routing, demonstrated for the Texas Gulf region. The example shows a 15-day-ahead forecast with an ensemble of 50 hydrographs for a specific reach catchment. This supports the claim that ensemble forecast systems can be developed using NHDPlus reaches.
supporting_quote: “the forecast is for 15 days ahead… results in an ensemble of 50 forecast hydrographs”
“they have also succeeded in executing this ECMWF-RAPID coupling for the 67,313 NHDPlus reaches in the Texas Gulf region”

chunks.text: The paper describes operational-style flood inundation mapping at NWS forecast points co-located with USGS gages, using a library of maps keyed to water surface elevation increments and rating curves. It provides Onion Creek at Highway 183 (forecast point ATIT2 / gage 08159000) as an example where map extent expands/contracts as stage changes. This illustrates a practical method for translating discharge forecasts into mapped inundation at selected sites.
supporting_quote: “a flood inundation map library is computed in uniform increments of water surface elevation such as one foot.”
“Onion Creek at Highway 183… Forecast Point ATIT2 and U.S. Geological Survey Stream Gage 08159000”

chunks.text: The first NFIE phase did not fully realize operational real-time inundation mapping and emergency response procedures, beyond conceptual framing. The author states these goals were not achieved in 2014–2015 but were achieved in a second phase culminating in a 2016 Summer Institute. This highlights that end-to-end decision support required additional research and development beyond hydrologic simulation.
supporting_quote: “The goals of having a real-time flood inundation map and flood emergency response procedure were not really achieved except in concept during the first phase of the NFIE in 2014-2015”
“but were achieved in the second phase of the NFIE research which culminated in the second Summer Institute in June-July 2016.”

chunks.text: Although prototype flood information services were created, the paper reports that a continuously operating flood information services framework was not achieved during the first phase. This limitation indicates that interoperable service publication is necessary but not sufficient; sustained operations require additional infrastructure, governance, and reliability work. The result also frames NFIE-Services as an early step rather than a finished system.
supporting_quote: “while some prototype output services for flood information were created, a continuously operating flood information services framework was not achieved during the first phase of the NFIE.”
“NFIE-Services is a set of standardized web services for water and weather observations and forecasts”

chunks.text: Coverage gaps in FEMA’s NFHL constrain reach-scale flood warning zone creation and nationwide linkage between forecasts and mapped floodplains. The paper explicitly notes NFHL absence over 40% of U.S. land area, including much rural land. This limits uniform implementation of flood warning maps based on intersecting reach catchments with flood hazard zones.
supporting_quote: “the NFHL does not exist for 40% of the land area of the U.S., including much of its rural lands.”
“The NHDPlus and NFHL can be intersected so that an elementary flood warning zone is created for each reach catchment where flood mapping has been done”

chunks.text: Real-time inundation mapping based on gage-linked map libraries covers only a small portion of national river mileage. The paper notes there are 134 real-time inundation sites, which is small relative to “about 4 million miles of rivers and streams” nationally. It concludes that additional methods are required to map inundation on ungaged reaches.
supporting_quote: “There are 134 of these real-time flood inundation mapping sites distributed across the nation”
“small compared to the total of about 4 million miles of rivers and streams… Another solution is needed”

chunks.text: The paper concludes that NFIE was a significant step in engaging academia with NOAA/NWS and demonstrating national-scale, near real-time, high-resolution flood modeling.
