It highlights the 10-minute computation over 2.7 million reaches as a milestone and as validation for building the National Water Model. The work established the principle of computing flows on the NHDPlus reach network, which is being maintained for the National Water Model.
supporting_quote: “the demonstration that the discharge could be forecast simultaneously in 2.7 million stream reaches… in only 10 min… was a milestone”
“This demonstration validated the concept of building a National Water Model”

chunks.text: The five-part conceptual framework (Geo, Hydro, River, Response, Services) is presented as a useful way to contextualize and assess progress across the end-to-end flood information pipeline. The paper concludes that WRF-Hydro plus RAPID performed solidly without unexpected failures in producing national flows. It also notes that some other components (inundation mapping, response, services) required additional phases to mature.
supporting_quote: “dividing the overall task… into five parts: Geo, Hydro, River, Response, and Services was very useful”
“Using the WRF-Hydro-RAPID combination to compute flows… proved to be very solid. There were no unexpected failures”

chunks.text: From a research viewpoint, the NFIE produced what the author calls the first comprehensive real-time common operating picture of streamflow conditions across the nation. This enables a ‘hydrology of now’ analogous to routine continental-scale weather forecasting. The paper argues that the National Water Center context will help transfer NFIE insights into future operational practice and partner coordination.
supporting_quote: “the first comprehensive real-time common operating picture of streamflow conditions across the nation.”

“a basis for what could be called the ‘hydrology of now’ in which continental-scale hydrologic forecasting is being treated in much the same way as is normal for continental-scale weather forecasting.”

chunks.text: The U.S. National Water Model (NWM) is an operational hydrologic modeling framework developed by NOAA that simulates streamflow across the U.S. and territories. It produces forecasts by modeling processes such as rainfall-runoff, snowmelt, infiltration, overland flow, and river routing. Outputs are produced at high spatial and temporal resolution and include streamflow for millions of river reaches, supporting both official river forecast locations and ungauged locations.
supporting_quote: The U.S. National Water Model (NWM) ... is a hydrologic modeling framework developed by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
The NWM outputs include simulated streamflow data for over 2.7 million river reaches

chunks.text: NWM operational forecasts span multiple horizons and update frequently. Short-term deterministic forecasts run for 18 hours at hourly timesteps and initialize every hour, while medium- and long-range ensembles initialize every 6 hours with coarser timesteps and longer durations. The system also includes analysis/assimilation nowcasts that incorporate gauge data, plus a run with no data assimilation.
supporting_quote: Forecasts include a short-term 18-h deterministic forecast ... on an hourly time step
a medium-term forecast with 10 days ... with a 3-h time step and a long-term 30-day four-member ensemble forecast on a 6-h time step
there is also an analysis and assimilation run ... includes data assimilation from streamflow gauges and a run with no data assimilation

chunks.text: Multiple distribution systems exist for NWM outputs (e.g., NOMADS, cloud archives on AWS/Azure/Google, and visualization portals), but their usability varies by focus and historical availability. Several sources provide operational data, while the AWS registry provides retrospective archives across model versions. Differences in storage formats and directory structures across providers complicate cross-platform access and downstream use.
supporting_quote: There are currently several data stores and methods for retrieving ... forecast data from the NWM.
The Amazon AWS registry provides a comprehensive archive ... spanning multiple model versions ... 1979–December 2020
each cloud provider stores the data in differing directory structures making cross platform access challenging

chunks.text: The study’s main objective is to design, develop, and deploy a cloud-based workflow that manages the terabytes of NWM operational forecast data and provides tools for effective public use. A key goal is restructuring NWM outputs into a queryable, analysis-ready and cloud-optimized (ARCO) dataset using BigQuery. The authors also aim to implement and deploy a REST API so users can retrieve forecasts as time series without needing to write complex database queries.
supporting_quote: Our primary objective is to research, design, develop, and deploy a comprehensive cloud-based data workflow that manages and provides tools to effectively use the terabytes of operational forecast data
We take full advantage of Google's BigQuery cloud database to restructure the data into a queryable dataset (i.e., ARCO format)
design and implement a REST-based API for querying and retrieving these operational forecast data

chunks.text: A further objective is to fill an unmet need for efficient access to complete historical and ongoing operational NWM forecasts. Prior solutions either served raw files or focused on retrospective data delivery via other protocols, but did not provide efficient use of the full operational archive. This work targets easily searchable access and retrieval for analysis, visualization, and third-party applications.
supporting_quote: To date, no service exists for efficient use of the complete historical and ongoing operational forecast data that are produced by the NWM.
Ultimately our research and tools aim to make these data easily searchable and available as time series forecasts for analysis, visualization, and other types of use within third party applications.

chunks.text: A central usability problem is that NWM outputs are stored as nationwide snapshots per time step, with one NetCDF file per time step. Extracting a time series for a single reach and a single initialization requires accessing many national-scale files and then subsetting them, which is data-transfer intensive and slow. This storage pattern reflects a common space-versus-time dilemma: formats optimized for spatial coverage hinder point-based time series use typical in hydrology.
supporting_quote: data are stored as nationwide time steps. In other words, each iteration of the NWM produces a nationwide forecast ... one per time step.
This makes it quite difficult and arduous to extract a single forecast for a single stream reach
This is an instance of the well-known space-versus-time dilemma of hydrologic and atmospheric modelling.

chunks.text: Even when data are available in cloud archives, users often must download entire nationwide datasets for each forecast time step to obtain values for a specific stream. Because each NetCDF represents one time step for all 2.7 million streams, per-reach retrieval becomes cumbersome and time-consuming. Cross-provider differences in directory structure further increase complexity for users trying to build repeatable workflows.
supporting_quote: each NetCDF file represents one time step of one forecast across all 2.7 million streams in the nation
if one is interested in a specific stream's forecast, one needs to download the entire dataset for every time step and then extract the relevant information
each cloud provider stores the data in differing directory structures making cross platform access challenging

chunks.text: Access does not guarantee usability for large hydrologic datasets, because traditional computing approaches struggle with the volume of NWM outputs. The authors argue the data need to be analysis-ready and cloud-optimized so users can directly access subsets without transferring large files or paying overhead to parse nationwide NetCDF for small extractions. This motivates transforming data into formats and services designed for cloud-based subset queries.
supporting_quote: Access does not guarantee usability as the data volumes involved pose significant challenges.
the data need to be Analysis Ready and Cloud Optimized (ARCO)
need to be stored in a cloud-optimized fashion that supports direct access to data subsets without the latency of transferring large contiguous bytes (i.e., files)

chunks.text: While BigQuery tables are public, practical access can still be limited because users may need a Google Cloud account and skills with cloud analytics and SQL. The paper positions an API as a way to lower barriers by enabling standard HTTP requests for common query patterns. Without such a service layer, many potential users may not be able to integrate NWM forecasts into applications or workflows.
supporting_quote: While the datasets are public, they may not be accessible to everyone because a Google Cloud account is required along with proficiency in cloud-based data analytics tooling (i.e., distributed processing frameworks and SQL).
Because the API does not require an account or proficiency in database queries, it allows researchers and practitioners a simple and efficient method to access these data using HTTP requests.

chunks.text: The workflow transforms NWM NetCDF outputs into an ARCO-friendly tabular structure. Data are processed into tabular form, written as Parquet files in Google Cloud Storage, and ingested into BigQuery as long tables. This restructures access from spatial time-step files to queryable time series by reach and time, enabling SQL filtering and efficient retrieval.
supporting_quote: we processed the NWM NetCDF file data into a tabular format, then stored the tabular data in a Parquet file format on Google Cloud Storage and in Google BigQuery in long-table format
By storing the NWM data in a structured table format rather than the raw NetCDF format, the data is made accessible using various queries based on logical filters (e.g., reach ID and time)

chunks.text: Apache Beam is used to define the parallel data processing pipeline for large-scale transformation. The pipeline can run on different execution engines, and this implementation uses Google’s internal execution engine Flume. Parquet is selected for efficient analytical querying and for straightforward ingestion into BigQuery, supporting high-throughput processing and downstream access.
supporting_quote: We used Apache Beam ... to define the transformation pipeline.
We used the Google internal execution engine Flume ... to run the processing pipeline.
We selected the Parquet file format to store the data because it is open source ... efficient for analytical queries, and is easily ingested directly into BigQuery

chunks.text: The workflow is automated to keep the operational archive current. The processing pipelines run once per day to batch process new NWM datasets and update the transformed products. This supports operational needs by continuously extending the Parquet and BigQuery holdings as new forecasts are published.
supporting_quote: We automated the data processing pipelines using Google infrastructure which is executed once per day to batch process every new NWM dataset provided during that period.
Therefore, the datasets are continuously updated for operational needs.

chunks.text: The REST API is implemented as a FastAPI server packaged as a Docker container and deployed on Google Cloud Run. Requests are routed and authenticated through Google API Gateway, which forwards calls to Cloud Run where the service issues BigQuery SQL queries and formats responses. Cloud Build and Artifact Registry are used to build, store, and deploy container images.
supporting_quote: We wrote the API server using the FastAPI framework
We packaged the FastAPI server as a Docker container image
The service is deployed on Cloud Run
We used Google's API Gateway service as the authentication and management layer for the API.

chunks.text: The system is designed for scalability and secure access using managed cloud services. BigQuery supports large, concurrent analytical queries; Cloud Run autoscales based on incoming requests; and API Gateway rate-limits and protects access using API keys. These design choices aim to maintain performance as usage increases while controlling unauthorized access.
supporting_quote: BigQuery supports performant queries ... with up to 1000 concurrent queries.
Cloud Run supports autoscaling
The API Gateway supports up to 10,000 requests per second ... using authentication and authorization mechanisms with API keys.

chunks.text: Benchmarking compares five access patterns to quantify performance improvements from the transformed dataset and API. The patterns include direct NetCDF via xarray, NetCDF with kerchunk metadata, Parquet with DuckDB, direct BigQuery SQL, and the API. Test queries include single-reach long-range forecasts, multiple-reach forecasts, and ensemble statistics for one or multiple reaches.
supporting_quote: We developed and tested five different access patterns:
Access original NetCDF data directly ... xarray
Access original NetCDF data ... with kerchunk metadata
Access through the processed parquet files ... DuckDB
Access the processed data tables on BigQuery ... and ... using our API.
Accessing a long-range forecast for a single reach ... multiple reaches ... ensemble statistics

chunks.text: The transformed NWM operational outputs are published in two primary forms: Parquet files in Google Cloud Storage and long-table BigQuery tables. The Parquet directory structure organizes by output type (e.g., channel_rt) and model run configuration (e.g., short_range), and aggregates dates within directories for easier multi-date reads. These formats are intended to support time-series extraction without reading nationwide NetCDF files.
supporting_quote: stored in two formats/locations: 1) the collection stored in parquet format on Google Cloud Storage and 2) the collection stored in tables as part of a Google BigQuery dataset
directory structure with the output type (e.g., channel_rt) ... and then model run configuration (e.g., short_range)

chunks.text: The BigQuery dataset is publicly available and organized so that each table corresponds to a model configuration and output type (e.g., short_range_channel_rt). Data are stored in long-table format so users can filter efficiently by forecast date, time range, and reaches. Ensemble forecasts are stored in the same table, creating extremely large tables that can reach trillions of rows.
supporting_quote: The data stored in BigQuery are publicly available as a dataset with the following ID: "BigQuery-public-data.national_water_model"
For example, "short_range_channel_rt" is the table for the short-range forecast and channel_rt dataset.
stored in a long table format where users can efficiently filter by forecast date, time range, and reaches
creates extremely large tables, on the order of trillions of rows

chunks.text: The API exposes multiple endpoints to retrieve reach geometry and time-series streamflow from analysis/assimilation runs and forecast runs. Returned data can be delivered as JSON for application integration or CSV for analysis. The documentation is accessible through a browser-based OpenAPI/Swagger interface, while data endpoints require an API key.
supporting_quote: The API has four access endpoints
"geometry/" retrieves the stream reach geometry and attribute information
"analysis_assim/" retrieves the streamflow data ... from the analysis and assimilation runs
"forecast/" retrieves the streamflow data ... and forecast run
The data returned ... can be in either JSON format ... or CSV format
The data access endpoints do require an API key

chunks.text: Benchmarking data requests focus on a Sacramento River test case within the HUC10 Curry Creek–Sacramento River watershed. The benchmarks filter stream feature IDs to include the Sacramento River and Curry Creek and exclude canals, resulting in 13 stream reaches. Tests were executed in Google Colab Enterprise on an n1-standard-4 machine in the us-central1 region.
supporting_quote: We selected the HUC10 Curry Creek-Sacramento River watershed (HUC10 ID = 1802016104)
This selection resulted in 13 stream reaches to query
We used Google's Colab Enterprise service ... an n1-standard-4 machine ... 15 GB of memory
tests were run using the us-central1 cloud region

chunks.text: Benchmarking shows that reading original NetCDF files directly from cloud storage using xarray is the slowest approach for the tested queries. Adding kerchunk metadata improves performance relative to native NetCDF access, but remains slower than using the transformed Parquet/BigQuery representations. Overall, restructuring the data yields major runtime reductions for common reach-based time-series queries.
supporting_quote: Using the original NetCDF files and reading them natively from cloud storage ... is the least efficient across all queries.
Using technologies like kerchunk ... improve speed compared to the native file access
still less efficient compared to using the transformed Parquet files and BigQuery.

chunks.text: Across the benchmark cases, accessing transformed data via BigQuery or the API is the most efficient. Parquet with DuckDB is faster than NetCDF-based methods but slower than BigQuery/API. The results indicate that pushing computation to BigQuery and retrieving filtered results is effective for the typical access patterns evaluated.
supporting_quote: Accessing the data using Parquet and DuckDB showed improvements over using NetCDF whereas accessing the data using BigQuery or the API were the most efficient.
The API accesses the data directly on BigQuery which consistently yielded the most efficient query time across the different methods.

chunks.text: API query runtimes are reported as consistent across different query types, with mean runtimes around 2.5 seconds for the benchmarked tests. This includes single-reach, multiple-reach (13 reaches), and ensemble-statistics cases, suggesting query type had limited effect on response time in this setup. The consistency is presented as evidence of robust performance for common requests.
supporting_quote: The query runtimes were consistent across the different methods with a mean runtime around 2.5s for each, no matter which query was run.
The Multiple Reach case includes the test for 13 reaches

chunks.text: The API introduces a small overhead compared with running SQL directly in BigQuery. The paper reports the API as slightly slower by less than 0.5 seconds, attributing the difference to gateway authentication, URL routing, and response formatting. Despite this overhead, API performance remains comparable to direct BigQuery access while simplifying usage.
supporting_quote: there is a slight increase in runtime (less than 0.5s) with using the API.
This is most likely caused by authentication through the API gateway, URL routing of the API, and/or logic to transform results into formats requested.

chunks.text: The published BigQuery dataset and Parquet outputs provide public access paths for different user needs. BigQuery tables are described as optimized via clustering and partitioning so queries scan only a few megabytes for typical requests. This setup reduces query costs and supports interactive data retrieval patterns for time-series extraction.
supporting_quote: The data stored in BigQuery are publicly available as a dataset with the following ID: "BigQuery-public-data.national_water_model"
The data are stored efficiently on BigQuery for use clustered and partitioned to where individual queries only scan a few MB of data.

chunks.text: The API implementation has a stated data transfer limitation tied to BigQuery interactive query results, capped at 10 MB per request. Large requests, such as long-range forecasts for more than about 200 reaches, should instead be executed directly in BigQuery with an export job. As an alternative workaround, users can issue concurrent parallel API requests while keeping each request under the 10 MB limit.
supporting_quote: there is a data transfer limitation to our implementation of only 10 MB requested from BigQuery using interactive queries.

If researchers require access to large amounts data (e.g., more than 200 reaches at a time for a long-range forecast), then queries would need to be run directly on the BigQuery tables with an export job.
users can run concurrent requests in parallel ... to keep individual requests under the 10 MB limit

chunks.text: The authors caution that benchmark results are sensitive to configuration and technology choices. Parquet formatting and kerchunk chunk sizes can affect read efficiency, and different tools rely on different implementation languages and backends (e.g., DuckDB in C++ versus Python libraries). Therefore, the timings are intended to indicate order-of-magnitude performance differences rather than definitive comparisons of technologies.
supporting_quote: multiple configurations can influence the results. Particularly the formatting of the Parquet files and chunk sizes used with kerchunk can have an influence
DuckDB backend is written in C++ whereas xarray and kerchunk are Python only libraries
should be interpreted as a general test that provide an order of magnitude ... rather than exact times

chunks.text: Although the dataset is hosted as a Google Public Dataset, querying in BigQuery can still incur costs in general BigQuery usage models. The paper notes a published price of $6.25 per TiB queried with 1 TiB per month free, and emphasizes that typical queries scan only a few megabytes when clustered/partitioned. CIROH provides API keys to project members, and third parties can deploy their own API for other user communities.
supporting_quote: querying data from BigQuery does incur cloud charges if it were implemented within an individual cloud tenant
BigQuery costs are $6.25 per TiB of data queried (with 1 TiB per month free)
CIROH provides data access keys for project members
a third party can implement our open-source API on the dataset

chunks.text: The work closes a key gap in NWM accessibility by transforming operational forecast outputs into ARCO long-table structures and publishing them in BigQuery and Parquet. This restructuring changes retrieval from downloading nationwide time-step files to querying reach-based time series, reducing effort and improving usability. The accompanying REST API further simplifies access by providing standard HTTP endpoints for common queries.
supporting_quote: We present data storage methods and an API that solves a major gap in the accessibility and use of the NWM data
We transformed the data from files representing nationwide time steps to long tables in ARCO formats
providing them as public datasets on the cloud with an API for querying to provide quick and easy access

chunks.text: The authors argue the approach is transferable to other large hydroinformatics modeling efforts that produce massive NetCDF time-step archives. They highlight GEOGLOWS as an example where similar NetCDF-to-structured-database processing and cloud-run query services could enable efficient reach-level forecast access globally. The paper frames this as advancing a Hydrologic Modeling as a Service (HMaaS) paradigm by delivering model results in user-ready formats.
supporting_quote: One example ... is the European Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) GEOGLOWS model
We anticipate that the approach used here could be readily adapted to GEOGLOWS
builds upon the Hydrologic Modeling as a Service (HMaaS) approach

chunks.text: While the reference deployment uses Google Cloud services, the implementation emphasizes open-source components that support replication. The API is built with Python, FastAPI, and Docker, and deployment automation is provided via Terraform, enabling reproducible infrastructure setup. The authors note that other cloud warehouses (e.g., Amazon Redshift or Azure Synapse) could substitute for BigQuery with additional deployment work.
supporting_quote: We developed the API service using Python, the FastAPI framework, and Docker for containerization, all open-source products.
The repository includes Terraform scripts to automate deployment
AWS and Azure have similar offerings (Amazon Redshift and Azure Synapse) that can be used as the data warehouse

chunks.text: Surface water is a key part of the Earth’s water cycle, and tracking its changes supports water resources management and disaster mitigation. Satellite remote sensing is widely used to monitor surface water extent and dynamics. Such monitoring also supports policy needs like SDG Target 6.6 concerning water availability and sustainability. Long time series collections (e.g., Landsat) have enabled multi-decadal analyses of surface water change.
supporting_quote: Surface water is a major component in the water cycle, and monitoring surface water dynamics is essential for understanding and managing water resources
These applications support the monitoring of surface water dynamics assisting in sustainable development goals... Target 6.6 under the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 6

chunks.text: Optical multispectral sensors are commonly used for surface water mapping with indices and classification approaches, but data quality is often degraded by clouds and related atmospheric artifacts. These issues can be especially problematic during floods, when peak inundation frequently coincides with cloud cover. Even with higher temporal optical constellations, thin clouds, aerosols, fog, and shadows still create substantial gaps and uncertainty in water detection.
supporting_quote: Optical multispectral sensors are commonly used to map surface water
However, clouds often obscure surface observations, particularly in the context of floods
the peak surface water extent during flood events occurs coincidentally with cloud cover, resulting in data gaps

chunks.text: SAR observations can be acquired in most weather conditions and can complement optical monitoring, but they require substantial preprocessing and may misclassify some land surfaces as water. SAR can yield false positives over pavement or dry sandy soils and false negatives when water is obscured by vegetation canopy or affected by geometry and terrain effects. Combining SAR with optical data provides an opportunity to leverage complementary strengths and reduce uncertainty.
supporting_quote: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data offer advantages over optical data because observations of surface conditions can be acquired in almost all weather conditions
SAR imagery relies on the specular reflectance of open water for detection, which can lead to errors of commission... pavement or dry sandy soils being mistakenly classified as water
errors of omission, when the water surface may be beneath vegetation canopies

chunks.text: The study aims to generate dense time series of surface water maps by fusing optical and SAR observations at the pixel level and filling optical gaps. The intent is to increase the temporal density of unobstructed observations while maintaining reliable water classification. The authors apply the workflow across diverse landscapes and climates and evaluate it with independent, hand-labeled reference data.
supporting_quote: This paper presents a method for generating dense time series of surface water observations using optical–SAR sensor fusion and gap filling.
In this study, we applied a pixel-level data fusion approach for creating a dense time series of surface water maps
We validated this approach using hand-labeled reference points for different sites

chunks.text: A stated objective is to provide contiguous time series information that captures both long-term dynamics and short-term changes such as flooding. The approach is designed to work across riverine, coastal, and floodplain settings, emphasizing high temporal variability. The workflow seeks to use SAR to fill cloud-occluded or poor-quality optical observations.
supporting_quote: we generated a contiguous, dense time series of surface water that (1) provided information on the spatial and temporal dynamics of surface water extent for different landscapes, including riverine, coastal, and floodplain regions
and (2) fused optical and SAR imagery to increase the temporal density of observations to monitor long-term dynamics and short-term changes in surface water (e.g., flood events)
Our approach fills optical surface water data gaps caused by clouds, cloud shadows, and other atmospheric conditions using SAR surface water estimates.

chunks.text: Optical surface water mapping is frequently impaired by clouds and related artifacts, creating missing observations precisely when flood extent information is most needed. These gaps limit optical-only flood mapping and time series completeness. Increasing optical revisit can help but does not eliminate cloud and haze impacts, motivating alternative approaches.
supporting_quote: cloud cover can obscure surface observations, particularly during flood events, hindering water identification
Often, the peak surface water extent during flood events occurs coincidentally with cloud cover, resulting in data gaps

chunks.text: SAR can observe through clouds but presents its own challenges, including intensive preprocessing and characteristic commission/omission errors. Low backscatter non-water surfaces can be confused with water, and vegetation can mask water from C-band SAR signals. These limitations reduce reliability if SAR is used alone, motivating fusion with optical data.
supporting_quote: substantial preprocessing is required to remove image artifacts such as radio frequency interference, terrain effects, and speckle effect
errors of commission, with large areas of pavement or dry sandy soils being mistakenly classified as water
errors of omission, when the water surface may be beneath vegetation canopies and not classified as water with a higher frequency radar signal

chunks.text: Several prior fusion approaches either require region-specific coefficients, rely on non-parametric methods that may not scale well across environments, or require coincident optical–SAR acquisitions that force temporal aggregation. These constraints limit near-real-time applicability and the ability to capture rapid event dynamics. The paper positions its workflow as avoiding coincident-acquisition requirements by gap filling optical observations with recent SAR.
supporting_quote: these methods are regionally tailored with specific coefficients requiring significant effort to fit coefficients for each study
requires coincident acquisitions as inputs into the classifier, resulting in data aggregation in time; this coincident requirement makes near real-time application infeasible
feature- and decision-level fusion... aggregates data in space or time, making the approach unsuitable for events that have high-temporal and high-spatial changes

chunks.text: The workflow is implemented in Google Earth Engine and processes optical and SAR streams separately before fusing them. Logistic regression models are applied independently to each sensor type to produce water probability maps. These probability maps are then thresholded and filtered into binary water/no-water classifications. A fusion step gap-fills optical masks using SAR-derived water estimates to create a dense time series.
supporting_quote: We used the Google Earth Engine (GEE) cloud computational platform (GEE) to implement the data fusion workflow.
Then, the logistic regression models are applied to each data type independently to estimate water probability maps.
Finally, the sensor fusion step combines the SAR and optical classifications to fill gaps in the optical data and produce a dense time series of surface water maps.

chunks.text: For model training, the authors use hand-labeled chips from Sen1Floods11 and treat each pixel as a training example. Because non-water pixels dominate, they undersample non-water to balance classes, producing around 20 million examples. They withhold 33% of the balanced dataset for validation. Stratified 5-fold cross-validation is used to select the best-performing logistic regression model.
supporting_quote: we flattened the images into vectors, treating each individual pixel as a training example. This resulted in approximately 96 million samples
randomly undersampled the non-water examples... resulting in a balanced dataset of around 20 million examples
randomly withheld 33% of the data for validating the final model
implemented stratified K-fold cross-validation with five folds

chunks.text: Input features include raw optical bands plus MNDWI, and SAR polarizations plus VV/VH ratio and texture statistics. SAR texture features are computed as mean and standard deviation within a 9×9 moving window. These features are used by logistic regression to output pixelwise water probabilities for each sensor. The feature set is explicitly enumerated for optical and SAR in the paper’s table of variables.
supporting_quote: we computed and included several indices as input features... the VV/VH ratio for SAR data
the Modified Normalized Difference Water Index (MNDWI) for optical data
computing the mean and standard deviation within a 9 × 9 moving window
Table 1. Variables used as features for the surface water prediction models

chunks.text: SAR imagery is further processed with established corrections to reduce artifacts and terrain effects, while optical imagery is masked for clouds and other contaminants. Specifically, SAR preprocessing includes border noise correction and angular-based radiometric slope correction. Optical data use CFMask to remove clouds, cloud shadows, and snow/ice. These steps aim to ensure that the downstream probability estimation and fusion operate on cleaner inputs.
supporting_quote: For SAR data... including border noise correction, and angularbased radiometric slope correction... to reduce terrain effects.
For optical data, we used the CFMask band to mask out clouds, cloud shadows, and snow/ice pixels

chunks.text: Water probabilities are converted to binary water maps using adaptive thresholding. The method uses the Edge Otsu algorithm to determine a threshold for classifying water pixels from probability maps. The binary outputs are additionally filtered by the maximum climatological extent for the corresponding month using JRC historical water data to constrain implausible false positives. This combination is intended to handle residual noise and masking errors.
supporting_quote: we used the Edge Otsu algorithm... to determine a threshold for classifying water pixels
We further filtered the classified water areas... based on the maximum climatological extent for the corresponding month, using historical surface water data from the JRC.

chunks.text: The fusion approach performs gap filling of optical classifications using recent SAR probabilities near the edges of optical gaps. SAR probabilities from the most recent 15 days prior to the optical acquisition are sampled where they intersect optical gap edges, then reduced to a single threshold via the 50th percentile. That threshold is applied to SAR to map water and fill optical gaps, producing a merged optical–SAR map for each observation. Aggregating across observations yields monthly surface water frequency products.
supporting_quote: sampled the SAR water probabilities from the most recent 15 days prior to the optical image acquisition that intersected with the edges of the optical image gaps
reduced the sampled SAR probabilities to a single threshold value using the 50th percentile
This threshold was applied to the SAR data... used to fill the gaps in the optical data.
By aggregating the resulting time series to a monthly scale, we obtained a final dataset representing the frequency of surface water observations for each month.

chunks.text: Evaluation uses standard classification metrics derived from confusion matrix counts. The paper defines overall accuracy (OA), false alarm ratio (FAR), probability of detection (POD), and critical success index (CSI). Metrics are computed across the full validation dataset and broken down by region and time. The goal is to diagnose spatial and temporal patterns in errors (false positives vs false negatives).
supporting_quote: We computed these metrics for the entire validation dataset
We also computed these metrics per region and over the time series
The overall accuracy is the percentage of pixels that were correctly estimated
The critical success index (CSI)... combines both the POD and FAR

chunks.text: The fusion workflow uses Sentinel-1 IW GRD SAR data in Google Earth Engine, relying on an analysis-ready collection. The study uses 10 m ground sampling distance data with VV and VH dual polarization. The GEE Sentinel-1 dataset includes SNAP-based preprocessing such as orbit updates, noise removal, and conversion to dB backscatter. These inputs provide frequent, all-weather observations used for gap filling.
supporting_quote: we used the Sentinel-1 Interferometric Wide (IW) swath mode at a 10 m ground sampling distance (GSD)... VV... and VH
We used the preprocessed analysis ready dataset (ARD) of Sentinel-1 Level-1 IW Ground Range Detected (GRD) data provided by GEE ("COPERNICUS/S1_GRD")
These steps included updating the orbit state vectors, removal of thermal and border noise, and conversion... to logarithmic decibels (dB)

chunks.text: Optical inputs come from Landsat 8 OLI surface reflectance in Google Earth Engine at 30 m resolution across visible, NIR, and SWIR bands. The SR product is produced with LaSRC atmospheric correction (6S) and standard reflectance conversions. The analysis filters to scenes with 75% cloud cover or less to ensure usable optical observations for fusion. Optical QA information is used later for gap identification.
supporting_quote: The Landsat 8 Operational Land Imagery (OLI)... at a ground sampling distance of 30 m
We used the preprocessed surface reflectance (SR) Landsat 8 collection ("LANDSAT/LC08/C02/T1_L2")
atmospheric correction using the 6S atmospheric correction algorithm... (LaSRC)
We only used Landsat scenes that had 75% cloud cover or less in this study

chunks.text: Training data are derived from Sen1Floods11, which provides Sentinel-1 SAR chips and corresponding water classifications designed for flood algorithm development. The dataset includes 4831 non-overlapping chips at 10 m resolution across 11 flood events. A subset of 446 chips is hand-labeled, and the paper uses only these hand-labeled chips for training to maximize label quality. Pixels are treated as individual samples during model fitting.
supporting_quote: we used water extent data from the Sen1Floods11 dataset
It consists of 4831 non-overlapping image chips... at 10 m resolution... span 11 distinct flood events
a subset of 446 chips were meticulously hand-labeled
We only used the hand-labeled chips from the dataset

chunks.text: Independent validation uses hand-labeled reference data derived from Planet imagery time series. Tottrup et al. provide monthly inland open surface water at 10 m for 2019 over four 100×100 km sites in Colombia, Gabon, Mexico, and Zambia. Markert et al. provide a 2019 inland surface water time series for Cambodia and Myanmar, which is aggregated to monthly scale to align with the other validation sources. Together these support cross-region assessment.
supporting_quote: an independent validation dataset of hand-labeled points derived from time series of Planet imagery from Tottrup et al.
represented monthly areas of inland, open surface waters at 10 m spatial resolution for 2019 over four sites (100 × 100 km)... Colombia, Gabon, Mexico, and Zambia
validation data from Markert et al.... Cambodia and Myanmar in 2019. We aggregated these data to a monthly time step

chunks.text: The study evaluates six geographically diverse regions chosen to represent different climates, landscapes, and mapping challenges. These include Colombia (Magdalena tributaries), Gabon (Ogooué outflow wetlands), Mexico (reservoir region), Zambia (Zambezi basin), Myanmar (Upper Irrawaddy), and Cambodia (Lower Mekong Tonlé Sap floodplains). The sites include conditions that can confound mapping, such as vegetation, topography, and permanent low-backscatter surfaces. Validation data availability for 2019 influenced site selection.
supporting_quote: This study focused on six regions spanning diverse ecological and climatological conditions across the globe
The regions include... Colombia... Gabon... Mexico... Zambia... Myanmar... Cambodia
selected to represent a variety of landscapes, climates, and surface water dynamics as well as to include major challenges for surface water mapping

chunks.text: The trained logistic regression models achieve strong accuracy during fitting and testing on withheld samples. The best K-fold model reports mean training accuracy of 0.8776 for SAR and 0.9599 for optical. When trained as a final model and evaluated on the withheld validation portion, testing accuracy is 0.8778 (SAR) and 0.9601 (optical). The authors attribute SAR’s lower performance to speckle, geometry, and land-surface effects compared with optical electro-optical discrimination.
supporting_quote: training mean accuracy of 0.8776 for the SAR model and 0.9599 for the optical model
The testing accuracy using the validation data was 0.8778 and 0.9601 for the SAR and optical datasets, respectively.
Errors in surface water mapping with SAR typically arise due speckle noise... side-looking geometry

chunks.text: The paper reports final fitted logistic regression equations with coefficients for both SAR and optical feature sets. In the SAR model, the mean and standard deviation texture terms have larger weights than raw VV/VH backscatter, indicating spatial context is important. The VV/VH ratio is weighted very low, implying minimal contribution in their fitted model. In the optical model, MNDWI has a much larger coefficient than individual bands, reflecting its central role in water discrimination.
supporting_quote: The final logistics regressions equation with fitted coefficients are: ... -0.0584 VV ... 0.1433 VV_mean + 0.4898 VV_std ... - 10.9985
The final logistics regressions equation... + 4.5892 MDNWI - 1.0033
the spatial statistics... are weighted greater than the original values
the VV/VH variable is weighted very low
the MNDWI variable has a much greater importance than the individual bands

chunks.text: Across the independent validation dataset, the fused gap-filled product attains high overall mapping quality. The reported overall accuracy is 0.9025, with FAR 0.0631 and POD 0.8394. The CSI is 0.8073, which the authors describe as a good score. Error balance indicates underprediction of water: false negatives are about 16% while false positives are around 6%.
supporting_quote: overall accuracy of our method based on the validation dataset was 0.9025 with a FAR of 0.0631 and a POD of 0.8394
The CSI metric was 0.8073, a good score
overall false positive rate was around 6% compared to the false negative rate of 16%
it slightly underpredicted water areas, that is, higher false negatives

chunks.text: Regional validation shows performance varies by site but remains broadly consistent. Accuracy ranges from 0.8656 (Zambia) to 0.9265 (Myanmar) in Table 2. FAR is lowest in Mexico (0.0000) and higher in Cambodia (0.0349), while POD spans from 0.4353 (Colombia) to 0.8261 (Gabon). The paper links Cambodia’s higher FAR to fallow agriculture/alluvium confusion and Colombia’s low POD to vegetation and terrain effects for C-band SAR.
supporting_quote: Zambia region had the worst overall accuracy of 86.56%, with the Myanmar region having the best accuracy of 92.65%
Mexico had the best FAR of 0.0%
The Gabon region had the highest POD metric of 82.61%, whereas the Colombia region had the lowest, of 43.53%
This may be due to the high amount of fallow agricultural areas and alluvium soils present in the Cambodia floodplain region
The Colombia region was heavily vegetated and had terrain that could obscure the land surface in C-band SAR data

chunks.text: Monthly accuracy is not statistically related to cloud cover for the 2019 evaluation period. The paper reports a correlation between accuracy and cloud cover across all regions of −0.0331 with a p-value of 0.8621. This suggests that at a monthly scale, the fusion and gap-filling strategy yields stable accuracy even during cloudier periods. The result supports the method’s goal of reducing cloud-driven degradation in optical monitoring.
supporting_quote: We found no statistical relationship between cloud cover and accuracy, with the accuracy correlation with cloud cover across all regions of −0.0331, which resulted in a p-value of 0.8621.
accuracy of the extracted water at a monthly timescale using our method was not impacted by cloud cover

chunks.text: The fusion workflow substantially increases the temporal density of valid observations relative to optical-only and modestly relative to SAR-only. Across validated months/regions, optical has an average of 11.462 valid observations and SAR has 55.354. Using both sensors yields 64.899 observations on average. This corresponds to a 466% increase over optical-only and a 17% increase over SAR-only, improving the ability to track dynamic water changes.
supporting_quote: On average, the regions had 11.462 valid observations
SAR data had an average of 55.354 valid observations
When using both optical and SAR data... increased to 64.899
a 466% increase over just using optical and a 17% increase over using SAR alone

chunks.text: A practical observation from the validation regions is that in Myanmar no optical scenes passed the initial cloudiness filter, so the method effectively relied on SAR-only observations there. The paper attributes this to filtering Landsat scenes to less than 75% cloud cover for fusion suitability. This illustrates how input data availability can constrain fusion benefits in persistently cloudy regions, even though SAR remains available.
supporting_quote: In Myanmar, there were no optical observations that met the initial filter of less than 75% cloudy for use, resulting in only SAR imagery being used for the region.
We only used Landsat scenes that had 75% cloud cover or less in this study

chunks.text: The method depends on having at least some valid optical water observations to define water edges and gaps; without them, gap filling cannot be performed reliably. If an optical image contains no water pixels, edge-based thresholding for SAR gap fill can be incorrect because water edges are not defined. Consequently, the approach can fail or degrade in periods/places where optical imagery is entirely unusable or where optical-derived water is absent. This reliance is a core constraint of the gap-filling design.
supporting_quote: First is the need for optical imagery for water observation to identify gaps that can be filled with SAR imagery. The algorithm does not work without water pixels computed from an optical image.
if there is an optical image, but there are no water pixels in the optical image, then the method can attempt to fill the gaps... as the water edges are not defined.

chunks.text: Gap filling is only applied where optical QA indicates poor-quality pixels, so QA mask errors can propagate into the fused product. If the QA mask fails to flag contaminated pixels, those areas will not be gap filled and may remain misclassified. This places strong dependence on CFMask/QA reliability for consistent performance. The paper notes that such omissions can introduce errors and prevent correction by the fusion step.
supporting_quote: Gap filling using SAR data only occurs where poor-quality data are identified in the optical imagery, as indicated by a quality mask.
If the QA masks have errors that omit poor-quality data, then the resulting water detection could have errors and the gap-filling process will not be performed

chunks.text: The SAR probability inputs used for filling inherit known SAR uncertainties, which can lead to incorrect filled areas. The paper cites issues such as mountain geometry effects and low-backscatter non-water surfaces (e.g., sandy soils) causing false positives. Because SAR is used to infer water where optical is missing, these SAR-specific errors can become embedded in the fused time series. This underscores that fusion reduces cloud gaps but does not eliminate sensor-specific ambiguities.
supporting_quote: The gap filling uses the surface water probabilities computed from SAR data, which include a number of uncertainties and known issues
cannot detect water on the lee side of mountains, can have false positives due to sandy soils

chunks.text: A tunable design choice is the percentile used to reduce sampled SAR probabilities into a single threshold for gap filling. The authors note this value may require local calibration to account for regional conditions and seasonality, but such calibration is not addressed in the study. This may limit optimal performance in specific environments without additional tuning. Future work could explore calibration strategies for the percentile threshold.
supporting_quote: We then reduced the sampled SAR probabilities to a single threshold value using the 50th percentile.
The percentiles used to reduce the sampled probabilities can be calibrated for local regions and seasonality; however, the calibration of this value was out of the scope of this paper

chunks.text: The validation is performed at a monthly time step, which does not fully match the method’s intended sub-weekly scene-based outputs. The paper states that there is a mismatch between available validation data and the higher temporal frequency products generated by the workflow. This limits the ability to verify performance for weekly or event-scale dynamics (e.g., floods). The authors identify the lack of high-temporal-frequency validation data as a broader community gap.
supporting_quote: Lastly, we validated our method using monthly data.
The improvement this method provides is a dense time series at a sub-weekly scale, but there is a mismatch of available data to validate weekly timescale water maps
The lack of high-temporal-frequency validation data is a gap in the community.

chunks.text: The approach’s dense fusion time series is constrained to the Sentinel-1 era, because Sentinel-1 provides critical SAR inputs for regular gap filling, particularly in cloudy regions. The paper notes Sentinel-1 has been operating since October 2014, implying dense optical–SAR fusion products cannot be generated earlier using this framework. This temporal limitation affects long-term historical analyses that would otherwise rely on Landsat-only archives. Extending further back would require other SAR missions or alternative strategies.
supporting_quote: The Sentinel-1 mission... has been in operation since October 2014; therefore, a dense time series of optical and SAR surface water observations can only be created from that time onwards.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that pixel-level optical–SAR fusion with gap filling can generate dense time series of surface water maps by filling optical cloud-related gaps using SAR estimates. The method is validated across six regions and achieves overall accuracy of 0.9025 with regional accuracies spanning 0.8656 to 0.9212. The approach is positioned as improving monitoring for rapidly changing events such as floods by producing more complete and frequent observations than single-sensor approaches.
supporting_quote: This study presented a method for generating dense time series of surface water observations using optical–SAR sensor fusion and gap filling.
validated the results... six regions... overall accuracy of 0.9025
accuracies ranging between 0.8656 and 0.9212
especially useful for monitoring surface water during events that change rapidly in time, such as floods

chunks.text: A key conclusion is that fusing optical and SAR increases the number of valid surface water observations substantially, improving temporal coverage. The study reports average increases of 466% over optical-only and 17% over SAR-only for the validated regions and months. The authors also conclude that monthly-scale accuracy is not impacted by cloud cover in their analysis. This supports the method’s role in reducing cloud-related observation gaps.
supporting_quote: We found that incorporating both optical and SAR data increased, on average, the number of valid observations by 466% and 17% for optical and SAR, respectively
we found cloud cover was not correlated with accuracy and had no effect on the accuracy at a monthly scale

chunks.text: The authors state that the resulting fused surface water products can support practical applications including flood monitoring, drought monitoring, and water resource management. They further suggest the outputs can serve as inputs to other predictive frameworks, specifically referencing use in the FIER framework for inundation extent forecasting. The conclusion frames the work as an advance over prior methods that either used a single sensor at high frequency or aggregated fusion products to coarser temporal scales.
supporting_quote: This method has the potential to be used for a variety of applications, such as flood monitoring, drought monitoring, and water resource management.
We plan to use the results of this study as inputs into the... (FIER) framework
Previous methods either used one sensor... or aggregated data fusion results at a lower temporal resolution.

chunks.text: Exchange of water and sediment between rivers and floodplains supports biogeochemical and ecological processes that yield societal benefits such as sediment/nutrient storage and flood-wave attenuation. Human activities can laterally and/or vertically disconnect channels from floodplains through encroachment and incision, degrading floodplain function and increasing erosion. These impacts motivate tools that can assess connectivity and erosion potential across many reaches to support planning.
supporting_quote: Frequent exchange of water and sediment between rivers and their floodplains supports a myriad of biogeochemical, physical, and ecological processes
human activities can vertically and/or laterally disconnect the channel from its floodplain

chunks.text: Specific stream power (SSP) has been used at large scales as an indicator of erosion potential, sediment transport characteristics, and channel stability. Many watershed-scale SSP approaches use DEM-derived slope and flow accumulation, but they often omit reach-specific geometric information that is encoded in high-resolution topography. HAND-based methods can approximate geometry and discharge, creating opportunities for broader, faster assessments.
supporting_quote: Specific stream power (SSP) has been successfully estimated at scale to approximate sediment transport characteristics and assess erosion potential and channel stability
These DEMbased models typically use slope and flow accumulation area ... but neglect reach-specific geometric information.

chunks.text: Restoration and conservation investments are substantial, yet projects can underperform because they are implemented without basin-scale, systems-based planning. Hydrodynamic modeling for flood attenuation and connectivity is often too costly to develop and run across large regions. Low-complexity modeling combined with high-resolution topographic data offers a pathway to evaluate connectivity status rapidly over wide areas.
supporting_quote: restoration projects often fall short of their objectives, in part due to the lack of systems-based strategic planning.
modeling flood wave attenuation often requires process-based hydrodynamic models that are costly to develop and apply at the basin scale.

chunks.text: The study aims to evaluate channel–floodplain (dis)connectivity and erosion/incision hazard at the basin scale by computing reach-specific SSP–flow relationships from a low-complexity, DEM-based hydraulic approach. The authors intend to extract measures from SSP–flow curves that reflect floodwater storage capacity (connected vs disconnected) and erosion hazard at design storm stages. They also seek to identify watershed-scale patterns in connectivity using these reach metrics.
supporting_quote: To evaluate channel-floodplain (dis)connectivity and erosion/ incision hazard at the basin scale, we calculate Specific Stream Power (SSP)
We extract measures from these curves that describe (dis)connected floodwater storage capacity and erosion hazard at individual design storm flood stages

chunks.text: A second goal is to benchmark the low-complexity SSP estimates against a calibrated process-based model to determine whether the simpler approach is accurate enough for planning. The comparison is performed against a calibrated 2D HEC-RAS model across multiple design events. This validation is positioned as a step toward enabling broad-scale screening where full process-based modeling is infeasible.
supporting_quote: we benchmarked the SSP calculated from probHAND using a calibrated two-dimensional ... (HEC-RAS) unsteady model
We ran the HEC-RAS model for 2-, 25-, 50-, 100-, and 500-year design events (Q2, Q25, Q50, Q100, and Q500)

chunks.text: A key challenge in basin-scale management is the lack of a direct, scalable method to quantify lateral channel–floodplain connectivity. While flood-wave attenuation can serve as a proxy for connectivity, computing it typically requires costly hydrodynamic models. This limits the ability to support strategic, watershed-scale restoration and conservation planning.
supporting_quote: a method for quantifying lateral channel-floodplain connectivity at basin scales has eluded most.
modeling flood wave attenuation often requires process-based hydrodynamic models that are costly to develop and apply at the basin scale.

chunks.text: Many existing DEM-based SSP assessments provide distributional patterns of energy but do not incorporate reach-specific geometry that influences how SSP changes with stage and discharge. This omission constrains their usefulness for evaluating connectivity features like spillover and floodplain storage. The paper frames its contribution as leveraging geometry encoded in DEMs to produce reach-specific SSP–flow curves.
supporting_quote: These DEMbased models typically use slope and flow accumulation area ... but neglect reach-specific geometric information.
Our approach leverages this information to generate reach-specific SSP-flow curves.

chunks.text: Restoration efforts are often executed in an ad hoc manner, which can reduce their intended contributions to river and floodplain function. Managers need tools that can rapidly evaluate and visualize connectivity status and erosion potential across many reaches. The paper motivates process-form metrics as a screening approach to better target further assessment and investment.
supporting_quote: these river and floodplain restoration efforts are often undertaken in an ad hoc manner that may limit their intended contributions
Management tools that can rapidly evaluate and visualize connectivity status and channel erosion potential over a wide spatial extent provide opportunities

chunks.text: The authors compute reach-averaged specific stream power (SSP) using probHAND, a low-complexity DEM-based model extending HAND and incorporating Monte Carlo uncertainty. SSP is calculated as (γQs)/W using reach-averaged discharge Q, slope s, water specific weight γ, and average channel width W. Discharge is estimated from reach-averaged Manning equation parameters derived from stage-dependent geometry and roughness.
supporting_quote: We calculated SSP using the probHAND model, a low-complexity DEM-based model that extends the HAND model
We calculated SSP (watts/m2 ) as the product of the reachaveraged flow rate (Q [m3 /s]), reach slope (s [m/m]) ... divided by the average channel width (W [m])

chunks.text: Reach-averaged discharge for each stage is computed with a Manning-based formulation using reach-averaged cross-sectional area A, hydraulic radius R, slope s, and weighted roughness n. This links stage-dependent geometry inferred from topography to flow estimates, which in turn drive SSP calculations. The method emphasizes extracting geometry from high-resolution DEM and relative elevation products.
supporting_quote: For a given stage ... reach-averaged discharge was calculated as: Q = (AR^{2/3}sqrt{s})/n_{ord}
The method of determining A, R, s, and n_w is described in Supplemental S.3.

chunks.text: To evaluate the impact of assuming normal-depth flow and to verify probHAND SSP, the study benchmarks against a calibrated 2D HEC-RAS unsteady model. The authors run HEC-RAS for Q2, Q25, Q50, Q100, and Q500 events and export SSP rasters. Reach-averaged SSP is computed by averaging the raster within reach Thiessen polygons, with additional channel vs overbank SSP separation using top-of-bank lines.
supporting_quote: we benchmarked the SSP calculated from probHAND using a calibrated two-dimensional ... (HEC-RAS) unsteady model
Average SSP was calculated for each reach by averaging the SSP raster within the probHAND Thiessen polygon

chunks.text: SSP–flow curves are generated by plotting probHAND SSP versus Q across 100 stage heights between 0 and 10 m above the channel. Discharge is normalized by the Q2 flow rate to compare curve shapes among reaches, and curves are examined up to six times Q2 to emphasize design-practice floods (Q2 through Q500). Channel and overbank components are separated using a 1 m land-use/land-cover layer.
supporting_quote: we plotted probHAND SSP versus Q for 100 stage heights between 0 and 10 m above the channel.
We normalized Q by the Q2 flow rates ... We display normalized Q values between zero and six times the Q2 flow rate

chunks.text: Spillover behavior is classified from SSP–flow curve shape into Gradual, Abrupt, or No Spillover categories based on curve slopes. Abrupt spillover corresponds to very-large-magnitude slope values, while gradual spillover corresponds to slope near zero. The stage where spillover first occurs is translated into a 'First Spillover Design Flood' to characterize how frequently a reach accesses floodplains.
supporting_quote: We automated the categorization of the spillover type based on the slope of the SSP-flow curves
called that the 'First Spillover Design Flood'.

chunks.text: Floodplain storage is quantified as specific volume capacity (m³/m), computed as total inundated volume divided by reach length to compare reaches of different lengths. Connected Specific Volume Capacity (CSVC) is associated with gradual spillover events and represents naturally connected storage. Disconnected Specific Volume Capacity (DSVC) is defined as the volume of closed topographic depressions ('pits') below a given stage, normalized by reach length, representing storage isolated by natural or anthropogenic barriers.
supporting_quote: We calculated floodplain storage capacity of each reach as a specific volume capacity (m³/m)—defined as the total volume in a reach divided by reach length
Disconnected Specific Volume Capacity (DSVC) is the volume of all 'closed topographic depressions' ... below a given flood stage normalized by the reach length.

chunks.text: DSVC is computed by identifying DEM pit-filled locations, extracting pit-fill depth, restoring pit topography to the HAND raster, and comparing inundation between restored and original HAND surfaces. Cells inundated in the restored HAND but not in the original HAND are considered disconnected. Disconnected volume for a stage is the sum of all such pit volumes below the flood stage.
supporting_quote: we extracted the DEM pit topography, restored that pit-filled floodplain topography to the HAND elevation raster
any pit topography cells inundated in the updated HAND raster, but not in the original HAND raster, were defined as disconnected.

chunks.text: Erosion hazard is evaluated by comparing in-channel SSP at design floods to a critical SSP threshold derived from bed grain size and slope. The study estimates SSPcrit using Ferguson (2005) with D50, D84, and slope s, and propagates uncertainty via 95% confidence intervals for D50 and D84 computed from pebble-count sample size. Threshold exceedance (including LCL/UCL) is then checked at each design flood to screen for channel-altering flows.
supporting_quote: we estimated the critical SSP threshold (SSPcrit) for the 84th percentile ... after Ferguson (2005)
The 95% confidence intervals for the D50 and D84 diameters were generated

chunks.text: The proof-of-concept is conducted in the Mad River watershed in central Vermont using Vermont Stream Geomorphic Assessment (SGA) reaches along the main stem. The study analyzes 25 SGA-defined reaches along a 38-km segment, excluding one impounded reach from further analysis. Reach drainage areas span roughly 31.9 to 373 km², capturing a range of geomorphic settings.
supporting_quote: 25 main stem reaches ... along a 38-km stretch of the Mad River.
Reach drainage areas range from 31.9 to 373 km2 .

chunks.text: The analyzed reaches include both bedrock-controlled and alluvial channels with wide variation in confinement and entrenchment. The paper reports 6 bedrock-controlled reaches and 18 alluvial reaches after excluding the impounded one. Valley confinement and entrenchment ratios span broad ranges, allowing assessment of how geometry influences SSP–flow behavior and storage metrics.
supporting_quote: Six (24%) are bedrock-controlled, and the remaining 18 (72%) are alluvial channels.
Reaches vary in their degree of valley confinement from 1.3 to 16 times the channel width. Entrenchment ratios varied from 1.13 to 12.

chunks.text: ProbHAND inputs combine high-resolution topography, land cover, channel geometry, sediment data, and design flows. The study uses LiDAR-derived DEM and land-use/land-cover rasters at 1 m resolution, plus reach polylines, channel bed grain-size distributions, and design flood flow rates per reach. This dataset supports stage-based hydraulic geometry extraction and SSP–flow curve generation.
supporting_quote: Inputs to the probHAND model included: LiDAR-derived DEM rasters (1 m resolution), a land-use land-cover (LULC) raster layer (1 m resolution)
stream reach polylines, channel bed grainsize distributions, and design flood flow rate data for each stream reach.

chunks.text: Model verification data come from a calibrated 2D HEC-RAS unsteady model of the study area. The study runs the model for 2-, 25-, 50-, 100-, and 500-year design events and exports SSP rasters for each event. Channel and overbank areas are distinguished with top-of-bank lines in HEC-RAS to enable component-wise comparison.
supporting_quote: using a calibrated two-dimensional ... (HEC-RAS) unsteady model of the study area
We ran the HEC-RAS model for 2-, 25-, 50-, 100-, and 500-year design events

chunks.text: Critical erosion thresholds are parameterized with pebble count data from SGA assessments. The critical SSP threshold uses D50 and D84 statistics and their uncertainty bounds derived from cumulative grain-size distributions and sample size N. This allows reach-specific comparison of SSP at design floods to nominal and confidence-bounded thresholds.
supporting_quote: Using pebble count data available from SGA assessments (VTANR, 2022), we estimated the critical SSP threshold ... for the 84th percentile
where N is the number of grains counted during the grainsize survey.

chunks.text: ProbHAND SSP agrees reasonably with 2D HEC-RAS at the reach scale, with systematic biases that offset when channel and overbank are combined. The low-complexity model overestimates channel SSP by about 22.6% RPD on average and underestimates overbank SSP by about 44.2% RPD on average. When channel and overbank are combined, the average difference is about 8% RPD, supporting use as a screening tool.
supporting_quote: probHAND model systematically overestimated SSP for the channel (22.6% RPD on average)
When considering the combined channel and overbank estimates ... differing by only 8% RPD

chunks.text: Spillover behavior differs strongly by reach type and confinement, with spillover absent in bedrock-controlled reaches. Among 18 alluvial reaches, 8 (44%) first experience spillover at or below Q50, representing more frequent floodplain access. Many remaining alluvial reaches do not spill over until Q100/Q500 or show none, implying disconnection or limited floodplain extent.
supporting_quote: Of the 18 alluvial reaches, 8 (44%) first experience spillover ... at or below the Q50
spillover was not observed in any of the bedrock-controlled reaches.

chunks.text: Spillover at flows below Q50 is statistically associated with entrenchment ratio, indicating that less entrenched channels more often access floodplains at smaller design floods. The Kruskal–Wallis test shows a positive association between below-Q50 spillover occurrence and ER at the 95% confidence level. This supports using SSP–flow curve features as indicators of connectivity tied to reach geometry.
supporting_quote: The occurrence of spillover at flow rates below the Q50 was positively associated with ER at the 95% confidence level (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.020).
We use the Q50 as a breakpoint between smaller events that are easier to design for

chunks.text: Floodplain storage metrics show clear magnitude ranges across the study area and relate to downstream position. CSVC ranges from 0 to 200 m³/m, while DSVC ranges from 0 to 31 m³/m. Upstream reaches often lack either CSVC or DSVC (less than 1 m³/m) at Q50 or smaller, while many downstream alluvial reaches have substantial storage available at these flows.
supporting_quote: The CSVC values for our study area range between 0 and 200 m3 /m and between 0 and 31 m3 /m for DSVC.
the six upstream reaches lack either CVSC or DVSC (defined as less than 1 m3 /m) at the Q50 or smaller

chunks.text: Entrenchment ratio is positively associated with the presence of connected and disconnected storage at or below Q50, whereas incision ratio is not. Statistical tests indicate ER is positively associated with CSVC presence (p = 0.049) and DSVC presence (p = 0.026) at or below Q50. Incision ratio shows no correlation with either DSVC or CSVC (p > 0.268).
supporting_quote: We found ER to be positively associated with the presence of both CSVC (p = 0.049) and DSVC (p = 0.026) at or below the Q50
Incision ratio was not correlated with either DSVC or CSVC (p > 0.268

chunks.text: Critical SSP threshold exceedance patterns vary longitudinally, with the greatest exceedance magnitudes in headwaters and reduced hazard in mid-watershed alluvial reaches. Headwater reaches (M17–M21) show the greatest threshold exceedances, including UCL exceedances, while mid-watershed reaches (M11–M16) show no exceedances of the LCL at or below Q50. Downstream reaches (M01–M10) show exceedances of nominal critical SSP but not UCL exceedances.
supporting_quote: The headwater reaches (M17–M21) experienced the greatest magnitude of threshold exceedances (including UCL exceedances)
The mid-watershed reaches (M11–M16) exhibited the least erosion hazard with no exceedances of the LCL at or below the Q50.

chunks.text: Higher in-channel SSP tends to occur in confined, steeper alluvial reaches. Six of seven confined alluvial reaches with slopes 0.010–0.018 m/m have higher SSP than unconfined, lower-gradient reaches. After two bedrock reaches (M17 and M18), slopes of downstream alluvial reaches flatten (< 0.005) and SSP decreases.
supporting_quote: Six of the seven confined alluvial reaches with greater than average slopes (0.010– 0.018 m/m) had higher SSP values than the unconfined reaches
slopes of the alluvial reaches flatten substantially (slopes < 0.005) leading to reduced channel SSP values

chunks.text: Reaches exceeding erosion thresholds at more frequent floods often lack storage capacity. Of 18 alluvial reaches, 10 exceed the LCL prior to Q50, and 6 of those 10 (60%) have CSVC/DSVC below 1 m³/m at these flows. In contrast, among eight reaches without LCL exceedance prior to Q50, only two (25%) have storage less than 9 m³/m.
supporting_quote: Of the 18 alluvial reaches, 10 exceed the LCL prior to the Q50; 6 of these 10 reaches (60%) lack connected storage capacity (CSVC/DSVC < 1 m3 /m)
only two reaches (25%) have storage capacities of less than 9 m3 /m.

chunks.text: Entrenchment ratio appears to relate to erosion threshold exceedance even when not statistically significant in the reported test. Among 12 entrenched reaches (ER < 3), 8 exceed the LCL prior to Q50, while only 1 of 6 nonentrenched reaches (ER > 3) exceeds a critical threshold prior to Q50. This pattern suggests that entrenchment and limited floodplain access coincide with higher erosion hazard at frequent floods.
supporting_quote: Of the 12 entrenched reaches (ER < 3), 8 exceed the LCL prior to the Q50, while only one of 6 nonentrenched reaches (ER > 3) exceeds a critical SSP Threshold prior to the Q50.
We also found no significant correlation between IR and Threshold Exceedances (p = 0.268

chunks.text: The authors argue that probHAND SSP differences from HEC-RAS are unlikely to change broad-scale planning interpretations, and note the bias may be conservatively oriented for screening. They emphasize that building calibrated 2D models over large basins is resource-intensive and could take years. They recommend using the low-complexity approach for prioritization, followed by process-based modeling for selected projects during detailed design.
supporting_quote: differences between the two methods are likely to not alter the interpretation as applied to broad-scale planning applications
Constructing, calibrating, and running 2D HEC-RAS ... for these areas is highly resource intensive and would likely require years

chunks.text: The study acknowledges limitations in sample size and representativeness of floodplain types. The non-bedrock reaches are characterized as 'equilibrium floodplains' with medium SSP and generally unconfined, moderate-to-low gradients. The authors note future work is needed to test whether their measures correlate to geomorphic metrics in other settings, including lower-energy environments.
supporting_quote: The sample size used to develop our method and illustrate proof-of-concept is admittedly small
Our non-bedrock study reaches would be classified as 'equilibrium floodplains' ... characterized by medium SSP (>10–300 watts/m2 )

chunks.text: DSVC derived from DEM pits can include naturally occurring microtopography and DEM noise, which may confound interpretation when volumes are small. The authors address this by using a DSVC threshold of 1.0 m³/m, noting smaller values appeared linked to micro-topography and/or DEM noise rather than meaningful disconnection. In their watershed, such small-pit contributions were typically minor compared to larger anthropogenic pits.
supporting_quote: We used a threshold of 1.0 for DSVC because small values appeared to be associated with micro-topography and/or noise in the DEMs
these were insignificant, typically accounting for <1 m3 /m of DSVC in any given reach.

chunks.text: The statistical analysis is intentionally limited to conditions at or below Q50 because higher-intensity, lower-frequency storms are often outside typical restoration design scope. The authors state they disregard CSVC, DSVC, and threshold exceedances above Q50 for this planning purpose. This framing limits conclusions about extreme-event behavior but aligns the tool with common project decision contexts.
supporting_quote: We disregarded the presence of CVSC, DSVC, and Critical SSP threshold exceedances above the Q50
designing for such low-frequency, high-intensity storms is typically outside the scope of restoration and conservation projects

chunks.text: The paper concludes that DEM- and HAND-derived information can be mined to produce reach-scale, process-form measures of connectivity and erosion hazard with relatively low computational and labor requirements. These measures enable broad-scale screening to target locations for restoration, reconnection, or conservation, and they reflect both natural geomorphic controls and impacts of built infrastructure. The approach is positioned as a practical regional planning tool that complements, rather than replaces, detailed process-based modeling for project design.
supporting_quote: Process-form measures describing channel-floodplain connectivity and fluvial erosion hazards can be calculated over a wide geographic area at relatively low computational and human labor costs
Information embedded in DEMs and relative elevation products, such as HAND, may be used to describe the condition and function of rivers and floodplains.

chunks.text: The authors emphasize that their suite of measures captures variability imposed by geomorphic setting and highlights the effects of infrastructure and land use through disconnected storage, abrupt spillovers, and heightened erosion hazards during regular floods. They also state that the framework can guide planners toward reaches needing detailed feasibility assessments and suggest future synthesis into a reach classification system for better usability.
supporting_quote: captures both the natural variability imposed by the geomorphic setting
Synthesizing these measures into a reach classification framework may improve user friendliness for planners.

chunks.text: Operational forecasting models support water management and hazard mitigation, and their quality depends strongly on channel flow routing. Routing influences predicted flood timing, magnitude, depth, duration, and extent along channel networks and adjacent floodplains. Routing methods typically solve the De St. Venant mass and momentum equations, with different simplifications yielding dynamic, diffusive, kinematic, and Muskingum-Cunge approaches.
supporting_quote: Channel flow routing significantly impacts the ability to accurately capture the timing and magnitude of flood elevations along the length of the channel network of a given watershed.
Routing methods are based on numerical solutions of the well-known De St. Venant equations for mass and momentum

chunks.text: Dynamic wave (full De St. Venant) routing can be computationally expensive and prone to numerical instability, which is problematic for large operational systems like the National Water Model. Bulk-wave approaches (diffusive and kinematic) omit some momentum terms and are typically faster and more robust, but can be inaccurate when conditions require inertia and backwater physics. Muskingum-Cunge is broadly efficient and includes diffusion-like behavior but still struggles with strong backwater effects.
supporting_quote: The dynamic wave approximation is computationally expensive relative to simpler approximation and requires a great deal of caution to avoid numerical instabilities
the Muskingum-Cunge method does not fully capture strong backwater effects — especially in lowgradient (hydraulically mild slope) channels

chunks.text: At continental scale, rivers exhibit a broad spectrum of hydraulic conditions, from steep and flashy to low-gradient systems with backwater. Prior work emphasized ranges of validity for wave approximations and suggested using wave celerity and dimensionless scaling parameters to assess whether friction, inertia, and pressure dominate.
