supporting_quote: We used a two-by-two contingency matrix ... true positive (TP) ... true negative (TN) ... false positive (FP) ... false negative (FN).
The F-statistic, also known as the Critical Success Index (CSI), ranges from 0 to 1
We used the median instead of the mean to summarize F-statistic which mitigates the influence of outliers

chunks.text: The experimental design uses an exhaustive pairing of DEMs and hydrography datasets to separate hydrography versus DEM effects. Within FABDEM or SRTM, switching RFS1 to RFS2 isolates hydrography refinement. Within RFS1 or RFS2, switching SRTM 30 m to FABDEM isolates DEM refinement. Additional evaluations include higher-resolution USGS and ALOS DEMs with both hydrographies.
supporting_quote: We conduct eight sets of trials using each possible combination of the four DEM datasets and the two hydrography datasets.
Comparisons between FABDEM-RFS1 and FABDEM-RFS2, and between SRTM-RFS1 and SRTM-RFS2, assess the impact of hydrography refinement while keeping the elevation model constant.
comparisons between FABDEM-RFS1 and SRTM-RFS1, and between FABDEM-RFS2 and SRTM-RFS2, isolate the effect of DEM resolution

chunks.text: Flood scenarios are designed to represent multiple event magnitudes by modeling four flow levels per site approximating 2-, 10-, 50-, and 100-year return periods. When USGS reference-map flows did not align directly with FEMA benchmark return-period discharges, the study used the closest USGS-modeled discharge or log-log interpolation between known return-period discharges to estimate the return period for the chosen flows.
supporting_quote: At each of the five sites, flood maps are simulated to match four different flow levels which approximate 2-, 10-, 50-, and 100-year return period level events.
we used the closest available USGS-modeled discharges
we used log-log interpolation between known return period discharges—typically between the FEMA-reported 2-year, 10-year, 50-year, 100-year, and 500-year events

chunks.text: The evaluation uses USGS flood inundation maps as reference datasets, built using observed flood information and high-resolution modeling inputs. The reference maps incorporate recorded flood events, LIDAR, gauge data, surveyed high water marks, and HEC-RAS 1D/2D models. These reference extents serve as the “ground truth” for pixelwise agreement metrics.
supporting_quote: We used maps from the USGS as our reference or "ground truth" flood maps.
They are based on recorded flood events, high-resolution LIDAR, stream gauge data, surveyed high water marks, and the Hydrologic Engineering Center's River Analysis System (HEC-RAS) 1D-or-2D models

chunks.text: Five U.S. study sites span varied hydro-climatic and geographic settings: Suncook River (NH), North Fork Kentucky River (KY), Nimishillen Creek (OH), Flathead River (MT), and South Platte River at Fort Morgan (CO). The paper reports site attributes including drainage area, gauge IDs, water-level ranges, and modeled domain lengths. These sites provide multiple contexts for comparing DEM and hydrography combinations.
supporting_quote: The study areas ... include the Suncook River in New Hampshire, the North Fork Kentucky River in Kentucky, Nimishillen Creek in Ohio, the Flathead River in Montana, and the South Platte River at Fort Morgan in Colorado.
Summary details of each site ... are given in Table 2.

chunks.text: Four DEM sources are tested: SRTM (30 m and 90 m), FABDEM (30 m), ALOS (12.5 m), and USGS 3DEP (10 m). The paper highlights differing vertical accuracies and that TanDEM-X underlies both FABDEM and the RFS2 hydrography derivation. This mix enables testing resolution, accuracy, and bare-earth representation effects on inundation skill.
supporting_quote: we evaluate flood inundation maps using four DEM sources ... SRTM ... FABDEM, ALOS DEM, and the USGS 3DEP 10 m DEM.
Table 1 summarizes several properties of the DEM datasets
the TanDEM-X DEM source is used to derive both the RFS2 hydrography and the FABDEM.

chunks.text: Two global hydrography inputs from GEOGLOWS RFS are compared. RFS1 is derived from SRTM/HydroSHEDS-aligned elevations, while RFS2 is derived from TanDEM-X Hydro (TDX-Hydro) with edits. The study uses these versions because RFS provides retrospective and forecast discharge simulations on the corresponding stream representations.
supporting_quote: We use the Group on Earth Observations' Global Water Sustainability (GEOGLOWS) River Forecasting System (RFS) datasets from their original and more recent second versions
RFS Version 1 (RFS1) is derived from the same elevation source as HydroSHEDS
RFS Version 2 (RFS2) is derived from the TanDEM-X Hydro (TDX-Hydro) dataset

chunks.text: Across all DEM and hydrography combinations, modeled flood map agreement generally improves as the modeled event magnitude increases. The paper reports that F-statistic tends to rise with increasing simulated return period, both when aggregated across sites and within individual sites, though the magnitude varies. This indicates the ARC/Curve2Flood workflow performs more reliably for larger floods than for smaller events.
supporting_quote: we found that, in general, F-statistic increased as the simulated return period increased regardless of which DEM and hydrography combination used.
This trend applied when aggregating F-statistic across all sites as well as for any individual site

chunks.text: Improving DEM quality produced larger accuracy gains than improving hydrography alone. When isolating effects, the study reports a mean F-statistic increase of 0.125 from DEM improvements compared to a mean increase of 0.015 from hydrography upgrades. This suggests terrain representation is the dominant driver of extent agreement in these experiments, although hydrography alignment can still matter in specific cases.
supporting_quote: most scenarios show more significant gains from DEM improvements (with a mean increase in F-statistic of 0.125).
most return periods and locations had mixed benefits from improved hydrography (with a mean increase in F-statistic of 0.015)

chunks.text: Using both improved elevation and improved hydrography together produced consistent benefits. The FABDEM-RFS2 pairing outperformed SRTM-RFS1 across all five sites and four return periods, with a mean F-statistic increase of 0.139 (38.9%). The paper highlights this as evidence that matching higher-quality DEMs with higher-quality hydrography—especially when derived from the same underlying elevation source—yields the most reliable improvements.
supporting_quote: The FABDEM-RFS2 pairing consistently produced a higher F-statistic than the SRTM-RFS1 combination across all five study sites and all four return periods.
there was a mean increase in the F-statistic of 0.139, or a 38.9% increase.
flood map agreement improves the most when both the DEM and hydrography datasets matched each other and were from higher resolution satellite missions.

chunks.text: In broader comparisons using multiple DEMs, higher-resolution elevation datasets generally produced higher F-statistics regardless of hydrography choice. The paper summarizes an overall ranking where USGS 3DEP 10 m typically performs best, followed by ALOS, then FABDEM, SRTM-30 m, and SRTM-90 m. The sharp decrease for SRTM-90 is attributed to its coarse resolution.
supporting_quote: The higher-resolution elevation data consistently yielded higher F-statistic values without respect to the underlying hydrography.
The USGS 3DEP 10 m DEM generally showed superior performance, followed by ALOS, FABDEM, SRTM-30 m, and SRTM-90 m.
The sharp drop in the F-statistic for the SRTM-90 DEM is expected because of its relatively low resolution.

chunks.text: At low return periods (small flood extents), hydrography alignment becomes more influential. The paper notes that switching from RFS1 to RFS2 can produce large gains at low return periods, because small spatial errors in stream placement can create disconnected or misplaced inundation patches. A Colorado 2-year example shows RFS1 centerlines misaligned with the DEM, contributing to false positives disconnected from the river, while RFS2 alignment reduces these errors when paired with FABDEM.
supporting_quote: for some locations the hydrography improvement produces large gains at low return periods (this is seen also in Figure 4).

At lower return periods ... The improved F-statistic with RFS2 and FABDEM reflects the importance of accurate placement of the hydrography within the DEM is particularly important for lower return periods.
RFS1′ s stream centerlines are not well aligned with the channel in the DEM ... false positive results shown in areas that are disconnected from the actual river.

chunks.text: The paper’s averaged auxiliary metrics indicate lower-return-period simulations tend to overpredict inundation and that bias improves toward 1 as return period increases. It reports that “the lower return periods do worse” partly because “the model is overpredicting,” and that “as the return period increases, the model's bias approaches 1.” This supports the observed increase in F-statistic with larger flows.
supporting_quote: The values for bias indicate that the reason the lower return periods do worse is because the model is overpredicting.
As the return period increases, the model's bias approaches 1.

chunks.text: Despite the general resolution-based ranking, FABDEM sometimes outperformed higher-resolution non-bare-earth DEMs in specific contexts, especially at the lowest return period. The paper identifies a 2-year outlier pattern where FABDEM often had larger F-statistic than ALOS or USGS DEMs, and provides a Kentucky example where FABDEM is superior for three of four return periods. This suggests bare-earth processing and dataset alignment can outweigh raw resolution in some locations.
supporting_quote: One relevant outlier is at the lowest return period simulated, 2-year, where the FABDEM option typically had a larger F-statistic than either the ALOS or USGS DEMs.
Figure 9 shows ... The performance at this location is superior to the USGS and ALOS DEMs for three of the four return periods.
We hypothesize that the impact of the bare earth DEM could make a larger difference in some locations

chunks.text: ARC/Curve2Flood’s simplified hydraulics lead to known weaknesses in certain physical settings and conditions. The paper states the workflow performs poorly for complex hydrodynamic systems (e.g., coasts, braided channels, culverts, bridges, low relief). It also notes that overestimation is more common in low-flow conditions, particularly in flatter terrain, due to simplified bathymetry representation and the lack of multidimensional hydraulics.
supporting_quote: for complex hydrodynamic systems like coasts, braided streams, culverts, low topographic relief, and bridges, ARC-Curve2Flood will perform poorly.
flood extent estimates tend to be overestimated, particularly in flatter terrain, due to simplified bathymetry representation and the lack of multidimensional hydraulic modeling

chunks.text: The authors caution that performance magnitudes observed here may not generalize because the evaluation includes only five U.S. sites selected based on availability of reconstructed USGS reference maps. They recommend expanding to more sites representing different physical characteristics and analyzing site properties to better explain where certain datasets perform best. Accordingly, the paper advises caution in expecting the same size of accuracy changes at untested locations.
supporting_quote: Future work should include more total sites and ideally many sites representative of different kinds of physical characteristics.
Because of the limited number of sites, we recommend caution expecting the specific magnitudes of increase or decrease in performance at other sites.

chunks.text: The paper highlights a need for site-specific investigation because dataset strengths can vary by location and flow regime. It reports cases where FABDEM (bare earth) combined with TanDEM-X-derived hydrography can outperform higher-resolution non-bare-earth DEMs at low return periods, implying that resolution alone is not always decisive. This variability motivates additional studies to identify when bare-earth processing and hydrography alignment are most impactful.
supporting_quote: the FABDEM sometimes outperformed higher-resolution non-bare-earth DEMs (like ALOS or USGS 3DEP) at the lowest return period (2-year flow).
This suggests that the bare-earth representation of FABDEM, combined with RFS2 hydrography derived from the same underlying TanDEM-X elevation data, is particularly important for lower flows

chunks.text: Overall, modeled flood map agreement (F-statistic) tends to increase with higher return periods across sites and dataset combinations. The largest and most consistent improvements occur when both the DEM and hydrography are upgraded together to higher-quality sources, particularly when they share an underlying elevation representation. The study emphasizes the paired improvement from SRTM30+RFS1 to FABDEM+RFS2 as a central finding.
supporting_quote: We observed that the F-statistic generally increased as the simulated return period increased, regardless of the DEM and hydrography combination used.
Using FABDEM with RFS1 or SRTM with RFS2 did not yield the same accuracy gains, underscoring the importance of using terrain and stream network data derived from same source
Overall, there was a 38.9% increase in mean F-statistic between the two pairings.

chunks.text: The study concludes DEM improvements have a stronger influence on accuracy than hydrography improvements alone, though hydrography refinement matters more for lower return periods. It reports that switching from RFS1 to RFS2 “played a more significant role” for the 2-year events, where small alignment errors alter floodplain connectivity and extent. This highlights a regime-dependent importance: hydrography for small floods and DEM quality for larger floods.
supporting_quote: Improvements to the DEM had a more pronounced impact on the F-statistic than hydrography alone
Switching from RFS1 to RFS2 played a more significant role in accuracy improvement at lower return periods, particularly the 2-year return period.
These results indicate that small errors in stream alignment and floodplain connectivity have a larger impact ... at low flows.

chunks.text: For practical recommendations, the paper suggests ARC and Curve2Flood with globally available FABDEM and RFS2 as a strong baseline for general flood extent mapping, particularly for lower flows. For higher flows, it notes that ALOS or better-resolution DEMs with RFS2 are usually best, although such DEMs may not be globally available. The authors encourage staying current with new global DEM releases and processing methods that improve vertical accuracy, resolution, and bare-earth representation.
supporting_quote: The ARC and Curve2Flood tools combined with the globally available FABDEM and RFS2 can be recommended as generally the best option for accurate flood maps at lower flows
while ALOS or better-resolution, but perhaps not global coverage, DEMs with RFS2 are usually best at higher flows.
Future flood inundation mapping initiatives should prioritize staying current with the release of global DEMs and advanced processing methods

chunks.text: Accurate estimates of channel bankfull depth and top-width are important inputs for large-scale hydrologic and hydraulic applications. They affect channel routing, generalized cross-sections, hydrological forecasting, and flood mapping products. Such estimates also help represent below-DEM channel volume that otherwise is poorly captured when bathymetry is missing.
supporting_quote: The use of accurate estimates of channel bankfull depth and top‐width improves channel flow routing models
precise estimates of bankfull depth and top‐width improve flood risk analysis and mapping.

chunks.text: Prior work has often relied on global power-law relations between discharge and channel geometry. An early example provides global equations for bankfull top-width and depth as functions of discharge. These approaches are widely used but can have substantial errors and limited applicability depending on latitude and resolvable channel widths.
supporting_quote: One of the earliest of these efforts was proposed by Moody and Troutman (2002) for global channels (Equations 1 and 2).

chunks.text: Machine learning has emerged as an alternative that can learn non-linear, multi-predictor relationships and utilize hydrographic networks and watershed attribute datasets. Prior ML work (e.g., random forest with many watershed predictors) improved estimates but raised issues of high dimensionality and collinearity, which can reduce interpretability and extensibility.
supporting_quote: ML models provide a superior alternative to simple regression models by efficiently learning from multidimensional and complex data, capturing non‐linear relationships
when using a large suite of 96 predictors, high dimensionality (referred to as the "curse of dimensionality") and high correlation between variables

chunks.text: The study tests whether an ensemble meta-learning approach that uses National Water Model simulated flow characteristics together with land-surface and climate variables can predict bankfull and in-channel top-width and depth with goodness of fit comparable to or better than previous methods. The goal includes improving predictive capability by incorporating NWM flow statistics (e.g., annual exceedance probability discharges) as explicit predictors alongside landscape attributes.
supporting_quote: we test the hypothesis that a meta‐learning (ensemble ML) methodology informed by National Water Model (NWM) simulated flow characteristics ... and a suite of land surface and climate variables can predict bankfull top‐width and depth

We hypothesize that the incorporation of NWM simulated flow characteristics and a suite of land surface and climate variables can significantly improve bankfull top‐width and depth predictive capability.

chunks.text: A further objective is to produce reach-scale predictions across the CONUS hydrofabric network, enabling an integrated, updatable channel geometry dataset. After training, the approach is applied to produce width and depth estimates for approximately 2.7 million river reaches, leveraging the National Hydrologic Geospatial Fabric as the prediction domain.
supporting_quote: Following the completion of model training, we utilize the reference fabric aggregated features ... to predict channel width and depth under both bankfull and in‐channel conditions for approximately 2.7 million river reaches across the CONUS.
The river network used in this study is the National Hydrologic Geospatial Fabric (NHGF; Bock et al., 2022)

chunks.text: Existing global and regional empirical relations can exhibit substantial error and limited coverage, especially when constrained by remote sensing resolution and geographic scope. Some global equations were validated with wide error ranges and are limited to reaches below 60°N and widths above Landsat’s resolution. These limitations motivate data-driven approaches that can leverage diverse predictors beyond simple discharge or drainage area scaling.
supporting_quote: these equations are limited to channel reaches below 60°N and top‐width greater than the 30 m resolution of Landsat scenes.
In their validation, they found errors ranging from 8% to 62%.

chunks.text: Remote sensing approaches for channel geometry are limited by spatial resolution, data quality constraints (e.g., cloud cover), and computational cost. Landsat’s 30 m resolution restricts estimation to wider channels, and SWOT’s 50 m resolution limits observable channels to those wider than about 100 m. As a result, tributary systems remain difficult to characterize with remote sensing alone.
supporting_quote: The major constraints on all remote sensing approaches are (a) the spatial resolution of the data, (b) the quality of the data (e.g., scan lines and cloud cover), and (c) the computational costs
the 30‐m resolution of Landsat products and algorithms limit estimation to channels greater than 50 m in top‐width
limiting the observable channels to those with top‐widths exceeding 100 m

chunks.text: Prior ML approaches using many predictors face issues of dimensionality and collinearity that can impair interpretability and extensibility. Highly correlated variables can create collinear predictors, which may confuse models and distort inferred responses even for algorithms like random forests. This study explicitly targets reducing predictor count and covariance while maintaining predictive skill.
supporting_quote: when using a large suite of 96 predictors, high dimensionality ... and high correlation between variables ... create collinear predictors within the model, impairing its interpretability post‐training
These challenges can lead to model confusion and a distorted representation of the actual responses, even in ML algorithms such as random forest methods

chunks.text: The authors filtered noisy multi-profile hydraulic observations at each site and fit at-a-station hydraulic geometry (AHG) relations linking discharge to top-width, depth, and velocity. They used the AHGestimation R package to remove statistical outliers and fit equations while preserving mass conservation constraints. Sites were retained only if fitted relationships had adequate explanatory power and did not show inverse discharge-depth behavior.
supporting_quote: we leveraged the AHGestimation R package ... to filter data based on statistical outliers prior to using an ensemble‐based fitting method to ensure massis conserved (Equations 7 and 8)
We took an arbitrary threshold of 0.6 ... and retained sites with a R^2 > 0.6 from AHG fit.
In total, 4,229 of the 6,226 initial sites were retained.

chunks.text: Bankfull and in-channel discharges were defined using annual exceedance probability conventions and estimated from gauge records via flood frequency analysis. The study labels 100% annual exceedance probability as in-channel and 50% as bankfull, and then uses the AHG relations to compute corresponding width and depth. Candidate extreme-value distributions were compared using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic to choose the best fit per site.
supporting_quote: we used the widely accepted definitions of discharge at 100% and 50% annual exceedance probability, respectively
we simplify our approach by labeling 100% and 50% annual exceedance probability as in‐channel and bankfull
the Kolmogorov‐Smirnov (KS) method was used

chunks.text: Predictors were compiled on the National Hydrologic Geospatial Fabric and aggregated to reach scale to reconcile varying spatial resolutions and time periods across datasets. The study averages gridded datasets to a consistent upstream drainage area and uses long-term aggregation (20+ years) to reduce temporal inconsistencies. Predictors include watershed characteristics (StreamCat), additional soil/landscape/weather datasets, hydrographic connectivity, and NWM flow statistics.
supporting_quote: we aggregate data over 20 or more years, which smooths out short‐term fluctuations
we resolve spatial resolution discrepancies by averaging gridded data sets to a consistent upstream drainage area and producing reach average input data.
In total, we used 58 watershed‐level predictorsfrom this data set.

chunks.text: The model incorporates NWM retrospective streamflow percentiles and flood-frequency discharge estimates as predictors, treating them as synthetic due to discrepancies with gauge measurements. During training, sites were split so half used NWIS-derived floods and half used NWM-derived floods, and a binary indicator flags absence of NWIS records. During testing, bankfull and in-channel floods are derived only from NWM.
supporting_quote: Streamflow statistics were generated ... from the NWM v2.1 retrospective simulation ... and include 20%–0.1% annual exceedance probability discharge

randomly split sites such that half only contained NWIS bankfull ... and the other half only contained NWM bankfull ... and introduced a binary variable as an indicator of the absence of NWIS records.
During the testing phase, bankfull or in‐channel floods are only derived from NWM.

chunks.text: To address high dimensionality (116 predictors), the authors reduced feature space using SHAP-based importance ranking and correlation clustering with PCA. PCA was applied to correlated variable groups, retaining components that explain 95% of variance. Using an elbow heuristic on R-squared, they selected a compact subset of 15 features while maintaining performance near 0.80.
supporting_quote: Given the large predictor set selected for this study (116), we used two approaches to reduce the number of variables
We specified a target explained variance of 95%
we identified a subset of 15 features while the R^2 value remained close to 0.80

chunks.text: Model development used a broad out-of-the-box screening of 40 algorithms and then selection and tuning of the top 10 candidates using repeated 5-fold cross-validation. Final predictions used ensemble approaches, including a meta-learner (stacking) and a voting model, built from the tuned base models. The meta-learner was ultimately reported as achieving the highest R-squared among the tested configurations.
supporting_quote: training 40 different ML models ... and the 10 top‐performing models were selected prior to hyperparameter tuning
fine‐tuned using a five‐fold cross‐validation with three repeats
The highest R^2 was obtained through the meta‐learner ensemble method.

chunks.text: The primary observation source is the HYDRoSWOT hydroacoustic dataset, consisting of over 200,000 ADCP measurements at 10,081 USGS gauging locations. The study uses recorded depth, top-width, velocity, and discharge from each campaign. After filtering and AHG fit quality control, 4,229 sites were retained for modeling.
supporting_quote: This data set is composed of 200,000+ Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler (ADCP) measurements collected at 10,081 USGS stream gauging locations
we use the recorded depth, top‐width, velocity, and discharge for each campaign.
In total, 4,229 of the 6,226 initial sites were retained.

chunks.text: The hydrographic network framework is the National Hydrologic Geospatial Fabric (NHGF), derived from NHDPlusV2 with improved topology and connectivity. Predictors are aligned to this reference fabric using stream segment identifiers and aggregated upstream drainage areas. The approach supports reach-scale prediction across the continental United States network.
supporting_quote: The river network used in this study is the National Hydrologic Geospatial Fabric (NHGF; Bock et al., 2022)
Following the completion of model training ... for approximately 2.7 million river reaches across the CONUS.

chunks.text: Watershed and landscape predictors were sourced from EPA StreamCat and additional gridded products aggregated using climateR. StreamCat contributed 58 watershed-level predictors spanning dams, land use, climate, hydrology, and geology. Additional datasets included TerraClimate, POLARIS, NLDAS/GLDAS, USGS 3DEP, and MODIS-derived variables, yielding 31 more predictors.
supporting_quote: we collected a range of landscape characteristics ... using the EPA StreamCat data set
In total, we used 58 watershed‐level predictorsfrom this data set.
In total, we built 31 predictors from these sources.

chunks.text: Streamflow predictors were derived from the NOAA National Water Model v2.1 retrospective archive, including flow percentiles and flood exceedance probability discharges. The study generated 20%–0.1% annual exceedance probability discharges and percentile summaries (minimum, 25th, 50th, 75th, maximum). The authors emphasize these are synthetic flow statistics when compared with gauge records.
supporting_quote: Streamflow statistics were generated ... from the NWM v2.1 retrospective simulation
include 20%–0.1% annual exceedance probability discharge ... and the minimum, 25th, 50th, 75th, and maximum flow percentiles.
these are regarded as "synthetic flow percentiles" due to discrepancies with the gauge measurements.

chunks.text: On the held-out test set, the meta-learner achieved strong goodness of fit for both bankfull and in-channel geometry predictions. Reported log-transformed R-squared values were 0.80 (bankfull depth) and 0.77 (in-channel depth). For width, log-transformed R-squared values were 0.76 (bankfull top-width) and 0.66 (in-channel top-width).
supporting_quote: achieved log-transformed R^2 = 0.8 predicting bankfull depth (R^2 = 0.77 for in-channel conditions)
R^2 = 0.76 predicting bankfull top-width (R^2 = 0.66 for in-channel conditions)

chunks.text: Model errors vary with river size: the models tend to underpredict both width and depth for smaller rivers. The authors attribute this to the skewed nature of observations and to small-scale runoff generation processes not well represented by the predictor set. They also note less training data for large river systems in HYDRoSWOT, which can limit model learning for the upper tail.
supporting_quote: the models underpredict both top‐width and depth as channel top‐width and depth decrease (smaller rivers; scatter dots located on the right side of the 1:1 line
there is a shortage of data for large river systems (in HYDRoSWOT), resulting in less training data for the machine learning model

chunks.text: Discharge-related features dominated the learned relationships. SHAP analysis identified bankfull discharge and the first flood-frequency principal component (NWM Flood pc 0) as the most influential predictors. For width, influential variables included cumulative upstream flowline length (Arbolatesu), topographic wetness index (TWI), and actual evapotranspiration (AET), generally increasing predicted width.
supporting_quote: The most influential feature identified is bankfull discharge and the 0th flood frequency principal component (Figure 4; NWM Flood pc 0).
Focusing on top‐width ... the most pivotal variables are the cumulative lengths of all upstream flowlines (Arbolatesu), the topological wetness index (TWI), and actual evapotranspiration (AET).

chunks.text: Depth predictions were most sensitive to topographic and hydrologic controls beyond discharge. SHAP feature importance highlighted mean catchment elevation, channel slope, and the base flow index as influential variables alongside bankfull flow estimates. The paper contrasts this with width models, where drainage area, stream length measures, wetness, and precipitation-related variables were more prominent.
supporting_quote: Concerning the feature importance of the depth prediction ... mean catchment elevation, channel slope (Slope), and the base flow index.
it's evident that channel depth is influenced by topographical factors (elevation and slope), groundwater recharge (base flow index)

chunks.text: Model performance depends on predictor magnitude, revealing systematic skill patterns. Width model errors decrease as channel width (and related discharge/PC0 magnitude) increases, and a similar pattern is present for Arbolatesu. For depth, skill improves as slope decreases, declines at smaller bankfull discharge, and worsens at higher elevations; depth performance is highest in runoff-dominated regions compared to groundwater-dominated ones.
supporting_quote: showing that as channel top‐width increases, modeling errors decrease.
as the channel slope decreases, model GOF (R^2) increases.
Higher elevations ... also tend to negatively impact model GOF (R^2)

chunks.text: SHAP dependence plots suggest non-linear thresholds in how hydrologic and landscape variables influence predicted geometry. For top-width, an inflection occurs near TWI = 810, where high-discharge sites with TWI below this threshold reduce predicted width, while TWI above it increases width. For depth, an inflection near AET = 65 indicates lower AET corresponds to shallower channels and higher AET to deeper channels.
supporting_quote: there is an inflection point near TWI = 810.
values above TWI > 810 correspond to an increase in channel top‐width.
an inflection point of AET = 65 ... AET < 65 contribute to shallower channels

chunks.text: NWM and NWIS flood discharge estimates show moderate agreement for the 2-year (bankfull) condition and weaker agreement for the 1-year (in-channel) condition. The paper reports log-transformed R-squared of 0.61 for the 2-year flows and 0.24 for the 1-year flows. These diagnostics motivate including broader flood statistics as predictors to compensate for low-flow skill limitations.
supporting_quote: the 2‐year flows show nice agreement (log‐transformed R^2 = 0.61)
the 1‐year flows show less (log‐transformed R^2 = 0.24).

chunks.text: Across hydrologic landscape regions and physiographic provinces, the proposed ML approach generally improves R-squared compared to regional regression relations from Blackburn-Lynch et al. (2017). For depth, the paper reports improvement across all HLR and most physiographic provinces, with specific exceptions noted (Adirondack and Southern Rocky Mountains). For HLR 20, the ML depth model does not improve over Blackburn-Lynch, with reported R-squared values close between methods.
supporting_quote: Results showed that the proposed depth modelshows a significant improvement in R^2 across all HLR and physiographic provinces ... except for physiographic provinces 1 (Adirondack) and 23 (Southern Rocky Mountains).
in HLR 20 ... the ML model did not show improved GOF ... (R^2 ≅ 0.77 of our model vs. R^2 ≅ 0.8).

chunks.text: A key limitation is that training data come only from USGS gauging locations, which may not represent full reach geometry because measurements are often taken in confined, high-bank sections for operational reasons. The authors also caution that HYDRoSWOT lacks ADCP measurements in estuaries near river mouths, making accuracy unreliable in these areas. Anthropogenically altered systems (e.g., dams and levees) may also have unreliable estimates due to limited representation in training data.
supporting_quote: training data and its general applicability, which are constrained to USGS sites only.
in estuaries, particularly near the river mouth ... there are no recorded ADCP measurements in HYDRoSWOT, and model accuracy is unreliable.
unreliable estimates near anthropogenically altered river systems (e.g., dams, levees, artificial irrigation canals, and ponds).

chunks.text: Reliance on NWM-derived 100% annual exceedance probability discharge introduces sensitivity to NWM performance, especially at lower-flow conditions where NWM skill is weaker. The paper notes diminished agreement between NWM and observed records for 1-year flows and states that this impacts overall model goodness of fit. As a result, predictive skill decreases at smaller discharge magnitudes, which are common in small streams and tributaries.
supporting_quote: Another limitation stemsfrom the primary significant feature of ML models, or the 100% annual exceedance probability discharge derived from the NWM, where the NWM diminished skill
the 1‐year flows show less (log‐transformed R^2 = 0.24)
it is pertinent to acknowledge that the model's GOF diminishes with reduced discharge levels.

chunks.text: Predictions are reach-averaged and constrained to reach-scale resolution, which can omit fine-scale channel complexities such as braiding, incision, and aggradation. While reach-scale averaging can reduce computational burden and integrate with DEM-derived products, it may be inadequate for applications requiring sub-reach variability. Achieving finer resolution would require substantially more diverse measurements and additional remote-sensing support, especially for depth.
supporting_quote: its resolution is constrained to the reach scale.
it may lead to limitations such as overlooking intricate channel features like braiding, incision, and aggradation.
resolving depth accurately at resolutions lower than reach scale remains a challenge

chunks.text: The approach’s transferability beyond the United States is limited by dependence on comprehensive long-term NWM retrospective simulations, which are not globally available. The authors note that data size and availability constrain global scalability, though alternative global hydrologic models could be substituted with reduced accuracy. They also flag that ML deployment is more complex than a single regression relation, potentially complicating adaptation to new networks.
supporting_quote: Substantial data challenges associated with using existing NWM retrospective data ... currently make this data set globally unavailable
our model's applicability could be constrained in global regions where a comprehensive long‐term historic modeled record is unavailable.
The ML modeling method's applicability extends beyond a singular regression relation

chunks.text: Using predictors derived from different source datasets can introduce inconsistencies due to differing assumptions and biases. The paper provides an example that changing the DEM source (e.g., AW3D/PRISM versus SRTM) could yield different elevation representations and thus different model predictions. This highlights sensitivity to upstream data choice and the need to match data products to landscape/application context.
supporting_quote: building an ML model using predictors from different data sets can result in inconsistencies due to each product's unique assumptions and biases.
training an ML model on an optical‐based DEM like AW3D ... instead of the SRTM ... can lead to significant differences in predictions.

chunks.text: The study concludes that an ensemble meta-learner ML approach can predict bankfull and in-channel channel geometry with high goodness of fit while using a reduced set of predictors. Leveraging NWM v2.1 flow characteristics and hydrofabric-aligned landscape variables, the authors report strong log-transformed R-squared performance for both depth and width. They also emphasize that performance decreases at lower discharge, underscoring ongoing challenges in small rivers and tributaries.
supporting_quote: Our study showcases the efficacy of the current ensemble ML model in minimizing the necessary predictors
achieved log-transformed R^2 = 0.8 predicting bankfull depth ... and R^2 = 0.76 predicting bankfull top-width
it is pertinent to acknowledge that the model's GOF diminishes with reduced discharge levels.

chunks.text: The authors conclude that their reduced-predictor, collinearity-mitigated ensemble approach improves upon regional and global alternatives and can be operationalized on the CONUS hydrofabric. They reduced predictors from 116 to 15 while maintaining R-squared near 0.80, and then generated predictions for about 2.7 million reaches. This supports integration into evolving U.S. hydrologic data systems and modeling workflows reliant on channel geometry.
supporting_quote: This process helped reduce the number of model predictors from 116 to 15.
we identified a subset of 15 features while the R^2 value remained close to 0.80
predict channel width and depth ... for approximately 2.7 million river reaches across the CONUS.

chunks.text: Snow functions as a natural reservoir, storing water in cold months and releasing it as temperatures rise, which is critical for sustaining river flows and groundwater recharge during periods of high demand. Snowpack variability can therefore translate into downstream water-availability variability. Recent declines in snowpack across multiple regions are linked to greater drought risk and disruption of streamflow patterns. These changes motivate deeper study of how snow conditions propagate into hydrologic outcomes.
supporting_quote: Snow plays a crucial role in water resource management, acting as a natural reservoir
water is stored during the colder months and released gradually as temperature rises

chunks.text: Observed snowpack declines are widespread and expected to continue under warming, raising concerns for water resources in snow-dominated regions. Evidence indicates declines at the vast majority of monitoring sites in the western U.S., including a reported 23% decrease in April snowpack from 1955 to 2022. Such declines can worsen drought severity and affect sectors such as agriculture and ecosystems. This context frames the need for robust snow datasets and analysis linking snow to streamflow and drought.
supporting_quote: declines in snowpack have been observed at over 90% of snow monitoring sites across the western U.S.
a 23% decrease in April snowpack levels at 93% of monitored sites from 1955 to 2022

chunks.text: Snow droughts are defined by below-average snow water equivalent and are distinct from meteorological, hydrological, and agricultural droughts because they directly reflect snowpack deficits. Although snow drought occurrence is increasing, the pathway and timing by which snow drought conditions turn into downstream hydrologic drought remain less explored. Understanding this progression is essential for drought early warning and management in basins reliant on snowmelt.
supporting_quote: This observed snowpack decline indicates an emerging and critical challenge known as snow drought.
While the occurrence of snow droughts has been increasing, the progression from snow drought to hydrologic drought remains less explored.

chunks.text: The study aims to quantify snow–streamflow relationships in snow-dominated watersheds using machine learning and probabilistic analysis. It seeks to evaluate multiple SWE datasets to identify which best explains streamflow variability, and to determine the time window (lookback) when SWE most influences streamflow. In addition, it aims to characterize spatial differences across basins and to estimate the probability that hydrologic drought follows snow drought over different lag periods. These objectives support improving drought anticipation and water management.
supporting_quote: this study aims to address several key research objectives: (i) to identify the most reliable SWE dataset
(ii) to determine the optimal lookback period that captures the maximum influence of snow on streamflow

chunks.text: A central goal is to estimate conditional probabilities of drought propagation: the likelihood that a hydrologic drought occurs after a snow drought within specified lag periods. By computing this relationship across many snow-dominated basins, the study targets a probabilistic early warning signal. The approach is intended to clarify timing and improve preparedness actions before hydrologic drought manifests.
supporting_quote: our study investigates the conditional probability that a hydrologic drought follows a snow drought within various lag periods.
we calculated the conditional probability that a hydrologic drought follows a snow drought within specific lag periods.

chunks.text: Despite extensive work on historical low snowpacks and future anomalies, many analyses have not sufficiently connected snow droughts to downstream water availability and runoff impacts. This gap is especially problematic in basins where snowmelt is a dominant contributor to streamflow. The study positions its contribution as explicitly quantifying how snow drought conditions translate to hydrologic drought risk over time.
supporting_quote: a significant portion of this analysis has overlooked the connection between snow droughts and their effects on water availability
particularly where snow plays a crucial role in runoff

chunks.text: SWE estimation is uncertain across products due to differences in spatial/temporal resolution and methodological choices, complicating consistent assessment of snow impacts on streamflow. These dataset-dependent uncertainties create challenges when comparing basins or establishing reliable snow–runoff linkages. The study addresses this by using multiple SWE datasets and comparing their ability to explain streamflow via modeling.
supporting_quote: there are uncertainties associated with the measurement and modeling of snow water equivalent (SWE) across different datasets
Variability in spatial and temporal resolution, data assimilation techniques, and interpolation methods among datasets introduce challenges

chunks.text: Snow-dominated watersheds were identified using a watershed-level criterion based on persistent SWE presence. A watershed is classified as snow-dominated if, in 95% of years, SWE exceeds 30 mm for more than 3 months per year. This selection ensures basins consistently depend on seasonal snow storage and melt processes, enabling focused analysis of SWE–streamflow relationships.
supporting_quote: a watershed is defined as snow-dominated if, in 95% of the years in the SWE records, the SWE exceeds 30 mm for more than 3 months in a year.
grid cells with more than 30 mm of snow water equivalent (SWE) for more than 3 months

chunks.text: The study uses LSTM models to analyze how well streamflow can be predicted using SWE inputs, treating predictive skill as evidence of the SWE–streamflow relationship strength. Inputs consist of historical SWE sequences with varied lookback lengths, and the output is next-day streamflow. The model is tuned to capture delayed snowmelt effects on runoff, emphasizing interpretive understanding of snow influence rather than operational forecasting alone.
supporting_quote: we employed Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models.
input to the LSTM model is the historical SWE data, and the output is the streamflow values for the next day.

chunks.text: The LSTM architecture is multi-layered with two LSTM layers separated by dropout and followed by a dense output layer. Hyperparameters (units, dropout rates, learning rates) are optimized using KerasTuner to minimize validation MSE. This configuration aims to reduce overfitting while capturing temporal dependencies relevant to hydrologic memory in snow-dominated basins.
supporting_quote: This is followed by a dropout layer to mitigate overfitting
Using Keras Tune[r82], a range of values is explored for the number of LSTM units in both layers, dropout rates, and learning rates.

chunks.text: Data are split into training, validation, and testing subsets to evaluate generalization. The study uses 85% of the record for training and 15% for testing, and within training, 20% is reserved for validation. This setup supports both model selection during tuning and final performance assessment across basins.
supporting_quote: The dataset is divided into training, validation, and test sets, with 85% used for training and 15% for testing.
Within the training set, 20% is further segregated as a validation set

chunks.text: Model skill is quantified using multiple hydrologic performance metrics: MSE, NSE, and KGE. These metrics evaluate error magnitude, explained variance relative to mean behavior, and combined correlation/bias/variability components. Using several metrics supports robust comparison among SWE products and lookback windows.
supporting_quote: The model's performance is evaluated using metrics including MSE, Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) coefficient, and Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE).

chunks.text: For drought identification, the study constructs daily climatologies for SWE and streamflow and computes daily percentile ranks relative to those climatologies. A 5-day moving window is applied to smooth anomalies, creating 165 values per calendar day (5 days × 35 years). Drought is defined for both SWE and streamflow as values below the 30th percentile, enabling consistent event detection for snow and hydrologic drought.
supporting_quote: a 5-day moving window was applie[d83]
Drought conditions are determined based on the calculated percentiles. For both SWE and streamflow, a value falling below the 30th percentile indicates a drought condition

chunks.text: The probability that hydrologic drought follows snow drought is computed as a conditional probability over lag windows. For each basin and lag time T, the method divides the number of snow drought events that are followed by hydrologic drought within T days by the total number of snow drought events. This produces basin-specific and lag-specific drought-propagation probabilities for temporal and spatial analysis.
supporting_quote: The conditional probability Pconditional that a hydrologic drought follows a snow drought within a given lag period
P_{conditional} = \frac{\text{Number of Snow Droughts Followed by Hydrologic Droughts Within T Days}}{\text{Total Number of Snow Drought Events}}

chunks.text: Streamflow and basin attributes come from the CAMELS dataset, which provides daily forcing and hydrologic response data for 671 U.S. basins from 1980 to 2014. Daily streamflow is compiled from USGS stations. The study selects snow-dominated basins from CAMELS for analysis of how SWE relates to streamflow.
supporting_quote: The CAMELS dataset ... includes daily forcing data and hydrologic response data for 671 small-to-medium-sized basins ... from 1980 to 2014.
daily streamflow data were compiled from the United States Geological Survey

chunks.text: Daymet provides daily gridded meteorological variables, including SWE, at 1 km resolution across North America. It spans 1980 to 2022 for most of its coverage and is produced via interpolation and extrapolation of daily observations. This product is used as one of the SWE datasets compared for explaining streamflow.
supporting_quote: produce gridded estimates of weather conditions on a 1 km×1 km resolution.
Spanning from 1980 to 2022 ... including ... snow water equivalent (SWE)

chunks.text: The University of Arizona (UAZ) Daily 4 km SWE and snow depth product integrates in-situ SNOTEL and COOP measurements with PRISM modeled temperature and precipitation. It provides daily SWE at 4 km resolution for 1981 to 2022 (also summarized as 1981–2021 in the dataset table). The study relies on UAZ both as an SWE input to LSTM models and for constructing SWE climatologies in the drought-probability analysis.
supporting_quote: Daily 4 km Gridded SWE and Snow Depth dataset ... covering the period from 1981 to 2022.
it integrates in-situ snow measurements from the SNOTEL and COOP networks ... with PRISM's modeled temperature and precipitation data.

chunks.text: SNODAS is a NOAA product providing daily snowpack properties such as SWE and snow depth at 1 km resolution across the United States. It uses data assimilation and has temporal coverage from September 28, 2003, to the present. SNODAS is included as an additional SWE product for comparison against UAZ and Daymet in the SWE–streamflow modeling.
supporting_quote: The SNODAS dataset ... updated daily ... temporal coverage from September 28, 2003, to the present, with a high spatial resolution of 1 km.
It encapsulates ... parameters such as depth, SWE

chunks.text: A dataset summary table specifies key resolutions and coverage used in the study, including CAMELS (daily, basin-scale, 1980–2014), Daymet (daily, 1 km, 1980–Present), and UAZ (daily, 4 km, 1981–2021). The table also lists GLDAS (daily, 0.25°, 2003–2023) as a referenced dataset summary item. These characteristics frame the multi-product SWE comparison and basin-scale streamflow modeling.
supporting_quote: Table 1. Summary of datasets used in this study.
University of Arizona (UAZ) | Daily | 4 km | U.S. | 1981–2021

chunks.text: Using the snow-dominance criterion, the study identifies 68 snow-dominated watersheds within the CAMELS basins across the contiguous United States. These basins are concentrated in western mountain regions (Sierra Nevada, Rocky Mountains, Cascades), with a smaller number in the northeastern U.S. This basin set forms the basis for subsequent SWE–streamflow modeling and drought-progression analysis.
supporting_quote: a total of 68 snow-dominated watersheds were identified across the contiguous United States
These watersheds are predominantly located in the western regions, including the Sierra Nevada, Rocky Mountains, and Cascade Range

chunks.text: Across three SWE products (UAZ, Daymet, SNODAS), UAZ produces the strongest streamflow prediction performance in LSTM models. Statistical testing indicates UAZ significantly outperforms Daymet and SNODAS (p < 0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test). Median KGE is 0.671 for UAZ versus 0.459 for Daymet and 0.345 for SNODAS, with UAZ showing 46.10% and 94.40% improvements over Daymet and SNODAS respectively.
supporting_quote: UAZ dataset consistently outperformed the other datasets
UAZ dataset significantly outperforms both Daymet and SNODAS (p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).

chunks.text: The analysis of lookback windows shows that model performance improves as lookback increases up to about 60 days, with limited additional gains beyond that. This suggests the characteristic snow-to-streamflow memory for these basins is roughly two months. The study interprets this as reflecting typical lag between snow accumulation and snowmelt contributions to streamflow, after which other hydrologic factors become more influential.
supporting_quote: performance of the models generally increased as the lookback extended up to 60 days
the optimal lookback ... is around 60 days

chunks.text: Seasonal evaluation indicates the SWE–streamflow relationship is strongest during spring and summer, when snowmelt drives runoff. Highest KGE values occur for lookbacks around 60–90 days in spring and summer, while winter and fall show lower and sometimes negative KGE at shorter lookbacks. The study recommends 60–90 days for targeted summer modeling, while 60 days is a strong year-round compromise.
supporting_quote: spring and summer seasons generally exhibit higher KGE values, particularly for lookbacks between 60 and 90 days.
For targeted summer modeling, a slightly longer lookback period (60–90 days) is recommended

chunks.text: Spatial performance mapping using the UAZ dataset shows strong model performance in many western U.S. basins. Most basins achieve KGE and NSE above 0.6, indicating SWE alone can explain a substantial portion of streamflow variability at seasonal scale in snow-dominated regions. The spatial patterns underscore that snow–streamflow linkages are particularly robust in the western United States.
supporting_quote: particularly in the western United States, where snow-dominated basins are more prevalent.
Most basins achieved KGE and NSE values above 0.6

chunks.text: The drought-progression analysis finds that hydrologic drought probability following snow drought is low for short lags and increases markedly for longer lags. Across basins, probabilities are relatively low at 7–14 days and increase substantially by 30–60 days, aligning with snowmelt timing. The box-plot summary reports a median probability rising from about 0.2 at 7 days to 0.95 at 180 days, with the largest increase between 30 and 90 days.
supporting_quote: For shorter lookback periods (7–14 days), most basins show relatively low probabilities
The median probability increases substantially from approximately 0.2 at 7 days to 0.95 at 180 days

chunks.text: Probability density analysis divides drought propagation into four phases with increasing mean probability over time. Early phase (0–14 days) has mean 0.32; medium (14–30 days) mean 0.36; transition (30–60 days) mean 0.53; late (60–90 days) mean 0.52 with wider spread. The transition phase shows the sharpest increase and is identified as a critical window when snow drought effects on hydrologic drought become most pronounced.
supporting_quote: Early Phase (0–14 days): ... mean probability of 0.32
Transition Phase (30–60 days): ... mean probability of 0.53

chunks.text: Sensitivity testing across seven drought thresholds (10th–40th percentiles) shows the temporal progression pattern is consistent even when absolute probabilities shift. Stricter thresholds yield lower probabilities (e.g., 0.26–0.32 at 14 days, 0.82–0.90 at 180 days), while more lenient thresholds yield higher probabilities (0.35–0.36 at 14 days, 0.93–0.94 at 180 days). Sensitivity decreases with longer lags, with coefficient of variation dropping from about 9.9% at 14 days to about 4.4% at 180 days.
supporting_quote: sensitivity analysis using seven different percentile thresholds ranging from the 10th to 40th percentile.
coefficient of variation across thresholds is highest at the 14-day period (~10%) ... reaching only~4% at 180 days

chunks.text: The study acknowledges uncertainties in remote sensing and reanalysis datasets used for SWE, which can influence drought characterization and modeled relationships. Performance variability across basins suggests that topography, land cover, and human interventions can alter SWE–streamflow dynamics. Because the modeling intentionally uses only SWE to quantify its standalone influence, it may not capture processes driven by other variables in some regions. These limitations motivate expanded datasets and multi-variable frameworks.
supporting_quote: Our analysis relied on remote sensing and reanalysis datasets, which contain uncertainties that could influence drought characterization.
Our LSTM modeling framework intentionally focused exclusively on SWE

chunks.text: The authors note the approach may not fully capture rapid snowmelt events caused by rain-on-snow, which could accelerate hydrologic responses beyond typical lag structures. They suggest future work incorporating more ground-based measurements (e.g., SNOTEL) and separating regulated from unregulated basins to quantify reservoir effects on drought progression. More comprehensive modeling that maintains interpretability while adding influential factors is proposed as a next step.
supporting_quote: it may not fully account for rapid snowmelt events triggered by rain-on-snow occurrences.
Future research may address these aspects by incorporating additional ground-based measurements from SNOTEL sites, separating regulated and unregulated basins

chunks.text: The study concludes that the UAZ SWE product is the most reliable among the tested datasets for relating SWE to streamflow in snow-dominated watersheds. It identifies an optimal SWE lookback of 60–90 days, with stronger relationships in spring and summer. Spatially, western U.S. basins show high model skill, and probabilistic analysis indicates snow drought provides an early warning for hydrologic drought with increasing likelihood over 60–90 days. These findings support improved drought anticipation and management in snow-dependent regions.
supporting_quote: The UAZ dataset consistently outperformed other SWE products (Daymet and SNODAS)
the optimal lookback period for SWE influence on streamflow is 60–90 days

chunks.text: The probabilistic assessment supports a systematic progression from snow drought to hydrologic drought, with probabilities rising from about 0.3 in early phases (0–14 days) to over 0.8 in later phases (60–90 days). This establishes snow drought conditions as a practical early warning indicator and suggests a preparedness lead time on the order of weeks to months. The conclusion emphasizes integrating these insights into drought early warning and proactive water management.
supporting_quote: Probabilistic analysis demonstrated a systematic progression from snow drought to hydrologic drought, with probabilities increasing from approximately 0.3 in early phases (0–14 days) to over 0.8 in later phases (60–90 days).
snow drought conditions can serve as an effective early warning indicator for impending hydrologic drought.

chunks.text: The National Water Model (NWM) is NOAA’s operational hydrologic forecasting system built on WRF-Hydro, producing hourly streamflow forecasts and other hydrologic states over the contiguous United States. It routes flows across a digitized national river network and uses gridded meteorological forcing. NWM has been updated multiple times, and performance improvements have been reported up through version 2.1, but many evaluations have focused on larger rivers rather than headwaters.
supporting_quote: The NWM is an operational hydrological forecasting system built upon the Weather Research and Forecasting Model Hydrological modeling system, WRF-Hydro (Gochis et al. 2020), which provides hourly streamflow forecasts ... at over 2.7 million river reaches across the contiguous United States.
Over the years, the NWM has been updated several times, from its initial version 1.0 in 2016 to the most recent version 3.0 in late 2023.
Additional assessments of versions 2.0 and 2.1 ... have primarily focused on large river networks.

chunks.text: Montane low-order streams are critical to river network function and hazards, representing much of total channel length and contributing substantially to drainage area. These headwaters respond rapidly to precipitation and snowmelt due to steep topography and elevation gradients in precipitation. Despite their importance for water quality and flood generation, they are often underrepresented in streamgaging networks and are challenging for prediction due to complex terrain and limited instrumentation.
supporting_quote: Low-order streams may account for as much as 70%–80% of the entire channel length of a river network (Wohl 2017) and drain 70%–80% of the total catchment area.
montane catchments exhibit steep gradients in precipitation with elevation and are characterized by rapid and dynamic responses to precipitation and snowmelt
headwater streams draining these montane catchments are not often represented in the streamgaging network and hydrological modeling

chunks.text: Machine learning post-processing is increasingly used in hydrology to capture nonlinear relationships and improve forecasts, including for NWM/WRF-Hydro outputs. Prior studies have shown that neural-network post-processing can substantially improve streamflow skill relative to physics-based simulations. Separate lines of work indicate that adding local stage (water level) sensor data can improve site-scale water level/streamflow prediction when coupled with NWM forecasts.
supporting_quote: Several studies have explored the use of ML to enhance the NWM and other applications of the WRF-Hydro model
Frame et al. (2021) developed three long short-term memory (LSTM) post-processing models ... The results indicated substantial improvements in model skill relative to NWM reanalysis version 2.0
distributed low-cost in-stream water level (gage height) sensors could substantially improve the forecast of streamflow and water levels on a local scale when coupled with current NWM flow forecasts

chunks.text: The study aimed to evaluate NWM performance in montane, low-order stream catchments across the northeastern United States using retrospective simulations compared to observations. It also sought to examine how performance varies across space, time, and flow regimes, including high-flow events. The evaluation was designed to identify systematic deficiencies that matter for flood warning and local decision-making in headwater basins.
supporting_quote: Our study sought to evaluate NWM performance in montane low-order stream catchments in the northeastern US.
The study goals were to quantitatively examine model performance across temporal and spatial scales as well as flow regimes

chunks.text: A central goal was to develop a machine-learning post-processing correction for NWM streamflow at selected Vermont basins using LightGBM. The approach intentionally differs from conventional bias correction and emphasizes interpretability and low computation compared with deep learning. The correction is framed as a practical pathway to improve hourly predictions in complex, under-gauged montane watersheds.
supporting_quote: subsequently, we developed a ML post-processing correction model for the NWM.

Our ML correction model uses ... a Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) learning algorithm that offers advantages such as interpretability and low computation requirements compared to deep learning approaches.
presenting a widely applicable, computationally efficient alternative for improving the accuracy of hourly streamflow predictions

chunks.text: The authors specifically investigated whether antecedent water level (gage height) observations can improve the ML correction model, including when water levels come from distant gages rather than the basin of interest. This tests the idea that low-cost supplemental sensors, or sharing stage data across basins, could meaningfully enhance NWM-derived predictions. The study aims to quantify the value of local versus remote antecedent water-level inputs.
supporting_quote: we investigate the potential of incorporating distant antecedent water level observations from within or outside the catchment of interest into our ML correction model
Including antecedent water level measurements as input, even from distant sites, greatly improved model performance

chunks.text: Montane headwater streams are systematically underrepresented in the national streamgaging and operational forecast network, leaving communities with limited local information during hazardous events. River Forecast Center products are typically issued at select streamgages on higher-order rivers, not along steep headwater reaches that can generate flash floods. This creates a gap between national-scale coverage and actionable local-scale flood intelligence.
supporting_quote: headwater streams draining these montane catchments are not often represented in the streamgaging network
NWS River Forecast Centers provide forecasts at select streamgages, often located on higher order rivers, resulting in little information for local communities living in montane settings
Flash flooding along high-gradient headwater streams can contribute to extensive erosion damage

chunks.text: NWM performance in montane, snow-affected catchments has not been comprehensively assessed, despite the model’s reach-scale coverage. Low-order montane streams pose prediction challenges due to complex topography, variable rainfall-runoff patterns, and limited gaging infrastructure. Without focused evaluation, users may not understand seasonal weaknesses and event-scale errors in headwater basins.
supporting_quote: yet a focused assessment of its performance in these settings has not been comprehensively undertaken.
present challenges for streamflow prediction due to complex topography, highly variable rainfall-runoff patterns, and limited gaging infrastructure

chunks.text: The retrospective NWM shows seasonal deficiencies, with especially poor skill during snowmelt/spring runoff and high-flow events, and a tendency to underestimate flow. These errors are particularly consequential for flood response because they affect peak magnitude, timing, and event volume. Improving these deficiencies requires approaches that can leverage observations without redesigning the entire physics model.
supporting_quote: particularly poor performance during snowmelt, spring runoff, and high flow events, with a tendency towards flow underestimation.
we further evaluated the NWM at an event scale ... focusing on extreme streamflow events exceeding the 97th percentile

chunks.text: The study evaluated NWM v2.1 CONUS retrospective simulations (Feb 1979–Dec 2020) against observed hourly streamflow at 19 montane catchments. Performance was assessed at hourly resolution and also summarized by month and season to diagnose temporal patterns. Only months with at least 80% complete observations were included to ensure robust comparisons.
supporting_quote: we used the retrospective simulation of the NWM (version 2.1) ... covering the period from February 1979 to December 2020
To evaluate NWM performance ... we conducted an assessment over the period of available hourly observed streamflow records.
Only months with at least 80% complete streamflow observation records were included in the analysis.

chunks.text: Model skill for streamflow was quantified using Pearson correlation, percent bias (PBias), Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), and Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE). Acceptable-performance thresholds were drawn from prior literature and used as interpretive guidance rather than strict pass/fail. Additional diagnostics included percent mean squared error (%MSE) decomposed by season and quartiles to emphasize flow-regime sensitivity.
supporting_quote: This analysis employed the Pearson correlation (Cor), percent bias (PBias), Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) and Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE)
Additionally, we conducted monthly and seasonal assessments
we used the percent mean squared error (%MSE) decomposed by season and quartiles based on Hodson et al. (2021)

chunks.text: Because USGS gages may not coincide with NHD reach endpoints, modeled and observed flows were normalized by drainage area before comparison. A special adjustment was applied where two Sleepers River gages (SR-W9 and SR-W3) share a single NHD reach, scaling flow by drainage-area proportion. This ensured consistent spatial matching between NWM reach outputs and gage observations.
supporting_quote: streamgages do not necessarily fall on an NHD reach end point. In these cases, both the predicted and observed streamflows were normalized by dividing them by the upstream drainage area
The NWM provides the same streamflow value for the SR-W9 and SR-W3 basins because these two gages are located on a single reach
Simulated streamflow at the high resolution of SR-W9 was estimated based on the proportion of its drainage area relative to SR-W3.

chunks.text: To diagnose possible forcing-data contributions to streamflow errors, the authors compared NWM-simulated precipitation and snow depth against observations at subsets of sites. Hourly precipitation and 3-hourly snow depth from 1 km grids were extracted at gage locations and converted to daily totals/means for comparison. For basins lacking in-catchment observations, the nearest station was used, again requiring at least 80% complete months.
supporting_quote: we compared and assessed ... daily precipitation and snow depth observations with their simulated counterparts at a subset of 11 sites for precipitation and 13 sites for snow depth
Daily estimated values were computed by summing the hourly precipitation estimates and averaging the 3-h snow depth estimates over each day.
For sites where observed values are not available within the catchment, the observed values were estimated from the available station nearest to the catchment of interest

chunks.text: Event-scale evaluation focused on five Vermont basins and extreme events above the 97th percentile of observed hourly flows. Events were identified with the hydroEvents R package using a local maxima method, requiring peaks to be at least five times neighboring trough flows and at least 12 hours apart. Event metrics included peak magnitude error, peak timing error, and percent volume error.
supporting_quote: focusing on extreme streamflow events exceeding the 97th percentile based on all observed hourly flows.
The hydroEvents R package ... and the local maxima method were used to identify these events.
An "event" was defined as having a peak flow at least five times greater than flow in the neighboring troughs, and a minimum spacing of 12h is observed between peaks.

chunks.text: A post-processing correction model was built for the five Vermont sites using LightGBM, a gradient-boosted decision tree framework designed for efficiency. Two configurations were trained: LightGBM using meteorological and NWM features, and LightGBM_WL which additionally uses antecedent water level (gage height) lags at 4, 6, and 8 hours. Feature engineering created window averages and lags up to 24 hours, with selection guided by LightGBM split-based importance and iterative removal.
supporting_quote: we developed a postprocessing correction model for the five sites in Vermont using a LightGBM model.
LightGBM_WL includes antecedent water level (gage height) values at 4, 6, and 8 h prior to the predicted streamflow
These features include average values for periods up to 24h and antecedent (i.e., lagged) values
feature importance, determined using the "split" importance type in LightGBM

chunks.text: Hyperparameters (n_estimators, num_leaves, min_data_in_leaf, max_depth) were optimized with cross-validation and Optuna using CMA-ES. Training spanned from the earliest observed streamflow date through 2015, with 2016–2020 used for testing (WB trained through 2017 due to limited data). Model evaluation used the same streamflow metrics as the raw NWM assessment, and gap-filled streamflow was not used in evaluation.
supporting_quote: The hyperparameters n_estimators ... num_leaves ... min_data_in_leaf ... and max_depth ... were optimized using cross-validation and the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy ... implemented in the Optuna package
2016–2020 designated for testing at all sites except for the WB basin ... training ... extended until 2017
no gap-filled streamflow observed data was used in the evaluation

chunks.text: To test applicability in data-scarce settings, additional experiments replaced local water-level inputs with antecedent water levels from remote USGS gages up to 80 km away. These experiments used the LightGBM_WL configuration and applied the same remote-water-level choice to both training and testing. Remote gages were selected by proximity and data availability, including sites inside and outside the basin’s HUC8.
supporting_quote: incorporating distant antecedent water level observations ... replacing the antecedent water level at each of the five sites of interest with antecedent water level values lagging 4, 6, and 8h from each of a series of remote (up to 80km distant) USGS streamgage locations
for both training and testing.
Sites inside the same hydrologic unit (HUC8) as the site of interest are shown as orange dots

chunks.text: The study analyzed 19 unregulated montane forested catchments across the northeastern United States, spanning stream orders 1 to 3 and drainage areas from 0.41 to 191 km². Most sites had more than 10 years of streamflow records; Wade Brook had 7 years through 2020. Five Vermont catchments (Sleepers River W5/W3/W9, Ranch Brook, Wade Brook) were chosen for the ML correction model development.
supporting_quote: The study area encompasses 19 catchments across the northeastern US
upstream drainage areas ranging from 0.41 to 191km2 and stream order from 1 to 3
except for Wade Brook, which has 7 years of streamflow gaging record up through calendar year 2020.
Sleepers River (W5, W3, and W9), Ranch Brook, and Wade Brook ... were selected as test cases for the development of the ML correction models.

chunks.text: NWM inputs/outputs came from the NOAA NWM CONUS Retrospective Dataset for version 2.1, which uses AORC forcing and does not assimilate USGS streamflow observations. The retrospective provides meteorological variables and hydrologic outputs on a national grid/reach network, enabling long-term comparison with gage data. Streamflow estimates were extracted from Zarr archives hosted on AWS.
supporting_quote: NOAA NWM CONUS Retrospective Dataset ... utilizing forcing data ... from the OWP Analysis of Record for Calibration (AORC; Fall et al. 2023) and does not assimilate USGS streamflow observations.
NWM streamflow estimations were extracted from the NOAA NWM CONUS Retrospective Dataset, stored in Zarr format on the Amazon Web Service cloud platform

chunks.text: Observed data included long-term USGS streamflow and water level, daily precipitation from GHCNd, and snow depth from NYS Mesonet, CoCoRaHS, and GHCNd. Wade Brook streamflow records were provided by the authors’ University of Vermont team. A long snow-depth record at Ranch Brook has been monitored daily since 1951 by the National Weather Service near the summit area.
supporting_quote: Data sourced for each site included long-term streamflow and water level records provided by the U.S. Geological Survey
precipitation from the Global Historical Climatology Network Daily (GHCNd) database
snow depth sourced from the NYS Mesonet network ... Community Collaborative Rain, Hail & Snow Network (CoCoRaHS) and GHCNd databases.
Records at Wade Brook were provided by our research team at the University of Vermont (UVM).
Snow depth at Ranch Brook ... has been monitored daily since 1951 by the National Weather Service

chunks.text: The ML feature set combined NWM simulated basin precipitation and NWM streamflow with observed meteorology and in-stream water level. Daily observed predictors included precipitation, snow depth, SWE, and max/min temperature, while hourly observed inputs included gage height. The target variable for ML training was observed hourly streamflow at Vermont sites.
supporting_quote: The hourly simulated values correspond to the mean precipitation over the basin estimated by the NWM (AORC) and NWM retrospective streamflow
hourly observed data correspond to water level (gage height)
Daily observed data include precipitation, snow depth, snow water equivalent (SWE), maximum temperature, and minimum temperature
Observed hourly streamflow values ... served as the target variable.

chunks.text: SWE inputs were constructed by relating snow depth to SWE using observations from a UVM snow station near the Mt. Mansfield summit. This produced a linear relation used to estimate historical SWE for model inputs. Because daily snow data were limited in the region, the same compiled snow depth and SWE time series were used across the Vermont sites.
supporting_quote: SWE observations from a snow station operated by UVM near the Mt. Mansfield summit were used to develop a linear relation between snow depth and SWE, enabling the estimation of historical SWE values
the same compiled snow depth and SWE values were used to develop the input features at each study site, as these are the only available daily data in the study area.

chunks.text: The compiled ML dataset contained missing records across variables, with streamflow missingness ranging from 8% to 33% and precipitation missingness from 3% to 76%. Missing data shorter than 30 consecutive days were filled using seasonal decomposition and interpolation, and streamflow gaps were filled by correlation with the closest streamgage station. The authors note limitations of linear interpolation for precipitation but used it due to insufficient overlap for regression approaches.
supporting_quote: missing records, with percentages ranging from 8% to 33% for streamflow, 3% to 76% for precipitation
Missing data (not greater than or equal to 30days of continuous missing records) were filled using seasonal decomposition ... and linear interpolation
linear interpolation of precipitation ... is not ideal as it can introduce uncertainties in the water budget.

chunks.text: Across the 19 montane catchments, NWM v2.1 retrospective streamflow exhibited a consistently negative bias relative to hourly observations. Many sites failed commonly used performance thresholds, particularly for NSE and KGE. Better performance tended to cluster in some southern/western mountain regions, while poorer performance occurred in parts of the Adirondack, White, and especially Green Mountains.
supporting_quote: At our study sites, the NWM had a consistently negative streamflow bias relative to hourly observations
performance metric values under the thresholds ... at 8 out of the 19 sites for PBias ... 10 sites for KGE, and 13 sites for NSE.
