NWM performance generally decreased in the eastern Adirondacks, White Mountains ... and northern Green Mountains, with notably poorer performance at RB and WB sites.

chunks.text: Monthly and seasonal analysis showed that NWM bias is lowest in fall and becomes most negative in spring. The paper reports median seasonal PBias values of −2.72% in fall, −22.68% in winter, −31.77% in spring, and −18.95% in summer. Underestimation is most pronounced during snowmelt and spring runoff, consistent with the model’s difficulty during the ablation period.
supporting_quote: This seasonal pattern shows notably lower bias ... in the fall with a median PBias of −2.72%, increasing to more negative values in winter (−22.68%), peaking in the spring (−31.77%), and slightly decreasing in the summer (−18.95%; Figure 4, panel e).
NWM performance varied seasonally, with the best performance during the fall and particularly poor performance during snowmelt, spring runoff, and high flow events

chunks.text: Error decomposition indicated that spring contributes the largest share of mean squared error, and the model performs worst during high-flow conditions. This pattern is consistent with spring being a period of higher runoff volumes at many sites. The findings reinforce that event-relevant errors are not evenly distributed across the hydrograph but concentrated in high-flow regimes.
supporting_quote: The overall analysis ... shows that spring contributes the most to the %MSE, followed by fall, summer, and finally, winter.
Notably, when %MSE is further analyzed using empirical quartiles, the model performs worst during high-flow conditions.

chunks.text: Forcing-data comparisons suggested that precipitation estimates are generally reasonable at monthly scales, with median correlations above 0.5 and modest bias within ±25%. In contrast, NWM snow depth dynamics are poorly captured during ablation, trending toward underestimation and producing an average underestimation of peak snow depth by about 22%. Streamflow underestimation from March to June (and later at some sites) coincides with this snow-related bias despite generally adequate precipitation patterns.
supporting_quote: monthly estimated precipitation generally follows the pattern of observed precipitation, exhibiting median correlations above 0.5 ... and modest bias within ±25%.
NWM fails to capture observed snow depth dynamics.
This results in an underestimation of peak snow depth by approximately 22% on average.
A similar pattern to snow depth is observed in the streamflow estimates with a notable underestimation of observed streamflow from March to June

chunks.text: Event-scale evaluation (97th percentile threshold) at five Vermont sites showed mostly negative peak magnitude and volume errors, indicating underprediction of flood peaks and runoff volumes. RB and WB showed large peak timing delays, with median delays of 7 hours and 4 hours, and wide uncertainty ranges. Errors tended to increase downstream in the nested Sleepers River basins.
supporting_quote: For the event-based analysis focused on high streamflows, median peak streamflow magnitude (Qpe) and runoff volume errors (PVe) are mostly negative across all sites, except for SR-W9
RB and WB consistently exhibit very large delays in peak time estimation with median values of 7 and 4 h, respectively
In the nested Sleepers River basins, the model errors ... were lower upstream and increased in the downstream direction.

chunks.text: When events were classified, snowmelt-driven events showed larger underestimation of peak magnitude than rain-driven events. Volume error percentages were similar across event types, but snowmelt-driven events had greater variability and higher volume-error percentages. Peak timing error distributions were broadly comparable between rain-driven and snowmelt-driven events.
supporting_quote: Events were classified as rain-driven or snowmelt-driven if rainfall occurred on top of at least 50 cm of observed snowpack
snowmelt-driven events tend to exhibit larger underestimations of peak magnitude compared to rain-driven events.
While both types of events show similar volume error percentages, snowmelt-driven events display greater variability with higher percentages of volume error.
In terms of peak timing error, both event types show comparable distributions.

chunks.text: ML post-processing substantially improved hourly streamflow skill at the five Vermont sites during the test period. Averaged across sites, PBias improved by about 61% relative to NWM, with LightGBM reducing PBias to −23% and LightGBM_WL to −11%. Correlation increased from 0.43 (NWM) to 0.81 (LightGBM) and 0.89 (LightGBM_WL), while NSE increased from about −0.01 to 0.58 and 0.70, respectively.
supporting_quote: On average, both LightGBM and LightGBM_WL improved upon the NWM's Pbias (−61%), reducing it to −23% and −11% respectively.
Correlation increased from 0.43 to 0.81 with LightGBM and to 0.89 with LightGBM_WL.
KGE improved from −0.06 to 0.52 with LightGBM and to 0.72 with LightGBM_WL, while NSE improved from −0.01 to 0.58 and to 0.70, respectively.

chunks.text: Site-level metrics show that LightGBM_WL often yields strong improvements over both NWM and LightGBM, especially for Sleepers River sites. For example, at SR-W9, NSE improved from −0.02 (NWM) to 0.63 (LightGBM) and 0.84 (LightGBM_WL), and PBias improved from −56.14 to −25.65 and −5.12. Similar large gains occurred at SR-W3 and SR-W5, demonstrating added value from including antecedent water level lags.
supporting_quote: SR-W9 | NWM—v2.1 ... NSE −0.02 ... LightGBM ... NSE 0.63 ... LightGBM WL ... NSE 0.84
SR-W9 | NWM—v2.1 ... PBias −56.14 ... LightGBM ... PBias −25.65 ... LightGBM WL ... PBias −5.12
Overall, performance exhibits a substantial improvement in correlation, NSE, and KGE when antecedent water level observations (4, 6, and 8 h) are included.

chunks.text: At event scale, the correction models reduced flood-relevant errors in peak magnitude, timing, and volume. Relative to NWM, LightGBM reduced peak magnitude error by about 41%, improved peak timing by about 3 hours, and reduced volume error by about 55%. LightGBM_WL performed even better, reducing peak magnitude error by about 63%, peak timing error by about 1 hour, and volume error by about 74%.
supporting_quote: Peak flow magnitude error, peak timing error, and runoff volume error decrease on average across all sites by approximately 41%, 3 h, and 55%, respectively, using the LightGBM configuration
and by 63%, 1 h, and 74% with the LightGBM_WL configuration.

chunks.text: Feature-importance analysis indicated that, without water level, the most important predictors were observed daily temperature (max/min), precipitation, and snow depth, followed by NWM precipitation/streamflow window averages. With water level included, the 4-hour antecedent water level (WL_lag_4h) dominated importance, followed by antecedent simulated precipitation over an 8-hour window and current NWM simulated precipitation and streamflow. This highlights the strong predictive value of high-frequency stage information for hourly streamflow correction.
supporting_quote: For the LightGBM model configuration, the most important features are the observed maximum and minimum daily air temperature, precipitation, and snow depth
For the LightGBM_WL model configuration, water level values in the previous 4h are the most important feature

chunks.text: The authors argue that the pronounced spring underestimation in NWM streamflow is likely driven by underestimation of snow depth and hence SWE during the ablation period. This is the time when spring rains, snowmelt, and saturated soils can synchronize to generate large runoff volumes and floods. Even where daily precipitation estimates are acceptable, snow-related biases can propagate into streamflow underprediction during critical months.
supporting_quote: much of the most pronounced underestimation that is evident in spring at all sites is driven by the general underestimation in snow depth and consequently SWE.
Much of the annual streamflow and flooding events of concern occur during this time frame when spring rains and snowmelt are synchronous, and soils are typically saturated

chunks.text: Beyond snow biases, the paper notes that streamflow errors may also stem from hydrologic-process representation issues in the model, such as subsurface/groundwater processes or atmospheric fluxes like evapotranspiration and sublimation. Elevation mismatches between modeled grid cells and station locations could influence precipitation and snow estimates. The authors emphasize that the negative bias is likely multifaceted rather than attributable to a single factor.
supporting_quote: poor performance in streamflow prediction could stem from inconsistencies in the hydrological model, such as the representation of subsurface or groundwater flow processes, and/or the representation of fluxes into the atmosphere like evapotranspiration/sublimation
The differences found between model and actual elevations at the snow-depth station locations might influence the biases found in snow depth and precipitation.
the reasons behind the general negative bias could be multifaceted

chunks.text: ML performance depended on data availability and record length; the WB basin, with much shorter training data, showed poorer correction performance. The authors highlight that longer records support better ML correction, and that limited overlap among precipitation stations constrained more rigorous gap-filling methods. This underscores a limitation for applying the approach in very short-record basins.
supporting_quote: Poorer performance in the WB basin, which had a much shorter training dataset (4 vs. ~25years at the other sites), underscores the value of long-term records
Linear regression with nearby stations was explored as an alternative, but insufficient overlapping data prevented its use.

chunks.text: The data-preprocessing strategy for missing values is a practical compromise that can introduce uncertainty, especially for precipitation. The paper notes that linear interpolation of precipitation across extended periods is not ideal because it may distort the water budget. These uncertainties can propagate into ML features and affect correction-model training and evaluation.
supporting_quote: linear interpolation of precipitation, particularly over extended periods, is not ideal as it can introduce uncertainties in the water budget.

chunks.text: Operational use of water-level-informed ML corrections may be challenged by maintaining reliable real-time stage measurements. The authors note potential issues such as sensor drift, backwater effects, and impacts of ice cover or sediment deposition, plus data transmission challenges in montane settings. While water-level sensors are cheaper than full discharge gaging, they still require maintenance and robust infrastructure.
supporting_quote: maintaining reliable real-time water level data ... still requires periodic field and data infrastructure maintenance and reliable data transmission can be a challenge in montane settings.
water level (gage height) data ... can be compromised by inaccuracies caused by sensor drift, backwater effects, and the impacts of ice cover or sediment deposition

chunks.text: Across 19 montane catchments, NWM streamflow performance was strongly seasonal, with the lowest bias in fall and the greatest underestimation during spring, particularly in northeastern mountain regions such as the Adirondack, White, and Green Mountains. The authors link these deficiencies primarily to underestimation of snow depth/SWE during the ablation period, which affects spring runoff and flood-relevant flows. Event-scale analyses showed substantial errors in peak magnitude, timing, and volume, reinforcing the need for improvements for operational usefulness in headwaters.
supporting_quote: The results revealed a seasonally variable performance, with the NWM generally underestimating observed streamflow.
lower bias was observed in the fall ... peaking in the spring with substantial underestimation
This pattern of performance appears to be primarily driven by the negative bias in snow depth estimation and, consequently, snow water equivalent during the spring runoff

chunks.text: LightGBM post-processing correction models markedly improved NWM hourly streamflow predictions at the Vermont test basins, including during high-flow events. Adding antecedent water level (gage height) lags (LightGBM_WL) produced the largest gains in correlation, NSE, and KGE and reduced event-scale peak and volume errors. The work demonstrates a computationally efficient, interpretable pathway to improve reach-scale forecasts in complex montane watersheds.
supporting_quote: These ML correction models markedly improved NWM streamflow simulation skill relative to observations.
The inclusion of antecedent water level (gage height) values at 4, 6, and 8h for LightGBM_WL
Peak flow magnitude error, peak timing error, and runoff volume error decrease ... by 63%, 1 h, and 74% with the LightGBM_WL configuration.

chunks.text: Including antecedent water level observations, even from distant gages, can substantially improve corrected streamflow skill, highlighting the potential value of deploying low-cost stage sensors and sharing data across basins. The authors propose that this approach could be implemented to post-process NWM forecasts in other regions and could align with future NWM/NextGen development. Overall, the study positions ML post-processing plus supplemental stage monitoring as a scalable way to improve local flood-relevant predictions in under-gauged headwaters.
supporting_quote: The inclusion of water level and snow depth observations, even from locations well outside the watershed of interest, substantially improved NWM streamflow simulation skill
incorporating antecedent water level data into the models (LightGBM_WL) markedly increased model performance
An approach like this could be implemented operationally to post-process NWM streamflow forecasts ... where antecedent water level data are available from nearby streams

chunks.text: Compound flood (CF) events occur when multiple flood drivers (e.g., rainfall–runoff and storm surge) coincide or occur in close succession, producing nonlinear water-level dynamics and impacts larger than individual drivers. In coastal-to-inland transition zones, interactions among tides, rivers, rainfall, wind, and geomorphology can strongly shape flood extent, duration, and depth. Process-based models are widely used for hindcasting because they represent local physical features and complex hydrodynamics, but they remain subject to multiple interacting uncertainties.
supporting_quote: Compound flood (CF) modeling enables the simulation of nonlinear water level dynamics in which concurrent or successive flood drivers synergize, producing larger impacts than those from individual drivers.
process-based models can simulate complex CF dynamics in coastal to inland transition zones where hydrological and coastal processes determine flood extent, duration, and inundation depth

chunks.text: Uncertainty in process-based flood modeling is commonly grouped into four sources: initial condition, forcing/boundary conditions, model parameters, and model structure. Initial-condition uncertainty includes DEM and bathymetry/topography errors (notably in wetlands), forcing uncertainty includes sensor limitations and operational simplifications (e.g., omitting freshwater inflow), parameter uncertainty includes roughness and soil moisture assumptions, and structure uncertainty includes reduced-physics schemes and coupling/configuration choices. These uncertainties can propagate through the modeling chain.
supporting_quote: uncertainties in process-based modeling can be classified into four main sources: (i) the initial condition, (ii) the forcing (or boundary) conditions, (iii) the model parameters, and (iv) the model structure
These sources of uncertainty, if not quantified and effectively reduced, cascade in series throughout the modeling chain

chunks.text: Galveston Bay, Texas is a shallow estuary connected to Houston and the Gulf of Mexico, making it vulnerable to both coastal and terrestrial flood drivers. The study focuses on Hurricanes Ike (storm-surge-dominant) and Harvey (rainfall–runoff-dominant with storm surge) as major recent compound events in the region. Harvey produced extreme precipitation and multi-day coastal flooding, making it a benchmark for analyzing CF uncertainties.
supporting_quote: We simulate two CF events in G-Bay, namely, Hurricane Ike and Hurricane Harvey
Hurricane Harvey... generated total cumulative precipitation amounts ranging from 0.64 m up to 1.52 m over southeastern Texas
a wind-driven storm surge triggered compound coastal flooding over the region that lasted 3–8 d

chunks.text: The study aims to characterize how uncertainty evolves and cascades during a compound flood event, using Hurricane Harvey in Galveston Bay as the case study. It seeks to quantify isolated versus total (cascading) uncertainty using linked process-based hydrodynamic models and regression approaches. A key objective is to estimate the relative and cumulative contribution of initial condition, forcing, parameters, and structure to total uncertainty over time.
supporting_quote: Here, we aim at characterizing the spatiotemporal evolution of uncertainty during a well-known CF event, namely, Hurricane Harvey in Galveston Bay, TX.
we are able to estimate the relative and cumulative contribution of the four sources of uncertainty to total uncertainty over time.

chunks.text: Another goal is to evaluate whether a process-based machine learning (PB–ML) model can better explain total uncertainty than conventional multiple linear regression (MLR). The authors hypothesize that nonlinear PB–ML models can capture hidden interactions among uncertainty sources that linear models miss. They use this comparison to support PB–ML as an alternative framework for CF uncertainty quantification.
supporting_quote: Results from this study show that the proposed PB–ML model captures "hidden" nonlinear associations and interactions among the sources of uncertainty, thereby outperforming conventional MLR models.
we conclude that PB–ML models are a feasible alternative for quantifying cascading uncertainty in CF modeling.

chunks.text: A key challenge is that uncertainties from different sources are often treated in isolation, even though they interact and propagate through the modeling chain. Without robust quantification and reduction, these uncertainties can cascade and compromise CF hazard assessments. The paper positions this as a barrier to reliable spatiotemporal characterization of uncertainty during compound events.
supporting_quote: These sources of uncertainty, if not quantified and effectively reduced, cascade in series throughout the modeling chain and compromise the accuracy of CF hazard assessments.
there is a fundamental gap in terms of understanding the evolution of uncertainty sources in CF modeling as well as their cascading effects propagating in the modeling chain

chunks.text: Operational coastal flood guidance may omit freshwater components, assuming river flow and local rainfall are small compared to storm surge. This can be invalid in estuarine and tidally influenced rivers where nonlinear interactions among drivers matter. Such simplifications introduce forcing-condition uncertainty that can bias CF hazard estimates in transition zones.
supporting_quote: under the assumption that river flow and local rainfall contributions to flooding are relatively small compared with that driven by storm surge
ignoring nonlinear interactions among flood drivers in freshwaterinfluenced stretches of the coast can lead to an underestimation of CF hazards

chunks.text: Two independent 2D hydrodynamic models were developed for Galveston Bay: Delft3D-FM (v2021.3) and HEC-RAS (v6.3). The intent is to represent compound coastal flooding and evaluate model-structure uncertainty by comparing outputs across software with different configurations and capabilities. Both models use unstructured finite-volume grids with similar refinement patterns and a Courant-controlled timestep, and outputs are saved hourly.
supporting_quote: we set up 2D models in Delft3D-FM (version 2021.3) and HEC-RAS (version 6.3).
The mesh consists of polygons of varying cell size and the numerical scheme to solve the shallow water equations is set to the Eulerian–Lagrangian (SWL-ELM) method.
The time step is controlled by the Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy condition, with a maximum value of 0.7 for both models.

chunks.text: Model calibration focused on Manning’s roughness coefficients mapped from NLCD land-cover categories and refined via Latin hypercube sampling (100 ensemble members). Tidal propagation was evaluated using a 1-year tide-only simulation in Delft3D-FM, including harmonic analysis of constituents, and then event-based calibration was performed for Hurricanes Ike and Harvey with a warm-up and a 1-week evaluation window. Both models were calibrated independently to support parameter and structure uncertainty analysis.

chunks.text: Coastal to inland transition zones (CTZs) experience flooding driven by interacting processes including rainfall/runoff, tides, surge, wind, and waves. Accurate total water level (TWL) prediction during extreme events is important for planning, emergency response, and flood risk management, and is a priority for U.S. federal forecasting efforts. Delaware Bay is a representative CTZ system with semidiurnal tides and frequent tropical cyclone impacts, making it a suitable testbed for evaluating TWL modeling approaches.

chunks.text: Prior work has compared other 2D hydraulic models and highlighted tradeoffs among mesh structure, sub-grid approaches, and computation time, but a direct 2D comparison between Delft3D-Flexible Mesh (FM) and HEC-RAS had not been established. Existing Delaware River Basin studies showed improved performance when models include atmospheric forcing, especially for wind-dominated surges, motivating a more balanced 2D-to-2D evaluation. This paper positions itself as a benchmark study to support ongoing inter-model comparisons and model selection for CTZ applications.

chunks.text: The study compares Delft3D-FM and 2D HEC-RAS for their ability to predict total water level (TWL) in a coastal-to-inland transition zone. It evaluates performance for two hurricanes in Delaware Bay using tidal analysis, observed-versus-simulated TWL comparisons, and spatiotemporal diagnostics across the entire 2D domain. It also compares computation time and time-step behavior under different forcing scenarios to inform practical model selection.

The paper aims to keep boundary conditions, domain extent, grid sizes, roughness fields, and topobathy consistent between models so that differences can be attributed primarily to model physics and available forcing terms. This is used to evaluate how forcing conditions (tide, surge/waves, river discharge, atmospheric forcing) affect TWL skill for each model.

In particular, accurate TWL prediction requires integrating atmospheric, continental, and oceanic inputs, and inadequate representation of wind setup can degrade storm-surge simulation. This creates uncertainty for stakeholders choosing between readily available tools such as HEC-RAS and more feature-rich systems like Delft3D-FM.

The paper addresses this by comparing both complete and reduced-forcing configurations.

chunks.text: The evaporation (EV) method (Wind method) estimates unsaturated hydraulic conductivity (UHC) and soil water retention (SWR) by monitoring soil weight loss and matric potential as a sample dries from surface evaporation. Schindler’s variant uses two matric potential measurement points and assumes a linear variation of flux in the sample. This linear-flux assumption is considered valid up to about 1,000 cm matric potential, and improved tensiometers and degassed water have historically extended measurement ranges by delaying cavitation.
supporting_quote: The evaporation (EV) method, also known as the Wind method, essentially records volumetric water content and matric potential data at different times as a soil sample is allowed to dry via surface evaporation.
The data analysis procedure assumes linear variation in water flux within the soil sample ... an assumption that is valid for matric potential values up to 1,000 cm

chunks.text: Wet-range UHC values are critical for modeling rapid soil water transport near saturation, such as infiltration under wet or ponded conditions. Because EV-derived UHC often becomes unreliable near the wet range, researchers sometimes merge EV with other techniques (e.g., double-membrane, multistep-outflow) to obtain wet-range data, though this reduces simplicity and increases equipment and procedural needs.
supporting_quote: Because the UHC values in the wet range are important for modeling rapid soil water transport near the wet range
researchers have combined the EV method with other techniques to collect data in the wet range... double-membrane method ... or multistep-outflow methods

chunks.text: Measured SWR and UHC can also vary due to sample preparation, especially incomplete saturation that traps residual air. Trapped air can significantly impact unsaturated hydraulic properties and degrade reproducibility, with literature examples showing noticeable variation in SWR near the wet range. Standardizing soil preparation to achieve full saturation is highlighted as a pathway to mitigate this variability.
supporting_quote: Incomplete saturation often results in residual air trapped in the soil, which can significantly impact unsaturated hydraulic properties
Standardizing the soil preparation procedure to fully saturate the soil can help mitigate this problem

chunks.text: The study aims to improve the EV method so it can accurately determine UHC and SWR in the wet range without needing expensive add-ons or cumbersome combined methods. The authors propose (1) a standardized saturation protocol and (2) a robust, on-sample calibration procedure to quantify and correct tensiometer offset errors. The intended outcome is to extend the working range toward near-saturated conditions while keeping the method simple and cost-efficient.
supporting_quote: we developed an improved EV method that utilizes a simple experimental protocol for standardizing the soil saturation procedure and a robust calibration method to quantify tensiometer offset errors.

This paper presents an experimental protocol that systematically quantifies and corrects tensiometer errors when using the EV method, thereby eliminating the need for a rejection criterion to remove wet-range data.

chunks.text: A specific objective is to directly quantify the magnitude and sign of offset errors in two tensiometers and correct the gradient calculations used by the EV method. By doing so, the authors intend to prevent systematic overestimation or underestimation trends in wet-range UHC that arise from small pressure measurement biases. The protocol is tested through repeat experiments to assess reproducibility of both UHC and SWR.
supporting_quote: We calibrated the tensiometer readings directly on the sample under hydrostatic conditions
We tested the robustness of the proposed protocol by repeating the experiment three times to quantify its reproducibility.

chunks.text: A key limitation of the conventional EV method is inaccurate UHC estimation near the wet range, where data often show large variation and inconsistent trends. Prior work attributes much of this issue to tensiometer measurement errors, including offset errors that distort hydraulic gradients. Because of these problems, researchers often discard many wet-range points using rejection criteria, shrinking the usable dataset and potentially biasing fitted UHC functions.
supporting_quote: the UHC data collected near the wet range tend to have considerable variation
Peters and Durner (2008) ... demonstrate numerically how tensiometer offset errors can lead to erroneous overestimation ... or underestimation
applying the criterion often results in discarding more than 50% of measured data points

chunks.text: Even small tensiometer offset errors can significantly distort EV-method hydraulic gradient estimates and thus UHC values. The paper reports that offset errors as low as about 1 cm can create major problems in wet-range measurements. This sensitivity restricts the EV method’s effective working range for wet-condition applications, motivating a correction protocol rather than discarding data.
supporting_quote: Our experimental study shows that when using the EV method, tensiometer offset errors as low as 1 cm can cause problems with wet-range measurements.
even a relatively minor tensiometer offset error, on the order of -1 cm variation ... can result in an order of magnitude error in the UHC estimates.

chunks.text: Another source of error is incomplete soil saturation during sample preparation, which can trap air and alter measured hydraulic properties. The paper notes that achieving uniform, complete saturation is challenging, especially for low-hydraulic-conductivity soils, and literature data show reproducibility issues near the wet range. Without standardized saturation, SWR and UHC measurements may be unstable across repeated tests.
supporting_quote: Achieving uniform and complete saturation across the entire sample can be a challenging task.
we found that achieving complete saturation can be a challenging task using this method, particularly for low-hydraulic-conductivity soils.

chunks.text: The experimental setup used a plexiglass sample box with internal dimensions 12.0 × 9.0 × 6.0 cm and a separate saturation–calibration assembly kit (12.0 × 9.0 × 10.0 cm) to extend wall height for saturation and calibration. The bottom had ten 4.5-mm holes covered by a fine mesh and sealable with rubber caps. Two miniature tensiometers (TEROS 31) were installed horizontally via predrilled holes with O-rings, positioned 1.5 and 4.5 cm below the soil surface.

chunks.text: Data acquisition used a ZL6 system to record tensiometer and sample weight measurements every 30 minutes. The tensiometers had a measurement range of −150 to 50 kPa, enabling measurement of both positive and negative pressures, with positive pressures used later for calibration. Saturated hydraulic conductivity was also measured independently via the falling head method across multiple runs.

chunks.text: The sample preparation protocol used Tuscaloosa silt loam dried at 105°C for 24 hours, then packed in three equal layers with vibratory compaction. To improve saturation, the sample box walls were extended with the assembly kit and placed in a bucket. A peristaltic pump gradually raised the external water level over 24 hours, forcing bottom-up seepage through the base holes while maintaining a small head difference to avoid boiling, expansion, or air trapping.
supporting_quote: Tuscaloosa silt loam soil ... dried for 24 h in an oven at 105°C
layered into the sample box in three equal layers with vibratory compaction
Using a peristaltic pump, we gradually raised the water level ... over 24 h
crucial to continuously maintain a low head difference ... to prevent soil boiling, sample expansion, or air-trapping problems

chunks.text: The EV data analysis followed Schindler’s formulation, using spatially averaged volumetric water content and average matric potential from two depths (zu = 0.25L and zl = 0.75L). Unsaturated hydraulic conductivity was computed via Darcy–Buckingham using the evaporated volume over each time interval and an average hydraulic gradient derived from tensiometer readings. The method assumes linear flux variation with maximum at the top and zero at the bottom, so the midpoint flux is half the surface flux.
supporting_quote: The EV method is based on the assumption that the flux varies linearly with a maximum value at the top and zero at the bottom.
where zu = 0.25L, and zl = 0.75L
K(havg Δt) = -ΔVw / (2AΔt iavg Δt)

chunks.text: Tensiometer calibration was performed directly on the saturated sample under hydrostatic ponded conditions to estimate offset errors. Ponded water was pumped out with a peristaltic pump at about 1 cm/h while recording tensiometer pressures and corresponding hydrostatic “actual” values. Offset errors were defined as εu = hu − hu(actual) and εl = hl − hl(actual), then gradients were corrected by subtracting the net offset (εl − εu) in the head difference term.
supporting_quote: We calibrated the tensiometer readings directly on the sample under hydrostatic conditions by establishing ponded water above the soil surface
The pumping rate was set to a low value to decrease the ponded free surface at the rate of about 1 cm/h.
εu = hu − huactual
(εl − εu) = net offset error

chunks.text: The experimental design included: (1) the calibration step to quantify offset sign and magnitude; (2) an EV experiment using corrected tensiometer data (Experiment 1 baseline); and (3) two derived datasets representing net-negative and net-positive offset cases by omitting corrections or reversing offset signs. Two additional EV experiments (Experiments 2 and 3) were conducted with the same soil and protocol to evaluate reproducibility.
supporting_quote: We then conducted the EV experiment to generate a baseline experimental data set after implementing proper tensiometer corrections (referred to here as Experiment 1)

chunks.text: The soil tested was Tuscaloosa silt loam sourced from a local quarry in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, and oven-dried before packing. The sample was placed in a plexiglass box and instrumented with two TEROS 31 tensiometers at 1.5 and 4.5 cm below the surface. Time-series data collected included tensiometer pressures and sample mass changes at 30-minute intervals, enabling calculation of SWR and UHC as the sample dried.

Two miniature tensiometers [TEROS 31, METER Group ...] were installed

chunks.text: Calibration data were generated by starting with ponded water about 3.5 cm above the soil surface and then lowering the free surface using pumping. Based on hydrostatics, initial actual pressures at the upper and lower tensiometer depths were 5.0 and 8.0 cm, respectively. Recorded pressure-versus-time (or free-surface level) data were used to fit lines and infer tensiometer intercept-based offsets for each instrument.

the initial actual values ... should have been 5.0 and 8.0 cm, respectively
The offset values were obtained from the intercept values of linear fits to the upper and lower tensiometer data.

The mean was about 15 cm/day with a standard deviation of 8 cm/day. This Ks estimate was used as an external reference to evaluate whether wet-range UHC values derived from EV calculations were physically plausible near saturation.

chunks.text: Three experimental datasets (Experiments 1–3) were produced using the proposed saturation and tensiometer-correction protocol. These datasets included UHC as a function of matric potential and SWR curves across wet to dry ranges. The comparative plots (Fig. 7) served as the primary evidence for assessing reproducibility across independently prepared samples.

chunks.text: The on-sample hydrostatic calibration revealed measurable offset errors in both tensiometers: εu = 0.27 cm (upper) and εl = −0.70 cm (lower). The net offset was therefore negative, εl − εu = −0.97 cm. The study emphasizes that this magnitude is small in absolute terms but consequential for wet-range gradient estimation in EV calculations.

chunks.text: After applying tensiometer offset corrections, the wet-range UHC estimates became more realistic and approached the independently measured saturated hydraulic conductivity. The corrected UHC function near saturation aligned with Ks ≈ 15 ± 8 cm/day rather than showing spurious departures. This indicates the calibration-and-correction step can extend the EV method’s useful range into wetter conditions.
supporting_quote: The corrected data set yielded more-realistic values in the wet range.

chunks.text: A net-negative offset error (here −0.97 cm) produced an overestimation trend in the wet-range UHC function, similar to problematic literature examples. The analysis showed that early-time hydraulic gradients became negative for about 2 days (~3,000 mins), which is inconsistent with the hydrostatic initial condition. This led to computed UHC values that were negative initially and then exhibited undershoot/overshoot behavior near the zero-crossing of the gradient.
supporting_quote: we simply used our observed data points without the tensiometer correction ... net-negative offset error of -0.97 cm
yielded negative hydraulic gradient values during the initial drying period [for about 2 days (3,000 mins)]

chunks.text: The spurious oscillation associated with net-negative offset arose when the hydraulic gradient transitioned from negative to positive and became extremely small in magnitude around the crossing. The zero-crossing occurred at about 3,000 min and corresponded to a matric potential of about 160 cm. Around this point, UHC values swung from extreme negative to extreme positive values, explaining wet-range overshoot artifacts often hidden in log-scale plots.
supporting_quote: At about 3,000 min, the data had spurious oscillations in which the UHC values swung from extreme negative values to extreme positive values.
The value of the matric potential measured at the zero-crossing point (about 3,000 min) was about 160 cm

chunks.text: A net-positive offset error (constructed as +0.97 cm by reversing the signs of εu and εl) caused systematic underestimation of wet-range UHC. In this case the hydraulic gradients were consistently positive from the beginning, which contradicted the intended hydrostatic start (gradient should be zero). The resulting UHC values in the wet range were nearly an order of magnitude lower than the corrected estimates.
supporting_quote: This resulted in a net-positive offset error of 0.97 cm
the hydraulic gradient values were consistently positive from the beginning

chunks.text: Across three independent EV experiments using the proposed saturation and calibration protocol, SWR curves were highly reproducible. The paper reports that the three SWR datasets were almost identical, with wet-range variability described as almost negligible compared with prior literature variability linked to incomplete saturation. UHC datasets still showed natural random variability, but within the same order of magnitude as measured saturated conductivity variability.

The UHC data did have some natural random variability, but these were of the same order of magnitude as that observed in the measured values of saturated hydraulic conductivity.

chunks.text: The paper argues that conventional EV practice often responds to wet-range instability by applying rejection criteria, which can discard a large fraction of measurements and still leave unrealistic trends. This approach can remove important wet-range information needed for modeling, and may bias fitted UHC functions. The authors position offset correction as a preferable alternative to discarding data.
supporting_quote: To address this problem, they proposed a rejection criterion to discard UHC data collected near the wet range.
applying the criterion often results in discarding more than 50% of measured data points

chunks.text: Achieving complete saturation using typical bottom-up pan methods can be difficult, especially for low-hydraulic-conductivity soils, increasing the chance of trapped air and variability. The authors found standard approaches challenging and therefore introduced a controlled head-difference saturation procedure. This discussion highlights that sample preparation is a practical limitation affecting reproducibility near the wet range.
supporting_quote: others have used a bottom-up saturation procedure ... However, we found that achieving complete saturation can be a challenging task using this method, particularly for low-hydraulic-conductivity soils.
Incomplete saturation often results in residual air trapped in the soil

chunks.text: When tensiometer offset errors are not corrected, the derived hydraulic gradients can be physically inconsistent with the experimental initial condition. In the net-negative case, gradients became negative even though the system started hydrostatic, and this caused negative UHC values and oscillations that are often obscured in log-scale presentations. This explains why wet-range artifacts may persist unnoticed and be handled only by ad hoc data screening.
supporting_quote: These negative values are unrealistic because we initiated the system under hydrostatic conditions, and hence the starting gradient should have been zero
Typically, in the published literature, researchers used a log-scale graph ... because these graphs ignore negative data, they cannot display the oscillation in the negative direction.

chunks.text: The study concludes that wet-range inaccuracies in EV-derived UHC and SWR primarily stem from tensiometer offset errors and incomplete saturation procedures. It presents evidence that even about a 1 cm offset can induce roughly an order-of-magnitude error in UHC near saturation. By calibrating tensiometers directly on the sample under ponded hydrostatic conditions and using a robust saturation protocol, the method yields more reliable wet-range UHC and reproducible SWR without relying on rejection criteria.
supporting_quote: variabilities in UHC and SWR data collected near the wet range originate from the errors associated with tensiometer calibration and sample saturation procedures.
even a relatively minor tensiometer offset error, on the order of -1 cm ... can result in an order of magnitude error in the UHC estimates.
the proposed protocol generates more-reliable and -stable UHC and SWR data in the wet range.

chunks.text: Repeating the improved EV procedure three times demonstrated strong reproducibility, especially for SWR, indicating that the standardized preparation and calibration steps stabilize results across samples. The protocol reduces both over- and underestimation errors in wet-range UHC by quantifying and correcting net offset in gradient computations. Overall, the work enhances EV-method reliability for characterizing unsaturated soil properties across the full suction head range.

accounting for this error significantly reduces both over- and underestimation errors in UHC data collected at the wet range.

chunks.text: The Amazon River basin is the world’s largest river system and is globally important for water and sediment delivery. It supplies roughly one-fifth of global freshwater discharge and a large share of Atlantic sediment flux. Deforestation has accelerated over recent decades and is known to modify hydrology and erosion by reducing evapotranspiration and increasing runoff and erosion. These changes can alter suspended sediment concentration in rivers, with implications for ecosystems and geomorphic processes.
supporting_quote: The Amazon River basin is the largest river system in the world, accounting for roughly one-fifth of global freshwater discharge
supplying 40 % of the Atlantic Ocean's sediment flux
From 1975 to 2018, the Amazon experienced an accelerated rate of deforestation, with roughly 20 % (788 353 km2 ) of the Amazon deforested

chunks.text: Intact forest cover can dampen runoff and erosion through interception, evapotranspiration, infiltration, and root stabilization. Deforestation removes canopy and roots, increasing erosion and sediment mobilization. The magnitude and spatial configuration of clearing (including fragmentation and edge effects) can influence how quickly and strongly sediment responses appear. Remaining vegetation, intact forests, or reforestation can mitigate erosion and delay or reduce sediment responses.
supporting_quote: An intact forest cover is known to reduce runoff through various mechanisms such as canopy interception
Deforestation, however, reduces these capabilities by removing the protective canopy cover and vegetation roots

chunks.text: Because observational sediment datasets in the Amazon are sparse and inconsistent, basin-wide comparisons of deforestation effects on sediment have been limited. National and regional monitoring networks often lack long-term records, and consistent basin coverage is limited. This has led many Amazon studies to rely on models rather than observations. Remote sensing and machine learning provide a path to consistent, spatially explicit sediment concentration time series across the basin.
supporting_quote: the relationship between deforestation and fluvial sediment dynamics in the Amazon has not been extensively studied using a basin-wide, comparative approach primarily due to lack of data
sediment concentration measurements are spatially sparse and limited in long-term records for trend analysis
Remote sensing remains the sole approach capable of generating consistent, spatially explicit, long-term (1984–2020) SSC observations across the Amazon Basin

chunks.text: The study aims to quantify how deforestation from 2001–2020 relates to suspended-sediment concentration (SSC) changes across large Amazon rivers and major tributary basins. It uses a lag-based approach to detect whether sediment responses occur immediately or after a delay. The work also evaluates whether deforestation intensity is associated with the presence or absence of response lags. The intent is basin-wide comparison using a consistent remote-sensing SSC dataset.
supporting_quote: utilize a novel remote-sensing-derived sediment concentration dataset to analyze the impact of deforestation from 2001 to 2020
These impacts are studied using a lag-based approach to quantify the spatiotemporal relationships between observed suspended sediment and changes in land cover over time
we explore deforestation–sediment concentration dynamics across the 34 major tributary basins of the Amazon River basin

chunks.text: A specific objective is to identify hydrogeomorphic response lags between annual deforestation and basin-median annual SSC, focusing on lags up to 2 years. The study uses time-lagged cross-correlation to choose the lag that maximizes correlation between deforestation and SSC time series for each basin. These lag assignments are then compared with deforestation magnitude categories to test whether more intensive deforestation corresponds to faster responses.
supporting_quote: a time-lagged cross-correlation (TLCC) analysis is used to identify lags in sediment response to deforestation
We confine the results presented here to a maximum of a 2-year lag
basins are categorized into two primary groups based on deforestation intensity: high deforestation, consisting of basins with over 5 % of their area deforested

chunks.text: Basin-wide studies of deforestation impacts on sediment in the Amazon have been constrained by limited, inconsistent in situ sediment observations. National datasets contain many gauges but SSC records are sparse and often short, limiting trend analyses across 2001–2020. A key challenge is compiling consistent sediment and land-cover change information across eight countries with differing methods and availability. This motivates use of remote-sensing SSC estimates for comparative basin-scale analysis.
supporting_quote: basinwide deforestation–hydrologic studies within the Amazon River basin remain limited due to a lack of high-quality water quality datasets
sediment concentration measurements are spatially sparse and limited in long-term records for trend analysis
As the Amazon River basin falls within the boundaries of eight different countries, it is difficult to compile the various national datasets available for a basin-wide analysis

chunks.text: Fine-scale (reach-level or minor-basin) analyses produced inconsistent and spatially non-uniform relationships between SSC and deforestation, likely because local variability and short-term fluctuations dominate at that scale. This sensitivity obscures broad patterns needed for comparative basin-wide inference. The authors therefore adopt major tributary basins as a more stable scale to reveal clearer spatial patterns of SSC–deforestation relationships.
supporting_quote: Initial trend and correlation assessments were conducted at the river reach level... However, these analyses often resulted in inconsistent findings that lacked spatial uniformity
an assessment on lags performed at the minor tributary basin aggregation scale yielded similar, non-uniform results
examinations at the larger major tributary basin scale... revealed clearer spatial patterns of SSC– deforestation relationships

chunks.text: Deforestation was quantified using the Global Forest Change dataset, which maps forest loss from 2000–2020 at 30 m resolution using Landsat imagery. Forest loss is defined as stand-replacement disturbance (forest to non-forest), and the study uses it as a proxy for non-natural forest loss (deforestation). Alternative datasets were considered but did not match the needed spatial coverage or temporal range. Forest loss was summarized as annual percent cleared within basins for 2001–2020.
supporting_quote: The Global Forest Change (GFC) dataset... identifies changes in forest cover from the year 2000 to 2020 (v1.8) at a 30 m resolution
Forest loss is defined as a stand replacement disturbance, or a change from forest to non-forest
these datasets did not have the spatial coverage or the temporal range desired for this analysis

chunks.text: SSC was estimated from Landsat surface reflectance using a machine-learning model (XGBoost) trained on satellite–field matchups. Reflectance was extracted over SWORD river reaches and cross-calibrated across Landsat sensors to enable time series analysis. The model training used 1112 matchups within the same day or ±1 day, incorporating data from ANA Hidroweb gauges and SO-HYBAM grab samples. Annual SSC for each reach was computed from dry-season observations due to wet-season cloud cover limitations.
supporting_quote: Suspended-sediment concentration (SSC; mg L−1 ) concentration data were acquired using Landsat Collection 1 and machine learning
An Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model was trained using 1112 matchups
Satellite imagery was captured mostly during the dry season... using wet-season imagery was not possible due to high levels of cloud coverage

chunks.text: To ensure SSC time series suitability, reaches with fewer than 10 years of SSC data were removed, then remaining reaches were aggregated to tributary basins. Major and minor basins were defined using the Amazon Aquatic Ecosystem Spatial Framework, selected for spatially uniform multi-scale comparisons. Basin median SSC, rather than outlet values, was used to better represent within-basin variability and reduce sensitivity to extremes. This aggregation supports comparative analyses across large basins with diverse internal sediment sources.
supporting_quote: reaches with less than 10 years of SSC data are removed from the dataset
grouped by their respective major and minor tributary basins defined by the Amazon Geographic Information System (GIS)-based river basin framework
the use of the median SSC and not the mean or maximum values provides resilience to extreme values

chunks.text: Precipitation trends were evaluated to limit confounding effects on SSC trends. Basin-averaged monthly precipitation totals from CHIRPS daily rainfall were computed for each minor tributary basin, and Mann–Kendall tests identified significant trends (p < 0.05). River reaches in minor basins with significant precipitation trends were excluded from the deforestation–sediment analysis performed at the major basin scale. This filtering aimed to focus on basins where SSC changes are less likely driven by precipitation trend changes.
supporting_quote: Mann–Kendall trend tests are performed over the Amazon's 172 minor tributary basins
daily rainfall data... CHIRPS Daily
reaches within minor tributary basins bearing significant precipitation trends are excluded from the deforestation–sediment analysis

chunks.text: Response lags between deforestation and SSC were estimated using time-lagged cross-correlation (TLCC) for each major tributary basin, correlating annual basin-median SSC with annual percent deforested. Deforestation was treated as the stationary predictor and SSC was shifted to identify the lag maximizing Pearson’s r. The analysis only considered lags up to 2 years because preliminary tests found no significant covariation for shifts of 3+ years. These lags define groups (L0, L1, L2) used in subsequent comparisons.
supporting_quote: a time-lagged cross-correlation (TLCC) analysis is used to identify lags in sediment response to deforestation
We use the annual deforestation percentages as a "stationary" predictor variable and test lag responses
We confine the results presented here to a maximum of a 2-year lag

chunks.text: To test whether deforestation intensity differs across lag groups and whether high/low deforestation is associated with lag presence, the study used Kruskal–Wallis and Fisher’s exact tests. High deforestation basins were defined as >5% cleared during 2001–2020 and low as <5%. Lag presence was grouped as lagged vs immediate response for the contingency analysis. Outliers with unusual deforestation dynamics (Curuá Una; Huallaga) were removed before the Kruskal–Wallis comparison.
supporting_quote: A Kruskal–Wallis (K–W) test is used to identify significant variations in deforestation intensity between all three lag groups
high deforestation, consisting of basins with over 5 % of their area deforested... low deforestation, consisting of basins with less than 5 % deforested
the Curuá Una sub-basin stood out... had 23 % of its area deforested... excluded... the Huallaga basin was also excluded

chunks.text: Annual SSC values were normalized to standardized anomalies to enable inter-basin comparison of year-to-year sediment changes. The normalization uses the 2001–2020 mean and standard deviation for each basin, producing positive anomalies for above-average years and negative anomalies for below-average years. These normalized SSC values were synchronized with deforestation years based on identified lags prior to correlation analysis. This setup evaluates whether deforestation relates to annual SSC deviations differently across lag groups.
supporting_quote: concentration values are normalized by measuring their deviation from the mean (i.e., standard anomaly) using Eq. (1)
Positive and negative SSCn indicate above and below 2001–2020 average SSC, respectively
SSC n values are synchronized with their expected deforestation year before conducting a correlation analysis

chunks.text: The forest-loss driver dataset is the Global Forest Change product (Hansen et al., 2013) in Google Earth Engine, providing annual forest cover loss from 2000–2020 at 30 m resolution. Forest loss is defined as a stand-replacement change from forest to non-forest. The study uses this dataset to quantify annual percent deforested within basins over 2001–2020. Its spatial scale and temporal continuity were key selection reasons over alternatives like PRODES or ALOS PALSAR maps.
supporting_quote: Global Forest Change (GFC) dataset... in GEE... from the year 2000 to 2020 (v1.8) at a 30 m resolution
Forest loss is defined as a stand replacement disturbance, or a change from forest to non-forest
these datasets did not have the spatial coverage or the temporal range desired for this analysis

chunks.text: The SSC dataset was built from Landsat Collection 1 surface reflectance (ETM+ and Landsat 8 OLI) extracted over 18,401 SWORD river reaches (median length ~10 km). SSC estimates are derived using an XGBoost model trained on 1112 satellite–field matchups. The usable analysis subset includes 10,932 reaches with at least one year of SSC data during 2001–2020, and annual values require at least 6 dry-season samples. Reaches with less than 10 years of SSC data were excluded for trend/statistical analyses.
supporting_quote: Landsat surface reflectance values were extracted over 18 401 river reaches (median length = 10 km) from the SWOT River Database or SWORD
An Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model was trained using 1112 matchups
Of the 17 182 river reaches in the Amazon, 10 932 reaches had at least 1 year of SSC data during the 20-year period (2001–2020)

chunks.text: Field observations for SSC model training came from both continuous gauges and manual grab samples across the basin. Data from 121 gauging stations were sourced from Brazil’s ANA Hidroweb, and grab samples from 14 SO-HYBAM gauging stations were used. These matchups provide ground truth for calibrating SSC predictions from satellite reflectance. Sampling points are distributed across the Amazon to represent diverse hydrological settings.
supporting_quote: Data from 121 gauging stations were sourced from ANA Hidroweb
grab sample data were collected from 14 SO-HYBAM gauging stations
Field observation data used in the match ups were obtained from both gauging stations and grab samples spread throughout the basin

chunks.text: Precipitation data used to assess and filter basin trends came from CHIRPS Daily at 0.05° resolution. Daily precipitation values were summed to monthly totals per pixel, then averaged within each minor tributary basin. Mann–Kendall tests on these basin-averaged monthly totals identified significant precipitation trends. Reaches in basins with significant precipitation trends were removed from deforestation–SSC lag analyses to reduce precipitation-driven confounding.
supporting_quote: daily rainfall data... CHIRPS Daily
Daily precipitation values are summed for each month for each 0.05° × 0.05° pixel

chunks.text: Spatial framework data include SWORD river centerlines for delineating reaches and an Amazon multi-scale basin framework for aggregations. Reaches are based on the SWOT River Database (SWORD) centerlines. Basins are defined by the Amazon Aquatic Ecosystem Spatial Framework (Venticinque et al., 2016a) and used to group reaches into minor and major tributary basins. These datasets enable consistent spatial aggregation for basin-wide comparative statistics.

major and minor tributary basins defined by the Amazon Geographic Information System (GIS)-based river basin framework (Venticinque et al., 2016a)
These basin delineations were chosen... due to its spatially uniform, multi-scale framework necessary for comparative statistical analyses

chunks.text: The SSC prediction model reported strong validation performance across a wide concentration range. It predicts SSC from 0.01 to 2500 mg/L and achieves MAE of 32 mg/L and relative error of 0.21 on hold-out test data. Additional metrics include SMAPE 30%, percent bias 11%, and RMSE 58.7 mg/L. These metrics are presented as benchmarks indicating suitability for analyzing relative SSC changes across the basin.
supporting_quote: predict over an SSC range from 0.01 to 2500 mg L−1
Specifically, the model exhibits a mean absolute error (MAE) of 32 mg L−1
RMSE of 58.7 mg L−1 , and a very low relative error of 0.21

chunks.text: Significant precipitation trends from 2001–2020 were concentrated in the western Amazon near the Andes. The analysis found 12 minor tributary basins with increasing precipitation trends and one with a decreasing trend. In contrast, significant SSC trends showed spatial clustering in the eastern Amazon, where multiple subbasins experienced increasing SSC trends. A separate cluster of increasing SSC trends also appeared in the north, where deforestation rates are lower than in the east.
supporting_quote: Significant trends in precipitation... were observed in the western portion of the Amazon near the Andes
A total of 12 minor tributary basins were noted as having increasing precipitation trends, while one basin had a decreasing trend
In the eastern portion of the Amazon, several subbasins showed significant increases in SSC trends

chunks.text: Before accounting for response lags, correlations between annual deforestation percentage and basin-median annual SSC were often weak in many basins, especially in the west with limited deforestation. Many basins even showed negative correlations, implying higher deforestation aligned with lower SSC. After adjusting SSC time series by the optimal lag from TLCC, correlations increased across much of the basin. However, five basins still retained negative correlations even after lag adjustment.

negative correlations were observed in many of these basins

chunks.text: The spatial pattern of optimal lags shows immediate (zero-lag) responses concentrated in eastern basins, aligning with regions of intensive deforestation and settlement. Basins with 1–2 year lags generally have lower deforestation levels. Overall, 61.76% of basins showed lagged responses and 38.24% showed no lag. Among lagged basins, approximately 85% had low deforestation (<5%), while among no-lag basins, 69% had high deforestation (>5%).

about 61 % of the basins analyzed have a lagged response

chunks.text: The contingency results quantify a strong association between deforestation intensity and lag presence. Low-deforestation basins (<5%) contain most lagged responses, whereas high-deforestation basins (>5%) are more likely to have no lag. In the table, lagged responses account for 52.94% in low-deforestation basins versus 8.82% in high-deforestation basins. Conversely, no-lag responses are 26.47% in high-deforestation basins versus 11.76% in low-deforestation basins.
supporting_quote: Sub-basins with "low" levels of deforestation (< 5 % of basin deforested) carry the majority of lags
basins with "high" levels of deforestation (> 5 % of basin deforested) tend towards an immediate hydrogeomorphic response
Low | Lag 52.94 ... High | No lag 26.47

chunks.text: Fisher’s exact test indicated a statistically significant association between high/low deforestation and lagged/non-lagged responses. The two-tailed Fisher’s exact test produced p = 0.002, indicating significance at 0.05. A one-tailed (right) Fisher’s exact test also returned p = 0.002, supporting a strong association between high deforestation and the absence of lags. These tests reinforce the link between deforestation intensity and faster SSC response timing.

Fisher's exact test | 2 | 0.002 | Yes
One-tailed Fisher's exact test (right) | 1 | 0.002 | Yes

chunks.text: After excluding two outlier basins (Curuá Una and Huallaga), the Kruskal–Wallis test found significant differences in total deforestation among lag groups. The test reported p = 0.0209 with H statistic = 7.734. Basins with zero lag (L0) had higher deforestation than L1 or L2. Summary statistics show mean percent deforested of 9.07% for L0, 4.02% for L1, and 3.20% for L2 (2001–2020).
supporting_quote: The Kruskal–Wallis Test demonstrated significant variations... (p value of 0.0209, H statistic of 7.734)
Sub-basins with 0 years of lag (L0)... exhibited a higher average percentage of deforestation
L0 | Mean percent basin deforested 9.07 ... L1 4.02 ... L2 3.20

chunks.text: Correlation between lag-adjusted annual deforestation percentages and normalized annual SSC anomalies differed by lag group. The no-lag group (L0) had a statistically significant but modest overall correlation (r = 0.184, p = 0.004, n = 240). The lagged groups were weaker and not significant (L1: r = 0.051, p = 0.508, n = 170; L2: r = 0.116, p = 0.089, n = 216). This suggests detectable annual coupling mainly in basins with immediate responses.

A Mann–Whitney U test comparing deforestation rates between above-mean versus below-mean SSC anomaly years showed significance only for the immediate-response group. In L0 basins, the test found p = 0.0022 and positive SSC anomaly years had higher average deforestation (0.294) than negative anomaly years (0.206). For lagged basins, the differences were not significant (L1 p = 0.3445; L2 p = 0.1556). This indicates clearer annual deforestation–SSC coupling where no lag is present.
