chunks.text: Large hydroclimatic datasets enable high-resolution analysis, but their time spans are limited to decades, motivating stochastic simulation to create alternative plausible scenarios for design, planning, risk assessment, and uncertainty quantification. Precipitation is especially challenging because it is intermittent, bounded below at zero, highly skewed, and governed by complex spatiotemporal dynamics. Existing methods are often mature for smaller domains but struggle when moving to large-domain, many-site settings.
supporting_quote: big datasets are inherently limited in their time span, which covers at most few decades.
precipitation is also quite difficult to model owing to its features, such as intermittency (rain/no rain), lower bounded highly skewed marginal distribution, and spatiotemporal dynamics

chunks.text: Large-domain multisite precipitation modeling faces practical constraints: CPU time increases sharply with the number of locations, and some established model classes require fine-scale multiresolution data that are rarely available over large areas. Time-series based parametric approaches are viable but are often applied to tens of sites rather than thousands. As a result, operational tools that can scale to many locations while retaining key dependence properties are still needed.
supporting_quote: large-domain modeling faces limitations such as the dramatic increase of CPU time with increasing number of locations
only few examples showed capabilities to simulate precipitation at a large number of locations

chunks.text: CoSMoS is a flexible simulation framework designed to preserve arbitrary marginal distributions and correlation structures (including intermittency), and can incorporate features like anisotropy and advection. However, in its original formulation, scaling CoSMoS to large domains is hindered by a key computational bottleneck related to correlation transformation functions (CTFs) when marginal distributions vary across sites.
supporting_quote: CoSMoS ... is a general stochastic modeling framework able to reproduce key properties ... marginal distributions, spatiotemporal correlation structures (STCS), anisotropy, and advection
a computational bottleneck for large-domain multisite simulations in CoSMoS is actually the estimation of the so-called correlation transformation function (CTF).

chunks.text: The study aims to advance CoSMoS so it becomes operational for large-domain multisite precipitation generation by dramatically reducing computational burden. The key idea is to work in an intermediate mixed (zero-inflated) Uniform space that simplifies correlation transformations while preserving marginal distributions, probability of zero, and inter-site correlations. The framework is demonstrated through long simulations across a very large set of rain gauges.
supporting_quote: This study proposes a methodological advancement in the CoSMoS framework ... to dramatically decrease the computational burden and make the algorithm fast enough to perform large-domain simulations
Introducing the mixed-Uniform CoSMoS allowing simulation in thousands of stations

chunks.text: A second goal is to provide an operational blueprint for multisite generation under different correlation-modeling strategies (nonparametric, parametric, semiparametric), including practical fitting of spatiotemporal correlation structures (STCS). The work also seeks to broaden dependence modeling beyond Gaussian by describing parent non-Gaussian processes with different tail dependence behaviors.
supporting_quote: we consider three main strategies, that is: Nonparametric ... Parametric ... Semiparametric
we extend CoSMoS incorporating parent non-Gaussian processes with different degrees of tail dependence

chunks.text: A core scalability problem in original CoSMoS is that CTFs depend on marginal distributions and must be estimated for each pair of locations when sites have different marginals, as commonly occurs over large and complex regions. This implies O(n^2) distinct CTF computations, which becomes infeasible as n grows to thousands. The bottleneck is not mainly matrix factorization, but repeated estimation of pair-specific CTFs.
supporting_quote: CTFs depend on the marginal distributions and need to be estimated for each pair of locations if one assumes different at-site marginal distributions
it requires estimating more than six million different CTFs

chunks.text: Fully reproducing observed multisite correlation matrices at multiple lags is technically difficult because empirical correlation matrices, especially lagged ones, may violate mathematical requirements such as positive definiteness needed for stable multivariate time-series simulation. This limits naive nonparametric strategies that attempt to preserve all observed correlations exactly, particularly at fine time scales and large numbers of stations.
supporting_quote: A fully nonparametric approach that exactly reproduces observed correlation matrices is technically impossible
the observed lag-0 correlation matrix is extremely unlikely to be positive definite (PD); ... Yet this is not the case for lagged correlation matrices.

chunks.text: Using a stationary and isotropic STCS over very large regions may be unrealistic because correlation behavior can vary spatially due to different climate regimes and weather systems. Such simplifications can smooth out true spatial heterogeneity, and may also miss advection-related phenomena like the dimple effect, where lagged correlations can exceed contemporaneous correlations.
supporting_quote: a stationary STCS over large regions is that it cannot reproduce variations in the correlation behavior at different locations.
lag-1 correlations can sometimes appear larger than lag-0 correlations, indicating a phenomenon known as the dimple effect in time due to advection

chunks.text: In semiparametric settings that try to preserve empirical lag-0 cross-correlations while allowing different at-site autocorrelation structures, exact preservation is generally impossible unless autocorrelations are the same at both stations. Differences in lag-1 autocorrelations across sites mathematically induce decreases in cross-correlation, creating an intrinsic mismatch between goals for spatial and temporal dependence.
supporting_quote: which shows that cor(Z_i, Z_j) = cor(\tilde{Z}_i, \tilde{Z}_j) only when \rho_{1,i} = \rho_{1,j}
it is impossible to preserve exactly the observed lag-0 correlation matrix and arbitrary ACSs that differ at each site.

chunks.text: The paper defines a one-parameter mixed (zero-inflated) Uniform distribution U(p0) on [0,1], with probability mass p0 at zero and a Uniform density on (0,1]. Analytical expressions for the pdf, cdf, and quantile function are given, along with mean and variance. This distribution serves as the intermediate marginal space enabling simplified dependence transformations.
supporting_quote: A random variable (rv) U follows a standard zero-inflated Uniform distribution U(p0) ... with probability mass at zero p0
The mean and variance of the U(p0) are given, respectively, by \mu_U = (1 - p_0)/2 and \sigma_U^2 = \frac{(1 - p_0)}{12} + \frac{p_0(1 - p_0)}{4}

chunks.text: Observed intermittent time series Y(t) are transformed into mixed-Uniform series U(t) by mapping nonzero values through the fitted (or empirical) cdf of positive values, while zeros remain at 0. This transformation standardizes diverse site marginals into a one-parameter family characterized only by p0, acting as a dimensionality reduction for large-domain inference. The transformation changes correlation structure, so correlation must be handled in the mixed-Uniform space.
supporting_quote: A stationary intermittent process {Y(t)} ... can be transformed to a mixed-Uniform process ... by U(t) = {0, Y(t)=0; F_X(X(t)), Y(t)>0}
Observed intermittent time series ... can easily be transformed into time series having zero-inflated Uniform marginal distributions. This acts as a sort of "dimensionality reduction"

chunks.text: To connect dependence between Gaussian parent processes and mixed-Uniform variables, the paper defines a Gaussian-to-mixed-Uniform transformation that thresholds at z_{p0}=Phi^{-1}(p0) and rescales probabilities above that threshold. A theoretical relationship between Gaussian correlations and mixed-Uniform correlations is expressed via a double integral over the bivariate Gaussian density. This establishes the basis for correlation transformation functions (CTFs).
supporting_quote: Transforming a standard Gaussian process {Z(t)} ... to one having a mixed-Uniform marginal distribution U(p0) is accomplished by setting U(t) = {0, Z(t) \le z_{p_0}; (\Phi(Z(t)) - p_0)/(1 - p_0), Z(t) > z_{p_0}}
C_U(\rho_{Z_{i,j}}; p_i, p_j) = ... \int ... \int ... \varphi_{Z_iZ_j}(z_i, z_j; \rho_{Z_{i,j}}) dz_i dz_j

chunks.text: Because numerically solving the theoretical double integral is expensive, the paper uses parametric approximations for autocorrelation and cross-correlation transformation functions: ACTF T_a and CTF T_c. These functions map desired mixed-Uniform correlations to the needed Gaussian correlations using three parameters (b, c1, c2). The shapes can be concave or convex depending on |p_i - p_j|.
supporting_quote: we modify the two-parameter ACTF and CTF ... as follows \rho_Z = \mathcal{T}_a(\rho_U; b, c_1, c_2)
the three-parameter CTFs (Equation 12) are concave when |p_i - p_j| < 0.5 ... and convex typically when |p_i - p_j| > 0.5

chunks.text: The key operational acceleration is to precompute ACTF/CTF parameters on grids of p0 (and pairs p_i,p_j) and store them in lookup matrices. For any station probabilities of zero, parameters (b,c1,c2) are obtained via linear interpolation rather than pairwise numerical integration. This converts a massive pairwise estimation problem into inexpensive interpolation driven only by p0 values.
supporting_quote: we estimate the parameters of the ACTF ... for p_0 = 0.01, ..., 0.99
we form three lookup matrices of points (p_i, p_j, b), (p_i, p_j, c_1), and (p_i, p_j, c_2) ... by linear interpolation.

chunks.text: For single-site generation, the algorithm stratifies by season (e.g., monthly), estimates p0 and fits a distribution for positive values, transforms observations to mixed-Uniform, fits an autocorrelation structure in mixed-Uniform space, and then uses ACTF to infer the Gaussian autocorrelation. Gaussian series are simulated using an AR(p) model, then transformed back to precipitation via the inverse of the fitted positive-value cdf combined with the mixed-Uniform threshold mapping.
supporting_quote: Stratify the observed time series values on a seasonal basis; estimate the probability of zero p_{0,m} and fit a parametric distribution function F_{X_m}(x)
Generate Gaussian time series {z_i(t)} ... by using an autoregressive model AR(p) fitted to the Gaussian ACS
Retrieve original time series {y(t)} by transforming the Gaussian ones according to ... (13)

chunks.text: For multisite simulation under the nonparametric strategy, all stations are transformed to mixed-Uniform, and empirical correlation matrices K_U(τ) are computed for required lags. These are transformed to Gaussian correlation matrices K_Z(τ) using CTFs and ACTFs based on each station’s p0. A vector autoregressive model VAR(p) is then fitted to K_Z(τ), and simulated Gaussian series are transformed back to site-specific precipitation using fitted positive-value distributions and p0 thresholds.
supporting_quote: Estimate the correlation matrices K_{U_m}(\tau) of the mixed-Uniform time series for desired lags
Generate parent Gaussian time series {z_i(t)} by using a vector autoregressive model VAR(p) fitted to the K_{Z_m}(\tau) matrices.
Retrieve original time series {y_i(t)} by transforming the Gaussian ones according to (14)

chunks.text: For the parametric strategy, observed correlations are summarized by a spatiotemporal correlation structure (STCS), and the paper uses the Clayton–Weibull STCS that couples copulas and survival functions. Parameters control spatial and temporal correlation ranges and the space–time interaction. This provides parsimonious correlation matrices that are positive definite, enabling VAR model fitting without treating every pairwise correlation as a parameter.
supporting_quote: we use the Clayton-Weibull STCS given by \rho_{\text{CW}}(\delta, \tau; \theta) = ...
the pairs of parameters (b_S, c_S)^T and (b_T, c_T)^T control the correlation intensity in space ... and time ..., while \theta controls the spatiotemporal interaction.

chunks.text: The case study simulates daily precipitation at 1,000 rain gauge stations in selected sub-basins of the Mississippi River basin. The records come from the serially complete dataset for North America (SCDNA), which provides precipitation and temperature series without missing values from 1979 to 2018. Stations span large distances, enabling evaluation of large-domain correlation behavior.
supporting_quote: simulate daily precipitation in 1,000 rain gauge stations located in selected sub-basins in the Mississippi River basin
SCDNA ... without missing values from 1979 to 2018

chunks.text: Model setup for the demonstration uses VAR(1) dependence, requiring at-site marginal distributions for positive precipitation, probability of zero, lag-0 and lag-1 cross-correlations, and lag-1 autocorrelations. Analyses are performed on a seasonal basis (monthly). This provides a practical configuration for large-scale daily simulations.
supporting_quote: we simulate using the mixed-Uniform CoSMoS with VAR(1) dependence structure.

the model setup requires information about at-site marginal distribution for positive precipitation values, probability of zero, and lag-0 and lag-1 cross-correlations, as well as lag-1 autocorrelations.

chunks.text: Positive precipitation marginals are modeled with the GE4 distribution from the Generalized Exponential system, parameterized by one scale and two shape parameters. The paper interprets shape parameter γ1 as controlling whether the pdf is J- or bell-shaped, and γ2 as controlling right-tail heaviness (sub-exponential vs hyper-exponential tails). Monthly parameter estimates are summarized across the 1,000 sites.
supporting_quote: The marginal distribution of positive precipitation is modeled by the ... GE4 ... The cdf is given by F_{GE4}(x;\beta,\gamma_1,\gamma_2)
the pdf is J- and bell-shaped for \gamma_1 < 1 and \gamma_1 > 1 ... \gamma_2 controls the right tail heaviness, with \gamma_2 < 1 and \gamma_2 > 1

chunks.text: Spatial separation among the 1,000 stations is wide, with distances ranging from 20 m to 2,062 km (median 553.5 km). This broad scale helps reveal strong distance decay in cross-correlations and challenges for stationary correlation modeling over a large basin.
supporting_quote: Distances among these stations vary from 20 m up to 2,062 km with a median distance of 553.5 km.
The cross-correlation values among the 1,000 stations clearly depend on the distance between any two stations.

chunks.text: The paper reports strong seasonal variation in precipitation intermittency and intensity across the 1,000 stations. Probability of zero is higher in winter and lower in summer, while the GE4 scale parameter is larger in summer, consistent with stronger convective events. Shape parameters show less systematic seasonality, with γ2 medians indicating heavier-than-exponential tails in many months.
supporting_quote: There is a clear seasonal variation in the probability of zero, with summer months being wetter than winter months (Figure 9a).
A contrasting pattern is observed in the estimated scale parameters ... with summer months having larger values
The parameter \gamma_2 ... medians varying from 0.72 to 0.88 ... indicate heavier than exponential tails

chunks.text: Empirical dependence across the basin is generally weak at daily scale due to large inter-station distances. Median lag-0 cross-correlations range roughly 0.02–0.24, lag-1 cross-correlations 0.01–0.09, and lag-1 autocorrelations 0.09–0.16, with summer showing weaker correlations. The study also notes subtle asymmetry between upper and lower triangular parts of the lag-1 matrix, potentially indicating weak advection.
supporting_quote: medians of lag-0 cross-correlations ... vary from 0.02 to 0.24
Lag-1 cross-correlations are even weaker, with medians ranging from 0.01 to 0.09
lag-1 autocorrelations are also weak, with medians ranging from 0.09 to 0.16
subtle differences shown might be due to weak advection

chunks.text: In the semiparametric 40-year simulation, marginal properties for January show little bias: probability dry, mean, and L-moment ratios are aligned near the 1:1 line across 1,000 stations, and monthly maxima are broadly unbiased though noisy. The paper emphasizes that the GE4 fit was obtained by minimizing cdf square error, yet still reproduces key summary statistics well in simulation.
supporting_quote: Figure 11 shows the scatter plots of observed versus simulated statistics (1,000 points for every month)
The probability of zero (Figure 11a) and mean of nonzero values (Figure 11b) are closely reproduced with low sample variation.
As expected, the monthly maxima points (Figure 11f) show remarkable scattering, but overall unbiasedness.

chunks.text: Semiparametric simulations reproduce spatial correlation patterns well for January: observed and simulated lag-0 correlation matrices show similar structure, and simulated-versus-observed lag-0 correlations cluster around the diagonal with differences centered near zero. Even though only diagonal lag-1 correlations are explicitly preserved, the simulated lag-1 correlation matrix and lag-1 correlations versus distance are reported as close to observations, with some months showing slightly larger simulated autocorrelations due to smoothing from fitted ACS functions.
supporting_quote: The patterns of the observed and simulated lag-0 correlation matrix ... match well
The histogram depicting the differences between observed and simulated values ... is also centered at zero
Although only diagonal lag-1 correlations (autocorrelations) are preserved explicitly ... the observed and simulated lag-1 correlation matrices are reproduced quite well.
the simulated lag-1 autocorrelation appears to be slightly larger ... due to ... fit parametric ACSs

chunks.text: For the parametric simulation using the Clayton–Weibull STCS, fitted parameters vary by month, with reported median vector θ_med=(588.1, 0.96, 1.09, 0.64, 0.46)^T. Under θ_med, the STCS yields cross-correlations of 0.42 (δ=500 km, τ=0) and 0.22 (δ=500 km, τ=1), and lag-1 autocorrelation 0.39 at δ=0 km. This summarizes the basin-scale correlation intensity implied by the fitted stationary STCS.
supporting_quote: a vector of median values \theta_{\text{med}} = (588.1, 0.96, 1.09, 0.64, 0.46)^T
yields cross-correlations equal to 0.42 and 0.22 for distance \delta = 500 km and lags \tau = 0 and 1
while the lag-1 autocorrelation is 0.39 for \delta = 0 km

chunks.text: Parametric simulations reproduce lag-0 correlation patterns and distance decay reasonably well, but the lag-1 dependence shows systematic discrepancies. The paper reports a positive bias of lag-1 correlations for most months and an even more prominent positive bias in lag-1 autocorrelations, with January’s density peak around observed 0.15 versus simulated 0.25. The lag-1 simulated matrix is smoother (less noisy) than the observed one, reflecting STCS smoothing.
supporting_quote: Figures 13i and 13j indicate a good reproduction ... although the simulated values are slightly less scattered.
Figures 13g ... indicate a positive bias of lag-1 correlations for most of the months. Such a bias is more prominent for lag-1 autocorrelations
the density pick in January ... corresponds to observed and simulated values approximately equal to 0.15 and 0.25, respectively.

chunks.text: The paper argues that fully nonparametric multisite simulation is not viable at large scales because empirical correlation matrices, especially lagged ones, may not satisfy positive definiteness and other technical constraints needed for VAR models. Treating each observed correlation as a parameter also leads to millions of parameters (for 1,000 stations), which is scientifically unappealing and sensitive to sampling variability. Observed correlation variability may partly reflect sampling noise rather than true spatial heterogeneity.
supporting_quote: A fully nonparametric approach that exactly reproduces observed correlation matrices is technically impossible
preserving the correlations among 1,000 stations is equivalent to preserving millions of parameters.
The observed correlations among stations are affected heavily by random sample variations.

chunks.text: Stationary and isotropic STCS assumptions can be problematic for very large regions where weather regimes differ, leading to spatial nonstationarity in correlation structures. In such cases, parametric STCSs may smooth out meaningful variability, contributing to reduced scatter and biases (notably at lag-1) in parametric simulations. The authors highlight the need for nonstationary STCS extensions and more complex space–time modeling components.
supporting_quote: a stationary STCS over large regions is that it cannot reproduce variations in the correlation behavior at different locations.
a stationary STCS might smooth out the variability due to spatial nonstationarity, which partly explains the results reported in Section 3.3.

chunks.text: Advection and anisotropy can induce features such as the dimple effect and asymmetry in lagged correlation matrices, which are not captured by simple stationary isotropic STCSs. Over basin-scale domains, weather systems may move in preferred directions over multiple days, making these effects more relevant. The paper suggests that missing these mechanisms can contribute to discrepancies in lag-1 cross-correlations in large-domain applications.
supporting_quote: lag-1 correlations can sometimes appear larger than lag-0 correlations ... the dimple effect in time due to advection
some large-scale weather systems can move systematically across the basin ... such movement can span days, thus generating the dimple effect

chunks.text: Semiparametric approaches that preserve empirical lag-0 correlations while prescribing different at-site autocorrelations cannot preserve cross-correlations exactly unless autocorrelations match across stations. The derived relationship shows cross-correlation decreases when lag-1 autocorrelations differ, but the decrease may be small when autocorrelations are similar (e.g., January range 0.16–0.44 producing less than about −4.6% decrease). This creates an inherent trade-off between local temporal realism and exact spatial correlation preservation.
supporting_quote: the transformed Gaussian lag-1 autocorrelations range approximately from 0.16 to 0.44 for January precipitation
will cause an insignificant decrease less than -4.6%.

chunks.text: Scaling to global-scale station counts (e.g., >100,000 sites) may be limited by operations on massive correlation matrices, despite improvements from mixed-Uniform CTF simplification. The authors identify matrix inversion as a remaining bottleneck and suggest sparse correlation matrices that keep only neighboring interactions because distant correlations are essentially zero. This points to a computational limitation beyond the CTF bottleneck addressed in the paper.
supporting_quote: Ideally yet, we need to expand the simulation capacity to more than 100,000 sites
The bottleneck in this case is inverting the huge correlation matrices.
such massive simulations are feasible by using sparse correlation matrices

chunks.text: The paper notes uncertainty about which multidimensional dependence structure (Gaussian vs alternatives) best represents precipitation, especially regarding tail dependence. While Student t and Bárdossy copulas can modulate tail behavior with similar overall correlations, evidence is limited and large-scale comparative studies are needed. This limits immediate guidance on selecting non-Gaussian dependence structures for operational precipitation simulation.
supporting_quote: the existing literature provides limited evidence of which dependence structure better describes precipitation.
other multidimensional dependence structures can be used instead of the Gaussian one (e.g., based on Student t and Bárdossy copulas).

chunks.text: The paper concludes that transforming intermittent series to mixed (zero-inflated) Uniform marginals enables operational large-domain multisite simulation by reducing CoSMoS computational cost by orders of magnitude. The key is that ACTF/CTF parameters depend only on probabilities of zero, enabling lookup-table interpolation rather than pairwise numerical integration. This allows CoSMoS to preserve marginal distributions, probability of zero, and correlations across many stations in practical runtimes.
supporting_quote: transforms intermittent time series with different marginal distributions to time series having mixed (zero-inflated) Uniform marginals

Since the parameters of such CTF only depend on the probabilities of zero ... computed ... by linear interpolation of lookup matrices. This technique reduces computational time by orders of magnitude.

chunks.text: Applying the mixed-Uniform CoSMoS to daily precipitation at 1,000 stations in the Mississippi River basin shows that simulations can preserve univariate distributional properties and correlation structures satisfactorily under semiparametric and parametric implementations. The work provides an operational blueprint for choosing among nonparametric, semiparametric, and parametric dependence modeling approaches, and introduces stepwise least squares fitting for STCS as a scalable estimation approach.
supporting_quote: The multisite CoSMoS is applied to simulate daily precipitation in 1,000 gauging stations located in the Mississippi River basin.
The results show that the simulated timeseries preserve both marginal distribution properties and correlations satisfactorily.
we introduce a new stepwise least-square method to fit a STCS to large sets of correlation values.

chunks.text: The authors identify future development directions: nonstationary STCSs, advection and anisotropy for subdaily scales, sparse-matrix approaches for very large station networks, and two-state occurrence–intensity modeling via CoSMoS-2s. They also highlight potential use of non-Gaussian parent dependence structures to better control tail dependence. These extensions aim to improve realism while maintaining scalability for increasingly large domains.
supporting_quote: Additional crucial extensions include the use of nonstationary STCSs, and advection and anisotropy components
future work will focus on implementing the mixed-Uniform version of CoSMoS-2s ... coupling multisite binary and continuous processes.
such massive simulations are feasible by using sparse correlation matrices

chunks.text: The NextGen Water Resources Modeling Framework is a standards-based, model-agnostic hydrologic modeling system that enables modular coupling of distinct hydrologic models. It achieves interoperability through the Basic Model Interface (BMI), which standardizes model inputs and outputs across components and languages. NextGen also applies OGC conceptual data models (Hy_Features) to ensure compatibility with key hydrologic datasets and to support a detailed hydrofabric representation for modeling.
supporting_quote: The Next Generation Water Resources Modeling Framework (Next-Gen) is a standards-based and model-agnostic system for hydrologic modeling that enables modular coupling of distinct hydrologic models
This is accomplished via the Basic Model Interface (BMI), which enhances interoperability between models and datasets by providing a standard format for inputs and outputs
NextGen uses WaterML 2.0, part 3, Surface Hydrology Features, otherwise known as "Hy_Features"

chunks.text: NextGen is positioned as a key standard because it is planned for inclusion in future versions of the U.S. National Water Model (NWM), which provides predictions over a very large river network. NWM v3.0 added multiple capability upgrades, but the operational model has been constrained by reliance on a fixed model formulation across its full domain. NextGen’s modularity is presented as a pathway to heterogeneous model formulations suited to differing hydro-climate regions.
supporting_quote: planned inclusion in the U.S. National Water Model (NWM), which provides hydrologic predictions for over 3.4 million miles of rivers and streams across the United States
However, these upgrades have been restricted by the NWM's reliance on a fixed model across its entire range.
Differing hydro-climate regions pose a range of unique needs and challenges, and the NextGen framework's modularity permits incorporation of different hydrology models most suited for those regions.

chunks.text: Containerization is motivated as a portability and reproducibility solution for complex scientific software stacks. The paper contrasts containers with traditional virtual machines, emphasizing lower overhead because containers share the host kernel. Docker is highlighted for broad cross-platform distribution, while Singularity is highlighted for secure, scheduler-integrated execution on HPC systems without root permissions.
supporting_quote: Containerization resolves compatibility challenges by encapsulating applications, their dependencies, and runtime environments into a single, portable unit.
Unlike traditional virtual machines (VMs)... containers share the host system's kernel. This reduces overhead and improves computational efficiency
Singularity's ability to run containers without root permissions greatly improves the security of HPC deployments

chunks.text: The research objective is to improve continental-scale operational flood and water resource prediction by enabling broader community contributions to NextGen-based modeling. The work evaluates whether containerization can effectively encapsulate the NextGen framework to support efficient testing, deployment, and distribution. A key goal is to help individual researchers customize and deploy their own instances with less time spent on setup and maintenance.
supporting_quote: Our overarching research objective is to improve continental-scale operational flood and water resource prediction.

this research specifically evaluates how containerization techniques can effectively encapsulate the NextGen framework to support efficient testing, deployment, and distribution, thereby lowering barriers to community participation
The goal is to enable individual researchers... to customize and deploy their own instances of the system effectively.

chunks.text: A major project aim is to bridge the gap between NextGen’s flexibility and the practical difficulties that prevent community adoption. The paper frames NGIAB as a means to promote community engagement and facilitate research-to-operations pathways by packaging NextGen with expected NWM v4.0 components and automating releases. This is intended to speed onboarding and allow users to focus on hydrologic research rather than software engineering tasks.
supporting_quote: To bridge this gap in community accessibility, we developed Next-Gen In A Box (NGIAB)
NGIAB comes pre-configured with most components expected in version 4.0 of the National Water Model
NGIAB utilizes a cloud-based continuous integration/continuous deployment pipeline to automate releases.

chunks.text: Deploying and running the NextGen framework is described as difficult due to complex installation, dependency management, compilation, and environment configuration. The paper reports multi-day onboarding times with direct support and even longer when users attempt independent compilation on HPC systems. These time and expertise burdens are presented as a barrier to widespread community participation and research use.
supporting_quote: Running the framework and achieving reliable hydrologic results remains challenging due to deployment complexities, steep learning curves, and dependency management issues
Anecdotally, onboarding new users in setting up the framework directly takes around three days of effort.
at a workshop at the University of Vermont, one graduate student reported spending two entire weeks attempting to compile the framework on their HPC cluster.

chunks.text: The framework’s software ecosystem requires managing many source dependencies, build libraries, and Python environments, and building distinct executables for serial and parallel modes. This level of compiler and dependency knowledge is a significant obstacle, especially for users unfamiliar with such tooling. The paper also notes that T-Route adds further complexity due to mixed Python and C components and the risk of environment conflicts when used alongside NextGen.
supporting_quote: installing a functional instance of the framework requires retrieving many source code dependencies via git, managing a host of supporting libraries, compiling the NextGen framework via an additional suite of build libraries, and managing a Python virtual environment.
the NextGen framework compiles different executables for serial and parallel processing, so both need to be compiled
T-Route lacks a straightforward installation procedure, requiring management of both Python and C-based components... heightened risk of environmental conflicts

chunks.text: Operational and research users need portability across local, cloud, and HPC contexts, but NextGen’s native installation workflow undermines reproducibility and ease of deployment. Conflicts between dependencies and differences across platforms can make setup unpredictable. This motivates a reproducible packaging approach that reduces manual configuration and troubleshooting.
supporting_quote: deploying NextGen models remains challenging due to a complex installation process.

This eliminates the laborious task of not just running all of these commands, but also of troubleshooting the many environmental conflicts that can occur while attempting to build the NextGen framework.
NGIAB leverages Docker and Singularity to streamline deployment, ensuring cross-platform compatibility, accessibility, reproducibility, and ease of use.

chunks.text: NGIAB is designed as a layered ecosystem that encapsulates NextGen and associated modeling components within containerized environments, supported by automated CI/CD and outreach tooling. The architecture is described as four layers: core modeling components, containerization, CI/CD pipeline, and applications/outreach. This structure is intended to ensure portability, reproducibility, maintainability, and community accessibility across local, cloud, and HPC deployments.
supporting_quote: NGIAB's ecosystem has been developed with a layered architecture
At its core (Layer 1) lies a suite of integrated hydrological modeling components.
This core is wrapped by the Containerization layer (Layer 2)... supported by the CI/CD Pipeline layer (Layer 3)... The outermost layer (Layer 4), Applications & Outreach

chunks.text: The NGIAB core framework is built in a Rocky Linux 9.1 container and compiles the NextGen framework into separate serial and MPI-parallel executables. The build includes compilers and key data libraries for hydrologic datasets, and uses Python virtual environments to manage numerical dependencies and prevent version conflicts. Default inclusion of multiple BMI modules is selected to align with likely NWM v4.0 components.
supporting_quote: The core framework is built within a Rocky Linux 9.1 container
The NextGen framework is compiled into two separate executables to support both single-threaded (serial) and parallelized runs (MPI-based)
scientific data management libraries... including NetCDF, HDF5, SQLite, and UDUNITS

chunks.text: NGIAB includes nine BMI-compatible modules by default, explicitly chosen for likely inclusion in NWM v4.0. The list spans conceptual and physics-based components as well as routing via T-Route. This pre-packaging aims to provide a practical, NWM-aligned starting point for users running NextGen-based workflows.
supporting_quote: Nine BMI-compatible modules are included within NGIAB's core framework by default, chosen for their likely inclusion in NWM v4.0.

These models include: Simple Logical Tautology Handler (SLoTH)... Conceptual Functional Equivalent (CFE)... NOAH-OWP-Modular... TOPMODEL... Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)... Soil Freeze-Thaw Model... T-Route

chunks.text: Execution is facilitated by a container entry script (HelloNGEN.sh) that retrieves a model configuration directory mounted from outside the container. The paper proposes a standardized run-directory format (ngen-run) containing hydrofabric, forcings, BMI parameters, and a NextGen realization file that defines the coupled model configuration. Decoupling run configuration from the container is presented as supporting reproducibility and interoperability across environments.
supporting_quote: execution is facilitated by a shell script (HelloN-GEN.sh) that runs automatically when the container is launched.
The directories (generically denoted as ngen-run) hold the source hydrofabric, forcings, BMI model parameters, and a NextGen realization file
the fully standalone nature of this format facilitates both reproducibility across environments and interoperability with other applications and workflows.

chunks.text: NGIAB uses a multi-stage build approach to reduce final image size by discarding build dependencies after compilation. The containerization routines automate a large number of installation and configuration steps spanning compilers, MPI, data libraries, Python, T-Route, and NextGen. This is intended to eliminate manual execution of many commands and reduce environment-conflict troubleshooting.
supporting_quote: NGIAB adopts a multi-stage containerization approach... minimizes the final container image size by discarding build dependencies once they are no longer needed
each of NGIAB's containerization routines automate the execution of over 50 commands... installing and configuring over 40 packages
including Fortran compilers, NetCDF, MPI libraries, HDF5, SQLite, Python, T-Route, and the NextGen framework itself.

chunks.text: Docker image packaging is implemented via a Dockerfile with staged steps: base dependency installation, environment configuration, T-Route compilation, and NextGen framework compilation. The build is parameterized using environment variables that specify GitHub repositories and branches, easing version control and updates. The build also creates links and PATH updates to improve usability inside the container.
supporting_quote: The build process is strategically divided into four steps.
The initial "Build Base" step... including CMake, Ninja, Python, NetCDF, and MPICH.
These commands reference environment variables that define the GitHub repositories and branches for relevant source code

chunks.text: Singularity packaging is designed for HPC equivalence and performance, with adjustments such as replacing MPICH with OpenMPI due to SLURM srun compatibility issues. The paper notes technical differences that require environment-variable handling changes, and that the current Singularity build is single-stage for simplicity. The approach aims to keep parity between Docker and Singularity through shared environment-variable-driven repository integration.
supporting_quote: For the MPI library, MPICH had to be replaced with OpenMPI... due to compatibility issues with the SLURM workload manager's srun command.
Notably, the Singularity image currently builds in a single stage for the sake of simplicity.
environment variables control key source repository integrations for NextGen and T-Route... making it far easier to maintain parity

chunks.text: NGIAB automates releases via CI/CD pipelines implemented with GitHub Actions using AWS runners. Tagged releases trigger automated multi-architecture builds (ARM64 and AMD64), testing, and cross-platform checks. Final images are published publicly to DockerHub and Sylabs Cloud Library for community access.
supporting_quote: NGIAB uses continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines with GitHub Actions using AWS Runners
it automatically performs builds for both the ARM64 and AMD64 architectures, runs tests to verify software stability
The final Docker and Singularity images are published on DockerHub, and Sylabs Cloud Library respectively.

chunks.text: The paper’s demonstration case study uses the Provo River near Woodland, UT basin (USGS Gage-10154200) with a multi-year forcing period spanning 2017–2022. The model run directory is produced via the Data Preprocess tool using AORC forcings and is stated to be reproducible via the shown CLI command. For external reproducibility, the prepared run directory is also published in HydroShare.
supporting_quote: We prepared a NextGen-based model run for the Provo River near Woodland, UT (USGS Gage-10154200)... including the six full calendar years of 2017 through 2022.
uvx ngiab-prep -i gage-10154200 –sfr –source aorc –start 2017-01-01 –end 2023-01-02.
The model run directory for Section 4.1 is available via HydroShare (Patel, 2025a)

chunks.text: Performance benchmarking data were collected for an end-to-end workflow including Data Preprocess, NGIAB model execution, and TEEHR preparation across four platforms: Windows, Mac Mini M2 Pro, JetStream2 cloud, and Pantarhei HPC. Benchmarks span multiple basin sizes (23–316 subcatchments) and three simulation windows (10 days, 30 days, and 4 months). Four specific gaged basins are listed to represent the range of watershed sizes tested.
supporting_quote: we gathered performance benchmarks... on four different platforms: Windows, Mac Mini M2 Pro, the JetStream2 cloud platform..., and the Pantarhei HPC cluster.
Benchmarks performance... across four basins with varying number of sub-catchments... 10 days... 30 days... and 4 months
Fish River near Fort Kent, ME (Gage ID: 01013500, 316 subcatchments)

chunks.text: The benchmarking includes explicit hardware and OS specifications for Windows and Mac Mini desktops and platform specifications for JetStream2 and Pantarhei. These include CPU models, RAM, and operating systems, enabling interpretation of runtime differences. The paper provides these details in Tables 2 and 3 to contextualize performance results across heterogeneous architectures.
supporting_quote: Table 2 Hardware specifications for the Windows and Mac Mini desktops used for these benchmarks.
Windows Server 2022 Datacenter Azure Edition... Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8171M CPU... Memory (RAM) 32 GB

chunks.text: The evaluation workflow data for NGIAB’s TEEHR integration uses modeled streamflow from NWM v3.0 retrospectives and observed streamflow from USGS, joined via a location crosswalk. chunks.text: Stream water temperature seasonality is a key control on water chemistry, drinking water treatment, and aquatic life, so characterizing the seasonal thermal regime matters for both ecology and management. Many studies represent the annual temperature cycle as roughly sinusoidal, with summer maxima typically in mid-to-late summer in the Northern Hemisphere. However, colder regions with snowmelt and freezing can create deviations from a simple sinusoid, motivating better representations of the full day-of-year mean cycle.
supporting_quote: Stream water temperature is a key factor for water chemistry, for example, dissolved oxygen (Caissie, 2006), drinking water treatment (Honey-Rosés et al., 2013), and aquatic life

The seasonal thermal regime of streams, in terms of the full cycle of day-of-year mean temperatures (annual temperature cycle), follows a generally sinusoidal pattern throughout the year (Caissie, 2006)
The annual temperature cycle can be affected by snowmelt and freezing in colder regions

chunks.text: The annual temperature cycle offers richer information than seasonal summary statistics because it preserves the full within-year pattern and provides context for comparing trends. Summary statistics can aid classification, but they omit time-series structure and can hinder interpreting whether similar seasonal changes arise from different physical causes. A continuous annual-cycle function can enable extracting multiple metrics (e.g., maxima or seasonal means) consistently from a common representation.
supporting_quote: Seasonal regimes can be captured in the annual temperature cycle (the mean temperature for each day of the year) or in summary statistics such as seasonal mean temperatures
Seasonal summary statistics are effective for classification but do not capture the full time series, preventing the use of lost time-series information

This context enables clearer distinction between patterns, such as increasing maximum temperatures as part of a general warming trend versus increasing maximum temperatures with constant mean temperatures

chunks.text: The study aims to identify consistent deviations from a traditional sinusoidal annual temperature cycle and use those deviations to build a more universally applicable function for stream thermal regime analysis. The authors pose two questions focused on high-elevation streams: how to quantify sinusoid anomalies in a function and whether anomalies show a generalizable pattern across the United States. The proposed solution is an improved annual temperature cycle function called the three-sine model, intended to increase accuracy and preserve interpretable seasonal structure.
supporting_quote: The purpose of this study is to identify consistent deviations from the sinusoid model and use them to construct a more universally applicable stream annual temperature cycle function for thermal regime analyses, herein called the "three-sine model."

we ask: (1) How can anomalies from a sinusoidal annual temperature cycle for high-elevation streams be quantified in a function, and (2) Do the anomalies reflect a generalizable pattern across the U.S.?

chunks.text: A standard sine/cosine model often fits stream annual temperature cycles well, but it struggles to represent major seasonal variations in certain settings. The paper highlights that colder, drier, and high-elevation regions show asymmetric seasonal behaviors (e.g., snowmelt-driven spring cooling or freezing-limited winter temperatures) that a single sinusoid cannot capture. As a result, relying only on mean and amplitude can miss meaningful seasonal timing and anomaly information.
supporting_quote: the sine function is unable to capture major seasonal variations, particularly for colder, drier, and high-elevation regions
large deviations at several times of year, particularly at higher elevations
we propose that the sine curve model, typically used to represent seasonal thermal regimes, can be improved to better capture distinct spring and autumn behaviors or variable timing

chunks.text: Using only seasonal summary statistics can limit analysis because they do not retain the full annual time series and reduce contextual interpretation of trends. The paper argues that this loss of information makes it harder to compare seasonal changes or distinguish different processes that can produce similar summary-statistic trends. This motivates a function-based approach that retains within-year structure.
supporting_quote: Seasonal summary statistics are effective for classification but do not capture the full time series, preventing the use of lost time-series information
and lack context for the comparison of trends, hindering distinction between different causes of similar seasonal trends

chunks.text: To detect elevation-dependent seasonal patterns, streams were divided into 10 equal-sized elevation quantile buckets, each containing 10% of gages. This stratification was used to prevent low-elevation dominance from masking higher-elevation behaviors. Annual temperature cycles were then compared across elevation buckets to guide anomaly identification and model development.
supporting_quote: the streams in the dataset were evenly distributed into 10 groups herein called "buckets," with each bucket containing 10% of gages, organized by elevation
Organizing the streams by elevation allows the identification of seasonal temperature patterns at higher elevations that may not be apparent overall in a low elevation-dominated dataset

chunks.text: The baseline annual temperature cycle was represented as a cosine with fixed phase such that the maximum occurs around Julian day 210. The baseline includes an intercept (mean annual temperature) and amplitude, fit by ordinary least squares. For baseline-only testing, sub-freezing predictions were clipped to 0°C to avoid a spurious penalty from negative modeled values.
supporting_quote: For a maximum on day 210, sinusoidal day-of-year temperature  Ts  is expressed ... as Equation (1).
T_{\rm s} = \overline{T} + A\cos\left((d - 210) \cdot \frac{2\pi}{365}\right)
For testing the baseline sinusoid alone, erroneous sub-freezing predictions were set to 0°C

chunks.text: Model anomalies were derived from residuals between observed annual temperature cycles and the best-fit baseline cosine. Residuals were smoothed using a 31-day centered rolling mean to reduce noise and highlight seasonal structure. Visual inspection identified four recurring anomaly segments (winter-high, spring-low, summer-high, autumn-low) that were paired into two anomaly sine functions (autumnwinter and springsummer) because paired amplitudes were similar and four independent anomaly sines performed worse.
supporting_quote: the new model was constructed based on the residuals of the annual temperature cycles compared to a best-fit cosine
we used the 31-day centered rolling mean ... residual to reduce noise and highlight general trends
there were four portions with a consistent trend of approximately sinusoidal form

allowing anomalies to be fitted as two sine functions (autumn-winter, spring-summer) instead of four independent components. Fitting four independent anomaly functions ... was tested, but showed worse performance.

chunks.text: The three-sine model combines a year-long main cosine with two limited-domain seasonal anomaly sine functions. For each stream, anomaly timing (phases) was determined from local maxima and minima in the annual cycle using a 31-day rolling mean; periods were set to twice the max-to-min time. Each anomaly sine applies only over one period and is zero otherwise, allowing independent amplitudes without interference; coefficients were then fit via ordinary least squares.
supporting_quote: the two sine functions are specified with appropriate phase (Equation 2) and a period equal to twice the maximum-to-minimum time
Each function is then applied only to a domain of one period and set to zero otherwise
Finally, the coefficients ... are fitted using ordinary least squares regression
we introduce the three-sine model ... with day-of-year mean temperature  Ta  (Equation 2)

chunks.text: In the three-sine formulation, anomaly sine terms are subtracted so that positive fitted amplitudes correspond by convention to the observed residual pattern (spring/autumn lows and summer/winter highs relative to the main cosine). The model includes parameters for mean temperature, main cosine amplitude, two anomaly amplitudes, and anomaly timing/period settings, yielding an eight-parameter seasonal description used for subsequent spatial analyses.
supporting_quote: the two anomaly sine functions are subtracted because the peak in each sine function (autumn, spring) corresponds to a low temperature anomaly
This convention allows  a1,2  to be reported as positive by default.
The three-sine model captures the stream annual temperature cycle with eight parameters

chunks.text: Model performance was evaluated using AIC for both the two-parameter sinusoid and the eight-parameter three-sine model, with log-likelihood computed using R's logLik. The authors also tested coefficient significance via R's lm outputs. To assess generalizability and potential overfitting, they performed fivefold cross-validation by year, training on 80% of years and testing on the remaining 20% for each fold.
supporting_quote: we obtained the Akaike information criterion (AIC) ... for both the traditional sinusoid model and the three-sine model
computing log-likelihood with the R function logLik
We also calculated the statistical significance ... using the significance test built in to the "Im" function in R
we used fivefold cross-validation ... by year ... other four partitions (covering 80% of years)

chunks.text: A discrete Fourier transform (FFT) reconstruction was used as a comparator to the three-sine model, examining how many frequencies are needed to match three-sine performance. The paper reconstructed annual cycles using a specified number of FFT components and compared median R^2 by elevation group. This provided a complexity-performance benchmark for an alternative harmonic decomposition approach.
supporting_quote: To compare the three-sine model and discrete Fourier transform performance and model complexity, we also reconstructed the annual temperature cycle time series using only a given number of frequencies from the fast Fourier transform
and determined how many components were needed to equal three-sine model performance in terms of median  R2  by elevation group.

chunks.text: For spatial trend analysis in the contiguous U.S., three-sine parameters were fit to all streams within two-by-two degree windows centered on integer coordinate pairs. The window size was chosen to balance noise reduction and preservation of regional contrasts. Parameters were reported with amplitudes normalized by mean annual temperature, and mapped to examine geographic patterns; parameters were also summarized by 100-m elevation intervals.
supporting_quote: we fitted the three-sine model to streams in a two-by-two degree area around each pair of integer coordinates
The two-by-two degree fitting area was selected after testing several area sizes
reported with the three sinusoid amplitudes normalized to mean annual temperature
We also computed the three-sine parameters for all streams within elevation buckets by intervals of 100 m

chunks.text: Stream water temperature data were sourced from the USGS National Water Information System using the dataRetrieval R package. Gages were screened to include those with at least 365 days of data and required metadata (elevation and drainage area information). After filtering, 2222 gages across the United States were retained, spanning October 1964 to January 2023.
supporting_quote: Stream water temperature data were retrieved from the USGS gage network through the National Water Information System
the gages were further screened for at least 365 days of data and available metadata (i.e., elevation, drainage area identification, and drainage area)
After filtering, 2222 gages met the conditions for use across the U.S.
for the period from October 1964 to January 2023

chunks.text: The dataset covers broad geographic and physical ranges, including elevations from below sea level to high mountains and day-of-year mean stream temperatures up to mid-30s Celsius. Reported ranges include elevation from -4 m to 2900 m and day-of-year mean stream temperature from 0°C to 36°C. Overall mean stream temperature ranged from 0.60°C to 28°C.
supporting_quote: Elevation (m) | Minimum value | -4 | Maximum value | 2900
Day-of-year mean stream temperature (°C) | 0 | 36
Overall mean stream temperature (°C) | 0.60 | 28

chunks.text: Gages were unevenly distributed by elevation and geography, with most sites at lower elevations and more in the eastern U.S. The paper notes that 80% of gages are below about 600 m and 50% are below about 240 m, motivating elevation-bucket analysis. It also reports that 64% of gages are east of 100 degrees West, while still including substantial representation in western mountains and other sparsely gaged regions.
supporting_quote: 80% of gages are located below ~600 m and 50% are located below ~240 m
a greater percent of the gages are located in the eastern U.S. (64% located <100 degrees West)
However, ~27% of gages were located in western mountain ranges of the U.S.

chunks.text: Across the full dataset, the traditional sinusoid model achieved a median R^2 of about 0.96 for day-of-year mean temperatures, while the three-sine model achieved about 0.99. Improvements were present at all elevations, and the advantage increased with elevation as sinusoid performance deteriorated. For the highest-elevation gages, the sinusoid median R^2 dropped to about 0.93, whereas the three-sine model remained near 0.99.
supporting_quote: The sinusoid model performed as expected for most gages, with a median  R2 ~ 0.96
When compared, the three-sine model (median  R2 ~ 0.99) outperforms the sinusoid model (median  R2 ~ 0.96)
For gages located at high elevation, the performance of the sinusoid model declined (to a median R2 ~ 0.93 for the upper 10%) while the median R2 of the three-sine model remained ~0.99.

chunks.text: The elevation dependence of fit improvements was quantified as a median R^2 increase of roughly 0.02 for the lower 60%70% of gages (up to about 300 m elevation), rising to about 0.06 for elevations above roughly 1300 m (about 10% of gages). The authors interpret this as a shift toward seasonal anomaly behavior not captured by the main cosine at higher elevations, potentially linked to snowpack effects.
supporting_quote: the median difference between the three-sine and sinusoidal R2 oscillated around 0.02 for the lower 60%–70% of gages (**300m elevation), then increased up to 0.06 for gages at elevations **1300m
The consistent performance of the three-sine model and diminishing performance of the sinusoid model suggest that stream thermal behavior shifted more toward the seasonal anomalies

chunks.text: AIC comparisons favored the three-sine model despite its higher parameter count. The AIC was lower for the three-sine model across the 10 elevation buckets, and for about 98% of individual streams. Because AIC accounts for complexity, this supports that the added anomaly terms provide justified explanatory power.
supporting_quote: The AIC was lower (better) for the eight-parameter three-sine model than for the two-parameter sinusoid model in the 10 elevation buckets
For ~98% of individual streams, the three-sine model had a lower (better) AIC than the sinusoid model.

chunks.text: The anomaly coefficients were often statistically different from zero. The autumnwinter coefficient was significant (p < 0.05) for about 95% of streams, with p < 0.001 for 92%. The springsummer coefficient was significant for 68% of streams (p < 0.001 for 63%), indicating that many streams exhibit systematic departures from the baseline sinusoid.
supporting_quote: the autumn–winter coefficient was statistically significant (p < 0.05) for ~95% of individual streams, with p < 0.001 for 92% of all streams
The spring–summer coefficient was statistically significant for 68% of streams, with p < 0.001 for 63% of all streams.

chunks.text: A discrete Fourier transform using three frequencies (1/year, 2/year, 3/year) matched the three-sine model's fit closely, with slightly higher median R^2 (about 0.002). The paper notes a complexity comparison: Fourier terms are complex-valued, so three complex components correspond to six real parameters, whereas the three-sine model uses interpretable real-valued seasonal terms.
supporting_quote: A discrete Fourier transform using three frequencies (1/year, 2/year, 3/year) had nearly identical performance to the three-sine model
with a marginally higher median R2 (by ~0.002).
three complex Fourier terms are equivalent in complexity to six real parameters for the three-sine model.

chunks.text: Cross-validation by year showed the three-sine model generalizes better than the sinusoid model while both lose accuracy due to interannual variability. Under fivefold cross-validation, the three-sine model outperformed the sinusoid by about 0.03 median R^2, and both dropped by about 0.09 in median R^2 relative to the overall fit (to about 0.87 and 0.90). The performance gap widened strongly with elevation, from about 0.01 at 0500 m to about 0.08 at 25003000 m.
supporting_quote: Using cross-validation, the three-sine model outperformed the sinusoid model by a similar margin to overall fit (median R2 difference of ~0.03)
both experienced a similar reduction in median R2 by ~0.09 (dropping to 0.87 and 0.90, respectively)
the median increase in R2 rising from 0.01 for gages at 0–500m elevation to 0.08 for gages at 2500–3000m elevation.

chunks.text: Spatial mapping of three-sine anomaly magnitudes revealed patterns not apparent in the traditional sinusoid parameters. In the northern Mountain West, the model captured substantially lower spring temperatures than the sine model, represented by large springsummer anomalies. The largest springsummer anomaly coefficients were about 20%40% of local mean stream temperatures and also appeared in parts of the Northeast.
supporting_quote: for the northern Mountain West (highest elevation streams), the three-sine model captured substantially lower spring temperatures compared to the sine model
large spring and summer anomalies, with magnitudes of ~20%–40% of local mean stream temperatures
parts of the Northeast exhibited large (~20%–40% of mean stream temperature) spring–summer anomaly coefficients

chunks.text: The autumn and winter anomaly coefficient showed a different geographic pattern, tending to be weaker in much of the eastern U.S. and stronger in the West and northern Midwest. Reported magnitudes ranged from under 10% of mean temperature in many eastern locations to 10%40% in western and northern areas. This demonstrates that seasonal asymmetry varies by region and season, not just by overall mean and amplitude.
supporting_quote: The autumn and winter anomaly coefficient also had a distinct trend, appearing weaker (<10% of mean stream water temperature) in much of the eastern U.S. and stronger (10%–40%) in the West and northern Midwest.

chunks.text: Timing parameters derived from anomaly peaks supported regional clustering of seasonality across CONUS. The paper reports earlier anomaly peaks in the Northeast and northern Midwest and later timing in the Southeast. It distinguishes "Continental" versus "Mountain" timing: summer-high around day 200205 for Continental and day 210240 for Mountain, while winter-high timing is around day 8095 for Continental and day 2540 for Mountain.
supporting_quote: anomaly peaks occurred relatively early in the Northeast and northern Midwest ("Cold North" cluster) and late in the Southeast ("Warm").
the summer high arrived early (day 200–205) for Continental sites and later (day 210–240) for Mountain sites
the winter-high timing had the reverse pattern, occurring around day 80–95 for Continental sites and day 25–40 for Mountain sites

chunks.text: Elevation gradients in fitted parameters showed systematic changes in mean temperature and seasonal structure. Mean stream temperature decreased by about 3°C per 1000 m elevation gain. Normalized main cosine amplitude increased from about 50% near sea level to 100%–125% above 2000 m, with >100% indicating winter freeze conditions; both anomaly coefficients rose toward ~30% of mean temperature near 3000 m.
supporting_quote: With every 1000 m of increasing elevation, mean stream temperature decreased by ~3°C.
The sinusoid amplitude ... increased from ~50% near sea level (~0 m) to 100%–125% at >2000 m elevation
Both anomaly coefficients reached ~30% of mean annual stream temperatures with increasing elevation, especially nearing ~3000 m.

chunks.text: Although the three-sine model improves interpretability, the paper notes it does not outperform a discrete Fourier transform of similar complexity; the key advantage is contextual interpretability of seasonal components. Explicit separation into springsummer and autumnwinter components with independent timing avoids interference between harmonic terms and makes spatial comparisons clearer than interpreting higher-frequency Fourier pairs. This frames the three-sine model as a pragmatic, interpretable alternative rather than a strictly best-fitting harmonic representation.
supporting_quote: We note that the three-sine model does not have a performance advantage over a discrete Fourier transform of similar complexity, but retains a context advantage in the interpretability of the results.

Dividing higher frequency components of the annual cycle into spring–summer and autumn–winter components, which have independent timing and do not interfere with each other, allows seasonal components ... to be considered explicitly

chunks.text: The authors caution that a continuous, stationary annual-cycle function cannot capture abrupt discontinuities or direct year-to-year variability. They note the model would miss near-instantaneous temperature jumps or drops due to anthropogenic activity, and that it does not directly represent interannual changes unless coefficients are fit for each year or moving windows. This limits applicability where nonseasonal disturbances or strong nonstationarity dominate.
supporting_quote: the three-sine model, being based on a continuous function, would not be able to capture major discontinuities in the temperature cycle
The three-sine model also cannot directly represent year-to-year variability, though one could fit three-sine coefficients for each year individually

chunks.text: The paper acknowledges potential overfitting risk due to the three-sine model's larger number of parameters compared to the traditional sinusoid. It argues this risk is mitigated by multiple indicators: sustained cross-validation and AIC advantages, a high observations-to-parameters ratio (365 to 8), and physically plausible explanations (e.g., snowpack). This discussion positions the model as more complex but still defensible for broad application.
supporting_quote: The performance advantage of the three-sine model with considerably more parameters than the traditional sinusoid runs the risk of overfitting, but this is mitigated by the combination of several factors
sustained performance advantage in cross-validation and AIC; large ratio of observations to parameters (365 to 8); and plausible physical explanations for model terms (e.g., snowpack).

chunks.text: Physical drivers of the anomaly terms are not resolved in this study, and the authors frame them as hypotheses for future work. They propose that cold-spring/warm-summer anomalies at high elevations may be influenced by snowmelt timing, and that warm-winter anomalies may result from streams freezing when the sinusoid predicts subzero temperatures. The need to link anomalies to covariates (e.g., precipitation, riparian cover, slope) is highlighted as a next step.
supporting_quote: there remains a need to investigate the physical causes of the anomalies
we hypothesize that, at high elevations, the cold-spring/warm-summer anomaly pair is influenced by snowmelt patterns
We also hypothesize that, in many streams, the warm-winter anomaly may be a result of streams freezing when the sinusoid predicts subzero water temperatures.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that annual stream temperature cycles show consistent deviations from a traditional sinusoid that can be captured by two anomaly pairs: autumn-low/winter-high and spring-low/summer-high. Encoding these as two limited-domain sine anomalies added to a main cosine yields an eight-parameter three-sine model that better represents asymmetrical seasonal behavior. This improved framework is intended to support thermal regime analysis and comparison across diverse geographies and elevations.
supporting_quote: there is a consistent pattern in annual temperature cycle residuals relative to the traditional sinusoid model, which can be characterized by two pairs of anomalies: autumn-low/winter-high and spring-low/summer-high
We proposed an improvement to the traditional sinusoid model, called the "three-sine" model
The three-sine model captures the stream annual temperature cycle with eight parameters

chunks.text: The authors conclude the three-sine model provides improved accuracy over the traditional sinusoid across elevations and most streams, with particularly strong benefits in high-elevation settings where the sinusoid degrades. They emphasize that the three-sine representation enables analyzing seasonal trends in the context of the full annual cycle rather than relying on isolated summary statistics. The model is positioned as a standardized, interpretable basis for future climate and management applications.
supporting_quote: the three-sine model (median  R2 ~ 0.99) outperforms the sinusoid model (median  R2 ~ 0.96)
For ~98% of individual streams, the three-sine model had a lower (better) AIC than the sinusoid model.
The three-sine model sets up an improved framework for investigating stream thermal regime characteristics in context

chunks.text: Stream water temperature is a central water-quality variable that influences aquatic biochemistry and ecosystem health. It affects organism growth and life cycles, dissolved oxygen, and drinking water treatment chemistry. Because of these broad impacts, stream temperature is an important target for assessing infrastructure effects, disturbances, restoration, and climate change. Prediction is needed to establish baselines and evaluate conditions relative to ecological thresholds.
supporting_quote: Stream water temperature (ST) is a crucial water quality variable with wide-ranging impacts on aquatic biochemistry
affecting aquatic organism growth and lifecycles..., dissolved oxygen..., and water treatment chemistry

chunks.text: Large-scale stream temperature modeling spans process-based, stream statistical network (SSN), and sitewise statistical approaches, each with tradeoffs. Process-based models represent physical processes but can be computationally intensive and data/calibration demanding. SSN models can be accurate but are computationally heavy and rarely used at sub-monthly scales. Sitewise models are more computationally efficient and can work with sparse gage networks, but do not explicitly represent stream-network dependence.
supporting_quote: Process-based numerical models explicitly model stream temperature processes... However, numerical simulations are computationally intensive
SSN models demonstrate high accuracy at monthly resolution... but SSNs are computationally intensive
Sitewise models... are significantly more computationally efficient than process-based or SSN models

chunks.text: The paper positions a point-focused statistical approach as operationally practical for large domains because it can minimize data requirements and computational cost. By relying on widely available point-scale gridded or remotely sensed predictors rather than full watershed or stream-network datasets, such a model can also be easier to generalize beyond the CONUS. This motivates using relationships between seasonal thermal regime and short-term weather response to estimate stream temperature.
supporting_quote: At large scale and high resolution, it is important for a potential model to minimize data requirements and computational intensity
These considerations can be met by a pointfocused statistical model... limits computation requirements

chunks.text: The study aims to develop a CONUS-wide model that estimates daily stream temperatures at high spatial resolution using satellite and gridded data. The intended outputs are daily mean and daily maximum stream temperatures at 1 km resolution for ungaged streams of any size. The approach emphasizes interpretability and computational efficiency compared with the authors’ prior machine-learning model.
supporting_quote: developing a satellite remote sensing-based spatial-statistical model, TempEst 2... to estimate daily mean and maximum temperatures at 1 km resolution for ungaged streams of any size across the CONUS
TempEst 2 also improves over TempEst 1 in interpretability and computational efficiency.

chunks.text: The research question is how to identify weather and climate relationships that approximate watershed-scale processes using widely available site and point-scale remotely sensed or gridded data. The authors hypothesize that stream temperature can be efficiently estimated by separating seasonal thermal regime from short-term weather-driven anomalies. This hypothesis is operationalized through the SCHEMA framework used in TempEst 2.
supporting_quote: For this study, we ask: how can weather and climate relationships approximating watershed-scale processes to estimate stream temperature be identified
We hypothesize that stream temperature can be efficiently estimated using seasonal thermal regime and short-term weather response

chunks.text: High spatiotemporal resolution stream temperature datasets are limited across the CONUS, especially for small and remote streams. Existing models are typically constrained by one or more of the following: regional (sub-CONUS) coverage, coarse spatial resolution (around 10 km or more), and/or monthly temporal resolution. This leaves a gap for daily, 1 km, CONUS-wide estimates usable at ungaged sites.
supporting_quote: such datasets are limited spatially and temporally across the CONUS, particularly for small, remote streams
Available models are limited in domain (regional), spatial resolution (≥10 km), temporal resolution (monthly), or a combination thereof.

chunks.text: Process-based models can be limited in scalability over large domains because stability requirements force very small timesteps at high spatial resolution. The paper gives an example of a global 10 km model using a 5-minute timestep, implying far more timesteps than daily models and long runtimes. Such computational burdens reduce practicality for near-continental or global applications and long time series.
supporting_quote: numerical simulations are computationally intensive, with numerical stability requiring temporal resolution that scales with spatial resolution
for 10-km resolution, Wanders et al. (2019) used a 5 min timestep.

chunks.text: SSN models are accurate but computationally intensive and have not, to the authors’ knowledge, been applied at sub-monthly resolution in academic literature. Sitewise models are efficient but cannot explicitly represent stream-network conditions. These limitations motivate a CONUS-wide daily approach that is both efficient and minimally dependent on detailed stream network data.
supporting_quote: SSNs are computationally intensive and, to our knowledge, have not been applied at sub-monthly resolution in academic literature
Sitewise models are limited by their intrinsic inability to consider stream network conditions

chunks.text: TempEst 2 uses the SCHEMA approach: it models stream temperature as the sum of seasonal conditions (day-of-year mean) and a daily anomaly (departure from the DOY mean). Seasonal conditions are estimated by predicting parameters of an annual temperature cycle function using long-term site data, then reconstructing DOY means. Daily anomalies are estimated from recent weather anomalies using smoothing functions, with site-specific sensitivity inferred from long-term site data. The model is implemented as a single CONUS-wide model rather than ecoregion sub-models.
supporting_quote: TempEst 2... fit stream temperature in terms of seasonal and daily anomaly (departure from day-of-year, DOY, mean)
We refer to this combined approach as Seasonal Cycle Historical Estimation with Modeled daily Anomaly (SCHEMA).
TempEst 2 is implemented as a single model over the CONUS

chunks.text: For spatial-statistical modeling, the authors compared multiple linear regression, generalized additive models, and universal kriging for each component using gagewise cross-validation. Universal kriging was selected because it generally performed best and provides interpretability by separating a fixed part from a spatial signal capturing autocorrelation. Covariance parameters are estimated via maximum likelihood using the fields package. All spatial models include latitude, longitude, and elevation as baseline covariates.
supporting_quote: three approaches were tested: multiple linear regression... general additive models... and universal kriging
Since kriging usually performed the best, all spatial models used universal kriging
The model included latitude, longitude, and elevation for every simulation

chunks.text: Covariates were selected iteratively by testing additions to a baseline model in cross-validation, adding one or two covariates at a time to avoid a combinatorial explosion. Beyond spatial coordinates, the team tested long-term statistics (mean, max, min, standard deviation) for weather variables, as well as monthly means and nonstandard summaries (e.g., anomaly standard deviation, sine amplitude, and below-freezing days). Monthly means were particularly valuable for capturing seasonal characteristics not represented by long-term summaries. The final seasonal model uses a set of variable categories summarized in Table 2.
supporting_quote: Model covariates were thus identified iteratively, starting from the baseline model with latitude, longitude, and elevation
We also tested the inclusion of monthly means... Several monthly means substantially improved model performance
Variables used in the final seasonal conditions model.

chunks.text: Seasonal conditions are modeled by predicting coefficients of a sinusoidal annual temperature cycle rather than predicting 365 daily means directly. The paper uses a three-sine function that requires eight parameters (mean temperature, amplitudes, and timing terms) and fits separate kriging models for each parameter. Cross-validation suggested predicting some parameters while setting spring, summer, and autumn timing to fixed average Julian days to reduce uncertainty. The seasonal model achieved a reported RMSE for the annual cycle after these design choices.
supporting_quote: We estimate DOY mean temperature using the three-sine function... The threesine function requires the estimation of eight parameters
Cross-validation performance was best when predicting the three-sine coefficients... while setting spring, summer, and autumn timing to average values (Julian day 160, 220, and 330, respectively).

chunks.text: The daily anomaly component regresses stream temperature anomaly against anomalies in land surface temperature and humidity. The response to LST anomaly was modeled with a sigmoid transform, which modestly improved performance especially for larger anomalies. The sigmoid sensitivity parameter k was selected by testing gage-level performance across candidate values and then fixed globally. The model also investigated lag effects using smoothed covariates over multiple prior days.
supporting_quote: the response of ST anomaly (ΔT) to LST anomaly (ΔLST) was loosely sigmoidal in form (Eq. (1)
regression model development used the sigmoid function of LST anomaly
the optimal for the LST sigmoid... was a fixed = 0.3 −1 across all gages.

chunks.text: Lagged weather influence is incorporated via smoothing over prior days rather than fitting separate coefficients for each lag day. The optimal specification used seven days of LST and two days of humidity, with explicit weighted smoothing terms.
