Coefficients controlling anomaly sensitivity are predicted spatially; the selected predictors for coefficient prediction included water fraction (as a proxy for river width) and the standard deviation of daily humidity anomaly, along with spatial coordinates and elevation.
supporting_quote: the optimal model used smoothed covariates over seven days of LST and two days of humidity (Eq. (7)
The best-performing model for weather coefficient prediction used water fraction, a proxy for river width, and the standard deviation of daily humidity anomaly

chunks.text: Daily maximum temperature is estimated by adapting the daily mean approach: the anomaly of daily maximum relative to the DOY mean is regressed on the LST sigmoid and humidity anomaly, but with an intercept term. The intercept is justified because maximum temperatures can exceed the DOY mean even when anomalies are near zero. The same general coefficient-prediction strategy is used to spatially predict these regression parameters.
supporting_quote: To estimate daily maximum temperature, we tested a modified version of the daily mean temperature method
for daily maximum temperature... we included an intercept term in the regression

chunks.text: Performance evaluation uses gage-based cross-validation and additional stress tests for extrapolation in space, time, and elevation. The main reported metrics include median (across gages) RMSE, percent bias, NSE, R², and absolute bias. Additional evaluations include leave-one-out validation on a 4×4 spatial grid, walk-forward validation by year (2003–2023), and training below 1800 m to test higher-elevation extrapolation. Sensitivity to training network density (10%–100%) and training timeseries length (5, 10, 20 years) is also quantified.
supporting_quote: model performance was assessed for ten-fold cross-validation over gages using median (across gages) root mean square error (RMSE)
we divided the CONUS into a four-by-four grid and conducted leave-one-out cross-validation
we conducted a walkforward validation... from 2003 to 2023
trained on data from the lower elevation gages (<1800 m; 95% of gages)

chunks.text: Training and evaluation data include daily mean and maximum observed stream temperature from the USGS stream temperature gage network, retrieved via the dataRetrieval R package. The CONUS implementation uses overlapping observations and predictor data for 1,316 gages spanning diverse land uses, climates, and geographies. The model is trained to gage measurement locations within the stream cross-section, which can introduce random variation because it is not necessarily a cross-section mean. Drainage area was retrieved but excluded from the final model due to negligible impact on accuracy.
supporting_quote: Daily mean and maximum observed stream temperature... were retrieved from the US Geological Survey (USGS)... using the dataRetrieval package
Overlapping gage observations and prediction data... were retrieved for 1,316 gages
Gage drainage area and precipitation were also excluded from the final model due to negligible effect on accuracy.

chunks.text: Predictor datasets were primarily retrieved via Google Earth Engine and include land surface temperature, humidity, precipitation, land cover, and elevation. MODIS LST is at 1 km resolution, land cover at 10 m, and elevation from a 90 m DEM; precipitation is from ERA5 daily at 1/4° and humidity from NLDAS-2. Data were collected as averages within a 500 m radius around each site, consistent with MODIS 1 km resolution, and inner/outer radii were tested for LST. The final model uses nearby (500 m) daytime LST only.
supporting_quote: Table 1 lists other data used that were retrieved from Google Earth Engine
data were collected in a radius of 500 m, following the 1-km resolution of MODIS LST
The final model implementation considers only nearby (500 m) and daytime LST

chunks.text: The paper specifies the core input data sources and their spatial resolutions: MODIS 1 km land surface temperature, NLDAS-2 humidity, ERA5 precipitation, ESA WorldCover 10 m land cover, and a 90 m global DEM. These predictors are used to build point-based outputs with an effective resolution dominated by LST (1 km). The land surface temperature dataset includes temperature over water, though at 1 km most streams cannot be separated into over-water versus over-land LST. This motivates using nearby radii to approximate water/land influence.
supporting_quote: Land surface temperature (LST) | °C | 1 km | Remote sensing - MODIS
Land cover | – | 10 m | Remote sensing (Zanaga et al., 2021)
Land surface temperature includes temperature over water.

chunks.text: The final seasonal-conditions model uses a defined set of covariate categories, including spatial coordinates, elevation, land-cover fractions, and several LST and humidity summaries. These include the number of days with below-freezing DOY mean LST, minimum and maximum DOY mean LST, humidity annual amplitude, and multiple monthly means of humidity, LST, and cumulative LST degree-days. Different three-sine parameters use different combinations of these variables. The list of variables is summarized in Table 2.
supporting_quote: Table 2 Variables used in the final seasonal conditions model.
Number of days with below-freezing DOY mean LST
Monthly means of LST cumulative degree-days (multiple months)

chunks.text: The seasonal conditions (annual temperature cycle) model achieved a median cross-validation RMSE of 1.85 °C when predicting DOY mean temperatures using the three-sine function approach. Best performance came from predicting coefficients for mean, amplitude, seasonal anomalies, and winter timing, while fixing spring/summer/autumn timing to average Julian days. The authors attribute this to high uncertainty in those timing parameters outweighing site-specific estimation benefits. This seasonal component provides the baseline upon which daily anomalies are added.
supporting_quote: The final seasonal model predicted the annual temperature cycle with a median (across gages) cross-validation RMSE of 1.85 ◦C.
setting spring, summer, and autumn timing to average values (Julian day 160, 220, and 330, respectively).

chunks.text: For the daily anomaly model, the optimal LST sigmoid parameter was fixed at k = 0.3−1 across gages. The selected lag structure used smoothed covariates over seven days of LST and two days of humidity. Coefficient prediction performance in cross-validation had R² = 0.77 for the LST sigmoid coefficient and R² = 0.53 for the humidity coefficient. As an anomaly time-series prediction, the model achieved NSE = 0.45 and RMSE = 1.3 °C.
supporting_quote: the optimal for the LST sigmoid... was a fixed = 0.3 −1 across all gages.
the optimal model used smoothed covariates over seven days of LST and two days of humidity (Eq. (7)
the model had an NSE of 0.45 with an RMSE of 1.3 ◦C
overall cross-validation R2 of 0.77 for the LST sigmoid coefficient and 0.53 for the humidity coefficient

chunks.text: In ten-fold gagewise cross-validation, the combined SCHEMA model estimated daily mean stream temperature with median RMSE of 2.0 °C. Reported median bias was 0.1%, with R² of 0.94 and NSE of 0.91. Aggregating daily predictions to monthly means improved performance to median RMSE of 1.6 °C with R² around 0.97 and NSE around 0.94. The model error did not correlate with water fraction (a proxy for stream width) and performed well for very small streams.
supporting_quote: full model for daily mean temperature had a median validation RMSE of 2.0 ◦C
median bias of 0.1%, R2 of 0.94, and NSE of 0.91
Monthly means... had a median RMSE of 1.6 ◦C, with an improved R2 ∼ 0.97 and NSE ∼ 0.94
Validation gage RMSE did not correlate with water fraction (a proxy for stream width)

chunks.text: Daily maximum temperature estimation achieved a median cross-validation RMSE of 2.3 °C with bias of 0.5%, R² of 0.93, and NSE of 0.89. Monthly maximum temperatures had similar accuracy to daily estimation (median RMSE 2.3 °C), unlike mean temperature where monthly averaging improved results. Mean monthly maximum temperatures improved to RMSE 1.8 °C with very high R² (0.98) and NSE (0.92). Annual maxima were less reliable by NSE (median −0.20), likely due to few annual observations.
supporting_quote: daily maximum temperature estimation had a median cross-validation RMSE of 2.3 ◦C, bias of 0.5%, R2 of 0.93, and NSE of 0.89.
monthly maximum temperatures had similar performance... with median RMSE of 2.3 ◦C
Mean monthly maximum temperatures had a median RMSE of 1.8 ◦C... R2 of 0.98, and NSE of 0.92.
Annual maximum temperatures... median R2 decreasing to 0.72 and NSE to −0.20.

chunks.text: Extrapolating to higher elevations produced a substantial penalty when the model was trained only on gages below 1800 m and tested on roughly 1800–2900 m gages. Median RMSE worsened from 2.0 °C to 3.1 °C and median bias increased to 25% (about 1 °C), while median R² remained 0.91. The paper notes biases are seasonally highest during days around 50–150 and 200–300. Cross-validation on the same high-elevation gages (without elevation holdout) performed better, implying the issue is extrapolation distance rather than elevation itself.
supporting_quote: trained below 1800 m elevation... produced a substantial performance penalty, worsening median RMSE to 3.1 ◦C (from 2.0 ◦C) and adding a substantial bias, at a median of 25%
The correlation remained strong, at a median R2 of 0.91
biases were highest... during days ∼50–150... and days ∼200–300

chunks.text: Spatial cross-validation using a 4×4 grid (leaving out contiguous regions) caused a modest performance decrease relative to gagewise cross-validation. Median RMSE increased from 2.0 °C to 2.3 °C, while median bias stayed low at 1.1%. The penalty varied by region, with some regions near baseline and others showing median RMSE around 2.5–3.0 °C. Median bias did not exceed about 15% in any region and was under about 5% for most.
supporting_quote: Spatial cross-validation showed a modest performance penalty, with median RMSE increasing to 2.3 ◦C (compared to 2.0 ◦C).
Median bias remained low at 1.1%.
other regions had median RMSE ranging from 2.5–3.0 ◦C

chunks.text: Walk-forward validation for predicting each year using training from preceding years showed a small-to-moderate performance penalty. The median RMSE was 2.2 °C and median bias was −1.3%, indicating slight underestimation. The authors interpret the bias as potentially connected to stationarity assumptions in the seasonal component. They emphasize that TempEst 2 is not designed for forecasting despite this evaluation.
supporting_quote: Walk-forward validation... with a median RMSE of 2.2 ◦C.
The median bias was... negative, at −1.3%.
TempEst 2 is not designed for forecasting.

chunks.text: Performance under infrequent events was generally similar to overall performance with some systematic biases. For infrequent heat (LST > 99.95th percentile) the model slightly underestimated ST, with median RMSE 2.1 °C and bias −1.0 °C. For infrequent cold (LST < 0.05th percentile) RMSE remained 2.0 °C with bias 0.28 °C. Flood conditions (discharge > 99.95th percentile) showed median RMSE 2.2 °C and bias 0.51 °C, while drought (discharge < 0.05th percentile) improved RMSE to 1.6 °C with bias −0.18 °C.
supporting_quote: With infrequent heat (LST >99.95th percentile)... median RMSE of 2.1 ◦C... bias of −1.0 ◦C.
Infrequent cold (LST < 0.05th percentile)... median RMSE of 2.0 ◦C and bias of 0.28 ◦C
Under flood conditions (discharge > 99.95th percentile)... median RMSE of 2.2 ◦C and bias of 0.51 ◦C.
Droughts (discharge < 0.05th percentile)... median RMSE of 1.6 ◦C... median bias of −0.18 ◦C.

chunks.text: Model sensitivity to training timeseries length was limited: using 5- or 10-year training periods slightly increased error relative to full-period training. In cross-validation, median RMSE rose to 2.2 °C for 5-year blocks and 2.1 °C for 10-year blocks, compared to 2.0 °C overall. This suggests TempEst 2 can be trained on shorter intervals when users are concerned about stationarity or regime shifts. The performance change was described as a small penalty.
supporting_quote: use of a 5- or 10 year training timeseries caused a small penalty (median validation RMSE 2.2 ◦C for 5 years and 2.1 ◦C for 10 years, up from 2.0 ◦C).
For applications where stationarity is a major concern... using a relatively short (e.g., 5–10 year) training timeseries

chunks.text: Reducing gage network density increased error but the model remained usable under sparse networks. The full network (~1300 gages for ~8 million km²) corresponds to ~160 gages per million km²; at 10% density (16 gages per 10^6 km²) median RMSE increased to 2.4 °C. Performance improved to about 2.2–2.3 °C at 25% density, with diminishing returns thereafter. The authors report that this sensitivity is lower than for TempEst 1’s random forest approach.
supporting_quote: full training gage network... had a density of ∼160 gages per million square kilometers
median validation RMSE increased to 2.4 ◦C for 10% network density (16 gages per 10^6 km^2)
improving to ∼2.2–2.3 ◦C at 25% density

chunks.text: Model performance can be poor immediately downstream of large dams, with clusters of high-error gages near major reservoirs. The paper states that the current model formulation cannot directly account for the presence of dams, though some effects might be indirectly reflected in LST and humidity. As a result, predictions right below dams should be treated as questionable. The authors suggest the model could instead be used to quantify anthropogenic impacts via departures between observations and estimates.
supporting_quote: the model does sometimes exhibit poor performance immediately downstream of large dams
the current form of TempEst 2 cannot directly account for the presence of dams
performance immediately downstream of dams should be considered questionable at best

chunks.text: Extrapolation to high elevations is identified as a key limitation, especially for sites above about 3,000 m for the pre-trained model. When trained on lower elevations, predictions at 1800–2900 m show increased RMSE and notable positive bias, indicating systematic overestimation while retaining high correlation. The authors recommend caution for high-mountain applications and note that adding a few training gages in the target elevation range can mitigate the extrapolation penalty. They also observe similar high-elevation extrapolation issues in TempEst 1.
supporting_quote: We thus recommend that TempEst 2 be used with caution when extrapolating to high elevations above 3,000 m (for the pre-trained model)
worsening median RMSE to 3.1 ◦C (from 2.0 ◦C) and adding a substantial bias, at a median of 25%
the performance penalty... is similar to TempEst 1

chunks.text: TempEst 2 embeds an assumption of static seasonal conditions by explicitly modeling a fixed seasonal cycle. This can limit fidelity under regime shifts that change the seasonal thermal regime without being directly reflected in short-term weather anomalies, such as changes in snowmelt timing. The anomaly term can address episodic weather events (e.g., heat waves) but cannot fully correct seasonal-cycle shifts. The authors suggest training on shorter intervals (5–10 years) to reduce stationarity concerns for historical analyses.
supporting_quote: The explicit embedding of seasonal conditions in TempEst 2 is based on the assumption of static seasonal conditions.
The anomaly component can account for a heat wave, but cannot account for shifting snowmelt timing
we suggest that users concerned with regime shifts could use a series of shorter intervals (e.g., 5–10 years) to train their models

chunks.text: The model is trained to USGS gage measurements, which may not represent a consistent cross-section mean temperature. The authors note predictions correspond to the gage’s location in the stream cross-section rather than a standardized measurement location like surface temperature. This introduces random variation that can inflate residual error independent of model structure. The issue is intrinsic to the available observational dataset used for training and validation.
supporting_quote: model predictions are based on wherever in the stream cross-section each gage was located, not a cross-section mean or consistent location... which introduces some random variation.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that TempEst 2 provides the first CONUS-wide daily stream temperature estimates at 1 km resolution, enabling higher-resolution large-domain analysis than previously available. The model is designed to work for ungaged locations with minimal data requirements and computational effort, including for small streams and urban areas. It is presented as complementary to more data-intensive or regionally limited models, trading some accuracy for scalability and ease of use. The authors also state it can be readily trained and applied outside the CONUS.
supporting_quote: TempEst 2... is the first model to provide highresolution (1 km), daily ST estimates across the entire CONUS
capable of estimating daily stream temperatures, for streams of all sizes and in urban areas across the CONUS, efficiently and with minimal data requirements
TempEst 2 can be readily trained for, and applied to, regions outside the CONUS and worldwide.

chunks.text: The authors emphasize robustness to practical constraints relevant for transfer beyond the CONUS, including shorter training periods and sparse gage networks. They state that performance remains robust with 5–10 year training periods and training networks as low as roughly 10–20 gages per million square kilometers. This supports the model’s intended use for large-domain historical analyses where dense monitoring is unavailable. The conclusion highlights generalization as a core contribution.
supporting_quote: The performance of TempEst 2 is robust with short (5–10 year) training periods
sparse (as low as 10–20 gages per million square kilometers) training gage networks.

chunks.text: Stream temperature changes have major ecological and human-use implications. Prior work shows land cover (e.g., riparian vegetation and urbanization), elevation, width, and climate factors can influence stream temperatures, but findings from local models may not generalize across regions. Large-scale modeling is challenged by data needs and computational burden, motivating approaches that leverage existing observation networks and remote sensing products.
supporting_quote: The influence of anthropogenic activity and land cover alteration on stream temperatures has major ecological implications, such as limiting fish survival.
These studies have consistently found that stream temperatures are sensitive to land cover impacts like riparian vegetation and urbanization.
This raises the fundamental challenge of collecting and processing enough data to run stream temperature models at very large (e.g. millions of square kilometers) scales.

chunks.text: Most of Earth’s stream length is made of small rivers, yet routine temperature observations are sparse for these systems despite extensive gage networks. Satellite data offer broad coverage, but common thermal infrared products (e.g., Landsat) remain too coarse to directly resolve narrow channels. This creates a gap in high-resolution temperature products for small rivers over large domains such as the contiguous United States.
supporting_quote: most smaller rivers lack routine temperature observations despite extensive gage networks.
even relatively high-resolution datasets (e.g., 30-m Landsat 8 data; USGS, 2023) are still too coarse to accurately study rivers smaller than 60–180 m in width
Rivers that are narrower than 60 m comprise roughly 97% of Earth's total stream length

chunks.text: Remote-sensing-based regression approaches can work when supported by sufficient gage density, and spatial stream-network models can be very accurate but can be computationally intensive and rely on dense observations and sometimes discharge. Existing prominent tools such as NorWeST demonstrate high accuracy for specific targets (e.g., August temperatures) but are limited in scope and often demand extensive training data. The paper positions a point-based, remote-sensing-driven approach as a complementary alternative emphasizing scalability and broad applicability.
supporting_quote: the Nor-WeST model (Isaak et al., 2017), which uses training data from ∼23,000 sites to model August stream temperatures
this approach, though highly effective, is computationally intensive, with reported computation times on the order of days to train NorWeST models.
remotely-sensed approaches can work without stream network data and therefore simplify the computation by analyzing each point independently.

chunks.text: The study asks how spatially distributed stream temperature information for small rivers can be made more accessible at large scale. It proposes a satellite-driven algorithm, TempEst, to estimate monthly mean stream temperatures for small (especially <60 m wide) rivers across the contiguous United States. The intent is to enable high-resolution seasonal analyses with minimal geospatial processing and without detailed watershed or hydrologic inputs.
supporting_quote: In this study, we ask: how can spatially-distributed stream temperature data for smaller rivers be made more accessible for any river across the globe?
develop an algorithm (''TempEst'') which estimates monthly stream temperatures for small (especially less than 60 m wide) rivers in the contiguous United States (CONUS).
Efficient nationalscale application is supported by the model architectural decision to use minimal, point-scale prediction data rather than full-watershed data.

chunks.text: Beyond model development, the study demonstrates an application to ecological management questions. Using TempEst predictions, it evaluates simple thermal suitability criteria for cutthroat trout at 100 ungaged locations in Colorado, illustrating how monthly estimates can inform habitat screening across many streams.
supporting_quote: We illustrate the application of TempEst to examine trends in a set of thermal suitability criteria for 100 ungaged locations in Colorado rivers for cutthroat trout (Oncorhynchus clarkii) habitat.
Monthly QRF models were used to investigate trends in the thermal suitability of Colorado, US rivers for trout.

chunks.text: Small rivers dominate stream networks but are under-observed for temperature, limiting large-scale analyses. While gage networks exist, they do not provide high spatial and temporal resolution coverage for small reaches, and many large regions lack modeled products for small streams. The paper frames this observation gap as a barrier to understanding land-use and climate effects across diverse geographies.
supporting_quote: rivers comprise a vast majority (∼97%) of total stream length, most smaller rivers lack routine temperature observations
most large regions including the contiguous United States do not have modeled data products at high spatial and temporal resolution for small rivers.

chunks.text: Existing stream temperature modeling approaches face tradeoffs that hinder global-to-national scale use. Process-based models can require flow and hydrologic inputs plus calibration, while interpolation and spatial network models can require concurrent observations, dense networks, and high computational cost. These constraints motivate methods that can run efficiently using widely available remote sensing data.
supporting_quote: high-accuracy, process-based stream temperature models ... depend on flow parameters such as surface runoff and subsurface flow, requiring extensive location-specific data
spatial interpolation of temperature timeseries ... depends on having concurrent observed timeseries for interpolation.
This approach, though highly effective, is computationally intensive, with reported computation times on the order of days to train NorWeST models.

chunks.text: Thermal infrared satellite products alone struggle for narrow rivers because pixels mix land and water signals. The paper notes that even 30 m Landsat remains too coarse for <60–180 m channels, and prior purely satellite-based estimates for small rivers can have large errors. This motivates fusing satellite LST with additional spatial predictors and machine learning.
supporting_quote: 30-m Landsat 8 data ... are still too coarse to accurately study rivers smaller than 60–180 m in width
purely satellite-based predictions with no field data have been found to have errors in the range of 7 ◦C (Handcock et al., 2006)

chunks.text: TempEst uses USGS in-stream temperature gage records paired with satellite and spatial predictors to train a machine learning model for monthly mean stream temperature. For each gage, the study retrieves land surface temperature, land cover, ecoregion, topography, and humidity, and then trains and evaluates a random forest approach. Models treat each gage-month as an independent supervised learning observation.
supporting_quote: we retrieved spatial data associated with the surrounding area ... including land surface temperature, land cover, Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) ecoregion, topography, and humidity.
Using these data, we trained, tuned, and tested a random forest model ... to estimate monthly mean stream temperatures.
For all models, each point and timestep (month) was considered as a discrete observation for supervised learning.

chunks.text: Predictor variables are largely summarized over a fixed spatial neighborhood to keep computation uniform across watersheds. Except for ecoregion and coordinates at the exact point, variables are averaged within a 1000 m radius around each gage. This choice targets bank coverage for retrieving land-only LST and yields an effective resolution of about 1 km for meaningful point-to-point variation.
supporting_quote: all variables were averaged over a 1000 m data collection radius around the gage location.
That radius was selected to ensure coverage of the river banks, in order to retrieve land-only land surface temperatures
based on the radius for which data are retrieved (1 km), its effective resolution is ∼1 km.

chunks.text: The study compares linear regression, generalized additive models, random forests, and quantile regression forests (QRF) using five-fold cross-validation. QRF is selected because it matches or outperforms alternatives in RMSE and offers conditional quantile outputs for uncertainty characterization (e.g., 5%, 50%, 95%). The final modeling strategy groups implementations by month.
supporting_quote: We tested the performance of linear regressions, general additive models ..., random forests ..., and quantile regression forests (QRF ... ) with five-fold cross-validation
the QRF model outperformed the linear regression and general additive models (GAM) and matched standard ... random forests with a median Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) by gage of 1.6 ◦C
All model implementations were grouped by month.

chunks.text: Hyperparameters are tuned using a grid search on a preliminary dataset to avoid overfitting while limiting computation. Most hyperparameters are found to be performance-insensitive, so defaults are retained. The main sensitivity is to mtry and sample size, with optima near defaults; a larger ntree mainly increases runtime.
supporting_quote: We optimized hyperparameters using a grid search over all combinations
Model performance was insensitive to most hyperparameters ... which were left at default values (5, true, and 500, respectively).
Performance was sensitive to mtry and sample size, but both were optimal near the default values

chunks.text: Feature importance is assessed using Mean Decrease in Accuracy from the R randomForest library. To understand controls within landscapes and seasons, the authors also create submodel schemes: monthly-only models and ecoregion-by-month models. Because subdividing improves runtime but ecoregion subdivision can reduce robustness in sparse regions, the final approach uses monthly submodels and selects a reduced predictor set.
supporting_quote: Feature importance was calculated using the default metric in the R randomForest library ... Mean Decrease in Accuracy.
we created two sub-models: one subdivided by month only, and one subdivided by both ecoregion and month.
we moved forward with monthly submodels to improve runtime while preserving robustness.

chunks.text: Model validation includes multiple stress tests beyond standard cross-validation. The study performs walk-forward validation by year, prediction for a long block (2001–2022) using early training years, leave-one-out validation over 16 contiguous spatial regions, a focused arid Southwest holdout, and an elevation extrapolation test by withholding gages above 1800 m. It also evaluates sensitivity to gage network density by training on random subsets (10–100%).
supporting_quote: we conducted a series of validation runs ... time frames without training data; contiguous regions without training data; elevation extremes without training data; and training gage network density.
we predicted 2001-2022 using a model trained on 1984-2000 and ran a walk-forward validation predicting each year from 1985-2022
To evaluate the importance of gage network density, we ran a five-fold cross-validation on randomly-selected subsets ... 10, 25, 50, 75, and 100%

chunks.text: An independent evaluation uses external observations primarily drawn from NorWeST processing units across diverse western environments, plus a small set of USGS gages not used in tuning. The authors subsample 10% of sites from selected NorWeST units to keep 1409 prediction points, and use RMSE as the comparison metric due to limited observations per site.
supporting_quote: an independent dataset not used for model design/tuning.
the bulk of this dataset (1409 sites) was retrieved from several NorWeST (Isaak et al., 2017) processing units
In the independent validation test, comparisons were based on RMSE, since the NorWeST observation sites typically had just a few observations each

chunks.text: Stream temperature observations come from USGS gages spanning 1984–2021 and covering a wide range of river sizes. The study initially retrieved 1300 locations, then removed sites lacking joint availability with remote sensing predictors, resulting in 1009 gages used for modeling. The number of active gages changes over time, from under 100 in 1984 to about 1000 in 2021.
supporting_quote: stream temperature gage data ... for 1300 locations in the United States between 1984 and 2021
resulting in the removal of 291 gages and leaving a final total of 1009 gages for use in this study.
the number of active training gages ranged from under 100 in 1984 to about 1000 in 2021.

chunks.text: Predictors combine satellite-derived temperature, land cover, vegetation, and gridded meteorology with location attributes. Inputs include Landsat-based land surface temperature (Ermida et al., 2020), ESA WorldCover land cover, EPA Level I ecoregions, USGS 3DEP elevation and aspect, MODIS NDVI, and a specific humidity dataset. Latitude and longitude are included as point coordinates.
supporting_quote: Independent variables and associated data sources ... Land surface temperature ... Land cover ... US EPA level I ecoregions ... Elevation ... Aspect ... NDVI ... Specific humidity ... Latitude and longitude
The land surface temperature algorithm ... uses Landsat ... 30 m ... 8- or 16-day
European Space Agency (2020) ... 10 m/single time

chunks.text: The Landsat land surface temperature product is built from a regression using thermal infrared brightness and emissivity and is validated in prior work. Its reported validation RMSE ranges from 1.4–3.7 °C, and the processing pipeline selects Landsat 8 (2014+), Landsat 7 (1999–2013), and Landsat 5 (1984–1998) based on year coverage. Monthly spatiotemporal means are used to match the study’s monthly prediction target.
supporting_quote: has a validation Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) in the range of 1.4–3.7 ◦C.
Landsat 8 from 2014 onwards, Landsat 7 from 1999–2013, and Landsat 5 from 1984–1998.
this study focuses on average monthly temperatures

chunks.text: Most predictors are aggregated over a 1000 m radius around each gage, and land surface temperature is computed both across the whole neighborhood and for land-only pixels (excluding water classes). Land cover is represented as 2020 abundances (fractions of area by class), while NDVI and weather variables use monthly means. The approach also derives an urban/non-urban label based on built-up fraction and an 'effective river width' proxy based on water abundance.
supporting_quote: all variables were averaged over a 1000 m data collection radius around the gage location.
Land surface temperature averages were measured across the data collection area as well as over area outside of the river channel
we computed an ''effective river width'' parameter ... defined as ... W = (pi/2) p_w · R

chunks.text: The training data span broad environmental gradients across CONUS and include many small streams. Land surface temperature covers about −50 to 50 °C, water temperature ranges from 0–60 °C, and gage elevation ranges from 0–3000 m. Water abundance indicates many narrow channels: about 60% of observations have abundance <4%, corresponding to an effective width around 60 m.
supporting_quote: Observed land surface temperature covered about −50 to 50 ◦C, water temperature ranged from 0–60 ◦C
gage elevation ranged from 0–3000 m
roughly 60% had abundance less than 4%, which is associated with an effective river width of about 60 m.

chunks.text: In preliminary model selection (2013–2021 development dataset), quantile regression forests provided the best overall accuracy compared to linear regression and generalized additive models. Median RMSE by gage is about 1.6 °C for the random forest approach, compared to 1.9 °C for GAM and 2.5 °C for linear regression. Median R² is also higher for the random forest (0.97) than for GAM (0.95) and linear regression (0.90).
supporting_quote: random forest model had a median RMSE of 1.6 ◦C, compared to 1.9 ◦C for the general additive model and 2.5 ◦C for the linear regression.
the random forest model had a median 2 of 0.97, compared to 0.95 for the general additive model and 0.90 for the linear regression.

chunks.text: Hyperparameter tuning indicates that most QRF settings have little influence on accuracy, and default values are generally adequate. Performance is mainly sensitive to mtry and sample size, but both are best near default settings. Increasing the number of trees primarily affects runtime, so the study retains default ntree in tuning, then uses higher ntree in the final monthly models.
supporting_quote: most hyperparameters were insensitive and had little effect on performance.
Performance was sensitive to mtry and sample size, but both were optimal near the default values
Increasing ntree mainly resulted in increasing runtime

chunks.text: The final tuned monthly QRFs achieve strong out-of-sample performance across CONUS in five-fold cross-validation. Median RMSE across gages is 1.5 °C with NSE 0.94 and R² 0.97, and percent bias is near zero (−0.2%). Training error is much lower (about 0.3 °C), highlighting the gap between in-sample fit and generalization.
supporting_quote: had a median RMSE, NSE, coefficient of determination, and percent bias ... of 1.5 ◦C, 0.94, 0.97, and −0.2%, respectively
For comparison, the median training RMSE was about 0.3 ◦C.

chunks.text: Accuracy varies by ecoregion but biases remain small. Median RMSE by ecoregion ranges roughly from 0.8–2.0 °C, with median R² about 0.88–0.98. The paper notes that excluding many land-cover variables, slope aspect, or even ecoregion often does not meaningfully reduce performance, while key predictors provide most of the gain.
supporting_quote: The median RMSE and R2 by ecoregion ranged from approximately 0.8–2.0 ◦C and 0.88–0.98, respectively.
All ecoregions had near-zero median bias (less than approximately 5%)
performance were not meaningfully impacted by excluding most land cover data, slope aspect, or ecoregion.

chunks.text: Model error varies seasonally, with larger errors during warmer months. Grouping by month shows median RMSE ranging from about 1–1.7 °C, with higher errors in summer and lower errors in winter. This aligns with seasonal temperature dynamics that are harder to predict during peak warming periods.
supporting_quote: Grouping by month ... shows that median RMSE ranges from about 1–1.7 ◦C by month, with higher errors in the summer and lower errors in the winter

chunks.text: Independent validation using NorWeST sites and unused USGS gages shows performance comparable to cross-validation for the western U.S., where the model tends to perform worse. Overall median RMSE in the independent dataset is 1.9 °C, similar to the western-CONUS cross-validation median of 1.8 °C. Median bias in the independent validation is 5%.
supporting_quote: In the independentdataset validation ... overall median RMSE was worse than general cross-validation, at 1.9 ◦C
this was comparable to the median RMSE of 1.8 ◦C for cross-validation gages in the western CONUS
Median bias in the independent validation was 5%.

chunks.text: Quantile predictions are well calibrated, suggesting useful uncertainty information even when median errors exist. In cross-validation, the median gage has 98% of observations within the predicted 95% interval, and most gages exceed 95% coverage. This supports using QRF outputs for confidence intervals in downstream analyses.
supporting_quote: predicted quantiles are extremely reliable.
with a median of 98% of observations within the confidence interval.
the majority of gages had more than 95% of observations within the predicted 95% confidence interval

chunks.text: Spatial holdout tests show modest degradation when predicting contiguous regions without training data. Leave-one-out cross-validation over 16 regions increases median RMSE by about 0.4 °C to 1.9 °C; two regions reach 2.5–3 °C, but biases remain near zero (absolute median bias <1%). A specific arid Southwest holdout yields median RMSE 2.4 °C with median bias −3%.
supporting_quote: median RMSE increased by about 0.4 ◦C to 1.9 ◦C, with two regions' median RMSE reaching 2.5–3 ◦C
All regions retained near-zero bias, with absolute median biases of less than 1%.
arid Southwest validation region ... median RMSE of 2.4 ◦C ... median bias of −3%.

chunks.text: Performance scales with training gage density, with diminishing returns at high density. At 10% gage network density (about 10 gages per 1,000,000 km²), median RMSE is around 2.0 °C while median bias remains near zero (about −0.03%). As density increases to 100%, median RMSE approaches a limit near 1.5 °C, suggesting the USGS network is near optimal for CONUS-scale modeling.
supporting_quote: At 10% gage network density, or about 10 gages per 1,000,000 km2 ... median RMSE was around 2.0 ◦C
median bias ... centered on about −0.03%.
With increasing gage network density up to 100%, median RMSE tended towards a limit of about 1.5 ◦C

chunks.text: Temporal generalization is strong once the gage network becomes sufficiently dense. In walk-forward validation, predicting one year ahead for 2001–2022 yields median RMSE 1.1 °C with median R² 0.98 and median percent bias −0.4%. Early years with sparse training (1985–1986) have higher RMSE (2.3–2.5 °C) but drop to 1–1.5 °C by 1990 and remain stable thereafter.
supporting_quote: In the walk-forward validation ... prediction years from 2001–2022, was 1.1 ◦C.
The median R2 was 0.98 and the median percent bias was −0.4%.
median RMSE was 2.3–2.5 ◦C for 1985 and 1986 ... but dropped into the range of 1–1.5 ◦C by 1990

chunks.text: A major limitation is missing predictors that govern stream temperature but are not readily obtained by satellite remote sensing. The large gap between training and testing RMSE (0.3 °C vs 1.5 °C) suggests omitted variables, and the authors highlight the inability to include drainage area or discharge. The model also does not explicitly represent downstream dam effects, and training labels reflect the unknown position/measurement characteristics of each gage rather than a standardized temperature definition.
supporting_quote: The large gap between training and testing performance (RMSE of 0.3 ◦C vs 1.5 ◦C) indicates a possible lack of some important predictors in the model
it is unable to incorporate a variety of important hydrologic data, such as drainage area or discharge
the inherent uncertainty of training gage position: the model is trained to wherever each gage happened to be

chunks.text: The reliance on random forests imposes theoretical constraints on extrapolation. The paper notes random forests are unsuitable for extrapolation, which likely contributes to weaker performance at high elevations where training coverage is limited. Empirically, the model works across most temperature ranges because training coverage is broad for key variables, but extrapolation beyond CONUS or to extremes may require local training data.
supporting_quote: the use of a random forest model is a fundamental theoretical limitation because such models are unsuitable for extrapolation
This likely plays a role in the weaker model performance at high elevation
the model would require local training data for use outside of CONUS

chunks.text: TempEst is better suited for large-sample analyses than for single-reach inference because typical errors can mask small trends. The authors caution that an RMSE of 1.5 °C can conceal year-to-year changes at a point or short-distance gradients along a reach, and individual rivers may show notable bias. They argue aggregate analyses become more reliable because the mean error is near zero and does not correlate strongly with predictors.
supporting_quote: At a finer scale, the errors may overwhelm useful information
An RMSE of 1.5 ◦C is quite likely, for example, to conceal year-to-year temperature trends for individual locations
since the error has a mean of approximately zero and does not correlate with any predictor variables to any meaningful extent

chunks.text: Model robustness declines at high elevations and should be treated cautiously there. While the authors note this may not be critical for many applications because most CONUS land is below 3000 m and human activity is limited at high altitude, the validation shows sizable penalties in error and bias for withheld high-elevation gages. Future work is suggested to address elevation-related shifts in thermal behavior.
supporting_quote: the model is notably less robust to extrapolation in elevation and should be used with caution in higher elevation rivers
median highaltitude RMSE of 3 ◦C and bias of 17%
the overwhelming majority of CONUS land area falls below 3000 m

chunks.text: The paper positions TempEst as complementary to network-based models like NorWeST, reflecting a tradeoff between information content and operational efficiency. Point-based modeling avoids stream-network processing and fixes the area of interest to 3.14 km², enabling all-month predictions at effective ~1 km resolution but limiting representation of watershed-wide processes. Thus, TempEst trades some accuracy for minimal data requirements and computational efficiency.
supporting_quote: TempEst complements the NorWeST dataset and model by providing predictions for all months of the year, for all of CONUS, with orders of magnitude reduced runtime.
the area of interest is always 3.14 km2 regardless of watershed area.
TempEst selects seasonal-focused (monthly) temporal resolution and trades off some accuracy in exchange for operational advantages

chunks.text: The study concludes that TempEst provides an efficient, remote-sensing-driven approach to estimating monthly stream temperatures across CONUS, including very small streams. It reports performance comparable to typical satellite LST uncertainty and to other large-domain statistical approaches while requiring minimal inputs and computation. The authors argue this improves accessibility of stream temperature information for large-scale analyses and can be adapted to other regions given training gage data.
supporting_quote: The resulting model, TempEst, matched the performance of machine-learning-based, local air temperature models
TempEst ran orders of magnitude faster than spatial statistical network models.
the developed model ... will facilitate the study of stream temperature behaviors ... across the contiguous United States and can be easily adapted to support global river systems.

chunks.text: The paper emphasizes that TempEst supports seasonal and spatial comparisons over broad extents rather than detailed reach-scale inference. With median validation RMSE around 1.5 °C and low overall bias, it is intended for aggregating patterns across many streams, enabling applications such as habitat screening and temperature trend analyses where field data are locally lacking.
supporting_quote: TempEst's median validation RMSE of about 1.5 ◦C
it is suitable for estimating temperatures in sparsely-gaged regions within a gage network
the error has a mean of approximately zero

chunks.text: River flooding is a major and growing hazard, and the discharge a channel can convey before overtopping depends strongly on channel geometry. Across the world, alluvial rivers show consistent downstream hydraulic geometry (DHG) scaling between bankfull discharge and channel dimensions, enabling estimation of width from discharge. However, reach-scale and cross-site variability around these empirical scalings complicates forecasting flood inundation and designing infrastructure or restoration projects.
supporting_quote: River flooding represents a significant and growing natural hazard globally
Alluvial rivers across the world exhibit remarkably consistent geometric scaling with increasing water discharge often referred to as hydraulic geometry

chunks.text: The Near-Threshold Channel (NTC) model provides a physical explanation for bankfull channel geometry by balancing sediment transport on the bed with bank stability at bankfull discharge. This framework supports an expected square-root relationship between bankfull discharge (Qbf) and bankfull width (Wbf). The model does not fully explain the observed scatter about the width–discharge trend, motivating analysis of additional controls and stochastic variability.
supporting_quote: The Near‐Threshold Channel (NTC) model provides a physically based, experimentally verified, and field‐validated model for alluvial channel geometry
The relation between bankfull discharge (Qbf) and width (Wbf) is well described by a square root relation

chunks.text: Bankfull width varies within river reaches and among rivers with similar bankfull discharges, and this variability has been attributed to multiple interacting factors (e.g., vegetation, hydroclimate, sediment supply, bank properties). The complexity and interdependence of these factors makes it difficult to identify dominant mechanisms. A key step toward progress is accurately quantifying reach-scale variability and linking it to hydrologic statistics.
supporting_quote: Variation in bankfull width has been observed both at the reach‐scale for a given channel and across channels with similar bankfull discharges
observed variations may result from a variety of processes and feedbacks

chunks.text: The study aims to quantify reach-scale variability in bankfull river width using high-resolution lidar-derived measurements across many sites. It seeks a probabilistic description of width within reaches and then evaluates whether deviations from mean width–discharge scaling relate to hydrologic regime. The work specifically tests whether flow duration above bankfull (intermittency) and related climate signals help explain why some channels are wider or narrower than expected for the same bankfull discharge.
supporting_quote: Here we quantify width variability in relation to hydrological variability by utilizing high‐resolution lidar topography to extract bankfull width at the reach‐scale.

Finally, we explore potential climatic and hydrological sources of the variation between rivers and find that river systems where bankfull flow is exceeded for a greater portion of the total hydrograph are wider for the same bankfull flow.

chunks.text: A central objective is to move beyond purely empirical DHG scaling by examining whether reach-scale variability has a common distribution that can be incorporated into models. By characterizing the distribution of widths within each reach, the authors aim to provide a practical statistical framework for representing uncertainty in channel geometry. This supports comparisons among rivers and potential incorporation into network-scale hydraulic geometry applications.
supporting_quote: We find that reach‐scale variability for bankfull river width can be quantified probabilistically through a lognormal probability distribution.
The determination of a common reach‐scale probability distribution allows for several practical analyses such as the inclusion of variability into downstream hydraulic geometry network models

chunks.text: Physics-based and empirical models can predict average bankfull geometry trends but do not explain the magnitude of observed variability around those trends. At the reach scale, channels can deviate substantially, and some rivers may be far wider than others for the same bankfull discharge. This unexplained scatter hinders reliable flood hazard forecasting and understanding how channels might adjust under changing hydroclimate or engineering controls.
supporting_quote: Physics-based models predict the average relationship between bankfull geometry and discharge to within an order of magnitude, however, observed variability about the prediction remains unaccounted for.
some channels are adjusted to be 10 times wider than others for the same bankfull discharge

chunks.text: A limitation of existing approaches is insufficient quantification of within-reach variability, which is necessary to determine channel response to climate or engineered flow-regime changes. The NTC model, as a first-order solution, does not represent within-reach variability in width or depth. This leaves a gap in connecting detailed morphology to mechanistic interpretations of flow and sediment thresholds.
supporting_quote: As a first‐ order solution, the NTC model does not account for within reach variability in bankfull width or depth

Quantifying the inherent stochasticity and sources of variability for channel size remains an essential unknown for determining how channels respond to climatic and/or engineered changes in the flow regime.

chunks.text: The authors selected 67 river reaches spanning the conterminous United States and Puerto Rico from a larger compilation and restricted reaches to avoid significant tributary inputs. Lidar point clouds from OpenTopography were processed into 1-m DEMs, and banks and centerlines were manually digitized based on elevation breaks and imagery. Width was computed every 2–5 m along the centerline by estimating local downstream direction via OLS regression and projecting orthogonal lines to the banks; erroneous large widths from curvature/bar effects were filtered.
supporting_quote: we selected 67 river reaches for high‐resolution analysis spanning the conterminous United States and Puerto Rico
All lidar point clouds were processed using OpenTopography's built‐in tools to produce a 1‐m DEM
River width is calculated at 2–5‐m (the 2‐m window is used for narrower rivers) intervals
Ordinary least squares (OLS) linear regression was used to determine the local downstream direction

chunks.text: To evaluate effects beyond discharge, the study computed width deviations (Wdev) for the full compilation by measuring distance from a LOWESS fit to ln-transformed discharge and width. Wdev was defined as ln(Wbf/Wbf-LOWESS), using geometric-mean Wbf for high-resolution sites. This approach makes deviations approximately symmetric and provides a scale-independent indicator of whether a site is wider or narrower than average at its discharge.
supporting_quote: we calculated the width deviations (Wdev) for all 1,372 sites within the compilation as the distance from a locally weighted LOWESS trend line (fraction = 0.25)
Wdev = ln(Wbf / Wbf‐LOWESS)

chunks.text: Hydrologic controls were assessed using USGS instantaneous (15-min) discharge records, because daily averages underrepresent peaks and durations in small catchments. Sites with less than 5 years of data were removed, leaving 544 sites (including 50 high-resolution sites) for hydrograph analysis. The authors tested correlations between Wdev and multiple normalized flow metrics, focusing on bankfull intermittency (Ibf) defined as the exceedance probability (time fraction) at which Qbf occurs.
supporting_quote: downloaded US Geological Survey (USGS) instantaneous hydrographs (15‐min resolution)
daily average discharge records do not accurately represent the hydrograph for smaller catchments
Sites were removed from the hydrograph analysis if the hydrograph record contained less than 5 years of data
leaving a total of 544 sites for the hydrograph analysis including 50 high‐resolution sites
Bankfull intermittency is calculated as the probability of exceedance at which the bankfull flow occurred for each hydrograph

chunks.text: Because Ibf is relatively independent of watershed scale compared to Qmean/Qbf, intermittency was used to explore potential climatic dependence. The authors related intermittency to bankfull runoff (Qbf/DA) and computed an aridity index at each gage as Ai = P/PET using 30-year normal precipitation and potential evapotranspiration datasets. This allowed joint interpretation of width deviations with runoff, intermittency, and water availability.
supporting_quote: We use intermittency when exploring the potential climatic dependence of the flow metrics because Ibf is independent of runoff and watershed scale
bankfull runoff, Qbf/DA

The aridity index (Ai ) is calculated as a point value at each gage as the ratio of the 30‐year normal mean annual precipitation (P... ) over the potential evapotranspiration (PET... ). Note that the aridity index (Ai = P/PET)

chunks.text: High-resolution width measurements were derived for 67 sites selected from a larger bankfull discharge/geometry compilation. Selected sites span 1.3 < Qbf < 2,607 m3/s, and reaches were chosen to avoid major tributary inputs. The resulting product is a spatial series of bankfull width measurements per site derived from 1-m lidar DEMs.
supporting_quote: we selected 67 river reaches for high‐resolution analysis
bankfull discharges (1.3 < Qbf < 2,607 m3 /s)
All lidar point clouds were processed... to produce a 1‐m DEM
The resulting data set (Phillips, 2024) represents a spatial series of bankfull channel width for each site

chunks.text: The wider compilation contains n = 1,372 bankfull discharge and geometry measurements used to define the LOWESS width–discharge expectation and compute Wdev. For flow-regime analysis, USGS instantaneous (15-min) hydrographs were assembled for sites with current or historical discharge data, initially n = 846. After removing short or poor-quality records, 544 sites remained, with the remaining hydrographs having a median of 34 years of data (IQR = 9 years).
supporting_quote: from a data compilation (n = 1,372) comprised of bankfull discharge and channel geometry measurements
downloaded US Geological Survey (USGS) instantaneous hydrographs (15‐min resolution)... (n = 846)
leaving a total of 544 sites for the hydrograph analysis
The remaining hydrographs have a median of 34 years of data (IQR = 9 years).

chunks.text: Sampling density within reaches was high: widths were measured every 2–5 m, yielding on average about 500 measurements per kilometer. Reach lengths averaged 109 times the geometric mean width and ranged from 0.54 to 10.88 km (24–408 times mean width). This design supports estimation of within-reach distributions rather than single-point width values.
supporting_quote: River width is calculated at 2–5‐m... intervals
contain on average ∼500 measurements per kilometer
a site length of 109 times the geometric mean width and range from 0.54 to 10.88 km (24–408 times the mean width)

chunks.text: Within individual reaches, bankfull width is typically well described by a lognormal distribution: after ln transformation, most sites are unimodal and often symmetric. Central tendency and spread are effectively captured by the geometric mean (GM) and geometric standard deviation (GStD). This provides a probabilistic representation of reach-scale width rather than a single deterministic value.
supporting_quote: Within an individual reach, bankfull river width is well-described by a lognormal distribution.
reach‐scale bankfull width is typically unimodally (62/67 sites) and symmetrically distributed (49/67 sites) following a natural‐log transformation
Each site's central tendency and variation is well‐described by the geometric mean (GM) and geometric standard deviation (GStD)

chunks.text: Reach-scale variability in bankfull width has a near-constant geometric standard deviation across sites. The average GStD is about 1.2 with a range of 1.08–1.5, implying similar relative variability independent of scale. Standardized ln-width PDFs across all sites align well with a normal distribution, reinforcing the lognormal model for width.
supporting_quote: The reach‐scale GStD is effectively constant across all sites with an average value of 1.2 (range of 1.08– 1.5).
Following standardization, the reach‐scale results are well‐described by a normal probability distribution

chunks.text: Within-reach variability is smaller than the overall scatter about the continental width–discharge trend. When error bars based on within-reach GStD are added to geometric-mean widths, the spread remains less than the deviations around the width–discharge relationship. This indicates that between-site differences, not just within-reach fluctuations, contribute substantially to the observed scatter in hydraulic geometry.
supporting_quote: Incorporating error about the mean Wbf value for each high‐resolution site indicates that variability within a reach is less than the observed variability (scatter) about the width‐discharge scaling trend

chunks.text: Width deviations (Wdev) increase with bankfull intermittency (Ibf): rivers that spend more time at or above bankfull tend to be wider than expected for their bankfull discharge. For the high-resolution subset (n = 50), a least squares power relation is reported with R2 = 0.35. This identifies flow duration/frequency above bankfull as a hydrologic correlate of cross-site width variability.
supporting_quote: Deviations in bankfull width scale with the bankfull intermittency
Blue points represent Wdev for the geometric mean of the high-resolution sites (n = 50)
The solid blue line represents a least squares fit power relation to the high-resolution sites (R2 = 0.35)
Rivers that spend a greater proportion of time above bankfull are wider for the same bankfull discharge

chunks.text: Among tested flow metrics, normalized geometric mean flow and mid-to-low flow percentiles show the strongest correlations with Wdev in the high-resolution sites. Reported Pearson correlations include rmean = 0.67 and r25 = 0.67, while intermittency shows rI = 0.59; peak flow has much weaker association (rpeak = 0.17). Regression examples include Wdev = 1.97 (Qmean/Qbf)^0.22 (R2 = 0.45) and Wdev = 2 Ibf^0.14 (R2 = 0.35).
supporting_quote: The strongest correlations... occurred for the geometric mean flow and 25% flow (rmean = 0.67 and r25 = 0.67 ), followed by the bankfull intermittency (rI = 0.59
r99 = 0.56, and rpeak = 0.17

chunks.text: Bankfull intermittency is not fixed across regions and appears scale independent in the sense that bankfull discharge does not occur at a constant percentile. In the compilation, intermittency can be collapsed by considering bankfull runoff (Qbf/DA), and intermittency exhibits a consistent negative power-law correlation with Qbf/DA. For the high-resolution sites, Ibf ranges from 0.00019 to 0.28.
supporting_quote: Bankfull intermittency appears to be scale independent when viewed over multiple climatic regions as the bankfull flow does not occur at a fixed flow percentile.
Intermittency... can be collapsed by considering the ratio of bankfull discharge and drainage area (bankfull runoff, Qbf/DA ).
Intermittency possesses a consistent negative power-law correlation with Qbf/DA
For the high-resolution sites Ibf ranges from 0.00019 to 0.28.

chunks.text: Runoff and aridity relate systematically to intermittency and width deviations, indicating a climatic imprint on channel geometry. Catchments with high runoff and wetter climates (higher Ai) spend the lowest fraction of time above bankfull and tend to be narrower than expected. Lower-runoff, drier climates have higher intermittency and wider-than-expected channels for the same bankfull discharge.
supporting_quote: gages with high runoff and wetter climates spend the lowest portion of their record above the bankfull level, and channels are narrower than expected.
Lower runoff sites occur in drier climates where a greater proportion of the hydrograph occurs during above bank flows, and channels are wider than expected
The aridity index (Ai = P/PET)

chunks.text: Some reaches deviate from unimodal lognormal behavior, often due to prominent bars, islands, or multi-thread features that create secondary peaks when widths are measured bank-to-bank. The authors attempted to avoid multi-threaded sections, but where present, outer-bank width can misrepresent effective wetted width. Experimental guidance suggests that braided/islanded cases should consider the sum of wetted widths rather than outer bank-to-bank distance.
supporting_quote: Non‐unimodal sites often exhibit a secondary peak... due to the presence of prominent lateral and mid‐channel bars or islands
The unimodal distributions are limited to single threaded reaches
incorporating islands or multi‐threaded channels should consider the sum of the total wetted widths rather than the outer bank‐to‐bank distance

chunks.text: Width extraction can produce erroneous large values in curved or bar-dominated sections when the local centerline direction causes orthogonal projections to point partly downstream. The study manually checked sites and filtered these errors, but the issue highlights sensitivity to planform complexity and the method’s assumptions. Such geometric artifacts can affect tail behavior of width distributions if not filtered.
supporting_quote: The calculation of larger than expected widths can occur where the local centerline direction deviates from the reach‐scale downstream direction
We analyze each high‐resolution site for these errors and filter out the larger erroneous measurements.

chunks.text: The lidar-derived DEMs generally lack bathymetry, preventing comparable high-resolution measurements of bankfull depth (Hbf). The authors infer depth behavior indirectly: continuity and hydraulic geometry suggest depth may mirror width and be lognormally distributed. This limits direct evaluation of how width variability couples with depth and velocity at reach scale.
supporting_quote: The majority of lidar‐derived DEMs don't include bathymetry, as such we are presently unable to produce a high‐resolution analysis of bankfull depth (Hbf).
However, continuity and hydraulic geometry indicates that depth may mirror width and be lognormally distributed as well.

chunks.text: Hydrograph metrics are inter-correlated, complicating causal interpretation of which aspect of flow regime drives width deviations. Although multiple correlations are significant, explained variance and regression exponents are low, indicating modest effects and likely missing controls. The paper notes that experiments with mobile channels and variable hydrographs are needed to disentangle flow-duration, sediment supply, and threshold-history mechanisms.
supporting_quote: the overall explained variance and regression exponents are relatively low indicating a moderate to modest effect.
A challenge with interpreting the various hydrograph metrics is that they are all inter‐correlated with each other.
Experiments with mobile channels and variable hydrographs are likely necessary to untangle the interrelations within a hydrograph and the reason for channel change.

chunks.text: The mechanism linking intermittency and width deviations remains unresolved, limiting predictive power under changing climates or management. The authors suggest plausible pathways (e.g., increased transport time, bank erosion frequency, history-dependent bed thresholds), but cannot test others like grain size due to data limitations. This motivates development of mechanistic models incorporating full hydrograph complexity and sediment-transport dynamics.
supporting_quote: Despite lacking a clear mechanism, these results indicate that flow intermittency and duration are potential dials that could be adjusted
The absence of a clear mechanism for channel variation and dynamic adjustment highlights the pressing need for a mechanistic understanding

chunks.text: The study concludes that reach-scale bankfull width variability can be represented with a lognormal distribution, enabling probabilistic treatment of channel geometry. It also concludes that deviations from average width–discharge scaling correlate positively with hydrograph metrics, especially the duration/frequency of flows above bankfull. These results imply that climate and flow-regime changes can influence channel geometry even when bankfull discharge is unchanged.
supporting_quote: we have demonstrated that reach‐scale bankfull variation in channel width can be quantified with a lognormal probability distribution.
Variations in width from observed DHG scaling are positively correlated with metrics of hydrograph flow
Rivers that spend a greater proportion of time above bankfull are wider for the same bankfull discharge

chunks.text: The authors infer a climatic imprint on river geometry through correlations among bankfull intermittency, runoff, and basin aridity, suggesting that wetter climates tend to have lower intermittency and narrower-than-expected channels. They emphasize relevance to managed rivers below dams and to climate-driven shifts in flood duration and frequency. Better mechanistic understanding is identified as necessary for robust prediction of future flood hazards.
supporting_quote: Bankfull flow intermittency, runoff, and basin aridity are correlated, representing an imprint of climate on river geometry
Changes to riparian morphology and habitats in rivers below dams, and in regions experiencing climate‐induced changes in flood frequency, could be more robustly predicted
Without such a model, a dynamic channel prone to threshold changes poses a significant challenge for predicting flooding hazards under uncertain future climates.

chunks.text: Flood maps translate river flow into actionable information about who and what is at risk, and they support early warning systems that reduce losses. Satellite observations provide global information for observing floods directly and for training data-driven methods that synthesize inundation maps. The paper situates this work in the context of widespread flood impacts and uneven availability of adequate early warning systems worldwide.
supporting_quote: Flood maps are a crucial tool to translate what, for most, is an abstract number indicating river flow into a more understandable and actionable representation of who and what is at risk.

Early warning systems for flooding events have been shown to reduce loss of life and property during flooding events [3], yet in many areas of the world, adequate early warning systems do not exist [4].
Satellites provide a global source of information that can be used to directly observe flooding or as a training dataset for regression methods to synthesize flood maps.

chunks.text: FIER is a data-driven approach that forecasts flood inundation maps by extracting spatial and temporal flood patterns from historical satellite imagery and correlating them with historical flows. It selects the most correlated discharge time series within a scene and builds regression equations to synthesize flood signals into flood inundation maps. Prior FIER applications include multiple large basins and floodplains, indicating transferability when satellite observations and discharge inputs are available.
supporting_quote: We will use the Forecasting Inundation Extents using the REOF (Rotated Empirical Orthogonal Function) Analysis (FIER) model [13].
FIER forecasts flooding inundation maps (FIM) by first extracting spatial and temporal patterns of floods from historical imagery.
It creates a regression equation that can use forecasted flows from the correlated station(s) and generate synthetic satellite imagery...

chunks.text: Satellite imagery suitability for flood mapping depends on sensor limitations including distortions and the tradeoff between spatial and temporal resolution. Optical imagery has frequent coverage but is affected by cloud masking and coarser resolution, while SAR can image through clouds at fine resolution but has revisit and coverage constraints. These characteristics shape whether floods are observed coincident with satellite acquisitions and whether events are discernable at the sensor resolution.
supporting_quote: Issues arise from atmospheric interference, cloud cover, backscattering, and topographical distortions [18].
The finer spatial resolution of the SAR images, 10 m, allows for much smaller rivers and flood events to be imaged.
Because the VIIRS sensors cannot penetrate cloud cover, they often have missing information, especially during flood events.

chunks.text: The study’s goal is to develop processes to determine which locations are suitable for creating satellite-based synthetic flood inundation maps using different satellites. It evaluates suitability for both SAR (Sentinel-1) and optical (JPSS VIIRS) imagery in the context of FIER, and tests whether these suitability categorizations align with actual FIER model performance. A further objective is to reduce reliance on gauge locations by training FIER with large-scale hydrologic model outputs (GEOGLOWS and NWM).
supporting_quote: the purpose of this research is to take a broader view and develop processes and methods to determine which areas are suitable for satellite-based synthetic flood models with different satellites.

we will evaluate areas that are suitable for satellite-based models using Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery from the Sentinel-1 satellites and Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) optical imagery
To determine which locations are viable for satellite-based flood mapping, we created FIER test cases using GEOGLOWS and NWM data.

chunks.text: A specific aim is to determine whether flood events are captured by satellite acquisitions frequently enough to support model training and to quantify the maximum flood magnitudes (via return period classes) likely usable for SAR-based synthetic FIM. For VIIRS, the goal is to produce a suitability metric based on observed flood occurrence frequency relative to permanent water. These tools are intended as screening methods to identify promising domains for synthetic FIM development.
supporting_quote: we created suitability processes to determine the locations that have flood events that were captured in satellite imagery and, therefore, were likely suitable for model creation.
we were able to determine the maximum return period that an area would be suitable for creating a SAR-derived synthetic FIM.
we derived a mean flood occurrence metric that effectively captures relative suitability for model generation.

chunks.text: Synthetic flood map generation methods require both hydrologic data and satellite observations of historical flooding, but many locations lack adequate stream gauges and/or suitable imagery capturing floods. Satellite limitations include cloud masking for optical sensors, revisit and mission coverage constraints for SAR, and sensor artifacts that complicate consistent water detection. These constraints reduce the chance that flooding is observed at times coincident with satellite acquisitions and at scales discernable given sensor resolution.
supporting_quote: they all require a source of satellite data and hydrological data.
Gauges are the preferred source of historical flow data... The biggest limitation of gauge data is that they are not available globally
For the satellite images to be most useful, the flooding must occur at a time coincident with the satellite's acquisitions and be extensive enough to be discernable, given the satellite's resolution.

chunks.text: Sentinel-1 SAR practical global suitability is reduced by operational tasking limits and reduced coverage after Sentinel-1B failed. Although theoretical revisit may be frequent, the operational baseline does not provide continuous global coverage and prioritizes Europe. This creates regions with few or no acquisitions, limiting the ability to capture a range of flood magnitudes needed for robust regression-based synthesis.
supporting_quote: data in Figure 3 are not accurate because each satellite is limited to 30 min of IW band capturing each orbit.
The satellites prioritize Europe and with the failure of Sentinel-1B, no longer have enough coverage to image the entire globe.
Notably, several regions of the globe no longer receive any images.

chunks.text: For VIIRS optical imagery, suitability is limited by coarse spatial resolution and cloud masking. Small streams may not be detectable at 375 m resolution, and clouded pixels yield no-data that can mask large areas when aggregating many images. These issues require careful thresholding and image-quality filtering when attempting to train FIER models from VIIRS water fractions.
supporting_quote: the coarser spatial resolution of the VIIRS images, 375 m, means smaller streams are not visible in the imagery.
Because the VIIRS sensors cannot penetrate cloud cover, they often have missing information, especially during flood events.
All pixels that have no data values in any image we use for calibrating the FIER model are removed from the final model.

chunks.text: The SAR-derived suitability workflow estimates feasibility of SAR-based synthetic FIM by matching Sentinel-1 image footprints to sampled river reaches and labeling each acquisition with modeled streamflow return period. The method uses GEOGLOWS retrospective daily discharge and classifies each image into return period bins (<2, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100 years). A reach’s suitability is then assigned based on the maximum return period observed while also requiring at least one observation in each preceding return period class to ensure coverage across flow ranges.
supporting_quote: We evaluated which areas were suitable for SAR-derived synthetic FIM.
We selected test areas around the world, and matched each image with the streamflow, then classified them into return periods.
We assigned every reach into a category based on the maximum return period of flow that it had observed, with at least one observation in every preceding return period category.

chunks.text: To approximate detectability and manage computation for SAR suitability, the study filters to larger rivers using Strahler stream order five or greater and samples 4700 diverse reaches globally. For each reach, the centroid is intersected with SAR image boundaries to obtain acquisition timing and identifiers without downloading full images. Lakes are excluded using a global lakes/wetlands dataset because lake inundation is not governed by streamflow and GEOGLOWS reports streamflow for lakes.
supporting_quote: As a substitute for river width, we filtered the river reaches to Strahler stream order five or greater [37].
This gave us a set of 4700 reaches to test that were spread across the globe on larger rivers.
We excluded any points that were inside of lakes using the World Wildlife Foundation's Global Lakes and Wetlands Dataset [39] because GEOGLOWS reports streamflow data for lakes

chunks.text: The VIIRS-derived suitability workflow creates flood-frequency rasters from daily VIIRS water fraction imagery, then aggregates them to modeling domains based on grouped catchments. VIIRS daily tiles are mosaicked into one image per day, converted to percent water fraction (open water set to 100%), and clouded pixels treated as no-data. Permanent water is derived from the JRC dataset, resampled to VIIRS resolution by averaging 30 m pixels within each 375 m pixel, enabling comparison in water-fraction space.
supporting_quote: We merged (mosaic-ed) the images (tiles) for each day into a single image. This resulted in 3529 daily images.
we changed the open water to represent 100% water and kept only the water fraction.
we resampled it to the VIIRS resolution by taking the mean of the JRC Permanent Water pixels inside of each VIIRS pixel.

chunks.text: Flooding in VIIRS is defined via a flood fraction threshold (FFT) above the local permanent water fraction. The process tests FFT values from 0% to 100% at 5% intervals by adding each FFT to the permanent-water fraction image to form threshold images. For each day, a pixel is counted as flooding if it exceeds its threshold, producing flood-occurrence rasters across the study period for each FFT.
supporting_quote: We assumed that flooding occurs when water is present in a certain fraction of the pixel above what it normally occupies. We will call this value the flood fraction threshold (FFT).
we ran the process with FFTs ranging from 0% to 100% at 5% intervals.
To determine the frequency of flooding, we counted the number of times each VIIRS pixel exceeded the flood threshold image.

chunks.text: To associate VIIRS flood frequency with river domains, the study groups GEOGLOWS catchments by contiguous areas of the same Strahler stream order (>=5), creating ~12,250 candidate model areas (average aggregation of 11 reaches). For each flood-frequency raster (per FFT), mean reduction by region computes the mean number of flood occurrences per catchment group, enabling comparability across differently sized groups. Higher mean flood occurrence is interpreted as higher suitability for VIIRS-based synthetic FIM.
supporting_quote: we filtered the river reaches to Strahler stream orders of five or greater [37].
we merged all contiguous catchments of the same stream order into a single polygon. This yields about 12,250 areas that could be used for flood modeling
We took the merged catchments and used a mean reduction by region... This calculates the mean number of flood occurrences

chunks.text: For validation of the VIIRS suitability metric, the authors create 20 FIER test cases spanning different mean flood occurrences and locations. VIIRS images are clipped to rectangles enclosing each catchment group, and multiple image quality thresholds are tested (99% to 99.99% valid pixels) to balance data quantity and pixel consistency. FIER regression models are trained using both NWM and GEOGLOWS historical flows for each case, and outputs are qualitatively categorized into five performance/error categories.
