supporting_quote: We selected 20 catchment groups from our study area with different mean flood occurrences
We prepared sets of images for each catchment group for image quality thresholds 99.99%, 99.95%, 99.9%, 99.5%, and 99%

we took the resulting models and placed them into categories based on performance and types of errors... Category 5 was for models that exhibited a spatial pattern consistent with the permanent water mask

chunks.text: Sentinel-1 SAR Ground Range Detected imagery is used as the SAR source, with 10 m resolution and ascending/descending passes. The paper notes that theoretical revisit can be frequent, but operational tasking and the loss of Sentinel-1B limit practical global coverage. These characteristics motivate a footprint-and-flow coincidence approach rather than full SAR flood extraction at global scale.
supporting_quote: The resulting SAR images from the Ground Range Detected product have a 10 m resolution
the images are marked as being collected during either the ascending or descending collection paths.
Sentinel-1B ceased to function on 23 December 2021.

chunks.text: VIIRS optical data are taken from NOAA’s JPSS/VIIRS Flood Mapping (VFM) product, providing daily global surface water fraction estimates derived from multiple JPSS satellites. VIIRS provides frequent coverage but is affected by cloud cover and has 375 m spatial resolution. The study downloads VFM data and processes daily mosaics for the United States, Canada, and Mexico.
supporting_quote: NOAA used the VIIRS imagery from the three satellites to produce an operational daily surface water fraction estimate for the entire globe [27] titled NOAA JPSS/VIIRS Flood Mapping (VFM) product.
the coarser spatial resolution of the VIIRS images, 375 m
For the scope of this paper, we only processed the images for the United States, Canada, and Mexico.

chunks.text: GEOGLOWS retrospective discharge provides daily average river discharge from 1 January 1940 to present for about 7 million stream reaches, supporting global analysis. The study uses GEOGLOWS retrospective flows and precomputed return periods to label SAR acquisitions by flow rarity. GEOGLOWS also provides ensemble forecasts at 3-hour timesteps, described as potential inputs for FIER forecasting beyond calibration.
supporting_quote: The GEOGLOWS retrospective simulation provides the daily average river discharge from 1 January 1940 to the present for 7 million stream reaches.
We downloaded the GEOGLOWS historical simulation, and the return periods for each of the sample river reaches.
GEOGLOWS also offers average streamflow ensemble forecasts... at 3 hourly timesteps with a 15-day lead time.

chunks.text: The United States National Water Model (NWM) retrospective simulation spans 1979–2020 with hourly timesteps and covers 2.7 million river reaches in CONUS, with expansion ongoing. This hourly temporal resolution can better match satellite acquisition times compared to daily means. The study uses NWM historical data as an alternative discharge input when building VIIRS-based FIER test models.
supporting_quote: The NWM retrospective simulation covers the period from 1979 to 2020 with an hourly timestep.
The NWM retrospective covers 2.7 million river reaches in the continental United States (CONUS)
We generated FIER regression models for each of the 20 catchment groups for both NWM and GEOGLOWS

chunks.text: To separate flood water from baseline water, the study uses the JRC Permanent Water dataset and resamples it from 30 m to VIIRS 375 m resolution using mean aggregation within each VIIRS pixel. The permanent water fraction is then combined with flood fraction thresholds to define flood conditions. The approach leverages the fact that VIIRS outputs percent water fraction and benefits from permanent-water masking.
supporting_quote: To differentiate flood water from normal water, we used the Joint Research Centre (JRC) Permanent Water dataset.
The JRC permanent water dataset has a 30 m resolution... we resampled it to the VIIRS resolution by taking the mean
we extracted all the pixels with permanent water and set their values to 100 so that they were on the same scale as the VIIRS images.

chunks.text: For SAR-derived suitability across 4748 tested reaches, most locations were only suitable for low return periods: about 72% had a maximum suitable return period of 2 years or less. Only a small minority were suitable for higher-magnitude events; less than 2% were suitable for return periods higher than 10 years. The highest category (100-year) was extremely rare at 0.32% of test cases.
supporting_quote: The majority of images, about 72%, were suitable for a 2-year return period or less.
Less than 2% of all our test cases were suitable for anything higher than a 10-year return period.
The areas that were classified as suitable for a 100-year return period totaled only 0.32% of the test cases

chunks.text: Table 2 quantifies SAR suitability counts by maximum return period category (Max column) for 4748 reaches: <2 years (1249; 26.31%), 2 years (2206; 46.46%), 5 years (848; 17.86%), 10 years (354; 7.46%), 25 years (64; 1.35%), 50 years (12; 0.25%), and 100 years (15; 0.32%). These values summarize how seldom high return-period flows coincide with SAR acquisitions at sampled global rivers, given the study’s constraints.
supporting_quote: Table 2. Count of test reaches with each maximum suitable return period and the maximum for each pass.

chunks.text: In the VIIRS suitability analysis, mean flood occurrence is computed for catchment groups across North America, and the paper highlights results for a 25% flood fraction threshold. The 25% FFT was selected because it reduces minor water bodies and minor flooding while producing similar spatial patterns to lower thresholds. The resulting map shows darker blue where catchment groups have higher mean inundation observations, indicating higher suitability.
supporting_quote: We computed the mean inundation observation for every water fraction threshold. The results for the 25% threshold are shown in Figure 10.
We chose 25% because it excludes minor water bodies and minor flooding; lower thresholds all provide similar results.
The darker the blue of an area shown in the figure, the higher the mean inundation observation across the catchment.

chunks.text: The VIIRS-based FIER case studies show that the suitability metric (mean flood occurrence) correlates with model performance: all Category 5 (best-performing) cases occurred where mean flood occurrence exceeded 200. Some lower-mean catchments still achieved Category 4, suggesting occasional usefulness despite lower observed flooding. From these cases, the authors propose a practical suitability threshold between 150 and 200 mean flood occurrences for VIIRS-based FIER modeling.
supporting_quote: We can see that all the test cases that achieved a performance Category of 5 occurred in areas that have a mean flooding occurrence of over 200.
A few of the test cases achieved a Category 4 performance on the catchments with lower means.
From the case studies, we can establish a suitability threshold between 150 and 200.

chunks.text: Differences between NWM- and GEOGLOWS-driven FIER results appear in some test catchments. The paper attributes cases where NWM finds better correlation to its shorter stream segments and more candidate reaches within the grouped catchment areas, while GEOGLOWS can succeed where NWM lacks data because GEOGLOWS reports data on every reach. This indicates that hydrologic data availability and network representation affect the feasibility of building data-driven inundation regressions.
supporting_quote: On some of the lower mean models, NWM provided a better correlation than GEOGLOWS.
Because the stream segments are shorter in NWM, it attempts to correlate more reaches per grouped catchment areas
This occurred because GEOGLOWS reports data on every reach, and NWM masks many areas, so data were not available for this area.

chunks.text: Using the VIIRS thresholded suitability, the paper identifies major river systems and coastal regions as highly suitable when mean flood occurrence is at least 150. The Mississippi River and tributaries are highlighted as likely suitable, aligning with prior FIER applications. The map also flags many East Coast and Gulf of Mexico catchments as highly suitable, though the authors caution these may reflect hurricane/tropical-storm flooding and not purely riverine processes.
supporting_quote: Figure 13 shows all areas that have a mean flood occurrence of 150 or greater.
The results show that the Mississippi River and its tributaries are likely suitable. Since FIER models have been created for those areas [14]
Many of the catchments along the East Coast and the Gulf of Mexico are shown to be highly suitable.

chunks.text: A central limitation is the need for coincidence between flood events and high-quality satellite imagery. For SAR-based synthetic FIM, the key constraint is spatial/temporal coverage: many regions are not imaged often enough to capture a range of flood magnitudes for robust model development. The discussion emphasizes that despite SAR’s high resolution and all-weather capability, practical viability is limited to regions with consistent tasking and frequent flooding.
supporting_quote: A central finding of the presented research is that the coincidence of flood events and high-quality satellite imagery remains a limiting factor.
For SAR-derived synthetic FIM, the primary constraint is spatial and temporal coverage.
only a small fraction—less than 2%—are viable for highmagnitude events such as 50- or 100-year floods.

chunks.text: The paper compares theoretical probabilities of observing return-period floods over 10–15 years with observed suitability based on SAR acquisitions, highlighting revisit-driven limitations. Table 3’s exceedance probabilities represent best-case scenarios because they ignore missed acquisitions, clouds (for optical), and other constraints. The authors note that although a 10-year flood might be expected with 65–87% probability over 10–20 years, fewer than 10% of sampled rivers had such an event observed by a satellite image.
supporting_quote: Probabilities are calculated using the exceedance probability formula shown in Equation (1)
The calculated probabilities consequently represent the best-case scenarios, and actual probabilities should be much lower

Table [3] suggests the probability... exceeding the 10-year return period threshold is between 65% and 87%. However, Table [2] shows that less than 10% of the sampled rivers had such a flood event that was also observed by a satellite image.

chunks.text: The SAR feasibility classification may overestimate actual flood observability because it uses modeled high flows as a proxy for flooding and does not process SAR imagery to confirm inundation. GEOGLOWS does not represent control structures, so modeled high return period flows may be mitigated in reality, yielding little or no flood signal in imagery. The approach also does not account for detection issues from terrain or urban environments.
supporting_quote: Since determining flooding in SAR imagery requires extensive preprocessing, we instead identify areas with observed high flows, expecting many of them to be floods.
the GEOGLOWS hydrologic model does not account for control structures.
Our methods do not account for any possible interference from mountain ranges or urban environments.

chunks.text: The paper stresses that the VIIRS and SAR suitability results are not directly comparable and should not be used to argue one sensor is superior. The analyses address different requirements and domains (VIIRS across ~12,250 catchment groups in North America vs SAR at discrete sampled global points). SAR global flood-frequency mapping is described as prohibitively time-consuming in GEE due to storage limits, preprocessing needs, and finer resolution increasing raster size.
supporting_quote: Because such different processes must be used, our analysis does not support conclusions suggesting either VIIRS or SAR is superior for synthesizing FIM.
The VIIRS-derived synthetic FIM suitability process examined about 12,250 catchment groups across North America.
All these factors make performing this analysis for SAR at the global scale prohibitively time-consuming.

chunks.text: VIIRS suitability maps can be confounded by non-riverine water dynamics and incomplete masking of lakes. Coastal catchments may reflect hurricane or tidal inundation rather than river flooding, and lake-elevation changes can be misinterpreted as flood suitability. The authors caution that some north-of–Great Lakes catchments should be discounted due to small lakes not included in the lakes dataset used for masking.
supporting_quote: many of these areas have experienced flooding from hurricanes or tropical storms over the study period.
Many of the areas around the lakes are shown to be highly suitable, but this can include the detection of changes in lake elevation
many of the catchment groups north of the Great Lakes... should be discounted because of the presence of lakes that were too small to be included in our lakes dataset.

chunks.text: The study develops and demonstrates workflows to assess where satellite-derived synthetic flood inundation maps are feasible, focusing on SAR (Sentinel-1) and optical (VIIRS) in the context of the FIER method. It uses simulated hydrology (GEOGLOWS and NWM) to reduce dependence on gauge availability and evaluates suitability based on coincidence between imagery and flooding indicators. The authors emphasize that suitability estimates represent upper limits for skillful synthesis for methods like FIER that may not extrapolate beyond observed training flows.
supporting_quote: We evaluated viable locations for creating satellite-derived synthetic flood maps.

We developed workflows that determine the suitability of an area for satellite-derived synthetic FIM model creation with imagery from VIIRS and SAR based on the coincidence of satellite imagery and flood extents.
For models of this type, including FIER, the suitability estimates presented represent the upper limits for skillful flood synthesis.

chunks.text: From VIIRS case studies, the paper concludes that higher mean flood occurrence is strongly associated with better FIER model performance and proposes a suitability threshold range between 150 and 200 mean flood occurrences. It notes that the Mississippi River and tributaries appear suitable under this criterion, consistent with previous FIER work. The paper frames VIIRS daily coverage as particularly useful for large-scale screening, with future work suggested to extend the VIIRS process globally.
supporting_quote: We can see that all the test cases that achieved a performance Category of 5 occurred in areas that have a mean flooding occurrence of over 200.
From the case studies, we can establish a suitability threshold between 150 and 200.
Future work could extend the process to be global by processing the rest of the VIIRS images.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that suitability is not static and should improve as longer records accumulate, additional sensors are incorporated, and data fusion approaches mature. It also suggests that combining optical and SAR (and potentially other datasets) can increase the number of suitable locations and improve synthetic inundation mapping methods, including FIER. The authors position the presented methods as adaptable screening tools that can be reapplied as satellite coverage and processing approaches evolve.
supporting_quote: Further research... may need to create or apply methods to incorporate many data sources, potentially including non-satellite acquired datasets.
it has been shown that optical and SAR data can be combined [41].
Suitability is expected to improve... as more data are collected, additional sensors are included, and data fusion methods are refined.

chunks.text: The Fundamentals of Engineering (FE) exam is a nationally recognized U.S. exam used to test foundational engineering knowledge across many topics. Passing the FE is an important milestone and is required to progress toward professional engineer licensure. The FE exam also serves employers as a benchmark for technical competence and safe engineering practice.
supporting_quote: The Fundamentals of Engineering (FE) exam is a nationally recognized exam in the United States that is designed to test the fundamental knowledge of engineering students and professionals
Passing the FE exam is a significant milestone for engineering students and is a requirement for becoming a professional engineer (PE) in the United States

chunks.text: The FE Environmental Computer-Based Testing (CBT) exam is positioned as a key certification for environmental professionals and evaluates broad competency areas such as air and water quality, waste management, and regulations. Its breadth and rigor make it central to professional development and licensure advancement in environmental fields.
supporting_quote: The Environmental Computer-Based Testing (CBT) Exam is a critical certification exam for environmental professionals
this exam evaluates an individual's competency in areas such as air quality, water quality, solid and hazardous waste management, environmental regulations, and sustainability

chunks.text: Prior research has examined ChatGPT on exams in medicine, business, and computer science, often finding near-passing or passing performance but with notable weaknesses in calculations and advanced reasoning. The paper argues engineering requires complex mathematical problem solving that may create unique challenges for large language models. It also notes a literature gap specifically for environmental engineering exam-style questions.
supporting_quote: Terwiesch (2023) explored ChatGPT's performance in the final exam of a typical MBA core course
Despite the promising results of ChatGPT in various educational domains, there is a noticeable knowledge gap in the literature regarding its performance in the engineering field.

chunks.text: The study aims to evaluate how accurately ChatGPT can answer FE Environmental CBT-style questions and whether it can achieve satisfactory performance without specialized training. A second goal is to test whether noninvasive prompt modifications can measurably improve accuracy, informing feasibility for exam preparation and assessment use cases. The work also seeks to surface implications for responsible integration of AI in licensing and education.
supporting_quote: This study explores the potential of ChatGPT to achieve satisfactory performance on the Fundamentals of Engineering (FE) Environmental Exam
with particular emphasis on the strength of different models for environmental engineering as well as the effectiveness of noninvasive prompt modifications in enhancing the model's accuracy.

chunks.text: The paper frames its objectives as three research questions: measuring ChatGPT accuracy on FE Environmental questions, assessing feasibility through prompt-based improvements, and discussing benefits and concerns of AI in licensing exams. These questions define the experimental and discussion structure of the study.
supporting_quote: RQ1. How accurate is ChatGPT in answering FE Environmental CBT exam questions?
RQ2. How feasible is it to utilize ChatGPT for exam preparation and assessment?
RQ3. What are the potential benefits and concerns of using AI in licensing exams such as the FE Environmental CBT Exam?

chunks.text: The authors identify a gap in evidence about large language model performance on engineering exams, particularly environmental engineering, where multidisciplinary content and quantitative problem solving are common. They argue that engineering questions may stress mathematical and applied reasoning more than many domains where ChatGPT has been tested. This motivates direct evaluation against an FE Environmental-style practice dataset.
supporting_quote: there is a noticeable knowledge gap in the literature regarding its performance in the engineering field.
Engineering disciplines often involve the application of complex mathematical concepts and problem-solving skills, which may pose unique challenges for AI models like ChatGPT.

chunks.text: The paper highlights credibility and integrity concerns if widely available AI systems can answer licensing-exam questions, potentially enabling cheating and reducing accountability. At the same time, AI could improve objectivity and fairness in assessment, creating a tension that requires investigation. This concern is especially salient for high-stakes certification contexts.
supporting_quote: concerns have been raised about its potential impact on the credibility of these exams
Some argue that the use of AI within this context could lead to cheating and a lack of accountability

chunks.text: A practical obstacle for evaluation is that the true FE passing score is not published and scaled scoring varies by exam form. As a result, the study cannot definitively claim whether a given accuracy equates to passing the real FE exam. This limits how results can be interpreted relative to actual licensing outcomes.
supporting_quote: NCEES does not publish a passing score
Therefore, there is no tangible pass/fail score for the FE exam. Hence, this study cannot claim for a fact that ChatGPT is or is not able to pass the FE Exam.

chunks.text: The evaluation used two test sets derived from the practice dataset: (1) verbatim questions with only formatting fixes and (2) noninvasively refined prompts that add guidance without changing question content. Verbatim questions were tested on GPT-3.5-Legacy, GPT-3.5-Turbo, and GPT-4, while refined prompts were tested on GPT-4 to isolate prompt-modification impact. Each question was asked in unique calls to avoid interference effects.
supporting_quote: The first test set comprised verbatim questions, with no modifications except for addressing formatting issues
The second test set involved noninvasively refined questions, wherein additive guidance was incorporated without altering the question's content.

chunks.text: A separate experiment varied the temperature parameter for GPT-3.5-Turbo using the verbatim test set to assess how output randomness affects accuracy. The study chose not to replicate temperature testing on GPT-4 due to rate limits, slower execution, and cost, asserting GPT-3.5-Turbo was sufficient for studying temperature effects. Temperature values ranged from 0 to 1.
supporting_quote: a separate experiment was conducted on GPT-3.5-Turbo, using the first test set to measure the effect of using different temperature values
The temperature parameter, which ranges from 0 to 1, influences the randomness of the model's output.

chunks.text: The experiments were run through a Python application using the OpenAI API to process test sets, query selected GPT variants, and save outputs for reproducibility. To score responses, an autograder component compared model answers to an answer key. The autograder used GPT-3.5-turbo with temperature 0 and returned a boolean label, after which results were manually validated.
supporting_quote: a Python application was developed using the OpenAI API.

The autograder function operates by submitting a 'user' response to the ChatGPT model, instructing it to evaluate the accuracy of a given response by comparing it to the correct answer (i.e., the 'answer key').

chunks.text: Prompt refinement approaches were tested to improve performance without changing question meaning. LaTeX formatting and textual diagram descriptions did not yield consistent gains, but adding a system message that requests clear explanations and an educated guess from provided options improved results. The final refinement used a specific system message to guide multiple-choice and non-multiple-choice responses.
supporting_quote: Utilizing LaTeX formatting to present questions or requiring ChatGPT to use LaTeX in its responses did not yield any significant improvements

Providing a system message instructing ChatGPT to focus on providing clear and concise explanations for its answers, and to make an educated guess from the provided options when in doubt... proved beneficial.

chunks.text: The FE Environmental exam is described as a comprehensive CBT exam with 110 questions and multiple item types, including multiple choice, multiple correct options, and fill-in-the-blank. The practice dataset used here was created for education and may not match the real exam’s section weights or item-type mix. The study focuses on using this dataset to test model proficiency across sections.
supporting_quote: The exam consists of 110 questions
In total, the preparation exam in the dataset consists of 134 questions.

chunks.text: The dataset is an unpublished practice exam curated by University of Iowa Civil and Environmental Engineering faculty, drawing primarily from FE prep books and other referenced materials. The practice exam was completed in Summer 2021, with faculty assigned by section and a lead coordinator managing contributions. The intended audience is undergraduate students preparing for the FE Environmental exam.
supporting_quote: The dataset used in this study represents an unpublished practice exam... prepared by the University of Iowa Civil and Environmental Engineering department faculty.
the FE Environmental practice exam preparation... was completed in Summer 2021.

chunks.text: The practice dataset totals 134 questions with a mix of formats: 1 drag-and-drop, 11 fill-in-the-blank, and the remainder multiple-choice. The paper notes the distribution across content areas is not representative of the real FE exam and is designed as a study and solution resource with worked solutions and videos.
supporting_quote: In total, the preparation exam in the dataset consists of 134 questions. Out of these 134 questions, 1 was a drag and drop, 11 were fill in the blank, and the remaining ones were multiplechoice questions.
the number of problems in each area is not representative of an actual exam

chunks.text: On the 134-question dataset, GPT-4 base (no vision) achieved an overall accuracy of 66.42% using verbatim prompts. When noninvasive prompt refinements were applied to the same GPT-4 model, accuracy increased to 75.37%. The authors note the questions were not invasively modified for the model and the model was not trained on the dataset.
supporting_quote: ChatGPT (GPT-4 Base Model - No Vision) achieved an overall accuracy of 66.42% on the dataset herein
When applying a refined approach to the same GPT-4 model, the accuracy improved to 75.37%

chunks.text: Section-level results show strong performance in some topics and persistent weaknesses in others. The model performed well in Ethics and Professional Practice, Thermodynamics, and Probability and Statistics (especially with refined GPT-4 prompts). In contrast, Ground Water Soil and Sediments and Surface Water Resources and Hydrology stayed relatively low even after refinement.
supporting_quote: ChatGPT performs exceptionally well in certain sections, such as Ethics and Professional Practice, Thermodynamics, and Probability and Statistics
the model's performance in sections like Ground Water Soil and Sediments and Surface Water Resources and Hydrology remains relatively low, even with the refined prompts.

chunks.text: Temperature tuning for GPT-3.5-Turbo affected accuracy on the engineering question set. The highest reported overall accuracy was 0.59 at temperature 0.75, while the lowest was 0.47 at temperature 0.5. Accuracies at other temperatures were close (e.g., 0.56 at temperature 1 and 0.56 at temperature 0).
supporting_quote: The highest accuracy (i.e., 0.59) was achieved with a temperature setting of 0.75, while the lowest accuracy (i.e., 0.47) was observed at a temperature setting of 0.5.
The accuracies for the other temperature settings were found to be relatively close, with TEMP = 1 at 0.56... and TEMP = 0 at 0.56.

chunks.text: Noninvasive prompt refinement (Approach 3 system message) yielded an average gain of 8.95 percentage points in accuracy for GPT-4 (no vision) compared to unmodified prompts. The paper reports refinements were especially impactful at higher temperatures and therefore used temperature 0.75 for the refinement experiment. Response patterns suggested the refinement reduced irrelevant outputs and encouraged selecting from provided options.
supporting_quote: demonstrated a mean accuracy percentage point increase of 8.95% compared to the control group that employed unmodified prompts.
we conducted the experiment at a temperature setting of 0.75.

chunks.text: The paper reports large section improvements with refined prompts in multiple areas, including Energy and Environment (25%), Engineering Economics (20%), Environmental Chemistry (15%), Fluid Mechanics and Hydraulics (14.29%), and Mathematics (26.67%). Some sections showed no improvement (e.g., Air Quality and Control; Surface Water Resources and Hydrology). In a few areas, refined prompts decreased performance, including Ethics and Professional Practice and Water and Wastewater.
supporting_quote: the refined test set led to a noticeable improvement in numerous sections, such as Energy and Environment (25%), Engineering Economics (20%), Environmental Chemistry (15%)
the application of refined prompts did not yield any improvement... Air Quality and Control... Surface Water Resources and Hydrology
the refined test set resulted in a decrease in performance for Ethics and Professional Practice and Water and Wastewater sections.

chunks.text: For math-heavy sections (Math, Probability and Statistics, Engineering Economics), newer ChatGPT versions improved substantially. GPT-3.5-turbo increased weighted accuracy from 41.38% (GPT-3.5-legacy) to 62.07%, with refinement reaching 65.51%. Refined GPT-4-base (no vision) achieved 86.21% weighted accuracy, outperforming prior variants.
supporting_quote: GPT-3.5-turbo exhibits superior mathematical capabilities compared to its predecessor, GPT-3.5-legacy, with an observed accuracy increase from 41.38% to 62.07%.
when refining GPT-4-base (no vision), the model significantly outperforms its predecessors, achieving an impressive accuracy of 86.21%.

chunks.text: The authors emphasize that FE scoring is scaled and NCEES does not publish a passing threshold, so they cannot definitively determine whether ChatGPT would pass the real exam. This limits claims to accuracy on the provided dataset rather than licensure outcomes. They also note the lack of public diagnostic reports prevents section-level comparisons to human test takers.
supporting_quote: NCEES does not publish a passing score
Thus, a section-specific comparison of success between human test takers and ChatGPT could not be made.

chunks.text: The dataset may not be large or fully representative of the real FE Environmental exam, and the authors are uncertain how closely it matches actual questions. Some exam item types (e.g., point and click) are missing, and lack of visual capability would make such questions infeasible. They also acknowledge the nonzero possibility that some questions exist online, potentially affecting model familiarity.
supporting_quote: the dataset used for testing ChatGPT's performance may not be considered large or completely representative in terms of the question distribution.
the dataset lacks point and click question types, which, given ChatGPT's current absence of visual input capabilities, would render answering such questions infeasible.
the probability of ChatGPT being aware of some questions in the dataset is nonzero.

chunks.text: The study notes that ChatGPT outputs can be sensitive to prompt phrasing and intrinsically random, requiring cautious interpretation. Minor changes in grammar or punctuation can significantly change responses, and repeated runs may yield different answers. Therefore, reported accuracies may fluctuate on reproduction, though the authors expect rates to remain broadly representative.
supporting_quote: the model's output is extremely sensitive to variations in the prompt's grammar, punctuation, and phraseology.
the model's responses are intrinsically random, resulting in diverse responses to similar or identical prompts.

chunks.text: Even when refined GPT-4 showed stronger conceptual understanding, the authors observed limitations in multi-step calculations for complex engineering problems. They report the model could often set up formulas correctly but fail in executing computations, leading to incorrect answers in calculation-intensive sections like Engineering Economics and Mathematics. They also note GPT-3.5 sometimes got correct multiple-choice answers despite incorrect formulations, indicating unreliable reasoning.
supporting_quote: its overall mathematical capability proved inadequate for complex engineering calculations.
the refined GPT-4-base (no vision) model successfully identified the relevant formulas and concepts but failed to accurately perform the required calculations
GPT-3.5 occasionally provided correct answers, even when its calculations and overall formulation were incorrect.

chunks.text: A prompt-refinement side effect was observed where requiring explanations sometimes reduced accuracy, potentially by reducing lucky guesses or exposing lack of underlying knowledge. The paper gives an example in the Ethics section where GPT-4 answered correctly verbatim but produced a wrong answer when forced to explain reasoning. This suggests explanation prompts can change performance characteristics and may reveal memorization versus reasoning.
supporting_quote: for one question in the Ethics section, GPT-4 consistently provided the correct answer when asked verbatim but never offered an explanation.
with the refinement, the model always explained its reasoning but arrived at the wrong answer.

chunks.text: The study concludes that ChatGPT shows potential as an exam-preparation and engineering problem-support tool, with GPT-4 (no vision) reaching 66.42% accuracy and prompt refinement boosting this to 75.37%. The authors emphasize that noninvasive prompt modifications can materially improve performance and that model generations show improved mathematical capability. They caution that some subject areas remain weak and that careful, responsible integration is needed.
supporting_quote: The GPT-4 base model with no vision achieved a notable overall accuracy of 66.42% on the FE Environmental Exam dataset
leading to a mean accuracy increase of 8.95% for the FE Environmental Exam, resulting in an overall accuracy of 75.37%.

chunks.text: The paper argues that the ability of a widely available, domain-independent AI to potentially achieve a passing-like grade has nontrivial implications for licensing exam integrity. It highlights both benefits (study support and accessibility) and concerns (cheating, validity, reliability), motivating future research and exam design responses. The authors also foresee that integrating tools (e.g., code execution) may further raise AI performance in the future.
supporting_quote: the fact that an unrefined, domain-independent, widely-available AI can potentially get a passing grade in an exam that is supposed to assess and prove the credibility and merits of future engineers is nontrivial
Future research should explore the development of efficient and user-friendly plugin systems to facilitate seamless interaction between AI models like ChatGPT and specialized tools

chunks.text: Compound flooding arises from the sequence and/or co-occurrence of multiple flood drivers such as river discharge and elevated sea level (storm surge), and it can produce severe societal impacts. The paper situates this challenge in the context of climate change and sustainable development, noting the importance of hazard communication for disaster risk reduction and SDG targets (e.g., SDG 11.5). The authors argue that effectively communicating evolving dependence among drivers is central for preparedness and mitigation in coastal communities.
supporting_quote: Compound flooding, caused by the sequence and/or co-occurrence of flood drivers (i.e., river discharge and elevated sea level), can lead to devastating consequences for society.
A comprehensive hazard communication strategy is essential in engaging stakeholders and informing decision-making and mitigation efforts

chunks.text: Standard bivariate dependence analysis in compound-flood studies typically starts with scatterplots in variable space and computes correlation metrics such as Pearson’s r, Kendall’s τ, or Spearman’s ρ. The paper notes this approach is widespread across compound flooding literature and is the prevailing means to visualize coincident extremes. The authors use this as a baseline for motivating an alternative visualization.
supporting_quote: Bivariate analysis usually begins with a scatterplot that displays the variables of interest graphically in the variable space
then calculation of the correlation coefficient between them, e.g., the linear Pearson's r or the non-linear Kendall's τ or Spearman's ρ.

chunks.text: The authors draw on the idea that multivariate statistics can be interpreted geometrically in Euclidean space, specifically via a “subject space” where each observation is treated as a dimension and variables become points/vectors. While known in statistics, this framing has rarely been applied in environmental sciences and compound flooding. The paper proposes leveraging this geometric intuition to better communicate dependencies and their evolution over time.
supporting_quote: In reality, multivariate statistics have a strong flavor of Euclidean geometry

if we think about the data in the "subject space" instead, where each subject (observation) of coinciding extremal pairs defines an axis (dimension), then the two variables can be represented as two points inside that space

chunks.text: The paper’s main goal is to introduce and evaluate the “Angles method” as a complementary visualization approach for communicating dependence between compound-flood drivers. It aims to test, for the first time in this context, how the subject-space geometry can be used to compute and visualize dependence, particularly under nonstationarity. The authors also seek to assess end-user perceptions via a survey spanning academic and non-academic stakeholders.
supporting_quote: This paper introduces the Angles method, based on Euclidean geometry of the so-called "subject space", as a complementary visualization approach
Here, we evaluate, for the first time, the utility of this geometric space in computing and visualizing the dependence structure of compound-flooding drivers.
To assess the effectiveness of this method as a hazard communication tool, we conducted a survey with a diverse group of end-users

chunks.text: A specific communication objective is to make temporal evolution in dependence (non-stationarity) easier to interpret than with traditional scatterplots. The authors frame the Angles method as an accessible first visual check that can precede more complex modeling (e.g., copulas). This goal emphasizes clarity for diverse end-users rather than replacing statistical dependence modeling.
supporting_quote: The Angles method complements these approaches by offering a more intuitive visual representation specifically designed for communicating the temporal evolution of dependencies.
The Angles method is not meant to replace statistical methods like copula modeling but rather to complement them by serving as an accessible first visual check

chunks.text: The paper identifies a communication gap: effective hazard communication remains a major barrier for anticipating and responding to compound flood events. Even when dependence can be quantified statistically, conveying evolving patterns to diverse stakeholder groups is difficult. This motivates the need for visualization methods that are intuitive and purpose-built for communication.
supporting_quote: Effective communication remains the main barrier to anticipating and responding to compound flood events

Current approaches for visualizing compound flood dependencies, including scatterplots and statistical measures, while mathematically sound, often struggle to effectively communicate evolving patterns to diverse end-users.

chunks.text: A limitation of variable-space scatterplots is that they emphasize individual observations rather than representing the variables as entities whose relationship is the inferential target. This becomes especially problematic when adding an additional time dimension to inspect nonstationary dependence, where evolving structure can be hard to see. The authors argue for a representation with minimal focus on individual subjects to aid interpretation.
supporting_quote: The variable space, however, does pose a limitation in studying the dependence structure in the sense that it places a strong emphasis on the individual observations (subjects) themselves

This is particularly important when the dimensionality of the problem increases, e.g., when an additional time dimension is introduced, to examine potential non-stationarities in the dependence structure

chunks.text: Non-stationarity in compound-flood driver dependence is difficult to communicate and is often neglected in practice, even though climate and anthropogenic influences can change relationships over time. The paper notes that dynamic, non-stationary copulas exist but are complex, and many studies default to moving windows or stationarity assumptions. This sets up a need for simpler visual tools to convey changing dependence to practitioners and the public.
supporting_quote: Another important aspect within the compound-flooding framework is non-stationarities of the dependence structure among flood drivers.
dynamic, non-stationary copulas offer one solution (Pirani and Najafi, 2023), yet their complexity means that most studies default to moving-window analyses or a stationary assumption

chunks.text: The Angles method reframes bivariate extremes in subject space, where each paired observation forms a dimension and each variable becomes a point/vector from the origin. After centering variables by subtracting the mean, the two vectors define a 2-D plane, and dependence is visualized via the angle between them. Pearson correlation is shown to equal the cosine of this angle, linking standard correlation to geometric interpretation.
supporting_quote: in the "subject space" instead, where each subject (observation) of coinciding extremal pairs defines an axis (dimension), then the two variables can be represented as two points inside that space
For the sake of simplicity, we can center the two variables by subtracting the respective mean value
The following equation represents the cosine of the angle between two vectors: r = cos(θ)

chunks.text: To emphasize dependence rather than scale, the method can standardize/scale vectors so that they have equal or unit length, making the angle the principal characteristic. In this form, uncorrelated variables correspond to perpendicular vectors (90°) and correlated variables to collinear vectors (0° or 180°). The area of the parallelogram between unit vectors provides an additional geometric summary tied to r.
supporting_quote: In the subject space, uncorrelated discharge and surge variables are displayed as perpendicular vectors (θ = 90°), whereas correlated discharge and surge variables are displayed as collinear vectors (θ = 0° or θ = 180°).
For convenience, one may choose to work with vectors of unit length |q| = |s| = 1
Area_parallelogram = sin(θ) = √(1 - r^2)

chunks.text: The authors acknowledge Pearson’s r limitations and extend the geometric interpretation to Spearman’s rank correlation. The extension uses rank-based pseudo-observations (empirical CDF ranks) and then applies the same cosine-of-angle formulation to the transformed vectors. This yields a geometric angle tied to Spearman’s ρ, supporting monotonic (not only linear) dependence visualization.
supporting_quote: This approach can be extended to Spearman's rank correlation coefficient
we first transform the data into ranks and then into pseudoobservations: q^S = F_Q(Q) = rank(Q)/(N+1)
The Spearman correlation coefficient (ρ) can then be expressed geometrically as the cosine of the angle between the transformed vectors

chunks.text: For more than two drivers, the subject-space approach is applied via pairwise projections: each driver pair is represented as two vectors on a 2-D plane, and their angular separation summarizes dependence. This provides a systematic alternative to attempting multi-dimensional scatterplots (e.g., 4-D), while retaining a consistent geometric intuition across pairs.
supporting_quote: It is inherently difficult to illustrate 4-D scatterplots
Euclidean geometry offers a systematic solution through pairwise analysis. Each pair of flood drivers can be represented as vectors in a 2-D plane

chunks.text: A stakeholder survey was designed as a sequential comparative evaluation to test clarity and communication effectiveness, including non-stationarity depiction. The online survey ran from 10 July to 10 September 2024 and used Likert-scale questions about understandability, applicability, usefulness, and likelihood of adoption. Responses were analyzed by grouping participants into academic versus non-academic categories.
supporting_quote: We conducted an online survey (see Supplement) between 10 July and 10 September 2024
Likert scale questions were used to capture the degree of agreement or disagreement
The responses were subsequently grouped into two categories: academic and non-academic respondents.

chunks.text: For Washington, DC and Baltimore, MD, still-water level components were taken from tide gauges in GESLA3, and storm surge was derived as the non-tidal residual via rolling-year tidal harmonic analysis using 60 constituents. River discharge series were obtained from GRDC for rivers draining to each city’s tidal river outlet. Coinciding extremes were defined as annual maximum discharge paired with maximum surge within ±1 day of the discharge-maximum timing.
supporting_quote: still-water level data... from tide gauges at Washington, DC, and Baltimore, MD, extracted from the GESLA3 database
we performed tidal harmonic analysis on a rollingyear basis, involving 60 major tidal constituents
we utilized discharge data... originating from the Global Runoff Data Center (GRDC)
pairs of annual maximum discharge (Q) and the respective maximum surge (S) within (±) a day of maximum-discharge timing

chunks.text: Data completeness rules were applied before dependence analysis: years with more than 20% missing data were excluded for both scatterplots and correlation computations. Sample sizes differed by location: Washington, DC used 83 years of measurements, while Baltimore, MD used 54 years. These sample sizes also define the dimensionality of the subject space for each case (83-D and 54-D).
supporting_quote: In the case of the freshwater-influenced tide gauge at Washington, DC, the scatterplot is constructed from all 83 years of available measurements
54 years of data from the Baltimore, MD, gauge yield weaker correlations
For both tide gauges, years with > 20 % missing data were excluded
subject space of the data at Washington, DC, which consists of 83 axes (dimensions)
Baltimore, MD, can be thought of as belonging to a 54-D subject space

chunks.text: A Galveston Bay, Texas example dataset was used to demonstrate temporal evolution in dependence. Annual maxima still-water levels at Galveston Pier 21 were paired with co-occurring discharge maxima at Buffalo Bayou within ±5 days. The analysis compared non-overlapping periods (1972–1996 vs 1997–2022) to illustrate changes in correlation and the corresponding angle shrinkage in subject-space plots.
supporting_quote: annual maxima still-water levels at Galveston Pier 21, TX
co-occurring (±5 d) maxima of discharge at Buffalo Bayou
correlation coefficient of the period 1997–2022 (r = 0.42, p value = 0.035) is greater than that of 1972–1996 (r = 0.21, p value = 0.393)

chunks.text: Survey data comprised 91 complete responses, with global participation concentrated in the United States. Respondents were split into academic (n=44) and non-academic (n=47) groups for comparative analysis. The U.S. responses spanned 20 states, with higher counts in Mississippi (14), Alabama (13), and Florida (10), reflecting distribution channels.
supporting_quote: The survey collected 91 complete responses.
academic (n = 44) and non-academic (n = 47) respondents
In the United States, the survey responses came from 20 states, with the highest numbers reported in Mississippi (14), Alabama (13), and Florida (10)

chunks.text: For Washington, DC, coinciding annual maximum discharge and surge show very strong dependence, with Pearson’s r=0.96 and Spearman’s ρ=0.84 (both p=0.000). Baltimore, MD shows weaker dependence (r=0.41, ρ=0.52; p=0.005 and p=0.000). These baseline results motivate contrasting dependence strength across sites in both scatterplot and angle-based visualizations.
supporting_quote: Washington, DC... Pearson's r correlation coefficient is found to be 0.96 (p value = 0.000), while the non-linear Spearman's ρ ... is 0.84 (p value = 0.000).
Baltimore, MD... Pearson's r and Spearman's ρ being 0.41 (p value = 0.005) and 0.52 (p value = 0.000), respectively.

chunks.text: In subject space, the dependence difference between Washington, DC and Baltimore, MD becomes an easily interpretable angular separation between unit vectors. Using cos(θ)=r, Washington’s r=0.96 corresponds to θ≈16°, while Baltimore’s r=0.41 corresponds to θ≈66°. The authors interpret the smaller angle as a tighter interplay between discharge and surge and the larger angle as less frequent coincidence for severe compound events.
supporting_quote: In Washington, DC, the smaller angle between the unit vectors indicates a tighter interplay
in Baltimore, MD, the larger angle suggests a lower degree of correlation

chunks.text: The Galveston Bay example shows that scatterplots alone make it difficult to visually assess whether dependence is strengthening over time. By contrast, the Angles method highlights a shrinking angle between vectors across periods, indicating increasing dependence. Numerically, the later period (1997–2022) has higher correlation (r=0.42, p=0.035) than the earlier period (1972–1996; r=0.21, p=0.393).
supporting_quote: From Fig. 3 alone, it is not evident if the dependence between the two flooding drivers is getting stronger with time.
observe the shrinking angle θ in Fig. 4
1997–2022 (r = 0.42, p value = 0.035) is greater than that of 1972–1996 (r = 0.21, p value = 0.393)

chunks.text: The survey indicates strong domain familiarity among many respondents but also a notable gap on non-stationarity for non-academics. Combining “very well” and “extremely well,” 68.1% of non-academics versus 59% of academics reported high familiarity with CCF. For non-stationarity, 34% of non-academics reported “not well at all” versus 13.6% of academics, while 25% of academics reported “extremely well” versus 14.9% of non-academics.
supporting_quote: 68.1 % of nonacademics versus 59 % of academics report high familiarity.
34 % of non-academics reported "not well at all" ... compared to the 13.6 % of academics
25 % of academics reporting "extremely well" ... compared to only 14.9 % of non-academics

chunks.text: When asked about understandability of correlation, academics were more favorable toward numerical correlation coefficients than non-academics (50% vs 35.9% agree/strongly agree). For the Angles method, academics showed 68.2% at least slightly agreeing with understandability, but non-academics had low top-box endorsement: only 19.2% “agree” or “strongly agree.” The authors interpret this as possible familiarity bias toward conventional coefficients.
supporting_quote: For the numerical approach, academic respondents showed a higher level of agreement (50 % agree or strongly agree) compared to non-academics (35.9 %).
When assessing the Angles method... academic respondents... 68.2 % at least slightly agreeing
among non-academics, the level of high agreement ("agree" and "strongly agree") dropped to 19.2 %.

chunks.text: For communicating non-stationarity (variations in dependence), scatterplots were not perceived as very clear—especially for audiences. Only 11.3% of academics and 4.3% of non-academics agreed/strongly agreed that scatterplots would clearly depict variations for a prospective audience. The Angles method increased perceived audience clarity to 34.1% for academics and 23.4% for non-academics, suggesting improved communicability for evolving dependence.
supporting_quote: for a potential audience... only 11.3 % of academics and 4.3 % of non-academics agreeing or strongly agreeing.
the Angles method enhanced the level of agreeing or strongly agreeing from 11.3 % to 34.1 % for academics
and from 4.3 % to 23.4 % for non-academics compared to scatterplots.

chunks.text: Respondents’ views on applying the Angles method differed by sector. For practical use, 75% of academic respondents expressed likelihood of applying it in work or research, while non-academics were more mixed, with 53.2% expressing some likelihood and 21.8% disagreeing or remaining neutral. For perceived effectiveness in CCF hazard communication, academics were somewhat more positive (31.8% agree/strongly agree) than non-academics (23.4%).
supporting_quote: Academic respondents showed a strong consensus... with 75 % expressing a likelihood of applying it in their work or research.
non-academic respondents... 53.2 % expressing some likelihood of applying it but with a notable 21.8 % disagreeing or remaining neutral
31.8 % agreeing or strongly agreeing versus 23.4 % of non-academics

chunks.text: The authors position the Angles method primarily as a communication aid rather than a full dependence modeling tool. They note it does not capture the full complexity of dependence structures such as tail dependence, which copula approaches can model. Accordingly, it is intended as a complementary, accessible visualization step before more complex bivariate probability modeling.
supporting_quote: While the Angles method does not capture the full complexity of dependence structures (such as tail dependencies) that copula approaches can model
the method presented here is primarily designed as a communication tool rather than as a statistical modeling technique.
not meant to replace statistical methods like copula modeling but rather to complement them

chunks.text: The paper highlights limitations of Pearson correlation that motivate extending the geometry to rank-based dependence. Pearson’s r may be restricted to linear associations, can have existence issues in some cases, and is not invariant under monotonic transformations. The authors therefore point to a Spearman-based derivation as a more robust alternative for non-linear relationships and outlier-prone, non-normal environmental extremes.
supporting_quote: it is important to acknowledge its limitations, including problems of existence in certain cases, restriction to linear associations between variables, and lack of invariance under monotonic transformations
extended to Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, which offers advantages in handling non-linear relationships

chunks.text: Adoption barriers may stem from user preference for familiar terminology and methods. The authors caution that describing the approach as “new” or “different” can bias audiences against it, implying that framing it as building on familiar correlation concepts may improve uptake. Survey patterns suggested non-academics were more hesitant to adopt without further familiarization.
supporting_quote: using language like "new", "groundbreaking", or "different" can sometimes bias people against trying or adopting unfamiliar methods
non-academic respondents were more divided... suggesting a hesitancy to adopt the method without further familiarization.

chunks.text: The study concludes that the Angles method is a useful complementary visualization for communicating evolving dependencies in coastal compound flooding. By turning correlation into an interpretable angle, it can make non-stationary dependence patterns more accessible than scatterplots for diverse stakeholders. Survey results support its promise, particularly for clarifying non-stationarity, while indicating that broader testing with non-expert audiences is a key next step.
supporting_quote: This study evaluates the Angles method as a complementary visual tool for communicating evolving dependencies in CCF hazards.
Comparisons between the Angles method and scatterplots revealed that the Angles method provided a clearer and more intuitive representation of non-stationarity
future studies should explore the effectiveness of the Angles method with broader audiences, including the public and students.

chunks.text: The authors emphasize the Angles method’s distinct purpose relative to sophisticated statistical approaches: it supports hazard communication by making temporal patterns of dependence visually intuitive, not by replacing copula modeling. They argue this kind of visualization can bridge scientific insight and practical applications, aiding adaptive planning that accounts for changing relationships among drivers. The method is positioned as an accessible step that can motivate awareness and support resilient decision-making.
supporting_quote: Rather than replacing sophisticated statistical methods like copulas, the Angles method serves a distinct purpose in making temporal patterns of dependence more accessible
the Angles method is not meant to replace statistical methods like copula modeling but rather to complement them

chunks.text: Tropical cyclones (TCs) can generate severe coastal hazards, and the impacts are often amplified when storms rapidly intensify. Rapid intensification (RI) is commonly defined by a large wind-speed increase over a short window, and it is associated with major damage and casualties. Recent research highlights that prolonged ocean warming anomalies, marine heatwaves (MHWs), can precondition the ocean to provide extra energy for intensifying storms.
supporting_quote: TC RI is defined as a process wherein the maximum sustained wind speed of a TC increases by at least 30 kt over a 24 hr period
The extensive impacts can be more severe when TCs undergo rapid intensification (RI)
The role of MHW as a precursor to TC RI has been highlighted in recent studies

chunks.text: Machine learning (ML) has become a prominent approach for RI prediction, with both deep learning and shallow supervised algorithms used in prior work. Tree-based methods (e.g., Random Forest, ExtraTrees, XGBoost) and logistic regression are frequently applied due to lower computational cost and simpler model design compared to deep architectures. However, RI prediction is typically an imbalanced classification problem, motivating resampling or algorithmic class-weighting.
supporting_quote: Over the last decade, machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) methods have emerged as viable means of predicting TC RI.
shallow ML‐based algorithms are more popular for RI predictions because of their simplicity and low computational demands.
Another limitation for predicting RI with more accuracy is the imbalanced data issue

chunks.text: Conventional RI predictor sets emphasize favorable environments such as high sea surface temperature (SST), but MHW characteristics may convey additional information beyond SST at a given time. Prior studies suggest TCs over MHWs can intensify faster, yet explicit use of MHW metrics as RI predictors has been largely missing. This motivates integrating MHW detection and intensity metrics into RI forecast models.
supporting_quote: While high sea surface temperature (SST) and ocean heat content... are generally recognized as favorable environmental conditions for triggering RI
the influential characteristics of MHW for initiating RI events have not yet been fully explored.
to the best of our knowledge, there is no research done on utilizing MHW characteristics as predictors of RI events.

chunks.text: The study’s overarching aim is to build a global predictive model for a subset of RI events that are impacted by nearby marine heatwaves. It first identifies global hotspots where MHWs and RI co-occur or occur in succession, then develops an ensemble ML framework using storm and MHW characteristics. The model is evaluated on an independent recent period to reflect contemporary warming conditions.
supporting_quote: The overarching goal of this study is to develop a global predictive ML model for a subset of RI events impacted by nearby MHWs.
we analyze the TC best track and sea surface temperature data from 1981 to 2023 to identify hotspot regions for compound events
we propose an ensemble machine learning model for RI forecasting based on storm and MHW characteristics.

chunks.text: A central objective is to quantify whether MHW metrics improve RI prediction compared to using SST alone, which is common in existing RI prediction approaches. The comparison emphasizes operational relevance by focusing on standard RI forecast verification metrics and false alarms. The paper specifically tests whether MHW-based predictors can control false-alarm behavior while maintaining useful detection.
supporting_quote: We quantify enhanced predictive skill achieved by using marine heatwave intensity metrics as predictors compared to sea surface temperature
we evaluate the actual improvement achieved by using MHW predictors compared to using pre‐storm SST as a predictor.
using MHW predictors instead of the conventional method of using sea surface temperature reduces the false alarm rate by 30%.

chunks.text: RI remains difficult to forecast because it depends on nonlinear processes and storm inner-core dynamics that are not well observed or represented. The paper notes that RI forecast errors can be substantially larger than typical intensity forecast errors. This creates an urgent need for improved predictors and models, especially for environments favorable to intensification.
supporting_quote: Predicting RI remains challenging because as it involves the understanding of internal dynamics, interplay of environmental parameters, and nonlinear processes
RI forecast errors are estimated to be 2–3 times larger due to limited observational data and lack of understanding and prediction of inner‐core processes
signals the urgent need for enhanced forecasting capabilities

chunks.text: Selecting informative predictors is a primary obstacle for data-driven RI forecasting. Standard environmental predictors (e.g., SST, wind shear) do not uniquely determine RI, and RI can occur even when some conditions are unfavorable. This implies that improved predictor sets are needed to better discriminate RI onset.
supporting_quote: The primary challenge of data‐driven RI forecasting models is choosing predictors that inform RI formation and evolution
their coexistence is not necessarily required for RI.
Hurricane Irma (2017)... underwent RI despite high vertical wind shear.

chunks.text: ML-based RI prediction is hampered by severe class imbalance because RI cases are far fewer than non-RI cases along TC tracks. Without rebalancing, models tend to bias toward the majority class and miss RI events. This necessitates explicit imbalance-handling strategies such as oversampling or class weighting.
supporting_quote: RI events are generally limited compared to non‐RI situations, resampling techniques should be used to prevent models from being skewed toward the majority class.
In ML, imbalanced data often leads to models being overexposed to the majority samples during training
SMOTE can successfully address and rectify the imbalance issue

chunks.text: The study constructs a compound MHW–TC dataset by pairing TC best-track points with nearby MHW conditions based on spatiotemporal criteria. A compound event is recorded when a TC track lies within 200 km of a MHW grid point and the MHW occurred within 10 days or less before the TC record time. Each 3-hour TC point is treated as an independent sample, labeled positive if RI occurs in the subsequent 24 hours.
supporting_quote: A compound event occurs if a TC track lies within 200 km of a MHW.
a MHW must be present 10 days or less before the TC record time.
Each location/time is considered an independent sample. For each location we determine certain MHW metrics... We also determine if RI occurs over the subsequent 24 hr

chunks.text: RI event detection is performed from processed IBTrACS best-track data using the National Hurricane Center definition. The workflow preprocesses multi-agency best-track records by selecting USA-agency wind speeds when available, otherwise choosing wind speeds from the closest agency location. Only tropical and subtropical cyclone points are retained, excluding extratropical and other disturbance types.
supporting_quote: we select a unique wind speed for each location. We use wind speed provided by the USA agencies where data is available and non‐zero.
RI occurs if the maximum sustained wind speed increases at least 30 knots in 24 hr
we included only those points... classified as tropical or subtropical cyclones, excluding all other storm types

chunks.text: Marine heatwaves are detected pointwise from daily NOAA OISST using a percentile threshold definition. A MHW is defined as SST above the local, seasonally evolving 90th percentile for at least five consecutive days, and events separated by less than 3 days are merged. A 1991–2020 baseline and smoothing procedures are used to compute thresholds and reduce noise.
supporting_quote: a MHW event is defined as a period in which SST is above the local and seasonally evolving 90th percentile threshold of SSTs for at least five consecutive days
two events less than 3 days apart are considered a single MHW event.
A 30 year baseline period, from 1991 to 2020, is used in our analysis.

chunks.text: The modeling strategy trains four tree-based binary classifiers (XGBoost, Random Forest, ExtraTrees, LightGBM) and then forms a weighted ensemble. Hyperparameters are tuned via grid search with fivefold time-based cross-validation and F1-score as the selection criterion to balance precision and recall. The final ensemble (“LightEX”) selects weights to maximize separation between POD and FAR while keeping FAR below 50% on the test set.
supporting_quote: Four tree‐based ML classification algorithms (namely XGBoost, Random Forest (RF), ExtraTrees (ET) and LightGBM)
we divide the input data from 1981 to 2020 into five equal time periods (a.k.a. folds).
the models are trained using solely the training sets, and their performance on the validation set is evaluated based on F1‐score
We select the best ensemble ML modelso that it performs on the testing set with a FAR <50%

chunks.text: To address class imbalance, the study applies SMOTE for Random Forest and ExtraTrees, generating synthetic minority samples using the 5 nearest neighbors. For XGBoost and LightGBM, the models also use an internal class-weight parameter (scale_pos_weight) tuned during hyperparameter search, which emphasizes the minority RI class in the loss function. The authors report that using scale_pos_weight is computationally faster than SMOTE for these boosting models in their configuration.
supporting_quote: we rely primarily on the original Synthetic Minority Over‐sampling Technique (a.k.a. SMOTE)
we set the neighborhood as the 5 closest instances around the sample of interest.
XGBoost and LightGBM algorithms also have an internal parameter, called "scale_pos_weight"
using the scale_pos_weight parameter results in about 20% faster runtime compared to the SMOTE option

chunks.text: Feature importance and selection are performed using SHAP to rank predictors and focus training on the most influential variables. From 31 candidate features, 12 are retained as most influential, combining storm characteristics (e.g., wind speed, distance to land, storm motion, location and time) with MHW intensity metrics. This selection is used to improve efficiency and predictive performance of the ML models.
supporting_quote: We employ the Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) model explainer... to rank the importance of various features
Among the total 31 features considered... the SHAP results indicate that the 12 listed in Table 1 are the most influential parameters
mean absolute intensity is the most important MHW metric.

chunks.text: TC intensity-change samples are derived from the International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS), using 3-hourly interpolated track data. The dataset provides maximum sustained wind speed and other storm attributes, with lat/lon rounded to 0.1° (~10 km). The analysis focuses on 1981–2023 to align with availability of daily SST used for MHW detection.
supporting_quote: The dataset is sourced from the publicly available International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS) dataset
This dataset contains 3‐hourly interpolated TC track data from 1841 to the present.
The latitude and longitude values in the dataset are rounded to the nearest 0.1°, which corresponds to approximately 10 km in spatial resolution.

chunks.text: Marine heatwaves are detected using the NOAA Optimum Interpolation Sea Surface Temperature v2.1 (NOAA OISST v2.1) daily SST product. The SST record spans 1 September 1981 through 19 October 2023 at 0.25° (~25 km) resolution. A 1991–2020 baseline is used to compute daily climatology and 90th-percentile thresholds.
supporting_quote: The NOAA Optimum Interpolation Sea Surface Temperature version 2.1 (NOAA OISST v2.1) dataset is used in this study for MHW detection.
from 1 September 1981 through 19 October 2023 at a spatial resolution of 25 km.
A 30 year baseline period, from 1991 to 2020, is used in our analysis.

chunks.text: The compound MHW–TC dataset is created by matching TC track points to proximal MHW conditions under explicit spatial and temporal windows. The spatial window is 200 km around the TC track point, intended to cover the inner and outer core. The temporal window requires that MHW conditions occurred within 10 days before the TC record time.
supporting_quote: A compound event occurs if a TC track lies within 200 km of a MHW. This distance spans the inner and outer core radii of a TC
a temporal condition must also be met... a MHW must be present 10 days or less before the TC record time.

chunks.text: Model development uses a time-split design with recent years reserved for out-of-sample testing. The 2021–2023 period is used as the independent test set and represents about 20% of compounding MHW–TC events. The training/validation period (1981–2020) is split into five equal time folds for cross-validation.
supporting_quote: the testing period (2021–2023) covers approximately 20% of the total compounding MHW‐TC events in the dataset
The rest of the dataset is used to train and validate the model.
we divide the input data from 1981 to 2020 into five equal time periods (a.k.a. folds).

chunks.text: The study identifies geographic hotspots where MHWs and RI co-occur, highlighting several coastal and western boundary regions as frequent locations for compound MHW-induced RI. The reported hotspots include the Caribbean Sea near the Lesser Antilles, westernmost Pacific waters, Bay of Bengal near India, eastern coasts of the Philippines, northwest coasts of Australia, and the eastern part of the Southwest Indian basin. These patterns summarize where MHW preconditioning and RI are most likely to compound.
supporting_quote: the spatial distribution results... suggest that theCaribbean Sea (nearthe Lesser Antilles), westernmost Pacific waters, coastlines of India in the Bay of Bengal, eastern coasts of Philippines, northwest coasts of Australia, and east of the Southwest Indian basin are the regional hotspots

chunks.text: Normalized frequencies of MHW-induced RI increase across most basins over recent decades, with the 2020s reaching or surpassing the 2010s in most regions. Some basins show sustained high activity levels since the 1990s (Australian and Northwest Pacific at roughly 0.6–0.7), while the East Australian basin shows low recent activity. The East Pacific displays consistently high activity in multiple decades.
supporting_quote: The decadal plots illustrate an increase in the ratio of MHW‐induced RI events over most basins.
For the Australian and the Northwest Pacific basins, we observe a nearly constant frequency since the 1990s at around 0.6–0.7.
In the East Pacific... exhibit consistently high activity... with RI frequencies of 06–0.8 per year

chunks.text: Feature-importance analysis indicates that both storm-state variables and MHW intensity metrics are key predictors for MHW-associated RI classification. The most influential feature is the starting wind speed at the TC point, followed by latitude and MHW mean absolute intensity. Distance to land and maximum absolute MHW temperature also rank highly, suggesting coastal proximity and extreme MHW warmth matter for prediction.
supporting_quote: the SHAP results indicate that the 12 listed in Table 1 are the most influential parameters
start_wind_speed... Mean  SHAP  value 1.05
intensity_mean_abs... Mean  SHAP  value 0.47
intensity_max_abs... Mean  SHAP  value 0.35
dist2land... Mean  SHAP  value 0.37

chunks.text: Among individual learners, LightGBM is much faster than the alternatives while maintaining comparable predictive skill, making it practical for large global datasets. The paper reports LightGBM runs 8× faster than XGBoost, 12× faster than ExtraTrees, and 24× faster than Random Forest in their HPC configuration. This computational advantage supports its use as the dominant component in the ensemble.
supporting_quote: The results show that the LightGBM model runs significantly faster compared to other models (8 times faster than XGBoost, 12 times faster than ET, and 24 times faster than RF)

chunks.text: The final ensemble model (LightEX) uses weights favoring LightGBM and excludes Random Forest because it does not improve the ensemble objective. The best weight set is reported as 0.3 (XGBoost), 0.0 (RF), 0.1 (ET), and 0.6 (LightGBM). Predictions are produced by a weighted average of class probabilities followed by argmax classification.
supporting_quote: The best ensemble model adopts a weightset of 0.3, 0.0, 0.1, and 0.6 for XGBoost, RF, ET, and LightGBM, respectively.
RF does not add value to the ensemble model therefore it is excluded
The weighted average ofthe probabilities assigned to each class by all modelsisthen calculated

chunks.text: On the independent 2021–2023 test set, the LightEX model achieves a balance between detection and false alarms that meets common RI-forecast usefulness thresholds. Reported skill is POD = 54% and FAR = 49%, with a bias near 1 (bias = 1.06), indicating little over- or underprediction. These values were used to justify the final ensemble selection criteria.
supporting_quote: LightEX exhibits a good balance between detection accuracy and precision (POD = 54% and FAR = 49%), and the results are provided without over‐ or underprediction (bias = 1.06).

chunks.text: Basin-wise evaluation on the unseen 2021–2023 data shows performance varies by region, without retraining the global model. The East Pacific achieves the highest POD among basins, while the Australian basin performs worst (POD = 44% and FAR = 55%). The North Indian basin shows similar POD to Atlantic and Northwest Pacific but about 20% lower FAR, implying fewer false positives in that region.
supporting_quote: we evaluated the performance of the LightEX model using the unseen data (2021–2023 events) from each individual basin without retraining the model
The predictions... East Pacific exceeds that of other basins
our model resulted in POD = 44% and FAR = 55% for the Australian basin, which shows the worst performance among all basins.
the model demonstrates similar POD in the North Indian basin... but with roughly 20% lower FAR.

chunks.text: Replacing MHW predictors with pre-storm SST substantially increases false alarms, showing that MHW metrics carry more actionable information for controlling FAR. For the LightEX configuration, POD improves slightly (~3%) but FAR worsens markedly, from about 50% to 68%. Other models also show FAR values exceeding 60% when using SST alone, making them less suitable for operational-style RI guidance.
supporting_quote: we repeated the training and testing processes... this time using SST at the location/time of the TC
we observe a slight improvement in LightEX's POD (∼3%), its FAR value deteriorates by 36% (50% compared to 68%).
The ML models exhibit a significant increase in false alarms, with FAR values exceeding 60%.

chunks.text: During 2021–2023, the paper reports 51 damaging TCs totaling about $360B, and the model captured RI phases for more than half of them. Specifically, 28 of the 51 storms’ RI phases (55%) were detected by the model. This demonstrates practical value but also indicates substantial missed events remain.
supporting_quote: During our testing period, there were 51 TCs with a total damage of $360 B
of which the RI phase of 28 TCs (55%) was captured by our model.

chunks.text: The authors attribute missed RI predictions to both input-data limitations and model limitations typical of ML classifiers. They categorize issues into (a) input quality (data availability, data quality, feature representation) and (b) model inadequacies (generalization limits, algorithmic limitations, bias–variance tradeoff). They suggest improvements via better data quality, adding environmental predictors, and refining algorithms.
supporting_quote: The inability to predict more TC RI events is rooted in the inherent limitations and complexities of ML classification models.
The reasons can be categorized into two main areas: (a) input quality... and (b) model inadequacies
Improving data quality, incorporating more environmental features, and refining algorithms could enhance the model's predictive capabilities.

chunks.text: The model focuses on MHW and storm characteristics, but the authors note other environmental variables likely matter for RI and should be included in future work. Examples include vertical wind shear, ocean heat content, convective potential energy, divergence at 200 hPa, and vorticity. They also mention the need to manage uncertainties and potential error propagation when integrating forecast model outputs for real-time use.
supporting_quote: other important environmental predictors, such as vertical wind shear, ocean heat content, convective potential energy, divergence at 200 hPa from the storm center, and vorticity, may also be important

Incorporating forecast data from reliable numerical weather prediction models enables real‐time applicability of the model. However, thisintroduces complexitiessuch as choosing the appropriate model, dealing with track forecast uncertainties

chunks.text: Observational uncertainties in the IBTrACS dataset and differences among reporting agencies can affect training labels and model performance. The paper notes position uncertainty around 10–15 km for strong TCs and intensity uncertainties of ±7–20% across basins, with methodological differences such as 1- vs 10-minute wind averaging. Such inconsistencies complicate RI detection and predictor reliability.
