supporting_quote: The IBTrACS data also has uncertainties in its reported position and intensity
The position uncertainty is estimated to be approximately 10–15 km for strong TCs (Ws > 100 kt).
The range of intensity uncertainties across ocean basins is ±7–20%
different agencies use varying averaging times for maximum wind estimates (usually 1 or 10 min)

chunks.text: Marine heatwave detection choices can influence results, and alternative definitions may alter compound-event statistics under climate change. The study uses the common Hobday definition and smoothing techniques, but the authors note arguments for shifting baselines to avoid artificially increasing detected MHW frequency and intensity. They also cite evidence that smoothing affects estimated MHW duration and intensity, implying sensitivity to methodological settings.
supporting_quote: In terms of MHW detection criteria, we adhered to the commonly used definition of MHWs
there are suggestions to use a shifting temperature baseline rather than a fixed one to avoid detecting more frequent and more intense MHWs
found that MHWs become shorter and less intense in the absence of smoothing techniques.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that a global ML approach targeting MHW-influenced RI is feasible and valuable, especially for recent warming-era events. The LightEX ensemble uses storm and MHW metrics, with mean and maximum absolute MHW SST emerging as reliable predictors, and is designed for 24-hour RI forecasts aligned with the RI definition. The model performs acceptably across major basins, particularly the Pacific and Atlantic.
supporting_quote: This study aims to develop a global predictive ML model for the occurrence of RI events that are influenced by proximal MHWs.
mean and maximum absolute SSTs during MHWs emerged as reliable predictors of compounding MHW‐TC events.
based on the availability of TC and MHW data, the developed model can aid 24 hr forecasts of RI.

chunks.text: The authors conclude that incorporating MHW characteristics helps keep false alarms within operationally meaningful bounds, whereas substituting SST alone produces undesirably high FAR. They emphasize that MHW predictors maintain FAR below the 50% threshold, while SST-based variants can increase FAR by more than 30%. This supports integrating MHW metrics into existing and future RI forecast frameworks.
supporting_quote: including MHW characteristics as predictors not only helps achieve favorable POD levels, but also maintains a FAR below the 50% threshold.
using SST as a predictor instead of MHW metrics... leads to undesirably higher FAR values (more than 30%).

chunks.text: The study highlights LightGBM’s effectiveness for TC intensity-change classification and notes it as a first application in this context, emphasizing major runtime advantages. LightGBM training time is reported as about one-eighth of XGBoost and about one-twentieth of Random Forest in their tests. The authors suggest the approach can scale as datasets and predictor sets grow.
supporting_quote: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study that used LightGBM to classify TC intensity changes.
LightGBM outperforms other decision tree algorithms with significantly lower computational costs (about one‐eighth of XGBoost and one‐twentieth ofRF).

chunks.text: Coastal flooding risk is increasing because many people and assets are concentrated near shorelines and multiple drivers can trigger floods. Drivers include tides, storm surges, heavy rainfall, river discharge, waves, and sea level rise. When inland and coastal drivers interact concurrently or sequentially, the resulting hazard is compound coastal flooding and can produce nonlinear amplification of impacts. Climate change further alters exposure and the likelihood of these drivers co-occurring, increasing socioenvironmental consequences.
supporting_quote: Approximately 40 % of the global population resides within a 100 km proximity to oceanic coastlines
coastal flooding may result from the concurrent or successive interaction of inland factors... and coastal drivers... known as coastal compound flooding (CCF)
climate change has further altered the exposure of coastal communities to various flood drivers such as sea level rise (SLR) and precipitation

chunks.text: Nature-based Solutions (NbS) are promoted as alternatives or complements to gray infrastructure for coastal protection. Compared to fixed defenses, NbS can provide co-benefits such as biodiversity, habitat conservation, lower maintenance costs, and reduced greenhouse gas emissions, while attenuating waves and surges. Examples include tidal marshes, mangroves, dunes, barrier islands, and maritime forests. Hybrid approaches combining green and gray measures are frequently proposed to enhance coastal defense.
supporting_quote: NbS have emerged as alternative solutions that can provide multiple benefits for ecosystem and flood protection, including biodiversity and habitat conservation, long-term sustainability, lower maintenance costs
Tidal marshes, mangrove forests, intertidal flats, dunes, barrier islands, and maritime forests are examples of NbS that can effectively dissipate wave energy
hybrid solutions involving elements of both gray and green

chunks.text: Process-based numerical models are widely used to evaluate NbS effectiveness because field and laboratory experiments can be difficult and costly under extreme hydrodynamic conditions. Modeling offers flexibility for representing feature evolution, roughness characterization, and wave attenuation at relevant spatial and temporal scales. As computational resources improve, numerical modeling is increasingly adopted for NbS assessment. However, much of the modeling literature has focused on single flood drivers rather than compound events.
supporting_quote: In field and laboratory experiments, it is quite challenging to simulate hydrodynamic conditions with strong waves and water depths of several meters
Numerical models offer more flexibility and advantages in terms of feature evolution, roughness characterization, and wave attenuation
most modeling investigations... have focused on individual flood drivers rather than CCFs

chunks.text: The study aims to review numerical, process-based modeling literature on NbS for coastal flood mitigation with emphasis on compound coastal flooding. It seeks to identify knowledge gaps that limit understanding of NbS efficacy under compound scenarios and to outline modeling pathways for improved characterization. The review also targets uncertainties in numerical modeling and barriers that prevent transition from research studies to operational implementation. The intended outcome is a framework that supports adequate representation of NbS within compound flood models.
supporting_quote: reviews the literature on process-based modeling of NbS for mitigating compound coastal flooding and identifies knowledge gaps to enhance future research efforts
We outlined potential modeling pathways to improve NbS characterization in the compound flooding framework
uncertainties associated with numerical modeling and steps to bridge the research-to-operation gaps were briefly discussed

chunks.text: Only a small fraction of numerical NbS studies explicitly evaluate NbS performance under compound flooding conditions, leaving limited evidence for decision-making. The literature largely concentrates on single drivers such as waves or storm surge without incorporating inland processes like river discharge, precipitation, or groundwater. This imbalance constrains understanding of NbS efficacy when nonlinear interactions among drivers occur. The deficit motivates the need for improved coupled modeling to capture compound hazards.
supporting_quote: Our review identified a dearth of research (9 %) investigating the performance of NbS against compound flooding scenarios
most modeling investigations... have focused on individual flood drivers rather than CCFs
the inclusion of inland processes, such as river discharge, precipitation, and groundwater level, has been conspicuously missing

chunks.text: Adequate representation of nature-based features in numerical models is difficult because multiple interacting processes and feedbacks must be captured. Compound flood models must represent offshore water levels, nearshore wave transformations, overland flow dynamics, and additional drivers such as precipitation and river discharge. Omitting any compound flood source can cause substantial prediction errors, making coupling approaches necessary. These complexities have hindered widespread evaluation of NbS functionality for compound coastal flooding.
supporting_quote: Adequate representation of nature-based features in a numerical model is challenging due to the difficulties in linking multiple processbased models

full representation of CCFs... requires a model that accounts for (a) wave generation, storm surge, and tide processes... (d) other processes like infiltration, precipitation, wind setup, and river discharge
Eliminating any of the CCF sources can result in substantial prediction errors; therefore, the use of coupling techniques is inevitable

chunks.text: Operational deployment of compound flood modeling that includes NbS remains limited despite progress in individual component models. While models for overland flooding and coastal water levels are operational for certain forecasting tasks, their coupled use for compound flood risk is not yet operational. This contributes to a research-to-operations gap where decision-makers lack consistent, actionable modeling outputs. Localized, research-phase efforts dominate, despite funding support.
supporting_quote: the coupling of these approaches to provide estimates of the compound flood risk is not operational
most efforts are local and in a research phase
The modeling community has yet to reach a point where they have consistent approaches to inform CCF decision-making

chunks.text: The review used an automated online database search in SCOPUS with a structured query built from multiple keyword substrings. Four search strings targeted NbS types, nature-based topic terms, flooding hazards (including related wave and sea-level terms), and mitigation scope terms. The initial results were screened by titles, abstracts, keywords, and full texts to ensure alignment with numerical modeling of NbS for coastal flooding. After screening, the authors compiled a final database of 141 relevant articles.
supporting_quote: an automated search strategy within the SCOPUS database, followed by a screening process that ultimately resulted in 141 publications
four search strings were developed to align with the key elements of our overarching goal
first the titles, abstracts, keywords, and then, the full texts of the initial results were reviewed... After this step, we identified 141 articles for the final database

chunks.text: To organize analyses, the final set of 141 articles was classified into six categories capturing study scale, geographic location, numerical tools, NbS type, hybrid solutions, and whether compound flooding was considered. Spatial scale categories included global, regional, local, and N/A for idealized or experimental studies. The classification supported quantitative summaries of publication trends, dominant study locations, common modeling tools, and ecosystem types. This taxonomy also enabled focused synthesis on compound flooding and hybrid structures.
supporting_quote: this collection of articles has been classified into six categories
The 1st category determines the spatial scale... (i) Global... (ii) Regional... (iii) Local... and (iv) N/A
Categories five and six determine whether the mentioned study addresses hybrid solutions... or compound flooding

chunks.text: The paper frames an ideal process-based modeling pathway for evaluating NbS under compound coastal flooding as an integration of multiple model components. It emphasizes coupling hydrologic, hydraulic, hydrodynamic (ocean circulation), wave, and ecological models and distinguishes coupling schemes including one-way, loosely/two-way, tightly, and fully coupled approaches. Fully coupled modeling is described as solving hydrologic, hydraulic, and hydrodynamic equations simultaneously with mutual feedback at each time step. The framework is presented as necessary to represent nonlinear interactions among compound drivers.
supporting_quote: A holistic process-based modeling framework demands the integration of various numerical models, including ecological, hydrologic, hydraulic, ocean circulation (hydrodynamic), nearshore, and deepwater wave models
This coupling can be achieved in a variety of ways, including one-way... loosely... tightly, and fully coupled schemes
Fully coupled modeling... the hydrologic, hydraulic and hydrodynamic models are fully integrated and solved simultaneously

chunks.text: The evidence base for the review consists of 141 publications identified from SCOPUS after screening for relevance to numerical modeling of NbS for coastal flooding mitigation. The final database is summarized in a supplementary table (Table S1) ordered chronologically. Articles span publication years from 2009 to 2023 based on the SCOPUS retrieval. The dataset is used for statistical summaries of scales, geographies, tools, NbS types, hybrid solutions, and compound flooding coverage.
supporting_quote: After this step, we identified 141 articles for the final database
The final database of 141 articles is summarized in Table S1, chronologically from oldest to newest
the oldest papers were published in 2009
published between 2009 and 2023

chunks.text: The review’s geographic metadata show study locations across 22 countries, with a strong concentration in the United States and the Netherlands. Within the U.S., Virginia and New York are most frequently studied, followed by Maryland and Florida, then Louisiana and New Jersey. The paper notes an absence of studies from Africa in the retrieved set. These location counts are based on the classified database of 141 articles.
supporting_quote: The research was conducted in 22 countries
Notably, there are no studies from Africa

chunks.text: The literature shows increasing publication activity on numerical modeling of NbS for coastal flooding since the first identified papers in 2009, with notable peaks around 2016 and 2022. The authors report a gradual upward trend over time, indicating growing interest and expanding research output. However, sharp increases are followed by significant declines the next year, suggesting episodic surges in publication rather than steady growth. This temporal pattern is summarized from SCOPUS-retrieved documents.
supporting_quote: the oldest papers were published in 2009
There has been a gradual upward trend over the years. However, two notable periods of increase in 2016 and 2022 culminate in sharp peaks

chunks.text: Most studies in the compiled database evaluate NbS at local spatial scales rather than regional or global scales. The paper reports that 61% of studies are local, typically focusing on a coast, bay, or city. Only a few studies address regional or mixed scales. This indicates that evidence on broader-scale transferability and regional system interactions is relatively limited.
supporting_quote: a large proportion of studies (61 %) are carried out at the local scale and focus on individual coasts, cities, or bays
Three studies examined the regional effects of vegetation patches

chunks.text: Research locations are heavily concentrated in the United States, which accounts for 53% of study locations in the relevant literature. The Netherlands is the second most studied setting with 12 articles, while China is third with five. Within the U.S., Virginia and New York are the most frequently studied, followed by Maryland and Florida, then Louisiana and New Jersey. This spatial skew suggests that many coastal settings remain underrepresented in modeling evidence.
supporting_quote: the US is the most studied country, accounting for 53 % of study locations in the relevant literature
Outside the US, 12 articles focused on the sites in the Netherlands. China is the third most frequently studied country, with five articles
Within the US, the coastal regions of Virginia and New York were the most frequently studied

chunks.text: SWAN is the most frequently used numerical tool across the reviewed NbS coastal flooding modeling studies. It appears in 36 articles, followed by finite volume/finite difference models (24) and ADCIRC (23). The coupling of ADCIRC and SWAN is also common, appearing in 16 studies. These tool-use patterns indicate that wave modeling and coupled surge-wave frameworks dominate process-based NbS simulations.
supporting_quote: Simulating WAves Nearshore (SWAN) was adopted as a numerical tool in 36 articles
Advanced CIRCulation (ADCIRC) was the third choice with 23 studies
the coupling of ADCIRC and SWAN was also widely used with 16 studies

chunks.text: For studies that consider compound flooding specifically, TELEMAC and SWAN are reported as the most common numerical tools, each appearing in four articles. In analyses that include hybrid solutions (NbS combined with hard structures), SWAN (9), TELEMAC (7), and Delft3D (5) are most common. This suggests that compound and hybrid-focused modeling draws from a somewhat different subset of tools than the broader NbS flood modeling literature.
supporting_quote: analysis... showed that TELEMAC and SWAN (4 articles) were the most common numerical tools in such studies
in the presence of hybrid solutions... it was more common to use SWAN (9 articles), TELEMAC (7 articles), and Delft3D (5 articles)

chunks.text: Marshes are the most frequently modeled NbS type in the reviewed literature, accounting for 43% of case studies. Swamps represent 22% and barrier islands 11%, while seagrass accounts for 8%. Reefs and dunes appear less often, at 8% and 5% respectively, and a substantial portion of publications refer generically to wetlands or idealized vegetation. This distribution highlights a strong emphasis on marsh ecosystems compared with other NbS types.
supporting_quote: marshes are the most frequent NbS type, responsible for 43 % of case studies
22 % and 11 % of the literature selected swamps and barrier islands as their NbS model
8 % and 5 % of publications focused on reef and dune models, respectively

chunks.text: A central quantitative finding is that only 9% of the reviewed numerical studies investigate NbS performance against compound flooding scenarios. The paper treats this scarcity as the main motivation for proposing a more comprehensive modeling framework and identifying research directions. The result indicates that current numerical evidence is largely insufficient for assessing NbS under interacting inland-coastal flood drivers. This gap underpins subsequent discussion of coupling, ecological feedback, and operational implementation.
supporting_quote: only 9 % have numerically investigated the performance of NbS against compound flooding
Our review identified a dearth of research (9 %) investigating the performance of NbS against compound flooding scenarios

chunks.text: Coupling process-based models to represent compound flooding with ecological feedback can become computationally burdensome, especially when hydrodynamic and hydrologic components interact. The paper notes multiple coupling schemes, but achieving an ideal two-way or fully coupled representation that includes upstream flood water, runoff, storm surge, and ecological feedback is challenging. Moving toward full coupling requires overcoming issues in mathematical representation, computational power, and reconciling different temporal and spatial resolutions. These barriers are presented as key reasons the field still lacks a holistic compound flood framework with NbS.
supporting_quote: The computational burden often rises when there is a need to capture the impacts of hydrodynamic and hydrologic components via coupling process-based models
Moving toward a full coupling model requires overcoming challenges related to the complex mathematical representation... the computational power required, and the temporal and spatial resolution
Current state-of-the-art modeling efforts still lacks a holistic framework

chunks.text: A unified, universal approach for representing vegetation and other NbS in numerical models is still missing, and multiple known challenges remain for wetland characterization. The paper highlights needs such as accounting for storm-induced wetland changes, improving friction/drag formulations, capturing wave setup with vegetation, handling three-dimensional vegetation, and representing sub-grid channels. These limitations complicate reliable evaluation of NbS effectiveness during extreme events and compound flooding. The review positions these as persistent obstacles despite increasing modeling research.
supporting_quote: a unified and universal approach for vegetation simulation is still missing
listed six challenges... considering storm-induced changes in wetland structure... enhancing frictional formulations... a method for capturing the wave setup when vegetation is present
modeling of the three-dimensional vegetation... considering sub-grid channels through vegetated fields

chunks.text: Common vegetation parameterizations based on enhanced bottom friction are widely used but can be inadequate when vegetation height relative to water depth is not negligible. The approach may not capture emergence/submergence effects and becomes uncertain for time-varying roughness in systems like seagrass and kelp. The paper suggests that 2D parameterization can be insufficient and that 3D parameterization may be needed to resolve flow through vegetation. These issues contribute to uncertainty in estimating NbS-induced attenuation under changing water levels and seasons.
supporting_quote: The bottom friction approach does not take into account the emergence and submergence levels (depth-dependent or height characteristics) of vegetation fields
this approach is uncertain for vegetations with time-varying roughness, such as seagrasses and kelps
The 2D parameterization is inadequate when the relative vegetation height... is not negligible... 3D parameterization can be used

chunks.text: Explicit drag-coefficient approaches can capture unresolved vegetation effects but introduce uncertainty because the bulk drag coefficient often requires calibration or prior selection. Many uncertainties affect the choice of drag coefficients, and the lack of universal formulations across vegetation types and wave conditions hinders standardization. Alternative formulations based on Reynolds number or Keulegan–Carpenter number exist, but omissions such as blade flexural rigidity and wave frequency limit adoption. The review frames these as barriers to robust and transferable NbS modeling.
supporting_quote: relies on a pre-defined bulk drag coefficient, CD, which is subsequently calibrated or obtained from similar studies and direct measurements
lack of a universal formulation for different vegetation types and wave conditions further hinders widespread application
Ignoring blade flexural rigidity... and absence of wave frequency... in most formulations impedes this alternative approach

chunks.text: Flexibility and seasonality of vegetation are repeatedly identified as difficult to represent, because many models assume rigid vegetation and overlook temporal variability. Yet temporal variability can arise from seasonal growth and decay, changing canopy cover between low and peak biomass and affecting drag and attenuation. The paper notes that these dynamics create uncertainty, especially when selecting implicit versus explicit dissipation models under different stem-submergence ratios. It recommends that future evaluations consider synthetic scenarios spanning vegetation morphologies, storms, and water levels to improve robustness.
supporting_quote: Most existing numerical models and tools are based on a rigid schematization of vegetation and avoid modeling flexible plants
temporal variability of vegetation properties... attributed to seasonal growth and decay... often overlooked in numerical modeling studies
evaluate NbS models using synthetic scenarios that include different ecosystem conditions and vegetation morphologies, storm characteristics, water level scenarios

chunks.text: The review emphasizes substantial uncertainty sources in compound flood modeling, spanning hydrologic parameter identifiability, structural/model discrepancy, and measurement errors, as well as hydrodynamic uncertainties from topobathy errors, forcing and boundary conditions, and roughness/drag parameters. Input data quality is described as a major source of uncertainty, with bathymetry in data-scarce areas highlighted as an example. The paper lists methods such as Monte Carlo sampling, GLUE, data assimilation, and Bayesian model averaging to address uncertainty. Vegetation parameterization and time-dependent updates are singled out as additional ecological uncertainty drivers.
supporting_quote: Parameter estimation problems due to nonuniqueness of model parameters... structural uncertainty... and measurement uncertainty... are important elements of hydrologic uncertainties
input data is recognized as a major source of uncertainty and error in the CCF modeling process
parametrization of vegetations... and time-dependent updating of vegetation characteristics represent a significant uncertainty

chunks.text: The paper concludes that expanding knowledge of NbS performance against compound coastal flooding requires stronger coupling among ecological, hydrological, hydraulic, and hydrodynamic components while explicitly simulating NbS. It highlights three main challenges: mimicking vegetation dynamics (dimensions, motion, flexibility, seasonality), selecting tools that represent relevant physics and morphology, and coupling models with effective information exchange during execution. The authors advocate collaborative model development with end users to produce actionable scenarios and accelerate transition to operational readiness. Addressing these needs is presented as essential for consistent compound-flood decision support that includes NbS.
supporting_quote: we recommend more efforts toward coupling various components affecting CCF while considering and simulating NbS

Major challenges... (a) sufficient mimic of vegetation dynamic... flexibility, and seasonality... (b) selection of a tool with adequate representation of underlying physics... (c) coupling of different model with effective information exchange
it is crucial to develop models collaboratively with end-users and ensure actionable results

chunks.text: The review emphasizes that although hybrid and data-driven approaches can help address high computational costs, they still face constraints from data availability, non-stationarity, and nonlinear interactions. It also notes that integrating non-stationarity into compound flood risk assessment remains limited and uncertain, partly due to short or non-overlapping records and common reliance on simple time-varying assumptions. The authors suggest that improved uncertainty quantification and consideration of time-varying vegetation properties are necessary for reliable projections. These conclusions motivate continued research on both process-based and hybrid compound flood modeling with NbS.
supporting_quote: Hybrid approaches can help with high computational costs... but they have limitations in data availability, non-stationarity, and nonlinear interactions
incorporating non-stationary extreme value analysis... has attracted considerable attention... However, the number of publications to date is very limited
uncertainty quantification is still an area of active research... particularly due to the timevarying properties of vegetations

chunks.text: Rapid intensification (RI) is a major forecast challenge because tropical cyclone intensity can change quickly under favorable conditions, and forecast errors are much larger during rapid intensity changes. RI is defined by the National Hurricane Center as a 35 mph increase in maximum sustained winds over 24 hours. Many major hurricanes undergo RI during their life cycle, making RI frequency an indicator of the most intense (Category 4–5) storms.
supporting_quote: intensity forecast errors are approximately 2–3 times larger for rapid changes in TC intensity than for nonrapidly intensifying events
rapid intensification (RI) of a TC ... is defined as a 35 mph ... increase in maximum sustained winds over a 24 h period
Approximately 79% of major storms ... undergo this intensification process during their life cycle

chunks.text: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are prolonged periods of anomalously warm sea surface temperatures that can precondition the ocean to supply heat and moisture to tropical cyclones. MHWs are commonly defined as at least five days with SST exceeding a high, seasonally varying threshold relative to a baseline. Because sustained high SSTs can increase enthalpy fluxes into storms, MHWs have been proposed as a catalyst for hurricane intensification.
supporting_quote: marine heatwaves (MHW) as an indicator of a contiguous period of ocean water warming
MHW events are commonly characterized by at least 5 days of warm SSTs exceeding a high seasonally varying threshold above a baseline period
Recent studies have highlighted the importance of MHWs as a catalyst for rapidly intensifying hurricanes

chunks.text: The Gulf of Mexico (GoM) and northwestern Caribbean Sea (NWCS) are highly exposed to landfalling hurricanes and associated rapid intensification. A large share of U.S. landfalling hurricanes since 1950 occurred along this region’s coastlines. Many of the costliest U.S. hurricanes had RI start locations within the GoM/NWCS study area.
supporting_quote: approximately 68% (93 out of 136) of all hurricanes that made landfall on the continental United States between 1950 and 2022 occurring along the coastlines of this region
Among them, the RI start locations of five costly hurricanes in US history were in the study area ... Katrina 2005 ... Harvey 2017 ... Ian 2022 ... Ida 2021 ... Michael 2018

chunks.text: The study aims to quantify whether rapid intensification events are more likely when marine heatwaves are present in the Gulf of Mexico and northwestern Caribbean Sea. The authors frame this as a probabilistic comparison of RI likelihood during MHWs versus non-MHW conditions. The work addresses how the likelihood of RI changes during MHWs using conditional probabilities over historical records.
supporting_quote: we conduct a probabilistic analysis to assess how the likelihood of rapid intensification changes during marine heatwaves in the Gulf of Mexico and northwestern Caribbean Sea
The overarching goal of this research is to determine if RIs are more likely during MHW events
compare it to the RI probability in the absence of MHW

chunks.text: The extent to which marine heatwaves amplify the occurrence of rapid intensification is not well established, despite evidence that warming oceans can fuel cyclone intensification. This uncertainty limits understanding of compound MHW–RI events at regional scales. With oceans warming due to climate change, the authors argue it is essential to quantify how MHWs affect RI likelihood and associated hazards.
supporting_quote: the extent to which marine heatwaves contribute to the potential of rapid intensification events is not yet fully explored
The extent to which the occurrence ofMHWs amplifies the occurrence of RI remains unclear
In light of the expected surge in frequency and intensity of both MHWs and TCs in future warming scenarios

chunks.text: Forecasting rapid intensity changes remains difficult and can lead to major societal impacts because preparedness often lags. The paper highlights that RI-associated forecast errors are substantially larger than for non-RI cases, contributing to higher risk of catastrophic damage. This motivates improved understanding of environmental preconditioning such as prolonged high SSTs.
supporting_quote: This phenomenon is complex and difficult to predict, making it a serious challenge for coastal communities
intensity forecast errors are approximately 2–3 times larger for rapid changes in TC intensity than for nonrapidly intensifying events
This unpredictability, coupled with a lack of appropriate preparedness, often leads to higher risk of catastrophic socioeconomic damage during such events

chunks.text: The authors extract rapid intensification events from best-track records using the National Hurricane Center definition: at least a 35 mph wind increase over 24 hours. Because 3-hourly intensities can produce overlapping sequential RI detections, they apply declustering with a minimum separation time (MST) of 24 hours between RI events along a storm’s track to support event independence. Spatial probabilities are computed on 1°×1° grid cells.
supporting_quote: a RI event is characterized by a minimum 35 mph increase in maximum sustained wind speeds over a 24 h period
an MST equal to 24-h was deemed sufficient to ensure independent events and avoid overlapping RI events
each 1°× 1° computational grid of the area of interest

chunks.text: Marine heatwaves are detected from daily-averaged SST using a percentile-based definition adapted from Hobday et al. The study identifies MHWs where SST exceeds a seasonally varying PC80 threshold for at least five consecutive days, and merges events separated by gaps shorter than 3 days. Thresholds are computed using an 11-day window and smoothed with a 31-day moving average, with separate baseline periods for 1940–1980 and 1981–2022.
supporting_quote: MHWs are identified ... where daily-averaged SSTs exceed the seasonally varying PC80 values for a minimum of five consecutive days
if there is a gap of less than 3 days between two events, they are treated as a single continuous MHW event
a moving 11-day window size was chosen for the threshold calculation
climatology and threshold were smoothed by applying a 31-day moving average
we deployed two climatological periods of 1940 to 1980 (41 years) and 1981 to 2022 (42 years)

chunks.text: To link MHWs to RI events, the paper uses a double-threshold approach defining an RI “impact area” in time and space. MHWs are considered influential if they occur within 10 days of the RI start date and within 125 miles (~200 km) of the RI start location. This filtering creates the pool of MHWs used to compute conditional RI probabilities given MHW occurrence.
supporting_quote: identified all MHWs that have occurred within 10 days and 125 miles of the beginning of RI events (hereinafter called impact area)
the temporal threshold is defined such that the time span of a MHW event must fall within 10 days of the beginning date of RI
we only include MHWs that are located within 125 miles (≈ 200 km) of the start location of RI event

chunks.text: The probabilistic framework includes empirical RI occurrence probabilities and conditional probabilities of RI given MHW presence. RI probability per grid is computed as the fraction of RI occurrences in a grid cell relative to all RI events. Conditional probability P(RI|MHW) is computed for compound RI–MHW co-occurrences meeting RI thresholds and the double-threshold impact-area criteria, and the amplification is summarized as a multiplication rate P(RI|MHW)/P(RI|¬MHW).
supporting_quote: we aim at calculating the gridded probability of RI occurrence, i.e., PRI(i,j), as presented in Eq. (1)
calculate P(RI|MHW) (see Eq. (2) in "Methods"), which represents the probability of RI occurrence given a MHW pre-condition
Multiplication rate = P(RI|MHW) / P(RI|\overline{MHW})

chunks.text: For mapping and inference, probability estimates are evaluated for statistical significance, using p-value ≤ 0.1 as the criterion for significant grids. Grids not meeting this confidence threshold are marked as statistically insignificant (hatched). This approach is used for interpreting spatial patterns in RI probabilities.
supporting_quote: the criterion to identify statistically significant grids is to have p value ≤ 0.1, which is equivalent to the confidence interval of 90%
hatched grids represent locations with a statistically insignificant probability estimate

chunks.text: To contextualize oceanic and atmospheric conditions surrounding RI, the study additionally analyzes Tropical Cyclone Heat Potential (TCHP), depth of the 26°C isotherm (D26), and mixed layer depth (MLD) from NOAA products, and computes vertical wind shear (VWS) and latent heat flux (LHF) from ERA5. These fields are summarized spatially as averages over the 10 days preceding RI onset for events between 2013 and 2022.
supporting_quote: we acquired TCHP, D26, and MLD from NOAA's operational satellite ocean heat content product
Values are averaged over a 10-day period before the onset of RI events occurred between 2013 and 2022
LHF data were sourced from the ERA5 hourly data on single levels
Data for VWS were calculated based on u and v component wind speeds at 200- and 850 hPa pressure levels

chunks.text: Tropical cyclone track and intensity data come from IBTrACS Version 4, which integrates multiple agencies into a unified best-track dataset with three-hourly information. The analysis focuses on the GoM and NWCS over January 1, 1950 through December 31, 2022, and includes 406 unique named storms after excluding entries marked NOT_NAMED.
supporting_quote: International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS) ... provides three-hourly information
The period of our analysis spans from January 1, 1950, through December 31, 2022, with 406 unique TCs on record (excluding those marked NOT_NAMED)

chunks.text: Marine heatwaves are characterized using ERA5 sea surface temperature, selected for its longer and consistent record and hourly resolution compared to daily products. The MHW analysis uses daily-averaged SST from January 1, 1940 to December 31, 2022 to support threshold estimation over multi-decade baselines aligned to the hurricane analysis period.
supporting_quote: ERA5 dataset provides a much longer and more consistent record of SST data with superior temporal resolution (hourly versus daily data)
we used it ... to provide a robust and comprehensive understanding of the impact of MHWs on TC RI
daily-averaged SST data from the ERA5 SST dataset from January 1, 1940 to December 31, 2022

chunks.text: NOAA OISST V2.1 is used to illustrate the regional seasonal cycle and recent anomalies (e.g., 2023 exceeding climatological bounds), while ERA5 is the primary SST source for MHW detection. The SST climatology in the seasonal-cycle figure is based on 1982–2011. This combination supports both contextual visualization and the longer historical MHW detection needs.
supporting_quote: Seasonal cycle of daily SST ... The climatological period is 30 years, ranging from 1982 to 2011
The data source is NOAA OISST V2.1
we used [ERA5] ... our analysis spans hurricanes from 1950 to 2022, necessitating a historical baseline period that adequately covers this timeframe

chunks.text: Ocean thermal-structure variables used for event-based summaries include TCHP, D26, and MLD from NOAA’s Operational Satellite Ocean Heat Content Suite at 0.25° resolution, available from Aug 27, 2012 onward. The study also uses ERA5 latent heat flux and derives vertical wind shear from ERA5 winds at 200 and 850 hPa. These datasets underpin Table 1 and Fig. 9 analyses for 2013–2022.
supporting_quote: TCHP, D26, and MLD from NOAA's operational satellite ocean heat content product that has a grid resolution of 0.25° with temporal extent from Aug 27, 2012 onwards
LHF data were sourced from the ERA5 hourly data on single levels
VWS were calculated based on u and v component wind speeds at 200- and 850 hPa pressure levels

chunks.text: Across the study region and period, a large portion of hurricanes were associated with marine heatwaves, and rapid intensification is more likely during MHW conditions. The paper reports that roughly 70% of hurricanes formed between 1950 and 2022 were influenced by MHWs, and that RI is on average 50% more likely during MHWs. This supports the premise that ocean warming episodes elevate RI risk.
supporting_quote: Approximately 70% of hurricanes that formed between 1950 and 2022 were influenced by marine heatwaves
rapid intensification is, on average, 50% more likely during marine heatwaves

chunks.text: From 1950–2022, the regional dataset contains 406 unique tropical cyclones and 119 unique hurricanes that underwent rapid intensification within the study’s spatial/temporal domain. Using a 24-hour minimum separation time, the study identifies 165 RI occurrences across the GoM and NWCS. Most storms with RI had one event, but some had multiple RI episodes along their tracks.
supporting_quote: The period of our analysis spans ... 1950 ... 2022, with 406 unique TCs
we found that ... 119 unique hurricanes underwent RI
The results indicate a total of 165 RI occurrences in the GoM and NWCS
81 hurricanes that encountered a single RI event, 31 hurricanes that underwent two RI events, 6 hurricanes that experienced three RI events

chunks.text: Rapid intensification in the GoM/NWCS occurs during the Atlantic hurricane season, with a strong late-summer peak. Historically, RI events in the region occur between May and November, and the number rises sharply in August and peaks in September. This seasonality aligns with warm-ocean conditions and high ocean heat content associated with the Loop Current and eddies.
supporting_quote: historical RI events in the GoM and the NWCS have occurred between May to November
the total number of RI events ... surging from 12 in July to 43 ... in August
The peak number of rapid intensifying TCs was observed in September with 53 TCs
areas characterized by very high ocean heat content originating from the Loop Current and its eddies

chunks.text: Spatially, the empirical probability maps identify three RI hotspots in the region: near the Cayman Basin in the NWCS, the Bay of Campeche (Campeche Canyon), and the Yucatán Channel. Track density and RI segments concentrate over these areas, and higher maximum sustained winds occur more frequently there. These hotspots provide targets for studying MHW–RI compounding.
supporting_quote: we have determined three hotspots ... near the Cayman Basin in the NWCS, the Bay of Campeche (Campeche Canyon) and Yucatán Channel in the GoM
a greater density of tracks and associated RI events converging over the hotspot regions
higher maximum sustained wind speeds occur more frequently in hotspot regions due to the higher probability of RI

chunks.text: The MHW climatology shows a marked increase from the earlier (1950–1980) to later (1981–2022) period in extent and persistence. During the cooler era, only limited hotspots exceed about three events per year, while in the warmer era the affected region expands across the NWCS and southern GoM, with frequent events along the Loop Current. Average MHW duration increases substantially, from 36.5 to 49.5 days per year.
supporting_quote: During the cooler era ... only a few hotspots of MHWs exhibit more than 3 events per year
during the warmer period ... the extent of the regions was expanded to the whole of the NWCS and the southern GoM
Climate change has led to a substantial increase in the average duration of MHWs ... rising from 36.5 to 49.5 days per year

chunks.text: Using the double-threshold impact-area filter (10 days, 125 miles), the study identifies 5,242 MHW events as potentially influential for RI formation. Under the adopted MHW settings (PC80, minimum duration 5 days, maximum gap 2 days, RI MST 24 h), about 75 unique TCs—around 69.44%—had at least one MHW within their impact area. Conditional probability maps show MHW impacts across most of the NWCS and parts of the GoM.
supporting_quote: within 10 days and 125 miles of the beginning of RI events
The pool of influential MHWs on RI events encompasses 5242 events
75 unique TCs (≈ 69.44% of all TCs) had at least a MHW within their impact area
MHWs have significant impacts on RI events in nearly all grids of the NWCS, as well as the southern and northwestern GoM

chunks.text: The amplification of RI likelihood due to MHW presence is strongest in the southwestern GoM, near the Yucatán Channel, and the Yucatán Basin. The multiplication-rate analysis indicates that MHW–RI interaction can increase RI likelihood by up to fivefold in hotspot regions, with an average amplification around 1.5-fold. This quantifies where MHWs most strongly elevate RI risk compared to non-MHW conditions.
supporting_quote: the interaction of MHWs and RIs can amplify the likelihood of experiencing rapidly intensified TCs up to 5-fold (on-average 1.5-fold) over the identified hotspot regions
in the southwestern GoM, near the Yucatán Channel, and the Yucatán Basin in the NWCS demonstrate the highest magnified likelihood in the presence of MHWs

chunks.text: Event-based summaries for several costly hurricanes show RI locations with high subsurface heat availability. For Harvey (2017), Michael (2018), Ida (2021), and Ian (2022), RI-point TCHP ranges from 83.1 to 183.8 kJ cm−2, exceeding the 50 kJ cm−2 level noted as favorable for strengthening in the Atlantic. The associated MHWs near RI start have i_max values near or above ~30°C.
supporting_quote: RI points of Hurricanes Harvey (2017), Michael (2018), Ida (2021), and Ian (2022)
TCs are prone to strengthening in areas where the TCHP exceeds 50 kJ cm−2 in the Atlantic Ocean

chunks.text: A key limitation is that the analysis is based on historical events, which can constrain statistical power and leave data-scarcity challenges for compound MHW–RI assessment. The authors suggest future work using synthetic tropical cyclone tracks and scenarios to enrich datasets for both historical and future climates. They also note machine learning approaches (e.g., LSTM) as potential tools to improve RI prediction and compound-probability quantification.
supporting_quote: A limitation of this study is that our findings are based on historical events
To bolster the statistical significance of the findings and address the data scarcity issue ... future work could incorporate physically-based synthetic TC scenarios
Machine learning algorithms, in particular LSTM ... can also be leveraged to predict RI events

chunks.text: The paper emphasizes that marine heatwaves are a necessary but not sufficient condition for rapid intensification because other atmospheric and oceanic factors must align. In particular, vertical wind shear and moisture conditions can suppress intensification even where TCHP is high. This helps explain why conditional RI probabilities given MHW are lower than unconditional RI probability patterns in some areas.
supporting_quote: the favorable conditions due to the presence of MHWs is a necessary but not a sufficient condition for RI formation
VWS values of less than 10 m s−1 ... favor rapid intensification
the LHF and VWS have the potential to suppress this phenomenon in some regions

chunks.text: The authors discuss uncertainty and potential mismatch between common MHW definitions and the thresholds relevant for cyclone rapid intensification. They argue that very strict ecosystem-focused thresholds may miss warming events that still support RI, motivating their use of PC80 instead of the more common PC90. They also highlight concerns about percentile definitions producing discontinuities at baseline edges and sensitivity to climatology calculations.
supporting_quote: The extremely high thresholds applicable to heatwave impacts on marine ecosystems may not apply to the RI of TCs
These observations led us to use the PC80 threshold instead of PC90
percentile-based definition raises concerns, particularly regarding the discontinuities in exceedance rates observed at the start and end of the baseline period

chunks.text: The double-threshold method intentionally simplifies the MHW–RI linkage and does not include several potentially important contributors to RI onset and magnitude. The authors note that SST anomaly length scales and storm translation direction and speed are not incorporated, even though they may affect the timing and strength of rapid intensification. They position their framework as a statistical screening approach rather than a full physical attribution.
supporting_quote: there are other factors such as length scales of SST anomalies and the translation direction and speed of the TC that contribute to the onset and magnitude of RI that were not included in the present analysis

chunks.text: The study concludes that marine heatwaves substantially increase the likelihood of rapid intensification in the GoM and NWCS, with particularly strong amplification in identified hotspots. Approximately 70% of storms experienced at least one MHW in their defined impact area, and RI likelihood can be amplified up to fivefold (about 1.5-fold on average) in hotspot regions. Given increasing MHW frequency under climate change, the authors infer that rapid intensification events may become more frequent in a warming climate.
supporting_quote: approximately 70% of TCs experienced at least one MHW within their impact area
amplify the likelihood ... up to 5-fold (on-average 1.5-fold) over the identified hotspot regions
As marine heatwaves are on the increase due to climate change ... more frequent rapid intensification events can be expected in the warming climate

chunks.text: Climate change has increased the frequency and intensity of droughts, elevating atmospheric water demand and depleting soil moisture needed for plant function. These dry spells affect forests and croplands and can disrupt water, nutrient, and energy cycling, with economic consequences. Reliable indicators of vegetation stress are therefore needed for monitoring and early warning to support management decisions.
supporting_quote: Global climate change in the recent decades has intensified both the frequency and intensity of the extreme drought events
Prolonged dry spells give rise to increase in atmospheric water demand that further depletes the soil moisture availability for plant's photosynthetic activity, thus inducing plant stress.

chunks.text: The ecosystem-level Evaporative Stress Index (ESI), also called Evaporative Stress Ratio (ESR), is widely used to infer vegetation stress and drought, and is commonly defined as the ratio of actual ET to potential ET (ET/PET). The term ESI is often used when derived from remote sensing, while ESR is used when ET and PET are from observed or reanalysis meteorology. Higher ESI/ESR indicates lower stress.
supporting_quote: Evaporative Stress Index (ESI), also sometimes referred as Evaporative Stress Ratio (ESR), has been widely used as an indicator of vegetation evaporative stress
These indices are defined as the ratio of actual ET to potential evapotranspiration (PET), i. e., ESI=ET/PET.

chunks.text: Total evapotranspiration (ET) includes soil evaporation (E) and plant transpiration (T), whose relative contributions vary in space and time. Because T is strongly influenced by plant physiology while E depends more on surface and meteorological conditions, their responses to soil moisture and atmospheric aridity can differ. This creates a conceptual risk that ET-based stress metrics may not reflect plant-level stress driven by constrained transpiration.
supporting_quote: ET, which is composed of two primary components: 1. abiotic component (E)... and 2. biotic component (T)

Given that T and E respond to hydrometeorological conditions differently, it is possible that the ESI, which uses ET, may not accurately represent the true evaporative stress experienced by vegetation

chunks.text: The study aims to test whether ecosystem-level ESI dynamics are representative of vegetation evaporative stress by comparing ESI to a vegetation-focused index (ESIv). It evaluates how differences between ESI and ESIv vary under regimes of soil moisture and vapor pressure deficit. It also assesses whether spatial patterns (rank ordering) of stress across sites inferred from ESI align with those from ESIv.
supporting_quote: The goal of this study is to assess the suitability of these indices for tracking vegetation evaporative stress.
we investigate whether the dynamics of ESI is sufficiently representative of evaporative stress in vegetation (ESI v , henceforth).

chunks.text: A core concern is that ESI uses ET, while vegetation stress is more directly linked to transpiration (T) constrained by stomatal conductance under hydroclimatic stress. Because E and T can evolve differently, ESI may misrepresent plant stress. Another issue is that potential loss in ESI is often computed with vegetation-agnostic PET, whereas vegetation stress ideally needs place-specific vegetation properties to define potential transpiration.
supporting_quote: it is hypothesized that ESI or ESR may not be sufficiently representative of the vegetation evaporative stress.
to capture the vegetation evaporative stress... the potential water loss should ideally be evaluated using place-specific vegetation properties instead of a vegetation-agnostic potential loss

chunks.text: The paper defines ecosystem ESI as ET/PET and vegetation stress index ESIv as T/PETv, both bounded between 0 and 1 where lower values indicate higher stress. ESI equals 1 when ET reaches its potential, while ESIv equals 1 when T reaches potential transpiration. The analysis compares these two indices after estimating ET, T, PET, and PETv.
supporting_quote: ESI = ET/PET
ESI v = T/PET v
Both ESI and ESI v can have values between 0 (high stress) and 1 (no stress).

chunks.text: ET and T are modeled using a dual-source Shuttleworth–Wallace (S-W) framework that represents total latent heat flux as the sum of soil evaporation and canopy transpiration components. The method computes separate Penman–Monteith-like fluxes for soil and canopy (PMs and PMc) and combines them using weighting factors (fs and fc). Available energy is split between soil and canopy using Beer's law with LAI and a net radiation extinction coefficient.
supporting_quote: ET is estimated utilizing a dual-source ET model based on Shuttleworth and Wallace (1985), where ET is computed as the sum of soil evaporation (E) and plant transpiration (T)
A = Rn - G
Rns = Rn exp(-kr · LAI)

chunks.text: Aerodynamic and boundary-layer resistances are computed following Wei et al. (2017), including raa (canopy to reference), ras (soil to canopy source height), and rac (canopy boundary layer). These depend on friction velocity (u*), canopy height (hc), displacement height (d0), roughness length (z0), and eddy diffusivity parameters. Mean boundary-layer resistance per unit vegetation area is used to estimate rac via r_b/(2 IAI).
supporting_quote: Aerodynamic resistance between the canopy source height and reference level (raa) is calculated as
Aerodynamic resistance between the substrate and canopy source height (ras) is calculated as
rac = rb/(2IAI)

chunks.text: Soil surface resistance (rss) is modeled as an exponential function of relative soil wetness with parameters α and β. Rather than using fixed α=8.2 and β=4.3, the study estimates site-specific α and β by first inverting Penman–Monteith to compute ecosystem conductance (Gs) from tower fluxes and then partitioning Gs into soil and canopy components via a conductance model involving GPP and VPD. Fitted soil conductance (Gss) is then mapped to rss=1/Gss to infer α and β; default values are used when fitted parameters are negative.
supporting_quote: rss = exp(α - β · θ/θs)
suggested values of 8.2 and 4.3 for α and β
Gs = Gss + G1 · GPP/VPD^m

chunks.text: Canopy stomatal conductance is computed using a photosynthesis–stomatal conductance model where conductance increases with gross assimilation rate and decreases with vapor pressure deficit via a term (1 + Ds/D0). Gross assimilation is modeled as a function of PAR, canopy temperature, and CO2 terms, and soil-moisture stress is applied to assimilation using f(θ) derived from β(θ). Leaf-scale conductance is upscaled to canopy scale and converted to stomatal resistance using rsc = 1/(1.6 gsc).
supporting_quote: gsc^l = gsc^min + a1 · Ag /((Cs - Γ)(1 + Ds/D0))
Ag = Ao* f(θ)
rsc = 1/(1.6gsc)

chunks.text: Potential evapotranspiration is evaluated using three methods: (1) S-W model PET and PETv obtained by running the model under unstressed conditions so predicted ET (T) equals PET (PETv), (2) Penman (1948) PET using radiation and aerodynamic terms, and (3) Priestley–Taylor PET with αPT=1.26. Only the S-W approach is used for PETv, enabling plant-specific potential transpiration estimates.
supporting_quote: we use three different methods for obtaining potential evapotranspiration
predicted ET (T) from S-W model is equivalent to PET (PETv) when the model is run under... unstressed conditions.
PET = αPT Δ(Rn - G)/(λ(Δ + γ))

chunks.text: Model parameters are optimized separately for each site using the Shuffled Complex Evolution algorithm to minimize mean square error between modeled and observed ET. The coupled S-W and stomatal scheme includes six unknown parameters: D0, km, Z0s, dl, Cd, and gscmin. This site-by-site calibration is intended to ensure robust ET (and hence T) estimates across diverse biomes.
supporting_quote: The S-W model is trained for each site individually
six unknown parameters, viz. D0, km, Z0s, dl, Cd, and gsc^min
These parameters are optimized using the Shuffled Complex Evolution approach

chunks.text: The analysis uses 49 eddy-covariance flux tower sites from the PLUMBER2 dataset spanning 9 land-cover types globally, producing 518 site years of data. Sites were selected to have soil moisture and other required variables for over 5 years. Data are half-hourly for 44 sites and hourly for 5 sites, and LAI is provided from MODIS MCD15A2H.006 at the same temporal resolution as flux measurements.
supporting_quote: Using eddy covariance flux tower data of 518 site years, distributed across 49-sites and 9 land covers globally
The S-W model is run at 49 flux tower sites... using the PLUMBER2 dataset
The sampling frequency of data is either half-hourly (for 44 sites) or hourly (for 5 sites)

chunks.text: Flux measurements of latent and sensible heat are corrected for energy balance closure when (LE+H)/(Rn−G) is less than 0.8 using a Bowen ratio method. Canopy heights and reference measurement heights come from site metadata. Basic soil properties (sand-silt-clay fractions) are taken from the Noah-LSM soil map, supporting estimation of soil hydraulic parameters like θs and θwp.
supporting_quote: measurements of LE and H are corrected for energy balance closure using a Bowen ratio method... when... (LE+H)/(Rn-G) is less than 0.8
Reference heights of flux measurement and mean canopy heights are obtained from site-specific metadata information.
Basic soil properties including sand-silt-clay fractions are obtained from the soil map used in Noah-LSM

chunks.text: Sap flow measurements from the SAPFLUXNET database are used to validate modeled transpiration at sites where such data exist. Sub-daily sap flow is aggregated to daily values, corrected by a factor 1.405, and upscaled to stand-level transpiration using species basal area information. Species included in sap flow measurements accounted for over 90% of the stand basal area at the sites used for this validation.
supporting_quote: To validate the transpiration estimates from the S-W model, sap flow data from SAPFLUXNET database
we apply a correction factor of 1.405 to the sap flow values
the species included in the sap flow measurements accounted for over 90 % of the stand basal area

chunks.text: Model outputs are generated at the native temporal resolution (30 min or 1 h) and then aggregated to daily ET, T, PET, and PETv to compute daily ESI and ESIv. Values deemed unrealistic (ESI or ESIv below 0 or above 1) are excluded for fair comparison. Regimes of high and low soil moisture and VPD are defined using site-specific 75th and 25th percentiles.
supporting_quote: we aggregate these fluxes to derive daily estimates of ET, T, PET, and PETv, and ultimately, ESI and ESIv.
we exclude such instances from our analysis both for ESI and ESIv.
These regimes are delineated using cutoffs at the 75th and 25th percentiles

chunks.text: Across sites, the S-W model shows generally good ET prediction performance at the flux-measurement timescale. R2 ranges from 0.36 to 0.94 with a mean of 0.69, RMSE ranges from 13.3 to 71.3 W m−2 with a mean of 32.4 W m−2, and MAPE averages 32.1%. Performance is best in croplands, mixed forests, and grasslands with mean R2 around 0.77–0.78.
supporting_quote: The coefficient of determination (R2) varies between 0.36 to 0.94 with an average value of 0.69.
The Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) varies between 13.3 W m−2 to 71.3 W m−2 with an average value of 32.4 W m−2.
The S-W model performs the best in cropland, mixed forest, and grassland settings with an average R2 of 0.78, 0.78, and 0.77, respectively.

chunks.text: Transpiration estimates from the S-W model align well with independent sap flow-based transpiration where available. At the three sites with sap flow data, modeled T has high correlation (0.76–0.87) with sap flow-derived T. This supports using the model’s T and PETv estimates to construct ESIv.
supporting_quote: When compared to independent sap flow measurements at the only three sites out of 49 with such data available, transpiration estimates from the S-W model show a high correlation (0.76–0.87)

chunks.text: During high VPD periods, ESI is consistently higher than ESIv across sites, implying ESI indicates less stress than vegetation actually experiences. Differences are statistically significant (Mann–Whitney U test p<0.05) during high VPD regardless of whether soil moisture is high or low. This pattern is reported as robust across PET calculation approaches.
supporting_quote: ESI is consistently higher... than ESIv under high VPD periods
ESI and ESIv are significantly different with p-value < 0.05 based on the Mann-Whitney U test during high VPD periods.
This is true irrespective of the PET method used

chunks.text: In dry, low-VPD conditions (low SM and low VPD), ESI tends to be lower than ESIv, implying ESI indicates more stress than plants exhibit according to transpiration-based stress. Under low SM and low VPD, ESI and ESIv are not significantly different (p-value > 0.05) when PET is from the S-W model. The sign reversal across VPD regimes indicates atmosphere-driven discrepancies between ET-based and T-based stress metrics.
supporting_quote: during low VPD and low SM periods, ESI is lower than ESIv
during low SM and low VPD periods, ESI and ESIv are not significantly different (p-value > 0.05) when considering PET from the S-W model.

chunks.text: Over all time periods pooled across sites, ESI is overall higher than ESIv, indicating a tendency for ecosystem-level ESI to underestimate vegetation evaporative stress. The paper notes that this conclusion holds across PET methods and remains after excluding sites with suboptimal ET-model performance. Thus, mismatches are not solely an artifact of a few poorly simulated sites.
supporting_quote: When all the time periods are considered, ESI is overall higher than ESIv, thus indicating that ESI underestimates vegetation stress
Even after excluding sites with suboptimal performance, our analysis reveals a consistent pattern in our findings

chunks.text: Case-study years show both indices detect higher stress in dry years, but ESIv responds more strongly than ESI, especially in croplands. At US-Ne3, reduction from wet to dry year is ~19% for ESI versus ~29% for ESIv, while at the forest site US-MMS reductions are ~8% for both. This suggests ET-based ESI can bias inferred fractional increases in plant stress during drought relative to transpiration-based metrics.
supporting_quote: at the site US-Ne3, the reduction in ESI (ESIv) from wet year to dry year is ~19 % (~29 %).
This reduction is about ~8 % for both ESI and ESIv at the forested site.

chunks.text: Seasonal behavior differs: differences between ESI and ESIv are larger early in the growing period and shrink later, consistent with increasing transpiration contribution to ET as the canopy develops. The study links smaller discrepancies at the forest site to higher transpiration fraction (T:ET). At US-MMS mean T:ET is 0.73 versus 0.58 at US-Ne3, corresponding to smaller ESI–ESIv divergence in the forest.
supporting_quote: the difference between ESI and ESIv is larger during the early growing period... and it reduces later in the growing season
mean T:ET for US-MMS... is 0.73, which is higher than at site US-Ne3 (mean T/ET=0.58).

chunks.text: Across all sites, the mean difference between ESI and ESIv increases where soil evaporation contributes more to ET (higher E/ET) and where LAI is smaller. The paper indicates that larger differences are governed primarily by T/ET rather than by PETv/PET. These patterns imply ESI’s representativeness declines in sparse canopies and periods with relatively high evaporation.
supporting_quote: site-averaged difference between the two indices increases for sites with higher E/ET ratio... or smaller overall LAI.
Larger difference in ESI and ESIv or high E/ET are largely governed by T/ET rather than PETv/ PET

chunks.text: Spatial rank correlation between site-mean ESI and ESIv is high during the growing season and weak during the non-growing season. The study reports correlations >0.8 during Apr–Sep and poorer covariation during Oct–Mar at daily, weekly, and monthly scales. This indicates ESI maps can identify relatively higher/lower stress areas in growing season despite magnitude biases.
supporting_quote: ESI and ESIv have high (> 0.8) spatial correlation in space during growing periods (Apr.-Sep.).
This covariation becomes poorer during non-growing periods (Oct-Mar).

chunks.text: A key practical limitation is that improving ESI’s representativeness may require accurate estimation of transpiration (T) and potential transpiration (PETv) in regions without in-situ observations. Modeling these variables is challenging because transpiration is modulated by plant physiological properties such as hydraulics and stomatal kinetics. The paper emphasizes the difficulty of deriving these properties over large areas in a spatially explicit way.
supporting_quote: Notably, this may entail accurate estimation of ecosystem T in systems lacking insitu data, a challenge that warrants further attention.
modeling T as well as potential transpiration flux (PETv)... is relatively challenging because T is modulated by plant physiological properties related to hydraulics and stomatal kinetics.

chunks.text: Validation of transpiration remains uncertain because common T data sources and ET-partitioning approaches have inherent uncertainties. The paper notes sap flux measurements and ET partitioning methods are “beset by uncertainties,” complicating evaluation of modeled T and stress indices built on T. This uncertainty limits straightforward operational deployment of ESIv without careful validation.
supporting_quote: validation of modeled T remains challenging as sources of T data... continue to be beset by uncertainties inherent in these methods.

chunks.text: A limitation for flash drought applications is that eddy-covariance records are often too short to robustly estimate long-term percentile-based distributions of ESIv needed for event identification. The study suggests extending both ESI and ESIv over longer periods to quantify differences in flash drought estimation. This highlights a gap between site-based evaluation and operational drought monitoring requirements.
supporting_quote: Limited length of data at the eddy-covariance sites pose challenge in assessment of such distributions for ESIv for a given period.
Further studies wherein both ESI and ESIv can be extended for long periods may allow quantitative assessment

chunks.text: Remote sensing implementation of ESIv would require multiple inputs (ET, soil moisture, meteorology such as Rn, VPD, wind) that often have mismatched resolutions and uncertainties. The paper argues that these issues necessitate thorough multi-product assessments for both ESI and ESIv. This limits immediate translation of the site-based framework to large-scale gridded monitoring.
supporting_quote: would require remotely sensed ET data, soil moisture data... and various other meteorological variables (e.g., Rn, VPD, wind speed, etc.).

Given the resolution mismatch among these data products and the inherent uncertainties in each dataset, a thorough assessment of remotely sensed ESI and ESIv across multiple data products is necessary.

chunks.text: The study concludes that conventional ecosystem ESI (ET/PET) does not reliably capture vegetation evaporative stress represented by transpiration-based ESIv (T/PETv). ESI tends to underestimate vegetation stress during high atmospheric demand (high VPD) and can overestimate stress in dry, low-VPD conditions. This motivates improving stress monitoring by better accounting for transpiration dynamics.
supporting_quote: our findings reveal underestimation of vegetation evaporative stress by ESI during periods of high vapor pressure deficit (VPD) and overestimation during dry, low-VPD periods.
Overall, the results from this study underscore the need to improve the representativeness of currently used evaporative stress index to monitor the evaporative vegetation stress.

chunks.text: Despite magnitude discrepancies, ESI and ESIv show strong spatial covariation during the growing season, implying ESI can still identify locations with relatively higher or lower stress during key periods. The paper reports high spatial rank correlation during Apr–Sep, with poorer agreement in non-growing months. Thus, ESI may remain useful for spatial drought mapping in growing season while still underpredicting true plant stress.
supporting_quote: ESI and ESIv have high (> 0.8) spatial correlation in space during growing periods (Apr.-Sep.).
though ESI underpredicts the plant stress, it can still be used to identify locations with relatively higher or lower stress during the growing season.

chunks.text: The authors propose that extending stress monitoring beyond ET-based indices will likely require remotely sensed or modeled estimates of T and PETv, validated at eddy-covariance sites. They emphasize that generating a robust remote sensing-derived ESIv is a future direction, but it depends on integrating multiple uncertain datasets. The work is positioned as a foundation for drought research and flash drought assessment where stress indices are percentile-threshold based.
supporting_quote: Future studies may focus on deriving remotely sensed data of T and PETv to extend the utility of ESIv beyond settings with in-situ data.
The goal should include generating the best remote sensing-derived ESIv after performing validation at eddy-covariance sites.

chunks.text: Evapotranspiration (ET) is a dominant component of the terrestrial water cycle and is essential for applications ranging from agriculture to water resources management and climate prediction. ET consists of direct evaporation and plant transpiration, and transpiration is regulated by stomatal conductance (gsc). Because gsc is tightly linked to plant water status and atmospheric demand, improving gsc representation is important for reducing uncertainties in water and carbon fluxes in Earth System Models.
supporting_quote: Around 60% of water falling over the land surface as precipitation is returned back to the atmosphere by evapotranspiration (ET) (Oki & Kanae, 2006).
ET is comprised of two distinct processes, namely direct evaporation (E...) and plant transpiration (T)... T is regulated by stomatal conductance (gsc)

chunks.text: Stomatal conductance has been modeled using empirical approaches and more mechanistic plant hydraulic (PH) approaches. Empirical models typically represent stomatal responses as independent stress functions of environmental variables (e.g., SM, VPD) and are widely used in land surface models. PH models instead link soil moisture to leaf water status through the soil–plant continuum and can better represent drought sensitivities, but they often require more parameters and input data.
supporting_quote: numerous efforts have been made to model gsc... from relatively simple empirical models... to more mechanistic but oftentimes data‐intensive plant hydraulic (PH) models that require many more model parameters and input data
Empirical models of gsc simulate stomatal kinetics as independent functions of environmental factors (e.g., SM, vapor pressure deficit (VPD), etc.)

chunks.text: Recent comparisons suggest differences between empirical and PH approaches in how soil moisture and atmospheric demand constrain transpiration and ET. Plant hydraulics approaches have been reported to improve ET estimation under drought, yet it remains unclear whether current empirical and PH formulations are fundamentally limited by their structures. The paper motivates evaluating structural constraints rather than only parameter uncertainty.
supporting_quote: Liu et al. (2020) showed discrepancy in the restriction effect of SM and VPD on ET between empirical and PH approaches.
it remains unknown whether, to what extent, and when, do the empirical and PH models are structurally constrained in their ability to predict ET.

chunks.text: The study aims to test whether structural constraints in representative empirical and plant hydraulic stomatal conductance models limit accurate ET prediction, even after local calibration at each site. It compares these physics-based formulations against a machine learning (ML) model that learns gsc directly from data without prescribed functional forms. The goal is to diagnose whether observed underperformance reflects structural error rather than poor parameterization.
supporting_quote: we assess whether, and the extent to which, the locally calibrated... empirical and plant hydraulic models underperform compared to the ML model.
Such underperformance would indicate inherent structural errors in empirical and plant hydraulic models

chunks.text: A second objective is to determine whether the structural constraints in current gsc models cause underutilization of hydrometeorological information available at eddy-covariance sites. The paper uses diagnostic tools (including RF/PDP and information-theory metrics) to evaluate both predictive accuracy and whether models capture functional coupling among ET, SM, and VPD. This separates “right answers” from “right reasons.”
supporting_quote: do the structural constraints... also lead to underutilization of the information inherent in the hydrometeorological data typically available at eddy‐covariance sites while predicting ET?
In addition to conventional model performance metrics... we also use an information theory‐based diagnostic method... to evaluate the considered models.

chunks.text: Current empirical and plant hydraulic stomatal conductance models may not fully exploit site-specific hydrometeorological data, leading to suboptimal ET prediction. Even with local calibration, simplifying assumptions in model structure can prevent models from reproducing observed gsc dynamics under varying stress conditions. The paper frames this as a structural limitation problem rather than solely a parameter estimation issue.
supporting_quote: Current stomatal conductance models underutilize the site‐specific hydrometeorological data
Even if these gsc models are calibrated locally, structural simplifications inherent in them limit their capability to accurately capture gsc dynamics.

chunks.text: Empirical models impose restrictive structures by representing stomatal responses as independent functions of drivers, which can miss interconnected responses among variables. For instance, VPD and soil moisture effects may compensate or interact in ways not represented by separable stress factors. This restrictiveness can cause incorrect sensitivities to SM, VPD, and other covariates.
supporting_quote: Structural constraints in empirical models are more restrictive compared to plant hydraulic models
Empirical models of gsc simulate stomatal kinetics as independent functions of environmental factors (e.g., SM, vapor pressure deficit (VPD), etc.)

chunks.text: Canonical explicit plant hydraulic models may still be structurally limited by simplified representations of the water potential gradient along the root–xylem–leaf pathway. Such simplifications can yield incorrect estimates of leaf water potential and hence gsc, even when many parameters are optimized. The paper therefore develops an implicit alternative to diagnose these structural issues.
supporting_quote: Enhancements are needed for the simplified depiction of the water potential gradient across the root‐ xylem‐leaf continuum in plant hydraulic models
the estimated Ψl and thus gsc may still have suffer from structural errors arising from the prescribed functions (Equations 5a–5e) as simplifications of the real plant hydraulic architecture.

chunks.text: ET is modeled using a two-source Shuttleworth–Wallace (S–W) framework where total ET is the sum of soil evaporation and canopy transpiration. The S–W model combines Penman–Monteith-like terms for soil and canopy, weighted by aerodynamic and surface resistances. Across model variants, the study changes only the stomatal conductance formulation to isolate structural impacts of gsc models on ET.
supporting_quote: ET is modeled using a two‐source ET model based on Shuttleworth and Wallace (1985) where ET is calculated as the sum of soil evaporation (Es) and plant transpiration (Tc or T)
ET is evaluated using four Shuttleworth‐Wallace (S‐W) models... with the only difference between them being the representation of stomatal conductance within each model.

chunks.text: Soil surface resistance (rss) is computed using the Sellers et al. (1992) exponential function of relative soil wetness. Because the empirical parameters (alpha, beta) can cause large uncertainty, the paper estimates them per site by fitting an ecosystem conductance model across soil-moisture percentiles, then mapping inferred soil conductance to rss. For sites with negative fitted alpha or beta, standard values (8.2, 4.3) are used.
supporting_quote: rss = exp(α - β · θ/θs) (2a)
For the few sites where either α or β is negative... we use standard values of 8.2 and 4.3 respectively

chunks.text: Observed canopy-scale stomatal conductance is obtained by inverting the S–W ET model using flux-tower ET (via a nonlinear solver). The inversion holds other resistances (rss, raa, rac, ras) computed consistently across models for fair comparison. Time points without feasible gsc solutions are discarded to avoid nonphysical inversions.
supporting_quote: Observed rsc... for each site is obtained by inverting Equation 3 given the observed ET of the site using a non-linear solver FSOLVE in Python.
Notably, these calculations are kept the same for all the models for fair model intercomparison.

chunks.text: The empirical (EMP) stomatal model follows a multiplicative structure with a VPD term, a soil-moisture-limited reference conductance, and radiation and temperature stress scalars. Key calibrated parameters are m (VPD sensitivity), gsref, and alpha (radiation response). Temperature reference is fixed at 298 K.
