supporting_quote: gsc = gs* (1 - m · ln(VPD)) × F1 × F2 (4a)
Here, the three parameters (m, gsref), and α are obtained using Markov-Chain Monte-Carlo (MCMC)... Tref is kept as 298 K.

chunks.text: The explicit plant hydraulic model (PHexp) uses stomatal optimality, coupling carbon gain and water loss with a marginal water-use efficiency parameter that depends exponentially on leaf water potential. Water supply is represented as whole-plant conductance times the soil-to-leaf water potential gradient, with conductance reduced by a vulnerability curve defined by gp,max, Psi50, and curvature parameter a. Soil water potential is derived from soil moisture and texture.
supporting_quote: gsc = argmax(fc(gsc) - λ fe(gsc)) (5a)
λ(Ψl) = λww* (ca/ca*) exp(β0 Ψl) (5b)
gsrp = gp,max [1 + (Ψl/Ψ50)^a]^{-1} (5d)

chunks.text: The implicit plant hydraulic model (PHimp) uses Medlyn’s stomatal conductance form with g0 assumed negligible and treats the slope parameter g1 as temporally varying with water stress. Instead of prescribing hydraulic equations for leaf water potential, g1 is learned using an ANN as a function of SM and VPD. Carbon assimilation Ac is computed using photosynthetic parameters obtained from the explicit PH model.
supporting_quote: gsc = g0 + (1 + g1/√VPD) Ac/ca (6a)
we use a feedforward Artificial Neural Network (ANN) ML method to estimate g1 based on SM and VPD.
Carbon assimilation rate (Ac) was calculated using the photosynthetic parameters obtained for PHexp above.

chunks.text: The pure ML gsc model is an ANN trained with nine hydrometeorological and vegetation variables: Ta, SRad, fPAR, USTAR, VPD, wind speed, atmospheric CO2, LAI, and SM. Data are split by day into 80% training and 20% testing to reduce leakage, with nested cross-validation for hyperparameter selection and early stopping to limit overfitting. Models are trained against log(rsc) because it is more normally distributed.
supporting_quote: We use 9 variables... including air temperature (Ta), solar radiation (SRad), fPAR, friction velocity (USTAR), VPD, WS, atmospheric CO2, LAI, and SM
randomly splitting the data for each site into training (80%) and testing (20%) sets... We find that the split-by-day strategy results in a better performance
all the models are trained against logarithmic value of rsc... because it is more normally distributed

chunks.text: EMP and PHexp parameters are estimated for each site using MCMC with adaptive Metropolized independence sampling (AMIS) and parallel tempering. The empirical model calibrates three parameters, while PHexp calibrates 11 parameters spanning hydraulic traits, soil parameter, and five photosynthesis parameters, plus an observation-noise standard deviation. Multiple chains and convergence diagnostics (Geweke and Gelman–Rubin) are used, and ensembles of parameter sets are propagated to ET for evaluation.
supporting_quote: In the empirical representation... we have three parameters; gsref, α, and m
In the explicit representation... we have 11 parameters... In addition... σlogrsc is also retrieved.
an adaptive Metropolized independence sampler (AMIS... ) is used... 10 independent MCMC chains... generating 20,000 samples.

chunks.text: The analysis uses the PLUMBER2 flux-tower dataset comprising 642 site-years across 84 sites distributed globally and spanning 10 land covers/plant functional types. Data are half-hourly or hourly and include meteorological forcings, fluxes, and remotely sensed vegetation indices. LAI is from MODIS MCD15A2H.006 and fPAR from MODIS MCD15A3H.
supporting_quote: eddy covariance flux tower data of 642 site years across 84 sites distributed across 10 land covers globally
In this study, we used data from 84 flux tower sites... in the PLUMBER2 data set
The data set also provides leaf area index (LAI)... derived from MODIS... (MCD15A2H.006)... The fraction of photosynthetically active radiation (fPAR) data is obtained... (MCD15A3H)

chunks.text: Sites were selected to ensure soil moisture data availability and at least one full year of required variables. The study applies strict filtering to focus on daytime, non-rain and non-interception conditions, removing high humidity periods and unstable or invalid flux conditions. LE and H are corrected for energy balance closure using a Bowen ratio method when the imbalance metric is below 0.8.
supporting_quote: Sites are chosen to ensure that SM data are available, and all other required variables are available for at least over one entire year.
We exclude data with relatively humidity (RH) exceeding 95%... data during rainy hours and within 6 hr after rainfall is removed
LE and H are corrected for energy balance closure using a Bowen ratio method... when the energy imbalance... is less than 0.8.

chunks.text: Aerodynamic and canopy structural variables are derived from site metadata and standard formulations, while soil properties are taken from a global soil map used in Noah-LSM. Additional drivers include canopy height and measurement height, used in resistance calculations within the S–W framework. These inputs support consistent computation of resistances across the four ET model variants.
supporting_quote: Measurement and canopy heights are obtained from site‐specific metadata information.
Soil properties are obtained from the soil map used in Noah‐LSM (Dai et al., 2019).

chunks.text: Across sites, the ML stomatal conductance approach yields the most accurate ET predictions, while empirical and explicit PH models are notably less accurate even after local calibration. Average ET performance is R2=0.84 with RMSE=34.46 W m−2 for ML, compared to R2=0.65 (56.63 W m−2) for EMP and R2=0.67 (54.85 W m−2) for PHexp. The implicit PH model improves over both (R2=0.73; RMSE=48.03 W m−2) but remains worse than ML.
supporting_quote: EMP and PHexp models show similar performance with an average R2 (RMSE) of 0.65 (56.63 Wm−2) and 0.67 (54.85 Wm−2), respectively.
The PHimp model... an average R2 (RMSE) of 0.73 (48.03 Wm−2)... pure ML model... average R2 (RMSE) of 0.84 (34.46 Wm−2).

chunks.text: Model differences are most pronounced under high-stress conditions (low soil moisture with high VPD), where PHimp and ML provide the largest improvements over EMP and PHexp. ML remains the best-performing model across all combinations of SM and VPD extremes. Under high SM and low VPD, models tend to behave more similarly because plants are least stressed and stomatal formulation has reduced influence on ET.
supporting_quote: Both PHimp and ML models demonstrate the most significant advantage over EMP and PHexp models during low SM and high VPD conditions, when plants are expected to experience the highest stress
ML model consistently perform the best among all the models during all extreme combinations of SM and VPD

chunks.text: PHimp outperforms PHexp, and the paper attributes much of this gap to limitations in the explicit depiction of water potential gradients along the root–xylem–leaf continuum. Because the main difference between PHexp and PHimp is how g1 (and indirectly leaf water potential) is obtained, better PHimp performance indicates structural errors in the canonical explicit hydraulic representation. This points to needed improvements in modeling the water potential gradient and associated dynamics.
supporting_quote: Given that the only difference between PHexp and PHimp is the approach used to evaluate the parameter g1 (or indirectly leaf water potential)... the relatively inferior performance of PHexp... is attributable to the simplified representation of water potential gradient along the root-xylem-leaf continuum.

chunks.text: Observed gsc patterns show heterogeneous, non-monotonic co-regulation by soil moisture and VPD, whereas EMP produces smoother and more gradually varying responses and PH models tend to be less sensitive to SM. The ML model most closely reproduces observed co-regulation patterns, including higher-order complexities that may reflect interactions with additional meteorological variables and lagged or hysteretic effects. This matching behavior helps explain ML’s superior ET performance.
supporting_quote: in the observed data... there is a decreasing trend... with decrease in SM, however the trend is non‐monotonic
the empirical model overall demonstrates a gradually varying co‐regulation pattern
due to independence of prescribed functional forms, the ML‐based gsc closely resembles the observed pattern with such higher order complexities.

chunks.text: Random-forest partial dependence diagnostics show ML captures observed gsc sensitivities to multiple drivers, while EMP and PH models misrepresent sensitivities. EMP is oversensitive to soil moisture and shows weak response to CO2, LAI, and air temperature. PH models better match observed sensitivities to VPD and SM than EMP but show discrepancies for other variables such as CO2 and LAI.
supporting_quote: the ML model most accurately captures the sensitivity of gsc to all variables.
gsc from the empirical model is oversensitive to SM... but barely responds to other variables including atmospheric CO2 concentration, LAI, and air temperature.
the PH models capture the observed sensitivity of gsc to VPD and SM relatively well, while showing discrepancies in the sensitivities to other variables

chunks.text: Information-theory diagnostics indicate ML has the best combined predictive and functional performance in representing ET and its coupling with SM and VPD. EMP shows the highest Ap (least desirable predictive performance), while ML shows the lowest Ap. Functional metrics suggest all models overestimate total information from VPD and SM about ET, with the overestimation largest for EMP and smallest for ML; models also tend to underestimate synergistic contributions of SM and VPD.
supporting_quote: Figure 5 indicates that EMP (ML) model shows the highest (lowest) Ap
Positive values of Af,T for all the models indicate that... is overestimated by all the models; this overestimation is the largest in EMP model and lowest in ML model
All the models underestimate the synergistic contributions of VPD and SM on ET, as reflected in negative Af,S

chunks.text: The paper emphasizes that it is not advocating ML-based ET models as replacements for physics-based models because ML can generalize poorly to ungauged sites or novel regimes. Concerns include extrapolation under climate nonstationarity and the need to ensure mass/energy balance constraints. Prior studies are cited noting ML failures outside the training distribution and challenges with physically constrained ML when training data contain errors.
supporting_quote: This study does not advocate that ML based ET models should be used over physics‐based ET models.
Other previous studies have already demonstrated poor generalizability of ML models (Sun et al., 2022)
ML models may fail for scenarios that are not seen in the training set.

chunks.text: The analysis has structural and data-related limitations, including excluding interception-loss periods and using inverted gsc as the observational target. The authors note uncertainties in the Shuttleworth–Wallace model, input data, and soil-moisture conductance estimation; however, these uncertainties are common across model variants and are argued not to change comparative rankings. The study also acknowledges noise and uncertainty in eddy-covariance derived variables such as GPP.
supporting_quote: our study have limitations, including restricting the analysis to no‐interception loss periods, use of inverted gsc as observations

certain uncertainties in stomatal conductance (gsc) and evapotranspiration (ET) are inherent due to the uncertainties associated with the Shuttleworth‐Wallace (S‐W) model structure, input data, and evaluation of SM conductance.

chunks.text: The paper discusses that big-leaf, one-layer canopy assumptions in the evaluated empirical and PH models can omit within-canopy structure, meteorology, and hydraulic architecture. This can misrepresent vertical variability in radiation, VPD, leaf temperature, leaf water potential, and trait plasticity (e.g., Vcmax gradients). Such simplifications may contribute to structural error in physics-based models and may not be fully compensated by parameter calibration.
supporting_quote: Another potential reason... could be attributed to the big‐leaf assumption which omits the canopy structure, and thus hydraulic architecture, radiative transfer, and within canopy meteorological conditions
The empirical and plant hydraulic models used in this study are one‐layer canopy models, which fail to capture the within‐canopy variability of several critical variables

chunks.text: Plant hydraulic model limitations discussed include reliance on stomatal optimization theory and simplified, time-invariant vulnerability curves that omit embolism refilling and new xylem formation. The paper also notes that assumed VPD exponents (e.g., proportional to VPD^0.5 in Medlyn-type forms) may vary across species. These issues point to missing flexibility and potentially incorrect process representations in current PH implementations.
supporting_quote: The stomatal optimization theory employed in the plant hydraulic model... can possibly be a one of the reasons of its subpar performance.
the model uses time‐invariant vulnerability curves and does not consider dynamic embolism refilling and the development of new xylem
Another example is the use of inversely proportional relation of gsc with VPD0.5 (see Equation 6a).

chunks.text: Across 84 flux-tower sites, the study concludes that both empirical and plant hydraulic stomatal conductance models have structural constraints that limit ET prediction, even when calibrated locally. A classic ANN ML model predicts ET more accurately, indicating that current physics-based formulations do not fully capture gsc dynamics or leverage available site data. The results highlight substantial opportunity to improve gsc model structures to reduce ET uncertainty in land surface and Earth system models.
supporting_quote: results... revealed that structural constraints in both empirical and plant hydraulic models of gsc limit their effectiveness for predicting ET.
ML model... predicted ET more accurately than any other model.
All the models were trained for each flux site individually to ensure that any error... is from the model structure and not from model parameterization.

chunks.text: By comparing explicit versus implicit hydraulic formulations, the paper concludes that conventional explicit plant hydraulics lacks flexibility for accurate ET prediction, pointing to needed improvements in representing the root–xylem–leaf water potential gradient and related process couplings. The study positions ML as a diagnostic benchmark to reveal missing relationships and motivate better process representations, not as an unconditional replacement for physical models.
supporting_quote: our results also revealed that the canonical implementation of the plant hydraulic model lacks the necessary flexibility for accurately predicting ET.
ML models help diagnose structural errors and highlight the potential for improvement by enhancing the process representations in current stomatal conductance models.

chunks.text: Stream temperature is a key variable for ecosystems, water quality, and human water uses, and it also encodes information about hydrologic sources contributing to streamflow. Groundwater typically has low annual thermal variability, surface runoff is closer to air temperature and more dynamic, and shallow subsurface flow is intermediate. These sources mix in channels and are modified by instream heat processes such as radiation, evaporation, and bed conduction, so temperature observations can contain signatures of pathways and thermal memory.
supporting_quote: Stream temperature (Ts , temperature of water in a river) is an important variable: it not only exerts a strong influence on ecosystem health
groundwater contribution to streams has a low annual thermal variability... surface runoff temperature is closer to air temperature... shallow subsurface flow is between these two extremes.

chunks.text: Process-based and statistical stream-temperature models often rely on simplifying structural assumptions, such as using fixed-window averages of recent air temperature to approximate source water temperatures. Examples include PRMS-SNTEMP assumptions of 1, 30, and 365-day air-temperature averages for surface, shallow subsurface, and groundwater contributions. Alternative models omit shallow subsurface components, apply multi-year averaging for groundwater, or add offsets and thresholds to account for rain cooling and minimum groundwater temperatures.
supporting_quote: SNTEMP... can assume that the temperatures of the surface runoff, shallow subsurface water, and groundwater are the averages of the air temperature in the most recent 1, 30, and 365 days, respectively
Meisner et al. (1988)... assumes no shallow subsurface component and sets the averaging length... to multiple years

chunks.text: Differentiable models connect neural networks to process-based equations and enable end-to-end gradient-based training, allowing outputs of untrained intermediate variables. The approach can reduce traditional calibration burdens by letting neural networks learn robust parameters across many sites. However, when neural components dominate, it is unclear whether structural priors are identifiable and whether intermediate flux estimates are physically meaningful without additional constraints or multivariate evaluation.
supporting_quote: a new class of physics-informed machine learning models—"differentiable models"—has emerged
it is not yet clear if the structural priors matter to the prediction accuracy or if better priors can be identified within a hybrid framework.

chunks.text: The study evaluates an NN-dominant hybrid differentiable model for daily stream temperature that also outputs internal hydrologic quantities such as water source fractions. It tests whether alternative structural priors for basin-scale thermal memory and instream heat processes can be distinguished using data, despite the flexibility of LSTM parameterization. The authors aim to assess model ability to predict both stream temperature and baseflow ratio, and to determine whether the resulting source fractions are physically meaningful under limited physics.
supporting_quote: we tested four alternative structural priors describing basin-scale water temperature memory and instream heat processes
We evaluated models' abilities to predict Ts and baseflow ratio.

chunks.text: The paper frames three research questions: comparing hybrid models trained on stream temperature to purely data-driven models while examining variance in baseflow estimates; testing the necessity of instream processes and the suitability of air-temperature averaging assumptions for inflow temperatures; and assessing whether different priors matter enough to identify better priors given LSTM’s adaptive capability.
supporting_quote: 1. How well can NN-dominant hybrid models trained only on Ts data predict Ts compared to purely data-driven models
2. Are instream processes necessary to achieve high simulation quality for daily stream temperature
3. Given the strong adaptive capability of LSTM, do different structural priors matter to the results of the hybrid model?

chunks.text: Structural uncertainty in stream temperature models is difficult to assess because it is intertwined with parametric uncertainty, data uncertainty, and calibration ambiguity. Poor performance can arise from inadequate structures, suboptimal parameters, or both, and exploring parameters for each structure is computationally expensive. Additionally, stream temperature models are often not benchmarked on common datasets, making conclusions data-dependent and hard to generalize.
supporting_quote: the structural uncertainty is intertwined with parametric uncertainty
stream temperature models are seldom benchmarked on the same data set

chunks.text: Pure deep learning models can achieve high predictive accuracy but are black boxes that lack interpretability and do not provide physically meaningful intermediate variables for diagnosing internal logic. This limits their use for understanding process contributions such as groundwater vs. surface flow fractions, and prevents direct comparison of inferred internal states against independent information.
supporting_quote: LSTM is also limited by its black-box nature: it does not provide an interpretable explanation of internal processes
its intermediate variables lack physical meaning and thus cannot be compared against observations

chunks.text: In NN-dominant hybrid systems, powerful neural components may compensate for weaknesses in different structural priors, potentially keeping final predictive accuracy high and making it hard to identify which priors are better. This raises concerns that priors may not be identifiable from output data, and that estimated internal fluxes may be unstable or non-physical when insufficient constraints are implemented.
supporting_quote: it is not yet clear if the structural priors matter... or if better priors can be identified
there is a risk that the NN components of the model will... adapt to and compensate for the unique weaknesses of each alternative structural prior

chunks.text: The framework follows differentiable parameter learning (dPL) where an LSTM predicts daily water source fractions, convolution parameters for mapping air temperature to source water temperatures, and physical parameters for instream processes. Source temperatures are computed by convolving air temperature with kernels and then mixed by flow-weighted averaging to create lateral inflow temperature. That lateral temperature is passed to the SNTEMP instream module to simulate downstream daily stream temperature, enabling end-to-end training via automatic differentiation in PyTorch.
supporting_quote: our hybrid model (LSTM + mixing assumptions + physical instream thermal processes) followed the dPL approach
given forcing and attribute data... an LSTM unit predicts (a) daily fractions of water sources... (b) convolutional parameters (θc)... and (c) some physical parameters (θ).
We used the PyTorch platform

chunks.text: Four structural prior options were evaluated: three that couple mixing with SNTEMP instream processes using assumptions from SMRA17, MRR88, and WVWBB19, plus a “LSTM + mixing” variant that omits instream processes entirely. The priors differ in number of water sources (two vs. three), how source temperatures are derived (averaging vs. daily air temperature with offsets), and whether groundwater thresholds or biases are applied. These priors define equations that constrain how LSTM-estimated fractions and temperatures combine to produce stream temperature.
supporting_quote: we considered three sets of basic assumptions... SMRA17... MRR88... WVWBB19
Thus we also evaluated a model option (called "LSTM + mixing") that did not involve the SNTEMP instream module

chunks.text: To support gradient-based training and allow flexible thermal-memory shapes, the study replaces simple air-temperature averaging with convolution using a cumulative gamma distribution. This produces a recency-weighted temperature estimate for groundwater and (when applicable) shallow subsurface water, but can become flat and revert to simple averaging. An optional groundwater temperature bias term is also explored to compensate for unmodeled heat fluxes such as geothermal conduction.
supporting_quote: we chose to convolve daily air temperature with a cumulative gamma function distribution (defined by θc parameters, and conv() in Table 1)
It can also have a large gradient to give higher weights to the most recent days.
we also explored adding an optional bias term bopt to the groundwater temperature part

chunks.text: A moving average (MA) adjustment operator is applied to raw LSTM outputs for groundwater and subsurface fractions to stabilize and smooth daily variability, then fractions are rescaled to sum to one. Experiments were run with and without MA and across multiple MA lengths to examine how smoothing affects baseflow plausibility and model selection. The operator is described as improving smoothness and reducing rapid unrealistic changes in inferred source contributions.
supporting_quote: we added a MA convolution filter to groundwater and subsurface flow
MA was tried with different lengths (MA_length) of 7, 15, 30, 40, 60, 75, and 90 days
MA_adj is a MA adjustment operator to improve the smoothness of the subsurface and groundwater fractions prediction.

chunks.text: Training uses end-to-end optimization with specified LSTM hyperparameters and time-windowing: 600 epochs, hidden size 256, and sequence length ρ = 365 days. Inputs include basin-averaged forcings and static attributes, and streamflow/precipitation are transformed using a log formula and standardized. Adadelta is used as optimizer, and one epoch corresponds to a forward run for all training basins.
supporting_quote: we ran all experiments with 600 epochs
The number of features in LSTM... was 256. The length of the time series... ρ, was selected as 365 days.
We used Adadelta (Zeiler, 2012) with adaptive learning rates

chunks.text: Model evaluation uses both target performance and an external hydrologic plausibility metric. Stream temperature performance is assessed with RMSE (used in the loss), and additional metrics including bias, NSE, and KGE. Baseflow index (BFI) is computed from modeled groundwater and subsurface fractions and compared via Pearson correlation (R_BFI) to an alternative BFI estimate from GAGES-II derived from hydrograph separation, treated as a soft constraint rather than ground truth.
supporting_quote: The metric used in the loss function... was the root-mean-square error (RMSE)
We calculated the spatial correlation between this estimate and the BFI from hydrograph separation (R_BFI)
R_BFI should only provide a soft constraint on model selection.

chunks.text: A grid of structural configurations was explored to characterize variance and limits: groundwater convolution length was set to 365 days; subsurface convolution length in SMRA17 was 30 days; MA smoothing was toggled and varied; an optional groundwater temperature bias was toggled; and many parameters were treated as either dynamic (daily varying) or static. In total, 144 experiments were run to understand how structural hyperparameters influence performance and inferred internal variables.
supporting_quote: The length of the convolutional filter in groundwater temperature (ngw) was set to 365 days for all models.
The length of the convolutional filter for subsurface flow temperature (nss) in LSTM-SMRA17 was 30 days.
In total, we ran 144 experiments with different configurations

chunks.text: The study uses 415 headwater basins across the conterminous United States drawn from GAGES-II, selected to have complete streamflow records from October 2010 to September 2016 and stream temperature data available for at least 10% of days in that window. Observed streamflow and stream temperature are sourced from the USGS National Water Information System. Basin-averaged meteorological forcings are derived from Daymet V4 by intersecting basin shapefiles with 1-km grid cells.
supporting_quote: We selected 415 headwater basins from the 9,017 basins... (GAGES-II)
observed streamflow data were fully available from October 2010 to September 2016, and stream temperature data were available for at least 10% of the days
Mean daily observed streamflow and stream temperature data were downloaded from the U.S. Geological Survey

chunks.text: LSTM inputs include 33 static basin attributes and seven daily forcings. Attributes span topography, long-term climate, dams/reservoirs, land cover, geology, and soils. Daily forcings include max/min air temperature, vapor pressure, observed streamflow, day length, shortwave radiation, and precipitation. SNTEMP additionally uses slope, drainage area, and estimated stream length, plus daily vapor pressure, solar radiation, and flows per source derived from modeled fractions.
supporting_quote: we used 33 attributes and seven forcings as inputs to the LSTM
Meteorological forcings... were maximum and minimum daily air temperature, vapor pressure, observed daily streamflow, day length, shortwave solar radiation, and precipitation.
SNTEMP attributes are slope, watershed drainage area, and stream (segment) length.

chunks.text: The training period spans 1 October 2010 to 30 September 2014, and the testing period is the subsequent two years through 30 September 2016. This split matches earlier national-scale LSTM stream temperature studies for comparability. Performance and analysis reported in the paper focus on the testing period results.
supporting_quote: The training time range... was from 1 October 2010 to 30 September 2014.
The testing period was the next 2 years, between 1 October 2014 and 30 September 2016.
All results discussed in this manuscript are the performance results in the testing period

chunks.text: Across 144 configurations, models show a mild tradeoff between stream temperature RMSE and baseflow correlation with external BFI estimates, producing sharp Pareto fronts for some priors. For a given prior, many configurations achieve similarly low RMSE but widely varying R_BFI, indicating large variance in inferred baseflow despite similar temperature accuracy. This suggests stream temperature alone does not fully constrain internal water source fractions in the NN-dominant setup.
supporting_quote: showing noticeable variance even for the same priors (Figure 2).
these models have almost equally good temperature predictive performance but widely different R_BFI values
the variance... suggests the internal dynamics are underconstrained by stream temperature alone.

chunks.text: Structural priors materially affect achievable performance despite LSTM flexibility, enabling identification of better priors. LSTM-SMRA17 yields the best overall RMSE and best R_BFI among priors, while LSTM-MRR88 is slightly worse and LSTM-WVWBB19 has higher minimum RMSE. Reported interquartile-like ranges show SMRA17 RMSE mostly 0.89–1.27°C with R_BFI 0.74–0.80, whereas MRR88 RMSE mostly 1.08–1.45°C with R_BFI 0.63–0.74; WVWBB19 has minimum RMSE 1.10°C.
supporting_quote: LSTM-SMRA17 gave the lowest error in terms of stream temperature as well as the best BFI correlation
More than half of the LSTM-SMRA17 stream temperature RMSE values are between 0.89°C and 1.27°C, and between 0.74 and 0.80 for RBFI.
LSTM-WVWBB19, on the other hand, has a minimum RMSE of 1.10°C.

chunks.text: Including a distinct shallow subsurface compartment improves both temperature and baseflow representation relative to a two-component structure. The comparison between LSTM-SMRA17 (surface + shallow subsurface + groundwater) and LSTM-MRR88 (surface + groundwater) suggests the shallow subsurface “bucket” adds necessary flexibility and physical realism. The paper links this to evidence that phase lag between air and stream temperature can reflect shallow subsurface pathways.
supporting_quote: a separate bucket for shallow subsurface flow... could improve both stream temperature accuracy and baseflow representation
Comparing the results between LSTM-SMRA17 and LSTM-MRR88 implies that a separate bucket for shallow subsurface flow... could improve both

chunks.text: Applying MA smoothing to LSTM-predicted source fractions improves BFI correlation and indicates fractions should not vary too rapidly. Many low-R_BFI models correspond to configurations without the MA operator. The smoothing is interpreted as representing buffering by transient storages along flow paths.
supporting_quote: Most of the models with lower accuracy in BFI correlations... are the ones in which the flow MA operator was not activated.
The benefit of MA operators in terms of BFI correlation suggests the water source fractions should not vary too rapidly.

chunks.text: Recency-weighted convolution (cumulative gamma) for source-water temperature outperforms simple averaging across the tested priors. Switching from simple averaging to convolution improved RMSE and R_BFI by about 11% and 13% on average. This supports a conceptual model where shallow layers and more recent temperatures exert stronger influence than a fully well-mixed reservoir implied by simple averaging.
supporting_quote: a cumulative gamma function (recency-weighted) outperforms a simple averaging function
switching from a simple average function to convolutional parameters respectively improved the RMSE and RBFI values by 11% and 13% on average

chunks.text: Dynamic (time-varying) parameterization of instream and related parameters is favored by multidimensional evaluation. Pareto-front models mostly use configurations where parameters are dynamic, consistent with seasonal variability in shading and evapotranspiration. All-static parameter models have larger median RMSE, indicating underfitting when seasonality is ignored.
supporting_quote: Almost all experiments in the Pareto fronts consist of dynamic θc or θ
The models with all static parameters... had relatively larger median RMSE values for stream temperature.

chunks.text: Selected differentiable models achieve high stream temperature skill close to a pure LSTM benchmark while providing process outputs. The chosen LSTM-SMRA17 configuration attains median NSE 0.970 and KGE 0.951, compared to earlier LSTM-only results of median NSE 0.98 and KGE 0.956. Bias for selected LSTM-SMRA17 is near zero (−0.23°C), though its median RMSE is 0.23°C higher than the LSTM benchmark.
supporting_quote: The chosen LSTM-SMRA17 model demonstrates outstanding performance with median NSE and KGE values of 0.970 and 0.951.
very close to the LSTM model... with median NSE and KGE values of 0.98 and 0.956.
The median bias was the closest to zero (bias = −0.23°C)

chunks.text: Instream heat processes are necessary for accurate daily stream temperature simulation; omitting them causes strong systematic errors. The LSTM + mixing model (no instream module) has much larger bias, mostly negative, and much worse RMSE compared to models that include SNTEMP. Time series examples show LSTM + mixing stays too close to air temperature and cannot correct bias via LSTM flexibility alone.
supporting_quote: Instream processes played a crucial role in simulating stream temperature, judged by the considerable difference in RMSE values between LSTM + mixing and the other models
The LSTM + mixing model incurred a much larger bias (mostly negative)

chunks.text: Multivariate model selection improves physical plausibility of internal fluxes: selected instream-process models correlate strongly with GAGES-II BFI, while LSTM + mixing does not. For selected models, LSTM-SMRA17 achieves R_BFI = 0.724, LSTM-WVWBB19 0.658, LSTM-MRR88 0.664, whereas LSTM + mixing has R_BFI = 0.234. This indicates that models may fit temperature but still yield poor hydrologic source fractions unless evaluated with additional criteria.
supporting_quote: LSTM-SMRA17 showed the highest Pearson correlation (RBFI) with GAGES-II BFI (r = 0.724).
The lowest RBFI was for LSTM + mixing with a value of 0.234

chunks.text: The NN-dominant hybrid system remains under-determined by stream temperature alone, leading to large variance in inferred water source fractions even when temperature RMSE is near-optimal. The paper cautions against interpreting internal dynamics from a single-target training setup and argues that additional data or process constraints are needed. Multivariate evaluation (e.g., using baseflow correlation) can narrow admissible models and improve physical significance of intermediate outputs.
supporting_quote: the variance of the predicted BFI remains large even within a small range of the optimal RMSE
the internal variables (water source fractions) may not be adequately constrained by a single target variable (stream temperature) alone.
To ensure the physical significance of the internal fluxes, one can either employ multivariate data for model selection

chunks.text: R_BFI is treated as a soft constraint because hydrograph separation and GAGES-II BFI are empirical and cannot clearly distinguish shallow versus deep subsurface contributions. Therefore, agreement with GAGES-II BFI does not constitute ground truth validation. This limits certainty about the correctness of inferred shallow subsurface vs. groundwater fractions, even when correlations are high.
supporting_quote: because the hydrograph separation approach used for comparison is also empirical and cannot clearly distinguish between shallow and deep subsurface outflow, RBFI should only provide a soft constraint

chunks.text: The modeling uses a single conceptual reach per basin, which simplifies computation but may not capture local heterogeneity in large basins. The authors note that the approach is most applicable to smaller headwater basins and that routing should be added for river networks. This structural simplification can limit physical realism in spatially complex systems.
supporting_quote: most applicable to smaller, headwater basins where the river network can be represented by a single conceptual reach, otherwise a routing section should be added
This lumped representation may not capture the local heterogeneities in large basins

chunks.text: Some regional discrepancies in baseflow patterns suggest missing processes such as snowmelt temperature effects and limitations of the assumed air-temperature-driven source temperature model. In the northeastern U.S. and Michigan Upper Peninsula, modeled BFI tends to be higher than GAGES-II BFI, and the authors hypothesize that snowmelt and glacial deposits may cause temperature behaviors not captured by the current priors. This points to the need for additional modules to represent cold-region processes.
supporting_quote: The main differences between LSTM-SMRA17 baseflow and GAGES-II BFI were in the northeastern United States and the Michigan Upper Peninsula
We hypothesize that... it lacks a module for modeling snowmelt and its temperature.

chunks.text: The study concludes that differentiable hybrid modeling can help identify better structural priors because different priors lead to distinct behaviors and Pareto fronts even with strong LSTM optimization, allowing focus on structure rather than parameter entanglement. The best-performing prior tested is LSTM-SMRA17, achieving temperature NSE 0.970 and R_BFI 0.724 for a selected configuration, though R_BFI varies widely across configurations. The approach demonstrates that structural assumptions—like including shallow subsurface flow and recency-weighted thermal memory—can be inferred and improved using large-scale data.
supporting_quote: The large differences in behaviors of models with different priors mean this hybrid modeling and parameter learning approach can be used to identify better physical assumptions
the LSTM-SMRA17 prior gave strong results... (temperature NSE = 0.970 and RBFI = 0.724 for the selected configuration

chunks.text: Key process conclusions include: adding a shallow subsurface bucket improves both temperature and baseflow modeling; recency-weighted averaging improves groundwater and subsurface temperature estimates relative to simple averaging; and in-stream heat processes are necessary for daily stream temperature accuracy. The paper also concludes that dynamical (seasonally varying) instream parameters are favorable, reflecting seasonal changes in shading and evapotranspiration. These results suggest more realistic, flexible process representations can be trained using big data with differentiable modeling.
supporting_quote: a separate bucket for the shallow subsurface improves both temperature and baseflow modeling
groundwater and subsurface flow temperature are better simulated by recency-weighted averaging, rather than a well-mixed reservoir
in-stream heat processes are necessary

chunks.text: Hydrology and environmental sciences rely on mathematical models and large datasets to analyze complex systems, but such models often require substantial computational resources, leading to long runtimes. Improving efficiency depends on understanding dependencies between simulation tasks to decide which can run in parallel versus must remain sequential. Prior work has explored parallel computing in hydrologic modeling using HPC standards (e.g., OpenMP/OpenACC), CPU/GPU hybrids, and MPI-based approaches. Recently, web technologies have become viable for porting computations to client-side environments, enabling near-native speed analyses in browsers.
supporting_quote: However, these models require significant computational resources, resulting in extensive processing times and resources.
By abstracting these dependencies, researchers can determine whether tasks can run in parallel or must be run sequentially.
Client-side web applications have become increasingly popular in environmental science and hydrology

chunks.text: Modern browsers provide a suite of standardized technologies relevant to scientific computing: Web Workers for concurrent threads, WebGPU for GPU access, WebAssembly for running compiled low-level languages, and WebRTC for peer-to-peer data transfer. These technologies allow computationally intensive tasks to be moved off the main UI thread, leverage heterogeneous CPU/GPU resources, reuse legacy code, and exchange large datasets without external servers. Together they create a foundation for high-performance, portable, in-browser computation for hydrology and environmental applications.
supporting_quote: Web workers are a feature in web browsers that enable concurrent and background execution of JavaScript code
In 2022, the WebGPU API was implemented, providing developers with an alternative way to access GPUs.
WebAssembly is a technology that allows low-level programming languages like C, C++, AssemblyScript, FORTRAN, and Rust to be used in web applications
WebRTC is a set of standards that allows peer-to-peer communication through a semantic API available in major web browsers

chunks.text: Traditional web-based analysis workflows typically rely on server-side computation while browsers mainly visualize outputs. With emerging in-browser HPC capabilities, client-side analysis can now execute near-native CPU/GPU code, but browser-based high-performance computing remains underexplored. The paper situates HydroCompute as part of a trend toward next-generation hydroinformatics applications that exploit modern computational architecture available directly in web environments.
supporting_quote: The traditional pathways to analyze data in web environments involve leveraging servers for data manipulation and analysis
with new technologies and applications allowing the porting of near-native speed code running on a CPU or GPU-based analysis, creating web applications for analysis has become a reality
high-performance computing on the browser is still an avenue to explore

chunks.text: The research goal is to present HydroCompute as a high-performance client-side computational library for hydrology and environmental science applications. The library aims to enable both sequential and parallel simulations, optimize computational efficiency, and support multiple compute backends (JavaScript, WebAssembly, WebGPU). It also aims to support local peer-to-peer data transfers via WebRTC and provide an open-source, flexible architecture that allows users to integrate their own code for decision-making and analysis workflows.
supporting_quote: We present HydroCompute, a high-performance client-side computational library specifically designed for webbased hydrological and environmental science applications.
the library facilitates both sequential and parallel simulations, optimizing computational efficiency.
HydroCompute enables the porting and utilization of various engines, including WebGPU, Web Assembly, and native JavaScript code.
the library supports local data transfers through peer-to-peer communication using WebRTC.

chunks.text: HydroCompute’s objectives include leveraging web technologies (Web Workers, WebGPU, Web Assembly, WebRTC) to provide scalable computation, efficient data management, and developer-friendly access in browsers. It targets researchers, practitioners, and educators needing computational tools for hydrological modeling, flood risk, water resources management, environmental monitoring, and education. The library is intended to be accessible for users with varied programming expertise while supporting integration of code written in different languages through WebAssembly and engine switching.
supporting_quote: HydroCompute aims to address the computational challenges in hydrology and environmental sciences by providing a high-performance client-side computational library.
HydroCompute targets researchers, practitioners, and educators in the fields of hydrology and environmental sciences
Applications of HydroCompute include, but are not limited to, hydrological modeling, flood risk assessment, water resources management, environmental monitoring, and educational applications

chunks.text: A central problem is that hydrologic and environmental models often take extensive time and resources, creating barriers to interactive or real-time decision support. Efficient execution requires identifying dependencies between tasks to determine what can be parallelized and what must remain sequential. Without a framework that manages these dependencies and execution modes, developers face complexity in structuring simulations and coordinating multi-threaded execution, especially within browser constraints.
supporting_quote: these models require significant computational resources, resulting in extensive processing times and resources.
The challenge lies in understanding the dependencies between different simulation tasks.
determine whether tasks can run in parallel or must be run sequentially.

chunks.text: Browser-based high-performance computing for hydrology is still emerging, and portability across browsers and execution engines is imperfect. Differences in JavaScript engines and incomplete adoption of standards like WebGPU can limit full in-browser portability. Additionally, large client-side computations must navigate browser limits on threads, memory, and array sizes, which can constrain how much data can be processed locally.
supporting_quote: high-performance computing on the browser is still an avenue to explore

There are two topics that limited the full in-browser portability of the library during the development process: the underlying engine that transpiles the JavaScript code ... and the full compatibility of the technologies used (in particular, Web Assembly and WebGPU).
ES6 allocates the maximum length of an array or array buffer to be about 4 billion elements and 2.5 GB of memory, respectively.

chunks.text: HydroCompute uses algorithmic optimization and dependency analysis to coordinate sequential and parallel execution of dependent functions. The development emphasizes graph-theory approaches using directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to model functional dependencies, plus dynamic memory strategies that prefer data transfer over cloning across contexts. The design supports mixed execution where some tasks run in parallel while others remain sequential, maintaining ordering constraints needed in hydrologic workflows.
supporting_quote: Techniques based on graph theory, memory allocation, and tradeoffs between correctness and speedup were employed
Graph-based algorithms, specifically using a directed acyclic graph (DAG), were set to analyze functional dependencies
the data is transferred, not cloned, between the threading environment and the main engine.

chunks.text: The system architecture is modular and organized around compute engines and a data-sharing engine. It comprises a computational scheme driven by JavaScript, Web Assembly, and WebGPU engines and a data-sharing scheme driven by a WebRTC engine. These are managed through four layers: connection layer, engine layer, threading layer, and scripts layer, enabling engine switching, configuration, and background execution through web workers.
supporting_quote: The HydroCompute library comprises two main approaches: a computational scheme driven by engines for JavaScript, Web Assembly, and WebGPU, and a data-sharing scheme driven by a WebRTC engine.
managed through four primary layers: a connection layer ... an engine layer ... a threading layer ... and the scripts layer

chunks.text: The connection layer is the central interface that tracks engines, runs, data management, results, and execution times. It transforms user-provided arrays into typed buffers (float 32) stored in the library for reuse and transfers data between main thread and worker contexts. It enforces workflow assumptions including data sharing between contexts, transferring rather than cloning to reduce overhead, and validating that inputs are numeric and non-empty.
supporting_quote: The connection layer keeps track of the number of engines available for use ... and the results from the simulation, as well as execution times.
The connection layer calls helper functions that clone the data and transform it into typed buffers
float 32 byte numbers were considered to have the maximum accuracy required and are used as typed arrays
The input data must not be an empty array or contain faulty characters or anything other than numbers

chunks.text: Engine management selects sequential versus parallel strategies based on dependencies, data sizes, and user inputs. Scheduling partitions data among engines or assigns multiple functions to the same data using user-accessible threshold functions, including arbitrary partition sizes. When dependencies exist between workers or functions, a graph algorithm coordinates execution and results are merged into a single result space.
supporting_quote: run required functions sequentially or in parallel, based on the dependencies of arguments, data sizes, and user inputs.
partitioning the input data among the available engines or by assigning multiple functions to the same data using threshold functions
If dependencies exist ... then a graph algorithm is implemented to ensure efficient thread coordination.
After each task is completed, the results are combined into a single result space

chunks.text: Step execution management supports parallel execution (multiple threads fired simultaneously), concurrent execution (ordered tasks within a step when dependencies exist), and DAG-based scheduling across functions or steps. Parallel execution is promise-based and uses batches to respect available thread limits and avoid race conditions. The DAG algorithm accepts functions, a dependency array, extra arguments, and execution type; it executes with promises, stores returned values, and passes them to dependent functions.
supporting_quote: A step handling function determines the linkage between steps, the number of functions, and their dependencies
A promise-based approach has been implemented when the execution context requires n-number of threads to fire up at the same time
Batches of work are created to run an n-number of workers per batch and fired up to avoid race conditions
A DAG algorithm was implemented to schedule the execution of multiple steps or functions in a specific order based on their dependencies

chunks.text: A thread manager class scaffolds per-thread execution by tracking time, results, data, and arguments inside worker contexts. Engines provide the worker locations and engine name so the thread manager can call engine-specific worker scripts. JavaScript and WebGPU workers use object-based script collections keyed by function name, while WASM workers interface with compiled binaries via glue code (e.g., EMSCRIPTEN for C/C++).
supporting_quote: The thread manager class creates a scaffold containing specific running implementations for each thread requirement
The thread manager is in charge of calling the worker scripts for all the available engines.
the WASM-compiled code uses the glue code generated by the specific language compiler—i.e., EMSCRIPTEN for C/ C++—to interface with the binary code

chunks.text: HydroCompute’s workers provide specialized execution contexts. The JavaScript worker is optimized for typed arrays and is efficient for small data with complex computations. The WebGPU worker manages adapters/devices, creates buffers and shader modules, and is best suited for large-scale data but can be inefficient for small data due to GPU overhead. The WebAssembly worker executes binary code from languages like C and AssemblyScript, allowing reuse of legacy code and producing small, fast bundles.
supporting_quote: JavaScript Worker: ... optimized for typed arrays. Not having to parse, the execution performance is considerably faster for small-sized data
WebGPU worker is best suited for analyzing large-scale data and becomes inefficient with smaller data
Web Assembly Worker: ... execute code directly from binary code compiled from different Web Assembly-compliant programming languages
C-implemented Web Assembly code allows for easy compiling through EMSCRIPTEN, outputting fast and small-sized bundles.

chunks.text: The WebRTC engine provides peer-to-peer data transfer for efficient sharing of large data or simulation results among machines on the same network. During initialization it sets parameters such as maximum message size (65 kB), data partitions, and connection type, then establishes a data channel in run(). Received data is saved into the connection layer’s shared structures so it can be directly used as simulation input.
supporting_quote: The WebRTC engine creates a wrapper around the WebRTC features for efficient data transfer, such as results from simulations on another machine
During initialization, the engine sets up connection parameters, such as the maximum message size (65 kB)
The received data is saved in the connection layer and readily accessible for use as input in simulations.

chunks.text: HydroCompute accepts input as JavaScript arrays of any size and transforms them into memory buffers for execution across engines. Data objects are stored in a namespace and can be referenced by a user-provided name (dataId) or used directly if only one object exists. Results are stored under a simulation name and can be retrieved as array buffers along with execution metadata such as times, order, and function names.
supporting_quote: Input data for the library are JavaScript arrays of any size
The data is transformed into memory buffers that can be moved throughout the streamlined processes
the given nametag (dataId) should be provided.
the results are saved in a separate namespace with the simulation name ... accessed through hydrocompute.engineResults.

chunks.text: Benchmarking data were generated as square matrices filled with random numbers between 0 and 1000 across a wide range of sizes. The evaluation used a naïve O(n^3) matrix multiplication implemented in JavaScript, WebAssembly, and WebGPU to compare CPU- versus GPU-backed execution. Testing occurred on an Intel Core i7-4790 CPU with 32 GB RAM and integrated Intel HD Graphics 4600, across Chrome Canary, Edge, and Firefox.
supporting_quote: square matrices of varying sizes (ranging from 42 to 56, 25^2) were generated and filled with random numbers between 0 and 1000.
we implemented a naïve matrix algorithm as scripts for all engines with both O (n^3 ) complexity
The implementation was executed on a machine with an Intel Core i7-4790 CPU @ 3.60 GHz, 32 GB of RAM, and an integrated Intel HD Graphics 4600

chunks.text: The Iowa streamflow dashboard case study used daily values from multiple hydrologic and climate data services. Data were queried via CUAHSI WaterOneFlow services from USGS, MOPEX, and NOAA GHCN, selecting stations within county boxes or user-drawn rectangles. Retrieved records spanned from 1900 through the day of analysis, with station time series sizes varying from 0 to over 40,000 daily records after cleaning.
supporting_quote: connects ... to CUAHSI WaterOneFlow services ... for daily values from USGS, MOPEX, and NOAA GHCN
obtain all the available streamflow stations with daily readings ... from 1900 through the day of analysis.
data sizes per station varied from 0 records to over 40,000

chunks.text: The streamflow analysis executed a fixed pipeline of time-series methods per station, totaling 33 algorithmic function calls per station. Computations included a 23-fold smoothing simple moving average, exponential and simple moving averages, autocorrelation, linear detrending, and ARMA estimation (including auto-parameter update). Functions were implemented in both JavaScript and C compiled using EMSCRIPTEN, with HydroCompute switching engines during the workflow.
supporting_quote: For each station selected, it calculates a 23-fold smoothing simple moving average
a parameter set ARMA and autoparameter calculated ARMA function
there were 33 algorithmic function calls per station done on the HydroCompute library
written in JavaScript ... and in C code compiled in EMSCRIPTEN (ARMA, moving averages, transformations, and autocorrelation functions).

chunks.text: Single-thread benchmarking showed that all engines behaved similarly for small matrices, but WebGPU became superior as matrix size increased. The paper reports similar performance for matrices smaller than 16^2, followed by increasing execution times for all engines with WebGPU performing best for larger computations. This demonstrates the expected crossover where GPU parallelism amortizes overhead only after data sizes become sufficiently large.
supporting_quote: Scenario 1 shows similar behavior for all engines for matrices smaller than 16^2, and a clear trend toward an increase for the three engines, with WebGPU performing best for larger matrix computations

chunks.text: In multithreaded benchmarking, the authors normalized FLOPs and execution time by thread count and derived empirical thresholds for choosing engines. They found JavaScript and WebAssembly are more efficient for matrix sizes below 124^2, and WebAssembly remains preferable up to 318^2. Beyond those sizes, WebGPU provides the best performance, supporting an engine-selection strategy based on problem scale.
supporting_quote: thresholds were found for when to use which engine; specifically, JS and WASM are more efficient for matrix sizes below 124^2 , and WASM for matrix sizes below 318^2 . Afterwards, the WebGPU engine has the best performance.
Fig. 13. Cutoff for JS and WASM engines in comparison to the WebGPU, at sizes (a) < 124 and (b) < 318 respectively.

chunks.text: WebGPU workgroup experiments for very large matrices revealed that, for the naïve shader implementation, a workgroup size of 1 performed best. The results showed a non-linear increase in execution time with matrix size and a notable jump at size 4096, attributed to GPU device memory allocation and paging behavior. The authors stress that this allocation behavior is vendor- and device-dependent.
supporting_quote: Given the naïve implementation, workgroup size 1 yields the best results in terms of performance.
there was a significant execution time jump at size 4096, which is linked to the data allocation driven by the device's hardware
this mechanism is highly dependent on the device's memory management and a specific vendor's GPU schemes.

chunks.text: The Iowa streamflow dashboard demonstrated that HydroCompute can run a multi-step analytical workflow fully on the client side while keeping the UI responsive. The workflow combined HydroLang for retrieval/cleaning/visualization with HydroCompute for heavy time-series analysis in background workers, using both JavaScript and WASM (C via EMSCRIPTEN). The system switched engines across simulations, starting with JS and then using WASM for computational routines such as ARMA and autocorrelation.
supporting_quote: All of this is done directly on the client side using the multiple functions and engines in the hydrocompute framework.
the Hydro-Compute library used to predict timebound streamflow using autocorrelation functions, the auto-regressive moving average (ARMA) process
The functions used for the analysis were written in JavaScript ... and in C code compiled in EMSCRIPTEN
initiating with the JS engine for the first two simulations and the WASM engine after.

chunks.text: Execution time in the streamflow case study scaled approximately linearly with the number of data points per station and the number of stations analyzed. For an example query of about 250 stations in northwestern Iowa, data retrieval and cleaning took roughly 9 minutes total, with about 3 minutes for retrieval/cleaning and 6 minutes for analysis. This indicates the client-side analytics can dominate runtime once data are obtained.
supporting_quote: The results of execution time show a linear relationship between time, the number of data points available at each station, and the number of stations within the selected area.

Querying a quarter of the state (around 250 stations in the northwestern part of the state) ... took approximately 9 min ... around 3 min for the data retrieval and cleaning and 6 min for the analysis.

chunks.text: Browser choice impacted measured execution time for the same analysis workload, reflecting differences in JavaScript engines and runtime behavior. For the same 10 stations near Iowa City, Mozilla Firefox took 34,221 ms, Chrome took 17,176.5 ms, and Edge took 19,412 ms. The authors attribute this primarily to SpiderMonkey versus Chromium V8 just-in-time engines, while noting the difference is negligible for small datasets.
supporting_quote: Mozilla yielded a total execution time of 34,221 ms, Chrome took 17176.5 ms, and Edge took 19,412 ms.
This difference can be attributed to the different just-in-time (JIT) engines for JavaScript in Mozilla (Spider Monkey) and Chrome/Edge (Chromium V8)

chunks.text: Workshop and survey feedback suggested HydroCompute is perceived as useful for web application development in hydrologic contexts such as flood forecasting, drought monitoring, and data management. Participants appreciated parallel/sequential execution and integration with other web tools such as HydroLang, while also asking for higher abstraction and emphasizing public repositories for accessibility. Reported responses showed many participants were neutral or positive on usability (50% and 75% neutrality/agreement cited).
supporting_quote: Users found the library suitable for web application development, particularly for tasks like flood forecasting, drought monitoring, and hydrological data management.
While 50% and 75% of participants expressed neutrality or agreement with the library's usability
Participants valued functionalities like parallel and sequential execution ... and compatibility with libraries such as Hydro-Lang.

chunks.text: WebGPU performance and stability were constrained by hardware and integrated GPU behavior in the tested environment. The authors observed that the integrated GPU adapter could lose connection with the WebGPU API during other graphical operations (e.g., clicking or switching tabs with video rendering). Shared GPU memory and concurrent CPU/GPU tasks in workers also influenced execution time, indicating that browser-GPU interactions can be fragile for heavy client-side workloads.
supporting_quote: Having shared GPU memory had a significant impact on the performance of the WebGPU
the adapter that the WebGPU API connected to got lost with no reconnection.
The combinations of CPU and GPU tasks running on a worker also heavily influenced the execution time.

chunks.text: The authors note portability constraints stemming from differences in browser JavaScript engines and incomplete implementation of WebGPU across browsers. Although ES6 modules improved portability, WebGPU was "not been fully implemented" during development, limiting consistent in-browser behavior. They developed the library anticipating broader standards adoption, but current cross-browser variability remains a practical limitation.
supporting_quote: the underlying engine that transpiles the JavaScript code (for example, Chromium V8 ... or SpiderMokey in Mozilla)
the WebGPU implementation has not been fully implemented.
the library has been developed with the anticipation that all these standards will be universally adopted

chunks.text: Very large client-side datasets may exceed practical resource limits in browsers, despite substantial theoretical maximums. The paper highlights constraints from runtime heap size per browser/tab and maximum allocated array sizes, noting ES6 limits of about 4 billion elements and 2.5 GB for an array buffer. Different isolated environments also have different maxima (JS 8–64 GB, WASM 4 GB, GPU 8–64 GB), which can restrict extremely large simulations and motivate hybrid server-client approaches or IndexedDB use.
supporting_quote: there may be limitations when dealing with extremely large datasets on the client side in terms of tens of gigabytes (Gbs).
ES6 allocates the maximum length of an array or array buffer to be about 4 billion elements and 2.5 GB of memory, respectively.
with JS ranging from 8 to 64 GB, web assembly runtime at 4 GB, and the GPU from 8 to 64 GB

chunks.text: Algorithm validity remains a key risk when porting and executing models through the framework. The authors report that an incorrect ARMA implementation initially produced low-reliability forecasting results until corrected, illustrating the need for clear problem statements and careful implementation. They warn that issues such as undefined instructions and memory leaks may arise from improper engine usage or unclear instruction definitions.
supporting_quote: During the implementation of ARMA processes for the case study, low reliability was observed in the forecasting results due to incorrect implementation, which was later corrected.
Any issues with the simulation run, such as undefined instruction definitions, uncaught or unhandled memory leaks

chunks.text: Endianness and bitwise organization were not fully considered during development due to uncertainty about how data types and compilation modes interact across engines. The authors state this will be addressed in future releases, implying potential cross-platform or cross-engine issues when moving binary data between JavaScript, WASM, and GPU contexts.
supporting_quote: computer bitwise organization, or endianness, was not thoroughly considered
This topic will be addressed in future releases of the project.

chunks.text: HydroCompute is concluded to be a high-performance, open-source client-side library that enables efficient and scalable computations for hydrology and environmental sciences within web applications. By combining Web Workers, WebGPU, WebAssembly, and WebRTC, it supports sequential and parallel execution and multi-language code integration. The case studies demonstrate performance tradeoffs across engines and show feasibility for real-time streamflow analytics on the client side, supporting improved processing and decision-making workflows.
supporting_quote: The HydroCompute library offers a powerful and versatile solution for addressing computational challenges in hydrology and environmental sciences.

By leveraging cutting-edge web technologies, such as Web Workers, WebGPU, Web Assembly, and WebRTC, the library enables users to perform efficient and scalable computations within clientside web applications.
The case studies demonstrate the library's performance capabilities and highlight its potential

chunks.text: The paper concludes that HydroCompute’s modular architecture and WebAssembly compatibility allow users to manage and deploy code written in different programming languages for fast web application development. It positions the library as community-oriented and intended to foster broader adoption and contributions, ultimately benefiting researchers, practitioners, and educators. The authors emphasize directives for structure and compilation that support rapid deployment and interoperability.
supporting_quote: The modular architecture, integration with existing frameworks, and compatibility with different programming languages through the WebAssembly standard enhance the library's adaptability
By providing an open-source, user-friendly, and high-performance computational library, HydroCompute aims to foster a community of users and developers
The library is able to read and manage code written in different programming languages by providing directives on structure and compilation that allow for fast deployment

chunks.text: Stream gauges are critical for building and calibrating hydrologic models, but most river segments lack active monitoring. This limits the ability to calibrate and evaluate large operational models and to predict floods and droughts, especially at local scales. In the U.S., the National Water Model covers millions of segments, but real-time monitoring exists for only a small fraction, motivating approaches that can infer flows where gauges are absent.
supporting_quote: less than 10% of the river segments are actively monitored using gauges
calibration and evaluation of this model is limited by the lack of real‐time streamflow monitoring data for more than 90% of these segments

chunks.text: Prior work has shown LSTMs can predict streamflow in ungauged basins from meteorological inputs and static basin attributes, often outperforming traditional models. However, many ungauged-basin approaches emphasize meteorological forcings and basin attributes, rather than using downstream observations to constrain upstream estimates in retrospective settings. This paper situates the upstream–downstream constraint as an opportunity specific to historic flow reconstruction.
supporting_quote: Kratzert et al. (2019) showed that LSTM networks can capture complex, non‐linear relationships between meteorological forcings and streamflow
many approaches emphasize parameter interpolation or purely meteorological inputs, rather than harnessing combined downstream flows to constrain upstream estimates

chunks.text: The paper frames the upstream estimation problem as a signal separation task, analogous to separating individual voices from a mixed audio recording. In this analogy, downstream discharge is a composite signal containing contributions from multiple tributaries, while physical/meteorological variables provide auxiliary features to help disentangle sources. This motivates using LSTM architectures for disaggregating tributary flows from a combined downstream record.
supporting_quote: the downstream flow is analogous to a "mixed signal," containing the combined contributions from multiple upstream tributaries
deep learning can parse a complex, composite signal into distinct components

chunks.text: The study aims to introduce and test an LSTM-based approach for estimating historical streamflow in ungauged basin segments by leveraging downstream gauge observations as constraints. The approach is designed to create surrogate gauges for unmonitored tributaries in a watershed network. A proof of concept is demonstrated using synthetic networks of leaky-bucket hydrologic models before future application to real basins.
supporting_quote: introduce a novel approach for estimating historical flows in ungauged basins by leveraging downstream gauge observations as additional constraints
we propose utilizing long short‐term memory (LSTM) networks to estimate historic streamflow in ungauged watersheds, effectively creating "surrogate gauges."

chunks.text: A central objective is to show that representing watersheds as connected upstream–downstream pairs is a generalizable framework for any ungauged portion of a basin. The work tests whether training on the combined downstream flow plus tributary attributes allows the model to recover individual upstream contributions. The intention is to provide a scalable concept that could be extended to real river networks.
supporting_quote: a novel conceptualization using pairs of connected basins (one gauged, one ungauged) as a generalizable framework applicable to any upstream‐downstream relationship within a river network
Representing watersheds with networks of two buckets allows for generalization to any ungauged portion of a basin.

chunks.text: Large-scale hydrologic models are difficult to calibrate because most stream segments lack real-time flow observations. Traditional ungauged-basin estimation methods transfer behavior from monitored locations to unmonitored ones using basin characteristics and meteorology, but this can ignore information contained in downstream observations. For retrospective (historic) reconstruction, downstream measurements are available and can potentially constrain upstream estimates more strongly than forecast-style methods.
supporting_quote: many places do not have enough gauge data to support accurate modeling
for historic flows, any downstream observations are particularly valuable for constraining estimates at the unmonitored location

chunks.text: A practical barrier to training models that infer upstream flows from downstream observations is the scarcity of fully monitored river networks with simultaneous upstream and downstream gauges. Because such datasets are rare, it is difficult to empirically validate upstream-disaggregation models directly on real-world systems at scale. The paper addresses this by using synthetic, fully monitored networks for proof-of-concept testing.
supporting_quote: such fully monitored networks are rare, limiting the practicality of directly applying this approach with real‐world data
we first employ synthetic data sets generated by simplified hydrologic models (Leaky Bucket networks)

chunks.text: The core methodology trains an LSTM to disaggregate individual upstream flows from a combined downstream flow time series, using meteorological and physical features of each tributary bucket as inputs. The model treats the downstream gauge as a mixed signal and learns to separate the tributary contributions. Training and evaluation are performed on synthetic bucket networks to test feasibility in a controlled environment.
supporting_quote: use of combined downstream flow data from networks of converging tributaries along with meteorological data to predict individual upstream flows
develop a LSTM model, designed to disaggregate the combined "downstream flow" back into the individual "upstream flows" of each tributary within the network

chunks.text: Each river segment is simulated with a leaky-bucket model that captures precipitation inputs and losses due to evapotranspiration and infiltration, plus outflows via spigot flow and overflow. Evapotranspiration is represented as a sinusoidal function modulated by a bucket parameter and noise, while infiltration is proportional to current water depth and an infiltration coefficient. Spigot outflow uses Torricelli-based velocity and multiplies by spigot area and timestep to compute discharge.
supporting_quote: ET = max(0, (A_bucket/ET_parameter) · sin(t) · noise(t))
Infiltration = h_bucket × K_infiltration
v = sqrt(2gh)
q_spigot = v × A_spigot × Δt

chunks.text: Watersheds are represented as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) called bucket networks, where tributary buckets converge into a downstream point. The combined downstream flow is computed by routing and summing tributary flows. For this proof of concept, routing is simplified to a null routing function to isolate the learning problem of separating upstream signals from the downstream mixture.
supporting_quote: A watershed can be represented as a directed acyclic graph (DAG)
Q_Total = sum_{i=1}^{n} f(Q_i)
For the purposes of this proof of concept, the upstream flows from each bucket were combined using a null routing function.

chunks.text: Model performance is assessed with RMSE, MAE, and Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) computed on validation (and then test) datasets. RMSE emphasizes large errors, MAE reflects typical absolute error, and NSE evaluates predictive skill relative to observed variance. Together these metrics are used to compare alternative training approaches and to select an optimized model.
supporting_quote: The effectiveness of the model was evaluated by applying three metrics: RMSE, MAE and Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE).
NSE = 1 - (sum (y_i - y_hat_i)^2) / (sum (y_i - y_bar)^2)

chunks.text: The LSTM is implemented in PyTorch and trained with Adam using Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss. Inputs are normalized with StandardScaler to zero mean and unit variance and later denormalized for interpretation. The chosen sequence length is 24 hourly steps (one day) to align with the simulated daily hydrologic cycle.
supporting_quote: the PyTorch 2.0.1 library was used to implement the LSTM network
For model training, the Adam optimization algorithm is used
during training, the model uses the Mean Squared Error (MSE) as a loss function
The model considers a sequence length of 24

chunks.text: Hyperparameter optimization explored different numbers of LSTM layers, cells per layer, and epochs. The best configuration (Model 13) uses 60 layers with 36 cells per layer and 30 epochs, and was selected using validation metrics for both spigot flow and overflow. Statistical comparisons via t-tests are reported to support that Model 13 performed significantly better across metrics.
supporting_quote: Model 13, with 60 hidden layers of 36 LSTM cells each, trained for 30 epochs, proved to be the best
The test showed that the performance of model 13 is significantly better across all six metrics ... with p‐values <0.0001.

chunks.text: Synthetic datasets are generated from bucket networks to provide fully monitored training examples. The main experiment uses a training set of 350 networks (two buckets each) with 7,000 hourly records per bucket (~291.7 days). Validation and test sets each contain 204 networks with 1,500 hourly records per bucket (~62.5 days), enabling out-of-sample evaluation on networks not used for training.
supporting_quote: The training data set consists of 350 unique bucket networks, each composed of two buckets
Each bucket has 7,000 records, simulating hourly measurements over 291.7 days
The validation data set contains 204 networks ... each bucket has 1,500 records, simulating a period of 62.5 days
a test data set of the same size and structure as the validation data set

chunks.text: An additional extreme-flow experiment uses a larger synthetic training dataset to broaden the range of hydrologic behaviors. It trains on 2,000 bucket networks with 10,000 hourly records per bucket (~417 days), with broadened precipitation parameters to induce extremes. Evaluation uses three separate test sets (Normal, Low-Flow, High-Flow), each with 300 networks and 1,500 hourly records (~62.5 days).
supporting_quote: A new training data set was created with 2,000 synthetic bucket networks
containing 10,000 hourly records per bucket (approximately 417 days of simulation)
three additional test sets ... Each comprised 300 synthetic bucket networks ... with 1,500 hourly records (about 62.5 days of simulation)
Precipitation parameters were also broadened to incorporate extremes in flow generation.

chunks.text: Model inputs include simulated physical bucket parameters and meteorological forcings, and the observed combined downstream flow for the network.
