Outputs are per-bucket predictions of spigot flow and overflow, corresponding to baseflow-like and stormflow-like components in the bucket formulation. This setup is explicitly designed to emulate recovering tributary hydrographs from a downstream gauge record.
supporting_quote: Each input sequence comprises the simulated physical and meteorological features of each bucket (e.g., precipitation, infiltration, evapotranspiration), along with the network's combined downstream flow
the model subsequently outputs separate upstream flows per bucket
outputs produced by the model, including bucket flow (q_spigot), overflow (q_overflow)

chunks.text: The optimized LSTM achieved strong test performance on the synthetic dataset, with spigot flow errors and skill indicating close agreement with bucket-model truth. Reported test metrics for the optimized model are RMSE 0.144, MAE 0.109, and NSE 0.886 for spigot flow. For overflow, the model achieved RMSE 0.210, MAE 0.087, and NSE 0.961.
supporting_quote: The visual comparison ... demonstrates a close correspondence between the predicted and true values.

chunks.text: Including downstream flow observations in training (combined bucket network approach) improved upstream flow estimation compared to training each bucket independently. On the test set, spigot flow performance improved from RMSE 0.194 to 0.144 and NSE from 0.788 to 0.886. Overflow improved from RMSE 0.396 to 0.210 and NSE from 0.876 to 0.961, demonstrating the value of downstream constraints for disaggregation.

The combined approach yields substantial relative improvements over the individual bucket approach across metrics. Reported percentage improvements on the test set include 26.06% (RMSE) and 26.72% (MAE) for spigot flow, and 46.87% (RMSE) and 41.88% (MAE) for overflow. NSE improvements are also reported as 12.44% (spigot) and 9.75% (overflow).

Bucket-level comparisons across the test networks show the downstream-informed combined approach improves performance for most individual tributaries. The paper reports better performance for 89% of all buckets (408 total), including improved spigot flow in 326 cases (~80%). For overflow, improvement occurred in 100% of cases, suggesting downstream flow strongly constrains episodic overflow dynamics in this synthetic setting.
supporting_quote: across the 204 networks in the test data set (408 buckets total)
combined approach yielded better performance metrics for 89% of all buckets, including 326 cases (approximately 80%) with improved spigot flow predictions and 100% of the cases for overflow

chunks.text: Under extreme-flow evaluation using NSE, the combined approach outperformed the individual approach in Normal, Low-Flow, and High-Flow scenarios. Spigot flow NSE increased from 0.739 to 0.834 (Normal), 0.683 to 0.793 (Low), and 0.655 to 0.755 (High). Overflow NSE increased from 0.867 to 0.956 (Normal), 0.452 to 0.755 (Low), and 0.823 to 0.935 (High).

chunks.text: The Po River Basin (PRB) in northern Italy is the country’s largest watershed and is hydrologically complex, including snowmelt-driven mountainous headwaters, rainfall-dominated internal systems with low summer flows, and a sensitive delta ecosystem. The basin supports major societal and economic activities, including a large share of Italy’s population, energy production, and agricultural output. Because of these dependencies, drought impacts in the PRB can be widespread and severe.

chunks.text: The 2022 spring–summer drought in the PRB drew substantial public attention and was quantified in prior work using the ~200-year Pontelagoscuro streamflow record. Earlier analysis found that 2022 had the lowest recorded streamflow for several spring–summer windows including AMJJ. This sets the context for evaluating whether recent drought conditions are anomalous or part of longer-duration drought behavior.

chunks.text: Tree-ring based drought atlases provide long records of hydroclimate variability in Europe that can be used as proxies to reconstruct streamflow beyond the instrumental period. This study uses the Old World Drought Atlas (OWDA) self-calibrated Palmer Drought Severity Index (scPDSI) grid, which spans 0–2012 AD, as predictors for reconstructing PRB seasonal streamflow. Such proxies support comparisons between recent observed droughts and earlier centuries to millennia.

chunks.text: The study aims to test whether the 2022 drought is the culmination of a longer multi-decadal drought in the PRB and to determine how recent multi-year periods rank within the ~200-year observed record. It also seeks to reconstruct gauge-specific AMJJ streamflow at Pontelagoscuro using tree-ring proxy information, enabling a paleo perspective on the 21st-century drought. Finally, the research targets evaluation of deficit/surplus dynamics and the frequency of wet–dry “whiplash” transitions across paleo and historical periods.
supporting_quote: we investigated longer-duration drought periods ranging from 2 to 30 years in the ~200-year Pontelagoscuro gauge streamflow record.

chunks.text: A core goal is the introduction and demonstration of PALEO-RECON, an open-source automated reconstruction tool intended to modernize and speed regression-based paleohydrologic reconstructions using scPDSI proxies. The tool is designed to standardize cell selection, prescreening, model fitting, and skill evaluation so that the workflow is reproducible. The authors also position PALEO-RECON as a foundation for later comparisons with machine learning and deep learning approaches.

chunks.text: While 2022 was identified as the lowest single-year spring–summer flow in the observed record, a key unresolved issue is whether longer-duration droughts (2–30 years) show that recent decades represent an extreme multi-decadal drought regime. This matters for understanding if 2022 is an isolated anomaly or part of an intensifying drought pattern potentially linked to climate change. The study frames this as a ranking and attribution-style question within the observed record.

chunks.text: Existing PRB reconstructions provided a basin-wide regional estimate, but the paper argues that a gauge-specific reconstruction at Pontelagoscuro is needed to quantify drought severity and ranking more precisely at the key outlet gauge across both observed and paleo periods. Without a gauge-specific reconstruction, integrating the ~200-year instrumental record with multi-century to millennial context is more difficult. This motivates the study’s reconstruction approach.

chunks.text: The reconstruction uses forwards–backwards stepwise linear regression (SLR) with AMJJ streamflow as the predictand and OWDA scPDSI grid cells as predictors. Predictor cells are prescreened for positive significance at p ≤ 0.01 and then tested for temporal stability using moving correlations; cells showing negative correlations are treated as unstable and excluded. Model selection proceeds with alpha-to-enter 0.05 and alpha-to-remove 0.10, followed by evaluation of skill and diagnostics.

Reconstruction windows of 30, 40, and 50 years are evaluated within the 1807–2022 observed record, and multiple retained models are combined. Skill metrics include R² and predicted R² via leave-one-out (drop-one) cross-validation, which is described as more rigorous than split-sample validation. Diagnostics include VIF for multicollinearity, Durbin–Watson for autocorrelation, and a sign test comparing reconstructed and instrumental direction of change.

chunks.text: Reconstructed annual AMJJ flows are bias-corrected to reduce systematic discrepancies between reconstructed and observed distributions. PALEO-RECON implements a quantile-mapping approach (RQUANT) as the bias correction module. This step aims to align reconstruction outputs more closely with observed streamflow characteristics.

chunks.text: Drought/deficit and surplus periods are defined statistically using departures from the long-term average of the historical period (1807–2022). A deficit or surplus event requires two or more consecutive years below or above the mean. For each event, duration and magnitude are computed, with magnitude defined as the cumulative departure from the mean.
supporting_quote: These periods are identified when two or more consecutive years of deficit flow (below average flow) or surplus (above average flow) occur.
For both deficit and surplus periods, the duration and magnitude (defined as the cumulative of the departure from the average) are determined.

chunks.text: Whiplash is analyzed as abrupt switching between hydrologic states that not only reverses sign (wet to dry or dry to wet) but also overcomes the previously accumulated anomaly. The method builds accumulated deficits or surpluses by summing consecutive years and then flags whiplash when the next accumulated period exceeds what is needed to offset the prior one. This provides an event-based measure of rapid hydroclimate transitions.
supporting_quote: Weather (or water) whiplash is defined when the hydrologic state shifts suddenly to overcome an accumulated deficit (or surplus).
Whiplash occurs when the accumulated surplus (or deficit) for the next state is greater than the amount needed from the opposite state in the previous accumulated period.

chunks.text: PALEO-RECON operationalizes the reconstruction workflow from site and radius selection through model fitting and diagnostics. Users provide observed data, site coordinates, a search radius, and reconstruction window length; the tool then selects scPDSI cells, screens them, runs stepwise regression, evaluates models, maps selected cells, and applies bias correction. It is intended to generalize to other locations covered by OWDA (Europe) and LBDA (North America).

The modern period has the largest number of whiplash years, interpreted as potentially indicating enhanced climate extremes.
supporting_quote: The whiplash analysis... shows a trend toward an enhanced number of whiplash years... during the historical record compared with the paleo record.
Overall, the number of whiplash years in a century increased by 2.4 episodes (deficit to surplus) and 2.2 episodes (surplus to deficit)

chunks.text: PALEO-RECON was independently validated by replicating previously published “manual” reconstructions for the Sava River. The tool produced identical results to the manual method for the Catez gauge when applying the same workflow, as reported in supplementary materials. This demonstrates consistency and reliability of the automated implementation for European scPDSI-based reconstructions.
supporting_quote: The same analysis was conducted using PALEO-RECON, yielding results identical to those obtained with the "manual" method (see Supplementary Materials).
This independent validation demonstrates that PALEO-RECON is a reliable and effective tool for generating tree ring-based proxy (scPDSI) reconstructions in Europe.

chunks.text: Comparison of standardized filtered streamflow reconstructions across the PRB, Inn, and Danube indicates similar timing of the most severe drought periods across these watersheds. The early–mid-16th century and late–19th century drought periods visually align among all three series. Differences are more pronounced for pluvial periods, where the PRB shows extreme wet periods not seen in the Inn or Danube reconstructions.
supporting_quote: A visual inspection... indicated that the most severe drought periods (early–mid-16th century and late–19th century) were similar across all three watersheds.
The primary difference... involved pluvials (wet periods). The PRB displayed extreme wet periods... that were not observed in either the Inn or Danube reconstructions.

chunks.text: The authors emphasize that uncertainty grows as reconstructions extend further back in time, which affects interpretation of ancient extremes. They caution that this increasing uncertainty may influence identification and comparison of very early deficit/surplus events and whiplash trends. As a result, conclusions about the most ancient periods should be treated carefully even when notable events are detected.
supporting_quote: It is important to note that the uncertainty of paleo records increases considerably as we analyze earlier periods, which may impact the interpretation of extreme events in ancient times.
the further back we go in the paleo record, the greater the uncertainty becomes, making it essential to interpret ancient whiplash trends with caution.

chunks.text: The discussion notes that the analysis focuses only on the AMJJ season and a 23-year 2000–2022 window, and that other seasonal windows and filter lengths could be evaluated. The authors suspect similar findings would occur for other spring–summer months/seasons and for filters such as 5-, 10-, 15-, and 20-year. This indicates that the presented results may not capture the full range of drought behavior across seasons and timescales.
supporting_quote: The current research focused exclusively on the 23-year 2000 to 2022 period... and the April–May–June–July (AMJJ) season.

We suspect reconstructions of additional spring–summer months and seasons would yield similar findings... additional filters... (5-, 10-, 15-, and 20-year filters) would show that the end year 2022 was indeed a historical, decadal, and multidecadal drought period.

chunks.text: When comparing PRB drought variability to other European reconstructions, the authors acknowledge a mismatch in temporal aggregation: annual streamflow reconstructions for the Inn and Danube versus AMJJ seasonal flow for the PRB. They state this was the best available data and proceed with standardized comparisons. This limitation means cross-basin similarity assessments may be influenced by differences between annual and seasonal hydrologic signals.
supporting_quote: it is acknowledged that the comparison involved annual streamflow for the Inn and Danube Rivers and AMJJ streamflow for the PRB, this represented the best available data for analysis.

chunks.text: The study concludes that 2022 marks the end year of multiple multi-decadal AMJJ droughts in the observed record, and that 2000–2022 is the driest 23-year period in the ~200-year instrumental series. Using multiple skillful reconstructions to quantify uncertainty, the authors infer that the 2000–2022 drought is the most extreme in about ~500 years. They also conclude that whiplash events appear to be increasing and may be linked to changing climate dynamics.
supporting_quote: 2022 represented the end year of several multidecadal spring–summer (AMJJ) streamflow droughts
this 23-year period was the most extreme dry (drought) period in the ~200-year observed record.
revealing that the 23-year period, 2000 to 2022, drought was the most extreme drought in ~500 years.
The paleo-observed record revealed increasing whiplash events, which may be associated with a changing climate.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that PALEO-RECON standardizes and streamlines scPDSI-based reconstruction workflows and supports reproducible paleoclimatic studies in Europe and North America. It is presented as an efficient open-source tool validated against prior manual work, and as a platform that could later integrate machine learning and deep learning models. This software contribution is positioned as enabling broader adoption of rigorous reconstructions in other regions covered by drought atlases.
supporting_quote: we introduce PALEO-RECON, an automated tool that standardizes and streamlines the reconstruction process, facilitating reproducible paleoclimatic studies across Europe and North America.
PALEO-RECON... provided an efficient and time-saving open-source tool for generating reconstructions using tree ring-based proxies (self-calibrated Palmer Drought Severity Index (scPDSI)).
offers a scalable foundation that could integrate advanced machine learning and deep learning models in future research

chunks.text: Groundwater is a critical resource, but extracting and managing groundwater data is difficult because monitoring well time series often contain large gaps and sparse spatial coverage. Groundwater levels typically exhibit temporal autocorrelation (seasonal patterns plus long-term trends) and spatial correlation, where nearby or similarly used wells show related behavior. These attributes suggest that both time-based and spatial information can be leveraged to reconstruct missing observations and better characterize aquifer-scale change.
supporting_quote: time series datasets representing groundwater levels at wells to have large gaps of missing data.
groundwater levels are generally temporally autocorrelated, meaning that they follow seasonal patterns with a long-term trend
Groundwater is also spatially correlated, meaning that groundwater levels near an observation well tend to be similar

chunks.text: Remote sensing is limited for directly monitoring subsurface hydrology, and GRACE primarily captures total water storage at coarse spatial resolution, limiting use for small-to-medium aquifers and long historical analysis. This motivates alternative approaches, including machine learning, to characterize groundwater dynamics when in situ observations are incomplete. Prior work showed Earth observation regressions can impute missing well levels, often requiring well-specific models due to local conditions and operations.
supporting_quote: Remote sensing techniques that automate the monitoring of other environmental processes do not accurately work on subsurface hydrology
GRACE has a low spatial resolution (>150,000 km2 )
each well behaves individually because of the local environment and well operations. They showed that, for imputation, a model should be developed for each well

chunks.text: The authors’ earlier satellite-based imputation used meteorological features and inductive bias via a prior estimate to improve gap-filling over long missing periods. However, the prior is not ground truth and deviations from original training patterns can be lost or exaggerated, leading to anomalies. The present work builds on this by adding a refinement stage that uses information from neighboring wells to correct and strengthen aquifer-consistent signals.
supporting_quote: we extended the Evans et al. approach using an extended Self-Calibrated Dai Palmer Drought Severity Index Penmen–Monteith (PDSI) and NASA's Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) data as the meteorological features
seasonal trends or natural variations that deviate from the original training data could be lost or overrepresented.
the initial prior used to constrain the structure of the signal used was not ground truth

chunks.text: The paper aims to improve groundwater level imputation by introducing an iterative refinement model (IRM) that can operate on a complete aquifer dataset containing both measured and previously imputed values. The idea is to repeatedly “re-impute” each well using information from correlated nearby wells, while anchoring predictions to available in situ observations. The authors also aim to describe when IRM is useful and demonstrate its value on the Beryl-Enterprise aquifer case study.
supporting_quote: presents a method for improving imputation predictions through an iterative refinement model (IRM) approach that can work on any complete aquifer dataset that is a mixture of measured and imputed values;
revisited the data from every well in the aquifer and "re-imputed" the missing values
The paper concludes with a study of the Beryl-Enterprise region in Utah that demonstrates the validity of the method

chunks.text: A stated goal is to leverage spatial correlations among wells to correct artifacts from initial satellite-based imputation and produce refined time series suitable for aquifer-scale analyses. By updating all wells synchronously over multiple iterations, the method is intended to allow measured information at some wells to propagate through the network of correlated wells. The end objective is a cleaner, more physically plausible dataset for mapping and storage-change estimation.
supporting_quote: we improved our initial predictions by using the spatial correlation among the wells.
We repeated this process for a predetermined number of iterations—updating the well values synchronously.
To compare our imputation results with these published values, we performed a geospatial interpolation of the imputed well values in the aquifer at each time step

chunks.text: Historic groundwater characterization is hindered by sparse well measurements with large temporal gaps and often poor spatial coverage. Monitoring programs can be curtailed or sensors break, creating gaps that last from months to decades. Without sufficiently complete and synchronized well datasets, aquifer-level analyses and mapping approaches that depend on consistent time steps and dense coverage become difficult to apply reliably.
supporting_quote: data at individual wells were generally sparse, with missing data and large time gaps between measurements, often with poor spatial coverage.
gaps that can span from months to decades
For this approach to work, it was critical to have a complete dataset for the individual wells in the aquifer using the same time step with relatively dense spatial coverage

chunks.text: Initial well-specific imputation can produce unrealistic excursions over large gaps when training data are limited and correlations are extrapolated beyond observed conditions. These outliers can be tens to hundreds of feet over short periods, which is physically implausible for groundwater. If such anomalies are used as inputs for spatial refinement, they can propagate errors to neighboring wells during iterative modeling.
supporting_quote: the effect of extreme data on model predictions over large gaps resulting in outliers
data will have changes to tens to hundreds of feet in groundwater levels within a few months.
If these anomalous data are used in the IRM process to refine groundwater predictions at neighboring wells, the method propagates these anomalous trends to other wells.

chunks.text: The prior used to impose inductive bias in satellite-based imputation is an assumption rather than ground truth, and it can be incorrect in magnitude or structure. When the prior is wrong, it may flatten trends or overconstrain predicted ranges, especially for wells with long post-observation gaps. This motivates a refinement approach that can override prior-driven artifacts using correlated signals from other wells with measured data during the missing intervals.
supporting_quote: the initial prior used to constrain the structure of the signal used was not ground truth
The satellite imputation model assumed that the prior estimate could not exceed about 85 feet.
This is an instance where the priors used as features were incorrect, but the IRM improved the imputation based on its correlation with other wells in the aquifer.

chunks.text: The IRM workflow starts with preprocessing to align wells on a common time step and performing an initial imputation to produce complete time series for each well. IRM then runs for a chosen number of iterations, and at each iteration it applies an outlier-smoothing step, selects correlated neighboring wells as features, retrains a model per well, and replaces predicted values with in situ observations where available. Outputs are updated synchronously only at the end of each iteration, and the refined dataset is used as input to the next iteration.
supporting_quote: We began by generating a complete dataset using independent imputation models for each well; then, we improved our initial predictions by using the spatial correlation among the wells.
Select the number of iterations, n, to pass through the entire data set.
Replace any predictions that have an observed value with the in situ measurement. The results of every model are updated synchronously at the end of the iteration.

chunks.text: To prevent unrealistic spikes from contaminating refinement, the authors apply a Hampel filter before each IRM iteration to detect and replace imputed outliers using a rolling-window local median and MAD-based thresholding. They define the threshold as three times the scaled MAD, and replace only values exceeding that threshold with the local median. A 36-month window is used, and in situ observations are never replaced, preserving measured extremes while smoothing only predicted anomalies.
supporting_quote: Before each iteration step, apply this filter to remove outliers.
We used a Hampel filter to detect and remove outliers
To apply the Hampel filter, we used a window size of 36 months. We did not replace in situ observations with Hampel-filter smoothed values

chunks.text: Each well is modeled with the same MLP architecture: two hidden layers (50 and 100 nodes), L2 regularization, and 20% dropout. Optimization uses ADAM, and models are trained on measured data at the target well using 19–25 features comprising well features, one prior feature, and 13 temporal features. Because many wells have limited observations, performance is assessed with 5-fold cross-validation using sequential splits; the average epochs are then used to train a final model on all available data.
supporting_quote: a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) model with two hidden layers of widths of 50 and 100 nodes
20% dropout between the layers to prevent over-fitting
we used a K-fold cross-validation with 5 folds

chunks.text: Feature wells for a target well are selected using a combined similarity metric R_w^2 that mixes squared Pearson correlation (r^2) and normalized Euclidean distance (d), weighted by w_c. Correlation is computed using only dates where the target has measured data, while feature wells can contribute measured or imputed values on those dates. The authors tune w_c by aquifer size (about 0.90–0.95 for small aquifers and 0.70–0.80 for large aquifers) to balance local environment effects with correlation strength.
supporting_quote: We define R_w^2 as a combination of the Pearson correlation coefficient (r^2) and the normalized physical distance (d) between the target well and the feature well using a correlation weight (w_c)
We computed the r^2 value... using only measured data from the target well
a reasonable range for w_c was between 0.90 and 0.95 for small aquifers and 0.70–0.80 for large aquifers

chunks.text: The number of feature wells is adaptively chosen based on the average R_w^2 of the five best candidate wells, with more wells added when average correlation is low. The procedure begins with the top five wells by R_w^2, computes the mean over these five, and then adds one feature well for every 0.10 below a 0.60 threshold. This is operationalized in a table that maps ranges of average R_w^2 to feature counts (e.g., 6 wells for 0.5–0.6, up to 11 wells for 0.0–0.1).
supporting_quote: First, we selected the best five wells based on R_w^2
We recommend that if R̅_w^2 is below 0.60, an additional feature well should be added for every 0.10 below the 0.60 threshold

chunks.text: A single prior feature is generated per well using a data-centric prior algorithm: PCHIP interpolation within the observed time range and linear extrapolation beyond it. Extrapolation averages slopes from four regressions (using 10%, 25%, 50%, and 100% of data on each side), with outliers removed beyond three standard deviations, and limits extrapolated values to six standard deviations from the overall mean. For IRM, the prior estimate is smoothed with a 24-month centered moving window and used as one model feature to encode broad trends without dominating well-to-well relationships.
supporting_quote: we interpolated within the temporal data range using a piecewise cubic Hermite interpolating polynomial (PCHIP) interpolation
we calculated four linear regressions for each side of the data using 10%, 25%, 50%, and 100% of the data.
For the IRM model, we only generated one prior feature using a 24-month centered moving window

chunks.text: Temporal behavior is encoded with 13 time features: 12 one-hot indicators for month-of-year and one sequentially encoded time variable normalized to [0,1] called Decimal Time. One-hot encoding allows the model to learn distinct seasonal effects for each month without imposing an ordinal month relationship. Decimal Time provides an ordered feature to support modeling long-term linear trends alongside seasonal components.
supporting_quote: We used thirteen temporal features
Twelve of these features were created using one-hot-encoding
We normalized the sequence between 0 and 1 and called that value "Decimal Time"

chunks.text: The case study uses historical in situ groundwater levels for the Beryl-Enterprise aquifer in Utah, obtained from USGS NWIS. The aquifer is described as approximately 433 square miles (1121.4 sq. km) in Utah’s Escalante desert. Within the aquifer boundary, 751 wells existed, but only 57 wells had at least 50 observations in unique months over the imputation window.
supporting_quote: We used in situ groundwater level observation data from the National Water Information System (NWIS) published by the United States Geologic Survey (USGS)
The aquifer has an area of approximately 433 square miles (1121.4 sq. km)
Of the 751 possible wells within the geographic boundary of the aquifer, only 57 had at least 50 observations in unique months

chunks.text: The main imputation window spans January 1948 to December 2020, and data are resampled to monthly time steps. Measurements are converted from depth-to-groundwater to groundwater levels, and outliers larger than three standard deviations from the mean are removed. PCHIP interpolation is used to resample to the beginning of the month and fill small gaps shorter than 120 days (4 months), enabling synchronous alignment with Earth observation datasets and across wells for refinement.
supporting_quote: over the imputation window from January 1948 to December 2020.
converting the measurements from depth-to-groundwater to groundwater levels, then removed outlier values that were larger than three standard deviations from the mean
used PCHIP to resample the groundwater data to the beginning of the month and interpolated the data over small gaps of less than 120 days (4 months)

chunks.text: For storage-change validation, the study creates monthly groundwater level surfaces using kriging interpolation for each month between 1948 and 2020. The kriging setup uses a model variogram with nugget 0 and a range of 25% of the aquifer’s maximum length, with sill set to the variance for each month. Monthly storage change is computed by differencing successive surfaces and multiplying by a storage coefficient of 0.2.
supporting_quote: We used kriging interpolation to build a surface of the aquifer every month between 1948 and 2020
We used a model variogram with a nugget of 0 and a range of 25% for the maximum length of the aquifer; we set the variogram sill to the variance of the data
multiplying the volume by a storage coefficient of 0.2

chunks.text: Examples highlight varying observation densities across wells, including a well with 550 monthly observations between January 1948 and March 1999 (plus 75 observations before the window) and another with only 135 unique monthly observations between 1950 and 1963. These well-level differences create diverse imputation difficulty, from moderate gaps (e.g., about 20 years after 1999) to extreme gaps (e.g., 57 years after 1963). The paper uses these wells to illustrate IRM behavior under different data availability regimes.
supporting_quote: The well had 550 monthly observations between January 1948 and March 1999 and 75 observations before the imputation window
The last 20 years have no measured data.
which had 135 unique monthly observations between 1950 and 1963. This well had no data after 1963, which leaves a 57-year gap.

chunks.text: Across the aquifer, IRM refinement removes obvious excursions from the initial satellite imputation and produces time series that better align with expected groundwater behavior. After refinement, the authors identify at least three distinct well-pattern groups: high-elevation mountain-base wells, agricultural-area wells with large declines, and far-from-field wells with lower levels and more stationary behavior. The visual differences between iteration 1 and iteration 2 are small, suggesting convergence after limited iterations.
supporting_quote: there is a clear change from the satellite imputation results to the IRM results, as the obvious data excursions that occurred in some wells were removed
there are at least three distinct well patterns in this aquifer.
Figure 10 shows that there are only small changes between the results for iterations 1 and 2.

chunks.text: The refined results show that wells near agricultural fields experienced substantial long-term declines, reaching as much as about 150 feet over the imputation window. In contrast, wells far from fields and away from mountains show lower groundwater levels but lack the same long-term decline. The elevation and behavior separation between mountain-base wells and other wells is interpreted as potential evidence for multiple aquifers, despite USGS assigning wells to a single aquifer.
supporting_quote: the wells are located near the agricultural fields, and the data shows that groundwater levels in these wells dropped up to 150 feet over the imputation window.
These wells have a lower groundwater level but did not exhibit a long-term decline in the group we assigned to agriculture.
could indicate that there are two aquifers here, though the USGS assigns all these wells to a single aquifer.

chunks.text: The authors report that two IRM iterations are generally sufficient: the first pass tends to remove noise and correct trends from satellite imputation, while the second strengthens spatial trends not captured in the first pass. Additional iterations often provide marginal improvement and can sometimes degrade results via feedback loops that swap patterns among subsets of wells. This finding motivates keeping the iteration count low for stability.
supporting_quote: We found that two iterations were generally sufficient to obtain good results.
The first iteration essentially removed any noise and corrected trends from satellite imputation, and the second iteration strengthened spatial trends
Using more iterations can also cause feedback loops where a particular pattern is swapped between a subset of wells for each iteration.

chunks.text: For well 373457113423801, the last roughly 20 years lack measured data, and satellite imputation suggested steady levels with seasonal variation. IRM refinement introduced a declining trend with rebounds around 2008 and 2011 that matches common features seen across multiple wells in the aquifer. Although fold-averaged RMSE increased and r2 decreased due to one poorly modeled fold, the authors argue the refined series is qualitatively more consistent with aquifer-wide behavior.
supporting_quote: The last 20 years have no measured data.
a trend appeared in the data where groundwater levels generally decreased with rebounds in 2008 and 2011.
The IRM shows an increase in RMSE and a decrease in r2 compared to satellite imputation.

chunks.text: For well 374504113370201, which has a 57-year post-1963 gap, satellite imputation produced a decreasing trend that flattened after hitting the prior-feature limit around 1972 and included large anomalies from 1993 to 2008. IRM continued the downward trend beyond the prior constraints, indicating the prior was too restrictive. The groundwater level range differed markedly between methods (about 5090–5135 ft for satellite vs about 5050–5135 ft for IRM), and the paper reports that RMSE and r2 improved considerably with IRM.
supporting_quote: This well had no data after 1963, which leaves a 57-year gap.
results demonstrate a long-term decreasing trend until the imputed results reached the limit placed on the prior features around 1972, after which the curve then flattens.
There is a significant difference in the range of groundwater levels between the satellite imputation (5090-5135 ft) method and iterative refinement (5050-5135 ft).

chunks.text: For well 373446113431102, the measured record is sparse and split into two short periods (1955–1961 and 1976–1978), making independent imputation difficult. Satellite imputation was broadly reasonable but generated unreasonably high excursions. IRM used correlated wells to generate more reasonable imputed behavior, transferring aquifer-consistent structure to the target well even with minimal direct observational context.
supporting_quote: had 110 observations; 79 occurred between April 1955 and October 1961, with 31 observations between April 1976 and October 1978.
the satellite imputation created several excursions that were unreasonably high.
After two iterations, the general structure shown in other feature wells was transferred to this well

chunks.text: Aquifer-scale validation via storage-change analysis produced depletion estimates consistent with prior published work. Using IRM-imputed surfaces and a storage coefficient of 0.2, the aquifer is estimated to have lost about 1.21 million acre-feet between 1948 and 1978. Over the full 70-year window, the cumulative loss is estimated at over 2.87 million acre-feet (1.49 km³), indicating steady decline and an increasing depletion rate in recent years.
supporting_quote: a storage coefficient of 0.2
groundwater storage was reduced by approximately 1.21 million acre-feet between 1948 and 1978.
Over the 70-year window, the aquifer lost over 2.87 million acre-feet of storage (1.49 km3)

chunks.text: The paper identifies three imputation situations that affect confidence in IRM results. Case I is best: target and feature wells overlap in measured periods and the feature well has measured data during target gaps, enabling reliable signal transfer. Case II is common and benefits most from IRM: overlap is partial and correlation may be supported by previous imputations, but the feature well has measured data inside target gaps. Case III is hardest: feature wells provide only imputed values during target gaps, making refinement rely on guesses rather than new measurements.
supporting_quote: there are three general cases that occur that can have significant effects on the accuracy of the imputation results and our confidence in the imputation (Table 3)
Imputation Case I is the best-case scenario for iterative refinement.
Imputation Case III is when the feature well and the imputation well only have measured values in their overlapping time range

chunks.text: IRM performance depends on the quality of the initial complete dataset and data cleanliness; if initial imputation is poor, iterative refinement can become a negative feedback loop and diverge. The authors emphasize that strong initial imputation with good priors is crucial for identifying correlated wells and stabilizing refinement. Satellite imputation provides independent estimates that, while imperfect, can be sufficiently informative for IRM to work effectively.
supporting_quote: Generally, if the initial imputation results are poor, iterative refinement acts as a negative feedback loop, and results may diverge.
Having a strong initial imputation with a good prior, as is conducted in the satellite imputation method [22], is crucial
Though the satellite imputation is imperfect, it produces independent results that are good enough for iterative refinement to work.

chunks.text: Using too many IRM iterations can introduce instability through feedback loops where patterns are repeatedly exchanged among wells, potentially degrading results. Because signals change during iteration and aquifers can contain many wells, tracking and diagnosing such feedback becomes difficult. The authors report improvements beyond two iterations are often marginal and sometimes worse, implying a practical limit on iteration count.
supporting_quote: improvements, if any, were marginal, sometimes even producing poorer results.
Using more iterations can also cause feedback loops where a particular pattern is swapped between a subset of wells for each iteration.
Because the resulting signal is changing, this problem is difficult to track when the numbers of wells become large.

chunks.text: Case III represents a common monitoring limitation: when feature wells also lack measured data during the target gap, the model is trained on ground-truth overlap but must predict using noisy imputed inputs. In such settings, IRM may converge multiple wells toward similar trends, but quality is difficult to assess due to limited measured data for comparison. Edge cases where no feature well has new measured information in gaps may yield no improvement or even negative feedback behavior.
supporting_quote: This is the most difficult case to obtain reliable results from and, unfortunately, is common due to limited aquifer monitoring.
the predictions may be inaccurate as the inputs used for prediction are noisy variations of the independent features on which the model was built.
In this case, there is no new information, so the IRM either does not improve the previous estimates or could become caught in a negative feedback loop with different results.

chunks.text: The study concludes that iterative refinement (IRM) can refine imputed groundwater time series by exploiting spatial correlations among wells in a complete dataset containing measured and imputed values. Applied to the Beryl-Enterprise aquifer, IRM produced more physically plausible series, reduced anomalous excursions, and enabled aquifer-scale analyses like storage depletion estimation. The authors suggest IRM can be used broadly wherever sufficient groundwater observations exist, and it can be paired with any initial imputation method.
supporting_quote: we developed the IRM data imputation refinement approach for the use of spatial correlations that could improve data imputation.
The IRM method demonstrated accurate results for the Beryl-Enterprise aquifer in Utah, where many wells were missing large periods of observations.
Though we only showed IRM when applied to Beryl-Enterprise, it can be used globally if sufficient groundwater observations exist.

chunks.text: IRM in conjunction with satellite-based imputation is presented as a way to gain insight into aquifer behavior even when individual wells have limited or no observations over long periods. By assuming wells in similar environments and pumping regimes exhibit similar changes, the method allows partial measured records from multiple locations to inform missing segments elsewhere. The authors highlight that the refined analysis revealed agricultural drawdown and long-term drying and suggested the possibility of overlapping aquifers not previously recognized.
supporting_quote: Using IRM in conjunction with satellite-based imputation provides valuable insights into aquifer behavior, even when limited or no data are available at individual wells.
This is based on the idea that wells in the same aquifer experiencing a similar environment (i.e., climate and pumping patterns) exhibit similar changes.
revealed the possibility of two overlapping aquifers not previously recognized.

chunks.text: Climate change is increasing the severity and frequency of flooding and other water-related hazards, making resilience planning a growing priority for US communities. Resilience planning aims to maintain critical services after disasters and reduce compounding future impacts. Because these plans require diverse climate and hydrologic information, communities can benefit from science-based tools and resources that translate data into usable decision support.
supporting_quote: Climate change is causing an increase in the frequency and severity of flood events and other water related hazards.

Resilience planning generally aims to achieve two goals: (1) ensuring that communities have access to critical services and needs following a disaster, and (2) mitigating the probability of communities suffering impacts from future disasters

chunks.text: Climate services are intended to provide scientifically grounded information products (historical patterns, forecasts, scenarios) that improve understanding and decisions. Despite their potential to help at-risk communities manage climate variability and reduce harm, climate services are often underutilized. Improving utilization requires better communication of value and fit with real decision contexts.
supporting_quote: These climate services provide information and products with a scientific foundation with the intent to improve the public's awareness and comprehension
While there is clearly practical value associated with predicting when and where water will be, climate services such as the NWM are generally underutilized

chunks.text: NOAA’s National Water Model (NWM) is a continental-scale hydrologic modeling framework that tracks and predicts key variables such as precipitation, snowmelt, soil moisture, and streamflow. It provides guidance across multiple forecast horizons (analysis/assimilation, short-, medium-, long-range) and offers broad spatial coverage. By producing stream outflow for 2.7 million reaches and complementing traditional forecast points, it can add information for underserved locations.
supporting_quote: The National Water Model is a mathematical modeling framework of water and weather cycles that tracks and predicts changes in precipitation, snowmelt, near-surface soil moisture, streamflow, and evapotranspiration across the continental US
in the continental United States configuration provides stream outflow results for 2.7 million river reaches.

chunks.text: The study sought to understand how NOAA’s National Water Model could be applied in community resilience planning and what prevents wider adoption. Using engagement with seven diverse US communities and NOAA/NWC staff, the project aimed to identify practical use cases and co-develop actions that would facilitate broader use of NWM data and visualization services by municipal and regional planners.
supporting_quote: From 2021 to 2023, seven geographically diverse US communities agreed to participate in a study to understand how the NWM might be applied in resilience planning.
This research yielded a set of recommendations, co-developed between the seven communities and NWC/ NOAA staff, for how these barriers could be overcome

chunks.text: A broader goal was to generate insights that extend beyond the NWM to climate services development more generally. The authors aimed to extract lessons about awareness, accessibility, and desired capabilities that could inform how other climate services are designed for resilience-related planning contexts, particularly across near-, medium-, and long-term time frames.
supporting_quote: developing insights that can be generalized to other climate services being developed for use in the resilience-related planning context.
identified actions to overcome the barriers to its use among municipal and regional resilience planners

chunks.text: The authors identify that community end-users are often not engaged in ways that lead to sustained adoption of climate-service tools like the NWM. Even when climate services are used, they may be applied incorrectly or not as intended. This gap motivates a bottom-up, co-development approach that directly involves developers and end-users to align tools with decision processes.
supporting_quote: community end-users were not being effectively engaged in ways that result in widespread tool use and adoption.
Even when climate services are used, communities frequently apply them incorrectly or in ways that are not as intended by their developers

chunks.text: Low awareness of the NWM among resilience stakeholders is a major barrier to uptake. In this study, most community interviewees had never heard of the model prior to participation. This limits the model’s ability to support planning, even when its capabilities could address recognized information gaps.
supporting_quote: most of the interviewees (60%) had never heard of the NWM prior to engaging with this study.
Since over 60% of the community stakeholders had never heard of the NWM

chunks.text: Resilience planning involves many practitioners who are not trained hydrologists, creating accessibility challenges for technical tools. Most stakeholders reported either no experience with hydrologic models or only experience using model outputs rather than running models. This implies that tool design and communication targeted primarily to specialists will miss key intended users in planning organizations.
supporting_quote: only 32% of the interviewees reported having experience running or working with hydrologic models themselves
the majority either reported no experience (23%) or only experience working with model output but not running/working with hydrologic models themselves (45%)

chunks.text: Stakeholders often prefer local hydrologic models over a national model due to perceptions of higher accuracy, calibration to local conditions, and stronger trust in known providers. This preference can create inertia against adopting the NWM, especially where communities already invested in locally informed tools and processes. The NWM must therefore show clear differentiation or complementary value to compete with established local practices.
supporting_quote: if they were given a choice between having access to a local water model and the NWM, they would prefer the local model.
The preference for a local water model stemmed from a perception of higher local accuracy and trust with the model.

chunks.text: The project used a community-engaged design consisting of four activities: interviews, community collaborative sessions, analysis, and participant validation. Interviews and sessions were conducted remotely, engaging community resilience stakeholders alongside NOAA/NWC staff. Collaborative sessions included an educational component and facilitated co-learning to produce actionable recommendations for NWM use and for NWC support.
supporting_quote: The methodology involved the research team undertaking a series of four activities: (1) conducting online interviews... (2) organizing and facilitating collaborative sessions... (3) completing an analysis... and (4) inviting each study participant to react
Once the community interviews were completed, a collaborative session for each community was held remotely via Zoom.

chunks.text: Seven communities were selected using criteria focused on resilience planning capacity, geographic diversity, recent experience of water-related hazards, and existing relationships enabling engagement. The selection strategy intentionally varied geographic, topographic, governance, and hazard contexts. This was designed to reflect a range of potential NWM end-users and improve transferability of lessons.
supporting_quote: selected against the following criteria: (1) they have engaged in resilience, adaptation, or climate planning... (2) each community is geographically diverse... and has experienced a water-related hazard within the past 5years
The geographic, topographic, water governance, and water hazard diversity of the seven communities was intentionally aimed to better represent the range of potential end-users

chunks.text: Stakeholders were recruited by identifying roles from public websites (e.g., planners, floodplain managers, engineers, GIS specialists) and using snowball sampling during interviews. Interviews were conducted via Zoom from February 2022 through June 2023 and covered resilience planning practices, information needs, experience with hydrologic modeling and the NWM, and ideas for NWM integration and NWC support.
supporting_quote: Target participants were initially identified from a search of public facing websites in roles such as city planners, floodplain managers, academics, engineers, and GIS specialists
All interviews were conducted remotely via Zoom between February 2022 through June 2023.

chunks.text: Analysis combined a qualitative content analysis to identify and quantify themes with a thematic analysis to generate recommendations. Codebooks were used to structure both analyses, and recommendations were synthesized by rephrasing coded statements while preserving intent. Recommendations were organized into community-directed use cases and NWC-directed actions (awareness, accessibility, and requested capabilities).
supporting_quote: The interview and collaborative session data were analyzed in two ways: (1) a qualitative content analysis to identify and quantify key themes, and (2) a purely qualitative thematic analysis to identify recommendations
the raw coded interview data was rephrased by the research team to form a recommendation or articulated need, while preserving the original intent of the interviewee.

chunks.text: To validate findings, participants received aggregated community-level summaries after collaborative sessions and were given two weeks to provide corrections or feedback. The team incorporated revisions based on participant responses. After this process, the results were treated as validated for each community.
supporting_quote: each participant received an aggregate, community-level summary of their community-specific results and then were asked to provide feedback within two-weeks.
After the twoweeks had passed and the feedback had been taken into account, the results from the study were considered "validated."

chunks.text: The dataset comprised remote interviews and collaborative session inputs from seven communities and NOAA/NWC staff. There were 95 community interviewees across the seven communities and 14 NOAA/NWC staff interviewees. Community response rates varied substantially, affecting strength of inference for some locations.
supporting_quote: There were 95 interviewees across a total of seven communities with an overall response rate of 28%.
The NOAA/NWC interviewees had an overall response rate of 56% (14 interviewees).

chunks.text: Charlotte had the lowest community response rate, limiting the robustness of community-specific interpretation compared with other sites. The paper notes that Charlotte results are still reported but should not be used for strong conclusions. This variability is an important characteristic of the study’s empirical base.
supporting_quote: Charlotte (6 interviewees) only had a response rate of 9%.
Due to Charlotte's low response rate, results for this community will be presented... but strong conclusions cannot be drawn.

chunks.text: Interviewees reported a set of direct and indirect water-related hazards, with flooding dominant across sites. Across communities, directly water-related hazards included flooding, water quality, water quantity, drought, erosion, landslides, and tsunamis; indirect hazards included earthquakes and wildfires due to downstream impacts on debris flow or infrastructure. The study quantified hazard mentions by percent of interviewees.
supporting_quote: there were seven directly waterrelated hazards... flooding (91% of interviewees), water quality (42%), water quantity (19%), drought (29%), erosion (29%), landslides (14%), and tsunamis (4%).
there were two indirect water-related hazards: earthquakes (8%), and wildfires (13%).

chunks.text: The study measured stakeholder experience with hydrologic modeling and familiarity with the NWM. Only about a third had experience running hydrologic models, and a majority had not heard of the NWM. These quantified indicators were used to assess accessibility needs and likely adoption barriers.
supporting_quote: only 32% of the interviewees reported having experience running or working with hydrologic models themselves
most of the interviewees (60%) had never heard of the NWM prior to engaging with this study.

chunks.text: Participants reported prioritized information needs that constrain resilience-related planning. The most common needs included better water-related modeling, climate change/future conditions, education/outreach resources, flood prediction, and flood-related mapping. The paper summarizes these needs across communities with counts and percentages.
supporting_quote: The top five water-related vulnerability information needs reported by the communities were: (1) better water-related modeling (42% of interviewees), (2) better information on climate change/future conditions (40%), (3) information/resources to better conduct education and outreach (41%), (4) better flood prediction information (31%), and (5) better mapping (specifically, flood-related mapping, 29%).
TABLE 3 A summary of the most common data/information needs in community resilience-related planning.

chunks.text: Flooding was nearly universal across interviewees and appeared as the top water-related hazard in every community. The study also documented other frequent concerns such as water quality, drought, and erosion, along with region-specific issues like wildfires in Boulder and earthquake/tsunami concerns in Portland. These hazard profiles framed how communities evaluated potential NWM applications.
supporting_quote: Across these communities... flooding (91% of interviewees), water quality (42%), water quantity (19%), drought (29%), erosion (29%), landslides (14%), and tsunamis (4%).
Examples of regional differences include a heightened wildfire concern in Boulder (50% of interviewees), and earthquake concern (44%) and tsunami (25%) concern in Portland.

chunks.text: Resilience planning was usually embedded across multiple plans rather than done as a standalone resilience plan. Hazard Mitigation Plans were common in all communities, and planning was often driven by project identification, prioritization, and eligibility for funding. Interviewees also highlighted constraints such as limited staff capacity, regulatory requirements, political will, community acceptance, and cost/benefit considerations.
supporting_quote: most pointed out that resilience was incorporated as a part of multiple planning efforts as opposed to preparing a dedicated resilience plan. Hazard Mitigation Plans (state, county, and local level) were highlighted across all communities.
Their planning is also about prioritizing projects and pursuing funding opportunities (74% prioritization, 60% funding).

chunks.text: The stakeholder landscape for resilience planning was highly diverse, extending beyond traditional hydrology roles. Interviewees included hazard mitigation planners, floodplain and emergency managers, consultants, academics, utility professionals, dam operators, hydrologists, and conservation districts. This diversity implies that climate services must be usable by practitioners with varying technical backgrounds and responsibilities.
supporting_quote: Those self-identified in the resilience-related planning landscape included hazard mitigation planners, floodplain managers, emergency managers, consultants... academics, water utility professionals, water quality experts, dam operators, hydrologists, and conservation districts.
This revealed a considerable diversity of individuals involved in resilience planning.

chunks.text: Awareness of the NWM was low among community stakeholders, while prior hands-on use was rare. The majority had never heard of the model, about a third had heard of it but not used it, and only a small minority reported prior experience. This finding directly motivated recommendations focused on awareness-building and training.
supporting_quote: most of the interviewees (60%) had never heard of the NWM prior to engaging with this study.
Only 6% (6 individuals) of the interviewees reported prior experience with the NWM and 34% of the interviewees reported having heard of the NWM before, but they had not used it.

chunks.text: Communities articulated major information needs that map onto potential NWM contributions, especially around modeling, flood prediction, and future climate conditions. Education and outreach needs were also prominent, reflecting challenges in communicating risk to the public and decision makers. The study’s synthesized needs provide targets for climate service enhancements and support materials.
supporting_quote: better water-related modeling (42% of interviewees)
information/resources to better conduct education and outreach (41%)

chunks.text: Stakeholders reported a general preference for local models over the NWM, primarily due to perceptions of better local accuracy and trust. However, they also recognized benefits of the NWM, including continual updates, free access, and its ability to fill gaps where no local models exist. This positions the NWM as a complementary tool rather than a replacement for local modeling systems.
supporting_quote: if they were given a choice between having access to a local water model and the NWM, they would prefer the local model.
the NWM is beneficial in that its use is free for communities and can fill in some data needs where currently none exist

chunks.text: The study synthesized community-directed use cases for integrating the NWM into resilience-related planning. Common categories across communities included emergency management, large basin/regional planning, scenario planning, preliminary assessments to target limited resources, filling information gaps, hindcast analysis, use as an additional data point, and as a convening/education tool. These use cases were also identified by NOAA/NWC staff, indicating shared views on near-term applicability.
supporting_quote: Key potential use cases... Emergency management (7/7+NOAA)

There was consistency between the recommendations that the communities had... and the ideas generated by NOAA/NWC staff; i.e., every hypothetical use case category identified by the communities was also identified by NOAA/NWC staff.

chunks.text: Recommendations for NOAA/NWC support clustered into awareness, accessibility, and requested capabilities. Awareness actions emphasized leveraging networks and partnerships, presenting at relevant venues, and using personal connections or local champions. Accessibility recommendations emphasized training, case studies, audience-tailored communication, tool differentiation, and improved visualizations to support non-specialist end-users.
supporting_quote: The recommendations for how the NWC could better facilitate the use of the NWM... fell into three broad areas: awareness, accessibility, and requested capabilities.
building awareness came down to communication strategies... identifying trusted connections or local champions

chunks.text: The authors note that the participating communities were selected for strong planning capacity, which may limit generalization to smaller or more rural communities that struggle to engage in resilience planning. They explicitly identify this as a need for future investigation. This constraint matters because tool accessibility and adoption barriers may differ substantially in low-capacity settings.
supporting_quote: The communities engaged in this study were intentionally selected for their capacity to engage in planning.
many smaller or more rural communities struggle to engage in resilience planning efforts.

chunks.text: The study emphasizes community engagement and use cases but does not explicitly address seasonality, uncertainty, or decision timing in relation to NWM forecasts. The authors argue these temporal factors affect usability and could lead to unintended or incorrect applications if not addressed. They propose future work to move from first-order questions about use to more contextual second-order questions about what makes information usable.
supporting_quote: it does not explicitly address the temporal and seasonal dimensions of resilience decisions or the uncertainties present in the models forecasts.
it is imperative to recognize the current limitations related to the NWM.

chunks.text: The paper highlights that NWM performance varies by geography, creating spatially heterogeneous uncertainty that influences decision value. This means that uncertainty is not only temporal (forecast horizon) but also spatial (where the model performs better or worse). The authors argue that acknowledging these factors is important to align the model with end-user needs and reduce misuse.
supporting_quote: the present version of the NWM... is known to perform better in certain geographies than in others.
not only is there a temporal aspect to the uncertainty associated with the NWM, but there is also a spatial aspect to the uncertainty.

chunks.text: Community-specific inference was uneven because response rates differed, especially the very low response rate in Charlotte. The paper cautions that, while Charlotte results are included, strong conclusions should not be drawn for that site. This limits comparative community-level interpretation within the seven-case design.
supporting_quote: Charlotte (6 interviewees) only had a response rate of 9%.
Due to Charlotte's low response rate... strong conclusions cannot be drawn.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that community engagement is essential for climate service developers to increase awareness, adoption, and improvement of tools like the NWM. It argues that engaging end-users can build trust, reveal practical applications, and surface new feature requests that developers may not anticipate. This supports a broader shift toward co-development to make climate services actionable for place-based decision support.
supporting_quote: Results from this study highlighted the importance of community engagement in the climate service space in three ways: (1) It can help to increase the awareness... (2) It can help increase the adoption... and (3) It can help improve the tool or service.
This study showed how community engagement can play an invaluable role in improving a climate service.

chunks.text: A key conclusion is that climate services should be made accessible to a wider range of resilience stakeholders beyond hydrologic specialists. The study found that many likely users are planners and other non-technical staff, and that communications and interfaces should be tailored to these audiences. Co-production with end-users can increase legitimacy and reduce inefficient or contradictory implementation.
supporting_quote: the wider audience of potential end-users in the resilience planning space than is often understood by the developers of climate tools and models.
"it [the NWM and its communications] looks like it was designed for water resources engineers, but the people who would use it are planners, city staff, etc. who use different terms."

chunks.text: The authors conclude that resilience planning spans multiple time horizons and that climate services need to support near-, medium-, and long-term planning, including future conditions. Although the NWM currently forecasts up to 30 days, it can still support shorter-timescale components of resilience planning such as prioritization, response planning, and identifying hotspots. They argue that a broader suite of tools is needed to cover longer-range timescales and their interactions.
supporting_quote: Climate services should also be capable of supporting the multiple timescales associated with resilience planning.
While the NWM has only a 30-day forecasting ability, interviewees identified that it can still support future-oriented resilience planning.

chunks.text: The paper frames integrated modeling as connecting models from different knowledge and sectoral domains to exchange information and represent feedbacks across a broader system. It argues that integrated models of social-ecological systems have historically been biased toward biophysical processes, with slower progress on integrating human and policy dimensions. The authors situate this within broader movements such as convergence research and transdisciplinary scholarship, emphasizing that integration should preserve the integrity of distinct knowledge systems rather than dissolving them.
supporting_quote: Integrated modeling is a process by which models of different but related systems, originating from different knowledge and sectoral domains, are connected to enable the exchange of knowledge and the representation of feedback mechanisms across a larger, more inclusive system.
the interdisciplinary links in integrated models of social‐ecological systems have arguably been biased toward biophysical processes
The goal of integration is not merely to dissolve knowledge systems into a modeling process, but rather to uphold and preserve their integrity

chunks.text: The authors advocate a shift in modeling philosophy from prescriptive, assumption-driven prediction toward exploratory modeling used to diagnose systems, test hypotheses, and surface new questions. In this view, integrated modeling is meant to navigate complexity and uncertainty in human-water systems by enabling cross-disciplinary adaptation of component models. This perspective is presented as an inversion of reductionism, emphasizing discovery and learning rather than producing a single “answer.”
supporting_quote: Integrated modeling moves away from the conventional, rather "prescriptive," approach to modeling ... to a more "explorative" approach.
we aim to shift our focus from using models to assert "answers," to using models as a means to explore "questions," diagnose systems
This shift is at the heart of the philosophy of exploratory modeling

chunks.text: A key conceptual distinction is drawn between warranted “systems complexity” and unjustified “computational complexity.” The paper argues that simply increasing resolution, numerics, or solver sophistication may not capture the interdependencies and feedbacks that matter for human-water systems. Instead, integrated modeling should be guided by careful consideration of scaling, nonlinear dynamics, thresholds, hysteresis, time lags, and legacy effects.
supporting_quote: investigating what constitutes warranted "systems complexity," as opposed to unjustified "computational complexity"
with careful attention to interdependencies and feedbacks, scaling issues, nonlinear dynamics and thresholds, hysteresis, time lags, and legacy effects.

chunks.text: The paper’s goal is to synthesize insights from diverse disciplines and stakeholders to identify persistent challenges and propose perspectives on the future of integrated modeling for human-water systems. It aims to push beyond standard framings of water problems by incorporating cross-boundary disciplines and diverse worldviews, including Indigenous knowledge. The authors also intend the paper to support concrete decisions in integrated modeling, such as selecting modeled components, choosing fidelity, interfacing models, handling uncertainty, and engaging societal actors.
supporting_quote: we seek to identify persistent challenges and offer a perspective on the future of integrated modeling of human‐water systems.
extend the frontiers to include contemporary, cross‐boundary disciplines and diverse worldviews.
we hope this paper helps readers when pondering the following decisions in the process of integrated modeling of human‐ water systems:

chunks.text: The authors propose that integrated modeling can help scope otherwise unbounded integration efforts by focusing on three guiding questions: modeling purpose, boundary judgment, and critical uncertainties. These questions are positioned as a way to keep integration relevant and defensible, while still enabling inclusive representation of natural and human processes. The intent is to improve how teams deliberate early and repeatedly about what to include, why, and what uncertainties most affect outcomes.
supporting_quote: integrated modeling can provide a focused approach to delineating the scope of integration, through the lens of three fundamental questions:
(a) What is the modeling "purpose"? (b) What constitutes a sound "boundary judgment"? and (c) What are the "critical uncertainties"

chunks.text: The paper argues that the move from rhetoric about convergence to actual implementation is obstructed by misalignments in semantics, methodologies, and discourse among disciplines and societal actors. Integrated modeling is therefore challenging not just technically but socially and epistemologically. The authors stress that these barriers are amplified in human-water systems because water is simultaneously physical, cultural, social, and spiritual, and because water systems are coupled to other sectors like energy, food, transport, and the economy.
supporting_quote: the transition from rhetoric to actual implementation is impeded by incongruence in semantics, methodologies, and discourse among disciplinary scientists and societal actors.
water is multidimensional in nature and are best understood not solely as a physical resource, but also as a cultural, social, and spiritual entity
water systems inherently interact with systems from other domains, such as energy, food, transportation, and the economy

chunks.text: The authors highlight a persistent risk that unclear modeling purpose can lead to misplaced effort, including an implicit drive toward a “model of everything.” They argue that such ambitions are usually infeasible due to limits in knowledge, data, and computation. Without an explicit purpose, models may be calibrated to appear acceptable while failing to represent the processes needed for diagnosis or scenario analysis.
supporting_quote: the modeling purpose must always be defined and articulated up front
the commonly‐implicit aspiration of developing a "model of everything" ... which is typically unachievable due to current limitations in knowledge, data, and computational resources.

chunks.text: Boundary judgment—deciding what is inside versus outside the model—is presented as a central obstacle to meaningful convergence. Poor boundary judgment can exclude pressing or controversial components (e.g., water rights) and create unintended consequences even if short-term predictive accuracy appears adequate. The paper emphasizes that boundary setting is not merely technical but ethical, and can be influenced by those who commission and use models.
supporting_quote: Boundary judgment relates to what is to be mathematically represented as relevant components within a model, that is, the assumptions about what is inside versus outside the model.
a poor boundary judgment in integrated water resources management, can result in the exclusion of the most pressing and controversial aspects of water rights
"the setting of model boundaries is not merely a technical issue—it is an ethical one"

chunks.text: The paper argues that uncertainty treatment becomes particularly difficult in integrated models because disciplines conceptualize uncertainty differently and because epistemic uncertainty may dominate. Probabilistic frameworks can become infeasible when uncertainty is high-dimensional and compounded, risking an “uncertainty explosion” that makes results unusable. This motivates approaches that identify which uncertainties matter most for a given purpose and boundary judgment.
supporting_quote: uncertainty and randomness may be perceived differently across disciplines and political contexts, rendering reconciliation within a single probabilistic framework infeasible.
there is the risk of an "uncertainty explosion" when attempting to account for all possible sources of uncertainty probabilistically.
the range of uncertainty can increase significantly, sometimes exponentially, due to compounding, cascading, or interaction effects

chunks.text: In hydrology–water management integration, the paper identifies a specific problem: hydrology-land surface models can be calibrated to regulated streamflow even with inaccurate or missing water management representations. This can occur because parameters like soil storage can be tuned to mimic reservoir store-and-release effects, producing superficially acceptable performance. The authors argue this reinforces the need to move beyond curve-fitting and toward system understanding aligned to modern societal questions.
supporting_quote: an H‐LSM with inaccurate—or even no—representation of water management can still be calibrated to data from a regulated watershed and yield what hydrologists might deem "acceptable" performance
model parameters associated with soil storage capacity can also be manipulated to represent (at least partially) the controlled store‐and‐release mechanisms of reservoirs.
it is now essential to shift attention from viewing modeling as a curve‐fitting exercise

chunks.text: The paper proposes a scoping framework built around three overarching questions to guide integrated modeling: purpose, boundary judgment, and critical uncertainties. It further classifies modeling purposes into nowcasting/forecasting, scenario analysis, and diagnostic learning, arguing that these purposes imply different requirements for process representation and human behavior modeling. The framework is meant to be revisited iteratively as integration progresses and new questions emerge.
supporting_quote: three fundamental questions ... Why do we model? What is a sound "boundary judgment" for a given purpose? What are the "critical uncertainties"
mathematical models may serve three general purposes: (a) nowcasting and forecasting, (b) scenario analysis, and (c) diagnostic learning
the three overarching research questions outlined in Section 2 should be frequently revisited

chunks.text: The authors argue for applying sensitivity analysis as a core instrument in integrated modeling, drawing on the Pareto principle (“vital few”). Sensitivity analysis is presented as a way to determine when, where, and how uncertainty matters, including for qualitative assumptions and narratives as well as quantitative inputs. They emphasize that sensitivity analysis should be used iteratively and can be applied at both submodel and integrated-system levels to reveal emergent sensitivities and interactions.
supporting_quote: The Law of the "Vital Few": Apply Sensitivity Analysis to Balance Complexity, Uncertainty and Computational Demands
The answer is through sensitivity analysis(SA).
SA needs to be an integral part of integrated modeling and be resorted to iteratively throughout the modeling processes.

chunks.text: Multi-fidelity modeling is proposed to handle scale incommensurability and to balance realism, computational cost, and data needs across coupled components. The authors define multi-fidelity modeling as using multiple models with varying complexity and accuracy for the same system or different components, allowing switching among fidelities within a model’s “trust region.” This is positioned as essential when different processes operate at distinct characteristic time and space scales in an integrated framework.
supporting_quote: To strike a balance between accuracy and efficiency in integrated modeling, "multi‐fidelity modeling" is essential.
Multi‐fidelity modeling ... involves multiple models of varying levels of complexity, accuracy, data requirement
Modelers, however, should only operate within the "trust region" of a model

chunks.text: The paper recommends stress-testing as an evaluation strategy for coupled models, especially when integration induces extrapolation beyond each component’s original data envelope. Stress-testing (or “assumption hunting”) involves exploring forcing scenarios and assumptions, including counterfactuals, to identify when and how an integrated model breaks down or generates surprising dynamics.
