chunks.text: The open-ended evaluation relies on cosine similarity thresholds, which the paper notes may not capture nuance in complex regulatory questions. While cosine similarity balances paraphrasing better than BLEU/ROUGE in this context, it still may miss deeper semantic correctness. The authors suggest future work with BERT-based or hybrid metrics, but note computational and data constraints.
supporting_quote: it relies heavily on cosine similarity for evaluating open-ended responses... it may not always capture the full nuance of complex regulatory questions or measure semantic accuracy
Future work could explore more advanced semantic similarity methods, such as BERT-based models
these methods require substantial computational resources and domain-specific training data, which are currently unavailable

chunks.text: Experts provided feedback that future improvements should include real-time policy updates, multilingual support, and enhanced retrieval quality for technical queries. Recommendations included automating policy updates through APIs/web-scraping and refining semantic search and ranking mechanisms. Integrating FEMA flood maps and spatial datasets was also proposed to strengthen practical learning through visualization.
supporting_quote: integration of real-time policy updates and state-specific regulations
Suggestions included automating policy updates through government APIs and web-scraping methods
The potential for multi-language support was also raised
integration of FEMA flood maps and spatial datasets into the tool

chunks.text: The paper concludes that the AI-powered FPM educational tool is an effective resource for CFM exam preparation, offering personalized and adaptive learning through flashcards, quizzes, and chatbot support. In evaluation, it achieved 91.03% accuracy for open-ended questions and 95.12% for multiple-choice questions. The authors position the tool as a scalable model for vocational and professional certification training beyond floodplain management.
supporting_quote: achieving 91.03% and 95.12% accuracy, respectively
the tool incorporates features like dynamic flashcard generation, adaptive quizzes, and real-time chatbot support
its underlying architecture and functionality hold significant potential for broader applications

chunks.text: Planned future enhancements include more detailed regulatory explanations, greater quiz customization, and improved interpretability and accuracy of AI-generated responses. The authors also plan to explore multidomain adaptability, real-time policy integration, GIS-based learning via FEMA flood maps, alternative similarity scoring methods, and multilingual support. These upgrades are tied to user feedback and expert recommendations.
supporting_quote: These improvements include more detailed regulatory explanations, expanded customization for quizzes, and refinements in AI-generated responses
future updates will focus on integrating real-time floodplain policy updates... incorporating FEMA flood maps... and expanding multilingual support

chunks.text: Higher education is changing due to digital technology and a diverse, globally distributed student population. Traditional instruction often cannot provide instant feedback and personalized support, especially in text-heavy, analytical qualitative fields. This motivates interest in AI/NLP tools that can augment teaching and learning experiences and outcomes.
supporting_quote: The landscape of higher education is experiencing a significant transformation, propelled by rapid advancements in digital technology and the evolving needs of a diverse and globally distributed student population
Traditional teaching methods... often struggle to provide personalized support and instant feedback, particularly in fields that demand a significant amount of text-based learning

chunks.text: AI-enabled virtual teaching assistants (VTAs) are positioned to bridge gaps in learning support by offering personalized help, instant feedback, and adaptive learning experiences. The paper frames VTAs as potentially improving engagement, satisfaction, and outcomes, while also extending to multimodal inputs (code, math, images, diagrams) as models advance.
supporting_quote: The advent of AI-enabled tools, such as virtual teaching assistants (VTAs), offers a unique opportunity to bridge the gap
VTAs can provide personalized support, instant feedback, and adaptive learning experiences, thereby enhancing student engagement, satisfaction, and learning outcomes

chunks.text: Web technologies enable embedding LLM-powered chatbots into engineering education platforms for real-time guidance, visualization, and troubleshooting. The paper argues that integration with web platforms and LMS environments is important to reach students in their normal learning workflows and expand pedagogical possibilities.
supporting_quote: Web technologies play a crucial role in embedding Large Language Models (LLMs) and chatbots into the intricate fabric of modern engineering education
Furthermore, the convergence of LLMs, chatbots, and web platforms has been instrumental in redefining pedagogical methods

chunks.text: The study introduces AIIA, a web-based AI-enabled Virtual Teaching Assistant framework intended to enhance student learning in qualitative disciplines. It aims to reduce cognitive load by improving access to course information, enabling knowledge assessment, and delivering personalized learning support. The system is built with a NodeJS backend and leverages AI/NLP to answer questions, generate quizzes/flashcards, and provide adaptive learning assistance.
supporting_quote: This study introduces a novel web-based framework for an AI-enabled Virtual Teaching Assistant (AIIA), designed to enhance student learning in qualitative disciplines.
The AIIA, built with a NodeJS backend, leverages the power of AI and Natural Language Processing (NLP)

chunks.text: A central objective is to create a discipline-independent, scalable assistant that can be integrated across institutions and communication channels. The framework is positioned to support self-regulated learning, improve student-faculty communication, and expand access to learning resources in postsecondary education.
supporting_quote: The AIIA aims to be discipline-independent, scalable, and seamlessly integrated across institutions
promoting self-regulated learning, fostering student-faculty communication, encouraging collaboration, and enhancing access to learning resources

chunks.text: The paper targets known gaps by integrating with LMS platforms, incorporating class recordings and interactions into the knowledge base, serving both students and instructors, and adding academic integrity safeguards. These goals are framed as necessary to make AI assistants more comprehensive and appropriate for higher education use.
supporting_quote: Proposed AIIA seeks to seamlessly integrate with existing LMS, utilize class recordings and class interactions, cater to the needs of both students and instructors
incorporate measures to ensure academic integrity and prevent cheating

chunks.text: Prior VTA research leaves key needs insufficiently addressed: scalability/adaptability across learning contexts, integration with Learning Management Systems, and broader impacts on higher education. The paper positions these gaps as barriers to deploying assistants that work reliably across courses and institutions.
supporting_quote: These include the scalability and adaptability of such systems across diverse learning contexts
and the integration of these systems with Learning Management Systems (LMS).

chunks.text: Most existing AI-based educational solutions do not incorporate class recordings and class interactions, despite their potential to enrich the assistant’s knowledge base. The paper treats these underused resources as important for improving coverage and the learning experience.
supporting_quote: most studies have not considered the incorporation of class recordings and class interactions in their AI-based solutions
which could potentially enrich the knowledge base of VTAs and provide a more comprehensive learning experience for students

chunks.text: Existing literature has not extensively addressed a solution that supports both students and instructors simultaneously. The paper highlights the need to balance personalized student assistance with instructor tools for managing resources, assessment, and oversight.
supporting_quote: existing literature has not extensively addressed the need for a solution that caters to both students and instructors
striking a balance between personalized assistance and instructor support

chunks.text: AI-based VTAs can increase opportunities for cheating and academic dishonesty, yet effective prevention mechanisms are underexplored. The paper frames academic integrity as a necessary design requirement for educational assistants rather than an afterthought.
supporting_quote: potential for cheating and academic dishonesty that may arise with the use of AI-based VTAs
Ensuring academic integrity and preventing cheating should be an integral part of any AI-enabled educational solution

chunks.text: The system uses GPT-3.5 via OpenAI APIs for natural language inference, selecting models based on task needs. The implementation used "text-davinci-003" (InstructGPT-based) and also employed "gpt-3.5-turbo" plus fine-tuned models for query classification and question generation. This design supports few-shot behavior and task-specific improvements through fine-tuning.
supporting_quote: For the study, we selected GPT-3.5 due to its user-friendly API and advanced natural language processing capabilities.
We utilized the "text-davinci-003" variant... Additionally, we also employed other GPT-3.5 models, including "gpt-3.5-turbo"

chunks.text: Course resources are transformed into embeddings using OpenAI’s text-embedding-ada-002 model, producing 1,536-dimensional vectors. The assistant converts materials (assignments, announcements, lecture notes, forum posts, recordings) into embeddings and uses cosine similarity for retrieval. This enables efficient document search without manually scanning documents.
supporting_quote: we used OpenAI's text-embedding-ada-002... to convert various classroom materials
provides embeddings with 1,536 dimensions

chunks.text: Retrieval uses cosine similarity between the query embedding and course data embeddings, selecting the top 10 most correlated documents. Only documents above a 75% similarity threshold are kept, and their text becomes the context for answering. This pipeline is intended to increase relevance and precision of responses.
supporting_quote: curates a list of 10 documents with the highest correlation to the user's query
Only those exhibiting a similarity score above 75% are retained, with their text forming the context for responding to the user's query.

chunks.text: To incorporate class recordings, the framework applies automatic speech recognition using OpenAI’s Whisper, trained on 680,000 hours of multilingual/multitask data. Recorded lectures are transcribed into text that can be embedded and searched like other course materials. This expands the assistant’s searchable knowledge beyond static documents.
supporting_quote: we adopted Whisper... trained on a substantial corpus... totaling 680,000 hours.
Whisper allows us to transcribe speech from recorded classes into textual data

chunks.text: AIIA architecture is organized into four components: Data Retrieval, Core Framework, Intelligent Services, and Communication. These collectively handle LMS ingestion and transcription, language services and server management, student/instructor assistants, and multi-platform user interaction. The architecture is described as enabling personalized and adaptive learning experiences.
supporting_quote: This architecture comprises four primary components: 1) Data Retrieval... 2) Core Framework... 3) Intelligent Services... and 4) Communication
This comprehensive architecture enables the AIIA framework to deliver personalized and adaptive learning experiences

chunks.text: Knowledge base generation acquires LMS resources (lectures, recordings, readings, assignments, discussions, quizzes, announcements), parses file-based text into ~800-character chunks, and encodes chunks as embeddings. Announcements and assignment details from the LMS API can bypass parsing because they are already structured JSON. The resulting embeddings form the chatbot’s course-specific knowledge base.
supporting_quote: breaks down the text into manageable chunks, each consisting of approximately 800 characters
Announcements and assignment details... are already presented in a structured JSON format. Their inherent structure eliminates the need for parsing

chunks.text: Before responding, the system performs query classification, context generation via embedding matching, and response generation with hallucination mitigation. Fine-tuned models are used for generating question types (open-ended, true/false, multiple-choice). The response pipeline includes prompt engineering to reduce hallucinations.
supporting_quote: Query Classification: The system begins by distinguishing the nature of the user's query
we selectively apply fine-tuning models... including open-ended, true/false, and multiple-choice questions... prompt engineering techniques are utilized to mitigate hallucination

chunks.text: The assistant includes an error prevention mechanism: if it lacks confidence, it withholds an answer and states uncertainty. This design is intended to prevent dissemination of incorrect information and improve reliability for students and instructors.
supporting_quote: If the model lacks confidence in the accuracy of its response, it refrains from providing an answer.
Instead, it communicates a message such as "I'm not sure," which aids in preventing the dissemination of erroneous information.

chunks.text: VirtualTA uses course-centric LMS resources as its primary data, including assignments, discussions, announcements, lectures (via transcripts), reading materials, and quizzes. These sources are intended to cover both administrative questions (deadlines, logistics) and course-content questions. The paper emphasizes that these resources are organized to support accurate responses.
supporting_quote: key resources... include but are not limited to Assignments, Announcements, Discussions, Lectures, and External Reading Materials
VirtualTA uses lecture transcripts to answer queries related to course content.

chunks.text: Resource types are categorized and prioritized so that primary materials (e.g., lectures) are consulted before secondary materials (e.g., external readings). This hierarchy is designed to improve response reliability and also provide traceability by disclosing which resources were used to answer a question.
supporting_quote: primary resources such as Lectures are given a higher priority compared to secondary resources like External Reading Materials
allowing the system to identify and disclose the resources it used to derive an answer

chunks.text: The system creates its knowledge base by chunking extracted text into approximately 800-character blocks and embedding those blocks into high-dimensional vectors. These embeddings constitute the searchable knowledge base used for retrieval-augmented responses and intelligent services. Some LMS API outputs already in JSON skip parsing.
supporting_quote: breaks down the text into manageable chunks, each consisting of approximately 800 characters
the resulting information is encoded into text embeddings... The set of embeddings created forms the fundamental knowledge base of VirtualTA chatbot.

chunks.text: Class recordings are incorporated as data by transcribing audio into text using Whisper ASR, enabling recorded lecture content to be processed similarly to other documents. This expands the assistant’s available course material beyond static files. The integration is motivated by the prevalence of recorded lectures after Covid-19.
supporting_quote: the recording of lectures and classes has become a prevalent practice
Whisper allows us to transcribe speech from recorded classes into textual data

chunks.text: The system provides a dynamic flashcard feature where students can request flashcards on any course topic. Flashcards include true/false and open-ended questions, and each answer includes an explanation or reasoning. The aim is to improve understanding and retention using an interactive study aid.
supporting_quote: incorporation of a flashcard feature, enabling students to request flashcards on any topic within the course
the flashcards encompass both true/false questions and open-ended questions... each answer is accompanied by a detailed explanation or reasoning

chunks.text: VirtualTA includes quiz generation for self-assessment on requested topics. Quizzes include true/false and open-ended items and are paired with an auto-grading function that provides immediate correctness feedback. When answers are wrong, the system supplies explanations to reinforce learning.
supporting_quote: allows users to request quizzes on specific topics from the course
implemented an auto-grading system... provides immediate feedback... In cases where the answer is incorrect, an explanation is provided

chunks.text: The assistant supports automated question-answering on both administrative and course-content topics using its knowledge base. Responses are designed to be prompt and accurate when matching information exists. The interface includes a disclaimer with confidence percentage and information source disclosure.
supporting_quote: feature that enables students to ask questions pertaining to administrative or course content topics
disclaimer includes the confidence percentage of the response and provides information regarding the source from which the information was obtained

chunks.text: A coding sandbox is embedded in the chatbot so students can request help with programming and execute code without separate IDE setup. The system detects the programming language and, upon a "run code" request, opens an in-chat sandbox. This is intended to support beginners and non-CS learners needing lightweight code experimentation.
supporting_quote: integrated a coding sandbox environment directly into the chatbot interface
The system automatically detects the programming language... upon the user's request to "run code," opens up a coding sandbox environment within the chatbot itself.

chunks.text: VirtualTA can generate summaries of course-related topics so students can quickly grasp key points. The summarization is powered by GPT-3.5 models and grounded in the course knowledge base. Similar to Q&A, summaries are accompanied by confidence and source information with a recommendation to consult experts for critical matters.
supporting_quote: implemented a summarization feature in the system
Leveraging the power of GPT-3.5 models... generate a relevant and concise summary
a disclaimer accompanies the response, indicating the confidence level and information source

chunks.text: The system supports context-aware conversation by adapting to a student’s communication style and maintaining conversation history through dynamic rewriting and rotation for token limits. It adopts an uplifting, helpful persona and attempts to recognize student emotional state to provide empathetic responses when appropriate.
supporting_quote: designed to replicate the communication style of the student
we employ a dynamic rewriting and rotation approach to maintain relevant context
incorporates techniques to identify the emotional state of the student

chunks.text: For instructors, an auto-evaluator supports streamlined grading by comparing student submissions against instructor-provided solutions. It can ingest student responses including PDFs, generate per-question scores, and provide explanations justifying the scores. A color-coded rubric highlights low (<=2), medium (<=5), and high (>5) scores to speed visual review.
supporting_quote: incorporated an auto-evaluator feature for assignments... upload PDF files
automatically evaluates... providing scores for each question... generates reasoning and explanations
score of less than or equal to two in red... less than or equal to five in yellow... greater than five in green

chunks.text: An automated homework detection mechanism enforces instructor preferences by blocking direct answers for designated off-limits assignments. When a query resembles homework, the system refrains from answering and instead directs students to relevant resources. This is intended to promote independent learning and protect academic integrity.
supporting_quote: When instructors designate certain assignments or homework as offlimits for direct answers
it refrains from providing a direct answer but instead guides the students towards appropriate resources

chunks.text: The system can generate diverse assessment questions for instructors to use in exams or quizzes. Instructors can specify question types such as True/False, Multiple Choice, or Open-Ended. This aims to reduce the time burden of question preparation while maintaining variety.
supporting_quote: empowers instructors to request VirtualTA to generate questions for exams or quizzes
specify the question type, selecting from options such as True/False, Multiple Choice, or Open-Ended questions

chunks.text: Handling PDFs is a major limitation because many PDFs are unstructured or scanned, requiring OCR for accurate parsing. The paper notes OCR was not implemented at the time of writing, limiting robust extraction from scanned documents. Addressing OCR is positioned as future work.
supporting_quote: handling of PDF files, which often contain unstructured data
scanned copies that require Optical Character Recognition (OCR)... we did not implement OCR functionality at the time of writing this paper

chunks.text: LMS integration is challenging because platforms often lack standardized methods to request or export data in desired formats. The authors report needing workarounds and a custom LMS library to retrieve and process information efficiently. This affects portability across different LMS ecosystems.
supporting_quote: LMS platforms typically lack standardized methods for requesting data in a desired format
we had to devise workarounds... development of a custom LMS library

chunks.text: Whisper API constraints limited transcription workflows because the API imposes a 25MB size limit while class recordings often exceed it. The system mitigated this by partitioning videos into smaller chunks or compressing files. This adds preprocessing overhead for incorporating large recordings.
supporting_quote: The API imposes a constraint of 25MB on the data size
To overcome this limitation, the videos were partitioned into smaller chunks or compressed to reduce the file size

chunks.text: Rapid updates to underlying models and APIs create maintenance challenges. The paper notes that as models evolve, the system must be upgraded to use new APIs and improvements, requiring continuous effort to remain aligned with state-of-the-art techniques.
supporting_quote: frequent updates and advancements in the underlying models posed another challenge
we needed to upgrade the APIs and adapt the system to leverage the latest technological improvements

chunks.text: The paper concludes that AIIA/VirtualTA integrates AI and NLP to support personalized and adaptive learning in higher education, particularly for qualitative disciplines. It provides student features (Q&A, flashcards, quizzes, sandbox, summarization, context-aware conversation) and instructor features (auto-evaluation, homework detection, question generation). The authors position the framework as a significant contribution while emphasizing ongoing refinement.
supporting_quote: This research has presented the design, implementation, and evaluation of an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Intelligent Assistant (AIIA) for personalized and adaptive learning in higher education.
capabilities span... responsive question-answering, flashcard integration, automated assessment, embedded coding sandbox, summarization... context-aware conversation

chunks.text: The work asserts that VirtualTA can help shape the future trajectory of higher education by fostering self-regulated learning, improving student-faculty communication, and expanding access to learning resources. It also acknowledges that challenges and limitations remain and should be addressed in future iterations.
supporting_quote: By fostering selfregulated learning, promoting student-faculty communication, and expanding access to learning resources
it is crucial to acknowledge the challenges and limitations encountered during the development process, which can be addressed in future iterations

chunks.text: The paper positions learning analytics (LA) and artificial intelligence (AI) as a joint shift in education that can reshape teaching and learning decisions. It argues that combining insights from learning sciences with modern AI methods can enhance pedagogical methodologies. The authors highlight the growing value of incorporating qualitative text via NLP into LA to provide richer context about learning processes.
supporting_quote: the confluence of learning analytics (LA) and artificial intelligence (AI) signifies a critical paradigm shift.
the incorporation of qualitative, textual data through NLP could introduce a richer, contextual understanding

chunks.text: Large language models such as GPT-4 are framed as an enabling technology for educational applications, including tailored assistants that integrate with learning management systems. Prior work cited suggests these models can perform well on complex tasks and can support personalized learning experiences in data-intensive domains. The paper uses this context to motivate applying GPT-4 capabilities inside LA workflows.
supporting_quote: large language models like GPT-4, have showcased potential applications in various educational contexts
tailored AI-enabled educational assistants that integrate with Learning Management Systems (LMS) to provide personalized learning experiences

chunks.text: The related work review describes LA as an interdisciplinary field using diverse data types and methods to improve learning and instruction. It notes recent advances such as deep learning for knowledge tracing and multimodal engagement indicators. At the same time, it emphasizes ongoing ethical and privacy challenges and the need for stronger ties to learning sciences.
supporting_quote: Learning analytics, an emerging interdisciplinary field, stands at the crossroads of various sophisticated domains
challenges persist in data tracking, evaluation, and analysis, along with ethical and privacy concerns

chunks.text: A central objective is to build an AI-empowered learning analytics tool that measures and analyzes student engagement to support pedagogical interventions. The tool is intended to monitor and quantify involvement and translate it into real-time, actionable insights for educators. The envisioned use is to improve instructional decision-making during a course rather than only after completion.
supporting_quote: develop an AI-empowered LA tool designed to effectively measure and analyze student engagement
enabling the delivery of pedagogical interventions based on real-time, actionable insights

chunks.text: The study aims to create an AI-based system that monitors students’ learning progression by mapping individual learning pathways. The authors propose using AI predictive and analytical capabilities to provide instructors with a nuanced view of each student’s trajectory. Bloom’s taxonomy is used as the organizing framework to interpret the cognitive level of student inquiries over time.
supporting_quote: construct a comprehensive AI-based system to monitor students' learning progression
employs Bloom's taxonomy to assess cognitive development based on student inquiries

chunks.text: Another objective is to assess affective states in learning using AI-derived indicators. The tool targets emotional context as an important contributor to cognitive processes and educational outcomes. It focuses on measuring indicators such as stress, curiosity, confusion, and agitation from student interactions.
supporting_quote: we aim to establish a mechanism to assess students' affective states
scores are given on a scale of 1 to 10 for stress, agitation, curiosity, and confusion

chunks.text: The research scope emphasizes inclusivity and access to AI-derived insights for diverse learners. The tool is described as focusing on engagement measurement, learning progression tracking, and affective state assessment, and it evaluates related metrics such as participation rates, progression speed, and emotional response. The goal is to improve educational outcomes while keeping interpretations bounded by known limitations of inferred metrics.
supporting_quote: our tool is designed with a focus on inclusivity, ensuring that insights derived from AI analytics are accessible
The specific elements under consideration include the measurement of student engagement, tracking of learning progression, and assessment of affective states.

chunks.text: The paper identifies a collaboration and knowledge gap between AI developers and learning sciences, limiting effective educational applications. It argues that many AI developers lack familiarity with learning sciences research, motivating closer collaboration among developers, educators, and researchers. This gap hinders designing AI tools aligned with pedagogical theory and classroom practice.
supporting_quote: a gap persists as many AI developers exhibit limited familiarity with learning sciences research
an imperative need to foster collaborative relationships among AI developers, educators, and researchers

chunks.text: It argues that current learning analytics methods often do not connect well to pedagogical theory and teaching practice, reducing educators’ ability to apply insights. The paper also notes scalability and generalizability problems across educational settings. These issues motivate an AI-enhanced LA tool designed to provide actionable insights informed by pedagogy.
supporting_quote: Current LA methods often lack integration with pedagogical theory and teaching practice
LA faces issues with scalability and generalizability across different educational settings.

chunks.text: The authors note that many LA tools do not adequately address affective aspects of learning even though they are crucial for understanding engagement. They argue that emotional indicators can enrich interpretation of student behavior and support more timely interventions. The proposed tool is positioned as filling this affective gap through AI-based inference on student interactions.
supporting_quote: many LA tools do not adequately address the affective aspects of learning, which are crucial for understanding student engagement.
sensitive to emotional states

chunks.text: Faculty adoption is constrained by concerns about student privacy and the accuracy of AI-generated insights. The paper reports that faculty see potential value but worry about how student data is handled and whether insights are reliable enough for teaching decisions. These concerns are treated as major barriers to real-world deployment.
supporting_quote: Faculty recognized the tool's potential to enhance instructional decision-making through real-time insights but expressed concerns about data security and the accuracy of AI-generated insights.
respondents expressed either very concerned or extremely concerned responses about both privacy (51%) and accuracy (59%).

chunks.text: The work develops a learning analytics tool as an extension to educational platforms, demonstrated within the VirtualTA intelligent assistant. VirtualTA answers course logistics and content questions and can generate flashcards and quizzes, providing interaction traces for analytics. The LA tool is designed to be flexible and compatible with other chatbots and LMS environments beyond VirtualTA.
supporting_quote: development of a novel LA tool, conceptualized as an extension to existing educational platforms
VirtualTA... can generate flashcards and quizzes

chunks.text: Data collection is built around capturing student-chatbot interactions plus an affective analysis of each input. The tool records topics, monitors engagement with flashcards and quizzes, and tracks time spent and outcomes. It also combines these interaction signals with LMS quantitative data and any available qualitative data such as surveys to create a holistic view of behavior and preferences.
supporting_quote: It captures all student interactions, including raw dialogues and an emotional analysis of each input.
tracks variables such as time spent on questions, overall duration on quizzes, and quiz outcomes

chunks.text: The pipeline preprocesses interaction data after a session ends, sending accumulated data to the backend in JSON for analysis of affective states and learning progression. Cleaning removes irrelevant, duplicated, or incorrect records, such as button clicks or incomplete quizzes that distort time measures. The system then updates or creates a student record and refreshes the instructor dashboard with the latest metrics.
supporting_quote: Once the session concludes... the accumulated data is forwarded to the backend in JSON format.
This involves pinpointing and rectifying or removing irrelevant, duplicated, or incorrect data entries.

chunks.text: Privacy-by-design is implemented by not storing the actual content of student messages. Instead, the tool computes metrics (e.g., emotional states) during active interactions and discards raw text afterward. It stores anonymized, aggregated time-series metrics to enable trend monitoring while protecting confidentiality.
supporting_quote: it does not store the actual content of student messages to protect privacy
Once these metrics are computed, the raw text data is discarded to maintain privacy.

chunks.text: GPT-4 is used for sentiment and topic analysis with few-shot learning and prompt engineering to score stress, agitation, curiosity, and confusion on a 1–10 scale. Prompt engineering is used to improve sensitivity to subtle emotional cues in educational queries. The tool also analyzes sessions using Bloom’s taxonomy to infer cognitive level from student questions after they exit the assistant.
supporting_quote: Leveraging the power of the GPT-4 model... scores are given on a scale of 1 to 10 for stress, agitation, curiosity, and confusion.
tracks the progression of learning by analyzing the questions using Bloom's taxonomy

chunks.text: For natural language inference, the system configures GPT-4 using few-shot learning with temperature set to 1.0, aiming for diverse yet relevant predictions. Due to GPT-4 token limits, conversation history is managed with a first-in-first-out approach so the most recent messages remain available. The approach is intended to consider prior communication while fitting within the model’s context window.
supporting_quote: we have employed few-shot learning with a temperature setting of 1.0
GPT-4's token limitation — with a maximum of 8192 tokens... we've adopted a first-in-first-out approach.

chunks.text: The system architecture includes a web dashboard implemented in vanilla JavaScript with Chart.js for visualization and a backend built on Express.js and Node.js. The backend interfaces with OpenAI’s GPT API and receives chatbot interaction data via APIs, using JSON as the data exchange format. Processed analytics are then relayed to the dashboard to provide instructors timely access to insights.
supporting_quote: The LA dashboard has been designed using vanilla JavaScript
integrated Chart.js
synergistic combination of Express.js and Node.js in the backend

chunks.text: Evaluation was conducted via an anonymous online survey of University of Iowa teaching faculty focused on perceived effectiveness and LMS compatibility (e.g., Canvas). Faculty did not directly interact with the tool; they responded based on described features. Survey topics included desired classroom insights, privacy/security concerns, and the importance of accurate tool outputs.
supporting_quote: evaluated through a survey distributed to teaching faculty at the University of Iowa.
It is important to note that the faculty did not interact directly with the tool

chunks.text: The tool’s data sources include detailed chatbot interaction logs and LMS-derived quantitative measures. Collected variables cover raw dialogues (temporarily), emotional analysis outputs, question topics, flashcard and quiz usage, time spent, and quiz outcomes. It also incorporates LMS metadata such as assignment scores, time on materials, and interaction frequency, plus optional qualitative inputs like surveys.
supporting_quote: It captures all student interactions, including raw dialogues and an emotional analysis of each input.
The strategy combines quantitative data (like student metadata, assignment scores, quiz results, time on learning materials, and interaction frequency from the LMS)

chunks.text: For demonstration and technical evaluation, the study used synthetic test data generated with ChatGPT rather than real student interactions. The synthetic dataset was used to show how the dashboard and analytics operate while avoiding real student privacy risks. The authors describe it as a proof-of-concept to illustrate engagement and emotional state analysis capabilities.
supporting_quote: synthetic test data generated using ChatGPT was utilized.
This data, devoid of any actual student interactions, serves to demonstrate the tool's ability

chunks.text: The case study dataset consists of faculty survey responses with varying response counts by question. The sample included 88 respondents for teaching area (Figure 8) and 86 for role (Figure 9), reflecting optional survey questions. Disciplines were diverse, with 38% in STEM and 27% selecting "Other" (e.g., Nursing, Health Sciences, Medicine, Pharmacy, Education).
supporting_quote: Primary Teaching Area of the Faculty (n=88)
a significant proportion (38%) representing STEM fields
27% of the respondents selected "Other," representing specialized fields like Nursing, Health Sciences, Medicine, Pharmacy, and Education

chunks.text: The survey also characterized respondent roles, with Assistant Professors, Professors, and Associate Professors forming the largest groups. Specifically, Assistant Professors were 30%, Professors 22%, and Associate Professors 22% among n=86. Smaller groups included Graduate Assistants (7%) and Lecturers (3%), with 15% selecting "Other" such as adjuncts and postdocs.
supporting_quote: Primary Role of the Teaching Staff (n=86)
Assistant Professors (30%), Professors (22%), and Associate Professors (22%) made up the majority of respondents

chunks.text: Using synthetic data, the tool demonstrated real-time scoring of affective indicators—stress, curiosity, confusion, and agitation—on a 1–10 scale from student questions. The dashboard can visualize these measures at class-wide and individual levels over time. The paper notes that such views can be aligned with academic events like quizzes and assignments to support timely interventions.
supporting_quote: scores are given on a scale of 1 to 10 for stress, agitation, curiosity, and confusion.
The dashboard shows both class-wide (Figure 2a) and individual (Figure 2b) stress levels over time

chunks.text: The system demonstrated topic analysis that identifies and records the main topics of student queries and removes duplicates for instructor usability. This produces an overview of unique topics asked by the class, intended to help instructors detect areas of interest and difficulty. The approach also supports analyzing questioning patterns (types, sentiments, sequencing) to infer learning journeys within a topic.
supporting_quote: The LA tool uses GPT-4 for topic analysis and tracking questioning patterns
duplicate entries are carefully removed from the table. Each row corresponds to a unique topic

chunks.text: The tool tracks study method preferences by recording interaction modes such as asking questions, creating flashcards, taking quizzes, and requesting summaries. Dashboards show class-wide and student-specific distributions of these study methods. These outputs are positioned as enabling instructors to adjust teaching strategies and helping the system tailor resources to student habits.
supporting_quote: recording activities like asking questions, creating flashcards, taking quizzes, or requesting summaries.
The graphs show class-wide (Figure 4a) and individual (Figure 4b) study methods

chunks.text: For quizzes delivered through VirtualTA, the tool demonstrated tracking of quiz topics, completion times, time per question, and quiz results. Visualizations include a bar chart of time spent per question and displays of correct versus incorrect responses. The paper argues these outputs can reveal question difficulty and topic mastery and support targeted instruction.
supporting_quote: recording quiz topics, completion times, time spent on each question, and quiz results.
Figure 5b shows quiz outcomes, distinguishing correct and incorrect responses.

chunks.text: The tool demonstrated learning progression tracking by analyzing student session messages through Bloom’s taxonomy. It extracts cognitive level indicators from queries, distinguishing early stages (recall/comprehension) from advanced stages (application, analysis, synthesis, evaluation). The mapping is described as using “digital planning verbs” within a GPT-4 analytical framework to monitor changes over time.
supporting_quote: analyzed through the lens of Bloom's Taxonomy
questions demonstrating application, analysis, synthesis, or evaluation suggest more advanced understanding.

chunks.text: A consolidated instructor dashboard was presented as an interactive holistic report that can display class-level or student-level analytics. The paper emphasizes the importance of visualization for translating complex metrics into actionable representations for educators. The dashboard is described as enabling navigation between individual student patterns and overall class performance for instructional decision-making.
supporting_quote: Presented in Figure 7 is the comprehensive instructor's dashboard
opting to delve into the learning patterns of a specific student or obtain an overarching understanding of the class's performance

chunks.text: Surveyed faculty prioritized specific classroom insights the tool could provide. The most valued were identifying frequently asked questions (80%), tracking learning progression over time (75%), and identifying common misconceptions (73%). These preferences suggest instructors want analytics that directly reveal confusion points and learning trajectories to guide teaching adjustments.
supporting_quote: identifying frequently asked questions (80%) and tracking the progression of student learning over time (75%).
identifying common misconceptions (73%)

chunks.text: Faculty expressed high concern about both privacy/security and the accuracy of AI-generated insights. The paper reports that 51% were very or extremely concerned about privacy and 59% about accuracy. This indicates that perceived tool value is tied to strong assurances in data handling and reliable outputs before classroom adoption.
supporting_quote: very concerned or extremely concerned responses about both privacy (51%) and accuracy (59%).
Faculty are especially cautious about the risks associated with handling sensitive student data and ensuring that the AI tools provide consistently accurate insights.

chunks.text: Open-ended faculty feedback was characterized as cautious optimism. Participants noted potential benefits such as saving student time and providing guidance similar to teaching assistants during office hours, while not simply giving answers. However, they also warned about over-reliance potentially stifling critical thinking and raised concerns about misinformation skills and the maturity of current AI tools.
supporting_quote: a clear theme emerges around the cautious yet optimistic stance towards the integration of AI in education.
Some participants worry that over-reliance on AI could stifle critical thinking

chunks.text: The discussion notes that emotional analysis insights may not fully capture the complexity of human emotions and external factors influencing engagement. While real-time emotional analysis was valued, faculty feedback suggested the tool needs refinement to provide more accurate and comprehensive affective interpretations. This is framed as an important limitation for using affective scores as actionable indicators.
supporting_quote: these features may not fully capture the complexities of human emotions and external factors affecting engagement.
need for further refinement to ensure the tool delivers more accurate and comprehensive emotional insights.

chunks.text: Accuracy and data security are discussed as critical barriers to real-world applicability. Faculty concerns are said to align with limitations observed in synthetic demonstrations, including issues of consistency and reliability. The paper argues that adoption, especially in precision-sensitive domains like healthcare and STEM, depends on stronger privacy measures and transparent data practices.
supporting_quote: Faculty expressed strong concerns around the accuracy of AI-generated insights and the security of student data.
revealed limitations in consistency and reliability.

chunks.text: The authors note usability constraints, emphasizing that instructors want intuitive data visualization and that the tool’s success depends on digital literacy. They suggest that training for educators and students is necessary so users can effectively interpret analytics and integrate them into teaching workflows. Without such support, even a technically capable tool may be underutilized.
supporting_quote: faculty emphasized the need for more intuitive data visualization to ensure ease of use.
the success of the tool depends on the digital literacy of both educators and students

chunks.text: The survey sample may be biased toward more favorable views because STEM faculty were overrepresented. The paper cautions that higher familiarity with technology in STEM could increase comfort with AI tools relative to arts and humanities, which were less represented. This limits the generalizability of faculty feedback across disciplines.
supporting_quote: the dataset may be biased toward a more positive outlook... due to the overrepresentation of STEM faculty in the survey responses.
fields like the arts, which were less represented in the sample.

chunks.text: A major limitation is the absence of classroom experimentation with real students. The study relied on synthetic data for technical demonstration and a faculty perception survey for feasibility feedback. The paper states that real classroom experiments are necessary to understand impacts on learning, workflow integration, and unforeseen challenges during active use.
supporting_quote: A key limitation of this study is the absence of classroom experimentation.
further evaluation is necessary in real classroom settings to fully understand its impact

chunks.text: The paper concludes that it developed and deployed a learning analytics tool that integrates with platforms like VirtualTA to capture and analyze student engagement and learning patterns. It highlights AI-driven features such as real-time sentiment analysis and Bloom’s taxonomy-based cognitive tracking as enabling more responsive, data-driven education. The tool is positioned as supporting timely interventions by providing nuanced views of participation and progression.
supporting_quote: successfully developed and deployed a novel learning analytics (LA) tool
leveraging AI-driven capabilities, including real-time sentiment analysis and cognitive tracking based on Bloom's taxonomy

chunks.text: The authors emphasize that additional evaluation is needed, particularly classroom-based experimentation, to validate effectiveness with real students. They also state that privacy and data security must be prioritized through stronger anonymization and transparent data usage policies and compliance with regulations. These are presented as essential next steps for practical adoption.
supporting_quote: further evaluations, particularly through classroom-based experimentation, are needed to validate its effectiveness
Privacy and data security concerns must be prioritized through stronger anonymization techniques, transparent data usage policies

chunks.text: Future directions include improving emotional analysis using real classroom data and exploring attention-tracking algorithms, alongside refining the user interface and visualization for actionable insights. The paper also proposes expanding applicability to different educational levels, including special education, and improving educator training and usability. It frames the work as a foundational step toward data-driven, personalized learning supported by emerging technologies.
supporting_quote: future research should focus on enhancing the tool's emotional analysis by integrating real-life classroom data and exploring attention-tracking algorithms.
Expanding the tool's applicability to various educational levels, including special education

chunks.text: Global hydrological models provide baseline streamflow information useful for water management, especially where local models or gauging are limited. They leverage centralized data and computing to offer broad coverage, but to be impactful their information must be usable at regional and local decision-making scales. Key operational challenges include managing big data, communicating outputs, enabling adoption, and ensuring validation credibility. These challenges motivate post-processing methods that can improve local usability without full model recalibration.
supporting_quote: A global hydrological model gives water managers a baseline of data ... providing hydrological simulations in regions without local models or adequate in situ gauging stations.
Several challenges must be addressed to make hydrological models useful at a local scale ... Big Data Management ... Communication ... Adoption ... Validation

chunks.text: The GEOGLOWS ECMWF Hydrological Model is a global streamflow service that routes ECMWF land-surface runoff to a high-resolution stream network. It uses ECLand/HTESSEL total runoff, applies grid-to-vector mapping, and routes flows with Muskingum routing in RAPID. Its historical simulation is driven by ERA5 reanalysis and produces daily average streamflow for nearly one million reaches starting in 1979. GEOGLOWS also provides cyberinfrastructure for storing and accessing results via web services and REST APIs.
supporting_quote: The GEOGLOWS model ... uses the ECLand ... gridded total runoff results ... uses Muskingum routing as implemented in the RAPID software ... The ERA5 reanalysis dataset produces historical streamflow for the approximate one million stream reaches
The GEOGLOWS model provides a global historical simulation, starting in 1979-01-01 and covering ~928,000 streams worldwide.

chunks.text: Traditional calibration and validation of GEOGLOWS are difficult due to limited observed discharge data access, heterogeneous agency data practices, and the need to calibrate distinct components (land surface and routing) separately. Additionally, much of the streamflow bias originates from precipitation forcing errors, so hydrologic calibration can mask meteorological biases rather than fix them. These constraints make bias correction a practical alternative for improving simulations after model runs, especially for local applications.
supporting_quote: traditional calibration and validation of the GEOGLOWS model is challenging ... shortage of adequate observed discharge data for calibration.
much of the bias stems from the precipitation forcings from the meteorological model. Traditional hydrological calibration would inherently adjust model parameters to account for that bias

chunks.text: The study aims to address seasonal, systematic biases in GEOGLOWS historical streamflow simulations by introducing a month-by-month flow duration curve quantile-mapping approach. It conducts a comprehensive evaluation of GEOGLOWS retrospective simulation performance before and after bias correction across a large global set of gauges. Performance is quantified using Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE) and its bias, variability, and correlation components. The method is named Monthly Flow Duration Curve Quantile-Mapping (MFDC-QM).
supporting_quote: we present a method for hydrologic model bias correction that addresses the problem of model bias that changes with seasons.
We evaluate the performance of the historical simulation both before and after applying the bias correction method, which we have named Monthly Flow Duration Curve Quantile-Mapping (MFDC-QM).

chunks.text: A further goal is to test the MFDC-QM method at global scale using an extensive station dataset and to understand whether improving bias and variability can raise overall skill. The evaluation uses more than 15,000 gauging stations and examines how KGE and its components change after correction. The work positions MFDC-QM as an alternative to calibration that can be performed locally after downloading GEOGLOWS results. It also emphasizes applicability beyond GEOGLOWS to other hydrologic models with streamflow outputs matched to gauges.
supporting_quote: We assess the model's performance using a dataset of more than 15,000 gauge stations.

The methodology presented in this study, MFDC-QM, involves a quantile-mapping bias correction approach independent of the underlying model structure. Therefore, it could be applied to any regional or global hydrological model

chunks.text: GEOGLOWS historical simulations exhibit systematic biases that reduce local accuracy, and these biases can vary by season. Coarse global forcings and model structure limitations lead to mismatches in magnitude and timing of events in some regions. The model is also uncalibrated for rainfall-runoff and routing in this setup and does not represent human interventions like dams and withdrawals. These issues motivate a post-processing bias correction approach tailored to seasonal behavior.
supporting_quote: revealing systematic biases that impact its accuracy.

It is important to acknowledge that the GEOGLOWS Model used in this study is an uncalibrated model ... It additionally does not account for human interventions in rivers, such as water withdrawals and the presence of dams.

chunks.text: Standard flow-duration-curve based bias correction applied across the full year fails to address seasonality. The Farmer et al. method maps simulated values to non-exceedance probabilities using an overall simulated flow duration curve and substitutes with corresponding observed values, but it does not account for seasonal biases. This limitation is important in globally diverse basins where seasonal flow regimes differ. The paper targets this gap with a monthly bias correction framework.
supporting_quote: Farmer et al. (2018) proposed a bias correction method ... This method is applied across the entire simulation period. Unfortunately, this method does not account for seasonal biases.
uses the flow duration curves calculated for each month ... to correct biases monthly, thus accounting for the different globally observed seasonal patterns.

chunks.text: The MFDC-QM approach requires that observed and simulated flow duration curves are similar in shape; otherwise quantile mapping may not yield accurate corrections. If the observed and simulated FDC shapes differ substantially, mapping probabilities to observed flows can distort results. The study explicitly checks this assumption by examining correlations between observed and simulated FDCs by month. This highlights that bias correction is not guaranteed to work in all hydrologic contexts.
supporting_quote: MFDC-QM method ... operates under the assumption that ... observed and simulated streamflow flow duration curves exhibit statistical similarity.
If the shape of the flow duration curves ... are significantly different, it is unlikely that the MFDC-QM method will produce accurate results.

chunks.text: Even with bias correction, ungauged locations remain a challenge because MFDC-QM needs observed data at the correction site. The paper notes that MFDC-QM improves accuracy where observations exist but does not automatically extend improvements to ungauged regions. This constraint limits the direct operational reach of the method despite its global evaluation. Related regional methods (e.g., SABER) are mentioned as extensions for ungauged correction but are outside MFDC-QM’s inherent capability.
supporting_quote: it does not automatically enhance model performance in ungauged regions.
The bias-corrected values from GEOGLOWS can only be generated in locations where observed data are available.

chunks.text: MFDC-QM performs bias correction through month-specific flow duration curves for observed and simulated daily streamflow. For each month, each simulated daily value is converted to a non-exceedance probability using the simulated monthly FDC, then mapped to an observed discharge value using the observed monthly FDC at the same probability. The mapped observed-equivalent value replaces the simulated value to form a bias-corrected hydrograph. This month-by-month structure is intended to correct seasonally varying biases.
supporting_quote: uses the flow duration curves calculated for each month in both the simulated and observed historical time series to correct biases monthly
For every month, the non-exceedance probability of each simulated value is determined and matched to the corresponding observed streamflow value.

chunks.text: The study connects gauging stations to the GEOGLOWS stream network by assigning a Reach ID using geospatial proximity rules and manual review when needed. Automated assignment is done when stations are within 2 m of a stream, or within 10 m with no competing streams inside a 20 m radius; ambiguous cases are flagged for manual revision. ArcGIS tools compute station-to-stream distances, and OpenStreetMap helps verify stream names and locations. This ensures observed and simulated series correspond to the same watershed reach for validation and correction.
supporting_quote: We connected the station network with the stream network by assigning the parameter Reach ID to each station based on its location on or near the stream network.
within less than 2 m ... assigned ... if a station was located less than 10 m ... and no other streams ... within a radius of 20 m

chunks.text: Historical simulated discharge for each station-reach pair is retrieved using the GEOGLOWS model REST API. The retrospective simulation is daily average streamflow driven by ERA5 reanalysis and updated nearly monthly with a two-month delay. The analysis uses the full time series even though the model starts with an initial condition of 0 m3/s, which can make early values unrealistic. The authors justify including all values to provide a comprehensive and honest performance assessment and because warmup completes quickly for all but the largest rivers.
supporting_quote: We used the GEOGLOWS model REST API to download historical simulations for the 15,586 gauging stations
The GEOGLOWS historical simulation has an initial condition of 0 m3 /s flow rate for every stream in the world

chunks.text: Model performance is evaluated with Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE) and its three components: Pearson correlation (r), bias ratio (β), and variability ratio (γ). KGE is computed as 1 minus the Euclidean distance from the ideal point (r=1, β=1, γ=1). The paper provides explicit formulas for KGE, r, β, and γ, using simulated and observed means and standard deviations. Metrics are computed at each station before and after applying MFDC-QM.
supporting_quote: To assess the performance ... we use the Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE) metric and the decomposition of its three components: bias, variability, and correlation.

chunks.text: To check the key MFDC-QM assumption of similar FDC shapes, the study compares monthly correlations between observed and simulated flow duration curves against KGE results. The rationale is that quantile mapping is most appropriate when simulated and observed distributions are similarly shaped apart from bias. Where shapes differ, MFDC-QM may fail to provide accurate corrections. This diagnostic step is used to interpret when and why corrections work or struggle.
supporting_quote: To verify this assumption, we used the average linear correlation coefficient between the observed and simulated flow duration curves for every month and compared with the calculated Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE).
assumption that ... simulated flow duration curve is similar to that of the observed flow duration curve, except for the bias.

chunks.text: Observed discharge data were compiled for more than 23,500 gauging stations worldwide across 113 countries from multiple programs and agencies (e.g., NASA GEOGLOWS/SERVIR, GRDC, IDEAM, ANA, USGS, WSC, BOM). Each station provides daily average streamflow with historical records averaging just over 50 years. Stations used for MFDC-QM had to align to the GEOGLOWS network and have at least one year of record. These observations underpin global validation and bias correction.
supporting_quote: we collected observed discharge data for more than 23,500 gauging stations worldwide ... across 113 countries.
Each station's data includes daily average streamflow values, providing a historical record of over 50 years.

chunks.text: After spatial matching, nearly 21,000 of 23,543 stations were assigned GEOGLOWS reach IDs, but only a subset met time-series criteria for validation. Final selection required at least one year of record and data availability after January 1, 1979, yielding 15,586 stations used in analyses. The observed series have about 10% missing daily values on average. This curated dataset is the basis for station-by-station metric computation before and after correction.
supporting_quote: Out of the 23,543 stations, we assigned reach IDs to nearly 21,000.
15,586 met the additional criteria and were used for the validation exercise ... On average, each station's time series has about 10% of its daily values missing.

chunks.text: Simulated discharge comes from the GEOGLOWS historical simulation, which starts on 1979-01-01 and covers approximately 928,000 streams globally. The series consists of daily average streamflow generated by ERA5 precipitation reanalysis and is updated nearly monthly with about a two-month delay. Simulations for the 15,586 selected stations were downloaded through the GEOGLOWS REST API. The model begins with 0 m3/s initial streamflow everywhere, affecting early-period realism.
supporting_quote: The GEOGLOWS model provides a global historical simulation, starting in 1979-01-01 and covering ~928,000 streams worldwide.
The GEOGLOWS historical simulation has an initial condition of 0 m3 /s flow rate for every stream in the world

chunks.text: Before bias correction, only a minority of stations met commonly cited “good” ranges for bias and variability ratios (0.8–1.2). Specifically, 23% of stations had bias ratio within 0.8–1.2, 33% had variability ratio within 0.8–1.2, and only 9% satisfied both simultaneously (mostly in Europe and North America). Median correlation was 0.46 with IQR 0.32–0.60, and 78% had correlation greater than 0.3. These results indicate moderate alignment in temporal patterns but substantial magnitude and variability issues at many sites.
supporting_quote: 3658 of 15,586 (23%) stations presented bias ratio between 0.8 and 1.2; 5215 ... (33%) ... variability ratio between 0.8 and 1.2; and just 1343 ... (9%) ... bias and variability ratio between 0.8 and 1.2 simultaneously.
The Pearson Correlation Coefficient has a median value of 0.46 and an interquartile range between 0.32 and 0.60.

chunks.text: Uncorrected GEOGLOWS simulations were generally skillful relative to the mean-flow benchmark at many stations but often only at low to moderate levels. Median KGE was 0.13 with IQR −0.42 to 0.36, and 75% of stations had KGE ≥ −0.41. Using the cited classification, 25% were unacceptable (KGE < −0.41), 15% very poor, 49% poor, 10% intermediate, and 1% good. Spatial patterns showed better performance in Europe and North America and poorer performance in several arid or mountainous regions.
supporting_quote: The calculated median KGE value is 0.13, and the IQR between -0.42and 0.36 ... 11,634 of 15,586 (75%) stations presented a KGE value greater than or equal to -0.41.
25% (3952 stations) are classified as unacceptable (KGE < -0.41) ... and 1% (124 samples) as good (0.75 < KGE ≤ 1.00).

chunks.text: MFDC-QM substantially improved bias and variability ratio distributions. After correction, 61% of stations had bias ratio within 0.8–1.2, 62% had variability ratio within 0.8–1.2, and 51% satisfied both simultaneously, with improvements now globally distributed rather than concentrated in Europe and North America. This indicates the monthly quantile-mapping approach effectively reduces systematic magnitude and variability errors across diverse hydroclimates. Remaining poor areas were noted in several regions, suggesting local data or process challenges.
supporting_quote: 9464 of 15,586 (61%) stations presented a bias ratio between 0.8 and 1.2; 9609 ... (62%) ... variability ratio between 0.8 and 1.2; and 7973 ... (51%) ... bias and variability ratio between 0.8 and 1.2 simultaneously
these stations are now globally distributed, contrasting with the previous concentration in Europe and North America

chunks.text: Correlation also increased after MFDC-QM, indicating better alignment of simulated and observed temporal dynamics. Median Pearson correlation rose from 0.46 to 0.52, with IQR shifting to 0.38–0.67. The number of stations with positive correlation increased to 15,543 (99%), representing 128 stations shifting from negative to positive. Stations with correlation greater than 0.3 increased to 85% (13,220), showing broader moderate linear agreement after correction.
supporting_quote: After bias correction, the Pearson Correlation Coefficient improved to a median value of 0.52 and the interquartile range between 0.38 and 0.67
15,543 of 15,586 (99%) stations presented a positive correlation which indicates the shift of 128 stations from a negative to a positive correlation.

chunks.text: Overall skill improved strongly after MFDC-QM as measured by KGE. Median KGE increased from 0.13 to 0.43, with IQR tightening and shifting from −0.42–0.36 to 0.20–0.61. The fraction of stations meeting KGE ≥ −0.41 increased from 75% to 94% (14,585 stations), meaning 2,951 stations moved above the benchmark. Classification counts improved to 9% good and 30% intermediate, with unacceptable stations decreasing to 6%.
supporting_quote: After the bias correction, the KGE median is 0.43, and the IQR is between 0.20 and 0.61.
14,585 of 15,586 (94%) stations presented a KGE value greater or equal to − 0.41 ... 2951 stations that previously fell below the − 0.41 benchmark now perform better

chunks.text: Box-plot summaries show MFDC-QM reduced systematic bias and narrowed dispersion in key components. Bias ratio median improved from 0.87 to 0.99, and its IQR shrank from 0.60–1.51 to 0.86–1.13. Variability ratio median stayed at 1.03, but IQR narrowed from 0.76–1.44 to 0.92–1.20. These component changes align with the observed increase in KGE and indicate more consistent performance across stations.
supporting_quote: Before bias correction, the bias ratio median is 0.87 ... After bias correction, the bias ratio median is 0.99
Before the bias correction, the variability ratio median is 1.03 ... After the bias correction, the variability ratio median is 1.03

chunks.text: MFDC-QM can adjust magnitude and improve seasonal patterns in corrected hydrographs. The authors report that corrected seasonal flows can better correspond to observed seasonality, even when the timing of simulated seasonal maxima differs from observed maxima. An example is provided for the Hayes River Below Gods River station (04AB001) in Canada, where daily and monthly seasonal patterns are corrected. This illustrates MFDC-QM’s month-based structure affecting seasonality as well as overall magnitude.
supporting_quote: We found that the MFDC-QM method adjusts the magnitude in the daily simulated streamflow and improves the seasonal patterns.
Fig. 8 shows the daily and monthly seasonal patterns correction for the gauging station 04AB001 HAYES RIVER BELOW GODS RIVER

chunks.text: Case studies suggest MFDC-QM can implicitly account for systemic anthropogenic influences absent from the original model, such as withdrawals and dam regulation, by matching observed distributions. At station 21207960 Puente Portillo (Bogota River), the bias-corrected series “learned” systemic interventions compared with the uncorrected simulation. Downstream of Betania Dam at station 21097120 La Esperanza, corrected flows reduced extremes and better matched regulated patterns, though abrupt operational changes remained smoother than observed. These examples show improvements but also remaining discrepancies in regulated systems.
supporting_quote: MFDC-QM method effectively incorporates adjustments for systemic anthropogenic influences ... such as irrigation withdrawals, industrial water use, and micro-hydropower plants.
The bias-corrected simulation ... appears to have "learned" the systemic anthropogenic interventions.

chunks.text: Using overlapping stations with published GloFAS evaluations, the paper compares KGE distributions via cumulative distribution functions. The bias-corrected GEOGLOWS model performed better than GloFAS v3.0 calibration for the lowest 40% of cases and was similar for the remaining 60%. It also outperformed GloFAS v3.0 validation overall, while GloFAS v2.1 (uncalibrated) performed better overall than uncalibrated GEOGLOWS. This situates MFDC-QM-corrected GEOGLOWS performance relative to another global system.
supporting_quote: bias-corrected GEOGLOWS model exhibited better performance than the GloFAS model version 3.0 calibration for the lower 40% of the cases
the uncalibrated GloFAS model version 2.1 still showed better overall performance than the uncalibrated GEOGLOWS model.

chunks.text: Users of global hydrologic services often cannot calibrate key model components because they lack control over meteorological drivers and internal model parameters. While results are accessible via REST APIs and web services, the inability to recalibrate rainfall-runoff or routing models motivates bias correction as a practical post-processing approach. Bias correction allows local adjustment using user-provided observed data without changing model parameters. This framing supports MFDC-QM as an accessible alternative to calibration for local decision-making.
supporting_quote: they do not have control over the meteorological drivers, rainfall-runoff model and/or the routing model that allows them to calibrate and/or validate the global models on their own.
using bias correction as a post-processing technique ... allows users to modify the model output directly and locally with their own data without changing the model parameters.

chunks.text: The MFDC-QM approach is limited to gauged locations because it requires observed streamflow to build observed monthly flow duration curves. The authors emphasize that bias-corrected values can only be generated where observations exist, leaving geographic gaps. They note related work (SABER) that extends bias correction to ungauged areas based on similar principles, but this is not inherent to MFDC-QM. Future efforts may use other observation types (e.g., water levels) to address sparse streamflow data.
supporting_quote: The bias-corrected values from GEOGLOWS can only be generated in locations where observed data are available.
future bias correction efforts may consider incorporating the more abundantly available water level estimates derived from ground or satellite-based sources

chunks.text: Because the study applies bias correction using the entire available observed dataset, it does not provide an independent validation of the bias correction procedure itself. The authors explicitly state that they lack “validation” results for MFDC-QM under this setup. They propose future work to apply MFDC-QM to GEOGLOWS forecast datasets and compare corrected forecasts to observations. This would complete evaluation across historical performance, calibration surrogate, and forecast validation contexts.
supporting_quote: As we used the entire available dataset to perform the bias correction, we do not have "validation" results on the proposed bias correction method.
In future work, we need to apply the MFDC-QM bias correction method to a GEOGLOWS forecast dataset and compare the resulting corrected values with the observed values

chunks.text: Some regions remain less accurate even after bias correction due to issues not resolved by quantile mapping. The paper attributes residual inaccuracies to factors such as nonstationarity in observed records (e.g., dam construction periods), data quality problems (spikes and outliers) affecting observed flow duration curves, and timing mismatches where MFDC-QM corrects magnitude but not timing. The authors suggest alternative preprocessing such as removing spikes/outliers and using more recent stationary portions. Addressing time mismatch may require methods beyond MFDC-QM.
supporting_quote: inaccuracies may be attributed to ... nonstationarity in observed time series, including periods with dam constructions
MFDC-QM method corrects the magnitude but not the timing of these processes.

chunks.text: MFDC-QM relies on the assumption of similar observed and simulated flow duration curve shapes, which may not hold universally. When shapes differ, the method is unlikely to produce accurate results, limiting reliability in certain basins or regimes. The paper acknowledges this and uses correlations between observed and simulated FDCs as a diagnostic. This limitation is inherent to distribution-matching approaches and affects generalizability without further safeguards.
supporting_quote: operates under the assumption that ... simulated flow duration curve is similar to that of the observed flow duration curve, except for the bias.
If the shape of the flow duration curves ... are significantly different, it is unlikely that the MFDC-QM method will produce accurate results.

chunks.text: GEOGLOWS historical simulations are valuable but contain systematic biases that limit accuracy, particularly in variable regimes and human-influenced rivers. The MFDC-QM monthly quantile-mapping approach effectively reduces these biases, improving simulated streamflow magnitude and seasonality and providing a practical surrogate for “calibrated” values. The authors emphasize that MFDC-QM improves simulations only where observed data are available. They also argue the approach is model-agnostic and could be applied broadly to other hydrologic models with gauge-linked outputs.
supporting_quote: The proposed MFDC-QM bias correction methodology effectively reduces these biases, improving the accuracy of the simulated streamflow and providing a surrogate to "calibrated" values
It is essential to recognize that the MFDC-QM method improves simulations only where observed data is available and does not ensure better performance in ungauged areas.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that MFDC-QM not only corrects magnitude but can also adjust seasonal patterns and reflect effects of human interventions such as hydraulic structures and dam-regulated flows. It reports that the method performs well across different regions, climate groups, watershed areas, and observed time-series lengths, with extended analyses provided in supplementary material. This supports use in applications like water resources management, flood/drought forecasting, and climate-change impact assessment. However, large geographic gaps without observations still limit where improvements can be computed.
supporting_quote: MFDC-QM method ... not only corrects the magnitude ... but also adjusts the seasonality, as well as accounting for human interventions in streams such as hydraulic structures and dam-regulated flows.
there are still large gaps where no hydrological information is available, and the assessment on the GEOGLOWS model cannot be carried out.

chunks.text: MFDC-QM is presented as a quantile-mapping bias correction independent of underlying model structure, enabling potential transfer to other regional or global hydrologic models. The key practical requirement is that model outputs can be associated with known streamflow gauge measurements and formatted for use (e.g., within the GEOGLOWS Python package). This portability is framed as a major contribution because it allows local post-processing improvements without modifying core model parameters. The conclusion highlights excitement about this general applicability.
supporting_quote: MFDC-QM, involves a quantile-mapping bias correction approach independent of the underlying model structure. Therefore, it could be applied to any regional or global hydrological model
The method requires that the hydrologic model outputs be associated with known streamflow gauge measurements and that the data be formatted for input and use within the GEOGLOWS Python package

chunks.text: The East and Gulf coasts of the United States have recently faced more frequent and intense tropical storms and hurricanes, which generate extreme precipitation and catastrophic flooding. These hydrologic extremes threaten public safety and major infrastructure assets, creating strong demand for reliable early-warning streamflow forecasts. Because flood impacts depend on local orography, geomorphology, and hydrology, forecasting skill must generalize across diverse basins.
supporting_quote: the East and Gulf coasts of the United States have experienced an increase in both the frequency and intensity of tropical storms and hurricanes
often leading to catastrophic flooding
Such hydrological extremes pose a significant threat to public safety, affecting over 40 % of the U.S. population

chunks.text: Hydrologic forecasting relies on rainfall–runoff models that may be physically based or data driven. Physically based models simplify complex processes and face uncertainties in initial conditions, forcing data, model structure, and parameters. Data-driven models can be accurate but depend heavily on training data and may lack physical interpretability, motivating hybrid and uncertainty-aware approaches.

chunks.text: Probabilistic forecasting is increasingly used because deterministic models can miss unprecedented extremes. The paper distinguishes epistemic uncertainty (reducible, knowledge-driven) from aleatory uncertainty (irreducible randomness, e.g., measurement/atmospheric variability). Probabilistic methods can provide predictive intervals that better support disaster preparedness and risk management.

Two types of uncertainties involved in hydrologic modeling are epistemic and aleatoric uncertainties.
