chunks.text: The study aims to develop a reliable one-step-ahead daily streamflow forecasting framework that explicitly accounts for both epistemic and aleatory uncertainties, emphasizing extreme events. The core model uses Monte Carlo dropout in an LSTM (LSTM-MC) to represent model uncertainty. The framework also uses wavelet decomposition of observed discharge and perturbation of forcing inputs to estimate total uncertainty.

The intent is to demonstrate real-world applicability for forecasting during extreme hydrologic events. Performance is compared against multiple deterministic and probabilistic baselines.

chunks.text: Deterministic rainfall–runoff models are limited in representing uncertainty, reducing reliability during extremes. This limitation is especially critical when forecasting unprecedented events where single-value predictions may miss peaks. The paper positions probabilistic predictive intervals as necessary to better capture the range of possible streamflow outcomes in extreme events.

chunks.text: A central challenge is jointly representing epistemic (model) and aleatory (input/measurement) uncertainty in daily streamflow forecasts. Epistemic uncertainty arises from lack of knowledge and can be reduced, while aleatory uncertainty reflects irreducible randomness such as measurement errors. Many approaches quantify only one uncertainty type, motivating a framework that estimates total uncertainty.
supporting_quote: Epistemic uncertainty stems from a lack of knowledge or understanding of the processes
aleatory uncertainty arises from inherent randomness in natural systems, exemplified by the measurement errors
PLSTM-WT1, quantifies only model uncertainty, while the second, PLSTM-WT2, includes input perturbation to account for aleatory uncertainty

chunks.text: Forecast accuracy during Hurricane Harvey-like extremes is hindered by limited historical examples of such rare events in training data. As a result, even accurate models for medium flows may underpredict peaks. The paper treats this as a key motivation for probabilistic intervals that still capture peak flows even when the ensemble mean is biased low.

chunks.text: The probabilistic backbone is an LSTM with Monte Carlo dropout (LSTM-MC), where dropout is activated during prediction to sample from an approximate Bayesian posterior. Multiple forward passes produce a distribution of outputs, and output variability indicates epistemic uncertainty. This supports probabilistic prediction intervals rather than a single deterministic forecast.
supporting_quote: The LSTM-MC employs Monte Carlo dropout, which involves randomly excluding a few neural network units during the testing phase
dropout could be leveraged as a sampling method for Bayesian inference, thereby giving rise to the term Monte Carlo (MC) dropout.
for a single input, the model is run multiple times with activated dropout, each time producing a slightly different output

chunks.text: Wavelet Transform (WT) is used to decompose observed discharge time series into components to help identify trends and improve forecasting. The study uses Discrete Wavelet Transform and selects an optimal wavelet and decomposition level based on prior methodology. The chosen configuration is Daubechies 5 (db5) with decomposition level 3.

Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) is often used to decompose hydrologic time series

chunks.text: To represent aleatory uncertainty in forcings and observations, the framework perturbs input datasets and uses an ensemble approach. Precipitation error is modeled multiplicatively using a lognormal distribution with zero mean and relative error 5–25%. Observed streamflow errors are assumed heteroscedastic normal with relative error 5–25%, enabling ensemble-based uncertainty propagation through the model.
supporting_quote: we perturb the model's forcings for a range of perturbation factors (5–25 %)
Recognizing the multiplicative nature of error in precipitation, we employed a lognormal error distribution with a zero mean and a relative error of 5–25 %

chunks.text: Two probabilistic model variants are constructed to isolate and then combine uncertainty sources. PLSTM-WT1 includes LSTM-MC with WT but no input perturbation, thus capturing only epistemic uncertainty. PLSTM-WT2 adds perturbed inputs to capture both epistemic and aleatory uncertainties, aiming to estimate total predictive uncertainty more reliably.
supporting_quote: The first framework, PLSTM-WT1, quantifies only model uncertainty
the second, PLSTM-WT2, includes input perturbation to account for aleatory uncertainty, providing a comprehensive estimate of total uncertainty.
PLSTM-WT1 is a probabilistic model without input perturbation, estimating only epistemic uncertainty

chunks.text: Perturbation factors and ensemble size are tuned per basin using validation performance, following Moradkhani et al. (2005). The process explores perturbation factors from 5% to 25% and ensemble sizes from 10 to 100, then selects settings based on probabilistic metrics such as NRR and Reliability. Selected settings are then applied to the testing dataset.

chunks.text: The overall probabilistic inference is computationally structured as nested sampling: an input ensemble and Monte Carlo dropout samples per ensemble member. The framework uses 100 ensemble members and an MC sampling size of 100, requiring 10,000 total model runs per forecast. This design produces predictive intervals capturing total uncertainty.

The Monte Carlo sampling size is set at 100

chunks.text: Deterministic baselines include Random Forest (RF), LSTM, LSTM enhanced with wavelet-decomposed streamflow (LSTM-WT), and a TCN with attention. Probabilistic benchmarks include LSTM-GMM (mixture density network) and the two proposed probabilistic frameworks. Hyperparameters are tuned using grid search and models are compared using metrics such as NSE, KGE, PCC, RMSE and probabilistic reliability measures.

Hurricane Harvey (2017) provides the focal extreme event, with extraordinary rainfall and severe flooding. Twenty-four basins are selected for case-study evaluation using USGS gauges in the region.

chunks.text: Across deterministic baselines, LSTM outperforms Random Forest, supporting the benefit of sequence modeling for streamflow. Reported improvements of LSTM over RF are 12% (NSE), 42% (KGE), 6% (PCC), and 2% (RMSE). This establishes LSTM as a stronger baseline for subsequent enhancements.

chunks.text: Adding wavelet-decomposed observed streamflow as an input feature substantially improves deterministic LSTM performance. The paper attributes these gains to WT’s ability to identify trends in the discharge signal.

chunks.text: The proposed PLSTM-WT2 probabilistic framework provides the best overall accuracy among all tested models, including deterministic alternatives. Compared with the basic LSTM, PLSTM-WT2 improves NSE by 45%, KGE by 40%, PCC by 9%, and RMSE by 40%. chunks.text: Hydrological models are essential tools for simulating the hydrologic cycle and supporting streamflow prediction, water resources management, and risk assessment for extremes such as floods and droughts. However, these models simplify complex processes and face a trade-off between simplicity and accuracy. As a result, their streamflow predictions are impacted by multiple uncertainty sources, motivating the use of downstream correction strategies.
supporting_quote: Hydrological models serve as mathematical frameworks that enable the simulation and prediction of various aspects of the hydrologic cycle.
The streamflow prediction generated by these models is prone to different uncertainties in forcing data, initial condition, model structure, and parameterization

chunks.text: Data-driven machine learning approaches can flexibly capture non-linear relationships and evolving system behavior without explicit physical knowledge. Prior work has shown strong performance for streamflow prediction using ML/DL models. Yet purely data-driven methods can be limited by reliance on training data and lack of explicit physical mechanisms, which can hinder causal understanding and extrapolation.
supporting_quote: Data-driven models are the alternative to physically based models with the advantage of being more flexible in handling complex relationships without the need for explicit knowledge of underlying physical principles.
However, these models are subject to some shortcomings as they fully rely on available training data and lack a physical mechanism, hindering their ability to comprehend causal relationships.

chunks.text: Hydrologic post-processing uses observed streamflow to correct model outputs and can be implemented with deterministic or probabilistic methods. Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA) is widely used to integrate multiple models, but its standard form often assumes Gaussian conditional distributions. Copula-Embedded BMA (COP-BMA) was introduced to avoid restrictive distributional assumptions and to estimate posterior predictive distributions more flexibly.
supporting_quote: Hydrological post-processing primarily leverages observed streamflow data to improve the accuracy of simulated streamflow outputs
The BMA approach, as outlined by Raftery et al., 2005, assumes that the conditional Probability Distribution Function (PDF) of each model follows a normal distribution.
Madadgar and Moradkhani, 2014 proposed the Copula-Embedded Bayesian Model Averaging (COP-BMA) method

chunks.text: The study aims to develop a two-step probabilistic post-processing framework that improves hydrologic-model streamflow predictions. It first applies multiple machine-learning/statistical postprocessors to deterministic hydrologic simulations and then integrates those postprocessed outputs via COP-BMA. The framework is intended to improve accuracy while producing probabilistic predictions that account for uncertainty across postprocessing structures.
supporting_quote: This study proposes a two-step probabilistic post-processing approach that combines different machine learningbased postprocessors through the Copula-Embedded Bayesian Model Averaging (COP-BMA) method

The proposed approach serves a two-fold purpose: firstly, it aims to enhance the accuracy of streamflow predictions, and secondly, it provides probabilistic results that implicitly address the structural uncertainty inherent in different postprocessing methods.

chunks.text: The framework is validated on extreme flooding conditions associated with Hurricane Harvey and tested across twelve watersheds in Southeast Texas at daily and monthly time scales. The evaluation includes overall performance and focused assessment in medium-to-high flow regimes (e.g., exceedance above 75th and 90th percentiles).
supporting_quote: We validate our approach by applying it to the Conceptual Functional Equivalent, a lumped hydrologic model utilized for simulating extreme floods during Hurricane Harvey.
The validation is conducted across twelve distinct watersheds in the Southeast Texas region at both daily and monthly scales.
evaluate the proposed framework in medium-to-high flow events in the studied watersheds.

chunks.text: Hydrologic predictions are affected by diverse uncertainty sources including forcing, initial conditions, structure, and parameterization. These uncertainties can degrade streamflow simulation skill, especially during extremes. Addressing uncertainty is therefore central to improving operational usefulness of model outputs.
supporting_quote: The streamflow prediction generated by these models is prone to different uncertainties in forcing data, initial condition, model structure, and parameterization

chunks.text: Many studies improve streamflow by coupling a single postprocessor to a hydrologic model, but postprocessors themselves are data-driven and prone to structural uncertainty. Relying on one postprocessor can therefore introduce additional model-form risk. The paper treats this as a motivation to integrate multiple postprocessors and quantify uncertainty in their outputs.
supporting_quote: Most studies couple a postprocessor with the hydrologic model to improve the streamflow prediction skill.
However, these postprocessors are data-driven models that are inherently prone to structural uncertainty.

chunks.text: Standard BMA often assumes Gaussian conditional predictive distributions, which may be invalid for hydrologic variables. When this assumption fails, careful distribution selection or transformations may be required, complicating postprocessing. COP-BMA is positioned as a remedy by estimating posterior distributions using copulas without assuming a specific parametric form.
supporting_quote: The BMA approach, as outlined by Raftery et al., 2005, assumes that the conditional Probability Distribution Function (PDF) of each model follows a normal distribution.
past studies demonstrated that this assumption may not hold for certain forecast variables
COP-BMA... allows for estimating the posterior distribution of model predictions without assuming the specific form of the distribution or performing data transformation.

chunks.text: The proposed workflow integrates a hydrologic model (CFE), multiple deterministic postprocessors, and COP-BMA to generate probabilistic streamflow at daily and monthly scales. Deterministic postprocessors first correct CFE simulations, and COP-BMA then combines these corrected series into a probabilistic predictive distribution. The process is implemented separately for each watershed and time scale.
supporting_quote: This study proposes an integration of a hydrologic model, i.e., CFE, multiple postprocessors, and the COP-BMA technique.
Subsequently, we employ COP-BMA to combine the outputs of various post-processing models and generate probabilistic predictions

chunks.text: At the daily time scale, three deep learning postprocessors are used: LSTM, CNN, and MLP. They are trained with simulated streamflow and meteorological variables (plus observed streamflow history) to predict improved daily streamflow. The resulting deterministic postprocessed series are then passed to COP-BMA for probabilistic combination.
supporting_quote: To enhance the accuracy of daily streamflow predictions, we employ three commonly postprocessor methods: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP).
The improved streamflow predicted by the postprocessors is fed into COP-BMA to train its parameters.

chunks.text: At the monthly time scale, three postprocessors are used: Quantile Mapping (QM), Copula-based bias correction, and Support Vector Regression (SVR). QM adjusts CDF-based quantiles between simulations and observations; copulas capture dependence structures; SVR uses nonlinear mappings with hyperparameter tuning. COP-BMA then integrates these monthly postprocessed outputs into probabilistic predictions.
supporting_quote: To improve monthly streamflow predictions, we utilize three widely used methods: Quantile Mapping (QM), Copula functions, and Support Vector Regression (SVR).
The QM approach involves identifying the prediction quantile for a specific time from the simulation CDF and then selecting the corresponding observed quantile
In the third monthly postprocessor, we use Copulas

chunks.text: Training/testing is organized with CFE calibrated on 2006–2016, then tested on 2017–2019. Postprocessors are trained during 2006–2016 using CFE simulations and meteorological inputs, with the last 20% of the training period used for validation. COP-BMA parameters are trained using postprocessor outputs, and multi-modeling is done separately for each month to account for seasonality.
supporting_quote: calibrating the CFE model using meteorological forcing data spanning from 2006 to 2016
In the test phase... for the years 2017 to 2019.
In this study the last 20 % of the training data is considered as the validation dataset.
Multi-modeling was conducted separately for each month of the year to account for seasonality effects.

chunks.text: To reduce missing-value issues in daily predictions, COP-BMA is implemented on five-day averaged predictions. Training lengths are varied and evaluated on the validation set to ensure stable BMA weights. This design is meant to improve robustness when gaps in daily time series are present.
supporting_quote: For the implementation of COP-BMA, we utilized five-day predictions (averaged daily predictions over five days) to lessen the issue of missing values in daily predictions.
we trained the BMA using various training lengths and evaluated it on the validation dataset to ensure that the BMA's weights were accurately determined

chunks.text: COP-BMA replaces Gaussian conditional PDFs in BMA with copula-based posterior estimation, yielding a predictive distribution as a weighted sum of copula-informed posteriors. Model weights are estimated via an Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm that maximizes a log-likelihood involving copula densities. Marginal distributions and copula families are selected via statistical tests (K-S, AIC) and a bootstrap-based Cramér–von Mises statistic.
supporting_quote: In the COP-BMA approach, the expression g(y|f_i,\sigma_i^2)... is replaced with a set of multivariate copula functions.
The Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm is used to determine the weights of the BMA.
the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) and the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) tests are used to find the best marginal distribution.
Five copula functions are tried: Gaussian and t... and Gumbel, Clayton, and Frank

chunks.text: The hydrologic backbone is the Conceptual Functional Equivalent (CFE), a simplified conceptual version of the National Water Model with seventeen parameters. CFE is calibrated using Dynamically Dimensioned Search (DDS) with RMSE as the objective. chunks.text: Floods are major natural disasters that cause large economic losses and fatalities, and accurate flood forecasting is important for early warning and risk reduction. chunks.text: Data-driven streamflow models, including deep learning, have shown promise but depend on learned patterns from historical training data. Their ability to forecast rare or unobserved extremes is limited when such events are scarce in the training record. This motivates approaches that increase training diversity and better represent extreme hydrologic behavior.

chunks.text: Standard GANs can generate realistic samples but are not inherently designed to preserve sequential temporal dependencies, which are critical for time-series forecasting. TimeGAN was developed to better preserve temporal dynamics in generated sequences by combining adversarial learning with sequence modeling, making it suitable for multivariate hydrologic time series generation.

chunks.text: The study proposes a generative machine learning framework to enhance streamflow forecasting accuracy during extreme events by augmenting scarce high-flow training data. It integrates TimeGAN for synthetic multivariate flood sequence generation (meteorology plus discharge), uses LSTM for multi-step forecasting, and incorporates wavelet transform decomposition to better capture multi-scale dynamics. The framework is validated on Hurricane Harvey impacts across 24 Southeast Texas basins.
supporting_quote: this study proposes a generative machine learning framework to enhance the accuracy of streamflow forecasting, with a particular focus on extreme events.

The framework integrates TimeGAN to augment the training dataset by specifically generating the synthetic multivariate sequence of high flow events, incorporating weather and observed streamflow data.
The proposed framework is validated through a real-world case study of Hurricane Harvey.

chunks.text: A specific objective is to quantify how wavelet transform preprocessing affects LSTM forecasting performance under different configurations. The study compares applying WT to discharge only versus applying WT to all input variables. This comparison is used to identify an effective and parsimonious way to leverage WT for streamflow prediction.

chunks.text: Flood forecasting models depend strongly on the length and quality of training data, but historical records often include too few flood events. When extreme events are scarce, both physically based models (calibrated to frequent flows) and data-driven models (learning dominant historical patterns) can degrade in skill for rare floods. The paper targets this data scarcity as a core barrier to accurate extreme flood forecasting.

chunks.text: The forecasting backbone is an LSTM trained for multi-step-ahead streamflow prediction using meteorological forcings and discharge history. Q = HBV(Xθ, θ)
we did not need any ground truth for the parameters — the only observational data used for model training was streamflow.

chunks.text: A fusion LSTM (NNf) generates time-dependent weights for three precipitation datasets and produces fused basin-mean precipitation as a weighted sum. NNf takes as inputs the three precipitation series plus Daymet temperature and PET, along with selected static attributes. The fused precipitation is then used as the precipitation input to HBV while other forcings remain from Daymet.
supporting_quote: an additional LSTM network (NNf, called fusion-LSTM henceforth) fuses the forcings datasets by generating weights (w)
Xf = [PDaymet, PMaurer, PNLDAS, TDaymet, PETDaymet]
Pfused = ∑ wi Pi
The forcings in Xθ thus become [Pfused,T, PET]

chunks.text: To reduce co-adaptation between parameter learning and forcing fusion, training is staged. NNθ is pre-trained with δHBV using Daymet forcings and streamflow observations, then its weights are frozen. Afterward, NNf (and a routing-parameter ANN) are trained using streamflow loss backpropagated through δHBV to adjust precipitation weights.
supporting_quote: to reduce coadaptation, we trained the two NNs in two separate stages — NNθ was pre-trained
NNf was trained after the weights of NNθ were frozen
The pretraining process aims to learn physical parameters that address (or compensate for) model structural errors

chunks.text: Routing parameters are re-estimated during fusion training to handle timing differences and aggregation effects across forcing datasets. A separate static ANN with three hidden layers (128, 64, 32) generates routing parameters for the intermediate fused precipitation. This ANN is trained jointly with NNf while NNθ remains fixed.
supporting_quote: the routing parameters, which can compensate for such errors, need to be retrained when a different forcing dataset is used.
we train a fully connected artificial neural network (ANN) network to generate routing parameters separately.
three hidden layers with hidden sizes of 128, 64, and 32
The fusion LSTM and the routing ANN shared the same optimizer.

chunks.text: A soft range-bound regularization term penalizes deviations of the sum of fusion weights from approximately mass-conserving bounds. The total loss is streamflow loss plus Lw, and Lw applies if the cumulative weights fall outside 0.95 to 1.05. The penalty strength α2 is tuned and set to 23.0 based on validation.
supporting_quote: introducing a penalty, Lw, to the precipitation weights in the loss function:
Ltotal = Lstreamflow + Lw
Lw imposes a penalty on the model if the cumulative summation of weights exceeds the specified range of 0.95 to 1.05.
a value of 23.0 was selected as the optimum factor based on validation.

chunks.text: A single-forcing correction baseline is tested where NN outputs a time-dependent multiplicative weight applied to one dataset’s precipitation. The corrected precipitation is then used in HBV, and a range-bound penalty constrains weights (e.g., 0.9–1.1 for Daymet/NLDAS and 0.8–1.2 for Maurer). This baseline assesses whether adaptive scaling alone can mitigate precipitation errors.
supporting_quote: We also tested a single-forcing data-correction approach where time-dependent weights for a single forcing dataset (wforcing) were output
Pcorrected = Wforcing Pforcing
A range-bound loss function (Eq. (8)) was employed to penalize any individual weight that deviated from the predefined ranges: (0.9–1.1) for Daymet, (0.9–1.1) for NLDAS, and (0.8–1.2) for Maurer.

chunks.text: Model evaluation uses multiple hydrologic metrics emphasizing overall fit and flow-regime errors. Reported metrics include median NSE and KGE, RMSE for low flows (bottom 30%) and high flows (top 2%), and absolute bias in low-flow and high-flow volumes (FLV, FHV). A data-driven benchmark uses the Kratzert et al. (2021) LSTM, including a variant that replaces Daymet precipitation with the fused precipitation.
supporting_quote: The models were evaluated based on Nash-Sutcliffe model efficiency coefficient (NSE)
Kling-Gupta model efficiency coefficient (KGE)
high-flow (top 2 % of flow) and low-flow (bottom 30 % of flow) root-mean-square error (RMSE)
percentage of absolute bias for low-flow volume (FLV) and high-flow volume (FHV).
we used the model developed by Kratzert et al. (2021)

chunks.text: The differentiable nature of the framework enables analysis of how fusion weights respond to inputs through automatic differentiation. Using PyTorch, the study computes sensitivities (gradients) of weights with respect to static landscape attributes such as elevation and slope. This supports interpretation of where and why each precipitation dataset is emphasized.
supporting_quote: Since the entire framework is differentiable, we can obtain the sensitivity of weights to the input variables using automatic differentiation supported in PyTorch.
found that elevation and slope were particularly impactful (Fig. 2).

chunks.text: Experiments use the CAMELS dataset covering 671 CONUS catchments, including basin-averaged forcings and observed streamflow. The fusion focuses on three precipitation products packaged in CAMELS: Daymet, NLDAS, and Maurer. Static basin attributes from CAMELS are used for parameterization and for selecting fusion-relevant predictors.
supporting_quote: CAMELS contains hydro-meteorological forcings, static attributes, and observed streamflow records for 671 distinct catchments
We fused the three basin-averaged datasets packaged with CAMELS, namely, Daymet, NLDAS, and Maurer
Aθ are the static location-specific attributes

chunks.text: The fusion model inputs include three precipitation time series (Daymet, Maurer, NLDAS) and uses Daymet temperature and PET. The subset of static attributes for fusion (Af) is chosen to reflect likely controls on precipitation error, including elevation, slope, fraction of precipitation as snow, aridity, and precipitation statistics (e.g., high/low event duration and frequency).
supporting_quote: Xf = [PDaymet, PMaurer, PNLDAS, TDaymet, PETDaymet]
NNf only used a subset of attributes (Af)... such as elevation, fraction of precipitation as snow, slope, and precipitation statistics
elev_mean
slope_mean
frac_snow_daily

chunks.text: Training and testing follow fixed time splits across basins. The model is trained from 1 October 1980 to 30 September 1995 and tested from 1 October 1995 to 30 September 2008. Optimization uses AdaDelta and sequence batching with one-year (365-day) windows.
supporting_quote: The model was trained from 1 October 1980 to 30 September 1995, and tested from 1 October 1995 to 30 September 2008.
AdaDelta was used as the optimization algorithm
a time series length of 365 days

chunks.text: Station-based precipitation observations from GHCN-D are used for independent evaluation of the fused basin precipitation in basins with overlap. The assessment mentioned focuses on 126 basins with available gauge-based data and compares correlation and bias across forcing alternatives. This provides an observational check beyond streamflow-based training.
supporting_quote: Based on an assessment in 126 basins that overlapped with available gauge-based (GHCN-D) data
GHCN-D can be downloaded from https://datadryad.org/stash/dataset/doi:10.5061/dryad.7tv80

chunks.text: Using fused precipitation in δHBV improves streamflow simulation compared with single-forcing δHBV (Daymet), with especially strong gains in high flows. Median NSE increases from 0.74 to about 0.77–0.78 and KGE from 0.76 to 0.77, while high-flow RMSE decreases from 3.86 to as low as 3.64 mm/day. Low-flow RMSE remains similar, indicating most benefits are in peaks and extremes.
supporting_quote: Compared to the single-forcing (Daymet) δHBV model, the NSE value for the fusion framework was improved from 0.74 to 0.77 while KGE increased from 0.76 to 0.77
the high flow mean RMSE was reduced from 3.86 to 3.64 mm/day, while low-flow mean RMSE stayed similar.
δHBV-Fused P ... Median NSE 0.78 ... Median KGE 0.77

chunks.text: Constraining the sum of fusion weights via the range-bound penalty has only minor effects and can slightly worsen RMSE. The paper notes that when applying the penalty, low-flow and high-flow RMSE became slightly worse, suggesting the regularization is not crucial for performance in this setup. This indicates the fusion already tends to near-mass-conserving solutions without strong constraints.
supporting_quote: The regularization function (Eq. (7)) applied to constrain the sum of weights in the fusion approach had a minor impact on the performance.
When we used the range-bound loss function as a penalty, the means of low-flow and high-flow RMSE became slightly worse
Lw imposes a penalty... if the cumulative summation of weights exceeds the specified range of 0.95 to 1.05.

chunks.text: Multi-forcing fusion in δHBV approaches but remains slightly below a multi-forcing LSTM benchmark. The LSTM achieves NSE around 0.80 (and KGE about 0.79–0.80), while the fused δHBV is slightly lower (median NSE about 0.77–0.78). The consistent performance gap suggests remaining constraints or structural differences between mass-conserving process-based modeling and unconstrained LSTM fitting.
supporting_quote: The δHBV model using the fusion framework approached but remained slightly below the multiforcing LSTM, which had an NSE of 0.80 and KGE of 0.79
δHBV-Fused P ... Median NSE 0.78
LSTM – Fused P ... Median NSE 0.79 ... Median KGE 0.80

chunks.text: Adaptive correction of a single precipitation dataset provides only minor improvements relative to using multiple datasets. Reported reductions in mean high-flow RMSE from single-forcing correction are small (0.11, 0.23, and 0.39 mm/day for Daymet, NLDAS, and Maurer), and low-flow RMSE decreases by only about 0.01 mm/day. This suggests the fusion benefit comes primarily from adding complementary information rather than scaling one dataset.
supporting_quote: utilizing an adaptive weight for a single precipitation source... had only a minor benefit for hydrologic simulations.
The mean high-low RMSE decreased only by 0.11 mm/day, 0.23 mm/day, and 0.39 mm/day with biascorrected Daymet, NLDAS, and Maurer precipitation, respectively
while the low-flow RMSE decreased by just 0.01 mm/day

chunks.text: Simple averaging of precipitation datasets is not effective and can degrade hydrologic performance. The δHBV-Average P configuration shows reduced performance relative to better single-forcing or fused approaches, indicating errors are not uniform across datasets. This supports the need for adaptive, learned weighting rather than static combination rules.
supporting_quote: the simple fusion method of averaging the three datasets was not at all suitable, as it actually reduced streamflow performance (δHBV-Average P in Table 1).
This indicates that the forcing errors were not uniform, highlighting the need for an adaptive fusion method

chunks.text: The learned fusion weights indicate Daymet is the dominant source, with CONUS-average effective weight around 0.6, while NLDAS and Maurer contribute around 0.2 each. Spatially, NLDAS weights increase in the humid eastern US, and Maurer gains weight in mountainous/northwestern regions. These patterns suggest the network selects datasets differently by region based on performance-relevant characteristics.
supporting_quote: Overall, Daymet had the highest weights (CONUS average ~ 0.6), while NLDAS and Maurer had comparably lower weights (CONUS average ~ 0.2)
NLDAS's importance rose in the eastern US, and Maurer was used more along the northwestern coast

chunks.text: The sum of effective weights is generally close to 1, implying the fusion emphasizes reweighting rather than large bias correction. The reported range is about 0.92–1.07 for most basins, with higher sums in the northern US and mountainous west. This suggests modest net amplification in snow-affected regions, consistent with the authors’ speculation about snow undercatch.
supporting_quote: The sum of learned effective time-integrated weights ... was generally between 0.92 and 1.07
Higher w' values (above 1.0) were observed in the northern half of the US, particularly in the Northeast and the mountainous regions

chunks.text: Against station-based GHCN-D precipitation in 126 overlapping basins, the fused precipitation has the highest correlation for the largest share of basins and near-smallest bias for large storms. Median bias for large-magnitude storms is essentially the same as Daymet and better than NLDAS, Maurer, or the simple average. This aligns with improved high-flow performance in streamflow simulation.
supporting_quote: in 126 basins that overlapped with available gauge-based (GHCN-D) data, the fused P showed the highest correlation with GHCN-D data
It also showed close to the smallest error for large-magnitude storms
For large-magnitude storms, the fused P's median biases were essentially the same as Daymet

chunks.text: The fused precipitation transfers to an external LSTM model, improving rainfall–runoff performance even outside the differentiable HBV context. When the Kratzert-style LSTM uses fused precipitation (with other forcings from one dataset), median NSE rises from 0.74 to 0.79 and KGE from 0.77 to 0.80 compared to Daymet precipitation. This suggests the fused precipitation captures generally useful precipitation information, not only HBV-specific compensation.
supporting_quote: As we trained an LSTM using the fused P, NSE increased from 0.74 to 0.79 and KGE increased from 0.77 to 0.80
LSTM – Daymet ... Median NSE 0.74 ... Median KGE 0.77
LSTM – Fused P ... Median NSE 0.79 ... Median KGE 0.80

chunks.text: Pre-training NNθ on the best single forcing (Daymet) yields the strongest subsequent fusion performance. Fusion-δHBV median NSE/KGE are 0.77/0.77 for Daymet-trained pretraining, compared with 0.74/0.73 (Maurer), 0.72/0.68 (NLDAS), and 0.67/0.71 (Average-P). This supports selecting the best-performing forcing for pretraining in the staged setup.
supporting_quote: Pre-training the parameterization network based on the best-performing single forcing (Daymet) yielded better results
Table A2  Performance ... Daymet-trained 0.77 0.77 ... Maurer-trained 0.74 0.73 ... NLDAS-trained 0.72 0.68 ... Average-P-trained 0.67 0.71

chunks.text: The fused precipitation is produced at basin scale and is not intended as a general gridded precipitation product. The authors caution that its main purpose is improving streamflow prediction, and its applicability to other uses requires careful testing. Basin aggregation limits direct transfer to other spatial scales without additional development.
supporting_quote: Because the fused P can only be produced at the basin scale, we do not regard it as a new precipitation product
we caution against using the fused precipitation for purposes other than streamflow prediction unless rigorously tested.

chunks.text: Some learned precipitation-weight patterns may reflect compensation for hydrologic model structural errors rather than true precipitation corrections. The paper explicitly notes that weights might adjust for HBV structural limitations, complicating interpretation. This ambiguity limits the ability to attribute changes solely to forcing quality improvements.
supporting_quote: However, one should note that the learned weights might compensate for structural errors rather than solely correcting precipitation bias.

chunks.text: Differentiable HBV faces known structural challenges in simulating zero or near-zero flows, contributing to higher low-flow RMSE and limiting improvements in low-flow regimes. The authors attribute this to HBV structure and mention potential mitigation using implicit numerical solutions and process updates. Thus, forcing fusion mainly improves peaks rather than addressing low-flow structural issues.
supporting_quote: Due to structural limitations of HBV, the differentiable models faced challenges in simulating zero or near-zero flows, leading to a higher low-flow RMSE value.
This structural issue can be alleviated using implicit numerical solutions and process updates (Song et al., 2024).

chunks.text: A remaining performance gap versus LSTM is attributed partly to physical constraints (e.g., mass conservation) and to fewer forcing variables used by δHBV. The paper suggests LSTM can exploit additional meteorological inputs (humidity/wind) while δHBV relies on PET and thus has less flexibility. This helps explain why δHBV fusion approaches but does not fully match LSTM performance.
supporting_quote: some physical constraints, e.g., mass conservation, that prevent δHBV from fully matching LSTM in performance.
this discrepancy might be partially attributed to the LSTM's capability to assimilate more forcing variables, e.g., humidity and wind speed
whereas δHBV only utilizes estimated potential evapotranspiration (PET).

chunks.text: The authors speculate that elevated total weights in snow-dominated regions may relate to snow undercatch, but they present this as a hypothesis requiring further testing. They suggest future work could assimilate high-precision snow data to validate whether snow processes explain the added weights and remaining streamflow errors. This indicates an unresolved attribution problem in cold regions.
supporting_quote: These patterns suggest that some of the added weights may be linked to the effects of snow undercatch
Future work can explore whether assimilating high-precision snow data improves streamflow simulation in snow-dominated regions to confirm our speculation.

chunks.text: A differentiable hydrologic modeling framework can learn hydrology-informed fusion of multiple precipitation datasets, yielding substantial streamflow improvements, especially for high flows. The fusion relies most on Daymet while selectively incorporating NLDAS and Maurer information, improving precipitation timing and agreement with gauges. The approach is positioned as a generic method to use multiple forcings for better streamflow prediction under physical constraints.
supporting_quote: Leveraging a differentiable hydrologic model, we trained a neural network to merge multiple forcings.
The new merged forcing greatly improved hydrologic simulations, especially for high flows
The fusion placed the most weight on Daymet
Overall, the differentiable hydrologic model offers a generic hydrology-informed method to utilize multiple sources of meteorological forcing data for improving streamflow predictions.

chunks.text: Fusion of multiple precipitation datasets is more effective than correcting a single dataset with adaptive scaling, implying each forcing source contributes complementary information. The network focuses on landscape attributes like elevation and slope when adjusting weights, and NLDAS and Maurer are emphasized regionally (eastern US and mountain ranges, respectively). This supports the interpretability of the learned fusion patterns within a differentiable framework.
supporting_quote: Fusion of multiple datasets was much more effective than a singleforcing-based correction
The network paid particular attention to static landscape attributes, as they captured the influences of factors like elevation and slope.
NLDAS's weighting increased in the eastern US
Maurer's weighting increased along mountain ranges.

chunks.text: Best practice for the staged training appears to be pretraining the parameterization network on the best-performing single forcing dataset. The paper reports that Daymet-based pretraining leads to the best fusion performance relative to pretraining on Maurer, NLDAS, or the simple average. This highlights the importance of separating structural-parameter learning from forcing fusion with a strong initialization.
supporting_quote: pretraining the parameterization networks on a best-performing single forcing dataset led to the best performance overall for the ensuing fusion process.
Table A2 ... Daymet-trained 0.77 0.77 ... Maurer-trained 0.74 0.73 ... NLDAS-trained 0.72 0.68 ... Average-P-trained 0.67 0.71

chunks.text: GIS processing is offered through desktop and web platforms, each with tradeoffs for raster analytics. Desktop systems can work without internet and leverage powerful computing, but are platform-dependent and hard to distribute and maintain. Web systems are platform-independent and user-friendly, yet commonly rely on servers and network communication for heavy processing and data management.
supporting_quote: Web-based applications are platform-independent, however, require the internet to communicate with servers for data management and processing
stand-alone desktop applications can usually function without relying on the internet, however, they are platform-dependent, making distribution and maintenance of these systems difficult

chunks.text: Growth in raster layer size makes storing, serving, and processing multidimensional gridded data increasingly difficult. Desktop GIS can access workstations or HPC, but development and user onboarding are costly and complex. These barriers also limit data sharing and integration because systems can act as black boxes.
supporting_quote: Since the size of raster layers keeps growing by orders of magnitude, it's difficult for applications to store, serve, and process large amounts of raster data.
difficulties from the perspective of the users, including a steep learning curve and the requirement of sophisticated procedures for installation to local machines

chunks.text: Advances in browser standards and client-side performance have enabled migrating GIS functionality from server to the browser. Progressive Web Applications (PWAs) combine web and native-app traits like offline usage and installation, and are increasingly used in geospatial and environmental domains. However, the full potential of modern web standards for geospatial storage and offline usage is not fully explored.
supporting_quote: Advancements in client-side web technologies and the evolution of web standards ... have propelled the migration of application logic and GIS functionality from server to client-side
The main characteristics of a PWA include, but are not limited to ... offline usage

chunks.text: The study aims to present RasterJS, a hybrid client-side geospatial processing library built as a Progressive Web Application to work in both Online and Offline modes. The goal is to bring raster analytics to the browser while minimizing reliance on external servers. A packaged distribution approach using Web Bundles is also introduced for offline access and sharing.
supporting_quote: This paper presents RasterJS, a hybrid client-side web library for geospatial data processing that is built on the Progressive Web Application (PWA) architecture to operate seamlessly in both Online and Offline modes.
A packaged version of this system is also presented with the help of Web Bundles API for offline access and distribution.

chunks.text: RasterJS is positioned as a proof-of-concept for interactive hydroinformatics tasks on large raster data, performed entirely on the client. The paper targets functions including flow direction computation with hydro-conditioning, watershed delineation, and raindrop flow tracking, plus real-time raster resampling. A large-scale watershed case study in Iowa is used to demonstrate capabilities and limitations.
supporting_quote: As a proof-of-concept, RasterJS is released with flow direction calculation, watershed delineation, and raindrop flow tracking functions
A large-scale case study is included in the study for watershed analysis to demonstrate the capabilities and limitations of the library.

chunks.text: Traditional web GIS often concentrates processing and data management on the server, leaving the client focused on UI. This creates performance bottlenecks from client-server communication, can cause conflicts under concurrent access, and increases server resource costs. The challenge becomes more severe with massive multidimensional raster data and mission-critical needs for timely results.
supporting_quote: client-side code focus on user interface and interaction whereas the server-side application encapsulates the geospatial data resources and functionality
The communication between the clients and the server does not only raise performance issues but also may lead to serverside conflicts or limitations in case of concurrent access

chunks.text: Web-based geospatial applications face difficulties handling large raster volumes when many users request data and processing simultaneously. Massive raster influx threatens affordability of server memory and compute. Data inconsistency and limited benchmark availability can further hinder timely, accurate responses.
supporting_quote: the influx of massive raster data from numerous concurrent users threatens the viability and affordability of utilizing server memory and resources for geospatial processing
Unavailability of large-scale benchmark datasets ... or inconsistency in the data sources may hinder the generation of the desired response effectively and on time.

chunks.text: Offline access is a key barrier for web GIS because internet connectivity may be unstable or absent in field settings. Desktop systems can run locally but are hard to distribute across platforms, while typical web systems depend on online server communication. The work targets bridging this gap to support productive analysis without stable connectivity.
supporting_quote: Web-based applications are platform-independent, however, require the internet to communicate with servers

the users can perform their activities without relying heavily on a stable internet connection as the users can continue analytical activities within the platform even when the internet connection is unstable or absent.

chunks.text: Client-side storage is limited and must be managed carefully, especially when attempting offline raster analytics. Browser caching capacity is constrained, making it unsuitable to cache all resources. Even IndexedDB, while larger, is limited by client disk space and browser-specific allocation policies.
supporting_quote: Since the resources are stored locally in the browser the storage capacity for caching is limited.
Browsers allocate a certain percentage of disk space to IndexedDB and this percentage is browserspecific ... changing between 5 GB to entire available space on the harddisk.

chunks.text: RasterJS is designed as a client-side PWA with three operational modes: Online, Offline, and Web Bundle. It relies on browser-supported JavaScript and web APIs to provide comparable workflows across connectivity conditions. The case-study scope is restricted to five Iowa counties to demonstrate feasibility under realistic data volumes.
supporting_quote: RasterJS is designed to be used via browsers with three modes of use (i.e., Online, Offline, web bundle)
As a case study, the scope/ region of interest of RasterJS is limited to five counties (i.e., Linn, Jones, Johnson, Cedar, Muscatine)

chunks.text: The system architecture combines 3-layer and component-based designs. Components are organized into Presentation, Application, and Data layers to improve modularity and scalability. Background work is separated into service worker and web worker contexts, while sequential logic stays in the main application context.
supporting_quote: The architecture of RasterJS is a hybrid of 3-layer architecture ... and component-based architecture
RasterJS components are distributed into three layers (i.e., Presentation, Application, and Data)

chunks.text: RasterJS uses a service worker to intercept resource requests and support offline functionality. Static resources and OpenStreetMap raster tiles are cached using Cache API during service worker installation and served on fetch events. Large georeferenced images are stored in IndexedDB rather than the Cache API to manage cache size limits.
supporting_quote: Whenever the request is made by the client to fetch resources from the external component it is intercepted by the service worker
Cache API is used ... to cache CSS ... JavaScript ... HTML ... application images, and OpenStreetMap raster tiles
georeferenced images are downloaded in indexedDB for Offline mode

chunks.text: IndexedDB is used as the primary client-side store for georeferenced raster images (as blobs) to enable offline use and lazy loading. The application checks IndexedDB first; if the image is missing in online mode it fetches from the server and stores it for future access. This shifts data management responsibility to the client while reducing repeated network requests.
supporting_quote: RasterJS creates an IndexedDB to store georeferenced images in the form of blobs for Offline mode and lazy loading.
the application first looks for that image in IndexedDB. If the image is found then it is retrieved ... otherwise it fetches the image from the external component and stores the image.

chunks.text: Web Workers are used to prevent UI blocking during computationally intensive raster analytics. Separate workers handle flow direction calculation, watershed delineation, and raindrop tracking. This design aims for a native-like, responsive experience despite heavy client-side processing.
supporting_quote: RasterJS uses this API to perform geospatial analysis calculations.
It uses web workers for the calculation of the flow direction, raindrop tracking and another for watershed delineation.

chunks.text: Mapping and interaction differ by mode: Google Maps API is used online, while OpenLayers renders cached tiles offline. Offline mapping requires specifying tile locations, supported zoom levels, and extent. Both modes support drawing a selection window, projecting georeferenced images, and visualizing watershed or raindrop results.
supporting_quote: Google Maps API is used in Online mode whereas OpenLayers JavaScript library powers the map in Offline mode.
in the Offline Mode, RasterJS provides static map tiles, the extent of these tiles, and a range of zoom levels supported

chunks.text: Georeferencing transforms the selected geographic bounds from EPSG:4326 to EPSG:3857, requests appropriate tiles at a zoom level, and then mosaics and crops them to the target area and resolution. Images are fetched from IndexedDB in offline mode or from a server in online mode. The resulting raster is projected over the map for subsequent analysis.
supporting_quote: These coordinates are then transformed from coordinate pairs (EPSG:4326) to projected coordinates in the Pseudo-Mercator coordinate system (EPSG:3857).
RasterJS then fetches these images either from IndexedDB (offline mode) or from the server (online mode). All of these rasters are mosaicked to form a single image

chunks.text: Flow direction is computed through hydro-conditioning and flat-resolution steps. RasterJS first fills depressions using the Priority Flood algorithm, then applies D8 for non-flat areas. Flat areas are categorized by adjacency to higher or lower terrain, gradients are constructed, and D8 is applied again to obtain final directions; the output can be downloaded.
supporting_quote: First, the georeferenced image is conditioned by using the Priority Flood algorithm.
After this preprocessing step, the D8 algorithm ... is employed for calculating flow direction for non-flat areas only
RasterJS makes this flow direction data available for download for future reference.

chunks.text: The case study focuses on a five-county region in Iowa covering 2,956 mi^2 (7,656 km^2), defined by latitude and longitude bounds. The region of interest is explicitly bounded to support offline tile caching and packaged distribution. This geographic constraint is central to the evaluation design.
supporting_quote: a 5-county extent within the State of Iowa was selected, encompassing an area of 2,956 mi2 (i.e., 7,656 km2 ).
The region of interest was defined by ranges of latitude (41.30, 42.33) and longitude (-92.31, -90.23).

chunks.text: Elevation inputs originate from the Iowa Department of Natural Resources and the Iowa LiDAR Mapping Project. DEM sections were provided as 1-meter ESRI GRIDs in UTM Zone 15N (EPSG:26915) with floating-point elevations. The full dataset size is about 570 GB before subsetting for the project.
supporting_quote: The original georeferenced images or digital elevation model (DEM) data was obtained from the Iowa Department of Natural Resources
The DEM sections were provided as 1-meter ESRI GRIDs projected into the UTM Zone 15 N coordinate system (EPSG:26,915)
Altogether, the file size for the entire dataset is about 570 GB.

chunks.text: For web use, the DEM was mosaicked, clipped to the case-study extent, and converted to GeoTIFF, then encoded into PNG. Elevations were integerized in US feet and stored in the Red and Green channels using a quotient/remainder encoding. The raster was reprojected to EPSG:3857 to display in web mapping frameworks.
supporting_quote: The DEMs were mosaicked into one large DEM ... the elevation values were converted into US feet as integers
We developed a method (Eq. 1) to encode the elevation in the Red and Green bands of the PNG
we reprojected the raster to the Spherical Mercator projection (EPSG:3857)

chunks.text: A tiling schema was created across multiple scales and resolutions, and more than 13,000 image tiles were generated for the five-county region. Offline basemap tiles were downloaded from OpenStreetMap for zoom levels 10, 11, and 12 using JTile-Downloader. Tiles were organized into folders by zoom level to support offline rendering.
supporting_quote: Using this tiling schema, over 13,000 image tiles were created for the selected region of interest
tiles were selected for 5 counties ... for three different zoom levels (i.e., 10, 11, 12).
All of these tiles were downloaded from OpenStreet-Map data ... with the help of the JTile-Downloader application.

chunks.text: RasterJS can operate on multiple device types with offline geospatial analysis by caching resources locally and using client-side computation. Lazy loading stores requested georeferenced images in IndexedDB after the first retrieval, and cached map tiles enable offline navigation. This architecture supports performing watershed and raindrop analyses even when connectivity is unstable or absent, assuming required data has been cached.
supporting_quote: To make the geospatial analysis feature available in Offline mode and to improve the response time of the application, a lazy loading strategy has been adopted. Requested georeferenced images will be cached in indexedDB once received.
The application caches map tiles so that the user can navigate the map in Offline mode.

chunks.text: The study reports client-side storage footprints for the complete five-county dataset on a device. Total space is 3,286 MB when all data are downloaded, dominated by georeferenced images in IndexedDB (~3,274 MB). Static resources and map tiles require 11.9 MB in Cache API, and the service worker itself uses 33.3 KB.
supporting_quote: if all the data ... is downloaded on the client-side, then it takes a total space of 3,286 MB
a large chunk of size (i.e., ~3,274 MB) is occupied by IndexedDB where georeferenced images are stored
static resources along with the map tiles take 11.9 MB of space in the cache, and Service Workers take only 33.3 KB of space

chunks.text: RasterJS introduces a Web Bundle distribution mode to enable standalone offline access and sharing. For the five counties, the packaged file is around 300 MB and includes resources necessary for offline mode, excluding large georeferenced images to keep size practical. The bundle can be transferred using offline methods such as Bluetooth and run directly in a browser.
supporting_quote: All the resources that are needed for the application to work in Offline mode are packaged in a single file.
The size of the packaged file is around 300 MB for the five counties
This file can be distributed to other devices using any Offline data transfer technology (i.e., Bluetooth).

chunks.text: The paper demonstrates a complete interactive workflow for georeferencing and hydrologic analytics in both online and offline modes. Users select resolution/area/elevation dataset, request georeferenced images, and then compute flow direction, watershed boundaries, or raindrop paths using web workers. Visualization overlays results on the georeferenced raster inside the selected window on the map.
supporting_quote: the user then selects elevation resolution, area dimension, elevation dataset, and navigates to the area of interest.
RasterJS then invokes a web worker for determining the flow direction of the georeferenced image.
it displays the watershed over the georeferenced image

chunks.text: Offline capability depends on client-side storage limits and careful caching. The Cache API has limited storage and is not recommended for all resources, while IndexedDB capacity depends on disk space and browser-specific quotas. These constraints require restricting offline datasets by area and zoom levels and influence scalability beyond the case study.
supporting_quote: Since the resources are stored locally in the browser the storage capacity for caching is limited.
Browsers allocate a certain percentage of disk space to IndexedDB and this percentage is browserspecific
storage capacity is limited with the hard disk size and browser specification, which encourages restricting the cached tiles to a certain area and zoom levels.

chunks.text: The Web Bundles approach is currently constrained by browser support and maturity. The paper notes Web Bundles are experimental and supported only in Chrome at the time described. This limits cross-browser portability of the packaged offline distribution method.
supporting_quote: Currently, web bundles are only supported in the Chrome browser and it is an experimental technology
As of 2021, Web Bundles are supported in Google Chrome as an experimental proposed feature

chunks.text: Some PWA features are not uniformly supported across mobile platforms, reducing the native-like experience in certain environments. In particular, iOS lacks support for push notifications and web manifest files as described. This affects engagement features and installation behavior on those devices.
supporting_quote: there are some limitations in iOS devices regarding nativelike experience as such devices do not support Push notifications and web manifest files.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that RasterJS demonstrates client-side raster processing for real-time geospatial analytics using PWA concepts and modern browser APIs. By transferring storage, management, and processing to the client, it targets reduced server dependence, lower costs, and better responsiveness. The system offers Online, Offline, and Web Bundle modes with comparable workflows across connectivity states.
supporting_quote: This paper presents RasterJS, a web-based geospatial processing library that is built using client-side web technologies and concepts of Progressive Web Application.
It transfers data storage, management and processing responsibility to the web-client as opposed to the conventional server-based architecture.
It provides three modes to suit different use cases: Online, Offline, and Web Bundle modes.

chunks.text: Future directions include integrating newer web technologies and extending functionality and formats. The authors highlight Web Assembly for performance, WebRTC for peer-to-peer distribution, and WebGL/WebCL for advanced visualization and acceleration. They also note potential expansion to other domains and supporting additional raster formats such as GeoPackage, ArcGrid, and ImageMosaic.
supporting_quote: Web Assembly is a technology that can be incorporated to improve the performance of the system.
The development of the RasterJS has opened the door for exploring peer to peer geospatial data distribution using WebRTC.
several other raster data formats (e.g., GeoPackage, ArcGrid, ImageMosaic) can be supported

chunks.text: Floods cause major damages and fatalities, and future risk is expected to grow with climate change and increasing populations in flood-prone areas. Accurate, real-time forecasts of flood-inundation extent are important for emergency response. This paper situates its contribution in the need for better operational flood-inundation mapping at large scales.
supporting_quote: Floods are one of the most damaging natural hazards.
Climate change and growing populations in flood-prone areas mean that the frequency and magnitude of floods can be expected to increase

chunks.text: The National Water Model (NWM) provides streamflow forecasts across the continental U.S. using Muskingum–Cunge routing that relies on continuity, but more accurate stage/inundation estimates generally require momentum effects as well. Backwater and other nonuniform-flow dynamics are not captured by Muskingum–Cunge alone, motivating hydraulically based augmentation for inundation mapping.
supporting_quote: NWM then applies Muskingum–Cunge channel routing techniques, solely based on the continuity equation
the momentum equation also needs to be considered to obtain more accurate estimates of streamflow and stage in rivers

chunks.text: SPRNT is a river-network model that solves 1D Saint-Venant equations for steady or unsteady flow and can operate efficiently at very large scales using the NHDPlus framework. Because SPRNT and NWM share the same stream-reach framework, SPRNT can potentially be coupled with NWM streamflow to improve stage estimates and downstream inundation mapping.
supporting_quote: Simulation Program for River NeTworks (SPRNT) is a model for large-scale river networks ... that solves the nonlinear SVE
SPRNT can handle river networks at continental scales 330 times faster than real time

chunks.text: The study aims to test whether driving a steady-state backwater (SPRNT) model with NWM streamflow improves flood-inundation mapping compared to using NWM with HAND synthetic rating curves alone. It evaluates performance for the Hurricane Matthew (October 2016) flood in the Neuse River near Goldsboro, North Carolina, using a remote-sensing inundation extent as reference.
supporting_quote: assess the applicability of using steady-state SPRNT driven by NWM streamflow to produce better stage forecasts, and convert them to inundated-area predictions using HAND
We evaluated SPRNT's and NWM's abilities to predict inundated area for the record flood of Hurricane Matthew in October 2016.

chunks.text: A specific contribution is comparing inundation extents generated with and without backwater effects against an observed inundation extent and discussing implications for operational flood forecasting. The work also includes a communication component by creating a web app to visualize and compare outputs.
supporting_quote: new contribution made by this research is its comparison of flood-inundation extents generated by different methods (with and without backwater effects) to observed inundation extent
developed a web app to visualize and communicate the results

chunks.text: A key modeling challenge is that NWM’s Muskingum–Cunge routing does not represent nonuniform flow dynamics, notably backwater effects, which can influence water surface elevations and inundation extent. Without momentum-based hydraulics, flood-inundation mapping derived from NWM flows can miss important spatial patterns, especially near junctions and low-slope reaches.
supporting_quote: Muskingum–Cunge routing does not capture the dynamics of backwater effects; solution to the momentum equation is needed
the momentum equation also needs to be considered to obtain more accurate estimates of streamflow and stage in rivers, especially for applications such as flood-inundation mapping

chunks.text: For inundation mapping, streamflow forecasts must be converted to stage and then to spatial flood extent. NWM outputs discharge, so the approach depends on synthetic rating curves and terrain processing (HAND), introducing additional uncertainty in stage and inundation estimates relative to hydraulically computed stages.
supporting_quote: NWM provides us with flow values and not river stages. We obtained river stages for NWM by converting the flow values using HAND rating curves
Synthetic rating curves can be produced ... to establish relationships between discharge and stage for each NHDPlus reach

chunks.text: River-geometry inputs derived from HAND/NHDPlus can violate monotonic requirements needed by SPRNT to build bathymetry, requiring data cleaning and interpolation. This highlights a practical barrier to large-scale hydraulic modeling when geometry estimates are constrained by catchment boundaries.
supporting_quote: SPRNT needs a minimum of five monotonously increasing points of data for A, P, and Y
A-P-Y-W data from NHDPlus does not always conform to this rule of monotonous increase

chunks.text: The study uses steady-state SPRNT, which solves steady-state continuity and momentum (Saint-Venant) equations to compute flow and stage along a river network. By incorporating momentum, the approach is expected to better represent backwater effects than NWM’s routing and HAND-only stage conversion.
supporting_quote: Steady-state SPRNT solves the steady-state continuity and momentum equations for flow and is therefore expected to simulate backwater effects more accurately than NWM.
we follow Yu et al. (2017) in using the steady-state version of the SVE as the governing equation

chunks.text: SPRNT river geometry is constructed from wetted area, wetted perimeter, stage, and top width (A-P-Y-W) datasets derived from HAND rating curves. Where A-P-Y-W sequences were not monotonically increasing, the authors removed problematic points; for reaches with insufficient points, they interpolated wetted area and assumed trapezoidal geometry to compute perimeter and top width.
supporting_quote: The river geometry was defined using SPRNT's intrinsic definition, which takes in the wetted area (A), wetted perimeter (P), stage (Y), and top width (W)
We resolved nonmonotonously increasing A-P-Y-W problem by removing the data points when one of the variables stopped increasing.

chunks.text: Boundary conditions for steady-state SPRNT were defined using NWM retrospective peak-flow timing for major rivers and a downstream stage boundary. Minor tributary headwaters used a synthetic inflow boundary derived from a nearby USGS gage discharge divided by the number of headwater streams to assign a uniform small inflow to all minor headwaters.
supporting_quote: Flow rate at 0000 h on October 10, 2016 (local time), at the upstream reach on Neuse and Little River was used for the upstream boundary condition
we divided the flow rate (385 m3/s) recorded at 1600 h on October 9, 2016 ... by the total number of headwater streams in our study area ... (9.2 m3/s)

chunks.text: Flood-inundation mapping is produced using the HAND method, which normalizes topography by subtracting elevation of the nearest drainage from each cell, producing relative height above drainage. A cell is classified inundated when stage exceeds its HAND value; otherwise it remains dry.
supporting_quote: In a HAND raster, the elevations are relative to the elevations along the drainage network.
If the stage is higher than the HAND value for a cell, that cell is inundated

chunks.text: To generate HAND rasters, the DEM was conditioned (sink filling), flow directions were computed using D8, and drainage networks were delineated. A nearest-drainage map linked DEM cells to outlet cells, and HAND values were computed by subtracting outlet elevation from each draining cell’s elevation.
supporting_quote: the DEM (10-m National Elevation Dataset) was conditioned by filling the sinks, defining flow directions (using D8), and delineating the drainage network
HAND operator, which subtracts the elevation of the drainage outlet cell from the elevation of all the cells draining to it

chunks.text: NWM stages were derived from NWM flows using HAND-based synthetic rating curves built by iteratively solving Manning’s equation over depth values. These curves use HAND-estimated inundated-zone water-surface area and reach length to infer cross-sectional area and wetted perimeter, with slope from NHDPlus.
supporting_quote: We obtained river stages for NWM by converting the flow values using HAND rating curves
Repeatedly solving Manning's equation to calculate streamflow for a range of different depth values results in a synthetic rating curve.

chunks.text: Observed inundation extent was derived from Sentinel-1 SAR imagery classified into water/nonwater using Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) with predictors VV, VH, and HAND. Training data consisted of 80 points derived using USGS high water marks and NHDPlus flowlines, and SAR was preprocessed with calibration, speckle filtering, and terrain correction.
supporting_quote: we leveraged a remote-sensing approach utilizing the European Space Agency's SENTINEL-1 C-Band (5.405 GHz) SAR data from October 12, 2016.
we used Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) ... three predictors (VV, VH, and HAND)

chunks.text: Model performance was evaluated using pixel-based binary comparison between predicted and remotely sensed wet/dry maps. The study computed confusion-matrix counts (TP, FP, TN, FN) and derived performance metrics (TPR, TNR, PPV, NPV, ACC), then tested differences between SPRNT and NWM using a two-tailed difference in proportions at 99.9% significance.
supporting_quote: The fundamental statistics for binary comparison of True Positive, False Positive (FP), True Negative, and FN were computed
two-tailed difference in two proportions with a high level of significance (0.001% or 99.9%)

chunks.text: The case study focuses on the Goldsboro, North Carolina region on the Neuse River, comprising five HUC12 watersheds. Hurricane Matthew rainfall in October 2016 produced record flooding, including a USGS gage stage of 9.05 m at Goldsboro (flood stage 5.18 m), providing a well-documented event for evaluation.
supporting_quote: Our study area was the region of Goldsboro, North Carolina ... consisted of five 12-digit hydrologic unit code (HUC12) watersheds
USGS gage on the Neuse River at Goldsboro experienced a record stage of 9.05 m (where flood stage is defined as 5.18 m)

chunks.text: NWM retrospective analysis outputs for the Neuse River at Goldsboro were used because NWM is not available for individual researchers to run directly. These NWM discharge simulations served as forcing and boundary conditions for SPRNT and were also converted to stage via synthetic HAND rating curves for inundation mapping.
supporting_quote: NWM is run ... and the model is not available for use by individual researchers. Accordingly, NWM retrospective analysis output ... were used as input for our models.
Streamflow simulations from NWM retrospective analysis were used as input for the SPRNT simulation.

chunks.text: SPRNT network inputs were based on NHDPlus flowlines and geometry derived from HAND-related A-P-Y-W data. The study notes that SPRNT uses a netlist (.spt) file describing channel geometry and forcing, enabling simulation over the 178-reach network within the five HUC12 basins.
supporting_quote: SPRNT requires NHDPlus flowlines, runoff data, and river geometry for the model to be set up.
A SPRNT preprocessor takes all these input data and produces a netlist (.spt) file

chunks.text: For HAND inundation processing, the authors used a 10-m National Elevation Dataset (DEM) to compute flow directions, drainage network, nearest drainage map, and HAND raster. This terrain product was then combined with reach-wise stage estimates to map inundated pixels.
supporting_quote: the DEM (10-m National Elevation Dataset) was conditioned
This HAND raster is used as a proxy for predicting flood events using the stage height in the nearest drainage channel

chunks.text: Remote-sensing validation used Sentinel-1 SAR imagery from October 12, 2016 in Interferometric Wide Swath mode with VV+VH dual polarization at ~10 m resolution. SAR predictors were supplemented with HAND as an auxiliary variable due to canopy and urban interference.
supporting_quote: SENTINEL-1 C-Band (5.405 GHz) SAR data from October 12, 2016
processed to the level-1 Ground Range Detected processing level with a spatial resolution of approximately 10 m

chunks.text: Training labels for the QDA remote-sensing classification were created from USGS high water marks and NHDPlus flowlines, producing 80 training points distributed across the study area. These points supported estimation of class means and covariance matrices for inundated vs noninundated classes.
supporting_quote: USGS report for Hurricane Matthew documents a series of high water marks (HWM)
derive 80 training points that are spatially distributed in the study area

chunks.text: Across the modeled network, SPRNT generally produced higher stages than NWM for the same NWM-derived flow forcing, consistent with representing backwater effects. Specifically, 126 of 178 reaches (71%) had higher SPRNT stages than NWM.
supporting_quote: In 126 reaches of the 178 reaches in the network (71% of reaches), SPRNT has higher river stages than NWM
SPRNT likely captures backwater effects.

chunks.text: HAND-based inundation maps derived from SPRNT stages showed larger inundation extent than maps derived from NWM stages. The additional inundation in SPRNT was especially evident along tributaries, while NWM inundation concentrated near the Neuse River mainstem.
supporting_quote: The inundation extent from SPRNT is larger than that of NWM.
most inundated areas from NWM are situated along or near the mainstream of the Neuse River, whereas most additional inundated areas from SPRNT are located along the tributaries

chunks.text: The remotely sensed classification indicated that about 47% of the study site was flooded, totaling about 154 km². This reference extent was used as the observed dataset for pixel-based validation of NWM and SPRNT inundation maps.
supporting_quote: Overall, the study site was 47% flooded with an area of 154 km2.
The observed dataset is taken to be the SAR remote-sensing classification

chunks.text: SPRNT correctly predicted more inundated area than NWM: 58.1 km² versus 49.9 km² of true positives. Expressed relative to the observed inundated area (153.6 km²), SPRNT captured 37.8% while NWM captured 32.5%, indicating improved detection of flooded pixels.
supporting_quote: NWM predicts 32.5% (49.9 km2/153.6 km2) of inundated area accurately, and SPRNT predicts 37.8% (58.1 km2/153.6 km2).
SPRNT obviously captures more flood than NWM

chunks.text: Performance metrics favored SPRNT over NWM for most indices: PPV 0.84 vs 0.81, NPV 0.63 vs 0.61, TPR 0.38 vs 0.32, and ACC 0.68 vs 0.65. TNR was essentially unchanged at 0.94 for both models, and statistical tests reported significant differences for all except TNR.
supporting_quote: p-values {SPRNT-NWM} ... TNR ... 0.07

chunks.text: Using backwater-capable steady-state hydraulics yielded a modest but meaningful improvement in overall inundation-map accuracy. The paper reports accuracies of 67.6% for SPRNT versus 65.1% for NWM when compared to the remotely sensed dataset.
supporting_quote: The inundated-area accuracies for NWM and SPRNT (based on comparison to a remotely sensed dataset) were 65.1% and 67.6%, respectively.
using steady-state SPRNT results in a modest improvement of inundation-forecast accuracy compared to NWM

chunks.text: A principal limitation is that SPRNT is driven by NWM flows, so any NWM discharge biases propagate into SPRNT. The authors suggest that underestimation of streamflow along smaller tributaries likely caused both models to underestimate the total inundated area, reflected in relatively low true positive rates.
supporting_quote: uncertainty in the NWM streamflow ... is propagated to SPRNT.
The most likely explanation for the underestimate of flooding by both models is uncertainty in the NWM streamflow, especially underestimates of flow along smaller tributaries.

chunks.text: The study’s steady-state SPRNT implementation is positioned as an initial step, and the authors note that future research should evaluate gradually varied and unsteady flow effects. This implies current results may not capture time-dependent hydraulics important for flood-wave evolution.
supporting_quote: We used steady-state SPRNT in the current work as a first step, but future research should explore the effects of using gradually varied and unsteady flow.

chunks.text: Due to sparse active USGS gages in the study area, the authors found it impractical to estimate headwater inflows directly and therefore assumed similar hydrologic conditions from a nearby gage to construct synthetic tributary inflows. This boundary-condition assumption can influence simulated stages and inundation patterns in minor branches and downstream reaches.
supporting_quote: Due to the sparsity of the active USGS gages in the study area, getting a reasonable estimation for the synthetic headwater inflow boundary is impractical.
we assumed that the hydrological condition at USGS gage 02091000 is similar to our study area

chunks.text: Remote-sensing inundation mapping using SAR faces classification difficulties under vegetation canopy and in urban areas due to backscatter interference. The paper mitigates this by including HAND as an auxiliary predictor, but the discussion notes that SAR-alone was not a valid predictor in the study area, indicating limits of purely SAR-based flood detection.
supporting_quote: Due to the forested and urban nature of the study area, SAR alone was found to not be a valid predictor of inundated areas
vegetation canopy affects the return signal for SAR, which can affect the classification accuracy (ACC)

chunks.text: For Hurricane Matthew flooding near Goldsboro, linking NWM streamflow forecasts to a steady-state hydraulic backwater model (SPRNT) and mapping inundation with HAND improved inundation predictions relative to NWM-based HAND mapping alone. Improvements were most apparent in smaller headwater tributaries and at channel junctions, consistent with better representation of hydraulic effects.
supporting_quote: The areas in which SPRNT most improved upon NWM were in smaller headwater tributaries and at channel junctions.
Linking NWM streamflow forecasts to hydrodynamic models like SPRNT is a potentially powerful way to generate flood-inundation forecasts

chunks.text: The study concludes that adding hydraulic formulation to hydrologic NWM predictions can improve river-channel flow/stage representation and thereby inundated-area forecasts, with potential benefits for emergency response. The authors suggest broader deployment may be worthwhile if similar performance gains occur in other regions with backwater effects.
