supporting_quote: we succeeded in adding a hydraulic formulation to the hydrologic NWM predictions to improve the flow predictions in the river channels, and hence improve inundated-area predictions.
The results suggest that this addition will improve inundation predictions in other areas with backwater effects

chunks.text: Geoscientific models are widely used for prediction and decision support across domains such as hydrology, vegetation, agriculture, geohazards, and biogeochemistry. Many of these problems are represented as nonlinear equation systems or ODE/PDEs driven by time-varying forcings and modulated by semi-static attributes. Model systems often chain multiple processes with varied certainty and uncertain parameterizations. The paper argues that differentiable implementations can more seamlessly connect process-based and machine-learning components within these model structures.
supporting_quote: Geoscientific models encompass a wide range of domains, with evolving scopes and ever-increasing societal importance, especially in the face of rapid climate change.
Many such problems can be described as systems of nonlinear equations, algebraic differential equations, or ordinary and/or partial differential equations (ODE/PDEs)

chunks.text: Process-based models (PBMs) provide interpretability, physical consistency, and the ability to simulate both observed and unobserved variables that support scientific narratives and stakeholder communication. They are useful for hypothesis testing and assessing cause–effect relationships because they respect physical laws. PBMs also enable controlled experiments by progressively improving process representations and evaluating them. These strengths motivate retaining PBM components as structural priors in hybrid approaches.
supporting_quote: Process-based modelling offers interpretability and physical consistency
Due to their physical basis, they can be leveraged in hypothesis testing to assess system responses, and cause-effect relationships
they can simulate a wide variety of observed ... and unobserved variables

chunks.text: Purely data-driven machine learning, especially deep neural networks, has achieved strong predictive performance across many geoscience variables, including streamflow, soil moisture, evapotranspiration, and water quality. Deep networks can exploit large datasets and scale favorably in accuracy and efficiency with more data. However, their success is tightly tied to the differentiable programming paradigm that enables training large numbers of parameters via gradient-based optimization. This computational foundation motivates extending differentiability to physical models.
supporting_quote: In geosciences, NNs have shown strong accuracy in predicting
NN training can scale up favorably with the amount of data (in terms of accuracy, generalizability, and efficiency)
The computing paradigm that enables efficient training of so many parameters is Differentiable Programming

chunks.text: The paper’s central goal is to position differentiable modeling as a pathway to unify process-based modeling and machine learning in geosciences. It proposes that end-to-end differentiability enables learning high-dimensional unknown relationships while incorporating physical knowledge. The authors aim to demonstrate the potential of this paradigm with hydrologic examples and argue it can improve interpretability, generalizability, and extrapolation. The perspective also emphasizes using such models to ask scientific questions and discover new physical relationships.
supporting_quote: we explore differentiable modelling as a pathway to dissolve the perceived barrier between process-based modelling and machine learning in the geosciences
‘Differentiable’ refers to accurately and efficiently calculating gradients with respect to model variables or parameters
Differentiable modelling approaches are primed to enable geoscientists to ask questions, test hypotheses, and discover unrecognized physical relationships.

chunks.text: A stated ambition is to develop differentiable geoscience models that simultaneously achieve ML-level predictive performance and retain physical consistency and diagnostic capability. The paper lists desired properties including transferability, structural evolution, conservation laws, consistent internal fluxes/states, and the ability to isolate uncertain components for learning. These goals reflect a shift from just calibration toward evolving process representations. The authors treat this as a guiding “wish list” for success.
supporting_quote: Success can be claimed if we obtain models with the following features:
(i) Predictive accuracy and transferability equal to or superseding purely data-driven models
(ii) Models capable of structural evolution
(iv) Conservation of mass/energy/momentum;

chunks.text: The paper frames differentiable geosciences as a means to broaden the kinds of scientific questions modelers can ask by placing a “question mark” precisely in a model: parameters, modules, or parts of governing equations. By retaining trusted parts as structural priors and learning uncertain parts, scientists can focus data and attention on the most unknown components. This is positioned as more flexible than fixed explainable-AI queries. The intent is to couple deductive reasoning with inductive learning in one framework.
supporting_quote: differentiable models allow us to ask questions about the functional form, i.e., " =?", by training a neural network
The unchanged parts (structural priors) ... critically serve as physical constraints, allowing us to isolate and focus our attention (and data) on the most unknown model components.
DG provides a framework for combining deductive reasoning and inductive learning.

chunks.text: A key limitation of process-based models is that they often cannot rapidly evolve to exploit big data because developing and testing process representations and parameterizations is slow and expensive. When mismatch remains after calibration, modelers iterate through hypotheses and structural changes, a labor- and time-intensive workflow dependent on intuition and legacy choices. This contributes to stagnation, with long periods between structural updates for specific processes. These barriers motivate approaches that can learn and update components more efficiently.
supporting_quote: Process-based models often cannot rapidly evolve with and fully exploit the information in "big data"
This iterative process is highly expensive (in both labor and time) and dauntingly complex, and is dependent on developer intuition and legacy
it is common for the structural representation of a specific process in a geoscientific model to stagnate, with years or decades passing between structural updates

chunks.text: Process-based models are also limited by knowledge gaps: representing and updating geoscientific processes requires extensive physical, biological, and socioeconomic understanding. Deficiencies in knowledge can amplify errors and ambiguity, especially where processes interact across disciplinary boundaries. Examples include interactions among vegetation, human management, and socioeconomic systems affecting water and biogeochemical cycles. The paper argues a new paradigm could enable faster progress despite these gaps.
supporting_quote: Process-based models are limited by knowledge gaps.
Extensive physical, biological, and socioeconomic knowledge is required
vegetation, human management, and socioeconomic systems all interact with each other and affect the water and carbon and other biogeochemical cycles

chunks.text: Purely data-driven deep networks are data hungry, which is problematic because many geoscience variables are measured sparsely in space and time. Water quality observations are highlighted as sparse and inconsistent, and rare extremes such as mega floods, droughts, and earthquakes have even less data. This limits the feasibility and robustness of black-box learning in many applications. The issue motivates incorporating physical structure to reduce data requirements.
supporting_quote: Deep networks are data hungry.
big data", which can, unfortunately, be sparse for many geoscientific pr oblems
For rare and extreme events such as mega floods, droughts, and earthquakes, available data is even scarcer.

chunks.text: Data-driven ML models are sensitive to errors, incompleteness, and bias in inputs and observations, inheriting issues such as implicit biases, inadequate resolution, and limited ability to handle non-stationarity due to short records. This can degrade performance when conditions change, which is central in climate-change contexts. The paper emphasizes that ML can replicate training patterns but may fail under shifted regimes. These concerns point toward models that incorporate stronger priors and physical constraints.
supporting_quote: ML has difficulties with errors, incompleteness, or bias in the inputs or observations.
it invariably inherits various issues from the training data including implicit or explicit biases, inadequate spatiotemporal resolutions
the inability to account for non-stationarity in time series due to the short data record.

chunks.text: Purely data-driven neural networks are hard to interpret, cannot predict untrained variables, and often learn correlations rather than causality. They cannot provide mechanistic narratives involving unobserved internal states (for example, attributing a flood to soil saturation if soil moisture is unobserved). This limits hypothesis formation, stakeholder communication, and reliability of projections when circumstances change. The paper frames these as major obstacles for using ML to answer scientific questions.
supporting_quote: Neural Networks remain challenging to interpret.
Purely data-driven ML models cannot predict untrained variables (those not provided as training targets).
Most geoscientific ML algorithms capture correlations and not causality

chunks.text: The paper defines differentiable programming as the computational paradigm enabling efficient gradient computation for models with many parameters, supporting backpropagation via the chain rule. It relies on automatic differentiation (reverse- or forward-mode AD) in ML platforms, though adjoint methods are another option. Differentiability is mainly needed for training, not forward runs. Cheap gradients enable first-order gradient-descent updates at scale, making large-parameter learning feasible compared to finite differences or evolutionary approaches.
supporting_quote: Differentiable Programming ... where accurate derivatives of the model outputs with respect to inputs and/or intermediate variables can be efficiently computed.
The chain rule can be applied to efficiently accumulate the derivatives in a process called "backpropagation"
Many alternative gradient estimation methods, e.g., finite differences, are intractable for any reasonably-sized NNs

chunks.text: The authors broaden the term to “differentiable modeling,” meaning any approach that can produce gradients rapidly and accurately at scale. Automatic differentiation differentiates through code and is problem-independent, while adjoint methods differentiate through equations and require manual derivations per problem. The key requirement is the ability to compute gradients end-to-end so that learning can occur through complex workflows. This framing is used to unify ML and process-based model training under similar optimization forms.
supporting_quote: Here we expand the scope and use the term differentiable modeling to include any method that can produce the gradients rapidly and accurately at scale.
AD differentiates through the code in an automated manner and is independent of the problem, while adjoint methods differentiate through the mathematical model equations
both ML and parametric physical models can be expressed in nearly identical mathematical forms

chunks.text: The paper proposes “Differentiable Geoscientific modeling” (DG), defined as models that intermingle process-based descriptions with neural networks while being fully programmatically differentiable end-to-end. DG retains trusted process-based components as structural priors and replaces or augments uncertain parts with learnable NN components. This enables parameter learning, process updates, uncertainty quantification, and sensitivity/trajectory analyses using gradients. DG is positioned as a branch of scientific ML that prioritizes improving process understanding while maintaining predictive strength.
supporting_quote: Here we advocate for a new modeling paradigm: "Differentiable Geoscientific modeling", or simply "Differentiable Geosciences" (DG).
A distinct feature of DG is its full programmatical differentiability
The process-based descriptions retained in the model can be called the structural priors.

chunks.text: DG models can be viewed from two equivalent perspectives: as ML models constrained by structural priors into a smaller searchable space, or as PBMs augmented with learnable NN components that expand searchable space. Structural priors act as physical constraints that reduce data demands and help isolate uncertain components. At the same time, DG preserves the scaling benefits of big data seen in ML. This dual view clarifies design choices about how much physics to embed versus learn.
supporting_quote: There are two perspectives from which we can view DG models (Figure 2):
(a) they are ML models constrained to a smaller searchable space by the structural priors.
(b) they are PBMs augmented with learnable and adaptable components

chunks.text: The paper provides a conceptual method for targeted learning: place a learnable NN where the main uncertainty lies—parameterization schemes, entire modules, or parts of governing equations/constitutive laws—while keeping the rest as a physics backbone. This allows asking “what should the function be here?” rather than only calibrating parameters. Learned relationships may be inspected directly or distilled to interpretable forms. The approach aims to reduce ambiguity by focusing learning on one uncertain component at a time.
supporting_quote: differentiable models allow us to ask questions about the functional form
(i) a parameterization scheme ... differentiable parameter learning
(ii) a module in a model ... replace ... with NN
(iii) a part of a governing equation or constitutive laws

chunks.text: One class of DG methods is to directly differentiate through numerical models and connect them to NNs using automatic differentiation. This requires reimplementing a process-based model on differentiable platforms, sometimes replacing non-differentiable operations with differentiable equivalents and improving parallel efficiency. The advantage is that the trained model is the same as the forward simulator, clearly enforcing physics and enabling use under arbitrary initial/boundary/forcing conditions. Learned relationships can also be migrated to operational implementations.
supporting_quote: Directly differentiating numerical models is the most straightforward method
one can reimplement an existing model to obtain a differentiable model version
Because the model being trained is the same one for the forward simulation, the physics is clearly enforced

chunks.text: Differentiable parameter learning (dPL) is described as connecting a process-based model to a neural network that predicts physical parameters from attributes, then training end-to-end by comparing model outputs to observations. This turns calibration into a machine-learning problem optimized across many sites simultaneously via backpropagation and gradient descent. The global loss encourages spatially coherent parameters and can improve extrapolation. It also enables efficient training and the ability to output unobserved variables while addressing equifinality.
supporting_quote: proposed differentiable parameter learning (dPL), connected the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) process-based hydrologic model to a neural network () that estimates physical parameters of VIC () using some widely available attributes (A)
trained on all sites simultaneously using backpropagation and gradient descent
dPL allows the combined model to output unobserved variables while addressing the notorious problem of parameter equifinality

chunks.text: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are presented as a gradient-based approach aligned with DG in that derivatives are used to enforce governing PDEs. PINNs train a network h(t,x) so it fits data at observed points and satisfies PDE residual constraints via dh/dx and dh/dt. Physical parameters can be included, and PINNs can be used for data assimilation and learning constitutive relationships from sparse observations. However, the learned solution is tied to the specified initial and boundary conditions and often requires retraining for different conditions.
supporting_quote: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs)101,140
train a neural network with space-time coordinates as inputs, h(t,x)
h(t,x) agrees with known data points ... and (ii) the derivatives dh/dx, dh/dt, etc. agree with the governing partial differential equations.

chunks.text: The paper highlights a core data challenge in geosciences: observations are imbalanced across space, time, and variables. Satellites provide broad coverage for some variables (for example leaf area index and surface soil moisture), while many key processes have limited site measurements, especially in Africa and Asia, and subsurface properties are poorly known. These constraints can bias or limit purely data-driven ML and motivate using physics to compensate for sparse measurements. Differentiable models can better leverage such heterogeneous data by embedding physical structure.
supporting_quote: geoscientific data are strongly imbalanced in spatial extent, temporal coverage, and in terms of variables of interest.
satellites can measure leaf area index ... or coarse-resolution surface soil moisture
there are a limited number of sites measuring photosynthesis rates or streamflow, especially in Africa and Asia

chunks.text: Water quality datasets are noted as sparse and inconsistent across time, space, and chemical coverage, which contributes to data scarcity for deep learning. Extreme events such as mega floods, droughts, and earthquakes also have very limited data, compounding the difficulty for purely data-driven approaches. These examples motivate hybrid approaches that can impose constraints and use fewer training targets. The paper uses these observations to justify differentiable modeling for data-scarce regimes.
supporting_quote: water quality data are sparse and inconsistent in temporal, spatial, and chemical coverage
For rare and extreme events such as mega floods, droughts, and earthquakes, available data is even scarcer.

chunks.text: DG models can exploit sparse and scattered observations through conditioning and data assimilation because the embedded process equations allow output of diagnostic (latent) variables. The paper gives examples where satellite soil moisture can condition hydrologic models to improve vegetation water use or productivity predictions, and streamflow can constrain snow water equivalent. Assimilation is described as using recent observations of one variable to improve short-term forecasts of another by updating model states. This relies on the availability of intermediate states/fluxes from the process-based backbone.
supporting_quote: As DG models can also output any diagnostic (latent) variable available from the process-based equations within the DG model
satellite-based soil moisture data can condition a hydrologic model to better predict vegetation water use
streamflow can constrain a model to better simulate snow water equivalent

chunks.text: Large-sample hydrology benchmarks and multi-site datasets are used as examples where differentiable models can learn from data at scale. The paper references the CAMELS streamflow benchmark and forcings such as NLDAS in reporting performance comparisons between differentiable PBM-NN hybrids and LSTM models. These datasets provide many sites for training and testing, enabling evaluation of generalization, including regional extrapolation. Such benchmarks are used to illustrate scaling and transferability claims.
supporting_quote: they approached the performance level of LSTM, giving a median Nash Sutcliffe model Efficiency coefficient (NSE) of 0.732 for the CAMELS streamflow benchmark
For temporal test using NLDAS forcings
in spatial extrapolation test cases, the differentiable model outperformed LSTM

chunks.text: The differentiable parameter learning example (dPL) uses multiple datasets spanning soil moisture, CAMELS streamflow, and global headwater runoff, combining observations across many sites with widely available attributes. The attributes are used by a neural network to estimate process-based model parameters, and the model outputs are compared to observations in an end-to-end workflow. The paper also references MODIS satellite products as comparison data for evapotranspiration (ET) during evaluation. These datasets support claims of spatial coherence and extrapolation.
supporting_quote: for three different datasets (soil moisture, CAMELS streamflow, and global headwater runoff).
estimates physical parameters of VIC () using some widely available attributes (A)
dPL better matches the MODIS satellite product for uncalibrated variable ET

chunks.text: A differentiable implementation of the conceptual hydrologic model HBV coupled with neural networks achieved near-LSTM performance on the CAMELS benchmark. Reported median NSE was 0.732 for the differentiable model versus 0.748 for LSTM on CAMELS streamflow, and 0.715 versus 0.722 under another forcing dataset. This demonstrates that hybrid differentiable PBM-NN approaches can approach state-of-the-art accuracy while retaining physical structure. The paper presents this as striking evidence for DG’s viability.
supporting_quote: they approached the performance level of LSTM, giving a median Nash Sutcliffe model Efficiency coefficient (NSE) of 0.732 for the CAMELS streamflow benchmark, compared to LSTM's 0.748
or 0.715 vs. 0.722 for another forcing dataset

chunks.text: The differentiable HBV-based model produced credible multiphysical outputs that were not directly trained, such as evapotranspiration and baseflow, and these outputs agreed with alternative estimates. This highlights a key advantage over purely target-driven ML: DG can provide intermediate states and fluxes that support physical narratives and downstream coupling. The figure caption explicitly emphasizes high-quality evapotranspiration estimates despite ET not being used in training. Such results support the claim that DG can deliver interpretable internal variables alongside accurate predictions.
supporting_quote: They also output untrained variables such as evapotranspiration and baseflow, which agreed well with alternative estimates
(d) δ models can predict high-quality evapotranspiration estimate (not used in training)

chunks.text: In spatial extrapolation tests (prediction in ungauged regions), the differentiable model outperformed LSTM on daily metrics and on decadal-scale trends due to structural constraints. The paper argues that physical priors improved reliability when transferring across regions and when evaluating long-term annual flow percentile trends. This is presented as evidence that DG can generalize better under extrapolation stress than purely data-driven methods. The results are used to motivate DG for global hydrologic modeling and climate-change assessments.
supporting_quote: in spatial extrapolation test cases, the differentiable model outperformed LSTM with respect to daily metrics and decadal trends
For prediction in ungauged regions (PUR; train in some regions and test in another large ungauged region), δ models can surpass the performance of LSTM;
δ models can predict long-term trends of annual flow percentiles more reliably than LSTM.

chunks.text: A differentiable river routing model trained on downstream discharge learned a parameterization for Manning’s roughness coefficient (n) and recovered a power-law-like relationship between n and catchment area consistent with expected behavior. This illustrates how DG can infer physically meaningful parameter relationships from data by training through a numerical routing model on a graph. The work demonstrates the feasibility of learning interpretable parameterizations rather than only improving black-box predictions. It also shows DG applicability beyond ODE-like conceptual models to network/graph domains.
supporting_quote: created a differentiable river routing model that was trained on daily discharge at a gauge downstream
to learn a parameterization scheme for Manning's roughness coefficient (n).
They obtained a power-law-like curve between n and catchment area that was consistent with the expected n behavior.

chunks.text: Differentiable parameter learning (dPL) is reported to produce spatially coherent parameter fields and improved spatial extrapolation compared with site-by-site calibration methods. The paper notes that dPL exhibits advantages across three datasets and that estimated parameters are spatially coherent. It also claims dPL better matches an independent MODIS ET product for an uncalibrated variable than SCE-UA. These results support the argument that end-to-end learning across many sites reduces regionalization uncertainty and helps address equifinality.
supporting_quote: dPL exhibits advantages over traditional calibration on multiple fronts, for three different datasets (soil moisture, CAMELS streamflow, and global headwater runoff).
The parameter sets are spatially coherent
dPL better matches the MODIS satellite product for uncalibrated variable ET than does SCE-UA.

chunks.text: The paper reports a substantial computational efficiency gain for differentiable parameter learning: a calibration job that typically requires a 100-CPU cluster for 2–3 days can be completed on a single GPU in about one hour. This exemplifies how gradient-based end-to-end training can scale favorably and reduce the practical burden of large inversion problems. The result supports the claim that differentiable models can be both accurate and efficient at scale. It also underscores a key operational advantage for large-domain geoscience modeling.
supporting_quote: dPL is hyper efficient: a job that normally takes a 100-CPU cluster 2-3 days now takes a single Graphical Processing Unit (GPU) one hour.

chunks.text: A geoscience PINN example demonstrates learning both a state field and a constitutive relationship accurately from sparse measurements under governing-equation constraints. In the unsaturated flow case, only sparse pressure head measurements are assumed, while the steady-state Richards equation is enforced via a residual network. The paper states that the method can learn the pressure head field and the unsaturated conductivity function as a function of pressure head “very accurately.” This supports the broader claim that differentiable, physics-constrained learning can infer unmeasured parameters and relationships.
supporting_quote: it was assumed that only sparse measurements of pressure head were available.
Substituting the NN approximations into this equation formed the axillary residual NN
These figures demonstrate that the PINN method can learn both the state variable and the constitutive relationship very accurately.

chunks.text: The paper emphasizes that PBMs face slow, expensive cycles of calibration and structural revision, often leading to stagnation of process representations over long time spans. This structural inertia is described as dependent on developer intuition and legacy, making it difficult to exploit big data and update model structures frequently. The discussion frames this as a fundamental limitation of traditional PBM workflows. It motivates the need for approaches that can update uncertain components more efficiently.
supporting_quote: This iterative process is highly expensive (in both labor and time) and dauntingly complex, and is dependent on developer intuition and legacy
it is common for the structural representation of a specific process in a geoscientific model to stagnate, with years or decades passing between structural updates

chunks.text: Purely data-driven ML is limited by data hunger, difficulty handling bias/errors, interpretability challenges, inability to output untrained variables, and weak causal grounding. These shortcomings can cause models to replicate training patterns without delivering mechanistic explanations or reliable projections when conditions change. The paper positions these as obstacles to using ML to answer scientific questions rather than just predict targets. This motivates hybrid differentiable approaches that enforce constraints and produce internal diagnostics.
supporting_quote: Deep networks are data hungry.
Neural Networks remain challenging to interpret.
Purely data-driven ML models cannot predict untrained variables

chunks.text: Directly differentiating numerical models can require significant up-front development effort because many existing PBMs are not implemented on differentiable platforms. The paper notes that reimplementation may require mathematical changes to handle non-differentiable operations (for example, replacing indexing with convolutions) and to improve parallel efficiency. Although GPU enablement can yield orders-of-magnitude speedups, it is acknowledged to have current challenges. This discussion highlights practical barriers to adopting DG despite its benefits.
supporting_quote: reimplementing a model does incur non-trivial initial development cost.
Mathematical changes may be required to adapt previously nondifferentiable mathematical operations to be mathematically differentiable, e.g., by replacing indexing with convolutions
enabling GPUs will improve the computational efficiency by orders of magnitude, notwithstanding some current challenges

chunks.text: Parameter estimation in geoscientific models is described as highly uncertain due to equifinality and sensitivity to resolution, making inference non-unique. Calibration at a location can yield similar outputs from different parameter sets, and extending parameters to unmonitored locations via regionalization adds further uncertainty. The paper frames this as a long-standing source of ambiguity and frustration. It argues that DG and machine learning can help, but the discussion clarifies why parameter inference is intrinsically difficult.
supporting_quote: calibration at a geographic location can often lead to nonunique inference (sometimes referred to as "equifinality")
Extending parameters to unmonitored locations requires "regionalization", which also introduces uncertainty.

chunks.text: For PINNs, the paper notes a limitation that the learned function h(t,x) is tied to the initial and boundary conditions, so models must be trained separately for different initial/boundary condition pairs. It also states that the input form limits network choice largely to multilayer perceptrons, which may be harder to train. Additionally, the fidelity of the trained network to physical equations must be carefully examined. These caveats indicate that DG methods vary in where generalization holds and require careful validation.
supporting_quote: the function h(t,x) is tied to the initial and boundary conditions so it needs to be trained separately for different initial/boundary condition pairs
the form of the inputs limits the neural network to certain types (multilayer perceptron network) that are not the easiest to train.
the fidelity of the trained network to physical equations must be carefully examined.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that differentiable programming is the core enabling feature behind neural networks and that differentiable modeling can serve as the basis for unifying neural-network and process-based geoscientific modeling. It argues that the divide between ML and PBM is largely legacy-driven now that differentiable tools are accessible. By implementing both components within differentiable workflows, their mathematical and code forms converge. This unification is presented as opening new doors to scientific discovery with minor conceptual and implementation changes.
supporting_quote: differentiable programming is the core distinguishing feature of neural networks, and differentiable modeling can serve as the basis for unifying NN and process-based geoscientific modeling.
the perceived divide is more of a legacy issue now that differentiable modeling is broadly accessible.
this unification requires only minor modifications ... but it opens new doors to scientific discovery.

chunks.text: The paper positions Differentiable Geosciences as a transformative paradigm for advancing process understanding while maintaining strong predictive accuracy. It emphasizes that full workflow differentiability enables learning unknown relationships, improving process representations, and interrogating models for scientific questions. The authors argue DG can enhance interpretability, generalizability, and extrapolation relative to purely data-driven ML, especially in data-scarce settings. It is presented as primed to enable hypothesis testing and discovery of unrecognized physical relationships.
supporting_quote: Differentiable modelling involves connecting (flexible amounts of) prior physical knowledge to neural networks
It offers better interpretability, generalizability, and extrapolation capabilities than purely data-driven machine learning
Differentiable modelling approaches are primed to enable geoscientists to ask questions, test hypotheses, and discover unrecognized physical relationships.

chunks.text: The paper calls for future work to address outstanding needs, including computational challenges, uncertainty reduction, and verifying the physical significance of model outputs. This frames DG as promising but requiring careful development and validation to ensure learned components remain physically meaningful. The conclusion thus combines optimism about DG’s potential with a concrete agenda for making the paradigm robust and trustworthy. These directions align with the perspective’s emphasis on process understanding and reliable inference.
supporting_quote: Future work should address computational challenges, reduce uncertainty, and verify the physical significance of outputs.

chunks.text: Large-scale climate risk assessments in hydrology have often emphasized large rivers and coarse spatial resolution. Yet water availability and excess depend strongly on catchment area through mechanisms such as runoff reinfiltration and groundwater flow. Because these scale effects are difficult to generalize, they have been under-represented in Earth System Models and global water modeling practice.
supporting_quote: Climate impact assessments for water supply with large spatial coverage have mostly focused on coarse resolution or large rivers
Water availability and excess are known to be tied to scale (here the basin area) due to processes like runoff reinfitration and regional groundwater flow

chunks.text: Empirical studies report that specific runoff and peak flow often decline with increasing catchment area in arid and semi-arid regions due to reinfiltration and transmission losses, but opposite or more complex patterns can also occur depending on environmental context and rainfall/soil properties. This diversity has prevented consistent “unifying laws” and systematic model representations of scaling. As a result, transferring hydrologic knowledge across scales remains challenging.
supporting_quote: as the catchment area goes up, specific runoff and peak flow typically go down in arid or semi-arid regions due to reinfiltration of surface runoff
However, positive runoff-scale relationships or more complex patterns have also been observed

chunks.text: Spatial scaling is described as a longstanding barrier that limits water management analyses and hydrologic modeling. It affects the reliability of calibrated models when applied at other locations within a basin and contributes to uncertainty when hydrologic processes are represented in Earth system models. The paper frames scaling as an unresolved community problem and links it to computational constraints in global modeling.
supporting_quote: In fact, spatial scaling is a decadal-scale (and still standing) nemesis of scientists
incorporating hydrologic process representations in Earth system models to support climate modeling remains a major source of uncertainty

chunks.text: The study aims to learn catchment-area scaling relationships directly from large-sample observations using a physics-informed AI framework. It targets how key hydrologic fluxes (mean flow, peak flow, and groundwater fractions) and their climate sensitivities vary with basin area. The goal is to provide interpretable, continent-scale scaling curves and identify where scaling most alters climate risk assessments.
supporting_quote: we learned scaling relationships from >3000 basins, highlighting overlooked climate risks
We specifically learn how fluxes (mean flow, peak flow, and groundwater fractions) and their sensitivities to climate change vary as a function of scale.

chunks.text: A further objective is to diagnose regions where scale dependence is particularly important and thus where coarse-resolution assessments may miss community-level risks. The work seeks to quantify characteristic length scales associated with processes like groundwater return flow and show how these scales change with aridity. These aims are positioned as guidance for Earth System Model parameterization and multi-scale water management.
supporting_quote: identify regions with large scaling impacts on climate sensitivities
we observe the length scale (� ) of 50 km as being around where groundwater return flow tends to balance water loss.

chunks.text: A key problem is that specific runoff measured at small catchments cannot be reliably extrapolated to larger basins (and vice versa), which increases error in climate risk analysis. This nontrivial scaling arises from runoff reinfiltration, channel losses, heterogeneity, and groundwater transfer. Such difficulty undermines the transfer of knowledge across scales for planning and assessment.
supporting_quote: specific runoff observed at small catchments cannot be linearly or otherwise easily extrapolated to larger scales or vice versa
which hampers the transfer of knowledge and information across scales and increases the errors in our climate risk analysis.

chunks.text: Deep learning can fit large hydrologic datasets but may be hard to interpret and can learn incorrect sensitivities, making climate-sensitivity interpretation risky. This motivates the need for models that combine data learning with physical structure and sensitivity constraints. The paper positions differentiable physics-informed approaches as a remedy.
supporting_quote: such deep networks cannot be readily interpreted and may acquire incorrect sensitivities to inputs, making interpretation of climate sensitivities risky
a new type of physics-informed DL technique termed differentiable modeling seamlessly connects deep neural networks (NNs) to process-based equations

chunks.text: Coarse global water models and computational limits complicate resolving scaling, and higher-resolution simulations may still fail to capture downstream integrative behavior. Additionally, outlet-calibrated models can produce large errors when diagnosing internal dynamics or other gauges. These limitations impede robust climate-impact assessment across scales.
supporting_quote: global water models (GWMs) were typically applied only at very coarse scales
models calibrated at a basin outlet encounter large errors when used to investigate internal dynamics or another gage

chunks.text: The study uses a differentiable hybrid hydrologic model (δHBV.CONUS3200.v1.1) that couples a neural network parameterization with the conceptual HBV model. An LSTM receives meteorological forcings and static attributes, including catchment area, and outputs scale-dependent HBV parameters. This design aims to retain interpretability while learning scaling effects from data at continental scale.
supporting_quote: we use a differentiable hybrid hydrologic model where we can learn the impacts of scale (defined as basin area) from big data using an NN.
The NN accepts catchment areas as inputs (along with atmospheric forcings and other attributes) and learns scaling relationships

chunks.text: Formally, parameters are produced by an LSTM and then passed into HBV to simulate streamflow. The paper describes this as end-to-end training on PyTorch to enable gradient-based learning from streamflow targets back to neural network weights. Only two HBV shape parameters are treated as dynamic to reduce overfitting.
supporting_quote: θ = LSTM_w( x̄, Ā_attr )
Q = HBV(x, θ)
To avoid overfitting, we only set two parameters as dynamic

chunks.text: The modeling framework is trained in a regionalized manner across thousands of basins, allowing the LSTM to learn general relationships between attributes and HBV parameters. Inputs are normalized by variable mean and standard deviation. The approach includes a structural update by adding a capillary rise flux to improve low-flow prediction.
supporting_quote: Training the NN over all basins in the domain (called 'regionalized parameterization') helps the network learn complex and general relationships
The inputs of the neural network are normalized with respect to each variable's mean and standard deviation.
we incorporated a capillary rise flux into the HBV model to enhance its performance in low flow prediction

chunks.text: A four-model ensemble is used to balance performance across flow regimes. Two members use an NSE-based loss and two use RMSE, each with and without log-transform normalization of precipitation. The ensemble mean is taken as the final simulation used for subsequent scaling and sensitivity analyses.
supporting_quote: we utilized a four-model ensemble approach
two models employed a loss function based on NSE ... while the other two models used the RMSE loss function
We used the mean of the simulations from 4 models as the ensemble simulation.

chunks.text: To evaluate scaling, the authors perturb catchment area values in the neural-network inputs to generate responses at different length scales. Climate sensitivities are computed by applying controlled perturbations of +1% daily precipitation and +1 degree temperature. The sensitivity metrics are then recalculated at multiple assumed basin areas to reveal how sensitivity changes with scale.
supporting_quote: We perturbed the catchment area ( ) values in the inputs of the learned neural networks
We tested increasing the daily precipitation by 1% and the daily temperature by 1 degree to calculate runoff climate sensitivities

chunks.text: Scaling analysis uses defined hydrologic quantities, including relative water supply, baseflow contribution, peak-flow dominance, evapotranspiration scaling, and climate sensitivities of flood and drought. The paper specifies evaluation definitions such as Q/QminA and Qbase/Q, and defines Q7 as the lowest 7-day average flow each year. These definitions standardize comparisons across scales.
supporting_quote: Q/QminA | Water supply | The total amount of runoff at different scales divided by the total amount of runoff at the minimal analysis basin area (5 km2).
Qbase/Q | Groundwater contribution | The ratio of the total amount of baseflow to the total amount of runoff.
Q7 represents the lowest average flow for seven consecutive days for each year.

chunks.text: The analysis uses 3,212 basins across the conterminous United States with relatively complete streamflow records in both training and testing periods. Basins are drawn from GAGES-II and overlap substantially with CAMELS used for benchmarking. Daily streamflow observations come from USGS gauges.
supporting_quote: predict daily streamflow in 3212 basins across the conterminous United States (CONUS)
selected 3212 basins with relatively-complete (>90%) observational time series data
The daily streamflow data was downloaded from the United States Geological Survey (USGS)

chunks.text: Meteorological forcings are basin-averaged precipitation and min/max temperatures from Daymet v4, used to derive mean temperature and compute potential evapotranspiration using Hargreaves with temperature and latitude. These daily forcings drive HBV within the differentiable model. The dataset enables consistent forcing across thousands of basins.
supporting_quote: basin- averaged precipitation, maximum temperature, and minimum temperature from the Daily Surface Weather Data on a 1-km Grid for North America (Daymet) Version 4
Potential evapotranspiration is calculated by the Hargreaves method with mean, maximum, and minimum temperatures and latitudes.

chunks.text: Static catchment descriptors include 28 attributes covering basin area, topography, climate, soils, land cover, and geology. Examples listed include catchment area, NDVI, open-water fraction, soil texture fractions (HWSD and SoilGrids), porosity/permeability (GLHYMPS), and snow-related indices. These attributes are inputs for LSTM parameter regionalization.
supporting_quote: Aattr contains 28 attributes, including information on basin area, topography, climate, soil texture, land cover, and geology
The inputs of the neural network are normalized with respect to each variable's mean and standard deviation.

chunks.text: Training and testing follow a split design with a temporal test and a spatiotemporal holdout test. The model is trained from Oct 1, 1980 to Sep 30, 1995 and tested from Oct 1, 1995 to Sep 30, 2010. In spatiotemporal testing, one-sixth of basins are held out from training and used for evaluation over the same periods.
supporting_quote: trained from October 1, 1980, to September 30, 1995, and subsequently tested from October 1, 1995, to September 30, 2010
In the spatiotemporal test, we randomly held out one-sixth of the basins from the training set

chunks.text: The δHBV ensemble achieves state-of-the-art streamflow prediction skill across 3,200+ basins, with strong daily and monthly performance. Reported median metrics include daily KGE 0.76, daily NSE 0.74, and monthly NSE 0.86 in temporal testing. Setting all catchment areas to a uniform 5 km² degrades performance, supporting that learned area dependence is important.
supporting_quote: median daily Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE) of 0.76, daily median Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE ... ) of 0.74, and monthly median NSE of 0.86 for 3,200 basins
assuming a uniform catchment area (all catchment areas = 5km2 ) ... median daily KGE dropped from 0.76 to 0.69

chunks.text: Mean specific streamflow supply exhibits strong aridity-dependent scaling. In arid basins, relative water supply (Q/QminA) declines to about 75% at a characteristic ~50 km length scale (~2500 km²), then stabilizes and can recover, consistent with groundwater return flow balancing channel losses. Semi-arid basins show a smaller decline (~5%) around 40 km and then increase at larger scales.
supporting_quote: Q/QminA ... for the arid group first declines noticeably to ~75% at 50 km length scale ... equivalent to 2500 km2 catchment size
At and above 50 km in length scale ... Q/QminA stabilizes and even recovers, and the only possible process ... is groundwater return flow.
semi-arid ... Q/QminA declines until around 40 km length scale ... only about 5%.

chunks.text: Groundwater contribution increases with catchment size, and the effect is strongest in arid regions. Above the minimum analyzed scale (5 km²), groundwater pathways can contribute around 70% of streamflow, increasing to as much as 95% in arid regions as basins get larger. This indicates a downstream shift toward groundwater-dominated flow regimes.
supporting_quote: fraction of water supply contributed by groundwater (Qbase/Q) increases as catchment size increases, but the effect is stronger for arid regions
groundwater pathways (Qbase/Q) can contribute 70% of total streamflow, increasing up to 95% in arid regions.

chunks.text: Peak-flow dominance declines substantially with increasing scale, especially in arid basins, implying strong attenuation and losses of flood peaks downstream. The annual maximum daily peak as a fraction of annual flow drops from about 3.3% at small scales to about 1.0% near 150 km length scale. Humid regions show different scale behavior, with relatively higher peak-flow dominance at large scales than arid regions.
supporting_quote: annual peak flow (Qmax/Qannual) decreases
largest daily peak of a year can account for a median of ~3.3% of total annual flow ... declines to ~1.0% at around 150 km length scale.

chunks.text: Flood sensitivity to precipitation is higher in headwater basins for arid and semi-arid regions, indicating elevated flash-flood risk upstream. The sensitivity (ΔQmax/Qmax per +1% precipitation) decreases from ~0.033 to ~0.028 moving downstream, a >10% relative difference. Humid regions show weaker or different downstream trends.
supporting_quote: higher flood sensitivity to precipitation ... for headwater basins for arid and semi-arid regions
The sensitivity decreases from ~0.033 to ~0.028, a >10% difference in sensitivity compared to downstream

chunks.text: Low-flow sensitivity to temperature is strongly scale dependent, particularly in arid and semi-arid basins. Downstream low flows become much more susceptible to warming, with sensitivity (ΔQ7/Q7 per +1 degree) changing from about -0.01 to about -0.05, described as a >200% change in sensitivity. This suggests warming-driven drought impacts may intensify downstream where groundwater dominates flow.
supporting_quote: low flow sensitivity to temperature ... downstream locations in arid and semi-arid regions are susceptible to larger low-flow changes due to warming
Low flow sensitivity to temperature decreases from -0.01 to -0.05 ... representing >200% change in sensitivity.

chunks.text: Scaling impacts show spatially coherent regional patterns and can exceed the aridity-aggregated averages. The paper reports regional scaling impacts reaching ~40% for mean water supply and ~50% for groundwater ratio, and very large relative changes in climate sensitivities (>300% for low-flow temperature sensitivity; >40% for high-flow precipitation sensitivity). Distinct clusters include eastern basins (small positive scaling), western arid basins (large, mixed impacts), and a “corn belt” region with strong scale effects.
supporting_quote: in some regions reaching ~40% for water supply, ~50% for groundwater ratio, and >300% (>40%) for low (high) flow runoff climate sensitivities
The "corn belt" cluster ... sees strong scaling impacts on baseflow ratio (>40%) ... and low flow sensitivity to temperature (>±200%)

chunks.text: Learned parameter trends indicate systematic downstream changes in modeled storage and release behavior. The neural network tends to reduce water release rates (K0, K1, K2), particularly in arid and semi-arid groups, and increase upper zone storage (UZL) downstream. These parameter shifts are interpreted as reflecting real gradient/storage changes and compensation for missing processes like in-stream losses and between-basin groundwater transfer.
supporting_quote: reduce water release rates (K0, K1, and K2), with the arid and semi-arid groups showing more rapid declines, and increase upper zone storage (UZL) as we go downstream
lack of explicit representations for in-stream water loss, between-basin groundwater transfer, and river-bank storage

chunks.text: The authors caution that parameter scaling curves should not be over-interpreted mechanistically because the model may be adapting to missing process representations. Specifically, the model lacks explicit treatment of in-stream water loss, between-basin groundwater transfer, and river-bank storage, which can be absorbed into learned parameter changes. They argue that more detailed process understanding will require more explicit parameterization and targeted testing.
supporting_quote: While we caution against reading too much into these parameter changes
the model also tries to internally adapt to the lack of explicit representations for in-stream water loss, between-basin groundwater transfer, and river-bank storage.

chunks.text: The scaling analysis is constrained at very small catchment sizes by gauge availability. The minimum analysis scale used is about 5 km² (~2.2 km length scale), which is larger than sheet-flow scales. The paper notes that channel-loss processes may occur at smaller scales, but they are not analyzed due to limited data below this threshold.
supporting_quote: minimum analysis scale on the plot (~5 km2 or ~2.2 km length scale)
water loss could have occurred at smaller scales than our minimum analysis scale, but we did not analyze that since we have few gauged basins below this scale
