supporting_quote: On the day of the beginning of the flood event, the forecast more closely aligns with the timing and magnitude of the event.
for both peaks, the mean predicted streamflow is significantly below the actual streamflow
Because the predicted series that was a standard deviation above the average had a peak flow above the 20-year threshold, a small purple warning point was generated.
because the peak flow of the average series was above the 2-year threshold a large yellow triangle was also generated.

chunks.text: A key limitation is streamflow initialization. The system starts at zero flow for the first prediction and then initializes subsequent cycles using the average of previously predicted flows, requiring multiple runs for model spin-up. The authors argue this approach may not match actual streamflow well and call for data assimilation using real-time gage data or reanalysis meteorological data to improve initial conditions.
supporting_quote: The most pressing need is improving the streamflow initialization.
The current method begins at zero flow for the very first prediction and then initializes the next prediction from the average of previously predicted flows.
This method requires multiple forecast runs in order for the model to "spin-up" the streamflow in the rivers.
data assimilation methods will need to be incorporated ... incorporating real-time stream gage data

chunks.text: The system requires additional improvements before it can be fully operational, including calibration and reservoir routing/operations. The authors explicitly identify calibrating the model and including reservoir releases as known needs. They also propose derived products such as predictive flood index maps and improved analyses of flood likelihood and warning timing.
supporting_quote: Additional known improvements include items such as methods for calibrating the model as well as a method for including reservoir releases in the modeling process.
New tools could be created ... predictive flood index maps derived from the instream forecasts

chunks.text: Computational scaling challenges remain for very large regions, particularly on the local cluster where performance degraded for the largest watershed. The paper reports that the Mississippi region’s local-cluster computation rate slowed relative to smaller regions and suggests environmental overhead or hardware differences. A proposed mitigation is subdividing the Mississippi watershed into two or three watersheds with 400,000–600,000 reaches each.
supporting_quote: This is especially true of the local cluster, where the rate of computation of the Mississippi region is half that of the Colorado region.
The efficiency of the system running on the local cluster could be improved significantly by dividing the Mississippi watershed into two or three watersheds with 400,000-600,000 reaches each.

chunks.text: Return-period generation was not completed for the NFIE Mississippi Region due to time and computational constraints, limiting warning generation based on those thresholds for that region. This highlights a practical limitation of computing historical statistics for very large, high-density networks. Completing nationwide return-period datasets would be required for uniform warning capability.
supporting_quote: Due to time and computational constraints, the NFIE Mississippi Region return period data were not generated in this study.

chunks.text: The Onion Creek case study indicates that forecast accuracy improves as lead time shortens, but also shows deficiencies in capturing event magnitude and timing across the network. The authors emphasize the need for broader evaluation and improvement to accurately capture events. They present the framework as enabling widespread assessment rather than claiming high skill everywhere.
supporting_quote: As expected, the case study illustrates that the predictions become more accurate, the closer to the time of the flooding event.
It is clear that the system needs further evaluation and improvement to accurately capture events over the broad stream network.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that a national-scale, high-resolution flood warning system with lead times of days to weeks is feasible. By downscaling ECMWF runoff forecasts and routing through NHDPlus V2 with RAPID, the authors produced high-density ensemble stream forecasts. They note that full functionality will require improvements in initialization and calibration and inclusion of reservoir operations.
supporting_quote: The creation of a flood warning system that can provide predictive information for floods days and even weeks in advance at a high spatial resolution at a national-scale is within reach.
By downscaling runoff forecasts generated by the ECMWF ... and routing the runoff using the RAPID model, we were able to produce high-density ensemble national-scale stream forecasts.
improvements in initialization and calibration as well as the addition of reservoir operations need to be incorporated.

chunks.text: The Streamflow Prediction Tool is presented as a decision-support interface that summarizes NetCDF ensemble forecasts, visualizes uncertainty up to 15 days, and enables comparison with NWS AHPS and USGS observations. The tool also displays warning points where 2-, 10-, and 20-year thresholds are exceeded on individual reaches. The authors argue that these warnings help make catchment-level predictions usable at national scale and simplify interpretation for decision-makers.
supporting_quote: This tool gives decision-makers information ... including a statistical summary of the potential streamflow up to 15 days in advance.
the tool displays warning points where the 20-year, 10-year, and 2-year thresholds have been exceeded in the predictions for each individual reach.
These warnings make the catchment level predictions applicable at a national-scale.

chunks.text: Extreme climate events such as floods are becoming more frequent and severe, increasing risks to communities and requiring rapid protective decision-making. Effective outcomes depend on how people receive, process, and act on information during these events. Coordination among federal, state, local officials, volunteers, and other groups adds complexity across preparation, response, recovery, and mitigation.
supporting_quote: Extreme climate events, such as floods are increasing in magnitude and frequency, putting entire communities at risk
Federal, state, local officials, volunteers, and other groups play unique and, at times, overlapping roles during the preparation, response, recovery and mitigation stages of a disaster.

chunks.text: The July 2023 Vermont storm produced rapid, high-volume rainfall and caused widespread flash and river flooding, with major impacts in the Winooski River watershed. Forecasts did not capture the storm’s severity, limiting preparation time and compressing the window for planning and communication by local officials. This event provides a real-world context to examine crisis and risk communication under time pressure.
supporting_quote: In July 2023, the state of Vermont experienced a powerful storm that rapidly unleashed as much as 9 inches of rain over the course of around 48 hours
Advanced forecasts failed to capture the severity of the storm, leaving communities with limited time to prepare

chunks.text: The paper distinguishes risk communication as dialogical—shaping decisions through dialogue about possible outcomes—while crisis communication is time-sensitive and addresses an unfolding event. Effective crisis messages should combine affect, cognition, and behavior: raise awareness, explain what is happening, and give clear actions. Warnings are more likely to prompt protective behavior when understood, believed, and personalized.
supporting_quote: Risk communication is a dialogical process.
effective crisis messages must include components of affect, cognition, and behavior.
"Warnings are more likely to be responded to with some protective action if they are understood, believed, and personalized"

chunks.text: The study aims to provide practical insight based on the perceptions of stakeholders who worked during the Vermont floods, focusing on communication, governance, and actions during major flooding events in the Winooski River watershed. By learning directly from emergency managers and related officials involved in response, the work seeks to identify barriers that influence public decision-making before, during, and after flood events.
supporting_quote: This study aims to provide practical insight based on the perceptions of stakeholders who worked during the Vermont Floods.
Learning from emergency managers who participated in the crisis response to a historic flood provides necessary context to flood response and mitigation measures

chunks.text: A key goal is to leverage a rare pre- and post-crisis design: an initial focus group occurred months before the July 2023 flood, followed by post-crisis sessions. This timing enables a temporal assessment of how preparation, response, recovery, and risk/crisis communication actually unfolded compared to expectations. The authors intend that the resulting learning outcomes inform recommendations to reduce harm in future floods.
supporting_quote: The first session (March 2023) occurred just a few months before the historic "Great Vermont Flood of 2023"
This allowed the collection of pre- and post-crisis data, which provided a unique temporal assessment of how preparation, response, and recovery, including risk and crisis communication, unfolded.

chunks.text: A major challenge during the July 2023 flood was that forecasts underestimated storm severity, which constrained preparation and compressed the time available for officials to plan and communicate. This created a fast-moving crisis environment where communities received less advance warning than needed. The situation highlights vulnerability in relying on forecast-dependent triggers for local readiness and messaging.
supporting_quote: Advanced forecasts failed to capture the severity of the storm, leaving communities with limited time to prepare
local officials had little time to plan and communicate.

chunks.text: Stakeholders perceived push warning messages from NWS and Vermont Emergency Management as invasive and sometimes less relevant because similar alerts are used for non-crisis events (e.g., highway crashes). Participants suggested these sender-focused messages assume accuracy alone is sufficient to drive public response. This can reduce motivation when audiences do not perceive personal relevance, making one-size-fits-all crisis communication ineffective.
supporting_quote: push warning messages used by the National Weather Services (NWS) and VT Emergency Management (VEM) were seen as invasive and perceived as less relevant in times of crisis
These communication methods are sender-focused and assume that sharing accurate messages is enough to ensure appropriate responses from the public.
A one-size fits all approach to crisis communication is, therefore, ineffective.

chunks.text: Communication gaps persisted for vulnerable populations, including residents in manufactured home parks near rivers and people facing language barriers. Despite increased awareness since COVID-19, participants reported that needs of those who spoke English as a second language were not effectively addressed during the July 2023 response. This indicates continuing inequities in crisis communication reach and accessibility.
supporting_quote: Some of the same communities also disproportionately experienced the impacts of this historic flood, specifically those living in manufactured home parks that tend to be adjacent to rivers.
participants shared that during the July 2023 flood response, the needs of people who spoke English as a second language were still not effectively addressed.

chunks.text: Researchers convened three focus groups with stakeholders involved in or supporting flood governance and response in the Winooski River watershed. The participants included emergency managers, regional planners, watershed and river managers, dam safety staff, and town officials. Sessions were designed to examine governance, communications, and actions across major flooding events, with one pre-crisis session and two post-crisis sessions.
supporting_quote: A group of professional emergency managers, regional planners, watershed and river managers, dam safety and town officials ... were convened for 3 focus groups
designed to study the governance, communications, and actions in response to major flooding events.

chunks.text: The first focus group was conducted in March 2023, prior to the July 2023 flood, enabling a comparison of anticipated versus actual crisis communication and response. The second and third focus groups focused on the historic July floods and assessed preparation efficacy and communication strategies as they played out during the real event. This structure supports a pre/post temporal assessment rather than a single retrospective view.
supporting_quote: The first session (March 2023) occurred just a few months before the historic "Great Vermont Flood of 2023"
The second and third focus groups concentrated on the historic July 2023 floods, including preparation efficacy, communication strategies

chunks.text: Each session lasted about three hours and followed prepared protocols tailored to pre-crisis experiences and post-crisis reflections. The first session focused on previous floods, public interactions, information needs, and threats, while later sessions revisited these topics in light of the July 2023 flood. This consistent protocol approach facilitated comparison across sessions with a similar participant set.
supporting_quote: Each focus group session lasted approximately 3 hours
Protocols were prepared in advance and guided the sessions.
The first session considered the participants' previous experiences with floods in the region.

chunks.text: All sessions were recorded, transcribed, and analyzed using grounded theory and thematic analysis to identify major themes. Researchers took extensive notes and coded notes and transcripts to derive findings. The team then conducted member checks by sharing themes with participants and collecting feedback via email and an online form to augment and rectify reports.
supporting_quote: All focus group sessions were video/audio recorded and transcribed.
These notes and transcriptions were coded, and major themes were identified using the grounded theory approach [8].
Themes and findings were then shared with participants for member checks

chunks.text: The dataset consists of three focus group sessions with largely the same participants, including one in-person pre-crisis session and two hybrid post-crisis sessions. Participation counts were n=12 for the March 2023 session and n=10 and n=11 for the post-crisis sessions. Hybrid participation reflected ongoing flood management duties that prevented some stakeholders from attending in person.
supporting_quote: The first session (pre-crisis) was held in person (n=12).
The post-crisis focus groups (n=10 and n=11) had a hybrid format (in person and virtual)

chunks.text: Primary materials included video/audio recordings, transcripts, and extensive researcher notes from each session. These qualitative materials were coded and thematically analyzed under a grounded theory approach, and then validated through participant member checks. Participant feedback was collected via email and an online feedback form to refine the reported themes.
supporting_quote: All focus group sessions were video/audio recorded and transcribed. Extensive notes were taken by the researchers.
Participants' feedback was provided through email and an online feedback form.

chunks.text: Before the July 2023 flood, stakeholders identified flash floods, erosion events, and major dam failures as the most concerning threats, particularly for impacts to life and property. They also anticipated significant social and psychological consequences, including trauma among those who experienced catastrophic flooding and anxiety about future threats. These perceptions shaped concerns about preparedness and communication needs.
supporting_quote: Flash floods, erosion events and major dam failures were perceived as the largest flood threats in the region
Participants also shared their concerns with the social trauma among those who experienced catastrophic flooding, and the anxiety that future flooding threats could cause.

chunks.text: Participants reported that conference calls and online meetings organized by Vermont Emergency Management as storms approach were useful for anticipating flood events. These sessions were described as widely attended and helpful for local leadership such as town officials, police chiefs, and fire chiefs. Stakeholders also emphasized nonprofits and community resilience groups as key partners for pre-flood communication with vulnerable populations.
supporting_quote: Conference calls and online meetings organized by VEM when storms approach the state were deemed as useful tools in anticipation to potential flood events.
These sessions are usually widely attended and viewed as helpful by town officials, police chiefs, and fire chiefs.

chunks.text: During the flood response, participants described Vermont Emergency Management as understaffed while handling many concurrent tasks. As the storm hit, the team monitored trends, answered information requests, developed maps and reports, and deployed assets for life-saving measures. This workload illustrates operational strain during high-tempo crisis communication and coordination.
supporting_quote: During the response to the Great Vermont Flood of 2023, the VEM team was understaffed.
the team was responsible for looking at trends, answering information requests, developing maps and reports, and deploying assets to assist with life-saving measures.

chunks.text: The National Weather Service contributed multiple daily briefs that guided resource deployment and acquisition. Regional Planning Commissions gathered information from towns and converted it into Situational Reports, supporting shared situational awareness. RPCs also played a role in reaching people without internet access and coordinating post-crisis webinars and trainings.
supporting_quote: The NWS provided multiple briefs per day, informing the deployment and acquisition of resources
Regional Planning Commissions (RPC) ... collected information from towns and converted them into Situational Reports (SitRpts).
RPCs were also instrumental in communicating with people without internet access

chunks.text: Stakeholders observed that post-crisis communication during the 2023 floods lacked coordination in some situations. A cited example was technical dam safety staff being tasked with crisis communication in addition to routine assignments. Participants viewed this as a potential risk because it could distract specialists from safety procedures and force them to manage communication logistics such as cell reception.
supporting_quote: post-crisis communication during the 2023 floods lacked coordination in some important situations.
technical staff responsible for dam safety were also responsible for crisis communication.
This added responsibility could potentially become a risk

chunks.text: A key issue was that much information was shared primarily with people who had consented or actively sought it, leaving others less informed. Participants highlighted reliance on opt-in channels such as Front Porch Forum. This suggests that information distribution mechanisms may not adequately reach residents who are not already connected to local information networks.
supporting_quote: A key post-crisis communication issue identified by the focus group participants was the volume of information shared only with those who provided prior consent or actively sought it.
"It's really whether or not people are tied into things like Front Porch Forum"

chunks.text: Mutual aid and volunteer support generally worked, with downtown associations helping recruit volunteers and build social capital for response. However, participation varied across the state, and some towns struggled to coordinate with volunteers. This indicates uneven local capacity to convert volunteer willingness into organized support.
supporting_quote: mutual aid from local communities appeared to have worked, although there was some variation in the levels of participation across the state.
There were designated downtown associations that helped recruit volunteers.

chunks.text: Participants argued that Vermont’s governance structure places heavy responsibility on local officials due to limited county infrastructure and strong local control. While local officials “stepped up,” the communication flow between local and state officials was identified as improvable during major crises. Variation in community risk-management capacity, limited social capital, and outdated or missing Flood Emergency Response Plans were highlighted as constraints on effective preparedness.
supporting_quote: The lack of county infrastructure and strong reliance on local control placed a great deal of responsibility on elected, appointed, or volunteer local officials
the communication flow between local and state officials could be improved, particularly during times of major crisis.
Pre-planning, such as having Flood Emergency Response Plans, is lacking or outdated.

chunks.text: The focus groups emphasized limited statewide emergency management capacity and the need for better resourcing and role clarity. Participants repeatedly noted the small number of regional emergency managers relative to the number of towns, and stressed that effective crisis response depends on speed and consistency. The paper recommends a gap analysis of roles and responsibilities across the emergency response and immediate recovery network.
supporting_quote: the observation that the state has just three regional emergency managers for 261 towns
when "simplicity, credibility, verifiability, consistency and speed" [5, p. 8] matter most
A gap analysis pertaining to the roles and responsibilities of actors in the emergency response and immediate recovery network across the state of Vermont is, hence, recommended.

chunks.text: Although communication channels were described as sufficient to yield good outcomes, the paper highlights the need for redundancy and clearer protocols across technical and emergency management roles. Specific emphasis is placed on improving real-time information exchange among dam engineers, hydrological modelers, emergency managers, and local/state officials to avoid misinformation or missing information. It also recommends translated, timely, comprehensible public messaging and strengthening two-way channels, plans, and logistics.
supporting_quote: redundant and clear channels of communication, particularly between dam engineers, hydrological modelers, emergency managers, and local and state officials, are needed.
Timely comprehensible, translated risk communication to the public and vulnerable communities during crisis situations is, therefore, recommended
need to assess gaps and generate recommendations for risk communication "two-way" channels, plans and protocols

chunks.text: The paper concludes that future flood events at or beyond the scale of the Great Vermont Flood of 2023 are inevitable, and complacency could increase losses of life and property. While the 2023 response was viewed as adequate/commendable, more action is needed to ensure capacity for effective response to severe floods. The authors emphasize moving from lessons learned to operational readiness and improved communication and coordination.
supporting_quote: Future flood events on the scales of The Great Vermont Flood of 2023 are inevitable.
While the emergency response to the Great Vermont Flood of 2023 was adequate, further action is needed to ensure that there is capacity in place

chunks.text: The study produced a policy brief shared with Vermont legislative committees, aiming to translate findings into policy change. The authors anticipate that combining these focus group insights with national-level surveys and simulation-based experiments will yield more generalizable recommendations. This reinforces an intent to connect research outputs to decision-making that can protect lives and infrastructure in future floods.
supporting_quote: This study resulted in a policy brief that was recently shared with members of Vermont's House Appropriations and Environment & Energy Committees, and Senate Appropriations and Natural Resources & Energy Committees.
The triangulation of this data with additional research conducted at a national level (surveys and simulation-based experiments) will lead to even more generalizable recommendations.

chunks.text: The National Water Model (NWM) is used operationally for U.S. flood forecasting and water management, combining multiple components such as WRF-Hydro, forcing preprocessing, and a national hydrofabric. Over time, NWM versions added calibration, data assimilation, reservoir representation, and coastal coupling, and expanded beyond CONUS. Despite strong physical foundations, operational needs include accurate streamflow prediction across diverse regions and scales, from headwaters to large downstream rivers.
supporting_quote: The National Water Model (NWM) is a key tool for flood forecasting, planning, and water management.

Updated versions have incorporated parameter calibration (v1.1), streamflow data assimilation (DA) (v1.2), reservoir representation (v2.0) ... and a total water level coastal coupling component (v3.0).

chunks.text: Differentiable models (DMs) are positioned as physics-based models that embed neural networks to learn parameters or replace components, while keeping process equations explicit and interpretable. Because the full pipeline is differentiable, they can be trained end-to-end with backpropagation across many basins, enabling rapid learning from large datasets. The paper contrasts DMs with PINNs and highlights advantages such as interpretability, extrapolation, and multi-output consistency due to physical linkages.
supporting_quote: DMs are real physical models that integrate neural networks (NNs) to infer parameters or replace specific components.
The entire system is differentiable and trained as a unified pipeline, enabling end‐to‐end optimization via backpropagation.

chunks.text: Prior national or large-domain DMs in hydrology were often spatially lumped, relying on basin-averaged inputs and producing outlet streamflow only. Operational applications often require spatially distributed streamflow along river networks to support inundation prediction. This motivates moving from implicit, unit-hydrograph-style routing to explicit routing that can generate a seamless, high-resolution streamflow product across a continental river network.
supporting_quote: previous DMs mostly were "coarsely spatially lumped," requiring the definition ofthe whole upstream catchment and basin‐averaged inputs
An external routing model capable of routing high‐resolution runoff across the entire continental river network is essential for generating a seamless high‐resolution streamflow product.

chunks.text: The study aims to test whether high-resolution differentiable hydrologic models with neural-network-based parameterization can substantially improve operational streamflow prediction across thousands of CONUS basins. A central objective is to use multiscale training, where parameters are learned at MERIT unit-basin scale but supervised by gage-basin observations, to better represent spatial heterogeneity. The work also targets producing a seamless, discretized streamflow simulation across the continental river network via explicit routing.
supporting_quote: Can an NN‐supported parameterization with a high resolution and multiscale training scheme significantly improve operational streamflow prediction for thousands of basins across the CONUS?
we developed a multiscale parameterization scheme to produce seamlessly discretized simulations across the entire high‐resolution CONUS river network.

chunks.text: The paper explicitly evaluates where multiscale training helps or hurts, and whether adding differentiable Muskingum-Cunge routing improves performance relative to implicit routing. It also frames a goal of contributing to the next generation of NWM by providing a model design compatible with integration standards. This includes assessing how DMs can be incorporated operationally while maintaining interpretability and multivariate outputs.
supporting_quote: Where does the newly introduced multiscale training scheme have advantages and disadvantages?
How can DMs contribute to and be integrated into the development of the next generation of the National Water Model?

chunks.text: A key challenge for the NWM is scaling calibration and parameter regionalization to thousands of gages, where basin-by-basin calibration is time-consuming and may not generalize spatially. Regionalization that transfers calibrated parameters to data-sparse regions can lead to large uncertainties at ungauged sites. The paper positions this as a "big data" learning limitation of traditional calibration strategies.
supporting_quote: Key challenges facing the NWM include calibration and parameter regionalization when confronted with big data.
This calibration strategy is time‐consuming and prone to both local overfitting and poor spatial generalization.

chunks.text: Earlier differentiable hydrologic models were typically lumped, using basin-averaged meteorological forcing and attributes. This coarse resolution prevents them from resolving fine-scale heterogeneity in forcings and basin properties within large basins, and restricts outputs to basin outlets. Such limitations are problematic for applications that require reach-scale streamflow estimates and distributed products.
supporting_quote: previous DMs mostly were "coarsely spatially lumped," requiring the definition ofthe whole upstream catchment and basin‐averaged inputs
They could only output lumped basin‐averaged fluxes, states, or streamflow at the outlet of the basin

chunks.text: Implicit unit-hydrograph routing used in earlier coarse DMs overlooks routing physics and channel characteristics, which can be important in large and complex river systems. Producing a seamless streamflow product across the entire CONUS network requires routing runoff across many connected reaches. This motivates incorporating an explicit routing model that is differentiable and scalable to continental domains.
supporting_quote: the coarse DMs used a unit‐hydrograph‐style routing formula for basin‐scale routing.
an external differentiable Muskingum‐Cunge routing model is incorporated to route flow across the high-resolution, continental, MERIT-based river network

chunks.text: Certain regions remain long-standing modeling challenges, especially where processes like wetlands, reservoirs, and human water use influence streamflow. The study notes that NWM3.0 includes reservoir and human impacts, while the δHBV models do not explicitly represent these influences. This gap can create biases, particularly in reservoir-dense areas like the downstream Mississippi and parts of Texas.
supporting_quote: These regions have high concentrations of reservoirs and human water use which exert major impacts on streamflows
Such influences are simulated in NWM3.0 ... but not explicitly included in δHBVs

chunks.text: The work compares three differentiable models: δHBV1.0 (coarse lumped), δHBV2.0UH (high-resolution MERIT unit basins with unit hydrograph routing), and δHBV2.0δMC (same runoff model but with explicit differentiable Muskingum-Cunge routing). The framework uses neural networks for parameterization while retaining HBV process equations as the structural backbone. The study focuses mainly on the two high-resolution δHBV2.0 variants and their end-to-end trainability.
supporting_quote: We discuss three DMs in this work... δHBV2.0UH ... and ... δHBV2.0δMC ... employs an external differentiable Muskingum-Cunge method for routing
Both versions use neural networks to provide a multiscale parameterization and process-based equations to provide a structural backbone

chunks.text: The coarse δHBV1.0 uses an LSTM to output basin-lumped dynamic and static HBV parameters from basin-averaged forcings and attributes, then simulates runoff with HBV and routes it with a gamma-distribution unit hydrograph. Dynamic parameters include shape coefficients for effective flow and evapotranspiration, while other HBV and routing parameters are static. Streamflow is produced at the basin outlet and can be converted from mm/day to m3/s with basin area.
supporting_quote: a neural network is utilized for regional parameterization ... HBV ... is employed for hydrologic modeling.

chunks.text: δHBV2.0UH operates at MERIT unit-basin scale (median 37 km2), predicting runoff for each unit basin using high-resolution forcings and attributes. Parameters are estimated at the unit-basin scale but trained using losses computed at the larger gage-basin scale by aggregating unit runoff upstream of each gage and applying unit-hydrograph routing to the outlet. The model uses an LSTM for dynamic parameters and an MLP for static parameters to reduce memory while retaining time-varying parameterization.
supporting_quote: inputs and outputs defined at the scale of MERIT unit basins (median size 37 km2 over the CONUS)
"Multiscale" means the parameters are estimated at the small MERIT unit basin level, while the training ... occurs at the larger gage basin scale.

chunks.text: For δHBV2.0UH training, the paper uses a normalized squared-error loss that divides each basin’s squared errors by the variance of observed runoff, reducing overweighting of large/wet basins and improving high-flow performance. The loss includes an epsilon to avoid division by zero. The study also notes adding a capillary flux (from prior work) to improve low-flow performance.
supporting_quote: we utilized a normalized squared-error loss function (Equation 10) to enhance the high flow performance

chunks.text: δHBV2.0δMC couples δHBV2.0 runoff with an explicit, differentiable Muskingum-Cunge routing scheme applied across the MERIT-based CONUS river network. The routing component uses Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) to estimate hydraulic and leakage-related parameters from reach attributes. For efficiency, the study uses an implicit routing scheme on GPU and maps unit-basin runoff to flowlines with ~2 km discretization for numerical stability.
supporting_quote: an external differentiable Muskingum-Cunge routing model is incorporated to route flow across the high-resolution, continental, MERIT-based river network
two Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) ... were employed to estimate the hydraulic parameters and leakage parameters

chunks.text: Model training uses large-sample learning across many basins with mini-batching and fixed hyperparameters largely inherited from prior δHBV1.0 work. δHBV1.0 and δHBV2.0UH are trained for 100 epochs on 2,807 basins over 1980–1995, while δHBV2.0δMC is trained for 5 epochs with 1980 used as warmup. The paper reports specific neural network sizes (e.g., LSTM hidden sizes and MLP hidden size) to balance performance and GPU memory constraints.
supporting_quote: Both δHBV1.0 and δHBV2.0UH were trained on 2,807 ... from 1 October 1980 to 30 September 1995.
Both δHBV1.0 and δHBV2.0UH were trained over 100 epochs ... δMC was only trained over five epochs

chunks.text: Evaluation is conducted on 4,997 GAGES-II basins over 1980–2019 with exclusions to avoid bias from δHBV training periods and NWM3.0 calibration periods. Streamflow metrics include NSE, KGE, Spearman’s rho, NNSE, and RMSE for low and peak flows. SWE is evaluated as an untrained variable using 525 SNOTEL sites by comparing daily SWE against NWM3.0 and δHBV2.0UH predictions at nearby grid points.
supporting_quote: We evaluated all models on observations from 4,997 GAGES‐II stations between 1 January 1980 and 31 December 2019
The following metrics were used ... Spearman's correlation ... Nash‐Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), Kling‐Gupta Efficiency (KGE)

chunks.text: The hydrography backbone is MERIT Hydro, which partitions the global river network into 2.97 million reaches and includes about 180,000 reaches across CONUS. The study uses MERIT unit basins with minimum size 25 km2 and median size 37 km2 to define model units for high-resolution simulations. The river reach median length is about 7 km, supporting network-scale routing in δHBV2.0δMC.
supporting_quote: MERIT Hydro ... divides it into 2.97 million reaches, including 180 thousand reaches across the CONUS
MERIT unit basins ... have a minimum size of 25 km2 and a median size of 37 km2 across the CONUS.

chunks.text: Meteorological forcings are derived from Daymet v4 R1, providing basin-averaged precipitation and temperatures for each MERIT unit basin. Potential evapotranspiration is computed using the Hargreaves method from daily temperature and latitude. Static attributes span topography, climate, land cover, soil, and geology, compiled from multiple datasets listed in appendices.
supporting_quote: Meteorological forcings ... were derived from Daymet version 4 R1
Potential evapotranspiration was estimated using the method from Hargreaves (1994) with daily temperature and latitude

chunks.text: Streamflow evaluation uses 4,997 CONUS basins where NWM3.0 simulations are available and where GAGES-II observations exceed 10% availability over 1980–2019. The paper starts from 5,084 basins with NWM3.0 data, then filters to 4,997 with sufficient observations. To reduce bias, the evaluation excludes time windows used for δHBV training (1980–1995) and NWM3.0 calibration (2016–2019) at corresponding stations.
supporting_quote: we selected 4,997 basins ... where National Water Model version 3.0 (NWM3.0) streamflow simulation data were available
4,997 have more than 10% valid daily observation data from 1 January 1980 to 31 December 2019.

chunks.text: Training for δHBV models uses 2,807 GAGES-II stations with relatively complete daily time series (>90%) from 1 Oct 1980 to 30 Sep 1995, with gages within 500 m of MERIT riverlines. δHBV2.0δMC is trained over 1981–1995 with 1980 as warmup. This setup supports multiscale learning of unit-basin parameters supervised by downstream gage observations.
supporting_quote: trained on 2,807 GAGES‐IIstations with relatively complete (>90%) daily observational time series data from 1 October 1980 to 30 September 1995.
δHBV2.0δMC was trained from 1 October 1981 to 30 September 1995 ... while the first year (1980) ... was used as the warmup year

chunks.text: SWE evaluation uses 525 in-situ SNOTEL sites over 2001–2019 to test an output variable that was not used for training. δHBV2.0UH SWE at SNOTEL is generated using inputs at the nearest grid points and compared to SNOTEL observations. NWM3.0 SWE is taken from its 1-km, 3-hr product and aggregated to daily for the same comparison.
supporting_quote: in‐situ SWE observations from 525 Snowpack Telemetry (SNOTEL) sites
comparing it with in‐situ measurements from 525 SNOTEL sites from 1 January 2001 to 31 December 2019.

chunks.text: Across 4,997 basins, all NN-supported differentiable models substantially outperform NWM3.0 on daily streamflow skill. Median NSE increases from 0.475 (NWM3.0) to 0.683 (δHBV2.0UH), with similarly strong KGE and Spearman correlation improvements. The gap remains large even though NWM3.0 is extensively calibrated, indicating the advantage is largely from NN-based parameterization and large-sample learning.
supporting_quote: the median daily Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency of all 4,997 basins is improved to around 0.68 from 0.48 of NWM3.0.
NWM3.0 ... Median NSE 0.475 ... δHBV2.0UH ... Median NSE 0.683

chunks.text: Performance gains generalize to sites not used for δHBV training and not used for NWM calibration. For the 1,836 “ungauged” basins subset, δHBV2.0UH achieves median NSE 0.519 versus 0.382 for NWM3.0, with higher KGE and Spearman’s rho. This suggests improved spatial transferability relative to traditional calibration/regionalization.
supporting_quote: The 1,836 "ungauged" basins are a subset ... not used in either the training of δHBV or the calibration of NWM3.0.
1,836 "ungauged" basins ... NWM3.0 ... Median NSE 0.382 ... δHBV2.0UH ... Median NSE 0.519

chunks.text: Hydrograph shape and total bias improve markedly under δHBV models relative to NWM3.0. The fraction of basins with poor shape (Spearman’s rho < 0.5) drops from 14% to 9%, and basins with large bias (ARTB > 1) drop from 9% to 4%. About 90% of basins fall into the “good” quadrant (high rho, low bias) for δHBV models versus 82% for NWM3.0.
supporting_quote: The percentage of basins with "bad shape" was reduced from 14% with NWM3.0% to 9% with δHBV2.0UH
the percentage of basins with "large bias" (ARTB larger than 1) was reduced by more than half, from 9% ... to 4%

chunks.text: Normalized NSE (NNSE) shows a pronounced distributional improvement: δHBV models have far more basins with high NNSE than NWM3.0. The paper reports over 30% of basins with NNSE > 0.8 for δHBVs versus 6% for NWM3.0, and roughly 80% of basins with NNSE > 0.6 versus 64% for NWM3.0. These results indicate widespread elevation in predictive accuracy.
supporting_quote: δHBVs had over 30% of basins with an NNSE value greater than 0.8 (compared to 6% with NWM3.0)
approximately 80% of basins had an NNSE over 0.6 (compared to 64% for NWM3.0).

chunks.text: NSE improves for most basins when moving from NWM3.0 to δHBV2.0UH. The appendix reports 3,990 basins above the 1–1 line in an NSE scatter comparison and 1,007 below. This indicates improvements are widespread rather than limited to a small subset of locations.
supporting_quote: The NSE values of streamflow predictions for 3,990 out of the 4,997 basins were improved compared to those of NWM3.0
There are 3,990 basins above this line, and 1,007 basins below this line.

chunks.text: Spatial patterns show the largest improvements in the western CONUS and the Prairie Pothole Region (PPR), both known as difficult areas for hydrologic models. Eastern basins improve more modestly because NWM3.0 already performs well there. Some locations along the downstream Mississippi and in the southern Great Plains show NWM3.0 advantages, consistent with reservoir and water-use influences that δHBV models do not include.
supporting_quote: including the eastern US and, more noticeably, the western US and the Prairie Potholes Region (PPR)
NWM3.0 shows some advantages ... along the downstream Mississippi River and the southern Great Plains (Texas)

chunks.text: Compared to the coarse basin-lumped δHBV1.0, the high-resolution multiscale δHBV2.0UH improves performance in northern and eastern regions and better captures high-flow behavior, particularly in challenging PPR basins. The paper highlights that δHBV2.0UH captures flow peaks in PPR that were significantly underestimated by basin-averaged δHBV1.0. Stratified analyses indicate larger benefits for larger basins and higher flow percentiles.
supporting_quote: Compared to δHBV1.0, the high‐resolution, multiscale parameterization in δHBV2.0 improved predictions in the northern and eastern US
δHBV2.0 well captured the flow peaks at sites in this region, which were significantly underestimated by the basin‐averaged δHBV1.0

chunks.text: Explicit routing with δHBV2.0δMC provides advantages for large basins, especially in arid and semi-arid regions, and can improve aspects like peak timing and water balance through channel leakage. However, it slightly degrades performance in some humid regions relative to δHBV2.0UH. The study attributes improvements to better downstream conveyance and leakage losses, with an example noting a one-day peak timing difference.
supporting_quote: it showed an advantage in large basins in terms of KGE
better describing the flow conveyance for downstream river reaches, which allowed for accurate prediction of peak timing ... (one day difference with δHBV2.0UH).

chunks.text: A key product outcome is a seamless, discretized streamflow dataset over the CONUS MERIT river network generated by δHBV2.0δMC. The paper states this covers about 180,000 MERIT unit basins and provides simulations from 1980 to 2020 without requiring basin-lumped inputs for each reach. This enables reach-scale streamflow availability for operationally relevant applications.
supporting_quote: With δHBV2.0δMC, we can provide a seamlessly discretized CONUS‐scale data set ... over the river network of ∼180,000 MERIT unit basins from 1980 to 2020
it does not need the inputs for the whole upstream catchment—each MERIT incremental basin and reach uses its own inputs.

chunks.text: For SWE, an untrained internal variable, δHBV2.0UH shows strong pointwise skill at 525 SNOTEL sites. Median daily SWE NSE is 0.670 for δHBV2.0UH versus 0.517 for NWM3.0, and median annual relative peak bias is −9.6% versus −33.0%. This indicates the hybrid model can produce credible multi-variable outputs even without direct SWE calibration.
supporting_quote: SWE ... demonstrated decent performance (daily NSE of 0.67, Table 2)
annual peak bias of SWE from δHBV2.0UH was reduced to − 9.6%, compared to − 33.0% from NWM3.0

chunks.text: The δHBV models do not explicitly represent reservoirs and human water use, which can dominate streamflow dynamics in certain regions. The paper notes this contributes to high bias that cannot be fixed by routing choices and helps explain where NWM3.0 performs better (e.g., reservoir-dense areas). It also cautions that performance metrics can be less reliable in poorly performing arid regions due to sampling uncertainty.
supporting_quote: Such influences are simulated in NWM3.0 ... but not explicitly included in δHBVs, which consequently could incur a noticeably high bias
metrics were less reliable ... due to fewer data points being available

chunks.text: Although δHBV2.0δMC enables seamless reach-scale outputs, it currently incurs a slight performance penalty versus implicit unit-hydrograph routing in many regions. The paper suggests causes including numerical dispersion in Muskingum-Cunge, structural limits (e.g., prismatic assumptions), and static parameters. It argues routing modules should be viewed as evolving, with future improvements like time-varying Manning’s roughness.
supporting_quote: Muskingum‐Cunge routing performed slightly worse than implicit unit hydrograph routing
The loss of accuracy could be due to numerical dispersion inherent with the Muskingum‐Cunge formulation ... and static parameters

chunks.text: The multiscale training scheme supervises unit-basin parameterization using aggregated outlet observations, which may underconstrain subbasin-scale dynamics. The paper states it is not clear whether δHBV2.0 accurately captures heterogeneous within-basin systems under this setup and invites community evaluation. It proposes that multivariate training or data assimilation could reduce distortions of fluxes within MERIT unit basins.
supporting_quote: It is also currently not clear whether δHBV2.0 accurately captures and simulates the heterogeneous hydrological systems within the basins
multivariate training or data assimilation could be used to reduce the distortion of fluxes within the MERIT unit basins.

chunks.text: Even at higher resolution, δHBV2.0 remains a conceptual rainfall–runoff model emphasizing vertical processes and simplified lateral/baseflow dynamics. The paper contrasts this with NWM’s more detailed 2D St. Venant overland flow and 2D saturated subsurface lateral transport at 250 m. As a result, δHBV2.0 focuses on capturing large-scale behavior with aggregated parameters rather than fully representing detailed flow mechanics.
supporting_quote: the rainfall‐runoff processes are still simulated using conceptual models (like HBV).
In contrast, NWMs solve a two‐dimensional (2D) St. Venant equation for overland flow ... and a 2D saturated subsurface lateral transport equation

chunks.text: High-resolution multiscale training increases computational demands versus basin-lumped models, particularly GPU memory. The paper reports δHBV2.0UH needs about 125 GPU hours and ~50 GB GPU memory to train, while δHBV1.0 needs 70 GPU hours and ~3 GB. This creates practical tradeoffs for training and model experimentation at national scale.
supporting_quote: δHBV2.0UH requires approximately 125 GPU hr and ∼50 Gigabytes of GPU memory
δHBV1.0 needs 70 GPU hr and ∼3 Gigabytes of GPU memory

chunks.text: The study concludes that NN-supported differentiable hydrologic models can substantially improve CONUS-scale streamflow simulation relative to NWM3.0, reaching a median daily NSE of about 0.68 across 4,997 basins and improving bias and hydrograph shape. Multiscale parameterization at MERIT unit basins enables better representation of heterogeneity in forcings and attributes. These benefits extend to challenging regions such as the western CONUS and the Prairie Pothole Region.
supporting_quote: They reached a median daily NSE of ∼0.68 for 4,997 trained and untrained gage stations
The multiscale parameterization ... enabled accurate runoff prediction at high resolution (MERIT unit basins, median 37 km2 )

chunks.text: The paper concludes that explicit Muskingum-Cunge routing, despite slight penalties in smaller basins, is important for major rivers and for producing a seamless discretized streamflow product across the river network. δHBV2.0δMC can provide reach-scale simulations over about 180,000 MERIT unit basins. This supports operationally relevant, spatially distributed streamflow products.
supporting_quote: δHBV2.0δMC, while currently experiencing a slight performance penalty compared to δHBV2.0UH in smaller basins, can produce superior streamflow predictions in major downstream rivers and a seamlessly discretized hydrologic product.
seamlessly discretized streamflow simulation over 180 thousand MERIT unit basins.

chunks.text: The work states the models are designed for integration into future NWM development through standard interfaces. Specifically, it implements a Python Model Interface and a CSDMS Basic Model Interface to align with the NextGen framework. This is presented as enabling immediate compatibility and modular incorporation of δHBV variants into operational modeling workflows.
supporting_quote: we have built two interfaces ... a Python Model Interface (PMI)
a Community Surface Dynamics Model System (CSDMS) Basic Model Interface (BMI) ... so that they can be incorporated into, and operated within, the NextGen framework.

chunks.text: Suspended sediment concentration (SSC) is central to aquatic ecosystem health and reservoir management, with both insufficient and excessive suspended sediment creating major environmental risks. SSC reflects a mix of landscape erosion and in-channel sources, and these sources interact through deposition and resuspension in river networks. Because sediment generation and transport vary strongly across space and time, predicting SSC consistently is difficult and often requires understanding multiple coupled processes.
supporting_quote: Suspended sediment concentration (SSC) is a crucial indicator for aquatic ecosystems and reservoir management but is challenging to predict at large scales.
Suspended sediment in rivers has two primary sources... soil erosion... in the landscape (type A), and... erosion in the river network (type B)

chunks.text: SSC dynamics are often nonlinear and hysteretic due to heterogeneous sediment distributions and complex interactions between rainfall, land cover, soils, and channel processes. Traditional rating-curve approaches often miss these dynamics and can substantially underestimate sediment loads without correction. Process-based approaches can represent mechanisms but are difficult to calibrate and may not transfer well between basins and climates.
supporting_quote: make the sediment dynamics hysteretic, nonlinear, and challenging to predict for both process-based and statistical approaches
sediment loads can be underestimated by up to 50 % using the rating curve without a bias correction (Ferguson, 1986)

chunks.text: Deep learning, especially LSTM networks, has shown strong performance on hydrologic and water-quality time series because it can represent temporal dependencies. Prior sediment deep-learning applications were often limited to single sites and sometimes relied on recent sediment observations, which makes prediction easier but reduces usefulness for forward simulation and generalization. Training across many sites can create a "data synergy" effect where pooled data improves robustness and accuracy.
supporting_quote: long short-term memory (LSTM) deep networks stand out... due to their inherent ability to retain information from previous inputs
there is often a "data synergy" effect, where pooling data from more numerous and more diverse sites resulted in more robust and higher-accuracy models

chunks.text: The study aimed to test whether daily SSC can be predicted at basin outlets using only basin-averaged meteorological forcings, readily available physiographic attributes, and streamflow (observed or modeled). It compared site-specific (local) LSTMs against a single continental (Whole-CONUS) LSTM trained across all basins. The work also examined whether a continental model can provide reliable SSC estimates in unmonitored basins where SSC is not measured.
supporting_quote: predict daily SSC at basin outlets given only basin-averaged forcings, readily-available physiographic attributes, and streamflow (from observation or model)
trained long short-term memory (LSTM) deep networks both separately... ("local models"), and on all the sites collectively (Whole-CONUS).

chunks.text: A core objective was to relate SSC predictability to the correlation between SSC and streamflow (Rs-q) across CONUS. The authors intended to use Rs-q as a diagnostic to infer likely sediment-source controls and to explain where models succeed or fail. This analysis was designed to yield continental-scale insights into SSC patterns and mechanisms.
supporting_quote: we investigated how model performance is related to SSC-streamflow correlations (Rs-q) across the entire CONUS
Rs-q can help us discern the sediment sources and can thus be used as an analysis framework.

chunks.text: The paper explicitly framed three questions: how accurate LSTM SSC estimation can be with minimal inputs, what causes poor SSC–streamflow correlation in low Rs-q basins, and whether widely available geospatial datasets can generically describe daily SSC time series. These questions connect predictive performance to process interpretation and transferability. The focus was on both temporal extrapolation and spatial generalization.
supporting_quote: (1) How accurately can LSTM-based models estimate daily SSC at the continental scale using minimal macroscopic forcings, basin landscape attributes, and (observed or simulated) streamflow?
(3) Can widely available geospatial datasets generically describe the daily SSC time series at the basin scale

chunks.text: Large-scale SSC modeling is constrained by scarce observations relative to streamflow gages, which limits training-site availability and complicates building transferable models. The authors found that only a small subset of GAGES-II basins had enough consecutive SSC samples to support their train/test protocol. This data scarcity motivates methods that can learn from many basins and still generalize.
supporting_quote: we only kept basins for which at least 50 consecutive SSC data points... were available. Therefore, only 377 basins remained out of the 9312 GAGES-II basins
approximately 8500 streamflow gages are available for streamflow modeling, highlighting the challenge posed by the lack of SSC data.

chunks.text: SSC is difficult to predict because it arises from both landscape and in-channel erosion, with drivers that vary in strength and nonlinearity. Landscape erosion depends strongly on rainfall intensity and within-basin heterogeneity, while in-channel erosion is more directly tied to streamflow magnitude and hydraulics. These mixed controls create complex SSC–streamflow relationships that can break simple predictive assumptions.
supporting_quote: soil source is more relevant to the rainfall intensity and sediment supply... resulting in a more nonlinear relationship with streamflow.
The in-channel erosion is driven by streamflow... This process is closely related to the magnitude of the streamflow.

chunks.text: Conventional statistical tools such as sediment rating curves can have substantial bias because they do not adequately capture dynamic sediment processes and hysteresis. Even mixed statistical–process approaches may not fully use information in the time series because they do not explicitly represent memory effects. These limitations motivate sequence models that can learn temporal dependencies from data.
supporting_quote: a rating curve is often used to express SSC as a power law function of streamflow
sediment loads can be underestimated by up to 50 % using the rating curve without a bias correction

chunks.text: Process-based sediment models are challenging to calibrate at scale due to equifinality and sensitivity to climate and basin differences, and they require accurate hydrologic simulation first. Parameters tuned in one basin may not work in another, limiting transferability. This creates an opening for data-driven approaches that can be trained across many basins using common datasets.
supporting_quote: calibration is often challenging for these models... as it often runs into non-uniqueness (or equifinality) issues
parameters calibrated for one basin may not perform well in different climatic conditions. They also first require the hydrology to be correctly simulated

chunks.text: The study trained two LSTM modeling strategies: local models (one LSTM per basin) and a single Whole-CONUS model trained across all basins. For local models, the longest consecutive SSC segment was split 80:20 into training and testing by time. For the Whole-CONUS temporal test, each basin used the same per-basin split; for the spatial test, the model trained on 252 basins and tested on 125 basins to assess prediction in unmonitored basins.
supporting_quote: a model was trained and tested locally for each of the 377 basins, resulting in a total of 377 LSTM-based "local" models.
trained with data... pertaining to 252 basins... and tested on the remaining 125 basins

chunks.text: Irregular SSC data gaps were handled by selecting the longest consecutive SSC sequence per site using the Maximum Sub-Array Sum algorithm, then splitting that sequence into training and testing. This ensured comparable periods across local and Whole-CONUS temporal experiments. The approach prioritized maximizing usable continuous information in sparse SSC records.
supporting_quote: the Maximum Sub-Array Sum algorithm (Takaoka, 2002) was implemented to find the proper training and testing periods for each site.
We firstly found the series of SSC with the maximum number of data points for each site, then split the selected series of SSC into training and testing periods with a ratio of 80:20.

chunks.text: The authors applied quality screening and transformations to stabilize learning across a wide SSC range. SSC values above 10,000 mg/L were capped due to sampling accuracy concerns, and SSC was log-transformed to reduce skewness. Streamflow was made dimensionless by normalizing with basin area and mean annual precipitation, then transformed using a log-sqrt function to approximate a Gaussian distribution.
supporting_quote: sample accuracy is considered inadequate at SSC values of 10,000 mg/L or above... we set the ceiling... to 10,000 mg/L
We also applied a logarithmic transformation... to the SSC data to minimize the skewness... (spanning from 0.1 to 10,000)

chunks.text: All inputs and outputs were standardized after transformation to improve optimization stability and comparability across basins. Model outputs were de-standardized and inverse-transformed to original units before reporting. This pipeline supports training across heterogeneous basins in a single model while still evaluating in physical units.
supporting_quote: A standardization procedure was used to normalize all the inputs and outputs.
All outputs from the model were de-standardized and transformed (if relevant) back into their original units before values were reported.

chunks.text: The LSTM architecture was implemented in PyTorch with an input transformation layer and standard LSTM gates (input, forget, output) and cell/hidden states. The paper emphasizes that LSTM can learn time dependencies and implicitly extract useful features such as hydrograph limb status without manual feature engineering. This temporal modeling capacity was leveraged to predict daily mean SSC from forcings, attributes, and streamflow.
supporting_quote: The LSTM networks were implemented in PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019)
LSTM stands out... because it considers the time dependency of the input and output series (memory in the sequences)

chunks.text: Model training used RMSE as the loss function and the AdaDelta optimizer to adapt learning rates automatically. Hyperparameters were fixed across experiments: batch size 100, dropout 0.5, hidden size 256, and 300 epochs. Training-instance length differed by scale (rho=30 for local models, rho=365 for Whole-CONUS) to cover varied training periods across basins.
supporting_quote: Root-mean-square error (RMSE) between the SSC prediction and observation was set as the loss function for all models.
For both the Whole-CONUS and local models, the batch size was 100 and the dropout rate... was 0.5... hidden size... was 256... trained for 300 epochs.

chunks.text: Performance evaluation used multiple statistics: relative RMSE, relative bias, Pearson correlation (R), coefficient of determination (R2), and NSE. In addition, the SSC–streamflow Pearson correlation (Rs-q) was computed as a mechanism-oriented diagnostic to interpret performance differences and infer source controls. Relative RMSE and bias were normalized by each site's maximum observed SSC.
supporting_quote: We computed five metrics to evaluate model performance: relative RMSE, relative bias, Pearson's correlation coefficient (R), the coefficient of determination (R2 ), and the Nash–Sutcliffe model efficiency coefficient (NSE)
we also used... the Pearson's correlation between SSC and streamflow, Rs-q

chunks.text: Daily SSC observations were sourced from USGS NWIS using parameter code 80154 and linked to GAGES-II basins. Due to data availability constraints, only basins with at least 50 consecutive SSC points were used, resulting in 377 training basins out of 9312 GAGES-II basins. This dataset formed the basis for both local and Whole-CONUS LSTM experiments.
supporting_quote: Historical daily mean SSC data were downloaded... from... NWIS... (parameter code 80154...)
only 377 basins remained out of the 9312 GAGES-II basins across the contiguous United States.

chunks.text: Meteorological forcings were obtained from Daymet at 1-km resolution for 1980–2019 and aggregated to basins. Variables included precipitation, minimum and maximum temperature, vapor pressure, solar radiation, snow water equivalent, and related fields listed in Table A1. Data were accessed via Google Earth Engine at daily resolution.
supporting_quote: Daymet, 1-km resolution... for the time period from 1980 to 2019 at daily resolution.
The variables, including precipitation, minimum and maximum temperatures, vapor pressure, solar radiation, and snow water equivalent

chunks.text: Static watershed attributes were drawn from GAGES-II to represent geology, land cover, soils, slope, and human regulation (e.g., dams and hydrologic disturbance). The input set was motivated by MUSLE and sediment transport mechanisms to capture erosion susceptibility and connectivity at basin scale. Table A1 enumerates these predictors, including land-cover fractions and soil texture variables.
supporting_quote: The static watershed characteristics were acquired from GAGES-II, which includes, but is not limited to, geology types, land cover, and reservoir attributes (Table A1).
Model inputs were inspired by inputs used by the Modification of the Universal Soil Loss Equation (MUSLE)

chunks.text: Streamflow was used as a key dynamic input, with missing observations filled using a pretrained LSTM streamflow model. The cited streamflow model achieved median Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency of 0.74 and was also used to provide streamflow inputs for unmonitored basins lacking SSC measurements. This enabled consistent SSC model forcing even with incomplete gage records.
supporting_quote: We used a pretrained LSTM-based model from Ouyang et al. (2021) (median Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency = 0.74 on streamflow prediction) to fill those missing streamflow observations.
This streamflow model was also employed to provide streamflow inputs for unmonitored basins

chunks.text: The full LSTM input list combined hydrometeorological forcings, streamflow, and many static attributes related to drainage area, precipitation climatology, dam metrics, land cover fractions, soil composition, infiltration groups, and slope. The paper provides these in Table A1, explicitly naming variables like prcp, swe, DRAIN_SQKM, NDAMS_2009, FORESTNLCD06, CLAYAVE, and SLOPE_PCT. This design aimed to represent both climatic forcing and erosion susceptibility using widely available datasets.
supporting_quote: The inputs of LSTM are summarized in Table A1, which include hydrometeorological forcings... static watershed attributes... and the streamflow rate
DRAIN_SQKM... NDAMS_2009... FORESTNLCD06... CLAYAVE... SLOPE_PCT

chunks.text: Across CONUS, mean SSC showed strong spatial structure: it was generally low in the humid eastern U.S. and northwestern mountainous regions but high in the arid southwestern U.S. The authors used this pattern to delineate a high-SSC southwestern region and a lower-SSC region elsewhere. They also observed that low-precipitation areas can still have low SSC where evergreen forest dominates, suggesting vegetation protection effects.
supporting_quote: The mean SSC was generally low in the more humid eastern US and northwestern mountainous area but very high in the southwestern US where the mean precipitation is low
A plausible reason is that these basins have evergreen forest as the dominant land cover... so that the soil erosion in the basin is light

chunks.text: Basins in the high-SSC southwestern region tended to have lower SSC–streamflow correlation (Rs-q), indicating disproportionate SSC peaks relative to streamflow peaks. The paper interprets this as evidence that large SSC responses can occur under low flow or that peak alignment is weak. In contrast, many low-SSC humid regions show higher Rs-q, consistent with more flow-driven sediment dynamics.
supporting_quote: In the high-SSC region (southwestern US), we observed that the SSC tends to have a lower Rs-q
in the low-SSC region... the SSC shows a relative higher Rs-q

chunks.text: For temporal extrapolation, the Whole-CONUS model outperformed local models in aggregate. The median R2 was 0.63 for Whole-CONUS versus 0.52 for local models, indicating improved predictive skill when pooling data across basins. The authors attribute this improvement to data synergy from training on more numerous and diverse sites.
supporting_quote: The Whole-CONUS and local models presented median coefficient of determination (R2) values of 0.63 and 0.52, respectively.
This comparison agrees with previously acknowledged "data synergy" effects for LSTM models

chunks.text: Error metrics also favored the Whole-CONUS temporal model, with lower median RMSE and relative RMSE than local models. Local models had median RMSE 80.55 mg/L and relative RMSE 11.4%, while Whole-CONUS had median RMSE 66.86 mg/L and relative RMSE 10.0%. Relative bias was near zero for both approaches (0.2% local; −0.5% Whole-CONUS).
supporting_quote: The median coefficient of determination (R2 )... local models was 0.52, with a median relative bias and relative RMSE of 0.2 % and 11.4 %
The model's median R2 value was 0.63... The median relative bias and relative RMSE were − 0.5 % and 10.0 %, respectively.

chunks.text: Model performance was strongly stratified by Rs-q: both local and Whole-CONUS models performed better where SSC–streamflow correlation was high. For local models, median R2 reached 0.70 when Rs-q exceeded 0.8, indicating strong predictability in more linear, flow-driven basins. When Rs-q was below 0.2, local-model median R2 dropped to 0.12, showing substantial difficulty in basins with weak SSC–flow coupling.
supporting_quote: The median R2... reached 0.70 when Rs-q was larger than 0.8
When Rs-q is less than 0.2, the median of local model R2 drops to 0.12

chunks.text: Basin seasonality and size were linked to lower Rs-q and poorer performance. Regions with higher snow water equivalent (SWE) were more likely to have low Rs-q, and local-model performance declined with increasing mean SWE. Larger drainage area was also associated with worse local-model performance, consistent with increased hysteresis and within-basin heterogeneity that are hard to capture with basin-averaged inputs.
supporting_quote: SWE... is used to roughly represent the seasonality of the basin, and the regions with high SWE are more likely to have low Rs-q.
the performance of local models tends to decrease with the increase of the drainage area

chunks.text: The Whole-CONUS model demonstrated spatial generalization to unmonitored basins in a PUB-style test. Training on 252 basins and testing on 125 basins, it achieved median R2 of 0.55 with relative bias −0.6% and relative RMSE 8.6%. This supports using a single continental LSTM to predict SSC where only forcings, attributes, and streamflow are available.
supporting_quote: trained with data... pertaining to 252 basins... and tested on the remaining 125 basins
Whole-CONUS model tested on unmonitored basins obtained... median... R2 ) of 0.55... relative bias and relative RMSE were − 0.6 % and 8.6 %

chunks.text: Performance limitations were concentrated in arid, high-SSC basins with low Rs-q, where SSC–streamflow relationships are highly nonlinear. The paper attributes low Rs-q to factors such as differing erosion mechanisms for snowmelt versus rainfall, hysteresis that varies with basin size, and heterogeneity in rainfall intensity, land cover, and soils. These complexities can cause high flows to produce minimal SSC at times, reducing predictability with basin-averaged inputs.
supporting_quote: The highly-nonlinear SSC-streamflow relationships seem related to seasonality, basin size, and heterogeneity of land cover and rainfall within the basins
At certain sites, not all high streamflow peaks lead to significant SSC.

chunks.text: The authors suggest that improving SSC prediction in arid basins may require higher spatial resolution modeling and additional inputs. They argue that basin-averaged predictors may miss localized erosion processes, and that better representation of seasonality-related erosion is needed. Proposed directions include high-resolution rainfall and land cover data and potentially a gridded LSTM rather than basin-based discretization.
supporting_quote: suggesting these basins need to be simulated at higher spatial resolution and may require additional inputs related to SSC induced by seasonality.
capturing sediment erosion in arid basins at a higher spatial resolution may be necessary... likely in the form of a gridded LSTM model rather than with a basin-based spatial discretization.

chunks.text: A key limitation is model opacity: the fully data-driven LSTM is difficult to interpret, and learned sensitivities to basin attributes may not be correct. The paper notes uncertainty in whether static attributes can entirely describe SSC heterogeneity across CONUS. This motivates combining deep learning with process-based priors using differentiable modeling to improve interpretability and extrapolation.
supporting_quote: it is still opaque in that it is difficult to understand the learned sensitivities to basin attributes, and it is uncertain if those learned sensitivities are correct.
even if the sensitivities to the static attributes are not entirely correct (i.e. if the static attributes can entirely describe the heterogeneity of SSC across the CONUS)

chunks.text: The SSC data quality and availability impose constraints on training and evaluation. The study capped SSC at 10,000 mg/L due to known sampling accuracy issues, which can truncate extremes important for hazard assessment. In addition, only 377 basins had enough consecutive data, limiting coverage of some hydroclimatic regimes and potentially biasing learnability toward better-monitored basins.
supporting_quote: sample accuracy is considered inadequate at SSC values of 10,000 mg/L or above... we set the ceiling... to 10,000 mg/L
only 377 basins remained out of the 9312 GAGES-II basins

chunks.text: The paper emphasizes that prediction is inherently easier when recent observations are used, but this work targets forward simulation using forcings, attributes, and streamflow instead of relying on recent sediment observations. Prior neural-network sediment studies often used past sediment values as inputs, which can inflate performance but reduces suitability for projection and unmonitored basins. This underscores why low Rs-q basins remain challenging even with strong deep learning models.
supporting_quote: when recent observations are used for forecasting, the problem is inherently easier and typically results in better prediction metrics than forward simulations
most existing models were not trained on multiple sites... cannot be used for predictions in unmonitored locations.

chunks.text: The study concludes that LSTM models can predict daily SSC at continental scale using minimal, widely available inputs: meteorological forcings, static watershed attributes, and streamflow. The Whole-CONUS model achieved higher temporal-test performance than local models, demonstrating benefits from pooled training data. The authors position this as an initial continental-scale, data-driven daily SSC modeling effort enabling analysis and gap-filling across decades.
supporting_quote: developed a Whole-CONUS LSTM model to accurately predict daily SSC... using only meteorological forcings, related static watershed attributes, and daily streamflow data
Whole-CONUS and local models obtaining median R2 values of 0.63 and 0.52, respectively

chunks.text: They conclude that model success is linked to SSC–streamflow coupling, with high Rs-q basins being more predictable and arid, high-SSC, low Rs-q basins being more challenging. The paper hypothesizes low Rs-q corresponds to greater influence of landscape soil erosion and complex seasonal and heterogeneous drivers. These insights are used to motivate future improvements such as higher-resolution representations and better seasonality-related inputs.
supporting_quote: We further analyzed the relationship between model performance and... Rs-q
We hypothesized that low Rs-q arises when SSC is more likely predominantly induced by soil erosion across the landscape.

chunks.text: The Whole-CONUS model can generalize to predict SSC in unmonitored basins, indicating practical utility where SSC measurements are unavailable but common forcing data exist. In spatial testing, the model achieved median R2 of 0.55, supporting large-scale sediment assessment and historical reconstruction. The authors suggest this capability could help identify spatiotemporal hotspots and trends in SSC over past decades.
supporting_quote: The Whole-CONUS model also performed well for spatial extrapolation... median R2 = 0.55
