chunks.text: Basins are represented using MERIT Hydro basin delineations as SUMMA grouped response units, with no sub-GRU discretization (one GRU equals one HRU). Gridded land surface data are remapped to basin GRUs using area-weighted averaging. Satellite snow products are also remapped similarly, but only time steps with at least 50% GRU pixel coverage are used to reduce missing-data effects from clouds. This yields consistent basin-scale inputs and evaluation data across 289 basins.
supporting_quote: we use the basin delineation as GRUs in this study and do not perform sub-GRU discretization (i.e., one GRU corresponds to one HRU).
Gridded data are remapped to basin GRUs using area-weighted averaging.
we only include samples for which at least 50% of the area of a GRU is covered by MODIS or AVHRR pixels for each time step.

chunks.text: The primary forcing uncertainties come from EM-Earth precipitation and air temperature ensembles, while other meteorological variables are taken deterministically from ERA5. EM-Earth provides 0.1° global land estimates from 1950–2019 and includes 25-member probabilistic daily estimates. ERA5 supplies hourly fields at 0.25° resolution and is used to disaggregate daily EM-Earth ensembles to hourly forcing for SUMMA. The study also selects specific ERA5 levels for some variables to avoid land-model coupling effects.
supporting_quote: This study uses precipitation and air temperature data from EM-Earth. Other meteorological forcing variables are taken from ERA5 at the hourly and 0.25° resolution.
EM-Earth provides ... at the 0.1° resolution from 1950 to 2019
the 25-member probabilistic estimates are provided at daily timesteps
We obtained air temperature, wind speed, and specific humidity ... (L137, 10 m above the land surface)

chunks.text: Basin and river network structure is derived from MERIT Hydro (MERIT-BASINS), which delineates roughly 3 million basins globally. The delineation uses a ~25 km² channelization threshold and is adopted here to define GRUs for modeling. This provides consistent hydrography and routing connectivity across the study domain. Basin sizes in the selected sample are constrained to support computational feasibility and data representativeness.
supporting_quote: We adopt the MERIT Hydro basin delineation and river network, which divides the globe into ∼3 million basins using a 25 km2 channelization threshold
For simplicity, we use the basin delineation as GRUs in this study

chunks.text: Land surface characterization uses multiple global gridded products: MERIT DEM (~90 m), MODIS land cover (500 m), and SoilGrids soil classes (250 m). These layers are processed and remapped to basin GRUs using area-weighted averaging. The combination supports parameter and process representations for snow, soil, and vegetation in SUMMA. Preparation steps follow established workflows referenced by the authors.
supporting_quote: The Digital Elevation Model (DEM) data are ... from the Multi-Error-Removed Improved-Terrain (MERIT) DEM ... at the ∼90-m spatial resolution.
The land cover data are from ... MODIS MCD12Q1 V6 at 500-m resolution
The soil class data are from SoilGrids at 250-m resolution
Gridded data are remapped to basin GRUs using area-weighted averaging.

chunks.text: Snow cover observations used for calibration/validation are from MODIS Terra daily snow cover (MOD10A1, Version 61) and ESA Snow_cci AVHRR daily global snow cover fraction (1982–2018). MODIS NDSI is converted to fractional snow cover using FSC = −0.01 + (1.45 × NDSI). Both products are remapped to GRUs, and samples are filtered to require at least 50% GRU pixel coverage per time step to limit missing-data impacts. These data constrain snow process simulation beyond streamflow alone.
supporting_quote: MOD10A1 provides daily Normalized Difference Snow Index (NDSI) data
The NDSI is converted to fractional snow cover (FSC) using FSC = −0.01 + (1.45 × NDSI)
AVHRR Snow_cci provides daily fractional snow cover from 1982 to 2018
we only include samples for which at least 50% of the area of a GRU is covered by MODIS or AVHRR pixels for each time step.

chunks.text: Streamflow observations are drawn from a global database compiled from international and national sources with more than 22,000 gauges. From this database, 289 cryosphere basins are selected, with basin areas constrained between 100 and 20,000 km². Basins must have at least 10 years of continuous streamflow data between 1950 and 2019 and limited human impacts based on reservoir capacity, urban fraction, and irrigation fraction thresholds. These criteria support consistent calibration/validation and emphasize natural hydrologic response.
supporting_quote: Streamflow observations come from a global database ... comprising in total of >22,000 gauges
We select 289 cryosphere basins with areas between 100 and 20,000 km2
the basin should have at least 10 years of continuous streamflow data between 1950 and 2019
None of the three indices should exceed 0.01.

chunks.text: Meteorological uncertainty patterns from EM-Earth vary regionally for precipitation and air temperature. Precipitation uncertainty is larger in North American prairies, Canada, and eastern Siberia, and uncertainty ratios tend to be larger in drier regions. Air temperature uncertainty is larger in complex terrain (e.g., Rocky Mountains, Andes, east Asia) where sparse gauges limit robust local regression. Flatter, well-instrumented regions such as eastern CONUS and Europe show smaller temperature ensemble spread.
supporting_quote: The precipitation uncertainty is larger in the prairies of North America, Canada, and eastern Siberia
The uncertainty ratio tends to be larger in regions with less precipitation.
The air temperature uncertainty is larger in regions with complex terrain such as the Rocky Mountains, Andes Mountains, and east Asia

chunks.text: Snowfall uncertainty can exceed precipitation uncertainty because snowfall depends jointly on precipitation and air temperature through precipitation-phase partitioning. The study notes that regions with modest precipitation uncertainty can still have increased snowfall uncertainty due to temperature uncertainty contributions, such as the U.S. west coast. This demonstrates that temperature uncertainty can strongly influence cryosphere-relevant fluxes. Deterministic humidity and pressure inputs may also reduce uncertainty in phase partitioning relative to a fully probabilistic forcing set.
supporting_quote: Snowfall is jointly affected by precipitation and air temperature, showing larger uncertainties than precipitation
on the west coast of the U.S., the precipitation uncertainty is smaller ... while snowfall shows increased regional uncertainties because of the contribution of temperature uncertainties

chunks.text: Ground snow variables (e.g., SWE, fractional snow cover, snow drainage) share similar spatial uncertainty patterns, with the highest uncertainty ratios often occurring in low-latitude regions. In such regions, small snowfall and short snow duration make snow accumulation and melt sensitive to meteorological uncertainty near the rain–snow threshold. In contrast, high-latitude regions can have large precipitation and snowfall uncertainties but smaller ground-snow uncertainties because large snowpacks dampen relative impacts. The result emphasizes that large forcing uncertainty does not automatically imply large hydrologic uncertainty.
supporting_quote: The highest uncertainties occur in low latitude regions ... because, in low latitudes, both snowfall and duration of ground snow are small
in high latitudes, the accumulation of ground snow is enormous, and the impacts of meteorological uncertainties on snow processes are offset/small
large meteorological uncertainties do not necessarily lead to large hydrological uncertainties in cryosphere basins

chunks.text: Total soil water uncertainty is generally small, consistent with slow soil-water response to atmospheric variability. The paper offers multiple mechanisms: saturated soils reduce sensitivity to forcing uncertainty, snow cover dampens propagation, frozen soil restricts variability, and deep soil acts as a reservoir that offsets event-scale variability. The authors suggest shallow soil may be more sensitive than deep layers and recommend more detailed soil-state analyses. Overall, meteorological uncertainties have limited impact on total soil water at the analyzed scales.
supporting_quote: The uncertainty of total soil water ... is small

meteorological uncertainties have little impact on total soil water: (a) if the soil is saturated ... (b) if the soil is covered by snow ... (c) soils can be frozen ... (d) deep soil can function as the reservoir

chunks.text: Runoff uncertainty is spatially heterogeneous, with particularly large uncertainties in North American prairie regions. Surface runoff shows large uncertainties in several regions (high-latitude Canada, eastern Europe near the Black Sea, and eastern Asia), while baseflow uncertainties are generally lower. Total runoff uncertainty tends to fall between surface runoff and baseflow uncertainty. The paper notes that basins with greater baseflow contribution could exhibit smaller total runoff uncertainty.
supporting_quote: All runoff components show large uncertainties in the prairie of North America.
Surface runoff also shows large uncertainties in high-latitude Canada, eastern Europe ... and eastern Asia.
The uncertainty of total runoff is generally between the uncertainty of surface runoff and baseflow.

chunks.text: Among energy-related variables, net radiation exhibits small uncertainty because it depends on shortwave and longwave fluxes that are not controlled by precipitation and air temperature in this setup. Latent heat and ET have near-identical spatial patterns and resemble precipitation uncertainty patterns in many regions, reflecting dependence on water availability. Sensible heat shows a smoother uncertainty field than latent heat/ET. In high-latitude North America, small magnitudes of latent heat and ET can produce large uncertainty ratios.
supporting_quote: Net radiation ... is not controlled by precipitation and air temperature and shows smaller uncertainties.
Latent heat and ET show almost the same spatial distributions
the latent heat (or ET) uncertainty distribution is generally similar to precipitation uncertainty distribution

chunks.text: Hydrologic signatures computed after full spatiotemporal averaging (ST-none)—baseflow ratio, runoff ratio, and snow-melt runoff ratio—are generally robust to forcing uncertainty. Most basins show uncertainty ratios smaller than 0.05 for these signatures, largely due to the scale effect of averaging. Larger uncertainties persist in prairie regions and around the Black Sea, and snow-melt runoff ratio uncertainty can be larger where snowfall amounts are small (e.g., south of the Great Lakes). The authors caution that small spread indicates robustness to forcing uncertainty, not necessarily accuracy.
supporting_quote: The signatures show uncertainty ratios smaller than 0.05 for most basins due to the scale effect
The three variables show relatively large uncertainties in the prairie regions and around the Black Sea
hydrologic signatures from models are generally robust with the existence of meteorological uncertainties

chunks.text: Uncertainty exhibits a strong scale effect: spatiotemporal averaging (ST-none) notably reduces both precipitation and air temperature uncertainty relative to raw ST-both calculations. The reduction mainly benefits from temporal averaging, which offsets uncertainty associated with meteorological variability. Spatial averaging slightly reduces precipitation uncertainty and has little impact on air temperature uncertainty at the basin sizes studied (100–20,000 km²). The effectiveness of spatial averaging increases with basin area, with Spearman correlations of 0.87 (precipitation) and 0.74 (air temperature).
supporting_quote: ST-none ... notably reduces the uncertainty compared to ST-both ... mainly benefiting from temporal averaging
Spatial averaging slightly reduces the uncertainty for precipitation ... and has little impact on air temperature
The coefficients are 0.87 for precipitation and 0.74 for air temperature

chunks.text: For hydrological variables, temporal averaging substantially reduces uncertainty, but the reduction differs by variable type. State variables (snow depth, SWE, snow cover, total soil water) show smaller reduction than many flux variables (snow drainage, surface runoff, total runoff), while baseflow behaves more like a slow state with smaller reduction. Streamflow shows smaller reduction than total runoff because routing smooths and slows the signal. Energy variables and meteorological fluxes (precipitation and snowfall) show the largest reduction ratios under temporal averaging.
supporting_quote: Temporal averaging can notably reduce hydrological variable uncertainties, while different variables exhibit different sensitivities
State variables ... show a much smaller reduction ratio compared to most flux variables ... except for baseflow
Streamflow shows a smaller reduction ratio compared to total runoff because the routing process makes streamflow a slower and smoother variable

chunks.text: Precipitation uncertainty generally dominates hydrological modeling uncertainty, but air temperature uncertainty is nonnegligible and can dominate for some variables. Across most variables and basins, RT/P is below 1, meaning UT is smaller than UP. Energy variables show high RT/P, with median RT/P values of 1.1 for sensible heat and 2.9 for net radiation, indicating temperature uncertainty can exceed precipitation uncertainty for these outputs. Snow drainage also has relatively high RT/P, highlighting stronger temperature influence during melt.
supporting_quote: Overall, for most variables and basins, RT/P is smaller than one
For sensible heat and net radiation ... the RT/P median values are up to 1.1 and 2.9, respectively.
Snow drainage shows the highest RT/P among all snow-related variables

chunks.text: The study acknowledges that it only analyzes precipitation and air temperature uncertainty, while other forcing variables (radiation, wind speed, pressure, humidity) are held deterministic. This is described as a simplification of real-world uncertainty propagation, and the authors call for future work on other variables and their propagation to hydrological forecasts. They also note that some phenomena, such as temperature uncertainty dominating in a few basins/variables, warrant deeper investigation. These limitations affect completeness of uncertainty attribution.
supporting_quote: Using probabilistic estimates of precipitation and air temperature, while keeping the radiation, wind speed, pressure, and humidity inputs constant, is a simplification of the real-world uncertainty propagation.
exploring the uncertainty propagation of various meteorological variables to hydrological forecasts is of great importance.
Some interesting phenomena ... can be further investigated and explained.

chunks.text: Geographic representativeness is limited by data availability, with weaker coverage in parts of Asia and missing coverage in key cryosphere regions. The authors explicitly note that basin coverage should be improved in Siberia, Central Asia, and the Tibetan Plateau, where open streamflow data are scarce. This constraint can bias global generalizations toward North America and Europe where gauges and ancillary data are more available. Expanding observations would strengthen inference about uncertainty in under-sampled cryosphere areas.
supporting_quote: The coverage of cryosphere basins should be improved in Asia (Siberia, Central Asia, and Tibetan Plateau) where the public streamflow database often has few or no stations.
Most basins are in North America and Europe ... completely absent (e.g., the Tibetan Plateau) due to the scarcity of station networks and the unavailability of open-access data.

chunks.text: The interaction between forcing uncertainties and parameter uncertainties is not examined. Calibration is performed using deterministic EM-Earth forcing rather than probabilistic ensemble calibration, primarily due to computational constraints across hundreds of basins. The authors note parameter changes could alter model sensitivity to forcing uncertainty and that exploring parameter–forcing uncertainty interactions is beyond scope. This limits conclusions about total predictive uncertainty under combined parameter and forcing uncertainty.
supporting_quote: The interaction between forcing uncertainties and parameter uncertainties also needs investigation.
we use EM-Earth deterministic ... rather than probabilistic estimates for model calibration ... it is beyond the scope of this study due to the large computational consumption in hundreds of basins.
It is possible that parameter changes can affect the response ... while exploring the interaction between parameter and forcing uncertainties is beyond the scope of this study.

chunks.text: The study highlights dependence on model and metric choices. SUMMA is process-based and realistic but computationally demanding, while simpler models might be more practical for extensive ensemble uncertainty analysis. The uncertainty metric used is the ratio of ensemble standard deviation to ensemble mean (or standard deviation for temperature), but alternative spread measures (quantiles, seasonal normalization, skewness-aware approaches) could yield different insights. The authors propose future work testing model dependence and alternative uncertainty metrics.
supporting_quote: This study uses a complex process-based hydrological model (SUMMA) ... but is also computationally demanding.
This study uses the ratio between ensemble standard deviation and ensemble mean as the metric to quantify uncertainties.
Exploring model dependence and testing other uncertainty metrics can help reveal modeling uncertainties more comprehensively.

chunks.text: The study concludes that real-world precipitation and air temperature forcing uncertainties can generate substantial hydrological modeling uncertainty in cryosphere basins, sometimes exceeding the magnitude of the modeled variables. It reports characteristic uncertainty rankings across process groups: snow variables show increasing uncertainty through process complexity; runoff uncertainty reflects low baseflow and higher surface runoff; and net radiation is least affected by precipitation and temperature. The results caution that deterministic simulations can be quite uncertain and should be interpreted carefully in cryosphere applications.
supporting_quote: The magnitude of uncertainties is nonnegligible, which can exceed 100% of the magnitude of hydrology variables in some cases.
ground snow variables with higher process complexity exhibit larger uncertainties ... (snow cover < snow depth ≤ SWE < snow drainage < snowfall)
uncertainty in runoff originates from the low uncertainty of baseflow and high uncertainty of surface runoff and is reduced after routing (baseflow < streamflow < total runoff < surface runoff)
net radiation only receives a limited impact from precipitation and air temperature (net radiation < sensible heat < ET ≈ latent heat)

chunks.text: A key conclusion is that uncertainty strongly depends on analysis scale due to averaging effects. Across the evaluated basin sizes and resolutions, the uncertainty magnitude generally ranks as ST-none < S-only < T-only < ST-both. Temporal averaging reduces uncertainty substantially, and variables with faster response to meteorological inputs show larger reductions than slow-response variables. This implies that coarse-scale analyses may underestimate uncertainty present at finer spatiotemporal scales and can change the relative uncertainty ranking among variables.
supporting_quote: For the basins and scales of this study, the uncertainty magnitude rank is ST-none < S-only < T-only < ST-both.

The response speed to meteorological inputs could decide the uncertainty reduction caused by temporal averaging: quick-response variables often show larger uncertainty reduction compared to slow-response variables

chunks.text: The paper concludes that precipitation uncertainty is typically the dominant driver of hydrological modeling uncertainty, but air temperature uncertainty is sometimes comparable or larger, especially for energy variables and snowmelt-related fluxes. Median RT/P values exceed 0.4 for several outputs, including snow cover (0.42), ET (0.44), latent heat (0.52), snow drainage (0.55), sensible heat (1.1), and net radiation (2.9). It also concludes that snow indicators (SWE, snowfall amount, snowfall fraction) can help anticipate where temperature uncertainty will matter more for certain variables. Finally, precipitation and temperature uncertainties can partially offset in joint simulations.
supporting_quote: The precipitation uncertainty is the dominant source of modeling uncertainties for most basins and variables.
the median ratio values of 289 basins are larger than 0.4 for six variables: snow cover (0.42) < ET (0.44) < latent heat (0.52) < snow drainage (0.55) < sensible heat (1.1) < net radiation (2.9).
it is possible to predict the impact of air temperature uncertainties ... based on the snow-related indicator variables
precipitation and air temperature uncertainties can offset each other in hydrological modeling.

chunks.text: Hydrologic modeling supports process understanding, water management, and hazard monitoring, but it is affected by multiple uncertainty sources. Among these, uncertainty from meteorological input data is often the most important, influencing parameter estimates and water-balance calculations. Global meteorological datasets remain uncertain due to sparse station networks, measurement errors (e.g., precipitation under-catch), imperfect atmospheric models, and limitations of remote sensing retrievals.
supporting_quote: Hydrologic modeling is affected by uncertainties originating from input data, model structures and parameterization, and output/calibration data
The uncertainty stemming from meteorological input data is arguably the most important uncertainty source

chunks.text: Uncertainty quantification in hydrology commonly uses either multiple forcing products (an ad hoc ensemble) or probabilistic/stochastic perturbation methods. Multi-product ensembles are easy to implement but may not represent real-world uncertainty. Probabilistic methods can better reflect real-world uncertainty when their assumed error distributions align with actual meteorological errors.
supporting_quote: The first approach ... quantify hydrologic modeling uncertainties is popular and easy to implement
However, the uncertainty derived from these methods provides an ad hoc "ensemble of opportunity" that is not constrained to represent real-world meteorological uncertainties
The second approach defines the probability distribution of errors ... and then perturbs meteorological data by sampling from these probability distributions

chunks.text: Probabilistic meteorological inputs have historically been rare in large-domain hydrologic modeling because producing reliable probabilistic forcings and running ensembles are computationally challenging. New probabilistic datasets now provide multiple equally plausible realizations, enabling explicit uncertainty quantification. EM-Earth is highlighted as a global dataset offering deterministic and probabilistic precipitation and temperature estimates over long periods.
supporting_quote: Probabilistic estimates of meteorological inputs are rarely used in large-domain hydrologic modeling due to the challenges
EM-Earth ... provides long-term deterministic and probabilistic estimates of four meteorological variables over global land for the first time

chunks.text: The study aims to quantify how real-world uncertainties in precipitation and air temperature propagate into global hydrologic simulations. It evaluates impacts on key hydrologic variables across approximately three million subbasins worldwide using ensemble forcings. It also introduces two complementary normalized metrics to identify uncertainty hotspots, one measuring uncertainty magnitude relative to climatology and another measuring uncertainty propagation relative to natural variability.
supporting_quote: we evaluate how uncertainties in spatial meteorological data affect uncertainties in simulations of hydrologic processes across the globe
assessing the impact of precipitation and temperature uncertainties across approximately three million subbasins globally
we defined two normalized uncertainty metrics (ψ and χ)

chunks.text: A key objective is to provide a coherent global picture of meteorological–hydrological uncertainty propagation, especially in remote regions such as the Northern Hemisphere high latitudes, the Southern Hemisphere, and mountains. The analysis is performed for 2004–2019 with ensemble-driven simulations to reveal spatial patterns and hotspots in uncertainties of modeled land and river variables.
supporting_quote: researchers lack a coherent and quantitative global picture of the magnitude and spatial variability of meteorological–hydrological uncertainty propagation
Simulations are performed for the period 2004–19

chunks.text: Global understanding of how real-world precipitation and temperature uncertainties affect hydrologic modeling remains limited. This gap is especially pronounced for remote areas where observations are sparse and terrain is complex. Without a global assessment, it is difficult to identify where uncertainty propagation is strongest and where improvements to forcing datasets would be most beneficial.
supporting_quote: the impact of real-world meteorological uncertainties on global hydrologic modeling has not yet been investigated
particularly in remote areas such as the northern land areas, the Southern Hemisphere, and the mountains

chunks.text: Most large-scale studies emphasize precipitation uncertainty because it dominates hydrologic variability, but temperature uncertainty can be important, especially for snow processes. The study frames temperature uncertainty as often overlooked despite its influence on cryosphere hydrology and potential relevance under climate change. This motivates considering both precipitation and air temperature uncertainty together.
supporting_quote: Most studies focus on the impact of precipitation uncertainties
Air temperature also substantially affects land surface processes, especially snow processes in cryosphere basins. However, the impact of air temperature uncertainties is often overlooked

chunks.text: Ideally, uncertainty in all forcing variables would be included, but probabilistic estimates are often unavailable for variables other than precipitation and temperature. This creates an incomplete characterization of meteorological uncertainty impacts in process-based models that require multiple forcings. The study therefore focuses on precipitation and temperature as critical water-cycle drivers while acknowledging missing ensemble forcings for other variables.
supporting_quote: Ideally, the uncertainties of all forcing variables should be considered
this study only uses ensemble estimates for precipitation and air temperature because EM-Earth does not provide ensemble estimates for other variables

chunks.text: The study uses EM-Earth, a 25-member ensemble dataset for precipitation and air temperature at 0.1° resolution, constructed by merging station-based SC-Earth and ERA5 via optimal interpolation. Uncertainty is estimated using a leave-one-out strategy and used to perturb deterministic fields to generate ensemble realizations. Spatial and temporal correlation is considered during ensemble generation, providing equally plausible forcing members.
supporting_quote: EM-Earth provides 25-member estimates of precipitation and air temperature at 0.1° resolution from 1950 to 2019
The leave-one-out strategy is employed to quantify the uncertainty of these spatial estimates
Ensemble realizations are then generated by perturbing the deterministic precipitation and temperature estimates

chunks.text: Daily EM-Earth precipitation and temperature are disaggregated to hourly to drive SUMMA, using ERA5 hourly series as reference. Precipitation uses multiplicative disaggregation based on the ratio of EM-Earth daily totals to ERA5 daily totals. Temperature uses additive disaggregation based on the difference between EM-Earth and ERA5 daily mean temperatures, added to ERA5 hourly temperatures.
supporting_quote: the daily EM-Earth estimates are disaggregated to the hourly scale using the hourly series of ERA5 as the reference
For precipitation, a multiplicative disaggregation approach is applied
For air temperature, an additive disaggregation method is used

chunks.text: Hydrologic simulation uses the process-based SUMMA model for land processes and mizuRoute for river routing across global land except Antarctica and Greenland. Each MERIT Basins subbasin is treated as a grouped response unit (GRU) with one hydrologic response unit (HRU) to reduce computation. Routing excludes lakes and reservoirs in the main experiments, producing streamflow for river segments from simulated runoff.
supporting_quote: SUMMA divides the modeling domain into grouped response units (GRUs, e.g., subbasins)
We do not perform HRU discretization ... (i.e., there is one HRU per GRU)
mizuRoute ... accepts the runoff outputs ... and generates streamflow for all river segments across the modeling domain

chunks.text: To improve global performance without full calibration, two sensitive SUMMA parameters are estimated: k_soil (soil hydraulic conductivity) and qSurfScale (surface runoff scaling factor). The globe is divided into 10°×10° boxes and representative basins are sampled (7379 basins). For each basin, 400 combinations (20×20) are evaluated, selecting parameter pairs that best match reference runoff and baseflow ratios, then transferring parameters to other basins by nearest match in soil and vegetation class.
supporting_quote: we select two parameters (k_soil as the hydraulic conductivity of soil and qSurfScale as the scaling factor in the surface runoff parameterization)
The number of selected basins is 7379
20 values ... resulting in 400 combinations of the two parameters
we transfer parameters from the closest calibrated basin with the same vegetation and soil classes

chunks.text: The ensemble experiment runs SUMMA/mizuRoute 25 times using EM-Earth precipitation and temperature members for 2004–2019 (and subperiods 2004–09 and 2010–19). SUMMA runs hourly but outputs are saved daily to match EM-Earth inputs and reduce storage. Uncertainty is computed on daily outputs at each basin or river segment using ensemble mean and ensemble spread.
supporting_quote: We run SUMMA/mizuRoute 25 times for the global domain
Simulations are performed for the period 2004–19, 2004–09, and 2010–19
SUMMA is run at the hourly time scale ... Model outputs are saved on the daily scale

chunks.text: Uncertainty is summarized using daily ensemble mean (μ_t) and standard deviation (σ_t) across 25 members, then aggregated to time-series statistics: mean of μ_t (μ̄), mean ensemble standard deviation (σ̄_e), and temporal variability of μ_t (σ_s). Two normalized metrics are defined: ψ = σ̄_e/μ̄ (relative to climatological mean) and χ = σ̄_e/σ_s (uncertainty propagation relative to natural variability). Values greater than one indicate uncertainty exceeding mean magnitude (ψ) or temporal variability (χ).
supporting_quote: we defined two normalized uncertainty metrics (ψ and χ)
ψ = \frac{\overline{\sigma_e}}{\overline{\mu}}
χ = \frac{\overline{\sigma_e}}{\sigma_s}
The ψ values greater than one indicate that the variability introduced by uncertainties ... is greater than the average magnitude

chunks.text: EM-Earth provides 25-member precipitation and air temperature estimates at 0.1° resolution for global land, with a long record. The dataset is built from SC-Earth station observations and ERA5 reanalysis, merged using optimal interpolation. Uncertainty is quantified through a leave-one-out procedure and used to generate ensemble perturbations; the authors note EM-Earth may underestimate true uncertainty because it does not include raw station bias like snowfall under-catch.
supporting_quote: EM-Earth provides 25-member estimates of precipitation and air temperature at 0.1° resolution from 1950 to 2019 for global land areas
EM-Earth is built on ... station observations from the serially complete Earth (SC-Earth) dataset ... and the reanalysis estimates from ERA5
EM-Earth could still underestimate the "true" uncertainties because it does not consider inherent biases in raw station measurements (e.g., under-catch of snowfall)

chunks.text: Other meteorological forcing variables required by SUMMA are taken from ERA5 at hourly and 0.25° resolution, while precipitation and air temperature come from EM-Earth. Daily EM-Earth values are disaggregated to hourly using ERA5 diurnal structure. The combination of EM-Earth and ERA5 introduces potential inhomogeneity, which the authors flag as requiring further investigation.
supporting_quote: Precipitation and air temperature estimates come from EM-Earth, while other variables are sourced from ERA5 at the hourly and 0.25° resolution
Combining data from different sources (e.g., EM-Earth and ERA5 in this study) ... while the potential influence caused by the inhomogeneity among datasets requires further investigation

chunks.text: The spatial modeling units are derived from MERIT Basins, providing a global basin and river network delineation with approximately three million subbasins. Each subbasin is a SUMMA GRU, and river segments are attributed with Strahler stream order for analysis and mapping. The global domain excludes Antarctica and Greenland for routing.
supporting_quote: MERIT Basins dataset (Lin et al. 2019) which has ∼3 million subbasins
Each subbasin is treated as a GRU in SUMMA
Each river segment in MERIT Basins is assigned a Strahler stream order

chunks.text: Topography, land cover, and soil properties are taken from global gridded products and remapped to basin units. Elevation comes from hydrologically adjusted MERIT DEM at ~90 m. Land cover uses MODIS MCD12Q1 v6 at 500 m and soil classes come from SoilGrids at 250 m; gridded variables are aggregated to basins by area-weighted averaging.
supporting_quote: DEM data are the hydrologically adjusted elevations ... from the MERIT DEM dataset ... at the ∼90-m spatial resolution
The land-cover data are from ... MODIS ... (MCD12Q1) v6 at 500-m resolution
The soil class data are from SoilGrids at 250-m resolution

chunks.text: The computational experiment is large: each ensemble member’s forcing volume is reported as 6.6 TB, and the 25-member raw model outputs total 24.3 TB. Simulations were executed on multiple high-performance computing platforms (Graham, Narval, and Cedar). These details contextualize why the ensemble size and variable coverage are constrained.
supporting_quote: The size of meteorological forcing is 6.6 TB for each ensemble member
The size of raw 25-member SUMMA/mizuRoute outputs is 24.3 TB
The global modeling was performed on three high-performance computing platforms (Graham, Narval, and Cedar)

chunks.text: EM-Earth precipitation uncertainty patterns broadly follow wet tropical regions, with high mean, variability, and uncertainty over the Amazon, Congo, and Malay Archipelago. Globally, precipitation’s χ is smaller than ψ because temporal variability exceeds the mean; the paper reports global mean/median χ of 0.37/0.35 versus ψ of 0.90/0.82. Relative uncertainties are also high in the Sahara for ψ, reflecting low mean precipitation.
supporting_quote: with the highest values in tropical regions including the Amazon rainforest, the Congo rainforest, and the Malay Archipelago
leading to smaller χ (global mean/median: 0.37/0.35) than ψ (global mean/median: 0.90/0.82)
The high ψ is partly attributed to the high values in the Sahara Desert

chunks.text: Air temperature uncertainty is largest in complex terrain and high latitudes, including the Tibetan Plateau, Rocky Mountains, Siberia, northern Canada, and Greenland. The study notes ψ becomes larger in colder regions because the same absolute uncertainty yields a larger ratio when mean temperature is low. In contrast, χ can be large in tropical regions where temperature’s temporal variability is low.
supporting_quote: air temperature exhibits the largest uncertainty in complex terrain such as the Tibetan Plateau and Rocky Mountains and in high-latitude areas such as Siberia, northern Canada, and Greenland
For temperature, ψ is larger in colder regions ... mainly because the same temperature uncertainty ... leads to larger ψ for low mean temperature
The χ is large in tropical regions due to the low temporal variability of air temperature

chunks.text: A comparison to a prior calibration-focused study in 289 cryosphere basins suggests that calibrating parameters can reduce uncertainty ratios, especially for χ. Median ψ across variables is often similar between calibrated and a priori parameters, but discrepancies are larger for snow-related variables. The authors interpret this as evidence that observational constraints can reduce the impact of input uncertainty in simulations.
supporting_quote: comparison ... in 289 cryosphere basins on the global scale
calibrated parameters often show smaller uncertainty ratios than a priori parameters, especially for χ
with large discrepancies for ground snow variables, especially snow drainage

chunks.text: For snow water equivalent (SWE), χ hotspots occur in Arctic coastal regions (e.g., Arctic Archipelago and Hudson Bay), Russia, High Mountain Asia, and North American prairies. ψ increases as SWE decreases, with a strong negative Spearman correlation reported up to −0.84, meaning relative uncertainty can match or exceed mean SWE in low-SWE regions. For basins with average daily SWE > 0.1 mm, global mean/median χ/ψ are 0.30/0.50 and 0.26/0.44, respectively.
supporting_quote: SWE shows higher χ values in Arctic coastal regions such as the Arctic Archipelago and Hudson Bay in Canada, Russia, High Mountain Asia, and the prairie regions of North America
with Spearman's rank correlation coefficient between them up to −0.84
for basins with average daily SWE larger than 0.1mm, the global mean and median χ/ψ values are 0.30/0.50 and 0.26/0.44

chunks.text: Total soil water shows highest χ in drier regions such as northern Canada, the Sahel, the Arabian Peninsula, and the rain shadow of the Andes. The global mean/median χ are 0.45/0.37, while ψ is much smaller (0.017/0.016) because total soil water integrates eight layers to 4 m depth, damping the relative effect on the total amount. The authors interpret χ and ψ as reflecting faster (shallow) versus slower (deep) soil-water responses.
supporting_quote: χ highest in drier areas such as northern Canada, the Sahel, the Arabian Peninsula, and in the rain shadow of the Andes
The global mean and median χ values are 0.45 and 0.37, respectively, much larger than 0.017 and 0.016 for ψ
total soil water ... calculated from eight layers with a depth of 4m

chunks.text: Total runoff uncertainty propagation (χ) is highest in tropical rain forests, including the Amazon, Congo, and the Malay Archipelago, matching forcing uncertainty hotspots. The paper reports global mean/median χ of 0.27/0.26, while ψ is higher at 0.77/0.68. Uncertainty in total runoff is dominated by surface runoff rather than baseflow because it is less smoothed by soil and aquifer storage.
supporting_quote: For total runoff, χ is the highest in the tropical rain forests, including the Amazon and Congo River basins and the Malay Archipelago
The global mean and median χ values are 0.27 and 0.26, respectively, much lower than 0.77 and 0.68 of ψ
This indicates that the uncertainties of total runoff mainly come from surface runoff

chunks.text: The study quantifies how extremes contribute disproportionately to uncertainty. Globally, runoff days in the 95%–100% percentile contribute 41.59% of total uncertainty, while days in the 0%–20% percentile contribute only 1.50%. This pattern is strongest in dry areas and is also observed for SWE, soil water, and ET (though weaker for soil water), implying increasing extremes could increase overall hydrologic uncertainty.
supporting_quote: days within the 95%–100% percentiles of runoff contribute 41.59% of the total uncertainty
days within the 0%–20% percentiles of runoff only contribute 1.50% of the total uncertainty
As more extreme events are expected in the future, the uncertainty in hydrologic simulations is likely to increase

chunks.text: For routed streamflow, μ, σ_s, and σ̄_e show highly consistent spatial distributions with cross correlation above 0.9, but ψ and χ are largely uncorrelated globally, emphasizing their different interpretations. Both metrics are low in high-latitude and high-altitude regions and are smaller downstream than upstream, consistent with cryosphere damping and routing-based aggregation reducing uncertainty ratios.
supporting_quote: The uncertainty magnitude ... the mean streamflow μ, and the temporal variability σs ... show highly consistent spatial distributions with the cross correlation between them above 0.9
the correlation between ψ and χ is negligible on the global scale
Both metrics are relatively low in high-latitude and high-altitude areas
downstream reaches have smaller uncertainty ratios compared to the tributaries and upstream

chunks.text: Streamflow hotspots differ by metric: ψ highlights arid regions (Sahara, Arabian, Australian, and South American deserts), while χ highlights tropical rain forests and Europe (except Scandinavia). The paper links this to dry-region characteristics (low mean runoff and low baseflow ratios) raising ψ, while high baseflow ratio regions have lower temporal variability, increasing χ. These patterns indicate baseflow ratio is closely linked to uncertainty-metric behavior.
supporting_quote: Areas with a dry climate (e.g., the Sahara Desert, Arabian Desert, Australian Desert, and South American deserts) are identified as uncertainty hotspots by ψ but not χ
Tropical rain forests ... and Europe (except the Scandinavian Peninsula) emerge as χ hotspots but not for ψ
These areas are characterized by high baseflow ratios (Beck et al. 2015)

chunks.text: Streamflow and its uncertainty increase with drainage area, but ψ decreases logarithmically with drainage area. For 1.48 million headwater basins (median area 45.57 km²), the 25%, 50%, and 75% of ψ are 0.45, 0.85, and 1.22. For major river outlets like the Amazon, Nile, and Yangtze, ψ drops below 0.1, indicating large-basin aggregation stabilizes relative uncertainty.
supporting_quote: streamflow and its uncertainty ... linearly increases with river drainage areas
The uncertainty metric ψ shows a logarithmic relationship with the drainage area
for the 1.48 million headwater basins (with a median area of 45.57 km2), 25%, 50%, and 75% of ψ are 0.45, 0.85, and 1.22
For the largest rivers ... Amazon, Nile, and Yangtze Rivers, ψ drops below 0.1

chunks.text: The modeling framework has uncertainties from simplified parameter estimation and limited calibration, as only two parameters are tuned and then transferred globally. Most parameters remain a priori, so uncertainty estimates may differ from calibrated regional models. The authors note that future work should compare uncertainty propagation under calibrated versus uncalibrated settings and consider ensemble parameter sets or model ensembles.
supporting_quote: two SUMMA parameters are fine-tuned in 7379 subbasins and then transferred to global subbasins
given most model parameters use a priori values since we cannot calibrate all parameters
Future study should compare the modeling uncertainties between calibrated and uncalibrated models

chunks.text: Lakes and reservoirs are not included in routing in the main analysis, even though they can regulate streamflow and affect uncertainty estimates. A sensitivity check using HydroLAKES excludes rivers where upstream storage capacity exceeds 0.1 of annual streamflow; only 6.2% of rivers exceed this ratio, and the ψ–area relationship remains stable. Nonetheless, the paper advises caution in regions with substantial regulation effects.
supporting_quote: In this study, lakes and reservoirs are excluded from routing
excluded rivers with ratios exceeding 0.1 ... Globally, 6.2% of rivers exceed this ratio
the relationship between uncertainty ratios and river drainage areas remains stable

chunks.text: The study does not separate precipitation and temperature uncertainty impacts because doing so would require more ensemble simulations and is prohibitively expensive. The authors note that combined effects can be additive in some studies but smaller than the sum of individual effects in others. This limits attribution of hotspots to a single forcing variable and motivates future work on interaction and dependency among forcing uncertainties.
supporting_quote: This study lacks a separate analysis of precipitation and temperature uncertainties which needs a larger ensemble of simulations but is prohibitively expensive
some studies indicate that the combined effect ... is additive
others suggest that the combined effect is smaller than the sum of the individual inputs

chunks.text: Only precipitation and air temperature are treated probabilistically because EM-Earth lacks ensembles for other variables (wind, pressure, humidity, radiation). This means the analysis underestimates the integrated impact of full meteorological forcing uncertainty on hydrologic outputs. The paper frames this as an important direction for future research, including examining dependencies among forcing variables, particularly in tropical regions.
supporting_quote: this study only uses ensemble estimates for precipitation and air temperature because EM-Earth does not provide ensemble estimates for other variables
Future research should investigate the combined impact of uncertainties from other forcing variables and explore the interactions and dependencies among them

chunks.text: Across global subbasins, the study reports average χ values of 0.30 (SWE), 0.45 (total soil water), 0.27 (total runoff), and 0.38 (ET), while corresponding ψ values are 0.50 (SWE), 0.017 (soil water), and 0.17 (runoff), with ET excluded for ψ due to sign conventions. This demonstrates that ψ and χ provide different but complementary perspectives and that metric choice affects hotspot interpretation. The authors emphasize selecting metrics based on user needs and application focus.
supporting_quote: the average χ values for SWE, total soil water, total runoff, and ET are 0.30, 0.45, 0.27, and 0.38, respectively
The corresponding ψ values for these variables (excluding ET) are 0.50, 0.017, and 0.17
metric selection and interpretation should be based on the specific needs of research and applications

chunks.text: Surface runoff is identified as the dominant contributor to total runoff uncertainty globally, exceeding baseflow uncertainty by a large margin. The paper summarizes that the average uncertainty of surface runoff is about six times larger than that of baseflow. This highlights the importance of fast runoff generation processes in transmitting forcing uncertainty to hydrologic outputs.
supporting_quote: For total runoff, surface runoff is the major source of its uncertainties on the global scale
The average uncertainty of surface runoff is about six times larger than that of baseflow

chunks.text: Streamflow uncertainty patterns show low ψ and χ in high-latitude/high-altitude regions and reduced uncertainty downstream, consistent with cryosphere damping and routing aggregation. The study also concludes that ψ flags arid regions as hotspots, whereas χ highlights tropical rain forests and Europe, reflecting differing roles of mean magnitude versus temporal variability and links to baseflow ratio. It further concludes that ψ declines logarithmically with drainage area, a relationship not observed for χ.
supporting_quote: Both ψ and χ are low in high-latitude and high-altitude areas
Downstream reaches have smaller uncertainty ratios than upstream areas
ψ identifies arid regions as uncertainty hotspots ... while χ highlights tropical rain forests and Europe
ψ shows a logarithmically decreasing relationship with upstream drainage areas, which is not observed using χ

chunks.text: Gridded meteorological datasets derived from station observations are widely used because they often provide the most accurate records, but spatial interpolation is imperfect and introduces uncertainty. Deterministic products are common, while explicit uncertainty estimates and ensemble products are comparatively rare. Recent ensemble datasets and tools exist, but well-tested open tools for ensemble meteorological estimation remain limited. GMET is a notable exception, providing ensemble analyses via locally weighted regression and has supported multiple regional-to-continental applications.
supporting_quote: Among these datasets, those based on ground-station observations offer the most accurate meteorological records

Yet spatial interpolation is an imperfect process that leads to ubiquitous uncertainties in gridded meteorological datasets. Few meteorological datasets provide explicit analytical uncertainty estimates, and even fewer provide probabilistic or ensemble estimates
A notable exception is the Gridded Meteorological Ensemble Tool (GMET)

chunks.text: GMET’s probabilistic framework represents variables with parametric distributions (e.g., normal), where the mean is a deterministic estimate and the standard deviation represents estimation uncertainty. For skewed variables like precipitation, transformations such as Box–Cox are used to approximate Gaussian behavior before sampling. The methodology is generic for any variable that can be represented in Gaussian space, either directly or via transformation.
supporting_quote: For mean air temperature and daily temperature range ..., the normal distribution is used by GMET in the form of X ∼ N (µ, σ2 )
For variables such as precipitation with skewed distributions, transformation methods such as Box–Cox are applied to convert variables into normal (Gaussian) space
it can also be applied to any variable that can be described using the normal distribution, either directly or through transformation

chunks.text: GPEP is positioned as a Python-based evolution of GMET, leveraging Python’s extensibility and access to method libraries such as scikit-learn. The tradeoff is slower computation relative to FORTRAN, but with benefits in flexibility, usability, and potential community contributions. The package aims to support both deterministic and ensemble geophysical estimation for research and operational contexts.
supporting_quote: we have developed the Python-based Geospatial Probabilistic Estimation Package (GPEP)
we view Python as providing a more convenient and extensible development environment
The major downside ... is its relatively slower computational speed

chunks.text: The study’s goal is to present GPEP v1.0 as a Python package that reproduces and expands GMET’s ensemble estimation capabilities while improving flexibility and usability. The paper describes the package design, summarizes the underlying methodology, and demonstrates capabilities through experiments estimating precipitation, temperature, and SWE ensembles. A key aim is broadening application scope beyond hard-coded GMET variables and enabling easier method extension through Python libraries.
supporting_quote: we have developed the Python-based Geospatial Probabilistic Estimation Package (GPEP) that offers GMET functionality along with additional methodological and usability improvements
This paper describes GPEP and illustrates some of its capabilities using several demonstration experiments
including the estimation of precipitation, temperature, and snow water equivalent ensemble analyses

chunks.text: A specific goal is to generalize GMET’s hard-coded assumptions by moving variable selection, predictors, weights, and I/O controls into user configuration files. This includes supporting arbitrary variables, allowing users to define event probabilities for any variable, and specifying linkages or transformations between input and output variables. The intent is to make the tool adaptable for diverse Earth-science estimation tasks.
supporting_quote: GPEP brings the variable selection and associated details into the user control ("configuration") file
generalize GMET to allow the user to specify arbitrary input and output variables and linkages and transformations between them
the concept of POP is generalized to "probability of event" (POE), which can be estimated for any variable

chunks.text: Another goal is to broaden spatial interpolation options by integrating scikit-learn methods for local and global regression, including machine learning models. GPEP aims to support both locally weighted regression and more computationally efficient global regression approaches, recognizing that performance tradeoffs may occur depending on the domain and method.
supporting_quote: GPEP expands the options ... to also support any supervised learning method from the scikit-learn package
Global regression builds one model for the entire study domain at every time step, which is far more efficient than the local regression methods
users need to caution that global regression may have degraded accuracy compared to local regression

chunks.text: Despite increasing interest in uncertainty-aware applications, probabilistic or ensemble gridded meteorological datasets are still uncommon relative to deterministic products. Uncertainty from interpolation is pervasive, but few datasets provide explicit uncertainty quantification, limiting robust characterization of extremes and risk-based applications. This motivates tools that can generate ensembles from station-based analyses in a reproducible and accessible way.
supporting_quote: spatial interpolation is an imperfect process that leads to ubiquitous uncertainties in gridded meteorological datasets
Few meteorological datasets provide explicit analytical uncertainty estimates, and even fewer provide probabilistic or ensemble estimates

chunks.text: Producing ensemble datasets is often difficult to replicate because methods are more complex than single-value interpolation and open-access routines are limited. Additionally, ensemble datasets can be large, creating burdens in downloading, storage, and processing. These barriers reduce community ability to generate custom ensemble datasets aligned with specific variables, periods, and resolutions.
supporting_quote: ensemble estimation is more challenging than single-value spatial interpolation, and open-access routines and tools are limited in this area
ensemble datasets often have large data sizes increasing with the number of members, posing challenges in downloading, storage, and processing
ensemble estimation methods generally have much higher complexity compared to singlevalue spatial interpolation methods

chunks.text: GMET’s FORTRAN implementation is computationally efficient but less convenient for extending methods and user control compared with Python ecosystems. GMET also contains hard-coded variable-specific assumptions (notably precipitation and temperature), requiring code modification for other variables. This restricts flexibility and slows adoption for broader geophysical applications.
supporting_quote: GMET's FORTRAN basis enables it to be computationally efficient and fast but is more cumbersome for adding or linking to new methodological modules
certain assumptions, functions, and settings specific to precipitation and temperature must be changed in the code if other variables are of interest
The major downside of pursuing future development in Python relative to FORTRAN is its relatively slower computational speed

chunks.text: GMET/GPEP ensemble estimation assumes a parametric distribution at each location and time, using a mean (µ) as the deterministic estimate and a standard deviation (σ) as uncertainty. Temperature variables are modeled as normal, and precipitation is transformed (e.g., Box–Cox) into Gaussian space. Ensembles are generated by sampling perturbations using correlated random fields, then back-transforming when needed.
supporting_quote: X ∼ N (µ, σ2 ), where µ and σ are the mean value and standard deviation
transformation methods such as Box–Cox are applied to convert variables into normal (Gaussian) space
Ensemble estimates can be obtained by sampling from the normal distribution

chunks.text: Deterministic estimation of µ is performed using locally weighted linear regression, relating station observations to predictors such as latitude, longitude, elevation, slope, and aspect. GMET v2.0 also allows time-varying predictors (e.g., model precipitation and temperature) to improve estimates. σ can represent either regression standard error or prediction error derived from cross-validation metrics such as RMSE.
supporting_quote: GMET adopts the locally weighted linear regression (LWLR) to obtain deterministic gridded estimates of µ
static terrain-related predictors such as latitude, longitude, elevation, topographic slope, and aspect
GMET version 2.0 added the ability to use time-varying dynamic predictors
σ is the uncertainty of gridded regression estimates µ based either on the standard error of the regression or the prediction error (e.g., root mean squared error from cross-validation)

chunks.text: For intermittent variables like precipitation, occurrence is modeled via locally weighted logistic regression to estimate probability of precipitation (POP), regressed on predictors. This separates event occurrence from amount estimation and can be generalized to other intermittent geospatial variables. In GPEP this concept is generalized further to probability of event (POE) for any variable with a user-defined threshold.
supporting_quote: GMET uses a locally weighted logistic regression to estimate the probability of precipitation (POP)
This method can be applied to other intermittent geospatial variables
the concept of POP is generalized to "probability of event" (POE), which can be estimated for any variable and can also use a user-defined event threshold

chunks.text: Ensemble generation uses spatiotemporally correlated random fields (SCRFs). Spatial correlation is modeled with an exponential function using a spatial correlation length (Clen), and random numbers are generated efficiently with a nested simulation strategy. Temporal dependence is introduced with lag-1 autocorrelation, and cross-correlation can link random fields across variables.
supporting_quote: GMET generates distributed, spatiotemporally correlated random fields (SCRFs)
c_{i,j} = exp(- d_{i,j} / C_{len})
The temporal correlation structure is represented using the lag-1 auto-correlation
the cross-correlation between the two variables can be used to correlate their SCRFs

chunks.text: Temperature ensemble members are generated by perturbing deterministic estimates with SCRF random numbers scaled by σ: xT = µT + R·σT. For precipitation, POP determines whether precipitation occurs; if it occurs, the SCRF value is converted to a scaled cumulative probability and mapped through the inverse normal CDF to perturb µP in Gaussian space, followed by back-transformation.
supporting_quote: x_T = µ_T + R · σ_T
a precipitation event occurs only when F_N(R) is larger than p_0
µ_P + F_N^{-1}(p_cs) · σ_P

chunks.text: GPEP expands spatial interpolation beyond GMET’s linear/logistic locally weighted regression by supporting scikit-learn supervised learning methods for both local and global regression. Examples include ridge regression, BayesianRidge, Lasso, ElasticNet for local approaches, and random forest, multi-layer perceptron, and SVM for global regression. Global regression trains one model per time step for the entire domain, improving efficiency but potentially reducing accuracy relative to local regression.
supporting_quote: GPEP expands the options ... to also support any supervised learning method from the scikit-learn package
Such techniques include ridge regression ... BayesianRidge ... Lasso ... ElasticNet
regressors and classifiers of random forest (RF), multi-layer perceptron, and support vector machine
Global regression builds one model for the entire study domain at every time step

chunks.text: To reduce computational cost in uncertainty estimation, GPEP uses cross-validation at station points only, then interpolates station RMSE to grid cells via distance-weighted averaging. It uses leave-one-out for local regression and N-fold (k-fold) for global regression. This aims to provide uncertainties similar to per-grid-cell k-fold approaches at lower cost, though similarity depends on data characteristics.
supporting_quote: GPEP adopts an alternative cross-validated uncertainty estimation strategy: (1) obtaining regression estimates at all station points, using leave-one-out validation for local regression and N-fold cross-validation for global regression; and (2) interpolating the resulting root mean square error from the station points to each grid cell
The GPEP method achieves generally similar uncertainties with the standard method at less computational cost
The similarity ... will depend on the nature of the station and grid datasets being used

chunks.text: GPEP adds flexibility in defining spatial correlation length for SCRF generation, allowing either user-prescribed values or data-driven estimation from station inputs. Users can apply thresholds (e.g., focusing on heavy precipitation) when computing correlations. Prescribed lengths are recommended for small datasets where correlation estimation is not robust.
supporting_quote: GPEP supports either user-specified correlation lengths or a data-driven option, in which the length is inferred from raw station inputs
a positive threshold such as 10 mm d−1 can be used to focus only on heavy precipitation
the prescribed option is useful for smaller datasets ... that are inadequate to define such correlation lengths

chunks.text: A primary comparison experiment uses the GMET v2.0 California test case, involving daily meteorological ensemble generation at 0.0625° resolution. The comparison focuses on locally weighted linear and logistic regression with static predictors only, examining agreement in transformed precipitation, precipitation probability, mean temperature, and temperature range outputs between GMET and GPEP.
supporting_quote: the GMET version 2.0 test case in California, USA
a 0.0625◦ resolution daily meteorological ensemble generation for California
focusing on the locally weighted linear and logistic regression method based on static predictors only

chunks.text: A high-resolution demonstration generates 1 km daily ensembles of precipitation, Tmean, and Trange for the US upper Colorado region for calendar year 2013. The experiment uses 864 precipitation and/or temperature stations, with quality control and gap filling via a four-pass iterative quantile mapping approach. Predictors include static terrain terms and dynamic ERA5-Land variables (2 m temperature, 2 m dewpoint, and precipitation).
supporting_quote: using a resolution of 1 km in the US upper Colorado region
meteorological data from 864 precipitation and/or temperature stations for the 2013 calendar year
filled using a four-pass iterative quantile mapping
we use the 2 m air temperature, 2 m dewpoint temperature, and precipitation from the ERA5-Land reanalysis product ... as dynamic (time-varying) predictors

chunks.text: The SWE demonstration uses the same upper Colorado domain and estimates SWE ensembles for water year October 2012 to September 2013. Observations come from the SNOTEL network, and only 71 serially complete stations are used because the authors did not quality control or fill SWE station data for this demonstration. The method uses Box–Cox transformation and locally weighted linear/logistic regression with terrain predictors.
supporting_quote: We estimate SWE ensembles for the water year from October 2012 to September 2013
The station observations come from the SNOwpack TELemetry Network (SNOTEL)
Only serially complete stations (71) in the study period are used
the transformation method was Box–Cox; and the locally weighted linear/logistic regression is adopted

chunks.text: Performance and computational benchmarks are reported for the upper Colorado 1 km case on NCAR’s Casper HPC. Using 36 CPUs, the run took 54.4 minutes for regression estimates and 37.3 minutes to generate 36 ensemble members for 2013, excluding one-time prior file generation. CPU-scaling tests were also conducted for California February 2017 with LWR variants and random forest.
supporting_quote: Using 36 CPUs on the Casper high performance computer (HPC) ... took 54.4 min to produce regression estimates and 37.3 min to generate 36 ensemble members for the year 2013
tested two locally weighted regression methods (LWR: LWR1 and LWR2) and a global regression method (i.e., RF) for the GMET version 2.0 test case ... February 2017 in California

chunks.text: GPEP reproduces GMET’s deterministic regression estimates closely for the California test case when configured with comparable locally weighted linear/logistic regression using static predictors. Scatter comparisons show near identity for precipitation, Tmean, and Trange, with most points along the 1–1 line. Small discrepancies (notably in precipitation probability) are attributed to numerical precision differences and can be amplified in logistic regression iterations.
supporting_quote: For precipitation, Tmean, and Trange, the GPEP and GMET estimates are almost identical
mainly located along the 1–1 line
minor discrepancies, especially in the probability of precipitation, come from slight numerical differences in data inputs, attributed to differences in double precision or single precision

chunks.text: In the California comparison, GPEP’s precipitation event probabilities differ slightly from GMET’s, with a small mean bias. The paper reports that GPEP tends to be lower at low probabilities and higher at high probabilities, but differences lack spatial patterns. The overall mean precipitation POE is slightly higher by 0.005 (about 1%), which the authors deem negligible.
supporting_quote: GPEP tends to generate lower precipitation POE than GMET for low precipitation probability, while for high POE GPEP generates higher probabilities
GPEP's mean precipitation POE is slightly higher than that of GMET by 0.005 (∼ 1 %), which is negligible

chunks.text: For the 1 km upper Colorado 2013 experiment, leave-one-out validation indicates precipitation accuracy is higher in flatter eastern areas and lower in complex western terrain with lower station density. Temperature metrics show different patterns: Tmean generally has better MAE and modified KGE" than Trange. The results highlight difficulty capturing diurnal temperature range compared with mean temperature.
supporting_quote: Precipitation estimates show higher accuracy in the relatively flat eastern areas
the vast western areas have lower accuracy due to the complex terrain and lower station density
Tmean having much better MAE and KGE" than Trange. This indicates the difficulty in capturing diurnal fluctuations

chunks.text: A method comparison between random forest (global regression) and locally weighted regression shows mixed skill outcomes in the upper Colorado case. Using default scikit-learn settings, RF improves correlation coefficient for precipitation and Tmean but yields higher MAE for all variables. KGE" differences vary across stations, producing broadly comparable overall performance.
supporting_quote: Compared to locally weighted regression, RF has better CC for precipitation and Tmean but a higher MAE for all variables
For KGE", the difference between the two methods varies across stations but has a comparable overall performance
we only use the default settings of the scikit-learn package

chunks.text: Ensemble outputs for 9–17 September 2013 show heavy precipitation with accumulated totals exceeding 500 mm at the event center, and large member-to-member differences at event centers. The paper attributes these differences to interpolation uncertainties and the limited ability of station networks and interpolation methods to capture extremes. Among variables, Tmean has the lowest ensemble spread, Trange is intermediate.
supporting_quote: heavy precipitation occurred with the accumulated amounts exceeding 500 mm at the precipitation centre
The large differences between members at event centres originate from the interpolation uncertainties
Tmean shows the lowest ensemble spread among the three variables, and Trange shows the intermediate ensemble spread

chunks.text: A Boulder County September 2013 time series illustrates how ensemble bounds convey uncertainty during an extreme event. Around 11 September, mean or median precipitation exceeds 60 mm d−1 and some ensemble members exceed 100 mm d−1. The uncertainty is largest during the flood period, with 5%–95% bounds ranging from less than 10 to greater than 150 mm d−1.
supporting_quote: mean or median precipitation going beyond 60 mm d−1 and some members going beyond 100 mm d−1 around 11 September
the 5 %–95 % bounds ranging between < 10 and > 150 mm d−1

chunks.text: An independent ensemble evaluation using 70% of stations for gridding and 30% for verification with 100 ensemble members suggests reasonable reliability but some bias. Rank histograms indicate precipitation ensembles have a slight tendency toward overestimation, while Tmean ensembles lean toward underestimation. The authors note departures from uniformity are present but not severe and could be improved via different predictors or methods.
supporting_quote: utilized 70 % of the randomly selected stations to generate the gridded estimates and used the remaining 30 % as a reference for evaluation
The number of ensemble members is 100
precipitation probabilistic estimates appear to have a slight bias toward overestimation
whereas Tmean probabilistic estimates lean toward underestimation

chunks.text: The SWE leave-one-out evaluation for the upper Colorado case shows that estimated SWE fields are spatially smoother than observations, producing large biases at a few stations. The paper reports a relative mean error of 2.94% for mean annual SWE at the displayed points but highlights an outlier station where estimated SWE is 375 mm versus observed 180 mm. Seasonal domain-average SWE is generally captured, except underestimation near the end of melt (June 2013).
supporting_quote: the estimated SWE is smoother in space, leading to large biases at a few points
the relative mean error for the points shown is 2.94%
the estimated SWE is 375 mm but the observed SWE is 180 mm
except for the underestimation of SWE at the end of the melt period (June 2013)

chunks.text: GPEP performance and scalability results indicate internal parallelization can improve run time, though Python remains slower than FORTRAN GMET. Benchmarks suggest GPEP may be 10–50 times slower overall, including about 10 times slower for least-square linear regression. CPU scaling shows substantial speedups for local regressions as CPU count increases (e.g., up to 25 CPUs) and high parallel efficiency for generating ensemble members up to 35 CPUs.
supporting_quote: GPEP's production of ensemble analyses overall appears to be between 10 and 50 times slower than GMET
Python is around 10 times slower than FORTRAN for leastsquare linear regression functions
significant speedup for LWR1/LWR2 when CPUs increased from 1 to 25
parallel efficiency remains high with increasing CPU numbers up to 35

chunks.text: The demonstrated experiments are not optimized for best achievable accuracy; predictor choices, parameters, and methods were selected for illustration. The authors emphasize that users should evaluate configurations for their specific applications, including station density and topographic or climatic influences. They note that biases in rank histograms may stem from regression inaccuracies and could be improved by trying alternative predictors or methods available in GPEP.
supporting_quote: predictor selection was for demonstration purposes and does not presume to offer optimal performance
The experiments showcased in this study illustrate examples of GPEP's capabilities without being tailored for optimal application-quality performance
These biases might stem from inaccuracies in spatial regression estimates and may be improved through a consideration of different predictors or methods available in GPEP

chunks.text: GPEP’s dependence modeling is limited: the implemented probabilistic formulation handles intercorrelation between two variables, while many Earth system applications require higher-dimensional multivariate dependence structures. Although multiple pairs can be configured, the approach is still pairwise through the existing formulation. The authors suggest expanding to multivariate correlation/covariance and exploring alternative probabilistic methods such as copulas and multi-site weather generator correlation structures.
supporting_quote: implemented to handle the intercorrelation relationship between two variables, while higher-dimensional multivariate formulations would likely be needed
GPEP only allows the dependencies of one variable on the other one through Eq. (4), although multiple pairs of dependencies can be defined
This formulation can be expanded ... to include multivariate correlation and covariance structures ... such as using Copula functions

chunks.text: The current transformation and random-field methods are limited and may not be ideal for all variables. The paper notes that Box–Cox may be insufficient for certain distributions and suggests adding more transformation options. It also points to potential improvements in constructing spatiotemporal correlation structures using copulas/survival functions and leveraging geostatistical libraries like GSTools.
supporting_quote: myriad options exist for variable transformation (the current Box–Cox transformation may not be ideal) and can be added in the future
benefit from the addition of a variety of methods, including the Papalexiou and Serinaldi (2020) technique
geostatistical tools such as the Python-based GSTools ... can be used to generate spatial random fields

chunks.text: Moving from FORTRAN GMET to Python introduces a major drawback in computational speed, which may limit large-domain and near-real-time operational use under local regression configurations. The authors anticipate this can be mitigated through algorithm optimization, hybrid programming for costly components, additional parallelism, and potentially GPU computing. They also mention future integration with deep learning frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow, Keras).
supporting_quote: A major drawback of the move from the FORTRAN-based GMET to GPEP is the significantly slower outcomes
may pose challenges for GPEP's local regression configurations if applied for large-domain and/or near-real-time operational applications
resolved through further algorithm optimization, hybrid programming ... additional parallel processing options, and even a shift toward GPU computing
future development may link to ML and deep learning packages such as PyTorch, TensorFlow, or Keras

chunks.text: The SWE example highlights a limitation for strongly auto-correlated variables: SWE lag-1 autocorrelation exceeds 0.99, so temporal linking can make random fields very similar across time steps, potentially underestimating ensemble spread. This increases sensitivity to the initial random field and to the spatial correlation length choice. The authors used 10 km for demonstration and encourage future studies to investigate optimal correlation lengths and better predictors for SWE variability.
supporting_quote: The lag-1 auto-correlation of SWE exceeds 0.99
the random field in all time steps will be quite similar to that in the first time step (Eq. 4), and the ensemble spread may be underestimated
For demonstration purposes, we have used a spatial correlation length of 10 km, but we would encourage future studies to investigate optimal settings for this length

chunks.text: The paper concludes that GPEP is a flexible Python-based tool for deterministic and ensemble probabilistic estimation of geophysical variables, expanding GMET’s capabilities and configurability. It supports local and global regression methods including machine learning and can generate ensembles using cross-validation-based predictive uncertainty. While slower than GMET, internal parallelization scales well, making it practical for research and some operational applications.
supporting_quote: GPEP is a flexible Python-based software for ensemble, probabilistic estimation of any geophysical variable
GPEP supports various local and global regression methods including ML techniques
Although GPEP operates more slowly than the original GMET, the tool's internal parallelization capability scales well

chunks.text: The authors emphasize that template configurations can emulate GMET and yield good results, but GPEP should be treated as a versatile framework requiring user expertise to tune predictors, weights, transformations, and methods. The showcased experiments demonstrate capabilities rather than optimal performance, and users are encouraged to extend configurations to suit their domains and variables. The tool is intended to support scientific exploration and uncertainty-aware applications across scales.
supporting_quote: The template configurations available ... can emulate GMET configurations and generally deliver commendable results
The experiments showcased in this study illustrate examples of GPEP's capabilities without being tailored for optimal application-quality performance
User expertise and domain knowledge are required for scientific explorations of various configurations

chunks.text: HydroShare is an open-source, web-based hydrologic information system designed for the hydrologic sciences community to share and publish research products. It supports not only data publication but also collaboration on data preparation, analysis, and management across the data lifecycle. The project was motivated by growing hydrologic data volumes and advances in computing and storage, with a philosophy of hydrology as a collaborative “team sport.”
supporting_quote: HydroShare ... is an open source, web-based hydrologic information system developed for researchers, scientists, and data managers ... to easily share and publish data, models, scripts, and applications
HydroShare supports not only data publication, but also collaboration on data preparation, analysis, and management throughout the scientific data lifecycle
Many of these challenges are alleviated and opportunities are multiplied when hydrology is viewed as a "team sport"

chunks.text: HydroShare evolved from the CUAHSI Hydrologic Information System (HIS), which established a service-oriented architecture for managing hydrologic time series. CUAHSI HIS includes the Observations Data Model (ODM), HydroServers, client tools, and a central metadata catalog (HIS Central), using protocols such as WaterOneFlow and WaterML.
