The HIS remains widely used and provides context for HydroShare’s broader publication and collaboration capabilities.
supporting_quote: HydroShare evolved out of the Consortium of Universities for the Advancement of Hydrologic Science, Inc. (CUAHSI) Hydrologic Information System (HIS) project ... which established a service-oriented architecture (SOA) for managing hydrologic time series data.
The CUAHSI HIS is comprised of ... the Observations Data Model (ODM) ... data servers called HydroServers ... client tools ... and a central catalog called HIS Central
nearly 100 registered data servers sharing time series data for more than 1.2M locations around the globe and over 10.3B individual data values

chunks.text: HydroShare was funded by NSF SI2–SSI in two major phases: an initial five-year project (2012–2017) and a subsequent expansion (2017–2021). The development team was intentionally multidisciplinary and distributed across many institutions to align the system with hydrology and water resources community needs while leveraging computer and information science expertise.
supporting_quote: Funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation's (NSF) ... (SI2–SSI) program, the first five-year HydroShare project (2012–2017) ... was followed by a subsequent project ... (2017–2021)
HydroShare was developed and is supported by a multidisciplinary team of hydrologists, modelers, software engineers, and computer and information scientists spanning several institutions.

chunks.text: The paper’s aim is to retrospectively synthesize a decade of HydroShare development and operation. It focuses on describing the system architecture and functionality, summarizing key scientific and cyberinfrastructure contributions, reporting usage metrics, and outlining future directions for the platform within water data science.
supporting_quote: This retrospective paper reviews a decade of HydroShare development and operation by presenting the general architecture, functionality, key contributions ... current usage metrics, and future directions.

chunks.text: HydroShare was conceived to complement CUAHSI HIS by enabling citable publication for a broader range of hydrologic research artifacts beyond time series. A central objective was to reduce scientists’ effort in data organization and management while enabling collaboration, sharing, and eventual publication under stable identifiers.
supporting_quote: HydroShare was conceived as a companion to the CUAHSI HIS with support for citable data publication of a broader array of data types beyond hydrologic time series
HydroShare was intended to reduce the effort for data organization and management by scientists.

chunks.text: Hydrologic research workflows are burdened by substantial time spent on data preparation. Survey results cited in the paper indicate that most researchers spend a nontrivial fraction of their research time preparing data, with a notable subset spending more than half their time. This inefficiency motivated an environment to streamline organization, sharing, and iterative metadata improvement.
supporting_quote: "more than 80% said they spend at least one-tenth of their research time on data preparation, and 12% of the respondents said they spend more than half their research time on this task"

chunks.text: Early HydroShare designs treated each content type as a distinct resource type, but this proved restrictive for real projects. Users commonly needed to publish multiple heterogeneous files together under one citation and identifier. This limitation drove the shift toward a composite resource approach.
supporting_quote: this resource type approach was found to be limiting because of the need to store multiple different content types in a single resource to preserve and publish under a single identifier and citation
specific resource types were later replaced with a more universal approach wherein content files are stored in a generic composite resource type

chunks.text: Common geoscience file-sharing approaches typically do not manage metadata explicitly, creating uncertainty about shared data content and context. The paper positions HydroShare’s structured metadata and packaging as addressing this gap, especially under growing emphasis on openness and FAIR principles.
supporting_quote: none of these approaches explicitly manage metadata about the shared files and hence can result in uncertainty about the data content being shared.
Given the growing calls for openness in the scientific community ... and momentum behind the FAIR data principles ... metadata management such as provided in HydroShare is essential.

chunks.text: HydroShare’s architecture is organized into three functional categories: resource storage, resource exploration, and actions on resources. Content storage is implemented with iRODS to provide a unified virtual file system and features like parallel transfer and replication for recovery. The main web interface is built with Django and also exposes a REST API so third parties can perform CRUD operations and build connected applications.
supporting_quote: The general architecture of HydroShare is organized into three categories: (1) resource storage, (2) resource exploration, and (3) actions on resources
Storage of content files in HydroShare is accomplished using the Integrated Rule Oriented Data System (iRODS)
The HydroShare website also provides a representational state transfer (REST) web service application programming interface (API) that enables ... create, read, update, and delete (CRUD)

chunks.text: HydroShare defines a “resource” as the granular object for content management and access control. Resources can be created, modified, versioned, shared, discovered, published, and acted upon by web apps. The system moved from multiple specialized resource types to a consolidated composite resource that can contain arbitrary files while still supporting recognized content types with value-added metadata extraction and specialized viewers.
supporting_quote: A resource is the granular unit of digital content used for data management and access control within HydroShare.
defines resources as objects that can be created, stored, modified, versioned, shared, annotated, discovered, accessed, published, and acted upon by web apps
specific resource types were later replaced with a more universal approach wherein content files are stored in a generic composite resource type

chunks.text: HydroShare packages each resource directory using the BagIt format, supporting transfer and preservation. Downloads are provided as zipped BagIt files containing payload data along with machine-readable metadata and manifests. The package includes OAI-ORE structures (e.g., resource maps) so a computer can discover relationships and structure within a resource.
supporting_quote: a resource is a directory in a file system that adheres to the structure of the BagIt format
When a user downloads a complete resource as a BagIt file ... it is retrieved as a zipped file
resourcemap.xml ... an Open Archives Initiative Object Reuse and Exchange (OAI-ORE) resource map

chunks.text: HydroShare manages metadata at two granularities: resource-level and content-level. Resource-level metadata is stored in resourcemetadata.xml and primarily conforms to Dublin Core elements, including title, abstract, keywords, creators, coverage, license, and citation. For known content types, content-level XML schemas allow metadata to be added and often auto-extracted from uploaded files to reduce user burden.
supporting_quote: HydroShare considers resource metadata at two levels of granularity ... resource-level metadata ... and content-level metadata
Resource-level metadata (resourcemetadata.xml file, Table 1) conforms primarily to standard Dublin Core Metadata Initiative elements
HydroShare automatically extracts much of the content-level metadata from the files uploaded by the user, alleviating some of the burden of metadata creation.

chunks.text: HydroShare discovery uses Apache Solr for keyword and faceted search over indexed resource metadata. Facets include author, owner, subject, contributor, type, and availability; titles and abstracts are also indexed. Public and discoverable resources are included in the search index, and metadata is exposed to external crawlers via a sitemap and JSON-LD using Schema.org vocabulary.
supporting_quote: Data discovery ... is enabled by an Apache Solr search engine
Specific facets supported ... include author, owner, subject, contributor, type, and availability.
HydroShare also embeds a JSON-LD encoding of the resource level metadata using the Schema.org vocabulary within the landing page for every resource.

chunks.text: HydroShare provides data services for geospatial and multidimensional datasets using standards-based servers. GeoServer automatically publishes OGC WMS/WFS services for public resources containing Shapefile or GeoTIFF content, generating endpoints shown on the landing page. For NetCDF multidimensional files, HydroShare registers public resources with a THREDDS server to enable remote access via OPeNDAP for subsetting and retrieval without downloading entire large files.
supporting_quote: HydroShare includes an instance of Geo-Server ... creating and exposing WMS and WFS services
Once the resource is taken out of editing mode and shared publicly ... the spatial datasets are automatically registered in the GeoServer application
After being made public in HydroShare, the resource is automatically registered on the HydroShare THREDDS server. This enables remote access using the OPeNDAP service

chunks.text: HydroShare’s web app connector enables external applications to be launched from a resource landing page using URL templates with dynamic variables. The “Open With” mechanism can pass parameters such as the invoking resource ID or file references. This approach supports integration with environments like JupyterHub, enabling cloud-based analysis workflows that can retrieve data from HydroShare and write results back through client libraries.
supporting_quote: The web app connector resource ... allows a web application or web site to be referenced via URL from HydroShare.
by including the variable name ${HS_RES_ID} ... HydroShare will dynamically insert the ID of the invoking HydroShare resource
HydroShare users can leverage JupyterHub computing environments using the "Open With" button on a resource landing page.

chunks.text: HydroShare resources are delivered in a defined BagIt package structure that includes payload content and supporting metadata and integrity files. The package contains manifests with MD5 checksums, a resource map, and resource-level metadata in XML. This standardized structure ensures resources remain self-documented and machine-readable after download.
supporting_quote: File and folder structure of downloaded HydroShare resources in BagIt format.
manifest-md5.txt ... provides a checksum for each file calculated using the MD5 algorithm.
resourcemetadata.xml ... XML document storing the main, resource-level metadata.

chunks.text: HydroShare’s discovery API accepts JSON-like filter parameters in the query string to retrieve matching resources. Example filters include availability (discoverable/public/published), type (e.g., Image), author name, and subject keywords. Parameters are case-sensitive and intended for programmatic discovery use cases.
supporting_quote: The HydroShare resource discovery API ... allowing a user to specify a particular search criterion using JSON-like namevalue pairs in a query string
Example filter parameters ... include author, owner, subject, contributor, type, and availability.
Filter parameters and parameter values are case-sensitive.

chunks.text: HydroShare usage and impact are monitored using operational metrics derived from internal tracking. The system tracks counts and volumes of stored resources, logons, active users, DOI issuance, and DOI citation counts. These metrics are computed from a database using custom Python scripts executed weekly to generate reports for the period June 2015 through September 2023.
supporting_quote: Usage of HydroShare is assessed based on extensive tracking of metrics including number of resources stored ... number of digital object identifiers (DOI) issued, and citation count of DOIs.
a set of custom Python scripts are executed weekly to generate usage reports.
All graphs summarize usage for the period June 2015 through September 2023.

chunks.text: HydroShare provides metadata exposure to external search engines by embedding JSON-LD on each resource landing page. The encoding uses the Schema.org vocabulary so web crawlers can parse dataset metadata. This supports discovery via systems such as Google’s Dataset Search.
supporting_quote: HydroShare also embeds a JSON-LD encoding of the resource level metadata using the Schema.org vocabulary within the landing page for every resource.
enables powerful external data discovery systems such as Google's Dataset Search

chunks.text: A key system outcome was the shift from specialized resource types to a composite resource model. The initial idea of one type per resource was too restrictive for publishing complete project or paper artifacts under one identifier. The composite approach allows arbitrary files in user-defined folder structures while preserving value-added behaviors for known content types (e.g., metadata extraction and app association).
supporting_quote: this resource type approach was found to be limiting ... to preserve and publish under a single identifier and citation
content files are stored in a generic composite resource type
Value-added functionalities for different content types include automated extraction of metadata ... and association of content files with specific external applications

chunks.text: HydroShare’s standardized packaging and metadata approach produces self-describing, machine-readable resources that retain documentation when downloaded. Resource-level Dublin Core-like metadata and content-level XML metadata remain with the data, addressing a common shortcoming of ad hoc file sharing. The paper frames this as a distinguishing feature relative to FTP/email or general cloud storage options that do not explicitly manage metadata.
supporting_quote: structured, selfdescribing, and machine-readable XML metadata documents that remain with the data when they are downloaded.
none of these approaches explicitly manage metadata about the shared files
Resource-level metadata ... conforms primarily to standard Dublin Core Metadata Initiative elements

chunks.text: HydroShare supports standards-based data services that lower the barrier for sharing geospatial and multidimensional datasets. For Shapefile and GeoTIFF, public resources can be automatically registered with GeoServer and exposed as WMS/WFS endpoints on the landing page. For NetCDF, public resources are registered with THREDDS to enable OPeNDAP-based remote subsetting and access, which is especially useful for large files.
supporting_quote: Once the resource is taken out of editing mode and shared publicly ... the spatial datasets are automatically registered in the GeoServer application
relevant URL endpoints for the associated web services are generated, and these end points are displayed on the resource landing page.
This enables remote access using the OPeNDAP service ... especially useful for sharing and analyzing large NetCDF files

chunks.text: HydroShare’s modeling support is organized around two content types: Model Program and Model Instance. The Model Program represents software used to run simulations, and the Model Instance represents the inputs for a specific run. Together with collections and composite resources, this supports publishing entire modeling workflows—data, scripts, inputs, and outputs—rather than only final results.
supporting_quote: HydroShare includes two content types specifically for models. First is the Model Program content type
Second is the Model Instance content type that represents the input files associated with a specific simulation model run
facilitates publication of an entire hydrologic modeling workflow – from raw data ... model results

chunks.text: Operational metrics show sustained growth in HydroShare usage and content volume through September 2023. The system stores approximately 4.6 TB of scientific data and grows by about 46 GB per month on average. It has 15,277 total resources with roughly 150 new resources created per month, and 1,220 total permanently published resources with about 12 new DOI publications per month.
supporting_quote: In total, HydroShare currently consists of approximately 4.6 TB of scientific data, increasing at an average of 46 GB per month.
Approximately 150 new resources are created every month (15,277 total)
approximately 12 resources are permanently published per month (1220 total).

chunks.text: Although iRODS was selected partly to support geographically distributed storage federation, this capability is not currently used in HydroShare. The paper notes that modern “bucket cloud storage” has prompted an ongoing modernization effort to transition toward cloud storage for scalable needs. Federation remains a future option rather than an operational feature today.
supporting_quote: The iRODS system was originally chosen ... because of a vision to use its federated file system
This capability is currently not used in HydroShare
a modernization project now underway to transition to the use of cloud storage for expansible storage needs.

chunks.text: HydroShare’s internal discovery is limited by the fact that a user must first learn about HydroShare before searching it. The paper suggests that enabling mainstream search engines to crawl HydroShare metadata is more impactful than only enhancing internal indexing. As a result, HydroShare uses sitemaps and Schema.org JSON-LD to support external discovery, including Google Dataset Search.
supporting_quote: A limitation of the discovery system in HydroShare is that a user first needs to know about or discover HydroShare itself.
enabling mainstream discovery engines like Google and Bing to crawl HydroShare metadata
HydroShare also embeds a JSON-LD encoding ... using the Schema.org vocabulary

chunks.text: Access to linked cloud computing environments is restricted to mitigate abuse of free computational resources. HydroShare uses a group-based authentication model in which users must be admitted to an approved group before using linked cloud resources such as JupyterHub. This creates a gatekeeping tradeoff between openness and operational protection.
supporting_quote: HydroShare uses a group authentication approach to prevent abuse of these free cloud computing environments
users can only access HydroShare's linked cloud resources if they have previously been admitted into an approved group

chunks.text: The paper concludes that HydroShare has matured substantially since inception, expanding in functionality, stability, and usage while also generating contributions to hydroinformatics and cyberinfrastructure. It emphasizes the project’s broad scholarly footprint, citing more than 20 Scopus-indexed articles and more than 1100 related documents in Google Scholar. HydroShare is positioned as both an operational platform and a continuing source of technical innovation for water science data and model publication.
supporting_quote: Since its inception in 2011 and first official release in 2015, Hydro-Share has grown in functionality, stability, and usage.
This is attested by > 20 journal articles in the Scopus database and >1100 ... documents in Google Scholar

chunks.text: With NSF-supported development concluded, CUAHSI has assumed operational responsibility for HydroShare as its flagship data management product. Future development is expected to be community-driven through open-source contributions, supported by ongoing projects that rely on HydroShare operationally. The paper notes there are no plans to charge users, though tiered storage fees are mentioned as a possible sustainability model.
supporting_quote: CUAHSI has taken over responsibility for operation of Hydro-Share as its flagship data management product.
As an open-source software system, future developments on HydroShare are expected to come from many directions.
As of this writing, there are no plans to charge users for access to HydroShare, though one sustainability model might include implementing fees for higher tiers of data storage requirements

chunks.text: River ice strongly affects hydrological processes and human systems in cold regions. Ice formation and breakup can trigger flooding, damage infrastructure, and disrupt water supply and hydropower generation. These impacts are particularly important at higher latitudes where river ice persists over much of the winter and controls many fluvial processes.
supporting_quote: River ice phenomena, which encompass ice formation, growth, and subsequent breakup can instigate flooding and inflict considerable damage to infrastructure
Here, river ice influences the hydrological patterns of nearly 60% of rivers for a significant portion of the winter

chunks.text: Traditional monitoring approaches rely on in situ and agency reports, but these are limited by accessibility and safety in winter and do not provide systematic continental-scale mapping. Existing U.S. sources include USGS reports and stream-gauging flags as well as the CRREL Ice Jam Database, but they are not designed to provide continuous spatial products. Satellite remote sensing is positioned as a key complement to fill these monitoring gaps.
supporting_quote: its systematic monitoring poses formidable challenges
There exists a notable deficiency in the systematic mapping of river ice at a continental scale
river freeze up and breakup and ice jam information is cataloged by the US Army Cold Regions Research and Engineering Laboratory (CRREL) and is available in the Ice Jam Database

chunks.text: VIIRS offers wide-swath, frequent coverage suitable for large-domain environmental monitoring, yet most VIIRS hydrology applications have focused on floods and snow rather than river ice. The paper argues that deep learning can improve scalability compared with threshold-based methods, enabling automated river-ice detection across large areas. The system is presented as unique in automating continental-scale mapping and supporting additional information products and user access.
supporting_quote: the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS)... offers repetitive and wide-ranging coverage
most extant studies employing VIIRS imagery for hydrological applications have predominantly focused on flood mapping and snow cover detection
most of these mapping algorithms continue to be predominantly threshold-based

chunks.text: The study aims to develop an automated satellite-based system that provides daily, near real-time river ice condition maps over northern U.S. watersheds and Canada. The goal is to address the operational gap in large-scale river ice monitoring and supply forecasters and decision makers with regular updates. A further goal is to generate complementary surface classes (e.g., snow, water, cloud) to support holistic hydrologic analysis and product verification.
supporting_quote: introduces a novel satellite-based system for river ice mapping using VIIRS imagery
provides forecasters and decision makers with daily updates on river ice conditions on a continental scale, covering northern watersheds in the US and the entire Canadian territory
generate additional classes such as snow, water, and cloud

chunks.text: A key design goal is to disseminate outputs operationally through a user-friendly platform so products can be queried, compared, and validated against other satellite imagery. The system is intended to run routinely during the freeze-up and breakup season window to capture river ice phenology. This supports both monitoring and potential downstream operational integration for forecasting workflows.
supporting_quote: all the generated images are disseminated in a Google Earth Engine (GEE) interface that allows the users to display, compare, and query the different products
The system is operational between October 1st and June 15th of the following year

chunks.text: In situ river ice observations are difficult to collect consistently due to harsh winter conditions and limited accessibility, making them insufficient for comprehensive monitoring. This leads to a lack of systematic, continuous mapping at continental scales. The paper positions automated satellite methods as necessary to overcome logistics and safety constraints inherent to ground-based measurements.
supporting_quote: While in situ observations hold substantial worth, their utility is curtailed by issues of accessibility, particularly during severe winter conditions
There exists a notable deficiency in the systematic mapping of river ice at a continental scale, primarily attributed to logistical constraints and safety concerns

chunks.text: Existing remote-sensing mapping algorithms for related hydrologic products are often threshold-based and dependent on terrestrial observations, limiting their adaptability in data-scarce regions. This constraint reduces scalability for continental-scale operational river ice products. The study proposes deep learning segmentation to reduce reliance on rigid thresholds.
supporting_quote: most of these mapping algorithms continue to be predominantly threshold-based, largely dependent on terrestrial observations
This factor considerably constrains their adaptability and scalability, particularly in regions where data is scarce

chunks.text: Quantitative validation is challenging because operational and official river-ice spatial products are scarce. The study highlights reliance on a unique set of georeferenced river ice charts in New Brunswick as a workaround for evaluation. This limitation motivates careful selection of dates and overlap regions to assess the binary ice/water mapping.
supporting_quote: In the absence of operational and official river ice products, the quantitative evaluation of the proposed system is challenging
the New Brunswick Department of Environment and the local Government in Canada generated river ice charts showing the extent of ice in the main rivers

chunks.text: The system performs semantic segmentation of VIIRS imagery using a U-Net encoder–decoder architecture. It integrates VIIRS channels with auxiliary surface layers to classify pixels into multiple surface and atmospheric classes. The output includes classes relevant to hydrology and quality control such as clouds and cloud shadow.
supporting_quote: leverages the sophisticated U-Net network architecture
facilitating an efficient image segmentation process... encompass clouds, river ice, snow, water, bare land, and vegetation
Flowchart illustrating the methodology with (A) data preprocessing, (B) segmentation using U-Net

chunks.text: A two-stage segmentation strategy is used to improve cloud handling. First, a cloud-specific network maps cloud and cloud shadow under prevailing cloudy conditions; second, a clear-sky network segments the cloud-free part into surface classes. This division is intended to reduce confusion between cloud contamination and surface ice/snow signatures.
supporting_quote: we propose a two-stage approach that consists of using the first cloud-specific net to map clouds
the cloud free part of the satellite image is segmented separately with the second net
So, the output of the first net is two classes, namely, cloud and cloud shadow

chunks.text: Cloud detection is guided by a temperature-based feature derived from auxiliary LST climatology and VIIRS thermal observations. The method uses the vertical temperature gradient between MODIS LST climatology and VIIRS I05 brightness temperature, where large differences indicate clouds. This feature is used as a key input variable for the first network.
supporting_quote: calculation of the vertical temperature gradient between LST climatology... and the I05 thermal band of VIIRS
A narrow gap between the climatology of LST and I05 indicates that the scene is cloud free
The vertical gradient of temperature corresponds to the difference between LST climatology and the observation in the thermal I5 channel

chunks.text: Training data are created by visually selecting representative cloudy and cloud-free scenes, then labeling pixels into target classes. Each scene is split into training, test, and validation subsets using fixed proportions. Both networks use the same hyperparameters and follow the same training/validation workflow.
supporting_quote: The scenes used in the training... were carefully examined visually to select those with various cloud types
The selected scenes that were used for the training of the UNet were labeled
Each scene used for the training of each net is divided into training, test, and validation fractions that cover 80%, 10%, and 10%

chunks.text: Ice extent is obtained directly from the U-Net segmentation, while ice concentration is computed independently using a linear reflectance model. The concentration uses two tie points in VIIRS I02 representing open water and pure ice reflectance. Tie points are updated adaptively per scene using quantiles to account for seasonal and spatial reflectance variability.
supporting_quote: the system calculates ice concentration... using a linear model that uses two tie points of the I02 channel
tie points used in the calculation of ice concentration are updated regularly... using the 10% and 80% quantiles
ice extent is solely a result of the U-Net segmentation

chunks.text: Quantitative evaluation compares model outputs to rasterized river status from New Brunswick ice charts using pixel-wise confusion-matrix metrics. Reported measures include Proportion Correct (PC), Bias ratio (B), Probability of Detection (POD), False Alarm Ratio (FAR), and Critical Success Index (CSI). These metrics summarize accuracy, bias, detection skill, and false positives for the binary ice/water task.
supporting_quote: quantitative verification... executed via a raster-to-raster comparison
evaluation metrics... encapsulated in a 2 × 2 confusion matrix
The Proportion Correct (PC)... Bias ratio (B)... Probability of Detection (POD)... False Alarm Ratio (FAR)... Critical Success Index (CSI)

chunks.text: The system uses VIIRS I-band imagery from NOAA-20 and Suomi-NPP, focusing on ascending daytime passes. Inputs include I01, I02, I03, and I05 plus viewing geometry layers (zenith and solar/satellite angles). Two similar-sensor platforms provide observations about 50 minutes apart, enabling compositing to reduce cloud obstruction.
supporting_quote: This study employs I-band images derived from the NOAA-20 and S-NPP satellites' ascending daytime passes
the following VIIRS I-bands are used: I01, I02, I03, and I05. In addition, the zenith, the satellite, and the solar angle layers are used
they are 50 min apart... useful to generate composites that should minimize the cloud coverage

chunks.text: Auxiliary inputs include MODIS land cover and MODIS LST climatology to improve segmentation and cloud detection. Land cover uses the MCD12Q1 product, while LST climatology is taken from MOD11C3 monthly LST&E. These layers provide context on surface type and expected surface temperature under clear-sky conditions.
supporting_quote: use the Terra and Aqua combined MODIS Land Cover Type (MCD12Q1) product as one of the input variables
The LST climatology was obtained from the NASA MODIS product MOD11C3 Version 6

chunks.text: A high-resolution land-water mask is used to delineate waterbodies and support reliable water/ice mapping. The mask is generated from Landsat imagery collected over roughly 20 years, intended to include floodplains by capturing extreme flooding conditions. This constrains water detection to plausible hydrologic areas.
supporting_quote: high-resolution land-water mask, which was generated using Landsat images collected over around 20 years
long enough to capture extreme flooding conditions to ensure that floodplains are included in the water mask

chunks.text: Qualitative validation uses multiple observation sources including USGS river cameras, NOAA NWS field and airborne surveys, and comparisons with other satellites. Additional cross-checking leverages high-resolution sensors (Sentinel-1/2) and moderate-resolution Sentinel-3. USGS streamflow station flags indicating ice presence are also used as supporting evidence.
supporting_quote: qualitative methods make use of collected on-the-ground observations from cameras deployed and maintained by USGS
comparison with other collocated satellite observations from high-resolution sensors such as Sentinel 1 and 2 or moderateresolution sensors such as Sentinel 3
USGS adds a flag that is indicative of ice presence

chunks.text: Quantitative validation relies on georeferenced river ice charts from New Brunswick, Canada, which depict ice extent and related characteristics for major rivers. The study evaluates performance on dates in 2023 when charts and cloud-limited VIIRS scenes overlap, focusing on the Saint John River and Aroostook River. This provides a rare reference dataset for pixel-wise assessment.
supporting_quote: the charts issued by the authorities in New Brunswick, Canada, were used for the quantitative assessment
Reference data for model evaluation were obtained on specific dates in 2023: 7 February, 9 February, 3 March, 10 March, 21 March, 11 April, 14 April, and 15 April
observed river statuses of open water and ice cover on the Saint John River and the Aroostook River

chunks.text: A case study over the Saint Lawrence River (14 January 2022) shows that the VIIRS ice extent product matches Sentinel-3 observations in capturing ice along banks and in Lake Saint-Pierre while keeping the central seaway largely ice-free. The ice concentration product is spatially consistent with observed patterns, with higher values near banks and lower values near the maintained shipping channel. Agreement between independently computed ice concentration and segmentation-derived ice extent supports product reliability.
supporting_quote: Ice extent... agrees reasonably well with the extent shown in the Sentinel 3 image
Ice concentration values are the highest along the northern and southern riverbanks and in Saint Pierre Lake
ice extent and ice concentration are calculated independently in the system

chunks.text: User-oriented qualitative assessment over three winter seasons indicates that the system maps river ice extent and concentration well, especially for large and moderately wide rivers. A Missouri River example (near Bismarck) shows rapid transition captured by the product, with estimated ice concentration dropping from about 90% to about 20% between 6 and 9 April 2023. The remaining nonzero concentration is attributed to snow presence near the riverbanks, illustrating interactions among classes.
supporting_quote: assessment of the product was conducted continuously for three winter seasons
capabilities to accurately map river ice extent and concentration, especially in large and moderately wide rivers
concentration dropped from around 90% (Figure 4b) to values closer to 20% (Figure 4e)

chunks.text: Quantitative evaluation against New Brunswick ice charts yields solid skill for binary ice/water mapping. Reported metrics include Proportion Correct (PC) of 0.747, Bias ratio of 0.870, Probability of Detection (POD) of 0.768, False Alarm Ratio (FAR) of 0.117, and Critical Success Index (CSI) of 0.697. These indicate good detection capability with relatively low false alarms and slight underprediction of ice.
supporting_quote: The Proportion Correct... was 0.747
The Bias ratio stood at 0.870
The Probability of Detection was measured at 0.768
the False Alarm Ratio was calculated as 0.117
the Critical Success Index was calculated as 0.697

chunks.text: A bias analysis shows the model is very accurate for open water but misses some ice-covered conditions, explaining underprediction. The False Positive Water (FPW) rate is reported as 0%, while False Negative Water (FNW) is 25%, meaning some ice-covered pixels are classified as open water. The paper notes that occasional snow classification over rivers can introduce additional bias in the binary comparison.
supporting_quote: FPW rate was a remarkable 0%
rate of FNW... stood at 25%
model predicted snow cover over some river stretches, which introduced an additional source of bias

chunks.text: The system can track seasonal transitions by mosaicking multiple VIIRS swaths to reduce clouds, demonstrated over Alaska in spring 2022. Weekly composites show statewide snow cover on 19 April 2022 and progressive snowmelt through May, with later melt in the north slope. This supports monitoring of snowmelt as a precursor to river ice breakup across large regions.
supporting_quote: weekly running composite of VIIRS scenes over Alaska that capture statewide progress in snow melt and river ice breakup
On 19 April 2022, VIIRS product shows the state of Alaska entirely covered by snow
It is only towards the end of May that snow and ice in the north slope region of Alaska... started to melt

chunks.text: Time-series analysis for the Tanana River watershed during the 2021 breakup season indicates a lag between snowmelt and ice-area reduction. Snow-covered area decreased by about 41% from 17–21 April, while ice-covered area decreased by about 16% in the following four days. The reported four-day delay highlights how the system’s daily mapping can help characterize watershed-specific breakup dynamics.
supporting_quote: from 17 April to 21 April, we observed a ~41% reduction in snow-covered areas
followed by only a ~16% decrease in ice-covered areas within the following four days
This four-day delay

chunks.text: Spatial resolution limits constrain performance for narrow rivers because VIIRS I-bands are moderate resolution (375 m). The current system is therefore better for large rivers and those wider than the pixel size, while narrow rivers require downscaling and mixed-pixel unmixing. The paper describes ambiguity cases where different land–water–snow–ice mixtures can produce similar observations, complicating retrievals.
supporting_quote: VIIRS images, which are of moderate 375 m spatial resolution
system is more suitable for large rivers and those of a moderately wide cross section, wider than 375 m
requires downscaling the collected observations over mixed pixels

chunks.text: Cloud and especially cloud-shadow detection remain challenging, with lower performance noted for low and thin clouds and for cloud shadows. The current approach relies on the DLST feature (difference between I05 temperature and LST climatology), which performs better for high and thick clouds. The authors suggest expanding cloud-shadow training samples and adding explanatory variables such as cloud base height and temperature profiles.
supporting_quote: The limitation faced in the case of low and thin clouds is common when optical images are used
works well with high altitude and thick clouds but requires further training in the case of low and thin clouds
a lower performance was noticed in the detection of cloud shadow

chunks.text: Region-specific false alarms arise from relief shade in Alaska when low sun angles create dark areas over snow that resemble water reflectance. These shaded snow areas can be misclassified as water due to reduced reflectance. A mitigation approach is to restrict water detection to within waterbody boundaries and a buffer corresponding to floodplains.
supporting_quote: false classification of relief shade issue was reported mostly in Alaska, where the sun angle can be relatively low
leads to their classification as water since their reflectance drops to the order of water pixels
allow water to be detected only within a waterbody's boundary and within a certain buffer area around it

chunks.text: Optical physics can limit separability of ice and water under some conditions, such as thin or dark ice. In a Peoria Lake example (10 January 2022), thin ice was not clearly visible in Sentinel-2, and the VIIRS ice extent product missed some thin-ice areas while ice concentration increased. The paper emphasizes analyzing both extent and concentration to better interpret such cases.
supporting_quote: NWS reported the presence of thin ice
system showed an increase in ice concentration... indicating a better sensitivity of the concentration to ice presence
The ice extent map did not include the thin ice part

chunks.text: Operational adoption would require integration into NOAA NWS workflows, beyond the current Google Earth Engine dissemination. The authors note that full integration would require transition into AWIPS, which forecasters use for analysis and reporting. This highlights an implementation gap between a research-grade web product and an operational decision-support system.
supporting_quote: Eventually, a full integration of the system in the decision-making process of NOAA NWS forecasters requires the transition of the system and its integration into the Advanced Weather Interactive Processing System (AWIPS)
generated river ice product was disseminated using a Google Earth engine interface

chunks.text: The paper concludes that an automated deep learning VIIRS-based system can address the gap in systematic, large-scale river ice monitoring by producing near real-time maps across northern watersheds. The system is presented as a first continental-scale river ice monitoring capability, validated via qualitative and quantitative assessments. It successfully captures river ice phenology, particularly onset and breakup, supporting hydrologic monitoring and risk management.
supporting_quote: addressing the gap in systematic, large-scale river ice monitoring via the development of an automated
culminating in the creation of the first continental-scale river ice monitoring system
maps generated by the system have proven to successfully capture the phenology of river ice, particularly during the onset and breakup periods

chunks.text: Evaluation over multiple seasons with NOAA end-users and independent observations indicates the system can track rapid changes in river ice conditions, which is important for monitoring potential ice jams and flooding. The Missouri River example demonstrates that product changes align with camera-observed transitions from ice-covered to ice-free conditions. This supports the product’s operational relevance for forecasters.
supporting_quote: evaluation of the river ice product was carried out continuously over three winter seasons
demonstrated the system's capability to accurately map river ice extent and concentration
swift transition from an ice-covered river to an ice-free one... The corresponding river ice map showed a similar trend

chunks.text: Quantitative verification indicates strong detection skill with moderate overall accuracy and low false alarms, while also revealing slight underprediction of ice. Reported values include PC = 0.747, POD = 0.768, FAR = 0.117, and Bias ratio = 0.870, suggesting room for refinement in sensitivity. The study positions the system as a valuable tool for future water resources management under changing conditions.
supporting_quote: overall accuracy (Proportion Correct) of 0.747
The Probability of Detection was measured at 0.768
False Alarm Ratio was calculated as 0.117
With a Bias ratio of 0.870, the model exhibited a slight under-prediction of river ice presence

chunks.text: Earthen dams and levees are widely used for water storage and flood mitigation, but they can fail and cause severe impacts. Breaching can occur by overtopping, piping, or slope failure, and overtopping often begins with a small channel that enlarges until full failure. Because physical modeling is costly and has scaling limits, validated numerical models are important for exploring dam breach scenarios and informing design and countermeasures.
supporting_quote: Earthen dams are utilized worldwide for water storage and flood mitigation.
Earthen dams may breach for various reasons including overtopping, piping, and slope failure. Overtopping is one of the main causes of dam failure

chunks.text: Many free-surface flow models emphasize the flow field with rigid boundaries, which limits their ability to represent evolving breach geometry. Capturing breach widening remains challenging, partly due to soil variability and incomplete representation of key processes. Recent work introduced a slumping-failure approach that incorporates slope stability concepts into morphodynamics to better represent breach deepening and widening.
supporting_quote: widely used free-surface flow models typically focus on the flow field by considering rigid boundaries
reproducing the key processes affecting the breach evolution, especially the breach widening, has remained poorly resolved

chunks.text: TELEMAC-MASCARET provides open-source modules for 2D shallow-water flow and sediment transport that can be coupled for morphodynamic simulations. TELEMAC-2D models depth-averaged shallow-water flow, while SISYPHE models sediment transport and bed evolution via the Exner equation. Their coupling offers various numerical and discretization choices that may be applied to dam breaching problems.
supporting_quote: This system contains TELEMAC-2D module for modeling two-dimensional open channel flow and SISYPHE module for modeling sediment transport
The coupling between TELEMAC-2D and SISYPHE may be utilized for investigating dam breaching through a broad set of options regarding the numerical schemes and discretization methods.

chunks.text: The study aims to compare breaching simulations from TELEMAC-2D/SISYPHE against an in-house slumping model for an overtopping failure case. Using field measurements from the Upper Rocky Ford Dam failure, the work evaluates how each model reproduces breach evolution and final dimensions after a prespecified failure time. The broader intent is to assess open-source feasibility for breach modeling and motivate integration of slumping physics into TELEMAC workflows.
supporting_quote: The current work aims to compare the simulation of the breaching process in dams due to overtopping by TELEMAC-2D/SISYPHE with that of the slumping model
The evolution of breach shape in time and space after a prespecified failure time is compared.

chunks.text: A key technical gap motivating this work is that common free-surface models often treat boundaries as rigid, limiting representation of evolving breaches in earthen embankments. Additionally, numerical dam-breach modeling struggles to reproduce important processes controlling breach widening, and variability in soil properties complicates prediction. These issues can lead to inaccurate breach evolution estimates needed for design and risk mitigation.
supporting_quote: widely used free-surface flow models typically focus on the flow field by considering rigid boundaries
a wide variability of soil characteristics poses a significant challenge to modeling the breaching of earthen embankments.

chunks.text: For morphodynamic breach modeling specifically, the breach widening process remains poorly resolved in many existing approaches. The paper frames this as a persistent limitation despite prior numerical developments, emphasizing the need for models that better capture the mechanisms shaping the breach in space and time.
supporting_quote: reproducing the key processes affecting the breach evolution, especially the breach widening, has remained poorly resolved

chunks.text: In TELEMAC-2D, the study solves the depth-averaged shallow-water equations using the Finite Volume option to better handle dry areas. The Courant number is targeted near 0.94, with time steps adjusted during the run to maintain stability and consistency. This hydrodynamic setup provides flow fields used by the morphodynamic coupling for breach evolution.
supporting_quote: FV is used in this study because it easily handles dry areas compared to FE in TELEMAC-2D.
The Courant number is set to be 0.94, and time steps are varied accordingly throughout the simulation

chunks.text: SISYPHE represents bed evolution using the Exner equation and computes bedload with the Meyer-Peter and Muller (1948) formula. The approach also adjusts transport direction for secondary currents and transverse slopes via the van Bendegom equation, and modifies critical shear stress using the Soulsby equation. These options define how sediment transport and erosion contribute to breach development in the coupled model.
supporting_quote: SISYPHE utilizes the Exner equation for bed sediment mass conservation.
The Meyer-Peter and Muller (1948) formula is used for modeling bedload transport.

chunks.text: The TELEMAC-2D and SISYPHE models are used in a fully coupled mode for this study. Fully coupled coupling solves both models at the same time step, which is preferred here to better capture rapid breach evolution during flooding, rather than using larger morphodynamic time steps typical of decoupled estuarine applications.
supporting_quote: TELEMAC-2D and SISYPHE are fully coupled in this study for better temporal and spatial estimation of breach evolution
In fully coupled applications, both models are simultaneously solved at each same time step.

chunks.text: The slumping model (SM) solves the shallow-water equations using an explicit MacCormak finite-difference scheme and adds a side-slope slumping component. Slumping is represented using submerged and emerged repose angles to reflect breach widening by slope failures. The study applies the same computational domain and boundary/initial conditions as used for TELEMAC-2D/SISYPHE to enable a like-for-like comparison.
supporting_quote: SM is a numerical model developed to simulate dam and levee breaching using SWE solved by the explicit MacCormak Finite Difference (FD) scheme
This is done by considering the embankment submerged and emerged repose angles.

chunks.text: For the TELEMAC-2D breach simulation, the upstream boundary condition is imposed as a constant discharge throughout the run, while the downstream boundary fixes water depth. For SISYPHE, the boundaries enforce zero sediment discharge, meaning no sediment inflow or outflow is prescribed. This setup isolates breach erosion to material mobilized within the modeled domain.
supporting_quote: the US BC is a constant discharge throughout the simulation, equal to 15.18 m3/s, while the DS BC is fixed at a water depth of 0.8 m.
For SISYPHE, US and DS BCs are constant zero sediment discharge (i.e., no sediment inflow or outflow).

chunks.text: The case study is the Upper Rocky Ford Dam (URFD) in the Gills Creek watershed, which failed by overtopping during the October 2015 flood in South Carolina. Field data were collected after failure, and the dam geometry and measured final breach dimensions are used as benchmarks. The reported final average top breach width is 24.6 m and the breach depth is 5.3 m.
supporting_quote: URFD was one of the several dams in Gills Creek watershed that failed by overtopping during the historic flood event in October 2015 in South Carolina, USA.
The top breach width was 24.6 m, and the breach depth was 5.3 m.

chunks.text: URFD site characteristics include a reservoir area of 132,954 m2 and a dam height of 6.1 m with 160 m length and 9.1 m crest width. The upstream and downstream slopes are 2:1 (H:V). These dimensions define the baseline embankment geometry for the numerical breaching simulations.
supporting_quote: URFD had an upstream reservoir area of 132,954 m2.
The dam was 6.1 m high, 160 m long, had a crest width of 9.1 m, and upstream and downstream slopes of 2:1 (H:V).

chunks.text: Hydrograph and failure timing inputs come from prior analysis of the event. The peak flood discharge is estimated as 15.18 m3/s, and the dam failure time is taken as 940 s (average of three empirical methods). The simulations apply the peak discharge throughout the failure time, following assumptions used in earlier work.
supporting_quote: Tabrizi et al. (2017) estimated the peak flood discharge as 15.18 m3/s
calculated the dam failure time using three empirical methods with an average of 940 s.

chunks.text: The breach initiation is represented by a pilot channel centered on the dam crest. The pilot channel has a bottom width of 4.8 m and a depth of 0.1 m, representing the incipient overtopping pathway. The initial condition includes an 8 cm head above the pilot channel invert, with a downstream water depth of 0.8 m over the domain.
supporting_quote: The pilot channel had a bottom width equal to 4.8 m and a depth equal to 0.1 m.
with an initial head of 8 cm above the invert level of the pilot channel while having a DS water depth for the entire domain equal to 0.8 m.

chunks.text: The computational domain idealizes upstream and downstream reservoirs as rectangles and uses a fine grid to resolve breach processes. The upstream reservoir length is 831 m and the downstream reservoir length is 400 m, both with width 160 m matching the dam. The grid resolution is 0.4 m longitudinally and 0.8 m transversely.
supporting_quote: the US reservoir and 400 m for the DS reservoir. Both reservoirs are considered to have the same 160 m width as that of the dam.
The grid size is set at 0.4 m in the longitudinal direction and 0.8 m in the transverse direction.

chunks.text: Key material and hydraulic parameters used for the TELEMAC-2D/SISYPHE runs include Manning’s n, friction angle, grain size, and porosity. The study sets Manning roughness to 0.025, maximum soil friction angle to 45°, median grain size to 0.88 mm, and porosity to 0.43. These parameters govern flow resistance, sediment mobility, and bed change rates in the coupled simulation.
supporting_quote: Manning roughness coefficient is 0.025
the angle of maximum soil friction is 45o , the medium grain size is 0.88 mm, and soil porosity is 0.43.

chunks.text: At the end of the 940 s simulation, TELEMAC-2D/SISYPHE and the slumping model produce different final breach dimensions relative to field measurements. TELEMAC-2D/SISYPHE predicts a width of 16.69 m and depth of 4.03 m, while the slumping model predicts a width of 29.20 m and depth of 3.70 m. Compared with the observed 24.60 m width and 5.30 m depth, TELEMAC-2D/SISYPHE underestimates both, while the slumping model overestimates width and underestimates depth.

Error metrics show that the slumping model is slightly closer to field-measured breach dimensions than TELEMAC-2D/SISYPHE. The reported average absolute error is 28.06% for TELEMAC-2D/SISYPHE and 24.45% for the slumping model when compared to field measurements. This quantitative comparison supports the paper’s claim that incorporating slumping physics improves agreement for this case.
supporting_quote: The average absolute error is 28.06% for T2D/SIS couple and 24.45% for SM with respect to field measurements.
showing that SM results agree better with the final breach measurements in the field.

chunks.text: TELEMAC-2D/SISYPHE produces an unsymmetric breach, with erosion deviating toward one side of the initial pilot channel. This is notable because the computational domain is symmetric, so a symmetric breach would be expected. The slumping model, in contrast, is described as producing a more symmetric breach development for the same setup.
supporting_quote: T2D/SIS couple tends to have a deviation in the erosion rate towards one side of the initial pilot channel
In contrast, a symmetric breach should be expected in such a symmetric computational domain.

chunks.text: Changing the TELEMAC-2D finite-volume numerical flux scheme did not materially improve the asymmetric breach outcome. The study reports trial runs using alternative FV schemes, including HLLC instead of the kinetic scheme. Despite these adjustments, the unsymmetric breach shape persisted, suggesting the issue is not resolved by simple scheme substitution.
supporting_quote: Additional trial runs were made ... such as the HLLC scheme instead of the kinetic scheme.
None of these trials improved significantly the unsymmetric shape of the breach.

chunks.text: A key limitation observed for TELEMAC-2D/SISYPHE in this application is its tendency to underestimate breach dimensions while generating an unsymmetric breach shape. The paper interprets this as indicating a need for improvement in hydrodynamic and erosion modeling within the TELEMAC-2D/SISYPHE framework for breaching problems. The persistent one-sided erosion bias, despite symmetric geometry and test runs, is highlighted as a concern for predictive reliability.
supporting_quote: TELEMAC-2D/SISYPHE tends to underestimate the breach dimensions while having an unsymmetric final breach
showing the need for improvement in the hydrodynamic and erosion models.

chunks.text: The study notes that attempting different finite-volume schemes within TELEMAC-2D did not fix the asymmetric breach prediction. This suggests that numerical scheme changes alone may be insufficient, and that other aspects of model physics or coupling may control the erosion bias. The finding limits confidence in using TELEMAC-2D/SISYPHE as-is for symmetric overtopping breach cases without further enhancements.
supporting_quote: Additional trial runs were made ... using other hydrodynamic FV schemes
None of these trials improved significantly the unsymmetric shape of the breach.

chunks.text: For the Upper Rocky Ford Dam case, the slumping model provides slightly better agreement with measured breach dimensions than TELEMAC-2D/SISYPHE. TELEMAC-2D/SISYPHE underestimates breach size and yields an unsymmetric final breach, motivating model improvements. The work recommends integrating the slumping model concepts with TELEMAC-2D to improve simulation of breach evolution and downstream inundation.
supporting_quote: The slumping model showed a slightly better comparison of the breach evolution with the final measured breach dimensions.
Integrating the slumping model with TELEMAC-2D is recommended for a better simulation of both dam breach evolution and downstream flood inundation

chunks.text: Flooding is among the most damaging natural disasters, and risks are expected to grow due to population growth, economic development, and climate change. Governments have long invested in structural and nonstructural mitigation, including flood forecast and early warning systems (FFEWS). In the US, the National Weather Service has operated River Forecast Centers for over 50 years, and states/localities also deploy early warning systems.
supporting_quote: flooding consistently is among the most damaging and costly types of natural disaster
exposures to flood risks are likely to continue increasing due to the combined effects of population growth, economic development, and climate change
for over 50 years the US National Weather Service has managed a nationwide network of River Forecast Centers

chunks.text: Cost-benefit analysis (CBA) is widely used by agencies such as USACE and FEMA to evaluate flood mitigation investments. However, valuing information-based approaches like FFEWS is harder than valuing physical infrastructure because benefits depend on human behavioral responses to forecasts and warnings. The paper frames VOI as a way to integrate forecasting, decision-making, outcomes, and valuation into one structure.
supporting_quote: cost-benefit analysis (CBA) has long been used, particularly by agencies such as the USACE and FEMA, to evaluate flood mitigation investments
measuring economic benefits and returns on investment (ROIs) for FFEWS continues to be particularly challenging
traditional economic valuation methods need to be integrated within a broader value-of-information (VOI) framework that accounts for human behavioral responses

chunks.text: Value-of-information (VOI) analysis is a decision-analytic approach for estimating the gains from reducing uncertainty that informs decisions, with applications across many domains including hydrometeorological forecasts. VOI emphasizes that information has value by helping decision makers avoid mistakes relative to fully informed choices, even under risk neutrality. The review notes VOI has been widely used for climate and weather, but less for flood forecast valuation to date.
supporting_quote: VOI analysis refers to a decision-analytic approach for estimating the gains (in monetary terms) from reducing uncertainty in parameters that inform decisions
VOI is derived from its ability to help even risk neutral or risk loving decision makers to avoid mistakes
its use for valuing FFEWS thus far has been more limited

chunks.text: The paper’s goal is to summarize and assess research on the economic benefits of flood forecast and early warning systems. It aims to identify key gaps and implications for future work. To guide this review, it articulates a VOI-based conceptual model linking forecast, decision, outcome, and valuation components as a framework for classifying and comparing studies.
supporting_quote: the purpose of this review is to provide a summary and assessment of research to date on the economic benefits of FFEWS, including identifying main gaps in the literature and implications for future research
I articulate and apply a VOI-based conceptual model connecting four main modeling components-forecast, decision, outcome, and valuation models

chunks.text: A central organizing objective is to categorize valuation methods used in the literature. The review distinguishes VOI-based approaches from prevented-damage approaches, and further differentiates among nonmarket valuation strategies (deductive vs inductive methods). This classification is used to evaluate how comprehensively studies represent the pathways from forecast information to actions and monetized outcomes.
supporting_quote: I also use the framework to categorize the methods used to assess FFEWS benefits, distinguishing between methods that focus specifically on prevented flood damage and those that take a more holistic VOI-based approach
it is useful also to distinguish between deductive and inductive nonmarket valuation approaches

chunks.text: A major problem for quantitative VOI analysis of flood forecasts is limited empirical data on how people and agencies respond to warnings, the costs of these protective actions, and the avoided damages they generate. This constrains the ability to parameterize outcome and valuation components of VOI models. As a result, many studies rely on assumptions or focus narrowly on damage prevention rather than full net benefits under forecast errors.
supporting_quote: Conducting detailed quantitative VOI analyses to assess the value of flood forecast is challenging for several reasons, including, most importantly, lack of data on response actions by emergency managers and flood-affected property owners and on the associated costs and avoided flood damages from these actions
very few of them included empirical estimates of avoided flood damages or flood avoidance costs

chunks.text: Traditional flood-mitigation valuation methods are well developed for physical projects but are insufficient for information-based mitigation. FFEWS benefits depend on how forecasts alter decisions and can create both underprotection and overprotection outcomes. Without integrating behavioral response and forecast error consequences, standard avoided-damages methods can miss key benefit and cost components.
supporting_quote: these traditional economic valuation methods need to be integrated within a broader value-of-information (VOI) framework that accounts for human behavioral responses to forecasts and warnings
the value of an imperfect flood forecast includes not only the expected value of avoided flood losses but also the expected value of avoiding unnecessary flood protection costs

chunks.text: Evidence on the economic benefits of flood forecasts and warnings is particularly limited for the United States. The review finds few US-focused studies overall, no deductive VOI applications in the US, and no US primary survey studies of households or businesses on warning response and avoided damages. Much of the US evidence relies on older expert-judgment studies emphasizing potential rather than observed benefits.
supporting_quote: Overall, only 11 of these studies focused on flood forecasts or warning system in the US, none of which involved primary data collection through surveys
Only one of the VOI studies... and none of the deductive VOI studies was conducted in the US
most of the US-based evidence is from older studies relying on expert judgment

chunks.text: The review uses a VOI conceptual framework that integrates four modeling components: forecast, decision, outcome, and valuation models. Forecast performance can be represented by a contingency table with hit rate and false alarm rate, and decision-making uses conditional probabilities such as p(s|f). Outcomes depend jointly on chosen action and realized state, and valuation converts outcomes into monetary payoffs (cost-loss framing).
supporting_quote: The VOI framework integrates four main modeling components (Fig. 1): forecast, decision, outcome, and economic valuation models
The forecast-based probabilities can be represented as conditional probabilities, p(s|f)
These payoffs often are referred to as a cost-loss model because the monetized outcomes fall into two main categories: (1) costs of protective actions... and (2) flood losses

chunks.text: The paper formalizes VOI with value of perfect information (VOPI) and value of imperfect information (VOII). Under imperfect forecasts, VOII depends on probabilities of forecast states and conditional flood probabilities, balancing avoided underprotection losses against overprotection costs. The framework also defines relative economic value (REV) as VOII/VOPI to compare forecast systems independent of absolute monetization.
supporting_quote: The VOI framework can be used to assess the value of perfect forecast information (VOPI)
The VOI framework also can be extended to assess the value of imperfect forecast information (VOII)

The VOI framework also can be used to assess the relative eco-nomic value (REV)

$$REV = VOII/VOPI$$

chunks.text: For binary cost–loss models, the paper presents a simplified computation of REV using four parameters: cost-loss ratio r, prior flood probability p, false alarm rate F, and hit rate H. It also notes that forecast skill scores relate to maximum obtainable REV and the range of cost-loss ratios where REV is positive. This provides a practical method for comparing forecast systems when cost and damage data are unavailable.
supporting_quote: the calculation of REV can be simplified to the following equation, based on only four model parameters:
where r = cost-loss ratio (C/L_p); p = prior probability, p(s), of flood; F = false alarm rate of the imperfect forecast; and H = hit rate of the imperfect forecast
the maximum obtainable REV for a forecast system... is equal to the difference between its hit rate and its false alarm rate

chunks.text: The review categorizes valuation studies into VOI methods and prevented-damage methods. VOI methods include deductive approaches that parameterize and simulate forecast-decision-outcome-valuation modules, and inductive nonmarket valuation approaches (revealed preference and stated preference). Prevented-damage methods focus on avoided damages and use surveys, expert assessment, flood risk modeling of temporary measures, or benefit transfer from prior studies.
supporting_quote: I first distinguish between (1) VOI methods... and (2) prevented damage methods
Within this category, it is useful also to distinguish between deductive and inductive nonmarket valuation approaches
four main approaches are used to estimate prevented flood damages... surveys... expert assessment... flood risk models... benefit transfer (BT)

chunks.text: The paper applies a systematic literature search and screening process. It uses keyword searches across Web of Science, Google Scholar, and Science Direct, then conducts title/abstract screening and full-text relevance ranking. High relevance studies are supplemented by backward and forward citation screening, leading to a final included set and a database of study characteristics.
supporting_quote: keyword searches using multiple online scholarly databases (Web of Science, Google Scholar, and Science Direct)
conducted more in-depth screening of the study contents to rank them as either high, low, or no relevance
For the studies ranked high relevance, I also reviewed their references and citations

chunks.text: The review dataset comprises 66 studies on the economic value of flood forecasts and warning systems. These studies span 1970 to 2023 and cover more than 15 countries. The author compiled a database summarizing each study’s publication type, region, and valuation method, and conducted deeper summaries for deductive VOI and empirical warning-response studies.
supporting_quote: I identified 66 articles and reports published from 1970 to 2023 in more than 15 countries
Through the previously described search process I identified 66 studies
I then created a database summarizing key features of the studies, including date and type of publication, geographic focus, and methods used

chunks.text: Publication patterns show most evidence is relatively recent and primarily journal-based. Roughly two-thirds of studies were published between 2005 and 2019, with 2005–2009 the most prolific five-year period (19 studies). Nearly 70% (45) are peer-reviewed journal articles and 26% (17) are reports.
supporting_quote: roughly two-thirds were published during the period from 2005 to 2019
The 5-year period providing the most studies (19) was 2005 to 2009
Almost 70% (45) of the studies were published as peer-reviewed journal articles, and 26% (17) were published as reports

chunks.text: Geographically, the literature is concentrated in Europe. About 60% (39) of studies focus on Europe, especially Germany (15) and the UK (14). The US accounts for a much smaller subset, and the table indicates only 12 US entries across method categories.
supporting_quote: Roughly 60% (39) of the studies focused on flood forecast or warning systems in Europe
most of these were conducted for Germany (15) and the United Kingdom (UK) (14)

chunks.text: Methodologically, the database includes relatively few VOI studies compared to prevented-damage approaches. Table 1 reports 12 deductive VOI studies and 3 inductive stated-preference VOI studies, totaling 15 VOI-method studies. In contrast, prevented-damage methods include 22 household/business survey studies, 10 expert assessments, and 8 benefit transfer studies, among others.
supporting_quote: only 23% (15) of the studies applied a deductive or inductive VOI approach

chunks.text: The review identifies 12 deductive VOI case-study papers published from 2006–2019, mainly in Europe (six) and Canada (five), plus one in Thailand. Many of these studies evaluate short-term streamflow forecast systems with lead times from 1 to 9 days, and most simplify continuous forecast outputs into binary flood/no-flood states for cost–loss evaluation.
supporting_quote: I identified 12 papers that applied a deductive approach to assess the economic value of flood prediction systems
All these studies were published during the period 2006–2019, and they predominantly involved case study applications in Europe (six) and Canada (five), along with one application in Thailand
lead times across these systems ranged from 1 to 9 days

chunks.text: Across the 66 included studies, only a minority uses VOI approaches. The review finds 15 studies applying deductive or inductive VOI methods (23%), while 51 focus on prevented damages and behaviors. This indicates that most of the literature does not model the full decision-analytic pathway from forecast errors to actions, costs, and net benefits.
supporting_quote: only 23% (15) of the studies applied a deductive or inductive VOI approach
In contrast, 51 studies focused on prevented damage values and behaviors

chunks.text: The review finds that prevented-damage studies dominate and frequently rely on surveys or expert assessments. It reports 23 studies that analyzed data collected through surveys of flood-affected households and businesses, and many others using expert elicitation. These studies often estimate warning receipt, protective action, and damage reduction ratios, but less often quantify net benefits including action costs and forecast errors.
supporting_quote: including 23 studies that analyzed data collected through surveys of flood-affected households and businesses
almost half of the studies used expert assessments or surveys of household or businesses to quantify the effectiveness of warnings for prompting protective actions and for reducing damages
few of these studies estimated the costs of protective actions or accounted for the effects of forecast errors

chunks.text: Deductive VOI applications are relatively few and often report value in relative terms rather than dollars. The paper notes that many deductive VOI studies estimate relative economic value (REV) instead of absolute monetary VOI. The REV approach is frequently implemented through simple 2×2 cost–loss models requiring assumed cost–loss ratios instead of empirical cost and damage parameters.
supporting_quote: relatively few of the studies (15) applied a VOI-based approach, and most of them estimated VOI in relative rather than absolute (i.e., monetary) terms
eight of them applied a simple 2 × 2 × 2 cost–loss framework to estimate and compare REV
it requires the specification of a generic cost–loss ratio... varied between the extremes of 0 and 1 as part of a sensitivity analysis

chunks.text: A recurring finding in deductive VOI studies is that probabilistic forecasts often yield higher economic value than deterministic forecasts. Multiple studies attribute this to probabilistic forecasts allowing decision makers to set action thresholds tailored to their own cost–loss circumstances. This result emerges despite differing decision contexts (warnings, reservoirs, emergency spending) across applications.
supporting_quote: several studies found that the VOI from probabilistic forecasts is greater than that from deterministic forecasts because they give decision makers the flexibility to define action thresholds that are tailored to their individual cost–loss conditions
seven of the studies compared VOI for deterministic and probabilistic forecasts

chunks.text: The review identifies three inductive stated-preference (SP) studies that elicit willingness to pay (WTP) for flood warning/forecast information, and no revealed-preference (RP) studies. One Philippines contingent valuation study estimates mean household WTP of about $3.50 per month for text-message warnings and reports a benefit–cost ratio above 30:1. A US farmer survey finds WTP of roughly $13 per year for improved spring flood predictions, with potential underestimation due to voluntary payment framing.
supporting_quote: identified three studies that used inductive VOI methods. Each study applied a SP approach
No studies using a RP approach to assess the value of FFEWS were identified
households were willing to pay the equivalent of $3.50/month on average
concluded that the system would provide significant net benefits... benefit–cost ratio of over 30∶1
respondents were willing to pay roughly $13/year on average

chunks.text: US evidence is sparse and lacks primary surveys of affected households or businesses. The review reports that only a small subset of studies focus on the US and that none include primary survey data collection. Consequently, US-focused estimates often rely on older expert judgment or benefit transfer rather than contemporary empirical measurement of warning response and damage reduction.
supporting_quote: Overall, only 11 of these studies focused on flood forecasts or warning system in the US, none of which involved primary data collection through surveys
No survey-based studies analyzing protective actions by households or businesses in the US were found
most of the US-based evidence is from older studies relying on expert judgment

chunks.text: Survey and expert assessment studies report wide ranges for damage reduction and related ratios. Table 6 includes expert-judgment estimates of potentially preventable residential damages, such as 34–36% with 12–24-hour warnings (Day 1970; Day and Lee 1976) and 24–49% avoided content damages for 6–48-hour lead times (Carsell et al. 2004). It also reports warning receipt and action rates such as 55% receipt and 75% able-to-respond in Parker (1991), with later UK and Germany surveys reporting a variety of receipt and action percentages.
supporting_quote: Day (1970)... Estimated ratio (%) 34 ... Potential preventable content damage with 12–24-h warning
Day and Lee (1976)... 36 ... Potential preventable content damage with 12–24-h warning
Carsell et al. (2004)... 24 ... with 6-h warning
Carsell et al. (2004)... 49 ... with 48-h warning
Parker (1991)... 55 ... Ratio type R
Parker (1991)... 75 ... Ratio type A

chunks.text: A notable empirical gap is limited robust evidence linking warnings to reduced damages, even in data-rich settings like Germany. The review notes that multiple statistical analyses of German household survey datasets did not find strong or robust effects of early warnings or protective measures on reducing flood damages. This suggests either difficulty identifying causal impacts or that effects are context-dependent and hard to isolate with available observational data.
supporting_quote: ultimately none of them found strong evidence or reported robust measures of the effects of early warnings or protective measures on reducing flood damages
surprisingly little evidence... has emerged linking flood warnings to reduced damages

chunks.text: Only one identified study uses hydraulic flood risk modeling to estimate community-level damages prevented by actions enabled by early warnings. Nofal et al. (2021) model Santa Clara County, California with a baseline without-FFEWS scenario and then simulate building-level protective actions such as barriers and elevation of components. Across more than 100 mitigation simulations, they find potentially prevented community-level damages in the millions of dollars.
supporting_quote: my search identified only one study that has used this method specifically to estimate prevented damages attributable to FFEWS
Nofal et al. (2021)... Santa Clara County, California
results from more than 100 mitigation simulations demonstrated millions of dollars in potentially prevented damages

chunks.text: The review emphasizes that detailed VOI analyses are constrained by missing empirical inputs on protective actions, their costs, and avoided damages. This limitation leads many VOI studies to rely on assumed cost–loss ratios and to report relative economic value rather than monetized benefits. As a result, current VOI applications often cannot fully quantify net benefits of FFEWS in realistic behavioral settings.
supporting_quote: lack of data on response actions... and on the associated costs and avoided flood damages from these actions
most (6) only estimated information value in relative terms (i.e., as REV), rather than providing absolute estimates of forecast benefits
it requires the specification of a generic cost–loss ratio... varied between the extremes of 0 and 1
