Under bankfull conditions, the developed models performed better than the RHGC method
These data and maps are valuable resources for water‐related experts, enabling further investigations

chunks.text: Flood forecasts are often communicated as deterministic inundation maps derived from a single discharge input to a hydraulic model. The paper emphasizes that these products do not reflect the full range of possible outcomes because uncertainty arises from forcing, initial conditions, parameter choices, and numerical limitations. Prior work suggests probabilistic mapping can better convey flood hazard and support decisions under uncertainty.
supporting_quote: Forecasted flood inundation maps are typically based on deterministic model output generated using a hydraulic model forced with a single discharge output from a hydrologic model
These deterministic flood inundation maps are subject to uncertainty due to imperfect forcing, initial conditions, model parameterizations, and numerical limitations

chunks.text: Ensemble approaches are presented as a common way to quantify prediction uncertainty, with options including time-lagged ensembles, perturbed initial conditions, varied physics, and multimodel ensembles. The paper highlights that multimodel ensembles face distributional challenges (each model having its own PDF), but improvements to the underlying models can improve the overall framework. Multimodel methods can also reduce the impact of subjective model selection by emphasizing areas where models agree.
supporting_quote: Three common approaches to generating an ensemble are to use statistical models to generate a time-lagged ensemble, perturb initial conditions of a single model, or vary the physics of the single model
Another ensemble generation approach is to generate a multimodel ensemble where the ensemble is composed of realizations from different models

chunks.text: Communicating forecast uncertainty must balance usefulness with potential information overload. The paper notes that probabilistic techniques can improve situational awareness and decision making, but too much information can cause users to abandon uncertainty products during time-sensitive situations. A proposed remedy is to augment existing products with probabilistic information so it integrates into established workflows.
supporting_quote: Frick and Hegg (2011) showed that the communication of forecast uncertainty improves end users' situational awareness and decision making
HEFS and other uncertainty visualization tools ... are confronted with the paradox of decreasing the end user's understanding of the situation by providing too much information

chunks.text: The study aims to develop an ensemble framework that quantifies and visualizes uncertainty in flood inundation forecasts. It combines a hydrometeorological ensemble streamflow forecast with a hydraulic multimodel setup to produce probabilistic inundation products. The intent is to generate uncertainty-aware flood extent, depth, and velocity maps that can be disseminated rapidly to support operational decision making.
supporting_quote: The objective of this study was to develop an ensemble framework for the quantification and visualization of uncertainty associated with flood inundation forecast maps
This study quantifies forecast flood inundation uncertainty using a combined hydrometeorological and hydraulic multimodel ensemble approach

chunks.text: A specific goal is to demonstrate dissemination of probabilistic flood risk information through an interactive web-based tool rather than requiring users to navigate complex GIS software. The framework is designed to link existing systems so probabilistic uncertainty can be integrated with current operational products. This is positioned as a way to help decision makers prioritize resources based on spatially varying flood risk.
supporting_quote: The incorporation of this flood inundation uncertainty information into an interactive webbased application will demonstrate new techniques for rapid dissemination of flood inundation forecast products
the framework allows for the seamless integration of uncertainty information into operational products

chunks.text: Deterministic inundation maps provide a single scenario and can misrepresent risk because they omit uncertainty from meteorological forcing, initialization, model parameters, and numerical behavior. The paper argues this limits decision support by failing to communicate the full range of plausible inundation outcomes. As a result, users may interpret deterministic extents as certain and allocate resources inefficiently.
supporting_quote: While deterministic forecasts provide a single realization of potential inundation, the inherent uncertainty associated with forecasts also needs to be conveyed
therefore, by not incorporating these uncertainties, deterministic flood inundation maps fail to communicate the full risk for potential flooding

chunks.text: Hydrologic and hydraulic modeling uncertainty is compounded by subjective choices in model development and calibration, and no single model is universally best. This makes model selection complex and potentially introduces modeler-dependent errors into forecast products. The paper motivates multimodel ensembles as a strategy to reduce subjectivity by focusing on areas of agreement.
supporting_quote: Subjective choices made by the modeler in developing and calibrating the simulational framework may generate substantial error
there is not a unique model that can be known as the "best" model for all conditions

chunks.text: Existing uncertainty visualization systems can overwhelm users, reducing comprehension during emergencies. The paper notes that in time-sensitive situations users may discard additional uncertainty information and revert to habitual routines. This motivates creating uncertainty products that are simple and augment existing maps rather than requiring major workflow changes.
supporting_quote: users often abandon the additional information and revert back to habitual routines
a more effective method for the communication of uncertainty is to augment current products with probabilistic uncertainty information

chunks.text: The framework links four major components: hydrologic ensemble prediction, hydraulic modeling, GIS postprocessing, and web-based visualization. An 11-member streamflow ensemble is used to force two hydraulic models, producing a multimodel ensemble of flood extent, depth, and velocity. The resulting ensemble spread is turned into probabilistic raster surfaces that represent exceedance likelihoods for hazard thresholds.
supporting_quote: The major components consist of the regional hydrological ensemble prediction system (RHEPS), hydraulic modeling, postprocessing, and web-based visualization
an 11-member ensemble streamflow forecast at lead times from 0 to 48 hr was used to force two hydraulic models to produce a multimodel ensemble

chunks.text: Ensemble streamflow forecasts are obtained from a regional hydrological ensemble prediction system (RHEPS) driven by GEFSRv2 weather ensembles and the HL-RDHM hydrologic model. The paper uses an 11-member, 48-hour (1-hourly) streamflow forecast ensemble at the upstream boundary for the selected event. This provides the hydrometeorological forcing needed to generate multiple hydraulic inundation realizations.
supporting_quote: The RHEPS uses weather ensemble forecasts ... from the National Centers for Environmental Prediction 11-member Global Ensemble Forecast System Reforecast version 2 (GEFSRv2) to force ... HL-RDHM
An 11-member, 48-h (i.e., lead times from 1 to 48 h at 1-h resolution) streamflow forecast ensemble was obtained

chunks.text: One hydraulic component uses the two-dimensional HEC-RAS shallow-water solver on an unstructured mesh and includes a subgrid bathymetry approach to reduce computation. The Darby Creek HEC-RAS mesh contains 82,349 irregular cells with average cell size 385 m². Roughness parameters use a channel Manning’s n initially 0.035 and floodplain n values derived from 2011 NLCD ranging 0.04–0.15.
supporting_quote: The 2D component of the model solves the shallow water equations over an unstructured computational mesh
the model mesh is composed of 82,349 irregularly shaped cells ... with an average cell size of 385 m2
The Manning's n value for the main channel was initially set to 0.035 ... it varied from 0.04 to 0.15

chunks.text: The second hydraulic component uses iRIC with the FaSTMECH quasi-steady, vertically averaged solver to simulate flood extent and compute depth and velocity fields. Terrain inputs match HEC-RAS (1 m LiDAR merged with NOAA bathymetry) but are mapped to an approximately 5×5 m grid to improve stability and reduce computation time. FaSTMECH requires both upstream and downstream boundary conditions because it assumes discharge variations in the momentum equation are negligible.
supporting_quote: FaSTMECH, a quasi-steady vertically averaged model, was used to simulate flood extent and to calculate depth and velocity domains
The topographic data used in iRIC were mapped over a grid mesh approximately 5 × 5 m2
the model requires both upstream and downstream boundary conditions

chunks.text: Both hydraulic models are calibrated using the August 30, 2009 flood event and USGS gage information at Mt. Moriah Cemetery. For HEC-RAS, Manning’s n is adjusted until water surface elevation matches observations with no further improvement. For iRIC, drag coefficients are initialized based on HEC-RAS roughness and then adjusted so upstream water surface elevation reaches the expected value, using consistent downstream boundary conditions across models.
supporting_quote: The flooding event of August 30, 2009 ... was selected for calibration. The Manning's n values were adjusted to ensure the model output matched the observed water surface elevation
the iRIC model was calibrated ... using the flood event of August 30, 2009
the spatial distribution of the frictional coefficients was set the same as HEC-RAS

chunks.text: Postprocessing converts model outputs to a common 5×5 m raster grid and reclassifies each cell into binary exceedance indicators for predefined hazard thresholds. Flood extent is defined as inundation exceeding 0.05 m depth to reduce sensitivity to DEM vertical errors. Composite probability rasters are created by summing binary layers across ensemble members and dividing by the number of members to produce percent agreement, which serves as a proxy for uncertainty at each grid cell.
supporting_quote: resample the output from the models to a common 5×5 m2 gridded raster format

Flood extent illustrates all flood inundation that exceeded a water depth of 0.05 m. A threshold of 0.05 m was selected because it described the flooding while removing potential vertical errors in the DEM
Each grid cell value in the composite rasters corresponds to the percentage of ensemble member agreement

chunks.text: The framework creates multimodel ensemble rasters by combining composite outputs from iRIC and HEC-RAS using the same agreement calculation. It also evaluates uncertainty in total inundated area using a nonparametric interquartile range (IQR) across ensemble members and compares 24-hour vs 48-hour lead time forecasts. The multimodel agreement surfaces are used to communicate spatially varying exceedance probabilities for extent, depth, velocity, and critical conditions.
supporting_quote: To help describe the uncertainty among ensemble members ... a nonparametric value called interquartile range (IQR) was used
the outputs from both the iRIC and the HEC-RAS ensemble members were combined into a single composite using the same procedures
This procedure created the final multimodel flood inundation ensemble rasters for flood extent, water depth, flow velocity, and critical conditions

chunks.text: For dissemination, probabilistic raster layers are delivered through a web-based interactive mapping app built using the open-source Tethys platform. The app, Flood Threat Viewer, lets users toggle between flood extent, depth, velocity, and critical-condition threshold layers and explore local risk by zooming and querying. This approach aims to simplify access to ensemble uncertainty information for rapid, user-driven flood risk assessment.
supporting_quote: the multimodel flood inundation ensemble raster layers were disseminated using a webbased mapping and decision support software development framework called Tethys
built an example web application called the Flood Threat Viewer in the Tethys platform

chunks.text: The study focuses on a 15 km reach of Darby Creek in urban Philadelphia, from Mt. Moriah Cemetery to the Delaware River. The reach is low-gradient (mean slope 0.001 m/m) with an average width of 50 m, and tidal impacts occur downstream. Because floodplains are highly urbanized, high-resolution terrain representation is emphasized.
supporting_quote: stretching from the Mt. Moriah Cemetery to its confluence with the Delaware River
The mean slope of the river is 0.001 m/m with an average width of 50 m. The length of the reach is approximately 15 km
Tidal impacts are apparent in the downstream portion of the Darby Creek segment

chunks.text: Elevation inputs include a 1 m LiDAR-derived DEM combined with NOAA bathymetry, with specific handling under bridges to maintain hydraulic connectivity. The river bed under bridges is set to the average bed elevation upstream and downstream of each bridge. These terrain preparations support both hydraulic models and improve stability and realism in the inundation computations.
supporting_quote: A high-resolution (1 m) LiDAR-derived digital elevation model (DEM) ... was used in combination with a bathymetry dataset collected by NOAA
The river bed elevation underneath bridges was set to average bed elevation of the upstream and downstream of the bridge to ensure the connectivity of the flow

chunks.text: The demonstration event is the April 30, 2014 flood, during which the USGS gage at Cobbs Creek near Mt. Moriah Cemetery recorded the second highest streamflow on record at 99 m³/s. The nearby Philadelphia International Airport precipitation gage measured 121.92 mm of rain during the last two days of April 2014, characterized as a five-year precipitation event. These observations provide context and a reference for evaluating baseline and forecast simulations.
supporting_quote: The flood event that occurred on April 30, 2014 was selected
measured the second highest streamflow on record ... reaching 99 m³/s
recorded 121.92 mm of rain during the last two days of April 2014, indicating a five-year precipitation event

chunks.text: Hydrometeorological forcing consists of an 11-member streamflow forecast ensemble generated by RHEPS for lead times up to 48 hours at hourly resolution. The ensemble originates from GEFSRv2 weather reforecasts and is routed through HL-RDHM to produce multiple streamflow realizations at the upstream hydraulic boundary. The study uses these ensemble inflows because National Water Model forecasts were not available for the 2014 event.
supporting_quote: Thus, 11 different realizations or ensembles of streamflow forecasts are generated
An 11-member, 48-h ... streamflow forecast ensemble was obtained
forecasts from the National Water Model (NWM) were not available for the selected flood event

chunks.text: Hazard metrics are derived by thresholding model outputs for flood extent, water depth, flow velocity, and a combined depth-velocity 'critical conditions' indicator. Flood extent uses a depth exceedance of 0.05 m, and depth/velocity thresholds include values such as >0.15 m, >0.30 m, >0.61 m for depth and >0.45 m/s, >0.90 m/s, >1.80 m/s for velocity. Critical conditions include combinations like >0.30 m water flowing at >1.80 m/s intended to represent dangerous situations for people and response operations.
supporting_quote: Flood extent is defined as any cell inundated by >0.05 m of water
These predetermined thresholds were based on hazardous levels for flood extent, water depth, flow velocity, and critical conditions
>0.30 m water flowing at >1.80 m/s

chunks.text: Both hydraulic models produced 24-hour inundation forecasts that visually matched their respective baseline inundation maps reasonably well. Agreement maps show uncertainty as lower ensemble agreement, with higher agreement interpreted as higher risk of exceedance at a location. This supports the feasibility of using ensemble agreement surfaces to communicate uncertainty spatially across an urban floodplain.
supporting_quote: Both iRIC and HEC-RAS produced quality 24-h lead time forecasts relative to the baseline map produced by each model
Greater uncertainty is illustrated ... as green, or where there is less agreement between the ensemble members

chunks.text: At 24-hour lead time, the iRIC ensemble displayed more spatial disagreement than the HEC-RAS ensemble for predicted inundation cells. The paper reports 4,529 grid cells where only one iRIC member predicted inundation, compared with 1,040 such cells in HEC-RAS. This indicates higher uncertainty in the iRIC-derived inundation footprint at that lead time under the study setup.
supporting_quote: the iRIC model ensemble members have greater disagreement ... than HEC-RAS
The iRIC 24-h lead time has 4,529 grid cells where only one ensemble member predicts inundation, whereas HEC-RAS has 1,040

chunks.text: Uncertainty increased substantially for iRIC at 48-hour lead time, while HEC-RAS agreement remained relatively consistent between 24 and 48 hours. For iRIC at 48 hours, 31,963 grid cells were predicted inundated by only one ensemble member, versus 608 such cells for HEC-RAS at 48 hours. This contrast highlights model-dependent sensitivity of inundation uncertainty to forecast lead time.
supporting_quote: the model agreement dropped substantially for the iRIC 48-h lead time forecast
For the iRIC 48-h lead time forecast, there are 31,963 grid cells where only one ensemble member predicts
the HEC-RAS 48-h lead time forecast ... with 608 grid cells where only one ensemble member predicts

chunks.text: Area-based uncertainty, measured by interquartile range (IQR) of inundated area across members, was small for iRIC 24-hour, HEC-RAS 24-hour, and HEC-RAS 48-hour forecasts but large for iRIC 48-hour forecasts. The paper reports IQR < 0.1 km² for the consistent cases, and nearly 0.4 km² for iRIC at 48 hours. This provides a quantitative indicator that the iRIC 48-hour inundation forecasts were much less consistent across ensemble members.
supporting_quote: the 24-h iRIC, 24-h HEC-RAS, and 48-h HEC-RAS ... produced IQR < 0.1 km2, the IQR for the 48-h iRIC lead time forecasts was nearly 0.4 km2
This inconsistency and lower agreement translates into higher uncertainty in the iRIC 48-h lead time flood inundation forecast

chunks.text: Compositing the two hydraulic model ensembles is presented as a way to reduce modeler subjectivity and increase confidence where model predictions converge. Compared with a deterministic map, the multimodel probability surfaces reveal different relative risks among nearby locations that appear similarly flooded in a single-run output. In the example, ensemble agreement indicates the highest inundation risk at Location 1, followed by Locations 2 and 3, guiding more nuanced resource prioritization.
supporting_quote: By compositing the ensemble flood inundation maps from both hydraulic models, modeler subjectivity is decreased
it turns out that the risk for inundation, based on ensemble agreement, is highest for Location 1, followed by Locations 2 and 3

chunks.text: The Flood Threat Viewer web application demonstrates interactive exploration of multiple probabilistic hazard layers, including flood extent, depth, velocity, and critical conditions. In a tank farm example, the app indicates moderate flood extent risk for some tanks but no risk of velocity exceeding 0.9 m/s and no risk of critical conditions requiring swift water resources. This illustrates how the framework can support rapid, location-specific interpretation of ensemble-based hazard thresholds.
supporting_quote: the rasters were incorporated into a web-based application, the Flood Threat Viewer app
There is no risk for the velocity of the water to exceed 0.9 m/s (2 mph)
no risk for exceeding the critical conditions that would require a swift water team

chunks.text: A key limitation is computational intensity of hydraulic models, which constrains the spatial scalability of the framework beyond local analyses. The paper suggests that adopting lower-complexity alternatives could expand applicability. Terrain-based approaches such as Height Above Nearest Drainage are proposed as possible substitutes when full hydraulic simulations are too expensive, though dynamic environments may still require hydraulics.
supporting_quote: the intensive nature of the hydraulic models limits the spatial applicability of the framework
future work can use terrain-based models such as Height Above Nearest Drainage, which could be a reasonable substitute

chunks.text: The evaluation is limited by lack of ground-truth inundation extent data for the selected event. As a workaround, baseline maps forced by observed discharge are treated as the best available representation for comparison, but these baselines still contain error and do not capture full uncertainty. The authors note a need for improved field data collection methods, including unmanned aircraft systems, to better validate inundation forecasts.
supporting_quote: In the absence of ground-truth data, baseline inundation maps were used for the comparison of model output
it is still subject to errors and, in that sense, it does not account for the full uncertainty of the inundation forecasts
it sheds light on the need for new methods to collect ground-truth flood extent data, such as unmanned aircraft systems

chunks.text: The paper emphasizes that successful uncertainty communication depends on end-user interpretation and integration into decision routines. Prior findings cited in the paper caution that too much uncertainty information can reduce understanding during emergencies, leading users to ignore additional products. The framework therefore focuses on simplified threshold-based layers and an interactive viewer to help users consume uncertainty without being overwhelmed.
supporting_quote: one of the most prominent caveats is the end user's understanding of how to use the uncertainty information to make decisions
HEFS and other uncertainty visualization tools ... are confronted with the paradox of decreasing the end user's understanding of the situation by providing too much information

chunks.text: The framework is presented as semiautomated and adaptable, but performance and operational value still require additional case studies and structured evaluation. The authors propose emergency management training exercises as one way to assess how access to the Flood Threat Viewer changes decisions relative to historical events. This indicates that human-factors validation is a remaining step for confirming practical benefits.
supporting_quote: With this process now semiautomated, there are opportunities to adapt the framework to new study areas
case studies are needed to provide a thorough assessment of this framework in flood preparation and planning activities

chunks.text: The study concludes that linking hydrometeorological ensembles with two hydraulic models can produce probabilistic flood inundation products that explicitly communicate uncertainty. Uncertainty is represented through ensemble agreement and probabilistic raster surfaces for extent, depth, velocity, and critical conditions, and delivered via a web-based tool. The framework is positioned as a viable approach to reduce modeler subjectivity and augment deterministic forecasts with actionable uncertainty information.
supporting_quote: an 11-member streamflow forecast ensemble was used as input in two hydraulic models, iRIC and 2D HEC-RAS
Uncertainty was quantified by assessing the spread among ensemble members and was visualized as probabilistic raster surfaces
this framework provides a viable approach for reducing modeler subjectivity, quantifying uncertainty

chunks.text: The paper highlights the integration of hydraulic models, GIS postprocessing, and web dissemination as an important outcome that can be adapted to other regions and potentially updated with new national forecast systems. It suggests future substitution of the regional hydrometeorological system with the National Water Model to extend to nationwide inundation uncertainty products. This underscores the framework’s modularity and potential for operational expansion.
supporting_quote: An important outcome from this project is a framework that links between existing hydraulic models, GIS, and web-based application platforms
with the implementation of the NWM, future work can substitute the regional hydrometeorological forecast system in the framework to produce nationwide flood inundation uncertainty information

chunks.text: The National Water Model (NWM) is a continental-scale hydrologic framework used for water-resource management, flood prediction, and drought monitoring across the U.S. While it performs well inland, it lacks direct representation of coastal water dynamics. In coastal zones, tides and storm surges can alter river discharge, storage, and backwater effects, which can affect downstream discharge and lateral flooding processes.
supporting_quote: The National Water Model (NWM) is a hydrologic modeling framework that simulates and forecasts water flow over the continental United States
its hydrological code base lacks a direct connection to coastal water dynamics... tidal and surge processes affect river discharge and storage

chunks.text: Operational NWM v3.0 includes a one-way coupling to the SCHISM coastal hydrodynamic model to produce total water-level predictions in coastal areas. In this setup, NWM provides upstream boundary conditions to SCHISM, but SCHISM does not feed information back to NWM. Similar unidirectional coupling patterns are common in other hydrologic–hydrodynamic integrations, limiting improvements to NWM streamflow.
supporting_quote: The latest operational implementation of the NWM (version 3.0)... coupling it to... SCHISM... However, this coupling is unidirectional
there is no feedback mechanism from the SCHISM to the NWM to improve discharge or streamflow modeling and forecasting

chunks.text: Two-way coastal–river coupling can improve not only streamflow but also multiple downstream NWM-derived products. Better coastal-aware streamflow can enhance soil moisture and groundwater representation, improve long-term water balance and forecasting, strengthen floodplain dynamics for risk assessments, and support water-quality modeling. These benefits rely on bringing tidal and storm-surge information back into hydrologic routing and state evolution.
supporting_quote: A two-way coupling... would offer benefits that extend far beyond merely improving the NWM's streamflow predictions
This improved streamflow modeling enhances soil moisture and groundwater representation in coastal areas... It leads to more reliable long-term waterbalance calculations

chunks.text: The study aimed to design and implement a two-way coupling method between NWM and SCHISM. The intended workflow keeps NWM as the driver of SCHISM via upstream boundary streamflow, while SCHISM returns coastal water-dynamics information to update NWM streamflow for subsequent time steps. The paper evaluates whether this feedback improves streamflow modeling in coastal regions during tides, surges, and storms.
supporting_quote: we aimed to design and implement a two-way coupling method between the NWM and the SCHISM
The SCHISM's total water modeling results would then be fed back to update the streamflow predictions in the NWM

chunks.text: The research examines improvements in NWM streamflow accuracy and reliability when coastal influences are incorporated through two-way coupling. The analysis targets multiple scenarios including storm events and tidal extremes, with a focus on how these coastal processes modify discharge timing, magnitude, and floodplain storage effects in the lower river network.
supporting_quote: This paper examines the gains in the NWM's streamflow modeling accuracy and reliability resulting from this two-way coupling
We analyze how incorporating coastal influences improved predictions in various scenarios, including during storm events and tidal extremes

chunks.text: A core limitation of NWM in coastal regions is the absence of tidal and storm-surge processes, which can change discharge and storage and produce backwater effects. Without these influences, predictions in lower river reaches may miss altered flow dynamics, lateral flooding behavior, and ultimate discharge during coastal extremes. This is especially critical where coastal water levels interact strongly with river routing.
supporting_quote: its hydrological code base lacks a direct connection to coastal water dynamics
The absence of these coastal influences in the model may affect predictions of backwater effects, altering flow dynamics in a river's lower reaches

chunks.text: One-way coupling approaches do not allow hydrodynamic feedback to improve NWM streamflow calculations. Even when SCHISM is driven by NWM discharge, the NWM hydrologic component remains unchanged and cannot adjust its routing based on tides, surges, or coastal backwater. This lack of feedback constrains improvements to NWM streamflow and its dependent products.
supporting_quote: this coupling is unidirectional—the hydrological component of the NWM does not receive updates from the SCHISM
The one-way coupling's lack of feedback limits the NWM as it does not incorporate coastal processes to update the NWM's streamflow modeling

chunks.text: A key coupling barrier is that hydrologic and hydraulic models represent common variables differently, causing magnitude and timing discrepancies. Even for small events, water depth/water level can differ between NWM and SCHISM, complicating direct exchange. This mismatch stems from NWM’s idealized trapezoidal channel representation versus SCHISM’s detailed hydrodynamic treatment of morphology and flows.
supporting_quote: variables such as water depth can exhibit significant differences in magnitude and timing between the NWM and the SCHISM, even for small natural events
The NWM relies on an idealized trapezoidal river channel described by parameters... In contrast, the SCHISM hydraulic model provides a more detailed representation

chunks.text: The two-way coupling uses an iterative, time-step exchange centered on converting discharge (Q) and velocity (V) at the NWM–SCHISM interface. NWM discharge is converted to SCHISM boundary velocity using V = Q/A. SCHISM then simulates coastal water levels and velocities, and its velocity field is integrated across a cross-section to compute discharge returned to NWM. NWM uses the returned discharge to update its next-step flow calculations.
supporting_quote: focusing on the conversion between discharge (Q) and velocity (V)... V = Q/A
integrating the velocity across the bathymetry-defined cross-section... Q = ∑(Vihiwi)

chunks.text: To reconcile spatial mismatch between SCHISM discharge cross-sections and NWM channel nodes, the coupling applies a distance-based weighting coefficient. For a SCHISM discharge location within a radius Rn of an NWM node, weights are computed as (Rn^2 − djn^2)/(Rn^2 + djn^2); otherwise weight is 0. The radius was set to 1000 m to include nearby links and smooth the transition of SCHISM feedback onto NWM nodes.
supporting_quote: a weighting coefficient... was introduced... calculated as (Rn^2 - djn^2) / (Rn^2 + djn^2)
In order to ensure smooth coupling, Rn was set as 1000 m to include a few links nearby

chunks.text: The coupling was implemented using the CoastalApp framework built on the Earth System Modeling Framework (ESMF). CoastalApp is described as a coupling framework for coastal applications and regional forecasts, enabling integration of different earth system model components. The study leveraged this framework to execute the iterative Q–V exchange between NWM and SCHISM.
supporting_quote: implemented and tested using the CoastalApp framework. CoastalApp [18] is a comprehensive modeling framework
built upon the Earth System Modeling Framework (ESMF) [19] to facilitate the coupling of various earth system model components

chunks.text: Three experiments were designed to test coupling impacts: EXP1 two-way coupling, EXP2 no-coupled validation using observed upstream discharge to drive SCHISM, and EXP3 one-way coupling from NWM to SCHISM without feedback to NWM. EXP2 primarily serves model validation by comparing SCHISM water levels to observations under reliable boundary conditions. EXP1 vs EXP3 comparison isolates benefits from two-way feedback.
supporting_quote: EXP1: two-way coupling between the SCHISM and the NWM
EXP2: no-coupled validation, with the SCHISM using USGS-observed discharge
EXP3: one-way coupling from the NWM to the SCHISM, without feedback from the SCHISM to the NWM

chunks.text: Model configuration included short time steps for stability and coastal dynamics. NWM used 10 s temporal resolution, SCHISM 20 s, and ROMS 30 s; SCHISM spatial resolution was ~100 m. Simulations covered 28 September–5 November 2016 for NWM and SCHISM with a 5-day spin-up, while ROMS ran 1 September–30 November 2016. SCHISM Manning roughness was set to 0.025, described as typical for flood plains with short grass.
supporting_quote: Temporal Resolution | 10 s | 20 s | 30 s
Simulation Period | 28 September–5 November 2016 (5-day spin-up)
The Manning roughness coefficient was set as 0.025 in the SCHISM

chunks.text: The study area is the northeastern coast of South Carolina, with SCHISM covering three major rivers flowing to the Atlantic and NWM covering the entire Pee Dee watershed. The NWM and SCHISM domains overlap in the coupling region. Upstream boundary information and validation stations were defined using USGS gauges, including upstream discharge stations 02135200 and 02110704 and water-level validation stations 02110802, 021108125, and 02110815.
supporting_quote: The SCHISM domain covered the northeastern coast of South Carolina, including three major rivers that flow into the Atlantic Ocean
USGS stations 02135200 and 02110704 were used to provide upstream discharge data... 02110802, 021108125, and 02110815 were used to provide water-level data

chunks.text: Hurricane Matthew (landfall 8 October 2016) was selected to test the coupled system under compound coastal–river forcing. The event included storm surge driven by strong onshore winds followed by offshore wind and negative surge, plus heavy rainfall. The paper reports rainfall intensity from 1 mm/h to 6 mm/h over 2 days and substantial damage estimates, making it a strong stress test for tide–surge–river interactions.
supporting_quote: Hurricane Matthew... was selected as the case study to test the coupled model
heavy rainfall from 1 mm/h to 6 mm/h over 2 days led to severe inland flooding
estimated costs reaching approximately USD 10.3 billion

chunks.text: Offshore boundary water levels for SCHISM were provided by a ROMS simulation for the northwestern Atlantic, coupled one-way into SCHISM. ROMS used atmospheric forcing from NCEP CFSR and CFSv2 and tidal forcing from TPXO9, with initial conditions from CMEMS GOPR. chunks.text: Two-way coupling introduced tidal oscillations into river discharge predictions that were absent in the one-way NWM results. The tidal signal attenuated upstream, representing a realistic transition from estuarine dominance to inland river dominance. At sampling points 9071860 and 9073930, backflows of −213.8 m3/s and −399.4 m3/s occurred immediately after the storm surge on 8 October. During peak flooding (11 October, 02:00 UTC), intense flow through this branch reversed Waccamaw flow and produced a backwater effect. The interaction evolved from normal merging (10 October, 12:00 UTC) to reversal during peak and then toward normalization (11 October, 12:00 UTC).

chunks.text: A central limitation is the absence of discharge observations within the SCHISM domain, restricting validation primarily to water levels. chunks.text: Variable dissimilarity between NWM and SCHISM is a major obstacle for two-way coupling, particularly for water level/depth exchange. The paper shows that water depth or water level can differ markedly in magnitude and timing between the models, creating conflicts during data exchange. Because of these discrepancies, the authors avoided using water level as the exchanged variable and instead used discharge, even though SCHISM does not directly output discharge.

chunks.text: The difference in how models represent river geometry contributes to mismatches in coupled variables and dynamics. chunks.text: The NWM’s Muskingum routing method has weaknesses for representing backflows, which become important once tidal and surge signals are introduced through coupling. The coupled system captured tidal influences, storm-surge-driven reversals, and river–river interactions that the one-way approach missed. chunks.text: A key conclusion is that discharge was the most workable exchange variable for two-way coupling because water level was not directly comparable across models. Since SCHISM lacks direct discharge output, the study developed an approach to compute discharge by integrating SCHISM velocities over predefined cross-sections. This methodological choice is presented as essential for operationalizing feedback despite model variable incompatibilities.

chunks.text: The authors conclude that while the approach advances coastal–riverine prediction, challenges remain, especially variable dissimilarity and routing limitations for backflows. chunks.text: Stormwater management ponds (SMPs), including wet retention and dry detention ponds, are key infrastructure for reducing flooding from heavy rainfall and runoff in coastal communities. These benefits motivate assessing SMP vulnerability under additional coastal hazards such as tropical-cyclone-driven seawater flooding.

The paper cites IPCC projections of global mean SLR of 0.43 m (RCP2.6), 0.55 m (RCP4.5), and up to 0.84 m (RCP8.5), each with stated likely ranges. These rising baseline water levels can increase the frequency and extent of coastal inundation impacts on built systems.

The paper notes evidence of rising TC destructiveness and increases in category 4–5 hurricanes across basins. It also cites projections that hurricane storm-surge flood elevations in the Gulf of Mexico could rise by 0.5 m by the 2030s and 1.8 m by the 2080s, underscoring future surge risk.

chunks.text: The study aims to quantify the risk that South Carolina stormwater management ponds lose function when submerged by tropical-cyclone storm surge and seawater inundation. It further targets identifying how sea level rise and future extremes can exacerbate SMP vulnerability across multiple return periods. The work includes locating coastal hotspots where redesign or additional SMPs may be needed.
supporting_quote: This study will quantify the risk of SMPs' loss of function after being submerged under storm surge and seawater inundation during tropical cyclones

chunks.text: A central objective is to develop and apply a modeling-and-analysis framework combining hydrodynamic storm-surge simulation with inundation mapping to assess SMP exposure. The framework is intended to be computationally efficient and transferable to other regions for evaluating sea level rise and related climate-change impacts on SMP facilities.
supporting_quote: A framework is developed to assess the impact of TC-induced storm surges and inundation on stormwater management ponds

chunks.text: SMPs can fail when inflows exceed their design capacity, and they may also fail during coastal compound flooding if seawater inundation submerges the pond system. During tropical cyclones, storm surge can overtop or inundate coastal land, compromising SMP ability to retain runoff. Climate change intensifies this challenge through higher sea levels and potentially stronger storm surges.
supporting_quote: Retention ponds fail to function when the rainfall exceeds the pond's capacity

chunks.text: Assessing storm-surge hazard is complicated by uncertain tidal phase when storm surge arrives. A given return-period surge can coincide with high tide or low tide, changing the total water level substantially. Because the tidal phase is uncertain, the study treats tides separately and later assumes a worst-case coincidence with high tide for inundation risk assessment.
supporting_quote: Astronomical tide is another important factor affecting the actual storm surge height
Due to the uncertain possibilities of the tidal phase coinciding with storm surge height... the astronomical tide-caused water level changes are not included

chunks.text: Historical tropical-cyclone storm surges along the South Carolina coast were simulated for storms spanning 1851–2018 to obtain maximum surge heights. Return periods for modeled surge heights were estimated using the classical Hazen method, ranking events over the 132-year record. A quadratic function in ln(t) was fit to relate surge height h(t) to return period t.
supporting_quote: From 1851 to 2018, 243 TCs in 132 years made landfall or caused storm surges on the South Carolina coast
The storm-surge-height return periods were calculated based on the classical Hazen method

chunks.text: Inundation extent was computed using a surge decay coefficient (SDC) approach that represents inland decay of storm surge. SDC is defined as (Hs - Hi)/(Wi - Wc), with Wc assumed to be 0 m so inundation begins at the coastline. Idealized 2D simulations at several surge heights were used to identify inundation width Wi and end inundation elevation Hi, which then parameterize GIS-based inundation mapping.
supporting_quote: The surge decay coefficient (SDC) is defined as follows: SDC = (Hs - Hi)/(Wi - Wc)
We assume that the inundation begins at the coastline so that Wc = 0 m
run an idealized 2D hydrodynamic model simulation by setting sea level to the storm surge heights... to determine the widths of the inundated area Wi and the end inundation elevation Hi

chunks.text: The study used Delft3D-FLOW to support inundation-parameter estimation and to produce flooding extent maps, driven by hurricane winds generated using the Holland model. Model configuration included variable grid resolution and a small time step intended to satisfy stability (CFL) constraints. These outputs supported deriving SDC values and validating inundation patterns for subsequent GIS calculations.

chunks.text: Inundation mapping and SMP exposure counting were performed in QGIS using DEM and coastline distance. For each inland raster cell, distance from coastline (RD) was computed, then water depth was calculated as WD = (Hs − RD × SDC) − DEM. Cells with WD > 0 were classified as inundated, and SMPs intersecting inundated areas were counted for each scenario.

Determine the water depth (WD)... WD = (Hs − RD × SDC) − DEM
WD > 0 indicates inundation

chunks.text: Scenario experiments combined storm-surge return periods with tide and SLR assumptions to estimate inundation and SMP exposure. The study evaluated six scenarios per return period, including no tide/no SLR and multiple SLR increments up to 2.0 m with tide. The tide treatment used a worst-case assumption by adding an average high tide to storm surge heights in the inundation assessment.

Modeled maximum storm surge heights from these events were used to estimate surge heights for 5-, 10-, 50-, 100-, and 1000-year return periods. The fitted relationship enabled extrapolating rare-event surge heights beyond observed maxima.

chunks.text: Flood inundation maps are important for emergency response and flood risk management, yet maps for real events are often unavailable or uncertain. Inundation mapping generally converts flows from hydrologic models or gages into flood extent/depth using topography. Approaches are commonly grouped into terrain-based methods that simplify physics to reduce computational cost, and dynamic hydraulic/hydrodynamic models that solve flow equations with higher data and computation demands.
supporting_quote: Accurate and timely inundation maps not only provide firsthand information for rescuing and emergency operations during floods but also potentially improve flood risk management
Flood inundation modeling approaches are essentially to convert flows from either hydrologic models or observation gages into inundation extent/depth based on topographic information.
In general, inundation models can be classified as terrain-based and dynamic-based approaches.

chunks.text: NHDPlus-HAND is a terrain-based inundation mapping approach that normalizes topography by computing each cell’s height above its nearest drainage. HAND inundation delineation requires discharge and rating-curve (stage–discharge) information, and its performance depends on accurate DEM and flowline data. The approach is attractive for large-scale mapping because HAND rasters can be precomputed and then paired with modeled discharge.
supporting_quote: Height Above the Nearest Drainage combined with National Hydrograph Dataset Plus (NHDPlus-HAND) is a terrain-based flood inundation model.
The HAND model normalizes topography based on relative heights found along the nearest drainage network
For delineating inundation maps, HAND needs discharge and rating curve information from hydrologic/hydraulic models.

chunks.text: Satellite remote sensing provides spatial observations of flood extent that can support validation of inundation models when field observations are limited. Landsat imagery has a long history of floodplain boundary delineation, and supervised classification can robustly identify water pixels. Cloud cover can cause underestimation, motivating postprocessing steps to fill likely inundated areas under clouds using elevation constraints.
supporting_quote: Lack of reliable observed spatial extents of flood inundation limits the validation and utility of both approaches in flood inundation mapping.
the advent of satellite-based remote sensing technology has become a key tool for flood monitoring
Supervised Classification has been proven as a robust method to classify features of interest (Frazier and Page 2000; Shalaby and Tateishi 2007).

chunks.text: The study aims to validate NHDPlus-HAND inundation simulation using National Water Model (NWM) streamflow information against inundation observed from Landsat 8 imagery for the May 2016 Brazos River flood. It also evaluates terrain-based (HAND) versus dynamic-based (iRIC-FaSTMECH) performance in accuracy, runtime, and real-time feasibility. A third aim is to test a modified HAND method to improve mapping and provide suggestions for future improvements toward large-scale inundation forecasting.
supporting_quote: This study is conducted to achieve the following objectives:
To validate the NHDPlus-HAND's simulation using streamflow information from the NWM along with the observation derived from the satellite imagery.
To evaluate the terrain-based (NHDPlus-HAND) and dynamic-based (iRIC-FaSTMECH) models with respect to modeling accuracy, modeling efficiency (running time), and feasibility in real-time mode.

chunks.text: A specific goal is to explore efficient ways to improve HAND by addressing catchment-network behavior during extreme floods. The authors test a modified HAND approach that redefines channel networks by stream order to reduce errors when inter-catchment flow interactions are important. This improvement is examined alongside iRIC and satellite-derived observations.
supporting_quote: A modified version of the NHDPlus-HAND model, considering networked catchment behaviors, is also tested
Better performance of NHDPlus-HAND can be achieved by considering the inter-catchment flows during extreme riverine flood events.
the modified HAND method is used to improve the HAND simulation in this study and compare with other inundation mapping results.

chunks.text: Existing FEMA flood risk maps primarily depict design events (e.g., 100-year flows) and do not necessarily provide inundation extents for real flood events. For real-time flood decision-making, agencies need event-specific inundation maps, but such maps can be limited by uncertainties in data sources or modeling frameworks. This motivates evaluation of methods that can be run efficiently and validated against observations.
supporting_quote: Although FEMA has produced ~100,000 flood risk maps based on 100-year return period flows (NFIP 2002), inundation maps for real events are unavailable or limited by uncertainties in data sources or modeling

chunks.text: The standard NHDPlus-HAND implementation treats each NHDPlus catchment independently using a uniform water depth or stage, which can overlook inter-catchment flow transfer. This limitation can lead to disconnected water surfaces and missed inundated areas, particularly where tributaries interact with the main stem during large riverine floods. The paper targets this deficiency through the modified HAND approach.
supporting_quote: with the assumption of applying uniform water depth for each catchment, NHDPlus-HAND cannot consider inter-catchment flow mechanisms, i.e., the flow transfer between adjacent catchments.
The disconnected water surface shown in Figure 7b indicates that the catchment-based calculation by HAND overlooks the inter-catchment flow.

chunks.text: Validation of inundation models is constrained by limited reliable observations of flood extent. Satellite imagery helps, but clouds can obscure flooded pixels and cause underrepresentation of inundation area. This creates a need for careful image processing and gap-filling strategies when using remote sensing as the observational benchmark.
supporting_quote: Lack of reliable observed spatial extents of flood inundation limits the validation and utility of both approaches

the presence of clouds is a common problem in remote sensing imagery, which hinders the identification of flooded water pixels beneath the clouds, leading to underrepresentation of flood water extents

chunks.text: The HAND workflow uses NWM hourly discharge for each NHDPlus flowline (ComID) and converts discharge to stage height using rating curves derived from channel properties via Manning’s equation. The resulting stage is applied to the HAND raster within each catchment to classify cells as wet if HAND values are below the computed stage. The procedure is automated with Python and ArcGIS tools, and results are later aligned to the observation grid for comparison.
supporting_quote: the NWM output provides hourly discharge information for each NHDPlus flowline (identified by a unique ID number – ComID).

These NWM flow information are then converted into stage height using rating curves (stage-discharge relationship). The rating curve for each reach is generated from channel properties in the HAND model based on Manning's equation.
HAND cells with lower elevation than the interpreted stage height information can be classified as "wet" cells.

chunks.text: A modified HAND approach is tested to address HAND’s inability to represent inter-catchment flow. Following prior work, the method uses stream order information to redefine the drainage network by deleting low-order streams, effectively allowing water depth in problematic low-order catchments to be replaced by adjacent higher-order catchments. The modification is applied strategically where original HAND overlooks catchment interaction.
supporting_quote: McGehee et al. (2016) developed the modified HAND method by taking stream orders into account when determining the nearest drainage.
the modified HAND method provides an approach to redefine channel network, i.e., deleting streams with low stream orders.
the modified HAND can essentially replace the water depth of the low-stream-order catchment ... with that of the adjacent catchment with high stream order

chunks.text: The dynamic-based model iRIC-FaSTMECH is configured using a 10 m DEM and set with boundary/initial conditions based on USGS gage data. The downstream boundary uses peak discharge and peak stage, while iterations converge to an upstream discharge. Manning’s n is assigned by land cover, drag coefficient is updated as a function of Manning’s and water depth, and rewetting is enabled to improve shallow-area inundation estimation.
supporting_quote: The terrain used to develop iRIC-FaSTMECH model is 10 m resolution DEM obtained from USGS database
assign a water surface elevation as the initial upstream condition and the peak discharge (4,445.7 m3/s) with stage information (49.7 m) from USGS gage (8111500) as the downstream boundary condition
Three Manning's coefficients (0.03, 0.05, and 0.035) are assigned to corresponding land cover types

chunks.text: Satellite-based flood mapping is produced from Landsat 8 imagery using supervised classification with a maximum likelihood classifier. Preflood and postflood images are preprocessed in ERDAS Imagine, then classified into water/nonwater. To mitigate cloud impacts, DEM-based elevation screening identifies likely wet pixels beneath clouds, and spatial filling plus a 3×3 high-pass kernel are used to sharpen boundaries and postprocess the classification.
supporting_quote: The preflood (March 25, 2016) and postflood (May 28, 2016) images are classified via Erdas Imagine 2015
Supervised Classification of flooded pixels based on the maximum likelihood classifier.
Each pixel with a lower height than that of the lowest height of an apparent flooded pixel in the neighborhood of the cloud is considered as "wet."

chunks.text: Model–observation agreement is quantified using the advanced fitness index (AFI), which accounts for both inundated and noninundated matches. Because model outputs and satellite classification differ in resolution and can be patchy, simulated inundation is resampled to 30×30 m and aligned to the observation grid. Pixel counts of agreement are computed with ArcGIS raster calculator operations.
supporting_quote: the advanced fitness index (AFI) method is applied in this study.
Advanced Fitness(%) = ... / Atotal × 100
the simulated inundation is further resampled to 30 × 30 m grids and aligned to be consistent with the observed inundation.

chunks.text: The study focuses on a 27 km Brazos River section upstream of the USGS gage near Hempstead (ID: 8111500), selected because a relatively cloud-free Landsat 8 image captured the May 2016 flood inundation. The gage recorded 255.8 mm rainfall in 25 hours and a peak stage of 16.78 m at 3 p.m. on May 27, 2016 (CDT). Landsat imagery was taken at 12 p.m. on May 28, 21 hours after peak, but the stage had decreased only 2.5%, so the image is assumed to represent peak inundation.
supporting_quote: The study area ... spanning 27 km of main stem distance upstream of the USGS gage near Hempstead (ID: 8111500).
recorded a total rainfall of 255.8 mm within 25 h, as well as the peak stage of 16.78 m ... at 3 p.m. on May 27, 2016
the stage elevation decreased from the peak stage elevation only by 2.5% ... the flood extent captured by satellite imagery is assumed to represent the peak inundation

chunks.text: Hydrologic forcing for HAND comes from preoperational National Water Model (NWM) discharge outputs, which provide hourly discharge for NHDPlus reaches and include nudging-based assimilation of streamflow at about 7,000 gage stations. The approach leverages the shared NHDPlus reach framework between NWM routing and HAND catchments, enabling automated conversion from discharge to stage and then to inundation extent.
supporting_quote: the NWM output provides hourly discharge information for each NHDPlus flowline
This study uses a set of the preoperational NWM discharge data that ingests the streamflow data assimilation capability at ~7,000 gage stations
the discharge from the NWM undergoes nudging-based data assimilation wherever/whenever gage-observed values become available

chunks.text: Topographic data for both HAND and iRIC modeling is based on a 10 m resolution DEM from the USGS EarthExplorer database. Using the same-resolution DEM supports a fair comparison of terrain-based and dynamic-based approaches. NHDPlus flowlines and catchments underpin the HAND framework for drainage network representation and reach identification.
supporting_quote: The terrain used to develop iRIC-FaSTMECH model is 10 m resolution DEM obtained from USGS database
the NHDPlus-HAND is developed using DEM of the same resolution (10 m).
The NHDPlus Version 2 dataset provides a reliable stream network consisting of ~2.7 million reaches

chunks.text: Remote sensing observations are derived from Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager multispectral imagery obtained via USGS EarthExplorer. The analysis uses a preflood image from March 25, 2016 and a postflood image from May 28, 2016. These images are preprocessed and then classified to produce a binary inundation map for AFI comparison.
supporting_quote: The remote sensing imagery used in this study is obtained from the Landsat 8-Operational Land Imager multispectral database
The preflood (March 25, 2016) and postflood (May 28, 2016) images are classified

chunks.text: The iRIC model configuration includes boundary and iteration settings tied to the flood peak. Downstream boundary conditions use peak discharge 4,445.7 m³/s and peak stage 49.7 m, while model iterations converge to an upstream discharge of 4,300 m³/s. The simulation uses 1,500 iterations, variable drag coefficient, constant upstream stage, and rewetting enabled.
supporting_quote: Downstream peak discharge: 4,445.7 m³/s Downstream peak stage: 49.7 m
Iteration 1,500
Upstream discharge 4,300 m³/s

chunks.text: Compared to Landsat-derived observed inundation, the HAND simulation achieved 56% AFI overlap, while iRIC achieved 70% and modified HAND achieved 67%. Visual comparison indicates iRIC and modified HAND overlap more with the observed inundation than original HAND. The modified HAND improved AFI by 11 percentage points relative to HAND, indicating benefits from accounting for networked catchment behavior.
supporting_quote: the HAND model has a 56% match with the observation, while iRIC and the modified HAND have higher AFI values of 70% and 67%, respectively.
the modified HAND method is found to improve the AFI value by 11% with capturing a few missed areas.

chunks.text: The satellite-derived inundation area was the smallest among the four maps, while model-based estimates were larger, particularly for modified HAND. Reported areas were 41.3 km² for satellite observation, 41.7 km² for HAND, 55.9 km² for iRIC, and 70.8 km² for modified HAND. The observation map showed discontinuities or gaps, yet it was treated as the best available representation of the true flood extent.
supporting_quote: the inundation classified from satellite imagery has the least area of only 41.3 km2
55.9 km2 for iRIC, 41.7 km2 for HAND, and 70.8 km2 for modified HAND
the authors consider the inundation from satellite imagery as the "true" flooded area during the study.

chunks.text: Detailed inspection showed that original HAND missed inundation where catchment interactions mattered, producing a disconnected water surface across adjacent catchments. In the example, a low stream-order tributary catchment (Catchment 2) differed from the main-stem catchment (Catchment 1). Modified HAND improved realism by effectively using the adjacent higher-order catchment water depth to correct the low-order catchment, addressing missed inundation areas.
supporting_quote: The disconnected water surface shown in Figure 7b indicates that the catchment-based calculation by HAND overlooks the inter-catchment flow.
Catchment 1 is located along the Brazos River main stem with a higher stream order than that of Catchment 2
the modified HAND can essentially replace the water depth of the low-stream-order catchment (Catchment 2 herein) with that of the adjacent catchment with high stream order (Catchment 1)

chunks.text: When problematic catchments were excluded from the comparison, HAND and iRIC produced similar agreement with observations. The AFI values under this exclusion were 65% for HAND and 68% for iRIC, suggesting that HAND’s main deficiency in this event was inter-catchment representation rather than the simplified flow physics. This supports the idea that terrain-based simplifications can still capture peak inundation reasonably well.
supporting_quote: If the problematic catchments in HAND simulation are excluded from the comparison, the HAND and iRIC models would generate comparable AFI values (65% and 68%, respectively).
Such results indicate that aside from HAND's deficiency to model inter-catchment inundation, it has equivalent capability as iRIC in terms of matching the observation.

chunks.text: Runtime differed substantially between approaches. iRIC required about 90 minutes (5,400 s) to run 1,500 iterations, while HAND required about two minutes (120 s) to generate inundation for 37 NHDPlus reaches. This large efficiency advantage highlights why HAND is attractive for coupling with the National Water Model for large-scale, near-real-time inundation mapping.
supporting_quote: the iRIC model needs ~90 min (5,400 s) to run 1,500 iterations, while the HAND model only takes about two minutes (120 s) for 37 NHDPlus river reaches to generate the inundation.

chunks.text: Although iRIC produced the highest AFI in this case, the paper emphasizes that dynamic 2D models often require intensive calibration and historical data to be reliable. This requirement can limit their use where such data are unavailable, especially for rapid deployment during events. HAND, by contrast, can be applied to river sections with limited historical calibration data, trading some physical detail for speed and scalability.
supporting_quote: the dynamic-based model represented by iRIC in this study provides more accurate estimates under high flow conditions, the model needs intensive calibrations using various historical data to achieve a reliable performance
the terrain-based model, as represented by HAND in this study, demonstrates a unique inundation mapping capability for a river section without much historical data.

chunks.text: HAND does not explicitly model interactions between the main stem and tributaries, and this issue is expected to be more pronounced in larger riverine floods. The authors suggest incorporating mass balance into the framework as a potential remedy in addition to the modified HAND approach. Without such mechanisms, catchment-based stage assignment can create unrealistic discontinuities in water surface between adjacent catchments.
supporting_quote: the HAND calculation does not explicitly reflect interactions between the main stem and its tributaries. This issue likely becomes more pronounced for larger riverine floods.
one remedy to this problem is to incorporate a mass balance process into the modeling framework as suggested by Bates and De Roo (2000).

chunks.text: The authors caution that HAND may be inferior to traditional hydraulic models in urban settings with complex infrastructure. Features such as culverts, pipes, and bridges can strongly affect flood hydraulics but are not explicitly represented in the HAND approach. Therefore, selecting an inundation model requires considering land cover complexity, accuracy needs, and data/computation constraints.
supporting_quote: the authors think that while not observed in this study, the accuracy of the HAND model would be inferior to a traditional hydraulic model if the flooded area has complex urban hydraulic components like culverts, pipes, and bridges.
extra caution should be taken when choosing proper inundation models for flood risk prediction due to the uncertainties in data requirement, computation demand, accuracy, types of land cover

chunks.text: Remote sensing inundation mapping can underrepresent flooding due to clouds, and the observed flood map can appear patchy with gaps. The study applies DEM-based filling under clouds and postprocessing to mitigate these issues, but the discontinuities still affect area estimates. This introduces uncertainty in treating the satellite classification as the true inundation extent for validation.
supporting_quote: the presence of clouds is a common problem in remote sensing imagery ... leading to underrepresentation of flood water extents
the inundated area appears to have some discontinuous features or gaps, leading to the reduced inundation area

chunks.text: All three modeled approaches achieved a fair fit with satellite observations, with iRIC performing best in this extreme event. The reported AFI values were about 70% for iRIC, 67% for modified HAND, and 56% for NHDPlus-HAND. The results support the feasibility of using HAND for large-scale inundation mapping, especially when enhancements address inter-catchment flow behavior.
supporting_quote: NHDPlus-HAND, the modified HAND, and iRIC generated a fair (>50% of AFI) fit with the satellite imagery.
iRIC performed slightly better (~70% in AFI) than the other two methods (NHDPlus-HAND and the modified HAND)
the HAND model has a 56% match with the observation, while iRIC and the modified HAND have higher AFI values of 70% and 67%, respectively.

chunks.text: The modified HAND method can remedy a key weakness of catchment-based HAND by addressing main-stem/tributary interactions when applied strategically. The paper concludes that simplifying flow dynamics has relatively minor influence on peak inundation prediction for extreme events, which supports using terrain-based models when computational efficiency is critical. This provides justification for HAND’s use in large-scale operational contexts.
supporting_quote: the modified HAND method provides a remedy to this issue when strategically applied to the areas overlooked by NHDPlus-HAND.
For extreme events, simplification of the intricacy of flow dynamics has relatively minor influence on predictions
This finding confirms that using a simple terrain-based model could adequately simulate the flood inundation area

chunks.text: Despite not being a superior option for complex urban inundation, NHDPlus-HAND is highlighted as promising for real-time, continental-scale forecasting because of low computational cost and ease of coupling with the National Water Model. The study suggests future work on observation uncertainty using additional imagery sources and classification techniques. Overall, the findings point to practical improvements and evaluation pathways for operational inundation mapping.
supporting_quote: its low computational cost and ease to couple with the NWM provide great potential to support realtime continental inundation forecast in the future.
there is room for future investigation in uncertainty analysis of observations using multiple sources of raw imagery along with various classification techniques.

chunks.text: Cross-View Geo-Localization (CVGL) estimates the location of a ground image by retrieving the most similar geo-tagged aerial image from a database. CVGL is commonly treated as an image retrieval and metric learning problem, where matched aerial-ground pairs are pulled together in embedding space and mismatched pairs pushed apart. The task is challenging because aerial and ground views differ drastically in viewpoint, time, and resolution, requiring understanding of image content and spatial configuration.
supporting_quote: Cross-View Geo-Localization (CVGL) estimates the location of a ground image by matching it to a geo-tagged aerial image in a database.
CVGL is considered an extremely challenging problem because of: (i) the drastic difference in the viewing angles ... (ii) the variance in capturing time ... (iii) very different resolutions

chunks.text: Prior CVGL methods largely rely on CNN features and aggregation modules, but struggle to explicitly capture global spatial configuration. Transformers have been introduced to model global contextual information, yet their attention tends to entangle spatial configuration with low-level appearance cues. This motivates a design that models geometric layout separately to avoid overfitting to low-level details and to better generalize.
supporting_quote: Such methods are limited in exploring the spatial configuration which is a global property ... due to the capacity of fully connected layers
Nevertheless, in these methods, the spatial configuration is unavoidably entangled with low-level features because the multi-head attention mechanism implicitly models those correlations.

chunks.text: Hard sample mining and data augmentation are used in CVGL, but each has limitations. In-batch mining lacks diversity within a batch, while global mining needs extra memory and compute to maintain a pool. Standard augmentations can disrupt fragile cross-view correspondence; this paper builds on augmentations that preserve correspondence while diversifying layout and appearance.
supporting_quote: in-batch mining methods are limited by the lack of sample diversity within a training batch, while global mining strategies require additional memory and computational resources
data augmentation ... is not fully explored due to the fragility of the spatial correspondence between aerial and ground images which can be easily disrupted

chunks.text: The paper targets improved generalization in CVGL when training and testing come from distinct geographic areas (cross-area evaluation). It asks how to generalize cross-view geo-localization algorithms with minimal supervision and aims to reduce reliance on low-level details by emphasizing geometric layout correspondence between views. The goal is to achieve strong cross-area performance without sacrificing same-area accuracy.
supporting_quote: This paper seeks to answer the question - how to generalize cross-view geo-localization algorithms with minimal supervision?
existing methods still suffer from poor performance in cross-area evaluation, in which the training and testing data are captured from completely distinct areas.

chunks.text: A specific objective is to enhance the earlier GeoDTR framework by improving geometric layout extraction and better leveraging layout simulation and semantic augmentation techniques. The work proposes to explicitly incorporate intra-batch contrastive signals through generated hard samples to strengthen training. The intended outcome is a substantial margin improvement in cross-area benchmarks on CVUSA, CVACT, and VIGOR.
supporting_quote: First, we improve the design of the geometric layout extractor module to better capture the spatial configurations
we extend LS techniques to explicitly include intra-batch contrastive signals in the current work ... We named this process the "Contrastive Hard Samples Generation" (CHSG) procedure.

chunks.text: A key problem is the large gap between same-area and cross-area performance in existing CVGL systems. Many methods achieve around 90% R@1 on same-area CVUSA yet only 30% to 40% R@1 on cross-area; on CVACT cross-area they can be 20% to 30% R@1 despite over 80% same-area. This indicates poor generalization when applied to unseen geographic regions.
supporting_quote: on CVUSA ... achieve around 90% R@1 accuracy on same-area evaluation but only achieve 30% to 40% R@1 accuracy on cross-area performance.
on CVACT ... can only achieve 20% to 30% R@1 accuracy on cross-area performance while achieving more than 80% R@1 accuracy on same-area performance.

chunks.text: The authors attribute cross-area degradation to models overfitting to low-level appearance and lacking explicit capability to extract geometric layout of visual features. Prior transformer and CNN-based modules capture correlations implicitly, entangling layout with low-level cues. The previous GLE design also risks information loss by compressing features into a saliency map before learning correlations.
supporting_quote: We attribute this deficiency to the lack of ability to extract the geometric layout of visual features and models' overfitting to low-level details.
such a mechanism suffers from information loss during the saliency map generation, leading to sub-optimal performance.

chunks.text: Training the geometric layout pathway is difficult because there is no direct ground truth supervision for geometric layout descriptors. As a result, the Geometric Layout Extractor would receive only indirect and insufficient signals if trained solely from retrieval losses. The paper introduces auxiliary supervision to avoid degenerate solutions.
supporting_quote: Due to the absence of ground truth geometric layout descriptors, the sub-module GLE would only receive indirect and insufficient supervision during training.
the counterfactual loss provides a weakly supervision signal to the layout descriptors

chunks.text: GeoDTR+ is a siamese CVGL network with separate branches for ground and aerial images. Within each branch, it uses two pathways: a backbone feature pathway producing raw latent features and a geometric layout pathway producing geometric layout descriptors (GLDs). The GLDs modulate the raw backbone features to form the final embedding used for L2 retrieval.
supporting_quote: GeoDTR+ ... is a siamese neural network including two branches for the ground and the aerial views
there are two distinct processing pathways, i.e., the backbone feature pathway and the geometric layout pathway.

chunks.text: The representation is decomposed into raw features and geometric layout descriptors via a modulation operation. The final embedding is computed by Frobenius inner products between each layout descriptor and each channel of raw features, yielding a CK-dimensional vector. This explicitly injects geometric layout into the latent representation used for matching.
supporting_quote: we propose the following decomposition of the latent representation f^v = q^v  r^v.
where p_m^v, r_j^v denotes the Frobenius inner product ... resulting f^v  R^{CK}

chunks.text: The enhanced Geometric Layout Extractor (GLE) avoids the earlier saliency-map bottleneck by operating on full C-dimensional patch features. It patchifies the raw feature into HW patches, applies positional encoding and a transformer to model relations among patches, reshapes back, reduces channels to K via point-wise convolution, and refines with a bottleneck using Sigmoid to output GLDs in [0,1]. This design aims to capture richer correlations and reduce information loss.
supporting_quote: Given a raw feature r  R^{H  W  C}, we first "patchify" r into HW of C-dimensional patches
we adopt a standard transformer module to learn the relations among these vectors
we choose the Sigmoid function ... maps q'  [-, ] into q  [0, 1]

chunks.text: Layout Simulation and Semantic Augmentation (LS) create augmented aerial-ground pairs while maintaining cross-view geometric correspondence. Layout simulation applies synchronized flips and rotations (90°, 180°, 270°) to both views to change layout while preserving low-level detail. Semantic augmentation modifies low-level features separately via color jitter and other photometric transforms (blur, grayscale, posterize).
supporting_quote: Layout Simulation: It is a combination of a random flip and a random rotation (90°, 180°, or 270°) that synchronously applies to ... aerial and ground images.
Semantic Augmentation: randomly modifies the low-level features ... A color jitter is employed ... random Gaussian blur, transform images to grayscale or posterized

chunks.text: Contrastive Hard Samples Generation (CHSG) builds batches that include multiple LS-augmented variants from the same original pair to create intra-batch hard negatives. For each original pair, CHSG samples two variants (e.g., Pb3 and Pb4) from the same subset S62 and constructs a batch containing both sets of variants. This emphasizes contrast among samples that share visual content but differ in layout/appearance, improving training efficiency without global mining pools.
supporting_quote: we propose Contrastive Hard Samples Generation (CHSG)
CHSG constructs a training batch as {P_{b3}^{(1)}, b2, P_{b4}^{(bs)}, P_{b4}^{(1)}, b2, P_{b4}^{(bs)}} ... the intra-batch contrast among hard samples is emphasized.

chunks.text: A counterfactual (CF) learning schema provides auxiliary supervision to geometric layout descriptors by replacing true descriptors with random imaginary ones and pushing the resulting representations apart. Imaginary layout descriptors are drawn from U[0,1], producing an imaginary feature c6f5b. The counterfactual loss maximizes the distance between f5b and c6f5b to discourage wrong solutions and improve descriptor quality.
supporting_quote: apply an intervention do(q^v=c6q^v) ... imaginary layout descriptors c6q^v ... drawn from the uniform distribution U[0,1].
we maximize the distance between f^v and c6f^v by minimizing our proposed counterfactual loss

chunks.text: Training uses a weighted soft margin triplet loss on matched versus unmatched pairs, combined with counterfactual losses for both aerial and ground branches. The triplet loss encourages d(f62g,f62a) to be smaller than d(f62g,f63a) for m62n. The final objective sums L_triplet + L_cf^a + L_cf^g.
supporting_quote: we also adopt the weighted soft margin triplet loss ... L_{triplet} = log(1 + e^{b1[d(f_m^g, f_m^a) - d(f_m^g, f_n^a)]})
Our final loss is L = L_{triplet} + L_{cf}^a + L_{cf}^g.

chunks.text: Experiments evaluate GeoDTR+ on CVUSA, CVACT, and VIGOR datasets. CVUSA and CVACT each contain 35,532 training pairs, with CVUSA having 8,884 test pairs and CVACT having 8,884 validation pairs plus a 92,802-pair test set. VIGOR includes 90,618 ground panoramas and 105,124 aerial images across four US cities and defines same-area and cross-area protocols.
supporting_quote: we conduct extensive experiments on three datasets, CVUSA [2], CVACT [3], and VIGOR [4]. Both CVUSA and CVACT contain 35,532 training pairs.
CVACT provides a challenging and large-scale testing set ... contains 92,802 pairs.
VIGOR ... collects 90,618 ground panorama images and 105,124 ... from 4 major cities

chunks.text: For evaluation, the paper uses recall at top-K (R@K) metrics, including R@1, R@5, R@10, and R@1%. R@K measures the probability that the ground-truth aerial match appears within the top K retrieved results for a ground query. This aligns with common CVGL benchmarking practice.
supporting_quote: we choose to use recall accuracy at top K (R@K) for evaluation purposes.
we evaluate the performance of all methods on R@1, R@5, R@10, and R@1%.

chunks.text: The authors identify duplicated pairs in CVUSA and adjust training data for fair comparisons. They report finding 762 repeated pairs in the training set and 43 in the testing set using an md5 hash on pixel values. They remove duplicates from training but keep duplicates in testing to match baselines.
supporting_quote: we identify 762 and 43 repeated pairs in the original training set and testing set of the CVUSA [2] dataset, respectively.
we remove the repeated pairs in the training set but keep those in the testing set.

chunks.text: Implementation uses ConvNeXt-T as backbone and a lightweight transformer in GLE. Training runs 200 epochs with AdamW at learning rate 10^-4, batch size 32, and images resized to 12271 (ground) and 256256 (aerial).
