The GLE uses 2 transformer encoder layers with 4 heads, K=8 descriptors, yielding a 3072-d embedding (8 x 384).
supporting_quote: The model is trained ... for 200 epochs with AdamW [41] optimizer and a learning rate of 10^{-4}.
The number of transformer encoder layers in the proposed GLE is set to 2 and each with 4 heads. The number of descriptors K ... is 8.
the latent feature f^v is a 8 x 384 = 3072 dimensional vector

chunks.text: GeoDTR+ achieves state-of-the-art cross-area performance on CVUSA and CVACT in both polar-transformed and non-polar settings. For CVUSAbcCVACT, it reaches 61.17% R@1 with PT and 60.16% without PT. For CVACTbcCVUSA, it reaches 53.89% R@1 with PT and 52.56% without PT, improving substantially over prior best numbers reported in the same table.
supporting_quote: GeoDTR+ (ours) ... CVUSA c2 CVACT ... R@1 61.17%
GeoDTR+ (ours) ... w/o PT ... CVUSA c2 CVACT ... R@1 60.16%
GeoDTR+ (ours) ... CVACT c2 CVUSA ... R@1 53.89%
GeoDTR+ (ours) ... w/o PT ... CVACT c2 CVUSA ... R@1 52.56%

chunks.text: On same-area benchmarks, GeoDTR+ is competitive and achieves strong results, including improvements on CVACT. With polar transformation, it reports 87.61% R@1 on CVACT_val and 67.57% R@1 on CVACT_test. Without polar transformation, it reports 87.76% R@1 on CVACT_val and 67.75% R@1 on CVACT_test, outperforming several baselines that use polar transformation.
supporting_quote: GeoDTR+ (ours) ... CVACT_val ... R@1 87.61% ... CVACT_test ... R@1 67.57%
GeoDTR+ (ours) ... w/o PT ... CVACT_val ... R@1 87.76% ... CVACT_test ... R@1 67.75%
our GeoDTR+ without polar transformation ... outperforms other models trained with polar transformation

chunks.text: On the challenging VIGOR dataset, GeoDTR+ achieves state-of-the-art performance under the reported comparison. The paper states it improves R@1 from the previous SOTA 22.35% to 36.01%, which is a 13.66% absolute gain. This is notable because VIGOR uses many-to-one correspondence between ground and aerial images, closer to real-world settings.
supporting_quote: GeoDTR+ achieves the SOTA performance by improving from the previous SOTA 22.35% to 36.01% which is a 13.66%
each ground query image in VIGOR [4] has two or more corresponding aerial images.

chunks.text: Ablations show CHSG significantly boosts cross-area accuracy while minimally affecting same-area performance. For CVACT with ConvNeXt-T and GLE v2, cross-area R@1 rises from 42.11% without CHSG to 53.89% with CHSG. For CVUSA with ConvNeXt-T and GLE v2, cross-area R@1 rises from 53.65% to 61.17% when CHSG is enabled.
supporting_quote: CVACT ... d7 ... v2 ... ConvNeXt-T ... Cross-area R@1 42.11%
CVACT ... c7 ... v2 ... ConvNeXt-T ... Cross-area R@1 53.89%
CVUSA ... d7 ... v2 ... ConvNeXt-T ... Cross-area R@1 53.65%
CVUSA ... c7 ... v2 ... ConvNeXt-T ... Cross-area R@1 61.17%

chunks.text: Varying the number of geometric layout descriptors trades off accuracy and embedding size, but cross-area remains strong even at low dimensions. With K=8, the embedding is 3072-d and achieves cross-area R@1 of 61.17% (CVUSAbcCVACT) and 53.89% (CVACTbcCVUSA). With K=2 (768-d), cross-area R@1 is still 59.21% (CVUSA) and 50.68% (CVACT), indicating robustness.
supporting_quote: CVUSA ... 8 ... Dimension 3072 ... Cross-area R@1 61.17%
CVUSA ... 2 ... Dimension 768 ... Cross-area R@1 59.21%
CVACT ... 8 ... Dimension 3072 ... Cross-area R@1 53.89%
CVACT ... 2 ... Dimension 768 ... Cross-area R@1 50.68%

chunks.text: CHSG outperforms simply increasing batch size when using LS techniques. On CVUSA cross-area, LS with batch size 32 yields 58.62% R@1 and LS with batch size 64 yields 57.18% R@1, while CHSG with batch size 32 yields 61.17% R@1. This suggests the gain is from intra-batch hard contrasts rather than more samples per batch.
supporting_quote: CHSG ... 32 ... Cross-area ... R@1 61.17%

chunks.text: Different CHSG configurations show that combining layout simulation and semantic augmentation as intra-batch contrast gives best cross-area gains. On CVUSA cross-area, Raw achieves 53.65% R@1, L only 58.09%, same S + L 59.46%, and L + S 61.17%. Same-area results remain near the Raw baseline, indicating limited harm to in-domain accuracy.

GeoDTR+ is computationally efficient relative to recent transformer-based CVGL methods. The paper reports it has the least trainable parameters among compared models and similar inference time and FLOPs to TransGeo. It also states GeoDTR+ has 50% and 45% fewer trainable parameters than GeoDTR and TransGeo, respectively, and avoids large pretrained ViT backbones.
supporting_quote: It is clear to see that GeoDTR+ has the least # of trainable parameters
Compared with GeoDTR [1] and TransGeo [7], GeoDTR+ has 50% and 45% less trainable parameters respectively.
GeoDTR+ does not require a large pretrained backbone such as ViT which is pretrained on ImageNet-21K

chunks.text: The paper notes GeoDTR+ may not always be best on same-area benchmarks, even though cross-area improvements are large. It acknowledges a slight drop in same-area evaluation and suggests the difference could arise from model scale and CHSG augmentations such as color distortions and geometric transformations. The authors indicate same-area performance might be further improved with a larger backbone, but that is not the focus.
supporting_quote: Although, GeoDTR+ does not achieve the best result on same-area evaluation.
there is a slight drop in same-area evaluation.
The same-area performance difference might come from both model scale and the augmentation in CHSG such as the color space distortion and geometric transformations.

chunks.text: Ablations suggest that upgrading the GLE/backbone without CHSG can degrade cross-area performance, implying that stronger supervision from hard samples is important for the enhanced layout pathway. The paper observes that cross-area performance degrades in some cases when training with the new GLE but without CHSG. It reports that CHSG mitigates this by adding strong supervision from additional hard aerial-ground pairs.
supporting_quote: It is noticeable that the cross-area performance degrades if training with the new GLE and without CHSG
Once training with CHSG, this degradation can be mitigated due to the strong supervision signal from the additional hard aerial-ground pairs.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that GeoDTR+ improves geometric layout extraction and explicitly disentangles layout correlations from raw backbone features via a novel GLE. It combines LS techniques with CHSG to generate hard pairs within a batch, eliminating the need for global mining pools. Experiments show state-of-the-art cross-area performance on CVUSA, CVACT, and VIGOR while keeping same-area performance comparable.
supporting_quote: we propose GeoDTR+ to explicitly disentangles the geometric layout correlations from the raw features ... via a novel Geometric Layout Extractor (GLE).
we take advantage of LS techniques and form a Contrastive Hard Sample Generation (CHSG) sampling strategy.
GeoDTR+ achieves SOTA performance on all cross-area benchmarks including, CVUSA [2], CVACT [3], and VIGOR [4]

chunks.text: GeoDTR+ forms latent representations by Frobenius products between raw features and learned layout descriptors, enabling strong performance even without polar transformation. The authors emphasize that CHSG generates hard pairs by varying geometric layout and low-level details, improving cross-area CVGL without extra mining memory. They suggest future work evaluating generalization across different environments such as low-light or seasons and applying CHSG to other retrieval tasks.
supporting_quote: The latent representation is a Frobenius product between the raw features and geometric layout extractors ... even without post-processing such as polar transformation.
CHSG aims to generate hard aerial-ground image pairs by varying the geometric layout and low-level details. Thus, there is no need to mine hard samples from a global pool
it is worth investigating the performance of GeoDTR+ under different environments, for example, low-light scenarios or different seasons.

chunks.text: Cross-view geo-localization estimates the location of a ground (query) image by retrieving the best-matching geo-tagged aerial (reference) image. It is commonly framed as an image retrieval problem where matched aerial-ground pairs are pulled closer in embedding space and mismatched pairs pushed apart. The task is difficult due to large viewpoint changes and other capture differences between the two views.
supporting_quote: Cross-view geo-localization aims to estimate the location of a query ground image by matching it to a reference geo-tagged aerial images database.

Cross-view geo-localization is considered an extremely challenging problem because of 1) the drastic change of viewpoints, 2) the difference in capturing time, 3) and the different resolutions between ground and aerial images

chunks.text: Many prior approaches use CNN-based features and local aggregation, which can miss global spatial configuration needed to align objects like roads and buildings across views. Transformer-based methods can model global context, but often do so implicitly through attention, entangling correlations with appearance features. This motivates explicitly handling geometry and appearance separately to better generalize.
supporting_quote: Most existing methods ... match ground and aerial images by exploiting features extracted from convolutional neural networks (CNNs).

Recently, with the advancement of Transformer ... explore extracting latent features from global contextual information. However, such methods solely rely on multi-head attention mechanism to implicitly explore correlations in the input features. Consequently, the correlations are unavoidably entangled in those approaches.

chunks.text: Cross-area evaluation, where training and testing come from different regions, remains challenging for existing cross-view geo-localization models. The paper attributes this weakness to poor extraction of spatial configuration and overfitting to low-level details from the training region. Improving robustness on cross-area benchmarks is emphasized as a key need.
supporting_quote: existing methods still suffer from poor performance on the cross-area benchmarks, in which the training and testing data are captured from two different regions.
We attribute this deficiency to the lack of ability to extract the spatial configuration of visual feature layouts and models' overfitting on low-level details from the training set.

chunks.text: The work aims to improve cross-view geo-localization generalization, especially under cross-area settings, by explicitly learning geometric layout correspondence between aerial and ground images. The goal is to disentangle spatial configuration from raw appearance features, then integrate them to form more discriminative representations. The approach also seeks training procedures and augmentations that preserve cross-view geometric correspondence while improving robustness.
supporting_quote: we propose GeoDTR which explicitly disentangles geometric information from raw features and learns the spatial correlations among visual features from aerial and ground pairs
These augmentations help to improve the performance of the cross-view geo-localization models, especially on the cross-area benchmarks.

chunks.text: The paper formulates cross-view geo-localization as retrieving the best-matching aerial reference image for a query ground image. Given ground-aerial pairs tied to distinct geo-locations, the system learns latent representations for each view and predicts the reference index minimizing an L2 distance. This frames learning as producing discriminative embeddings robust to severe view changes.
supporting_quote: Considering a set of ground-aerial image pairs  ${(I_i^g,I_i^a)}$, i=1,\ldots,N,
we seek discriminative latent representations  $f^g$  and  $f^a$
where  $d(\cdot, \cdot)$  denotes the  $L_2$  distance.

chunks.text: A major challenge highlighted is poor cross-area performance: models trained in one region often fail to generalize to another. The authors argue this is caused by models overfitting to low-level appearance details and failing to capture stable spatial configurations that persist across views and regions. Addressing this requires extracting global spatial correlations among visual features.
supporting_quote: existing methods still suffer from poor performance on the cross-area benchmarks, in which the training and testing data are captured from two different regions.
We attribute this deficiency to the lack of ability to extract the spatial configuration of visual feature layouts and models' overfitting on low-level details from the training set.

chunks.text: Data augmentation in cross-view geo-localization is constrained because many augmentations break the geometric correspondence between aerial and ground views. The paper notes that rotating or shifting only one view can sabotage spatial alignment, limiting the ability to regularize training without harming correspondence. The work targets augmentations that vary layout or semantics while maintaining cross-view geometric consistency.
supporting_quote: data augmentation in cross-view geo-localization is very limited due to the vulnerability of the spatial correspondence between aerial and ground images which can be easily sabotaged by a minor interference.
most existing methods ... randomly rotate or shift one view while fxing the other one.

chunks.text: GeoDTR represents an image by combining raw backbone features with learned geometric layout descriptors. It decomposes the final representation as a modulation of raw latent representations by a set of K layout descriptors, producing a CK-dimensional vector used for retrieval with L2 distance. This design aims to treat spatial configuration separately from low-level appearance, then integrate them to improve discriminative matching across views.
supporting_quote:
Specifically, we propose the following decomposition of the latent representation

$$f^v = \mathbf{p}^v \circ \mathbf{r}^v. \tag{2}$$
the resulting  $f^v \in \mathbb{R}^{CK}$  are referred to as the *geometric layout modulated representations*

chunks.text: The architecture is a siamese network with separate branches for ground and aerial images, and within each branch it has two pathways: a CNN backbone pathway and a geometric layout pathway. The backbone produces raw latent representations, while the layout pathway generates geometric descriptors based on those raw features. The descriptors modulate raw features to form the final embedding used for cross-view retrieval.
supporting_quote: GeoDTR ... is a siamese neural network including two branches for the ground and the aerial views, respectively.
Within a branch, there are two distinct processing pathways, i.e., the backbone feature pathway and the geometric layout pathway.

chunks.text: The geometric layout extractor is built on a transformer to capture global contextual information among visual features and produce K geometric layout descriptors. It starts with channel-wise max-pooling to form a saliency map, embeds it into K vectors, adds positional information including an index-aware positional embedding, then applies a transformer to model correlations. A second embedding layer projects the transformer output into the final set of K layout descriptors.
supporting_quote: the geometric layout extractor is built on top of the standard transformer.
the network consists of a max-pooling layer along channels, a transformer module, and two embedding layers that locate before and after the transformer.
After projecting by the second embedding layer, our geometric layout extractor generates a set of K geometric layout descriptors  $\mathbf{p}$ .

chunks.text: GeoDTR introduces an index-aware positional embedding that augments standard learnable positional embeddings with information derived from the raw feature channel index of the maximum response. The method combines embeddings using a HardTanh nonlinearity and a learnable linear mapping of the index map into K distinct subspaces. This is intended to better condition the transformer on spatial saliency structure tied to the backbone features.
supporting_quote:
we introduce an extra index-aware positional embedding adding to E

$$\hat{E} = E + \text{HardTanh}(E_{pe} + W_{LN}M^{idx}), \tag{4}$$
where  $M_{mj}^{idx}=\frac{1}{C} {\rm arg} \max_{c\in 1,...,C} r_{mj}^c$ .

chunks.text: A counterfactual-based learning schema is used to provide auxiliary supervision to the layout descriptors without ground-truth layouts. The method replaces learned descriptors with random imaginary descriptors sampled from U[-1,1] to create an imaginary representation, then encourages the real and imaginary representations to be far apart by minimizing a counterfactual loss. Training uses the sum of triplet retrieval loss and counterfactual losses for both aerial and ground branches.
supporting_quote: we apply an intervention  $do(\mathbf{p}^v = \hat{\mathbf{p}}^v)$  which substitutes  $\mathbf{p}^v$  for a set of imaginary layout descriptors
Elements of  $\hat{\mathbf{p}}^v$  are drawn from the uniform distribution U[-1,1].

Our final loss is

$$L = L_{triplet} + L_{cf}^a + L_{cf}^g. (7)$$

chunks.text: The retrieval objective uses a weighted soft margin triplet loss that pulls matched ground-aerial embeddings closer than mismatched pairs. Distances are computed using L2 distance between the modulated representations. This aligns with common cross-view geo-localization training where embeddings are optimized for retrieval ranking.
supporting_quote: we also adopt the weighted soft margin triplet loss which pushes the matched pairs closer and unmatched pairs further away from each other
$$L_{triplet} = \log\left(1 + e^{\alpha[d(f_m^g, f_m^a) - d(f_m^g, f_n^a)]}\right),\tag{6}$$

chunks.text: Layout simulation is a correspondence-preserving augmentation that synchronously applies a random flip and a random rotation (90°, 180°, or 270°) to both the aerial and ground images in a matched pair. By transforming both views together, it changes the geometric layout while keeping low-level details intact and maintaining cross-view correspondence. The paper presents it as a generic method that can be applied to other geo-localization models.
supporting_quote: Layout Simulation It is a combination of a random flip and a random rotation  $(90^{\circ}, 180^{\circ}, \text{ or } 270^{\circ})$  that *synchronously* applies to ground truth aerial and ground images.
our LS does not break the geometric correspondence among visual features in the two views.

chunks.text: Semantic augmentation changes low-level appearance separately in aerial and ground images to reduce overfitting to textures and colors. The method uses color jitter for brightness, contrast, and saturation, and may apply Gaussian blur, grayscale conversion, or posterization. This encourages reliance on spatial configuration rather than view-specific appearance cues.
supporting_quote: Semantic augmentation randomly modifies the low-level features in aerial and ground images *separately*.

We employ color jitter to modify the brightness, contrast, and saturation in images. Moreover, we also randomly apply Gaussian blur and randomly transform images to grayscale images or posterized images.

chunks.text: Experiments use two standard cross-view geo-localization datasets: CVUSA and CVACT. Both datasets contain 35,532 training pairs; CVUSA has 8,884 test pairs and CVACT has 8,884 validation pairs (CVACT_val). CVACT additionally provides a large-scale test set (CVUSA_test) with 92,802 pairs as described in the paper.
supporting_quote: we conduct extensive experiments on two datasets, CVUSA ... and CVACT ... Both CVUSA and CVACT contain 35, 532 training pairs.
CVUSA provides 8, 884 pairs for testing and CVACT has the same number of pairs in its validation set (CVACT_val).
CVACT provides a challenging and large-scale testing set (CVUSA_test) which contains 92, 802 pairs.

chunks.text: The paper reports removing duplicated training pairs in CVUSA to avoid contamination while keeping the test set unchanged for fair comparison. Specifically, it identifies 762 repeated pairs in the training set and 43 repeated pairs in the testing set; only training duplicates are removed. This adjustment is described as preserving benchmark comparability.
supporting_quote: In CVUSA, we identify 762 and 43 repeated pairs in the original training set and testing set, respectively.
We remove the repeated pairs in the training set but keep the testing set unchanged for fair comparisons.

chunks.text: Evaluation is performed using retrieval recall at top K, reporting R@1, R@5, R@10, and R@1%. R@K measures how often the correct aerial reference is ranked within the top K predictions for a query ground image. This metric is used consistently across same-area and cross-area experiments to compare methods.
supporting_quote: we choose to use recall accuracy at top K (R@K) for evaluation purpose.
In the following experiments, we evaluate the performance of all methods on R@1, R@5, R@10, and R@1%.

chunks.text: On CVUSA same-area evaluation, GeoDTR with layout simulation achieves competitive or best performance compared to prior work, especially when polar transformation is applied to aerial images. The table reports that “Ours w/ LS†” reaches R@1 of 95.43% and R@1% of 99.86%. Without polar transformation, “Ours w/ LS” still attains strong performance, indicating robustness.

On CVACT, GeoDTR with layout simulation improves same-area performance, including on the challenging CVACT_test split. With polar transformation, “Ours w/ LS†” reaches 64.52% R@1 on CVACT_test and 86.21% R@1 on CVACT_val. These results are reported as improvements over prior state-of-the-art methods on CVACT_test.
supporting_quote: To be noticed, GeoDTR achieves 64.52% on R@1 of CVACT_test which is a 3.23% increase from previous SOTA (CDE (Toker et al. 2021))

chunks.text: Cross-area generalization improves substantially with GeoDTR. When training on CVUSA and testing on CVACT, the best reported GeoDTR configuration (“Ours w/ LS†”) achieves 53.16% R@1, exceeding the listed baselines in Table 3. The results indicate the combination of explicit layout modeling and correspondence-preserving augmentation benefits transfer to unseen regions.
supporting_quote: On CVUSA  $\rightarrow$  CVACT, GeoDTR achieves 53.16% on R@1
Ours w/ LS† ... CVUSA ↓ CVACT ... 53.16%

chunks.text: For the harder direction (CVACT → CVUSA), GeoDTR also leads by a large margin. Table 3 reports “Ours w/ LS†” reaching 44.07% R@1 and 64.66% R@5, notably higher than the baselines shown in the same table. This supports the claim that learned geometric layout descriptors plus LS reduce overfitting to low-level details from the source area.
supporting_quote: Ours w/ LS† | CVACT ↓ CVUSA | 44.07% ... | 64.66%
we consider CVACT  $\rightarrow$  CVUSA to be a more challenging task. We observe that GeoDTR outperforms all other methods by a substantial amount.

chunks.text: Ablation over the number of geometric layout descriptors K shows consistent gains, especially for cross-area evaluation. In Table 5, cross-area R@1 increases from 39.93% (K=1, CF, w/ LS) to 53.16% (K=8, CF, w/ LS). This indicates that richer geometric descriptor sets improve generalization beyond what augmentation alone provides.

Counterfactual (CF) learning improves retrieval accuracy in the ablation study, with clearer benefits on cross-area performance. For example in Table 5 (cross-area, w/ LS), adding CF increases R@1 from 49.18% (8, noCF, w/ LS) to 53.16% (8, CF, w/ LS), and R@5 from 71.96% to 75.62%. This supports CF as an auxiliary supervision signal for the layout extractor.

The layout simulation (LS) augmentation is shown to be broadly useful beyond GeoDTR. The paper applies LS to L2LTR and observes that it “greatly boosts” cross-area performance with only minor same-area decrease. This supports the claim that correspondence-preserving augmentations help models rely more on spatial configuration rather than low-level appearance.
supporting_quote: we apply the LS technique to L2LTR ... by comparing the recall accuracy training with or without LS.
We notice that LS greatly boosts the performance of L2LTR on the cross-area benchmark with only a minor decrease on the same-area benchmark.

chunks.text: The authors note that the learned geometric layout descriptors are not yet fully interpretable, even though visualizations suggest alignment between aerial and ground descriptors. They identify the interpretation of these descriptors as an open direction, aiming for more explainable models. This limitation frames future work around analyzing what the descriptors encode and why they transfer well across views and regions.
supporting_quote: Presently, the interpretation of geometric layout descriptors in our model has not been fully explored.
In the future, we will keep investigating their properties and work towards more explainable models.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that GeoDTR improves cross-view geo-localization by disentangling geometric layout from raw features and explicitly modeling spatial correlations among visual features. It also concludes that layout simulation and semantic augmentation improve generalization and can benefit other methods. Finally, it claims that the counterfactual-based learning process helps train better geometric descriptors and boosts performance across same-area and cross-area benchmarks.
supporting_quote: we propose GeoDTR which disentangles geometric layout from raw input features and better explores the spatial correlations among visual features.
we introduce layout simulation and semantic augmentation which improve the generalization of GeoDTR and other existing cross-view geolocalization models.
a novel counterfactual-based learning process is introduced to train GeoDTR.

chunks.text: Flooding is a major global hazard causing large fractions of disaster impacts and fatalities, and projected losses are expected to rise with climate change and urbanization. Inundation maps are essential for emergency response, but their accuracy depends on representing channel and floodplain geometry well. Traditional hydraulic modeling relies on surveyed cross sections and detailed local HEC-RAS models, which are costly and difficult to scale nationally. This motivates terrain-based approaches that can be automated over large domains.
supporting_quote: Flooding is the most threatening natural disaster worldwide considering the fatalities and property damage it causes. It makes up about 40% of all natural disasters worldwide
Inundation maps show the spatial extent of flooding and play an important role in emergency response during flood events

chunks.text: HAND (Height above Nearest Drainage) is a hydrologic terrain descriptor derived from a DEM that measures each cell’s elevation relative to the stream cell it drains to. A cell is inundated when the channel water level exceeds its HAND value, and the resulting depth grid can be used to characterize inundation. Prior studies demonstrated HAND for inundation mapping, but its use for deriving hydraulic geometry and stage–discharge relationships had not been explored in this work’s framing. The paper positions HAND as a way to derive hydraulic parameters directly from terrain.
supporting_quote: Height above Nearest Drainage (HAND) (Rodda 2005; Renno et al. 2008), which is defined as the height of each grid cell with respect to the nearest stream cell it drains to.
However, its application in describing river geometry information and retrieving stage–discharge relationships has not been explored.

chunks.text: Existing remote-sensing and statistical river-geometry datasets provide useful large-scale summaries but have limitations for local flooding studies. Key shortcomings include insufficient stream-network resolution for small local streams and providing only bankfull geometry rather than continuous stage-dependent hydraulic properties. Because remotely sensed imagery captures transient planform conditions and regressions may miss local physiographic uniqueness, the authors argue for terrain-based extraction. This context supports developing continuous stage–geometry relations from DEMs.
supporting_quote: numerous local streams, which are critical during flood events, are not detected in the existing global river width and depth database.
only the bankfull width and depth are provided instead of a continuous relationship between stage height and channel properties

chunks.text: The paper aims to estimate reach-averaged channel hydraulic geometry and build synthetic rating curves using HAND derived from high-resolution terrain data. The goal is to relate discharge and water level in stream reaches without requiring surveyed cross sections, enabling application to ungaged basins. The approach is evaluated by comparing stage–geometry relationships and rating curves to calibrated HEC-RAS models and to USGS gage observations. The authors also test whether HAND-derived inundation can capture FEMA 100-year floodplains.
supporting_quote: we describe a method for developing a synthetic rating curve to relate flow to water level in a stream reach based on reach-averaged channel geometry properties developed using the Height above Nearest Drainage (HAND) method.

We evaluate the method's performance by comparing the reach-average stage-river geometry relationships and rating curves to those from calibrated Hydrologic Engineering Center's River Analysis System (HEC-RAS) models and USGS gage observations.

chunks.text: A central objective is to create a workflow that can be executed with national-coverage datasets to support continental-scale applications such as the National Water Model. The authors intend to compute HAND aligned to NHDPlus reaches, derive hydraulic properties per reach, and then estimate rating curves using Manning’s equation. The work emphasizes automation and scalability while maintaining comparability to more data-intensive hydraulic modeling where available. This is positioned as an alternative route to inundation mapping when cross-sectional data are absent.
supporting_quote: We implement this conceptual framework in the continental U.S. with the 1/3 arc-second (10 m) USGS 3D Elevation Program (3DEP) dataset and the NHDPlus dataset
This paper has presented a new method for the determination of reach-average hydraulic properties from a DEM based on the HAND approach.

chunks.text: A main challenge is that surveyed cross sections and locally built HEC-RAS models cannot be easily extended across ungaged basins and large geographies. Efforts to merge many local HEC-RAS models have struggled due to inconsistent model development, overlaps, and gaps in coverage. These issues limit the ability to create consistent, national-scale representations of channel geometry for inundation and hydraulic analysis. The paper frames this as a need for a new, terrain-driven approach.
supporting_quote: Traditional approaches to quantifying river geometry rely on measurements of river cross sections, which cannot be extended to ungaged basins.

Attempts to combine many independently developed local Hydrologic Engineering Center's River Analysis System (HEC-RAS) models have failed due to variations in model development, overlaps in cross sections from one local model to another, and gaps in coverage

chunks.text: NHDPlus flowlines do not always align with valleys in high-resolution DEMs, and direct rasterization of NHDPlus streams can produce spurious HAND values. This misalignment arises because NHDPlus is mapped at a nominal 1:100,000 resolution while the 1/3 arc-second DEM is finer and depicts valley positions more accurately. Because HAND requires the stream raster to be aligned with DEM flow directions, the authors must reconcile hydrography with terrain. The problem directly affects the validity of inundation and geometry derived from HAND.
supporting_quote: NHDPlus streams, however, do not always align with valleys in the 1/3 arc-second NED DEM.

To avoid the spurious HAND values that would result from calculating HAND to a direct rasterization of NHDPlus flowlines, we derived a stream raster at the same drainage density as the NHDPlus stream network, but aligned with 1/3 arc-second NED DEM.

chunks.text: DEM representations of channels can be biased because elevations are smoothed and may include water surfaces, and DEM conditioning steps like pit filling can introduce additional errors along streams. This creates a “shelf effect” where HAND-derived geometry shows nonzero width at zero water level, indicating missing bathymetry. Such biases require adjustments such as a bottom shift to better match thalweg elevations and observed geometry. The problem influences both channel geometry estimation and rating-curve accuracy.
supporting_quote: Because DEMs are smoothed versions of land surface topography, and because the DEM may have been created when the channel was partly filled with water, the DEM channel elevation is generally higher than the minimum channel elevation.
it is useful to introduce a bottom shift into the HAND-derived water levels reflecting the "shelf effect" where the bottom of a DEM channel is actually flat over a finite area.

chunks.text: HAND is computed using the D∞ flow-direction model and a recursive weighted-average vertical drop-to-stream formulation. The method defines drop(i,k) as z(i) − z(k) and aggregates drops using flow proportions P_ik to obtain h(i). Stream cells are assigned distance zero and the function is evaluated upstream as downslope values become available, enabling parallel computation. The authors choose D∞ because it smooths sharp HAND differences that can arise from D8.
supporting_quote: Our method uses the D∞ approach for the computation of HAND (vertical distance or drop to a stream
h(i) = ( (∑ P_ik(drop(i,k) + h(k))) / ∑ P_ik )
The D∞ approach with weighted average distance to the stream is used here as it provides a smoothing of the HAND values

chunks.text: To align streams with the DEM while keeping NHDPlus drainage density, the authors build a stream raster starting from NHDPlus first-order channel heads. Channel-head cells are encoded as weights, and a weighted D8 flow accumulation is computed; stream cells are those with weighted flow accumulation > 1. This produces a DEM-aligned raster stream network that follows valleys while preserving the NHDPlus-originating topology. This stream raster is then used as the target set for HAND calculation.
supporting_quote: identifying the upstream channel head of each first-order NHDPlus stream and representing this as a grid cell with value of 1
This weight grid was then used as input to a weighted flow accumulation calculation using D8 flow directions
Stream grid cells were mapped where the weighted flow accumulation was >1.

chunks.text: The preprocessing and HAND workflow is implemented with TauDEM tools. The DEM is hydrologically conditioned by pit removal, D8 and D∞ flow directions are computed, channel-head sources are defined from NHDPlus, and weighted D8 contributing area delineates the stream raster. Finally, HAND is computed as D∞ distance down to the stream with the vertical drop option. The paper lists these steps as a complete processing chain for repeatable computation.
supporting_quote: Fill pits using TauDEM pitremove function.
Calculate D8 flow directions using TauDEM D8flowdir function.
Calculate HAND using D∞ distance to stream function with the vertical drop option.

chunks.text: For a reach R, inundation at a reach-average water level y is defined by selecting all catchment cells with HAND h(s) ≤ y. Water depth at an inundated cell is computed as d(s,y) = y − h(s). From the inundated set F(y), the method derives water surface area S(y), channel bed area B(y) using local slope, and flood volume V(y). These are converted to reach-averaged width W(y)=S(y)/L, cross-sectional area A(y)=V(y)/L, wetted perimeter P(y)=B(y)/L, and hydraulic radius R(y)=A/P.
supporting_quote: the inundated zone F(y), which is a subarea of the reach catchment C.
d(s,y) = y - h(s), s ∈ F(y)
W(y) = S(y)/L
R(y) = A(y)/P(y)

chunks.text: Synthetic rating curves are generated by applying Manning’s equation to the HAND-derived reach-average hydraulic geometry. Given reach slope S and assumed roughness n, discharge is computed as Q(y)=(1.00/n)·A·R^(2/3)·S^(1/2) for each stage y. Evaluating this over a range of y produces a stage–discharge relationship y(Q) per reach, intended to convert modeled discharges into water depths. The approach assumes uniform flow along the reach.
supporting_quote: the Manning's equation can be applied to obtain a discharge Q(y) corresponding to the water depth of y at uniform flow
Computing the discharge Q(y) for different water depths y results in a synthetic rating curve for reach R.

chunks.text: Integrity checking is performed by comparing HAND-derived results to HEC-RAS outputs for the same reach. The paper compares minimum channel elevation profiles, channel width vs. stage, and rating curves, using HEC-RAS cross-section samples to define reference “sample spaces.” A bottom shift is introduced to address DEM shelf effects, and a roughness n is calibrated by minimizing RMSE or mean stage-difference relative to a median HEC-RAS rating curve. This provides a structured validation and parameter-tuning procedure.
supporting_quote: One way of checking the integrity of the HAND-derived information is to compare the results with those derived from a HEC-RAS model of the same river.
it is useful to introduce a bottom shift into the HAND-derived water levels reflecting the "shelf effect"
The optimal roughness value is selected for the HAND-derived rating curve by minimizing the root-mean-square error (RMSE)

chunks.text: The main study uses 10 m terrain data from the USGS 3D Elevation Program and NHDPlus hydrography. The 1/3 arc-second DEM is described as having RMSE vertical accuracy of 1.5 m. Reach length and channel bed slope are taken from the NHDPlus flowline attribute table to support hydraulic computations. These national datasets enable the method to be executed broadly while maintaining reach indexing via NHDPlus identifiers.
supporting_quote: using 10-m terrain data from the United States Geological Survey (USGS) 3D Elevation Program (3DEP) dataset.
The DEM used in this study is the 1/3 arc-second DEM from the USGS 3DEP dataset with horizontal resolution of about 10 m. The RMSE is 1.5 m
The reach length and channel bed slope come from the attribute table of the flowline feature class in the NHDPlus dataset.

chunks.text: A detailed validation case study is conducted on the Blanco River watershed in Central Texas. The watershed includes 170 medium-resolution NHDPlus reaches, about 1,100 km2 drainage area, and about 540 km total river length. A calibrated HEC-RAS steady-flow model for the lower half of the main channel is used as reference, and a specific reach (COMID 1630223) with eight cross sections is selected for focused comparison. The reach’s HEC-RAS main-channel Manning’s n is 0.045, and floodplain n ranges from 0.06 to 0.1.
supporting_quote: The network of the Blanco River watershed is composed of 170 medium-resolution NHDPlus reaches. The total drainage area is about 1,100 km2
In particular, we implemented the approach for a single NHDPlus reach with COMID 1630223.
The main channel Manning's n value is 0.045 for all the cross sections, while the floodplain Manning's n varies from 0.06 to 0.1.

chunks.text: For reach 1630223, the rating-curve computation uses NHDPlus attributes for hydraulic slope and length along with a chosen roughness value. The paper reports the segment length as 2.1 km and the channel bed slope as 0.00198. Water levels are sampled from 0 to 18.3 m (60 feet) at 0.3 m (1 foot) intervals to generate depth grids and hydraulic-property tables. This discretization underpins the stage-dependent geometry and discharge computations.
supporting_quote: In this study for reach 1630223, the segment length is 2.1 km, and the channel bed slope is 0.00198.
we create the water depth grids that correspond to a series of threshold water levels from 0 to 18.3 m (60 feet) at an interval of 0.3 m (1 foot).

chunks.text: For broader evaluation against observed rating curves, the Tar River watershed in North Carolina is used. Within areas covered by local hydraulic models, nine USGS stream gages provide measured rating curves. The comparison uses 100-year flood discharge estimates from local models and roughness ranges from FEMA flood insurance study reports by county. These inputs enable testing both default n=0.05 HAND curves and tuned n values at multiple gage sites.
supporting_quote: The Tar River watershed in North Carolina was selected as the test bed (Figure 15).
observed rating curves are collected from nine USGS stream gages.
the Manning's n range for channel and overbank zone from FEMA flood insurance study reports organized by county

chunks.text: For Blanco River reach 1630223, DEM-based thalweg profiles are close to HEC-RAS minimum channel elevations, but pit removal introduces additional positive bias. The DEM-derived profile is 0.13 m higher than the HEC-RAS profile on average (standard deviation 0.12 m) for the reach, while the pit-removed DEM profile is 0.88 m higher on average (standard deviation 0.95 m). Over the full modeled 82 km segment, mean differences are 0.49 m (DEM) and 0.99 m (pit-removed DEM). This shows conditioning steps can materially affect HAND-based geometry.
supporting_quote: For the profile comparison of reach 1630223 (shown in Figure 10a), the DEM-derived profile is 0.13 m higher than the HEC-RAS profile on average with a standard deviation of 0.12 m.
The profile derived from the pit-removed DEM... is 0.88 m higher than the HEC-RAS profile on average, with a standard deviation of 0.95 m.
For the entire 82-km modeled segment, the DEM-derived profile is 0.49 m higher... the pit-removed DEM is 0.99 m higher

chunks.text: HAND-derived geometry initially indicates a nonzero channel width at zero water depth due to missing bathymetry (“shelf effect”). For reach 1630223, the HAND method yields a bottom width of 38 m at water level 0 m. By matching this width to the HEC-RAS reach-average depth–width relationship, the authors estimate a bottom shift of 0.64 m to adjust HAND-derived geometry. After adjustment, the HAND depth–width curve lies within the sample space of individual HEC-RAS cross sections.
supporting_quote: when the water level is equal to zero... a corresponding channel width of 38 m is derived from the HAND raster for reach 1630223.
From Figure 11, a depth of 0.64 m is interpolated... This depth is treated as the bottom shift needed to adjust HAND-derived river geometry

chunks.text: After bottom-shift adjustment, HAND-derived reach-average widths agree closely with HEC-RAS-derived reach-average widths over a wide depth range. The HEC-RAS reach-average channel width is reported as 12.04 m wider than HAND on average between depths 0.92 m and 15.24 m, with a 19.33 m standard deviation. Normalized by the HEC-RAS reach-average width, this corresponds to a relative mean difference of 3.2%. This supports that HAND can capture reach-scale geometric behavior reasonably.
supporting_quote: The RAS-derived reachaverage channel width is 12.04 m wider than the HAND-derived reach-average width within the depth range from 0.92 m (3 feet) to 15.24 m (50 feet).
The standard deviation of the width difference is 19.33 m.
the relative mean difference is 3.2%

chunks.text: For reach 1630223, HAND-derived rating curves require an initial shift to account for missing channel bottom when compared to HEC-RAS median rating behavior. Using the 0.64 m depth shift, the discharge added to the bottom is identified as 22 m3/s, and both depth and discharge are shifted accordingly. With Manning’s n = 0.05, HAND stages are 0.52 m higher than the HEC-RAS median on average (standard deviation 0.09), equivalent to 7.7% mean difference. This quantifies rating-curve discrepancy under a default roughness.
supporting_quote: For the depth shift of 0.64 m, the discharge added to the bottom of the HAND-derived rating curve is 22 m3/s.
For the case with the Manning's n of 0.05, the water level read from the HAND-derived rating curve is 0.52 m higher... with a standard deviation of 0.09.
it represents a mean difference of 7.7%.

chunks.text: Calibrating Manning’s n improves agreement between HAND-derived and HEC-RAS median rating curves for the Blanco reach. Searching n from 0.040 to 0.06 (step 0.001), the mean stage-difference absolute value is minimized to 0.02 m at n = 0.043. This calibrated value is close to the HEC-RAS channel roughness 0.045, and adopting n = 0.045 yields a mean difference of 0.17 m deemed acceptable for inundation mapping. The proximity of calibrated and HEC-RAS n supports the method’s plausibility.
supporting_quote: searching across Manning's n values between 0.040 and 0.06 at an interval of 0.001.
The mean stage height difference absolute value is minimized to 0.02 m at a Manning's n of 0.043
If the actual 0.045 Manning's n value is adopted, the mean difference is 0.17 m

chunks.text: Across nine USGS gages in the Tar River watershed, a single default Manning’s n does not yield high accuracy everywhere, but tuning n within FEMA-reported ranges can closely match observed 100-year depths. The paper compares depths derived from USGS observed rating curves to HAND-derived synthetic rating curves with n=0.05 and with an optimized nbest per site. Examples include site 02081747 where HAND depth changes from 8.82 m (n=0.05) to 7.04 m (nbest=0.031) against USGS 7.07 m, and site 02083000 where optimized depth matches 5.65 m exactly. This indicates roughness calibration materially improves depth conversion.
supporting_quote: The results (Table 2, Figure 16) show that... tuning Manning's n within a reasonable range can achieve near-real water depth prediction

chunks.text: HAND-derived inundation extents for Tar River catchments generally capture most of the FEMA 100-year floodplain, even without calibrating Manning’s n. Reported F-index values are often high, for example 0.90 at site 02081500 and 0.94 at site 02083000 when using USGS-derived depths, and 0.97 at site 02083000 using initial n=0.05 depths. Some sites show larger differences (e.g., 02081747 has FInitial 0.54). Overall, the comparison suggests robust floodplain coverage with occasional overprediction.
supporting_quote: the inundation extent produced with the HAND approach is able to capture the majority of FEMA floodplain, even without a calibration of the Manning's n coefficient.

chunks.text: A key limitation is the assumption that the input DEM adequately represents channel shape, even though bathymetry is often missing and DEM elevations may be biased high. The authors note that base elevation adjustments may be necessary, and they expect improvements as better bathymetric data become available (e.g., water-penetrating lidar or sonic measurements). Without bathymetry, HAND may overestimate water depth relative to actual conditions, influencing rating curves and inundation mapping. This limitation is central to the need for bottom shifts and calibration.
supporting_quote: We assumed, for example, that the input DEM represents the shape of the river channel and comparison with HEC-RAS showed that adjustments of the base elevation may be needed in certain cases.
we expect that as DEMs are improved... especially if and when channel bed bathymetry is obtained... the need for such adjustments may be reduced
Due to the absence of the bathymetric portion... the water depth computed... is often higher than the actual water depth.

chunks.text: The pit-filling step required for hydrologic conditioning can create incorrect elevations along stream corridors, especially near artificial barriers. The paper highlights artifacts such as road/rail crossings where the DEM reflects the barrier crest rather than the underpass elevation where water flows. Such errors can propagate into flow directions, HAND values, and derived hydraulic properties. The authors propose exploring adjustments using higher-resolution hydrography to enforce nonincreasing elevation along mapped flowlines.
supporting_quote: the pit-filling process... can result in incorrect DEM values along the streams.
for example, the DEM representation of the elevation of road/railway crossings and not of the elevation beneath these crossings at which water passes.
use high-resolution hydrography information... to adjust the DEM so that elevation is nonincreasing along hydrographically mapped flowlines.

chunks.text: Despite using channel-head-based DEM stream delineation, perfect reconciliation between DEM-derived networks and NHDPlus reaches/catchments is not guaranteed. The authors note that drainage areas to DEM stream segments may not align with NHDPlus catchments, producing edge errors when clipping HAND rasters by NHDPlus boundaries. This reflects a broader need for improved alignment between national hydrography and elevation datasets. The paper points to NHDPlusHR as an example of ongoing effort.
supporting_quote: even with this approach, a one-to-one mapping between stream segments in the DEM delineated network and NHDPlus is not guaranteed
areas draining to DEM stream segments may not align exactly with NHDPlus catchments, resulting in errors around the edges when clipping the HAND raster
An example of ongoing effort is the NHDPlusHR (Viger et al. 2016).

chunks.text: The approach assigns a uniform water depth to a reach during inundation mapping, which can be unrealistic for long reaches. While reaches can be split into shorter segments, the paper leaves open the question of optimal segment length and notes interactions with 1D modeling practices such as cross-section spacing. Sudden shape changes at confluences may also cause instability in large-scale models if properties are organized only at reach scale. The authors suggest segment-level organization could help but requires further research.
supporting_quote: Channel properties are currently organized by reach and a uniform water depth is assigned to a reach during the inundation mapping process. Sometimes reaches are quite long and assuming a uniform depth is unreasonable.
It is possible to split reaches into shorter segments, but we leave to future work the exploration of the best length to use.
Organizing hydraulic properties in a segment unit smaller than a reach also has the potential to help resolve the instability problem in large-scale hydraulic models

chunks.text: HAND-based inundation and rating curves are approximate and may perform worse in settings dominated by artificial structures or complex channel–floodplain momentum exchange. The authors state the method should primarily serve as a screening tool to identify where detailed studies are warranted. They observe better performance in hilly rural catchments where topography controls routing, and worse in flat urbanized catchments where structures affect hydrodynamics. This limits operational use without additional physics or data.
supporting_quote: We also acknowledge the preliminary and approximate nature of the proposed method, particularly in areas where artificial hydraulic structures or momentum interaction between channel and floodplain controls the propagation of flood waves.
we suggest that this method should be used primarily as a screening tool for identifying locations where more detailed studies are warranted.
performs better in the hilly, rural catchments... compared to the flat, urbanized catchments where artificial structures significantly affect the hydrodynamic process.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that a DEM-based HAND workflow can compute reach-average hydraulic geometry and synthetic rating curves with inputs of a DEM, channel heads (or a stream network), and a Manning’s n value. In the Blanco River example, HAND-derived hydraulic geometry and rating curves are generally consistent with cross-section and HEC-RAS outputs after addressing base-elevation issues. Calibrated roughness values are close to those used in HEC-RAS, supporting validity. The authors argue the approach is promising for continental-scale hydraulic modeling using national datasets.
supporting_quote: a workflow for computing river geometry and estimating channel reach rating curves based on DEM-derived HAND was presented.
The workflow requires as input a DEM, the channel heads (or a stream network from which they can be extracted), and a Manning's n value.
Overall, our proposed method was shown to hold promise for supporting quantitative hydraulic modeling at continental scale using readily available national datasets.

chunks.text: The authors emphasize that while limitations remain due to terrain-only information and a one-dimensional steady-flow assumption, the approach is useful for approximate inundation mapping in areas lacking detailed hydraulic studies. They point to operational and community uptake, including use during Hurricane Harvey to produce real-time flood maps over large stream lengths. This illustrates practical value and scalability despite acknowledged approximations. The paper encourages broader testing across flow and terrain scenarios to better characterize performance.
supporting_quote: Although limitations exist in our method due to the terrain-only consideration and the one-dimensional steady flow assumption, we think it is a valid approach for approximate inundation mapping especially in those areas where detailed hydraulic studies are not available.
NOAA National Water Center implemented the HAND workflow during Hurricane Harvey to produce real-time flood maps for over 60,000 km of streams

chunks.text: Food, energy, and water (FEW) systems are tightly interconnected, and focusing policy on only one domain can create unintended consequences elsewhere. Prior work has recognized these couplings, but integrating them into computational models that can support policy and risk management remains an active area. Ecosystem service degradation further amplifies risks at the FEW nexus, especially under global environmental change.
supporting_quote: any strategy that focuses on one part of the food-energy-water nexus without considering interconnections risks serious unintended consequences.
computational modelling that reflects those convergent and divergent interconnections and can inform policy development and risk management requires far more research and resource investments
the degradation in ecosystem services also poses a monumental risk at the nexus of food energy and water systems

chunks.text: Extreme hydro-meteorological events (e.g., temperature and rainfall variability) are central drivers of FEW insecurity, and their impacts depend on antecedent landscape conditions. Poor understanding of responses to “primary” extremes can trigger “consequent” hazards such as floods, droughts, wildfires, and contamination events. Scientific consensus anticipates changes in the frequency, intensity, and duration of primary extremes under climate change, but projection uncertainty remains high at multiple scales.
supporting_quote: changing risk from extreme hydro-meteorological events, such as extreme temperature and rainfall variability, poses a fundamental scientific and policy challenge

Poor understanding of biogeochemical, landscape and policy responses to "primary" extreme events typically leads to "consequent" extreme events such as floods, droughts, wildfires, and water contamination events
there is considerable uncertainty surrounding the projection of the changing frequencies and intensities of these events at multiple scales

chunks.text: Early warning systems (EWS) have been deployed for many hazards across a wide range of lead times, from minutes to years. A FEW security EWS must span much broader horizons—from hours to decades or longer—to support operational, tactical, and strategic decisions. Communicating uncertainty and clarifying nexus trade-offs and synergies are emphasized as key goals for next-generation systems.
supporting_quote: The temporal scales (early warning lead times) range from minutes in the case of earthquake and tsunamis... and at times months and even years in the case of drought.
Food, energy, water security early warning systems must encompass lead times from hours to decades and perhaps even centuries
Effective communication of uncertainty embedded in Nexus-EWS and improved understanding of synergies and trade-offs in the nexus

chunks.text: The chapter frames Nexus-EWS as convergent technologies intended to help societies adapt to more frequent and intense extremes under climate change. The intended benefit is improved stakeholder understanding of FEW interactions and the ability to forecast and manage social-ecological risks. The approach is positioned to support both public and private decision-making by making nexus synergies and trade-offs transparent under multiple scenarios.
supporting_quote: The goal of designing convergent technologies, such as Nexus-EWS, is thus driven by critical global environmental policy need to adapt to increasing frequency and intensity of extreme events
Deployment and continual improvement of such convergent technologies may enhance stakeholder understanding of nexus interactions, couplings, and processes
facilitate both the private and public decision making by enabling transparent understanding of synergies and trade-offs

chunks.text: A central hypothesis is that Nexus-EWS can function as resilience technologies that project shifting risks to safe and secure FEW provision under alternative climate, socio-economic, and land-use scenarios. The focus includes national and regional scales, explicitly including Central and South Asia. The projected outputs are meant to inform early action capabilities as risks evolve.
supporting_quote: A central hypothesis is that Nexus-EWS could be harnessed as convergent resilience technologies that can project, under different climate change, socio-economic, and land-use scenarios, the shifting risk from extreme events on safe and secure provision of food, energy, and water
including but not limited to communities in the Central and South Asia

chunks.text: The chapter’s stated purpose is to review and discuss Nexus-EWS, highlight application examples emphasizing Central and South Asia, and examine challenges to deployment and improvement. It also aims to discuss the role of open-source big data (satellite data) and AI, and to surface geopolitical and ethical issues tied to convergent technology deployment. This positions the chapter as both a synthesis and a forward-looking research and policy agenda.
supporting_quote: This chapter presents a brief review and discussion of Nexus-EWS as convergent technologies
provides promising examples of Nexus-EWS applications with specific focus on Central and South Asian countries
The growing role of open-sourced big data, such as remotely sensed satellite data and artificial intelligence (AI)... Geopolitical and ethical issues arising from the deployment

chunks.text: Uncertainty in projecting changes in extreme events at watershed-to-regional scales limits the ability of decision-makers to incorporate risk into FEW planning. This uncertainty affects actors involved in production and consumption of FEW resources and constrains preparedness. The chapter argues that such uncertainty is a major barrier to local-to-regional decision processes for climate resilience.
supporting_quote: there is considerable uncertainty surrounding the projection of the changing frequencies and intensities of these events at multiple scales
Large uncertainty about changes in extreme events hinders local- to regional-scale efforts to incorporate the risk from extreme events in the decision-making processes

chunks.text: Existing early warning efforts in Central and South Asia are fragmented by hazard and sector (e.g., flood, drought, famine) rather than integrated across the FEW nexus. As a result, they often fail to represent cross-sector couplings needed for nexus security planning. This fragmentation is presented as a key gap in moving from single-domain EWS to Nexus-EWS.
supporting_quote: a variety of fragmented early warning systems are deployed at various scales

These fragmented EWS do not necessarily account for the nexus, rather the EWS are operational in separate domains, e.g., flood early warning systems, drought early warning systems, and famine early warning systems.
no nexus EWS application has yet been derived from the SERVIR program

chunks.text: The chapter highlights deficiencies in understanding non-linear processes, thresholds, tipping points, and controllability in complex adaptive FEW systems. Conventional optimization and top-down control approaches may not be suitable when systems exhibit emergence, adaptation, and irreversibilities. Poorly understood micro-scale decision processes (households, firms, utilities) further complicate effective nexus risk management.
supporting_quote: Inadequate understanding of non-linear processes and threshold effects pose fundamental challenges in distinguishing controllable from non-controllable processes
properties of complex adaptive systems, such as emergence, adaptation, and self-organization... do not necessarily lend to top-down control and dynamic optimization
the controllability in the decision-making processes at micro-scale levels, such as households and firms (farmers, utilities, etc.), is poorly understood

chunks.text: Regional-scale Nexus-EWS development is constrained by limited data sharing among riparian countries in transboundary basins and by narrower geopolitical goals. Conflicts and sectoral securitization reduce access to field data needed for model calibration and validation. Without consistent field-data assimilation, forecast reliability and accuracy are difficult to determine.
supporting_quote: lack of cooperation in data sharing and management planning among riparian partners in transboundary river basins
Due to ongoing geopolitical conflicts in Central and South Asia (e.g., Kashmir, Afghanistan), field data on nexus being collected by national level agencies is not yet shared
Without concurrent assimilation of field data in the nexus forecast models, the forecast reliability and accuracy cannot be readily determined.

chunks.text: Satellite observations enable new Nexus-EWS opportunities but are limited by spatial, temporal, radiometric, and spectral constraints, plus cloud cover and cost barriers for private data. These limitations can increase uncertainty unless complemented by in situ measurements of water, food, and energy variables. The chapter frames these as practical constraints on high-resolution operational and tactical Nexus-EWS.
supporting_quote: the satellite data could be limiting due to limits in their spatial, temporal, radiometric, and spectral resolutions
Satellites with higher spatial resolutions tend to have lower temporal resolutions and vice versa.
Challenges associated with cloud cover limit the accuracy of Nexus-EWS.

chunks.text: Nexus-EWS is conceptualized as a convergent technology grounded in social-ecological systems theory and complex adaptive systems theory. It emphasizes explicit modeling of interconnections and dynamics across consistently defined eco-hydrological regions. This framing highlights that exogenous shocks and endogenous surprises can cause abrupt critical transitions, which Nexus-EWS should help anticipate and manage.
supporting_quote: The food, energy, and water early warning systems (Nexus-EWS) approach is embedded in social ecological systems theory
and complex adaptive systems theory (Holland 1992) that explicitly models the interconnections and dynamics of various nexus components
social ecological systems do not necessarily go through gradual change, but rather critical transitions (tipping points and thresholds) may abruptly change the trajectory

chunks.text: The chapter defines resilience in the social-ecological sense and uses it to motivate Nexus-EWS design for extreme-event risk. Resilience is framed as disturbance absorption capacity and the ability to self-organize and adapt. This definition supports the need to model thresholds and transitions rather than relying only on smooth, incremental change assumptions.
supporting_quote: resilience refers precisely to the magnitude of disturbance that can be absorbed before a system changes to a radically different state, as well as the capacity to self-organize and the capacity for adaptation
Tipping points, thresholds, nonlinearities, and irreversibilities... need to be adequately accounted for to effectively model social ecological resilience and vulnerability to extreme events.

chunks.text: A governance-oriented methodological stance is advanced: polycentric governance is proposed as better suited for integrating across issues and scales in nexus management. It balances bottom-up, top-down, and lateral pathways of influence and is assumed to support adaptive capacity. This is positioned as a governance complement to bottom-up modeling in Nexus-EWS.
supporting_quote: Polycentric governance systems balance bottom-up and top-down (multi-level) and lateral (intersectoral) pathways of influence
They are assumed to have high performance with respect to integration across issues and scales and regarding adaptive capacity

chunks.text: The chapter contrasts top-down nexus optimization models with bottom-up approaches informed by social-ecological theory. Top-down methods commonly assume global control, objective functions, and constraints to find optimal pathways. Bottom-up computational modeling is argued to better capture distributed decision-making, non-linear interactions, and landscape dynamics that influence resilience to extreme events.
supporting_quote: Zhang and Vesselinov (2017) developed a Water Energy Food Security Optimization model, an example of a top-down approach, that minimizes cost
These top-down, integrated assessment approaches assume global control of societal preferences
bottom-up approaches informed by social ecological systems theory have the potential to generate actionable convergent technologies for managing risk at spatially distributed scales

chunks.text: One highlighted application method is a World Bank-funded hydro-economic modeling approach for basin-scale nexus analysis under alternative climate scenarios. It evaluates synergies and trade-offs induced by FEW management decisions and explores alternative water allocation mechanisms and infrastructure developments. This approach is presented for both Indus and Brahmaputra basins.
supporting_quote: Under the World Bank funding, a top-down hydro-economic modelling approach was used to ascertain the synergies and trade-offs
Impacts of a range of climate change scenarios on the nexus in the Indus Basin were modeled
Yang et al. (2016b) present details of this calibrated hydro-economic water system model of the Brahmaputra basin

chunks.text: A second highlighted approach under development is an Integrated Regime Shift Assessment Model (IRSAM) intended to build tactical and strategic Nexus-EWS capacity. IRSAM integrates eco-hydrological and socio-economic modeling to anticipate impacts of hydro-climate regime shifts and support multi-governance resilience mechanisms in multiple transboundary basins. It is described as a bottom-up model co-designed with stakeholders.
supporting_quote: develop a bottom-up Integrated Regime Shift Assessment Model to build tactical and strategic Nexus-EWS capacity
anticipating the impact of hydro-climate regime shifts on food, energy, and water security
scenarios co-designed with stakeholders in focal riparian countries

chunks.text: IRSAM’s computational structure integrates a hydrological model (e.g., SWAT) with an agent-based model to simulate endogenous basin dynamics and governance regimes. It aims to represent interacting regime shifts driven by climate change and ENSO, and to simulate socio-economic stability regimes such as migration or conflict/cooperation. The workflow is planned for implementation using a workflow management system such as Pegasus.
supporting_quote: The IRSAM will integrate a hydrological model, e.g., SWAT with an Agent Based Model (ABM)
simulate endogenous dynamics of (1) water, energy, and food availability and socioeconomic stability
implemented in a workflow management system such as the Pegasus Workflow Management System

chunks.text: Nature-based solutions and ecological design are presented as complementary interventions that can reduce extreme-event risks in the nexus, especially under urbanization pressures. Examples include wetland and riparian buffer conservation for flood mitigation, rooftop and vertical gardens, micro-hydro, biomass/biowaste projects, and conservation tillage. These interventions are framed as landscape design alternatives to business-as-usual urbanization.
supporting_quote: nature-based solutions and ecological design approaches to reduce the risk from extreme events

Such nature-based solutions may include: agro-ecological practices... wetland and riparian buffer conservation for flood mitigation... micro-hydro power generation projects... cover crops and conservation tillage
assess the differences between "business as usual" urbanization scenarios versus natural infrastructure landscape design scenarios

chunks.text: For Indus Basin analysis, Yang et al. (2016a) used a hydroagro-economic model extended with an agricultural energy use module to simulate impacts of climate change scenarios and management options. The modeling outputs reported include annual crop production and hydropower generation under alternative climate, dam development, and allocation scenarios. The chapter notes additional datasets and model components needed for refinement, including groundwater, energy markets, and demographic demand changes.
supporting_quote: using a hydroagro-economic model extended with an agricultural energy use module
Indus basin annual crop and hydropower production under the impacts of climate change... dam development... and alternative water allocation scenarios
integration of a groundwater model and an energy market model was needed... Explicitly addressing changes in food and energy demand as a result of demographic dynamics

chunks.text: For upper Indus climate impacts, the chapter cites simulations using a baseline period (2000–2007) and a future period (2046–2065) under the A1B SRES scenario. The projection reported is a mean 8.4% decrease in upper Indus water supply. These scenario-based simulations are used to motivate the need for finer-resolution, calibrated basin models.
supporting_quote: simulating mean upper Indus discharge for the baseline (2000–2007) and future climate for A1B SRES scenario (2046–2065)
projected a mean 8.4% decrease in the upper Indus water supply

chunks.text: The SERVIR program is described as providing Earth observation-based geospatial services and supporting regional drought and flood monitoring/forecasting in the Hindu Kush Himalaya. The flood service is planned to include an operational 15-day flood forecast and warnings for 24–48-hour high-intensity rainfall and flash floods. These systems represent data and service infrastructure that could support future Nexus-EWS development.
supporting_quote: SERVIR maintains a large, diverse collection of user-tailored geospatial services that use Earth observations and NASA data
include an operational 15-day flood forecast
issue warnings on 24 to 48-hour high intensity rainfall events and flash floods

chunks.text: FEWS NET is described as producing monthly reports and maps of current and projected food insecurity, and issuing alerts on emerging crises. It also publishes special reports on drivers related to weather and climate-induced water variability, markets, conflict, livelihoods, nutrition, and humanitarian assistance. These reporting products constitute recurring data streams relevant to food-security early warning in the broader nexus.
supporting_quote: The FEWS NET issues monthly reports and maps detailing current and projected food insecurity and alerts on emerging or likely crises.
issues special reports on factors that contribute to or mitigate food insecurity, including nexus factors pertaining to weather and climate changing induced water variability

chunks.text: The chapter identifies satellite datasets such as Landsat (NASA) and Sentinel (ESA) as key open sources, but notes that their spectral and other design choices are driven by western agency science goals. It stresses the need for field-scale in situ measurements for water (stream data), food (crop data), and energy (hydropower, wind data) to develop high-resolution Nexus-EWS. These data needs are framed as essential for calibration and uncertainty reduction.
supporting_quote: Spectral resolutions of satellites, e.g., Landsat (NASA) and Sentinel (ESA), are driven by science goals of western agencies
field scale in situ data on water (e.g., stream data), food (e.g., crop data) and energy (e.g., hydropower, wind data) must be made available

chunks.text: In Indus Basin hydro-economic modeling, scenarios with hotter and wetter conditions increased modeled water and energy use. The analysis suggests that more flexible surface water allocation policies can mitigate negative climate impacts and allow larger crop and hydropower production. However, the same flexibility may increase inter-annual variability, shifting use toward surface water while reducing groundwater and energy use.

more flexible surface water allocation policies can mitigate negative climate change impacts... allowing for larger crop and hydropower production
such policies might also increase the inter-annual variability of resource use... surface water use... while groundwater and energy use would be lower

chunks.text: In Brahmaputra Basin modeling, results indicate that whether future development remains “free of conflict” depends strongly on future precipitation in the basin. The chapter highlights that decreases in precipitation combined with large upstream diversions could prevent downstream Bangladesh from securing enough water to meet desired energy and food production. Trade-offs are illustrated between flood affected area and rice production under precipitation change and upstream diversion scenarios.
supporting_quote: Results indicate that the ability of future development to remain free of conflict hinges mostly on the amount of precipitation falling in the basin in the future.
decreases in precipitation coupled with large upstream diversions... would leave downstream Bangladesh unable to secure enough water to produce their desired energy and food
Precipitation change and Chinese diversion cause tradeoff between FAA and rice production in Bangladesh.

chunks.text: For upper Indus projections, a cited climate-impact study projected a mid-century mean reduction in water supply. The reported estimate is an 8.4% decrease in mean upper Indus discharge for 2046–2065 relative to a 2000–2007 baseline under an A1B SRES scenario. This reduction is linked to downstream implications for irrigation and reservoir storage supporting Pakistan’s agriculture.
supporting_quote: projected a mean 8.4% decrease in the upper Indus water supply for this mid-century scenario
Upstream water supply is crucial to sustaining water storage capacity in Tarbela dam, which in turn regulates the largest irrigation network in the downstream Indus.

chunks.text: The chapter reports an estimate that reduced upstream water availability would translate into fewer people being fed in the Indus basin. Using linkages to irrigation requirements, crop yields, caloric values, and human energy consumption, the cited analysis estimates 26.3 ± 3.0 million fewer people could be fed. The chapter emphasizes that uncertainty is substantial and sensitivity to glacial melt timing is important.
