The paper specifically compares flood extent extraction strategies (AOI, Smallest Extent, Convex Hull) and reports their influence on metrics such as CSI, POD, F1, and FPR across different events and scales.
supporting_quote: We have utilized all the methods of flood extent extraction i.e. Smallest Extent (SE), Convex Hull (CH) and Area of Intereest (AOI)
We tested the influence of data-imbalance on the scores using two inbuilt methods.
This paper demonstrates the impact of data imbalance on the performance scores through the application of SE and CH across difference case studies.

chunks.text: Evaluating model-predicted flood maps is challenging due to the lack of standardized metrics, uncertain model inputs, and limited ground truth. Reported scores can be highly sensitive to the wet/dry pixel ratio (class imbalance), which can inflate true negatives and bias some metrics. These issues complicate comparisons across diverse geographic settings and flood events.
supporting_quote: Numerous challenges exist while evaluating the accuracy of M-FIM... including the lack of standardized evaluation metrics
sensitivity to the ratio of the wet to dry (W/D) pixels, i.e., imbalance between flooded and non-flooded classes
lack of accurate ground truth information

chunks.text: Existing workflows for pixel-based geospatial evaluation often require labor-intensive GIS preprocessing, including aligning rasters and removing permanent water bodies. This manual effort becomes a bottleneck for evaluating many case studies quickly. The paper argues that such barriers hinder scalability for large benchmark databases.
supporting_quote: manual pre-processing of M-FIM and B-FIM (in GIS platforms), removal of permanent water bodies (PWB) for analyses, can be extremely laborious and time-consuming
thus hindering evaluation against a large number of case studies in a short time.

chunks.text: Pixel-based validation depends strongly on how the evaluation domain is defined, especially when benchmark and model rasters have mismatched extents or contain no-data regions. If evaluation is performed over overly large domains dominated by dry pixels, true negatives can dominate and distort some scores. Conversely, restricting the domain can omit over- or under-predicted flooded areas.
supporting_quote: AOI selection relates to: (a) original extents of M-FIM and B-FIM not identical
A large bounding box dominated by dry pixels can inflate the TN, thereby generating biases in the scores.
In some cases of FIM, this method may exclude areas where flooding occurs in one dataset but not in the other

chunks.text: Evaluation tools may miss operationally relevant impact information. The paper notes that NOAA's GVAL computes skill scores but lacks impact-based assessment with building footprints, limiting insights into exposed assets. This motivates adding building-hit evaluation as a complementary assessment layer.
supporting_quote: GVAL lacks the capability for impact-based assessment utilizing building footprints, whereas FIMeval incorporates a dedicated module for building-hit evaluation.
The disaster management authorities are more likely concerned with the impact-based assessment of buildings and transportation

chunks.text: FIMeval evaluates flood maps using pixel-to-pixel comparison between model-predicted (M-FIM) and benchmark (B-FIM) rasters. Both datasets are converted to binary flooded/non-flooded rasters, permanent water bodies are masked, and the rasters are superimposed to create a confusion matrix raster. The confusion matrix raster is then used to compute evaluation metrics and to support building-footprint-based impact analysis.
supporting_quote: FIMeval's underlying principle is based on a pixel-to-pixel comparison between Model-predicted and Benchmark FIMs (M-FIM and B-FIM).
Next, the permanent water bodies (PWB) are eliminated from the binary rasters
binary rasters M-FIM and B-FIM are superimposed and compared against each other to create a confusion matrix raster

chunks.text: The framework implements a seven-step processing chain: reprojection/resampling, binary conversion, area-of-interest selection, permanent-water removal, confusion matrix raster generation, metric calculation, and building-footprint impact analysis. This modular pipeline allows comparison of multiple M-FIMs against one benchmark and supports batch processing across many case studies for consistent evaluation.
supporting_quote: The FIMeval framework processing chain follows the seven steps: (1) Reprojection and Resampling, (2) Conversion to Binary FIM, (3) Selection of Area of Interest, (4) Removal of Permanent Water Bodies, (5) Generation of the Confusion Matrix Raster (6) Calculation of the evaluation metrics (7) Impact analysis using Building Footprints.
FIMeval allows the comparison of multiple M-FIMs... against one benchmark.
support the comparison of multiple case studies at once

chunks.text: For raster alignment, FIMeval reprojects and resamples inputs to a common grid using rasterio and pyproj. For CONUS data, the default target projection is EPSG:5070, and if no resolution is specified, rasters are resampled to the coarsest resolution among inputs. The paper reports that resampling to the coarsest resolution led to only trivial changes in pixel-based statistics (up to the third decimal place).
supporting_quote: For datasets within CONUS, the framework will reproject both B-FIM and M-FIM rasters to EPSG:5070.
If no resolution is provided, the framework will automatically resample all rasters to match the coarsest resolution among them
pixel-based statistics remain consistent, with only trivial variations (up to the third decimal place)

chunks.text: Binary encoding is designed to enable map-algebra-based confusion matrix creation. B-FIM uses flooded=2 and nonflooded=0, while M-FIM uses flooded=2 and non-flooded=1, with no-data optionally represented as 0. Superimposing these layers yields confusion matrix classes mapped to TN, FP, FN, and TP, plus separate classes for PWB and no-data.
supporting_quote: For the B-FIM, the class of flooded pixels is assigned as 2; for the nonflooded pixels, 0.
For the M-FIM, the class of flooded pixels is assigned as 2, and non-flooded pixels as 1.
the final confusion matrix raster generates six distinct classes: PWB: 5; No-Data: 0; TN: 1; FP: 2; FN: 3; TP: 4.

chunks.text: FIMeval offers three strategies for defining the evaluation domain (AOI): user-defined polygon, Smallest Extent (SE), and Convex Hull (CH). SE uses the intersected bounding box of M-FIM and B-FIM to reduce extent mismatch and dry-pixel dominance. CH creates a minimum bounding polygon around benchmark flood pixels by converting flooded pixels to points and generating a convex hull polygon.
supporting_quote: FIMeval offers three strategies for AOI selection
The Smallest Extent (SE): The framework detects the region that is the intersected bounding box among the B-FIM and M-FIMs.
Convex Hull (CH)... will convert all the flood pixels of the B-FIM into vector point features. From these features, the convex hull is automatically generated

chunks.text: Permanent water bodies (PWB) are removed to avoid counting non-flood water as flooded. By default, a pixel is excluded as PWB if more than 50% of it overlaps a user-provided PWB polygon layer. The study uses the ESRI USA Detailed Water Bodies dataset, hosted in an AWS S3 bucket for streamlined access and automated integration.
supporting_quote: PWB needs to be removed to ensure that only flood water is evaluated.
By default... if more than 50 % of a pixel overlaps with the PWB layer, it is considered part of the PWB and excluded
The ESRI USA Detailed Water Bodies dataset... is hosted in an AWS S3 bucket

chunks.text: Evaluation metrics are computed from pixel counts of TN, FP, FN, and TP derived from the confusion matrix raster. The framework supports a broad set of metrics and highlights four used in the paper: FPR, F1, POD, and CSI, with explicit formulas. The paper notes that CSI penalizes false alarms while POD does not.
supporting_quote: A set of evaluation metrics is calculated, including the Accuracy, Precision, Sensitivity, Critical Success Index (CSI)... False Positive Rate (FPR)
For the application shown in this paper, we utilized four metrics: FPR, F1 score, POD, and CSI.
The metric POD does not penalize the false alarms, whereas the metric CSI penalizes the false alarms.

chunks.text: Impact-based evaluation overlays building footprints with the confusion matrix raster to quantify building hits and spatial agreement. FIMeval uses the Microsoft building footprint dataset and can also ingest user-provided building vectors; it can automate footprint extraction using the msfootprint PySpark-based engine. The Building Deviation Ratio (BDR) is defined to compare building hits between M-FIM and B-FIM.
supporting_quote: Using a building footprint layer, FIMeval can calculate the number of buildings impacted by B-FIM.
FIMeval employs the 'msfootprint' framework... which optimizes building footprint extraction through a PySpark-based computational engine.
The Building Deviation Ratio (BDR) measures how well an M-FIM captures building hit compared to the B-FIM (Eq. (1)).

chunks.text: The benchmarking database used with FIMeval is organized into four quality tiers spanning remote sensing and synthetic model products. Tier 1 includes hand-labelled 40 cm rasters from NOAA Emergency Response Imagery. Tier 2 and Tier 3 use Planet and Sentinel-1 flood maps with a gap-filled algorithm, and Tier 4 includes 10 m synthetic flood maps from FEMA BLE at HUC-8 scale.
supporting_quote: The Benchmarking FIM Database consists of four tiers of benchmark FIM
Tier 1 FIM includes the hand-labelled rasters generated from NOAA's Emergency Response Imagery with a resolution of 40 cm.
Tier 4 features the synthetic FIM from FEMA's BLE with a spatial resolution of 10 m on HUC-8 scale.

chunks.text: For observed flooding, the paper evaluates Hurricane Matthew impacts along the Neuse River, North Carolina, using Planet-based high-resolution benchmark flood maps for Oct 9, 10, 14, and 15, 2016. These Planet flood maps were enhanced by gap-filling using a hydrologically guided region-growth algorithm and a high-resolution DEM. The model-predicted maps for comparison are produced using NOAA OWP HAND-FIM.
supporting_quote: flooding in the Neuse River, North Carolina, US... due to Hurricane Matthew in October 2016.
Planet satellite extracted from the FIM database (Tier 2) were utilized for 9th, 10th, 14th, and October 15, 2016.
gaps... were filled with a hydrologically guided region-growth algorithm incorporating high-resolution DEM

chunks.text: A second historical case uses the 2016 Midwest flood on the Arkansas River with a very high resolution (40 cm) benchmark derived from NOAA Emergency Response Imagery. Multiple image classification algorithms were tested and then an expert GIS analyst manually corrected the map to produce a high-quality benchmark. The candidate M-FIM is generated using NWM discharge during the flood period and the OWP HAND-FIM workflow.
supporting_quote: The second case study considered the 2016 Midwest flood that occurred on the Arkansas River (FIM Database Tier 1).
generate the final high-quality benchmark flood map of 40 cm
For the generation of the M-FIM, we used the NWM discharge corresponding to the flood period and generated a series of flood maps.

chunks.text: Synthetic benchmarks come from FEMA Base Level Engineering (BLE) flood maps provided at HUC-8 watershed scale. The study uses publicly available BLE 100-year (S1) and 500-year (S2) flood maps and associated streamflow for FEMA Region 6, covering 45 HUC-8 watersheds. OWP HAND-FIM is generated for the same watersheds for comparison.
supporting_quote: The FEMA BLE simulation results are provided at HUC-8 watershed scales.
we used publicly available BLE 100-year and 500-year synthetic flood maps and the associated streamflow data for FEMA Region 6
We generated OWP HAND-FIM for 45 HUC-8 watersheds, for S1 and S2 scenarios

chunks.text: Model-predicted flood maps are produced using OWP HAND-FIM and generated through the FIMserv toolset. The workflow identifies HUC-8 boundaries, extracts NWM retrospective streamflow linked to river IDs from hydrofabrics, and uses hydrofabric attributes such as HAND/REM rasters and hydraulic parameters to map discharge to inundation at 10 m resolution.
supporting_quote: We used the OWP HAND-FIM 'as a service' (FIMserv... )... to generate the model-predicted flood maps (M-FIM).
extracting the NWM retrospective streamflow data linked to the unique 'River-IDs' from the FIM' hydro fabrics.'
Using the NWM streamflow data, flood inundation maps are generated at a spatial resolution of 10 m.

chunks.text: For masking permanent water bodies, the study uses the ESRI USA Detailed Water Bodies dataset for CONUS and integrates it via AWS S3. For impact analysis, the paper uses the Microsoft building footprint dataset under the Open Data Commons Open Database License, with optional automation via GEE global buildings or user-provided building vectors.
supporting_quote: The ESRI USA Detailed Water Bodies dataset... is used in this study.
The mentioned PWB shapefile... is hosted in an AWS S3 bucket
The Microsoft building footprint dataset is used under the Open Data Commons Open Database License

chunks.text: On the 2016 Midwest flood case, FIMeval produced performance scores broadly consistent with NOAA's GVAL while reducing total elapsed time. GVAL took 127.68 s after manual GIS preprocessing, whereas FIMeval took 100.33 s including reprojection, resampling, PWB removal, and output generation. POD was ~0.710 for GVAL and ~0.709 for FIMeval-AOI, and CSI was 0.637 vs 0.634, indicating similar detection skill.
supporting_quote: The total computational time of GVAL... was around 127.68 s. However, for FIMeval, the total elapsed time took 100.33 s
Both frameworks exhibit a similar true positive rate, with Probability of Detection (POD) remaining consistent at around 71 %
GVAL... CSI (0.637)... FIMeval-AOI (0.634)

chunks.text: For the Midwest flood, evaluation domain choices influenced some metrics, especially those involving true negatives. FIMeval-SE produced a much lower FPR (0.035) compared to GVAL (0.107) and FIMeval-AOI (0.105), which the paper attributes to increased true negatives in the selected domain. CSI and F1 also changed modestly across AOI, SE, and CH methods, demonstrating sensitivity to extent delineation.
supporting_quote: a significant change in the FPR is observed for FIMeval-SE (0.035)
GVAL (0.107), FIMeval-AOI (0.105), and FIMeval-CH (0.108)
Since FPR is calculated as FP/(FP + TN), a higher TN count reduces the overall ratio.

chunks.text: In the Midwest flood building-impact analysis, the candidate M-FIM slightly underpredicted benchmark building hits. The Building Deviation Ratio (BDR) was −0.05, corresponding to about 5% fewer buildings impacted by M-FIM relative to B-FIM. Using building hit/miss statistics, the paper reports CSI=0.34, FAR=0.472, and POD=0.49 for the building-level assessment.
supporting_quote: underpredicts the benchmark (B-FIM)... by 5 % (BDR = − 0.05).
Considering the building hit/ miss statistics, the scores of CSI, FAR, and POD were estimated as 0.34, 0.472, and 0.49, respectively.

chunks.text: For Hurricane Matthew benchmarks on four dates, CH versus SE produced noticeable differences in pixel-based scores. Across dates, the CH method showed an average 7.7% difference compared to SE in CSI, POD, and F1. Including FPR, mean differences were 10.92% (Oct 9), 11.88% (Oct 10), 14.50% (Oct 14), and 2.73% (Oct 15), highlighting the sensitivity of evaluation outcomes to domain extraction.
supporting_quote: On average, the CH method demonstrated a 7.7 % difference compared to SE in CSI, POD, and F1 scores across all four dates.
When including FPR, the mean difference was 10.92 % on October 9th, 11.88 % on October 10th, 14.50 % on October 14th, and 2.73 % on October 15th.

chunks.text: For Hurricane Matthew, CH reduced false positive rate substantially compared with SE. The paper reports an average FPR reduction of about 24.6% across dates, with the largest reduction on Oct 14 (48% decrease). Despite these changes, POD remained unchanged between CH and SE, implying the same TP and FN counts while FP and TN varied with the domain definition.
supporting_quote: The overall reduction in the FPR with the CH method averaged approximately 24.6 % across all the dates.
The most significant reduction in FPR was observed on October 14th, with a decrease of 48 %
the POD values remained unchanged regardless of the methods employed.

chunks.text: Hurricane Matthew building-impact results varied by date and method, with mostly negative BDR indicating underprediction of exposed buildings by the model. Table 3 reports BDR(SE) values of −0.729, 1.246, −0.974, and −0.833 for Oct 9, 10, 14, and 15, respectively, and BDR(CH) values of −0.856, 1.189, −0.977, and −0.833. The peak flood date (Oct 10) was an exception where M-FIM overpredicted building hits (positive BDR).
supporting_quote: The negative BDR indicates that for most dates, the number of buildings detected by M-FIM underpredicts
an exception was observed on October 10th, where M-FIM detected a high number of building hits

chunks.text: Pixel-based building hit/miss agreement for Hurricane Matthew was low, indicating poor spatial match between predicted and benchmark building impacts. The paper reports very low scores (CSI/POD/F1 range about 0.02–0.39) across dates. The highest values occur on Oct 10, with CSI 0.141 (SE) vs 0.144 (CH) and F1 0.246 (SE) vs 0.25 (CH), while POD showed no change between methods.
supporting_quote: estimated scores were very low (0.02–0.39) for all the mentioned dates, highlighting poor agreement with B-FIM
F1 Score (0.246 (SE); 0.25 (CH))... no change was observed in the POD

chunks.text: For the 45 HUC-8 synthetic BLE comparisons, CH and SE produced nearly identical performance, indicating limited sensitivity to domain method at large watershed scales. The overall difference between CH and SE was about 0.31% for the 100-year scenario (S1) and 0.32% for the 500-year scenario (S2). FPR values ranged from 0.002 to 0.073, suggesting false positives had minimal influence on overall performance.
supporting_quote: The overall difference between CH and SE was estimated as 0.31 % for S1 and 0.32 % for S2
The values of the FPR differ from a minimum of 0.002 to a maximum of 0.073
magnitudes of the FPR values are remarkably low, which indicates that the false positives have a minimal impact

chunks.text: Across HUC-8 watersheds, OWP HAND-FIM achieved moderate to high pixel-based accuracy against BLE for both scenarios. The paper reports CSI and F1 ranges of roughly 0.4 to 0.89, with slightly higher medians for the 500-year scenario (S2). CH produced small improvements (e.g., CSI +0.59% in S1 and +0.63% in S2), while POD was least influenced by the method and yielded the same TP counts.
supporting_quote: The values of all the scores except FPR range from 0.4 to 0.89
median values were increased for S2
Both methods yielded the same number of TP, irrespective of the methods employed.

chunks.text: Computational timing for Hurricane Matthew indicates tradeoffs between SE and CH evaluation domains. Table 4 shows SE times of 70–91 s with 4.4–7.7 million pixels, while CH times were 89–96 s with fewer pixels (1.5–3.4 million), reflecting overhead from geometry creation despite reduced pixel counts. The paper also reports about 4 min 2 s for building footprint assessment for the case study.
supporting_quote: Computational Time (secs) (SE) ... 70 ... 91
Computational Time (secs) (CH) ... 89 ... 96
it took around 4 min and 2 s to assess the building statistics

chunks.text: Both automatic evaluation-domain methods have limitations tied to flood geometry and can bias results. SE (intersection of bounding boxes) can omit areas flooded in only one dataset, potentially neglecting overprediction or underprediction. CH can overgeneralize by ignoring concavities in flood shapes, such as meandering rivers or floodplains with indentations, which may affect accuracy metrics.
supporting_quote: In some cases of FIM, this method may exclude areas where flooding occurs in one dataset but not in the other
The CH ignores concavities in flood shapes (e.g., meandering rivers or floodplains with indentations), thereby overgeneralizing the true extent.
This simplification may affect accuracy metrics.

chunks.text: Impact-based evaluation using only total building counts can be misleading because similar counts may correspond to different spatial flood extents. The paper addresses this by overlaying building footprints on the confusion matrix raster to obtain spatially explicit building hit/miss statistics. Even with this, building-impact metrics depend on settlement patterns and building density, affecting interpretability across regions.
supporting_quote: identical building counts may sometimes correspond to spatially different B-FIM and M-FIM flood extents.
FIMeval also supports a pixel-based evaluation approach that overlays the building footprints dataset onto the confusion matrix raster.
pixel-based building hit/miss statistics are influenced by multiple factors including the type of settlement area (urban, suburban, rural), building density

chunks.text: Pixel-based evaluation metrics can be biased by class imbalance between flooded and non-flooded pixels, especially when large dry areas inflate true negatives. The paper highlights that domain selection interacts with this imbalance and recommends metrics that are independent of true negatives (CSI, POD, F1) for more reliable comparisons when AOI is uncertain. It also notes a lack of standards for selecting and interpreting these metrics in FIM evaluation.
supporting_quote: Flood extent comparison suffers from imbalances between dry and wet pixels. A large bounding box dominated by dry pixels can inflate the TN
metrics such as CSI, POD, and F1 Score, which are independent of true negatives, may be less affected by large dry areas
There is a lack of standards for utilizing these metrics.

chunks.text: The building-footprint processing stack introduces practical deployment constraints. FIMeval’s msfootprint uses a PySpark-based engine for parallel footprint extraction, but the paper notes compatibility issues on Windows, where PySpark may not function as on macOS or Linux. This limits out-of-the-box portability for some users.
supporting_quote: FIMeval employs the 'msfootprint' framework... through a PySpark-based computational engine.
the PySpark library often encounters compatibility challenges on Windows systems and may not function properly as it does on macOS or LinuxOS.

chunks.text: The paper emphasizes that pixel-based statistics alone may not capture true flooding impact and can lead to incomplete interpretations. It argues for additional impact-based assessment and suggests that object-based evaluation could reduce biases of traditional pixel-level comparisons. The authors plan to incorporate object-based strategies in future versions of FIMeval.
supporting_quote: evaluating FIM solely based on these statistical metrics may not generate a comprehensive understanding of the actual flooding impact.
additional evaluation of FIM based on impact-based assessment is necessary.
We plan to incorporate an object-based FIM evaluation strategy into future versions of FIMeval

chunks.text: OWP HAND-FIM predictions used in demonstrations have known structural limitations that can cause over- or underprediction of flood extents. The paper notes that the approach is largely static and that 10 m DEMs miss detailed channel geometry and bathymetry, which can overpredict inundation. Errors are also linked to reach-averaged slope and Manning roughness used in discharge-to-stage calculations.
supporting_quote: This model mostly represents a static flow, unlike the hydraulic models
The 10 m resolution DEMs currently used in inundation mapping do not capture detailed channel geometry... can lead to overpredictions of inundation extent.
two other major contributors to FIM extent error are the reach-averaged slope and the roughness coefficient used in Manning's equation.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that FIMeval provides a modular, open-source framework for scalable evaluation of flood inundation maps across diverse benchmarks and case studies. It automates key preprocessing (reprojection/resampling, PWB removal) and supports both pixel-based and building-impact-based analyses. The framework is available as a Python package, Jupyter notebook, and ArcGIS Pro toolbox to broaden usability.
supporting_quote: We present a novel framework for the evaluation of Flood Inundation Maps (FIM). The framework, FIMeval, streamlines evaluation procedures for a large number of case studies
Apart from the statistical analysis of the flooded pixels using the confusion matrix, FIMeval also offers an evaluation procedure based on building impact.
FIMeval is currently available as (a) a Python package, (b) a Jupyter notebook, and (c) an ArcGIS Pro Toolbox.

chunks.text: A central takeaway is that pixel-based FIM performance metrics are highly sensitive to the evaluation extent, especially for historical floods. The paper reports that CH versus SE produced about 7.7% differences for historical benchmarks, while differences were only about 0.3% for simulated HUC-8-scale benchmarks. This indicates that domain definition has a larger effect when flood extents are localized or fragmented.
supporting_quote: significant differences in the scores were observed while applying the two methods, Convex Hull (CH) and Smallest Extent (SE).
overall difference... with CH was estimated to be approximately 7.7 % compared to SE, for the historical benchmarks.
For the simulated benchmarks, the rate of change of CH with respect to SE was only about 0.3 % on average.

chunks.text: The authors conclude that combining pixel-based and impact-based assessments is necessary for more comprehensive evaluation. They recommend using AOI when the true flood domain is known and favor metrics less sensitive to dry-area dominance (CSI, POD, F1) when SE/CH must be used. Planned enhancements include integrating the benchmark database, linking with FIMserv, and incorporating evaluation strategies that exclude enhancement-algorithm flooded pixels.
supporting_quote: Among the available approaches, the method 'AOI' is the most accurate as it clearly distinguishes between flooded and non-flooded pixels.
Metrics such as CSI, POD, and F1 Score, which are independent of true negatives, may be less affected by large dry areas
Future work also involves linking FIMeval with FIMserv

chunks.text: Seasonal mountain snow is a major source of water supply, especially in the western United States, and changes in climate have reduced available snow-derived water. Because runoff and water management depend on knowing snow conditions, there is strong motivation to measure snowpack accurately at basin scales. Existing monitoring networks provide valuable data but do not fully represent complex mountain terrain and its heterogeneity.
supporting_quote: The majority of the water supply for many western US states is derived from seasonal snowmelt in mountainous regions.
over the last century, much of the West has observed decreasing available water from snow, and more rapidly over the past 20 years

chunks.text: In situ monitoring via SNOTEL is widespread but sparse relative to mountainous snow-covered areas, limiting spatial representativeness. Station observations can differ from surrounding-area means and vary in accuracy across accumulation and melt seasons. Basin-scale snow distribution is affected by terrain, wind, and canopy, and may deviate from Gaussian behavior in certain periods or terrains.
supporting_quote: nearly 900 snow telemetry (SNOTEL) in situ monitoring sites throughout the western US
there is, on average, one SNOTEL site per approximately 4000 km2 of potential snow-covered area
station measurements often did not align with mean values from surrounding areas

chunks.text: Airborne lidar can map snow depth at high resolution by differencing snow-on and snow-free DEMs, but repeat acquisitions are costly and constrained by weather, and performance can diminish under forest canopy or shallow snow. A practical alternative is to acquire snow-free lidar once to derive static terrain features and combine those with sparse snow depth point measurements for estimation across a basin. Citizen-scientist observations can provide low-cost point measurements, but safe collection methods are necessary in avalanche-prone terrain.
supporting_quote: By subtracting a baseline snow-free DEM from a lidar-derived snow-on DEM, the resulting difference between the two precisely measures the snow depth
The financial costs of lidar instrumentation and acquisition, especially for repeat or large-area surveys, also pose a significant constraint.
it is imperative to develop sampling methods in remote regions that address and protect the safety of the individuals collecting data.

chunks.text: The study aims to rapidly generate high-resolution, basin-scale snow depth estimates by combining sparse snow probe measurements with static terrain features derived from a single snow-free lidar acquisition. A central design requirement is reducing danger to field personnel by selecting sampling locations that minimize exposure to avalanche terrain. The approach is intended to be low-cost and scalable, potentially leveraging citizen-scientist measurements.
supporting_quote: generate basin-scale snow depth estimates using a multistep, Gaussian-based machine learning model that combines snow probe depth measurements with static lidar terrain features from a single snow-free date
focus on reducing personnel danger by modifying the algorithm to minimize the exposure of field sample collectors to avalanche-prone terrain

chunks.text: A key objective is to validate whether the model is universal across subbasins with differing spatial characteristics when only a limited number of in situ measurements are available. The authors test performance across multiple subbasins and compare optimized sampling to random sampling. They also examine sensitivity to the number of sampling locations.
supporting_quote: validate the model's universality by sampling separate subbasins with differing spatial characteristics using a limited number of in situ measurements
We also investigate how the number of sampling locations affects model accuracy by testing sparse measurements (e.g., 10 sites) against a more extensive dataset (e.g., 100 sites).

chunks.text: Another objective is to estimate snow depth beyond the subbasin where samples are collected, including using training sites outside the modeled basin. The work evaluates whether sparse subbasin samples can provide accurate basin-scale estimates. This explicitly targets the point-to-basin representativeness problem.
supporting_quote: investigate the accuracy of basin-scale estimation beyond a smaller sampling domain with sparse sampling locations both within and outside of the modeled basin
we apply the validated model to estimate snow depth across the larger Franklin Basin, using sampling sites from selected subbasins

chunks.text: The study tests whether excluding high-avalanche-risk terrain from the sampling candidate set affects snow depth estimation accuracy. The authors create feature spaces both including and excluding avalanche-prone cells and compare downstream prediction performance. This is intended to demonstrate a safety-preserving sampling strategy without large accuracy penalties.
supporting_quote: determine if estimation accuracy is affected by the exclusion of high-avalanche-risk terrain when selecting measurement locations.
we explore the impact of excluding avalanche-prone terrain from the sampling locations (Objective iii).

chunks.text: Basin-scale snow depth estimation is difficult because mountainous basins have strong heterogeneity in elevation, slope, aspect, vegetation, and wind exposure, all influencing snow distribution. Point observations may not represent surrounding terrain well, especially across accumulation and melt seasons. This makes both accurate modeling and representative sampling challenging.
supporting_quote: Accurately representing basin-scale (30–200 km2) snowpack is challenging due to scale and geographic heterogeneity.
A single basin can exhibit broad slope, elevation, and land cover differences, all influencing snow distribution.

chunks.text: Existing in situ monitoring is too sparse to capture mountain snow variability at relevant scales. The paper notes that SNOTEL sites are widely used for forecasts but their density is low relative to snow-covered area, motivating additional observations and methods to provide continuous spatial estimates.
supporting_quote: Within the contiguous US, there is, on average, one SNOTEL site per approximately 4000 km2 of potential snow-covered area
The low density of sites highlights the need for additional observations or techniques to produce an accurate and continuous snowpack estimate.

chunks.text: Remote sensing alternatives have limitations: SNODAS is coarse and can be inaccurate in complex or forested terrain, while repeated snow-on lidar is expensive and operationally constrained by weather. These constraints limit near-real-time or frequent mapping across seasons at low cost. The study therefore targets a method that depends on one snow-free lidar acquisition plus sparse field measurements.
supporting_quote: SNODAS and similar products have their limitations, including a relatively coarse spatial resolution (1 km)
The financial costs of lidar instrumentation and acquisition, especially for repeat or large-area surveys, also pose a significant constraint.

chunks.text: Collecting snow depth samples in remote terrain can expose observers to avalanche risk, and most avalanche fatalities occur in uncontrolled terrain due to human triggering. This creates a need for sampling designs that avoid or minimize time spent in avalanche-prone areas while still producing representative observations. The paper operationalizes this safety challenge by excluding slopes at or above a threshold angle from candidate sampling locations.
supporting_quote: access to remote sampling locations often can require a researcher or recreationist to travel in, under, or above avalanche terrain
Nearly all avalanche fatalities occur in remote, uncontrolled terrain
Cells with a slope angle of 30° or greater are defined as having potential avalanche risk.

chunks.text: The workflow is a two-step machine learning approach. First, an unsupervised Gaussian mixture model (GMM) selects physiographically representative sampling locations using snow-free lidar-derived features. Second, a supervised Gaussian process regression (GPR) model predicts gridded snow depth across the domain using point snow depth measurements at those sites and the same static features.
supporting_quote: we apply a multistep, Gaussian-based machine learning algorithm
using an unsupervised Gaussian mixture model (GMM) to identify sampling locations
We model basin snow depth distribution throughout the study domain by applying a Gaussian process regression (GPR) model

chunks.text: The GMM represents the feature space as a mixture of K Gaussian clusters with mixing coefficients and parameters fit via Expectation-Maximization. The authors run multiple random initializations and select the best solution by maximizing the log-marginal likelihood, using spherical covariance and subsampling for efficiency. Cluster centers are mapped to real grid cells using a nearest-neighbor ball-tree search in feature space.
supporting_quote: The EM algorithm iteratively adjusts parameters for the mixture of components until it arrives at a maximization of the log-likelihood function
we run a grid search of randomized algorithm initializations with either 10 or 50 restarts
For each cluster center defined by the GMM, a ball-tree nearestneighbor search method is applied

chunks.text: Sampling effort is constrained to 10 locations so a small team can collect data in a single day. To assess sensitivity to training data size, the model is also executed with increasing numbers of clusters from 5 up to 100. Comparisons are made between optimized locations from the GMM and randomly selected locations.
supporting_quote: We defined the total number of clusters (sampling sites) as 10
we run the model initially with five clusters and increase the number of clusters with each iteration to 100
compare the accuracy of snow depth estimates obtained from optimally located sites versus those from randomly selected sites

chunks.text: Avalanche-prone terrain is operationally defined using slope angle, with cells at or above 30° flagged as potential risk and optionally excluded from the candidate sampling domain. The GMM is run twice—once including and once excluding these cells—and if an excluded risky location is selected in nearest-neighbor mapping, the next most similar safe neighbor is used instead. Avalanche cells can be reinstated during gridded prediction for evaluation against lidar.
supporting_quote: Cells with a slope angle of 30° or greater are defined as having potential avalanche risk.
We run the GMM twice for each feature space: once including cells defined as avalanche-prone and once excluding them.
When avalanche terrain is excluded, the next most similar neighbor is selected instead

chunks.text: The GPR model uses topographic and canopy-related predictors and an RBF (squared exponential) kernel, with the length-scale selected by grid search to maximize log-marginal likelihood. The method is designed to work with minimal training data and to output a probabilistic function relating features to snow depth. Training uses field probe depths in Hell’s Kitchen Canyon and lidar-derived point depths as synthetic samples in other domains.
supporting_quote: We use a radial basis function (RBF) (also referred to as a Gaussian or squared exponential covariance function)
we perform a grid search across a range of [0.01, 1] ... maximizes the log-marginal likelihood.
In Hell's Kitchen Canyon, field-measured snow depths from 10 locations are used as training data
lidar-derived snow depths at the GMM-identified locations are used to train the GPR model

chunks.text: Model performance is evaluated against lidar-derived snow depth maps using bias and error metrics and distribution similarity. The paper reports mean bias error (MBE), root mean squared error (RMSE), and Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE) to capture correlation, variability, and bias. A Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic is also used to compare estimated and reference snow depth distributions.
supporting_quote: The standard mean bias error (MBE) ... and root mean squared error (RMSE) metrics are used
Additionally, we report the Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE) score
we define distribution similarity using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) test to define the KS statistic (D)

chunks.text: The study area is Franklin Basin on the Utah–Idaho border, including three subbasins (Hell’s Kitchen Canyon, Boss Canyon, Peterson Hollow). Franklin Basin spans 72 km² with elevations from 2115 to 2940 m, while subbasins are about 7.7–9.3 km². The paper also quantifies the proportion of avalanche terrain in each domain.
supporting_quote: The limits of the study span an area within the Bear River Range
Hell's Kitchen Canyon | 8.9        | 2077        | 2830        | 2400         | 9.7

chunks.text: Snow-free airborne lidar was collected in fall 2020 using an Optech Galaxy T2000 and Prime, with about 10.1 points per square meter and stated absolute vertical accuracy of < 0.03–0.25 m RMSE. DEM and DSM rasters were derived and typically upscaled from 1.5 m to 50 m to reduce computational demand. Terrain features including slope, aspect-derived northness/eastness, canopy height, and wind shelter were computed and normalized.
supporting_quote: We collected snow-free lidar data of the Franklin Basin in the fall of 2020.
An average flight density of 10.1 points per square meter was captured with a stated sensor absolute vertical accuracy of < 0.03–0.25 m RMSE
upscaled the resolution from its native resolution of 1.5 to a 50 m grid cell size
we extract the physiographic parameters of slope, aspect, and canopy height
we normalize the physiographic features from 0 to 1 with a min-max scaler

chunks.text: A snow-on lidar survey was flown on 28 March 2021, and snow depth was computed by subtracting the bare-earth DEM from the snow-on DEM. The resulting basin snow depth was approximately normally distributed, with mean 1.28 m and standard deviation 0.44 m. Snow-on lidar did not cover Hell’s Kitchen Canyon due to flight constraints.
supporting_quote: On 28 March 2021 ... the flight crew collected snow-on lidar data
developed a snow depth TIFF for the basin by raster subtracting the bare-earth DEM from the snow-on DEM
mean depth of 1.28 m and a standard deviation of 0.44 m.
Due to flight pattern constraints, snowon lidar was not captured for the Hell's Kitchen area.

chunks.text: A field snow depth survey was conducted in Hell’s Kitchen Canyon on 28 March 2021 at the 10 GMM-identified locations. Two researchers navigated to the coordinates with a handheld Garmin inReach GPS and used graduated probes. Each researcher took four measurements per site, and the average of eight measurements was recorded as the site depth.
supporting_quote: two researchers conducted a snow survey of the Hell's Kitchen Canyon study subbasin
The researchers reached the 10 locations at coordinates retrieved via a handheld Garmin inReach GPS device.
Each researcher took four measurements ... and recorded the average of the eight measurements.

chunks.text: Dataset handling differed by domain: Franklin Basin, Boss Canyon, and Peterson Hollow rasters were upscaled to 50 m for efficiency, while Hell’s Kitchen Canyon retained 1.5 m resolution to guide field sampling. The paper summarizes inputs as lidar snow depth, DEM/DSM, and in situ probe depths (10 sites) and clarifies coverage differences among domains.
supporting_quote: In Franklin Basin, Boss Canyon, and Peterson Hollow, raster data were upscaled to improve computational efficiency.
Hell's Kitchen Canyon raster data were maintained at 1.5 m for accurate locating of physical sampling locations.
In situ snow depth | Manual probes  | Point-based (10 sites)       | Hell's Kitchen Canyon

chunks.text: Within-subbasin validation showed that GMM-optimized sampling locations consistently outperformed random sampling for snow depth estimation. With 10 optimized sites, RMSE was 0.37 m in Boss Canyon and 0.19 m in Peterson Hollow, compared to 0.43 m and 0.33 m using 10 random sites. Across scenarios, modeled snow depth was slightly underestimated on average.
supporting_quote: With 10 training sites optimally located by the GMM, the snow depth estimate results in RMSEs of 0.37 and 0.19 m for Boss Canyon and Peterson Hollow, compared to 0.43 and 0.33 m for random sites
For each scenario, modeled snow depth was slightly underestimated.

chunks.text: Increasing the number of optimized sites from 10 to 100 produced only modest improvements in subbasin accuracy, indicating diminishing returns relative to the additional sampling effort. For Boss Canyon, RMSE improved from 0.37 m (10 GMM) to 0.31 m (100 GMM) when avalanche terrain was included. For Peterson Hollow, RMSE changed from 0.19 m (10 GMM) to 0.18 m (100 GMM).
supporting_quote: The resulting estimate is only slightly improved when increased to 100 optimally located sites.
Boss Canyon     | 10 | (GMM)    | 0.37
Boss Canyon     | 100 | (GMM)    | 0.31
Peterson Hollow | 10 | (GMM)    | 0.19
Peterson Hollow | 100 | (GMM)    | 0.18

chunks.text: Random sampling could perform substantially worse than optimized sampling even when many more points were used. In Boss Canyon, 100 random sites increased RMSE to 0.66 m, worse than 10 optimized sites. In Peterson Hollow, 100 random sites improved over 10 random sites but still did not match 10 optimized sites (0.28 m vs 0.19 m RMSE).
supporting_quote: Boss Canyon     | 100 | (Random) | 0.66
Boss Canyon     | 10 | (GMM)    | 0.37
Peterson Hollow | 100 | (Random) | 0.28
Peterson Hollow | 10 | (GMM)    | 0.19

chunks.text: Excluding avalanche-prone terrain from the candidate sampling domain had minimal impact on subbasin-scale estimation. In Boss Canyon, excluding high-risk cells increased RMSE by 2.7% for 10 training locations and reduced KGE from 0.54 to 0.47. In Peterson Hollow, excluding avalanche terrain increased RMSE by 11% for 10 sites and reduced KGE, but the model remained robust when increasing to 100 sites.
supporting_quote: When the high-risk cells are excluded ... for Boss Canyon, the RMSE ... increases by 2.7 % ... KGE is slightly reduced from 0.54 to 0.47.
For the 10 sites within Peterson Hollow ... the subbasin estimate RMSE expresses an increase of 11 %

chunks.text: The approach successfully estimated snow depth across the larger Franklin Basin using training sites from subbasins, demonstrating extrapolation beyond the sampling region. With 10 sites and excluding avalanche terrain, basin-scale RMSE was 0.34 m for Franklin Basin sampling, 0.37 m for Boss Canyon sampling, 0.45 m for Hell’s Kitchen Canyon sampling, and values were stated as similar within 28%. KGE ranged from 0.39 (Hell’s Kitchen) to 0.59 (Peterson Hollow) in these basin-scale scenarios.
supporting_quote: Expanding the estimation domain beyond the smaller subbasin sampling spatial bounds results in effective snow depth modeling at the greater basin scale.
For the Franklin Basin sampling instance ... RMSE of 0.34 m ... KGE of 0.72.
Boss Canyon providing the lowest RMSE (0.37 m) ... Hell's Kitchen Canyon providing the largest (0.45 m).
Hell's Kitchen Canyon also provides the lowest KGE (0.39), while Peterson Hollow maintains the highest (0.59).

chunks.text: Distribution similarity analyses showed that some subbasin-trained estimates matched the basin snow depth distribution better than others, even when RMSE differed. Hell’s Kitchen Canyon had a relatively low KS statistic (DHK = 0.13), close to the Franklin Basin-trained estimate (DFB = 0.10). Boss Canyon had the greatest mismatch in distribution (DBC = 0.28) and showed overestimation in the distribution plot.
supporting_quote: The Hell's Kitchen Canyon estimated snow depth exhibits a DHK of 0.13
only the Franklin Basin derived estimate is more similar ... with DFB = 0.10
the greatest KS statistic of DBC = 0.28

chunks.text: Across subbasin-to-basin estimates, error tended to increase with elevation, indicating that higher-elevation areas were harder to predict accurately from limited sampling. The paper notes this trend explicitly and visualizes it in elevation-binned error distributions. This suggests remaining sensitivity to elevation-driven processes and representativeness of the training domain.
supporting_quote: For all subbasin estimates, errors increase with elevation (Fig. 10).
Estimate variance is greater, particularly at higher elevations

chunks.text: The focus on 10 sampling sites reflects practical constraints: increasing the number or spatial range of sites can make it infeasible to collect measurements in a single day, and rapid collection is needed before melt or new accumulation changes the snowpack. The authors observed incremental performance variation when adding sites but no large improvements beyond 10 in overall trends. They hypothesize the optimal number of sites depends on basin size and complexity and leave determining lower bounds to future work.
supporting_quote: increasing the number or spatial range of sites makes it infeasible for a group of samplers to collect snow depth samples in a single day.
The ability to collect data quickly is critical to accurately representing the snowpack before changes occur
increasing the number of points did not significantly improve model performance over a smaller sample, such as 10

chunks.text: Sensor and measurement uncertainty may be nontrivial relative to the snow depth in the region. The lidar’s specified accuracy range could affect comparisons, and the Hell’s Kitchen Canyon scenario adds potential probe measurement errors because it trains on field data but validates against lidar. The authors note that synthetic sampling (lidar-to-lidar) in other domains reduces additional uncertainty, and they call for further validation with diverse lidar sources and ground-truth datasets.
supporting_quote: stated sensor absolute vertical accuracy of < 0.03–0.25 m RMSE
errors in lidar data or in the depth probe measurements may lead to biases in the overall snow depth estimate.
Further research should involve validating the model with diverse lidar sources and additional ground-truth datasets

chunks.text: Avalanche terrain identification is simplified to a 30° slope threshold, but real avalanche hazard can extend beyond this definition due to runout zones and propagation into lower-angle terrain. The paper cautions that in steeper, more complex regions the safe sampling domain may be much smaller than in Franklin Basin, potentially reducing performance. Future work is proposed to test the method in additional steep terrain to find limits of exclusion.
supporting_quote: Cells with a slope angle of 30° or greater are defined as having potential avalanche risk.
Avalanches may run out to flatter areas beyond the risk terrain analyzed in this study or may propagate horizontally to areas of slope angles below the threshold.
Future work will aim to apply the model to additional regions of steep terrain

chunks.text: Model performance depends on similarity between the sampling domain and estimation domain feature spaces. Hell’s Kitchen Canyon canopy height distribution differed notably, attributed to resolution differences: Hell’s Kitchen retained higher resolution while other domains were upscaled, likely affecting feature variance and performance. The authors posit that uniform resolution could make feature spaces more analogous and improve results.
supporting_quote: Hell's Kitchen Canyon's canopy height distribution appears very dissimilar to the other canopy distributions.
This is due to the spatial resolution difference between Hell's Kitchen Canyon and the other domains.
we posit that with uniform resolution, the feature space would present more analogous to Franklin Basin's and thus improve results.

chunks.text: The study’s modeling assumptions and evaluation scope are constrained: the target snow depth distribution was near-Gaussian on the study date, aligning with GPR assumptions, but non-Gaussian snow distributions occur in other environments. The analysis is performed for a single date near the end of the season, and the authors state that more dates—especially after accumulation events—are needed to test temporal robustness and transferability to different snow climates.
supporting_quote: The snow distribution of Franklin Basin at the time of sampling presented as near-Gaussian
Application of the model in more diverse snow environments ... is needed to understand transferability
this study is performed for a single date towards the end of the snow season. More sampling dates and periods throughout the snow season

chunks.text: The paper concludes that a low-cost workflow combining one-time snow-off lidar-derived physiographic features with a small number of point snow depth measurements can produce accurate, high-resolution snow depth maps at subbasin and basin scales. The two-step approach uses a GMM to locate representative sampling sites and a GPR to generate gridded estimates. With about 10 optimized samples, the method remained effective and supports rapid surveys and potential citizen-science contributions.
supporting_quote: we introduce a methodology leveraging physiographic features derived from one-time-captured snow-off lidar and a small number of in situ sampling points to generate region-scale snow depth estimates
First, a Gaussian mixture model is used to locate optimal sampling locations
used to train a Gaussian process regression algorithm to estimate broadscale snow depths.
We find that with few (i.e., 10) optimized sampling points, the model is effective

chunks.text: A key conclusion is that excluding avalanche-prone terrain from sampling site selection does not substantially degrade estimation performance, allowing safer field campaigns. The authors report minimal performance loss when high-risk terrain is removed, supporting the goal of reducing personnel danger. This demonstrates that representative sampling for snow modeling can be achieved while systematically prioritizing safety.
supporting_quote: When high-risk terrain is removed, we observe that the model produces snow depth estimates with minimal performance loss.
prioritizing safety and systematically reducing personnel danger in the field.

chunks.text: Snow is a key freshwater storage component in the western US, releasing water seasonally to support streamflow, groundwater recharge, and water supply. Traditional SWE monitoring relies heavily on point observations (e.g., SNOTEL), which do not capture spatial variability in complex terrain. This has driven development of spatial SWE products from models, reanalyses, remote sensing, and machine learning approaches.
supporting_quote: Snow is a critical component of freshwater resources, storing water seasonally and releasing it gradually to sustain streamflow, groundwater recharge, and water supply
SNOTEL... provides automated in situ measurements of mountain snowpack. While valuable, point-based observations do not measure spatial variability across complex terrain

chunks.text: SWE estimation methods in practice fall into major categories with different assumptions and resolutions: physically-based models, reanalysis/analysis products, data-driven models, and remote sensing-derived SWE. Reanalysis systems can assimilate observations (e.g., fSCA), while data-driven approaches learn relationships using station data and gridded meteorology. This diversity creates a need to understand strengths and weaknesses across approaches.
supporting_quote: SWE estimation methods can be categorized into four main approaches... physically-based models, reanalysis products, data-driven models, and SWE derived directly from satellite remote sensing imagery.
Data-driven models, such as Snow Water Artificial Neural Network (SWANN... and ...SWEML... leverage historical observations and machine learning

chunks.text: Community benchmarking has accelerated progress in streamflow modeling through standardized datasets and conventions (e.g., CAMELS). The paper positions SWE estimation as lacking comparable shared protocols, making inter-study comparisons difficult. A SWE benchmarking framework analogous to CAMELS could enable more consistent evaluation and tracking of progress across methods.
supporting_quote: The potential utility of such standardized intercomparison has been strongly demonstrated previously for streamflow... with the widespread adoption of the Catchment Attributes and Meteorology for Large-Sample Studies (CAMELS)
Such datasets enable direct comparisons between diverse modeling results... due to a lack of standard experimental conventions

chunks.text: The study’s primary goal is to propose and demonstrate a standard protocol for evaluating SWE products at catchment scale using ASO SWE as a benchmark reference. It processes many distributed SWE products, aggregates them consistently to catchments, and compares performance across multiple spatially variable metrics. The work also aims to motivate community convergence on shared experimental conventions for SWE benchmarking.
supporting_quote: The overall objective of this paper is to propose and illustrate the use of a standard protocol for SWE product evaluation, using ASO SWE as a benchmark
This study aims to expand on the success of the CAMELS community benchmarking activities in developing a similar focal point for SWE estimation

chunks.text: Two explicit aims guide the paper: (1) evaluate multiple SWE estimation methods against ASO SWE and (2) propose potential experimental protocols that can be reused to assess existing and new SWE products. The emphasis is on catchment-based SWE spatial averages that align with hydrologic management scales. The protocol concept is positioned as a starting point toward CAMELS-like community benefits for SWE estimation.
supporting_quote: In particular, we (1) evaluate the performance of multiple SWE estimation methods with respect to ASO SWE observational estimates
and (2) discuss and propose potential common experimental protocols for evaluating SWE that can be used to assess existing and new products.

chunks.text: A central challenge is that SWE products vary widely in resolution, extent, and temporal coverage, which prevents direct comparisons without standardization. Many studies use different basin selections, time periods, and metrics, limiting reproducibility and cross-paper synthesis. The paper frames the lack of a common community standard for SWE evaluation as a barrier to systematic benchmarking and adoption guidance.
supporting_quote: Noting the lack of a common community standard for SWE product and model evaluation
Because each of these SWE products differ in spatial resolution and extent, we must first implement a common spatial basis for comparison.

chunks.text: ASO provides high-resolution SWE snapshots but has discontinuous timing and limited basin/year coverage driven by funding and client purchase. These constraints complicate building a universally representative evaluation dataset and require careful scene selection and quality control. The paper addresses this by filtering problematic flights and using the remaining ASO scenes for benchmarking.
supporting_quote: ASO SWE... presents temporally discontinuous snapshots of SWE (with typically 1-5 scenes obtained in a basin per year).
ASO coverage is not continuous, as flight frequency depends on funding and client purchase.

chunks.text: The evaluation uses ASO-flown western US basins from 2013–2024, but excludes specific scenes with incomplete coverage or known issues. After these removals, 405 ASO flights remain for analysis. This curated set serves as the verifying reference against which all other SWE products are compared after spatial standardization.
supporting_quote: The evaluation was conducted across basins... surveyed by the Airborne Snow Observatory (ASO) from 2013–2024.
After removal of these flights, a total of 405 ASO flights remained for evaluation.

chunks.text: To compare products with different grids, the study aggregates all gridded SWE datasets to a common catchment unit using the NOAA NextGen Hydrofabric (median area ~7 km²). Catchments not fully contained within a flight domain are excluded to avoid partial-area bias. Area-weighted overlaps between raster cells and catchment polygons produce catchment-average SWE for each scene and product.
supporting_quote: These are spatially aggregated to a catchment scale (using the NOAA NextGen hydrofabric catchments dataset (median area ~7 km²
Gridded SWE datasets were spatially aggregated to the catchment resolution... by computing area-weighted overlaps between raster grid cells and hydrofabric polygons.

chunks.text: Two remapping workflows are used for computational efficiency and reproducibility. For large-domain datasets, the study applies areally-conservative remapping with the Python-based grid2poly tool. For small-domain single-date analyses (e.g., ASO, SWEMLv2), it uses xESMF to perform weighted averaging to catchment polygons.
supporting_quote: For large-domain datasets, areally-conservative remapping was performed with the Pythonbased grid2poly tool
For small-domain, single-date analyses (e.g., ASO, SWEMLv2), the Python package xESMF was used to implement weighted averaging.

chunks.text: Performance is evaluated per ASO scene across all catchments, producing one metric value per scene per product. The metric set includes relative mean absolute error (rMAE), percent bias (PBIAS), Kling–Gupta Efficiency (KGE), and R² computed from Pearson correlation. These metrics jointly quantify magnitude error, systematic bias, correlation, and variability agreement.
supporting_quote: SWE products were evaluated using relative mean absolute error (rMAE), percent bias (pbias), Kling-Gupta Efficiency... and  R^2
Metrics were calculated across all catchments in a scene, yielding one value per metric per scene.

chunks.text: The paper situates SWE benchmarking within the CIROH Hydrologic Prediction Testbed (CHPT) concept, which defines standard protocol elements such as objectives, verifying observations, reference baselines, experimental design, and metrics. It emphasizes protocol features like harmonizing spatial/temporal domains and enabling seen/unseen testing (temporal and spatial holdouts). This structure is intended to facilitate community-wide benchmarking across datasets and methods.
supporting_quote: This study follows a testbed framework... termed the CIROH Hydrologic Prediction Testbed (CHPT).
Ideally, an experimental protocol would: (1) use a subset of ASO SWE data for testing products in both "seen"... and "unseen" catchments

chunks.text: An example protocol is proposed that withholds 50 ASO scenes for testing from prominent basins over three years (WY2019–WY2021). The intent is to capture a representative range of snowpack conditions while leaving most ASO data available for training or assimilation. The example protocol is also summarized via a basin list and protocol elements table.
supporting_quote: A protocol could have a subset of 50 ASO SWE scenes from prominent basins... over 3 years (2019–2021) that would be withheld
The protocol uses roughly 10% of all currently available ASO SWE data (Table 3)

chunks.text: ASO SWE is used as the quasi-observational reference dataset, providing 50 m gridded SWE derived from lidar snow depth differences and modeled density (iSnobal). The paper notes reported depth errors (<8 cm at 3 m and <2 cm at 50 m) and density agreement (within 5–8%). ASO scenes are temporally discontinuous snapshots, but remain among the most detailed distributed SWE references available.
supporting_quote: ASO provides highresolution (50 m) SWE estimates derived from lidar-based snow depth and modeled snow density
The ASO snow depth mean absolute error is reported to be <8 cm at 3 m resolution and <2 cm at 50 m resolution... modeled density produces results within 5- 8%

chunks.text: The study benchmarks a broad suite of 12 SWE products spanning reanalysis/analysis, models, and data-driven methods. Products include SNODAS, SWANN (4 km and 800 m), NWM SWE, CONUS404, UCLA-SWE, ERA5-Land, SWEMLv2, NLDAS-2 LSMs (Noah, Mosaic, VIC), and Daymet. These datasets differ substantially in spatial resolution (50 m to ~12 km) and temporal coverage (1950–present to 2014–2023).
supporting_quote: Utilizing lidar-based ASO... evaluates the performance of multiple SWE products, including SNODAS, SWANN... NWM... UCLA-SWE, SWEMLv2, NLDAS-2... ERA5-Land, Daymet and the CONUS404 dataset.
The SWE datasets used in this procedure have varying designs and resolutions, as summarized in Table 1.

chunks.text: The common spatial framework is the NOAA NextGen Hydrofabric v2.2, a national dataset of connected rivers and catchments refined from NHDPlusV2. Catchments are designed as hydrologically meaningful units, typically 3–10 km², and the median catchment area used is about 7 km². Hydrofabric attributes (elevation, slope, aspect, land cover) support additional stratified analyses such as elevation bands.
supporting_quote: Standardization was achieved using the NOAA NextGen Hydrofabric
catchments typically measuring 3–10 km² in area... This study uses Hydrofabric v2.2

chunks.text: Quality control removed a small set of ASO scenes with missing/incomplete SWE data or metadata errors before evaluation. Exclusions include three 2019 Kaweah flights, one 2016 Rio Grande flight, and one 2014 Uncompahgre flight with erroneous geolocation, plus select other problematic scenes. After filtering, the evaluation uses 405 ASO flights.
supporting_quote: three flights in the Kaweah River Basin during the 2019 season, one 2016 flight in the Rio Grande River Basin, and one 2014 flight in the Uncompahgre River Basin were removed
After removal of these flights, a total of 405 ASO flights remained for evaluation.

chunks.text: Across all basins and ASO scenes at the catchment level, UCLA-SWE and SWANN 800 m show the strongest overall agreement with ASO, including the lowest rMAE and high correlation/efficiency. Reported values include rMAE of 29.8% (UCLA-SWE) and 31.8% (SWANN 800 m), R² of 0.88 and 0.84, and KGE of 0.88 and 0.89, respectively. Both have percent bias of 7.4% in this all-scenes comparison.
supporting_quote: UCLA-SWE and SWANN 800m performed similarly well with the lowest rMAE values (29.8% and 31.8% respectively), high R^2 values (0.88 and 0.84 respectively) and KGE values (0.88 and 0.89 respectively)
and the lowest percent bias (each 7.4%)

chunks.text: Boxplot summaries indicate UCLA-SWE has the best median performance for rMAE, KGE, and R² with a relatively small spread, suggesting consistent skill across regions. SWEMLv2 shows similarly small spread in KGE, rMAE, and R², indicating stable performance across scenes. Percent bias differences are smaller among top products, while some models show systematic underestimation.
supporting_quote: UCLA-SWE achieved the best median performance for rMAE, KGE, and R², with a notably small spread
SWEMLv2 has a similarly small spread for KGE, rMAE, and R^2

chunks.text: CDF analysis of KGE ranks UCLA-SWE, SWEMLv2, and SWANN as the highest-performing products, with median KGE values at or above 0.6. SNODAS is competitive but slightly lower, with a reported median KGE of 0.57. ERA5-Land and NLDAS-2 Noah LSM are among the worst performers in this catchment-scale analysis.
supporting_quote: UCLA-SWE, SWEMLv2 and SWANN products showed relatively higher performance, yielding median KGE values of 0.6 or above, with SNODAS also ranked competitively but slightly lower (0.57).
The ERA5-Land and products involving NLDAS-NOAHLSM datasets exhibited the worst performance

chunks.text: Elevation-stratified comparisons show systematic patterns linked to resolution and forcing limitations. ERA5-Land tends to overestimate SWE at low elevations and underestimate at high elevations, while NLDAS-2 LSMs consistently underpredict with low bias increasing at higher elevations. UCLA-SWE, SWEMLv2, and SWANN generally show lower errors across elevation bands, with SNODAS degrading somewhat at higher elevations.
supporting_quote: ERA5-Land generally overestimates SWE at low elevations and underestimates at high elevations
The NLDAS-2 LSMs consistently underpredict SWE, with a low bias increasing at higher elevations.
UCLA-SWE, SWEMLv2 and the SWANN products (4 km and 800 m) exhibit the lowest errors across all elevation bands, with SNODAS performing slightly worse

chunks.text: Regional analysis separating California and Colorado indicates that California basins have higher overall SWE and therefore larger absolute errors, while Colorado basins show lower MAE but modestly reduced correlation (KGE) for most products. SWEMLv2 and Daymet, and even NLDAS-2 Noah LSM, perform better in Colorado relative to their California performance. The paper suggests regional skill differences may be influenced by forcing quality and snow-event characteristics.
supporting_quote: Across the California basins, higher overall SWE leads to larger errors, whereas Colorado basins... exhibit lower MAE but modestly reduced correlation (KGE)
NLDAS-2 Noah LSM. SWEMLv2, and Daymet show better performance in Colorado.

chunks.text: At basin-average scale, several coarse products perform much better than at catchment scale, indicating compensating spatial errors. ERA5-Land and NLDAS-2 Mosaic and VIC are reported as comparable to finer-resolution products for basin-mean SWE across basins with ≥20 ASO scenes. NLDAS-2 Noah LSM remains a poor performer even at basin scale.
supporting_quote: we also assess the performance of the products for basin-mean SWE
ERA5-Land, NLDAS-2 Mosaic, and NLDAS-2 VIC LSM performed comparably to finer-resolution products at the basin scale
NLDAS-2 Noah LSM... generally underperformed relative to other datasets

chunks.text: SNODAS is consistently competitive and particularly valuable for operational applications at basin scale. The basin-average evaluation notes that, despite a small overestimation bias, SNODAS ranks among the most skillful products across evaluated basins in terms of R² and rMAE. This contrasts with several non-assimilating process-model products that lag in catchment-scale skill.
supporting_quote: Despite a small overestimation bias, SNODAS was also competitive (among the most skillful) in all of the basins evaluated in terms of R^2 and rMAE
SNODAS emerged as more competitive than previously reported, even rivaling non-operational approaches

chunks.text: A Tuolumne River Basin time-series illustration (WY2014–2016) highlights differing melt timing and peak SWE behaviors among products. NLDAS-2 Noah LSM shows notably early meltout, while ERA5-Land tracks ASO most closely in that example. SNODAS and SWANN generate the highest peak SWE, whereas Daymet shows the lowest peak but a prolonged melt period.
supporting_quote: Across all SWE products, the NLDAS-2 Noah LSM exhibited notably early meltout
ERA5-Land tracked ASO most closely.
SNODAS and SWANN produced the highest peak SWE, whereas Daymet showed the lowest peak but the most prolonged melt period.

chunks.text: In the proposed protocol subset (WY2019–WY2021; 50 scenes), results broadly mirror the all-scenes evaluation but with some shifts. UCLA-SWE remains the top performer, with its median KGE increasing to 0.73 in this subset. SWANN 4 km median KGE decreases to 0.44, while NWM and CONUS404 improve by 0.14–0.16 compared to earlier results.
supporting_quote: based on 2019 to 2021 ASO SWE in protocol basins.
UCLA-SWE KGE (0.73) slightly increased, SWANN 4km decreased to 0.44, and NWM and CONUS404 improved by 0.14–0.16.

chunks.text: ASO SWE is treated as an observational benchmark but is not a direct observation because it combines lidar snow depth with modeled density. Its uncertainties in depth and density propagate into the reference SWE used for evaluation. The study cautions that ASO’s limitations should be considered when interpreting product performance.
supporting_quote: It's important to recognize that ASO SWE is not a direct observation (due to its combination of lidar-based depth and model density)
We highlight again that ASO SWE is not a direct observation but rather a modeled estimate based on lidar-derived snow depth and modeled snow density

chunks.text: ASO data availability is uneven in space and time, creating potential representativeness issues for broad western US conclusions. Most basins have only a few years and 1–5 scenes per water year, driven by funding and purchase decisions. This limits continuous temporal evaluation and may bias analyses toward better-sampled basins like Tuolumne.
supporting_quote: ASO provides... temporally discontinuous snapshots of SWE (with typically 1-5 scenes obtained in a basin per year).
As a result, most basins have only a handful of years of record.

chunks.text: The paper notes that protocol adoption is challenging because products differ in whether they can comply with a holdout strategy (e.g., models trained on ASO basins). Aligning records with differing temporal spans and discriminating products that incorporate ASO in training are cited as hurdles. The authors suggest community consensus and transparent caveats as ways to make comparisons still useful.
supporting_quote: Multiple challenges are present in defining a protocol... such as discriminating products that incorporate ASO in training, aligning records with differing temporal spans
It is likely to be difficult to strike a balance that allows all datasets contributed by researchers for evaluation in the protocol to adhere completely to the protocol

chunks.text: A key interpretive limitation is that SWEMLv2 is trained on ASO scenes, which can complicate comparisons even with temporal cross-validation. The paper explicitly notes this caveat when interpreting SWEMLv2’s competitive performance. Such training dependence is an example of why benchmark protocols must track innovation metadata and data usage.
supporting_quote: SWEMLv2 is unique amongst the products in having been trained on ASO scenes (notwithstanding temporal crossvalidation).
SWEMLv2 is also highly competitive, with the caveat being its training on the basins in question (even though the testing years are out of sample).

chunks.text: The study concludes that snow reanalyses, particularly UCLA-SWE, provide the most accurate SWE estimates among reviewed products in catchment-scale comparisons to ASO. SNODAS, an operational assimilating system, is competitive with newer data-driven methods and often outperforms non-assimilating process-model systems like NWM/CONUS404/NLDAS Noah. Many products show mid-to-high elevation underestimation, and coarse-resolution products can still provide useful basin-average SWE skill.
supporting_quote: Applying this framework to 12 SWE products revealed... (1) snow reanalyses such as UCLA-SWE are currently the most accurate
(4) most of the products studied underestimated SWE at mid-to-high elevations; ... (6) coarse resolution products... showed skill at estimating SWE on a basin-wide scale

chunks.text: A major takeaway is that standardized, catchment-based benchmarking protocols for SWE could improve consistency and comparability across studies and products, similar to CAMELS for streamflow. The paper provides an example protocol using the NextGen Hydrofabric and ASO scenes and argues that shared conventions can help track progress and support decision-making. It encourages extensions to additional protocols (grid/point-based, other variables like fSCA) as data and community adoption grow.
supporting_quote: This study applied a standard approach for catchment-scale SWE evaluation... and further outlined and demonstrated an example of an community evaluation experimental protocol
Future protocol and study extensions could include grid- and point-based protocols... or protocols for other variables such as fSCA.

chunks.text: Flood mapping is essential for disaster response, recovery, and hydrologic science, but traditional offline remote-sensing workflows often introduce delays that reduce usefulness during active events. Cloud platforms like Google Earth Engine (GEE) provide near real-time access to preprocessed satellite archives and scalable computation, enabling faster mapping over large regions. SAR imagery is particularly valuable because it can observe floods during cloud cover and precipitation when optical sensors fail.
supporting_quote: Rapid and accurate flood mapping and monitoring are essential for effective disaster management, response, and recovery, as well as for advancing hydrological sciences.
Traditionally, remote sensing data were processed offline to produce flood maps, which usually took a day or more after a flood event.
In contrast, SAR remote sensing has become increasingly important for flood mapping and monitoring, due to its capabilities in operating day-andnight

chunks.text: GEE hosts a large, continuously updated archive of Earth observation data, including Sentinel-1, and provides preprocessing and analysis tools that reduce barriers to rapid flood mapping. Sentinel-1 GRD data in GEE are already processed with calibration and terrain correction, and new acquisitions are typically available within about two days. These characteristics support global flood monitoring without local downloads or high-performance hardware.
supporting_quote: GEE is an innovative cloud platform with an extensive archive of near-ready-to-use level geospatial data.
Many datasets, such as Sentinel-1 SAR images, have already gone through the preprocessing procedure for noise filtering, radiometric calibration, terrain correction, and geo-referencing
new acquisitions being available within two days.

chunks.text: ML and DL approaches can improve SAR-based flood mapping by incorporating additional information beyond single-band thresholding. CNN models (e.g., U-Net) can capture spatial context but are computationally heavy and hard to deploy in GEE due to missing DL APIs. In contrast, MLPs can be implemented with per-pixel inputs using simple matrix operations, which makes them more deployable for interactive GEE applications.
supporting_quote: Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) methods have been increasingly applied to SAR-based flood mapping, which offer improved flood mapping accuracy
GEE's APIs only support a limited number of traditional machine learning models, and deep learning models are not included in current GEE's APIs.
MLPs are computationally lightweight, require only per-pixel inputs, and can be fully re-implemented using simple matrix operations available in GEE's JavaScript API.

chunks.text: The study aims to build DeepSAR Flood Mapper, a fully automated, publicly accessible flood mapping web application running directly on GEE. The goal is to enable interactive, near-real-time global flood inundation mapping by deploying an offline-trained MLP model for on-demand online prediction. The application is intended for both experts and non-technical users, requiring only an AOI and target date.
supporting_quote: This study introduces DeepSAR Flood Mapper, a novel, fully automated deep learning-based flood mapping application on the GEE cloud platform as an operational, publicly accessible tool
enabling interactive and near-real-time capabilities globally.
requiring only the geographic area and target date of the flood event to be specified by users.

chunks.text: A further goal is to demonstrate that a lightweight MLP with SAR and HAND inputs can achieve strong accuracy and generalization while being deployable in GEE through an Offline Training and Online Prediction (OTOP) strategy. The work targets reduced latency by eliminating data transfer bottlenecks common in loosely coupled workflows, while improving mapping accuracy over thresholding and classic ML baselines.
supporting_quote: we adopted an OTOP coupling strategy (Figure 2). Specifically, we train the MLP model offline
then re-implement and deploy the trained MLP model within GEE for real-time or interactive flood prediction
Performance evaluation demonstrates that DeepSAR Flood Mapper significantly improves flood mapping accuracy compared to traditional approaches

chunks.text: Most public-facing GEE flood mapping apps rely on thresholding approaches that require manual parameter selection or fail in complex landscapes. Thresholding effectiveness can degrade in mountainous terrain, irrigated fields, and dense forests, creating false positives and negatives. This limits reliability and scalability for global, user-driven flood mapping.
supporting_quote: previous studies have almost exclusively relied on thresholding-based methods
requiring manual input
