the effectiveness of the thresholding method and its variants diminishes in the complex terrain, particularly in mountainous areas, irrigated agricultural fields and densely forest covered areas

chunks.text: Loosely coupled DL workflows with GEE typically run model training and prediction outside the platform, then transfer outputs back to GEE for visualization. This introduces significant latency due to data transfer and prevents real-time or interactive applications. The paper frames this as a key operational barrier for deploying sophisticated DL flood models for rapid response.
supporting_quote: core modelling processes (training and prediction) occur outside of the GEE platform
this offline strategy requires significant time for data transfer between GEE and the external environment, precluding real-time or interactive flood mapping applications
heavy local computations and data transfers between local systems and the GEE cloud platform introduce significant latency

chunks.text: Deep learning models such as CNNs are difficult to deploy directly within GEE because relevant APIs are not available and CNNs are computationally heavy. This constraint blocks close coupling for DL and pushes developers toward offline inference, undermining interactive mapping. The paper positions model deployability within GEE as a central design constraint.
supporting_quote: deep learning models are not included in current GEE's APIs.
they are computationally heavy and difficult to reimplement directly within the current GEE environment because they involve deep convolutional layers and large parameter sets.
the absence of relevant APIs, along with the inherent complexity and computational demands of CNNs precludes their direct deployment within the GEE environment.

chunks.text: DeepSAR Flood Mapper uses an MLP classifier with three input variables: Sentinel-1 VV, Sentinel-1 VH, and HAND. The selected architecture has four layers (input, two hidden, output), with two hidden layers of 4 neurons each and Leaky ReLU activations. The output layer uses a sigmoid function to produce a per-pixel flood probability for binary classification.
supporting_quote: our MLP model consists of four layers of neurons, including one input layer, two hidden layers, and one output layer.
two hidden layers, each comprising 4 neurons.
The output layer has a single neuron with a sigmoid activation function, which is well suited for the binary classification tasks.

chunks.text: Model training is performed offline in TensorFlow using supervised learning with backpropagation. The authors use stochastic gradient descent with binary cross-entropy loss and tune an optimal learning rate of 0.01. Input variables are standardized as Z-scores to normalize feature ranges before training and later during online prediction.
supporting_quote: we train the MLP model offline in a local computing environment with the TensorFlow framework
We utilised a Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) optimiser
we identified an optimal learning rate of 0.01
The input variables are standardised as Z-scores

chunks.text: The study adopts an Offline Training and Online Prediction (OTOP) coupling strategy to deploy the trained MLP within GEE. Optimal model parameters (weights) are transferred to GEE in JSON format, and the MLP computations are re-implemented using the GEE JavaScript API. This design enables rapid, on-demand flood inference directly in the web app without external computation.
supporting_quote: we adopted an OTOP coupling strategy (Figure 2).
transferring the optimal model parameters (weights), obtained from offline training of the MLP deep learning model, onto the GEE in JSON format.
re-implemented the architecture and computational algorithms of the MLP model within the GEE environment using its JavaScript client library

chunks.text: Training samples are generated using stratified random sampling from labeled image chips, with measures to address class imbalance. All chips from one Sen1Floods11 event (Bolivia) are held out as an independent test set, and remaining chips are split 60-20-20 into training, validation, and test subsets. Within each chip, equal numbers of flooded and non-flooded pixels are sampled to balance classes.
supporting_quote: we first set aside all chips from one flood event (Bolivia) in the Sen1Floods11 dataset as an independent test set.
randomly split into training, validation, and test subsets following a 60-20-20 ratio.
Within each chip, equal numbers of flooded and non-flooded pixels were randomly selected to mitigate class imbalances.

chunks.text: In the GEE app workflow, the tool searches for Sentinel-1 images within a 30-day window around a user-selected target date, then users choose the closest acquisition. Inputs (VV, VH, HAND) are standardized to Z-scores and passed through the two hidden layers and sigmoid output to create a binary flood map. The GUI also displays AOI area, flood area, and supports exporting GeoTIFF outputs.
supporting_quote: DeepSAR Flood Mapper searches and lists all available Sentinel-1 SAR images within a 30-day window around the target date.
The VH and VV bands of Sentinel-1 SAR GRD images and HAND elevation data layer ... are standardised to Z-scores
Users may also export the resulting flood maps and corresponding Sentinel-1 SAR imagery as GeoTIFF files

chunks.text: Performance is evaluated using precision, recall, and F1-score, with comparisons against Otsu thresholding, RF, SVM, and a compact U-Net. Otsu is applied with chip-specific local thresholds on the Sentinel-1 VV band to ensure fair comparison. Two evaluation settings are used: an in-distribution random test split and an out-of-distribution Bolivia event test set.
supporting_quote: Model performance is evaluated using precision, recall, and F1-score
including a thresholding method, two conventional machine learning methods and a CNN-based deep learning method.
Otsu's thresholding was applied to the Sentinel-1 VV polarisation band.
The second is an independent dataset from a Bolivia flood event, which was excluded from the training phase.

chunks.text: The model inputs are Sentinel-1 SAR backscatter in VV and VH polarizations and HAND topographic data, all available in the GEE catalog. Sentinel-1 GRD in GEE is radiometrically calibrated and terrain corrected, and pixel values are σ0 in dB derived via σ0 = 10 log10(I). HAND provides relative elevation above nearest drainage to reduce false positives in elevated areas.
supporting_quote: The MLP model uses three input layers, Sentinel-1 SAR VV and VH backscatter, as well as HAND topographic data
The pixel values of Sentinel-1 Level-1 GRD images are the backscatter coefficient (σ0) in decibels (dB)
HAND terrain model describes the relative elevation of a point on the landscape above the nearest drainage

chunks.text: HAND is sourced from the MERIT Hydro dataset in GEE, which provides hydrologically adjusted elevations along with other hydrography layers. MERIT Hydro is derived from MERIT DEM and water body datasets, and MERIT DEM has ~90 m resolution. This topographic layer is used as an auxiliary input to help mitigate commission errors from low SAR backscatter surfaces.
supporting_quote: the HAND band of the Multi-Error-Removed Improved-Terrain (MERIT) Hydro dataset was used
MERIT DEM is a multi-source fused DEM with a spatial resolution of ~90 m
The use of HAND data can help to mitigate these commission errors (false alarms) in elevated or steeply sloped regions

chunks.text: Training labels come from two sources: Sen1Floods11 and an in-house US historical flood chip dataset. Only 446 manually labeled Sen1Floods11 chips are used because automatic labels contain many misclassifications. The in-house dataset includes 104 flood events (2017–2019) across 20 US states and produces 1,624 labeled 512×512 chips, each with 10%–90% flooded pixels.
supporting_quote: only the 446 manually labelled image chips were used for our model training.
an in-house dataset of historical flood maps across the continental United States, derived from 104 flood events happening between 2017 and 2019
clipped into 512 × 512 pixel image chips, resulting in 1,624 labelled chips, each containing between 10% and 90% flooded pixels.

chunks.text: The training sample construction uses per-pixel feature vectors containing VV, VH, HAND, and the flood label, with Z-score standardization. The study uses 131,777 sample pixels from the in-house dataset and 74,725 from Sen1Floods11 for training, while 2,111 Bolivia samples are reserved as an independent test set. This setup targets broad climate and terrain coverage for generalization.
supporting_quote: training vectors comprising four variables (VV, VH, HAND, Flood-Label)
In total, 131,777 sample pixels from the in-house dataset and 74,725 sample pixels from the Sen1Floods11 dataset were used for model training
2,111 Bolivia samples were reserved as an additional independent test set

chunks.text: Across four example flood events, the MLP consistently improves over Otsu thresholding, especially by reducing false positives and balancing precision and recall. Reported event-level F1-scores for MLP are 0.86, 0.79, 0.77, and 0.89, while Otsu yields 0.76, 0.73, 0.61, and 0.72. The improvement is notable in cases where Otsu produces erroneous patches or misclassifies smooth surfaces as water.
supporting_quote: Table 1. Performance comparison of MLP deep learning method with otsu thresholding method.
Event #1 ... Otsu's thresholding ... F1-score 0.76 ... MLP ... F1-score 0.86
Event #3 ... Otsu ... F1-scores of 0.61 ... MLP ... F1-score of 0.77
Event #4 ... Otsu ... F1-score of 0.72 ... MLP ... F1-score of 0.89

chunks.text: On the in-distribution test set, the MLP achieves the highest F1-score (0.77) compared with RF (0.72), SVM (0.74), and compact U-Net (0.71). The MLP’s precision and recall are both 0.77, indicating balanced performance. The comparisons suggest a lightweight per-pixel MLP can match or exceed heavier baselines under the study’s training data conditions.
supporting_quote: Table 2. Performance comparison of proposed MLP deep learning method with Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Mathine (SVM), and a compact U-Net architecture.
MLP ... Precision 0.77 ... Recall 0.77 ... F1-score 0.77
RF ... F1-score 0.72 ... SVM ... F1-score 0.74 ... U-Net ... F1-score 0.71

chunks.text: On the out-of-distribution Bolivia event, the MLP shows better transferability than RF, SVM, and U-Net. The MLP reaches precision 0.96, recall 0.55, and F1-score 0.70, while RF and SVM suffer strong recall drops (0.34 and 0.27) and lower F1-scores (0.50 and 0.42). This indicates the MLP generalizes more robustly to an unseen geographic and hydrologic setting in this evaluation.
supporting_quote: Accuracy based on Bolivia dataset
MLP ... Precision 0.96 ... Recall 0.55 ... F1-score 0.70
RF ... Recall 0.34 ... F1-score 0.50
SVM ... Recall 0.27 ... F1-score 0.42

chunks.text: The application demonstrates retrospective mapping for Hurricane Matthew flooding near Goldsboro, North Carolina. Using October 12, 2016 as the peak date, the tool estimates a flood area of approximately 21 km2. The example illustrates that the app can compare pre-flood and peak-flood dates and identify permanent water bodies versus event inundation.
supporting_quote: Hurricane Matthew brought heavy rainfall and severe flooding in and around Goldsboro, North Carolina.
October 12, 2016, the observed peak flood date, was specified as the target date.
captures extensive inundation during peak flooding, with an estimated flood area of approximately 21 km2 on October 12.

chunks.text: For the 2024 Bangladesh monsoon flood example over Sylhet, DeepSAR Flood Mapper reports extensive inundation across multiple dates. Flooded areas are measured at 8,736 km2 (June 19), 8,402 km2 (June 22), and 7,473 km2 (June 24) within an AOI of 65,059 km2. The case shows the app’s capability to handle large AOIs requiring multiple Sentinel-1 scenes and to support temporal tracking of flood evolution.
supporting_quote: The flood maps for June 19, 22 and 24 showed extensive inundation, with flooded areas measured at 8,736 km2 , 8,402 km2 , and 7,473 km2 , respectively within total AOI covering 65,059 km2
Due to the large spatial extent of the AOI, multiple Sentinel-1 image scenes from adjacent orbits were required to cover the AOI.

chunks.text: The authors report low-latency performance for interactive use in GEE, with typical AOIs processed in seconds. A 50–100 km AOI takes about 5–10 seconds, and larger 100–250 km AOIs take 10–15 seconds. Reported latency scales from 5 seconds for 25×25 km to 16 seconds for 500×500 km AOIs, supporting operational responsiveness.
supporting_quote: generating a flood map for a typical 50−100 km AOI requires approximately 5−10 seconds
For larger AOIs (100−250 km across) ... typically 10−15 seconds.
Table 3. Empirical latency and scalability measurements for DeepSAR Flood Mapper.
500 × 500 ... Observed latency (seconds) ... 16

chunks.text: The tool depends primarily on Sentinel-1 C-band SAR, which has known limitations for flood detection in some land covers. The paper notes limited vegetation penetration, ambiguity with smooth urban or bare-soil surfaces, and reduced sensitivity to shallow inundation. The authors propose future integration of NISAR L-band and S-band observations to address these issues.
supporting_quote: The current version of DeepSAR Flood Mapper primarily relies on ESA's Sentinel-1 C-band SAR imagery

C-band SAR has known limitations, including limited penetration through vegetation, difficulties in distinguishing floodwater from smooth urban or bare-soil surfaces, and reduced sensitivity to shallow inundations.
we plan to incorporate NISAR's dual-frequency observations into DeepSAR Flood Mapper.

chunks.text: The current system does not incorporate multimodal fusion of SAR with optical imagery, despite potential accuracy gains. The authors cite practical challenges: needing large volumes of co-registered SAR-optical training pairs, expanded feature space, and limited availability of cloud-free optical observations during floods. As a result, multimodal fusion is identified as important but non-trivial for a globally operational workflow.
supporting_quote: the multimodal integration of optical and SAR data poses practical challenges for DeepSAR Flood Mapper.
Incorporating multimodal inputs would require retaining the model with large volumes of co-registered SAR-optical pairs
cloud free optical observations are not consistently available during major floods

chunks.text: Using an MLP is partly driven by GEE constraints, but it creates architectural trade-offs. MLPs classify each pixel independently and cannot explicitly model spatial dependencies, texture, or boundary continuity that CNNs can learn through convolutions. The paper suggests that future versions could transition to CNNs if larger labeled datasets and GEE-compatible DL APIs or inference pathways become available.
supporting_quote: GEE's existing built-in API infrastructure only supports a limited number of conventional machine learning models and does not yet accommodate deep learning models such as CNNs.
MLP models process input features of each pixel independently, lacking the ability to explicitly model spatial dependencies
once ... larger and more representative labelled flood datasets become availabe and ... APIs for complex deep learning models become available in the GEE

chunks.text: The study notes that CNN performance is constrained by training data volume and model capacity choices. To avoid overfitting with the available data, a tiny U-Net was used, which limited generalization to new regions. This highlights that more expressive spatial models likely require substantially larger and more diverse labeled flood datasets to realize their advantages.
supporting_quote: with only 1,233 labelled image chips for training, we implemented a tiny U-Net architecture to prevent overfitting.
the insufficient amount of training data to support a deeper, more expressive model.

chunks.text: The paper concludes that DeepSAR Flood Mapper is an interactive, globally scalable GEE web app for near real-time SAR-based flood mapping. It integrates an offline-trained MLP with Sentinel-1 VV/VH and HAND via OTOP deployment, enabling fast online inference without local computation. Evaluations show the MLP outperforms Otsu thresholding, RF, SVM, and a compact U-Net, including on an unseen Bolivia event.
supporting_quote: This study developed DeepSAR Flood Mapper, the first deep learning-based SAR flood mapping application deployed as an interactive GEE Web App for global, near real time flood monitoring.
The proposed system integrates an MLP model with Sentinel-1 SAR imagery and HAND topographic data using an OTOP strategy.
outperforming traditional thresholding methods, conventional machine learning models (e.g. SVM, RF), and a compact U-Net

chunks.text: The authors emphasize remaining limitations and planned enhancements. They note that MLPs cannot model spatial context, reliance on C-band SAR can miss sub-canopy flooding and confuse low-backscatter surfaces, and multimodal fusion is challenging operationally. Proposed future work includes adding NISAR L- and S-band data, exploring optical-SAR fusion, and adopting CNN architectures when GEE support and training data improve.
supporting_quote: The MLP architecture cannot explicitly model spatial context
Reliance on C-band SAR imagery also leads to difficulties in detecting sub-canopy flooding
Future enhancements include incorporating NISAR's L- and S-band SAR observations, incorporating multimodal optical-SAR inputs, and transitioning to more expressive CNN architectures

chunks.text: Extreme events such as floods are increasing in magnitude and frequency, forcing communities to make rapid protective decisions. How people receive and process communications about these hazards is central to protecting lives and infrastructure. Decision-making is shaped by experience, perceptions, and trust in both sources and information. Effective flood risk management therefore depends not only on structural and planning measures but also on communication that motivates protective action.
supporting_quote: Extreme events, such as floods, fires, and heat waves are increasing in magnitude and frequency
The way communities receive, process and respond to communication about extreme events is crucial to saving lives and infrastructure

chunks.text: Flood risk governance and response involve many stakeholders whose roles can overlap across preparedness, response, recovery, and mitigation. This multi-actor setting makes coordination and communication difficult, and it can shape the distribution and convergence of warning messages. Because protective action is influenced by how risks are communicated, integrated and strategic communication approaches can amplify the effectiveness of top-down interventions. Governance complexity and legislative context add constraints that can make risk-related decisions harder.
supporting_quote: Federal, state, and local officials, volunteers, nonprofit organizations and other groups play their unique but, at times, overlapping roles
the ability and willingness of people to take protective actions is influenced by how these risks are communicated

chunks.text: The Great Vermont Flood of 2023 (GVF23) created a rare opportunity to compare pre-crisis and post-crisis perspectives on readiness and communication. Vermont received as much as nine inches of rain over about 48 hours, causing flash and river flooding with major impacts in the Winooski watershed. Flash Flood Warnings were issued through early July 11, with the last River Flood Warning canceled July 13. The event was described as "historic and catastrophic" and resulted in two fatalities.
supporting_quote: a severe storm rapidly delivering as much as nine inches of rain within approximately 48 hours
"Flash Flood Warnings"... continued to be issued by the National Weather Services (NWS) through the early morning of July 11

chunks.text: The study aimed to provide a temporal assessment of risk and crisis communication before, during, and after the GVF23 event. By using focus groups held pre-crisis and post-crisis, the authors sought to compare perceived readiness with observed response and recovery experiences. The work intended to generate practical recommendations for warning message content, governance of risk communication, and support for vulnerable populations. This design addresses a gap in crisis communication research that often emphasizes post-crisis analysis.
supporting_quote: This study presents a temporal assessment of how the risk and crisis communication process unfolded before, during and after a catastrophic event.
collecting data relative to the readiness of communities to natural hazards pre and post disaster events provides for a unique opportunity

chunks.text: The authors posed two research questions focused on perceptions and improvements. The first asked how Winooski watershed professionals perceived flood threats and the dissemination of risk and crisis communication across the pre-, during-, and post-flood periods. The second asked what actions should be taken to improve coordination and communication given likely increases in flood frequency. These questions were designed to identify challenges in regional risk management and communication operating systems.
supporting_quote: RQ1: What were the perceptions of the Winooski watershed emergency managers, regional planners, and river coordinator managers about flood threats and the dissemination of risk and crisis communication prior, during and after the GVF23 flood?
RQ2: What actions should be taken to improve coordination, risk and crisis communication given the likelihood of increased flood frequency?

chunks.text: A key issue identified is that warning terminology and common flood instructions are often confusing, ambiguous, and not intuitively obvious. Terms such as flash flood watch, warning, and emergency can be misunderstood by lay audiences, and generalized directions may not provide context-based steps. Ambiguity can lead to conflicting interpretations and unnecessary concern, especially in fast-changing flash flood situations. The paper argues messages should minimize ambiguity and better specify what actions to take in the local context.
supporting_quote: Terms such as flash flood watch, flash flood warnings, and flash flood emergency may sound confusing and ambiguous.
Messages such as: "move to a higher ground now"; "never drive through flooded roads"; and "turn around, don't drown", currently being sent across the country, are ambiguous

chunks.text: Communication and response are constrained by complex governance and unclear accountability across multiple actors. The Incident Command System depends on hierarchical authority, but the designation and preparedness of local incident commanders may be unclear or uneven. Such governance challenges can affect how messages are distributed and whether they converge across sources. Failures in accountability can produce conflicting information for the public during disasters.
supporting_quote: The designation of authority is not always clear, which can affect the distribution and consequent convergence of messages
Accountability failures during the crisis response process can result in lack of convergence of the messages shared with the public.

chunks.text: Vulnerable populations are frequently not adequately considered in risk and crisis communication planning. The literature and participants emphasize the need for long-term pre-crisis engagement so that messages are understood and feasible for those at greater risk. Communication-related factors can themselves increase vulnerability, and additional research is needed to show how this varies across crisis types. The study positions its contributions partly in addressing these gaps related to vulnerable populations.
supporting_quote: the characteristics and demands of these audiences are not always—in fact, infrequently—considered when planning and implementing risk and crisis communication
there is a need to develop long-term engagement with vulnerable populations during the pre-crisis stage

chunks.text: The study used three Regional Impact-Based Focus Groups to examine governance, communications, and actions related to major flooding events in the Winooski watershed. One focus group occurred pre-crisis in March 2023 and two occurred post-crisis in September 2023 and February 2024. Sessions were semi-structured and followed pre-established protocols, with later sessions revisiting themes from the first and focusing on the GVF23 experience. The work emphasized a temporal evaluation of preparation, response, and recovery communication.
supporting_quote: three Regional Impact-Based Focus Groups (one pre- and two post-crisis)
The second (September 2023) and third (February 2024) focus groups convened after the historic event

chunks.text: Each focus group session lasted three hours and included professional emergency managers, regional planners, watershed and river managers, dam safety, and town officials. The first session was held in person, while the second and third used a hybrid format due to ongoing flood management demands. The study also included a semi-structured interview when a participant could not attend a session. Data collection was approved by an Institutional Review Board and consent procedures were conducted at each session.
supporting_quote: Each focus group session lasted 3 hours.
The collection of data was approved by the Institutional Review Board (STUDY00002236)

chunks.text: Analysis was organized around three thematic areas: message content, roles and responsibilities affecting distribution and convergence, and support to vulnerable communities. The researchers coded transcripts and notes by hand and identified themes using a grounded theory approach. They conducted a thematic analysis structured around the major themes and supported with illustrative examples from transcripts. Findings were shared with participants through technical briefs for member checks and then corrected based on feedback.
supporting_quote: Data is analyzed considering three main aspects: the content of risk and crisis messages, the governance, roles and responsibilities regarding the distribution of these messages, and the outreach to vulnerable communities
These notes and transcriptions were coded by hand, and major themes were identified using the grounded theory approach

chunks.text: The dataset consisted of recordings and verbatim transcripts from three focus group sessions across pre- and post-crisis periods. The March 2023 session included 12 participants; the September 2023 session included 10; and the February 2024 session included 11, with most participants attending all sessions. Audio and video were recorded using Zoom and a Meeting Owl device and then transcribed word-by-word. Researchers also took extensive notes during sessions to complement transcripts.
supporting_quote: The first session (March 2023) was held in person (n = 12). The second (n = 10) and third (n = 11) focus groups had a hybrid format
All focus groups were recorded (audio and video)... and transcribed word by word.

chunks.text: Participants represented a core group of stakeholders involved in flood and emergency management in the Winooski watershed, including planners, river managers, and dam safety officials. Among the core participants, 66% were male and 34% were female. Roles spanned local/state government and nonprofits, such as floodplain manager, hazard mitigation manager, river corridor manager, and dam safety engineer. This mix was intended to capture perspectives of those directly involved in preparation, communication, and response.
supporting_quote: Among the core participants (those who participated in all sessions), 66% were male and 34% were female
These core stakeholders included professional emergency managers, regional planners, watershed and river managers, dam safety and town officials

chunks.text: Before the flood, participants agreed the region’s largest threats were localized flash flooding and fluvial erosion, often occurring in short time windows with limited warning. They expressed less concern about inundation flooding, noting it was rare compared to erosion impacts. Participants also noted that FEMA flood lines can miss erosion risk affecting properties outside mapped zones. They highlighted dam failure as the most serious potential threat to life and property, requiring evacuation planning.
supporting_quote: Agreement was reached among participants that the largest flood threat facing the region is localized flash flooding and fluvial erosion
Several participants shared that a potential major dam failure is the flood hazard that creates the most serious concern about threat to life and property

chunks.text: Participants reported that NWS warning terminology is not intuitive, and that broad instructions can be interpreted differently depending on local conditions. They argued warnings should minimize ambiguity and provide clearer, context-based action steps. Post-crisis, ambiguous information about Wrightsville Dam contributed to misinterpretations among community members about breach risk, even though experts said it was never the case. This reinforced that unclear technical communication can create unnecessary concern and influence protective action decisions.
supporting_quote: Terms such as flash flood watch, flash flood warnings, and flash flood emergency may sound confusing and ambiguous.
some community members interpreted the messages as a possible risk of breaching, even though experts share this was never the case

chunks.text: Mapping tools were viewed as important but mismatched to local hazard types and unevenly adopted. Participants noted FEMA maps are inundation-centric and do not include erosion information, limiting applicability for Vermont’s erosion-focused flood impacts. They expected new FEMA maps and suggested integrating them into community conversations. Awareness of USGS Flood Inundation Maps existed, but participants were unsure how much they were used by emergency managers or the public where available.
supporting_quote: It was noted that these maps are inundation-centric (not including erosion information), which makes them less applicable to other types of flood hazards.
Participants were asked about their awareness of the United States Geological Services (USGS) Flood Inundation Maps (FIMs). Some were aware

chunks.text: During GVF23, participants widely recognized coordination problems that led to overlapping or conflicting responsibilities and reduced message convergence. Vermont’s limited county-government structure leaves local communities reliant on incident commanders with varying preparedness, while Vermont Emergency Management resources were described as limited. Understaffing required temporary support from Regional Planning Commissions, partnering states, and other agencies. Dam safety managers sometimes also had to handle crisis communication, adding burden during monitoring-intensive periods.
supporting_quote: It was widely recognized by the participants that communication during the GVF23 suffered from a lack of coordination in certain key instances.
During the GVF23 response, the VEM team... was understaffed

chunks.text: Participants described mixed effectiveness of alerting systems: NWS and VT Alert can push messages broadly, but frequent alerts can reduce engagement. They also reported that geo-targeting was insufficient, with messages sometimes reaching people outside affected areas and creating confusion when multiple sources broadcast simultaneously. Participants emphasized messages should clarify consequences (a clear “so what”) and be tailored to specific audiences and locations. Human resource capacity constraints were highlighted as a factor affecting governance and message convergence.
supporting_quote: there were complaints that these alerts occur too often, and become less engaging due to its use in non-crisis situations
Participants discussed the importance of sharing messages that are better targeted to the receiver's location.

chunks.text: Support to vulnerable populations relied heavily on nonprofits and community resilience groups, often mobilized reactively after the crisis. Participants identified a post-crisis communication gap where critical information reached mainly people who had consented or actively sought it out (e.g., via Front Porch Forum). They observed a digital divide when official information was shared via platforms like Facebook and Twitter, leaving others without consistent internet access out of the loop. They also noted that limited English proficiency needs were not adequately met during the GVF23 response.
supporting_quote: critical information was often shared only with individuals who had either given prior consent or actively sought it out
Participants noted that during the GVF23 flood response, the needs of individuals with limited English proficiency were not adequately met.

chunks.text: Comparing pre-crisis and post-crisis discussions, pre-existing concerns about confusing warning terminology and coordination limitations were confirmed and intensified during the actual event. Participants reported that ambiguity led to real-world misinterpretations, particularly around dam safety communication. Coordination gaps and overlapping responsibilities persisted post-crisis, and understaffing made capacity limits more visible during response. Nonprofits helped post-crisis, but structural improvements for outreach (including language and accessibility) were still seen as lacking.
supporting_quote: Pre-existing confusion in terminology led to real- world misunderstandings
Understaffing and resource limitations were evident; response efforts stretched thin during crisis.

chunks.text: In discussion, participants judged the GVF23 response as generally adequate but warned that a slightly more severe crisis could have produced catastrophic outcomes given communication system gaps. They emphasized that messages must be audience-driven and location-based, with clear protective action steps, and that access to experts varies across Vermont. The paper notes that experts and response officials can be overburdened, indicating a need for increased resources. The authors suggest these issues may be relevant beyond Vermont as flood frequency rises.
supporting_quote: it was widely recognized that had the crisis been even slightly more severe, gaps in communication systems could have led to catastrophic results.
The assessment of the relevance of the messages that are shared was considered by the participants as a key challenge.

chunks.text: The study’s main limitation is geographic: data were collected only in Vermont, which constrains direct generalization. However, the authors argue that floods on the scale of Irene (2011) and GVF23 (2023) are increasingly likely elsewhere, so lessons should be considered through broader lenses. They propose triangulating these findings with a national survey conducted by the research group to improve generalizability. Additional research in other states is presented as the best way to contextualize recommendations.
supporting_quote: This study's limitations include the matter that data was collected only in the state of Vermont.
triangulation of this data with a national survey conducted by the same group of researchers can help to make this data more generalizable

chunks.text: The paper concludes that learning from disasters is essential for community resilience and that pre- and post-event focus groups can reveal gaps between perceived readiness and actual response. It argues that solutions to enhance resilience exist but require resources and political and social will to change planning and communication norms. The authors emphasize that flood communication should be audience-driven and context- and location-based. They assert that improving these systems can help save lives and protect infrastructure during future floods.
supporting_quote: Learning from disasters is key to any community's resilience.
ensuring that flood communication is audience driven, context and location-based, which will, ultimately help to save lives and infrastructure.

chunks.text: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are a major contributor to high-impact precipitation and water resources, and they commonly occur within the warm sector of extratropical cyclones. Explosively deepening cyclones (“bomb cyclones”) are frequently associated with ARs, indicating potential dynamical links between moisture transport and rapid cyclogenesis. Prior research also notes that cyclone deepening can be modulated by the magnitude of water vapor flux along the AR, motivating case-based physical process studies.
supporting_quote: Atmospheric rivers (AR) are responsible for 85% of intense precipitation and major flooding along the U.S. West Coast, and 30%–50% of the region's water supply
Extratropical cyclones that undergo a central sea‐level pressure drop exceeding 24 hPa in 24 hr are defined as "bomb cyclones"
AR‐related extratropical cyclones ... intensify with deepening rates that are directly modulated by the magnitude of water vapor flux along the AR

chunks.text: Warm conveyor belts (WCBs) are Lagrangian airstreams that transport warm, moist air into cyclones and ascend rapidly from the boundary layer to the upper troposphere. ARs defined by Eulerian thresholds of IWV or IVT can comprise a portion of a WCB, especially when low-level jet transport exceeds cyclone propagation speed. Diabatic processes along the WCB, particularly latent heat release, can redistribute potential vorticity (PV) and influence cyclogenesis and downstream ridge amplification.
supporting_quote: The WCB denotes a Lagrangian airstream ... ascends >600 hPa from the boundary layer to the upper troposphere ... within a period of 48 hr
ARs ... may comprise a portion of the WCB
mid‐tropospheric LHR along the WCB that can influence the vertical redistribution of potential vorticity (PV) and cyclogenesis

chunks.text: Atmospheric rivers over the Central US are not rare and are linked to extreme precipitation and flooding, typically involving poleward moisture flux from the Gulf of Mexico combined with baroclinic forcing. However, the March 2019 case featured IVT magnitudes far above typical values for the region and ranked among the strongest AR events in a multi-decadal reanalysis record. This exceptional intensity provides a natural laboratory for diagnosing AR–cyclone interactions inland.
supporting_quote: Atmospheric rivers over the Central US are not uncommon
occur in association with ∼50% of extreme precipitation events
widespread values >1,400–1,500 kg m−1 s−1 on 13 March 2019 ... ranking as the highest or top‐3 AR events ... between 1959 and 2023

chunks.text: The study aims to diagnose how an intense Gulf of Mexico–originating AR influenced the rapid deepening of a Central US lee cyclone in March 2019. The authors frame the central question as whether the record-breaking AR intensity contributed to the record-breaking cyclone intensity. They target the physical pathways connecting AR moisture transport, latent heat release, PV evolution, and storm-scale feedbacks during explosive cyclogenesis.
supporting_quote: The purpose of this study is to investigate the influence of an intense AR in the development of a bomb cyclone

The purpose of thisstudy wasto investigate the influence of the AR on the evolution of the midlatitude cyclone. In other words, did the record‐breaking intensity of the AR result in the record‐breaking cyclone?

chunks.text: A secondary goal is to quantify how changes to AR moisture and diabatic heating alter WCB behavior and synoptic structure, including the trough–ridge couplet and associated Rossby wave. The authors use controlled numerical experiments to separate the effects of reducing initial moisture (as a proxy for weaker AR development) from suppressing microphysics-driven latent heat release. This is intended to clarify which mechanism more strongly shapes cyclone structure and downstream impacts.
supporting_quote: four Weather Research and Forecast (WRF) model simulations in order to analyze the potential contributions of the AR and LHR to cyclogenesis
two runs where the moisture within the initial conditions ... are reduced by 20% ("RH20off) and by 50% ("RH50off")
a run with no late heat release ("NoLH") ... LHR associated with microphysical processes is turned off

chunks.text: Despite strong statistical links between ARs and explosively deepening cyclones, fewer studies have examined how ARs interact with continental cyclones and influence inland extreme weather. The paper highlights this gap as a motivation for a detailed case study over the Central Plains. Understanding such interactions is important because ARs can contribute both directly through moisture supply and indirectly via circulation changes tied to diabatic processes.
supporting_quote: Few studies have explored interactions between ARs and continental cyclones
ARs can interact with weather systems across various scales, contributing to extreme weather both directly and indirectly

chunks.text: The authors conduct four WRF simulations using the CW3E West-WRF configuration to analyze AR and latent heating contributions to cyclogenesis. The setup includes a 9-km outer domain and 3-km inner domain over the Central US, with 100 vertical levels and hourly output. All simulations are initialized at 0000 UTC 11 March 2019 for 96 hours and run without nudging, allowing differences to emerge from the specified sensitivity modifications.
supporting_quote: This study uses a nested WRF V4.3.1 configuration with an outer "Domain 1" containing 9‐km horizontal grid spacing and an inner "Domain 2" containing 3‐km horizontal grid spacing
Vertical levels 100 levels
All four simulations were initialized at 0000 UTC on 11 March 2019, spanned 96 hr ... and were configured without nudging

chunks.text: A control simulation is compared against three experiments designed to isolate diabatic and moisture effects. NoLH turns off microphysics-associated latent heat release, while RH20off and RH50off reduce relative humidity in initial and boundary conditions by 20% and 50%, respectively. The moisture-reduction experiments are intended to slightly impede AR development without fully removing it, enabling assessment of nonlinear storm responses.
supporting_quote: The Control run serves as the benchmark
a run with no late heat release ("NoLH") ... LHR associated with microphysical processes is turned off
the moisture within the initial conditions ... and the boundary conditions during the simulation are reduced by 20% ("RH20off) and by 50% ("RH50off")

chunks.text: The analysis uses a potential vorticity (PV) framework to compare cyclone structure across experiments, emphasizing upper-level PV hook development, ascent, and jet divergence. Plan-view PV and irrotational wind diagnostics are combined with cross sections of PV and potential temperature to assess coupling of upper- and lower-tropospheric anomalies. This approach links diabatic heating to PV generation/depletion patterns that can strengthen the low-level jet and amplify downstream ridging.
supporting_quote: The differences in cyclone structure from the PV perspective are observed via plan view analyses
featured a trough of high upper‐tropospheric PV air ... a prominent "PV hook"
low static stability air ... coincides with ... low (∼0–1 PVU) PV air atop the frontal zone ... high (>2–3 PVU) PV air in the lower troposphere

chunks.text: Lagrangian air-parcel trajectories are computed from hourly WRF output using the RIP4 software to identify air-mass sources and WCB ascent characteristics. Trajectories are run 24 hours backward and 24 hours forward from 0600 UTC 13 March 2019 within the AR core over Nebraska, Kansas, and Oklahoma. Parcels are initialized at five altitudes (1.5–4.5 km), allowing separation of near-AR-core inflow and elevated pathways.
supporting_quote: air parcel trajectories derived from the Read Interpolate Plot (RIP4) software package
Backward and forward air parcel trajectories (24 hr in each direction) were initiated at 0600 UTC on 13 March 2019
at five different altitudes above the surface (1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, and 4.5 km)

chunks.text: Warm conveyor belt (WCB) trajectories are objectively identified using the criterion of ascending more than 600 hPa within 48 hours. The authors then compare the number of WCB trajectories among experiments as a proxy for WCB strength and its sensitivity to moisture transport and latent heating. This provides a quantitative bridge between AR moisture pathways, condensational heating, and cyclone intensification.
supporting_quote: WCB denotes a Lagrangian airstream ... ascends >600 hPa ... within a period of 48 hr
only 12 of 495 were objectively classified as a WCB ascending more than 600 hPa in 48 hr
81, 66, and 41 of the air parcel trajectories in the Control, RH20off, and RH50off simulations met the criteria for a WCB

chunks.text: ERA5 reanalysis is used to characterize the observed AR and cyclone evolution and to provide initial and boundary conditions for WRF simulations. The paper cites ERA5’s advanced 4D-Var assimilation and its performance for synoptic/mesoscale features, including extratropical cyclones. ERA5 IVT and sea-level pressure fields underpin the event overview and ranking of the AR intensity.
supporting_quote: The reanalysis ... and the initial and boundary conditions for the WRF simulations were provided by the ECMWF ERA5 reanalysis data set
featuring a sophisticated 4D-Var ensemble data assimilation system
The ERA5 data set reliability resolves extratropical cyclones

chunks.text: The West-WRF simulations use specific physics and resolution settings designed for AR depiction and associated extremes. Key configuration elements include Morrison 2-moment microphysics, MYNN PBL and surface layer schemes, RRTMG radiation, and Noah land surface. Output is hourly and includes nested domains at 9 km and 3 km resolution with 100 vertical levels.
supporting_quote: Microphysics Morrison 2 Moment
PBL Scheme Mellor–Yamada–Nakanishi–Niino (MYNN)
Horizontal Resolution 9 km/3 km

chunks.text: Storm impacts are documented using National Weather Service watches/warnings/advisories and local storm reports, summarized across Colorado, Nebraska, Kansas, and Oklahoma. The paper reports counts exceeding 1,000 for both warning products and local storm reports during 12–14 March 2019. These datasets contextualize the meteorological analysis with observed hazard outcomes.
supporting_quote: necessitated over 1,000 watch, warning, and advisory statements
produced over 1,000 local storm reports
within four key states: Colorado, Nebraska, Kansas, and Oklahoma

chunks.text: Trajectory analysis relies on RIP4 driven by hourly WRF fields to compute parcel paths and along-trajectory diagnostics such as altitude, pressure, and latent heat release. The trajectory ensemble consists of 495 trajectories (five height groups) initialized within a defined AR-core box. This design enables comparison of transport pathways and ascent behavior across experiments.
supporting_quote: using hourly WRF simulation output as input for air parcel trajectories derived from the Read Interpolate Plot (RIP4) software package
at five different altitudes ... (1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, and 4.5 km)
495 trajectories in total

chunks.text: The March 2019 event featured rapid cyclogenesis in Colorado coincident with an intense AR and strong low-level moisture transport from the Gulf of Mexico. The cyclone deepened by more than 24 hPa in 24 hours and reached about 970 hPa near Lamar, Colorado around 1800 UTC 13 March. The AR corridor narrowed and intensified along the low-level jet, with IVT magnitudes exceeding roughly 1,400–1,500 kg m−1 s−1 over the Southern Plains during peak development.
supporting_quote: The cyclone rapidly intensified ... with a decrease in sea‐level pressure >24 hPa in 24 hr–970.4 hPa near Lamar, Colorado at 1800 UTC 13 March 2019
narrowed into an intense AR with IVT magnitudes >1,400 kg m−1 s−1 by 1200 UTC 13 March 2019
IVT magnitudes >1,500 kg m−1 s−1 over the Southern Plains

chunks.text: In the control simulation, the modeled cyclone and AR were broadly consistent with reanalysis but somewhat stronger. At 1200 UTC 13 March, the control cyclone had an MSLP near 977 hPa and IVT about 400 kg m−1 s−1 higher over central Oklahoma than ERA5. The control run later deepened below 964 hPa around 1900 UTC 13 March, indicating an over-intensification relative to ERA5.
supporting_quote: the Control simulation develops ... an MSLP of ∼977 hPa over Colorado
with an IVT magnitude that is ∼400 kg m−1 s−1 higher over central Oklahoma
produce a stronger cyclone than observed in the ERA5 with an MSLP below 964 hPa at 1900 UTC 13 March 2019

chunks.text: Suppressing latent heat release (NoLH) substantially weakened and altered the cyclone evolution. At 1200 UTC 13 March, NoLH produced an MSLP of 989 hPa over western Kansas and lower IVT near 1,300 kg m−1 s−1. The minimum cyclone pressure stayed above about 977 hPa through 14 March, and the system was more progressive, shifting farther east than the control.
supporting_quote: NoLH simulation ... an MSLP of 989 hPa over western Kansas
lower IVT magnitudes of ∼1,300 kg−1 m−1 s−1
NoLH simulation produced a cyclone with an MSLP below 977 hPa through 14 March

chunks.text: Reducing moisture in the initial and boundary conditions produced more modest changes than removing latent heating, and responses were not proportional to the RH reduction. RH20off remained close to control with similar IVT (~1,800–1,900 kg m−1 s−1) and similar MSLP (979 vs. 977 hPa) at 1200 UTC 13 March. RH50off produced IVT below 1,500 kg m−1 s−1 and a weaker cyclone (987 vs. 977 hPa), demonstrating sensitivity but not a simple linear scaling with moisture reduction.
supporting_quote: RH20off simulation ... similar IVT magnitudes ... (∼1,800–1,900 kg m−1 s−1) and similar MSLP values ... (979 hPa vs. 977 hPa)
RH50off simulation contained lower IVT magnitudes ... (<1,500 kg m−1 s−1) and a weaker cyclone (987 hPa vs. 977 hPa)
the reductions in AR intensity and the magnitude of cyclone weakening did not show a linear relationship

chunks.text: From a PV perspective, the Control, RH20off, and RH50off runs developed a prominent upper-tropospheric PV hook, while the NoLH run did not. The PV hook’s eastern flank aligned with a south-to-north maximum in mid-tropospheric ascent in the inferred WCB region and with upper-level divergent outflow. The control also showed the strongest upper-level divergence signature in the jet left-exit region, consistent with enhanced diabatic-PV feedbacks.
supporting_quote: Control, RH20off, and RH50off simulations all featured ... a prominent "PV hook"
contained a south‐to‐north oriented maximum in mid‐tropospheric ascent in the inferred region of the cyclone WCB
Control run ... suggesting the strongest upper‐level divergence among all simulations

chunks.text: Cross sections indicated strong diabatic-PV structure in the simulations that allowed latent heating, including low PV aloft over the frontal zone and enhanced PV in the lower troposphere. In these runs, low static stability air coincided with ~0–1 PVU aloft above a frontal zone with >2–3 PVU in the lower troposphere. The RH20off case showed a deeper, more vertically coupled PV structure than RH50off, supporting stronger cyclone dynamics even with modest moisture reduction.
supporting_quote: low static stability air ... coincides with relatively low (∼0–1 PVU) PV air atop the frontal zone containing relatively high (>2–3 PVU) PV air in the lower troposphere
cross sections illustrate ... more robust dynamics ... in the cyclone produced by the RH20off simulation with better coupling

chunks.text: Trajectory analysis in the control run indicated dual moisture source regions feeding the cyclone warm sector. About 54% of trajectories originated over the eastern Pacific and 46% from the Gulf of Mexico. Gulf-origin parcels below 3 km traversed the AR core and then split into two airstream branches consistent with WCB segmentation: one terminating poleward of the low in cyclonic flow (W2) and another emerging anticyclonically downstream (W1).
supporting_quote: Approximately half (54%) of the air parcel trajectories ... originated over the eastern Pacific while the other half (46%) originated from over Gulf of Mexico
originated at altitudes below 3 km, traversed through the AR core, and split into two distinct groups
a primary segment "W1" ... downstream upper‐level ridge, and a secondary segment "W2" ... poleward of the cyclone center

chunks.text: Latent heat release along Gulf-fed trajectories in the control run peaked in the mid-troposphere and aligned with rapid cyclogenesis signatures. The study reports strong LHR exceeding about 8 K day−1 near ~3 km (~600 hPa) on trajectories that terminate north of the low in cyclonic flow. This behavior was consistent with the inferred upper-tropospheric PV depletion and lower-tropospheric PV generation described for the intensifying storm.
supporting_quote: featured strong LHR (at a rate of more than 8 K day−1 ) at ∼3 km above the surface (∼600 hPa)
consistent with the aforementioned upper‐tropospheric PV depletion, lower tropospheric PV generation and rapid cyclogenesis

chunks.text: WCB strength differed markedly by experiment, supporting a key role for diabatic heating and AR moisture supply in enabling deep ascent. Only 12 of 495 trajectories in NoLH satisfied the WCB criterion (>600 hPa ascent in 48 hr), while Control, RH20off, and RH50off had 81, 66, and 41 WCB trajectories, respectively. Except in NoLH, WCB trajectories passed through the AR core, linking AR transport to deep ascent during cyclone intensification.
supporting_quote: only 12 of 495 were objectively classified as a WCB ascending more than 600 hPa in 48 hr
81, 66, and 41 of the air parcel trajectories in the Control, RH20off, and RH50off simulations met the criteria for a WCB
Except for the NoLH simulations, WCB trajectories in all other groups pass through the AR core

chunks.text: The study does not quantify the role of upstream Pacific/Baja moisture and antecedent wave-breaking processes that helped establish the large-scale pathway for the Gulf-origin AR. The authors note that anticyclonic Rossby wave breaking and PV-streamer evolution favored the early Baja low and the subsequent lee cyclogenesis, but these processes were not examined in the sensitivity experiments. This limits attribution of the event solely to Gulf moisture and local diabatic feedbacks.

chunks.text: This corrigendum updates the previously published study on deep learning rainfall–runoff prediction for extreme events. It preserves the original section numbering but only reprints text and figures that changed after correcting an experiment setup issue. The focus is on how corrected train/test splits affect benchmarking of peak flows and return-period-based evaluations.

Corrigendum to

"Deep learning rainfall–runoff predictions of extreme events" published in Hydrol. Earth Syst. Sci., 26, 3377–3392, 2022
This corrigendum maintains the same section names and numbering as the original publication but only includes text and figures that have been corrected.

chunks.text: The authors discovered an error in the experiment setup code that caused an incorrect splitting of training and testing data. Specifically, the notebook responsible for splitting used the wrong start date for the annual period, which undermined the intended 1-year separation between training and testing years. This required code correction and replotting of affected figures.
supporting_quote: An error in the experiment setup code was found by the authors that led to an incorrect splitting of training and testing data.

chunks.text: A description of the third training/test split in the original paper was also inaccurate. The earlier phrasing implied that all CAMELS water years with a 5-year-or-lower return period peak flow were used for training, but the actual procedure only used a specific early window of years. This corrigendum clarifies that discrepancy to align the text with what was implemented.
supporting_quote: It was also stated, in the original publication, that the third training/test period split used all water years in the Catchment Attributes and Meteorology for Large-sample Studies (CAMELS) data set

After fixing the split logic in the experiment code, the authors replotted the affected benchmarking figures in the results and appendix. The corrigendum highlights that this change slightly alters performance estimates derived from the return-period-based split.
supporting_quote: used the date 10 January (yyyy-01- 10), rather than 1 October (yyyy-10-01), as the beginning of the annual period when splitting basin years into training, validation, and test sets.
